## ATHENAEUS’S THE LEARNED BANQUETERS
## IN FIFTEEN BOOKS.

# OF ATHENAEUS
### THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS, THAT IS,
->those who discuss matters acutely and skillfully at a banquet. In 15 Books.<-

->How much labor and diligence has now been applied to these will be sufficiently evidenced by the fact that never before has the<-
->reader used this author more integrally or more conveniently, whether you look at the correction of the text or the gathering<-
->of fruits <note>original: "fructuum", referring to the useful knowledge or "harvest" extracted from the text</note> from his writings. To this end,<-
->we have taken care to provide, First:<-

**A TABLE** <note>original: "ELENCHON"</note> of the titles, by which what is discussed and in which book it is discussed is easily recognized. Then:

**A CATALOG** of the authors whom Athenaeus himself cites: where innumerable monuments of antiquity are read.

**A COLLECTION** <note>original: "SYLVVLAM", literally "a little forest," a common Renaissance term for a miscellany or gathering of related items</note> added to these, of proverbs of singular beauty. Also:

**ANNOTATIONS** on the same, observed from the scholarly labors of learned men. Finally:

**INDICES**, two of them, one Greek and the other Latin, by which a ready and prompt abundance of all things treated in these books will be made available to you.

<meta>This page provides a biographical introduction to the author Athenaeus, following the title page translated previously. It serves to establish the historical context of the author and distinguishes him from other famous figures of the same name, a common scholarly practice in Renaissance editions of classical texts.</meta>

# THE LIFE OF ATHENAEUS.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'D' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

VERY little has been found among writers concerning Athenaeus. Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia that preserved much ancient history.</note> says he was a native of Naucratis <note>A Greek city in the Nile Delta of Egypt.</note> and flourished during the time of Marcus <note>Refers to the Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius, reigned 161–180 AD.</note>; Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a famous Renaissance scholar whose encyclopedic works were widely cited.</note> repeats this same information from him. In addition to this work, *The Learned Banqueters* <note>original: "dipnosophistarū"</note>, which is both diverse and scholarly, he also wrote a history titled *On the Kings who Reigned in Syria* <note>original: "περὶ τῶν ἐν συρίᾳ βασιλευσάντων"</note>, which is mentioned in Book 5, where the banquet of Alexander is described. The first two books of *The Learned Banqueters* do not survive; for what we have are only a summary <term>epitome|A condensed version or summary of a larger work, often created when the original was too long or expensive to copy.</term> left to us by Hermolaus of Byzantium, if we believe Volaterranus. Truly—and I say this with all due respect to such a great man—I believe his memory has failed him here. For Suidas does not record that Athenaeus was condensed into a summary by Hermolaus, the grammarian of Byzantium, but rather Stephanus [of Byzantium], who wrote the *Ethnica* <note>original: "ἐθνικὰ", a geographical dictionary of place names and the peoples who lived there</note>, a summary of which still survives today, though it is by no means complete. There were also two other men named Athenaeus: one from Seleucia in Cilicia <note>A region on the southern coast of modern-day Turkey.</note> during the time of Augustus, who was a most learned Peripatetic <term>peripatetic|A follower of the philosophy of Aristotle, so named for the "walkways" (peripatoi) where the scholars would walk while discussing philosophy.</term> philosopher; Volaterranus records some things about him from Book 14 of Strabo's *Geography*. The other was indeed the famous physician from Attalia <note>original: "Attaleus"</note>, and it is reported by Galen <note>The most famous physician of antiquity, whose writings were the standard for medical knowledge until the 19th century.</note> that no one among the more recent doctors has better recorded the whole system of medicine. Indeed, Galen often mentions him, especially in Book 2 of *On the Causes of Symptoms* and in his book *On the Elements*. So much for Athenaeus.

<summary>This page presents a brief biography of Athenaeus of Naucratis, clarifying his historical period and his authorship of "The Learned Banqueters." It also corrects a common scholarly error regarding the summary of his work and distinguishes him from a philosopher and a physician who shared his name.</summary>
<keywords>Athenaeus of Naucratis, Suidas, Volaterranus, The Learned Banqueters, Hermolaus of Byzantium, Stephanus of Byzantium, Galen, medical history, Peripatetic philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the biographical introduction. It is a preface by the scholar-editor Hieronymus Bebelius (Jerome Bebel) to the reader, explaining the origins of this new edition of Athenaeus, its relationship to the famous 1514 Aldine edition, and the difficulties of correcting a text that survives in such poor manuscripts.</meta>

# JEROME BEBEL
## sends his best greetings to the kind reader.

<image-desc>A large historiated drop cap 'A' depicting a scholarly scene with three figures in a room; one is seated at a desk writing or reading, while others appear to be in discussion or looking at books.</image-desc>ABOUT twenty years ago, more or less, Athenaeus was published from the workshop of Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius (c. 1449–1515), the famous Venetian printer who pioneered small, portable editions of Greek and Latin classics.</note>. But as the reality of the work itself cries out, and as the <term>title|original: "epigraphe"</term> of Musurus <note>Marcus Musurus (c. 1470–1517), a Greek scholar and editor who worked closely with Aldus.</note> also testifies, it was mutilated in many places. This should by no means be blamed on Aldus—who deserves the highest praise from the world of letters—but rather on the manuscripts, which were so corrupted that without the freedom to engage in reckless guessing, no one has yet been able to provide a more corrected version. Truly, best reader, I have not chosen to say this in the preface because we wish, perhaps in an ambitious rivalry, to equal or prefer this new edition of Athenaeus over the Aldine one. Rather, I say it so that you may understand what plan led us to encourage the printer to publish this writer, and what work we have put into it. 

I was moved, above all, by the rarity of such an excellent book. For it has been seen by very few in our Germany, let alone read. Therefore, so that students of philology might finally possess such a precious treasure, and at a tolerable price, I encouraged the printer Johann Walder, <term>who was himself eager for the task|original: "syntheonta kai auton"</term>. Nor did he take this on reluctantly, since he has once and for all dedicated his workshop to publishing the best authors; the elegantly printed Plato and many other works testify to this, and shortly both the <term>Almagest|original: "megale syntaxis" (the "Great Treatise" on astronomy) by Ptolemy</term> and Plotinus, published in their own language, will testify to it as well. 

However, in correcting Athenaeus—to be honest about the matter—I was able to achieve less than I had initially hoped. For the more accurately I began to examine the corrupted and mutilated parts, the less the result matched my efforts. And although clever conjectures often strongly appealed to me, I felt a great religious duty not to exercise "Aristarchan tyranny" <note>A reference to Aristarchus of Samothrace, a famously rigorous ancient critic; the phrase implies making harsh or aggressive editorial changes.</note> over such an illustrious author; or, to speak more modestly, I did not want to seem more clever than is fair in another man's book. This is especially true since Athenaeus cites so many and such varied writers that, had they not been praised by our author, no mortal would even know they had been born. 

Indeed, I had some hope of healing many errors from a manuscript copy which they boasted lay hidden in the library of Reuchlin <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew.</note>, a man worthy of memory in every age. But when I inquired more carefully into its quality from the most trustworthy eyewitnesses, I discovered it was not unlike the Aldine version. The nearly identical word choices, mutilations, and <term>alterations|original: "paragogai"</term> make this more than clear. To put it in a word, it is reported to be of such a nature that Reuchlin himself explicitly testified it was never of any use to him. Since I had learned enough to know that this manuscript would offer nothing worth the effort, I did not want to beg any more shamelessly from those <term>book-buriers|original: "bibliotaphis" (a term for people who hoard books and refuse to share them with scholars)</term>, whoever they may be. 

In the same way, I was cheated of another hope that had appeared convenient at the time. For I happened to come across a book by Paolo Giovio <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician, historian, and biographer.</note> titled *On Roman Fishes*, and I found him mentioning his friend Sanga, the Roman poet, by whose benefit (so he says) we owe a Latin Athenaeus. Thinking I had found a prize <note>original: "in faba pueri", literally "the boy in the bean," a Latin idiom referring to finding a lucky charm or a hidden treasure.</note>, I strongly urged those who frequently do business in Rome to obtain the book for me, hoping indeed that no small...

<meta>The catchword "pa=" suggests the next page begins with "partem" (part) or a similar word, continuing the sentence about the Roman book.</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Jerome Bebel explains the necessity of a new edition of Athenaeus, citing the rarity and high cost of previous versions like the Aldine edition. He recounts his failed attempts to find better manuscript sources in the libraries of Reuchlin and through contacts in Rome.</summary>
<keywords>Jerome Bebel, Aldus Manutius, Johann Walder, Marcus Musurus, Johannes Reuchlin, book production, philology, textual criticism, printing history, Greek classics</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues Jerome Bebel’s preface to the reader. He is discussing the difficulty of acquiring a clean manuscript from Rome to assist in his editing of Athenaeus’s *Deipnosophistae* (The Learned Banqueters).</meta>

...[I believed] that many things could probably be corrected by guessing through a comparison with the Latin translation. But the longer I wait, the more I feel frustrated in my wishes. For they solemnly declare that nowhere in Rome is such a book for sale. I have chosen to mention these things, kind reader, so that you may see it happened through no fault of mine that everything in this author was not rendered <term>completely restored|original: "farta ac tecta", a legal phrase meaning a building is in good repair</term>. 

Yet, lest you suspect we have done nothing in the meantime, I would dare to boast that several hundred errors have been removed. Furthermore, whatever passages Athenaeus cites from Aristotle, Plato, Xenophon, Herodotus, and others, we have corrected according to the reliability of the original authors from whom they were taken. You will find, I believe, that the same has been done in many places which he quotes from the ancients—as is quite often the case—where the words are almost always slightly changed. 

As for how much trouble we had to swallow in the indexes—which we added to serve as a commentary for students—it will be for you, most fair reader, to judge. However, because according to the saying of the tragic poet, "the battle of a single hand is weak" <note>original: μίας χειρὸς ἀσθενὴς μάχη; a quote from Euripides</note>, and fearing to face so many "monsters" <note>He refers to the many corruptions and errors in the text as monsters to be fought.</note> alone, I joined to myself as a partner in this labor Christian Herlin, a young man distinguished by rare erudition. I would wish you to credit him for much of whatever has been more accurately observed. 

Our intention in this matter was to look out for the interests of students to the best of our ability; they will perhaps be grateful for our work now that they are permitted to enjoy such a great treasure, and one so easily obtainable. Indeed, this book should not wrongly be seen as a treasure, for from it so many learned men in our own time have greatly enriched their own supplements, commentaries on civil matters, dialogues on Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek geographer</note>, ancient readings, various histories, their own editions of Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, author of *Varia Historia*</note>, and almost every other work with a grand title that exists. 

But lest I delay you any longer from these banquets of learned men, which are full of

->various and wonderful things<-
->most worthy of being known, Farewell:<-
->and may you enjoy this without envy.<-
<note>original: καὶ ὄναιο ἀφθόνως</note>

<summary>In this concluding part of the preface, Jerome Bebel describes his collaborative effort with Christian Herlin to correct the corrupted text of Athenaeus by cross-referencing quotations. He presents the work as a vital "treasure" that has secretly fueled the scholarship of many other famous writers.</summary>

<keywords>textual criticism, Jerome Bebel, Christian Herlin, Greek literature, Athenaeus, editing, classical scholarship, bibliography</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion by Jerome Bebel regarding the difficulty of finding clean manuscripts in Rome to a formal dedicatory preface written by the famous printer Aldus Manutius. While the previous page focused on the labor of editing, Aldus here addresses the recipient of his edition of Athenaeus, Janus Vyrthesi, celebrating the young man's progress in Greek studies under the tutelage of Marcus Musurus in Venice.</meta>

# ALDUS PIUS MANUTIUS TO JANUS
# VYRTHESI OF PANNONIA, GREETINGS.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a scholar seated at a desk in a study, with a window looking out onto a landscape.</image-desc>

**I** could not easily say how much I congratulate you, Janus, how much I congratulate your kinsmen in Hungary, and Hungary itself: because you have already made such progress in Greek literature, having not yet spent a year listening to <term>Marcus Musurus|a leading Greek scholar of the Renaissance who worked closely with Aldus</term> of Crete. This has happened in Venice, so that you seem likely soon to return to your homeland as the first to bring back the <term>Greek Muses|the personification of the arts and sciences</term> speaking in the Attic style. <note>original: "Macte noua uirtute puer, sic itur ad astra"; a quote from Virgil's Aeneid meaning "Blessings on your fresh courage, boy; this is the way to the stars."</note> You know that you have taken up a heavy burden from Venice and from Musurus: the former can increase you in knowledge, the latter by examples. You know that line of Homer, <note>original: "αὐτὸν ἀνδρῶν τε μέσσην, χροίην τε πιθή"; likely a reference to Homeric character or appearance, often used to discuss the "middle way" or physical excellence.</note> You know how much you are spurred toward virtue by Thomas, the Cardinal and <term>Legate a latere|a high-ranking papal representative</term> of our Lord, and the most venerable Archbishop of Esztergom, your uncle, who can truly say to you that line of Aeneas to Ascanius: <note>original: "Disce puer uirtutem ex me uerumq; laborem"; "Learn virtue and true labor from me, my boy."</note> You know how much you are also encouraged by Philip Cyulanus, the king's secretary, a most serious and excellent man. While he acts as an ambassador to the Venetians with the highest faith and integrity, he constantly advises you whenever you go to greet him out of duty—which you do often—saying: "Janus, <note>original: "pauci quos æquus amauit Iuppiter, aut ardens euexit ad æthera uirtus"; "there are few whom impartial Jupiter loved, or whose burning virtue carried them to the heavens."</note> Pray, take care that you are one of those few, and most like your uncle the Cardinal." "Proceed, my son, as you have begun," and other such sayings full of love for your country. You know, moreover, how much you are inspired by that other Janus, the Bishop of Pécs, the great glory and ornament of Hungary (for you also share the name Janus), on whose tomb this elegant <term>distich|a pair of poetic lines</term> is read:

->Here lies Janus, who was the first to lead the<-
->laurel-bearing goddesses from Helicon to his native Danube.<-

That man, who can never be praised enough, was the first to bring the Latin Muses back to his country; you, with Musurus as your teacher, seem likely to bring back both the Latin and the Attic Muses. Nor do I doubt that you will complete what you have so gloriously begun: both because you have started well—for "he who has begun has half the deed done"—and "the beginning is half of the whole," <note>original: "ἀρχὴ ἥμισυ παντός"</note> and also because you have already made so much progress. Therefore, moved by your sharp intellect, your frequent study, your wonderful love for good literature, and your most holy character, I wanted these books by <term>Athenaeus|An ancient Greek author whose work preserves fragments of hundreds of lost books</term> concerning the banquets of learned men—full of varied, marvelous, and most worthy things to know—to go out from our printing house into the hands of students under your name, so that you may become more eager for the sacred study of letters. For these books, besides the varied and wonderful knowledge of things they contain—such as fish, herbs, trees, and almost countless others—will help you and other students in correcting other books, based on the very many authors he cites. 

Evidence of this can be found in a passage in <term>Theophrastus|An ancient Greek philosopher known as the "father of botany"</term> in the fourth book of his *History of Plants*, where he treats Median and Persian apples <note>citrons and peaches</note>. Although that passage is mutilated and corrupt—both in the book which <term>Theodore Gaza|A Greek scholar who translated many scientific works into Latin</term> translated from Greek into Latin no less elegantly than learnedly, and in the Greek edition printed by our care—it can easily be corrected from what Athenaeus cites in the third book of the *Deipnosophistae* [The Learned Banqueters]. For in the printed Greek edition and in Theodore’s translation, after "it is also a vegetable," <note>original: "ἐστὶ καὶ λάχανον"</note> there is missing "that of the <term>purslane tree|original: ἀδράχνης (adrachnes)</term>," and "and walnuts" <note>original: "καὶ κάρυας"</note> is missing. For *adrachne* without the 'n' is the purslane tree, while *andrachne* <note>original: "ἀνδράχνη"</note> with the 'n' is the purslane herb—a fact which Pliny also confirms. And after "basil or quite," <note>original: "ὤκιμον ἢ πάνυ"</note> "and itself" <note>original: "καὶ αὐτό"</note> is missing. Likewise, after "basil is a deadly poison," there is missing, "it remained to rinse the belly with wine, or even as a medicine." <note>original: "λοιπὸν ἦν ἐν οἴνῳ διακλύζειν τὴν κοιλίαν, νῆστιν ἢ καὶ φάρμακον"</note> Furthermore, where the printed edition has "whenever the purslane... what difference," <note>original: "ὅταν ἡ ἀδράχνη * τί διαφέρειν"</note> it should read "whenever the purslane is transparent," <note>original: "ὅταν ἡ ἀδράχνη, διαφάναι"</note> without the asterisk. That "it is also a vegetable" and "it remained to rinse the belly with wine, and some good medicine" are missing is confirmed by the verses of Virgil in the second book of the *Georgics*:

| | |
|---|---|
| Media produces the bitter juices and lingering flavor | Of the lucky apple, than which no aid is more present, |
| If ever cruel stepmothers have infected the cups, | And mixed herbs with not-harmless spells, |
| It comes as a help, and drives the black venom from the limbs. | The tree itself is huge and most like a laurel in appearance, |
| And if it did not cast a different scent far and wide, | It would be a laurel: its leaves do not fall in any winds: |
| Its flower is exceptionally tenacious; with it the Medes cherish | Their breath and smelly mouths, and heal gasping old men. |

For Virgil seems to have taken the whole thing from Theophrastus. Athenaeus proves this tree to be the <term>citron|original: citrium</term> for many reasons, and adds how it was first found in Media: that the venom is driven from the limbs by the fruit of this tree, and that it cannot harm those who have eaten the citron. I have said these things at some length so that you might know how useful these books of Athenaeus will be to you and other students. Our Musurus has so accurately revised them, compared with many copies and with the <term>epitome|a condensed summary used when the full text was lost</term>, that he has corrected them in almost infinite places and restored the poems—which were read as prose in other versions—to their proper meters. Add to this that the first and second books, which were missing in others, have been added from the epitome along with a good part of the third book; for this work was "without a head" <note>meaning the beginning was missing</note>. Thus, these books can be considered almost the same as the originals, since the subject matter is such that not much could have been subtracted from them. You have, therefore, the complete books of Athenaeus. Other authors who are desired will also be given, I hope, in a short time; may God favor it.

->Therefore, everything will be in abundance for you,<-
->so that you may gloriously bring the<-
->Attic Muses back to your homeland. Farewell. Venice.<-
->In the month of August. In the year 1514.<-

<meta>This page transitions from the alphabetical index of proverbs to philological annotations on specific passages of Athenaeus's "Deipnosophistae" (The Learned Banqueters). These notes provide textual corrections and cross-references to other classical authorities like Pliny, Galen, and the lexicographer Suidas.</meta>

ANNOTATIONS.

### ON CERTAIN PASSAGES IN ATHENAEUS
Annotations diligently collected from the studies of Budé, Erasmus of Rotterdam, and other learned men.

## ON BOOK I.

*Until now.* <note>original: "Εἰσούκβις" (likely for εἰσόκις)</note> 1. 31.) In Suidas, these words are read slightly differently.

*Thrice with those joined in the wagon.* <note>original: "Τρὶς δ᾽ ἐμαξαμβύνοισι"</note> 1. 4. 5.) Erasmus explains the proverb "to rub the face." He mentions the same in the adage, *Spit into your own bosom.* <note>original: "In tuum ipsius sinum inspue"</note>

*Asteropaeus.* <note>original: "ἀστροπαῖον"</note> 2. 4.) Since Homer mentions the hero Asteropaeus as being ambidextrous—namely, one who used the left hand as skillfully as the right—the phrase *the hero Asteropaeus, because he was ambidextrous* <note>original: "ἥρως ἀστροπαῖος ἐπεὶ περιδέξιος ἦν"</note> came to be used for those of a quick and ready wit for doing many things. The sophist Libanius attributes this same quality to the consul Montius in the introduction to his arguments on Demosthenes.

*Winding and...* <note>original: "ἑλίκᾱ κ' ἐδ'υνίες"</note> 2. 19.) Child. <note>original: "puer"</note> This passage is corrupt. <note>original: "Nihil sanum"</note>

*Som Som.* <note>original: "Σόμ Σόμ"</note> 2. 40.) See below in Book 4. Also the proverb, *I know not whether you are white or black.* <note>original: "Albus an ater sis nescio"</note> And Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, an Italian humanist</note> in Book 2, chapter 233.

*Seasonal things.* <note>original: "ὠρᾶια"</note> 2. 40.) For what kind of salted fish these were and from which fish they came, see the same Hermolaus, Book 2, chapter 233.

*The moray eels of Sicily.* <note>original: "ψ' τῶ σικελικῶ μυραίνας"</note> 2. 46.) Pliny, in Book 9, chapter 14, mentions that the moray eels in Sicily are the best.

*And of those without crests.* <note>original: "κ' τῶν ἀσλόφων"</note> 2. 48.) Caelius, Book 15, chapter 7.

*The banissades from Thebes.* <note>original: "Τὰς ἐκ θηβῶν βανιάδας"</note> 2. 49.) Hermolaus testifies in his *Corollarium* that Theban mustard is highly approved.

*Leg of a partridge.* <note>original: "πέρδικος σκέλος"</note> 5. 21.) Erasmus translates this as the proverb, *Legs of a partridge.*

*But... with.* <note>original: "π'ες δ'ὲ μεά"</note> 3. 2.) Corrected by Hermolaus, Book 28, chapter 2.

*For it raises the body.* <note>original: "τὸ γὰρ δέμας ἀνορθοῖ"</note> 3. 18.) The bulb <note>likely an onion or similar root</note> is effective for stimulating lust. See the proverb, *The bulb would be of no use.* <note>original: "Nihil pfuerit bulbus"</note> And below in Book 2 of Athenaeus.

*Vigil from...* <note>original: "βίγλη δ' ἐκ"</note> 3. 22.) See the proverb *Hecate’s supper.* And below in Book 7, folio 121.

*Pithymon.* <note>original: "πίθυμον"</note> 3. 46.) The same is found in Suidas.

*Regarding Apicius.* <note>Apicius was a famous Roman gourmet</note> 4. 10.) Mentioned after others by Caelius in Book 5, chapter 10, and by Budé <note>Guillaume Budé</note> near the end of Book 1 of *On the As.*

*Regarding Aristoxenus.* 4. 19.) Suidas reports the same things, in whose work one should read *flat cakes* <note>original: "πλακῶντας"</note> rather than *floating.* <note>original: "πλέομοντας"</note> The same is said of Nicomedes, but slightly differently under the entry *small fry.* <note>original: "ἀφύα"</note>

*To release the oil.* <note>original: "ἀπὸ λύσαι δ' ἔλαιον"</note> 4. 10.) One should read *onto the wood* <note>original: "ἐπὶ ξύλας"</note> following the proverb, *Small fry to the fire.* <note>original: "Aphya ad ignem"</note>

*Dying away.* <note>original: "ἐπιδαυαίονθς"</note> 4. 14.) One should read *gasping.* <note>original: "ἀσπαίονθς"</note> Erasmus translates the passage as the proverb, *A Myconian neighbor.*

*No longer honorable...* <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι τίμομ ἀσυνέγκους"</note> 4. 18.) It seems it should be read as *no longer honorable...* <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι τίμιον ἀσύνεγκας"</note>

*Meat for all.* <note>original: "πᾶσιν κρέα"</note> 1. 6.) Servius, commenting on the first book of the *Aeneid*, says that in heroic times, they did not eat boiled meat.

*The Thessalian trick.* <note>original: "Θεσσάλου σόφισμα"</note> 6. 11.) See the proverb, *The Thessalian device.*

<column-break/>

*Agallis.* <note>original: "ἄγαλλις"</note> 7. 46.) In Suidas, it is called *anagallis.*

*Phaininda.* <note>original: "φαινινδ'α"</note> 7. 52.) A proverb: *Returning the ball to one another.*

8. 19.) A proverb: *Displaying the Pyrrhic dance.*

*Upon the tongues.* <note>original: "ἐπὶ ταῖς γλώσσαις"</note> 8. 31.) The commentator on Aristophanes’s *Plutus* has almost the same thing: *The tongue of the victims is given to Hermes during public sacrifices.* <note>original: "Γλώττων ἡ γλῶττα τῷ ἑρμῇ δίδοτ'..."</note> *And Homer cast the tongues into the fire.* Didymus, in his commentary on the *Odyssey*, Book 3, says: *It was the custom in sacrifices for the priests to cut off the tongues and burn them for the gods.* Erasmus also mentions this in the proverb, *The tongue is cut out separately.*

*Theophrastus.* 9. 41.) Pliny records the same things from Theophrastus in Book 26, chapter 10.

*Entry.* <note>original: "ἔμβασις"</note> 12. 16.) This is a tub or basin; Dioscorides uses this word in Book 6, chapter 1.

*Cloud.* <note>original: "νεφέλη"</note> 11. 8.) This is a type of hunter’s net, according to Suidas.

*With the habits.* <note>original: "ψ'ν ταῖς ἔξεσιν"</note> 10. 30.) Linacre <note>Thomas Linacre, physician and scholar</note> testifies that this word is often used by Galen—and also frequently in Athenaeus—to mean the physical mass of an animal, which in Latin is also called the "body."

*But the tawny is five.* <note>original: "ὁ δὲ κίῤῥος πέντε"</note> 13. 33.) Galen, in Book 1 of *On Preserving Health*, says that wine for the elderly should be of the thinnest substance and of the color that Hippocrates calls *tawny* <note>original: "κίῤῥον"</note> (that is, reddish-yellow). He could also have called it *yellow* <note>original: "ξανθόν"</note> (that is, golden). Others translate *tawny* differently. See Marcellus, the commentator on Dioscorides, Book 1. Hermolaus translated most of the sections on the types of wine in Book 5 of his *Corollarium*.

*The partridge...* <note>original: "ψ' π'α' περδ'ικα"</note> 14. 20.) See the proverb, *Ships loaded with insults.*

*The beauty at Marathon.* <note>original: "ἡ' τὸ καλὸμ μαραθῶνι"</note> 14. 58.) He means Athens, which erected a trophy after the Barbarians were defeated at Marathon under the leadership of Miltiades.

15. 21.) Regarding *Elaterium* <note>a medicinal juice from the squirting cucumber</note>, see Dioscorides.

*Projecting one over another.* <note>original: "πρόκροσοι ἄλλος ἐπ' ἄλλῳ"</note> Suidas.

16. 24.) What Athenaeus cites here agrees with what Pliny has in Book 14, chapter 18, but not at all with the works of Theophrastus translated by Gaza.

## ON BOOK II.

*Inner chamber.* <note>original: "θάλαμος"</note> 19. 10.) This is the lowest part of a ship. See Pollux, Book 1.

*The Muses are the turners of Dionysus.* <note>original: "Διόνυσ' στροφοὶ αἱ μοῦσαι"</note> 12. 33.) It seems one should read *nymphs* rather than *Muses.* See the proverb, *You have ruined the wine by pouring in water.* And *A third for the Savior.*

*Having made the...* <note>original: "δ'ὴ ποιήσας τὸ"</note> 19. 12.) This epigram also exists under the title of Niceratus in Book 1 of his *Epigrams*. Someone translated it into Latin as follows:

> Bacchus is the poet's swift-footed horse in song;
> For without him, fluid virtue cannot exist.
> So says Cratinus, not breathing of a sweet wine-skin,
> But smelling of many a great jar.
> Crowned with ivy, he sang his joyful songs,
> For he has a brow wreathed like yours, O Liber <note>Bacchus</note>.

# ANNOTATIONS.

### ON BOOK I.

*Very persuasive* <note>original: "ἐπακτικώτατα"</note> (28. 28. 31.) Dioscorides says the same regarding almonds. <note>original: "De amygdalis idē Dioscorides"</note> See also Suetonius in his life of Tiberius.

*More medicinal* <note>original: "ἰατροφώτερος"</note> 19. 27.) They translate this as "medicines," that is, things which heal more than they nourish. <note>original: "Medicamenta uertūt, hoc est quæ plus medentur, quàm nutriūt"</note>

*Having handled* <note>original: "ἀφάσας"</note> 28. 15.) "Drinking eagerly." <note>original: "Auide hauriēs"</note> He also uses this at the beginning of Book 14; Diogenes Laertius reports the same regarding Zeno.

*But when it thunders* <note>original: "ὅταν δὲ βρονταί"</note> 31. 21.) Juvenal alludes to this in Satire 5: "And the long-awaited thunders will make the dinners larger," etc. <note>original: "Et facient optata tonitrua cœnas maiores"</note> See Pliny, Book 19, chapter 3.

*The wood-dwelling, harmless thorn* <note>original: "ὑλοχυνὴς ἀκάκανθος"</note> 31. 48.) Cicero, in Book 2 of *On Divination*, recites a riddle of this kind regarding a tortoise, taken from the poet Pacuvius.

*Nothing would benefit you* <note>original: "οὐδὲν ἂν σ’ ὀνήσοι"</note> 32. 19.) See the proverb: "The wild onion will be of no use." <note>original: "Nihil profuerit bulbus"</note>

*Having snapped off* <note>original: "ἀπορὰξαντος"</note> 34. 41.) "Not branched from the stalks." <note>original: "Nec brachiati a caulibus"</note> For this is how Hermolaus translates it in Book 2 of his *Corollarium*.

*Un-tongued* <note>original: "ἀγλῶδες"</note> 35. 29.) What if you read it as *sticky/viscous* <note>original: "γλοιῶδες"</note>, which is a word he also uses in Book 3. See Hermolaus in his glosses on Pliny.

->IN BOOK III.<-

*...or Thyramis* <note>original: "πτὰ ἢ θύραμιρ"</note> 36. 35.) It should be read as *Thyamis* <note>original: "θύαμιμ"</note>, as Hermolaus corrects this passage in Book 3 of his *Castigations of Pliny*.

*Geaionia* <note>original: "γεαιωνίαν"</note> 38. 52.) It should be read as *Geonia* <note>original: "γεωνίαν"</note>. Stephanus of Byzantium mentions this city citing Thucydides.

*Skiale* <note>A plant, likely a squill</note> <note>original: "σκιάλη"</note> 39. 2.) Theodore Gaza translates this as *Scylla* in Theophrastus's *History of Plants*, Book 2, chapter 7.

*Mydos* <note>original: "μυδὸς"</note> 39. 38.) See Stephanus of Byzantium's *On Cities*.

*A Pharian drug* <note>original: "φαριακὸν φάρμακον"</note> 41. 12.) See Marcellus, the commentator on Dioscorides, Book 6, chapter 19.

*Relieving fatigue* <note>original: "ἄκοπα"</note> 42. 17.) And these are said to conveniently preserve things unharmed. <note>original: "eaqȝ commodè illęsa præseruare dicitur"</note>

*Much the gelded pig* <note>original: "πολὺ τὴω ἐκτομίδα"</note> 51. 19.) See Hermolaus in his *Castigations of Pliny*, Book 11, chapter 37.

*From the pinna-shells* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶ πίνναι"</note> 46. 34.) See Aelian, Book 15, chapter 31.

*Laconian* <note>original: "λακωνα"</note> 46. 23.) Erasmus translates this story in the proverb: "Rougher than a sea-urchin." <note>original: "Echino asperior"</note>

*Eating* <note>original: "κατεσθαίωμ"</note> 49. 11.) *Gaping* <note>original: "ἀποχάωμ"</note> according to Hesychius.

*Rest-harrow* <note>A thorny shrub</note> <note>original: "ἀνώνις"</note> 49. 52.) Leonicenus translates this story in Book 2, chapter 86.

*One raised from the dust* <note>original: "συγκονιοδίης"</note> 57. 43.) One who is the first to make something from a new harvest; for this is how Hermolaus interprets it. <note>original: "qui primus è nouella messe cōficit"</note>

*Set down boiled, not...* <note>original: "θὲς ἐφ’θὸς μηδ’ ὸς"</note> 57. 49.) That which is made from crushed but not sifted wheat, according to the same author, Hermolaus. <note>original: "q ex cōfracto nec excreto fit tritico"</note>

*Washed millstone* <note>original: "ῥίπταμον μλύον"</note> 58. 4.) That is, excellently kneaded. <note>original: "hoc est egregiè subactum"</note> Hermolaus.

*Those having growth-marks* <note>original: "τοὺς ἔχοντας φυτομάς"</note> 58. 7.) Square and surrounded by notches. <note>original: "quadratos ac incisuris præcinctos"</note>

*A certain day of burning* <note>original: "ἐγκαιὼ τις ἡμέρα"</note> 59. 22.) It should be read as *a day of pregnancy*. <note>original: "ἐγκυιστις ἡμέρα"</note> See Erasmus’s *Adages*.

*It would be better for my blood* <note>original: "βέλτιον δ’ ἦν μοι αἷμα"</note> 61. 37.) These are verses from Aristophanes' *The Knights*. See the commentator on this author.

*Kephisodoros* <note>original: "κηφισόδωρος"</note> 61. 40.) What follows, Erasmus translates in the proverb: "The smell of profit is good." <note>original: "Lucri bonus est odor"</note>

*If then he turns me* <note>original: "ἐὰν δ’ ἄρα σρέφη μι"</note> 62. 13.) See the proverb: "There is no remedy against the bite of a sycophant." <note>original: "nō est remediū aduersus sycophātę morsū"</note>

<column-break/>

*Enamored of things belonging to others* <note>original: "ἐρωμλν ἀλλοτρίωμ"</note> 62. 31.) There is a similar sentiment in Pliny, Book 8, in his letter to Gallus: "Either because it is so arranged by nature that, indifferent to things close at hand, we pursue things far off; or because the desire for all things languishes when the opportunity is easy." <note>original: "seu quia ita natura comparatū, ut proximorū incuriosi, longinqua sectemur, seu quod omniū rerū cupido lāguescit, cū facilis occasio est"</note>

*Acting like a sycophant* <note>original: "συκαπάζει"</note> 63. 53.) A Syrian mimicking the Attic style. <note>original: "Syrus atticissans"</note>

->IN BOOK IV.<-

*Loosening the barriers* <note>original: "χαλῶν των φραγμάτων"</note> 65. 27.) That is, through secret mechanical devices, with the sails or boards pulled back, or led away, or lowered. <note>original: "id est per clādestina machinamēta reductis uelis aut tabulatis, uel deductis, uel demissis"</note> Budé.

*Upright, as the saying goes* <note>original: "ὀρθαὶ τὸ δὴ λεγόμενοψ"</note> 65. 51.) See the proverb: "Erect/Standing." <note>original: "erecti"</note>

*Eunuch or Fool* <note>original: "βάκηλου"</note> 67. 28.) See the proverb: "Similar to a Bacelus." <note>original: "Baceli similis"</note>

*A suckling piglet* <note>original: "γαλαθηνὸς ὀρθαγορίσκος"</note> 69. 40.) Sucking pigs, and those still at the breast, are so named from *early morning* <note>original: "ὄρθρος"</note> and *to go to market* <note>original: "ἀγοράζεσθαι"</note>, because they are carried around for sale in all the morning hours. Hermolaus.

*They say 'mappyen'* <note>original: "μαππύην φασί"</note> 70. 32.) Read the proverb: *to eat quickly* or *to gobble*. <note>original: "μαππυᾶν"</note>

*Through deer* <note>original: "δι’ ἐλάφος"</note> 71. 29.) Which is also called *eleaphos* <note>original: "ἐλέαφος"</note>; see Ammonius's *On Similar but Different Words* and Suidas. Athenaeus uses this later in the same book.

*Into the account* <note>original: "εἰς ὑπόλογον"</note> 73. 25.) Just as those who perform military service in Greece are accustomed to earn pay, so these receive sustenance from the king, which goes toward their wages and is charged to the account. Budé.

*But Alexander the Great* <note>original: "ὁ δὲ μέγας ἀλέξανδρος"</note> 73. 39.) Budé translates and diligently examines this passage in Book 3 of *On the As* [De Asse].

*Antamnos* <note>original: "ἄνταμνος"</note> 75. 3.) Herodotus calls it not *Autumnus* [Autumn], but *Attaginus* [a francolin].

*Minced meat* <note>original: "περίκομμα"</note> 75. 15.) According to Budé, this is a type of food.

*Dough for wiping hands* <note>original: "ἀπωμαγδαλίαμ"</note> 75. 20.) See the proverb: "A dog living off the dough-scraps." <note>original: "Canis uiuens è magdalia"</note>

*Within the trench* <note>original: "ὠθὶ τῆ χαραβάδῃ"</note> 74. 40.) Leonicenus translates this in Book 1, chapter 90 of his *Various History*: "Since through all the dining rooms of those reclining, heaps of leaves stood out here and there on all the floors, a cubit in measure." Therefore, perhaps it should be read as: *to a depth of a cubit*. <note>original: "ὠθὶ πήχεα βάθη"</note>

*Spending on pay* <note>original: "καταμιδοφορῶν"</note> 84. 12.) Instead of "to be spent on soldiers' wages." <note>original: "εἰς μισθὸν στρατιωτῶν καταδανανᾶσθαι"</note>

->IN BOOK V.<-

*Gatherer or Interrupter* <note>original: "ἀγνύρας"</note> 95. 32.) That is, gracefully taking up the conversation and speaking between, which means interrupting the middle of the speech, inserting one's own words as if intercalating them. Budé.

*Collecting fine words and showing technical skill* <note>original: "δἰροσσιλογῶν κὴ φιλοτεχνῶν"</note> 97. 16.) That is, discussing art and pouring out words. Budé.

*Tebenna* <note>An Etruscan garment, precursor to the toga</note> <note>original: "τήβενναν"</note> 97. 20.) A toga. See Baïf’s *On Clothing*. <note>original: "de re uestiaris"</note>

*Over-mantles* <note>original: "ἐφαπτίδας"</note> 97. 50.) "All the cavalry mentioned, however, were dressed in purple cloaks. Some indeed even had robes that were patched and woven with the figures of various animals," etc. Leonicenus, Book 2, chapter 9.

*A procession, or shortly wanting of two hundred* <note>original: "θεωρία ἠ βραχὺ λέπεσαι διακοσιῶν"</note> 98. 1.) Lo...

# ANNOTATIONS.

The passage is corrupt; perhaps it should read *spectacles* <note>original: "θεωριαί"</note>. For Leonicus translates it thus: "and three hundred spectacles of various dishes."

*The cabins* <note>original: "τὼ θαλάμκον"</note> (103. 9.) See Budé, Book 1 of *On the As* <note>Guillaume Budé’s influential 1514 treatise on ancient weights and measures</note>.

*Red copper* <note>original: "ἐρυθροῦ χαλκοῦ"</note> (103. 27.) Like copper gilded in fire <note>original German: "us Kupffer im feur uergult"</note>.

*The Gabinian War* <note>original: "γαβινικὸν πόλεμον"</note> (104. 8.) He understands the war by which Ptolemy was restored, concerning which see the first book of Cicero’s *Letters to his Friends*.

*Samines* <note>original: "σαμίνες"</note> (104. 19.) Budé translates this as "roasted meats" <note>original: "assamenta"</note>.

*Agradina* <note>original: "ἀγραδινή"</note> (104. 40.) See Stephanus; Livy mentions the place now and then in his history of the Punic War.

*Of a lysiode* <note>original: "λυσιοδοῦ"</note> (106. 42.) Guarino translates *lysiode* as a "singer of Bacchic songs" <note>original: "Bacchanaliū cantorē"</note> in Plutarch’s life of Sulla.

*Enrolled fraudulently* <note>original: "παρεγγραφος"</note> (102. 6.) A false and honorary citizen, or someone who has obtained citizenship by any means whatsoever. Budé.

*Turning his eyes aside* <note>original: "παραβαλὼν τὼ ὀφθαλμώ"</note> (109. 10.) That is, Socrates alone had stood firm, looking askance and grimly out of pride. This is taken from Aristophanes’s *Clouds*. See Budé in the *Commentaries*.

*If you should acquire a portion* <note>original: "εἰ τὸ μέρος κτήσαιο"</note> (110. 42.) The passage is explained by the proverb: "Would that those things which are between Corinth [and Sicyon] might happen to me" <note>A common Greek proverb for wishing for great wealth</note>.

*Monosyllables* <note>original: "μονοσύλλαβοι"</note> (112. 22.) So grammarians are called out of contempt, because they lurk in corners like silkworms, and because they treat of the minutiae of words. See the proverb: "Every master is a monosyllable to his slave" <note>Implying that masters give only short, curt commands</note>.

### IN BOOK VI.

*Brauron* is a deme of Attica, named after the hero Brauron, from whom Artemis also takes the name Brauronia. Stephanus. (112. 44.)

*Aporrhaphanti* <note>original: "ἀπορραφαντὶ"</note>—an aversion, "lest I be turned to stone." (113. 26.)

*Tarops* <note>original: "τάρωψ"</note>—instead of *tetraps* <note>four-eyed</note>. (113. 32.)

*You will cast it down for yourself* <note>original: "αὑτῷ καταβαλῖς"</note> (113. 44.) Erasmus thinks it should read *for yourself* <note>original: "αὑτῷ"</note>; see the proverb: "Here is Rhodes, here is the jump" <note>A famous Aesopic proverb used to challenge someone to prove their boasts on the spot</note>.

*Taking up the dead* <note>original: "νεκρῶν ἀναίρεσιν"</note> (114. 5.) "To take up the dead" <note>original: "ἀναιρεῖσθαι τοὺ νεκρούς"</note> is to bury the corpses of the slain. See Budé.

*It is according to the custom* <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὸ νομιμόν ἐστι"</note> (115. 1.) Erasmus elegantly translates these verses of Diphilus in his book of proverbs: "He makes a way for boldness" <note>original: "pteruiā facit"</note>.

*Beggar-boaster* <note>original: "πτωχαλαζόνα"</note> (116. 14.) That is, a displayer of riches. See the proverb: "Live according to your own harvest" <note>original: "Messē tenus ppria uiue"</note>.

*He came revelling* <note>original: "ἐπικώμασε"</note> (116. 47.) This word signifies "to enter rudely." See Budé in the *Commentaries*.

*And to praise everything* <note>original: "κὴ πάντα ἐπαινεῖν"</note> (120. 41.) The same is found in Juvenal’s third Satire: "Ready to praise, if he has belched well, if he has urinated straight," etc.

*Caryatids* <note>original: "καρυάτιδες"</note> (121. 31.) From which the "Caryatid columns" are named. Read Vitruvius, Book 1, Chapter 1.

*Oak-lover* <note>original: "φιλόδρυος"</note> (121. 32.) See the proverb: "Among the unlearned even the Lark sounds [like a Nightingale]."

*And those who were hungry* <note>original: "οἱ δὲ λιματωδῶντες"</note> (126. 21.) Read Erasmus’s proverb: "Beautiful at the door."

*Some were shaving* <note>original: "εἶχ’ οἱ μὲν ξυρόμενοι"</note> (131. 7.) It seems it should be read

<column-break/>

as: "and some were shaving and smoothing themselves, being at last delicate."

*Manes, just like a sack* <note>original: "μαύης ἅτε σάκις"</note> (132. 21.) Names of slaves.

*Discordant* <note>original: "ἀσυμφώνους"</note> (133. 16.) Thus also Cato the Elder, according to Plutarch, took care that there were always mutual quarrels among his slaves, because he held their goodwill and agreement of mind in suspicion, and feared it greatly.

*Someone to gush* <note>original: "κοχυδεῖν τις"</note> (135. 31.) To gush <note>original: "κοχυδεῖν"</note> means to overflow <note>original: "ὑπερχεῖν"</note>. Hesychius.

*Cleanings* <note>original: "ἐκφαντίσματα"</note> (136. 3.) In Hesychius it is incorrectly read as *ekphantismata*. According to the same author, they are the things thrown out when they clean the mangers.

*Go, found your strength* <note>original: "ἴσχυν γ’ ἴθι κτίσιν"</note> (135. 51.) Alludes to that saying of Socrates: "One must eat to live, not live to eat."

*Choenix-measurers* <note>original: "χοινικομέτρας"</note> (136. 53.) See the proverb: "Do not sit upon a choenix" <note>A choenix was a dry measure; the proverb warns against laziness or living only for the day's food</note>.

*Those having been benefited* <note>original: "εὐεργετημένων"</note> (137. 17.) By those with whom he had acted advantageously: whom he had favored with benefits, and who were indebted to him. Budé.

*Those having leisure* <note>original: "εὐκαιρούμενοι"</note> (138. 30.) Those who were most abundant in the things necessary for life, yet raised their children to be abstemious; or those who inhabited places most opportune for seeking life’s necessities, and who had plenty of leisure to acquire the necessities of life. Budé.

### IN BOOK VII.

*A Thessalian horse* <note>original: "ἵππον θεσσαλικήν"</note> (140. 17.) This oracle was given to the people of Aegitium when they asked which of the Greeks were the most excellent. See the proverb: "The Megarians are neither third nor fourth" <note>A proverb regarding those of no account</note>.

*For when they betray pleasures* <note>original: "τὰς γὰρ ἡδονὰς ὅταν προδώσιν"</note> (141. 5.) This passage proves how corrupted the published copies of books are—besides infinite other testimonies—having been emended and explained by that most learned man Joachim Camerarius in the scholia with which he illustrated Sophocles’s *Antigone*. The same verses are repeated below in Book 12.

*Having changed* <note>original: "μεταθέμενος"</note> (141. 39.) Diogenes Laertius in the *Life of Zeno* testifies that this Dionysius was so nicknamed.

*The season for loving* <note>original: "ὤρη ἐρᾶν"</note> (141. 41.) See the proverb: "Evil is good."

*And Themison, the favorite of Antiochus* <note>original: "κὴ θεμίσων τὰ αὐτιόχε παιδικά"</note> (145. 29.) That is, Themison was the darling of Antiochus. See Budé.

*Either into the chambers, or into the jar* <note>original: "ἢ εἰς θαλάμας, ἢ εἰς κεράμιον"</note> Gaza translates this as: "Either in the bed-chambers, or in the pottery."

*Metalochas* <note>original: "μεταλόχας"</note> (157. 39.) These verses are read a little differently below on page 163, line 33.

*I sacrifice in a rushing manner* <note>original: "θύω θυώνως"</note> (162. 1.) Here I think it should read: "Thyoneus" <note>a name for Bacchus</note> comes from *thyein* [to rush/sacrifice], because he is impetuous, etc.

# ANNOTATIONS.

The passage is a bit obscure, or the Greek is corrupt; I have chosen to add Erasmus’s Latin translation. Stratonicus had sailed into the Black Sea <note>original: "Pontum"</note> to King Berisades, where he stayed for a long time. He wished to flee from there back to Greece, though the king did not seem likely to allow it. "You have a fine plan, O King," said Stratonicus, "deciding to stay here yourself" <note>A clever way of implying he himself was leaving</note>.

*How pleasantly mocked* <note>original: "ὡς ἡδέως ἐπεσκημμένα"</note> (174. 28.) After no one cheered, he applauded in the popular fashion and approved the rumor with a seconding shout. See Budé.

*He said, "I think/It seems of a man"* <note>original: "ἀνδρὸς ἔφη δοκῶ"</note> (174. 37.) Erasmus says this cannot be rendered in Latin, for the passage relies on an ambiguity <note>a pun or double meaning</note>. *Doko* <note>original: "δοκῶ"</note> sounds like "to be a beam" if you include the subscript iota, but without it, it means "I think." Unless perhaps it should be read with an acute accent, meaning "these are beams."

*You do not have, but are had* <note>original: "οὐκ ἔχεις ἀλλ' ἔχη"</note> (174. 44.) This signified that the student was the master, or that the chorus was more learned than the leader himself.

*Inquiring in Ilium* <note>original: "πυνθανόμενος δ' ἐν ἰλίῳ"</note> (174. 45.) Erasmus thinks this passage is not free from error. See the proverb: *Always evils for Troy* <note>original: "Semper Ilio mala"</note>.

*Inhabiting* <note>original: "φυτοῖχιοῦσι"</note> (174. 50.) Should be read as *phytochonti* <note>original: "φυτοχόντι"</note>. Erasmus translates: "When by chance he had come to Miletus, which was then inhabited by a gathered crowd."

*He said, "to Macedonia"* <note>original: "εἰς μακεδονίαν ἔφη"</note> (177. 2.) Used instead of what others say, "to the blessed ones" <note>original: "εἰς μακαρίαν," a euphemism for the dead</note>, if one prays for someone's destruction. In passing, he also noted the barbarism of the Macedonian people.

*But the things of the bath-man in the heart* <note>original: "τὰ δὲ βαλανέως ἐν καρδίᾳ"</note> (175. 15.) Erasmus translates this as "in Arcadia," although according to Stephanus, Cardia is a city in the Thracian Chersonese.

*Timotheus the law/mode* <note>original: "Τιμόθεος ὁ νόμος"</note> (175. 27.) He seized upon the ambiguity of the word: for *nomos* <note>original: "νόμος"</note> to the Greeks means both "law" and "musical modes." Therefore, it is dangerous to defeat a king.

*From the land of Sibyra* <note>original: "ἐκ γῆς σιβύρας"</note> (180. 37.) See the proverb: *You ruined the wine by pouring in water*.

*They are saved together.* Alciatus. (181. 1.)

*A contribution feast* <note>original: "ἔρανΘ" / "eranos"</note>. See Budé. (180. 50.)

### IN BOOK IX.

*A stalky rug* <note>original: "πασὸν καυλωτόν"</note> (184. 42.) According to the interpretation of Hermolaus, this is something "plucked, full of shoots, common, and white."

*To desire a little leek* <note>original: "κιπῆσαι γηθυλλίδος"</note> (185. 21.) Because a pregnant woman had a craving for a headed leek during a period of calm weather <note>original: "malacia"</note>. See Hermolaus in the *Corollarium*.

*Unshorn* <note>original: "ἄπεκτον"</note> (186. 43.) Philochorus also mentions this in Book 1. *Apekton* is derived from *pikein*, which means "to comb."

*Of the surrounding months* <note>original: "τῶν περιφρομηνίων"</note> (189. 1.) Elsewhere he uses the word *polyphromenion*, but for the same thing. Regarding this matter, see Budé in his *Commentaries*.

*Lest the flute-player...* <note>original: "ἵνα μὴ ὁ αὐλητήρ"</note> (189. 10.) See the proverb: *The flute-player is beaten*.

*To the gates* <note>original: "ἐς τὰς πύλας"</note> (192. 19.) Erasmus’s proverb: *Evils af-*

<column-break/>

*-ter evils.* Nicolaus Leonicenus seems to have read "woods" <note>original: "ὕλας"</note> in Book 5 of *Various History*; he translates it as "Thermopylae."

*Gulping down the pinna-shell* <note>original: "κάπτων δὲ πῖνα"</note> (192. 35.) This is, as Pliny translates it, "the Porphyrio bird drinks by biting."

*To sacrifice quails to Hercules* <note>original: "θύειν τῷ ἡρακλεῖ ὄρτυγας"</note> (194. 41.) See the proverb: *The Quail and Hercules*.

*Gluttonous* <note>original: "λαμυριτόσης"</note> (196. 8.) Should be read as "salty" <note>original: "ἁλμυριτόσης"</note> according to Gaza’s version and the translator of Aelian.

*Celestial goat* <note>original: "αἶξ οὐρανία"</note>. See the proverb: *They beheld the celestial goat rising*.

### IN BOOK X.

*And that he sacrificed a hecatomb* <note>original: "κᾀὶ θύσαι αὐτὸν ἑκατόμβην"</note> (207. 11.) Cicero, in Book 3 of *On the Nature of the Gods*, says: "Although Pythagoras is said to have sacrificed an ox to the Muses when he had discovered something new in geometry." In Vitruvius, Book 9, Chapter 2, this discovery of Pythagoras is mentioned, not so much described as depicted.

*Whomever he might pick out* <note>original: "οὓς δ' ἂν ἐξέλοι"</note> (210. 5.) See the proverb: *The ill-advised rashness of the Athenians*.

*A two-choenix cup* <note>original: "ποτήριον δίχοινον"</note> (214. 14.) Budé translates this as a "two-congius cup" in Book 5 of *On the As*, where he discusses the heavy drinking and death of Alexander the Great.

*Effeminate* <note>original: "γύννις"</note> (214. 41.) A "soft hermaphrodite," according to Suidas.

*By the cold* <note>original: "ὑπὸ τοῦ ψύχους"</note> (215. 46.) See Aristotle’s *Problems*, problem 10 of the first section.

*Airodone* <note>original: "αἰροδώνη"</note> (217. 45.) According to Stephanus, *Airodora* is a city of Megara, and perhaps this wine is named after it.

*That false opinions...* <note>original: "ὅτι ψευδεῖς δόξαι"</note> (220. 18.) See the proverb: *In wine there is truth*.

### IN BOOK XI.

*Amorgian* <note>original: "ἀμόργιον"</note> (227. 14.) Amorgos is an island, the homeland of Simonides the Iambic poet, according to Stephanus and Suidas.

*To those who have despaired of the truth* <note>original: "ἀπεγνωκόσι τ' ἀληθείας"</note> (229. 24.) That is, those who have turned further away from the truth and are wandering. Budé.

*Entrust* <note>original: "ἐπιθέα"</note> (229. 44.) To mandate or enjoin a province; that is, "he did not hesitate to entrust it to those suited for it." Budé.

*Erytheia* <note>original: "ἐρύθεια"</note> (231. 42.) The island of Geryon near the Ocean, according to Stephanus.

*Publicly sold* <note>original: "δημοπρατα"</note> (235. 3.) Things which the people sell; things sold publicly or in a public manner. Suidas.

### IN BOOK XII.

*And to Sophocles...* <note>original: "καὶ τῷ σοφοκλῆς"</note> (251. 9.) Sophocles responded well when someone asked him, as he was now of a worn-out age, whether he still enjoyed sexual matters. "The gods forbid!" he said. "In truth, I have gladly fled from that, as if from a fierce and furious master." Cicero, *On Old Age*.

*Shrunken* <note>original: "συσέλλοντ"</note> (252. 21.) They are of a lowered mind and dejected spirits. Budé.

*To be brought up in the shade* <note>original: "σκιατραφῆσαι"</note> (254. 15.) A word said concerning "those who live luxuriously," namely those accustomed to the delights of shady places who do not wish to be scorched by the sun. Budé.

*Not only are the Lydian women set free* <note>original: "οὐ μόνον λυδῶν γυναῖκες ἄφετοι"</note> (254. 24.)

# ANNOTATIONS.

It was not only the women of the Lydians who lived without supervision and were available to all for the sake of Venus <note>original: "Venerisq; omniũ obuię"</note>, but also those of the Locrians and those inhabiting Cyprus. In short, to put it once and for all, the women whose custom it is to consecrate their girls to Venus the harlot <note>original: "Veneri meretrici"</note> and the prostituted, seem to be a monument to a certain injury actually perpetrated, for which they now pay the penalty. **Budé**. See **Herodotus**, Book 1.

*The things of Massanassa* <note>original: "μασανάσσης ὁ τῶν"</note> (256. 21.) **Plutarch** reports that **Caesar** said the same thing at the beginning of his *Life of Pericles*.

*Wishing for Sybaris* <note>original: "βουλόμενοι γὴ συβαρί"</note> (256. 33.) Read **Erasmus’s** *Proverbs*: "He who does not wish to die before his time," and "Sybaritic calamity."

*A privately-fitted ship* <note>original: "ἰδιόστολον πλοῖον"</note> (257. 8.) is said of a ship which someone has hired for himself alone. **Budé**.

*I have stipulated/agreed* <note>original: "προσδιεσελαλάμην"</note> (257. 11.) that is, "I have agreed," "I have specifically excepted," "I have provided by stipulation." **Budé**.

*Pythoretos* <note>original: "πυθόρρητος"</note> (263. 47.) He was nicknamed "The Versatile," as if "circular" or "moving around," according to the interpreter **Hermolaus**. See the proverb, "Versatile Artemon."

*Those who are most healthy in Larissa of Thessaly wander about* <note>original: "ἀλύουσι οἱ γὴ λαρίσση τῆς θετταλίας ὑγινέστατοι"</note> (264. 4.) From **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>.

*The city of the boobies [fools] for this very man* <note>original: "εἰς τοῦτον αὐτὸν πόλις κεπφ"</note> (261. 36.) That is, a life of pleasure turned the man's fortune around into the opposite to such an extent. **Budé**.

<column-break/>

*At the sweet elbow* <note>original: "ἀγκῶνι γλυκεῖ"</note> (267. 36.) See the proverb "Sweet elbow" <note>An idiom for taking one's ease</note>.

*Begging priests* <note>original: "μηραγυρτῶν"</note> (268. 9.) These are the *Mēragyrtai* who collected alms for the Mother of the Gods while carrying drums. **Budé**.

*Of much abuse* <note>original: "πολυβροείας"</note> (268. 25.) That is, affected by every kind of injury. **Budé**.

*By way of addition* <note>original: "ἐπισηκώμασιν"</note> (270. 14) That is, they introduced themselves among the virtues: they were deemed worthy of the same name. This was brought forth enviously under the persona of one advocating for pleasures. **Budé**.

*Thrace-travelers* <note>original: "θρακοφοῖται"</note> (327. 18.) I think this denotes ambassadors who were constantly traveling from Athens to Thrace.

*Because of the linden-tree* <note>original: "διὰ τὸ φιλύρας"</note> (273. 26.) That is, he is said to have been so slender that he supported his weakness with linden-wood slats <note>original: "tiliaceis asseribus"</note> wrapped around his body. For so **Hermolaus** translates in his *Corolla*, where "moth-eaten" <note>original: "tineaceis"</note> is wrongly read instead of "linden-wood."

->IN BOOK XIII.<-

*Judges through a man* <note>original: "δι' ἀνδρὸς δικασαὶ"</note> (303. 11.) **Budé** explains this passage in Book 1 of *On the As* <note>original: "de assis," his treatise on ancient coinage and weights</note> where he discusses interest.

->IN BOOK XIIII.<-

*And a pillar or Babys* <note>original: "καὶ κίων ἢ βάβυς"</note> (319. 13.) **Erasmus** thinks it should be read "Babys sings worse," etc. See the proverb, "Babys sings worse."

->END OF THE ANNOTATIONS.<-

<meta>This page serves as the "Errata" or list of corrections for the volume. It follows the alphabetical Latin index and precedes the main Greek text of Athenaeus’s "The Learned Banqueters." The printer, Johannes Walder, addresses the reader to explain the necessity of these corrections in a work of such immense complexity.</meta>

# JOHANNES WALDER TO HIS STUDIOUS READERS, GREETINGS.

<sig>f 2</sig>

Even if the greatest part of those things which follow are of such a kind that they ought to show a varied reading left to each person’s judgment, rather than any negligence of mine: nevertheless, since I have once resolved to do everything for the sake of your studies, I did not wish to pass over anything that I considered to be even the slightest part of my duty. Therefore, if by chance some lighter matters, not greatly worthy of notice, have been noted and described here, I would wish them to be accepted in this spirit: that you may understand how much care I have taken so that this writer might reach the hands of students as corrected and unencumbered as possible. At the same time, you may see what a great task it is to "clean the Augean stable." <note>A proverbial expression referring to a near-impossible task of cleaning up a massive mess, referencing the Labors of Hercules.</note> Regarding detractors, I take no trouble; I desire to help the study of letters as much as I can, expecting no greater rewards than if I know this intention of mine is recognized and approved by good men.
->Farewell.<-

<summary>This page contains a formal Latin greeting from the printer Johannes Walder to his readers, followed by a dense list of errata (textual corrections) for the Greek edition of Athenaeus’s "The Learned Banqueters." Walder frames the editing process as a Herculean labor, emphasizing his dedication to providing a clean and accurate text for scholars.</summary>

# FROM MACROBIUS'S SATURNALIA
# BOOK VII. CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure in classical robes, possibly a scholar, holding a book or scroll within an ornamental frame.</image-desc>
When the first courses were already removed after the banquet, and as the circulation of smaller cups began to vary, Praetextatus <note>Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, a prominent 4th-century Roman senator and polymath</note> said: "It is often the case that food, when consumed, makes men silent, but drink makes them talkative. Yet we remain silent over our cups, as if such a gathering should lack holiday discussions, or even philosophical ones." And Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a famous Roman orator and statesman</note> replied: "Do you really feel this way, Vettius, that philosophy should be present at banquets, and not be kept within her own inner chambers like some censuring and overly modest mother of the house? Should she not avoid mixing with Bacchus <note>original: libero; referring to Liber/Bacchus, the god of wine</note>, for whom rowdiness is a family trait, while she is of such modesty that she admits no noise—not only of words, but not even of thoughts—into the sanctuary of her own quiet? Let even a foreign custom and discipline sought from the Parthians teach us: they are accustomed to enter banquets with concubines, not with wives, as if they believe the former are fit to be brought out into the public and to behave playfully, while the latter should be kept hidden at home to protect their cloistered modesty. Should I think philosophy ought to be brought out, when even the art of rhetoric—a popular profession—blushed to go there? For Isocrates, the Greek orator—who first compelled words, previously free, to follow rhythmic patterns—when he was begged by his companions at a banquet to bring forth something from the fountain of his eloquence, pleaded for this excuse: 'What the present place and time require,' he said, 'I am not skilled in; what I am skilled in is suited neither for the present place nor time.'" To this Eustachius replied: "I approve of your intention, Symmachus, in that you venerate philosophy with that highest regard you think she deserves, believing she should be adored only within her own inner shrine. But if she is to be exiled from banquets for this reason, then her foster-children must also depart far from here—I mean honesty and modesty, and no less piety along with sobriety. For which of these would I say is less venerable? Thus it would happen that, if such a chorus of matrons were banished from these gatherings, the freedom of the banquet would be surrendered solely to concubines—that is, to vices and crimes. But far be it from philosophy, which in its schools treats so carefully the duties of banquet-goers, to dread the banquets themselves, as if it could not prove in reality what it is accustomed to teach in words; or as if she did not know how to keep a middle ground <note>original: modum; referring to the classical ideal of moderation</note>, she who has established the boundaries for all the acts of human life. For I do not invite philosophy to the tables in such a way that she does not moderate herself, since her discipline is to teach the moderation of all things. Therefore, let me settle the matter between you and Vettius as if by an arbitral judgment..."

<summary>This page concludes a detailed list of Greek textual corrections for Athenaeus and introduces a excerpt from Macrobius's Saturnalia, where Roman elites debate whether philosophy is appropriate for a dinner party.</summary>
<keywords>Macrobius, Saturnalia, Symmachus, Praetextatus, Eustachius, Isocrates, philosophy, banquets, moderation, Greek philology, Aldine edition</keywords>

--- Page 70 ---
<meta>This page continues from a list of textual corrections for Athenaeus’s "The Learned Banqueters." It transitions into a dialogue from Book VII of Macrobius’s "Saturnalia," where the character Eustachius discusses whether philosophy has a place at a dinner party.</meta>

For, I will indeed open the doors of the dining rooms <note>original: "tricliniorum"; the formal dining room of a Roman house, named for its three couches</note> to philosophy; but I promise she will be present in such a way that she does not exceed the measure of the distribution known to her and her followers.

Then Furius said: "Since our age has produced you, Eustachius, as the sole follower of philosophy, please reveal to us the manner of this 'distribution' <note>original: "dispensationis"; here meaning the appropriate way to manage or share something</note> you grant her while she dines."

And Eustachius replied: "First, I know she will observe this: to assess the natural talents of the guests present. If she finds several skilled men, or at least lovers of her art, in the dinner party, she will allow herself to be the subject of conversation. Just as a few mute letters, scattered among vowels, easily blend into the company of the voice, so the few unskilled guests, enjoying the company of the skilled, either harmonize as best they can or are captivated by hearing such matters.

If, however, the majority are strangers to the teaching of this discipline, she will command the wise (who are the minority) to conceal her presence, and she will allow a talkativeness more pleasing to the majority to join in, lest a rare nobility be disturbed by a more boisterous crowd. And this is one of the virtues of philosophy: for while an orator is only proven by speaking, a philosopher philosophizes no less by keeping silent as the occasion demands <note>original: "pro tempore"</note> than by speaking.

If there are only a few learned men present, they will move into agreement with the unrefined company, while keeping the notion of truth quiet among themselves, so that any suspicion of discord vanishes. It is no wonder if a learned man does what Pisistratus, the tyrant of Athens, once did. When he failed to gain his sons' agreement by giving them right advice, and was therefore in a state of hostitility with his children, he discovered that this gave his rivals cause for joy. They hoped that from that discord, some revolution might arise in the house of the ruler. So, having called a general assembly of the citizens, he said: he had indeed been angry with his sons for not yielding to the will of the fatherland, but it later seemed more fitting for a father's devotion <note>original: "pietati"</note> that he himself should concede to the opinion of his children. Let the city know, therefore, that the king's offspring are in harmony with their father. By this trick, he removed the hope of those plotting against the ruler’s peace.

Thus in every kind of life, and especially in the joy of a banquet, everything that seems discordant must be reduced to a single harmony of sound, while preserving innocence. Thus Agathon's banquet—because it included Socrates, Phædrus, Pausanias, and Eryximachus—and that dinner which the most learned Callias gave—I mean with Carneades, Antisthenes, and Hermogenes, and others like them—heard not a single word that was not philosophical. 

But the table of Alcinous or Dido, being suited as if for pleasures alone, had in the one case Iopas, and in the other Polyphemus, singing to the lyre. Nor were there lacking dancing men at Alcinous’s house, and at Dido’s there was Bitias, draining the unmixed wine <note>original: "merum"</note> so thoroughly that he drenched himself in its excess. If anyone had mixed conversations drawn from wisdom into the banquet stories among either the Phaeacians or the Carthaginians <note>original: "Poenos"</note>, would he not have both lost the grace appropriate to those gatherings and rightly moved everyone to laughter? 

Therefore, her first observation will be to judge the guests. Then, where she sees a place open to her, she will not speak of the deep secrets of her profundity over the wine cups, nor will she raise knotty and anxious questions, but rather useful and easy ones. For just as among those who practice dancing in the midst of banquets, if someone—in order to exercise himself more—challenges his companions to a race or a boxing match, he will be sent away as someone unfit for the cheer of the company; so at the table, when it is permitted, one must philosophize with appropriate subjects, so that the mixing bowl of liquid born for joy may be treated with an infusion not only of the Nymphs <note>representing water</note> but also of the Muses <note>representing the arts and wisdom</note>.

->tempes<- <note>Catchword for "temperamento" (with a temperament/blending) on the next page</note>

<summary>Eustachius discusses the decorum of philosophy at dinner parties, arguing that wisdom should only be shared when the company is receptive, otherwise, a philosopher should remain silent to maintain social harmony.</summary>
<keywords>Macrobius, Saturnalia, Eustachius, banquet etiquette, Pisistratus, silence, social harmony, Agathon's Symposium, Dido, Alcinous</keywords>

--- Page 71 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Macrobius’s "Saturnalia," Book VII. The character Eustachius is explaining how philosophy can be integrated into social gatherings by adjusting its tone to match the company, much like the "drug" Helen used in the Odyssey to soothe guests.</meta>

balance. For (as one must admit) in any gathering, one must either keep silent or speak. Let us ask whether silence or timely speech is better suited to a dinner party. For if, as with the Areopagites <note>The members of the high court of Athens, known for their gravity and silence</note> in Athens who judge in silence, it were necessary to always be silent among the dishes, there would be no further question as to whether one should philosophize between courses or not. But if banquets are not meant to be mute, why is it that where base talk is permitted, honorable speech is forbidden? Especially since words gladden a feast no less than the sweetness of wine. For if you search more deeply into the hidden wisdom of Homer, that soothing charm <note>original: "delinimentum"; in the Odyssey, this is the "nepenthe," a drug that banishes sorrow</note> which Helen mixed with the wine was not an herb, nor a juice from India, but the opportunity for storytelling, which turned the guest from his forgotten sorrow toward joy. For she told of the noble deeds of Ulysses while his son was present.

> I could not tell or name all the deeds
> of the stout-hearted Odysseus.
> But what a thing this was that the strong man did and endured
> in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans were suffering.

Therefore, by speaking of his father’s glory and his individual brave deeds, she made the son’s heart more cheerful, and in this way, she was believed to have mixed a remedy against sorrow with the wine. One might ask: "What does this have to do with philosophy?" On the contrary, nothing is so closely related to wisdom as adapting one’s speech to the place and the time, taking into account the character of those present. For some are stirred by recounted examples of virtue, others by acts of kindness, and some by modesty—so that even those who were acting otherwise might be led to self-improvement by hearing such things often. In this way, if the flow of conversation at a banquet requires it, philosophy will strike those entangled in vices without them even feeling it—just as Father Liber <note>another name for Bacchus or Dionysus, the god of wine</note> strikes with his thyrsus <note>a staff tipped with a pine cone and wrapped in ivy, used by followers of Dionysus</note> through the slanting cover of the surrounding ivy, with the point hidden. This is because philosophy will not act like a censor at a feast by openly punishing vices. Otherwise, those guilty of these faults will resist, and the resulting uproar at the banquet would be such that the guests would seem to have been invited under an order like this:

> For what remains, men, take care of your bodies
> gladly after your success, and look forward to the fight, prepared.

Or as Homer said more briefly and clearly:

> Now go to your meal, so that we may join the battle.

Therefore, if the opportunity for a necessary rebuke arises, it will be delivered by the philosopher in such a way that it is both veiled and effective. Is it any wonder if the wise man strikes, as I said, without them feeling it, when he sometimes rebukes in such a way that the person being corrected is gladdened? Through his stories and his questions, he will show the power of philosophy, which speaks nothing foolishly. Let no honorable act, place, or gathering exclude her; she adapts herself so that she appears necessary everywhere, as if it were a sin for her to be absent.

<summary>In this excerpt from Macrobius's Saturnalia, Eustachius argues that philosophy is a vital part of a banquet, acting as a "medicine" for the soul that provides subtle moral guidance through storytelling and timely conversation.</summary>

## FROM THE FIRST BOOK OF THE *DEIPNOSOPHISTS* OF ATHENAEUS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a scene with several figures in classical robes, possibly scholars or diners at a table.</image-desc>ATHENAEUS, the father of this book, addresses his discourse to Timocrates. The title of the work is *The Deipnosophists* <note>original: "Deipnosophistēs"; literally 'The Dinner-Table Philosophers' or 'The Banquet of the Learned'</note>. The setting of the dialogue is the home of Larensis, a Roman man of illustrious fortune, who was second to none in his vast experience of every branch of learning <note>Larensis is the Roman official Publius Livius Larensis, who hosted the fictionalized intellectual gathering</note>. At his own expense, he hosted these guests as diners. There was not a single beautiful thing of which he did not make mention. Indeed, the book includes fish—their uses and the explanations of their names—various kinds of vegetables, and all sorts of animals. It mentions historians, poets, and generally wise men; it describes musical instruments, countless types of jokes, various drinking cups, and the wealth of kings. It even relates the sizes of ships and so many other things that I could not easily recall them all, or the day would fail me if I tried to go through them species by species. The arrangement of the discourse mimics the luxury of the banquet itself, and the structure of the book corresponds to the preparation of the meal. Athenaeus, this wonderful steward of the word, introduces a conversation as vast as the sea, and surpassing even himself—just like champion orators—the warmth of his style gradually increases as he moves toward the subsequent parts of the book. Those who supposedly stayed for the dinner were "Dinner-Table Philosophers." Among them was Masurius, an interpreter of laws and a man who had pursued every branch of education, not merely as a side interest <note>original: "enkyklion"; referring to 'encyclopedic' or 'well-rounded' education</note>. In every subject he displayed, he seemed to have practiced that alone; such was the polymathy in which he was raised from childhood. He was a poet of iambics, second to none—as he says—of the poets after Archilochus. Also present were Plutarch, Leonides of Elis, Aemilianus the Maurusian, and Zoilus, the most graceful of the grammarians. Among the philosophers present were Pontianus and Democritus of Nicomedia, who surpassed everyone in their wide learning. There was also Philadelphus of Ptolemais, a man not only raised in philosophical theory but also tested in the rest of his life's conduct. One of the Cynics <note>Cynics were a school of philosophers known for their asceticism and biting social critiques; the name derives from 'Kyon' or dog</note> was there, whom he calls Cynulcus <note>Dog-leader</note>. He was not just followed by two "idle dogs," as is said of Telemachus when he went to the assembly <margin>Odyssey, Book 2</margin>, but by many more than those of Actaeon <note>In myth, Actaeon was a hunter torn apart by his own massive pack of hounds</note>. There was also a gathering of orators who were in no way inferior to the Cynics. Among them, and attacking anyone who spoke, was Ulpian of Tyre. Because of his constant inquiries, which he made at every hour in the streets, walkways, bookstores, and baths, he earned the nickname "Keitoukeitos" <note>This is a pun on the Greek phrases "Keitai" (is it found?) and "Ouchi keitai" (it is not found). Ulpian earned this name by constantly asking if a word was attested in classical literature before he would use it or eat.</note>. He had a rule never to take a bite of anything until he had asked whether the term "is found" or "is not found." For example, if "hour" is found as a division of the day, or if it is not found as a term for edible food; or if "wild boar" is found as a compound word for a pig. Among the physicians present were Daphnus of Ephesus, who was devoted to his art and practiced it according to the principles of Academic discourse, and Galen of Pergamum, who published so many works on philosophy and medicine that he surpassed all who came before him, being inferior in memory to none of the ancients. There was also Rufinus of Nicaea. A musician was present, Alcides of Alexandria. One might say this catalog sounds more like a military roll-call than a guest list for a symposium. Athenaeus fashioned the dialogue as a drama in the Platonic style. Thus, he begins:
