## THE SCHOLARLY HOST AND HIS LIBRARY

...acting not by chance, but as far as possible with a kind of critical and Socratic knowledge, so that everyone wondered at the precision of his inquiries. It is said that he was even appointed over sacred matters and sacrifices by the most excellent King Marcus <note>This is the Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius (reigned 161–180 AD), known for his Stoic philosophy</note>, and that he did not neglect the traditions of his ancestors while also mastering the learning of the Greeks. He calls him a kind of "Light-bringer," as he produced both languages <note>Latin and Greek</note> with equal skill. He also says that he was an expert in the established sacred rites—both those of Romulus, who gave the city its name, and of Numa Pompilius—and was a master of civil laws. All these things he discovered solely from the study of ancient decrees and doctrines, and furthermore from collections of laws, some of which are no longer practiced, but which he came to know through study; as the comic poet Eupolis says, "they were already silenced by the lack of refinement among the many."

<margin>Ancient Libraries.</margin>
In particular, he says that Larensis possessed such a collection of ancient Greek books that he surpassed all those who have been admired for their collections: Polycrates of Samos, Peisistratus the tyrant of Athens, Euclides (also an Athenian), and Nicocrates of Cyprus. He even surpassed the kings of Pergamum, Euripides the poet, Aristotle the philosopher, and Neleus, who preserved their books. From Neleus, he says, our own King Ptolemy—called Philadelphus—purchased all of them, and along with those from Athens and Rhodes, he transported them to beautiful Alexandria. Therefore, someone might say of that city what Antiphanes said: "where he was always present with the Muses and learning." There, the work of wisdom is examined. He makes the place shine with music, such as we play when we gather often around a friendly table to celebrate, and like the "Thesean red-paint-maker" <note>This is an obscure reference to a joke or a specific trade associated with Athens</note>. 

And when inviting guests to feasts, he declares Rome to be the "homeland of all." For who would long for home when living as a guest there, since he keeps his house open to his friends? For according to the comic poet Apollodorus, "When someone enters a friend's house, one can see the friend’s goodwill immediately upon entering the doors: first, the porter is cheerful; 

<margin>The style of Demosthenes.</margin>
the dog wags its tail and comes forward; someone meets you and immediately sets out a chair; and no one says 'Wait' or 'He is busy.'" One might say to those who do not act this way, "Why are you so stingy? The wine-pourers have long been ready; prepare a rich feast for the elders." 

Therefore, in his magnanimity, he was like Alexander the Great. And Conon, after defeating the Lacedaemonians in the sea-battle at Cnidus and rebuilding the walls of the Piraeus, sacrificed a true hecatomb <note>A sacrifice of 100 oxen</note>—and not just in name—and feasted all the Athenians. Alcibiades also, having won the chariot race at Olympia—taking first, second, and fourth place, for which victories Euripides wrote an ode—sacrificed to Olympian Zeus and feasted the entire assembly. Leophron did the same at the Olympics, 

<margin>The Ox of Empedocles.</margin>
when Simonides of Ceos wrote his victory ode. Empedocles of Akragas, after winning at Olympia with his horses, being a Pythagorean and abstaining from living things, fashioned an ox out of myrrh, frankincense, and the most expensive spices, and distributed it to those who attended the assembly. Ion of Chios, after winning a tragedy contest at Athens, gave every Athenian a jar of Chian wine. For as the saying goes, "Each man should pray to the gods that he might abound in wealth, rather than building a stone wall around his friends, so that he may sow the fruit of the sweetest grace from the gods." For both doing and eating have their pleasures, but as Antiphanes says, "hunger is not present at brilliant dinners." 

Furthermore, Tellias of Akragas, being a lover of guests and keeping watch at his gates, once hosted five hundred horsemen from Gela who arrived in winter; he gave each of them a tunic and a cloak. 

<margin>Unattributed verses.</margin>
The sophist Clearchus says that Charmus of Syracuse adapted little verses from proverbs for each of the dishes served at dinner. 

<margin>Iliad 1.</margin>
For the fish, he said: "I have come leaving the Aegean's salty depth" <note>A parody of a line from Euripides</note>. For the herald-fish <note>A type of shellfish</note>: "Hail, heralds, messengers of Zeus." For the sausages: "twisted." For the fire: "healthy fire." For the well-wrapped squid: "Wise, wise indeed." For the seasonal fish served with others: "He did not depart after preparing a crowd." For the eel: "not veiling her curly locks." He says that because many people enjoy feasts, they bring "contributions" <note>original: "symbolas"</note> consisting of letters from the menus. He also says that Charmus, by having something ready for every dish served, seemed to the Messenians to be highly educated; just as Calliphanes (nicknamed "The Apprentice") wrote down the beginnings of many poems and memorized up to three or four lines to create the appearance of great learning. Many others also had on the tips of their tongues the praises of Sicilian moray eels, the floating eels, the hereditary tunny of Pachynus, the swordfish of Mulo, and the mullets of Symaethus. Also the giant clams, the sprats from Lipara, the Mantinean turnip, and the beetroots from Thebes. And the beets from the people of Ascra. Cleanthes of Tarentum, as Clearchus says, said everything in meter during drinking parties. And Pamphilus the Sicilian also said things like: "Pour this for me and the Persian slipper; let someone give a chamber pot, or let someone give a cake." Aristophanes says, "They do not live a stable life, but carry baskets full of decrees."

Lynceus and Callimachus attribute it to **luxury**, while Clearchus calls it **scarcity of speech**, and others **culinary art**. The poem is an epic, the beginning of which says: "We make this demonstration of history for all of Greece." He says that all should dine at a single **luxurious table**, and that the total number of guests should be three or four, or at least no more than five. For any more would already be a "mob of mercenary soldiers plundering life." He is unaware that those in **Plato's** <note>The philosopher Plato, in his famous dialogue the *Symposium*</note> communal meal were as many as twenty. These men do not look toward the city in their dinners. And Antiphanes says they are cleverly made "uninvited guests" for these occasions. He adds that those who eat from common funds nourish the people, and they say they always behave like the mice at the Olympic games, "cutting down oxen uninvited in every place." The Syracusan poet says: "Some things happen in summer, others in winter." It is not possible to prepare everything at once, though it is said to be easy.

<margin>Records of Banquets.</margin>
That others have also made records of banquets, including **Timachidas of Rhodes** in verse, across eleven books or even more. Also **Numenius of Heraclea**, the student of Dieuchas the physician; **Mestreus of Potanae** the parasite <note>In antiquity, a "parasite" was a professional dinner-guest who provided entertainment or flattery in exchange for a meal</note>; and **Hegemon of Thasos**, nicknamed "Lentil-soup," whom some imagine to be a character in Old Comedy.

<margin>Delicacies.</margin>
Furthermore, **Plato the Comic** <note>A poet of Old Comedy, not the philosopher</note> mentions the *Dinner of Philoxenus of Leucas*, saying: "And I here in this solitude want to go through this book by myself." And he asks: "I beg you, what is it?" "A certain new art of cooking by Philoxenus." "Show me what it is." "Listen then: 'I shall begin from the **bulb** <note>original: *bolbos*; likely the tassel hyacinth bulb, a common ancient appetizer</note> and end at the **tuna**.'" "At the tuna? Then that is the last thing." "It is best to be stationed in this rank. Taming as many bulbs as possible with a sauce, devour them; for it straightens the body. These things are so, but I go again to the children of the sea." Then after a bit: "Nor is a casserole a bad thing, but I think the frying pan is better." And after a little: "Do not cut the shimmering sea-perch or the jagged shark, lest a divine nemesis breathe down upon you. But roast it whole and serve it, for it is much better. You shall again take the coils of the polyp <note>original: *poulipodos*; likely an octopus or squid</note> in season, and if it were roasted or larger, it would be much stronger. If they are roasted, I tell you to weep. The beet does not wish to be without its head-piece, for it belongs to Artemis of Garespous, and it hates allies. The scorpion <note>A type of venomous fish</note> again will stop you, coming up under your backside." From this Philoxenus, certain **Philoxenean cakes** were also named.

<margin>Philoxenus or certain sons of Pythinus.</margin>
Concerning him, **Chrysippus** <note>The Stoic philosopher</note> says: "I knew a certain glutton who had fallen so far into not caring for those near him at the table, that he openly practiced in the baths, accustoming his hand to the heat by dipping it into hot water, and gargling his mouth with hot water, so that he would be hard to move by hot things." For they said that he even bribed the cooks to serve the dishes at their hottest, so that he alone might consume them while the others were unable to follow. They record the same things about **Philoxenus**, and **Archytas**, and many others, of whom someone in the works of **Crobylus the Comic** says: "I drink these hot things to excess; I have fingers like wood, and I most pleasantly steam my throat with pieces of meat—a furnace, not a man." **Clearchus** says that Philoxenus would go around houses before bathing, with boys following him carrying oil, wine, vinegar, and other seasonings. Then, entering another's house, he would season what was lacking for the others, adding whatever was needed. Only then would he return and feast. Having sailed to Ephesus and finding the fish market empty, he asked the reason. Learning that everything had been bought for a wedding, he bathed and went uninvited to the groom's house. After dinner, he sang a wedding hymn beginning, "O most brilliant of the wedding gods," and charmed everyone. He was a **dithyrambic poet** <note>A composer of choral hymns, often wild and ecstatic in nature</note>. The groom said, "Philoxenus, will you dine here tomorrow too?" And Philoxenus replied, "If the fishmonger doesn't sell any fish." **Theophilus** says, "not like Philoxenus the son of Eryxithius." For he, as it seems, blaming nature for his enjoyment, once prayed to have the neck of a **crane**, but much more generally to become a cow or a camel or an elephant in terms of digestion. For in this way, the desires and pleasures would be much greater and more intense. For they take their pleasures according to their powers. **Clearchus** says that **Melanthius** prayed for this, saying: "Melanthius seems to deliberate better than Tithonus. For Tithonus, desiring immortality, hangs in a chamber deprived of all sweet things by old age. But Melanthius, being a lover of pleasures, prayed to have the neck of a long-necked bird, so that he might linger as long as possible over the sweet things." The same author says that **Githyllus**, called "The Taster," not only wore leather finger-guards but also encased his tongue in a membrane for his enjoyments, and finally cleaned it by rubbing it with fish-skin. He alone of the pleasure-seekers is said to eat the delicacies using **finger-stalls**, so that the wretch might deliver the food to his tongue as hot as possible. Others say that Philoxenus himself was the fish-lover. **Aristotle** simply calls him "dinner-lover." He writes somewhere: "They spend the whole day among the crowds at the spectacles. And to those sailing from the **Phasis** <note>The Rioni River in modern Georgia, a distant boundary of the Greek world</note> or the **Borysthenes** <note>The Dnieper River in modern Ukraine</note>, they have read nothing, except perhaps the *Dinner of Philoxenus*, and even that not in its entirety." **Phanias** says that Philoxenus the Cytherian poet, being passionately devoted to delicacies, once at a dinner...

<meta>This page transitions from the general anecdotes of gourmands to a specific philosophical and literary analysis of the Homeric diet. # BOOK 1.

<margin>The diet of the heroes according to Homer</margin>
God, the provider of all good things, wishing to implant virtue again from the beginning, and so that men might thereafter spend their leisure and zeal on noble deeds, and be beneficent and communal toward one another, established for all a simple and self-sufficient life. He considered that desires and pleasures become most powerful regarding food and drink. If they had remained in a state of simple good order, they would not have become less self-controlled than in other ways of life. He simply assigned the same diet to all—alike to kings, private citizens, the young, and the old—serving them all roasted meats. These were mostly beef, both at festivals and weddings, and at other gatherings. Though Homer mentions honey-cakes for the kings as a special honor, he primarily serves those things which would nourish the body and the soul. After the duel, he honors Agamemnon with the "chines of oxen" <note>original: "νώτοισι βοῶν"; this refers to the choice cut of the back, a mark of high honor</note>, and to Nestor—not because of his old age— <margin>Iliad 7</margin>
and to Phoenix he gives roasted meat, and to Alcinous, who lived a delicate life, he sets aside such things to turn us away from disordered desires. And Menelaus, when celebrating his children's weddings, served Telemachus the chine of an ox, <margin>Odyssey 4</margin>
for they served him roasted meats as his prize of honor. You will also find Nestor sacrificing oxen by the sea, as did his <margin>Odyssey 3</margin>
dearest and most intimate children, though he was a king and had many subjects. For this sacrifice is the most holy and pleasing to the gods, being performed by one's own kin and most pious men. He does not even depict the Suitors—though they were insolent and devoted to pleasures—as eating fish, or birds, or honey-cakes. For he removed from every tribe the "magical tricks of the kitchen" <note>A reference to complex, overly-seasoned culinary arts</note> and those "appetite-stirring foods" as Menander calls them, and those dishes that Chrysippus says are "wrapped in many coverings" <note>likely referring to complex pastries or stuffed meats</note>, or those whose preparation is quite laborious. Priam also, at one point in the poet's work, even reproaches his sons for consuming things not permitted by custom, calling them <margin>Iliad 24</margin>
"robbers of lambs and kids from the public stock." Philochorus records that it was even forbidden at Athens to kill an un-shorn lamb, because once these animals had become scarce. Though Homer refers to "small fish," and makes the Phaeacians most fond of luxury, and though in Ithaca there are many harbors and many nearby islands in which there is an abundance of fish and wild birds—and even when counting sea-fish among the signs of prosperity—nonetheless, he never depicts the heroes as eating them. And though some provide fruit and a great feast, and he mentions these most pleasantly, preparing them to be "immortal" for all time—saying "pear upon pear" <note>A reference to the eternal garden of Alcinous in Odyssey Book 7</note> and so forth—yet he never depicts them wearing wreaths, or being perfumed with myrrh, or burning incense. Instead, by freeing men from all these things, he restores kings especially to a state of freedom and self-sufficiency. To the gods he simply assigned a diet of nectar and ambrosia. He makes men honor the gods through their own diet, removing frankincense, myrrh, and wreaths, and the great luxury associated with them. One should not think they enjoyed this simple diet without pleasure, but rather, like the best of physicians, it removes surfeits. "But when they had put away the desire for drink and food," <margin>Odyssey 1</margin>
and had satisfied their desire, some would turn to athletic practice, "taking their pleasure with the discus and the javelin," practicing every serious skill through play. Others would turn to the lyre, recounting heroic deeds in melody and rhythm. Thus it is a wonderful thing that those nourished in this way kept their bodies and souls free from inflammation. Even when considering "good order" <term>eutaxia</term> <note>A Greek term for disciplined behavior and social harmony</note> as healthy, beneficial, and common, he has the most wise Nestor offer wine to Machaon the physician, who was wounded <margin>Iliad 11 and 9</margin>

Yet he does not sit and drink by nature, but scrapes goat's milk cheese into it, and provides an onion as a relish for the drink, so that he might drink more. Elsewhere he says that wine "dissolves strength and unnerves the limbs." <margin>Iliad 6</margin>

the wine, but he, coming from battle, pushes it away. He does not think it right to drink after making a libation while covered in blood, as that would be impious. Homer knows both the benefit and the advantage of wine. To those whom it "burns," he says it is harmful. <margin>Odyssey 21</margin>
And he certainly knew different ways of mixing it. Thus Achilles tells them to "mix it stronger," <margin>Iliad 9</margin>

# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS

[The poet] made him [Eurytion] perish through this [drunkenness], as he did Eurytion the Centaur; and at Circe’s palace, he depicts the lions and wolves as those who had followed their pleasures. But he saves Odysseus, who was educated by Hermes—that is, by Reason <note>original: "λόγῳ"; here the author interprets Hermes as a personification of 'Logos' or rational discourse</note>. Therefore, Odysseus remains unaffected. But Circe, hoping that he too was soft and luxurious, tries to cast him down. And Antinous, even while saying to <margin>Odyssey 21</margin> Odysseus, "Wine wounds you, honey-sweet," did not himself refrain from the drink. Therefore, being struck, he perished while still <margin>Odyssey 22</margin> holding the cup. He also depicts the Greeks getting drunk at the [Cicones], which is why <margin>Odyssey 9</margin> they perish. He also records that the most formidable Aeneas among the Trojans was nearly killed <margin>Iliad 20</margin> because of the frankness and threats brought on by drunkenness—which he promised the Trojans while drinking wine—where he endured the rush of Achilles and nearly perished. And Agamemnon, saying of himself: "But since I was blinded, yielding to my <margin>Iliad 19</margin> wretched mind, either drunk with wine, or the gods themselves harmed me." He places <margin>Iliad 9</margin> drunkenness on the same scale as madness. This is how Dioscurides, the student of Socrates, interpreted these verses. And <margin>Iliad 1</margin> Achilles, reproaching Agamemnon, says: "You wine-heavy man, with the eyes of a dog." This is the "Thessalian trick" <note>original: "θεσσαλὸν σόφισμα"; a proverbial expression for a clever or deceptive maneuver</note>, which originated in Thessaly. He plays perhaps—but how could a wretched man like me be playing?

->**The food of the heroes in Homer, and of later generations.**<-

<margin>The food of the heroes in Homer, and of later generations.</margin>
The ancients used early meals; in Homer, first is the so-called <term>akratisma: a light early meal consisting of bread dipped in unmixed wine</term>, which he calls <term>ariston: in Homeric times, this refers to an early morning meal, though it later came to mean lunch</term>, and which he mentions once in the *Odyssey*: "Odysseus and the divine swineherd, having kindled a fire, were preparing their *ariston*." <margin>Odyssey 16</margin> And he mentions it once in the *Iliad*: "They quickly prepared themselves and made ready their *ariston*." He refers to the morning morsel, which we call *akratisma*, because they soak and consume bread in unmixed wine (*akratos*). As Antiphanes says: "An *ariston* while the cook is busy." Then he adds: "How do you feel about having an *akratisma* with me?" and Cantharus: "Will we not then have an *akratisma*?" <gloss>(the very smile)</gloss>. Nor do we dine in private. Someone says: "To have a little *akratisma*, then out again, biting a piece of bread twice or thrice." But Philemon says that the ancients used these meals: *akratisma*, *ariston*, *hesperisma* (afternoon snack), and *deipnon* (dinner). They called the *akratisma* "dianekismos," and the *ariston* "dorpismos," and the dinner "epidorpis." The order of names is also found in Aeschylus, where Palamedes is made to say: "I appointed commanders of ranks, of armies, and of hundreds, and I defined the knowledge of food: to take *arista*, *deipna*, and *dorpa* third." Homer perhaps mentions a <margin>Odyssey 17</margin> fourth meal: "But you come after the *deielie*" <note>original: "δειελίησας"</note>, which some call <term>deilinon: an afternoon meal between lunch and dinner</term>. This is between what we call *ariston* and *deipnon*. The *ariston* is taken at dawn; the *deipnon* is at midday (what we now call *ariston*); and the <term>dorpon: the evening meal or supper</term> is the evening meal. Perhaps *ariston* is also a synonym for *deipnon*. For he says of any morning meal: "And then they took their *deipnon*, and they themselves put on their armor." For immediately after sunrise, having made their *deipnon*, they went forth to battle. They feast in Homer sitting down. Some think that a table was placed next to each of the feasters individually. At least, they say when Telemachus arrived <margin>Odyssey 1</margin> and the tables were already set, "a table was placed for the guest." It is not clearly shown whether it was a permanent fixture. It is passed over in silence whether Athena dined from Telemachus's table. For throughout the whole gathering, tables stood nearby full of food, as is still the custom among many of the barbarians.

->**Tables set nearby.**<-

<margin>Tables set nearby.</margin>
And food of all kinds of good things for Anacreon. After the departure, the handmaids "carried away the bread and the table and the cup." The banquet at Menelaus's house is unique. For he makes them talk after waking up, then after washing, he makes them feast again, and then mentions <margin>Odyssey 4</margin> "suppers (*dorpa*) again" along with the lamentation. The fact that the tables were not removed seems apparent in the *Iliad*: "Eating and drinking, and the table still stood nearby." One should read it thus: "eating and drinking still, and the table was fixed," or blame the timing of the events. For how was it appropriate for Achilles, while mourning, to have a table set nearby, just as for those feasting <margin>Iliad 24</margin> throughout the whole gathering? Loaves of bread were served in baskets, and the meals were meat only and roasted. Homer did not have them making broth when sacrificing oxen, nor boiled meat. Nor brain; he roasted even the entrails. So very anciently, Antiphanes says, "portions of meat were made." He calls the <margin>A feast or an 'equal portion' in Homer.</margin> feasts *themistas* <note>original: "θέμιστας"; meaning 'customs' or 'decrees', here used to imply an orderly meal</note> because of their equality. For they called dinners <term>daitas: feasts</term>, from <term>daiesthai: to divide or distribute</term>, because not only was the meat distributed, but also the wine: "Because we are satisfied with the equal feast (*dais*)." "Well, hail Achilles, we do not lack an equal feast." From these things, since they are very life-giving, an "equal feast" is said to be a good one. Since food is good for man at every hour, he says "equal" <note>original: "ἰσία"</note> as an intensifier. For since the first men, for whom food was abundant and just appearing, rushed upon it all together and seized it by force and took it from those who had it, and murders occurred with disorder, which might likely be called "recklessness" <note>original: "ἀτασθαλία"</note>, because in the festivities <note>original: "θαλίαι"</note> men first committed sins against one another. But as plenty from Demeter <note>Goddess of the harvest</note> advanced for them, they distributed an equal portion to each, and so the suppers (*dorpa*) came into order for men. Therefore, the bread is an "artos," a concept of a pastry divided into equal parts, and for those drinking together, an ointment. For where these things were shared equally, joy occurred. Thus food is called a *dais* from *daiesthai*, which is to be divided equally, and he who roasts the meat is a <term>daitros: a carver or distributor of meat</term>, since he gave an equal portion to each. And the poet uses the word *dais* only for men, but no longer for wild beasts. Being ignorant of this word's...

-># BOOK 1<-

<margin>Iliad 1</margin>Zoilus <note>A famous ancient critic known as "Homer’s Scourge" for his harsh critiques.</note> behaves destructively in his edition regarding the line: "And he made them spoils for dogs and a feast for birds." He claims that "all vultures and other birds are wise or beautiful," and only man rejoices in his own food through a chosen violence. For this reason alone, food is called a "feast" <note>original: "dais"</note>, from the "portion" <note>original: "moira"</note> given to each. Those who feasted in Homer's poems did not carry away leftovers to their homes, but having been satisfied, they left them where the feast was held. If one person took a portion, it was so that if a stranger arrived, they would have something to give him. Homer represents people using fish <margin>Homer’s fishermen</margin> even then—but not as a primary meal. For instance, in Thrinacia, the companions of Odysseus go hunting for "fish and birds, and whatever came to their hands with curved hooks." For these hooks were not forged in Thrinacia, but were carried along on the voyage, clearly showing that they had the care and skill for catching fish. He also likens the companions of Odysseus being snatched by Scylla to fish caught with a long rod and cast out of the water. In this, he is more precise in the art of fishing than those who published poems and treatises having practiced such things—I mean Cecilius the Argive, Numenius of Heraclea, Pancrates the Ar-<margin>fishing treatises</margin>cadian, Poseidonius of Corinth, and Oppian the Cilician, who lived a little before our <margin>Oppian</margin> time. For we have encountered so many epic poets who wrote on fishing. He also lists Seleucus of Tarsus and Leonidas of Byzantium. Yet, he does not mention such food at banquets, as it was not considered appropriate for the dignity of heroes, just as he does not mention the meat of young animals. They used not only fish, but <margin>Theory of the Homeric banquet</margin> also shellfish. Even though eating these is very beneficial and pleasant, they lie in the depths and the deep. They do not use any other art for these things, unless a man is "very light, who dives into the deep." He says such a man could satisfy many by searching for these. At the Homeric banquet, a basket and a table are set before every guest, and a cup is ready whenever the heart <margin>Iliad 10</margin> commands. The mixing bowls are "crowned with drink," meaning the bowls are filled to the brim so that they appear to be crowned by the liquid. They did this for the sake of a good omen, and "the young men distributed the wine to all, having begun with the cups." The word "all" refers not to the cups, but to the people. Alcinous says to the herald, "pour wine for all throughout the hall." And he follows this with, "He distributed to all, having begun with the cups." There are also "honorary meals" for the best men. Tydides <note>Diomedes</note> is honored with meats and more frequent cups, and Ajax is honored with "continuous chines" <note>The long cut of meat along the backbone, a prize portion.</note>. And for the kings, "they set before them the chine of an ox, which they had placed for him," as Menelaus noticed. He also honors Agamemnon with more frequent cups. He honors Sarpedon among the Lycians <margin>Iliad 1</margin> with the same things, and with the best seats and meats. There was also a kind of greeting through toasts. For the gods "greeted one another with golden cups." They did this by drinking to one another with their right hands, and someone "welcomed Achilles and pledged him with his right hand," which means to drink to him, giving the cup with the right hand. They also gave <margin>Iliad 9</margin> portions of food from their own shares to whomever they wished, as Odysseus, "having cut off a portion of the chine, set it before Demodocus." They also featured cithara players and dancers at their banquets, like the suitors did. At Menelaus's house, <margin>Homer’s Bard</margin> "a divine bard sang." At the start of the song among the well-robed women, they showed "the dance," meaning the play. The race of bards was a sober one, holding the disposition of philosophers. Agamemnon, for example, <margin>Odyssey 3</margin> left the bard as a guardian for Clytemnestra; by advising her and recounting the virtues of women, he instilled a certain ambition for excellence. Since bards lived a quiet life, they distracted the mind from wicked thoughts. Therefore, Aegisthus did not seduce the woman until he had killed the bard on a desert island. Such is also the bard among the suitors, who served by necessity, and who loathed those who were plotting against Penelope. In general, he says all bards are held in honor by men: "Therefore the Muse taught them songs and loved the race of bards." When Demodocus sings for the Phaeacians about the union of Ares and Aphrodite, it is not because he approves of such passion, but to turn them away from lawless desires, knowing they were raised in a luxurious life, and thus offering them songs most similar to their ways to provide rest. And Phemius, singing to the suitors according to their own will, sang of the "Return of the <margin>Odyssey 12</margin> Achaeans." Even the Sirens, singing to Odysseus the things that would most delight him and which suited his ambition and great learning, said: "For we know all things that happen upon the fruitful earth." There are also dances in Homer—some of tumblers, and others with a ball. The invention of the ball is attributed to Nausicaa by Agallis, the female grammarian of Corcyra, as a favor to her fellow citizen. But Dicaearchus attributes it to the Sicyonians, and Hippalus to the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, who were the first to use both the ball and the gymnasia. Homer introduces only Nausicaa among the heroines as playing with a ball. Famous for ball-playing was Demoteles, the brother of the philosopher Theognis of Chios, and a certain Chaerephanes. The latter once followed a lewd young man who was talking, but he prevented the youth from acting. When it was said, "If you stop following Chaerephanes, everything will be yours from us," the youth replied, "Would I even speak to you?" When asked why he followed him, he said, "I enjoy watching him, but I do not approve of his character." The game played with a ball called "snatching" <note>original: "harpaston"</note> used to be called "phaininda," which I enjoy most of all. There is much tension and fatigue in the contest of ball-playing.

-># FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS<-

This practice of ball-playing is a vigorous exercise for us. The comic poet Antiphanes describes the game of **Phaininda** <note>A fast-paced ball game involving deceptive throws; the name likely comes from 'phenakizein', meaning 'to deceive'.</note> in this way: "Taking the ball, he delighted in giving it to one, while dodging another; he knocked it away from one, while setting another player up with loud cries." It was called *phaininda* from the "sending away" <note>original: "aphesis"</note> of those playing ball. Its inventor, as Juba of Mauretania <note>A scholar-king of the 1st century BCE known for his vast writings on history and art.</note> says, was Phainestios the physical trainer. Antiphanes also says: "Playing *phaininda* was once called *phenakis*." Ball-players were very concerned with rhythm and grace. Demoxenos tells us: "A certain youth was playing ball, perhaps seventeen years old, from the island of Cos. The island seems to produce gods <note>A reference to Cos being the birthplace of many famous figures, including the physician Hippocrates.</note>, for whoever he looked upon among the spectators was transfixed. Whether receiving or passing the ball, we all broke into cheers. What rhythm, what character, and what perfect order there was!" He appeared to reach the very limit of beauty in everything he said or did; I have never heard of or seen such grace before. "I would have suffered some greater harm if I had stayed longer," the speaker says, "but now I think I am healthy again." Ctesibius of Chalcis, the philosopher, played ball rather unpleasantly, and many people associated with him and King Antigonus’s friend because of his skill in ball-games <margin>Ball-games.</margin>. Timocrates the Laconian also wrote a treatise on the art of ball-playing.

The Phaeacians in Homer's poems <margin>Odyssey, Book 8</margin> also danced without a ball. They danced in turns, frequently tossing the ball high <note>original: "tarph' ambolēmenoi"</note>, while others stood by and snapped their fingers <margin>Iliad, Book 13</margin>, as the poet says. The poet also knows of dancing accompanied by song. For instance, while Demodocus sang, young men in their prime danced. For even during the preparation of the meal, some played the lyre <note>original: "kitharizontes"</note> while others joined in with song and dance. The "hyporchematic" <term>hyporcheme: a lively mimetic dance performed to a choral song</term> style of dance is suggested here, which flourished in the time of Xenodemus and Pindar. This kind of dance is an imitation of things interpreted by words. As the noble Xenophon says regarding the festivities and the banquet at the home of Seuthes the Thracian <margin>The Dance in Xenophon.</margin> <margin>Book 6, Chapter 1</margin>: "After the libations were made and they had sung the paean <note>A song of praise or triumph.</note>, the Thracians rose up first and danced in armor to the sound of the flute, leaping high and lightly, and using their daggers. Finally, one struck the other, so that everyone thought he was hit. He fell down quite artfully, and the others cried out. Then the one who 'struck' him stripped the other of his weapons and went out singing the 'Sitalkas' <note>A traditional Thracian song named after one of their kings.</note>. Other Thracians carried the 'dead' man out, though he had suffered nothing."

After this, the Aenianes and Magnesians rose and performed the dance called the **Karpaia** <note>A mimetic dance representing a farmer defending his oxen from a robber.</note> while in armor. The manner of the dance was this: one man puts down his arms and sows and drives a yoke of oxen, turning back frequently as if in fear. A robber approaches. The farmer, seeing him, snatches up his arms and fights in front of his yoke, moving rhythmically to the flute. Finally, the robber binds the farmer and drives off the team. Sometimes, however, the plowman binds the robber. Another man, they say, performed the "Persian dance," clashing his shields together, crouching down, and rising up again—all in rhythm to the flute. The Arcadians, too, rose up in full armor and marched rhythmically to the sound of the flute. They sang the paean and danced.

The heroes also used flutes and pan-pipes <margin>The entire diet and lifestyle of the Homeric banquets.</margin> <margin>Iliad, Book 10</margin>. Agamemnon, for instance, hears the sound of flutes. He also introduces them into the wedding feasts in the description of the Shield of Achilles, though he attributes the flute primarily to the "barbarians" <note>To the Greeks, 'barbarian' simply meant non-Greek speakers.</note>. At the end of dinners, when they were breaking up, they would make libations to Hermes, and only much later to Zeus the Completer. This was because Hermes was thought to be the patron of sleep. They also offered the tongues of the animals to him as they left the feast, as tongues are dedicated to him because of his role in eloquence and interpretation.

Homer also knew of varied foods. He mentions "food of all kinds" and "delicacies" such as those served to kings raised by Zeus. He was aware of the great luxury of houses, such as the brilliant home of Menelaus. Polybius describes the palace of a certain Iberian king, which he says was built in imitation of the Phaeacians' luxury, except that in the middle of the house stood silver and gold mixing bowls <note>original: "krateres"</note> full of barley-wine <note>An early reference to beer.</note>. Homer, describing Calypso’s home, says even Hermes was amazed by it. The life of the Phaeacians was also devoted to pleasure <margin>Odyssey, Book 8</margin>. "Ever is the feast dear to us, and the lyre," and so on. Eratosthenes <margin>Luxury of the Phaeacians.</margin> says these lines were written for a purpose: "For I say there is no goal more graceful than when gladness possesses all the people" <margin>Odyssey, Book 9</margin>, and the guests in the halls listen to the singer. When he says "all the people," he is referring to their wisdom, for it is impossible for the Phaeacians not to be wise, as they are very dear to the gods, as Nausicaa says.

The suitors in Homer's poems <margin>The games of the suitors in Homer.</margin> <margin>Odyssey, Book 1</margin> amused themselves with **pessoi** <note>A game played with tokens or "men" on a board, similar to checkers or backgammon.</note> before the doors. Diodorus of Megalopolis or Theogenes, who mastered the game, describe it. Mention is also made of Leon of Mytilene, who was undefeated at this game, as Phanias says. Apion of Alexandria says he heard from Cteson of Ithaca what the game of the suitors was like. Since the suitors were one hundred and eight in number, they arranged their pieces opposite one another, equal in number to the suitors themselves—fifty-four on each side. Between these two sides, they left a small empty space. In this middle ground, they placed a single piece, which they called "Penelope." This was their target, to see if someone could hit it with another piece. They would cast lots to see who would aim at it first. If someone hit the Penelope-piece and knocked it forward, he would place his own piece in the position of the one he hit and...

# BOOK I.
->A.<-

When she had looked upon the land, or before she went there... and again, everything regarding Penelope, where the contest took place, for from there she was to cast the other. <note>Refers to the contest of the bow in the *Odyssey*, where Penelope challenges the suitors to shoot an arrow through twelve axe-heads.</note> And if it should happen that she did not touch any of the others, he would win, having great hopes that he would marry her. He suggests that Eurymachus had invented this game and was hopeful about the marriage. Yet the suitors had such soft hands due to their luxurious lifestyle <note>original: *tryphe*, meaning luxury, softness, or over-indulgence</note> that they were not even able to string the bow; they were surrounded by extravagance, as were those who served them. In Homer's poetry, the fragrance of perfumes is portrayed as extremely powerful. "Not even when Zeus moves toward his bronze-floored house does the scent fail to reach the earth and heaven alike." <margin>*Iliad* 14</margin> <note>original: "Οὐ δὲ κινυμένοιο Διὸς..." The text cites the fragrant atmosphere of the gods' dwellings.</note> He also knows of magnificent bedding. Arete orders such bedding to be spread for Odysseus, and Nestor boasts to Telemachus of having an abundance of fine rugs. However, some of the other poets <margin>Poets who project their own contemporary customs onto the Trojan era.</margin> projected the luxuries and laziness of their own times back into the era of the Trojan War. <margin>10</margin> Aeschylus, for instance, indecorously introduces the Greeks as being so drunk that they break chamber pots <note>original: *amidas*</note> over one another’s heads. He says: "This is the one who once threw at me a 'laughter-making' missile, that foul-smelling 'sky-pot,' and he did not miss. It broke against my head, shattering like a shipwreck, and it breathed a scent over me that was anything but perfume." And Sophocles says in *The Gathering of the Achaeans*: "But in his anger he threw the foul-smelling 'sky-pot' and did not miss; against my head the vessel was shattered, smelling of no perfume. I was startled by the far-from-pleasant odor." Eupolis, having introduced the name of the chamber pot in a mild way, says as a rebuke: "I hate to practice the Spartan way; I would rather talk fast or even buy... I think many are now being violated." <note>This passage from Eupolis is fragmentary and contains obscure slang regarding Spartan habits and sexual behavior.</note> The person who first invented drinking first, he gave us a great deal of "Laconian-doing" <note>original: *lakopraktian*, likely referring to Spartan-style drinking or coarse behavior</note> when he found it. They had those [vessels] for the chamber pot, and while drinking first among them all, I prayed for something milky, equal, and wise. The heroes in Homer's works, however, dine in an orderly fashion in Agamemnon's tent. Achilles and Odysseus show their rivalry, <margin>20</margin> and Agamemnon rejoices in his mind; their ambitions were useful, for they sought to benefit the cause at Troy through either speech or battle. Even when the suitors are introduced as being drunk, Homer never introduced such disorder as Sophocles and Aeschylus have done; rather, he mentions only a cow’s foot being thrown at Odysseus. <margin>Sitting vs. Reclining at banquets</margin> The heroes at these banquets sit rather than recline. <note>In later Greek history, it became the custom to recline on couches (*klinai*), but in the earlier Homeric age, they sat on chairs or stools.</note> Yet Duris says this changed under King Alexander. On one occasion, when he was feasting four hundred commanders, they sat on silver chairs and couches covered with purple cloths. Hegesander says it was not the custom in Macedonia for anyone to recline at dinner unless they had killed a wild boar without using a net; until then, they dined sitting. Cassander, for example, even though he was thirty-five years old, continued to eat sitting next to his father, being unable to accomplish that feat, despite being brave and a good hunter. Homer, looking to what was fitting, did not show the heroes eating anything other than meat, and that which they prepared themselves. <margin>30</margin> For they were not ashamed to be seen providing for themselves in abundance. They practiced self-service <margin>Self-service</margin> and, as Chrysippus says, they took pride in their dexterity in these matters. Odysseus, for instance, says he is second to none at stacking wood and lighting a fire. In the *Embassy* <note>The scene in *Iliad* Book 9 where an embassy is sent to Achilles.</note>, Patroclus and Achilles prepare everything decorously. And at the wedding of Menelaus, the bridegroom Megapenthes pours the wine. But now we have fallen so far that we recline while feasting. Recently, even baths <margin>Baths</margin> have been introduced, whereas originally they were not even allowed within the city. Antiphanes shows their harmful nature: "He has completely boiled me and worn me away. Anyone who takes me by the skin will find it a warm matter like water." Hermippus says: "By Zeus, a good man should not get drunk, nor take hot baths, as you do." The excess of cooks will also be criticized, as will that of perfumes, to the point that Alexis says someone could be satisfied with "diving into a pool of perfume." <margin>40</margin> Also criticized are the elaborate creation of cakes and the excessive efforts regarding sexual intercourse, such as the use of artificial means to maintain a pale complexion. For it is said that the bed is provocative, leading to an abundance of sexual desire. Theophrastus says <margin>Sexual powers</margin> that there are certain "coupling powers" that allow for up to seventy sexual encounters, after which blood is finally secreted. Phylarchus says that Sandrocottus <note>The Greek name for the Indian Emperor Chandragupta Maurya.</note>, the King of the Indians, sent Seleucus among his gifts certain aphrodisiac powers of such a nature that when placed under the feet of those having intercourse, they would produce an impulse like that of birds in some, while stopping it in others. The corruption of music has now increased, as has that of clothing. Extravagance in footwear has also been honored. <margin>Perfumes<br/>*Iliad* 22</margin> Homer, however, knowing the nature of perfume, did not introduce the heroes as being anointed with it, except for Paris. In those passages, he says he was "shining with beauty," just as Aphrodite cleanses her face with beauty. But he does not even introduce them <margin>Garlands</margin> wearing garlands. Nevertheless, they indicate the concept through metaphor, as with those who wear a crown. For they say, "an island which the vast sea had crowned," <margin>50</note> and "everywhere the crown of war is ablaze." I was mistaken when I said that he makes Odysseus wash his hands before eating. In the *Iliad*, one cannot find them doing this. For the life of Odysseus was one of leisure, and they lived luxuriously because of the peace. Therefore, they took care of their bodies through baths and ointments. This is also why they play with knucklebones in that city.

### FROM ATHENAEUS'S BANQUET OF THE LEARNED
->A.<-

In the [Homeric] state, they both dance and play ball. Herodotus <note>Herodotus, *Histories* 1.94, attributes the invention of games like dice and ball to the Lydians during a famine.</note> did not speak correctly when he said that games were invented in the time of Atys because of a famine; for the heroic times are far older. In the Iliadic state, they almost

<margin>Book I.</margin>
alone shouted "Hear the battle-cry, daughter of the war-god, the prelude to those with skillful hands." <note>A poetic invocation to the battle-cry (*Alala*), personified as the daughter of Ares.</note> Note that the Athenians made Aristonicus of Carystus—Alexander the Great’s ball-player—a citizen because of his skill, and they even erected a statue of him.

<margin>Honoring manual arts.</margin>
For later on, people began to value the "vulgar" arts <note>original: *banausous technas*, referring to manual or mechanical labor, which was usually looked down upon by the upper classes.</note> much more than intellectual pursuits. Thus, the people of Histiaea and Oreus dedicated a bronze statue in the theater to Theodorus the "juggler," <note>original: *psephokleptou*, literally a "pebble-thief," a term for a sleight-of-hand magician.</note> depicted as holding a pebble. In the same way, the Milesians honored Archelaus the cithara-player. In Thebes, while there is no statue of Pindar, there is one of Cleon the singer, which bears the inscription: "This is Pytheas's son, Cleon, the Theban singer, who won more crowns than any mortal by his own strength, and whose fame reaches heaven. Rejoice, Cleon, you who brought glory to your fatherland, Thebes." It is said that when Alexander destroyed Thebes, a man fleeing the enemy hid gold in the hollow of the statue's cloak; when the city was resettled thirty years later, he returned and found the gold still there. Herodotus the writer <note>original: *logopoios*. Not the famous historian, but likely a teller of tales or mimes.</note>—who was, as they say, a "man of the fountain"—and Archelaus the dancer were among the most honored friends of King Antiochus. His father, Antiochus, even made the son of Sostratus the flute-player a member of his bodyguard.

<margin>And flute-players.</margin>
Matreas the buffoon <note>original: *planos*, a wandering performer or charlatan.</note>, an Alexandrian, was admired by both Greeks and Romans. He used to say he was raising a beast that ate itself—and even today people still wonder what Matreas’s "beast" was. He also wrote parodies of Aristotle’s *Problems*, which he read in public, such as: "Why does the sun set, but never dive?" and "Why do descendants drink together, but never 'clink' together?" and "Why can four-drachma coins be changed, but never get angry?" <note>Matreas uses puns: *katallattetai* means both "to be exchanged" (as money) and "to be reconciled" (as an angry person). The "clinking" refers to a specific type of drinking party noise.</note> The Athenians gave Goreanus the puppeteer

<margin>Charlatans. Wonder-workers.</margin>
the use of the stage from which Euripides’s followers used to perform in their divine frenzy. Xenophon the wonder-worker was also admired; he left behind a pupil, Cratisthenes of Phlius, who could make fire appear spontaneously and engineered many other illusions that astonished the minds of men. Such a man was Nymphodorus the wonder-worker, who, having offended the people of Rhegium, was the first to mock them for their lifestyle, as Duris says. Eudicus the jester was famous for mimicking wrestlers and boxers, according to Aristoxenus. Straton of Tarentum was admired for mimicking the dithyrambs. And those around Oenonas from Italy mimicked songs sung to the lyre, even introducing living people into their performances. Nausicaa, the daughter of Naucyes, says himself that he portrayed Odysseus speaking with a foreign accent. Diopithes the Locrian, as Phanodicus relates, came to Thebes wearing a belt full of bladders containing wine and milk; by squeezing them, he made it appear as if these liquids were flowing from his mouth. There were also "philosophical" wonder-workers in the service of Alexander: Scymnus of Tarentum, Philistides of Syracuse, and Heracleitus of Mitylene. There were also "philosophical" buffoons, such as Cephisodorus and Pantaleon. Xenophon mentions the jester Philippides.

Note that he calls Rome the "people of the world." He also says that one would not be far from the mark in calling the city of Rome the "epitome of the inhabited world." Within it, one can see every city settled,

<margin>Rome as the epitome of the world.</margin>
and many of them individually: such as "Golden" Alexandria, "Beautiful" Antioch, or "Exceeding Fair" Nicomedia. Furthermore, it contains the most brilliant of all cities that Zeus makes manifest—I mean Athens. A single day would not suffice to count the cities found within the "Heavenly City" of Rome. Indeed, all are counted as one within this beloved place because of its vast population. For whole nations are settled there together: Cappadocians, Scythians, people of Pontus, and many others. These together form the entire populace of the world. 

He says that the "philosopher-dancer" of our time was called Memphis, because his bodily movements reflected the ancient and royal nature of that city—the city of which Bacchylides says, "Winterless Memphis and the reed-beds of the Nile." This man demonstrates what the philosophy of Pythagoras is, showing us everything in silence more clearly than those who profess to teach the art of speech. The first to introduce the dance of "equals," <note>original: *ison*, likely referring to a balanced or rhythmic style.</note> also called the "tragic" dance, was Bathyllus of Alexandria, whom Seleucus says danced according to strict rules. From there,

<margin>Dances. Pylades.</margin>
Aristonicus and Pylades mention Bathyllus. Pylades, who wrote a treatise on dancing, established the "Italian dance" by combining the comic dance (called the *kordax*), the tragic dance (the *emmeleia*), and the satyric dance (the *sikinnis*). Thus the Satyrs are called *sikinnistai*, named after a barbarian named Sicinnus, though some say he was a Cretan. The Pyladean dance was grand, passionate, and very intense. The Bathyllan style was more cheerful, resembling the *hyporchema* <note>A lively choral song and dance.</note>. Sophocles, in addition to being beautiful in his youth, was trained in dance and music as a boy under Lamprus. Indeed, after the naval battle at Salamis, he danced naked and anointed around the trophy while playing the lyre. Some say he wore a cloak. When he produced his play *Thamyris*, he played the cithara himself, and he played ball with great skill when he staged the *Nausicaa*. Socrates the Wise also loved the dance of Memphis and was often caught dancing, as he says...

# BOOK I.

As Xenophon says, he told his acquaintances that dance was an exercise for every limb of the body. For they used to define dancing as being "moved and stirred up." Anacreon <note>Anacreon (6th c. BCE) was a famous lyric poet known for themes of love and wine.</note> writes: "The fair-winning breezes of Zeus danced lightly." And Ion says: "He set his heart dancing beyond all expectation." 

<margin>Theophrastus teaching gestures.</margin>
Hermippus says that Theophrastus used to arrive at the *Peripatos* <note>The "walkway" at the Lyceum in Athens where Aristotle and his followers, the Peripatetics, taught.</note> at a set hour, looking splendid and well-groomed. Then, sitting down, he would deliver his lecture, holding back from no movement or gesture. Once, while imitating a glutton, he even stuck out his tongue and licked his lips. 

Those of that era also cared deeply about wearing their clothes decently; they would mock those who failed to do so. Plato, in the *Theaetetus*, <note>Plato, *Theaetetus* 175e. Plato contrasts the man who is clever in practical matters but cannot dress himself like a gentleman.</note> speaks of one who is able to serve quickly and sharply in all things, yet does not know how to throw his cloak over his shoulder like a free man, nor how to catch the harmony of words to rightly hymn the blessed life of gods and men. Sappho observes the foot of Andromeda, <note>Sappho (6th c. BCE), the famous poet of Lesbos. Andromeda was one of her rivals or pupils.</note> or what "wild-hearted thing" charms her mind, since she does not know how to pull her rags over her ankles. Amphis, a more affectionate critic, says: "You wretched man, will you not let your fair-flowing robe hang down? Do not hitch it up rustically above the knee!" Hermippus says that someone blamed the cloak of Anaximenes of Chios as being unrefined. 

And Callistratus, the follower of Aristophanes, spoke poorly of Aristarchus in a treatise because he did not dress himself with "good rhythm." <margin>Good rhythm in dressing.</margin> <note>original: *eurythmia*. The Greeks believed that physical grace and dressing well reflected an inner moral and intellectual harmony.</note> Some viewed this as a test of one's education. Therefore Alexis says: "For I believe it is a mark of the unfree to walk without rhythm in the streets when it is possible to do so gracefully. No one should be made to pay us a fee for this, nor should we receive it through others. To those who use it well, it brings a certain sense of dignity; to those who see it, it brings pleasure. For who, claiming to have a mind, would not want to possess such an honor as an ornament for his life?"

Aeschylus not only invented the beauty and dignity of theatrical costume—which the high priests and torch-bearers at the mysteries imitated when they dressed themselves—but he also invented many dance gestures, <margin>dance.</margin> <note>original: *schemata*. In ancient Greek dance, these were specific poses or symbolic gestures that conveyed meaning.</note> providing them to the chorus members themselves. Chamaeleon, at least, says that Aeschylus was the first to choreograph his choruses without employing professional dance-teachers. He personally created the dance figures for the choruses and, in short, took the entire management of the tragedy upon himself. His dramas certainly seem to reflect this. Aristophanes (for among the comic poets is kept the truth about the tragic ones) makes Aeschylus say: "I myself made the dance figures for these choruses." And again: "I saw the Phrygians <note>A lost play by Aeschylus where Priam comes to ransom the body of his son Hector.</note> when they came to Priam to help ransom his dead son; they made many such gestures, moving this way and that." 

Telesis (or Telestes), the dance-teacher, also invented many gestures to clearly demonstrate with his hands what was being spoken. Aristocles says that Telestes, Aeschylus’s dancer, was such an artist that when he danced *The Seven Against Thebes*, he made the events clear through his dancing alone. 

They also say that the ancient poets—Thespis, Pratinas, Cratinus, and Phrynichus—were called "dancers" because they did not only relate their own plays to dance via the chorus, but they also taught those who wished to learn how to dance outside of their own poems. Chamaeleon says that Aeschylus used to write his tragedies while drunk. Sophocles reproached him for this, saying: "Even if you do what is right, you do it without knowing it."

There are also national dances, such as the Laconian, the Troezenian, the Epizephyrian, the Cretan, the Ionian, and the Mantinean, which Aristoxenus prefers because of the movement of the hands. Dance was so highly regarded and considered so wise that Pindar calls Apollo a "dancer": "Dance, O Apollo, lord of splendor, with your wide quiver." And Homer (or one of the Homeridae) in the *Hymns to Apollo* says: "Apollo, holding the lyre in his hands, played beautifully and gracefully, stepping high." Eumelus (or Arctinus of Corinth) brings dance even to the King of the Gods, saying: "And in the midst, the father of men and gods danced." 

Theophrastus says that Anthron of Catana was the first to create rhythmic body movements while playing the flute. From this comes the term "to act the Sicilian," <note>original: *sikelizein*. In the ancient world, Sicilians were famous for their lively and expressive style of dancing.</note> which among the ancients meant to dance. After him came Cleophantus of Thebes. Famous dancers include Bolbus (mentioned by Cratinus and Callias) and Zenon the Cretan, who was a great favorite of Artaxerxes, according to Ctesias. Alexander, in his letter to Philoxenus, mentions Theodorus and Chrysippus.

<margin>The Museum.</margin>
Regarding the Museum: Timon the "Sillographer" <note>A writer of *silli*, or satirical poems. Timon of Phlius was a Skeptic philosopher.</note> mocks the philosophers supported there, saying that they are fed like the most prized birds in a "basket" or "cage," <note>original: *talaros*. Timon is making a famous joke that the scholars at the Museum of Alexandria were like pampered birds in a cage, being fed by the king just to sit and argue with each other.</note> as if in some communal trap. He writes: "Many are fed in populous Egypt, bookish scribblers, quarreling endlessly in the Museum’s cage." They escape their "word-feasts"—or rather, these table-orators, through their talkativeness, seem to me to have forgotten the Pythian oracle recorded by Chamaeleon: "Twenty days before the Dog-star, and twenty days after, use Dionysus as a physician in a shaded house." <margin>Dionysiac manner.</margin> <note>The "Dog-star" is Sirius; the oracle suggests drinking wine (Dionysus) as medicine during the intense summer heat.</note> 

Mnesitheus of Athens also says that the Pythia commanded the Athenians to honor Dionysus as a physician. Alcaeus, the poet of Mytilene, says: "Wet your lungs with wine, for the star [Sirius] returns; the season is harsh and everything is parched with heat... let us drink, for the star returns." And Eupolis, in his play *Callias*, says people are forced by Protagoras to drink so that "before the Dog-star they may carry a relaxed lung." For us, it is not only the lung that is dried up, but our heart is in danger too. As Antiphanes says: "Tell me, what is life? I say it is drinking!" You see how all things that drink along the winter-torrents...

### FROM THE *DEIPNOSOPHISTAE* OF ATHENAEUS
<meta>catchword: enjoyment</meta>

...to be soaked through both night and day; what size and beauty results! For this seeks nourishment, as if it had a certain thirst; but if it suffers from dryness, it perishes root and branch. So he says these things, having "gnat-picked" <note>original: *konologēsas*. This refers to sifting through tiny details or being overly meticulous with words.</note> to drink. The term "to soak" <note>original: *brechein*</note> is also used for the act of drinking. Antiphanes says: "For if, having eaten, one soaks oneself abundantly." Eubulus writes: "I, Sicon, have come well-soaked and well-potted." To drink is thus called "to soak," and it is also called "to Medize." <note>original: *mēdizein*. A play on words; "to Medize" usually meant to side with the Persians (Medes), but here it implies drinking heavily like a Persian.</note>

<margin>Falling back</margin>
The word "to fall back" <note>original: *anapipten*</note> is properly used for the soul—that is, to lose heart or to be negligent. Thucydides says in his first book: "When defeated, they fall back the least." <note>Thucydides 1.70.5. He is describing the resilient character of the Athenians.</note> Cratinus uses the word for rowers: "Splash the oars and fall back!" And Xenophon says in his *Oeconomicus*: "Why are rowers not a nuisance to each other? Is it not because they sit in order, lean forward in order, and fall back in order?"

<margin>To be dedicated</margin>
We say "to be laid up" <note>original: *anakeisthai*</note> when referring to a statue. Therefore, when people used this word for a person reclining at a meal, they were mocked. Diphilus says: "But while I was reclining..." <note>The joke here is that *anakeisthai* usually refers to a statue "dedicated" in a temple, not a person lying down to eat.</note> "How could your companion be annoyed?" he asks, "Stay dedicated like a statue!" Philippides writes: "And always dining while reclining next to him." He adds: "Was he eating a statue?"

<margin>To recline</margin>
One should instead say "to lie down" <note>original: *katakeisthai*</note> or "to be reclined" <note>original: *katakeklisthai*</note> as used for banquets by Phrynichus and Plato. Alexis says: "How it is a misfortune to lie down before dinner, for sleep never takes hold of one." One would not say this in any other way, for the person is now near the table. It is possible to find, however, that everyone eventually used the term "to recline" <note>original: *anakeisthai*</note> through a certain favor of usage. Satyrus, in a play by Sophocles, says of Heracles reclining in the middle: "I would enter into his neck." Aristotle, in his *Customs of the Etruscans*, says: "The Etruscans dine with their wives, reclining under the same blanket." Theopompus says: "After this, Epinomus was reclining most softly on a couch of Telamonian blankets, while they groaned out songs to one another." Philonides says: "I lie down, as you see, like a glutton." <note>original: *lekaptalai*. A rare word for someone who licks the dishes clean.</note> Euripides says in the *Cyclops*: "He fell back, letting out a heavy breath from his throat." <note>Euripides, *Cyclops* 410.</note> Alexis says: "After this, I ordered her to recline next to me."

<margin>To taste</margin>
The word "to taste" <note>original: *pasasthai*</note> is used for sampling something. Phoenix says to Achilles: "I was unwilling to taste food with another in the halls." And elsewhere: "When they had tasted the inner parts." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 1.464. "Inner parts" or "viscera" refers to the ritual tasting of organs after a sacrifice.</note> For they taste only the inner parts, since a large crowd is sharing a few things. And Priam says to Achilles: "Now I have tasted food." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 24.641. Priam had been fasting in grief for Hector; here "tasting" implies breaking a fast with a small amount.</note> For it is appropriate for someone in misfortune to merely sample food. Grief does not allow one to eat to fullness. Therefore, the "fasting person" <note>original: *sōkouros*</note> who has not tasted food lies hungry for the whole time. Homer never uses "to taste" for those who are being filled, but uses words that indicate satiety, such as: "But when I was satisfied with food," and "they put away the desire for food." However, the later poets use "to taste" even for being filled. Callimachus says: "I would taste of the story more sweetly." Eratosthenes writes: "They tasted roasted meat from the embers." "They chose to go to the banquet, like a wooden foot to a wooden leg," says the Theban lyric poet.

Seleucus says that what Homer calls a "banquet" <note>original: *dais*</note> or "festivity" <note>original: *thalia*</note> is, by a transposition of letters, a "way of life" <note>original: *diaita*</note>. To derive it from "to speak" <note>original: *lexasthai*</note> is a bit more forced.

In Homer, not only men but also women play with balls. They also used discuses and javelins with a certain rhythm. "They diverted themselves with discuses and by throwing javelins." For pleasure lightens hardship.

<margin>Homeric Heroes' Hunting</margin>
The young men also go out for hunting as a practice for the dangers of war. Through all kinds of hunting, they become stronger and healthier. They prepare themselves as if facing a tower, and they throw javelins while standing opposite one another.

<margin>Baths</margin>
They also know of baths as a relief from labor. They wash away exhaustion in the sea, which is especially beneficial for the sinews. By entering the water, they relax the silent tension of the muscles; if they did not wash away the salt spray, their bodies would become hardened. Those returning from a lookout point "washed away the heavy sweat in the sea, from their shins and neck and thighs." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 10.572-573.</note> Having thus cooled themselves, they went into "well-polished tubs" and bathed, and having anointed themselves with olive oil, they sat down to dinner. There is another way of relieving fatigue: by pouring water over the head, "delightful to the head and shoulders." <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 10.362.</note>

<margin>Iliad 10, Odyssey 10</margin>
For baths, by surrounding the pores from all sides with water, block the secretion of sweat, just as if a strainer were thrown into water. For water will only pass through if one lifts it up to allow the pores to breathe and provides an exit to the outside. As Aristotle said in his *Physical Problems*, <note>Aristotle, *Problems* 2.1.</note> he asks why those who have sweated and then entered hot or cold water no longer sweat until they leave the bath.

They eat lunch first, and they also eat vegetables. That they knew of vegetable gardens is clear from the "well-ordered rows of greens" in the garden of Alcinous. <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 7.127.</note> Moreover, they used tree-fruits, and from "tree-fruit" comes every kind of side-dish. He introduces them as taking care of the fruits: "Pear upon pear grows old, and fig upon fig." <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 7.120.</note>

<margin>Tree-fruits. Odyssey 10, Odyssey 11</margin>
For this reason, he calls the fruit-bearing trees "beautiful," saying "tall trees grew there in bloom: pears and pomegranates and apple-trees." Those used for timber he distinguishes by different epithets: "Tall trees grew there in bloom: alder and poplar and fir that reached to heaven." The use of pomegranates was even more ancient than these. Tantalus, therefore, even in death is not free from the desire for them. God punishes him by placing them near him, just as those who lead irrational animals by holding out green branches. He hides him away from such fruits...

### BOOK I

<margin>Odyssey, Book 24</margin>
...of enjoyment, whenever it might come near to hope. <margin>Homeric heroes hunting fish and birds.</margin> And Odysseus, reminding Laertes of what he gave to him when he was a child, says: "You gave me thirteen pear trees," <note>original: *ongchnas*. Odyssey 24.340.</note> and so forth. That they also ate fish is made clear by Sarpedon, who likens their capture to a hunt with an all-catching net. Yet Eubulus, speaking with comic wit, says jokingly: "As for fish, Homer has not said that any of the Achaeans ate them. He only showed them roasting the sacred victims, for he has not made any of them boiling meat, nor did anyone see even a single mistress among them; rather, they fed themselves with ten bowls of wine. They saw a bitter campaign, those who, having taken a single city, departed far more active in the marketplace for delicacies <note>original: *opsopraktoteroi*. A play on the word *opson*, meaning a relish or gourmet side dish, implying they became foodies after the war.</note> than the city they took then." Nor did the heroes leave the air free for the birds, setting traps and nets for thrushes and doves. 

<margin>Iliad, Book 23</margin>
They also practiced fowling, hanging the dove by a cord from a ship’s mast and shooting at it from a distance with arrows, as is described in the funeral games. <note>original: *epitaphio*. Referring to the games for Patroclus in Iliad 23.</note> Homer omitted the use of vegetables, fish, and birds because of their association with gluttony, and additionally because of the impropriety in their preparation, judging such things to be beneath heroic and divine deeds. However, that they also used boiled meats is shown where he says, "as the cauldron boils, melting the fat of a tender-fed hog." <note>Iliad 21.362-363.</note> And the ox-foot thrown at Odysseus was seen at a banquet, for he intended to roast the ox-foot. And the phrase "they set before them platters of all kinds of meats" <note>Odyssey 1.141.</note> indicates not only a variety of victims—speaking of birds, pigs, kids, and oxen—but also that the preparation was varied and not of one kind, but quite elaborate. This suggests the emergence of Sicilian, Sybaritic, and Italian tables, and even Chian ones; for the Chians are also recorded as being the first of those mentioned to excel in the art of dressing meat. In Homer, not only the young men but also the old men, such as Phoenix and Nestor, sleep with women. Only for Menelaus is no woman mentioned as sleeping with him, because he had undertaken the campaign for the sake of his abducted wedded wife. 

<margin>Old wine and differing colors. Pindar, Olympian Ode 9.</margin>
Pindar praises "old wine, but the flowers of newer songs." <note>Pindar, Olympian 9.48.</note> Eubulus says it is strange for old wine to be always in good repute with courtesans, but for "flowers" <note>meaning songs or young men</note> not to be old, but newer. Alexis says almost the same thing, with only the word "always" standing prominently in his verse. Truly, old wine is not only more pleasant but also more beneficial for health. For it digests the food better, and being thin-textured, it is easily absorbed, imparts strength to bodies, makes the blood healthy and well-circulated, and provides undisturbed sleep. Homer praises the wine that admits a sufficient mixture of water, such as that from Maron. <margin>Odyssey, Book 9</margin> Old wine admits more mixing because it becomes hotter as it ages. 

<margin>Dionysus taking refuge in the sea.</margin>
Some say that Dionysus fleeing into the sea signifies the making of wine, which has been known for a long time; for wine is very sweet when seawater is poured in. Homer, in praising black wine, often calls it "sparkling" <note>original: *aithopa*, meaning fiery or glowing.</note> or "fiery." For it is most enduring, and lasts a very long time for those who drink it regularly. Theopompus says that black wine first appeared among the Chians, and that the Chians were the first to learn how to plant and tend vines from Oenopion, the son of Dionysus, who also settled the island and shared the gift with other men. White wine, however, is weak and thin. But the tawny wine <margin>Italian wines.</margin> <note>original: *kirrhos*, an amber or yellowish-orange color.</note> digests more easily, being drier. Regarding Italian wines, Galen <note>original: *Gallikos*. In Athenaeus, this refers to the famous physician Galen, who is a character in the dialogue.</note> says in the presence of this sophist: Falernian wine is drinkable from ten years of age, and is at its peak from fifteen until twenty. But one who drinks it beyond this time suffers a headache and it affects the nervous system. There are two kinds of it: the dry and the sweetish. The latter occurs when south winds blow during the vintage, which also makes it darker. That which is not harvested this way is dry and tawny in color. Of Alban wine, there are two kinds: one sweetish and the other harsh; <note>original: *omphakias*, wine made from unripe grapes.</note> both are at their peak at fifteen years. Surrentine wine begins to be drinkable at twenty-five years; for being without fat and very thin, it ripens with difficulty. When aged, it is almost the only wine suitable for those who use it continuously. Rhegian wine, being fattier than Surrentine, is useful from fifteen years. Priaernian is also useful, being of a thinner texture than Rhegian and very little affecting the head. Formian is similar to this, but it peaks quickly and is fattier than it. Trifoline peaks more slowly and is more earthy than Surrentine. Setine is among the first wines, similar to Falernian but lighter and more pungent. Tiburtine is thin, does not easily evaporate, and peaks at ten years; it becomes better as it ages. Labican is sweet, fatty to the taste, and between Falernian and Alban. It is drinkable at ten years. Algidian wine is scarce and very fine, moreover vigorous and thick, being fattier than Praenestine and Tiburtine. Marsian is very dry, but that which is called Alban produced in and around Cumae in Campania is drinkable and light from fifteen years. Oenian is good, and Vicentine is somewhat fatty, similar to Alban in being harsh. The latter is sweet to drink but hard on the stomach; its peculiarity is that it does not seem to be "running off," <note>meaning it has a lingering finish or body.</note> appearing as if something else were mixed with it. Lacinian is light, but more difficult than Falernian. Caecuban is also noble and pungent.
