# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS

...pungent, and causes shortness of breath. Among the wrestlers, <note>Perhaps a metaphor for wines that "wrestle" with the drinker's senses.</note> after sufficient years, the Pablian, Fannian, and Huspian wines are multifaceted, affecting both the head and the stomach. These are often drunk at symposia. Lighter than all of these is the Rabinian wine, which is suitable for drinking from seven years of age up to eighty. Signine wine is useful up to six years, but it becomes much more beneficial as it ages. Numentan wine reaches its peak quickly and is drinkable from five years; it is very sweet and light. Apulian wine is sweet to the taste and golden in color. Capuan wine was very similar to Surrentine. Barbinian wine is very harsh but always improves with age. Caucinian is a noble wine, similar to Falernian. Bruttian wine is "hard to fight" <note>original: *dysomachos*, meaning harsh or overwhelming.</note> and fatty. Trebellian wine from Naples is well-balanced in its potency, good for the stomach, but harsh to the taste. Erebellian wine is dark at first, but after not many years it becomes white; it is very light and delicate. Massilian wine is mild, produced in small quantities, but is thick and fleshy. As for Tarentine wines, all those not from this specific climate are soft; they do not strike the head, though they cause some distress, <note>likely referring to a hangover or digestive labor</note> being sweet and good for the stomach. Mamertine wine comes from outside Italy.
<margin>Italian, as Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a Renaissance scholar who corrected many ancient texts.</note> reads.</margin>
Produced in Sicily, it is called Iotaline; it is sweet, light, and vigorous. Note that among the Indians, a deity is honored—as Chares of Mitylene says—who is called Zoroades. This name is interpreted in the Greek tongue as "Wine-maker."

Note that Antiphanes <note>A famous Athenian poet of Middle Comedy.</note> lists the specialties of each city as follows: A cook from Elis, a cauldron from Argos, wine from Phliasia, and blankets from Corinth. Fish from Sicyon, and flute-girls from Aegia.
<margin>Specialties of each city.</margin>
Cheese from Sicily, perfume from Athens, and eels from Boeotia. Hermippus <note>A poet of Old Comedy and rival of Aristophanes.</note> speaks thus: "Tell me now, O Muses who dwell in Olympic homes, since the time Dionysus began sailing upon the wine-dark sea, what good things he has brought here for men in his black ship: From Cyrene, the <term>silphium</term> stalk <note>A medicinal plant, now extinct, highly prized in antiquity.</note> and ox-hide. From the Italians, mackerel and all kinds of salt-fish. From Italy, groats and ribs of beef. From Sitalcas <note>A powerful King of Thrace.</note>, mange for the Spartans. From Perdiccas <note>King of Macedon, often mocked for his shifting alliances.</note>, lies in very many ships. Syracuse provides pigs and cheese. And may Poseidon destroy the Corcyraeans in their hollow ships, because they have a divided heart. These things come from there. From Egypt, hanging sails and papyrus rolls. From Syria, frankincense. Beautiful Crete provides cypress for the gods. Libya provides much ivory for sale. Rhodes provides raisins and dried figs that bring sweet dreams. Furthermore, from Euboea, pears and fat apples. Slaves from Phrygia, and mercenaries from Arcadia. Pagasae provides slaves and branded men. Acorns and shining almonds are provided by the Paphlagonians, for these are the ornaments of a feast. Phoenicia provides the fruit of the palm and fine flour. Carthage provides carpets and embroidered pillows." Pindar, in his ode to Hiero, asks: "Are the Laconian hounds the cleverest of beasts? Seek the most skilled dog, the Scyrian goats for milking, arms from Argos, a Theban chariot from the fertile earth, and a finely crafted carriage from Sicily." Critias <note>An Athenian politician and writer, leader of the Thirty Tyrants.</note> speaks thus: "The <term>Cottabus</term> <note>A popular drinking game involving throwing wine dregs at a target.</note> is a distinguished feat from the land of Sicily, which we set up as a target for the shots of wine-drops. Next is the Sicilian carriage, the most beautiful and strongest of vehicles.
<margin>Specialties of each country.</margin>
A Thessalian throne is the most delicate seat for the limbs. A bed for sleep has exceptional beauty in Miletus and Chios, the coastal city of Oenopion. The Etrurian gold-beaten bowl is the best, and all the bronze that adorns a house for any use. The Phoenicians discovered letters that preserve speech. Thebes first joined together the chariot-frame. The Carians, masters of the sea, made the merchant ships. But the one who established the beautiful trophy at Marathon discovered the potter's wheel, the offspring of the earth and the kiln—the most famous ceramic ware, a useful household steward." Indeed, Attic pottery is highly praised. Eubulus says: "Knidian jars, Sicilian platters, Megarian small vats." Antiphanes mentions mustard from Cyprus, juice of the scammony, Milesian cress, Samothracian onions, stalks from Carthage, <term>silphium</term>, Hymettian thyme, and Tenedian oregano.
<margin>Wines.</margin>
Note that the King of the Persians drank only Chalybonian wine, which Posidonius says is also produced in Damascus in Syria, the Persians having planted the vines there. On the island of Issa in the Adriatic, Agatharchides says a wine is produced which is found to be better when compared to all others. Epilycus mentions Chian and Thasian wine: "Chian and Thasian, sweet-washing." Lesbian wine, which I think Maro himself made, says Clearchus. "There is no other wine sweeter to drink than the Lesbian draft," says Alexis. For those who spend their days with Thasian and Lesbian wines,

But whoever is caught sending it to another city, even a bean’s worth, his property shall be declared sacred <note>confiscated by the state</note>. Ephippus says: "Loving Lesbian wine, a hearty wine." Much of the "Lesbian mantle" <note>likely a metaphor for the wine's froth or color</note> is drunk to excess. Antiphanes says: "There is a wine that is very alluring; Thasian wine, smelling of perfume or cinnamon. For in plenty there is desire, but among those faring poorly, there is no urge for Aphrodite among mortals." Eubulus says: "Taking Thasian or Chian, or old Lesbian smelling of nectar." # BOOK 1

Anaxandrides says: "Yesterday you drank a mixed cup." <note>Likely referring to wine diluted with water, the standard practice at Greek symposia.</note> Note that Aristophanes titles his play *The Second Thesmophoriazusae*, while Demetrius of Troezen titles his *The Women Who Have Celebrated the Thesmophoria*; in this work, the comic poet mentions sweet wine: "I will not let you drink Pramnian wine, nor Chian, nor Thasian, nor Peparethian, nor any other wine that rouses the <term>embolon</term> <note>original: *embolon*, literally a ship's ram; here used as a phallic double-entendre common in Old Comedy.</note>." Eubulus mentions "the Leucadian and Milesian" wines. Archestratus, in his *Gastronomy*, speaks of "Oeniscus, so pleasant to drink." He then says: "Then, whenever a full cup is raised to Zeus the Savior, you must drink a sweet and venerable, grey-haired wine, heavily laden with white blossoms on its liquid mane <note>A poetic description of the 'crust' or foam on aged wine.</note>. Let it be from sea-girt Lesbos. I also praise the Byblian wine from sacred Phoenicia, though I do not equal it to the Lesbian. For if you taste it suddenly without being accustomed to it, it will seem more fragrant than the Lesbian, as it retains its scent for an immense length of time. But in the drinking, it falls far short."
<margin>Wines.</margin>
"It is not wine, but seems to hold a rank equal to ambrosia. If some boastful, empty-headed fools mock me, saying Phoenician wine is the sweetest of all, I pay them no mind." Regarding Thasian wine, he says it is noble to drink "if it is aged for many beautiful seasons in well-aimed jars." I know also of "vine-clusters from other cities" that one could praise, though their names escape me. But simply nothing compares to Lesbian wine. Some people, however, delight in praising their local varieties. 
<margin>Book 2.</margin>
Ephippus also mentions Phoenician wines: "Nuts, pomegranates, dates, and other dainties, and jars <note>original: *samnakia*, a type of vessel.</note> of Phoenician wine." And again, "a jar of Phoenician wine was opened," which Xenophon also mentions in the *Anabasis*. Cratinus also mentions it: "And again we saw what kind of little wines they were enjoying just now, following and accompanying them." He says: "Oh, how soft and white! Is it possible?" <note>Referring to the color and texture of a specific vintage.</note> Hermippus somewhere portrays Dionysus mentioning several wines: "The gods themselves know Mendean wine on soft blankets; and Magnesian, a honey-sweet gift. And Thasian, which carries the scent of apples. I judge this to be by far the best of all wines, after the faultless and painless Chian." There is also a wine they call <term>saprias</term> <note>literally "rotten" or "mellowed by age," used for very old, high-quality wine.</note>, of which "whenever the jars are opened, there is a scent of violets, roses, and hyacinths—a divine fragrance that fills the high-roofed house. It is ambrosia and nectar combined; this is the true nectar. One should drink this at a flourishing banquet with friends, but give the Peparethian to enemies." Phanias of Eresus says that when the grape clusters are full, they sprinkle them with <term>elatreion</term> <note>likely a juice or extract from the wild cucumber, used as a preservative or to soften the flavor.</note> on the vine, which makes the wine soft.

Note that Themistocles received Lampsacus as a gift from the King <note>The Persian Great King Artaxerxes I, to whom the exiled Athenian general fled.</note> for his wine, Magnesia for his bread, Myus for his meat, and Percote and Palaeskepsis for his bedding and clothing.
<margin>
Gifts given long ago by the King of the Persians. Strabo 14 & Plutarch.
</margin>
The King ordered him to wear a barbarian robe, just as he had formerly given to Demaratus and his son-in-law, on the condition that he no longer wrap himself in Greek clothing. Cyrus the Great also gifted seven cities to his friend Pytharchus of Cyzicus, as Agathocles of Babylon says: Pythiasos, Olympios, Mamantion, Skeptra, Artypsion, and Pertyrian. But they say that out of insolence and folly, Pytharchus attempted to become a tyrant over his homeland, gathering an army. The Cyzicenes set out against him and fought him in the meadows. Priapus is honored among the Lampsacenes, being the same as Dionysus, called so by epithet, just as he is called Thriambos and Dithyrambos. Note that the Mitylenaeans call their local sweet wine *prodromos* <note>the "forerunner" or "precursor."</note>, while others call it *protropos* <note>the juice that flows from the grapes before they are pressed.</note>. 
<margin>
Pramnian wine. Icarian.
</margin>
Icarian wine is also admired. As Amphis says: "Oil from Thyrea, and lentils from Gela. Icarian wine, which is close to Kimolian." Eparchides says the Pramnian wine is produced in Icarus; this is a specific kind of wine. It is neither sweet nor thick, but austere, hard, and possessing exceptional strength. Aristophanes, speaking to the Athenians, says that the people of Athens do not like poets who are "sweet," but prefer those who are "harsh and unrefined," like "harsh Pramnian wines that knit the brows and the belly." Instead, they should prefer "fragrant wine, ripe and nectar-filled." Semus says there is a rock in Icarus called "Pramnian," and near it a great mountain from which the Pramnian wine gets its name, which some also call "medicinal." Icarus was formerly called *Ichthyoessa* <note>literally "Abounding in Fish"</note> because of the abundance of fish around it. Similarly, the Echinades are named from sea urchins (*echinoi*), Skepias point from its many cuttlefish (*skepiai*), and the Lagoousae islands from their hares (*lagoi*). Others are named "Seaweed-filled" and "Dock-leaf-filled" from similar causes. Eparchides says the vine that bears the Icarian Pramnian is called "Sacred" by strangers, but "Dionysian" by the locals. Didymus says Pramnian wine is named after a "Pramnian vine," though some say it is specifically a dark wine. Others say it refers to any wine suitable for long preservation <note>original: *paramenion*, a pun on *pramnion*.</note>. Others say it "soothes the spirit" (*praunonta to menos*), since those who drink it become mild. 
<margin>Acanthian wine.</margin>
Amphis also praises the wine from the city of Akanthos, saying: "Tell me, of what country is he? Acanthian. Then why, as a citizen of such excellent wine, are you such a great cup? You have the very name of your fatherland, but you do not have the character of its citizens." Alexis mentions Corinthian wine as being harsh: "Foreign wine was present. For the Corinthian variety is a torture." Regarding Euboean wine, someone is described as "having drunk much Euboean wine." Archilochus compares Naxian wine to nectar, saying: "In my spear is my kneaded bread..."

<header>FROM ATHENAEUS' DEIPNOSOPHISTS</header>

...and to him, Ismarian wine <note>A famous wine from Thrace, mentioned by Homer as the wine Odysseus used to intoxicate the Cyclops.</note> seems best. "I drink while leaning on my spear." And Stratis praises Sciathian wine: "The wine is making a sound like a cuckoo <note>original: *kokkyzei*, perhaps referring to the sound of pouring or the effect of the drink</note> when I drink it with travelers. Dark Sciathian wine, mixed equal-to-equal <note>A very strong mixture of half wine and half water; Greeks usually diluted wine much further.</note>." Achaius mentions the 
<margin>Byblian wine.</margin> Byblian wine: "Byblian cups of drunkenness for Euetis." This is named after certain places from which it is called. And Philinus says that he will provide Lesbian, Chian, Thasian, Byblian, and Monosian wine, so that there may be no hangover. But Epicharmus says it was named after certain Byblian mountains. Armenidas says there is a region of Thrace called Byblia, which was later renamed Tisara. Thrace was 
admired as a land of sweet wine, as were the areas near it. From the island of Lemnos, wine was also brought. Hippias says that a vine called "orchine" or "eileos" is also called Byblian. Pollis the Argive, who ruled as king of the Syracusans, was the first to bring it to Syracuse from Italy. Thus, the wine called "Pollian" among the Sicilians would be this Byblian wine. An Oracle says: "Drink wine with the 
lees, since you inhabit Aethone, and not sacred Hyperia, where you used to drink wine without the lees." It was also named among the Troezenians, as Aristotle says in his *Constitution*, a vine called "authenthonias" or "hyperias," named after a certain Anthus and Hyper, or according to some, from a certain Alpheia, one of the descendants of Alpheus. Alcman somewhere speaks of 
"unfired wine" <note>original: *apyron*, wine that has not been boiled down to a syrup</note> and "scented with flowers," coming from the Five Hills, a place seven stadia <note>About 0.8 miles</note> from Sparta. He also mentions wines from the Denthiades (a type of fortification), and from Oenus, and from Onogla and Stathmoi. These are places near Githana. He says: "wine from Oenentiades, or Psithian, or Onoglis, or Stathmites," 
and that from Carystus, which is near Arcadia. He called it "unfired" because it was not boiled; for they often used boiled wines. Polybius says a distinct wine is produced in Capua called "climbing-vine wine" <note>original: *anadendriten*, referring to vines trained to grow up trees rather than along the ground</note>, with which none can compare. Alciphron of Maeander says that near Ephesus there is a mountain village formerly called 
Lythisia, but now Lagoreia (after the Amazon Lagoreia), where Pramnian wine is produced. Timachidas 
of Rhodes calls a certain wine in Rhodes *hypochytos* <note>A wine mixed with must or boiled wine</note>, which is similar to sweet wine. And a wine is called *glytris* when it contains boiled-down must. Polyzelus says that a wine in Rhodes is called *antitites*. Plato the comic poet mentions "smoky wine" <note>original: *kapnias*, likely referring to a wine aged in a smoky room to accelerate maturity</note>. Mallius says this variety is produced in Briventum, a city in Italy. Amphis says poor wine is called *trimma* <note>original: *trimma*, literally something "rubbed" or "ground," referring to a spiced drink</note> by 
<margin>Spiced drink. Book 9, chapter 10.</margin> Sosicrates. The ancients also used a drink prepared with aromatics, which they called *trimma*. 
<margin>Pliny, Book 14, chapter 18.</margin> Theophrastus in his *History of Plants* says that in Heraea in Arcadia a wine is produced which, when drunk, makes men mad but makes women fertile. But around Cerynia in Achaea, there is a vine from which the wine causes pregnant women to miscarry; even if they eat the grapes, they miscarry. He says the Troezenian wine makes those who drink it sterile. In Thasos, he says, 
they make a certain wine that induces sleep, and another that causes wakefulness in those who drink it. In some cities, they prepare "flower-scented" wine <note>original: *anthosmias*</note>. Phaenias of Ephesus says: "Pour in sweet wine to the water-drinkers in the sea-mixture, which becomes flower-scented." And again: "flower-scented wine becomes stronger from a young vine than 
<margin>Preparation of flower-scented wine.</margin> from old ones." Some say they store away grapes that were trampled while unripe, and it becomes flower-scented. Theophrastus says that in Thasos, the wine given in the Town Hall <note>original: *Prytaneion*</note> is wonderful for its pleasure. For they mix it with care; they put into the jar dough kneaded with honey, so that the wine takes its fragrance from the dough and its sweetness 
from the honey. And he says further: "If one mixes hard and foul-smelling wine with soft and fragrant wine, such as the Heracleote and the Erythraean, the one provides softness and the other provides fragrance." Myrtle-wine <note>original: *myrrhites*</note> or myrrh-wine is mentioned in Poseidippus; "the precious myrrh-wine of Diphilus." 
<margin>Characteristics of wines.</margin> And "Hermes" is a kind of drink in Stratis. Chaereas says that in Babylon a wine is produced called "nectar." For this word is true, that there is not only a share of water, but also wine that provides a certain light. For the Cean poet says that neither the gifts of Dionysus nor the grape-stones are to be cast away. Of wines, some are white, some 
tawny <note>original: *kirrhos*, a yellowish-orange color</note>, and some black. The white is naturally the thinnest, diuretic, hot, and aids digestion, but it makes the head burn, for wine rises upward. The black wine that is not sweet is the most nutritious and astringent. But the sweet wine, whether white or tawny, is the most nutritious of all, for it smooths the passage through the body. And by thickening the 
fluids more, it troubles the head less. For the nature of sweet wine lingers in the lower digestive tract and is productive of phlegm, as Diocles and Praxagoras observe. Mnesitheus the Athenian says: "Black wine is the most nourishing, but white is the most diuretic and thinnest, while tawny wine is dry and helps more in digesting food." Wines that are more carefully treated with sea-water 
<margin>Sea-treated wines.</margin> do not cause hangovers; they loosen the bowels, sting the stomach, cause flatulence, and assist in the 
digestion of food. Such is the Myidian wine and that from Halicarnassus. The comic poet Menippus calls the Myidian "brine-drinking." The Coan wine is also sufficiently treated with sea-water. Rhodian wine has a smaller portion of 
sea-water, but its age is significant. The island wine is well-suited for drinking and not out of place for daily use. Knidian wine generates blood, is nourishing, and makes the bowels loose and 
calm. But if drunk in large quantities, it relaxes the stomach. Lesbian wine has less astringency and is more 
diuretic.

<header>BOOK I</header>

...is sought after. But the Chian wine is more pleasant, and among the Chians, that which is called Ariusian. There are three varieties of it: 
<margin>Wine among others.</margin> for one is dry, another is sweetish, and the one that is between these in taste is called "autocrat" <note>original: *autokratōr*, meaning "self-ruled" or perfectly balanced</note>. Now, the dry kind is good for the stomach, nourishing, and quite excellent. The sweetish kind is nourishing, filling, and softens the bowels. The one used as the "autocrat" is the Chian wine commonly known; it is digestive, nourishing, produces good blood, and is very mild and filling because of its great potency. Of the wines of Italy, the most pleasant are the Alban and the Falernian. However, when these are aged, they can become overly pungent or medicinal in nature as they quickly reach their peak. The wine called Albian is a cause of sleeplessness and is difficult to digest, but generally causes no pain. It should be made some time in advance and placed in an open area to allow its excessive potency to evaporate. The Corcyraean <note>From modern Corfu</note> is the most pleasant wine for aging. But the Zacynthian and Leucadian wines, because they contain gypsum <note>Gypsum was often added to wine in antiquity to clarify it and reduce acidity</note>, are harmful to the head. The wine called *abates* from Cilicia is similar; it only serves to soften the bowels. The Sicilian wines, such as the *eodes*, the *mandonios*, and the *halicarnassios*, are excellent when the water is sufficiently salted, specifically with hard waters like spring or rain water, if it has been filtered and settled for a long time. These are useful in Athens and Sicyon, for in those places the waters are very bitter. For sea-wines and spring-wines, mix them sufficiently with Chian and Lesbian varieties, as the harshness of the waters is dissolved thereby. "The tongue having aged well over a long time..." How then could such a great thing be hidden then? "Necessity is nothing if not heavy. Under which the hidden things of the palace were made manifest," says Sophocles <note>A fragment from a lost play, possibly *Inachus*</note>. 

The Mareotic wine, an Alexandrian variety, 
<margin>Chian and Mareotic.</margin> took its name from Lake Mareia in Alexandria and the city of the same name nearby, which was formerly very large but is now a village. It received its name from Maron, one of those who accompanied Dionysus on his campaigns. The vine is abundant in this land, and its grapes are very pleasant to eat; from them, a most excellent wine is produced. It is white and fragrant, easily absorbed, thin, does not affect the head, and is diuretic. Some call 
<margin>Taeniotic wine.</margin> another variety Taeniotic; Taenia <note>meaning "Ribbon" or "Strip"</note> is a long strip of land in the same region, from which the wines produced are slightly greenish, showing something oily in them which dissolves when mixed with water, much like Attic honey when diluted. This Taeniotic wine, besides being sweet, has something aromatic and slightly astringent. The vine around the Nile is as extensive as 
<margin>Egyptian.</margin> the river itself. Many of the wines have unique colors and qualities. But the wine from the city of Antylla—which is not far from Alexandria—surpasses these; the kings of that time, both Egyptian and Persian, gave the taxes from this city to their wives for their girdles <note>essentially "pin money" for the queens</note>. The wine of the Thebaid, and especially that from the city of Coptos, is so thin, so easily absorbed, and so quickly digested that it is given to those suffering from fever without causing harm. "You praise yourself like Anydamas, woman." <margin>Anydamas.</margin> Anydamas was a practical poet. 

<margin>Discovery of wine.</margin> Theopompus of Chios records that the vine was discovered in Olympia by the Alpheus River, and that there is a place in Elis eight stades away where the locals, during the festival of Dionysus, shut up three empty bronze cauldrons and seal them in the presence of the residents. Later, upon opening them, they find them filled with wine. Hellanicus says that the vine was first discovered in the city of Plinthine in Egypt. Because of this, Dio of the Academy says that the Egyptians became wine-lovers and drinkers, and a remedy was found among them so that those who lacked wine due to poverty could drink 
<margin>Barley wine.</margin> wine made from barley <note>an early form of beer</note>. Those who use this are so delighted that they sing, dance, and do all the things that those intoxicated by wine do. Aristotle says that those who are drunk from wine fall on their faces, but those who have drunk barley wine fall on their backs; for wine makes the head heavy, but barley wine causes a stupor <note>original: *karōtikos*, causing a heavy sleep or numbness</note>. That the Egyptians are wine-lovers is also shown by the fact that they alone have a custom at dinners of eating boiled cabbage before all other foods, and this is observed to this day. Many people also add cabbage seed to preparations intended to prevent drunkenness. Indeed, in whatever vineyard cabbages grow, the wine produced is duller. For this reason, Timaeus says the Sybarites eat cabbage before drinking. Alexis says:
> "Yesterday you were drinking, and now you have a hangover.
> Go to sleep. For you will cease if someone gives you cabbage to eat."
And Eubulus says somewhere:
> "Woman, bring cabbage to me; you are going to 
> take away this whole hangover, so it seems to me."
That the ancients called the hangover-remedy "rhaphanos" <note>usually "radish," but here used for "cabbage"</note> is shown by Apollodorus of Carystus: "I know that we call it *rhaphanos*, but we foreigners call it *krambe* <note>cabbage</note>; for women it makes no difference." Anaxandrides says:
> "And now, by eating much cabbage, you will cease your chatter at the table,
> and you will scatter the weight of the cloud that is now upon your brow."
Nicochares:
> "Tomorrow we will boil cabbage for her from the baths, so that it may suffice for the hangover."
Amphis:
> "It seems there is no medicine for drunkenness 
> like a sudden grief falling upon one;
> for it drives out the nonsense so thoroughly that even cabbages seem like nothing in comparison."
Concerning this power which the cabbage possesses, Theophrastus also records that the very smell of cabbage kills the vine even while it is growing.

# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS
## FROM THE SECOND BOOK

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "O" at the start of the main text, enclosed in a square frame with ornate foliate and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

<margin>About wine.</margin>
O you who measure out so much of the day in sleep, it does not seem to me that the varied discourses you have recounted allow any leisure for sleep. For Nicander of Colophon says that wine <note>original: *oinos*</note> was named after Oeneus. He says: "Oeneus, having squeezed the juice into hollow cups, called it wine." Hellanicus of Miletus also says that the name is an eponym, for each man calls wine "the gift of Oeneus." Hecataeus of Miletus, speaking of the vine being discovered in Aetolia, says the following: "Orestheus, the son of Deucalion, came to Aetolia to take the kingship, and a dog of his gave birth to a piece of wood; he ordered it to be buried, and from it grew a vine laden with grapes. Because of this, he called his son Phytios <note>A name derived from *phyein*, meaning "to grow" or "to plant"</note>." Then Oeneus was born, named after the vines; for the ancient Greeks, he says, called the vines *oinai*. Oeneas was an Aetolian. Plato, in the *Cratylus*, when providing an etymology for wine <note>original: *oinos*</note>, says it is "mind-possessing" <note>original: *oionous*, a play on *oiēsis* (thought/opinion) and *nous* (mind)</note>, because it fills our minds with self-importance. Or perhaps it is named after "benefit" <note>original: *onēsis*</note>. For Homer, playing on the word, says: "And then you yourself will have benefit <note>original: *onēseai*</note> if you drink." Indeed, he is accustomed to calling foods "benefits" <note>original: *oneiata*</note>, and to saying that we are benefited. "The gods made wine the best thing for mortal men to scatter their cares." Diphilus the comic poet says: "O Dionysus, most dear to all who are wise, and most clever, how sweet you are! When you alone make the humble feel great, 
<margin>The nature of wine.</margin> making the one who knits his brows laugh, and making the weak daring, and the coward bold." And Philoxenus says: "Wine is a creature of many voices, bringing joy." Chaeremon the tragic poet says that wine provides those who use it with laughter, wisdom, learning, and good counsel. Ion of Chios says: "Wine, the unconquered child, bull-faced <note>original: *tauropōnion*, an epithet of Dionysus as a bull-god</note>, not a young or insulting attendant of loud-thundering loves, the wine that lifts the spirit, the presiding official of men." 
<margin>10</margin> Mnesitheus said that the gods revealed wine to mortals as a greatest good for those who use it rightly, but for those who use it in a disorderly fashion, quite the opposite. For it provides nourishment to those who use it, and strength to their souls and bodies. Indeed, it is most useful in medicine, for it is mixed with liquid drugs, and it brings benefit to those who are wounded. In daily social gatherings, to those who drink it in moderation and mixed with water, it brings cheerfulness; but if you exceed the limit, it brings insolence. If you take it equal parts wine and water <note>original: *ison isō*, a very strong mixture as Greeks usually diluted wine significantly</note>, it produces madness; and if taken pure, it produces paralysis of the body. For this reason, Dionysus is called a physician everywhere. And the Pythian oracle told certain people to call Dionysus the "Healer." Eubulus
<margin>20</margin> represents Dionysus as saying: "I mix only three bowls <note>The *krater*, a large vessel for mixing wine and water</note> for those who are wise: one for health, which they drink first; the second for love and pleasure; and the third for sleep, after drinking which, those who are called wise go home. The fourth is no longer ours, 
<margin>30</margin> but belongs to insolence; the fifth to shouting; the sixth to revelry; the seventh to black eyes; the eighth to the legal process-server; the ninth to bile; and the tenth to madness, so that it even makes people throw things. For much wine poured into one small vessel easily trips up the feet of those who have drunk." Epicharmus says: "From a sacrifice comes a feast; from a feast, drinking; from drinking comes revelry; from revelry, a brawl; from a brawl, a lawsuit; from a lawsuit, a conviction; and from a conviction, chains, collapse, and a fine." Panyasis the epic poet assigned the first 
<margin>40</margin> drinking to the Graces, the Seasons, and Dionysus; the second to Aphrodite and again to Dionysus; but the third to Insolence and Ruin. As Euripides says: "The revel brings blows and insulting insolence." For this reason, some say that for Dionysus, the golden cup and the cup of insolence are the same. Alexis says somewhere: "In a way, the nature of wine is most similar to that of men. For new wine must first ferment and insult and lose its bloom, and again become harsh; but when it has chewed through all these stages I mention, and has shed that superficial folly that floats on the top, then it becomes drinkable and settles down again. But the remainder stays the same for everyone." And according to the poet Antimachus: "Wine has a strength equal to fire when it comes upon a man; it surges like the Libyan sea under the North wind or the South wind. It reveals things that were hidden in the depths, and shakes the entire mind." 
<margin>50</margin> On the other hand, Alexis says the opposite: "Man is not at all like wine in nature. For as he grows old, he becomes unpleasant; but we welcome the oldest wine. The old man bites, but the old wine makes us cheerful." Panyasis says: "For wine is a benefit equal to fire for those on earth, a good warder-off of evil, a companion to every sorrow. For it is a lovely part of the feast and the splendor, and in the dance. It is in the desirable love; therefore you must drink it, having received it at the feast with a cheerful heart, and not be sated with food like a child, or drink to excess, forgetting your good spirits." And again: "Wine is the best and most splendid gift from the gods to mortals. To it all songs are fitted, and all dances, and all lovely loves. It drives all sorrows from the hearts of men when drunk in measure; but beyond measure, it is worse." Timaeus of Tauromenium says that in Akragas <note>Modern Agrigento in Sicily</note> there is a house 
<margin>60</margin> <margin>The Trireme House.</margin> <margin>70</margin> called the "Trireme" <note>A Greek warship with three banks of oars</note> for the following reason. Certain young men were getting drunk in it, and they reached such a point of madness...

# BOOK II

...heated by a madness born of drunkenness, they imagined they were sailing in a trireme <note>A standard ancient Greek warship with three banks of oars.</note> and were being tossed by a violent storm at sea. They became so delirious that they began throwing all the furniture and bedding out of the house, believing they were jettisoning cargo into the sea to save the ship from the storm, as they had told the "captain." Even as a crowd gathered and began looting the items being thrown out, the young men did not cease their madness. On the following day, when the generals <note>The *strategoi*, or high-ranking city officials.</note> arrived at the house, the young men—still feeling "seasick"—answered the officials' questions by saying they had been distressed by a storm and were forced to throw the excess cargo into the sea. While the generals marveled at the men’s delusion, one of the youths, who appeared to be the eldest of the group, said: "As for me, men of the trireme, I was so terrified that I threw myself under the benches and lay as low as possible." The officials, realizing the men were out of their minds with drink, let them go with a warning not to indulge in so much wine in the future. The youths, expressing their gratitude, replied: "If we ever reach a harbor after escaping such a great surge, we shall set up statues of you in our homeland as Manifest Saviors alongside the sea deities, for appearing to us so auspiciously." From this event, the house became known as "The Trireme." Philochorus says that those who drink not only reveal who they are themselves, but also uncover the character of everyone else

<margin>Wine and truth.</margin>
<margin>Epa.</margin>
by practicing frankness. Hence the saying "wine and truth." It is also said that wine "shows the mind of a man." Furthermore, the prize for Dionysus <note>The god of wine and theater.</note> is a tripod <note>A three-legged stand or vessel, often given as a victory prize.</note>, for we say that those who speak the truth speak "from the tripod." However, one must understand that the tripod of Dionysus is actually the mixing bowl <note>The *krater*, where wine and water were blended.</note>. In ancient times, there were two kinds of vessels called tripods: both were cauldrons, but one was for the fire <note>Used for heating water or cooking.</note> and the other for pouring baths. Aeschylus says:

> A household cauldron, acting as a tripod,
> Received him, always keeping 
> Its place above the fire.

But the other kind is what we call the mixing bowl. Homer says:

<margin>Iliad, Book 9.</margin>
> Seven tripods untouched by fire.

It is not by chance that wine is associated with these, for the tripod of truth is its proper home. Thus, it belongs to Apollo because of the truth found in prophecy, and to Dionysus because of the truth found in drunkenness. Semus of Delos says that the bronze tripod was not the Pythian one <note>The famous tripod used by the oracle at Delphi.</note>, but what they now call a cauldron. Some were "untouched by fire," in which they used to mix the wine; others were for pouring baths, in which they heated water and set over the fire. Some of these stood on three legs, and because of this base, they were called tripods. Ephippus says somewhere:

> A great quantity of wine forces much talk.
> Therefore they say that those who are drunk speak the truth.

Antiphanes says:

> Friends, one could hide 
> Everything else, except for two:
> Drinking wine and falling in love.

For both are revealed by looks and by words, even by those who try to deny it. These things make the heart clear to many. Philochorus says that Amphictyon, the King of the Athenians, having learned from Dionysus the art of mixing wine, was the first to mix it. 

<margin>Dionysus the Upright.</margin>
Because of this, men were able to stand "upright" <note>original: *orthos*</note> when drinking this way, whereas previously they were bent double by the unmixed wine; for this reason, he established an altar to "Dionysus the Upright" in the temple of the Seasons <note>The *Horai*, goddesses who oversaw the natural cycles and the ripening of fruit.</note>, for it is they who nurture the fruit of the vine. Near him, he built an altar to the Nymphs, providing a reminder to those who drink of the proper mixing <note>The Nymphs represent water; the Greeks almost always diluted their wine with water.</note>. Indeed, the Muses are said to be the nurses of Dionysus. He also established a law that after the meal, only a small taste of unmixed wine should be offered, as a sample of the power of the Good God. 

<margin>Give nothing unmixed to the Savior.</margin>
The rest of the wine was then served mixed, as much as each guest desired. During this, the name of Zeus the Savior was invoked, as a reminder to the drinkers that by drinking in this manner, they would be kept safe and sound. Plato, in the second book of the *Laws*, says that the use of wine is for the sake of health. However, people also compare the states of drunkenness to a bull and a leopard, because those who have had too much wine turn toward violence. Alcaeus says:

> Sometimes like honey-sweet wine, sometimes sharper 
> Than the juice of wild berries.

And some people become spirited or angry; such is the nature of the bull. Euripides says:

> A bull, ready for insolence, its heart enraged in its horns.

And because of the fighting spirit and wildness some display, they are called "leopard-like." Ariston of Ceos rightly says that the most pleasant drink is one that shares both sweetness and fragrance. For this reason, some people near Mount Olympus in Lydia prepare what is called "nectar," mixing wine and honeycombs with fragrant flowers. I know that Anaxandrides says nectar is not a drink, but the food of the gods:

<margin>Nectar.</margin>
> I eat the nectar, chewing it well, and I drink the ambrosia;
> I serve Zeus, and I am dignified whenever I speak to Hera
> Or sit beside Cypris <note>Another name for Aphrodite, the goddess of love.</note>.

Alcman also says that the gods "eat nectar." And Sappho says:

> The mixing bowl was filled with ambrosia; 
> Hermes took the ladle and served the gods.

However, Homer knows nectar as the drink of the gods. Ibycus says that ambrosia has a sweetness nine times that of honey, stating that honey is only a ninth part of ambrosia in terms of pleasure.

<margin>Nectar and ambrosia.</margin>
> No man who loves drink is evil. For Bromios <note>A common epithet for Dionysus, meaning "the noisy one."</note>, who dispels hunger,
> Delights in being with honest men, not in an uneducated life.

So says Alexis. And wine is called "ambrosia" because it makes all those who drink plenty of it "lovers of learning" <note>original: *philologos*</note>. The author of the epigram on Cratinus <note>A famous Athenian comic poet known for his heavy drinking.</note> says:

> Wine is a great horse for the gifted singer;
> But if you drink water, you will give birth to nothing good.
> These things Cratinus said, O Dionysus, smelling 
> Not of just one skin, but of the whole jar.

-># FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS<-

Therefore, he nourished the house with a wreath. He had a forehead like yours, "saffron-colored" with gardens. Polemon <note>A 2nd-century BCE geographer and Stoic</note> says that in Monychia, a hero named the **Unmixed-Drinker** <note>original: "akratopotes," referring to someone who drinks wine without water</note> is honored. Among the Spartans, the heroes **Mathon** and **Kyrbon** <note>Names derived from "kneading" and "mixing," appropriate for kitchen work</note> were established by certain cooks who served at the communal meals <note>original: "phiditia," the Spartan public mess-halls</note>. In Achaia, **Deipneus** <note>The "Dinner-God"</note> is also honored, named after dinners <note>original: "deipnon"</note>, which led to the title of his village. If there should be mockery about dry things, let the poems follow them. Yet there is neither boasting nor arrogance of soul here. Homer, therefore, spoke well when he said that all the vows you made before the harbor, while eating much meat and drinking full bowls of wine, were empty. The grammarian Aristarchus <note>The famous librarian of Alexandria</note> marked these verses with a sign of disapproval, as he believed the Greeks were not characterized by such gluttony <note>original: "aristophagia"</note>. For boasting, mocking, and joking do not come from every kind of cheer and fullness; rather, the alteration of the mind toward what is fittingly false occurs during drunkenness. Therefore, Bacchylides <note>A Greek lyric poet</note> says: "A sweet necessity, arising from the cups, warms the heart with the gifts of Aphrodite <note>original: "Kypris"</note>. Hope flutters the mind when mixed with the gifts of Dionysus. It sends the thoughts of men to the heights; a man thinks he is tearing down the battlements of cities and imagines he will rule over all people. Houses gleam with gold and ivory, and ships carrying grain across the shimmering sea bring back vast wealth from Egypt—so does the heart of the drinker surge." Sophocles says that being drunk is a "releaser from pain." Other poets call wine the "sober fruit of the field." And

<margin>Iliad, Book 3.</margin>
<margin>The discovery of Comedy.</margin>
the King of Poets <note>Homer</note> portrays Odysseus saying that when a man is sated with wine, he fights all day with a courageous heart, and so on. From drunkenness also came the discovery of **comedy** and **tragedy** in Ikaria, a village in Attica, and it happened during the very time of the vintage <note>original: "tryge"</note>. From this, comedy was first called **vintage-song** <note>original: "trygoidia," a pun on "tragoidia" or tragedy</note>, because the vine was a "pause-to-sorrow" for mortals. "When wine is gone, Aphrodite exists no more, nor any other pleasure for mankind," as Euripides says in the *Bacchae*. Astydamas says: "To mortals, the wine-mother vine appeared as a healer of grief." For a man who is constantly filled up becomes negligent, but one who drinks in moderation becomes quite thoughtful. Antiphanes says: "I do not intoxicate my wisdom, but only my life," and Alexis says that "the letters of life are clearly defined to the body" by moderation.

<margin>Etymology of feast, festivity, and drunkenness.</margin>
Seleucus says that in ancient times, there was no cheer where they offered wine or other luxury unless they were doing so for the sake of the gods. Because of this, they used the terms **feasts** <note>original: "thoinas"</note>, **festivities** <note>original: "thalias"</note>, and **intoxication** <note>original: "methas"</note>. The first, because they believed one ought to be "wined" for the sake of the gods <note>A pun on "theos" (god) and "thoine" (feast)</note>; the second, because they gathered and sunned themselves for the gods' grace. This is where the term "flourishing feast" <note>original: "daite thaleian"</note> comes from. Aristotle says that **to be drunk** <note>original: "methyein"</note> is so named because it is what happens "after the sacrifice" <note>original: "meta to thyein"</note>. Euripides says that those who offer small sacrifices to the gods while being burdened with heavy matters are the most impious.

<margin>The End/Goal.</margin>
One should also note the term **End** <note>original: "telos"</note> and "sacrifice," as used by Homer. "For I say there is no 'end' more graceful than when joy holds the whole people." We also call **mysteries** <note>original: "teletas"</note> those festivals associated with battles or those handed down with music, because of the expenses involved; for to "complete" <note>original: "telein"</note> means to spend. Those who spend much are "expensive" <note>polythelos</note>, and those who spend little are "economical" <note>eutelos</note>. Alexis says: "Those who are fortunate should live conspicuously and make the gods' gifts visible. For the Giver of good things thinks he is being thanked when he sees men enjoying them; but those who hide their fortune and claim to be doing only moderately well appear ungrateful. When they live meanly, He takes back what He gave long ago." He does not rejoice in the drink of the first offering, drinking moderately. For it is sweet in the feast and

<margin>Waters.</margin>
the flourishing banquet to be delighted with stories after men are sated with the meal. Hesiod, in the *Melampodia*, speaks of the desire for **water** that comes upon us in equal measure to the wine from which it grows. Pindar, in his most grand voice, says that "water is best of all." Homer knows it to be most nourishing, which is why he speaks of a grove of "water-nourished poplars." He also praises its clarity: "Four springs flowing with **white water**" <note>meaning clear or bright</note>.

<margin>Iliad, Book 10.</margin>
That which is quiet and of greater value he calls "lovely." He calls the Titaresios river "lovely" where it mixes with the Peneios. The art of washing also mentions water, which Prathagoras the Cean accepts, saying it is good: "It flows forth beautifully to cleanse that which is very filthy." He also distinguishes "sweet water" from "broad water," saying the former is lesser than the latter, as he describes in another place: "They moored the ships near the **sweet water**." He also knows the nature of **warm water** for wounds.

<margin>Iliad, Book 40 <note>likely error for Book 11</note>.</margin>
He washes Eurypylus, who was wounded, with this; yet if the bleeding were swift, cold water would have been more suitable to constrict and tighten the wound. But to soothe the pain, he used warm water as a healing treatment

<margin>Iliad, Book 30 <note>likely error for Book 11 or 22</note>.</margin>
in a heated state. In his work, "tepid" <note>original: "liaron"</note> is clearly shown as the water at the source of the Scamander. For they say one spring flows with **tepid water**, and smoke rises from it as if from a burning fire. Thus, it has a tepid appearance, from which fire-vapor and fiery smoke are carried up. Again, he speaks of another spring that "in summer flows like hail, or cold snow, or ice from water." He is also accustomed to saying

<margin>Iliad, Book 80 <note>likely error for Book 11</note>.</margin>
that the freshly wounded are covered in blood; in one place he says of Agamemnon, "while the **warm blood** still welled up from the wound." But of a deer fleeing after being hit, he translates it as "while the blood is **tepid** <note>original: "liaron"</note> and the knees have strength." The Athenians call lukewarm water "mixed-after" <note>original: "metakeras"</note>, as Eratosthenes says. Of other waters, those that come from rocks he calls "dark," as Achaeus...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of natural wonders and dietary observations found in Athenaeus’s "The Deipnosophists" (The Banquet of the Learned). Having previously discussed the social and mythological aspects of wine, the text now turns to a scientific and geographical survey of the various types of water found throughout the ancient world, citing poets, historians, and philosophers like Theophrastus.</meta>

-># THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS, BOOK II<-

...as things that are clearly ancient. But he prefers spring waters, especially those that flow through much earth and infertile ground, over all others. As **Hesiod** <note>A Greek poet from the 8th century BCE</note> says: "Of a spring ever-flowing and unpolluted, which is untroubled." And **Pindar** <note>A lyric poet famous for his odes</note>: "Honey-sounding ambrosial water." The waters of **Tilphossa**, the beautiful spring in Boeotia; it is from this spring that **Aeschylus** <note>The famous tragic playwright</note> says **Tiresias** <note>The blind prophet of Theban myth</note> drank and, because of his great age, died from the intense coldness of the water. <margin>Book 9, Chapter 10</margin> **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle’s successor and a keen observer of nature</note> says in his treatise *On Waters* that the water of the **Nile** is the most fertile and the sweetest. For this reason, it also loosens the bowels of those who drink it, as it contains a salty <note>original: "nitron," referring to alkaline mineral salts</note> mixture. In the same region, he says that in some places the water becomes "child-producing," as it is in **Thespiae**, whereas in **Rhyrra** it causes sterility. Among sweet waters, he notes some are sterile and others highly fertile, such as those in **Pheta** and **Tarra**. 

When droughts once occurred around the Nile, the water flowed "violet-colored" <note>original: "iodes," likely referring to a toxic or mineral-heavy discoloration</note>, and many Egyptians perished; they say that not only do bitter waters change, but even salty ones, as do entire rivers. Just as <margin>10</margin> on **Cithaeron**, near where there is a sanctuary of Zeus and Poseidon. The cause is that lightning often strikes that spot. Other waters are very "fleshy" <note>original: "somatodestata," meaning dense or heavy-bodied</note> and have a kind of weight in themselves, like the water in **Troezen**. For everything that is produced there immediately fills the body. The waters near **Mount Pangaeon** produce a sweet effect in the mines; in winter, a cup <note>original: "kotyle," a measure of about half a pint</note> weighs six units, but in summer it weighs forty-six. For the cold itself makes the water more compact. Because of this, when it flows in water-clocks <note>original: "gnomon," here referring to the clepsydra</note>, it does not accurately show the hours in winter, but flows more slowly at the outlet because of its thickness. They say these things occur in **Egypt**, where the air is softer; but salty water is more "earthy" and requires more processing <note>meaning it is harder for the body to digest</note>. Sea water, having a warmer nature, is not as thick. 

One of the salty springs that stands out is that of **Arethusa** <note>The famous spring in Syracuse, Sicily</note>. I say this because the heaviest, hardest, and coldest waters are so for the same reasons: they are harder to process. Some have too much earthy matter, while others are excessively cold. <margin>20</margin> Waters that heat up quickly are light and healthy. In **Crannon**, there is water that warms up gently and, when mixed with wine, preserves it for two or three days. Running waters, such as those from conduits, are generally better than stagnant ones, becoming softer through their lightness. This is why water from snow is thought to be good; for the most potable part is drawn upward <note>referring to evaporation and precipitation</note>. Water is "beaten" by the air. Therefore, rain water is better, as is water from ice, because it is lighter. The proof of this is that ice itself is lighter than other water. 

Cold waters are hard because they are more earthy. Dense water, when heated, becomes hotter, and when cooled, becomes colder. For this same reason, water in the mountains is more potable than that in the plains, for it is less mixed with earthy matter. The earthy quality also gives color to water; for instance, near the lake in **Babylon**, the water turns red for several days. The **Borysthenes** <note>The modern Dnieper River</note> becomes violet-colored at certain times, despite being exceptionally white. This is a sign of what was said above, due to the lightness of the northern waters. <margin>30</margin> In many places there are springs that are quite potable and even "wine-like," such as the one in **Paphlagonia**, which they say makes the locals who come to it slightly intoxicated. There are also salty-acidic waters in **Sicanos** in Sicily. 

In the territory of the **Carthaginians**, there is a spring where the substance floating on top is like oil, but darker in color; they skim this off into balls and use it for their sheep and cattle. Elsewhere there are "fatty" springs, like the one in **Asia** about which **Alexander the Great** wrote, saying he had found "oil-springs." Some naturally warm waters are sweet, such as those in **Aegae** in Cilicia, or near **Tragasae** in the Troad region of **Larissa**. Also near **Magnesia**, and on **Melos**, and **Lipara**. In **Prusa**, near the Mysian Olympus, are the so-called "Royal" waters. Those in Asia near **Tralleis**, and the river of **Charakoma**. Furthermore, the city of **Nysa** is so oily that those who bathe there do not need olive oil. Similar are the waters in the village of **Daskylus**. 

The waters in **Carrae** are dry and extremely hot. Those near **Mino's village**, which is in Phrygia, are rougher <margin>40</margin> and more fatty, as are those in the so-called **Lion's village** in Phrygia. But those near **Dorylaeum** are the most pleasant to drink. However, the waters near **Baiae** or the harbor of Baiae in Italy are completely undrinkable. 

By weighing it, I found the water from the spring called **Peirene** in Corinth to be the lightest of all in Greece. For I do not believe the comic poet **Antiphanes**, who says that Attica is superior to other lands in many things and has the finest water. For he says: "What a land produces, surpassing the whole inhabited world, O Hipponicus! Honey, bread, figs." By Zeus, it certainly produces figs! "Cattle, wool, myrtle, incense, cheese. And water so excellent that I would know it was Attic water immediately upon drinking." **Eubulus**, the comic writer, says that the tragic poet **Chaeremon** called river water the "body of the river," since it flows from the river. Just as we speak of the "enclosure of a fold," he says: "We crossed the river’s body." And our whole strength is nourished by waters. In **Tenedos**, there is a spring whose water does not mix with wine. **Herodotus** <margin>50</margin> says in his fourth book that the **Hypanis** river, for five days' journey from its source, is small and sweet, but after another four days it becomes quite bitter, because a certain bitter spring flows into it. **Theopompus** <note>A 4th-century BCE historian</note> says that near the **Erganes** river the water is acidic, and those who drink it become intoxicated just like those who drink wine. **Aristobulus of Cassandreia** says that in **Miletus**...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the properties of different waters. Having previously mentioned the Nile and regional springs, the text now catalogs specific springs associated with myths and historical figures, transitioning into a discussion on "water-drinkers"—individuals who abstained from wine.</meta>

-># FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS<-

In **Miletus**, it is said there is a spring called the **Achilleion** <note>Named after the hero Achilles</note>, whose flow is extremely sweet, yet the water sitting on the surface is salty. The **Milesians** say they first purified themselves from this spring after they killed **Strambelus**, the king of the **Leleges** <note>An indigenous people of the Aegean</note>. They also say that the water around **Cappadocia**, though abundant and very beautiful, putrefies in its runoff in a certain place, unless it flows beneath the peak. **King Ptolemy** <note>Ptolemy VII Euergetes II</note>, in the seventh book of his *Memoirs*, says that as they were advancing toward **Corinth** through the pass called **Contoporeia** <note>The "Pole-way," a rugged mountain path</note>, upon reaching the summit, they found a spring sending forth a stream colder than snow. He says many people hesitated to drink from it, expecting it would be too much to bear, but he says he drank from it himself.

<margin>Water-drinkers.</margin>
**Phylarchus** <note>A 3rd-century BCE historian</note> says that in **Cleator** there is a spring from which those who drink can no longer endure even the smell of wine. **Clearchus** <note>A philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> says that water is said to be "white," just as fire appears in milk. Wine, like nectar, is described as red. Honey and oil are yellow-green <note>original: "chloron"</note>. But the juice squeezed from perfumes is black. **Eubulus** <note>A poet of Middle Comedy</note> says that water makes those who drink only it "inventive," while wine obscures our wisdom. **Philitas** <note>A scholar-poet from Cos</note> says the same in his iambic verses, mentioning how many "water-drinkers" the orators were. After resting for a short while, **Amphis** the comic poet says something like this:

> "There is, it seems, reason even in wine."

But some who drink water are foolish. **Antiphanes** <note>A prolific comic playwright</note> says: "Drive out wine with wine, a weary task with another task, a trumpet with a trumpet, a shouter with a herald, noise with noise, a prostitute with a three-obol coin <note>A small Greek coin; the price of a cheap prostitute</note>, stubbornness with stubbornness, a sword with a **Callistratus** <note>likely a reference to a specific famous sword or soldier</note> blade, sedition with sedition, battle with battle, and beatings with bruises, labor with labor, a lawsuit with a lawsuit, and a wife with a wife." Note that the ancients also used the term "unmixed" <note>original: "akratos," usually reserved for strong wine</note> in reference to water. **Sophron** says, "Unmixed water into the cup." **Phylarchus** says that **Theodorus of Larissa** was a water-drinker, a man who was always hostile toward **King Antigonus**.

<margin>Water and frugality.</margin>
He also says that all the **Iberians** <note>People of the Spanish peninsula</note> are water-drinkers, even though they are the wealthiest of men. He says they always eat only one meal a day due to their frugality <note>original: "mikrologian," implying a strict or stingy management of resources</note>, even though they wear the most expensive clothing.

<margin>Water-drinkers.</margin>
**Aristotle** and **Theophrastus** record that a certain **Philinus** never used any drink or other food throughout his whole life except for milk alone. **Pythermus**, in his account of the tyrants of **Piraeus**, records **Glaucon** as a water-drinker. **Hegesander of Delphi** says that **Anchimalus** and **Moschus**, who were sophists in **Elis**, were water-drinkers their whole lives; they ate only figs and, despite this <unclear>with hollow</unclear> bodies, they were quite robust. However, their sweat was so foul-smelling that everyone avoided them in the public baths. **Matris the Athenian**, for as long as he lived, ate nothing except a few small grey mullets. He abstained from wine and everything else except water. **Lamprus** the musician was also a water-drinker, about whom **Phrynichus** says that "the gulls wail among those where Lamprus died, himself a water-drinker." **Minyrus**, a man who looked down on fine food, was a "skeleton of nightingales" and a shiver of fever; a hymn to himself. **Machon** the comic poet mentions **Moschion** as a water-drinker. **Aristotle**, in his treatise *On Drunkenness*, says that some who ate salty foods remained without thirst, one of whom was **Archonides of Argos**. **Mago the Carthaginian** crossed the desert three times eating dry barley and not drinking. **Polemon the Academic**, starting from age thirty, drank only water until his death, as **Antigonus of Carystus** stated. **Demetrius of Scepsis** says that **Diocles of Peparethus** drank cold water until the end of his life. A worthy witness to this habit is the orator **Demosthenes**, who claimed he drank only water for a certain time. **Pytheas** at least says: "But look at the popular leaders of today, **Demosthenes** and **Demades**, how contrary they are in their lives. For one is a water-drinker and meditates through the nights, as they say; while the other is a pimp and a drunkard, and every day he comes before us in the assembly belly-first."

<margin>Lasyrtras the non-drinker.</margin>
**Euphorion of Chalcis** writes something like this: **Lasyrtras the Lasionian** did not even require drink as others do, yet he passed liquid <note>original: "eremon," likely a euphemism for urine</note> just as all men do. And many, out of a desire for honor, tried to catch him in a lie, but gave up before finding out how it was done. For in the summer season, even when it was foul weather, they watched him closely; and while no one saw him abstaining from salty food, his bladder remained <unclear>truthfully</unclear> silent as if he had drunk, but nonetheless he would then accept various kinds of foods. **Antiphanes** says: "If something is sweet, and is in the middle of things often talked about and is an <unclear>unusual thing</unclear>, it provides a double pleasure."

<margin>Choaspian royal water, and more.</margin>
The **King of the Persians**, as **Herodotus** says in his first book, carries water with him from the **Choaspes** <note>A river in Persia</note> that flows by **Susa**, which is the only water the King drinks. Great numbers of four-wheeled mule wagons follow him, carrying this water, which has been boiled, in silver vessels. **Ctesias of Cnidus** also records how they boil the "royal water" and how, once placed in the vessels, it is carried for the King; he says it is both the lightest and the sweetest. Also, the second **King of Egypt**, surnamed **Philadelphus**, when he gave his daughter **Berenice** in marriage to **Antiochus**, the King of Syria, took care to send her water from the **Nile**, so that his child might drink from this river alone, as **Polybius** records. **Heliodorus** says that **Antiochus Epiphanes** (whom Polybius calls "Epimanes" or "The Madman" because of his actions) mixed the spring in **Antioch** with wine, just as **Theopompus** says the Phrygian **Midas** did when he wanted to capture the **Satyr** by getting him drunk. That spring is...

-># BOOK II<-

<margin>Melampus on the mixing of wine.</margin>
There is a spring, as Bion says, called **Misomede** <note>Meaning "hating counsel"</note> at which people call out with a **Paean** <note>A hymn of praise or healing, usually dedicated to Apollo</note>. **Staphylus** <note>A writer on wine whose name appropriately means "grape-cluster"</note> says that **Melampus** <note>A legendary healer and seer</note> was the first to discover the mixing of wine with water. **Pleistonicus** says that water makes wine more drinkable. Note that for those who drink excessively, the stomach is not well-disposed but is rather damaged, and this often causes the food taken to spoil. Therefore, one who cares for their health must use moderate exercises—because of the much sweating they cause—and baths, so that the body might be dried out and softened. After these things, one should drink the best quality water; however, it should be cold in the summer and as warm as possible in the spring. He says it should be cold in the summer so as not to drench the stomach too much. One should drink in proportion to the quantity of wine, for the sake of replenishing the constitution, so that the power of the wine is not given off in its pure state, nor does it bite at the ends of the vessels while one is awake. 

If any of you feels unwell after seeing this, let him first take sweet or warm water, <margin>The use of waters.</margin> especially the so-called **protropos** <note>original: "protropon"; this refers to the "first-run" juice that flows from the grapes before they are pressed</note>, the sweet **Lesbian** wine, which is good for the stomach. Even wine that is slightly sweet does not weigh down the head, as **Hippocrates** says in his *On Regimen*. Some people title this work *On Acute Diseases*, others *On Barley-Groats*, and others *Against the Cnidian Sentences*. He says that sweet drink is less likely to cause a heavy head than wine-like drink, and it affects the mind less, being more naturally laxative than others. 

**Posidonius** <note>A Stoic philosopher and polymath</note> says the **Carmanians** <note>A people from the region of modern-day Iran</note> drink to one another in friendship. For while they are being friendly at their banquets, they cut the veins on their faces and, mixing the blood that flows down into the drink, they consume it, considering it the ultimate mark of friendship to taste each other's blood. After this consumption, they rub their heads with ointment, especially rose oil. If that is not available, they use quince oil to ward off the effects of the drinking and to avoid being harmed by the vapors of the wine. If not that, then iris or nard ointment. **Alexis** <note>A poet of Middle Comedy</note> says not badly: "Anointing the nostrils is a great part of health, providing good scents to the brain." 

One should avoid bitter ointments and drink water that is clear and transparent to the sight, <margin>Which waters are best.</margin> which is light in weight and has no earthy sediment in it. Water that is moderately heated and cooled is good, and when poured into a bronze or silver vessel, it does not produce rust <note>original: "iōdes"</note>. **Hippocrates** also says that water which heats up and cools down quickly is always lighter. He says those waters are bad which are slow to boil legumes; such are the alkaline and salty waters. In his *On Waters*, **Hippocrates** says good and useful water is very valuable. Stagnant waters are difficult, such as those from lakes and marshes. Most spring waters are also quite hard. 

**Erasistratus** <note>A famous ancient physician and anatomist</note> says that some people test waters by weight, but they are mistaken. For look: if the water of **Amphiaraus** and that from **Eriphia** are compared, one is poor and the other is truly excellent, yet there is no difference in their weight. **Hippocrates**, in his *On Places*, says the best waters are those that flow from high places and dry hills. For these are white and sweet, and they can bear a little wine <note>i.e., they are strong enough to be mixed with wine without losing their character</note>; they are warm in winter and cool in summer. He especially praises those whose springs break toward the rising sun, particularly toward the summer sunrise. For these are inevitably bright, fragrant, and light. 

**Diocles** says that water is digestive, prevents flatulence, is moderately cooling, sharpens the eyesight, and is least likely to cause a heavy head, being a mover of both soul and body. **Praxagoras** says these same things and praises rain-water. **Eunor** says cistern-water is good, and that the water from the **Amphiaraus** spring is excellent when compared to that of **Eriphia**. 

That water is admittedly nutritious is clear from infants, <margin>Watery nutrition.</margin> and some animals live on it alone, such as **cicadas**. Many other liquids are also nutritious, such as milk, barley-water, and wine. Indeed, sucklings are sustained by milk. Many nations of animals are milk-drinkers. 

There is a story about the diet of **Democritus** <note>The "laughing philosopher" who proposed the atomic theory</note>: when old age had weakened him and he decided to leave life, he reduced his food each day. But when the days of the **Thesmophoria** <note>A festival in honor of Demeter and Persephone celebrated by women</note> arrived, the women of his household begged him not to die during the festival so that they might celebrate. He was persuaded and ordered a jar of honey to be placed near him; the man lived for many days <margin>The use of honey.</margin> using only the scent of the honey. After those days, when the honey was taken away, he died. Democritus always delighted in honey. To someone who asked how one might live healthily, he said: "By wetting the inside with honey and the outside with oil." 

Bread with honey was also the food of the **Pythagoreans**, as **Aristoxenus** says, who notes they were always satisfied with what was served and remained healthy. **Lycus** says that the **Cyrnians** <note>People of Corsica</note> (who live near **Sardinia**) are long-lived because they always use honey. Unmixed water is also found among them. 

Observe the use of the word *anathemenōn* for "postponing" or "putting off" an inquiry. Note that *auxis* or *anēsis* <note>meaning "increase" or "growth"</note> occurs with a pleonasm of the 'a', like *stachys* and *astachys* <note>both meaning "ear of grain"</note>. It is found in **Cratinus**: "For you are not the first to come here to dinner *authis* <note>again</note>." As for the word *oxupeinos* <note>sharply hungry</note>: "I am delighted to see the *oxupeinas* <note>hungry man</note> naked," and in another place, "to know those who are always *deuthiontas* <note>hungry/longing</note>." **Antiphanes** also says: "He has a disease. For he is always *oxupnos* <note>sharp-minded or perhaps a corruption of hungry</note>." You say he is a **Thessalian** <note>Thessalians were stereotyped as gluttons</note>... And **Eubulus** says: "Coming to the holy plain of **Thebes**, he orders the house-servant..." For indeed, it seems the seasonings are worthier...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the Deipnosophistae (The Learned Banqueters). ### FROM THE ATHENAEAN "LEARNED BANQUETERS"

...cheeses. And you, keen-eyed one, or most musical Amphion, who brings the famous city of Athens from its cups. It is not easy to pass through the night
<margin>those who eat once a day</margin>
by those who eat only once. The "sons of Cecrops" <note>An archaic name for Athenians, after their legendary first king Cecrops</note> are hungry and "inhaling the breeze, feeding on hopes." The term **monositon** <note>original: "monositon"; one who eats only one meal a day</note> is found in Alexis: "Whenever you see a common man eating one meal a day, he either does not care for poetic songs or melodies." Believe that such a man has lost half of his life, and half of his art; both live with difficulty.

<margin>Sweetmeats</margin>
They called sweet foods **nogalismata** <note>original: "nogalismata"; dainties or sweet treats</note>. Araros says: "These elegant sweetmeats." Alexis says: "With Thasian wine-shoots he will be soaked for the rest of the day and enjoy **nogalizein**" <note>To snack on dainties</note>. Antiphanes mentions: "Grapes, pomegranates, dates, and other dainties." Philonides uses the word **apositos** <note>Having no appetite or fasting</note>, while Crobylus says **autositos** <note>Bringing one's own food</note>. Eupolis uses the term **anaristeton** <note>Going without lunch</note>, and Crates uses **anankositon** <note>One who eats by necessity or a parasite</note>. Nicostratos also speaks of a youth who by chance had a "bowl-cut" hairstyle and wore a short cloak: "I eat by necessity <note>original: "anankosito"</note> beneath the earth." Alexis mentions **aristhypnos** <note>original: "aristhypnon"; a deep sleep after lunch</note>, from which we might briefly understand the term.

After these things, we arose and reclined as each of us wished, not waiting for the
<margin>the usher</margin>
**nomenclator** <note>original: "onomakletor"; a servant whose job was to call out the names of guests and assign their seats</note>, the "commander" of the dinners. Note that among the ancients, there were rooms with two couches, three couches, seven couches, and so on according to the numbers. Antiphanes says: "I have gathered the three of you into a **triklinon**" <note>A three-couch dining room, common in Greek and Roman homes</note>. Phomylus says: "The seven-couch room was beautiful, even the nine-couch one." It was common even if you made Sicilian couches. He says, "But tell me, why five Sicilian pillows? Never was a three-couch room spread so poorly." Anaxandrides says: "The insolence of the **triklinon** was gathered together, or a flute-playing party for an old man. But open the guest rooms and spread the beds in order, and let the fire gleam with wine, the bowl be full, and the horn most sweet." 

They distinguish the arrangement or the covering of the bedding, and the "under-layer," as Plato the philosopher says.
<margin>Couches</margin>
The poet of the same name <note>Plato Comicus, a comic playwright</note> says: "And then we reclined on ivory-footed couches adorned with purple-dyed coverlets and Sardian crimson cloths."
<margin>Decorated bedding</margin>
The weaving of decorated fabrics reached its peak; they were especially crafted by **Acesas** and **Helicon**, the sons of Cyprians. These were famous weavers, as Hieronymos says. Indeed, at Delphi, on one of their works is inscribed: "Helicon, son of Acesas of Salamis, whose hands the mistress Pallas <note>The goddess Athena</note> endowed with divine grace." Such was also Pathymias the Egyptian. "As if on a skip, I long ago spread rose-breathing coverlets, and I wash myself, being sprinkled with perfumes," says Ephippus. Aristophanes says: "Whoever spends the night on sweet coverlets, having fallen in love with a mistress." Sophron mentions the "rolls" <note>original: "eligmata"</note> of a "soap-scrubbed" rug. Homer, the most wonderful of poets, describes the lower bedding as "smooth" <note>original: "lita"</note>, meaning white and not dyed or decorated. The
<margin>The spread linens honored by the Persian King</margin>
outer covers he calls **rhegea** <note>Rugs or blankets</note>. The Persians were the first, as Heraclides says, to invent the so-called "spreads" <note>original: "strotas"</note>, so that the arrangement would be elegant. 

Therefore, Timagoras, or Entimos as Phanias the Peripatetic says, was highly honored. Out of envy for Themistocles, he went up to the King <note>The Persian King Artaxerxes</note>. Artaxerxes gave him a tent of extraordinary beauty and size, and a silver-footed couch. He also sent luxurious bedding and a servant to spread it, claiming that "the Greeks do not know how to spread a bed." This Entimos was even invited to the "kinship breakfast" to entertain the King, an honor which had been given to no Greek before or after. For this honor was reserved for the King's relatives. Timagoras the Athenian, who performed prostration <note>original: "proskynesis"; the Persian act of bowing/prostrating before a superior</note> before the King and was greatly honored, did not receive this specific privilege. Of the dishes set before the King, some were sent to him from the table. To Antalcidas the Spartan, the King dipped his own garland into perfume and sent it to him. But for Entimos, he did many such things and invited him to the "kinship breakfast." The Persians took this badly, seeing it as a diminishing of their honor and a sign that another campaign against Greece might occur. He also sent him a silver-footed couch, bedding, a flower-patterned tent with a sky-canopy, a silver throne, a gilded sunshade, gold vessels set with stones, a hundred large silver vessels, silver mixing bowls, a hundred slave girls, a hundred slave boys, and six thousand pieces of gold—aside from the daily provisions given for the victory feasts—and ivory-footed tables made from so-called "maple" <note>The OCR "σφρυσίου" is likely a corruption of "σφενδαμνίνου" (maple)</note>. Cratinus says: "Maple
<margin>Tables are tripods</margin>
tables."

When someone in a comedy called a table a **tripous** <note>original: "tripoda"; a "three-foot" or tripod</note>, Ulpian the Sophist <note>A regular character in this dialogue</note> grew annoyed and said: "Today I shall have trouble with difficulties. Where did this man get 'tripod'? Unless he called it a tripod by counting Diogenes' staff along with his two feet! For everyone else calls these serving-stands 'tables' <note>original: "trapezas"</note>." However, Hesiod in the *Marriage of Ceyx*—even if the "sons of grammarians" <note>A mocking term for scholars</note> reject these verses, they seem ancient to me—calls tables "tripods." Xenophon, the most musical, writes in the seventh book of the *Anabasis*: "Tripods were brought in for everyone, about twenty of them, full of served meats." He adds: "Especially the tables <note>original: "trapezai"</note> were always placed for the guests." Antiphanes: "When the tripod was removed, we washed our hands." Eubulus: "Tripods are ready for you, and I shall become a collector of the fiftieth." Epicharmus: "What is this? A Sicilian tripod."
