# BOOK II

...and what monster has [four] feet. "Oedipus, going there, do you not understand the riddle?" <note>This refers to the famous riddle of the Sphinx, usually answered by "man," but here adapted to a joke about furniture.</note> Aristophanes says: "Bring us a table having three feet. Do not look for one with four." And: "Where will I get a three-legged table?" It was the custom at dinners for the host, once reclined, to be given a small tablet <note>original: "grammation"; a precursor to the modern menu</note>
<margin>Damsons, also called plums, or *brabyla*.</margin>
containing a list of the prepared dishes, so that he might know what the cook was about to bring. **Damsons** <note>original: "Damaskena"; plums from Damascus</note> are mentioned by many of the ancients, Damascus being a hospitable and great city. Since the land of the Damascenes produces the plum-tree <note>original: "kokkymelon"</note> in abundance and it is cultivated most beautifully, the fruit is specifically called a "Damson," as it is distinct from those produced in other regions. These are a type of plum, which others mention, such as Hipponax: "Wearing a crown of plums <note>original: "kokkymelon"</note> and mint." Alexis says: "Indeed, in my sleep, I think I have seen a victory-prize. Tell him, pay close attention now. In the stadium, one of my rivals seemed to come to me naked and crown me with a twisted crown of plums. By Heracles! You have seen a son of the ripe fruit again, well-prepared, or perhaps stuffed with a plum-filling." The gathering of ripe plums gives such a look to the forehead. Nicander says, "He shall call it the cuckoo's apple" <note>original: "melon ho kokkygos"; a pun on "kokkymelon"</note>. Clearchus the Peripatetic <note>A student of Aristotle's school</note> says that the Rhodians and Sicilians call plums **brabyla**, as does Theocritus the Syracusan: "The branches were weighed down to the ground with *brabyla*." And again: "As much as an apple is sweeter than a *brabyla*." The fruit is always smaller in circumference than the plums, but the same in eating, except a little more tart. Seleucus, in his *Glossary*, says that *brabyla*, *kla*, *kokkymela*, and *mabyla* are all the same thing. He says *mabyla* are like "apple-bursts," while *brabyla* are so named because they are "easy on the bowels" <note>original: "eukoilia"; referring to their laxative properties</note> and expel food. *Kla* are like apples, as Demetrius Ixion says in his *Etymology*. Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany"</note> speaks of plums and *spondiai*, which are similar, like wild plums. He unclearly calls the tree the "plum-tree" <note>original: "kokkymelea"</note> and the fruit the "plum" <note>original: "kokkymelon"</note>. Diphilus of Siphnos 
<margin>Book 3, Chapter 13. Cherries and ground-cherries.</margin>
says these are moderately juicy, easily digested, easy to excrete, and provide little nourishment.

**Cherries.** <note>original: "Kerasia"</note> Theophrastus, in his *History of Plants*, says: "The cherry tree is a tree of a peculiar nature and grows to a large size; for it reaches even twenty-four cubits <note>About 36 feet</note> in height. Its leaf is similar to that of the medlar <note>original: "mespile"</note>, but hard and thicker. Its bark is like the linden tree. Its flower is white, similar to the pear or medlar, composed of small flowers in a cluster, very numerous. The fruit is red, similar to the 'double-fired' <note>original: "disapyros"</note> fruit in shape. In size, it is like a bean, but whereas the 'double-fired' fruit has a hard stone, the cherry has a soft one." Again, he mentions the *praiatagos*; some call it *praitagos*. It has a long leaf, like the medlar, though it is larger and broader, or more oblong, with the same serration. The tree does not grow very large or thick. Its wood is variegated, yellowish, and strong. It has smooth bark like the medlar, and usually has a single root going deep. Its fruit is round, the size of a *dastinos* <note>An unknown fruit or measurement</note>. When ripe, it is yellowish and then turns black. It has the taste and juice of a medlar, so it might seem to be more like a wild medlar. "From these descriptions," says the philosopher, "it seems he is describing what is now called the **cherry**." Asclepiades of Myrlea says that some call a certain tree the **ground-cherry** <note>original: "chamaikerasos"</note>: "In the land of the Bithynians, the ground-cherry grows, whose root is not large, but it is not a tree, but a shrub. The fruit is in all other respects similar, but is more mealy inside, and like wine it weighs down the head and causes pain." 
<margin>Mimaikyla.</margin>
These things Asclepiades says seem to me to refer to the **mimaikyla** <note>The fruit of the Arbutus or strawberry tree</note>. For such trees bear them, and anyone who eats more than seven of the fruits gets a headache. Aristophanes says: "In the mountains, many *mimaikyla* grow spontaneously." Theopompus: "Myrtles and ripe *mimaikyla* for the goats." Crates: "For the girl whose breasts are as ripe as an apple or *mimaikyla*." Amipsias: "Wherever you see a furnace of mulberries, the fruit of the *apyle*, the arbutus, or *mimaikyla*." Theophrastus: "The arbutus, which bears the edible *mimaikylon*." 

Since **agloai** <note>An obscure fruit name</note>, a kind of satyric food, are discussed, like the poem made by the man from Catania, or Byzantium, or even King Alexander himself. Larensis <note>The Roman host of the banquet</note> says among the rhetoricians: "You Greeks claim many things as your own, either naming them or being the first to find them. You are ignorant that Lucullus, the Roman general who defeated Mithridates and Tigranes, was the first to bring this plant to Italy from Cerasus, a city of Pontus. He is the one who called the fruit the **cherry** <note>original: "kerasion"</note> after the name of the city, as our historians record." How then can a man like Daphnus say this? For a man much older than Lucullus, the distinguished 
<margin>Cherries.</margin>
Diphilus of Siphnos, who lived in the time of King Lysimachus (one of Alexander's successors), mentions cherries, saying: "Cherries are good for the stomach, juicy, provide little nourishment, and when taken cold, are good for the stomach; the redder ones and those from Miletus are better, for they are purgative."

The term *sykamina* is also used for the fruit of the Egyptian fig tree, which some call "sycamore-figs" <note>original: "sykomora"</note>. The locals graze them slightly with an iron tool and leave them on the trees. When moved by the wind, they become ripe and fragrant within three days...

# FROM THE ATHENAEUS DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...they are produced, especially when the West Winds blow, and they are edible because they have a gentle coolness. For those with fevers, when applied with rose oil, it benefits the stomach, and it is no small comfort to the sick. The Egyptian sycamore <note>original: "sykaminos"; specifically the *Ficus sycomorus*, which produces fruit directly on its trunk</note> bears this fruit from its wood, and not from the fruit-bearing branches.

<margin>Mulberries.</margin>
Aeschylus says that mulberries <note>original: "mora"</note> are the same as sycamines; in his play *The Phrygians*, speaking of Hector, he says: "He was riper than a mulberry <note>original: "morōi"</note> dropped from the branch." And in *The Cretan Women*:
> For it teems with mulberries, both white and black,
> And those that look like vermilion, this golden thing.

Sophocles says:
> First you will see the white blooming stalk,
> Then the rounded mulberry <note>original: "moron"</note> turning blood-red.

And Nicander in his *Georgics* shows that it appears before other "peak-fruits" <note>original: "akrodryōn"; fruits that grow on the tips of branches, generally meaning nuts or fruits with hard shells</note>, saying: "I always look for the beautiful mulberry-tree <note>original: "moreō"</note>... it is a delight to young children, being the first to announce the sweet autumn to mortals." Phanias of Eresus <note>The OCR reads "Ephesian," but Phanias was from Eresus</note>, the student of Aristotle, calls the fruit of the wild sycamore a "mulberry," which is very sweet and pleasant when it has ripened. He writes as follows: "The mulberry of the bramble, when the sycamore-like sphere has dried, has riddling mulberry-like divisions, as if woven together, and has differences that are crumbly and juicy."

<margin>Sycamines.</margin>
Parthenius says "abrona" are sycamines, which some call mulberries. Salmonius calls these same things "batia" <note>original: "batia"; bramble-berries or blackberries</note>. Demetrius Ixion says sycamines and mulberries are the same, saying: "The mulberries are flowing and better than figs." Diphilus of Siphnos, the physician, writes as follows: "Sycamines, which are also called mulberries, are moderately juicy, but provide little nourishment; they are good for the stomach and easily excreted." Specifically,

<margin>Epidemic of a 'devouring' disease.</margin>
the juice of these will expel intestinal worms. Pythermus, as Hegesander relates, records that in his time the sycamore trees did not bear fruit for twenty years, and such an epidemic occurred that not only were **men** chilled by the suffering, but also beardless boys and girls, and even women. The dread reached such a point even among the goat-herds that two-thirds of the sheep were chilled by the same condition.

<margin>Nuts.</margin>
Nuts <note>original: "Karya"; a general term for walnuts, hazelnuts, or any hard-shelled nut</note>: the Attic writers and other authors generally call all "peak-fruits" *karya*. Epicharmus specifically calls almonds "crunchy-eating nuts." Philyllius mentions "eggs, nuts,

<margin>Almonds.</margin>
almonds." Heracleon of Ephesus says: "They used to call almonds *karya*, as well as what are now called chestnuts <note>original: "kasianua"</note>." These nuts also appear in Sophocles: "Nut-bearing ash trees." Eupolis mentions "beech-mast, nuts, and small nuts." Some are also called "musk-nuts." As for **almonds**, those from Naxos were remembered by the ancients, and indeed various kinds are produced on the island of Naxos, as I have been persuaded. Phrynichus says: "He knocked out all my molars, as if he were breaking a Naxian almond." Different almonds are also produced on the island of Cyprus; for compared to those elsewhere, they are both elongated and curved at the tip. Seleucus says in his *Glossary* that the Spartans call large nuts "mykeras," and the Tians call sweet nuts by that name. Ameipsias says the almond is called "mykeros." Eating almonds before drinking is very effective at preventing drunkenness. Eupolis says: "Give him Naxian almonds to chew, and wine to drink from Naxian vines."

<margin>Bitter almonds for sobriety.</margin>
There is also a certain vine called "Naxian." Plutarch of Chaeronea says that in the company of Drusus, the son of Tiberius Caesar, there was a certain doctor who surpassed everyone in drinking; he was caught eating five or six bitter almonds before the drinking session. When he was prevented from taking these, he could not withstand even the smallest amount of drink. The cause is the bitterness, which has a drying power and consumes the moisture in the body. Herodian of Alexandria says they are called "almonds" <note>original: "amygdalai"</note> because after the green husk they have many "scratches" <note>original: "amykas"</note> on the shell. Among these, they are the "kings" of the dried fruits <note>original: "tragēmatōn"</note>, as Philemon says. A "wooden statue of the god Pan" made of beech-wood. Nicander says in the second book of his *Georgics* that they are also called "edible." Diphilus mentions: "Sweetmeats, myrtle-berries, honey-cake, almonds."

<margin>The accent of 'almond'.</margin>
Regarding the pronunciation of the accent on the word *amygdale*: Pamphilus thinks that for the fruit, the accent should be on the third-to-last syllable, just like the word for the tree (*amygdalos*). For the tree is meant to be feminine, like "rose-bush" (*rodē*). And Antilochus says: "The beautiful flower of the rose-bush." But Aristarchus pronounces both the fruit and the tree with the acute accent on the same syllable. Philoxenus supports both. Eupolis says: "You will destroy me, yes, by the almond!" Aristophanes: "Come now, take these almonds and break your own head with a stone." Phrynichus says: "An almond is a good medicine for a hiccup." Others treat *amygdalas* as a common noun. Tryphon says in *Attic Prosody* that the fruit is *amygdalē* (with a heavy accent), which we call *amygdalon* when eating it, while the tree is *amygdalē*. We use the character of the fruit as the standard for the name.

<margin>Pontic nuts.</margin>
Pamphilus says in his *Glossary* that the "nut-cracker" bird is called a "mykērobatos" by the Spartans. This is because the Spartans call almonds "meikēroi." Nicander mentions **Pontic nuts** (hazelnuts), which some call "peelable." Hermonax and Timachidas say in their *Glossaries* that the Pontic nut is called "Zeus's acorn." Heraclides of Tarentum asks whether these sweetmeats should be served beforehand, as happens in some places in Asia and Greece, or not until after dinner. If they are served after dinner, it leads to a greater consumption of food...

# BOOK II

...found in the belly and the intestines, the nuts served for the sake of drinking <note>The practice of eating salty or oily nuts to encourage more wine consumption</note> being mixed with the meals, produces flatulence and spoilage of the food, because their nature is such that they float on the surface of the stomach and are difficult to digest; from these come indigestions and bowel troubles. Diocles says that almonds are nourishing and good for the bowels, but heating because they have a certain pungency. However, green ones are less troublesome than dry ones, and soaked ones less than unsoaked, and roasted ones less than raw. Those called Heracleotic nuts <note>original: "hērakleōtika"; hazelnuts, named after Heraclea in Pontus</note> and "Zeus's acorns" <note>original: "Dios balanoi"; chestnuts</note> do not nourish in the same way as almonds, but have a somewhat grainy and floating quality. If eaten in excess, they weigh down the head, though the green ones are less bothersome than the dry. <margin>Peaches.</margin> Persian nuts <note>original: "persika"; usually refers to peaches, though treated here among the nuts</note> are no less headache-inducing than the chestnuts. They are more nourishing, but they roughen the throat and mouth. When roasted, they become more beneficial. They pass through the bowels best of all nuts when eaten with honey. The flat ones are more flatulent. Boiled ones are more beneficial than raw or roasted ones, and roasted ones more than raw. Philotimus, in his works *On Food*, says: "The flat nut called the Sardian <note>Another term for the chestnut</note> is <margin>The virtues and vices of various nuts.</margin> difficult to digest when raw, and all are hard to break down when held by phlegm in the belly, having a certain harshness. The Pontic nut <note>Another term for the hazelnut</note> is oily and hard to digest. The almond is less hard to digest; therefore, if we eat more of them, we are not bothered. They appear oilier and yield a sweet and oily juice." Diphilus of Siphnos says that royal nuts <note>original: "basilika"; walnuts</note> cause headaches and float in the stomach. Of these, the tender ones that have been peeled are better and have better juice. Those roasted in ovens are less nourishing. Almonds are thinning, diuretic, and purgative, but provide little nourishment. Since the green ones have worse juice and are more moisture-bearing, the dry ones are much more flatulent and float more in the stomach. The tender ones, being full and peeled, are milky and have better juice. Of the dry ones, the Thasian and Cypriot types, being tender, are more easily broken. Pontic nuts cause headaches, but float less than the royal walnuts. Mnesitheus of Athens, in his book *On Edibles*, says of the Euboean nuts or "castanas" <note>original: "kasana"; chestnuts. This is an early reference to the word 'chestnut'</note> (for they are called by both names) that the processing in the belly is hard to digest, and the digestion becomes flatulent. They make the physical condition thicker if one can master them <note>i.e., if the stomach can actually digest them</note>. Almonds, Heracleotic nuts, Persian nuts, and others of this kind are worse than these. One should not eat anything of this sort raw at all, except for green almonds; rather, one should boil some and roast others. For some of them are oily by nature, like dry almonds and chestnuts. Others are dry and harsh, like the acorns of the beech tree <note>original: "phēgoi"</note> and all that kind. Now, fire removes the oil from the oily ones—for the oilier they are, the worse they are—while the harsh ones are ripened if one uses a small and gentle fire. Diphilus calls the "castanas" Sardian acorns, saying they are both very nourishing and have good juice, but are hard to manage because they stay a long time in the stomach. The roasted ones become less nourishing but easier to manage, while the boiled ones cause less gas and nourish more than the others. Some have called them the "peelable nut" among the Euboeans, and others have called them "acorns." Nicander of Colophon says in his *Georgics*: "Agelochus calls the 'castanas' *amota*; where the Sinopean nuts grow, those people there call them *amota*." Chickpeas. Crobylus, roasting some green chickpeas, is entirely empty-headed <note>A line from a lost comedy</note>. "These sweetmeats <note>original: "tragēmata"</note> are for a monkey, surely a wretched thing." <margin>Chickpeas.</margin> Homer says: "The black-skinned beans or chickpeas leap." Xenophanes of Colophon in his *Parodies* says:

> By the fire one should say such things in the winter season,
> Reclining on a soft couch when one is full,
> Drinking sweet wine and munching on chickpeas.

"Who are you, and from where among men? How many years have you, my brave friend? How old were you when the Mede arrived?" <note>A reference to the Persian invasion of 480 BCE</note> Sappho says: "Golden chickpeas grew upon the banks." Theophrastus in his *History of Plants* calls certain chickpeas "rams" <note>original: "krieious"; likely due to their shape resembling a ram's head</note>. And Sophilus says: "The father of this girl is a very great man, a 'ram' chickpea." Phanias says in his *On Plants*: "Sweetmeats have their place; the tender ones are the bitter vetch, the bean, and the chickpea. The dry ones are almost all boiled or roasted." Alexis says:

> I have a husband who is poor, and I am an old woman, and a daughter, and a son's child,
> who are my whole concern. You recognize all these; three of us dine, and two of us share

> pale because we are without food.

The parts of our composition of life are the bean, the lupin, the green vegetable, the turnip, the vetch, the grass-pea, the beech-nut, the bulb, the *pipēx*, the chickpea, the wild pear, and that god-fixed care of my mother, the dried fig, the discovery of the Phrygian fig-tree. Pherecrates says: "Making the chickpeas tender immediately." Again: "Once, while munching roasted chickpeas, he was choked." Diphilus says: chickpeas are hard to digest, cleansing, diuretic, and flatulent. And according to Diocles, they are productive of flesh <note>i.e., they help build muscle or body mass</note>. The white ones are better than the black ones and the pea-like ones. The Milesian ones are better than those called "rams," and the green ones are better than the dry, and the soaked ones better than the unsoaked. They say chickpeas are an invention of Poseidon. # FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS

"In the porch, the leftovers that he left behind. But he did not choke from eating too much." Cleaenetus certainly did not... I know that the tragic poet himself never lost a witty word. Thus he is a lucky man. Lycophron of Chalcis, in a satyr play which he wrote against the philosopher Menedemus (from whom the Eretrian school <note>The Eretrian school was a minor philosophical sect founded in the 4th century BCE</note> was named), mocks the dinners of the philosophers and says: "And for Democritus, a parched lupin <note>original: "thermos"; a common, cheap legume often eaten by philosophers</note> danced, a companion of drinkers and couches." Diphilus says: "There is no trade more destructive than the pimp's; I want to walk along the road selling radishes <note>original: "rhaphanidas"</note>, hot beans, and olive-skins <note>original: "semphyla"</note>. Anything else rather than raising these [women]." And note, he says "hot beans" <note>original: "thermokyamous"; literally "hot-beans," likely referring to lupins prepared as a snack</note>, because they are still called that today. Polemon says that the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> call them *lysilaïdas*. 
<margin>Book 4, chapter 16.</margin>
Theophrastus relates in *Causes of Plants* that the lupin, the vetch <note>original: "orobos"</note>, and the chickpea are the only legumes that do not breed worms, because of their sharp and bitter nature. He says the chickpea becomes large when it decays. The same author says in the fourth book of that work that caterpillars appear in chickpeas. Diphilus of Siphnos says that lupins are cleansing and very nourishing, especially those that have been sweetened by thorough soaking. For this reason, Zeno of Citium <note>The founder of Stoic philosophy</note>, who was harsh and very irritable toward his acquaintances, became sweet and mild after drinking more wine. When people asked about the reason for the change, he said that he suffered the same thing as lupins: for they too, before being soaked, are most bitter, but once watered they are sweet and very mild. 

**Kidney Beans.** <margin>phasēloi.</margin>
The Lacedaemonians, at the feasts called *kopides* <note>A Spartan festival featuring meat and snacks</note>, give as treats dried figs, beans, and green kidney beans <note>original: "phasēlous chlōrous"</note>. This is recorded by Polemon. Epicharmus says: "Eat the kidney beans quickly, for Dionysus loves them." Demetrius says: "Either a fig, or a kidney bean, or something of that sort." 

**Olives.** <margin>Olives.</margin>
Eupolis says: "Skips and shriveled olives <note>original: "thoupiteis"</note>." These are what the Romans call *drupae* <note>original: "throuppas"; referring to overripe or wrinkled olives</note>. Diphilus of Siphnos says that olives provide little nourishment and cause headaches; the black ones and those that have been kept too long are heavy for the head. However, those called "swimming olives" <note>original: "kolymbades"; olives preserved in brine</note> are better for the stomach and act as a tonic for the bowels. The black "crushed olives" <note>original: "thlasas"</note> are also better for the stomach. Aristophanes mentions crushed olives: "Making crushed olives." Again: "The same does not apply to brined olives and olive-skins." And a little later: "For it is better to have crushed olives than brined ones." Archestratus in his *Gastronomy* <note>A famous ancient poem on fine dining</note> says: "Let wrinkled and shriveled olives be set before you." So that for the rest of time people might remember Marathon for a good reason, they always put fennel <note>original: "marathon"; a pun on the site of the famous battle</note> into the brined olives. So says Hermippus. Philemon says: "The cheap olives are called *pityeideis*, and the black ones are called *semphylides*." 

Callimachus, in his *Hecale*, gives a catalog of olives, including the *pityein*. They called the shriveled olives and dried figs "shriveled" <note>original: "thoupiteis"</note> because they were gathered after they had fallen, as Didymus says. And even without the word "olive," they used the word "shriveled" by itself. Teleclides says: "In time, the richest oil will be mixed with shriveled olives, barley-cakes, and wild chervil." The Athenians called the pressed olives *semphyla*. But we call the grape-skins *brytia*, which are the remnants of the grape after pressing; the word comes from the word for a cluster of grapes (*botrys*). 

**Radishes.** <margin>Radishes.</margin>
They are named thus because they "appear easily" <note>original: "rhadiōs phainesthai"; an ancient folk etymology</note>. They are also called *keteutamenas*, and the term *sysollo* is used among the Attics. Cratinus says: "He manages with radishes, but not with other vegetables." Eupolis: "Unwashed radishes and cuttlefish." That the word "unwashed" refers to the radishes and not the cuttlefish is shown by Antiphanes, who writes: "To snack on ducks, honey-cakes, shellfish, eggs, eels, unwashed radishes, turnips, groats, and honey." Specifically, "unwashed radishes" was the name for those they called Thasian. Pherecrates says: "There was an unwashed radish, and hot baths, and steamed salt-fish, and nuts." Plato says diminutively, in an exaggeration: "A little leaf or a little radish <note>original: "rhaphanidion"</note>." 
<margin>Book 7, chapter 4.</margin>
Theophrastus, in his works *On Plants*, says there are five kinds of radishes: the Corinthian, the Leiothasian, the Cleonaean, the Amorean, and the Boeotian. He says the Leiothasian is called Thracian by some. The Boeotian is the sweetest and round in shape. Generally, he says that those with smooth leaves are the sweetest. Callias used the word *rhaphanos* to mean a radish. In some place where he discusses the antiquity of comedy, he says: "Pea-soup, fire, turnips, radishes, shriveled olives, and flat-cakes." That he used *rhaphanos* to mean radish is made clear by Aristophanes, who, writing about such antiquity in *The Danaïds*, says: "The chorus would dance having rubbed themselves with stones and bedding... having girded himself with legs, sausages, and radishes." The radish was a very cheap food. Amphis says: "Whoever wants to buy radishes when it is possible to buy real fish from the market is mad." 

**Pine Cones.** <margin>Cones.</margin>
Mnesitheus the Athenian physician, in his work *On Edibles*, calls the seeds of the cones <margin>Ostrakides.</margin> *ostrakides*, and also calls them cones. Diocles of Carystus calls them "pine-nuts," while Alexander of Myndus calls them "pine-cones." Theophrastus calls the tree a "pine" <note>original: "peukē"</note> and the fruit a "cone" <note>original: "kōnon"</note>. Hippocrates, in his work *On Barley-Gruel*, says... [the text becomes fragmented]... are called *kokkaloi*.

# BOOK II.

...kernels. Most people call them *pyrenas* <note>original: "πυρηνᾶς" (pyrenas); typically refers to the pits of fruit or kernels</note>, as Herodotus does when speaking of the Pontic fruit. For he says: "it has kernels <note>original: "pyrena"</note> which are thrown away when it is eaten." Diphilus of Siphnos says: "pine nuts are very nourishing, they soothe the windpipe, and they cleanse the chest, because they contain a mixture of resinous quality." Mnesitheus says they fatten the body, and for everyone, those that are easy to digest are harmless; they are also diuretic and do not irritate the bowels. <margin>Eggs.</margin> Regarding eggs: Anaxagoras says in his *Natural Philosophy* that what is called "bird's milk" <note>A proverbial Greek expression for something rare or exquisite; here applied literally to the egg white</note> is the white found in eggs. Aristophanes says: "Night first laid a wind-egg." <note>original: "hypenemion"; an unfertilized egg produced without a mate</note> Sappho calls it by a three-syllable name <note>likely *oïon* or *oeon*</note>. They say that Leda once found an egg, and again, "one much whiter than a sheep." Epicharmus called them *oea*: "hollow *oea* and those of certain hens." Simonides, in the second book of his *Iambics*, says: "like a goose's egg <note>original: "oëon"</note> of the Meander." The word has been applied in four different ways. Anaxandrides used the diminutive *oaria* [little eggs]. And Ephippus says: "small jars of wine and Phoenician dates, little eggs, and many other toys for gambling." Alexis mentions "half-cut eggs." They called them not only "wind-born" but also "unfertilized." They also used to call what we now call the upper rooms of houses <note>original: "hyperoa"</note> "egg-rooms" <note>original: "oïa"</note>. <margin>How the egg was born.</margin> Clearchus says in his *Erotics* that Helen, being raised in rooms under the eaves <note>high up in the house</note>, gained the reputation among many that she had been born from an egg. But Neocles of Croton spoke incorrectly when he said that the egg fell from the moon <note>original: "Selene"</note>, and from it Helen was born; for he claimed that the women on the moon lay eggs and that those born there are fifteen times larger than us. <margin>Plutarch, Opinions of the Philosophers, Book 2, ch. 3. The Molionidae.</margin> As Herodorus of Heraclea records. Ibycus, in the fifth book of his *Lyrics*, says of the Molionidae <note>Legendary twin brothers, sometimes depicted as joined together</note>: "those riders of white horses, the silver-haired youths, the children of Molione, whom I killed—equals in age, equal-headed, single-bodied, both born in a silver egg." Ephippus says: "Honey-cakes, sweetmeats, wheat-cakes, groats, a hecatomb <note>sacrificial offering of a hundred</note> of eggs—all these were gaped at." Nikomachus mentions "sipping eggs": "For when my father left me his property, I rounded it off and shelled it in a few months, just as someone might sip an egg." Chionides says: "An egg, a kid, white eggs indeed, and large, fresh ones, as it seems to me." He says Leda bore these. Heraclides of Syracuse, in his *Art of Cookery*, says in his praise of eggs that those of peacocks are preferred, after which are those of the fox-goose <note>likely the Egyptian goose</note>, and he lists chicken eggs third. <margin>Appetizer.</margin> The appetizer <note>original: "propoma"; a drink or snack served before the main meal</note>. When this was being carried around during the dinner, the steward Ulpian asked if the word *propoma*, as we now say it, is found in any author. While everyone was searching, he said: "I will tell you." Phylarchus the Athenian (or Naucratite), where his discourse is about Zelas, the King of the Bithynians—who, having invited the leaders of the Galatians to a feast, plotted against them and was destroyed himself—says this (if I remember correctly): "a certain appetizer was carried around before the dinner, as is the custom at the start." Having said this, Ulpian asked to drink from a cooler, saying he was pleased with himself for remembering so readily; and he says that among the appetizers, eggs are prepared along with other things. <margin>Mallow.</margin> Mallows. Hesiod says: "nor how much benefit there is in mallow and asphodel." This is the Attic form; but I found in many copies of Antiphanes the spelling with an 'o' <note>moloche instead of malache</note>, on account of how it was written: "chewing a root of mallow." And Epicharmus: "I am gentler than mallow." Phanias says in his *Plants* that the seed-pod of the cultivated mallow is called a *plakous* <note>a type of flat cake</note> because it resembles one; for its star-like part is analogous to the crust of a cake, and in the middle of the cake-like mass is the umbilical center. And when the base is included, it becomes similar to the delineated sea urchins. Diphilus of Siphnos records that mallow is good for the humors, soothes the windpipe, and tempers surface sharpness. He says it is suitable for irritations of the kidneys and bladder, and that it is easily excreted and nourishing. The wild variety is better than the garden kind. Hermippus and the followers of Callimachus say that mallow is most useful and is added to what is called "the hunger-less and thirst-less food." <margin>Hunger-less food. Gourds.</margin> Gourds <note>or cucumbers/squash</note>. Euthydemus of Athens, in his book *On Vegetables*, calls the gourd the "Indian cucumber" because the seed was brought from India. The people of Megalopolis call it "Sicyonian." Theophrastus says there is no division of species among gourds, but some are better and some are worse. Mnesitheus, a friend of Erasistratus, says of gourds: "One is the Indian, which is also called *sikya* [cucumber], and the other is the *kolokynte* [gourd]." The Indian one is boiled if it is to be eaten, while the gourd is also roasted. To this day, the people of Knidos call gourds "Indians." The people of the Hellespont call long ones *sikya* and the round ones *kolokyntai*. Diocles says the best gourds (or *kallisa*) are found around Magnesia; additionally, he mentions a very large, sweet, and stomach-friendly turnip. In Antioch, they call it *sikyon*; in Smyrna and Galatia, they call it *thridax* [lettuce]; and *peganon* [rue] among the perfumes. Diphilus says the gourd causes little gas and is easily spoiled; it moistens the constitution, is easily excreted, and is good for the humors. It is better for the stomach when taken with water and vinegar. It is more nutritious when seasoned, and more thinning when taken with mustard. It is easier to digest and more laxative when...

### FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS

...kernels. Mnesitheus <note>A 4th-century BC physician from Athens known for his dietary expertise</note> says that certain plants are naturally well-suited to being prepared by fire, such as the cucumber <note>original: "σίκυος" (sikyos)</note>, the gourd <note>original: "κολοκύντη" (kolokynte)</note>, quinces, small quinces, and the like. When these are served cooked by heat, they provide the body with nourishment that is not plentiful, but is easy to digest and rather moist. All of these are also effective for the bowels. For this reason, it is better to take them boiled. The Attics alone call it the *kolokynte*. Hermippus says: "What a head he has, as big as a gourd!" Phrynichus uses the diminutive: "Either a little piece of cake or a little gourd." Epicharmus says: "He is even much healthier than gourds."

The comic poet Epicrates says: "What are Plato, Speusippus, and Menedemus doing now? In what pursuits or what kind of discourse are they engaged? Tell me accurately, by the Earth, if you have come with any information." <note>This is a fragment of a comedy mocking the Platonic Academy's obsession with scientific classification (diaeresis)</note> "But I know how to tell you clearly. For at the Panathenaic festival, seeing a herd of youths in the gymnasia of the Academy, I heard unspeakable and strange talk. For they were defining the nature of things, distinguishing the lives of animals, the nature of trees, and the various kinds of vegetables. And among these, they were examining the gourd, asking what genus it belonged to." "And what did they define it as, and of what genus did they say the plant was? Reveal it, if you know." "First, they all stood speechless and remained bowed for a long time, thinking. Then suddenly, while the youths were still bowed and searching, one said it was a round vegetable, another a grass, and another a tree. Hearing this, a certain doctor from the land of Sicily farted <note>original: "κατεπέρδετ'" (kateperdet); a common comic trope for total dismissal or contempt</note> at them for talking nonsense. They were terribly angered and cried out at being mocked. But Plato, who was present, very mildly and without any agitation, ordered them to start again and define what genus it belongs to. And so they continued their divisions." Alexis the charming...

<margin>The Appetizer.</margin>
...serves a whole appetizer <note>original: "πρόπομα" (propoma); a preliminary dish or drink served before the main meal</note> to those capable of handling it. "I took it just as the matter required. Water was given for the hands. He came bringing the table, upon which lay neither cheese nor kinds of olives,"

> "Nor side-dishes and trifles that provide us with no more than a smell. But there was served up a magnificent dish, smelling of the seasons. It was like the vault of the entire hemisphere, containing everything! For there were all the fine things from there: fish, young goats. A scorpion-fish ran through them. There was a snowy egg-dish, like a half-moon of the seasons. We laid our hands on it. The man talking to me was busy drinking at the same time. But now the contest comes down to me. The end did not let up until, by digging into the dish, I showed it to be a sieve." <note>meaning he ate it so thoroughly it was full of holes</note>

<margin>Mushrooms.</margin>
Mushrooms <note>original: "μύκητες" (myketes)</note>. Also, the best ones. "And at the mushrooms, a stone tub resounded." Poliochus says: "A small, kneaded, dark loaf of bread. Each of us had it twice a day from the bitter mill. And small figs and a mushroom would occasionally be roasted. And a snail, emerging after a drizzle, would be woken up again, along with native vegetables. And a crushed olive, and a little wine of doubtful quality for a drink." Antiphanes says: "That the bread is without life because it is fenced in with chaff, how cheaply it is equipped! And one bulb and some side-dishes of sow-thistle or some mushroom, or such wretched things as the place gives to us wretched people. Such is a life without fever, having no inflammation. No one eats meat when thyme is present, not even those who seem to follow Pythagoras <note>A reference to the vegetarianism of the Pythagoreans</note> when they go forth. For who among us knows what is fated for each of our friends to suffer soon?"

<margin>Cephisodotus, four books against Aristotle.</margin>
"Roast these two oak-mushrooms." Note that Cephisodotus, the pupil of Isocrates, in his works against Aristotle—and there are four books of these—reproaches the philosopher for not having collected the proverbs of Antiphanes, who wrote an entire play entitled *The Proverb*, from which the following is cited. "For I would eat it myself; I think I would even eat raw mushrooms and tart apples and any food that might choke one." Mushrooms grow from the earth, and only a few of them are edible. For most of them cause choking. Therefore Epicharmus said jokingly, "May you be choked as if by dry mushrooms." Nicander, in his *Georgics*, lists them and tells which of them are deadly, saying:

> "The hostile offshoots of the gnarled olive, the oak, and the reed lie there, these are the heavy-choking, sticky lumps of mushrooms."

He also says that when the stump of a fig tree is buried deep in manure and watered with ever-flowing waters, harmless mushrooms grow at the base, from which you should not cut any nourishing mushroom from a low-growing root. "As for the others, I will not allow you to read of them, and why you should then fear mushrooms," says the same Nicander in the same work. Ephippus says: "So that I might choke you just like mushrooms." Eparchides says that the poet Euripides visited Icarus, and because a certain woman with her children in the fields—two grown males and one maiden—ate deadly mushrooms and was choked along with her children, he wrote this epigram:

> "O Sun, cutting through the unaging vault of the ether,
> have you ever seen such a tragedy before your eyes?
> A mother and a virgin daughter and two brothers
> perishing together in their fated light."

Diocles of Carystus says in the first book of his *Health*: "Wild boiled vegetables: beet, mallow, sorrel, nettle, orach, bulbs, truffles, mushrooms."

<margin>Water Parsnip.</margin>
Water Parsnip <note>original: "σία" (sia); likely *Sium angustifolium*</note>. Speusippus, in the second book of his *Similar Things*, says it grows in water, with a leaf resembling marsh celery. Because of this, Ptolemy II Euergetes <note>Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, who was also a scholar and commentator on Homer</note>, who reigned over Egypt, thinks one should write in Homer: "around the water-parsnip..."

# BOOK II. 61

...if they are soft like sorrel <note>original: "λαπάνοις" (lapanis), a genus of plants including dock and sorrel</note>, nor like celery. For water-parsley grows with celery, but violets do not. Diphilus <note>Diphilus of Siphnos, a 3rd-century BC physician</note> says that mushrooms are pleasant to the taste, pass easily through the bowels, and are nourishing, but they are difficult to digest and cause flatulence. <margin>Mushrooms.</margin> Regarding these, those found on the island of Ceos often kill those who eat them. It seems that the most suitable ones are the thinnest, most tender, and easily broken, particularly those that grow under pitch-pines and pines. Unsuitable ones are the black, dense, and hard ones, and those that become discolored <note>original: "ὑποσόλωνοι" (hyposolonoi), perhaps meaning "livid" or "muddy-colored"</note> after being boiled and served; some of these, if eaten, are fatal. Relief is found by drinking hydromel <note>a mixture of honey and water</note>, or oxymel <note>honey and vinegar</note> with nitre, or pure vinegar. After drinking these, one should vomit. For this reason, it is especially necessary to prepare them with vinegar, oxymel, honey, or salt; for in this way, their "choking" <note>original: "πνιγῶδες" (pnigodes), referring to the poisonous sensation of constriction</note> quality is removed. Theophrastus <note>The father of botany, student of Aristotle</note> writes in his *History of Plants*: "Such things grow both below and above ground, like those which some call puffballs <note>original: "πέζικας" (pezikas)</note>, which grow alongside mushrooms." For these too happen to be rootless. But the mushroom has the beginning of its attachment in a long stalk, which extends as a root-like growth from it. He also says that in the sea around the Pillars of Heracles <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note>, when there is heavy rain, mushrooms grow near the sea, which he says are turned to stone by the sun.

Phainias also says in the first book of *On Plants* that some things do not sprout, and others do not even produce a flower, nor any trace of a seed-bearing head or germination, such as the mushroom, the truffle, the puffball, and the *helix* <note>perhaps a type of ivy or a specific mushroom</note>. The same author says that the puffball is called "ion" <note>original: "ἰὼ" (io), likely a typo for "ἴον" (violet) or a specific local name</note> by some, and "blachnon" <note>original: "βλάχνον" (blachnon), a type of fern</note> by others. Theophrastus in his *Plant Explanations* mentions smooth-skinned plants, such as the truffle, the mushroom, the puffball, and the *geraneion* <note>literally "crane-plant," here a type of truffle</note>. <margin>Truffles.</margin> Truffles. These also grow spontaneously from the earth, especially in sandy places. Theophrastus says concerning them: "The truffle, which some call *geraneion*, and any other underground plant." And again: "The birth and nature of these 'earth-born' things <note>original: "ἐγχροτόκων" (enchrotokon), things produced in the soil</note>, such as the truffle and the plant that grows around Cyrene, which they call *misy*." This is thought to be very sweet, with a meat-like smell, as is the *iton* that grows in Thrace. Something peculiar is said regarding these: they say they appear when the autumn rains come and there are heavy claps of thunder; and especially when there is thunder, as this is the primary cause. He says they are annuals <note>original: "ἐπέτειον" (epeteion)</note> and reach their peak in the spring. However, some believe they grow from a seed. At least on the shore of the Mityleneans, they say they did not exist before a heavy rain brought the seed down from Tiarae <note>a mountain or region near Mitylene</note>. There are certain places where they grow in abundance. They grow mostly on the shores and in sandy soil—for these are suitable conditions. They also grow near Lampsacus in the Acarnian soil, in Alopeconnesus, and in Elis.

Lynceus of Samos <note>A 4th-century BC student of Theophrastus and writer of comedies</note> says: "The sea sends up the anemone <note>original: "ἀκαλήφην" (akalephen), usually meaning a nettle on land, but a sea-anemone in a marine context</note>, and the earth sends up the truffle." And Matron the parodist says in his *Dinner*: "To bring mountain-bred truffles of Thetis the Nereid." Diphilus says that truffles are naturally hard to digest, but succulent and slightly soothing, and moreover, they are laxatives. Some of them are similar to mushrooms. Hegesander of Delphi says that in the Hellespont, neither truffles, nor the *glaukiskos* fish, nor thyme are found. Therefore, Nausicleides says of that wasteland: "It has neither spring, nor a friend." <margin>Truffle-leaf.</margin> Pamphilus in his *Glossary* says that *hydnophyllon* (truffle-leaf) is the plant that grows above the truffle under the grass, by which the truffle is identified. <margin>Sea-anemone.</margin> The "sea-anemone" is so called among the Attics because it is plant-like and causes itching <note>original: "κνησμῶν" (knesmon)</note>. Aristophanes in the *Phoenician Women*: "First of all there grew sea-creatures, then next the rugged anemones." <margin>Asparagus.</margin> Asparagus. These are also called marsh-dwelling <note>original: "ἑλλοὶ" (helloi)</note> and mountain-dwelling <note>original: "ὄρξιοι" (orxioi)</note>. Of these, the good ones and others were all medicinal for the internal organs. In Libya, they say those in the marshes grow as thick as a Cyprian reed and twelve feet in length. In the mountain and "ptokeanitid" <note>unclear term, perhaps a specific region</note> regions, they grow as thick as large giant-fennel stalks and twenty cubits <note>approx. 30 feet</note> long. Cratinus mentions the "aspharagos" <note>an older spelling of asparagus</note>. And Theopompus: "And then seeing an asparagus in some thicket." Ameipsias says: "A sea-urchin, an asparagus, and branches of laurel." Diphilus says that the "cabbage-asparagus," specifically called *ormenos* <note>the sprouting shoot of a plant</note>, is better for the stomach and more diuretic, but harmful to the eyes. <margin>Shoot.</margin> The *ormenos* is also a creeping plant and is harmful to the kidneys and bladder. The Attics are those who use the word *ormenos* for the sprout from the cabbage. Sophocles in the *Trackers*: "It shoots out stems <note>original: "ἐξερμενίζει" (exermenizei)</note> and comes to the surface." A "blastos" is that which comes from the first growth and sprouting. Antiphanes mentions asparagus: "The asparagus was blooming, and someone threw out the bitter vetch." Aristophon lists: "Capers, pennyroyal, thyme, asparagus, rue, buckthorn, sage, and tambourine." <margin>Snail.</margin> Snail. Philyllius says: "I am not a cicada, nor a snail, O woman." And again: "Sprats, mackerel, snails, and gurnards." Hesiod calls the snail the "house-carrier." And Anaxilas says: "You are much more untrustworthy than snails, who carry their houses through distrust." Achaeus says: "The snails, having mixed with one another, were crushed." A riddle <note>term: "γρῖφος" (griphos), a banquet riddle</note> is proposed at symposia concerning snails: "Wood-dweller, spineless, bloodless, path-moistener." Aristotle in the fifth book of *On Animals* says: "Snails appear to be pregnant in the autumn and the spring. They are the only ones among the testaceans observed to mate." Theophrastus says in his work *On Hibernating Animals*: "Snails hibernate in the winter, and even more so in the summer. For this reason, they appear in the greatest numbers during the autumn rains. Their summer hibernation is on the ground and under trees." Some of these snails are called "estidioi" <note>an unclear dialectal or specific species name</note>. Epicharmus says: "They exchange locusts for all of these."

# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS

Regarding the snail, it is not called *sisilos* just once, but quite often. Apillas, in his work *The Lacedaemonians*, says that they call the snail <note>original: "καχλίαν" (kachlian), a variant of "κοχλίαν"</note> a *sisilos*. Apollodorus, in the second book of his *Etymologies*, says that some people call snails "dinner-stoppers" <note>original: "κωλυσιδείπνους" (kolysideipnous), perhaps because they were difficult to eat or filled the stomach quickly</note>. <margin>Bulbs.</margin> Bulbs. When Hercules is eating these in Eubulus’s play *Amaltheia*, he rejects them, saying:
> "Whether it is hotter, or milder, or in between, this is a greater task for each man than capturing Troy. For I have not come here to stuff myself with stalks, nor with silphium <note>an extinct medicinal and culinary plant from Cyrene</note>, nor with those sacrilegious and bitter side-dishes, nor with bulbs. But as for the first of foods and the peak of strength, and that which somehow provides health in all its power—give me a great piece of boiled beef, and a sweet little pig’s trotter, and three fat roasted piglets."

Alexis, showing the power of bulbs as an aphrodisiac <note>original: "τὴν τῶν βολβῶν πρὸς τὰ ἀφροδίσια δύναμιν"</note>, says: "Pine-nuts, sea-crayfish, bulbs, snails, whelks, eggs, and trotters; one might find just as many medicines as these, but for a man in love with a courtesan, other things are more useful." Xenarchus says: "The house wastes away when used by masters with no whistling <note>this passage contains several corruptions in the original Greek; it appears to be a poetic or comic fragment</note>... but the boiled bulb, the roommate of the earth, is a supreme helper for friends." By the goddess! The many-footed octopus <note>original: "πουλύπους" (poulypous)</note>, caught in the dark eddies of the sea, the turner of veins, which with twisted necessities fills the vessel of the dish with its firm-bodied flesh for mortals.

Archestratus says: "I say farewell to bulbs and stalks served in vinegar-cups, and to all other such side-dishes." Heraclides of Tarentum <note>a famous physician of the Empiric school</note> says in his *Symposium*: "The bulb and the snail and the egg, and things similar to them, seem to be productive of seed <note>i.e., they increase semen</note>, not because of their primary natures, but because their powers are like an enigma." Diphilus says: "Bulbs are difficult to digest, but very nourishing and good for the stomach. Furthermore, they are cleansing and sharpen the eyesight, and are stimulants for the sexual organs." And the proverb says: "A bulb will do you no good unless you have a woman." Some bulbs truly stimulate the sexual appetite, particularly the ones called "royal," which are superior to others; after those come the red ones, while the white and Libyan ones are like squills <note>original: "σκυλλώδεις" (skyllodes), referring to the sea onion, often considered too bitter or medicinal</note>. The Egyptians enjoy all of them.

The so-called *bulbinai* are more succulent than the common bulbs, though not as good for the stomach, because they have a certain sweetness and thickness. Indeed, because of their great hardness, they are easily excreted. Matron mentions the *bulbina* in his parodies: "I could not tell of nor name the companions, the marrowy sprout with hair-like thorns. The *bulbinai* are the singers of Olympian Zeus, which the wingless rain <note>original: "ἄπτερος ὄμβρος" (apteros ombros), a poetic metaphor for water/moisture</note>, the son of Zeus, nourished on the dry land, similar to the flour-cakes of Leucothea. For these, the mistress belly yearned."
<margin>chap. 1</margin>

Nicander of Megara also praises bulbs. Theophrastus, in his *History of Plants*, says in several places that bulbs are so sweet that they can even be eaten raw, as they are in the Tauric Chersonese <note>the modern Crimean Peninsula</note>. Phanias records the same things. Furthermore, Theophrastus speaks of "wool-bearing" bulbs <note>original: "ἐριφοόρων" (eriphooron)</note> which grow on the seashores. He says there is a wool-like substance under the first layers <note>original: "χιτῶνας" (chitonas), literally 'tunics'</note>, situated between the edible part of the plant and the outer skin. Socks and other garments are woven from this material, as Phanias also states. Among the Indians, this substance is hair-like.

Concerning the preparation of bulbs, Philemon says: "If you want to see how much a bulb costs to be successful, consider: cheese, honey, sesame, oil, cabbage, vinegar, and silphium. By itself, it is wicked and bitter." Heraclides of Tarentum, in his *Symposium*, describes bulbs, or rather describes the excessive eating of them, and especially of those that have something viscous and sticky, such as eggs, bulbs, trotters, snails, and the like. <margin>Thrushes.</margin> For these require more time for the stomach to process, and staying there, they retain the bodily fluids.

**Thrushes.** These and other flocks of birds were served among the appetizers <note>original: "προπόμασι" (propomasi)</note>. Teleclides says: "Roasted thrushes with small cakes flew into the throat." The Syracusans call thrushes *leichēlas*. Epicharmus says: "The thrushes <note>original: "λειχήλας" (leichēlas)</note> that eat olive leaves." Aristophanes also mentions them <margin>lib. 9. cap. 20.</margin> in *The Clouds*.

Aristotle records that there are three kinds of thrushes. The first and largest is the missel thrush <note>original: "κίσση" (kisse), literally a jay, but here identifying the 'ixophagos' or mistletoe-eater</note>, which is about the size of a jay; it is called the mistletoe-eater because it eats mistletoe. The second is the size of a blackbird, which is called the *trichas* <note>the Redwing</note>. The third and smallest is the *ilias* <note>the Fieldfare</note>. Some call it the *tylas*, as Alexander the Myndian records; he says it is a gregarious bird and builds its nest like the swallows.

The short poem <note>original: "ἐπύλλιον" (epyllion)</note> attributed to Homer, entitled "The Song of the Thrushes" <margin>Epikichlides.</margin> <note>original: "ἡ ἐπικιχλίδου" (he epikichlidou)</note>, received this name because Homer, when singing it to children, received thrushes as a gift. Menaechmus records this in his work *On Artists*.

**Fig-peckers.** <margin>Sykalis.</margin> Alexander the Myndian records that they are a type of titmouse; some call them the "olive-bird" <note>original: "ἐλαιὸς" (elaios)</note>, and some the "fire-bird" <note>original: "πυρείας" (pyreias)</note>, but it is called a "fig-pecker" <note>original: "συκαλὶς" (sykalis)</note> when the figs are at their peak. There are two kinds: the fig-pecker and the blackcap <note>original: "μελαγκόρυφον" (melankoryphon)</note>. Epicharmus mentions "splendid fig-peckers." And again: "O herons with long curved necks, and seed-gathering hawks, and all-plaintive fig-peckers." These are caught during the fig season. Therefore, it is better to spell the name with one 'l' <note>i.e., *sykalis*</note>, but for the sake of the meter, Epicharmus spelled it with two.

**Chaffinches.** <margin>Spinoi.</margin> Eubulus, in his *Amaltheia*, names them among the things he mentions: "Roasted ones and cheese from the Chersonese cut in slices. Cabbage boiled in oil...

# BOOK II.

...let there be an abundance of lambs. Pluck wood-pigeons and thrushes together with them; and at the same time, let them nibble on small cuttlefish with their sprats <note>original: "μαινίσι" (mainisi) - a small, salted fish similar to a sardine or sprat</note>, and many tentacles of squid, served with care. And let them drink many cups of the strongest wine.

<margin>Blackbirds.</margin>
Blackbirds. Nicostratus (or perhaps Philetaerus) says: "What then should I buy? Tell me, after you have considered it. But go back and clean them thoroughly if you happen to buy them. Buy as many ducks as you wish, and thrushes, and blackbirds <note>original: "κοψίχους" (kopsichous)</note>. And as for those wild birds, buy plenty of them, and be merry." Antiphanes also lists starlings among the foods: "Honey, partridges, wood-pigeons, ducks, geese, jays, mackerels <note>Though "koliose" usually refers to mackerel, in this list of birds it may refer to a similarly named bird or reflects a mixed grocery list</note>, blackbirds, quails, and a hen. You demand an account of everything from us, and it is not possible to say a single thing without being held responsible." Furthermore, the "small sparrow" is mentioned by others, and especially by Eubulus: "Take four or even five small sparrows <note>original: "πορδικία" (pordikia) - likely a humorous or local term for a small bird</note>, three hares, and some well-fed little sparrows, goldfinches, parrots <note>original: "βιτάκους" (vitakous)</note>, ducks, and whatever else you might happen upon."

<margin>Brains.</margin>
Pig brains. The philosophers did not allow us to eat these, claiming that participating in them was no different than eating beans <note>Pythagoreans famously abstained from beans for spiritual and physical reasons</note>. They avoided the heads not only of pigs, but of all other "profane" animals. They believed that none of the ancients ate them because all the senses—which are the most vital part of the soul—are located therein. Apollodorus of Athens says that none of the ancient writers even used the word "brain" <note>original: "ἐγκέφαλον" (enkephalon)</note>. For instance, when Sophocles in his *Women of Trachis* depicts Hercules throwing Lichas into the sea, he does not name the "brain," but calls it "white marrow," avoiding the forbidden word: "The white marrow was scattered from his hair, as his skull was shattered and blood mixed with it." He names everything else explicitly, but avoids that. And Euripides, introducing Hecuba mourning for Astyanax after he was thrown by the Greeks, says: "O wretched one, how miserably Fate sheared the towers of your father’s head, which your mother tended with many curls! From the broken bones, the murder flows—lest I say something shameful." This interpretation of the poems is subject to scrutiny, for Philocles does use the word "brain": "Not even if I were to eat the brain." And Aristophanes says: "I would destroy your brain, and others too." So Sophocles might have said "white marrow" poetically, and Euripides perhaps wanted to avoid a shameful image when he spoke of the "broken bones." That the ancients considered the head sacred is clear from the fact that they swore by it. They also worshipped sneezes, which come from the head, as sacred. Furthermore, agreements were confirmed by a nod of the head, as the Homeric Zeus says: "Come now, I will nod to you with my head."

<margin>81. a.</margin>
They also added these things to the appetizer <note>original: "πρόπομα" (propoma) - a spiced drink or first course taken before the main meal</note>: pepper, scented leaves, myrrh, cypress, and Egyptian ointment. Antiphanes says: "If someone brings pepper for a price, they record it as a gift of a spy." Again: "But now they go around with pepper and the fruit of the blite <unclear>ictam</unclear>." Eubu-

<margin>pitch.</margin>
-lus says: "Taking a grain of Cnidian berry <note>a type of spurge flax used as a spice or medicine</note>, or even pepper." "Together with myrrh, sprinkle the path." Ophelion says: "Libyan pepper is incense, and a book of Plato has been struck by lightning." Nicander in his *Theriaca* says: "Or the many-poured leaves of fine-set savory. Often, having crushed fresh pepper, or cardamom from the Medes." Theophrastus in his *History of Plants* says: "The pepper is a fruit, and there are two kinds. One is round like the pod of a vetch <note>original: "ὀροβίου" (orobiou)</note>, and is reddish. The other is elongated and black, having seeds like a poppy. This one is much stronger than the other, but both are heating. Therefore, they are useful as remedies against hemlock." In his *Medicinal Matters*, he writes: "Or the application of vinegar and pepper, or Cnidian fruit rubbed together." We should know that there is no Greek name ending in the letter 'i', except for *meli* (honey). For *peperi* (pepper), *kommi* (gum), and *koiki* (doum palm) are foreign words.

<margin>Oil.</margin>
Oil. Antiphanes (or Alexis) mentions Samian oil: "And this for you is the whitest of all oils, Samian oil, because it is the best." Ophelion mentions Carian oil: "With Carian oil for the deer." Amyntas, in his *Persian Stations*, says: "The mountains bear terebinth and mastic and Persian nuts, from which they make much oil for the King." Ctesias says that in Carmania there is "thorny oil" <note>likely oil from the moringa or a similar desert shrub</note> which the King uses. He, in listing everything prepared for the King’s dinner in the third book of his *Taxes of Asia*, mentions neither pepper nor vinegar, which is the best of seasonings. However, Deinon in his *Persian History* says that ammoniac salt was sent from Egypt to the King, as well as water from the Nile. Theophrastus mentions "wild-pressed" oil <note>original: "ὠμοτριβοῦς" (omotribous) - oil made from unripened olives</note> in his work *On Odors*, saying it comes from inferior olives and even almonds. Amphis mentions how much the oil made in Thurii differs: "In Thurii there is oil, in Gela there is lentil soup."

<margin>Garum.</margin>
Garum <note>the famous fermented fish sauce of antiquity</note>. Cratinus says: "The wretched man among us will be full of garum." Pherecrates in *Triptolemus*: "Of salted garum." Plato says: "Dipping me in rotten garum, they will choke me." That the name is masculine is shown by Aeschylus, who says "the garum of fish."

<margin>Vinegar.</margin>
Vinegar. The Attics call this alone of all the seasonings a "form" of vinegar. The philosopher Chrysippus says the best vinegars are the Egyptian and the Cnidian. Aristophanes in his *Plutus* says: "Dipping it in wasp-vinegar." Didymus, explaining the iambic verse, says:

# BOOK II

...Pamphilus says in his *Glosses* that it is called lettuce <note>original: "thridaka"</note>. But Cleitarchus says that the Phrygians call it this. Ibycus the Pythagorean says that they call the broad-leaved lettuce, which grows from seed, "titanis"; it is called "eunuch" <note>original: "eunouchon"</note> by the Pythagoreans, and "astytis" <note>original: "astytida" – literally "non-erect," referring to its supposed effect on male libido</note> by women. For it is not at all diuretic, and it dampens sexual desire. It is, however, excellent to eat. Diphilus says that the stalk of the lettuce is very nourishing, though harder to digest than the leaves. The leaves are more thirst-quenching, more nourishing, and better for the constitution. Generally, lettuce is good for the stomach, cooling, easy on the bowels, sleep-inducing, flavorful, and an inhibitor of sexual urges. The more tender lettuce is better for the stomach and more sleep-inducing. The harder and less flavorful kind is also good for the stomach and bowels and causes sleep. Black lettuce <note>A variety of darker-leaved romaine</note> is more cooling and good for the bowels. Summer varieties are more flavorful and nourishing, while autumn varieties are less nourishing and lack flavor. The stalk of the lettuce seems to quench thirst. A lettuce similar to the "ever-growing" kind, cooked in a pan like asparagus, is, as Glaucias relates, superior to all other garden vegetables. In other works, Theophrastus says that "after-sown" plants include beet, lettuce-radish, arugula, mustard, dock, coriander, dill, and cress. Diphilus says generally that all greens are non-nourishing, thinning, and produce poor humors, and furthermore, they sit on the stomach and are difficult to digest. Epicharmus mentions summer vegetables.

**Artichoke.** <note>original: "Kinara"</note> Sophocles calls these "kynara" along with snails. Regarding the artichoke <note>original: "kinaran"</note>... "the thorn of the Artichoke <note>original: "Kinaros"</note> fills all the fields." Hecataeus of Miletus mentions it in his *Description of Asia*, if the book is indeed a genuine work of that author—for Callimachus attributes it to a person from the islands. The author, whoever he was, says: "Where the so-called Arkanian sea is, there are high mountains thick with forests, and on those mountains grows the artichoke thorn <note>original: "akantha kynara"</note>." And further on: "The Khorasmians live toward the rising sun, possessing land in the plains and mountains. In the mountains there are wild trees: thorn, artichoke, willow, and tamarisk." He also says that the artichoke grows near the Indus river. And Skylax, in his *Description*, says that in the mountains a different kind of artichoke plant grows. And further: "A mountain range extends along the river, high and thick on both sides with wild woods and the artichoke thorn."

Didymus the grammarian, explaining the phrase "artichoke thorn" in Sophocles, asks if perhaps he means the "dog-briar" <note>original: "kynosbaton" – the wild rose</note> because the plant is thorny and rough. For the Pythian priestess spoke of it as a "wooden dog" to the Locrian who received an oracle to found a city where he was bitten by a "wooden dog"; after his leg was scratched by a dog-briar, he founded the city. The dog-briar is between a shrub and a tree, as Theophrastus says; it has a red fruit similar to a pomegranate and its leaf is bright. Phanias, in the fifth book of *On Plants*, calls a certain Sicilian "cactus" a thorny plant, as does Theophrastus in his sixth book *On Plants*.

<margin>Cactus <note>In antiquity, "cactus" referred to the prickly cardoon, a relative of the artichoke, not the desert plants of the Americas.</note></margin> The so-called "cactus" grows only around Sicily and is not found in Greece. It sends up stalks directly from the root along the ground. It has a broad and thorny leaf. The stalks, which alone they call "cactus," are edible when peeled; they are slightly bitter and people preserve them in brine. It also sends up another straight stalk which they call "pternika," and this too is edible. The seed-pod, once the downy parts are removed, is similar to the "brain" <note>the edible pith</note> of a palm tree. This is also edible, and they call it "askaleron." Who, trusting these descriptions, would not confidently say that this "cactus" is the same as what the Romans call "carduus" <note>thistle/artichoke</note>, since they are not far from Sicily, and what the Greeks clearly name "kinara"? 

<margin>Thistle <note>original Latin: "Carduus"</note></margin> For if you change the letters, "cardos" and "cactus" would be the same thing. Epicharmus also teaches us clearly, listing the cactus among the edible vegetables: "poppy, fennel, and the rough cactus." While for others it is one of the foods eaten as greens, when cooked well it is sweet. And again: "lettuces, fir-cones, radishes, cacti." And again: "someone seems to be bringing wild fennel and cactus, sorrel, dock, <unclear>otosyllon</unclear>, scolymus, chicory, <unclear>thradaktylon</unclear>, fern, cactus, and donkey-thistle." And Philetas of Cos says: "A fawn might bleat, having lost its life after failing to guard against the wound of the sharp cactus." Furthermore, 

<margin>Artichoke <note>original: "kinara"</note></margin> Sopater of Paphos named the artichoke much as we do. He lived during the time of Alexander the son of Philip, and continued until the time of the second King of Egypt <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus</note>, as he himself makes clear in one of his writings. Ptolemy Euergetes, King of Egypt, who was one of the pupils of Aristarchus the grammarian, writes as follows in the second book of his *Commentaries*: "Near Berenice in Libya is the Lethon river, in which are found sea-bass, gilt-head bream, and a multitude of eels, and those called 'royal eels,' which are half again as large as those from Macedonia or Lake Copais. The whole stream is full of diverse fish. Since much artichoke <note>original: "kinaras"</note> grows in those places, the soldiers following us would all gather them and bring them to us, having stripped off the thorns." I also know of an island called Kinaros, which Semus mentions.

FROM ATHENAEUS'S *THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED*

<margin>Palm hearts</margin>
**Palm heart.** <note>original: "enkephalos phoinikos" – literally "the brain of the palm." This refers to the edible growing bud at the top of the palm tree.</note> Theophrastus, writing about palms in his work on plants, states: "The method of planting from the fruit is as described, but another method involves taking the part from the top which they call the 'brain'." And Xenophon, in the second book of his *Anabasis*, writes: "There, the soldiers for the first time ate the brain of the palm, and many marveled at both its appearance and the unique nature of its sweetness. However, this was also found to cause severe headaches." He adds that the palm tree entirely withers away once the "brain" has been removed. Nicander says in his *Georgics*: "With the palm-shoots from which they cut the brain, they carry a deceptive food for the young." <note>Likely referring to the sweetness that hides the fact that the tree must die for the food to be harvested.</note> Diphilus of Siphnos records: "Palm hearts are filling and very nourishing, yet they are heavy and difficult to digest; they cause thirst and can cause constipation." He says to us, friend Timocrates: "How much 'brain' <note>A pun on the food and the intellect</note> will I have until the end if we conclude our discussion of the collections here?" <margin>10</margin>

### FROM THE THIRD BOOK

<margin>Lotus pods and taro</margin>
Callimachus the grammarian used to say that "a big book is equal to a big evil." <note>A famous ancient proverb suggesting that brevity is better than long-windedness.</note> **Lotus pods.** <note>original: "kiboria" – these are the seed-vessels of the Egyptian bean or sacred lotus.</note> Nicander says in the *Georgics*: "Having sown the Egyptian bean, so that you may harvest the flowers for wreaths in summer... but the fallen pods of the ripe fruit provide for those who take them; pour them out into jars to offer to those who have long desired them, and I set out the parched roots at feasts." By "roots," Nicander means what the Alexandrians call **taro**. <note>original: "kolokasia"</note> He himself calls them "smooth beans" and "growth-buds." In Sicyon, there is a festival called the *Kolokasia*. **Kiboria** <note>the lotus pods</note> are also a type of drinking cup. Theophrastus writes in his *History of Plants*: "The bean grows in Egypt in marshes and lakes; its stalk is at its longest four cubits <note>About six feet</note> <margin>20</margin> and a finger's breadth in thickness, resembling a long, jointless reed. Inside, it has distinct partitions throughout, similar to a honeycomb. Upon this sits the 'head' <note>the seed pod</note>, which is twice the length of a thumb and has a color like a deep rose. Large leaves grow alongside it. The root is thicker than the thickest reed and has partitions similar to the stalk. People eat it boiled, raw, and roasted, and those living near the marshes use it for food. It also grows in Syria and Cilicia, but those regions do not bring the fruit to ripeness. However, around Torone in Chalcidice, in a moderately sized lake, it does ripen and produce fruit."

Diphilus of Siphnos says: "The root of the Egyptian bean, which is called *kolokasia*, is good for the stomach and nourishing, but difficult to pass through the system because it is fibrous. The variety that is least 'wooly' is better." Those who have seen them say the beans that come from the pods are green when fresh and are "washy," cause dizziness, are laxative, and produce much gas. When dried, they are less flatulent. From these pods comes what is called the <margin>30</margin> *phanotikos* <note>meaning unclear, likely a specific variety or preparation</note>. The Egyptians call it the **lotus**. My fellow citizens of Naucratis, says Athenaeus, call it the **honey-lotus** <note>original: "meliloton"</note>, from which honey-lotus wreaths are made; they are very fragrant and very cooling in the heat of summer.

Phylarchus says that Egyptian beans were never sown or grew spontaneously anywhere except Egypt until the time of King Alexander, son of Pyrrhus. Then, in a certain marsh near the Thyamis river in Thesprotia, Epirus, they happened to grow. For two years they bore fruit abundantly and grew well, but when Alexander set a guard over them and forbid anyone not only from taking them but even from approaching the place, the marsh dried up. Ever since, it has not only failed to bear that fruit, but it seems to never even hold water. A similar thing happened in Edessa. Apart from the other waters, a small spring of cold <margin>40</margin> water appeared far from the sea; those who were sick and drank it were greatly benefited. Consequently, many came from far away to use the water. The generals of King Antigonus, wishing to be "efficient," ordered those who drank it to pay a fee, and from that time the spring dried up. In the Troad, those who wished to take salt from Tragasae previously did so without charge. But when Lysimachus imposed a tax, the salt disappeared. When he marveled at this and made the place tax-free again, it increased once more. **Cucumber.** <note>original: "sikyon"</note> There is a proverb: "Woman, weave the cloak while eating the cucumber." Matron says in his parodies: "And I saw a cucumber, son of the glorious earth, lying among the greens; it stretched across nine tables." And Laches says: "As when a cucumber grows in a breezy place." The Attics always use the form with two syllables. Alcaeus, however, uses the form *sikys* as the nominative, like *stachys* <note>ear of corn</note>. Pherecrates uses the diminutive *sikydion* in his *Persians*. <margin>50</margin>
