# BOOK THREE.
## CUCUMBERS. FIGS.

<margin>Aristotle, History of Animals, Book 7, chapter 4.</margin>
<margin>Theophrastus, History of Plants, Book 3, chapter 11.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, History of Animals, Book 7, chapter 1.</margin>
...more radishes and four cucumbers. Phrynichus uses the diminutive form "little cucumber" <note>original: "sikydion"</note> in his tragedies. Theophrastus, in his work *On Plants*, says there are three kinds of cucumbers: the Laconian, the Scytalian, and the Boeotian. Of these, the Laconian variety is better when watered, while the others prefer no water. He also notes that cucumbers can be grown to be more flavorful if the seeds are soaked in milk or honey-water <note>original: "melikrato"</note> for a short time before being planted. He records these facts in his *Plant Explanations*, saying they grow faster in water, especially if they were soaked in milk before being put into the earth. Euthydemus, in his book *On Vegetables*, says there is a species of cucumber called the "dragon-cucumber" <note>original: "drakontias"</note>. Demetrius Ixion, in the first book of his *Etymologies*, says the cucumber <term>sikyon<gloss>The Greek word for cucumber, which the author derives from 'seuesthai' (to hasten) and 'kiein' (to go)</gloss></term> is so named because it "hastens and goes" rapidly in its growth, as it has a pungent quality. Heraclides of Tarentum, in his *Symposium*, calls the cucumber "earth-sweet." Diphilus of Carystus says that if cucumbers are eaten as a first course, they cause distress, as they repeat on the eater like radishes; but if eaten last, they are less troublesome and more easily digested. They are also considered moderately diuretic. Diphilus also states that the cucumber, being cooling, is difficult for the stomach to manage and hard to digest. Furthermore, it is said to "make the mind" <note>This may imply it makes one dull or, conversely, according to some ancient theories, that it settles the mind by cooling it.</note>, generate bile, and suppress sexual desire. Cucumbers in gardens grow according to the full moon, showing a visible increase in size just like sea urchins. 

**The Fig Tree.** I would not yield to any argument regarding cucumbers, even if I were to be hanged for it! Philoxenus—and by Zeus, I will not speak in a divine manner, though I have been shaped by it—says: "The growth of the fig tree was a dear guide for the life of humans in the countryside." This is clear from the fact that the Athenians call the place where the fig was first discovered "The Sacred Fig." They call the fruit of this tree the "Leader" <note>original: "hegeterian"</note> because it was the first discovered form of civilized food. 

There are many kinds of figs. Among the Attic varieties, those mentioned by Antiphanes in his *Namesakes* are praised. Commending the land of Attica, he says: "What things this land bears, surpassing the whole inhabited world, O Hipponicus! The honey, the loaves, the figs. By Zeus, it certainly bears figs!" Istros, in his *Attic History*, says that it was forbidden to export dried figs from Attica, so that only the inhabitants could enjoy them. Because many people informed on those who smuggled them out, those who denounced them to the judges were first called "sycophants" <term>sycophant<gloss>Literally "fig-shower" or "fig-informer" (from sykon 'fig' and phaino 'to show')</gloss></term>. Alexis says in *The Poet*: "The name of 'sycophant' is rightly most wicked as it is now applied. For whoever was an honest and sweet man should have 'attached the figs' <note>This is a play on words suggesting that a 'good' informer would be sharing the sweetness of figs rather than legal accusations.</note> in a just manner. But now, why has Apollodorus made it so that 'sweet' is attached to 'wicked'?" 

Philomnetos, in his work *On the Sminthians in Rhodes*, says: "The sycophant was so named from this: because at that time, fines and taxes consisted of figs, wine, and oil, from which they managed public affairs. Those who processed these items and brought them in were called, it seems, sycophants, and they chose the most trustworthy citizens for this task." Aristophanes mentions Laconian figs in his *Farmers*, saying: "I plant all kinds of fig trees except the Laconian. For this fig is hostile and tyrannical; it would not be so small if it were not a great hater of the common people." He calls it "small" either because it is literally small or because the plant itself does not grow large. Alexis, in *The Olynthian*, mentions Phrygian figs, saying: "That which is eaten by gods, my motherly care, the discovery of the Phrygian fig tree—dried figs." 

Many comic poets mention the so-called Phibalian figs. Pherecrates, in *The Krapataloi*, says: "O wonderful men, you shall suffer having cared for nothing. Eat Phibalian figs in the summer, and when you are full, sleep through the noonday; then get a cramp, swell up, and scream!" Teleclides, in *The Amphictyons*, speaks of how beautiful the Phibalian figs are. They also call myrtles "Phibalian," as Antiphanes does in *Leptinis*: "First of all, those myrtles of the Bacchic kind which we want, which we chew whenever we need to deliberate—these Phibalian ones, very beautiful for wreaths." Epilycus mentions "swallow-figs" <note>original: "chelidonion"</note> in *Brevity*: "Then there comes, after a little while, a small plate of tough swallow-figs." Androstion, or perhaps Philip or Hegemon in his *Georgics*, lists the types of figs as follows: "In the plain one should plant swallow-figs, wild figs, Lucerians, and Phibalians. But the 'royal-sparrows' <note>original: "sparobasilidas"</note> should be planted everywhere, for each kind has something useful. For the most part, the Kolkoroi, the Phormunioi, the twice-bearing figs, the Megarian, and the Laconian figs are beneficial if they have water." 

Lynceus mentions the figs grown in Rhodes in his *Letters*, making a comparison between the finest Athenian figs and those of Rhodes. He writes: "The wild figs seem to compete with Laconian figs just as mulberries compete with figs. And these are not served after dinner, as they are there, when the sense of taste is already distorted by fullness, but are served before dinner while the appetite is still untouched." If Lynceus had tasted the figs called "beautiful-sparrows" <note>original: "kallistrouthion"</note> in beautiful Rome, as I have, he would have become much more sharp-sighted regarding the namesakes. These figs have such a superiority over all others produced in the whole inhabited world.

### FIGS.

Other types of figs are also highly praised; among those found in Rome are the so-called Chian figs, the Libian, and those known as the Chalcidian and African varieties. This is attested by Herodocus the Lycian in his treatise *On Figs*. Parmenon of Byzantium, in his iambic verses, praises the figs from Caunus—an Aeolian city—as being of superior quality, saying: 

"I have come across the wide sea, bringing a cargo of Caunian figs." 

We certainly know that those from Caunus in Caria were also highly esteemed. Heracleon of Ephesus mentions a variety called "Toxalian" figs, as does Nicander of Thyatira, who quotes 
<margin>1</margin> Apollodorus of Carystus from his play *The Dowry-Hunter* (or perhaps *The Clothes-Seller*): "The little wine was very sweet; it was sharp and bad, so that I nearly choked. For the other Toxalian regions bear fig-trees, but my own land bears vines." Regarding the figs on the island of Paros (for excellent figs are produced there as well), 
<margin>10</margin> the Parians call them "Haemonian" <note>The name "Haemonian" likely derives from the Greek word *haima*, meaning blood, referring to the deep red color of the fruit's flesh.</note>; these are the same as those called "Lydian" by others, receiving this name from their blood-red color. Archilochus mentions them, saying: 

"Leave Paros and those figs and the life of the sea." 

These figs have as much variation across the many places they grow as the meat of a wild boar has compared to that of domestic pigs.

The "Leukerineos" <note>original: "leukerineos," literally meaning "white wild-fig."</note> is a specific kind of fig tree, and it is likely the one that bears white figs. Hermippus mentions it in his iambic verses: "Aside from the dried white wild-figs." As for "wild figs" <term>erineoi<gloss>The fruit of the wild fig tree, often used to help ripen domestic figs through a process called caprification</gloss></term>, Euripides mentions them in his play *Sciron*: "The sacred branches of the wild figs." And Epicharmus in *The Sphinx*: "But they are not at all like wild figs." Sophocles, in *The Marriage of Helen*, used the word "dusky" <note>original: "orphnos"</note> metaphorically to describe the fruit, saying: "The wild fig, though it is ripe and ready for eating, ripens others only by its reputation." <note>This refers to the practice of hanging wild figs in domestic fig trees so that wasps from the wild fruit will pollinate and ripen the garden fruit.</note> Alexis says in *The Cauldron*: 
<margin>20</margin> "And why do we still speak of ourselves, the ones who always sell figs in the baskets? They always place the hard and wretched figs at the bottom, but the ripe and beautiful ones on top."

And if someone has been cheated by buying such things... Timem[archus?] having swallowed a small coin into his jaw, sold wild figs while swearing they were garden figs. The late-born wild fig tree is called "erineos" in the 
<margin>See Homer.</margin> masculine gender. Strattis in *Troilus* says: "A certain wild fig tree of yours being nearby." And Homer says: "There stands a great wild fig tree, flourishing with leaves." Ameipsias calls the early, unripe figs "erinakas." Hermonax, in his *Cretan Glosses*, lists varieties of figs called "amadia" and "nikylea." Philemon, in his *Attic Words*, says that certain figs are called "Royal" <note>original: "Basileia"</note>, from which the "Royal dried figs" also get their name; he adds that fully ripe figs are called "kilypra." Seleucus, in his *Glosses*, says a variety called "glykysidê" <note>Likely meaning "sweet-skin."</note> exists, which closely resembles a fig in shape. He notes 
<margin>30</margin> that women avoid eating them because they cause "follies" <note>original: "mataismous," referring to delusions or silly behavior.</note>, as the comic poet Plato says in *Cleophon*. As for winter figs, Pamphilus says the Achaeans call them "Cydonian," and he mentions that Aristophanes says the same in his *Laconian Glosses*. Hermippus, in *The Soldiers*, records a variety called "Korakian" <note>Literally "Raven figs."</note> in these lines: "Especially Phibalian figs, or the Korakian ones." Theophrastus, in the second book of his *History of Plants*, says there are types of figs such as the "Chariteios" and the "Krateios." 
<margin>cap. 17.</margin> In the first book of his work *On Trojan Affairs*, he says that on Mount Ida there grows a shrub-like fig tree with leaves similar to the linden tree. It bears red figs, the size of an olive, but more rounded, and the taste is like a medlar. Regarding the so-called "Cypriot fig" in Crete, the same Theophrastus, in 
<margin>cap. 2.</margin> the fourth book of his *History of Plants*, writes the following: "The so-called Cypriot fig in Crete bears its fruit from the trunk and the thickest branches. It sends out a small leafless shoot, 
<margin>40</margin> like a little root, upon which the fruit grows. The trunk is large and similar to a poplar, but the leaf is like an elm. It ripens four crops of fruit per year, as many as its periods of new growth. Its sweetness is similar to a garden fig, but the interior is like a wild fig; it is the size of a plum." Regarding the "early figs" <note>original: "prodromoi," meaning "forerunners."</note>, Theophrastus writes in the third book of *Plant Explanations*: "When the air becomes soft, moist, and warm, it calls forth the growth, which is why they are called forerunners." He continues: "Again, some trees bear these early figs—such as the Laconian and the 'white-navel' variety—while many others do not." Seleucus, in his *Glosses*, says that a tree which bears early fruit is called "proterikê." Aristophanes also mentions "exceptional" figs in *The Assemblywomen*: "As if you had received divine things from an exceptional fig tree."

And Antiphanes in *The Hardships*: "For there is a way down right past that exceptional fig tree." 
<margin>50</margin> Theopompus, in the fifty-fourth book of his *Histories*, says that during the reign of Philip, near Amphipolis in Bisaltia and Graesonia in Macedonia, in the middle of spring, the fig trees bore figs, the vines bore grapes, and the olives bore fruit at a time when they would normally only be in bloom; however, this was considered an ill omen.

BOOK III

# FIGS.

...Philip to bury everything. In his second book *On Plants*, Theophrastus says that the wild fig tree <note>original: "erineos"</note> bears fruit twice a year. Some say it even bears three times, as it does on the island of Keos. He also notes that if a fig tree is planted in the shade, 
<margin>ch. 7</margin>it perishes more quickly and the worms do not destroy it; indeed, all plants 
<margin>ch. 14</margin>planted in the shade grow faster but are difficult to digest. Again, in his second book of *The Causes of Plants*, Theophrastus says that the so-called "Indian fig," though marvelous for its size, has small and scanty fruit, as if it consumes all its nourishment in its excessive growth. In the second book of his *Natural History*, 
the Philosopher <note>Aristotle is often referred to simply as "the Philosopher."</note> says there is another kind of fig tree—not found in Greece, but in Cilicia and Cyprus—which is an "early-bearer" <note>original: "olynthophoron"</note>. This tree produces the mature fig at the front of the branch and the early fig <note>original: "olynthos," a fruit that often fails to ripen or ripens very early.</note> at the back. These grow entirely from 
<margin>10</margin>the old wood and not from the new growth. This is the first of the figs to ripen and is very sweet, unlike the varieties we have here. This fruit grows much larger than standard figs. The season for it follows shortly after the initial growth. I also know of other names for figs: "Royal" <note>original: "basileia"</note>, "Royal-figs," "Yellow-bellies," "Wood-figs," "Deer-fleshed," "Shell-figs," "Nikridians," "Ithakontians," "White-faces," "Black-faces," "Hermes-figs," "Mill-figs," and "Ashkelonians." Regarding the name for figs, Tryphon says in his second book of *The History of Plants* that Dorion, in his *History of Agriculture*, tells a story: a Titan named Sykeus <note>A name derived from "syke," the Greek word for fig tree.</note> was being pursued by Zeus when his mother, Gaia (Earth), received him and brought forth the plant from the ground to provide a place of rest for her child. From him, the city of Sykea in Cilicia takes its name. However, the epic poet Pherenicus, a native of Heraclea, says that the name comes from Syke, the daughter of Oxylus. For Oxylus, son of Oreius, lay with his sister Hamadryas and, among others, fathered the Walnut tree, the Oak, the Cornel, the Mountain-ash, the Poplar, the Elm, the Vine, and the Fig tree. 
<margin>20</margin>These were called the "Hamadryad Nymphs," and many trees took their names from them. From this, Hipponax also says, "the black fig, sister of the vine." Sosibius the Laconian, demonstrating that the fig tree was a discovery of Dionysus, says that for this reason the Spartans honor "Dionysus of the Fig" <note>original: "Sykitis"</note>. The people of Naxos, according to Andriscus and Agatharchides, report that Dionysus is called "The Gentle" <note>original: "Meilichios"</note> because of his gift of the fig fruit. For this reason, among the Naxians, the face of the god called "Bacchic Dionysus" is made of vine-wood, but that of "Gentle Dionysus" is made of fig-wood. Indeed, they call figs "gentle-fruits" <note>original: "meilichia"</note>. Herodotus the Lycian demonstrates at length in his treatise *On Figs* that of all the so-called "woody fruits," figs are the most beneficial to humans, stating that nursing infants become much heartier when fed on fig juice. Pherecrates (or whoever wrote the play *The Persians*) says: "One of us, seeing a fresh fig after a long time, pressed it against his eyes as if it were a healing medicine for children." This was not just any ordinary fig. That most wonderful and gentle historian Herodotus, in the first book of his *Histories*, says that figs are a great luxury, writing as follows: "O King, you are preparing to campaign against men who wear leather trousers (and their other clothing is also made of leather) and who eat not as much as they want, but as much as they have, for they inhabit a rugged land. Furthermore, they do not drink wine, but are water-drinkers. They have no figs to eat, nor any other good thing." Polybius of Megalopolis, in the twelfth book of his *Histories*, says that Philip (the father of Perseus), when he was overrunning Asia and was short of supplies, accepted figs from the Magnesians for his soldiers because they had no grain. For this reason, when he gained control of Myus, he granted the territory to the Magnesians in exchange for the figs. 
Ananius the iambic poet also said: "If one were to lock up much gold in a house, and a few figs, and two or three men, he would soon realize how much better figs are than gold." After Magnus had collected so many 
<margin>40</margin>facts about figs, Daphnus the physician spoke: Philotimus, in his first book *On Diet*, says that soft figs have many differences in their juices, the seasons in which they ripen, and their medicinal properties. Generally speaking, those that are moist and ripe are dissolved quickly by the body and are more easily processed than other autumn fruits; they do not hinder the digestion of other food. The juices they contain are sticky, sweet, and slightly alkaline <note>original: "hyponitrodes," suggesting a cleansing or salt-like quality.</note>; they make the bowel movements more frequent and fluid, and they provide this relief quickly and without pain. They produce a salty or pungent juice if eaten with salt. They are indeed dissolved rapidly, which is why, even if we eat a large volume of them, we feel empty and light again after a short time. It would be most troublesome if the figs remained and were 
<margin>50</margin>not quickly dissolved. They are processed better than other fruits, not only because we can consume many times more of them than other autumn fruits without discomfort, but even when we eat our usual amount of regular food alongside them, we feel no heaviness. It is clear, then, that we can handle both: the figs are digested more easily and do not prevent the rest of our food from being processed. Their properties are...

ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS.

->FIGS. APPLES.<-

<margin>Figs.</margin>
...are so called. We observe that the "sticky" and "salty" varieties are named from their tendency to stick to and cleanse the hands, while the "sweet" variety is named for the sensation it produces in the mouth. Regarding their effect on the bowels—how they cause significant movement and disturbance, and make the passage more frequent, faster, and softer—we believe no further explanation is needed. Their form is not much altered [during digestion], not because they are indigestible, but because they are swallowed quickly without being chewed thoroughly. This makes their passage, so to speak, rapid. They produce a salty juice because it has been shown that figs contain an alkaline <note>original: "nitrōdes," referring to natural soda or salt-like minerals</note> quality; this will produce a saltier or hotter effect depending on what is consumed after them. For while salt increases a salty humor <note>original: "chymon," referring to the four bodily fluids of ancient medicine</note>, vinegar and thyme increase a pungent humor. Heracleides of Tarentum, in his *Symposium*, investigates whether one should take hot or cold water after consuming figs. Those who say one should take hot water argue that it is recommended because hot water quickly cleanses the hands; therefore, it is plausible that figs are also quickly dissolved in the stomach by heat. Furthermore, even on the outside of figs, heat dissolves their consistency and breaks them down into fine parts, whereas cold water congeals them. Those who say one should take cold water claim that the intake of a cold drink easily carries down the things sitting in the stomach. For figs do not sit well in the stomach, making it feverish and more irritated; for this reason, some people also drink undiluted wine immediately after. After this, it readily pushes forward the contents of the belly. They use a larger and more frequent drink after eating figs so that they do not remain in the stomach but are carried into the lower parts of the intestines. Others say that one should not eat figs at midday, for they are unhealthful then, as Pherecrates said in *The Small Heracles*. Aristophanes says in *The Rehearsal*:
"Once seeing him sick in the summer,
he gobbled figs at noon so that he might stay sick."
And Eubulus in *The Sphinx-Cario*:
"By Zeus, for you were weak, my good man,
having eaten figs at noon the day before."
Nicophon in *The Sirens*:
"If any of us eats green figs at midday 
and then sleeps, a fever immediately
comes running—not worth three obols <note>A small coin; a way of saying the fever is 'cheap' or common, but undesirable.</note>—
and then falling upon us, it produces bile."
Diphilus of Siphnos says that among figs, the soft ones provide little nourishment and have bad juices; they are difficult to judge, they float in the stomach, and are more difficult for the body to manage than dried ones. Those produced near winter, being ripened by force, happen to be worse. Those in the peak of the season are better, as they are ripened according to nature. Those with much milky sap and those that are unusual are better for the stomach but heavier. The "Heraclean" figs correspond to the "Rhodian" ones. The "Chian" and all others are of worse juice than these.

<margin>Mnesitheus.</margin>
Mnesitheus of Athens, in his book *On Eatables*, says: "Regarding all things eaten raw by those who are drinking—such as peaches <note>original: "pika," likely a variant for "persika" or peaches</note>, figs, Delphic apples, and such—one must watch for the right season, when the juices in them are neither undigested, nor rotten, nor too dried out by the weather."

Demetrius of Skepsis, in the fifteenth book of *The Trojan Array*, says that those who do not eat figs become "two-voiced" <note>This may refer to a clearer or more resonant voice.</note>. He says that Hegesianax of Alexandria, the historian, was originally poor and became a tragic actor and performer with a beautiful voice because he did not taste a fig for eighteen years. I also know of proverbs said about figs, such as these: "A fig after fish, later after meat." "They do not wish to plant figs for bird-lovers."

<margin>Apples.</margin>
Apples. Mnesitheus of Athens, in his book *On Eatables*, says "Delphic apples are good." Diphilus says that among apples, the green and not yet ripe ones have bad juice, are bad for the stomach, float in the upper belly, generate bile, cause illness, and are a source of shivering. Among the ripe ones, the sweet are colder and easier to pass because they do not cause decay. The sour ones have worse juice and are more restrictive; those that are slightly sweet but take on a bad smell through unhealthy decay are worse for the stomach. The so-called "Orbiculata" <note>A Roman variety of apple, named for its round shape.</note> apples, having a pleasant ripeness and sweetness, are difficult for the stomach. The so-called "Setania" and "Platania" types have good juice and are easy to pass, not being hard on the stomach. The so-called "Mordiana" apples are produced most beautifully in the place called Apollonia Mordia; they are similar to the Orbiculata. Quinces <note>original: "kydōnia"</note>, some of which are commonly called "sparrow-apples" <note>original: "stroutheia"</note>, are the most difficult for the stomach of all apples, especially when ripe. Glaucides says that the best of the tree-fruits are quinces, "Phaulian" apples, and sparrow-apples. Philotimus, in the first or tenth book *On Diet*, says that spring apples are much harder to digest than pears—the raw vs. the raw, and the ripe vs. the ripe. Regarding the properties of their juices: the sour and unripe ones are more astringent and acidic to drink, and they yield to the body the humor called "natural." In general, apples are harder to digest than pears, because we digest them better if we eat fewer of them, and worse if we take in more. A natural humor is produced 

<meta>from them.</meta>

BOOK 3

# APPLES.

Regarding these, there is the opinion expressed by Praxagoras <note>A famous 4th-century BCE physician from Cos</note>, who argues that fruits not properly digested will produce thicker humors <note>original: "chymous," referring to the bodily fluids that ancient doctors believed regulated health</note>. It has been demonstrated generally that apples are more difficult to digest than pears, and that those with a harsh, astringent taste tend to make these humors even thicker. Among the winter varieties of apples, the Cydonian <note>The "Cydonian apple" is what we call a **quince**</note> types are more astringent, while the *strouthia* <note>original: "strouthia," a smaller, sweet variety of quince, literally "sparrow-apples"</note> yield less juice and are more astringent to the palate, though they possess more digestive power. Nicander of Thyatira claims that Cydonian apples are actually called *strouthia*, but he is mistaken. Glaucides, in fact, provides a better account, stating that the best tree-fruits <note>term: "akrodrya" (tree-fruits), a category including fruits with a hard outer shell or firm flesh like nuts and pomes</note> are Cydonian apples, *phaulia* <note>a common, everyday variety of apple</note>, and *strouthia*. Stesichorus mentions Cydonian apples in his *Elena* as follows:
> Many Cydonian apples they once threw 
> toward the king’s chariot, and many myrtle leaves 
> and rose petals, and braided crowns of violets.

And Alcman says:
> And a beetle was watching 
> for Cydonian apples upon her breasts. 

Furthermore, Philemon, in his play *The Rustic*, calls Cydonian apples *strouthia*. Phylarchus, in the sixth book of his *Histories*, says that Cydonian apples, because of their fragrance, can even dull the effects of deadly poisons. He claims that when the Phariacan poison <note>A specific toxic substance mentioned in ancient texts, likely from Illyria</note> was placed near a small pomegranate, it became harmless due to the composition of these apples, losing its natural power. Indeed, if it were mixed and given to those who usually die from it, they would remain unharmed. This was discovered later during the interrogation of the man who sold the poison, who realized what had happened due to the proximity of the apples. Hermon, in his *Cretan Glosses*, says that Cydonian apples are called *kodýmala* <note>original: "kodýmala," a regional Cretan word for quince</note>. Polemon, in the fifth book of his *Response to Timaeus*, records that some people use the term *kodýmalo*. Alcman also calls the *strouthion* apple simply an "apple" or *kodýmalo*. Apollodorus and Sosibius both understand this to mean the Cydonian apple.
<margin>20</margin>
Theophrastus, in the second book of his *History of Plants*, clearly showed that the Cydonian apple differs from the *strouthion*. Excellent apples are grown in Sicyon; this is a village near Corinth, as Euphorion or Archytas says in *The Crane*:
> Like a mountain apple on the clay-rich banks, 
> the Porphyrian variety is found and nurtured in Sicyon.

Nicander also mentions them in his *Transformations* as follows:
> Straightaway he cut green apples from Sidoeus’ garden, 
> many of which are still grown for the benefit of Cadmus' descendants.

That Sicyon is a village of Corinth is stated by Arrian in the first book of his *History of Heracles*, and by Apollodorus of Athens in the sixth book of his *Catalogue of Ships*, and by Antigonus of Carystus in his *Antipatros*: 
> Far dearer is the winter season of ripe apples, 
> even the Porphyrian seaweed-red ones that grow in the windy air.

Teleclides mentions the *phaulian* <note>meaning "common" or "cheap"</note> apples in his *Amphictyons*:
> O you who are elegant in some things, 
> but in others more common than a *phaulion* apple.
<margin>30</margin>
Theopompus also mentions them in his *Theseus*, and Androtion in his *Work on Farming* says that some apple trees are *phauliai* and others are *strouthiai*. For the apple does not fall far from the... <note>The Greek text here is slightly corrupted or technical regarding the botanical grafting of these varieties</note>. As for the spring varieties, whether Laconian or Sicyonian, they were unknown. I myself have wondered most of all at the apples sold in Rome called "Mattian" apples <note>named after Gaius Matius, a friend of Julius Caesar who was famous for his gardens</note>, which are said to be brought from a certain village situated in the Alps near Aquileia. Not much inferior to these are the apples from Gangra, a city in Paphlagonia. That Dionysus <note>The god of wine, also associated with vegetation and orchards</note> is the discoverer of apples is attested by Theocritus of Syracuse, who says something like this:
> May apples be kept in the lap of Dionysus.

Cratinus, in his *Laws*, mentions a "sacred apple-tree of Heracles." Neoptolemus of Parium, in his *Dionysiad*, also records that apples were discovered by Dionysus, just like other tree-fruits.
<margin>40</margin>
Pamphilus says that a certain kind of pear is called *epimēlis*. Timachidas, in his fourth book, says that certain apples are called "Apples of the Hesperides" <note>The Hesperides were nymphs who guarded a garden of golden apples in Greek mythology</note>, and Pamphilus says these are offered to the gods in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>. They are fragrant and not meant for eating, and are called the Hesperides' apples. Aristocrates, in the fourth book of his *History of Lacedaemon*, says there are also apples called "Persian" <note>This term was often used for peaches or citrus fruits newly introduced from the East</note>. Theophrastus, in his second book of the *History of Plants*, writing about those whose fruit is not obvious, says: "In the larger plants, the beginning is clear in all of them, as in the almond and the nut and others of that kind, except for the 'Persian' apple, where it is least clear." And again, he mentions "pomegranates and female pears." Diphilus of Siphnos, in his work on food for the sick and the healthy, says:
> What are called Persian apples, 
> and by some 'Persian plums,' have a moderate amount of juice 
> and are more nourishing than common apples.

Philotimus, in the thirteenth book of *On Food*, says the Persian apple is more oily and grainy; it is porous, and when squeezed, it yields a great deal of oil. Aristophanes the Grammarian, in his *Laconian Glosses*, says the Laconians call plums "Persian acid-apples," 
<margin>50</margin>
which are also called *asbia*. There is much inquiry among the "learned banqueters" regarding the "Citron" <note>original: "Kitrion," a large, fragrant citrus fruit</note>, and where it is mentioned by the ancients. Myrtilus said that Hegesander of Delphi mentions the word in his *Commentaries*, as if sending those of us searching for it off on a wild goose chase <note>literally "sending us to the wild goats"</note>, but he does not actually remember the passage. Plutarch, speaking in opposition, said: "But I certainly..."

ATHENAEUS: THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

### APPLES.

...I am convinced that Hegesander <note>An author of historical commentaries from Delphi, 2nd century BCE</note> never said this at all, for I have read through all his commentaries specifically to find it. However, since another of our companions insisted it was so, relying on certain scholarly notes of no small reputation, you must look for another witness, my dear Myrtilus. Aemilianus then said: "You know that the King of Mauretania <note>Juba II, a Roman-appointed king and famous scholar who wrote in Greek</note>—a man of immense learning—mentions the citron in his *History of Libya*. He claims it is called the 'Hesperic' apple by the Libyans, and that from there, Heracles brought to Greece those fruits called 'golden apples' because of their appearance. Asclepiades, in the sixtieth book of his *Egyptian History*, says that the Earth produced these for the wedding of Zeus and Hera." Democritus looked at these claims and said: "If he records these things as mere opinions, let him enjoy his Libyan books. They are full of the same old wanderings. However, I say that although the name 'citron' <note>original: "kitrion"</note> was not used by the <margin>Book 3, chapter 4.</margin> ancients, the actual thing is described by the follower of Aristotle, Theophrastus <note>The 'father of botany,' 4th century BCE</note>, in his *History of Plants*. This forces me to understand the 'Median apple' as meaning the citron. For the philosopher says in the fourth book of his *History of Plants* as follows:

'The land of Media and Persia has many other products, including the one called the Persian or Median apple. This tree has a leaf similar to and as large as that of the laurel, the arbutus, or the walnut. It has thorns like those of a pear or hawthorn, but they are smooth, very sharp, and strong. The fruit itself is not eaten, but it is very fragrant, as are the leaves of the tree. If the fruit is placed among clothes, it keeps them from being moth-eaten. It is also useful if someone has happened to drink a deadly poison; for when given in wine, it upsets the stomach and draws out the poison. It is also used for sweetening the breath; for if one boils the inner part of the apple in a broth or some other liquid, squeezes it into the mouth and swallows it, it makes the breath pleasant. The seed is sown in carefully tilled garden beds; it is then watered every four or five days. When the plant is sturdy, it is transplanted again in the spring into a soft, well-watered spot where the soil is not too thin. It bears fruit in every season; for while some are being harvested, others are blossoming, and others are ripening. Of the flowers, those that have a sort of distaff <note>term: "ēlakatē" (distaff) — the ancient term for the prominent central pistil of the flower</note> projecting in the middle are fertile, but those that do not are sterile.'

He also mentions the distaff and fertile flowers in the first book of the same work. Moved by these descriptions, my friends—what Theophrastus says about the color, the smell, and the leaves—I am convinced that the 'citron' is what is being described. And let none of you wonder that he says it is not eaten; for even up until the time of our grandfathers, no one ate it, but they stored it in chests with their clothes as a great treasure. That the plant came down to the Greeks from that upper country <note>meaning the Persian Empire</note> can be found in the works of the comic poets, who mention the citrons while remarking on their great size. Antiphanes says in *The Boeotian*: 

> 'And again, a dish that is quite sweet,' as someone might say simply. 
> But take these:
> 
> "Girls, these apples are beautiful! Beautiful indeed, by the gods!"
> "For the seed has only recently arrived 
> In Athens from the Great King." 
> "I thought they were from the Hesperides, lady," says the Light-
> bearer; "they say these golden apples are only three."
> "The beautiful is rare; it is everywhere 
> and highly prized."

And Eriphus, in his play *Meliboea*, quotes these very same iambic lines, presenting the words of Antiphanes as his own:

> "I thought they were from the Hesperides," says Artemis, "they say these golden apples are only three.
> The beautiful is rare; it is everywhere
> and highly prized."

I do not place much weight on these poets, but it should be noted that these fruits are healthy. For they say that Aphrodite planted this tree in Cyprus... [text becomes fragmented] ...Berenice highly honored... brought these three only... for there were no more. If anyone can argue against this, that the fruit now called 'citron' is not what is meant, let him produce clearer evidence. Indeed, Phanias of Eresus <note>A student of Aristotle</note> gives us the idea that the 'citron' <note>original: "kitrion"</note> might have been named after the 'cedar' <note>original: "kedros"</note>. For he says in the fifth book of *On Plants* that the cedar has thorns around its leaves. That this is also true of the citron is clear to everyone. Furthermore, I know well that the citron, when added to any food or drink, is an antidote to every deadly poison; I learned this from a fellow citizen of mine who was entrusted with the government of Egypt. He had sentenced some criminals to be eaten by wild beasts, as they were to be thrown to the animals as a punishment. As they were entering the theater designated for the execution of the robbers, a woman selling fruit took pity on them and gave them some of the citron she was eating. They took it and ate it, and not long after, when they were thrown to those enormous and most savage beasts—the asps—they suffered no harm when bitten. A sense of helplessness seized the governor. Finally, questioning the soldier who guarded them to see if they had eaten or drunk anything, he learned that the citron had been given to them just as they were. On the following day, he ordered that citron be given to one man, but not to the other. And the one who had eaten...

<meta>catchword: eaten...</meta>

BOOK 3

## SHELLFISH.

...for though he was bitten, he suffered no harm. However, another man who was struck at that same moment died instantly. After this phenomenon was tested many times, it was discovered that the citron is an antidote <note>original: "antipharmakon"</note> for every deadly poison. If one boils a whole citron in its natural state in Attic honey, along with its seeds, it dissolves into the honey; a person taking two or three finger-scoops of this in the morning will suffer nothing from poisons.

If anyone doubts these facts, let him learn from Theopompus of Chios <note>A 4th-century BCE historian known for his detailed, though often biting, accounts</note>, a man who loved the truth and spent much money on accurate historical inquiry. He says in the thirty-eighth book of his *Histories*, while recounting the story of Clearchus of Heraclea <note>A tyrant of Heraclea Pontica who famously carried a pet snake</note>—one of those who ruled as tyrants in the Black Sea region—that he used to kill many people by force. He often gave most of them aconite <note>a highly toxic plant, also known as monkshood or wolfsbane</note> to drink. He says that when everyone realized this cruel obsession with the poison, they would not leave their houses without first eating rue <note>original: "peganon," an herb long used in antiquity as a defense against venom</note>. For those who had <margin>10</margin> eaten it beforehand suffered nothing even when drinking the aconite. He says this is true because the plant grows in a place called Akonai, which is a city belonging to Heraclea. After Democritus said this, many of the guests, marvelling at the power of the citron, began to eat it, as if they had never eaten or drunk anything before. Gamelion says that in the Roman tongue, they call it *citrum*.

Next after the foods previously mentioned, many legumes and various other shellfish <note>original: "ostrakodermon," literally "shell-skinned" creatures</note> were served to us individually. We find almost most of them worthy of mention in Epicharmus’s <note>A Greek comic playwright from Sicily</note> *The Marriage of Hebe*, in these lines: "Come then, all sorts of shells: limpets, *aspedioi*, sea-snails, *enkybaloi*, sea-squirts, barnacles, purple-shells, and oysters huddled together. Some are difficult to open but easy to eat: mussels, sea-snails, *marykas*, <margin>20</margin> and *skisyberia*." He says the sweet ones are on the surface, while the sharp ones are within: "The long-shells, razor-clams, or black cockles, which are called 'little shells' by all and cost three-obols. Other cockles from the sand are poorly regarded and are called 'dogs.' Humans call them *anthrophytidas*, but we gods call them 'whites.'" In the middle of his verses he writes: "Instead of a cockle, we call it an *autillo*." This refers to the *adeion* shell, or perhaps what are called *tellinae*, which the Romans name *mutulus* <note>mussels</note>. 

Aristophanes the Grammarian <note>A famous scholar and librarian of Alexandria</note> mentions this in his treatise *On the Grieved Scytale*, saying that limpets are similar to what are called *tellinae*. Callias of Mitylene, in his work *On the Limpet in Alcaeus*, says there is an ode by Alcaeus <note>A lyric poet from Lesbos</note> beginning, "Child of the rock and the grey sea," at the end of which is written: "O sea-limpet, you distract the mind from shells." But Aristophanes writes "turtle" <note>original: "chelys"</note> instead of "limpet," and says Dicaearchus <note>A student of Aristotle</note> is wrong to interpret them as limpets. <margin>30</margin> These are the shells children play with; when they take them in their mouths, they blow through them as we do with the "word-gatherings" <note>original: "spermológia," perhaps a reference to small talk or trivia</note> of children using these *tellinae*. As Sopater the phlyax-writer <note>A writer of farcical parodies</note> says in the play titled *The Edible Bacchis*: "But wait, for suddenly a melodic sound of a *tellina* has reached my ears." Again, Epicharmus says in *Pyrrha* or *Prometheus*: "Someone would be amazed at how many limpets are there." 

In the works of Sophron <note>A writer of mimes from Syracuse</note>, the shells are called *melanitides* (black-ones): "For black-ones conquer my hunger, even though it is small." In the work titled *Fisherman*, he calls the rustic ones "stony shells" <note>original: "cheradas"</note>. Archilochus <note>An early Greek lyric poet</note> also mentions the "stony shell." The word *anarita* <note>a type of sea snail</note> is mentioned by Ibycus. It is also called *anartas*; it is a small shell-creature that clings to the rocks just like limpets. Herondas in *The Women Working Together* says: "Clinging like a sea-snail to the reefs." Aeschylus in *The Persians* calls the islands "snail-nurturing." Homer mentions sea-squirts. 

<margin>40</margin> Diocles of Carystus <note>A prominent physician of the 4th century BCE</note> says in his *Healthful Things* that among shellfish, mussels, oysters, scallops, and clams are best for digestion and urination. Archippus <note>A comic poet</note> in *The Fish* mentions: "Limpets, sea-urchins, *echarai*, pipe-fish, and scallops." Diocles says that cockles, purple-fish, and whelks are stronger than other small shells. Regarding whelks, Archippus says: "The whelk, nursling of the sea, son of the purple-shell." Speusippus <note>Plato’s successor at the Academy</note> in the second book of *Resemblances* says that whelks, purple-fish, sea-snails, and cockles are very similar. Sophocles <note>The tragic playwright</note> mentions sea-snails in *The Camicians* thus: "This child of the sea-snail, if we could find any." Speusippus goes on to list specific types: cockles, scallops, mussels, fan-mussels, and razor-shells. In another part, he mentions oysters and "little-limpets," and he says of the "curved ones"—meaning these elegant delicacies: "Cockles and razor-shells, and the curved shrimp leaped like dolphins." <margin>50</margin> 

Sophron in his *Mimes* says: "What a sweet-bitter shellfish, the craving of widowed women." Cratinus mentions fan-mussels in *The Archilochoi*: "Or like fan-mussels and useless things." Philyllius, or Pherecrates, or Aristophanes in *The Cities* mentions: "Small octopus, a *skipidarion*, a bitter *raboumas*, oysters, clams, limpets, razor-shells, mussels, fan-mussels, and scallops from Methymna. Lift up then the *thranidas*, *rigla*, sea-bream, *melrous*, turbot, and the *korakinos*." Agias and Dercylus in their *History of Argos* call the sea-snails *asrabélous*, mentioning them as being suitable for use as trumpets.

->ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED.<-

# SHELLFISH.

The word for mussel-shells <note>original: "lonchas," though likely a variation or error for "konchas," the standard word for bivalve shells</note> can be found used in both the feminine and masculine genders. Aristophanes <note>The famous comic playwright of Athens, known for his biting satire</note> says in *The Babylonians*: "They gaped at everything, looking like mussel-shells <note>original: "konchaisin"</note> over the coals." Teleclides says in his *Hesiods*: "He calls the shell <note>original: "konche"</note> double-valved." And Sophron <note>A writer of "mimes," short dramatic scenes of everyday life</note> says in his *Mimes of Women*: "Mussel-shells, just like a goat at a single command. All of them have gaped for us. This one is quite salty compared to the others." Using the masculine form, Aeschylus <note>The great tragedian</note> says in *Glaucus of the Sea*: "Shells <note>original: "konchoi"</note>, mussels, and oysters." Aristonymus says: "The shell was like another dyed one." Phrynichus likewise mentions them in his *Satyrs*.

Hicesius <note>A physician following the school of Erasistratus, focused on how food affects the body's 'humors'</note> says that regarding their juice, some are called "rough" and others "Royal." He states that the rough ones have poor juices, provide little nourishment, and are difficult to digest <note>original: "dyskritous," meaning hard for the body to separate or process</note>. Those who fish for purple-dye mussels use them as bait. Among those called "Royal," the best are distinguished by their size. Hegesander <margin>10</margin> says in his *Commentaries* that these rough shells are called *korykoi* by the Macedonians, but *kreioi* by the Athenians. 

Hicesius also says that limpets <note>original: "lepadas"</note> are more easily digested than the aforementioned types. Oysters <note>original: "ostria"</note>, however, provide less nourishment and are "washy" and even harder to digest. Scallops <note>original: "ktenes," literally 'combs'</note> are more nutritious but produce worse juices and are difficult to pass through the system. Among mussels <note>original: "myes," literally 'mice'</note>, those from Ephesus and others similar to them are superior to scallops in the quality of their juices, though their flavor is thinner. They are more diuretic <note>promoting the passage of urine</note> than they are moving to the bowels. Some of them are "squill-like" <note>referring to a bitter sea-onion</note>, having bad juices and being unpleasant to the taste. The smaller ones, which are hairy on the outside, are more diuretic and have better juices than the squill-like ones, but they are less nutritious because of their size and their natural constitution.

The "necks" of the trumpet-shells <note>original: "kerykon," whelks used for food and trumpets</note> are good for the stomach but less nutritious than mussels, scallops, or their juices. For those <margin>20</margin> who have a weak stomach and do not easily pass food into the lower gut, these are useful as they do not spoil easily. Indeed, foods that are universally acknowledged as hard to digest are, conversely, helpful for this condition because they resist corruption due to being firm rather than soft and easily dissolved. For this reason, their "poppy-heads" <note>original: "mekones," the soft internal organs</note> are not unsuitable for stomach ailments, and they are useful for those with a weak bowel. More nutritious and enjoyable than these are the poppy-heads of the purple-murex, though they are more "squill-like." Indeed, the whole purple-fish is of this nature. It is a peculiar trait of these and the razor-clams <note>original: "solesi"</note> that the seaweed-like substance they contain makes the broth thick. The necks of the purple-murex are also well-suited for stomach conditions. 

Poseidippus <note>A comic poet</note> mentions them in *The Lepers* as follows: "It is time to serve the eels, the lobsters, the shells, fresh sea urchins, poppy-heads, mussels, necks, and muscles." Barnacles <note>original: "balanoi," literally 'acorns'</note> of the larger sort are hard to pass and <margin>30</margin> unpleasant. The "little ears" <note>original: "otaria," likely abalone or a similar ear-shaped shell</note>—which are found near the island called Pharos at Alexandria—are more nutritious than all the types mentioned before, but not easily passed. Antigonus of Carystus <note>A 3rd-century BCE writer on art and natural history</note> says in his work *On Vocabulary* that this shellfish is called the "Ear of Aphrodite" by the Aeolians. The boring-mussels <note>original: "pholades"</note> are very nutritious but have a strong smell; in other respects, they are similar to those mentioned above. 

There are also some called "wild" oysters. They are very nutritious and pungent, yet quite poor in flavor. Aristotle <note>The philosopher and father of biology</note> says in his *History of Animals* that the following are shellfish: the pen-shell <note>original: "pinne"</note>, the oyster, the mussel, the scallop, the razor-clam, the shell, the limpet, the sea-squirt <note>original: "tethos"</note>, and the barnacle. Among the purple-producing ones are the trumpet-shell, the purple-murex, the "clatter-murex," the sea urchin, and the land-snail. He notes that the scallop has a rough shell and is ribbed. The sea-squirt is not ribbed and has a smooth shell. The pen-shell is thin-mouthed. The oyster is thick-mouthed, having a single valve <note>literally "one door"</note> and a smooth shell. The limpet has two valves and a smooth shell. The mussel is naturally joined together, while the razor-clam and barnacle have a single structure and a smooth shell. The word "shell" <note>original: "konche"</note> is a common name for both. 

<margin>40</margin> Epainetus says in his *Art of Cookery* that the internal part of the pen-shell is called the "poppy-head." In the fifth book of *History of Animals*, Aristotle says that purple-murex are produced around springtime, and trumpet-shells at the end of winter. In general, he says that all "shell-skinned" creatures <note>original: "ostrakoderma"</note> appear to have what are called "eggs" in the spring and in the autumn, except for the edible sea urchins. These are at their best in those seasons and always thrive more during the full moon and on warm days, except for those in the Euripus <note>The narrow channel between Euboea and Boeotia</note> which are reddish; those are better in winter and, though small, are full of eggs. Snails also appear to be pregnant at the same time. 

Continuing, the philosopher says that purple-murex gather together in the spring and produce a substance called *melikra* <note>original: "honeycomb-mass"</note>. This is like a honeycomb, though not as smooth, looking instead as if many white pea-husks had been glued together. None of these have an open passage. Purple-murex do not grow from these egg-cases; rather, they and other shell-skinned creatures grow from mud and decay. This substance is like a purging for them and for the trumpet-shells, for they also produce these "honeycombs." When they begin, they release a slimy stickiness from which the husk-like parts are formed. All these are then cast off. They release a fluid <note>original: "ichora"</note> into the earth, and in that spot they are produced...

# BOOK III

<meta>The catchword "coals" from the previous page referred to a quote about mussels being roasted; this page begins mid-sentence discussing the reproduction of the purple murex.</meta>

## SHELLFISH.

...are produced in the earth, having birthed small purple shells which the larger purple murex-shells <note>original: "porphyrai," the gastropods from which the famous Tyrian purple dye was extracted</note> possess when they are caught. If they are caught before they have finished spawning—sometimes in wicker baskets—they go silent, as it were, and spawn, producing something like a cluster of grapes.

There are several kinds of purple murex. Some are large, such as those found around Sigeum <note>A promontory in the Troad, near ancient Troy</note> and the Lecton. Others are small, like those in the Euripus <note>The narrow channel between Euboea and mainland Greece</note>. Regarding their "flowers" <note>original: "anthos," the pigment-producing gland</note>, most have a dark color, but some have a small amount of red. Some of the large ones even weigh a *mna* <note>A Greek unit of weight, roughly 430 grams</note>. Those found on the beaches and around the shores are not large in size but have a red flower. Furthermore, those in northern regions are mostly black, while those in southern regions are generally red. Apollodorus of Athens says in his writings *On Sophron* that there is a proverb regarding the greediness of the purple murex, saying that it "does not come from the dye." For it does not draw wounds toward itself by touch, but it imparts a brilliance of color to those things it strikes against. Others say the name comes from the animal itself. Aristotle says they are caught in the spring, but not during the "Dog Days" <note>The hottest part of summer, associated with the rising of the star Sirius</note>, for they do not feed then, but hide themselves and hibernate. They have their "flower" located between the "poppy" <note>original: "mekonos," referring to the dark digestive gland resembling a poppy head</note> and the neck. Both the murex and the trumpet-shell <note>original: "keryx," the triton or whelk shell</note> have opercula <note>The "lid" or trapdoor that seals the shell</note> in the same manner, as do all spiral-shelled creatures from birth. They feed by extending what is called the "tongue" from under the operculum. The size of the purple murex's tongue is greater than a finger's width; with this, it feeds and bores through other shells, and even its own shell. Both the purple murex and the trumpet-shell are long-lived, surviving for about six years. Their growth is visible from the coils in the shell.

Mussel-shells <note>original: "longchai," a variation of "konchai"</note>, clams, razor-shells, and scallops reach their full development in sandy areas. The pen-shells <note>original: "pinnai," large fan-shaped bivalves</note> grow upright from the sea floor. They contain within themselves the "pinna-guard" <note>original: "pinnophylaka"</note>, which is sometimes a small shrimp and sometimes a small crab. If they are deprived of these, they perish more quickly. Regarding this, Pamphylus of Alexandria says in his *On Names* that these creatures are naturally grown together. Chrysippus of Soli, in the fifth book of his *On the Beautiful and Pleasure*, says that the pen-shell and the pinna-guard work together, being unable to survive individually. The pen-shell is a shellfish, while the pinna-guard is a small crab. When the pen-shell opens its valves, it stays still, watching for small fish that enter. The pinna-guard, standing by, bites the pen-shell as a signal when something enters, and once bitten, the shell snaps shut. Thus, they consume what is trapped inside together. Some say they are even born together from a single seed. Aristotle says again that all shellfish are also produced in the mud: oysters in the slimy mud, mussels and scallops in the sandy mud. The "beasts" in the hollows of rocks include barnacles and those that live on the surface, such as limpets and sea-snails. In the same way, those without shells are produced among the hard-shelled ones, such as the *telunidai* <note>small bivalves, likely tellins</note> and the "homeless" ones <note>original: "atochoi," perhaps referring to certain anemones or soft-bodied rock dwellers</note> in the hollows of rocks.

There are two kinds of sea nettles <note>original: "knidai," referring to sea anemones</note>. Some are in the hollows and do not detach from the rocks, while those on smooth, flat surfaces detach and move around. Eupolis calls sea nettles *akalēphai* in his *Autolycus*. Likewise, Aristophanes says in *The Phoenician Women*: "First of all, let him have the power to grow mussels; then, in order, the smooth nettles." And in *The Wasps*. Pherecrates says in *The Deserters*: "If you were crowned with nettles for the same length of time." Diocles of Carystus, the physician from Siphnos, says the sea nettle is good for the bowels and is a diuretic, but is hard on the stomach. It causes an itch for those who handle it if they do not oil themselves beforehand. Indeed, they [sting] those who hunt them. From this [stinging quality], they are now called *akalēphe* by corruption; perhaps even the plant <note>the stinging nettle</note> is named for this reason. It is named by euphemism through contradiction, for it is not mild (*praeia*) or soft to the touch, but rough and unpleasant. Philippides mentions the sea nettle in *Limocrates* thus: "He served me oysters, nettles, and limpets." The passage in Aristophanes' *Lysistrata* is a joke: "O most courageous of grandmothers <note>original: "tethon," which also means "oysters"</note> and motherly nettles."

For oysters are categorized this way. He mentions them comically in relation to "grandmother" (the mother), and regarding other shellfish, Diocles says the following: Among the thick clams, the small ones with thin flesh are called oysters. They are hard on the stomach and difficult to eliminate. The thick ones, called "Royal" by some and "monstrous" <note>original: "peloriai," giant clams</note> by others, are nourishing, difficult to eliminate, full of juice, and hard on the stomach, especially the larger ones. Tellins <note>original: "Tellinai"</note> are found in great numbers at Canopus <note>A city on the Nile Delta</note>, and they abound during the rising of the Nile. The "Royal" variety of these is thinner, laxative, and light. They are also nourishing. Those from the river are sweeter. Mussels <note>original: "myes"</note> are moderately nourishing, laxative, and diuretic. The best are from Ephesus, especially those in the autumn. The *muiskai* <note>small mussels</note>, being smaller than the regular mussels, are very sweet, full of juice, and also quite nourishing. Those called "razor-shells" <note>original: "solenoi"</note> by some, and "flutes," "reeds," or "nails" by others, are very juicy and have poor juice—there are many of them. The males are striped and sky-blue in color; they are helpful for those with kidney stones and other urinary difficulties. The females are of a single color and very sweet. they are eaten boiled or fried. The best are those caught before they gape...

->ATHEN. DEIPNOSOPH.<-

### SHELLFISH.

...roasted on coals; those who gathered these shellfish were called "razor-clam fishers" <note>original: "solenisai," from "solen," meaning a pipe or tube, referring to the razor clam's shape</note>, as Phanias of Ephesus records in his work titled *The Overthrow of Tyrants by Vengeance*, writing as follows: "Philoxenus, the so-called 'razor-clam fisher,' rose from a popular leader to become a tyrant. He was originally a creature of the sea, a hunter of razor-clams, but having found an opportunity and engaged in trade, he acquired a fortune." Of the scallops <note>original: "ktenes," literally "combs"</note>, the white ones are more tender, for they are not without a certain scent. The black and reddish ones are larger, and the crumbly ones have a foul smell. Generally, all scallops are hard on the stomach but easy to digest and good for the bowels when taken with cumin and pepper. Archippus also mentions them in his play *The Fishes*: "with limpets, sea urchins, grilled meats, garfish, and scallops." 

The "acorn-shells" <note>original: "balanoi," or barnacles</note>, so named because of their resemblance to oak acorns, differ according to their location. The Egyptian ones are sweet, tender, smelly, nutritious, very juicy, diuretic, and good for the bowels. Others are saltier, and their "ears" <note>referring to a specific part of the barnacle's anatomy</note> are hard to digest, though they are more nourishing when fried. The *pholades* <note>piddocks or rock-borers</note> are smelly, pungent, and produce poor juices. 

Sea urchins <note>original: "echinoi"</note> are tender and have good juice, but they are smelly, filling, and hard to digest. When eaten with oxymel <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note>, celery, and mint, they are good for the stomach, sweet, and provide good juices. The best ones are the red and the yellow-orange ones, as well as the thickest ones and those that release a milky substance when scraped. Those found around Cephalonia, Icaria, and parts of the Adriatic are somewhat bitter. Those from the reefs of Sicily are laxative to the bowels. 

Aristotle says there are several kinds of sea urchins. One is the edible kind, in which are found the so-called "eggs" <note>the roe or gonads, the only edible part</note>. There are two other kinds: the *spatangi* <note>heart urchins</note> and those called *bryssi*. Sophron mentions the *spatangi*, and Aristophanes says in his *Merchant Ships*: "Tearing apart, mincing, and mangling the lower parts of my heart-urchins." <margin>10</margin> Epicharmus also says in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "From where do the sea urchins come? The sea-urchin comes with the *markinos* <note>an unidentified sea creature</note> through the salty brine." He distributes them equally, but they travel alone. 

Demetrius of Scepsis, in the twenty-sixth book of *The Trojan Array*, says that a certain Spartan <note>Laconian</note> was once invited to a dinner, and when sea urchins were placed on the table, he took one, not knowing how to eat the dish. Not paying attention to how his fellow-diners were opening them, he put the urchin into his mouth shell and all, and began to crunch it with his teeth. Struggling with the eating and finding the resistance of the rough shell disagreeable, he said: "O foul food! I will not let you go now and go soft on you, but I would never take you up again!"

As for the fact that urchins—and I mean both the land hedgehogs and the sea urchins—are protective of themselves by projecting their spines like a palisade against those who hunt them, Iophon of Chios testifies in his *New Phoenix*, saying: "But whether on land she rouses the lions, or rather the urchin's well-fortified arts. As you might learn the scent of other beasts, the hedgehog <note>original: "strobilos"</note> having rolled its body around its spines, it is impossible to sit upon or touch." <margin>20</margin>

Regarding limpets <note>original: "lepades"</note>, Diphilus says some are small and some are like legumes. They are tough, have little juice, are not overly pungent, but are smelly and somewhat difficult to digest. The *pinna* shells <note>large fan mussels</note> are diuretic, nutritious, but hard to digest and slow to be absorbed. Trumpet shells <note>original: "kerykes," or whelks</note> are similar to them. Their "necks" <note>the muscular foot</note> are hard on the stomach and difficult to chew—which is why they are suitable for those with weak stomachs—being difficult to pass and only moderately nutritious. The so-called "poppy-heads" <note>the soft internal organs</note> at the bottom of the shells are tender and easily digested, making them suitable for those with weak bowels. Purple murex shells are between the *pinna* and the trumpet shell. Their necks provide much juice but are smelly; the rest of them is salty and sweet. In a mixture <note>original: "andochos"</note>, they are well-suited for tempering other flavors.

Oysters <note>original: "ostria"</note> are born in rivers, lakes, and the sea. The best are those from the sea when a lake or river is nearby, for they become juicier, <margin>40</margin> larger, and sweeter. Those near shores and muddy rocks, where the water is unmixed, are small, hard, and biting. Spring oysters and those at the beginning of summer are superior, full of brine, yet possessing a sweetness; they are hard on the stomach but easy to pass. When boiled with mallow or dock, or with fish, or by themselves, they are nutritious and good for the bowels.

Mnesitheus of Athens says in his work *On Edibles*: "Oysters, mussels, and similar shells have flesh that is difficult to digest because of the raw moisture within them. Therefore, when eaten raw, they are laxative to the bowels due to their saltiness. When boiled, they release all or most of their brine into the surrounding liquid. Consequently, the liquids in which any of these shellfish have been boiled are disruptive and laxative to the bowels, but the flesh of the boiled shellfish themselves causes gas once it has been deprived of its moisture. Roasted shellfish, if one roasts them well, are the least harmful because they have been acted upon by fire. For the same reason, they are not as difficult to digest as raw ones, their moistures having been dried out. Thus the bowels become loose, and they provide a moist nourishment; yet every shellfish is difficult to digest and somewhat foul-smelling after boiling. Sea anemones <note>original: "akalephe"</note> or sea urchin eggs and such things provide a small amount of moist nourishment, but they are effective at loosening the bowels."

## SHELLFISH. PEARLS.

...and stimulate urination. <note>This continues a list of health benefits from the previous page.</note> Nicander of Colophon, in his *Georgics* <note>A poem on farming and nature</note>, lists the various types of shellfish as follows:
"All these the deep sea nourishes in the brine:
The nerites, the whelks, the giant clams <note>original: "peloriades"</note>, and mussels,
And the sticky ones of the shade, and the nest of the pinna-shell itself."
And Archestratus says in his *Gastronomy*:
"Ainos has large mussels, Abydos has oysters <note>original: "ostreia"</note>,
Parion has 'bear-crabs,' and Mitylene has scallops <note>original: "ktenas," literally 'combs'</note>.
Ambracia provides the *glastes* and many others with them.
Messene provides giant clams from the narrow straits.
And in Ephesus you shall take the clams <note>original: "chemas"</note>, because they are poor.
Chalcidon has sea-squirts, but as for the whelks <note>original: "kerykas"</note>,
May Zeus destroy them, both those born in the sea and those in the market!
Except for one man’s, and he is my companion;
He dwells in Lesbos rich in grapes, and is called Agathon."
And Philyllius, 
<margin>10</margin> or whoever was the author of the play *The Cities*, says: "Clams, limpets, razor-clams, mussels, pinnas, and scallops from Methymna." 
The ancients used only the word *ostreia* for shellfish in this way. Cratinus says in *The Archilochuses*: "Like to 'ginnoi' <note>a stunted animal</note> and oysters." And Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe* mentions "clustered oysters," though he uses *ostreon* as a word similar to *orneon* <note>bird</note>. Plato in the *Phaedrus* says we are "fettered in the manner of an oyster." And in the *Timaeus* he speaks of "the whole race of oysters." In the tenth book of the *Republic*, he describes "oysters and seaweed" grown onto a body. 
The giant clams <note>original: "peloriades"</note> were named for their "monstrous" <note>original: "pelorion"</note> size, for they are larger than a common clam and quite different. Aristotle says in his *History of Animals* that they are formed in the sand. Ion of Chios mentions clams <note>original: "chemas"</note> in his *Arrivals*; perhaps they are so named because of their "gaping" <note>original: "kechemenai," to yawn or gape</note>. 

Regarding the oysters found in the region of India—for it is necessary 
<margin>Pearls.</margin> to mention them because of the use of pearls—Theophrastus writes as follows in his treatise *On Stones*: "Among the stones held in wonder is the one called the pearl <note>original: "margarites"</note>, which is translucent in nature. 
<margin>20</margin> They make expensive necklaces out of it. It is produced in a certain shellfish similar to the *pinna*, but smaller. In size, it is about as large as a good-sized fish eye." 
Androsthenes, in his *Circumnavigation of India*, writes: "Of the whelks, the 'pig-shells,' and the rest of the bivalves, the varieties are many and quite different from ours. There are purple-fish and a great multitude of other oysters. There is one they call 'berberi,' from which the pearl-stone comes. This is very expensive throughout Asia and is sold among the Persians and the upper regions for gold. The appearance of this oyster is similar to a scallop. It is not striated, but has a smooth, hairy shell. It does not have two 'ears' like the scallop, but only one. The stone grows in the flesh of the oyster, just as a 'hailstone' <note>original: "chalaza," referring to a cyst or growth</note> grows in pigs. Some are very gold-like in color, so that they are not easily distinguished when placed next to gold. Others are silver-like, and others are perfectly white, similar to the eyes of fish."

<margin>30</margin> Chares of Mitylene, in the seventh book of his *Histories of Alexander*, says: "It is hunted in the Indian sea, and likewise in the Armenian, Persian, Susian, and Babylonian seas, being similar to an oyster. It has a name like 'dromon' <note>meaning 'runner'</note>, being long in shape and containing a large, white, and very sweet-smelling flesh. From these, they extract the white parts and call them pearls. They make necklaces from them, and bracelets for the hands and feet, which the Persians, Medes, and all Isaurians value much more than those made of gold." 

Isidore of Charax, in his *Description of Parthia*, says there is a certain island in the Persian Sea where many pearls are found. Therefore, there are reed rafts around the island, from which men dive into the sea to a depth of twenty fathoms <note>original: "orgyas," about 6 feet each</note> and bring up double shells. They say that 
<margin>40</margin> when there are continuous thunders and heavy rains, the *pinna* 'conceives' more, and the pearl becomes better formed and larger. In winter, the *pinnas* tend to sink into the deepest parts of the sea, but in summer they spend the nights 'gaping' <note>open</note> while swimming, though they close during the day. Those that attach themselves to rocks or 
<margin>Pearls.</margin> mud take root. Staying there, they produce the pearl. They are living creatures and are nourished through the part attached to the flesh. There is a creature grown into the body of the shell which has claws and brings in food; this is similar to a small crab and is called the 'pinna-guard' <note>original: "pinnophylax"</note>. The flesh extends from this through the middle of the shell like a root. Growing alongside this root, the pearl increases through the solid part of the shell and is nourished for as long as it remains attached. When the flesh slips away from the root and, growing soft, separates the pearl from the shell, the pearl no longer receives nourishment, but this makes it smoother, more translucent, and purer. The deep-sea *pinna* produces the most translucent, pure, and large pearls. Those that stay 
<margin>50</margin> near the surface and rise up are discolored and inferior because they are struck by the rays of the sun. Those who hunt for pearls run a great risk when they stretch their hand directly into a gaping shell, for it then snaps shut, and often their fingers are cut off; some even die instantly. But those who happen to put their hand in from the side can easily pull the shells away from the rock.
