# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS.

...to them. Menander mentions the "Maragdion" <note>An emerald-colored gem or perhaps a green-tinted dish</note> in his play *The False Substitute* <note>original: "Pseudybolimaios"</note>; these "Maragdions" are certain types of delicacies.
This might be the same thing as the *sardion* <note>the carnelian or sard stone</note>.
Regarding this, it should be said that the word for "shining" <note>original: "marmairein"</note> is used because of its translucent nature. After these things were discussed, 
plates were brought in containing many "sacred items from the water" <note>A humorous way to refer to boiled meats or offal</note>: feet, heads, ears, and 
jaws. There were also guts, tripe, and tongues, just as is the custom in the so-called "boiled-meat shops" <note>original: "ephthopolia"</note> in 
Alexandria.

<margin>Boiled-meat shop</margin>
->B O I L E D - M E A T  S H O P .<-

For the term "boiled-meat shop" has been used, Ulpian, by Poseidippus in *The Little Boy*. And again, when the guests were searching for those who had named these items, someone said: Aristophanes mentions edible tripe <note>original: "koilia"</note> in *The Knights*: "Selling tripe and bladders that are not quite right." And following that: "Why, my good man, do you not let me wash the tripe and sell the sausages, but instead you mock me?" And again:
> "I, having swallowed a cow’s abomasum <note>original: "hynustron"; the fourth stomach of a ruminant</note> and a sow’s belly, and then drinking the broth without washing my hands, will throttle the orators and throw Nicias into confusion."
And again:
> "And the daughter of Brimos <note>A title for Hecate or Demeter</note> took boiled 
> meat from the broth."
He also mentions intestines <note>original: "cholix"</note>, the abomasum, and a slice of stomach. Regarding jaws <note>original: "siagonon"</note>, Cratinus in *The Wealth-Gods* speaks of fighting over a beef jaw. And Sophocles in *Amycus* says: "He makes the jaws soft." Plato writes in the *Timaeus*: "And he bound the extremities of the jaws to them, beneath the nature of the face." Xenophon in *On Horsemanship* mentions: "A long, narrow jaw." Those who pronounce the word "jaw" <note>original: "siagona"</note> with the letter 'u' <note>as "suagona"</note> do so by analogy from the word for "hog" <note>original: "hyos"</note>. Epicharmus mentions guts <note>original: "chordōn"</note>, which he calls *oryai* <note>sausages</note>, even entitling one of his works after this food. Aristophanes in *The Clouds* says: "Setting a sausage <note>original: "chordon"</note> before the deep-thinkers." Cratinus in *The Flagon*: "How thin it is, and what a slice of sausage this is!" Eupolis in *The Goats*. Alexis in *The Woman from Leucas*, or *The Runaways*: "A slice of sausage has arrived, and some appetizers." Antiphanes in *The Marriage*: "Cutting out the middle of the sausage, and the feet, and the ears, and even the snout <note>original: "rhynchous"</note>." Alexis in *The Priesthood* or *The Pharmacist*: "I will set out the evidence a little later, which contains many of the names we are looking for." Theophilus in *The Professional Wrestler*:
> "Of boiled meats, speak of nearly 
> three minas' weight of another snout, 
> of legs, four hog's feet. By Heracles, what a cow's belly!"
Anaxilas in *The Cooks*:
> "To me, the poems of Aeschylus 
> seem much better than roasted little fish. What do you mean 'little fish'? You are going to treat the whole mess-hall as if it were sick, with as many pork-shoulder cuts <note>original: "aprokōlia"</note> as there are snouts and feet."
Anaxilas says in *Circe*:
> "For it is a terrible thing, my friend,
> to have a pig’s snout."
And in *The Charming Men*:
> "Wearing a pig’s snout, they swore an oath together."
Anaxandrides also called them "little ears" in *The Satyr*. Lebanicus says in *The Chalcidian*: "To make hot fish broth by reshaping it, putting together half-eaten remains." <note>The following passage is corrupt in the original Greek manuscript</note> † They think that for every other sausage I cut a sausage with silphium. I bring forward a slice of sausage and I press the snout upward. So that everyone agrees the day after the wedding was the best. Aristophanes in *The Rehearsal*: "I washed the sausage of a miserable child. How can I look upon a scorched snout?" Pherecrates in *Trifles*: "Pig, is this not a pig's snout?" And a certain place is also called "Snout" <note>original: "Rhynchos"</note>, near the army of Aetolia, as Polybius says in the sixth book of his *Histories*. Stesichorus says in *The Boar Hunters*: "To hide the tip of the snout beneath the earth." That the word "snout" is properly used for pigs has been stated before. But that it is also used for other animals, Archimachus has said in his second *Amphitryon* in a playful manner. And concerning the face: "And having that snout of his so long." And Araros in *Kekinōdia*: "For the god turns his snout toward us." Aristophanes mentions pork-shoulder cuts in *Aiolo-Sicon*: "One thing is certain, four tender pork-shoulder cuts have been boiled for you." And in *The Gerytades*: "Pork-shoulder cuts, loaves of bread, crayfish." Antiphanes in *The Corinthian Woman*: "Then you are ignorantly mocking a pork-shoulder cut of pig offered to Aphrodite." In Cyprus, they so delight in pigs that they devour the whole animal, but they forced the oxen <note>to be the primary sacrifice instead</note>. That a pig is indeed sacrificed to Aphrodite is witnessed by Callimachus, or Zenodotus, writing thus in his *Historical Commentaries*: "The Argives sacrifice pigs to Aphrodite, and the festival is called the 'Pig-festival' <note>original: "Hysteria"</note>." Pherecrates in *The Miners*: "Whole meaty ribs <note>original: "schelides"</note> nearby, most tender, upon small plates, and fat pork-shoulder cuts." Alexis in *The Dice-Players*: "We were finding, I think, some pork-shoulder cuts of a certain sow. Even if it's an all-night festival or for the laborers, the meat is half-roasted, and the mincemeat is loose. The conger eel is boiled, but I am eating the pork-shoulder cuts." Pherecrates mentions boiled feet in *The Slave-Teacher*, saying how a dinner is prepared: "How would you describe it to us? Every slice was an eel for us, a squid, lamb meat, a slice of sausage, boiled trotters <note>original: "pys ephthos"</note>, liver, a rib, many birds in abundance, cheese in honey, and a portion of meat." Antiphanes in *The Parasite*: "Hog's skin, reddish-brown. The woman deserves the holy best, much boiled cheese is spread over it." Ecphantides in *The Satyrs*: "And if the grain-buyers purchase feet of a boiled pig to devour." Aristophanes mentions the tongue in *The Fry-pan Cookers*: "For them, at least, enough of the small fry for me, it shall cease. For they gulp down the fatty bits. But bring the under-layer. Or some kind of boar's meat joined in a new way. If there isn't a rib or a tongue, or anything else, either of a sheep, or a pig, or snouts, or tripe, bring them here with warm rolls." After so many things were said about these and where they come from, not even the physicians...

# BOOK III
# THE DESSERT

The doctors who were present, participating without having to pay a contribution <note>original: "asymboloi"; guests who contribute conversation instead of money</note>, took up the discussion. Dionysiocles said that Mnesitheus the Athenian, in his book *On Eatables*, stated that the heads and feet of pigs do not have much edible or fatty matter in them. And Lynceus <note>OCR reads "Lynides"</note> of Samos, in the fourth book of his *History of Attica*, says that when Apheidas was king of Athens, his younger brother Thymoetes—who was a bastard—killed him and took the throne for himself. During his reign, Melanthus the Messenian was exiled from his homeland and consulted the Pythian oracle about where he should settle. The oracle told him he should stay where he was first honored with guest-gifts <note>original: "xenia"</note> consisting of a pig’s foot and head at a dinner. This happened to him at Eleusis. For the priests were performing a traditional festival and had consumed all the other meat; since only the head and feet remained, they sent these to Melanthus. 

Immediately following this, a sow's womb <note>original: "metra"; considered a great delicacy in antiquity</note> was brought in. It was truly a "mother" of a dish—the mother of the "pigs of Hippocrates," whom I know are mocked in comedies for their swinish nature. Looking at it, Ulpian said: "Come now, my friends, 'in what sense' <note>original: "pra tini"; Ulpian is asking for a linguistic precedent for the word's usage</note> is this womb laid before us? For we have gorged our bellies sufficiently, and it is now time for us to speak." He claimed we should follow the advice given to the comic poets: to remain silent once we are shamelessly stuffed—unless, of course, they wish to gnaw on the jawbones and heads like dogs, for no one begrudges them enjoying the bones. For there is water, and they pray to be called. It is the law to throw the scraps to the dogs; as Euripides said, use it. For they want to eat and drink everything, but they understand nothing, just as the divine Plato said in the *Protagoras*: that discussing poetry at a banquet is very similar to the parties of low-class and common people. For these people, because they are unable to converse with one another through their own resources during their drinking—not even through their own voices or their own words due to their lack of education—make flute-girls expensive, paying high prices for a "foreign voice" (the sound of the flutes), and they converse with each other through that sound. But where there are noble, good, and educated banqueters, you will not see flute-girls, dancing-girls, or harpists; they are sufficient in themselves to converse without such nonsense and childishness, speaking and listening in turn in an orderly fashion, even if they drink a great deal of wine. 

"I see that you, Cynulcus, are doing the opposite while you drink—or rather, while you gulp it down. Like the flute-girls and dancing-girls, you obstruct the pleasure that comes through conversation, living (as Plato says in the *Philebus*) not the life of a human, but that of a lung-fish or one of those sea creatures that live in shells."

Cynulcus, becoming angry, replied: "You belly-worshiper, you 'stomach-demon' <note>original: "koiliodaimon"</note>! You know nothing else; you cannot deliver a proper discourse, you cannot remember a history, nor can you ever offer any grace in your words. Instead, you spend all your time searching for whether a word 'is laid down' <note>original: "keitai"; a common pedantic question: is this word found in classical texts?</note> or not, and whether it has been said or not. You scrutinize every little thing that comes up in conversation, gathering thorns like a hedgehog, and you are always sawing away at names, never gathering any of the actual juice of the state. Or is it not you who—by the 'Selloi' as the Romans call them <note>likely referring to the Salii priests</note>, according to some Paphian tradition—hires out your friends, calling it 'extra-grazing' <note>original: "epinomidia"</note>? If you are emulating Plato, we want to learn. But if you found this word 'in some sense' used elsewhere, show us the whole context. For I know that a certain part of a trireme <note>a Greek warship</note> is called 'epinomidia,' as Apollonius records in his work on *Biremes*. 

And you—what was it? Something new, or not yet in common use—you spoke of a 'cloak' <note>original: "phainoles"; the Latin *paenula*</note>. For you said, 'My good man, the cloak is mentioned,' saying: 'Boy, give me the unbreakable cloak.' But while you were going into the bath, you didn't say to the man asking 'Where are you going to perish?' where you were being led. And on that day, your beautiful 'causinus' <note>a Macedonian hat</note> was snatched by clothes-thieves, so that there was great laughter in the bath because you were looking for a useless cloak. And another thing, my dearest companions—for I will tell you the truth—he struck his leg against a stone and cut it. When he was treated and came out, what did he say to those asking, this Ulpian? He called it a 'black eye' <note>original: "hypopion"</note>. And I (for I was with him), being unable to bear the laughter, had a doctor friend smear the area under my eyes with a thick ointment, and when people asked, I said, 'What was your stumbling-block?' <note>Cynulcus is mocking Ulpian's use of a word for a facial bruise to describe a leg injury</note>."

<margin>Word-hunters.</margin>
There is another pursuer of this same wisdom, Pompeianus of Philadelphia, a man who is not without cunning, but a 'word-hunter' <note>original: "onomatotheras"</note> himself. When speaking to his servant, he called out the name in a loud voice: "Sbombichides! Bring me my slippers here to the gymnasium—the 'unbearable' ones—and the 'unbreakable' outer garment. For after I have put on my beard <note>a strange way of saying he will act like a philosopher</note>, I will greet my companions. For I have a piece of roasted salt-fish. And bring the oil flask; for first we will 'dibiate' and then 'apoleumastha' <note>deliberately obscure or invented words used to mock Pompeianus's style</note>." 

This same sophist says that in the month of February, as the Romans call it—this month, says Juba the Moor, is named after the 'underworld terrors' <note>referring to *Februa*, instruments of purification</note> and the killing of victims, in which the winter is at its peak; and it is the custom to bring libations to the deceased for many days—he said to one of his friends: "You haven't seen me for many days because of the 'heat-waves' <note>using a word for summer heat in the middle of winter</note>." And when the festival of the Panathenaia was being celebrated, for which the law courts do not meet, he said: "It is the birthday of the..."

# ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

### W O M B

...of Athena’s rooster <note>original: "alektoros Athenas"; perhaps a reference to a specific breed or a cryptic proverb</note>, and "the day today is unjust." He also once used to call our comrade who had returned from Delphi—to whom the god had given no oracular response—"unprofitable" <note>original: "achreston"; a pun on "chrao" meaning to give an oracle</note>. On another occasion, while making a public speech, he did not proceed with a traditional eulogy for the ruling city <note>Rome</note>, but instead said: "The Roman empire is an irresistible wonder." Some of his companions are the "sophists of Ulpian," those men who call the device the Romans call a *miliarium* <note>a water heater; Latin: "miliarium"</note>—which is constructed for the preparation of hot water—an "oven-kettle" <note>original: "ipnolebetas"</note>. These men are creators of many names, delighting in numerous exaggerations.

Then there was Dionysius of Sicily, who used to call a woman who did not "breathe sweetly" <note>i.e., had bad breath</note> a "Menander," because she "waited for a man" <note>a pun on "Menei-andra"; the poet Menander's name is used as a joke</note>. He called a pillar "Menecrates," because it "stays the strength" <note>pun on "menei-kraten"; Menecrates was also a famous physician</note>. He called a javelin a "purse" <note>original: "ballantion"</note>, because it is "thrown against" <note>pun on "enantion balletai"</note> something. And the holes where mice creep in he called "mysteries," because they "keep the mice" <note>pun on "mys-terein"</note>. 

Athanis, in the first book of his *History of Sicily*, says that this same Dionysius called an ox a "fat-earner" <note>original: "garotan"</note> and a pig an "Iacchus" <note>a name associated with the god Dionysus</note>. Alexarchus was of a similar character; he was the brother of Cassander, the King of Macedonia, and the founder of the city called Ouranopolis <note>"City of Heaven"</note>. Heracleides Lembus tells of him in the thirty-seventh book of his *Histories*, saying the following: "Alexarchus, the founder of Ouranopolis, introduced a private dialect, calling a rooster an 'upright-shouter' <note>original: "orthoboas"</note>, a barber’s shop a 'mortal-cutter' <note>original: "brotokermen"</note>, a drachma a 'silver-piece' <note>original: "argyris"</note>, a *choenix* <note>a dry measure</note> a 'day-waster' <note>original: "hemerophthis"</note>, and a herald a 'shouter' <note>original: "apytes"</note>." Once, Alexarchus wrote the following letter to the magistrates of the Cassandrians: 

"Alexarchus the Master <note>original: "marmar"; an obscure term</note> to the chiefs of the earth: I consider the salt-creatures... leaving the... masters of the works of the spectators, having washed them in the god’s drinking-cups by a destined fate, and the mountain-born guards."

What this letter signifies, I believe not even the Pythian Apollo could discern. For as Antiphanes says in his *Cleophanes*: "Is it worth being a tyrant, or whatever 'self-given' is? To follow strife in the Lyceum with the sophists, or thin-skinned, starving, fig-tree-like men, saying: 'This thing is not, but it becomes. For it is not possible that a thing becoming what it becomes, should be what it was before it became it. For what is, is not, and what is not... and what has not yet happened is not, just as what has happened is not what has not yet happened. For it happened out of being. But if it came from nothing, then how did it happen? From non-existence? For how is that possible? But if it happened from itself, it will not be again. And how will something happen from afar? Non-being cannot go into non-being.'" Even Apollo could not understand this when it is spoken! 

I also know that the poet Simonides called Zeus "Arisarchos" <note>Best-Ruler</note>, and Aeschylus called Hades "Agesilaos" <note>Leader of the People</note>. Nicander of Colophon called the venomous spider a "hip-breaker" <note>original: "ischiairan"</note>. Because of these and similar things, the marvelous Plato in his *Statesman* speaks of "dry-walking" animals and "soot-walking" ones, and adds terms like "razor-turning" and "fluid-turning," and "dry-pasturing," in reference to land animals, and cold ones, and gray ones. It is as if he were advising these name-makers to beware of novelty, writing these words exactly: "And you will preserve yourself from taking names too seriously, and so appear richer in wisdom as you reach old age."

I also know that the Attic orator Herodes named a "wheel-drag" <note>a block for a wheel</note> a "wheel-shackle" <note>original: "trochopede"</note>, used when he traveled through steep places in a carriage. And Simaristus, in his *Synonyms*, called the wood used for a screw a "timber-swelling." Sophocles the poet once called a guard a "bolt" <note>original: "mochlon"</note> in these lines: "Be of good courage, for I am a great bolt against this fear of yours." In other places, he has called an anchor "dried figs" <note>original: "eschadia"</note> because it holds the ship back. "The sailors hauled in the ship’s fig." And the orator Demades said that the walls of Piraeus were the "city’s belt," and Samos was a "fragment broken off the city," and he called the young men the "spring of the people," and the city walls the "city’s garment," and the trumpeter the "common rooster of the Athenians."

But this "name-hunting" sophist <note>Ulpian</note> called a woman "unclean" when she was experiencing her menses. Where did it occur to you, Ulpian, to use the word "foddered" <note>original: "kechortasmenoi"; usually used for feeding cattle</note> for people who have eaten their fill, when you ought to have used "satiated"?

At this, Ulpian perhaps laughed pleasantly and said: "Do not bark, my friend, nor grow fierce, putting forward this Cynic madness <note>a pun on 'Cynic' and 'canine'</note> during the 'dog days' of summer. You should rather call us together and be gracious to your fellow-diners, lest we perform some 'Dog-Killing' festival <note>original: "kynophontin"</note> like the one celebrated among the Argives. The word 'to be foddered' <note>original: "chortasthenai"</note> has been used of humans, my divine man! By Cratinus in his *Odyssey* like this: 'Already all day long foddering themselves on white milk.' And Menander said in his *Trophonius*: 'having been foddered.' Aristophanes in his *Gerytades* says: 'Serve him and fodder him on monodies.' Sophocles in his *Tyro* says: 'We who entertained them with all-fodder.' Eubulus in his *Dolon* says: 'I have been foddered on men not badly, but I am full, so that I can hardly move; I have put on my shoes, doing everything.' Sophilus in his *Phylarchus*: 'There will be a lavish gluttony, I see the preludes, I shall be foddered, by Dionysus, men, already it is sharp.' And Amphis in his *Heaven*: 'In the evening being foddered with all good things.' I have these examples ready at hand now, Cynulcus. Tomorrow, I will give you... 

<margin>in book 2</margin> for as to the third day, Hesiod spoke thus: 'I will fodder you with blows,' unless you can tell me where the phrase 'bloody belly' <note>original: "koiliod' aimon"</note> is found." When the other man remained silent, Ulpian continued: "But I myself know and will tell you, you dog: Eupolis in his...

# BOOK 3

## THE NAME-HUNTER

...he called them flatterers in the play of the same name. But I delay the proof of this until I pay you back the "blows" <note>This likely refers to a playful threat of academic rebuttal or a pun on "paying back" a debt of information</note>. One could answer jokingly in this way; however, Ulpian would say no, so I will provide the account concerning the womb <term>metra: the womb of a sow, considered a luxury meat in antiquity</term>. 

For Alexis, in the play titled *The Man from Pontus*, mocks the orator Kallimedon—who was nicknamed "The Crab" <note>original: "karabos"; Kallimedon was a real politician and orator known for his gluttony</note> and was one of the politicians active in the time of the orator Demosthenes—saying:

"While someone else may wish to die for his fatherland <note>original: "patra"</note>, 
Kallimedon 'The Crab' wishes to die for a womb <note>original: "metra"; a pun on "patra" (fatherland) and "metra" (sow’s womb)</note>. 
Perhaps you were quick to die at the hands of the Italians."

<margin>5</margin>
Kallimedon was always notorious for his excessive fondness for fine fish and delicacies. Antiphanes also mentions the womb in his play *The Mother-Lover* <note>original: "Philometor"; another pun on the dish and the character trait</note> as follows:

"If the wood is in measure, it contains the olive; 
it is a 'mother-city' <note>original: "metropolis"</note>, not a 'father-city' <note>original: "patropolis"</note>. 
Some sell the womb as the sweetest of meats. 
Metras the Chian is a friend to the people."

<margin>10</margin>
And Euphron says in *The Hand-over*:

"A spirited teacher, having prepared a womb, 
served it to Kallimedon along with a small jar; 
it made him jump, which is why he was called 'The Crab'."

Dioxippus, in *The Pimp of His Own Accord*, says of the musical-like foods someone desires: "Abomasum, wombs, and intestines." He also used the term "isoscigraphos" <unclear>meaning uncertain; possibly a scribe of equal weight</unclear>, and "soau" <unclear>corrupt text</unclear>. Amphikles says: "Having shown him two wombs hanging there, send him," he says, "if you see them." Eubulus, in his *Deucalion*, mentions: "Small livers, the fasting-gut, lungs, 

<margin>15</margin>
and the womb." And Lynceus of Samos, a student of the philosopher Theophrastus, mentions its use in his work *On the Use of Silphium-Juice* <term>silphion: a now-extinct medicinal and culinary herb from Cyrene, highly valued for its resinous juice</term>. Describing the banquet of Ptolemy, he says: "While a certain womb was being carried around with vinegar and silphium-juice." Antiphanes also mentions the juice in *The Lovesick Man*, speaking about Cyrene: 

"I bid farewell to everyone from the voyage where I returned; 
to all the horses, the silphium, the chariots, the stalks <note>original: "kaulos"; referring to the stalk of the silphium plant</note>, 
the racing-horses, the breasts, the fevers, and the juices."

<margin>19</margin>
Regarding the difference of the "castrated" <note>original: "ektomidas"; referring to sows that were spayed to improve the quality of the meat</note> womb, Hipparchus, who wrote the *Egyptian Iliad*, mentions it in these lines:

"May you delight me with the beautiful faces of a mother’s womb, 
the castrated sow in the pan, and oh, how it might smell!"

Sopater, in *The Man Released*, says: "But like a womb of beautiful fruit, the castrated sow, twice-boiled, white-flowered, and cheese-like in body." And in *The Physiologist*: "A slice of a sow’s womb, not un-touched. Holding the double-hearted one with the eye of the skin." And in *The Silphae*: "So that you may eat a boiled slice of sow's womb, pushing a sharp bit of rue <note>original: "pegauie"; a bitter herb</note> into the bile."

<margin>25</margin>
However, all the ancients did not serve wombs, nor lettuces, nor anything of that sort during the main dinner as people do now. Archestratus, at least, that master-crafter of delicacies, speaks of the time after the dinner, the toasts, and the use of perfumes:

"Always crown your head with all kinds of wreaths at the feast, 
whatever the blessed soil of the earth brings to bloom; 
and tend your hair with rich, steeped perfumes. 
And throw myrrh and frankincense, the fragrant fruit of Syria, 
upon the soft ashes of the fire all day long. 

<margin>30</margin>
And for your drinking, let someone bring you this kind of 'after-dish' <term>tragemata: dessert or sweetmeats served during the drinking session</term>: 
The belly and the womb of a sow, served in cumin, 
and in sharp vinegar and silphium; 
and the tender race of roasted birds, as they may be available in season. 

Do not mind the customs of the Syracusans, who only drink like frogs, eating nothing. But do not believe them; eat what I tell you. All those other 'after-dishes' are merely 

<margin>35</margin>
the miserable scrapings of a 'fine' boiled poverty: chickpeas, beans, apples, and dried figs. But praise the flat-cake <note>original: "plakounta"</note> produced in Athens. If you cannot find one there, go and seek Attic honey, for that is what makes the cake insolently good; thus one lives the life of a free man! Otherwise, let one go beneath the earth, into the pit and Tartarus, to destruction, and be buried under countless miseries."

Lynceus, describing the banquet given by the flute-player Lamia when she entertained Demetrius the Besieger <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes, a Hellenistic king</note>, immediately 

<margin>40</margin>
shows those entering the dinner eating all kinds of fish and meat. Similarly, in the banquet of King Antigonus during the Aphrodisia festival, and in the account Ptolemy gives us, Archestratus—who became the guide to pleasure for the wise philosopher Epicurus—just like the poet of Ascra <note>Hesiod</note>, gives you advice in the form of maxims: he tells you not to trust some people but to pay attention to him, and he commands you to eat everything. 

These things are no different from the cook in the play of Damoxenus the comic poet, who says in *The Foster-Brothers*:

<margin>45</margin>
"You see me as a disciple of the wise Epicurus, 
under whom, in not even ten full years and months, 
I have compressed four talents <note>A massive sum of money</note> for you. 
And tell me, what is this? To be a leading cook? 
Even he did not know! Gods, what a cook—it is the nature of every art! 
There is someone for whom it is a sacrilege from the beginning. 
Nothing is wiser than hard work; the matter was easy, 

<margin>50</margin>
since I have the book of this discourse. For many things contribute; 
therefore, when you see an illiterate cook 
who has not read everything by Democritus, 
or rather, does not have it mastered, laugh him down as empty! 
And I will clearly hire out the 'Canon' of Epicurus <note>Epicurus’s work on logic and criteria of truth</note>, 
as if from a will. For one must know what difference it makes, 
my best friend, between the 'glauciskos' fish in winter and in summer." 

Again: "What kind of fish is naturally gathered here? It is most useful during the solstices, for the changes and the movements..."

# EPICUREANISM

...shaking that steep evil <note>original: "kakon helibaton"; likely a reference to indigestion or a heavy, poorly prepared meal</note> for men, they produce alterations in the digestive turnings—you understand—but that which
is taken in its proper season gives back its grace. Who follows these things? Truly, very
frequent and tiny breaths <note>original: "pneumatia"; here referring to flatulence or digestive vapors</note> make the guest feel heavy, but with me, the food is
better prepared, and it is thinned out, and it breathes out correctly. Therefore, into the pores the juice
is settled evenly everywhere. You speak of juice, Democritus <note>The cook is likely addressing a guest named Democritus, or referencing the philosopher of atoms</note> says; nothing makes the one
who has eaten more malnourished than these modern things, and how much of the medical art do you think I share in? And all this knowledge of nature,
while the ignorance of current cooks is apparent to the sight, what kind of smell do you perceive when you look at
fish. They do the opposite, making them one. And throwing sesame seeds into this, having taken
each of them in part, he will adjust it, just as you have used me; for how could anything turn out well, if its 
<margin>10</margin>identity were mixed with another? And those entanglements which are not harmonious touches—to see through these things
is the task of a spirited art, not just mincing dishes, nor smelling of smoke. For I do not 
enter the kitchen, but I observe something sitting nearby. Others do the work, but I tell you
the causes, and the resulting sharpness; the mincing is the work of a musical arranger <note>original: "harmonikos"</note>, not a mere cook; let him increase the fire,
let him level the coals. First the dish boils, but you do not understand the pattern of those that follow in harmony,
O Apollo! And what an art it appears to be! Then I set nothing at random before my fellow-diners—no,
but having mixed everything according to harmony. How is it for them? Those things which have fellowship through the frying-pan through the whole,
through all the strings <note>original: "dia pason"; a musical pun meaning an octave, suggesting the meal has a full range of flavors</note> again, these I bring to the intervals themselves,
and I weave them immediately in a fitting way with the desserts; and sometimes I command unsparingly: from where
are you coming? What should you mix with these things more? Have you tasted the laurel? It does not overflow the wise man;
Epicurus thus used to thicken pleasure.
<margin>20</margin>He kneaded it carefully; he alone saw "the Good" as it truly is; but those in the Stoa <note>The Stoic philosophers</note> seek it passionately,
not knowing what it is. Therefore, since they do not have it, they are ignorant. Nor could they manage otherwise—does it 
seem so to you? Let us leave the rest; it is clear as of old. And Plato <note>Plato Comicus, the comic poet, not the philosopher</note> in *The Summarizer*,
having represented a youth being stained, corrupted from the traditional path in his lifestyle by his
pedagogue, says: "You have destroyed my youth after taking him, you filthy man, and you have compelled him
to enter a life foreign to him; and now you rasp him with morning drinking-bouts, previously unaccustomed."
"If he has learned something, master, he lives; do you complain?" "Is such a thing 'living'?" "As the wise say."
"Epicurus, for instance, says the Good is pleasure, surely; it is not possible if one does not have this
from somewhere; but from living well, O Sosia, in every way you will perhaps give it to me." Have you ever seen
a philosopher of mine getting drunk? With these things you say, everyone is enchanted. Those who 
<margin>30</margin>now have their eyebrows raised <note>A common Greek idiom for being arrogant or pretentious</note>, and are seeking "the wise man" in the walks <note>original: "peripatois"; the covered walkways where philosophers taught</note> and the
discussions, as if he had run away—yet if a small grey-fish <note>original: "glaukiskos"</note> is served to them, they know 
at what spot they must first touch it, and they seek the head as if it were a matter of great state, so that
everyone is stunned. And in Antiphanes' *The Soldier*, you might find advice being brought in;
he is such a man. He says: "Whoever considers any possession in life to be a secure thing,
has erred greatly. For either a tax has snatched everything away, or falling into a lawsuit,
he is ruined. Or having served as general, he paid a fine; or chosen as choregos <note>a wealthy citizen who funded the public chorus</note>, providing garments and gold
for the chorus, he wears rags himself. Or as a trierarch <note>commander of a warship</note> he hanged himself, or sailing he was captured somehow, or walking, or sleeping
he was cut down by his servants. There is nothing stable, except what a man happens to spend
pleasurably on himself day by day. Nor are even these things very much; for a thief might snatch the table
<margin>40</margin>having approached again; but when you have already swallowed the morsel within 
the teeth, consider this alone of your possessions to be secure." The same thing is said in *The Water-
Pitcher*. Looking at these things then, dear friends, one might reasonably praise the noble Chrysippus <note>A famous Stoic philosopher</note>,
who saw the nature of Epicurus accurately and said that the "mother-city" <term>metropolis: the parent city/source</term> of his philosophy 
was the *Gastrology* of Archestratus <note>Archestratus of Gela (4th c. BCE), the first "food critic" who wrote a poem on fine dining</note>, which all the gluttons among the philosophers say is a kind of "Theogony" <note>An account of the birth of the gods</note> for them,
this beautiful epic poem. Against whom Theognetus says in *The Phantom*, or *The Miser*:
"Man, you will destroy me. For being filled with the little logic-choppings of the Painted Stoa,
you are sick. You will say: 'Is wealth foreign to man? It fattens him. But wisdom is one's own ice
<note>original: "krystallos"; here meaning something cold or crystalline/pure</note>,
no one who took this ever lost it.' O miserable me! Alas, my fate has housed me with a philosopher!
You have learned your letters backwards, you rogue; your books have turned your life upside down.
<margin>50</margin>You have played the philosopher, talking to the earth and sky, which care nothing for your words." <margin>Still</margin>
While Ulpian was still speaking, servants entered carrying crayfish <note>original: "karabous"; spiny lobsters</note> on platters, larger than Kallimedon
the orator, who because of his love for this food was nicknamed "The Crayfish." Alexis then mentions him
in *The Female Deer*...

<header>BOOK III</header>

## CRUSTACEANS

...in *Darcis*, or as some say, he commonly reports him to be a pleasure-seeker, just as other comic poets do, saying the following:
> It has been decreed by the fishmongers, so they say, to set up a bronze statue of Callimedon <note>original: "Kallimedontos"; a politician nicknamed "the Crab" due to his fondness for seafood</note> at the Panathenaic festival among the fish, holding a roasted spiny lobster in his right hand, as if he were the only Savior of their trade. But to all others, he is a loss.

And there was a whole group of people devoted to the eating of the spiny lobster <note>original: "karabou"; refers to the Mediterranean spiny lobster, which lacks the large claws of the common lobster</note>, as can be learned through many parts of comedy. For now, Aristophanes will suffice in the *Thesmophoriazusae*, speaking thus:
> Someone has bought a fish, or a small stingray, or some of the broad prawns, or an octopus, or a "fasting-fish," or a roasted shark, or squids; by Zeus, not even a ray, I say. Neither a sow’s womb, nor lungs, nor a boar’s liver,
<margin>10</margin> nor a crop, nor a three-year-old piglet’s haunch, nor an eel-let, nor a large spiny lobster—come to the aid of weary women!

By "broad prawns," he likely means those called lobsters <note>original: "astakous"; the European lobster, distinguished by its large claws</note>, which Philyllius mentions in *The Cities*. Indeed, Archestratus, in his famous poem, does not name the spiny lobster at all, but addresses it as a lobster, as in these lines: "But for much nonsense, buy a lobster, the one having long and heavy hands <note>original: "cheiras"; referring to claws</note>, but small feet, and which leaps slowly upon the earth. They are the best of all in excellence at Lipara, though the Hellespont gathers many of them." And Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe*, before the introduction of the lobster by Archestratus, shows that it is the spiny lobster, saying thus: "There are lobsters, and leaden-colored ones having small little feet, but long hands, and the one named spiny lobster." There is a distinct species of spiny lobster and another of lobsters, and still another of prawns. The Athenians say "astakos" <note>lobster</note> with the 's', just as they say "astaphidas" <note>raisins</note>. For Epicharmus also
<margin>20</margin> calls them "sea-creatures, soft and crook-taloned." Speusippus, in the second book of *Similar Things*, says that among the crustaceans, the "korakos," lobster, "nymphē," "arktos" <note>bear-shrimp</note>, "markinos," and "pagouros" <note>crab</note> are similar. Diocles the physician says: "prawns, crabs, spiny lobsters, and lobsters are difficult to pass but act as diuretics." Epicharmus also mentions "arktoi" <note>bear-shrimps</note> in *The Marriageable Girls*, which Nicander says is the "sea-aeolian," but Heracleides in his *Art of Cookery* says it is a type of prawn. Aristotle, in the fifth book of the *History of Animals*, says that among the crustaceans—spiny lobsters, lobsters, prawns, and the like—they mate in the same way as the backward-urinating quadrupeds. They mate at the beginning of spring near the land. For the mating of all such creatures has already been observed. They spawn when the
figs begin to ripen. Spiny lobsters are found in rough and rocky places, but lobsters in smooth places. Neither is found in muddy areas. For this reason, lobsters are found in the Hellespont and around Thasos, while spiny lobsters are found around Sigeum and Mount Athos. All spiny lobsters are long-lived. Theophrastus,
<margin>30</margin> in his work *On Creatures that Live in Burrows*, says that lobsters, spiny lobsters, and prawns shed their "old age" <note>original: "gēras"; a poetic term for the exoskeleton shed during molting</note>. Concerning prawns, Ephorus says in the first book of his *History* that there were many prawns at the city of Chios on the island, claiming it was founded by those saved from the flood of Deucalion after the blessed ones, and even until now the place is called "Karides" <note>Prawns</note>. The culinary-master Archestratus advises the following:
> If you ever come to the city of Iasus, you will get a prawn of great size, but they are rare to buy. In Macedonia and Ambracia, there are very many.

Araros has spoken at length of the prawn, though not as "the curved one":
> The curved prawns leap high like dolphins into the wicker-woven vessel.

And Eubulus in *Orthannes*:
> I let down the little prawns, and they went back up again.

Anaxandrides in *Lycurgus*:
> And he plays with the little prawns along with partridges and "therētidia," and with small roasted fish along with "lōbidaria," and with "skindaria" along with "kabidia" <note>These appear to be diminutive or local names for various small fish and snacks</note>.

He also says they are "all-tails" <note>original: "panourō"</note>:
<margin>40</margin> 
> You will be better off standing straight, not bent over; but this body of a prawn is curved and is a veritable anchor of a body.

And in *The Weaver's Shuttle*:
> I will show you to be redder than a roasted prawn.

Eubulus in *The Grandmothers* says of the hunchbacked prawn:
> And you, "kallaïchos," and the curved prawns together in a red dish.

And in the *Lament*:
> They danced like prawns on coals, the curved ones rejoicing.

Eupolis spoke of them in a contracted form in *The Goats* thus:
> Except once I ate prawns at Phaeax's house.

And in *The Demes*: "having the face of a peeled prawn."
They were named prawns <note>original: "karides"</note> from the head <note>original: "kara"</note>. For the head takes up the greatest part of the body. The Athenians use the form "karides" with a short vowel by analogy. For it comes from "karē" <note>head</note> because it has a larger head. Just as from "graphē" comes "graphis," and "bolē" comes "bolis," so from "karē" comes "karis." When the penultimate syllable was shortened, the end was lengthened. It is spoken similarly to "psēphis" <note>pebble</note>, "krēpis" <note>boot</note>, and "teuthis" <note>squid</note>.
<margin>50</margin> Concerning these shell-skinned creatures, Diphilus of Siphnos writes as follows: "Among the shell-skinned, the prawn, lobster, spiny lobster, crab, and 'sea-lion' belong to the same genus but differ. The 'sea-lion' is larger than the lobster. Spiny lobsters are also called 'graphaei.' They are meatier than crabs. The crab is heavy and difficult to digest." Mnesitheus of Athens, in his book *On Edibles*, says spiny lobsters...

# ATHENAEUS: THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

### THE FRYERS

...and crabs, and prawns, and similar things. These are indeed hard to digest, but they are much more sleep-inducing than other fish. They are more suitable when tender rather than boiled. Sophron, in his *Mimes of Women*, speaks of prawns as *lourias* <note>original: "lourias"; a local or dialectal name for prawns</note> in this way: "See, beautiful prawns; see, lobsters; see, look here, my friend, how red they are and how finely whiskered they are." And Epicharmus, in *Earth and Sea*, mentions "crimson prawns" and, in his descriptions, speaks of "fry-fish" and "curved prawns." Simonides says, "Squid for the tunnies, prawns for the gobies." Next, there were brought in "fried livers" <note>original: "tagēnista hēpata"</note> wrapped in what is called the omentum <term>omentum: the fatty membrane surrounding the internal organs, known in Greek as the "epiplous"</term>, which Philhetaerus mentions in *The Cheese-man* as "omentum-wrapped." Looking at all of this, Cynulcus said: "Tell us, O wise Ulpian, if the liver is recorded anywhere as being wrapped up in this way." And if you can show it first in some author, the omentum... <unclear>aricōn ōthi</unclear> ...the fat and the membrane. Regarding these things, Myrtilus said:

<margin>10</margin> It appears once in Epicharmus’s *Bacchae*: "Behold, he has wrapped his own in the omentum," and in *The Ambassadors*: "concerning the loin and the omentum." And Ion of Chios, in his *Travels*, used the word "wrapped." My dear friend Ulpian, keep yourself far from that omentum, lest you ever be wrapped up in it and burnt to a crisp, which would certainly relieve us all from your endless inquiries! You are the one who ought to remember the evidence for how these livers are prepared, especially since it was declared to you long ago that we were seeking information about the "ears" and "feet" <note>referring to common appetizers of pig extremities</note>. Alexis, in *The Dictatress* or *The Druggist*, has spoken of this. The whole selection is useful for many things. Since you cannot keep it in your memory now, I myself will go through it. The comic poet speaks thus: "First, he brought many oysters to a certain private citizen, an old man clothed in seaweed; then I took some sea urchins. For these are a pleasant prelude to a dinner for one who has visualized them well. After these were cleared away, there were small fish, trembling with fear—what are they all? He bid us be bold... these things, he said, were destined to do no harm, and I bought a large grey-fish <note>original: "glaukon"; possibly a bluefish or sea-perch</note>. Then I took an electric ray <note>original: "narkēn"; known for its numbing sting</note>, whispering that it was for a woman who, bringing her tender fingers near the spine, might not find what she sought.

<margin>20</margin> Onto the frying pan went some 'fasting' wrasses, a prawn, a seaweed-fish, a goby, a perch, and a needle-fish; he made the dish more colorful than a peacock. Then there were small meat-bits, feet, certain snouts, ears, and a liverling wrapped up. For it is ashamed and turns dark in color—will the cook not chop these? By Zeus, he will surely lament! I say clearly, I will manage these things elegantly and with variety. For where else could one find such a side-dish <term>opson: a generic term for any savory dish eaten with bread, often fish</term>, that I make the diners fall out over the leftovers? Sometimes they even lose their teeth because of the pleasure of the preparations. I am ready to explain the preparation of all these things, teaching it for free if anyone wishes to learn." That it was the custom to wrap livers in the omentum is also stated by Hegesander of Delphi in his *Commentaries*; he says that Metaneira the courtesan received her nickname because of the "wrapped livers" she was associated with. ❧ As she was putting on her sandals... "I am undone, I have perished; he has destroyed me by wrapping me in the omentum." Perhaps even Crobylus the comic poet called such a liver "shameful" <note>wordplay on the red, "blushing" color of the liver</note>. Just as Alexis says in *The False Supposititious Child*: "And you will be very glad of a twisted tentacle, or if you find a 'shameful liver' anywhere, devour the old things."

<margin>30</margin> Aristophanes mentions the "liverling" in *The Fryers*, and Alcaeus in *The Wrestling School*, and Eubulus in *Deucalion*, using a rougher breathing for the word "liver." For even the "fig-liver" <note>original: "sykalophē"; likely a liver from a bird fattened on figs</note> is found in Archilochus with a rough breathing. For he says, "For you have no gall in your liver." And if there is a certain fish called the "liver-fish" <note>original: "hēpatos"</note>, which Eubulus says in *The Laconians* has no gall... "as much gall as I had, so did he speak to me about the liver-fish. But I am still a 'Black-butt' <note>original: "Melampygou"; a reference to Heracles or a tough, tanned person</note>." Hegesander, in his *Commentaries*, says that in the heads of the "liver-fish" there are two stones, similar in luster and color to oysters, but rhomboid in shape. Alexis mentions "fried fish" in *Demetrius*, just as in the aforementioned passage.

<margin>40</margin> Eubulus, in *Orthanes*, says: "Every beautiful woman, a child of the morning and a companion of the frying pans. Tribal-bread and honey-cakes, and together with them the squid, and the Phaleric maiden <note>a poetic term for the Phaleric anchovy</note>, mixed with lamb’s innards; the foal dances like a piglet under the yoke. The fan <note>used to blow the fire</note> rouses Hephaestus’s guardian dogs, breathing hot breath onto the frying pan. The smell rises to the nostrils, kneaded... the hollow of the throat pressed by a finger, imitating the rams of a trireme, a precursor to an excellent dinner." Nothing is sweeter than fried cuttlefish. Philhetaerus, or perhaps Nicostratus, says in *Antyllus*: "Never again would I be moved to eat cuttlefish from the frying pan alone." Hegemon, in *Philinne*, makes them eat the "fry" <note>original: "gonon"; the young or spawn of fish</note> from the pan in these lines: "Very quickly buy some octopus, and give us the fry from the pan to devour." At these words, the sweet Ulpian was annoyed, and looking at us... ❧ ...the iambics of Eubulus’s *Orthanes*, saying, as if in the women's quarters at the frying pan, "O enemy of the gods!" Myrtilus added:

<margin>50</margin> "For I know well that he never bought any of these things to eat, as someone once told me, citing these iambics of Eubulus about a pimp: 'A heavy bag of a man feeds me, a miser and a scoundrel, a gourmet who buys side-dishes for only three obols.'" Since the young man was well-educated and brought up...

# BOOK III
## BREAD.

...not just about Myrtilus, but from wherever else someone might find it. When I asked him how he happened upon the subject of Myrtilus, he recited these lines to me from Antiphanes’s *The Fledgling*: "How could I have come here to Athens with my sister, brought by some merchant, being Syrian by birth? But this man here, a proclaimed usurer <term>obolostatēs: literally a 'weigher of obols,' a derogatory term for a petty money-lender</term>, met us and bought us—a man of unsurpassable wickedness. He is the sort who brings nothing into the house, not even the things that the famous Pythagoras used to eat; the thrice-blessed man would never carry anything through the doors." While he was still playing around with these Urapian-style <note>The Greek "oulapiana" is obscure; it may refer to a specific style of dance or buffoonery</note> jokes, the Cynic <note>original: "ho Kyklikos"; likely referring to Cynulcus, one of the banquet guests</note> cried out: "We need bread, and not that of King Messapius!" <note>Messapius was a legendary king of the Iapygians in Italy</note>

I say this because Iapygia is a city, and there is also a treatise on it by Polemon. Thucydides also mentions him in his seventh book, as does the comic poet Demetrius in the play entitled *Sicily*, through the characters of the Bytae: "And from there we crossed the sea to the Messapians with a south wind. Bread <note>original: "Artos"; here personified or used as a name</note> then took us up and welcomed us kindly; he is a great and splendid guest-friend there." But this was not the "Bread" of the current occasion, but rather those types discovered by Demeter, who is called *Pisitis* <note>meaning "of the grain-grinding"</note> and *Simalis*. For this is how the goddess is honored among the Syracusans, as Polemon himself records in his *Treatise on the Masticator*. In the first book of his *Reply to Timaeus*, 

<margin>10</margin> he says that in the Boeotian Skolos, statues of "Great-Bread" and "Great-Cake" have been established. Under these names, loaves of bread were brought in, and a multitude of all kinds of food accompanied them. Looking at these, he said: "How many traps for bread have miserable mortals set!" as Alexis says in *The Well*. Let us now say what and of what kind these are.

Forestalling him, Pontianus said: Tryphon of Alexandria, in his works entitled *On Plants*, sets out the various types of bread which I will list from memory: leavened bread <note>original: "zymitēn"</note>, unleavened bread <note>original: "azymon"</note>, bread made of fine flour <note>original: "semidalitēn"</note>, bread made of coarse emmer-wheat <note>original: "chondritēn"</note>, and unbolted or whole-grain bread <note>original: "synkomiston"</note>. He says that this last one is more laxative than pure bread. Then there is bread made of spelt <note>original: "olyra"</note>, bread of one-grained wheat <note>original: "tiphē"</note>, and bread of millet <note>original: "melinē"</note>. He says that the coarse emmer bread is made from emmer wheat <note>original: "zeia"</note>, for groats <note>original: "chondros"</note> cannot be made from barley. 

<margin>20</margin> Others are named after the method of baking, such as *ipnitēs* <note>oven-baked, from "ipnos"</note>, which Timocles mentions in *The False Robbers* like this: "Having learned of the hot tray of the oven, nothing is sweeter than hot oven-bread." Then there is *eschariitēs* <note>hearth-baked bread</note>; Antidotus mentions this in *The Master-Pourer*: "Taking hot hearth-cakes—how could you not? Dip them into sweet wine and devour them." And Crobylus in *The Man who Hanged Himself*: "And taking a certain tray of pure hearth-cakes." 

Lynceus of Samos, in his *Letter to Diagoras*, comparing the foodstuffs produced at Athens with those in Rhodes, says: "Furthermore, the city which prides itself on its market-bread provides it at the beginning and middle of the meal, lacking nothing in its delivery. But when people have finished eating and are full, they bring in the most pleasant pastime, called the 'divided hearth-cake' <note>original: "diachokton eschariitēn"</note>, which is so mixed with sweetening agents and made so soft that it creates a harmonious symphony with sweet wine even for one who is already stuffed. It is a marvel how it restores a sober man and often even a drunken one." In the same way, it brings rest to the one eating it. 

<margin>30</margin> There is also *talaritēs* <note>basket-bread, from "talaros"</note>; Sopater mentions it in *The Woman from Cnidus*: "and the basket-bread was jaw-stretching." *Achainas*: Samos mentions this bread in the eighth book of his *History of Delos*, saying it is produced for the Thesmophoria <note>a women-only festival in honor of Demeter</note>. These are large loaves, and the festival itself is called the *Megaglartia* <note>Great-Bread Festival</note> because those carrying the bread cry out: "Achainen!" It is filled with the fat of a goat. 

Then there is *kribanitēs* <note>bread baked in a "kribanos," a portable earthenware oven</note>. Aristophanes mentions this in *Old Age*. He depicts a bread-seller speaking after her loaves have been snatched away by those who have cast off their old age: "What was this business? They were hot, my child! Are you out of your mind? These were very white pot-baked loaves, my child!" 

*Enkryphias* <note>ash-baked bread, literally "hidden" in the embers</note>: Nicostratus mentions this in *The Hierophant*, as does the master-chef Archestratus, whose testimony I shall provide at the appropriate time. 

*Dipyros* <note>twice-baked, similar to a biscuit</note>: Eubulus in *Ganymede* mentions "hot twice-baked loaves." But there are also certain 

<margin>40</margin> unfired <note>original: "apyroi"</note> loaves. Alcaeus in *Ganymede* says: "And we need a light thin-cake <note>original: "laganon"</note>, easy to digest." Even better than this is what is called the *apanthrakis* <note>charcoal-seared cake</note>. Aristophanes also mentions it in *The Assemblywomen*, saying: "the thin-cakes are baked." Concerning the *apanthrakis*, Diocles of Carystus says in his *Health Treatise*: "The charcoal-seared cake is softer than the thin-cakes." It seems this too is cooked on coals, just like the Athenian ash-baked bread. The people of Alexandria dedicate this to Cronus <note>Saturn</note> and set it out for anyone who wishes to eat in the Temple of Cronus. 

Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe* and *The Muses* (the latter play is a revision of the former), sets out several kinds: pot-baked bread <note>original: "kribanitēs"</note>, *homoros*, *saititēs*, *enkrida* <note>a fried dough with honey</note>, *alaphatitēs*, and the *hemiartion* <note>half-loaf</note>. Sophron also mentions these in his *Mimes of Women*, saying: "Dinner for the aunts: pot-baked loaves, *homoroi*, and half-loaves." I know, my friends, that the 

<margin>50</margin> Dorians use the letter 'r' and say *kribanos* and *kribanitēs*. However, Herodotus in the second book of his *Histories* wrote "in a transparent *klibanos*." Sophron too said: "some *saititai*, and *klibanitai*, and half-loaves, why not?" He also mentions a certain "flat-bread" <note>original: "plakita"</note> in his *Mimes of Women*: "for the night, give me a flat-bread." And Sophron mentions "cheese-bread" <note>original: "tyrōnta"</note> in the play entitled *The Wicked Women*: "I advise you to eat a bread that is freshly cheesed for the children." Nicander of Colophon in his...

# ATHENAEUS: THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

### BREADS.

In the *Dialects* <note>original: "glōssais"; likely referring to a dictionary of regional terms</note>, unleavened bread is called *slaratos*. Plato the Comedian, in his play *The Long Night*, gives the name *kilikios* <note>original: "kilikios"; literally "Cilician," suggesting a rough or coarse style</note> to large, "dirty" loaves in these lines: "And then he came having bought breads, not the very pure kind, but large *kilikioi*." In the play entitled *Menelaus*, he calls certain breads "common" <note>original: "agelaious"</note>. Whole-wheat bread <note>original: "autopurou artou"</note> is mentioned by Alexis in *The Cyprian*: "Having just now eaten the whole-wheat bread." Phrynichus, in *The Weed-Gatherers*, calls them *autopuritai*, saying: "With whole-wheat breads and fat companions." Sophocles mentions "bird-bread" <note>original: "ornithou artou"</note> in *Triptolemus*, which is either made from rice or from a seed that grows in the land of Ethiopia, which is similar to sesame. 

Aristophanes mentions *kollabos* <note>a type of small roll or bun</note> in *The Fryers*: "Each man receives a *kollabos*." And again: "Either bring a late-autumn piglet here, or a trident with warm *kollaboi*." <margin>10</margin> These breads are made from new wheat, as Philyllius demonstrates in the same play: "He himself bringing the offspring of three-month wheat, milk-colored, warm *kollaboi*." Alcman, in his fifteenth book, remembers "poppy-breads" <note>original: "makonidiōn artōn"</note> thus: "Seven couches, and as many tables heaped with poppy-breads, crowned with linseed and sesame, and in grayish bowls." *Chrusokolla* <note>literally "gold-glue"</note> is a small snack made with honey and linseed. 

Aristophanes mentions the bread called *kollura* <note>a coarse, rounded loaf</note> in *Peace*: "And a large *kollura*, and a 'knuckle' <note>original: "kondylon"; a fist-sized piece of meat or bread</note> of relish upon it." And in *The Merchant Ships*: "They pass the *kollura* twice, because of the trophy at Marathon." <note>This refers to the "Marathonian" bread ration or a specific victory custom</note> 

The "spit-bread" <note>original: "obelias artos"</note> is so called either because it is sold for an *obol* <note>a small Greek coin</note>, as in Alexandria, or because it is roasted on small spits <note>original: "obeliskous"</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Glosses*: "Then do you happen to be roasting a spit-bread?" Pherecrates in *The Forgetful Man*: "You give back a whole spit-bread, but you do not value the bread." Those who carried this bread on their shoulders in processions were called "spit-bread-bearers" <note>original: "obeliaphoroi"</note>. <margin>20</margin> Socrates, in the sixth book of his *Invocations*, says that Dionysus invented the spit-bread during military campaigns.

"Tunny-bread" <note>original: "thunitas artos"</note> is what is called "yolk-bread" <note>original: "lekithitas"</note>, as Eucrates says. There is also *panos* bread; the Messapians call a certain payment *pania*, and the wrappings are *pania*. Blesus in *The Filter-Hater*, Archilochus in *Telephus*, and Rhinthon in *Amphitryon* mention it. The Romans also call bread *pana* <note>original: "pana"; a reference to the Latin "panis"</note>. 

*Nastos* bread is a large, leavened bread, as Polemarchus and Artemidorus say. Heracleon, however, says it is a type of cake. Nicostratus says in *The Couch*: "Master, a *nastos* of such a great size, and white!" For its thickness hides the basket, and a "springing" smell <note>original: "pidēlme"</note>—once the cover was removed—rose up, a certain steam mixed with honey reached the nostrils, for it was still warm. 

*Lēknos* bread is common among the Ionians, as Artemidorus of Ephesus says in his *Ionian Memoirs*. *Thronos* <note>literally "throne"</note> is the name of a bread. Neanthes of Cyzicus, in the second book of his *Greek History*, writes: "But Codrus takes the so-called 'throne' of a slice of bread, and meat, and they distribute it to the eldest." <margin>30</margin> There is also *bakchylos* bread, called *apoditēs* among the Eleans, as Nicander relates in the second book of *Dialects*. Diphilus also mentions it in *The Erring Woman*: "Having rubbed the *apoditēs* breads with oil..." 

There is also a type of bread called *apopurias* <note>literally "from the fire"</note>, which is roasted over coals; some call this "leavened bread" <note>original: "zumitēs"</note>. Cratinus in *The Softlings*: "First I have an *apopurias*, full of the 'son of leaven' <note>original: "zumētamiadou"; a playful personification of leaven</note>, like a cushion." 

Archestratus, in his *Gastronomy*, sets out the following regarding barley-meal and bread: "First, dear Muse, I shall remember the gifts of fair-haired Demeter, and you should cast them in your mind. For it is possible to get the best and finest of all things—all items cleanly prepared from fruitful barley. In Lesbos, by the famous wave of Eressos, the gods bring forth barley-meal whiter than driven snow; Hermes himself goes there to buy it. It is also fair in seven-gated Thebes, and in Thasos, and in some other cities, but those seem like grape-stones <margin>40</margin> compared to the Lesbian meal. You shall know it by the touch. Let there be a Thessalian *kollix* <note>a large loaf</note> for you, which the Kanoi call *krimmatian*, and others call a 'gristle-bread' <note>original: "chondroibon"</note>. Then I praise the bread of fine flour <note>original: "semidaleos"</note> from Tegea. As for the bread baked in the ashes <note>original: "enkruphian"</note>, and the bread made for the market, glorious Athens provides the most beautiful for mortals. In the red-soiled, grape-bearing Erythrae, coming from the oven <note>original: "klibanou"</note>, white bread, flourishing in its delicate seasons, will delight you at dinner." 

Archestratus, the glutton, says these things while away, and he advises having a "Phoenician" or "Lydian" for a variety of breads. Or perhaps he was ignorant that the bread-makers of Cappadocia are the best? He says: "Let there be a Phoenician or Lydian man in your house, who will be knowledgeable of your mind day by day, preparing all sorts of special breads <note>original: "panthias idias"</note> as you command." 

Antiphanes also mentions Attic breads as being superior in *Omphale*: "For how could any well-born man <margin>50</margin> ever be able to leave this roof, seeing these white-bodied breads, filling the oven in crowded ranks? Seeing their shapes changed by the baking-pots <note>original: "kribanois"</note>—an imitation of the Attic hand, which Thearion <note>A famous baker in 5th-century Athens, mentioned by Plato and Aristophanes</note> first revealed in his creations." This is the same Thearion the baker whom Plato mentions in the *Gorgias*, listing him alongside Mithaecus, writing: "Those who have become, or are, healers of bodies. You spoke to me very disparagingly of Thearion the baker..."

# BOOK III

### BREADS

---

The baker, and Mithaecus <note>a famous 5th-century BC cook and author of a Sicilian cookery book</note>, who wrote the *Sicilian Cookery*, and Sarambus the tavern-keeper—all these were marvelous "healers of bodies," the first by preparing wondrous breads, the second seasoning, and the third wine. Aristophanes mentions this in his plays *Gerytades* and *Aeolosicon* with these words: "I have come from Thearion’s, leaving the bakery where I ate bread from the pans" <note>original: "kribanōn"; earthenware baking pans</note>. Eubulus mentions Cyprian bread as being exceptionally fine in these lines: "It is a terrible thing for a man to see and then pass by Cyprian breads; for like a Magnesian stone <note>a magnet</note>, they pull in the hungry." Regarding "roll-breads" <note>original: "kollikiōn"; small buns or rolls</note>, which are the same as *kollaboi*, Ephippus mentions them in his *Artemis* thus: "Having eaten a roll of pan-baked bread from Alexander of Thessaly." And Aristophanes in *The Acharnians* says: "Greetings, you little Boeotian roll-eater!" <note>original: "kollikophage"</note>. After these things were said, one of the grammarians present named Hadrian spoke up: "These foods are ancient history <note>original: "kronika"; literally "from the age of Kronos," implying old-fashioned or outdated</note>, my friends. For we take no joy in barley-groats—since the city is full of bread—nor in this catalog of breads." But since another work by Chrysippus of Tyana exists, titled *The Art of Bread-making*, and having had experience with the names mentioned there among many of my friends, I myself shall say something about breads. 

The bread called "pan-baked" <note>original: "artopikinos"; likely from the Latin "artopticius"</note> differs from that baked in a portable oven <note>original: "klibanikios"</note> or a fixed oven <note>original: "fournakios"</note>. If you work the dough stiffly, it will be bright and good for "dry-eating" <note>eating bread without accompanying sauces or meats</note>. If you make it from soft dough <note>original: "amalthunēs"</note>, it will be light but not bright. Portable-oven and fixed-oven breads prefer a softer dough. Among the "rolled" types, there is a bread called "soft," seasoned with a little milk, oil, and enough salt. Because of the preparation, the dough must be left to rise. This bread is called "Cappadocian," since soft bread is most commonly made in Cappadocia. The Syrians call this type of bread *lachma* <note>original: "lachmau"; related to the Semitic "laḥm" for bread</note>, and it is the finest in Syria because it is eaten very hot. It is similar to the bread of our own region. The bread called *balikinos* is shaped like a *boulētēs* <note>a mushroom-shaped loaf</note>; the kneading trough is greased and sprinkled with poppy seeds, upon which the dough is placed, and because it is leavened, it does not stick to the trough. When it is put into the oven, some groats are sprinkled on the bottom, and then the bread is placed inside, taking on a beautiful color, like that of smoked cheese. "Spiced-pan" bread <note>original: "srēpipikios"</note> is made with a little milk, pepper, and a little oil (or fat, if oil is unavailable). For what is called "bread-wafer" <note>original: "artolaganon"</note>, a little wine, pepper, milk, and oil (or fat) are added. For the so-called "dry-biscuits" <note>original: "kapuria"</note>, one mixes the dough as for bread, but then treats them according to the "doctrines" of the Great Roman Sophist <note>referring to a cook or author of high reputation</note>. 

At this, Cynulcus <note>one of the Cynic philosophers at the banquet</note> exclaimed: "O Mother of Wisdom! Do you not know that the wonderful Blepsias has countless <note>original: "psammakosious"; literally "sand-hundreds"</note> students, and has carried off more wealth from this 'beautiful wisdom' than Gorgias or Protagoras? I hesitate to say whether he himself is blind, or if those who hand their students over to him have no eyes, seeing as they can barely see through the crowd. I say they are blessed—or rather, departed souls—for listening to such lectures from their teachers." Then Magnus, being a lover of tradition and surpassing even the sweat of grammarians, replied: "These 'barefoot ground-sleepers' <note>mocking the Cynics' lifestyle</note> are, according to the comic poet Eubulus, 'unholy gullets, unsparing of others' property.' Did not your forefather Diogenes, once eating a cake greedily at a banquet, tell someone who asked that he knew well-made bread when he saw it? But you, 'dish-chokers' <note>original: "lopad’anchoi"</note> as the same poet Eubulus calls you, do you not speak with the voices of gluttons? Why don't you keep quiet until someone brings you bread or holy offerings, as they do in comedies? How could you know that *kyboi* <note>literally "cubes" or "dice"</note>—not the ones you always handle—are actually square breads seasoned with dill, cheese, and oil, as Heracleides says in his *Book of Seasonings*? 

Blepsias describes another, the *thargēlos*, which some call the *thalysios* <note>a harvest-offering bread</note>. Crates, in the second book of *The Attic Dialect*, says the *thargēlos* is the first bread made from the harvest, as is the *samitēs*. He has not even seen the bread called *nasos*, which is made for the *Arrhephoroi* <note>young girls who carried sacred vessels in Athenian festivals</note>. There is also the *pyramous* bread, made with sesame seeds; it is perhaps the same as the *sēsamitēs*. Tryphon mentions all of these in the first book of *Plants*, as well as the so-called *thiagones*. These are breads made for the gods in Aetolia. *Dramikes* and *araxis* are names for certain breads among the Athamanians. The lexicographers also list names of breads: Seleucus mentions the *boaiē* among the Macedonians, and the *ōtos* among the Thessalians. He says the *enitan* is a bread made of pulse or yolks, also called *erikitan*. The *erregmenos* is made of unbolted, cracked wheat and is coarse. Amerias calls the whole-wheat bread *xēropyritan*. Timachidas says the same. Nicander says that breads called *thiagones* are made by the Aetolians for the gods. The Egyptians call a slightly sour bread *kyllastis*. Aristophanes mentions it in *The Danaids*: 'And you speak of *kyllastis* and *peitosiris*.' It is also mentioned by Hecataeus, Herodotus, and Phanodemus in the seventh book of his *History of Attica*. The...

# BREADS. SALTED FISH.

Nicander of Thyatira says that the bread made from barley by the Egyptians is called <term>kyllastis</term> <note>a sour-dough barley bread common in ancient Egypt</note>. Regarding "dirty" breads, Alexis in his play *The Cyprian* calls them "gray," saying: "Then how they came, barely like crab-apples, they took them all, but as for those you carry, I will bring sixteen here—eight white, and as many gray ones." Seleucus says that crumbled bread is called *blima*, and also *thermos*. Philemon, in the first book of *Various Usages*, says that <term>pyrnos</term> is the name for bread made from unbolted wheat, containing all the bran. He also says that breads with incisions, which the Romans call <term>quadrati</term> <note>original: "kodratos"; bread loaves scored with a cross into four sections</note>, are called *blamilii*. Bran-bread is called *erotike*, which Amerias and Timachidas call *eukonos* or *teukonos*. Philetas, in his *Miscellany*, mentions a bread called *apolia*, which is consumed only by locals. One can also find various types of <term>maza</term> <note>barley-cakes, the staple food of the ancient Greeks</note> 
<margin>10</margin>
recorded by Tryphon and many others. Among the Athenians, there is the <term>physte</term>, which is not overly kneaded; also the *kardamame*, the *berax*, the *tolypai*, and the *achilleion*—this last one is likely made from "Achillean" barley. There are also "lettuce-cakes" (*thridakinas*), "wine-cakes" (*oinoutte*), "honey-cakes" (*melitoutta*), and something called a "lily-cake" (*krinon*), which is also the name of a figure in choral dancing, as seen in Apollophanes’ *Dalinidi*. The cakes called *thridakiskai* by Alcman are the same as the Athenian lettuce-cakes. Alcman says: "Lettuce-cakes and oven-baked breads." Sosibius, in his third book *On Alcman*, says that *kribana* are certain cakes shaped like breasts. There is also a barley-cake called *hygeia* <note>meaning "Health"</note> given during sacrifices for people to taste. Hesiod calls a certain cake "amolgaean," saying: "An amolgaean cake and the milk of goats drying off," referring to a shepherd's cake at its prime, for <term>amolgos</term> means "the peak of perfection." I will avoid listing 
<margin>20</margin>
the rest of the catalog. My memory is not so fortunate as to recall every honey-cake and pastry mentioned by Aristophanes the Athenian in the third book of his work *To the Priestesses*. 

<note>A transition occurs here where the dining guests interact.</note>

We ourselves know the "Flower" <note>likely a reference to a specific wine or youth</note> is too young for a heavy pounding. Now, there was a performer of Old Comedy, a freedman of the most cultured King Hadrian, whom the king called *Athletopedix*. Ulpian asked, as the freedman was serving: "Does a drama have a title even if everyone stays silent?" He then asked again, "How does a freedman differ?" These matters were deferred for the moment. And Galen, just as we were about to touch the breads, said: "I will not be silent until you hear from us what the sons of Asclepius <note>physicians</note> have said regarding breads, pastries, and barley-meal."

Diphilus of Siphnos, in his treatise *On Food for the Sick and the Healthy*, says: "Breads made from wheat are more nourishing, more easily managed by the body, and generally superior to those made from barley. 
<margin>30</margin>
First in quality are those made from fine flour (*semidalitai*), then those from ordinary flour (*aleuritai*), and finally the 'unbolted' ones (*synkomistoi*) made from unsifted meal. These last ones seem to be the most nourishing." Philistion of Locri says that for strength, those made from fine flour are naturally better, followed by grit-bread (*chondrites*), then ordinary flour-bread. Breads made from the finest "dust" flour (*gyros*) are poorer in juice and less satisfying. Those that are well-leavened are airy and easily digested, but once cooled, they become filling and hard to process. Bread that is completely old and cold is less nourishing, binds the bowels, and has poor juices. Bread baked in the ashes (*enkryphias*) is heavy and hard to digest because it is baked unevenly. That called "large-oven bread" (*ipnites*) or "furnace-bread" (*kaminites*) is hard to digest. Griddle-bread (*escharites*) and that from the frying pan (*teganites*), due to the addition of oil, pass through the system more easily, but because of the greasy smoke, they are bad for the stomach. However, the bread baked in a portable oven (*klibanites*) excels in all virtues; 
<margin>40</margin>
it is flavorful, good for the stomach, easy to digest, and very easily absorbed. It neither binds nor relaxes the bowels. Andreas the physician says there are certain breads in Syria made from mulberries which make the hair of those who eat them stand on end. Mnesitheus says that bread is more digestible than barley-cakes, and those made from <term>tiphe</term> <note>einkorn or spelt</note> are sufficiently nourishing, for they are digested without much effort. Bread made from <term>zeia</term> <note>emmer wheat</note>, if eaten in abundance, is said to be heavy and hard to digest, so those who eat it are not healthy. We should know that grain foods that are not properly baked or nourished cause gas, heaviness, cramps, and headaches. 

After so much discussion, it finally seemed time for us to dine. Just before the dish called "prime-season" <note>original: "horaion"; refers to prime pickled fish</note> was brought in, Leonidas said: "My friends, Euthydemus the Athenian, in his book *On Salted Fish*, says that Hesiod spoke of all pickled foods as follows: 'Either the first body of the double-edged one, or the choice one, or the thionne, which they snatched from the jaws of the fish-striker. Truly, from Asia comes the race of the evening-claw for mortals, which the grinders bring both whole and sliced. Byzantium is the mother of the prime tunny, and of the mackerel of the depths and the lush marshes. And the famous little town of the shore was the nurse of the Spanish mackerel. The Ionian wave will bring from the belly of the deep the Brentian or Campanian or that from sun-scorched Tarentum, the triangles of the large tunny and those placed in Samian jars...'" These verses do not seem to me to be the work of the most musical Hesiod, but rather of some cook. For how could...
