# BOOK 3.

### BREADS. SALTED FISH.

For he can know the way, or Byzantium. Furthermore, having visited Tarentum, Brundisium, and many cities of Campania, being older than these men, I think I shall remind myself of the poems. And Dionysicles said, "Where the poems are good, Leonides, it is for us, the most esteemed grammarians, to judge. But since the conversation is about salted fish <note>original: *tarichos*; any fish preserved by salting, smoking, or drying</note>, much might be known even from a proverb deemed worthy of memory by Clearchus of Soli: 'Stale salt-fish loves the oregano.' I too am coming to say what I know about them (the matters of the craft)." Diocles of Carystus, in his writings titled *On Health*, says that among salted fish, the "seasonal" ones (*horaea*) are best when they are very fatty. Of the fatty ones, the tunny-bits are best. Hicesius reports that neither *pelamides* <note>young tunny fish</note> nor the "seasonal" ones are easy on the stomach. He notes that the younger tunnies have a similar proportion to the *kybia* <note>fish cut into cubes for pickling</note>, and there is a great difference compared to all those called "seasonal." He says the same regarding the
<margin>10</margin>
seasonal fish of Byzantium compared to those taken from other places, and not only regarding the tunnies, but also the other fish caught in Byzantium. Diphilus of Siphnos would add to these. Archestratus, the man of great learning regarding the lands of the inhabited world for the sake of the belly and the things beneath it, says:

> And let a slice of Sicilian 
> Tunny be cut, when they are about to be preserved in jars;
> But let the *saperdae* <note>a type of salted fish from the Black Sea, often considered inferior</note> go hang with their Pontic stench,
> And those who praise them. For few men 
<margin>15</margin> 
> Know that it is a poor and feeble food.
> But have a mackerel three days old, before it goes into 
> Salt water, a friend to the jar, newly half-salted;
> And if you come to the holy city of famous Byzantium,
> Eat a slice of seasonal fish for me again. For it is noble,
> And soft.

The gourmet Archestratus left out, though he listed them for us, the one mentioned by Crates the comic poet in *The Samians*, called "ivory salt-fish."
<margin>20</margin>
He does not say from where it comes:

> Once in a leather pot, an ivory salt-fish,
> Or from the sea-turtle in the thick waves, crabs moving their feet,
> and long-winged wolves, men fighting in the water, offerings of heaven. Everyone throttled that basket, scorched in the day.

That the "ivory salt-fish" of Crates was famous is witnessed by Aristophanes in *Thesmophoriazusae* through these lines:

> Truly the music of the tragic poet is a great thing,
> Which thought Crates’ ivory salt-fish was a bright thing laid out without effort,
> But he chuckled at ten thousand other such things.

<margin>25</margin>
Alexis has called it "raw salt-fish" (*omotarichon*) in *The Man Deprived of Sight*. The same poet in *Wicked Busybodying* introduces a certain cook speaking these words about salt-fish:

> Nevertheless, I want to calculate for myself,
> Sitting here, the grocery bill,
> And at the same time arrange what must be brought first,
> And how I must season each one.
> First, here is this seasonal salt-fish; it costs only an obol, it is for very rich men.
> Then, having strewn seasonings into a small pan,
<margin>30</margin> 
> Putting in the slice, pouring over white wine,
> And sprinkling oil, then boiling it until
> I took off the "marrow" <note>likely the richest, softest part of the fish</note> after glazing it with <term>silphium</term> <note>a prized, now-extinct medicinal and culinary herb from Cyrene</note>.

And in *The Man Deprived of Sight*, someone being asked for his contribution says:

> If you do not give me everything piece by piece,
> You would not get back a twelfth part of a copper coin.
> The logic is just; read the counter on the tablet:
> For raw salt-fish, five coppers; say another;
> Mussels, seven coppers—nothing impious there—say none;
> For salt-fish, an obol—it is still pure;
> From which after these things comes the cabbage, which was still useful.
> Stop, for I did not give us these obols.
<margin>35</margin> 
> Why? He gave to me; the *kybion* <note>cubed salt-fish</note> for three obols.
> I always benefited while rejoicing, and he did not charge, nor was it—
> I do not know, O blessed one, the market—
> The "eye-neighbors" <note>possibly a slang term for greedy people or small fish</note> have devoured the vegetables,
> Because of this, you have set the salt-fish at double.
> The salt-fish seller is here; go ask him.
> Conger eel for ten obols—not much; say another;
> I bought the roasted fish for a drachma—bah!
> Just as a fever let go, then it came back again;
> Add the wine, if we take it from those who are drunk. For you, three pitchers at ten obols a pitcher.

<margin>40</margin>
Hicesius, in the second book *On Matter*, says that *pelamides* are large *lybia*. Poseidippus mentions *kybia* in *The Transferred Man*. Euthydemus, in his work *On Salt-fish*, says the fish called *silkanos* takes its name from the Delkon river, from which it is caught, and when salted it is extremely foul-smelling. Dorion, in his work *On Fish*, calling the *lepinos* a *levianos*, says some people claim it is the same as the *silkanos*. The *korakinos* <note>the "crow-fish," possibly a variety of perch or drum</note> is called *saperdes* by many, and the best is from Lake Maeotis. 
<margin>45</margin>
He says the mullets (*kestreis*) caught around Abdera are wonderful, but those around Sinope, when salted, are extremely foul-smelling. He says some fish called *mylloi* are called *gnosidia* by some, and *platisakas* by others—being the same fish, just like the *chilleres*. For this fish, being one kind, has received many names: it is called *bakchos*, and *aniskos*, and *chilleres*. Now, the larger ones among them are called *platisakoi*. Those of middle age are *mylloi*. 
<margin>50</margin>
The small ones in size are *agnotidia*. Aristophanes also mentions the *mylloi* in *The Merchant Ships*: "mackerel, *koliai*, *lybioi*, *mylloi*, *saperdae*, young tunnies." After Dionysicles fell silent upon these words, the grammarian said there was no end to it. But truly, Antiphanes the poet in *Deucalion* says: "And for me to mention salt-fish, salt-fish..."

<meta>This page continues the catalog of preserved fish, focusing on specific regional varieties like those from Byzantium and Egypt, and transitions into a grammatical debate over whether the word "salt-fish" is masculine or neuter in Attic Greek, before concluding with medical advice on eating before drinking.</meta>

ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED.

# SALT-FISH.

If anyone wants *autakabion* <note>original: *autakabion*; a type of salted fish, possibly a whole small fish cured without being cut</note> or Gadric <note>from Gades, modern Cadiz in Spain</note>. He delights in the scents of Byzantine tunny. And in *Pasitus*, it says: "a salted *autakabion* in the middle; fat, pure white, and warm." Nicostratus (or perhaps Philetaerus) says in *The Little Ant*: "He celebrated a Byzantine slice. Let a Gadric belly-cut be served." And further on: "But I bought it from a man—O earth and gods!—a salt-fish seller, a very fine and good man: a *tiliton* <note>a specific cut or type of salt-fish</note> worth a drachma for only two obols, which we couldn't finish in three days." As for the *kateidontis* <note>another variety of cured fish</note>, it is not just twelve, but more; for it is of great size.

Following these remarks, Ulpian looked toward Plutarch and said: "Has anyone among you Alexandrians, my friend, ever mentioned these things? For no mad dog would ever taste what you call 'fine half-halves' or your salted *silouros* <note>original: *silouros*; the sheatfish or catfish of the Nile</note>." 

Plutarch replied: "As for the 'half-half' <note>original: *hemineros*</note>, how does it differ from the 'half-salted' fish mentioned earlier? Your own fine Archestratus 
<margin>10</margin> 
mentions it. However, Sopater of Paphos named the 'half-half' in his play *The Sordid Servant* thus: 'He received an *autakabion*, which the great Nile nourishes, a half-half pleasure for the scraps.' And the same author catalogs the Mendesian variety like this: 'A Mendesian fish is in its prime when lightly salted, a grey mullet roasted by the golden rays of the fire.' These foods were eaten in great quantities by the spendthrift sons of the teachers in your city, as they well know when they serve a little scale-fish. 

So, tell us also, is the word for salt-fish <note>original: *tarichos*</note> used in the masculine by the Attic writers? For we know it is used that way by Epicharmus." 

Myrtilus, anticipating the question, said: "Cratinus says in *Dionysalexandros*: 'I will bring Pontic salt-fish in baskets.' Plato says in *Zeus Ill-Treated*: 'So that I may lose this salt-fish I have.' Aristophanes says in *The Telmessians*: 'Not to behave unseemly toward this salt-fish here.' Plato says in *All Those Things* that it is bad for him. 
<margin>20</margin> 
Crates says in *Wild Beasts*: 'And we must have radishes, and roast fish, and hold our salt-fish in our hands.' It is uniquely phrased in Hermippus's *The Bread-Sellers*: 'And a fat salt-fish, an Egyptian corpse to look upon' <note>a joke comparing dried Egyptian salt-fish to mummies</note>. 

Aristophanes uses the diminutive in *Peace*: 'Buy something good for the farm, some little salt-fish' <note>original: *tarichion*</note>. And Cephisodorus says: 'A bit of cheap meat, or a little salt-fish.' Pherecrates says in *The Deserters*: 'Our wife cooked a mash for each of us—remind me, a lentil soup—and she roasts a small, lonely piece of salt-fish for you.' Epicharmus also used it in the masculine, 'the salt-fish' <note>original: *ho tarichos*</note>. 

Herodotus, in his ninth book, says: 'The salt-fish lying on the fire were leaping and quivering' <note>referring to a miraculous omen where dried fish acted as if alive</note>. The proverbs also use the masculine: 'Roast salt-fish immediately looks back at the fire' and 'Stale salt-fish loves oregano,' and 'Salt-fish would not suffer if it were worth its brine.' 

But the Attic writers also use the neuter form, and the genitive becomes 'of the salt-fish' <note>original: *tou tarichous*</note>. Chionides says in *The Beggars*: 'O gods, would you not eat even salt-fish?' And in the dative: 'Therefore, one must chop upon this salt-fish.' The dative is 'to the salt-fish' <note>original: *tarichei*</note>, like 'to the sword' <note>original: *xiphei*</note>. Menander says in *The Ephesian*: 'He sprinkled salt on the salt-fish, as it happened.' When it is masculine, the 's' in the genitive is extended. 

The Athenians took such an interest in salt-fish 
<margin>30</margin> 
that they even enrolled the sons of Chaerephilus the salt-fish seller as citizens, as Alexis says in *Epidaurus*: 'The sons of Chaerephilus are Athenians because he imported salt-fish.' Timocles, seeing them on horseback, said in *The Satyrs* that they were 'two mackerels' <note>a joke about their fishy origins</note>. Hyperides the orator also mentions them. 

Antiphanes mentions the salt-fish seller in *The Young Girl*: 'How they waited for the fish-slice seller, from whom I usually buy.' And Euthynus, accounting for it there: 'Provide something good, bid him not to overcharge.' And regarding Phadippus, for he too was a salt-fish seller. Alexis says in *The Little Horse*: 'And with mocks, another Phadippus, a foreign salt-fish carrier.' 

While we were eating the salt-fish and many were at the peak of their drinking, Daphnus said, raising his hands: 'Heraclides of Tarentum, my friends, in the work entitled *The Symposium*, says that one should take a moderate amount of food before drinking, and especially to set out the "sweets-and-savories" <note>original: *hadismylas*; appetizers meant to prepare the palate</note>. For if they are brought in after an interval, once people have been shaken by the wine, they settle in the stomach and cause inflammation.' 
<margin>40</margin> 
Some think that these same things are bad for the stomach—I mean types of vegetables and salt-fish—possessing a certain biting quality. They are suitable for sticky and slippery foods, though people are unaware that many things that aid excretion are actually good for the stomach, among which is the so-called *sisaron* <note>skirret or a type of parsnip</note>, mentioned by Epicharmus in *The Rustic*, *In the Land and Sea*. 

Diocles, in the first book of *Health Matters*, lists: 'asparagus, white beet'—for the black kind holds back excretion—'mussels, razor-clams, sea-mussels, clams, scallops, and finally salt-fish, provided it is not foul-smelling, and types of succulent fish.' It is also beneficial to set out the so-called *phyllida* <note>leafy greens</note> and little beets. Furthermore, as for salt-fish, one should not enjoy the various types in the same way, but avoid large draughts of drink at the beginning. For it is difficult to manage the intake of more liquids. 

The Macedonians, as Ephippus of Olynthus says in his work *On the Burial of Alexander and Hephaestion*, did not know how 
<margin>50</margin> 
to drink in an orderly fashion, but immediately used large toasts, so that they were drunk while the first tables were still set out and were unable to enjoy the food. Diphilus of Siphnos says: 'Salt-fish made from sea, lake, and river fish are low in nutrition, provide little juice, are "burning" <note>likely meaning they cause thirst or heartburn</note>, but are easy on the bowels.'

<meta>This page continues the technical and culinary discussion of various types of salted and cured fish (tariche), moving from specific species and regional varieties to their medical properties, and then transitioning into a spirited debate between the guests about linguistic purity and the use of "barbaric" or non-Attic loanwords in literature.</meta>

BOOK III. 61

### SALT-FISH

<margin>1</margin>
...indeed, they are good for the bowels and stimulate the appetite. The best of the lean varieties are the *kybia* <note>original: *kybia*; small cubes of salted tunny</note>, the *horaia* <note>seasonal fish caught at their peak</note>, and others of similar flavor. Among the fatty ones, the best are those made from tunny and the *kordyle* <note>a young tunny fish</note>. Older salt-fish is better and sharper, especially the varieties from Byzantium. He says that the *thynnion* <note>little tunny</note> comes from the larger *pelamys* <note>young tunny</note>, and from this comes a smaller portion proportional to the *ianthion* <note>possibly a specific cut or a violet-colored part of the fish</note>, from which the *horaion* juice is derived. The *sardia* <note>sardine</note> resembles the *kolias* <note>Spanish mackerel</note> in size. The *skombros* <note>Atlantic mackerel</note> passes through the stomach lightly and quickly. 

The *kolias* is easily digested and pungent, but has a poorer juice and is caught early in the season. Better is the *amyklanos*, also called the *iapanos* or *seisitanos*, as it is thinner and sweeter. Strabo, in the third book of his *Geography*, says that near the Heracleian Islands and the city of New Carthage in Seisitania <note>modern Spain</note>, there are salt-fish named after that region. In another passage, he mentions "Mackerel Island" <note>original: *Skombroasia*</note>, named for the mackerel caught there, from which the finest *garum* <note>a fermented fish sauce used as a ubiquitous condiment in antiquity</note> is prepared. 

<margin>10</margin>
There are also the so-called *melandryai* <note>original: *melandryai*; literally "oak-black," referring to the dark, firm meat of the tunny</note>, which Epicharmus mentions in *Odysseus the Deserter* like this: "so that the slice is of a dark-oak color." One should eat the *melandryas* from the largest tunny, as Pamphilus notes in his work *On Names*. Its slices are quite fatty. Diphilus says that some call the "raw salt-fish" <note>original: *omotarichon*</note> an *ekantema*. It is heavy, produces bile, and is difficult to digest. 

The river-born *korakinos* <note>original: *korakinos*; literally "crow-fish," a type of catfish</note>, which some call the *pheltios*, comes from the Nile; those around Alexandria specifically call it "half-fresh" <note>original: *hemineros*</note>. It is somewhat fatty, not at all bad-juiced, fleshy, nourishing, easy to digest, and easily absorbed—in every way superior to the *myllos* <note>mullet</note>. 

As for the roe <note>original: *oa*; fish eggs</note> of all fish and salt-fish, they are hard to digest and slow to pass, especially those from the fattier and larger fish. They remain firm and do not break down easily. They become foul-smelling when prepared with salt and roasted. One should wash all salt-fish until the water becomes fresh or sweet. Salt-fish taken from the sea becomes sweeter. Salt-fish is more pleasant when served hot. 

<margin>20</margin>
Mnesitheus the Athenian, in his book *On Edibles*, says: "Salty and sweet juices certainly move the bowels. Sour and pungent ones dissolve them. Bitter ones are more diuretic. Some of them also loosen the bowels, and the foul ones clear out the excretions." 

Xenophon, the most musical of authors, in the work titled *Hiero* or *On Tyranny*, criticizes such decadent foods, saying: "Why," said Hiero, "do men prepare all these many inventions—the sour, the pungent, the astringent, and their kin—which are served to tyrants?" "Indeed," said Simonides, "these seem to me entirely contrary to human nature." "But do you think," said Hiero, "that these dishes are anything other than the cravings of a soft and sickly soul? For those who eat with a healthy pleasure, as you well know, have no need for these 'sophistries' of the kitchen."

Upon these words being spoken, Cynulcus called for a "mattock" <note>original: *dikella*; a metaphor for a tool to dig into the conversation</note> for everyone, saying that "salty words should be washed away with sweet streams." 

<margin>30</margin>
At this, Ulpian, becoming indignant and striking his pillow with his hand, said: "How much longer will you not stop using such barbaric language? Or shall I leave the banquet and go, if you continue to bring me words that I cannot bear? You, who live in imperial Rome, now use the common dialect of the locals, my good man!" 

Cynulcus replied: "In the works of the ancient poets and writers who wrote in the purest Greek, one can find Persian words used because of common habit, such as *parasang* <note>a Persian measure of distance</note>, *asaphes*, and *schoinos* <note>an Egyptian measure</note>. This last is a measure of distance used by many even now. I also know that many Attic speakers 'Macedonize' <note>adopt Macedonian idioms</note> due to social mixing. 

It would be better for me to drink 'bull's blood'—for the death of Themistocles is preferable to falling into your hands! I won't say 'bull's water' <note>Cynulcus is mocking Ulpian's obsession with precise terminology</note>, as I don't know what that is. You don't even realize that even among the best poets and writers, some things are said poorly. Cephisodorus, for instance, the student of the orator Isocrates, says in the third book of his *Against Aristotle* that one can find poorly phrased things in the works of other poets or tragedians. 

<margin>40</margin>
For example, in Archilochus, there is the phrase 'to strip everything bare.' In Theodorus, the command 'to have more but praise the equal.' In Euripides, the famous line 'the tongue has sworn' <note>original: *he glotta omomoken*; from *Hippolytus*: "The tongue has sworn, but the mind remains unsworn." This was a controversial line in antiquity</note>. And in Sophocles, the phrase used regarding the Ethiopians. He speaks of 'grace and force' to everyone, yet you, like the 'wise' ones, praise justice while clinging to profit. Elsewhere, the same author said that 'nothing is bad if it brings profit.' And in Homer, there is the plot of Hera against Zeus and Ares committing adultery—things for which everyone accuses them. 

If I have made a mistake, O hunter of beautiful names and words, do not be harsh. For even Timotheus of Miletus, the poet, used to say that one shouldn't sing the old songs, for 'new songs are better; young Zeus reigns, while Cronus was the ruler of old; let the old Muse depart!' 

<margin>50</margin>
Antiphanes says in *Alcestis*: 'Since innovation brings profit, even that man saw, knowing that a new undertaking, even if it be daring, is much more useful than old ones.' And that the ancients knew of this so-called 'water' <note>referring back to the bull's blood/water joke</note>, I will show you, lest you be annoyed again, by quoting Lycophron. For as one of those who think themselves clever says in the *False Heracles* of Pherecrates: 'And I, in turn, these very things...'"

FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS

## DRINK.

Do not be so meddlesome; rather, if it pleases you, pay close attention and listen. "But do not be begrudging," said Ulpianus. "I have no need even for 'bull’s water' <note>original: *taureion hydōr*; likely a reference to river water, as rivers were often personified as bulls, or a specific spring</note>, which is what she thirsts for. For I myself thirst for the sweetest of voices." And the comic poet says: "But I drink to you a toast of friendship." <note>original: *philotesia*; a 'loving-cup' or toast shared between friends</note> You are indeed 'thirsting for words' in Alexis’s play *The Woman Following Pythagoras*: "Having taken a cup of boiled-down water... but if one drinks it raw, it is heavy and causes distress." My dear Sophocles, he called it "bull's water" because of the river Tauros <note>original: *Tauros*; meaning 'Bull'</note> near Troezen, beside which there is also a spring called Hyöessa <note>meaning 'the Rainy one'</note>. The ancients were well aware of the practice of drinking cold water during toasts; but I will not speak of it unless you also teach me whether the ancients drank hot water at their banquets. For if the mixing bowls <note>original: *kratēres*</note> happened to receive their name from the 'mixture' <note>original: *kerasthentos*</note> that filled them, they did not provide a boiling drink, heated from below like cauldrons. <margin>10</margin> For that they knew of hot water is shown by Eupolis in *The Demes*: "The bronze vessel is being heated for us, and someone is sacrificing; we must order that we share in the entrails." And Antiphanes in *Omphale*: "See that the water is boiled for me in a pot, for I will eat nothing. For I have no ailment, and may I have none! But if indeed a cramp twists me around the stomach or the navel, I have a ring from a most excellent person worth a drachma." In *The Sinner*, he says: "the food, as in Alexis... if you create a frightening fire in your stomach, pour over it... the two of them, the great ladles of yours and the middle ones, having dipped them into the boiling water of the cauldron." If I should never drink 'free-man's water'! <note>possibly a reference to unmixed or high-quality water</note> Plato says in the first book of the *Republic*: "Desire exists also in the soul, just as thirst is. Thirst, then, is for a hot drink, or a cold one, or for much or little of some kind of drink. If heat is added to the thirst, it would provide a desire for the cold; if coldness is added, then for the hot. If because <margin>20</margin> of a great presence of thirst, it will provide a desire for much; if for a little, then for little. But is 'thirsting' itself ever called anything other than a desire for that drink for which it is naturally intended, just as hunger is for food?" Semus of Delos says in the second book of his *History of the Islands* that on the island of Kimolos, cooling-pits <note>original: *psygeia*</note> are prepared in the summer, dug into the earth, where they place jars full of lukewarm water, and they bring it out no different from snow. The Athenians call lukewarm water *metakeras* <note>original: *metakeras*; literally 'after-mixture'</note>, as Sophilus says in *Androcles*. Alexis in *The Locrians* says: "The slave girls provided it, one the hot, the other the lukewarm." Philemon in *The Corinthian Woman*, and Amphis in *The Bathhouse*, shouted: "Bring hot water!" and another, "Lukewarm!" But intending to provide some comic repairs to these matters, Pontianus said: "The ancients knew, O dearest of men, also the drinking of very cold water." Alexis, at any rate, says in *The Parasite*: "For I wish to give you a taste of water; I have a thing within the well that is colder than anything unmentionable." He also names water <margin>30</margin> that falls into a well 'well-water' <note>original: *phreatiaion hydōr*</note>. Furthermore, they even drank snow, and Alexis says in a speech: "Then is man not a meddlesome plant, using things most contrary to his nature? We fall in love with strangers, we overlook our kin; having nothing, we are wealthy for our neighbors by bringing contributions, and we bring them only for ill. We have the nourishment of the grain, yet every day we crave the barley-cake so that it may be white. But for this we engineer a black broth. We dye the beautiful color with a staining-dye, and we prepare ourselves to drink snow. But as for the whole matter, if it is not hot, we mock it. And we spit out the sharp wine, yet we revel over spicy sauces. Is it not then as many of the wise have said: 'The best thing is never to be born, but once born, to reach the end as quickly as possible'?" <note>A famous pessimistic sentiment found in Theognis and Sophocles</note> Dexicrates says in the play entitled *The People Wandering by Themselves*: "If I am drunk and drink snow, and anoint my body with the best perfume Egypt produces..." Euthycles says in *The Prodigals* or *The Letter*: "He first <margin>40</margin> saw if snow was for sale; I write that he must certainly eat that cold thing." Even the noble Xenophon in his *Memorabilia* knows of the drinking of snow. Chares of Mytilene, in his *Histories of Alexander*, even tells how snow should be preserved; recounting the siege of the Indian city of Petra, he says that Alexander dug thirty large pits, which he filled with snow and covered with oak branches. For in this way, he says, the snow lasts for a longer time. That they also cooled wine so that they might drink it colder, Strattis says in *The Souls*: "For he would not accept to drink wine hot, but quite the opposite, cooled in the well, mixed with snow." And Lysippus in *The Bacchae*: "Hermon, what is it? How are we? What else, than that it does not seem right for your father to lower himself into the well from dawn, just like the wine in summer?" Diphilus says in *The Little Monument*: "Cool the Doric wine." Protagorides, in the second book of his *Comic Histories*, describing the voyage of King Antiochus <margin>50</margin> down the river, says something about the engineering of cold waters in these words: "During the day they expose it to the sun, and at night they strain off the thickest part; the rest they set out in the open air in ceramic water-jars on the highest parts of the house, and through the whole night two boys sprinkle the vessels with water. At dawn they take them down, and again drawing off the sediment..."

<summary>This page discusses the ancient Greeks' preferences for water and wine temperatures, detailing methods for heating water and, more extensively, techniques for cooling drinks using deep wells, excavated pits, and preserved snow.</summary>

### BOOK 3 OF THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...and making it thin, and how they place the water-jars in chaff <note>original: *achurois*; the husks of grain used as insulation</note> to keep them at their best for health. But if they use snow in this way, they have no need of anything else in their service. Anaxilas mentions "cistern water" <note>original: *lakkaia hydata*; water collected in underground tanks</note> in *The Flute Player* like this: "And as for cistern water, it is the sweetest thing you have." And again: "Perhaps the cistern water has perished." Apollodorus of Gela also mentions the "cistern" <note>original: *lakkon*</note> itself, just as we do, saying: "Anxious about the cistern, Lysa, you have properly arranged the ropes of the well." Upon hearing these things, Myrtilus said, "I, being a 'lover of salt-fish' <note>original: *philotarichos*</note>, my friends, wish to drink snow 'according to Simonides'." 

And Ulpianus said, "The word 'lover of salt-fish' is found in Antiphanes' *Omphale* as follows: 'I am by no means a lover of salt-fish, my girl.' And Alexis, in *The Rule of Women*, has called someone a 'sauce-fish-lover' <note>original: *zōmotarichon*</note> in these lines: 'The Cilician, and Hippocles the sauce-fish-loving actor.' But as for this 'according to Simonides,' I do not know what it means." 

"Because," said Myrtilus, "history is of no concern to you, you glutton. For there was once a 'steam-licker' <note>original: *knisoloichos*; one who hangs around the smell of roasting meat</note> according to the Samian poet Asius—that ancient one—the 'steam-flatterer' <note>original: *knisokolax*</note>. Callistratus, in the seventh book of his *Miscellanies*, says that when the poet Simonides was feasting with some people during a season of oppressive heat, and the cup-bearers were mixing snow into the drinks for the others but not for him, he improvised this epigram:

'This snow, which once covered the flanks of Olympus, 
rising swiftly from Thrace as the North Wind, 
and bit the hearts of men without cloaks, yet was subdued, 
clothed in the limbs of the dappled Earth—
if someone pours a portion of it for me, for it is not fitting 
to offer a warm toast to a dear friend.'"

When he had drunk again, Ulpianus asked where the word "steam-grasper" <note>original: *knisouchos*</note> is found, or what the verses of Asius are regarding the "steam-flatterer." 

Myrtilus replied, "The verses in Asius are these: 'Lame, branded with marks, and very old, perhaps the steam-flatterer came as a wanderer when Meles was celebrating his marriage; uninvited he came, craving the sauce, and stood among the guests like a hero rising out of the mud.' The word 'steam-licker' is found in Sophilus' *Philarchus* as follows: 'You are a glutton and a steam-licker.' And in the play titled *The People Running Together*, he uses the term 'steam-licking' in these lines: 'For the pimp, out of steam-licking, ordered me to prepare a certain blood-sausage for him.' Antiphanes also mentions 'steam-licking' in *The Buzzing Insect*." 

They also drank sweet wine while eating, as Alexis says in *The Man from Thrace*: "The courtesan entered carrying the sweet wine in a silver five-fingered cup—an Asiatic style—not a 'pro-drink' <note>original: *proubion*</note> nor a bowl <note>original: *phialē*</note>, but something between the two shapes." Next, a cake made of milk, wafers <note>original: *itria*</note>, and honey was brought in, which the Romans call *libum*. And Cynulcus said, "Fill yourself up, Ulpianus, with your ancestral 'groat-cake' <note>original: *chondrolibon*</note>, which is written of by none of the ancients, by Demeter, unless perhaps by those who wrote the Phoenician histories, Suniadicus and Machon, your fellow citizens."

<margin>Groats.</margin>
And Ulpianus said, "As for me, I have had enough of the 'burning of honey-cakes' <note>original: *kauiōma melipēktōn*</note>; I would gladly eat groats <note>original: *chondron*</note> made of shellfish or cockles, of which there is an abundance. And give me some 'scoop-food' <note>original: *komiadion*</note> of bread-scraps <note>original: *mystilōn*</note>; for I would call the tool a 'spoon-scoop' <note>original: *mystron*</note>." 

"This word was used by none before us," added Aemilianus. "O wonderful Aemilianus, you who have admired the epic poet Nicander of Colophon as a lover of antiquity and a man of great learning, and who overlooked him even when he named 'pepper'—this very man, in the first book of his *Georgics*, showing the use of groats, also named the 'spoon-scoop' <note>original: *mystron*</note> in these lines:

'But whenever a newly-slaughtered lamb of the air comes, 
or a goat, or a bird, it is a good thing to prepare: 
stretch out a pot, laying it in the hollow vessels, 
and mix in fragrant oil together. 
Let the broth roar over them, and stifle it by putting on a lid, 
for he praises heavy groats toasted for them; 
then gently in the warmth, feast with hollow spoon-scoops.'

Through these lines, most wonderful one, Nicander describes the use of both groats and hulled barley, ordering one to pour over them the broth of a lamb, a kid, or a bird. He says: 'Crush the young grains in a mortar, and having mixed oil with them, stir them together when it boils. Let the broth roar in the vessels of the equipment, mixing it with the thick movement of the ladle; do not pour in any other liquid, but drawing from the broth itself, see how nothing boils over the fatty part.' Therefore, he says, stifle the boiling by putting on a lid, so that the toasted groats swell up. Finally, when it is gently warm, serve it with the 'hollow spoon-scoops' <note>original: *mystrois*</note>. Furthermore, Hippolochus the Macedonian, in his letter to Lynceus, in which he describes a Macedonian banquet that surpassed all others in luxury, mentions that golden 'spoon-scoops' were given to each of the guests. And since you wish to be a lover of antiquity and say you will utter nothing that is not of the Attic dialect, my dear friend, what is it that Nicophon, the poet of the Old Comedy, says in *The Hand-Gluttons*? For I find him mentioning the spoon-scoops there too, when he says: 'Sellers of small fry, sellers of capers, fish-mongers, leather-sellers, barley-sellers, spoon-sellers <note>original: *mystropōlai*</note>, book-sellers, sieve-sellers, scrap-sellers, seed-sellers.' For of what would they be 'spoon-sellers' if not those who sell spoon-scoops? Having learned from these things the use of the spoon-scoop, which you call 'Syracusan,' fill yourself..."

FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS.

# GROATS.

...eat some groats <note>original: *chondrou*; a type of hulled grain or porridge</note>, so that you do not say you are "weak and strengthless." I am amazed that you did not ask: where are these groats from? Are they from Megara, or are they Thessalian? As Myrtilus says later. And Ulpian said, "I shall stop eating unless you teach us which people produce the best groats." Aemilianus replied, "I will not begrudge you. For seeing the most magnificent preparation of a dinner, I want you to be filled with groats and to swell your neck like a rooster. You should teach us about the dishes we are about to partake in." But he, for the sake of health, asked where it came from, for he was always seeking rest, [asking] "Why do you puff yourself up like a late-learned man?" But Aemilianus said, "I will not even withhold the account of this. I will say first where Antiphanes mentions groats, setting them out from his own works: 'And in those same ones, what is it, my dearest?'

'Among the three is good Megarian groats.' Not that he would call the Thessalian kind good, but they say that the fine flour <note>original: *semidalis*</note> of Phoenicia is very thoroughly sifted from much grain. This same food is reported, as Alexis says, to differ very little. But Alexis says again, poorly, 'And there is much Thessalian groats inside.' Aristophanes mentions the sipping of groats in the *Daitales* <note>original: *Daitalesin*; a lost play titled 'The Revellers'</note> like this: 'Boiling groats, then throwing in a fly, he gave it to him to sip.' And he mentions fine flour, even if I hold the evidence. For Stratis in *Anthroporestes*, and Alexis in *Isostasion*. Stratis mentions fine flour in a cup in the same drama like this: 'Fine flour from twin offspring.' And Antiphanes named the dishes in *The Parasite* <note>original: *Didymois* (likely a scribal error for a play title like *Parasitos* or *Homoiis*)</note> thus: 'He enjoyed many and beautiful dishes; there were perhaps three or four toasts, having somehow devoured the food of perhaps four elephants.' Let this book have its end here, having its conclusion with the discussions about dishes. For we shall make the beginning <margin>20</margin> of the dinner from the next [book]. But not before, O Athenaeus, you have recounted for us the Macedonian banquet of Hippolochus. But if this is also pleasing to you, Timocrates, let us prepare ourselves thus."

# ATHENAEUS’S DEIPNOSOPHISTS
## BOOK FOUR.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Π (Pi) featuring a figure and scrolling foliate ornamentation within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
The prologue is Macedonian, my friend Timocrates. In the times of Lynceus and Duris of Samos, who were students of Theophrastus of Eresus, there were agreements made with Lynceus, as can be learned from his letters; he explained to him in what kind of costly dinner he had been involved, and the other man would reciprocate in kind. Thus, some "dining-letters" of both are preserved. Those of Lynceus describe a dinner taking place in Athens <margin>30</margin> for King Demetrius, surnamed Poliorcetes <note>Demetrius the "Besieger," a prominent successor to Alexander the Great</note>, given by Lamia the Athenian flute-player. For Lamia was the mistress of Demetrius. But the letter of Hippolochus to Caranus the Macedonian describes a wedding. We also encountered other letters of Lynceus, written to the same Hippolochus, describing at that time the dinner of King Antigonus when he celebrated the Aphrodisia festival in Athens. And that of King Ptolemy. We shall give you the letters themselves. Since the letter of Hippolochus is rarely found, I will draw out for you what was written in it for the sake of sharing it now, and for your entertainment. 

In Macedonia, as I said, when Caranus was hosting a wedding feast, the invited men were twenty, to whom, as soon as they reclined, silver bowls <note>original: *phialai*</note> were given—one to each as a gift. He had also crowned each man before they entered with a gold headband worth five gold pieces. When they had drained the bowls, a bronze platter of Corinthian manufacture was given to each man, the same width as the bread, <margin>40</margin> and upon it were chickens and ducks. Moreover, there were ring-doves and a goose, and such a great abundance of other things piled up, which each man took together with the platter and gave to those standing behind him <note>It was customary for guests at such lavish feasts to pass surplus food to their personal attendants</note>. Many and varied other things were carried around. After these, another silver platter [was brought] on which there was again a large bread, and geese, and hares, and kids, and other crafted breads, and pigeons, and a turtle-dove, and partridges, and whatever other multitude of birds there was. 

"We gave these too," he says, "to the slaves, and when we had our fill of eating, we washed our hands." And many crowns of all kinds of flowers were brought in, and for everyone there were gold headbands equal in weight to the first crown. Now at this point Hippolochus mentions that Proteas, a descendant of that Proteas the son of Lanice (who was the nurse of King Alexander), was drinking excessively. For he was a heavy drinker. And he mentions how his grandfather Proteas used to drink with Alexander. And that he toasted everyone; he writes these things next. "While we were already drinking pleasantly and with moderation, there entered flute-<margin>50</margin>girls, and musicians, and some Rhodian sambuca-players <note>original: *sambykistriai*; women who played the sambuca, a triangular harp</note>. To me, they seemed naked, though some said they wore tunics. After they performed their opening pieces, they departed, and others entered carrying flasks of perfume <note>original: *lykythous myrepsikou*</note> tied with a gold thong, one silver and one gold, holding about a cup's worth <note>original: *kotyliaias*; roughly half a pint</note>, and to each...

<meta>catchword: ...they gave.</meta>

# BOOK IV.

...they gave, and then a great abundance was brought in instead of a meal: a silver platter <note>original: *pinax*; a large, flat serving dish</note> of no small thickness, large enough to receive the size of a roasted pig, and a very large one at that, which lay on its back, showing its belly upward, which was full of many good things. For inside it were roasted together thrushes, sow’s paunches, and a vast number of fig-peckers <note>original: *sykallidōn*; small songbirds considered a delicacy</note>, and egg yolks poured over them, along with oysters and scallops; and to each guest, a platter was given served in this scorching manner. After this, having drunk, we each received a boiling kid <note>original: *eriphon*; a young goat</note> on another such platter with golden perfume flasks. Seeing the difficulty of handling these, Caranus ordered that small shields and bread-baskets woven with ivory straps be given to us, at which we clapped our hands in delight and cheered the bridegroom, for the gifts we had been given were so well-supported. Then came another crown, and a double-flask of golden perfume, and silver vessels equal in weight to the previous ones. When silence was restored, those athletes who had served at the pots <note>referring to the previous courses</note> came in. After them entered ithyphallic dancers <note>performers wearing phallic costumes</note>, jugglers, and some wonder-working women who tumbled among swords and spat fire from their mouths while naked. 

When we were finished with these, a warm and stronger drink took us up again—Thasian, Mendaean, and Lesbian wines being served to us in very large golden cups. After the drinking, a platter two cubits in diameter <note>about three feet</note> was brought in, resting on a silver stand, full of roasted fish of all the sweetest kinds roasted together; and to everyone was given a silver bread-basket of Cappadocian bread <note>original: *artōn kappadokiōn*; a soft, refined luxury bread</note>, some of which we ate and some we gave to our attendants. Having washed our hands, we were crowned again, and once more received golden scrapers twice the size of the previous ones, and another double-flask of perfume. 

When silence fell, Proteas leaped from his couch and asked for a large cup <note>original: *skyphon*; a deep drinking vessel</note>, and having filled it with Thasian wine and sprinkling a little water in it, he drained it. Then he said that whoever drinks the most will be the most gladdened. Caranus said, "Since you were the first to drink, you shall have the cup as a gift; and this shall be the prize for the others as well, whenever they drink." After this was said, everyone rose up and snatched at them, each trying to beat the other in beauty. But one of our fellow guests, wretched and silent from hunger, sat up and wept because he was left without a cup. And Caranus graciously gave him the empty vessel. 

Following this, a chorus of a hundred men entered, singing the wedding hymn in harmony, and after them dancers dressed in the manner of bridesmaids, and others as nymphs. As the time went on and the hour grew dark, they threw open the room where everything was partitioned in a circle by white linens; and when these were drawn back, there appeared hidden by machinery statues of the Graces, Loves, Artemis, Pan, and Hermes, and many such images shining among silver lamps. While we were wondering at the craftsmanship, wild boars—veritable Erymanthian boars <note>a reference to the massive boar hunted by Heracles</note>—were brought around to each guest on square platters with golden centers, pierced through with silver skewers. 

And the wonder was that we, already acting like crabs from drunkenness, when we saw the things being brought in, we all stood upright. As the saying goes, we asked for more. In this feast, the servants continued the fortunate gathering until the trumpeter sounded the signal for the end of the dinner; for I know this is the Macedonian custom at large banquets. Caranus, having started with small cups, ordered the servants to circulate quickly. We drank opportunely, as if taking an antidote to the previous unmixed wine. At this moment, the jester Mandrogenes entered—the descendant, they say, of Straton the Athenian—and he moved us to much laughter. After this, he danced with his wife, who was already over eighty years old.

Finally, the dessert tables were brought in. Foods in woven ivory baskets were given to all, and cakes of every Cretan variety. And yours, my friend, were the Samian and Athenian lamps, with their own specific cases for the crumbs. After this, we rose and departed sober, by the gods, because of the fear of the wealth we had received. 

But you, remaining only among the Athenians, think yourself happy, listening to the lectures of Theophrastus on "Sacrifice" and "The Broth," and eating your fine twisted bread and looking at lentils and pots. We, however, having feasted on wealth instead of mere portions at Caranus’s dinner, now seek—some to buy houses, some lands, others slaves. Looking at these things, friend Timocrates, with what Greek dinner can you compare this banquet? Especially since Antiphanes the comic poet said in *Oenomaus* or *Pelops*, poking fun: "What could these small-tabled, food-loving Greeks do, where you get four tiny pieces of meat for an obol? But among our ancestors, they roasted whole oxen, deer, and lambs. Finally, the cook, having roasted a whole beast for the Great King, served him a hot camel." Aristophanes too, in the *Acharnians*, showing the magnificence of the barbarians, says: "Then he entertained us and served us whole oxen from the oven." And who ever saw "oven-baked oxen" except as a boast? "And by Zeus, he served us a bird three times the size of Cleonymus; its name was the Quack <note>original: *phenax*; a pun on 'hoaxer'</note>." And Anaxandrides, in *Protesilaus*, ridiculing the wedding banquet of Iphicrates when he married the daughter of Cotys, king of the Thracians, says: "And there you do as I say, with splendid..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of famous banquets in antiquity, transitioning from the lavish wedding of Caranus to the historical wedding of the Athenian general Iphicrates to the daughter of the Thracian king Cotys. It explores the differences between regional dining customs, specifically contrasting the heavy, "barbaric" feasts of the Thracians with the refined, multi-course, but sometimes meager portions of the Athenians.</meta>

-># FROM THE ATHENAEAN DEIPNOSOPHISTS<-

Your feasts are nothing like those of Iphicrates in Thrace. They say those were prepared with a true love of beauty. Throughout the marketplace, purple rugs <note>original: *halourga*; literally "wrought from the sea," referring to the expensive murex dye</note> were spread all the way to the north. They say countless thousands of long-haired men dined on butter <note>To the Greeks, butter was a "barbarian" food, as they preferred olive oil</note>. The bronze kettles were larger than cisterns meant for twelve couches. Cotys himself was girded with an apron, carrying broth in a golden bowl, and as the mixing bowls were tasted, he became drunk before those who were supposed to be drinking. There was the constant sound of flutes and the singing of poets, and Cephisodotus of Acharnae played the lyre, singing songs now of wide-spaced Sparta, and then changing his tune to seven-gated Thebes. The dowry included two herds of chestnut horses, a gold-shining shield, a fat-smeared bowl, a pitcher for snow, a pot of millet, a twelve-cubit pit of bulbs, and a hundred-fold sacrifice <note>original: *hekatomb*; traditionally a sacrifice of 100 oxen</note> of octopuses. They say this is how Cotys prepared the wedding in Thrace for Iphicrates. But the feasts among our own guests will be much more venerable and more brilliant than those. For what is lacking in our house? What kind of goods—the scents of myrrh, Syrian odors, and the breath of frankincense. We have the sight of tender-skinned cakes, fine breads, octopuses, tripe, fat, sausages, broth, beets, stuffed fig-leaves, egg yolks, garlic, small fry, mackerel, "whispering" cakes, barley groats, porridge, beans, peas, yellow peas, kidney beans, honey, cheese, pork, eggs, nuts, groats, roasted lobsters, roasted cicadas, boiled prawns, boiled cuttlefish, boiled eel, boiled gobies, roasted young tuna, boiled wrasse, frogs, perch, sea-breams, hake, rays, flatfish, dogfish, gurnard, sardines, torpedo fish, slices of ray, turtle, grapes, figs, flat-cakes, apples, cornel berries, pomegranates, thyme, wild pears, safflower, olives, grape-pressings, pancakes, leeks, scallions, onions, blowing-onions, bulbs, stalks, silphium <note>An extinct medicinal and culinary herb highly prized in the ancient world</note>, vinegar, fennel, lentils, roasted grasshoppers, cress, sesame, trumpet-shells, salt, mussels, limpets, mice <note>Likely referring to a type of shellfish</note>, oysters, scallops, and large tuna. In addition to these, a multitude of unspeakable small birds: ducks, wood-pigeons, "chips" <note>An unidentified small bird</note>, sparrows, thrushes, larks, jays, swans, pelicans, wagtails, and cranes—which, as it gapes, is cut through the rump and the sides to the forehead. And there is wine: white, sweet, local, and a most pleasant "smoky" wine.

<margin>Rug. Attic.</margin>
Lynceus, in his play *The Centaur*, mocking Attic dinners, says: "The cook who is sacrificing and leaving me hungry is a Rhodian, and I, the guest, am a Corinthian. Neither of you takes pleasure in these Attic dinners. For there is an 'Attic unpleasantness' about them, like a foreign funeral feast. For he brings a large platter containing small dishes, as if they were little plates; in one of these is garlic, in another two sea-urchins, in another sweet little scraps, in another ten mussels, and in another a small piece of sturgeon. While one man is eating those, and another is eating these, I have already finished mine! I want, my best friend, to work together with you, for I want things that are otherwise impossible: for I do not have a thousand mouths or lips. Such a variety looks impressive to the eye, but it is nothing to the belly. For it amazed the gullet, but it did not fill it. Why do you have so many little side-dishes? Set one large platter of these before me, all by itself. Do you have a sea-urchin? Let there be another platter for you. For I bought this for myself for eight obols. This little dish is for pleasure alone, so that I can be cheerful, and not so that one man gets it while the other does not." 

<margin>Difference of banquets.</margin>
Dromeas the parasite, when someone asked him (as Hegesander of Delphi says) whether the dinners in the City <note>Athens</note> or in Chalcis were better, said that the "prelude" to the dinners in Chalcis was more charming than the whole preparation in Athens, meaning by "prelude" the quantity and variety of the shellfish. Diphilus, in *The Deserter*, introduces a cook who says: "How many in number are those invited to the wedding, my good man? And are they Athenians, or some from the merchant quarter, or what? This is a part of the cook's art. It is a kind of leadership, father, to know the tastes of the eaters beforehand. For instance, if Rhodians are coming, give them a large, hot, boiled silurus <note>a large catfish</note> or a labrax <note>sea bass</note> right as they enter, with which they will be much more pleased than if you poured myrrh over them. It is a disgrace to serve a 'silurus-style' dish to Byzantines; give them things with plenty of wormwood, and make everything salty and garlicky. For because of the multitude of fish among them, they are all full of bile and phlegm." Menander, in *The Trophonius*, says: "The dinner is for the reception of a guest. Where he is from makes a difference to the cook. For these islanders are like little foreigners, raised on fresh little fish. They are not easily caught by all kinds of salted meats, but are only incidentally attracted by them. They prefer stuffed dishes and greasy delicacies. But if someone from Arcadia comes, it is the opposite."

<margin>Digestives/Appetizers book 12.</margin>
...is caught in little dishes. An Ionian rich man, making a feast, provides "Kandaulos" <note>A rich Lydian dish of meat, broth, cheese, and breadcrumbs</note> and food that makes one hungry. For the ancients also used foods for opening the appetite <note>original: *anastomōsis*; stimulating the digestion or 'opening' the stomach</note>, such as olives in brine, which they call "swimmers." Aristophanes, in *Old Age*, says: "O old man, do you love the 'ox-buttock' harlots, or the young 'virgin' olives in brine, like small shriveled olives?" Philemon, in *The Petitioner*, says: "A boiled fish appears to you, small—oh, you have heard!—and a brine that is white and exceedingly thick, and it does not smell of the pot or of seasonings; they all seemed to think it was a good..."

# BOOK IV

...you make it simple. I also saw cicadas <term>tettiges; large cicadas</term> and *kerkopai* <term>a smaller species of cicada</term> served for the sake of opening the appetite <term>anastomosis; the culinary theory that sharp or light foods "opened" the passages of the body to stimulate hunger</term>. Aristophanes says in *The Anagyros*: "How, by the gods, do you desire to eat a cicada and a *kerkope* caught with a lime-twig?" The *kerkope* is a creature similar to a cicada and a small turtledove <note>original: *trygonion*; likely a reference to size or sound</note>, as Speusippus notes in the fourth book of *Similars*. Epilycus mentions them in *The Little Girl*. Alexis says in *Thrason*: "I have never yet seen you, woman, nor a *kerkope*, nor a jay, nor a nightingale, nor a turtledove, nor a cicada." And Nicostratus in *The Handmaid* says:

->the first large tray will be brought out containing sea urchin, raw salted fish, capers, crumbs,<-
->a slice of fish, and a bulb in a sharp sauce.<-

That these things are more pleasant for opening the appetite, as well as turnips in vinegar and mustard, is clearly shown by Nicander in the second book of his *Georgics*, saying:

> For the turnip and the offspring of the radish appear in the garden beds,
> both long and wide.
> You should preserve these in the north winds <note>original: *boreesi*; cold northern winds</note>
> as favorites for the winter and for idle house-keepers;
> they come back to life when placed in hot water.
> Cut the roots of the turnip and the dry
> skin, or after cleaning those dried in the sun,
> after you have soaked them slightly in the sun, dip them in hot
> water and then immerse them in brine.
> At other times, mix white sweet sesame
> with vinegar, in equal parts. After hiding the inner layers in salt,
> and often pouring in raisins and rubbing them,
> add the pungent seeds of mustard;
> pour in vinegar and mix it together, and also with raw
> <unclear>korsē</unclear>. This brine is a timely seasoning for your diet.

Diphilus or Sosippus in *The Deserted Woman* says: "Therefore vinegar is something sharp; I suppose, my boy, we have taken the juice." Aristotle <note>This citation of Aristotle is likely a fragment from a lost work on banquets</note> says: "I will persuade everyone, and frequently, whether tribes or individuals, to be surrounded by incense. For these of the older seasonings open the senses most quickly, and the drowsy and dull <margin>The dance of the fellow-guests.</margin> state is shaken off, and they will bring one to eat with pleasure." Alexis says in *The Tarentines* that in their symposia <term>symposium; a formal drinking party</term> the Athenians even dance after they have drunk a little. "For this is now the local custom for you in beautiful Athens; everyone dances immediately if they only catch the scent of wine. You speak of a disaster! From which you might appear, entering a banquet suddenly, and to the rustics perhaps some grace is present. But you will stop the babbling Theodotus, or seeing the one chewing beside him, drinking white wine from a bowl, I would gladly fix him to a piece of wood!"

Perhaps Antiphanes in *The Seasons*, following the Athenian custom of dancing, mocks one of the wise men for dancing during dinner, saying: "Do you not see him dancing with his hands, the one who is not ashamed of the ears of Bacchus? He who explains the works of Heraclitus to all, who alone knows the art of Theodectas, who writes the summaries for Euripides!" No one, after opening their appetite, would bring in the kids <note>young goats</note> mentioned in *The Aeolus*: "For there is an old saying that is not bad: they say wine makes old men dance, O father, even when they do not want to." Alexis, in the play titled *Equal to the Gods* <note>original: *Isosasios*</note>, says: "From the contributions <term>symbolōn; a meal where guests pay a share</term> it is only for those who look on to dance, and having nothing else but the names of the dishes and foods: crayfish, and gudgeon, and fine flour."

# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS

I saw the white, and I know the black; and I saw Tityos <note>A giant in the Odyssey who covered nine acres; here, he is a giant eel.</note>, the glorious conger eel of the lake, lying upon 
<margin>Iliad, Book 11</margin> platters; and he lay across nine tables. Following in his footsteps came the white-armed fish, the 
<margin>In the catalog</margin> Eel, who boasted of having been joined in the arms of Zeus, in the bed from which the race of wild eels 
sprang—a creature of immense size, whom no fisherman would dare mock. So great were her coils and 
her resistance that men could easily have hoisted her from the ground onto a wagon. For they were three spans 
wide, and in length they were full nine cubits. And everything was turned upside-down and the cook came in silence, 
<margin>Iliad, Book 2</margin> shaking his dish-bearing trays over his sturdy shoulder. Behind him followed forty black pots, and 
along the straight paths just as many platters were brought in with force. Then Iris came as a messenger, the wind-footed, 
swift vapor <note>The "vapor" or "steam" is personified as the messenger goddess Iris.</note>, along with the dark-skinned Perch, and the common Black-tail, who—though not a mortal among 
immortal fish—would not have stayed his head as a chamberlain. <margin>Iliad, Book 10</margin> Turning away without his shield, the 
angry one <note>Likely the Murex or a similar shellfish</note> because of the armor they were stripping; and the gods 
appointed this misery for men. Of the Snails <note>original: *Rinon*</note>, whom the master-craftsmen love above all flowers, 
rough but a good nurse of youth <note>A parody of Homer's description of Ithaca</note>. For I could not find anything sweeter than her flesh, but it will swell. 
And the armored one, the monstrous knight Ivy-fish <note>original: *Kisseus*</note>, not alone, for with him followed 
the swift-footed hares. And with them the great dark-skinned Bonito, who knows all the depths of the 
entire sea as a servant of Poseidon, and the singers of Olympian Zeus were there; these indeed were curved, 
but anciently they were golden. The Gilt-head <note>original: *Chrysophrys*</note>, who stands as the most beautiful fish among 
others; and the Spiny Lobster <note>original: *Karabos*</note>, who in turn longed to be armored for the banquets of the blessed. 
Then laying their hands upon the food, they placed it in their mouths, and brought one thing after another. Among them, 
the famous ruler of the platters led the way, not being at all weak in his hand; he reached out, 
yearning for the knees <note>A parody of a suppliant's gesture</note>, and it gave me the smell of ambrosia. 
Oh, the gods of the blessed who live forever! And he brought the Moray Eel, lifting the cover of the 
table; she wore a belt, exalting in her speckled skin <margin>20</margin> when she went to the bed of the great-hearted 
serpent <note>A reference to the folk belief that moray eels mated with land snakes</note>. And they placed golden sandals 
on the feet of the immortals, so that the noisy Tongue-fish <note>The Sole fish</note> might shine in the murmuring salt-sea. 
And Thrushes in a row, like high-flying birds, and ducks from the grazing lands, and water-dwelling divers; 
and mixed in were Sargos-fish, and Horse-mackerel, and the Owl-fish, and the Striped Bream 
in turn, great children of the sea, which the cook brought and served sizzling, and the house was filled 
with the steam. He told them to feast, and to me they seemed to be the food of women <note>meaning delicate or sweet</note>; 
but when they moved on to other things, there lay some greenery which no one had yet seen at a banquet 
in a clean place, where the space of the platters was visible. Next came the Blackbird alone, sweet and 
ready. I was not left untouched by it, and others learned of it too. Every man protected the 
mackerel, and the mustard burned nearby, even sweeter, like gold when it is stripped. When I tasted it, 
I wept, thinking that tomorrow I would no longer see these things; but he urged me on, and the barley-cake 
urged me, and pitiless hunger did not hold back. For he was forced by the scraps, and the broth and the 
boiled trotters <term>akrokōlia; the extremities of an animal, like pigs' feet</term> subdued him. And there was a 
certain earth of the platter, thirteen ducks, very fat from the sacred lake, which the cook <margin>30</margin>
brought and set down, where they lay in ranks like an Athenian phalanx. And Chaerephon <note>A well-known parasite and friend of Socrates</note> 
stood among his friends, looking forward and backward to recognize the birds and to feed upon the 
fated food. He rushed like a lion, and his hand gripped the leg of the bird, so that he might have 
it for his supper when he went home again. And there was the fair-faced Groats <term>chondros; a type of grain mush</term>, 
which Hephaestus <note>The god of fire/craft; here meaning the cook or the heat of the oven</note> labored over, 
<margin>Iliad, Book 11</margin> ripening it in a ceramic jar for thirteen months. But when they had put away the desire 
for honey-sweet supper, and washed their hands in the flows of the ocean. Stratos the boy came 
carrying sweet, fragrant perfume. And another in turn gave garlands to all, moving from left to right; 
they were entwined with roses, adorned with various flowers. And the mixing bowl of Dionysus 
was mixed, and the Lesbian wine was drunk, of which no man could drink too much. Then 
the second tables were prepared, fully laden. And on them were for me fat apples and fat sheep <note>Matron plays on the word *mēla*, which means both apples and sheep</note>, 
pomegranates, and grapes, the nurslings of the god Dionysus, and the fresh fruit they call the *amamaxis* <note>A type of vine or grape</note>. <margin>40</margin>
I ate none of these simply, but lay back full. But when I saw the yellow, sweet, large, circular, 
rain-like child of Demeter, the Cake <term>plakous; a flat, layered cheesecake with honey</term>, which had come up. 
I could not keep myself away from the god-like cake; not even if I had ten hands and ten mouths, 
and an unbreakable belly, and a heart of bronze within me. And then prostitutes entered, two 
prostitutes who performed wonders, whom Stratocles drove like swift-footed birds.

Alexis, mocking Attic dinners in his *The Fellow-Guest*, says: "I want to take cooks who are 
the most sophisticated in the city. For they are not going to serve a Thessalian meal, not 
simply, nor precisely. To pass by hunger, but to serve each thing to them grandly one by one. 
For the Thessalians are still wealthy." Just as Eriphus says in *The Peltast* that: "Things in 
Corinth, when you see them, O Syros, the food for guests does not even compare to a Thessalian 
feast, of which no hand was without a share." The same author in *The Little Snow-Man* mentions 
the variety of the poor, saying that the Athenians, when they <margin>50</margin> set out a meal for the Dioscuri in the 
Prytaneion <term>Town Hall; the civic heart of Athens where official guests were fed</term>, they place upon the table cheese, 
a barley-cake, leeks, and olives, making a reminder of the ancient way of life. And Solon 
orders that for those who eat in the Prytaneion, they should be served barley-cake, but that wheaten 
bread should be added on feast days, imitating Homer.

### BOOK IV

For that author, when gathering the best for Agamemnon, says he "stirs the barley-meal." And Athenaeus 
relates that when two dinners were held by men who were not at all of the old school—one in the Lyceum and one in the Academy—the cook who brought a dish to the Academy was told how he had broken every other rule of the pottery trade. This was because of an unpleasant tradition of long standing, that one should keep far away from this "lion" <note>This likely refers to a specific type of dish or perhaps a cook nicknamed "The Lion."</note>. Meanwhile, the cook in the Lyceum, who tried to dress up cured meat to look like fresh, was whipped for being a scoundrel who behaved 
basely. But Plato, in the second book of his *Republic*, provides a feast for his new citizens in this way, writing: "It seems," he said, "you are making these men feast without any relish." "You speak the truth," I said, "I had forgotten that they will also have relish: salt, obviously, and olives, and cheese, and bulbs, and green vegetables, such as they boil in the fields. And we shall set before them desserts of figs, chickpeas, and 
<margin>10</margin> beans; and they will toast myrtle-berries and acorns at the fire, drinking in moderation. Thus passing their lives in peace and health, they will likely hand it down to their children." Next, we must speak of the Laconian <note>Laconian is another word for Spartan.</note> banquets. 
Herodotus, in the ninth book of his *Histories*, speaking of the equipment of Mardonius <note>A Persian general during the invasion of Greece.</note> and mentioning <margin>Lacedaemonian diet</margin> 
Laconian banquets, says that when Xerxes fled from Greece, he left his own royal equipment to Mardonius. When Pausanias <note>The Spartan commander who defeated the Persians at Plataea.</note> saw Mardonius's equipment, furnished with gold, silver, and 
<margin>15</margin> embroidered hangings, he ordered the bakers and cooks to prepare a dinner exactly as they would for Mardonius. When they had done what was ordered, Pausanias saw 
golden and silver couches beautifully spread, silver tables, and a magnificent preparation for a banquet. Struck with amazement, he then ordered his own servants, as a joke, to prepare 
a Laconian dinner. When it was ready, Pausanias laughed and sent for the 
<margin>20</margin> generals of the Greeks. When they arrived, he showed them the preparation of both dinners and said: "Men of Greece, 
I have gathered you because I wished to show you the folly of the leader of the Medes <note>The Persians.</note>, who, though he had such a 
way of life, came to us, who live so miserably, to take away what we have." Some say that a man from Sybaris <note>A city famous for extreme luxury.</note> who 
visited Sparta and ate at their common messes <note>original: *phiditia*</note> said: "Naturally the Lacedaemonians are the bravest of all 
men; for any sane person would choose to die ten thousand times rather than partake of such a wretched diet." 
<margin>25</margin> Polemon, in his work on the wicker-carriages mentioned in Xenophon, says that the feast called the *kopis* <note>A ritual meal, the name implies a "cutting" or "cleaver."</note> by the Spartans is mentioned by Cratinus in his *The Wealthy*: "Is it truly possible for strangers, as they say there, 
for all who come to feast well at the *kopis*? And in the bags, they have parched grain besides, 
and they let fall a bit of cake for the old men." And Eupolis says in his *Helots*: "And let there be 
a *kopis* for those today." The *kopis* is a dinner of a particular kind, just like the one called 
<margin>30</margin> the *aiclon* <note>The Spartan term for an after-supper or evening meal.</note>. For the *kopis*, they first set up tents near the temple of the god. In these, 
they make beds of brushwood, and over these they spread rugs, upon which they recline and feast—
not only the locals who arrive, but also any foreigners who are staying there. They sacrifice 
goats at these *kopis* feasts, but no other victim. They give out portions of the meat, and the so-called 
*physikillos*, which is a small round loaf, somewhat like a ball in its specific shape. They also give to each person who 
<margin>35</margin> comes together: green cheese, a slice of tripe and sausage, and desserts such as dry figs and beans, 
and green kidney-beans. Anyone who wishes may also have other appetizers. This same dinner is also held in 
the city, and at the festival called the *Tithonidia* on behalf of the children. For the nurses carry the male children 
at this time into the fields and to the temple of Artemis Corythallia, whose sanctuary is near 
the place called Piasos; there they perform the *kopis* in a manner similar to what has been described. 
<margin>40</margin> They also sacrifice suckling pigs, and they serve "oven-loaves" at the feast. What is called *aiclon* 
is called "dinner" by the other Dorians. Epicharmus, at any rate, says in his *Hope*: "For someone invited me to an *aiclon* 
willingly." The word "willingly" <note>original: *ekon*</note> is used like "moistening." He says the same in 
*Periallos*. In Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, for those who enter the common mess, the servant follows with a portion, and 
announces the "aiclon," adding the name of the person who sent it. These are the words of Polemon. But 
<margin>45</margin> Didymus the Grammarian—whom Demetrius of Troezen calls the "Book-forgetter" <note>original: *bibliolathan*</note> because of the vast number of books 
he published (for they number three thousand five hundred)—contradicts him, saying: "Polycrates, in 
his *Laconian History*, records that the Spartans celebrate the sacrifice of the Hyacinthia over three days. 
Because of the mourning that occurs for Hyacinthus, they do not wear crowns at the dinners, nor do they 
bring in bread, but they give out cakes and things that go with them, and they do not sing the paean to the god, 
<margin>50</margin> nor do they introduce anything else of that sort, as they do in other sacrifices; but after dining with great 
orderliness, they depart. But on the middle of the three days, there is a varied spectacle and 
a festival notable and large. For boys play the lyre, wearing girded tunics, and singing to the flute,

### FROM THE ATHENIAN DINNER-PHILOSOPHERS

...singing, running over all the strings at once with the plectrum <note>A small tool used to pluck or strum a stringed instrument like a lyre.</note>, they sing to the god in a restful rhythm but with a sharp tone. Others pass through the theater on decorated horses, and vast choirs of young men enter, singing some of their prize-winning poems. Dancers are mingled among them, performing their movements and their song in an ancient style to the accompaniment of the flute. As for the young women, some are carried in *kanathra* <note>original: κανάθρων; ornate wooden wicker-work wagons</note> with wooden arched roofs, which are very luxuriously constructed; others join the procession in racing-chariots yoked together. The entire city is established in the movement and joy of this spectacle. They sacrifice a great number of victims on this day, and the citizens give a dinner to all their acquaintances and to their own slaves. No one misses the sacrifice; rather, it happens that the city is emptied for the sake of the sight. Aristophanes—or perhaps Philyllius in *The Cities*—mentions the *kopis* <note>original: κοπίς; a specific type of Spartan sacrificial feast</note>, as does Epilycus in *The Little Boy*, saying: "so that if I imagine a *kopis*, a half-choenix <note>A dry measure, roughly a quart.</note>..." They bring many "barikas" <note>Probably a type of cake or fowl, though the text here is corrupted.</note> and very pleasant bundles, explicitly stating that barley-cakes are served at the
<margin>10</margin> *kopis* feasts. For he said "abarakas" <note>original: ἀβαράκας; possibly a type of unleavened bread or a specific snack</note> with a sweet drink—not "sorrows" as Lycophron says, nor the pre-mixtures of the barley-cakes as Eratosthenes claims. There is also bread and a certain seasoned broth to be served. What exactly the *kopis* is, Molpis clearly sets out in *The Constitution of the Lacedaemonians*, writing as follows: "they also hold the so-called *kopis* feasts. The *kopis* is a dinner consisting of barley-cake, bread, meat, raw vegetables, broth, figs, treats, and lupines." Moreover, there are "orthagoriskoi" <note>original: ὀρθαγορίσκοι; literally 'early-morning pigs'</note>, since they are sold towards dawn, as Sosibius records in *Laconian Customs*, as well as Dioscorides in the second book of his *Constitution*, Aristocles in his first book, and also in the *Constitutions of the Laconians*. Furthermore, Polemon says that dinner is called *aiklon* <note>original: αἴκλον; a Dorian/Spartan term for a meal</note> by the Lacedaemonians, or that almost all Dorians call it something similar.
<margin>20</margin> For Alcman says: "and then the mills, the ox-eaters, and at the weddings," still calling them communal dinners. And again elsewhere, Alcman arranged it; and the Spartans call the portion after the dinner the *aiklon*. But this is not the same as what is given to the *phiditia* <note>original: φιδιτίοις; the Spartan public messes or communal dining clubs</note> after the meal; for that is bread and meat, but he calls these things *epaikla* <note>original: ἐπαίκλα; literally 'extra-meals' or dessert-additions</note>, which are the contributions brought into the *phiditia* messes. For I believe the word is formed by the sound. And the preparation of these so-called *epaikla* is not simple, as Polemon supposed, but twofold. For what they provide for the boys is quite simple and cheap: it is barley-meal soaked in oil, which Nicocles the Spartan says they themselves eat after the dinner wrapped in laurel leaves—for which reason the leaves are called *kammatides* and the cakes themselves are called *kammata*. That it was the custom for boys to snack on laurel leaves, Callias or Diocles says in *The Circles*: "you might finish the leaves of the dinners." The other type, which is purely for 
<margin>30</margin> money, and which they bring to the men's *phiditia*, is prepared from certain specified animals, either by handing them over to the members of the mess through one of the servants, or sometimes more than one. Molpis says that the *epaikla* are also called *matyllon*. Regarding the *epaikla*, Perseus writes in his *Laconian Constitution*: "And immediately, therefore, he fines the wealthy for *epaikla*." These are treats after dinner. He orders the poor to bring reed, or a dry branch, or laurel leaves, so that they may have *epaikla* to eat after dinner. For it consists of barley-meal sprinkled with oil, and the whole thing is like a small political arrangement. For according to whoever sits in the first or second place, or sits upon the pallet, they all do such things for the *epaikla*. Dioscorides records similar things. Regarding the "plucking of the cake" and the cakes themselves, Nicocles writes: "The Ephor <note>A high-ranking Spartan magistrate.</note>, having cut through all of them, either released or condemned them, and the winner fined them lightly either in cakes (*kammata*) or laurel-cakes (*kammatides*)."
<margin>40</margin> The *kammata* are barley-cakes. The *kammatides* are the leaves in which they bake the cakes. Regarding the dinner of the *phiditia*, Dicaearchus records the following in the work entitled *The Tripoliticus*: "The dinner is first served to each person separately, having no sharing with another; then as much barley-cake as each person wants, and a drink. Again, whenever each person has a mind for it, the cup is set before them. The relish for this is always boiled pork for everyone, and sometimes nothing else except a small piece weighing about a quarter <note>About 1/4 of a Spartan pound.</note>, and nothing else besides this except the broth from these, which is sufficient to accompany the entire dinner for all of them; and perhaps an olive, or cheese, or a fig. But if they receive any additional gift, such as a fish, or a hare, or a wood-pigeon, or something similar, it is brought around later after they have already dined; these are called the *epaikla*." Each person contributes to the mess about three Attic half-medimni <note>A medimnos was about 1.5 bushels; three half-medimni is roughly 2.25 bushels.</note> of barley-meal, and some twelve choes <note>A chous was about 3 liters; 12 choes is roughly 9 gallons.</note> of wine. Besides these, a certain weight of cheese and figs. Further, for
<margin>50</margin> buying relish, about ten Aeginetan obols <note>A high-value currency at the time.</note>. Sphaerus writes in the third book of the *Laconian Constitution*: "The members of the mess also bring *epaikla* to them, and the many take pride in those things they have caught themselves. However, the rich also bring bread and whatever is in season from the fields, providing as much as they consider necessary for that particular gathering, and preparing more than enough, for it is a provision not intended to be consumed entirely."
