# BOOK IV

Molpis says: "After dinner, it is a constant custom for something to be brought to the table from someone—sometimes even from several people—which has been prepared at their own homes with *mattuē* <note>original: ματτύα; a spiced dish of meat or poultry, often considered a delicacy</note>, and they call this an *epaiklon* <note>original: ἐπαίκλον; literally an 'after-meal' or additive dish</note>. Of those who bring these items, no one is allowed to bring things bought from the market. For they do not bring them for the sake of pleasure or gluttony, but to provide evidence through their own efforts that they have been successful in the hunt. Many who also raise their own flocks share the offspring generously. These *mattuai* include: wild pigeons, young pigs, turtledoves, thrushes, blackbirds, hares, lambs, and kids. The cooks announce the names of those who bring something to the mess, so that all may know the industry of the hunter and his diligence toward them."

Demetrius of Scepsis, in the first book of *The Trojan Array*, says that the festival of the Carneia among the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> is a mimicry of military 
<margin>Spartan Carneia.</margin> 
training. For there are nine locations in number, and these are called *skiades* <note>original: σκιάδες; 'shades' or temporary tents</note>, having something closely resembling tents; nine men dine in each, and everything is conducted according to the herald's command. Each 'shade' contains three brotherhoods, and the festival of the Carneia lasts for nine days.

Later, having abandoned such rigor for the sake of luxury, the Laconians drifted into indulgence. Phylarchus, 
<margin>Spartan Lifestyle</margin> 
at any rate, writes the following about them in the twenty-fifth book of his *Histories*: "The Lacedaemonians used to go to the *pheiditia* <note>original: φειδίτια; the Spartan communal mess-halls</note> according to ancestral custom. But when they began to bring small additions to share, a sense of grace was prepared along with them. And again: Their couches were so expensively adorned with such large and elaborate coverings, varied in color, that some of the foreign guests who were invited hesitated to lean their elbows on the cushions. Those who previously had endured sitting upright on the bench throughout the entire gathering, or at most leaned an elbow once, had now come to the aforementioned luxury, with displays of many drinking cups and servings of all kinds of varied foods. Furthermore, they used exquisite perfumes and even flavored their wines and desserts." 

This luxury was first introduced by those who reigned shortly before Cleomenes, namely Areus and Acrotatus, who sought to emulate the authority of a royal court. Some private citizens in Sparta at that time even surpassed them in their lifestyle, so much so that Areus and Acrotatus seemed to exceed all the simplest men of former times in their frugality. 

<margin>Plutarch in the Life of Cleomenes.</margin>
Cleomenes, however, differed greatly from them, for he was conscious of the state of affairs, and being young, he became very simple in his way of life. When leading such great affairs, he would show those who visited how he performed the sacrifice, demonstrating that the arrangements at his home were no more meager or lavish than theirs. Though many embassies came to him, he never held a gathering more pompously than the occasion required; he would have a five-couch arrangement spread out, or occasionally more. When no embassy was present, there was no command for a three-couch arrangement through the ushers, nor would anyone know who would sit down first. Instead, the eldest led the way to the couches, unless Cleomenes himself invited someone. He was usually found reclining with his brother or one of his peers. 

Upon the tripod stood a bronze cooler, a small tray, and a silver bowl holding two *kotylai* <note>A unit of liquid measure, roughly half a pint.</note> and a small ladle, while the pitcher was made of bronze. Wine was not offered unless someone asked for it. One ladle-full was given before the dinner. For the most part, when he had finished his first cup, the others drank as well. The items served from the table were for each person according to what was available, and the rest was managed so as neither to exceed nor fall short, but to be sufficient for everyone so that those present required nothing more. For the dinner was not like those in the *pheiditia* where they were served black broth and pieces of meat in a plain fashion. Nor again did it so exceed as to waste anything, surpassing the symmetry of a balanced diet. For he considered one way to be illiberal and the other to be arrogant. 

The wine was slightly better when guests were present. After they had dined, everyone remained silent. The boy stood by with the mixed drink and offered some to each. In the same manner after dinner, if more than two ladles were given, they were offered only when he nodded. No musical entertainment was ever introduced. Instead, he spent the time conversing with each person, encouraging everyone not just to listen, but to speak themselves, so that everyone was delighted by the interaction. 

Satirizing the Laconian dinners, Antiphanes says the following in the play entitled *The Archon*:

> "Since you have been to Lacedaemon, you must follow those laws. Go to dinner at the *pheiditia*, enjoy the black broth, wear those rough cloaks, do not be fastidious, and do not seek other fine things. In their customs, stay old-fashioned."

<margin>Cretan Lifestyle</margin>
Regarding the Cretan communal meals, Dosiadas, recording in the fourth book of his *Cretica*, writes: "The Lyctians gather for their common meals in this way: each person brings a tenth part of his crops to his 'fellowship' <note>original: ἑταιρείαν</note>, as well as the city revenues, which the city leaders distribute to each household. Each of the slaves brings an Aeginetan stater per head. All citizens are divided into 'fellowships.' A woman has charge of the communal meals, taking three or four of the common people to assist with the service. Two servants called wood-bearers <note>original: καλοφόρους</note> follow each of them. Everywhere in Crete there are two houses for the communal meals, one of which they call...

### FROM ATHENAEUS'S *THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED*

...called the "men’s hall" <note>original: ανδρεῖον / andreion; the communal dining room for male citizens</note>. The other building, where they lodge guests, they call a "sleeping quarters." In the communal dining house, two tables are placed first, called "foreign tables," at which any visiting foreigners sit. Next are the tables for the others. An equal portion of the food provided is served to each person present, but the younger men are given half a portion of meat, and they do not touch any of the other dishes. Then, a cup of diluted wine is placed on each table. All those at the common table drink from this together; and after they have finished dinner, another cup is brought. A mixing-bowl is filled for everyone in common. The elders are given permission to drink more if they wish. From the table, the woman in charge of the mess <note>original: προεστηκῦια γυνή; it is notable that women managed these Cretan male dining clubs</note> takes the best of what is served and openly places it before those who have distinguished themselves in war or through their wisdom. After dinner, they are accustomed first to deliberate on public affairs. Then, after this, 
<meta>line 10</meta>they recount deeds of war and praise those men who have proven themselves brave, encouraging the young toward manliness. Pyrgion, in the third book of *Cretan Customs*, says regarding the communal meals that the Cretans dine while sitting <note>rather than reclining, which was the more common Greek fashion for formal banquets</note>, and that food is provided to orphans without expense, and that the youngest among them stand and serve. After prayers are offered to the gods, they distribute portions of what is served to everyone. They also assign portions to guests according to their seat and rank of hospitality—half of what is served to the men. The orphans do not receive equal portions; instead, they are served a mixture of the customary items without fear of being overlooked. There were also "foreign seats" and a table at the first right as one enters 
<margin>Book 10.</margin>the men's halls, which they called the "Table of Zeus Xenios" <note>Zeus the Hospitable</note>. Herodotus, in comparing the banquets of the Greeks 
<margin>Persian Diet</margin>with those of the Persians, says: "Of all days, the Persians honor most that on which each was born. On this day, they think it right to provide a more plentiful meal than on others. The 
<meta>line 20</meta>wealthy among them serve an ox, a donkey, a horse, and a camel, all roasted whole in ovens. The poor among them serve the smaller kinds of livestock. They use little bread, but many side-dishes <note>original: ἐπιφορήμασι / epiphorēmata; often translated as dessert or appetizers</note>, and not all at once. Because of this, the Persians say that the Greeks stop eating while still hungry, because nothing worth mentioning is served to them after dinner; if anything were served, they would not stop eating. They are very much devoted to wine. They are not permitted to vomit or urinate in the presence of another. These rules are strictly observed. While drunk, they are accustomed to deliberate on their most serious affairs. Whatever they decide while deliberating, the head of the household <note>original: σιγέαρχος / sigearchos; literally "leader of silence" or master of ceremonies</note> proposes to them again the next day when they are sober; if they still approve it while sober, they act upon it. If not, they set it aside. Whatever they first deliberate on while sober, they re-examine while drunk." Concerning the luxury of the Persian kings, Xenophon writes in his *Agesilaus*: "For the Persian king, they travel over every land searching for what he might 
<meta>line 30</meta>pleasantly drink. Ten thousand people devise what he might pleasantly eat; and as for how he might sleep, one could never describe all the trouble they take. Agesilaus, however, because he loved hard work, drank everything that was available with pleasure and ate whatever he happened upon with pleasure. To sleep contentedly, any place was sufficient for him." And in the work titled *Hiero*, speaking about the preparations made for tyrants compared to those for private individuals regarding food, he says: "And I know," said Simonides, "that most people judge by this—that we drink and eat less than private individuals, because they think they themselves would more pleasantly dine on the dinner served to us than on their own. For that which exceeds the usual provides pleasure. This is why all men look forward to festivals with pleasure, except for tyrants. For their tables are always prepared to the full. They have no extra abundance at festivals, so in this first joy of expectation, they are at a disadvantage compared to private individuals." Then he said, "I know this well, as you are also experienced in it, that the 
<meta>line 40</meta>more someone is served beyond what is sufficient, the more quickly they feel a fullness of eating. So, in the duration of pleasure, the one served much is at a disadvantage compared to those who live moderately." "But by Zeus," said Simonides, "as long as the soul accepts it, those fed with more costly preparations feel much more pleasure than those served the cheapest food." Theophrastus, in his work *On Kingship* addressed to Cassander—if the writing is genuine, for many say it is by Sosibius, for whom Callimachus the poet wrote an elegiac victory poem—says that the Persian kings, out of luxury, offered a great sum of silver to those who could invent a new pleasure. Theopompus, in the twenty-fifth book of his *Histories*, says that Thuys, the king of the Paphlagonians, had a hundred of everything served on the table when he dined, starting with oxen; and when he was taken away as a prisoner like a king and 
<meta>line 50</meta>was under guard, he again had the same things served, living magnificently. Because of this, when Artaxerxes heard of it, he said that this man seemed to live as if he were soon to die. The same Theopompus, in the fourteenth book of his *Philippics*, says that whenever the King [of Persia] visits some of his subjects, twenty talents <note>An enormous sum; one talent could pay a trireme's crew for a month</note> are spent on his dinner. Sometimes even thirty. Some spend even much more. For each of the cities, according to its size, has the cost of the dinner fixed of old, just like their tribute.

### BOOK IV

Heraclides of Cuma, the author of the *Persian History*, in the second book of his work titled *Preparations*, writes: “And those who attend the Persian kings when they dine are all bathed and serve in beautiful clothing, spending nearly half the day preparing the dinner. Of those invited to dine with the king, some dine outside in public view, where anyone who wishes may see them; others dine inside with the king. Even these, however, do not dine at his actual table. Instead, there are two rooms facing one another: in one, the king has his meal, and in the other, his guests. The king sees them through the curtain at the door, but they cannot see him. On festival days, however, they sometimes all dine in a single room, the Great Hall, alongside the king. Whenever the king holds a drinking party—which he does often—his drinking companions are at most twelve in number. 
<margin>10</margin> When they have finished dinner (the king dining by himself and the guests by themselves), one of the eunuchs calls in the drinking companions. When they enter, they drink with him, though they do not drink the same wine. They sit on the floor, while he reclines on a couch with golden feet; they then depart after having drunk with him. For the most part, the king breakfasts and dines alone. Sometimes his wife dines with him, and occasionally some of his sons. During the dinner, his concubines sing and play the harp for him; one leads the song, and the others sing together in a chorus. The 'King’s Dinner,' as it is called,” he continues, “will seem magnificent to those who only hear of it, but when examined closely, it is shown to be arranged economically and with great precision, just as it is for other Persians of high rank. For the king, one thousand animals are slaughtered every day. These include horses, camels, oxen, asses, deer, and mostly sheep. Many birds are also consumed, including Arabian ostriches <note>original: στρουθοὶ οἱ ἀράβιοι / strouthoi hoi arabioi; literally "Arabian sparrows," the common Greek term for the ostrich</note>—which are massive creatures—geese, and roosters. 
<margin>20</margin> Only a moderate portion of these is served to each of the king’s guests, and each of them carries away whatever is left over from his meal. But the greatest part of these meats and provisions is carried out into the courtyard for the bodyguards and the light-armed infantry whom the king maintains. There, everything is divided into equal portions of meat and bread. Just as mercenaries in Greece receive their pay in silver, these men receive their food from the king in place of wages. Similarly, among other Persians of high rank, all the food is placed on the table at once. When the guests have finished dining, whatever is left over from the table—mostly meat and bread—is given by the head waiter to each of the servants, who then has his daily food for himself. For the most distinguished guests go to the king’s court only for breakfast <note>original: ἄριστον / ariston; the midday meal</note>, to avoid 
<margin>30</margin> making the journey twice; however, they themselves then host their own dinner guests.” Herodotus says in his seventh book that those Greeks who received the king and hosted Xerxes at dinner were reduced to such extreme distress that they were driven from their homes. For instance, when the people of Thasos hosted the army of Xerxes on behalf of their cities on the mainland, Antipater, one of their citizens, spent four hundred silver talents on that single meal. Silver and gold drinking cups and mixing bowls were provided, and these were all carried off after the dinner. If Xerxes had stayed for breakfast as well as dinner, those cities would have been utterly ruined. In the ninth book of his *Histories*, Herodotus also says that the King provides a "Royal Dinner." This is prepared once a year, on the day of the king's birth. 
<margin>38</margin> The name of this dinner in Persian is *Tykta*, which in Greek means "Perfect" <note>original: τέλειον / teleion; likely referring to the completion of a year</note>. On that day alone, the king washes his head with soap and gives gifts to the Persians. Alexander the Great, whenever he dined with his friends, as reported by Ephippus 
<margin>40</margin> of Olynthus in his work *On the Deaths of Alexander and Hephaestion*, spent one hundred minas a day, with perhaps sixty or seventy friends dining with him. But the Persian king, according to Ctesias and Dinon in their *Persian Histories*, used to spend four hundred talents on his dinner, with fifteen thousand men present. This amount, converted to Italian currency <note>original: ἰταλικοῦ νομίσματος; referring to the Roman denarius</note>, comes to 2,400,000 denarii. When this is divided among fifteen thousand men, it results in one hundred and sixty denarii per man. Thus, it turns out to be equal to Alexander's expenditure, for he spent one hundred minas, as Ephippus recorded. Menander, in his play *The Drunkenness*, describes the cost of a very great banquet as one talent, saying:

> “I wish our fortunes matched our sacrifices!
> For to the gods, I bring a humble sheep
> Bought for twelve drachmas. But for the rest—
> The flute-girls, the perfume, the harpists,
> This Thasian wine, the eels, the cheese, the honey—
<margin>50</margin>> It adds up to nearly a talent by the account.”

He mentions a "Talent" here to signify an extravagant expenditure. And in *The Grouch* <note>original: Δύσκολος / Dyskolos</note>, he says:

> “The way these thieves sacrifice!
> They bring picnic-beds and wine-jars, not for the gods’
> Sake, but for their own. The incense is 'pious,'
> And the cake is 'religious' because the god gets it
> All on the fire. But as for the loin-end
> And the gall-bladder—since they aren't edible—they give those to the gods...”

In preparing their dinners, they served stuffed fig-leaves <note>original: "thria"</note>, boiled meats, small fry <note>original: "aphyas"</note>, cross-cut sausages, regular sausages, small birds, and pea soup. With these dishes, Attaginus <note>The Greek text reads "Automonos," but this is likely an error for Attaginus of Thebes, who famously hosted the Persians as described in Herodotus.</note> feasted Mardonius <note>A leading Persian military commander during the Persian Wars.</note> and the other fifty Persians. <margin>An Arcadian dinner.</margin>
Hecataeus of Miletus <note>An early Greek historian and geographer.</note>, in the third book of his *Genealogies*, describes an Arcadian dinner, saying it consists of barley cakes and pork. Harmodius of Lepreum, in his work *On the Customs of Phigalia*, says that the official appointed as the grain-provider <term>sitarchos: a magistrate in charge of grain supplies</term> among the Phigalians would bring three <term>choes: a liquid measure, roughly 3 liters each</term> of wine for the day, a <term>medimnus: a dry measure, roughly 50 liters</term> of barley meal, and five <term>mnai: a unit of weight, roughly 430 grams each</term> of cheese, along with other things suitable for the seasoning of the priests' meals. The city provided three sheep for each of the choruses, as well as a cook, a water-carrier, tables, and benches for seating. The choregos <note>The wealthy citizen who financed the public performances.</note> provided all such preparations, except for the cook's utensils. The dinner was as follows: cheese, kneaded dough, and barley cake served—according to custom—on bronze platters, which are called *mazonomoi* <note>Literally "barley-cake distributors."</note> by some because of their use. Along with the barley cake and the cheese, they served entrails and salt as a relish. After they had chewed these, they were required to drink a small amount from an earthenware cup, while the one serving would say, "Against indigestion." Then, for the common meal, there was broth and a dish of pulse. Two pieces of meat were ready for each person. At all dinners, a cake called a *phthois* was served, especially at those called "barley-cake feasts," for that is still the name of the Dionysian assembly. To the younger eaters, they would more generously pour more broth and set out barley cakes and loaves of bread, for their lifestyle was noble and generous. Indeed, their large appetites were a source of wonder and were famous among them. After the dinner, they performed libations without washing their hands; instead, they wiped them with bread crumbs <note>original: "apomagdalia"</note>, and each person carried these crumbs away. They did this because of the "nightly fears" that occur at crossroads <note>A reference to Hecate or spirits that were thought to be appeased by these bread-scrap offerings.</note>. After the libations, a paean <note>A song of praise or triumph.</note> was sung. When they sacrifice to the heroes, a great ox-sacrifice occurs, and everyone feasts together with the slaves. The children dine with their fathers at these feasts, sitting on stones, and they dine naked. Theopompus, in the forty-seventh book of his *Philippic History*, says that the Arcadians at their feasts receive neither masters nor slaves, but prepare one table for everyone, placing the food in the center for all and mixing the same wine-bowl for everyone.
<margin>A dinner of the Naucratians.</margin>
Among the people of Naucratis <note>A Greek colony in the Nile Delta of Egypt.</note>, as Hermeias says in the second book of his work *On the Gryneian Apollo*, they dine in the Prytaneion <note>The seat of government and the "hearth" of the city.</note> on the birthdays of Hestia of the Prytaneion and during the Dionysia. Also, at the festival of Apollo Komaios, everyone enters in white robes, which even to this day they call "Prytaneion garments." After reclining, they rise to their knees and join in the prayers as the sacred herald recites the ancestral petitions. After this, they recline and each receives two <term>kotylai: a cup holding about 0.25 liters</term> of wine, except for the priests of Pythian Apollo and Dionysus, for to each of these a double portion of wine is given along with other portions of the meal. Then, a pure loaf of bread made in a broad shape is set before each person, upon which is placed another loaf which they call "oven-bread" <note>original: "kribanites"</note>. There is also pork, a small bowl of barley-groat soup <note>original: "ptisane"</note> or seasonal vegetables, two eggs, a slice of cheese, dried figs, a flat cake, and a garland. Any sacrificial official who prepares anything beyond these is fined by the magistrates. Furthermore, it is not permitted for those dining in the Prytaneion to bring in any food from the outside. They consume only these items and give whatever is left over to the servants. On all other days of the year, any of those entitled to feed there who wishes to go up to the Prytaneion to dine may do so, having prepared for himself at home some vegetable or pulse, a piece of salt-fish, or some fish. He receives a very small piece of pork and a cup of wine. No woman is permitted to enter the Prytaneion, except for the flute-girl alone. No chamber-pot is brought into the Prytaneion either. If any Naucratian hosts a wedding feast, it is forbidden—as written in the marriage law—to give eggs or honey-cakes. What the reason for this is, Ulpian <note>One of the characters in Athenaeus' dialogue.</note> is the right person to teach us.
<margin>An Egyptian dinner.</margin>
Lynceus, in his *Egyptian Notes*, prefers the Egyptian dinners to the Persian ones. He says that when the Egyptians campaigned against Ochus <note>Artaxerxes III, King of Persia.</note> and were defeated, and the Egyptian King <note>Nectanebo II.</note> was taken prisoner, Ochus treated him kindly and invited him to dinner. When a magnificent preparation was made, the Egyptian laughed at the Persian's lifestyle as being too frugal. "If you wish, O King," he said, "to see how prosperous kings ought to dine, permit my former cooks to prepare an Egyptian dinner for you." When the King ordered it and it was prepared, Ochus was so delighted with the feast that he said, "O Egyptian, may the gods destroy you miserably, for you who left behind such dinners and yet yearned for a more frugal meal." What these Egyptian dinners were like, Protagorides teaches us in the first book of his *On the Daphnic Contests*, saying: "There is a third type of dinner, the Egyptian, where tables are not set...

Regarding the Galatians <note>The Greeks referred to the Celtic peoples of both Gaul and Asia Minor as Galatians.</note>, Phylarchus says in his sixth book that many broken loaves are set out in heaps upon the tables, along with meat from the cauldrons. No one tastes these until they have first seen whether the king has touched what is set before him. 

<margin>A Galatian dinner.</margin>In his third book, the same Phylarchus says that Ariamnes, a Galatian who was exceptionally wealthy, announced that he would feast all the Galatians for a year, and he accomplished this in the following way. He divided the most convenient parts of the roads throughout the country into stations. At these spots, he erected tents made of stakes, reeds, and osiers <note>flexible willow branches</note> that could hold four hundred men or more, depending on the capacity of the locations, intended to receive the multitude that would flow in from the cities and villages. There he set up large cauldrons of all kinds of meat, which he had commissioned from smiths he brought from the cities a year before the undertaking began. He ordered that many victims—bulls, pigs, sheep, and other livestock—be slaughtered every day. He also prepared jars of wine and a great quantity of kneaded barley meal. And not only, he says, did the Galatians coming from the villages and cities enjoy this, but even passing strangers were not allowed to leave by the attending servants until they had shared in the meal. 

Xenophon mentions the prepared dinners in the sixth book <note>Modern editions place this in Book 7</note> of the *Anabasis*, describing the banquet at the court of Seuthes <note>A Thracian prince who hired Xenophon’s "Ten Thousand" mercenaries.</note> in these words: "When they had all entered for the dinner, and they were all seated in a circle, then tripods <note>small three-legged tables</note> were brought in for everyone. These were about twenty in number, slender and full of sliced meats, and large leavened loaves were skewered to the meat. Tables were always placed especially for the guests, for it was the custom—and Seuthes was the first to do this—that he would take the loaves lying near him, break them into small pieces, and throw them to whomever he pleased, doing the same with the meat, leaving only enough for himself to taste. The others also did the same where the tables were placed. But a certain Arcadian named Aristas, a terrible glutton, let the throwing business go. Taking a loaf as large as three <term>choinikes: a dry measure, roughly 3 liters</term> into his hand and placing the meat upon his knees, he proceeded to dine. Horns of wine were carried around and everyone accepted them. When the wine-bearer came to him with the horn, Aristas, seeing that Xenophon was no longer eating, said: 'Give it to him! For he is already at leisure, but I am not yet.' At this, there was an outburst of laughter. 

<margin>A Thracian dinner. Book 7.</margin>As the drinking progressed, a Thracian man entered leading a white horse; taking a full horn, he said: 'I drink to your health, O Seuthes, and I give you this horse, upon which you may pursue and catch whomever you wish, and in retreat you need not fear the enemy.' Another brought in a boy and gave him as a gift with a toast, and another gave clothes for Seuthes’ wife. Timasion, drinking a toast, gave him a silver bowl and a rug worth ten <term>mnai: a high value, roughly 4.3 kilograms of silver</term>. A certain Gnesippus of Athens stood up and said that there was an ancient and excellent law that those who have should give to the king as a mark of honor, but to those who do not have, the king should give. Xenophon, being at a loss but emboldened, took the horn and said: 'I give you, O Seuthes, myself and these my companions, to be your faithful friends, and no one against his will. They are here now asking nothing of you, but rather wishing to labor for you and to face danger on your behalf.' Seuthes stood up and drank with him, and splashed the rest of the horn's contents over himself with him. After this, musicians entered, playing upon horns made of raw ox-hide <note>original: "keratistai"</note>, signaling rhythms as if they were blowing a trumpet <term>magadis: typically a stringed instrument, but here used to describe a type of trumpeting</term>."

<margin>A Celtic dinner.</margin>Posidonius <note>A Stoic philosopher who traveled to Gaul in the 1st century BCE.</note>, in the twenty-third book of his *Histories*—which he composed in a manner not at all foreign to the philosophy he chose, recording many customs and laws among many peoples—says: "The Celts set out their meals by spreading hay on the ground and using wooden tables raised slightly above the earth. Their food consists of a few loaves, but much meat, either boiled in water or roasted on coals or spits. They partake of this cleanly, but in a lion-like manner, taking up whole limbs with both hands and biting off pieces. If any part is difficult to tear away, they cut it with a small knife which lies in its own sheath in the scabbard. Those living near the rivers or the inner and outer sea also eat fish, which they roast with salt, vinegar, and cumin. They also add this cumin to their drink. They do not use olive oil because of its scarcity, and because they are unaccustomed to it, it seems unpleasant to them. When many dine together, they sit in a circle, with the most powerful man in the middle, like the leader of a chorus, excelling the others either in military skill, birth, or wealth. The host sits beside him, and the others in order on either side according to their rank. Their shield-bearers stand behind them, while the spearmen sit in a circle opposite them and feast together like their masters. The attendants carry the drink around in vessels resembling jars <note>original: "ambikoi"</note>, either of clay or silver. For the platters on which they serve the food are of the same materials, though some use bronze, and others use wooden or wicker baskets. The drink among the wealthy is wine brought from Italy or the region of Marseille; this is unmixed—"

They sip from the same cup a little at a time, no more than a *cyathus* <term>cyathus: a small measure or ladle, roughly 1.5 ounces</term>, but they do this frequently. The servant carries the drink around to the right and to the left; this is how they are served, and they 
<margin>Strabo, Book 4</margin>worship the gods by turning to the right. Furthermore, Posidonius, in recounting the wealth of Luernius, the father of Bituitus <note>Bituitus was a king of the Arverni who was defeated by the Romans in 121 BCE</note> who was deposed by the Romans, says that in his bid for popular favor, Luernius would ride in a chariot across the plains, scattering gold and silver to the thousands of Celts following him. He even constructed a square enclosure twelve *stadia* <note>About 1.4 miles</note> long, in which he filled vats with expensive drink and prepared such a vast quantity of food that for several days anyone who wished could enter and enjoy the feast, being served without interruption. Once, after he had set a deadline for the end of the feast, a certain barbarian poet arrived late. Meeting the king, the poet sang a song praising his excellence but lamenting his own late arrival. Luernius, delighted, asked for a bag of gold and threw it to him as he ran beside the chariot. The poet picked it up and sang again, saying that even the very tracks of the earth over which he drove his chariot brought gold and blessings to men. This is recorded in the twenty-third book of his *Histories*. 

In his fifth book, when discussing the Parthians, he says: "The man called the 'Friend' 
<margin>A Parthian dinner.</margin>does not share the king’s table, but sits on the ground while the king reclines on a high couch. He eats what is tossed to him like a dog. Often, for any chance reason, he is dragged away from his meal on the floor and scourged with rods and knotted thongs. Covered in blood, he then falls prostrate on the ground and worships the one who punished him as if he were a benefactor." 

In the sixteenth book, speaking of King Seleucus <note>Seleucus II Callinicus</note>, he relates how the king went up into Media and, while warring against Arsaces, was taken prisoner by the barbarian. He remained with Arsaces for a long time, being treated in a kingly manner. He also writes of the Parthian banquets: "The king had his couch, on which he reclined alone, higher than the others and set apart; he also had his own table, like a hero <note>Comparing the king's solitary, elevated status to the ritual offerings made to deceased heroes</note>, laden with barbarian delicacies." 

In his account of Heracleon of Beroea—who, having been promoted by King Antiochus 'the Hook-nosed' <note>Antiochus VIII Grypus</note>, nearly drove his benefactor from his kingdom—Posidonius writes the following in the fourth book of his *Histories*: "He arranged for the soldiers to feast in groups of a thousand in the open air. The dinner consisted of a large loaf of bread and meat, and the wine served was the local variety mixed with cold water. They were served by men carrying swords, and the meal was conducted in orderly silence." 

In the second book, he says that in the city of the Romans, 
<margin>A Roman dinner.</margin>whenever they feast in the Temple of Hercules to honor those who have celebrated a triumph, the preparation of the banquet is exceptionally lavish. Honey-wine <term>oinomeli: a mixture of wine and honey, often served as an aperitif</term> is poured, and the food consists of large loaves, boiled smoked meats, and a great abundance of roasted meats from recently consecrated sacrifices. 

Among the Tyrrhenians <note>The Greek name for the Etruscans</note>, luxurious tables are prepared twice a day, with floral coverings, silver drinking vessels of every kind, and a multitude of servants standing by, adorned in costly clothing. Timaeus, in the first book of his *Histories*, even says that their female servants serve them naked until they are fully grown. 

Megasthenes, in the second book of his *Indica*, says that among the Indians, a table is set before each individual at dinner. This table is like a cabinet, and upon it is placed a golden bowl into which the guest first puts boiled rice (prepared like a thick porridge) and then many side dishes prepared according to Indian recipes. 

<margin>A German dinner.</margin>The Germans, as Posidonius records in his thirtieth book, eat roasted meat for breakfast, divided into joints, and they drink milk and unmixed wine. 

Some of the Campanians engage in gladiatorial combat during their symposia. Nicolaus of Damascus, one of the Peripatetic philosophers, in the hundred-and-tenth book of his *Histories*, records that the Romans also hold gladiatorial matches at dinner. He writes: "The Romans held gladiatorial shows not only at festivals and in theaters—having adopted the custom from the Tyrrhenians—but also at their banquets. They would often invite friends to dinner for various reasons, but specifically to see two or three pairs of gladiators. When they were full from dinner and intoxicated, they would call in the combatants. As soon as one was slaughtered, the guests would clap, delighting in the sight. Someone even wrote in his will that the most beautiful women he owned should fight as gladiators; another requested young boys he had loved. However, the people would not tolerate such lawlessness and declared the will invalid." 

Eratosthenes, in the first book of his *Olympic Victors*, says that the Tyrrhenians box to the sound of the flute. Posidonius, 
<margin>Gladiators and dancing</margin>in the twenty-third book of his *Histories*, says that the Celts sometimes engage in single combat during dinner. For, rising up with their arms, they engage in shadow-boxing and spar with one another. Sometimes this goes as far as a...

### Page 78

...they advance with their spears, and from this a quarrel arises; if those present do not intervene to calm them, they go as far as killing one another. It is said that in ancient times, when the joints of meat were served, the strongest man would take the marrow. If anyone else laid claim to it, they would stand up to engage in single combat until death. Others, having received a sum of silver or gold—or sometimes a certain number of jars of wine—would secure the promise of the gift and distribute it among their close friends and family. Then, they would lie flat on their backs upon their shields, and someone standing by would cut their throat with a sword. 

Euphorian of Chalcis <note>A 3rd-century BCE poet and librarian</note> writes in his *Historical Commentaries* that among the Romans, five *minae* <term>mina: a unit of currency worth 100 drachmas</term> were offered to anyone willing to undergo decapitation by an axe, so that their heirs might collect the prize. He notes that often, when many people registered for this, they would argue over who among them had the best right to be beaten to death.

Hermippus, in the first book of his work *On Lawgivers*, declares that the Mantineans <note>Inhabitants of Mantinea in the Peloponnese</note> were the inventors of single combat, following the advice of one of their citizens named Demonax, and that the people of Cyrene became their imitators. Ephorus, in the sixth book of his *Histories*, says that the Mantineans and Arcadians practiced military exercises, including the "heavy-armed" style of fighting and ancient equipment, as if they were the inventors; even now, people call such gear "Mantinean." He adds that the formal teaching of "hoplite-fighting" <term>hoplomachia: fighting in heavy armor</term> was first discovered in Mantinea, after Demeas introduced the art. 

That the practice of single combat was ancient is mentioned by Aristophanes in *The Phoenician Women* as follows:
*Against the sons of Oedipus, two boys trained in boxing, Ares has fallen with the weight of single combat, a contest they now understand.*

It seems the word "single-combatant" <note>original: "monomachos"</note> was formed not from the noun for "battle" <note>original: "machē"</note>, but rather from the verb "to fight" <note>original: "machesthai"</note>. For whenever the word for "battle" is used in a compound, the accent usually shifts—as in "ally" <note>symmachos</note>, "first-fighter" <note>prōtomachos</note>, or "vulnerable" <note>epimachos</note>, and as Pindar uses "war-loving race" <note>philomachon genos</note> in reference to Perseus. However, when the accent remains on the middle syllable, it contains the verb "to fight," as in "boxer" <note>pugmachos</note> or "sea-fighter" <note>naumachos</note>. Stesichorus was the first to use "boxer," as well as "heavy-armed fighter," "wall-fighter," and "tower-fighter."

The comic poet Poseidippus says in *The Pimp*:
*He who has never sailed has seen no evil. We are more wretched than the gladiators.*

That even distinguished men and leaders engaged in single combat by challenge is something we have mentioned elsewhere. Diaetus the Athenian says in the ninth book of his *Histories* that Cassander, upon returning from Boeotia and burying the King and Queen at Aegae (along with Cynna, the mother of Eurydice), and having paid them all the proper honors, established a contest of single combat in which four of his soldiers competed.

Demetrius of Scepsis, in the twelfth book of *The Trojan Array*, says that at the court of Antiochus (the one called "The Great"), everyone at dinner used to dance in armor—not only the King’s friends, but even the King himself. When it came time for the turn of Agesianax of Alexandria (the historian from the Troad) to dance, he stood up and said: "O King, do you wish to see me dance poorly, or would you rather hear me recite my own poems well?" Being ordered to speak, he pleased the King so much that he was deemed worthy of a grant and became one of the King’s "Friends" <note>A formal title for high-ranking courtiers in Hellenistic kingdoms</note>.

Duris of Samos, in the seventeenth book of his *Histories*, says that Polysperchon, although he was quite elderly, would dance whenever he had been drinking—he who was second to none of the Macedonians in either generalship or status. He would put on a saffron robe <note>original: "krokōtos," a garment usually associated with women or the god Dionysus</note> and Sicyonian sandals, and continue dancing.

Agatharchides of Cnidus relates in the eighth book of his *History of Asia* that those who hosted Alexander the Great (son of Philip) used to gild the food that was to be served. When they wished to eat, they would strip off the gold and throw it away with the scraps, so that the guests might see the extravagance, but the servants would benefit by keeping the gold. These men had forgotten—as Duris also records—that Philip, Alexander’s father, possessed only one gold cup weighing fifty drachmas, which he took with him every night to bed and placed under his pillow.

<margin>Nooses.</margin> Seleucus says that certain Thracians at their banquets play a game of "hanging." They hang a noose from a high pulley, beneath which is placed a stone that easily tips over. They draw lots, and the one who loses stands on the stone and puts his neck into the noose. Another man comes by and tips the stone; if the man hanging does not quickly cut the rope with a knife, he dies. The others laugh, considering his death to be a great joke.

After saying these things, the friends and fellow-diners felt that the Greeks were by far the foremost in knowledge regarding ancient banquets. The wise Plato describes this accurately in the first book of the *Laws*, speaking as follows: "You would see nothing of the kind in the countryside or in the cities under Spartan care—no drinking parties, nor the things that follow them and stir up every kind of pleasure to the best of their power. There is no one who, meeting a man walking in a state of drunkenness, would not immediately inflict the greatest punishment; nor would the excuse of the festival of Dionysus save him, as I once saw among our people on the wagons, and in Tarentum among our colonists, where I saw the whole city..."

Then Cynulcus said, "I wish I had been destroyed playing that Thracian game rather than being led here by you as if we were keeping a fast, waiting for that 'self-invited white token' <term>aspron: literally 'white,' likely referring to a piece of white bread or a small coin/token required to begin a meal</term>. > For it is no bad thing to take dinner in due season.
And the fine **ARISTOPHANES** said in his play *Cocalus*:
> But it is exactly midday, father, when the younger men ought to dine.
It would have been much better for me to dine according to the *Cynic Banquet* of Parmeniscus than to stay here and see everything being carried around like people pacing with fevers." When we laughed at this, someone said, "But, my good man, do not begrudge us; tell us about that banquet of Parmeniscus." And he, raising himself up, said:
> I swear to you by the god himself, born of this soil,
> From whom the state of drunkenness comes to you all,
> That we live our lives choosing for ourselves,
> Rather than the superiority of King Seleucus,
> To sup on lentils, letting the sweet things go without fear,
> Than to sleep softly while fearing misery.
<margin>A Cynic Banquet.</margin>
But Parmeniscus began his account this way: "Parmeniscus to Molpis, greetings," abounding in addresses to you, a city of famous names. I am anxious lest, falling into an un-satiated state, you imitate [him]. Therefore, I also wish to share with you the dinner at the house of Cebes the Cyzicene. Having drunk a preliminary cup, return to the feast as if it were the fourth hour <note>Roughly 10:00 AM, though timing for meals varied</note>. For during the Dionysia at Athens, I was taken to his house. I found six Cynics reclining there, among whom were Cynulcus and Carneius the Megarian. As dinner was delayed, a discussion arose as to which food is the sweetest. While some praised the 'holy thing of Lerna' <note>Likely a reference to local shellfish or a specific delicacy from the Lerna region</note> and others the food from Garynus, Carneius said that a "friend to guests" <note>original: *philoxenon*</note> should, as need requires, praise the table when it is set; and to us, they poured out lentil soup <margin>Lentils.</margin>. Then more was brought in, and then again lentils were served, as many as if they had been soaked, and Ditrephes, quoting poetry, said:
> May you not fail to live [well], whoever is the cause of these lentils.
And another shouted out in turn:
> May a lentil-demon and a lentil-fate seize you!
As for me, according to the comic poet **Diphilus**—who says this in his play *The Bracelets*:
> The little dinner was flowery and very refined:
> A large bowl of lentil soup in the middle for each man.
> First of all, not bringing it in like chaff,
> A great *saperdes* <term>saperdes: a type of salted fish, likely a perch</term> danced into the middle,
> Smelling of the sea-eagle's island,
> Which he always tells the thrushes about.
When laughter broke out, Melissa ("the honey-delight") and Nikion ("the victress") appeared. These were among the notable courtesans. Looking at what was set before them and being amazed, they recognized the situation. And Nikion said: "None of you knows how to eat chosen fish. Or perhaps like your ancestor Meleager of Gadara, in his work entitled *The Graces*, you say that Homer, being Syrian by race, followed his ancestral customs by making the ancients abstain from fish? Or is it because fish were so cheap at the Hellespont? Or is his writing merely a riddle containing a comparison of egg-yolk and lentils? For I see among you a great preparation of lentils. Looking at it, I would advise you, in the Socratic manner, to lead yourselves out of life <note>A common euphemism for suicide</note> rather than eat such food." "How so?" asked Carythus. "Eurithius the Pythagorean, O Nikion," as Clearchus the Peripatetic says in the second book of his *Lives*, "said that God punishes the souls of all in the body and in this insulting life. For if they do not remain alone in these [bodies] until he willingly releases them, they will fall into more and greater outrages. Therefore, all should guard against the 'rising of the masters' <note>original: *anastasin* — this may refer to the stationing of divine guards over the soul</note> and fear to depart from life willingly. Only those who have gladly accepted death upon the earth, believing the release of the soul to be toward the Lord, should go forth with purpose. We are persuaded by these doctrines. But as for you, there is no envy for any of the three evils you may hope for. For you do not know, you wretches, that these heavy foods block the 'leading faculty' <term>hegemonikon: in Stoic and Greek philosophy, the rational part of the soul that governs behavior</term> and do not allow wisdom to exist within it." Theopompus, then, in the fifth book of his *Philippics*, says: "For eating much and devouring meat takes away reasoning and makes souls slower. It fills them with anger and much awkwardness." And the wonderful Xenophon says that it is great to eat barley-cake and cress when hungry, and sweet to drink water drawn from a river when thirsty. Socrates, too, was often found walking about late in the evening in front of his house. To those who asked what he was doing at such an hour, he would say he was "gathering relish for his dinner" <note>He meant he was building up an appetite so that simple food would taste like a delicacy</note>. For us, the portion we receive from you would be sufficient, and we do not grow angry if we receive less, like the Hercules in Anticleides' account. For he says in the second book of his *Returns* <margin>Macrobius, book 1, chapter 13, On the Dream of Scipio <note>A Latin marginal reference to a later Roman author who discussed similar themes of the soul</note>.</margin> that after Hercules completed his labors, Eurystheus was performing a sacrifice and invited him. When Eurystheus' servants were setting out the portions for each guest, they set a lowlier one before Hercules. Perceiving himself to be dishonored, Hercules killed three of Eurystheus' sons: Perimedes, Eurytius, and Eurypylus. We, however, are not so fierce in our temper."

### LENTILS.

...even if everyone is an emulator of Heracles <note>Heracles was famously depicted in comedy as a glutton with a particular fondness for simple, hearty foods like lentils</note>. For Archagathus said that "the lentil is a tragic thing" <note>This likely refers to lentils being served at funerals, or perhaps a joke about the mock-seriousness with which poets treat humble food</note>. Sophilus, the comic poet, says that people "fear the diseases of Orestes have ceased" <note>Orestes, the mythical prince, was famously mad; the joke implies that eating simple lentils is a sign of returning to sanity or, conversely, a new kind of misery</note>. Strattis, laying down a doctrine, says that one must do everything wisely, and even "season a dish of lentils prudently." Because of this, Timon of Phlius <note>A skeptical philosopher and poet known for his satirical "Silloi"</note> said: "And he touched the Zenonian lentils," meaning one who has not learned to live prudently, as if lentils cannot be properly cooked except according to the instructions of Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism, who was famously austere</note>. Zeno said: "Throw into the lentils a twelfth part of coriander." And Crates of Thebes <note>A famous Cynic philosopher who gave away his wealth to live in poverty</note> used to say: "Do not, by exalting a pot of lentils, cast us into discord." Chrysippus <note>The third head of the Stoic school</note>, in his work *On the Beautiful*, introducing certain opinions to us, says: "Never eat an olive when you have a nettle in the winter season; oh, oh, for a dish of bulb-lentils! > Whoever you are who slanders the lentil, that most delicious seasoning.

I also know that the sister of Odysseus, that most prudent and intelligent man, was named "Lentil" <note>original: "Phake"</note>, though others call her Callisto, as Mnaseas records in the third book of his *History of Europe*, and Lysimachus says in the third book of his *Returns*. At these remarks, Plutarch <note>One of the guests at the banquet, not necessarily the famous biographer</note> laughed brightly and said, "You did not fail, you white-livered fellow, to set forth your great learning concerning the lentil!" Euripides, in his *Suppliants*, says of Capaneus <note>One of the Seven against Thebes, usually depicted as arrogant, but here praised for his simplicity</note>: "This is Capaneus, who had a great livelihood, yet he was least of all proud of his wealth.

He held a spirit no greater than that of a poor man, shunning those who puffed themselves up too much at their tables, and praising what was sufficient. For Capaneus was not the sort of man the fine Chrysippus describes in his work *On Things Not to be Chosen for Their Own Sake*, where he says: "Some people fall so far into the love of money that it is recorded that one man, near his end, swallowed not a few gold coins and died. These men and those like them die almost shouting: "O Gold, most beautiful welcome to mortals! Neither a mother, nor children in the house, nor a dear father possess such pleasures as those who have you in their dwellings. If Aphrodite has such a look in her eyes, it is no wonder she has ten thousand lovers." Such was the love of money among the people of that time. When someone asked Anacharsis <note>A Scythian philosopher known for his outsider's perspective on Greek culture</note> what the Greeks use money for, he said: "For counting." Diogenes, in his *Republic*, legislated that knucklebones <note>original: "astragaloi," small bones used as dice or gaming pieces</note> should be the currency. Euripides also spoke well on these matters: "Do not speak to me of wealth; I do not admire a god whom even the worst man easily acquires." Chrysippus, in the introduction to his treatise *On Good and Evil*, says that a certain young man from Ionia came to Athens being very rich, wearing a purple robe with gold fringes. When someone asked him where he was from, he replied: "I am rich." Perhaps Alexis <note>A prolific poet of Middle Comedy</note> mentions this same man in his *Thebans*, saying: "Of what race is this man? Rich. Everyone calls these men the most ignoble and poor; they are not well-born, and no one looks at them." After saying this, Cynulcus, when he was not applauded, became angry. My own ancestor Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, the Roman polymath</note>, called the Menippean, also mentions it, as do many of the Roman grammarians. Those who have not conversed with many Greek poets and writers do not know where Varro took this iambic line from. Archestratus <note>A 4th-century BC Greek poet from Sicily known as the "Hesiod of Diners" for his mock-epic poem on gastronomy</note> and his "laughter in the belly-treatise"—it is not only rhapsodies that you "wise men" embrace, but this Pythagorean practice of silence, perhaps because you have no words of value. Consider the *Art of Love* by Sphodrias the Cynic, or the erotic lectures of Protagorides. And Persaeus the "Beautiful Philosopher" <note>A Stoic philosopher and student of Zeno</note> wrote *Sympotic Dialogues*, compiled from the memoirs of Stilpo and Zeno. In these, he investigates how to keep guests from falling asleep and how one should manage the pouring of wine. He asks at what time one should bring in the young men and women to the banquet, and when they should be accepted in their finery, and when they should be dismissed as being unskilled, and where the side-dishes should be placed, and the bread, and all such overly-curious details.

Sophroniscus's son, the philosopher <note>Persaeus is meant here, though the text calls him "Sophroniscus's son," which usually refers to Socrates—likely a satirical comparison or an error in the source</note>, also spoke of kisses—he who always turned these things over in his mind. As Hermippus says, he was entrusted by Antigonus with the Acrocorinth <note>The high citadel of Corinth</note>, but he was driven out while drunk, losing Corinth itself when he was out-maneuvered by Aratus of Sicyon. This is the man who previously contended in dialogues with Zeno, claiming that "the wise man would be a good general in all things," proving it only through his actions as Zeno’s "beautiful servant." For Bion of Borysthenes wittily remarked when seeing a bronze statue of him inscribed *Persaeus, son of Zeno of Citium*: "The engraver made a mistake. It should have read: *Persaeus, Zeno’s household slave*." <note>original: *oiketieus* (slave/servant) instead of *Kitieus* (man from Citium). This is a pun on his status; Persaeus was originally Zeno's slave before becoming his student.</note> Indeed, Nicias of Nicaea in his *History of Philosophers* and Sotion of Alexandria in his *Successions* both record that he was Zeno’s servant.

We have encountered two books by Persaeus on this "wise" subject, entitled *Sympotic Dialogues*. And Ctesibius of Chalcis, the friend of Mnesidemus, as Antigonus of Carystus says in his *Lives*, was asked by someone what he had gained from philosophy. He replied: "To dine <term>asymbolos</term> <note>original: *asymbolos*, meaning without paying a 'symbola' or contribution to a communal meal; essentially dining for free.</note>." Because of this, Timon said of him: "Dinner-mad, with dead eyes, but a heart that never stops rolling." Ctesibius was a eunuch, yet he had a certain grace for wit. Therefore, everyone used to invite him to banquets—unlike you, O Cynic, who has never sacrificed to the Graces, nor even to the Muses. Virtue has fled from you and those like you, and now sits beside Pleasure, as Mnasalcas of Sicyon says in his epigrams:

> But I, the wretched one,

The wise man should follow Pythagoras <term>pythagorizein</term> <note>To live in the ascetic, silent, or vegetarian manner of Pythagoras</note> with restraint among them. This Diodorus was by birth an Aspendian, a Pythagorean, who chose to live in the manner of you Cynics, being filthy and barefoot. From this, some believed that the custom of wearing long hair among the Pythagoreans began with Diodorus, as Hermippus states. Timaeus of Tauromenium, in the ninth book of his *Histories*, writes of him: "Diodorus of Aspendus introduced this unrefined appearance, presenting a false image of the Pythagoreans." How then did Stratonicus, in a letter, order the messenger to tell the man with the "beast-cloak mania"—full of insolence—that he was a follower of Pythagoras?

Sosicrates, in the third book of the *Succession of Philosophers*, records that Diodorus used a deep beard, wore a tattered cloak, and let his hair grow long. He introduced this practice out of a kind of vanity <term>typhos</term> <note>original: *typhos*, meaning vanity, smoke, or delusion; a common term used by critics to describe the perceived arrogance of philosophers</note>, whereas the Pythagoreans before him wore splendid clothes and used baths and ointments, following the common customs. It is clear that you philosophers truly embrace self-sufficiency <term>autarkeia</term> and the cheapness of meals; why then do you appear where you aren't even invited? Is it to learn how to leave the kitchenware in a mess, or to recite the main points of some gluttonous manual? For in Sophocles' *Cydalio*, there are "whip-scarred slaves, dog-eaten, and eaters of others' food."

### BOOK IV

They devour the food of others. Indeed, you philosophers always keep your mind on dinner, when you ought to be asking for something from the manger <note>original: "epifatnio," referring to a trough or manger, implying they eat like cattle</note> or some of that Cynic fodder. It is not lawful for you to use "grace-tongued" speech <note>original: "charitoglossein," meaning to speak purely to please or flatter</note>. This is made clear by what Alexis <note>An important poet of Middle Attic Comedy</note> records in the play entitled *Linus*. He depicts Heracles being educated by Linus; Heracles is told to choose one book from many lying nearby. He reaches out and takes a cookbook <note>term: "opsartytikon biblion" — a manual for the seasoning and preparation of delicacies</note> in his hands. Linus says the following:

> Take a book,
> Whichever of these you wish; go ahead and take it.
> Then you shall read it, looking closely
> At the titles laid before you, and at your leisure.
> Here is Orpheus, Hesiod, tragedy, Choerilus, Homer,
> Epicharmus, and all sorts of writings.

Linus shows his nature by asking, "At what did he most eagerly rush?" Heracles replies: "I am taking this one. Which one is it? Show me first." Linus answers: "It is *The Art of Cookery*, as the title says." You are a philosopher, Evangelus, yet you passed over so many books and took the "Art of Simus." Simus was a very <margin>they who and others | these</margin> ugly man who has now rushed into tragedy, and of the actors, he is by far the strongest. He is a cook, as it seems to those who employ him, and of cooks, Beliscus is an actor—say whatever you like, for I am hungry just looking at these things.

After Magnus said these things and sat down, Cynulcus looked at the philosophers present and said: "If you look at the sacrifices of others who walk in abundance, how quickly and immediately they pay the price! The blind man does not seem to speak into a deaf ear, as Cratinus said in his *Archilochoi*. For forgetting the fine iambic verses in the law-courts where he makes his displays, he—driven by his innate gluttony and love of sweet-talk—reads aloud the speeches of flatterers and drinking songs, and the clashing of cymbals. After this unmusical chatter, he goes around the houses searching for where grand dinners are being prepared, imitating that famous Chaerephon <note>A real-life follower of Socrates often mocked in comedy as a 'parasite' who lived off the meals of others</note> among the Athenians. Regarding him, Alexis says in *The Fugitive*:

> Chaerephon is always finding some new trick.
> Even now, he provides himself with meals for which he pays no share <note>original: "asymbola," meals without a financial contribution</note>.
> For wherever there is a rental of pottery
> For the professional cooks,
> He stands there from early dawn; if he sees a cook
> Being hired for a feast, he asks the name of the host,
> And through the yawning door he enters first,
> Uninvited and unforgotten.

Nor does this man hesitate, just like our "beautiful" Magnus here, to travel abroad for the sake of his stomach. As Alexis himself said in *Those Whose Bodies are Dying*:

> Chaerephon went to Corinth for a dinner,
> Uninvited; for he flies across the sea.

In this way, eating what belongs to others is sweet. And Theopompus said in his *Odysseus*:

> It is not a bad thing, as the excellent Euripides says,
> To spend what belongs to others and to be beautifully happy.

When everyone laughed at this, Ulpian said: "Whence comes this 'sweet-talking' <note>original: "hedylogia," meaning pleasant or flattering speech</note> for these pleasure-loving gluttons?" Cynulcus replied: "O you seasoned with pig-sauce! For the comic poet in *Ephialtes* mentions sweet-talking through these lines:

> It is a most difficult task to guard against them now.
> For they have a sort of sting in their fingers,
> A misanthropic nature hidden within.
> If they are sweet-talkers to everyone,
> Always wandering the marketplace on the benches,
> It is there that they give great scratches to those they sweet-talk.
> When someone has been stung and has hidden it all, they laugh."

Aeschylus mentioned being "grace-tongued" <note>original: "charitoglosson"</note> in *Prometheus Bound*:

> Know that these things are true; for it is not in me
> To be grace-tongued in vain.

When Ulpian spoke again, he asked: "What kind of things are the cooking utensils, my friends? For these were mentioned in the Arcadian dinners as being worthy of memory. And where is the word for 'profligacy' <note>original: "asotion"</note> located? For I know of 'wastefully' <note>original: "asobos"</note> serving. Alexis mentions 'chips' <note>original: "psia," small scraps or crumbs</note> in *The Woman from Knidos*. Diodorus says in *The Heiress*:

> He turned his paternal estate into a ball,
> So quickly did he chew through everything.

And in *Phaedrus* he says:

> You say that at your leisure, under the sun.
> Little Epichaerides, in five days,
> Made a ball of his father’s inheritance,
> So boldly and quickly did he round it all up.

Ctesippus, the son of Chabrias <note>Chabrias was a famous Athenian general; his son became a notorious spendthrift</note>, reached such a point of profligacy that he even sold the stones of his father's monument—upon which the Athenians had spent a thousand drachmas—to pay for his luxuries. Diphilus says in *Those Who Draw Lots*:

> If Ctesippus, the son of Chabrias,
> Had not happened to be a Scythian and a bright man,
> I would have introduced a law of chaff, as it seems to me.
> So that his father’s monument might finally be completed
> Each year with a 'crumb-stone' <note>original: "psia lithon," a play on words suggesting the stone is as small as a crumb</note>
> Of wagon-size—and I mean that very cheaply.

Timocles says in *The People of the Satyrs*:

> Nor is Ctesippus, son of Chabrias, any longer
> Shaving his head; he is brilliant among the women, but not among men.

And Menander says these things about him in *The Anger*:

> And yet I too was once young, woman,
> But I did not wash five times a day
> Back then, though I do now. Nor did I have a fine cloak,
> But I do now. Nor did I have perfume, but I do now.
> I will even dye my hair, by Zeus, and pluck my skin,
> And I will become Ctesippus—not a man—in a short time.
> Just like him, I will devour even the stones,
> Every single one of them, for I won't stop at just the land.

Perhaps because of this great profligacy and effeminacy, Demosthenes omitted his name in the speech *Against Leptines*. Those who have devoured their paternal estates should be punished just like the sea-captain in Menander's play.

# ATHENAEUS: THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

<margin>For those who now possess a thing of great value</margin>
...live. For he says: "O dearest mother earth, how exceedingly venerable you are." And as it was necessary, I said that whoever received a paternal inheritance and devoured it <note>original: "katephagoi," literally "ate it down," a common Greek metaphor for wasting an inheritance on food and luxury</note> should sail away for good. 

<margin>Like a good thing not tasted by the sea.</margin>
And not even set foot on land, where he was so...

<margin>This Pythodelus, equal to Ballion</margin>
Axionicus, in the play *The Etruscan*, mentions a certain profligate <note>term: "asotos" — literally "one who cannot be saved," referring to someone whose lifestyle is so extravagant it leads to ruin</note> in this way:

<margin>And the very wise "Woman of the Drum," being drunk from behind, follows at his heels. Polyductus and Anaxandrides in the play *The Tyrant*, mocking him. A bird shall chirp, he says, why and how at the feast, having perhaps devoured his paternal estate.</margin>

He approaches, being called the most profligate of all. For just as the handsome son of Lycon, but he was nothing but... because you were cut down by women. Theopompus, in the tenth book of his *History of Philip* <note>Theopompus of Chios was a 4th-century BC historian known for his biting social commentary and focus on moral character</note>—from which some have separated the final part containing the accounts of the Athenian demagogues—says that Eubulus the demagogue was profligate. He used this very word, and says he differed so much in profligacy and greed from Akimus the Tarentine, that while the latter was merely unrestrained regarding banquets, Eubulus spent his time distributing even the public revenues of the Athenians as pay.

Callistratus, the son of Callicrates, who was himself a demagogue, he says was also unrestrained in his pleasures, though he was diligent in political affairs. Regarding the Tarentines, he writes as follows in the fifty-second book of his *Histories*: "The city of the Tarentines offers sacrifices of oxen almost every month and holds public feasts. The mass of private citizens is always occupied with social gatherings and drinking bouts. The Tarentines even have a saying to this effect: that while other men, because they are industrious and spend their time in labor, are preparing themselves to live, they themselves, because of their social gatherings and pleasures, are not about to live, but are already living."

Regarding the profligacy and life of Philip, and that of his companions, Theopompus writes these things in the forty-ninth book of his *Histories*: "When Philip became master of great wealth, he did not spend it quickly, but rather cast it out and threw it away, being the worst manager of all men. This applied not only to him, but also to those around him. For simply no one among them knew how to live correctly or to manage a household soberly. He himself was the cause of this, being greedy and extravagant, doing everything impulsively—whether acquiring or giving. For being a soldier, he did not calculate his income and expenses because he was unable to do so due to his lack of leisure. Furthermore, his companions had flocked together from many places; some were from his own country, some from Thessaly, and others from the rest of Greece, not selected for their excellence. Rather, if there was anyone among the Greeks or the barbarians who was lewd, or loathsome, or bold in character, almost all of these gathered in Macedonia and were called 'Friends of Philip.' Even if someone arrived who was not of this sort, he quickly became like them due to the life and habits of the Macedonians. For wars, military campaigns, and extravagances encouraged them to be bold and to live not in an orderly fashion, but profligately and like those driven mad by their way of life."

Duris, in the seventh book of his *Macedonian History*, speaking of Pasicyprus, the King of Cyprus, says that he was profligate and writes these things: "Alexander, after the siege of Tyre, while dismissing Pnytagoras, gave him other gifts and the land which he requested. For previously Pasicyprus, who was then king, had sold his kingdom and the land for fifty talents <note>A talent was a massive unit of currency; fifty talents would be roughly equivalent to the weight of 1,300 kg of silver</note> because of his profligacy to Pymatos the Citian, and having taken the money, he grew old in Amathus." 

Aethiops the Corinthian was also such a man, as Demetrius of Scepsis says, whom Archilochus mentions. For because of his love of pleasure and lack of self-control, he too, while sailing to Sicily with Archias when he was about to found Syracuse, sold to his messmate the allotment of land <note>term: "kleros" — the plot of land assigned by lot to a new colonist</note> he was destined to have in Syracuse for a honey-cake. 

Demetrius, the descendant of Demetrius of Phalerum, reached such a point of profligacy, as Hegesander says, that he kept Arisagora the Corinthian as his mistress and lived extravagantly. When the members of the Areopagus <note>The ancient and venerable high court of Athens, which also oversaw public morals</note> summoned him and ordered him to live better, he said, "But even now I live as a free man. For I have the most beautiful mistress and I wrong no one. I drink Chian wine and I provide myself with everything else sufficiently, as my private income covers these things. I do not live by taking bribes as some of you do, nor by committing adultery." And he listed some of those who committed such acts by name. When King Antigonus heard these things, he appointed him a *Thesmothete* <note>term: "Thesmothetes" — one of the six junior archons/law-givers in Athens</note>. During the Panathenaic festival, while he was an official, he erected a platform near the Herms <note>sacred pillars topped with the head of the god Hermes</note> for Arisagora, higher than the Herms themselves. And during the mysteries at Eleusis, he placed a throne for her near the sanctuary, saying that those who tried to prevent it would regret it.

Phanodemus, Philochorus, and many others record that the Areopagus used to summon and punish those who lived profligately and without visible means of support. At any rate, when Menedemus and Asclepiades the philosophers were young and poor, the court sent for them and asked how they could spend their whole days at leisure with philosophers despite possessing nothing, yet they remained so healthy in their bodies. They ordered one of the millers to be summoned. When he arrived, he said that every night they came down to the mill and by grinding grain they both earned two drachmas. The Areopagites, being amazed, [rewarded them] with two hundred...

# BOOK 4

<meta>catchword: ...not</meta>

# PROFLIGATES.

...they honored them with drachmas. And the people of Abdera brought Democritus <note>Democritus (c. 460–370 BC), the "Laughing Philosopher," best known for his atomic theory. He was famously accused of wasting his inheritance on travel and research.</note> to public trial on the grounds that he had squandered his paternal estate. However, after he read to them his work *The Great Cosmology* and his writings on those in Hades—stating that he had expended his fortune on these eternal things—they acquitted him. There are others who are not quite so profligate, of whom Amphis says: "Every day they live two days' worth of life, their temples throbbing from the effects of unmixed wine." And according to Diphilus, they "have three heads like an Artemisium <note>Likely referring to a triple-faced statue of Hecate-Artemis; here a metaphor for the 'swelling' or confusion of a heavy hangover</note>, existing as enemies of sacrifice," as Satyrus says in his work *On Characters*. They overrun the countryside, plunder the household, and sell off their possessions as if they were war-spoils. They consider not what *will* be spent, but what *must* be spent; not what *will* be sold, but what *must* be sold. In their youth, they consume the provisions intended for old age, delighting in their mistresses rather than their friends, and in wine rather than their fellow-drinkers. 

Agatharchides of Cnidus, in the eighth book of his *History of Europe*, says that the Ephors in Sparta forbade Gnosippus—who was a profligate by nature—from associating with the young men. Among the Romans, it is mentioned (as Posidonius says in the thirty-ninth book of his *Histories*) that a certain Apicius <note>This is the first of several famous Roman gourmands named Apicius; this one lived in the early 1st century BC and was associated with the exile of Rutilius Rufus.</note> surpassed all men in profligacy. This is the same Apicius who was responsible for the exile of Rutilius, the man who published a Roman history in the Greek language. We have already spoken in the first books about the other Apicius, who was equally notorious for his profligacy.

Diogenes the Babylonian, in his treatise *On Nobility*, says that Phocus, the son of Phocion, did not escape the hatred of the Athenians. Whenever someone met him, they would say: "O you who bring shame upon your lineage!" For he squandered all his paternal inheritance on profligacy, and afterward, he flattered the governor of Munychia <note>The Macedonian commander of the fortress guarding Piraeus; Phocus was seen as a collaborator</note>, for which he was again rebuked by everyone. Once, when a public contribution was being made, he came forward into the assembly and said: "I also contribute." And the Athenians cried out with one voice: "To your own debauchery!" Phocus was also a heavy drinker. For instance, when he won the horse race at the Panathenaic games and his father hosted his friends, the preparations were magnificent; as the guests entered, they were offered foot-basins filled with spiced wine. When his father saw this, he called Phocus and said: "Won't you stop your friend from ruining your victory?" 

I know of many other profligates about whom I leave you to inquire, except for Callias the son of Hipponicus, whom even the children’s tutors know. As for the others I have already put forward, if you have anything to say, I have the gates of my ears wide open. So speak, for I am searching. 

And Magnus mentioned the "upper theater" and "eating on top." And Aemilianus said: You can find the term *asotion* <note>term: "asotion" — a place of debauchery or a "den of profligacy"</note> in Statidius, or in Chrysippus who says: "If he does not even have leisure to relieve himself, nor can anyone meet with him to talk." 

<margin>Cooking Utensils</margin>
Anaxippus, in *The Lyre Player*, lists cooking utensils as follows: "You are carrying soup-ladles, twelve small spits, a meat-hook, a mortar, a child-sized cheese-grater, a handle, three basins, a steamer, and four cleavers. You won't understand any sooner, you god-forsaken man! You are falling behind again with the little cauldron, the pot, and the 'sleeper' <note>original: "hypnēlē," a rare term for a specific vessel or perhaps a joke about a slow-cooking pot</note> competition-winner." Aristophanes, in *Women in Tents*, uses the word *kakkabos* <note>term: "kakkabos" — a three-legged cooking pot or cauldron</note> in this way: "For the *kakkabē* is a teacher of... and in the *Banqueters*, he says 'with the *kakkabos*'." Antiphanes, in *The Friend of Thebes*, says: "We have everything. For the eel, synonymous with the flute-playing Boeotian girl, was mixed in the hollow depths of the *kakkabē*. It is always being warmed, boiled, and bubbling." 

Antiphanes also mentions a *batanion* <note>term: "batanion" — a shallow dish or pan</note> in *Autolycus*: "Then a sliced octopus, boiled in shallow dishes (*bataniois*)." Alexis in *Asclepioclides* says: "I myself learned to cook so skillfully in Sicily that I make the guests sometimes knock their teeth out of their mouths from the pleasure of the dishes (*batania*)." Antiphanes uses the spelling *bataneion* with an 'e' in *The Woman of Samos*: "Dishes (*bataneia*), beet, silphium, pots, lamps, coriander, onions, salt, oil, a bowl." Philetaerus in *The Wine-Drinker*: "This cook with a dish (*bataneio*)." 

And in *The Parasite*, Antiphanes also said these things: "Another large one here, a six-quart earthen vessel, noble... you speak of the offspring of a cooking-pot, earth-born and boiling. Then wouldn't you say, 'Away with you, I call it a *kakkabos*!' But you perhaps would call it a flat dish (*lopada*). Do you think the name makes a difference to me, whether some people delight in calling it a *kakkabos* or a *sitybos*? Except that I know you are talking about a vessel." Eubulus, in *Ion*, mentions both *bataneia* and *patania* <note>note: dialectal variations of the word for dish/pan</note> in these lines: "Bowls and dishes (*bataneia*), and cauldrons (*kakkabia*), and flat pans (*lopadia*), and platters (*patania*), thick and frequent, and I could not stop listing them." 

<margin>Seasonings</margin>
Alexis made a catalog of seasonings in *The Cauldron* as follows: "And don't give me excuses there, or say 'I don't have it.' But tell me, for I will not list them all again. First, go and get some sesame. But there is also the leaf and chopped raisin. Fennel, dill, mustard, silphium-stalk, silphium-juice, coriander, bird-vetch, sumac, cumin, boiled wine, hartwort, rue, and leeks." And in *The All-Night Festival* (or *The Wool-Workers*), he makes a cook say: "I shall have to run in circles and shout for what I need. You will come and ask me for dinner now, but it happens that I have no vinegar, no dill, no oregano, no fig-leaf, no oil, no..."
