<meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of profligate spenders to the technicalities of the ancient kitchen, specifically focusing on the specialized roles of kitchen staff and food tasters.</meta>

...not <note>original: "αρ", likely the end of a word like "λιπαρ-" (fatty/sleek) or similar, continuing from the previous page</note>, not almonds, no garlic, no boiled wine, no leek, no bulb, no fire, no cumin, no salt, no egg, no wood, no tub, no frying pan, no rope, no pit of Hades, no well, no jar is here; and I stand empty-handed, holding a knife, and moreover girded with a belt. And miserable.

> First, place some oregano into a fresh pot; the dressing sings with much rhythm, having been colored with boiled wine vinegar and struck with a thick dose of <term>silphium</term> <note>Silphium was a highly prized medicinal and culinary herb from Cyrene, now extinct, similar to giant fennel or asafoetida</note>.

Teleclides mentions "eating afterwards" to the <term>prytanes</term> <note>Executive members of the Athenian Council</note> in this way. Eupolis says to the <term>taxiarchs</term> <note>Military commanders of a tribal infantry division</note>: "to eat nothing afterwards, except looking at an onion and three half-dried figs." Aristophanes in *Wealth* says: "before this, he used to eat everything because of his gluttony." Among the cooks, there were certain distinct types called <margin>Table-Arrangers</margin> <term>Table-Setters</term> <note>original: "τραπεζοποιοί" (trapezopoioi), literally "table-makers" or those who arrange the dining space</note>. Antiphanes clearly shows the purpose for which these were employed in *The Resident Alien*: "I went and brought this

> Table-Setter, who will wash the dishes, prepare the lamps, perform the libations, and do all the other tasks."

This is their proper duty. It should be investigated whether the <term>Table-Arranger</term> <note>original: "τραπεζοκόμος" (trapezokomos)</note> is the same as the Table-Setter. For King Juba <note>Juba II of Numidia (c. 48 BC – AD 23), a scholar-king who wrote extensively on history and linguistics</note> says in his *Similarities* that the Table-Arranger is the same person as the one called a <term>structor</term> <note>original: "στρουκτόρα", a Latin term for a servant who arranged dishes or carved meat</note> by the Romans. He cites this from the play by Alexander entitled *Labor*:

> For tomorrow I must get a flute-girl and I shall hire a Table-Setter/Artisan. My master sent me from the country for this purpose.

They called the one in charge of the tables and other orderly arrangements a Table-Setter. Philemon says that the preparation does not happen around a wandering person who enters: "The Table-Setter is there for the serving." They also called the food placed upon the table "table-toppings." Plato <note>Plato Comicus, the playwright, not the philosopher</note> says in *Menelaus*:

> How few of the table-toppings are left!

They called the person who bought the delicacies a <term>Market-Buyer</term> <note>original: "ἀγοραστήν" (agorasten)</note>, though now they call him a <term>Provisioner</term> <note>original: "ὀψωνάτορα" (opsonatora)</note>, as Xenophon says in the second book of the *Memorabilia*: "We would want to take such a servant and market-buyer for free." In Menander’s *Phania*, the word is used more generally: "He was a thrifty and moderate market-buyer." Aristophanes mentions a "caterer" in *The Frying-Pan Cookers* through these words: "It seems our caterer has wasted our breakfast." Cratinus in *The Women of Cleobuline* used the term "to buy side-dishes," and Alexis in *The Runaways* used "to buy snacks." 

According to Pamphilus, those who invite people to the royal table are called <term>Eleatroi</term> <note>original: "ἐλεατροί", a specialized term for royal stewards</note>, named after the <term>eleos</term> <note>A kitchen table or meat-board</note>. Artemidorus calls them <term>Dinner-Callers</term>. They say they also called the <term>Pre-Tasters</term> "eleatroi," as they were part of the kings' provision for safety. Now, the *eleatros* has become the overseer of the entire service. This role was once illustrious and honorable. Chares, at least, in the third book of his *Histories*, says that Ptolemy Soter <note>Ptolemy I, the founder of the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt and former general of Alexander the Great</note> was appointed as Alexander’s *eleatros*. Perhaps the one the Romans now call a <term>pre-taster</term> <note>original: "προγύστην" (progusten)</note> was then called a <term>fore-taster</term> <note>original: "προτένθην" (protenthen)</note> by the Greeks, as Aristophanes says in the first version of *The Clouds*:

> You know they receive the court-fees on the new moon, but also the old and new, because the fore-tasters seem to me to suffer so that they might snatch the court-fees as quickly as possible.

Because of this, they "fore-tasted" one day early. Pherecrates also mentions them in *The Wild Men*:

> Do not wonder, for we are among the fore-tasters; but I do not know them.

And Philyllius in *Heracles*:

> Do you want me to tell you who I am? I am called 'Dorpia' of the fore-tasters.

I also find a decree passed at Athens in the year of the Archon Cephisodorus <note>366/365 BC</note>, in which the "fore-tasters" are listed as a sort of association, just like those called the <term>parasites</term> <note>In this context, "parasites" were not leeches, but honored officials who ate at the public expense in the temple or town hall</note>. It reads: "Phocus said, so that the Council may celebrate the <term>Apaturia</term> <note>A major three-day family festival in Athens and Ionia</note> with the other Athenians according to ancestral custom, it was decreed by the Council that those serving as councilors be dismissed for the days—just as the other Councils are dismissed—starting from that day on which the fore-tasters celebrate for five days." 

That the ancients also had people called "Pre-Tasters" is stated by Xenophon in the work entitled *Hiero* or *The Tyrant*: "The tyrant lives distrusting his food and drink; instead of offering the first portions to the gods, they command the servants to taste them first, because of their distrust that they might eat or drink something harmful." Anaxilas says in *Calypso*:

> The old woman will taste the drink for you first.

Those who brought the pastries were called "bread-servants," whom they previously called <term>Artisans</term> <note>original: "δημιουργούς" (demiourgous), literally "public workers"</note>. Menander, in *The False Heracles*, criticizing the cooks for pouring sauces even where they shouldn't, says:

> Cook, you seem very unpleasant to me. How many tables are we going to make? Tell me. You ask about the day? We are sacrificing a piglet. Make eight tables; two as one—what does it matter to you? Set this as one. It is not possible to make <term>kandylas</term> <note>A rich Lydian dish made of milk, fat, honey, and bread</note>, nor the kind of things you usually mix together—honey, fine flour, and eggs. For everything is the opposite.

Now, for dinner, the cook in *Pythaitus* makes the cakes, roasts them, boils the groats, and brings them after the salted fish. Then comes the fig-leaf wrap and grapes. The female Artisan, standing in opposition, says:

> Roast the meats and thrushes, and the sweetmeats.

Since he is occupied with Athens, and Myrisambyos, having crowned himself again, says:

> Dine on the honey-cakes with the thrushes.

Because the duties of service were divided, the Artisans looked after the pastries, while the cooks looked after the seasoning of delicacies, as Antiphanes clarified in *Chrysid*:

> Four flute-players have...

# BOOK IV

...and twelve cooks. And "Makers of Honey" <note>original: "Δημιουργοὶ μέλιτος" (Dēmiourgoi melitos), likely a specific guild or professional title for honey-confectioners</note> asking for tubs. Mnesimachus says to a <term>honey-maker</term>: "What then of the boy? For, by Zeus, he has served us in a most servant-like manner through the night; we have been awake, and even now..."

Seleucus or Panyassis says that he was the first to mention these things, in the passage where he recounts human sacrifices among the Egyptians. He says they offered many pastries and many "brood-hens" <note>original: "νοσσάδας ὄρνις" (nossadas ornis)</note>. Before him, Stesichorus or Ibycus, in the works titled *The Labors*, said: "bring gifts for the maiden: bathing tubs, groats, and oil-cakes <note>original: "ἐγκρίδας" (enkriddas), dough fried in oil and seasoned with honey</note>, and other pastries, and fresh honey." The poet Simonides is a most sufficient witness that this poem belongs to Stesichorus; in his account of Meleager, he says: "who surpassed everyone with the spear, huling it from the banks of the Dinante... beyond Polybotrys from Iolcos." For thus Homer, or Stesichorus, shall sing to them. 

<margin>Delian cooks</margin>
For Stesichorus spoke thus in the aforementioned songs in *The Labors*: "Amphiaraus leaping, but you, Meleager, win with the javelin." I am also not unaware of what Apollodorus of Athens said concerning the Delians: that they provided the services of cooks and table-makers to those who came for the sacred rites. They even had names derived from their actions, such as <term>magadis</term> <note>originally a musical instrument, here likely referring to a type of bread or a kneading tool</note> and <term>gongylos</term> <note>literally "round," perhaps referring to round rolls</note>. Aristotle says that at festivals they would spend the whole day kneading the barley-cakes, just as "round cakes" are mixed for women. Even until now, some of them are called <term>choirakoi</term> <note>little pigs</note>, <term>amnoi</term> <note>lambs</note>, <term>artysilaoi</term> <note>seasoners of the people</note>, <term>spasmoi</term> <note>spasms/convulsions</note>, <term>artysitragoi</term> <note>goat-seasoners</note>, <term>neokoroi</term> <note>temple-wardens</note>, and <term>ichthymboloi</term> <note>fish-striker</note>. Among the women, they are called <term>kyminanthai</term> <note>cumin-flowers</note>. Collectively, they are all called <term>eleodytai</term> <note>table-creepers</note>, because they "duck under" the kitchen tables while serving at the feasts. The *eleos* is the cook's table or dresser. As Homer says: "But when he had roasted it, he placed it upon the dressers <note>original: "ἐλεοῖσιν" (eleoisin)</note>." From this, Polycrates the Cretanian, when writing the indictment of Rhenaea, does not call them "Delians," but uses the collective term "Table-Creepers" to bring the charge. The law of the Amphictyons also commands the <term>eleodytai</term> to provide water, signifying the table-setters and those who act as servants for the cups. Crito the comic poet, in *The Busybody*, calls the Delians "parasites of the god" in these lines:

> Having made a captain of a great master's purse unable to sail in the harbor, and having forced two transport ships to go to Delos from Peiraeus, hearing from everyone that this is the place for <term>parasites</term> <note>In this context, "parasite" refers to an official who eats at the public or sacred expense, rather than a social leech</note>, where one seems to possess good things by force alone: a market full of fish, inhabited by a motley crowd.

<margin>Delphic sauce-makers</margin>
Again, he calls the Delians "parasites of the god." Achaeus of Eretria, in his satyr play *Alcmaeon*, calls the Delphians <term>karykkopoioi</term> <note>sauce-makers or seasoning-crafters</note> in these lines: "I loathe looking at sauce-makers, who stand by the sacrificial victims," clearly implying that they cooked them and made them into seasoned sauces. Looking at this, Aristophanes also said: "O Phoebus, who sharpens the most knives of the Delphians, and teaches your attendants..." And in the following lines, Achaeus says: "Who is this hidden one concerned with the meat-cleavers of the <term>sarabakoi</term> <note>an obscure term, possibly referring to a specific group or type of luxury</note>, you who share a name with the body?" For the Satyrs mock the Delphians for always lingering around the sacrifices and feasts. Semus, in the fourth book of the *Deliad*, says that the Delians provide salt, vinegar, oil, wood, and bedding to the Delphians who come to Delos. Aristotle or Theophrastus, in the *Commentaries* concerning the Magnesians who live by the Maeander river, says they are colonists of the Delphians and perform similar services for visiting strangers, saying: "The Magnesians dwelling on the Maeander river, being sacred to the god and colonists of the Delphians, provide to those who reside there <term>gingy</term> <note>an unidentified seasoning or vegetable</note>, salt, oil, vinegar, a lamp-wick, beds, bedding, and tables." Demetrius of Skepsis says in the sixteenth book of the *Trojan Array* that in Laconia, on the road called Hyacinthian, there are shrines to the heroes *Daiton* <note>The Feaster</note> and *Keraon* <note>The Mixer</note>, established by the servants who make the barley-cakes and mix the wine in the <term>phiditia</term> <note>the Spartan communal mess halls</note>. The same author records in the twenty-fourth book of the same work that a hero named *Daitas* <note>Feast</note> is honored among the Trojans, whom Mimnermus mentions. Hegesander of Delphi says that in Cyprus, Zeus is honored as "The Banqueter" and "The Inward-Parts-Cutter" <note>original: "σπλαγχνοτόμον" (splanchnotomon)</note>.

While many such things were being said, from nearby was heard the sound of a <term>hydraulis</term> <note>a water organ, an instrument using water to regulate air pressure</note>, very 

<margin>musical instruments</margin>
sweet and delightful, so that all of us turned around, enchanted by its melody. Ulpian, looking toward the musician Alcaides, said: "Do you hear, most musical of men, this beautiful harmony which has turned us all, enchanted by the music? It is not like the <term>monaulos</term> <note>a single-pipe flute</note> common among you Alexandrians, which brings pain to the listeners rather than any musical pleasure." Alcaides replied: "Indeed, this instrument, the <term>hydraulis</term>—whether you wish to classify it as a stringed instrument or a wind instrument—is the invention of a countryman of ours, an Alexandrian, a barber by trade. His name was Ctesibius. Aristocles records this in his work *On Choruses*, saying something like this: 'It is debated whether the <term>hydraulis</term> is a wind instrument or a stringed instrument.' Aristoxenus, at least, did not know. It is said that Plato gave a small spark of the idea for the construction, having made a night-time..."

### ATHENAEUS: THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

A water-clock resembles the hydraulic organ, appearing like a very large clepsydra <note>A clepsydra was an ancient device that measured time by the regulated flow of water</note>. Indeed, the hydraulic instrument itself is thought to be a type of clepsydra. It is a "cast" instrument, and one might not think it a wind instrument, though perhaps it is rightly called so because the instrument is "blown into" by the action of the water. For the pipes are turned down into the water, and as the water is agitated by a certain youth, and as pivots move through the instrument, the pipes are filled with air and produce a delightful sound. The instrument itself resembles a rounded altar. They say this was invented by Ctesibius the barber, who lived in the district of Aspendia during the reign of Euergetes II <note>Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, who reigned in the 2nd century BCE; Ctesibius was a famous inventor in Alexandria</note>, where they say he gained great fame. He is also said to have taught his own wife, Thais, to play it. Tryphon, in the fifth book of *On Names* and in his treatise *On Flutes and Organs*, says that Ctesibius the engineer wrote a work concerning the hydraulic organ. I do not know, however, if he is mistaken about the name. Aristoxenus, meanwhile,
<margin>10</margin> prefers "cast" instruments <note>original: "chyta" (χυτά), likely referring to percussion or fixed-pitch instruments made of metal</note> over wind instruments, claiming that wind instruments are too easy. For he says so many people play the flute and pipe without being taught, just like shepherds. These are the things I have to tell you, Ulpian, concerning the hydraulic organ. For the Phoenicians, as Xenophon says, used "gingras" <note>original: "γίγγραι" (gingrai)</note>, flutes about a span in length <note>approximately 9 inches</note> that produced a shrill and mournful sound. These are used by the Carians in their laments—unless, of course, Caria was once called Phoenicia, as can be found in the works of Corinna and Bacchylides. These flutes are called "gingroi" by the Phoenicians after the laments for Adonis; for you Phoenicians call Adonis "Gingras," as Democleides records. These gingras flutes are mentioned by Antiphanes in *The Physician* and Menander in *The Carian Woman*. Amphis also says the following in his *Dithyramb*: "I

> ...take the gingras, that most clever thing,"

<margin>20</margin>
> "And who has not heard of the gingras, our new invention? Which has never yet been shown to the theater-goers at Athens, but is most pleasant when played in a relaxed style at drinking parties. Why do you not bring it before the crowd? Because the tribe desires it. It is like a certain wild, rustic thing, for I know that they reveal everything with their clapping."

And Axionicus in *The Lover of Euripides* says:

> "For they both suffer so much from the songs of Euripides that everything else seems to them to be merely gingras-tunes and a great evil."

How much better, O most wise Ulpian, is this hydraulic organ than the instrument called the "nablas," which Sopatros the parodist says is a Phoenician invention in his play titled *The Gates*. He speaks thus:

> "The Sidonian nablas <note>A Phoenician stringed instrument, perhaps a harp or lyre</note>, that throat-voiced type, has not been unstrung."

And in *The Slave of the Mystic* he says:

> "The nablas, though unmelodious in its joints of letters, which stands soulless and fixed in its sides, yet it rouses the breathing Muse of the flutes when someone joins the double chorus of pleasure-melodies."

Philemon in *The Adulterer* says:

> "There will be a flute-girl from the Garmunians or a certain Nablas-player."

But as for what the nablas is—"I do not know, you thunderstruck fool!" "By Zeus, you say you don't know the nablas? Even now I don't know anything good..."
<margin>30</margin> "Nor even a sambuca-player <note>The sambuca was a high-pitched triangular harp</note>." As for the instrument called the "trigonon" (triangle), Juba, in the fourth book of his *Theatrical History*, says it is a Syrian invention, as is the sambuca, which is called the "lyro-phoenix." Regarding this instrument, Neanthes of Cyzicus says in the first book of his *Annals* that it was an invention of Ibycus the poet of Rhegium, just as the "barbiton" <note>A deep-toned lyre</note> was an invention of Anacreon. But among us Alexandrians, there is a tendency to dismiss these as unmusical, and you constantly name the "monaulos" <note>A single-pipe flute</note> as being native to our land. Listen to what I have to say about that, which I have ready at hand. For Juba, in the aforementioned work, says the Egyptians claim the monaulos was an invention of Osiris, just like the cross-flute called the "photinx," which I recall a certain famous man mentioning. For the photinx flute is also common among us. Sophocles mentions the monaulos in *Thamyras* like this:

> "For the rattled songs of the harps are gone, the lyre and the monaulos which, like a ship filled with storms, is the desolation of the reveler."

Araros in *The Birth of Pan* says:
<margin>40</margin>
> "He snatched up a monaulos and immediately, you wouldn't believe how lightly he leaped up."

Anaxandrides in *The Treasure* says:

> "Taking up a monaulos, I played the wedding song."

And in *The Bowl-Bearer*:

> "Where have you brought that monaulos, you Syrian? What monaulos? The reed-pipe!"

Sopatros in *Bacchis* says, "and the monaulos sounded its melody." Protagorides of Cyzicus, in the second book of *On the Festivals at Daphne*, says: "The whole place was filled with the sound of castanets under the torchlight of the festival, and one hums the sweetest harmonies on the monaulos." Posidonius the Stoic philosopher, in the third book of his *Histories*, describing the war of the Apameans against the Larissaeans, writes: "They carried daggers and small spears, hidden away, but they wore hats and veils that provided shade but did not stop their necks from being cooled; they dragged along donkeys laden with wine and all sorts of food, alongside which lay the photinx and small monauli—instruments of revelry, not of war."
<margin>50</margin> I am not unaware that Amerias the Macedonian says in his *Glossary* that the monaulos is called a "tityrinos." There you have it, noble Ulpian, even the reference to the photinx. That the monaulos was the same as what is now called the "kalamaules" <note>A reed-flute (from "kalamos," meaning reed)</note> is clearly shown by Hedylus in his epigrams, speaking thus:

> "Here lies Theon the monaulos-player, the sweet flute-player of the mimes and the grace of the stages, blind from old age..."

### BOOK IV

| He had, and a sweet skip-dance, | And called him "Little Child," | A skip-dance of the hand | To sing him a birthday song. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| For he held, he had | <unclear>Gau marpan</unclear> <note>original: "Γαῦ μάρπαν," likely a corrupt or dialectal poetic fragment</note> a sweet sign | The owl played, intoxicated by the hemlock | Like the toys of the Muses |
| By Earth, the unmixed wine of Bacchus | The sweet-drinker. | Either Kota-pipe or Paka-pipe. | But Theon— |

->To Theon the reed-flutist, say "Farewell."<-

Just as people today do not use the term "reed-pipers" for those who play the reed-flute, they also used the term *rapaulas* <note>original: ῥαπαύλας</note>, as Amerias the Macedonian says in his *Glossary*, to describe those who play upon the reed. I want you to know, most excellent Ulpian, that there are no others more musical than the Alexandrians—not even those who live in equal-governed cities. I am not speaking only of singing to the lyre <note>original: κιθαρῳδίαν (kitharodia)</note>, an art with which even the lowliest commoner among us—who might even be illiterate—is so familiar that he can instantly detect any errors made in the rhythmic striking of the strings. They are also most musical regarding the flutes. They play not only the so-called "maiden" and "boy" flutes, but also the "manly" flutes which are called "complete" and "super-complete," as well as those used to accompany the lyre and the "finger-style" flutes.

As for the *elymoi* flutes <note>A type of boxwood flute associated with Phrygian music</note>, which Sophocles mentions in his *Niobe* and in *The Drummers*, we hear that they are none other than the Phrygian flutes, which the Alexandrians are also expert in playing. They are also familiar with the "twin" flutes, the "single-cut" flutes, and the so-called "under-pierced" flutes. Callias also mentions the *elymoi* flutes in his play *The Shackles*. These are said to be an invention of the Phrygians and are also called "little sticks" <note>original: σκυταλίας (skutalias)</note> because of their thickness. Cratinus the Younger says in his *Theramenes* that the Cyprians also use them. We also know of the "half-holed" flutes, about which Anacreon says: "Who, having crushed his heart with desire, is leaping so as to dance to the half-holed flutes?" These flutes are smaller than the "complete" ones. 

Aeschylus, at any rate, introduced characters who were "out of step" with the meter. Xenophon also mixed in certain commoners. Homer, however, did much better by presenting diverse types of banquets. For through comparison, the differences are more clearly seen. To him, the banquet of the Suitors is the sort of thing that happens when young men are devoted to drunkenness and lust. That of the Phaeacians is more refined than theirs, yet still full of human kindness. In contrast to these, he placed the banquets held during military campaigns and those conducted more temperately for political purposes. Again, he distinguished between those that were public and those that were private family banquets. Epicurus, however, described only a banquet of philosophers. Homer also taught us whom one ought not to invite, but who should come "of their own accord" <note>original: αὐτομάτους (automatous)</note>, taking the presence of like-minded kin as a necessity.

<margin>Iliad 2.408</margin>
<margin>Concerning those who came unbidden</margin>
"And Menelaus, good at the war-cry, came to him of his own accord." For it is clear that one does not need to invite a brother, or parents, or a wife, nor anyone whom one might bring to a sacrifice as an equal in honor. Indeed, to do so would be cold and unfriendly. Yet some writers have added a line to the poem to provide a reason: "For he knew in his heart how his brother was toiling." I think, however, that every brother would come to a dinner of his own accord, for a persuasive reason is already given. Does the poet mean that Agamemnon did not know his brother was coming? How could that not be ridiculous, since there was a great sacrifice and it was known to everyone? How would he have come if he did not know? Or, by Zeus, perhaps he says that Menelaus was persuaded by a shared sense of shame because he had not been invited, and so he came of his own accord as a fellow-traveler. It is like the one who said he came uninvited so that they wouldn't look askance at each other in the morning—the one feeling ashamed and the other feeling reproachful. But it would be ridiculous for Agamemnon to forget his brother, especially since he was sacrificing not just for the present, but for a brother who had been hand-picked for the war and who had invited those who were not even kin or close associates. Athenocles of Cyzicus, listening more closely to Homer's verses than Aristarchus did, says that Homer leaves us with a more subtle point: that Menelaus held a closer, more necessary bond. Demetrius of Phalerum, calling the omission of the verse "clumsy" and foreign to the intimacy, suggests that the line "For he knew in his heart how his brother was toiling" adds a certain pettiness to their characters. For I believe, he says, that every refined man has both kin and friends to whom he would go when there is a sacrifice without waiting for an invitation.

Plato, in his *Symposium*, speaks about these same matters as follows: "So that we may even destroy the proverb by changing it, saying that 'good men go to the feasts of good men unbidden.' For Homer seems not only to destroy the proverb but to insult it. For having made Agamemnon 'good at the works of war' but Menelaus a 'soft spearman,' when Agamemnon was making a sacrifice, the 'inferior' man came uninvited to the 'superior' man's feast." 

<margin>Menelaus is soft</margin>
Bacchylides, speaking of the house of Ceyx, says: "He stood upon the stone threshold. And they were preparing a feast, so he spoke: 'Just men come of their own accord to the rich feasts of the good.'" As for the proverbs, one says: "Good men go of their own accord to the feasts of the good." Another says: "Good men go of their own accord to the feasts of the base." At any rate, Plato did not properly strip Menelaus down to a coward, whom Homer calls "preeminently a friend," and who alone fought heroically over Patroclus, and who was eager to fight Hector in single combat before all others—even though he was inferior in strength—about whom alone of those on the campaign it was said: "And he himself went, trusting in his own eagerness." If his enemy spoke of him as a "soft spearman" as an insult, and because of this Plato...

# ATHENAEUS, THE DINNER-PHILOSOPHERS

If one truly considers him "soft," one might as well go as far as placing Agamemnon among the base men, 
<margin>Iliad, Book 1</margin> whom Agamemnon himself calls "noble," if indeed this verse was spoken against him:
"Heavy with wine, having the eyes of a dog, but the heart of a deer." <note>original: "Οἰνοβαρές, κυνὸς ὄμματ᾽ ἔχων, κραδίην δ᾽ ἐλάφοιο." This is Achilles' famous insult to Agamemnon in Iliad 1.225.</note>

For it does not follow that if something is said in Homer, Homer himself is saying it. After all, how could Menelaus be "soft"—the man who alone kept Hector away from Patroclus's body, and who killed Euphorbus and stripped him of his armor in the midst of the Trojans? It is absurd not to fully understand the very verse one finds fault with, through which Menelaus is called "good at the <term>war-cry</term>" <note>original: "βοὴν ἀγαθὸς" (boen agathos), a standard epithet for Menelaus</note>. For Homer is accustomed to use this term for those who stand their ground, since the ancients called war itself a "cry." Homer is precise in all things, and he neglected no detail, even the small matter of a guest tending to his body and bathing before going to dinner. Thus, he said of Odysseus's son among the Phaeacians: "And then the housekeeper commanded him to wash himself." And regarding the companions of Telemachus: "Having gone into the well-polished tubs, they bathed." For it was unseemly, as Aristotle says, to arrive at a banquet covered in sweat and dust. A person of refinement ought not to be filthy, nor parched with dirt, nor "delight in mud," according to Heraclitus. Moreover, the first person arriving at another's
<margin>Decorum of the Homeric dinner</margin> house for dinner should not immediately rush to the banquet to gorge his belly, but should first indulge his love of beauty and observe the house. The poet did not neglect this either:
<margin>Odyssey, Book 4</margin> "And they themselves entered the divine palace. And seeing it, they marveled at the house of the Zeus-nourished king."
"For there was a radiance like that of the sun or the moon throughout the high-roofed house of glorious Menelaus."

Aristophanes also depicts the wild old man and lover of lawsuits being reshaped into a civilized life by his son:
"Come now, recline here and learn how to be a social and companionable guest." <note>A reference to Aristophanes’ play *The Wasps*, where the son tries to teach his father high-society manners.</note>

And after teaching him how to recline, he says:
"Next, praise some of the bronzework; gaze at the ceiling and admire the tapestry of the hall."

Homer also teaches us what we must do before the feast: to distribute the "first fruits" of the food to the gods. 
<margin>Odyssey, Book 9</margin> For instance, those with Odysseus, even though they were in the Cyclops’ cave:
"There, having lit a fire, we sacrificed, and we ourselves took of the cheeses and ate."

And Achilles, even though the ambassadors were in a hurry,
<margin>Iliad, Book 9</margin> having arrived in the middle of the night, nevertheless commanded his companion Patroclus to sacrifice to the gods, and he cast the offerings into the fire. And the diners always perform libations:
"The youths filled the bowls to the brim with drink. And they distributed it to all, having poured the first drops into the cups. But when they had poured the libation..."

Plato also observes these customs in his *Symposium*. For after dining, he says they made libations and sang a hymn to the god with the customary honors. Xenophon speaks similarly. But in the works of Epicurus, there is no libation, no first fruit offered to the gods—rather, as Simonides said of the unruly woman: "She often eats unconsecrated sacrifices." For the Athenian writer says that the moderate mixing of wine was ordained by King Amphictyon. For this reason, he established a shrine to "Upright Dionysus." For a man is "upright" in reality and not stumbling when he drinks in a moderate and mixed fashion. "For wine commands the foolish man, and sends even the very wise to sing." It also prompts one to "laugh gently" and "to dance," and "to let slip a word that was better left unsaid." For Homer does not call wine "foolish" like a wooden bolt, or a maker of vanities. Nor does he command one to be sullen, or speechless, or never to laugh, nor ever to turn to rhythms and the dance, as if such things were rustic; rather, he shows the refined man. Simultaneously, through these descriptions, he shows the difference in both quantity and quality. Hence, it is not that wine makes the wise man sing, but "to sing too much"—that is, immoderately and excessively, like a nuisance. Nor is the laughter or the dancing criticized in itself, but by applying the word "gentle" to both, he signals a fall into an unmanly character: "to laugh gently and to dance." In Plato, however, they do nothing of this in a measured way, but they drink so much that they cannot stand on their own feet. Look at the drunken revel of Alcibiades, how disgracefully he behaves! The others drink from an eight-pint cooler, taking it as a pretext because Alcibiades himself led the way. It was not like those in Homer: "But when they had made libation and drunk as much as their heart desired." One should know what must be entirely discarded. For those who find moderation useful, they look upon these things as ornaments, just as 
<margin>Odyssey, Book 1</margin> Homer has said:
"Song and dance, for these are the ornaments of a feast."

On the whole, this inclination toward such things remained with the Suitors and the Phaeacians, but not with Nestor or Menelaus. Regarding the wedding feast, the school of Aristarchus was not silent, noting that the banquet was continuous and the peak days had passed—days in which the bride had already gone out to the bridegroom. The wedding of Megapenthes had reached its end, and they were living in seclusion, Menelaus and Helen. They were not all together, but were deceived by the first verse: "And they found him celebrating a wedding feast for many kinsmen," to which some added certain verses:
<margin>The Symposium of Homeric Menelaus</margin> "So they were feasting through the high-roofed great house, the neighbors and kinsmen of glorious
<margin>Odyssey, Book 4</margin> Menelaus, enjoying themselves. And among them a divine singer sang, playing the lyre, and two tumblers among them, leading the song, whirled through the middle."

These lines they transferred from the "Making of the Shield" <note>Referring to the description of Achilles' shield in Iliad 18, suggesting these verses were erroneously moved from the Iliad to the Odyssey.</note> along with...
<meta>catchword: with</meta>

# BOOK 4

...for the error regarding the wording at that time. For the tumblers were not the "leads" <note>original: ἐξάρχοντες (exarchontes); those who initiate a song or dance</note>, but rather they danced while the singer led. Indeed, leading is a characteristic specific to the <term>phorminx</term> <note>An ancient Greek stringed instrument, similar to a lyre</note>. For this reason, Hesiod says in *The Shield*: "and the Pierian Muses were beginning the divine song." And Archilochus says: "I myself am the leader of the Lesbian <term>paean</term> <note>A song of praise or triumph</note> to the accompaniment of the flute." Stesichorus calls the Muse "leader of the dance," and Pindar calls the preludes "leaders of the choir." Therefore, Didymus <note>The OCR reads "Διὸ δίωρος" (Dio-dioros), likely a corruption of the name of the scholar Didymus Chalcenterus</note>, the follower of Aristophanes, used to mark the entire description of the wedding as spurious, claiming it ended at the first days and its conclusion. Furthermore, he argued that the "day-old" remains of the symposium were not being accounted for. Then he commands us to write: "and two tumblers," for to write "by themselves" <note>original: καθ' αὑτοὺς (kath’ hautous)</note> in the text is necessarily a grammatical error. For "by themselves" means "among their own group," but to say "themselves" as a reflexive is a solecism <note>A grammatical mistake or absurdity</note>. But as I was saying, the introduction of these entertainers into this temperate banquet is a passage transferred from the description of the Cretan dance. It is missing from
<margin>Iliad, Book 18</margin>
the description of the making of the armor. "Therein the renowned God of the Two Strong Arms <note>Hephaestus</note> fashioned a choir, similar to the one that Daedalus once crafted in broad Knossos for Ariadne of the beautiful hair. There, young men and maidens who earn many oxen for their parents were dancing, holding one another's hands at the wrist." For he adds to these: "A great crowd stood around the lovely dance, enjoying themselves. And two tumblers among them, leading the song <note>original: Μολπῆς ἐξάρχοντες (Molpes exarchontes)</note>, whirled in the middle." For among the Cretans, both dancing and tumbling are native customs. This is why he says to the Cretan Meriones: "Meriones, though you are a dancer, my spear would quickly have stopped you forever, had I but hit you." From this also comes the name "Cretan" for the <term>hyporchemes</term> <note>A type of choral song accompanied by mimetic dance</note>. They call it the Cretan style, but the instrument is called "Molossian." And those who are called "Laconizers" <note>People who imitated Spartan customs</note>, as Timaeus says, "delight in square-shaped dances." In general, music was different among the various Greeks. The Athenians preferred the Dionysian and <term>cyclic</term> <note>Circular</note> choruses, while the Syracusans preferred the iambic ones, and others preferred other types. For this reason, Aristarchus—the only one (since he felt Menelaus's banquet was, conversely, not as it should be)—even made the Spartan kingship something alien, as well as the King’s temperance, and he even cut the poems short regarding the leader of the lyrical chorus or songs in this manner: "A great crowd stood around the lovely dance, enjoying themselves. And two tumblers among them, leading the song, whirled in the middle." Thus, the phrase "leading the song" becomes entirely incurable, since the reference to the singer is no longer even implied. But that a song was a plausible entertainment before reaching Menelaus is clear from the fact that the whole banquet was softened by social interaction. No name of a song was found by me, nor should one pay attention to those who say Telemachus was there with him. For they were more like people observing the house in a kind of silence and stillness. And indeed, how is it not improbable that the most prudent men, such as the sons of Odysseus and Nestor, should be introduced in such a clumsy way? It would be the manner of boors not to pay attention to these refined entertainments. Odysseus, at least, pays attention to the song-makers of the
<margin>Odyssey, Book 8</margin>
Phaeacians: "But Odysseus gazed at the twinkling of their feet, and he marveled in his heart," even though he had many things weighing on him and was capable of refusing. It was more settled in my mind that there were songs. How then would Telemachus not have been foolish if, with a singer and a tumbler present, he was instead looking toward
<margin>Iliad, Book 18</margin>
his belly and arranging the vessels? But Homer, like a good painter, made Telemachus in every way like his father. He has represented both—the one with Alcinous and the other with Menelaus—being recognized through their tears. In the banquet of Epicurus, there is a gathering of flatterers praising one another. That of Plato is full of sneering at those mocking one another. I will remain silent about the speech of Alcibiades. But in Homer, temperate banquets are heralded. And once, someone praised him, saying to Menelaus: "I do not dare to speak against you, for your voice is like that of a god, so that we may be delighted."
<margin>Odyssey, Book 4</margin>
But if someone said or did something incorrectly, he would forget it. "And now if something is lacking... for I am delighted to mourn after dinner." And he said again: "Telemachus, what word has escaped the barrier of your teeth?" Using a metaphor from the <term>ixios</term> <note>Likely referring to a species of fish or a trap</note>, he says: "The great one quickly swallows the half-sized and the smaller ones." These are the same as those called "boyish," which they used as competitions during feasts. For this reason, Anacreon called them "delightful." You also know other kinds of flutes: the tragic, the <term>lysiode</term> <note>Accompaniment for a specific type of mime or song</note>, and those for the <term>kithara</term>. Euphronius mentions these in his *Discoveries*, as does Euphanor the Pythagorean in his work *On Flutes*. The reed-flute is called <term>tityrinos</term> among the Dorians in Italy, as Artemidorus the follower of Aristophanes records in the second book of his *Doric Dialect*. The flute called the <term>magadis</term>—which is also called the "old-magadis" at the same time—displays both a high and a deep tone, as Alexandrides says in *The Heavy-Armed Soldier*: "I will speak to you a little on the magadis, both small and great at once." And those called "lotus-flutes" are the ones called <term>photinx</term> by the Alexandrians. They are constructed from reed and lotus; this is a wood that grows in Libya. He says the Thebans discovered the <term>iobas</term>, which is a flute constructed from the legs of a fawn. And Hyphon says that the one called the "ivory flute" was first seen around Phoenicia. You know that the <term>magadis</term> is a plucked instrument, just like the kithara, the lyre, and the <term>barbiton</term>. Euphorion the epic poet says in his work *On Dialects* that those now called <term>nablas</term>-players, <term>pandura</term>-players, and <term>sambuke</term>-players...

# ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS
<meta>catchword: -lesi (from "daitalesi," guests)</meta>

And they use no new instrument. For the <term>barbytos</term> <note>original: βάρβυτον; a deep-toned string instrument similar to a lyre</note> and the <term>barbitos</term>, which Sappho and Anacreon mention, as well as the <term>magadis</term> and the <term>trigona</term> <note>triangular harps</note> and the <term>sambucae</term> <note>small, high-pitched harps</note>, are all ancient. At any rate, Euphorion <note>OCR reads "ου γουν Μιτυληνη", likely a corruption of "Euphorion" or a reference to a Mitylenean source</note> says that a statue in Mitylene, made by Lesbothemis, shows a Muse holding a <term>sambuke</term>. Aristoxenus calls certain instruments "foreign," such as Phoenician pipes, the <term>pektides</term> <note>a type of harp or lute</note>, the <term>magadides</term>, <term>sambucae</term>, and the <term>trigona</term> called <term>klepsiamboi</term> <note>original: κλεψιάγγους; likely a string instrument used to accompany iambic poetry</note>, as well as <term>skindapsous</term> and the one called the <term>phoinikarchon</term>. Plato, in the third book of the *Republic*, says: "Then," I said, "we shall have no need of many-stringed instruments or 'pan-harmonic' instruments <note>instruments capable of playing in many musical modes</note> in our songs and melodies." "It does not seem so to me," he said. "Therefore, we shall not maintain makers of <term>trigona</term> and <term>pektides</term> and all such instruments that are many-stringed and pan-harmonic." The <term>skindapsos</term> is a four-stringed instrument, as Matron the parodist says in these lines:
> Nor did they hang me on a peg where you were stretched,
> O four-stringed <term>skindapsos</term> of a woman who spins.

Theopompus the Colophonian, an epic poet, also mentions it in the poem titled *The Chariot*:
> Shaking in his hands the great, lyre-like <term>skindapsos</term>,
> Made from the wood of a sturdy wild willow.

And Anaxilas in *The Lyre-Maker*: "I am stringing <term>barbitoi</term>, <term>pektides</term>, <term>kitharas</term>, lyres, and sharp-toned <term>skindapsoi</term>." Sopater the parodist, in his work titled *The Initiates*, says the <term>pektis</term> has two strings, speaking thus:
> The <term>pektis</term>, pride of the barbarian Muse
> With its two strings—how did it find its way into my hand?

Epicharmus, in *The Periellos*, mentions the <term>psalriam bides</term> <note>original: ψαριαμβιδῶν; likely an obscure stringed instrument</note> in this way:
> Semele dances, and a clever man accompanies her
> On the <term>psalriambis</term> with his lyre. She rejoices,
> Listening to the rapid, rhythmic plucking.

As Juba says, Alexander of Cythera perfected the <term>psalterion</term> <note>original: ψαλτήριον; a stringed instrument played with the fingers, not a plectrum</note> with more strings; when he grew old in the city of Ephesus, he dedicated his invention to Artemis as a masterpiece of his craft. Juba also mentions the <term>lyrophoenix</term> and the <term>epigoneion</term>, which has now been refashioned into an upright <term>psalterion</term>, though they preserve the awkwardness of the string arrangement. <term>Epigonos</term>, the inventor, was by birth from Ambracia but was made a citizen of Sicyon. 
<margin>Alexander, most skilled in music</margin>
Being most skilled in manual playing, he plucked the strings with his bare hands without a plectrum. The Alexandrians are expert and artistic in all these aforementioned instruments and the pipes. If you wish to test me on any of them, I will demonstrate it myself, though there are many others in my homeland far more musical than I. Indeed, my fellow citizen Alexander, who died not long ago after performing publicly on the instrument called the <term>trigonon</term>, made all the Romans so "music-mad" <note>original: μουσουμανεῖν; a pun implying they became obsessed with the Muses</note> that many could even play his tunes from memory. Sophocles also mentions this <term>trigonon</term> in his *Mysians*:
> Much the Phrygian <term>trigonon</term> and the plucked
> Lydian songs sound in harmony with the <term>pektis</term>.

And in *Thamyras*. Aristophanes mentions it in *The Banqueters*, and Theopompus in *Penelope*, and Eupolis says in *The Dippers*: "He who beats the drum well and plucks the <term>trigona</term>." The instrument called the <term>pandouros</term> <note>a long-necked lute, ancestor of the mandolin</note> is mentioned by Euphorion as previously stated, and by Protagorides in the second book of *The Festivals at Daphne*. Pythagoras, who wrote about the Red Sea, says the Troglodytes <note>a "cave-dwelling" people mentioned by ancient geographers</note> construct the <term>pandoura</term> from the laurel that grows in the sea. The horn and the trumpet are inventions of the Etruscans, while Metrodorus of Chios in his *History of Troy* says that Marsyas invented the <term>syrinx</term> <note>panpipes</note> at Celaenae, though previously men used to pipe on a single reed. Euphorion the epic poet, in his work *On Song-Makers*, says Hermes invented the single-reed <term>syrinx</term>, though some record that Silenus and Rhonaces of the Mydians did so; but Silenus invented the many-reeded pipe, and Marsyas the one joined with wax. There you have it from us Alexandrians, O Ulpian, hunter of words—this information regarding those devoted to the single-pipe. For you may know that Menicles of Barca, the historian, and Andron in his *Chronicles of Alexandria* say that the Alexandrians were the ones who educated all the Greeks and the barbarians when general education had already failed due to the continuous upheavals in the times of Alexander’s successors. Thus, there was a renewal of all learning during the reign of the seventh Ptolemy of Egypt, the one called "Malefactor" <note>original: κακεργέτην (Kakergetes); a mocking nickname for Ptolemy VII Euergetes II</note> by the Alexandrians. For he, having slaughtered many Alexandrians and exiled not a few who had reached manhood under his brother, filled the islands and cities with grammarians, philosophers, geometers, musicians, painters, athletic trainers, physicians, and many other craftsmen. These men, forced to teach what they knew because of their poverty, produced many famous scholars in turn. Music was a concern 
<margin>The zeal of the ancients for music</margin>
for all the ancient Greeks; therefore, the art of piping was also studied with zeal. Chamaeleon of Heraclea, in his work titled *Exhortation*, says the Spartans and Thebans all used to learn to pipe, as did the people of Heraclea in Pontus even in his own day, and the most eminent Athenians, like Callias the son of Hipponicus and Critias the son of Callaeschrus. Duris, in his work *On Euripides and Sophocles*, says Alcibiades learned the art of piping, not from just anyone, but from Pronomus, who had the greatest reputation. Aristoxenus says that Epaminondas the Theban also learned to pipe from Olympiodorus and Orthagoras. Many of the Pythagoreans also practiced piping, such as Euphranor, who left behind a treatise on pipes; likewise, Archytas did the same. Aristophanes also shows this in *The Banqueters*...

# ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS
## BOOK FIVE

<margin>Ancient banqueters</margin>
**B**ut since such a great discussion of symposia has been shared with you, Timocrates, in the preceding books, we left out the most useful parts—those which do not weigh down the soul but benefit it during a "all-feast"—which the divine Homer introduced. I shall mention what was said about these things by the excellent Masurius <note>one of the fictional scholars at the banquet</note>. For we, according to the beautiful Agathon, "make the side-work our main work, and treat the main work as a side-work." <note>A famous quote from the playwright Agathon about the reversal of priorities.</note> So, the poet [Homer], when speaking of Menelaus, says: <margin>The Dinner of Menelaus</margin> "They found him feasting <margin>20</margin> a wedding-banquet for many kinsmen for his son and his noble daughter in his own house." <note>Homer, Odyssey 4.3–5</note> For it is common to have banquets at weddings, both for the sake of the wedding sacrifices and for a kind of public testimony. As for how a banquet for strangers should be, the Lycian King showed what kind it ought to be when he received Bellerophon magnificently: "For nine days he entertained him and sacrificed nine oxen." <note>Homer, Iliad 6.174</note> <margin>Wine</margin> For I think wine has a certain "attractive" quality of friendship, warming the soul and opening it up. Therefore, they did not even ask who the guests were beforehand, but later, honoring the hospitality itself, rather than the individual person.

Taking thought for modern dinners, legislators established the "Phiditia" <note>the Spartan common meals</note> and the democratic dinners. Furthermore, there are the <term>thiasoi</term> <note>religious social clubs</note> and the <term>phratries</term> <note>tribal kinship groups</note>, and again what are called "Orgeonic" associations. There are, at any rate, many gatherings of philosophers in the city, some called "Diogenists," others "Antipatristers," and others "Panaitians." <margin>30</margin> Even Theophrastus <note>successor to Aristotle</note> left money for such a gathering—by Zeus, not so they could be debauched when meeting together, but so they might conduct the business of the symposium temperately and with education. The <term>Prytaneis</term> <note>leading government officials</note> also dined together daily, meals that were temperate and preserved the city. Regarding such a banquet, Demosthenes says he read about the capture of Elateia. <note>original: Ἐλάτεια; a strategic city whose capture by Philip II of Macedon caused panic in Athens</note> "For it was evening," he says, "and someone came reporting to the <term>Prytaneis</term> that Elateia had been captured." <note>Demosthenes, On the Crown 169</note> It was also a concern for philosophers who gathered the youth with them to behave decorously according to a set law. For instance, there were certain "sympotic laws" <note>rules for drinking and conduct</note> under Xenocrates in the Academy, and again under Aristotle. The Spartan common meals and the <term>Andreia</term> <note>literally "men's meals"</note> among the Cretans were gathered by the cities with all diligence. Therefore, someone said, and not badly: "One should not keep friends away from banquets... for this is the most pleasant reminder of friendship."

The philosopher Antipater, when gathering a symposium once, instructed those coming that they would "contribute" <note>original: ἐράσειν; like a potluck but for ideas</note> concerning sophisms. <margin>40</margin> They say that when Arcesilaus was invited to a banquet and reclined among those eating greedily, he himself was unable to enjoy anything; when one of those present asked him to speak, he said: "May it go well for you, but I am in the struggle of Telephus." <note>A reference to the tragic hero Telephus, who was often depicted as a beggar or in distress; Arcesilaus is joking that the greedy eaters are like a battle he cannot win.</note> It happened that the greedy eater was actually named Telephus. And Zeno, when one of those present was a <term>relish-eater</term> <note>original: ὀψοφαγῶν; someone who greedily eats the delicacies rather than the bread</note> and stripped the top off the fish as soon as it was served, Zeno himself turned the fish over and stripped the other side, saying: "So that the other side might be finished off too." Socrates, seeing someone using the <term>opson</term> <note>delicacy or relish</note> immoderately, said: "O you present, which of you uses bread as a relish and the relish as bread?" 

We shall now speak about the Homeric symposia. For the poet defines their times, persons, and causes. From this, Xenophon and Plato correctly modeled their own works. Those writers at the beginning of their works set out the cause of the symposium and who the participants were. Epicurus, however, defines neither place nor time. He pre-announces nothing. One must therefore divine how a man suddenly holding a cup proposes problems, as if speaking in a lecture; Aristotle says the symposium was like someone "unwashed and full of dust" rushing in. Furthermore, Homer teaches whom one should invite, saying that one must invite the best and most honorable: "He called the elders, the best of the Pan-Achaeans." Not in the manner of Hesiod; for he thinks one should mostly invite neighbors, "whoever dwells near you." For a symposium of that kind is truly one of "gluttonous insensibility," and belongs to the most misanthropic of proverbs...

# 94 ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...fitting for [friendships]. "Friends living far away are not truly friends." For how is it not irrational for friendship to be judged by location rather than by character? Therefore, in Homer's works, after the drinking, **"Among them the old man first began to weave his counsel."** <note>original: Τοῖς δ᾽ ὁ γέρων πάμπρωτος ὑφαίνειν ἤρχετο μῆτιν; a reference to Nestor in the Iliad</note> But among those who do not gather for temperate symposia:

<margin>The Homeric and Platonic Symposia</margin>
Among them the flatterer first began to weave his mockery. Furthermore, Homer introduces guests who differ in age and in their chosen paths, such as Nestor, Ajax, and Odysseus; generally, they all cling to virtue, but they have set out toward it by different roads. Epicurus, however, introduced only "prophets of atoms." He did this even though he had models like the variety found in the Poet’s <note>Homer</note> banquets and the grace of Plato and Xenophon. Of these, Plato introduces Eryximachus the physician, Aristophanes the poet, and others from various walks of life. For he did not think it seemly to be either too specialized or focused on sneering. Again, Epicurus in his *Symposium* conducts an inquiry about dysentery—hardly a good omen!—and then discusses fevers in order. One must speak of the lack of rhythm that runs through his style. Plato, on the other hand, describes those troubled by hiccups being treated by gargling water, or the instruction to tickle the nose with a straw to induce a sneeze; in doing so, he intended to satirize and mock, ridiculing Agathon's use of <term>isocola</term> <note>clauses of equal length</note> and <term>antitheses</term> <note>opposing ideas in parallel structure</note>. He also brings in Alcibiades, who says he is completely beaten. Yet despite writing such things, they banish Homer from their cities! But as Demochares said, a good man is not made by a spear from a theater-altar, nor from such speeches. He did not only mock Alcibiades, but also Charmides, Euthydemus, and many other young men. He acts like a comic poet against the city of Athens, the "Museum of Greece," which Pindar called "The Greece of Greece" and the Pythian oracle called the "Hearth and Town Hall of the Greeks." Why then does he speak falsely of these youths? One can see this from Plato himself. For he says of Alcibiades in the dialogue of the same name that he was past his prime when he first began to talk to Socrates, because all those who desired his body had left him. He says these things at the very start of the dialogue. And as for the falsehoods regarding Charmides, anyone who wishes can learn them from the dialogue itself. For he portrays him inconsistently: at one moment dizzy and "drunk" with love for the boy, becoming a "waiting player" <note>original: ἔφεδρον; a term from wrestling for someone who waits to take on the winner</note> and falling like a fawn under the strength of a lion; yet at the same time, he says Socrates looked down on the boy's beauty.

<margin>The Symposium of Xenophon and Homer</margin>
Furthermore, Xenophon’s *Symposium*, though it is praised, is subject to no fewer criticisms. Callias gathers the banquet because his favorite, Autolycus, was crowned for the <term>pankration</term> <note>a brutal ancient Greek combat sport combining wrestling and boxing</note> at the Panathenaic Games. Immediately, those reclining at the table focus their minds on the boy, even while his father is sitting beside him. Just as when a light appears in the night and draws all eyes toward it, so does the beauty of Autolycus draw the gazes of everyone to himself. There was not one of us present whose soul was not affected by him. Some became more silent, while others struck poses. But Homer never attempted anything of the sort. From where did we learn of Helen's beauty, and which of her enemies saw her? He spoke, overcome by the truth:

<margin>Iliad Book 3</margin>
> **"No shame that Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans**
> **Should suffer grief for a long time for such a woman;**
> **She is dreadfully like the immortal goddesses to look upon."**

<margin>The Homeric Banquet of Menelaus</margin>
Then he says, **"But even so, let her go back in the ships."** Consider the young men who come to Menelaus—Nestor’s son and Telemachus—they do not spend their time in wine and a wedding feast [improperly], and with Helen sitting there, they maintain a proper silence as is fitting, and they do not "shout down" that famous beauty. But Socrates, for what reason did he abstain from the flute-girls and the dancing and lyre-playing boy? Moreover, he unbecomingly rejected the perfume from the tumbling woman. He surely did not have those "splendid things" <note>Homer's descriptions of luxury</note> in mind.

<margin>Aristophanes in The Clouds</margin>
**"You speak of the pale ones, the barefooted ones, of whom the miserable Socrates and Chaerephon are numbered."** <note>original: Τοὺς ὠχριῶντας τοὺς ἀνυποδήτους λέγεις, ὧν ὁ κακοδαίμων Σωκράτης καὶ Χαιρεφῶν</note> Indeed, what follows is also inconsistent with his austerity. For Critobulus, an elegant youth, mocks his old teacher Socrates, saying he is far uglier than the Sileni <note>wild, tutor-like spirits of the forest, often depicted as bald and snub-nosed</note>. Socrates, in turn, engages in a "beauty contest," choosing the boy and the dancing girl as judges, and proposes that the winner receive kisses from the judges. Who among the youth, encountering these things, would not be corrupted rather than led toward virtue? In Homer, however, in the banquet of Menelaus, they propose questions to one another as if in a school, and by conversing like citizens, they delight each other and us. When Telemachus and his companions arrive from the bath and the food is set before them, Menelaus invites them to partake, saying:

<margin>Odyssey Book 4</margin>
> **"Take food and be glad; and then,**
> **After you have tasted dinner, we shall ask who you are."**

Then he offered them the portions set before him as an act of kindness. **"So he spoke, and set before them the fat back of an ox, which he had taken in his hands, which they had set before him as a portion of honor."** Having eaten in silence, as is fitting for youths to converse with one another, they leaned in quietly and spoke, not about the food, nor about the meat—

# 95 ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

### BOOK V

...maids of the host, by whom they were washed, and concerning the possessions of the host:
**"Such possessions lie within the halls of Zeus."** <note>original: Ζηνός που τοιαῦτα δόμοις ἐν κτήματα κεῖται; Odyssey 4.74</note> For Seleucus <note>A 1st-century grammarian and Homeric commentator</note> says it is better to write it this way, whereas Aristarchus <note>The famous librarian of Alexandria known for his critical editions of Homer</note> writes it improperly as: **"Somewhere within is the courtyard of Olympian Zeus."** For they do not marvel at the beauty of the house alone. For how could amber, silver, and ivory be part of the walls? Rather, these things have spread around the house like "echoing halls." For such things are indeed water-carrying and large. And concerning the vessels: **"of gold, amber, silver, and ivory."** To which the following is appropriately added: **"Such possessions lie within the halls of Zeus; many such things are here—wonder takes hold of me as I look upon them."** It is not consistent to follow the line **"Somewhere within is the courtyard of Olympian Zeus"** with the phrase **"many such things are here"**; it is <term>solecistic</term> <note>a grammatical error or absurdity</note> because of the unusual reading. Furthermore, to what part of the house does "courtyard" <margin>courtyard</margin> fit here? For an open, airy place is called a "courtyard" (*aule*). And we say "to channel through" (*diaulanizein*) a place that receives a breeze from both sides. Moreover, a flute (*aulos*) is the instrument through which air passes, and we call anything extended into a straight shape an *aulos*, such as a stadium or a jet of blood. For example: **"immediately a thick jet (*aulos*) of blood came through his nostrils,"** <note>Iliad 22.18</note> and we call a helmet *aulopis* <note>meaning "with a tube-like socket" for a crest</note> when it extends straight up from the middle. Certain sacred valleys (*aulones*) are also mentioned in Athens, which Philochorus refers to in *On the Women*. They use the word *aulon* in the masculine, as Thucydides does in his fourth book and all prose writers, but poets use it in the feminine. Carcinus in his *Achilles* says: **"Into the deep valley (*aulona*) surrounding the army."** And Sophocles in *The Scythians*: **"The cliffs and caves, and the coastal valleys (*aulonas*)."** One should also note that in Eratosthenes’s *Hermes*, it is spoken in the feminine: **"A deep valley (*aulon*) grows between,"** instead of the masculine form. Just as one says **"tender dew."** Every such thing is called both *aule* and *aulon*. But nowadays they call royal palaces *aulai*, as Menander says: **"To serve in the palaces (*aulas*) and satraps,"** and Diphilus: **"To serve in palaces is, it seems to me, the fate of an exile, or a starving man, or a scoundrel."** This is either because they have large open-air spaces in front of the houses, or because the bodyguards keep watch and sleep beside the royal quarters. Homer, however, always assigns the "courtyard" (*aule*) to open-air places where the altar of Zeus, the Lord of Thunder, was located. Peleus, for instance, is found **"in the grass of the courtyard, holding a golden cup, pouring sparkling wine upon the burning sacrifices."** <note>Iliad 11.773</note> And Priam is **"rolling in the filth in the grass of the courtyard."** And Odysseus, having given orders to those around Phemius: **"But go out from the well-built halls, from the slaughter into the courtyard."** That Telemachus praised both the house and the possessions together is made clear by Menelaus: **"Dear children, truly no mortal could rival Zeus,"** <margin>Menelaus</margin> **"for his halls and possessions are immortal."** But we must return to the symposium, <margin>symposium</margin> in which the young man <note>Telemachus</note> skillfully found an opportunity for conversation, so as to compare his friend to himself. For Menelaus does not propose this as a problem, but graciously consoles him after hearing the praises; he does not deny being wealthy. Here, fighting against envy, he says he possesses these things after much suffering. However, he does not deem himself worthy to be compared to the gods: **"for your halls and possessions are immortal."** Having displayed a brotherly <note>original: *Philadelphon*</note> character and saying he was wealthy as if by necessity, he countered with the logic of friendship: **"I wish I lived in my halls with only a third share of these things, if only those men were safe who then perished in broad Troy, far from horse-rearing Argos."** Who among the descendants of those who died for such a cause would not choose glory, with the grief over the loss of a father being corrected by the grateful memory of that father? So that he might not seem to be common to all who showed goodwill to him in a similar way, he added: **"I do not mourn so much for all of them, though I am grieved, as for one, who makes sleep and food hateful to me."** To ensure he did not seem to be neglecting any of that man's kin, he mentioned them by name: **"They would mourn him tonight: the old man Laertes, and constant Penelope, and Telemachus whom he left as a newborn in his house."** While he was weeping at the memory, the other observed him. And at this point, during Helen's entrance, she too judged by the likeness. For women, because they observe one another's modesty, are very clever at tracing the likenesses of children to their parents—a conversation which Pisistratus also joined. For it is necessary that an equal should not be present merely in the manner of a bodyguard; and after Telemachus had spoken gracefully about his modesty, Menelaus again added remarks about his friendship with Odysseus, saying that he would have liked to grow old with him above all others. As is natural, they began to weep, but Helen, being the daughter of Zeus and having learned many things from the wise people in Egypt, threw into the wine a "panacea," a truly all-healing drug, and began to tell stories about Odysseus while they were finishing their work. She did this not to please them, but because such was her natural disposition. At any rate, Aphrodite, coming to her after the duel <note>The duel between Paris and Menelaus in Iliad 3</note>, is likened to **"an ancient woman, a wool-comber, and addressed her."**

# ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

<margin>Odyssey, Book 4</margin>
The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> were wool-workers, yet even they did not practice the making of fine wools. Helen’s industriousness is displayed here as no casual matter; as the poet says, **"And for her, she placed a well-wrought couch."** <note>original: "τῇ δ’ ἄρ’ ἅμ’ ἀσπασίη κλισίην εὔτυκτον ἔθηκε" — Odyssey 4.123</note> **"Alcippe brought a rug of soft wool, and Phylo brought a silver basket, which Alcandre, the wife of Polybus, had given her. This the handmaid Phylo brought and set beside her, filled with dressed yarn; and upon it was laid the spindle, holding violet-dark wool."** It seems that she even kept track of her own craftsmanship. For instance, when she gives a robe as a gift to Telemachus, she says:
> **"A gift for you also, dear child, I give this, a memento of Helen’s hands, for the hour of your much-desired marriage."**
> **"To be worn by your wife."**

<margin>Iliad, Book 3</margin>
This very industriousness reveals her <term>sophrosyne</term> <note>temperance or modesty</note>. For she is not introduced as someone luxurious or made frivolous by her beauty; rather, she is found somewhere weaving a web and decorating it. **"He found her in the hall, and she was weaving a great double web, shining. And she was embroidering into it the many struggles of the horse-taming Trojans and the bronze-clad Achaeans, which they suffered for her sake at the hands of Ares."**

<margin>Odyssey, Book 4</margin>
Homer also teaches us that those invited to a feast should be the ones to ask their hosts for permission to depart. Telemachus, while staying with Menelaus, says:
> **"But come, send us to bed, so that even now we may take our fill of sweet sleep, lying down."**

<margin>Odyssey, Book 3</margin>
And Athena, pretending to be Mentor, says to Nestor:
> **"But come, cut the tongues of the victims and mix the wine, so that after we have poured libations to Poseidon and the other immortals, we may think of sleep; for it is the hour for it."**
At the festivals of the gods, however, it is considered holy to remain for a longer time. Athena speaks proverbially in Homer:
> **"For already the light has gone beneath the darkness, and it is not fitting to sit long at a feast of the gods, but to depart."**
Even now, it is the law to depart from certain sacrifices before the sun sets. Among the Egyptians, too, in ancient times, the style of symposia was conducted soberly, as Apollonius has written somewhere: they would dine sitting down, using the simplest and most healthful food, and only as much wine as was sufficient for good cheer—which Pindar asks for from Zeus:
> **"What should I do to be dear to you, O mighty-thundering son of Cronus, and dear to the Muses? In the cheerfulness of songs, I would be; this I ask of you."**

<margin>The Symposium of Plato and Homer.</margin>
Plato’s *Symposium*, however, is not a formal assembly, nor a council, nor a gathering of philosophers. For Socrates does not even want to leave the symposium. Indeed, even when Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others have left, he stays awake with Agathon and Aristophanes, drinking from a **"silver well."** <note>original: "ἀργυροῦ φρέατος" — a metaphor for an exceptionally large drinking cup</note> (Someone aptly named large cups this way.) He drinks from the bowl in turn from left to right. It is said that after this, the other two began to nod off, and Aristophanes fell asleep first. Then, as day was breaking, Socrates, having put Agathon to sleep as well, got up and went away to the Lyceum.

<margin>Odyssey, Book 8</margin>
Herodicus says, regarding those who slave over Homer:
> **"There a sleepless man might have earned a double wage."**
Every gathering for a symposium among the ancients referred its cause to a god. They used wreaths appropriate to the gods, and hymns and songs. There were no slaves to serve them; instead, the young men of the free class poured the wine, just as the son of Menelaus did even when he was a bridegroom, performing the service at his own wedding. In the works of the beautiful Sappho, even Hermes pours the wine for the gods. The guests would depart while it was still light. In some cases, the councils of the Persians were held at symposia, as was the case with Agamemnon during the campaign. As for the symposium of Alcinous, to which the speech of Odysseus is directed:
> **"For I say that there is no goal more graceful than when gladness possesses the whole people, and the feasters throughout the house listen to a singer."**
This had a certain reception, as the Phaeacians themselves were luxury-loving, which someone comparing it to the symposia of the philosophers might find to be more orderly. And yet, it contained both cheerfulness and jesting. For after the gymnastic contest, the singer sings about the love of Ares, a story mixed with mockery. And indeed, the slaughter of the suitors is suggested to Odysseus by the way Hephaestus and the "Limping One" <note>Hephaestus</note> overcame the strength of Ares.

<margin>Odyssey, Book 1</margin>
The people of that time also sat while dining. Homer says in many places:
> **"They sat in order on the couches and chairs."**
For the **"thronos"** <note>throne/high chair</note> is a chair for free men, used with a footstool—which they called a *thrynys*. They named it a "thronos" from the word *thrasasthai* <note>to sit down</note>, which means "to settle one’s essence," as Philitas says:
> **"to sit [thrasasthai] under the shade of a plane tree."**
The **"klismos"** <note>easy chair</note> was decorated with a reclining back. More humble than these was the **"diphros"** <note>stool</note>. For Odysseus, appearing to be a beggar, they set out a **"shabby stool and a small table."** Their mixing bowls <note>krateres</note>, as the name implies, stood by already mixed. From these, the youths serving would provide cups that were always full to the most honored guests, but distributed wine equally to the others. Agamemnon says to Idomeneus:
<margin>Iliad 4 <br/> Iliad 4</margin>
> **"Your cup stands always full, just as mine does, to drink when your heart bids you."**
They toasted one another, not as we do (for we must drink it all first), but by filling the cup to the brim: **"he filled the cup with wine and took it to Achilles."** How often they took their food, we have already touched upon. Because...
