# BOOK 5

There were three meals; for the same meal was sometimes called "breakfast" and sometimes "dinner." Those who claim that the ancients took four meals are being ridiculous. For when the poet says, "But you, go after you have spent the afternoon," <note>original: "σὺ δ’ ἔρχεο δηϊελήσας" — Odyssey 17.599. The speaker implies spending time until evening, not a separate meal time.</note> the intelligent reader understands he is saying to spend the late afternoon hours. Nevertheless, one will find in the poet’s work that people take food three times a day.

<margin>Odyssey, Book 1</margin>
Those who place the following lines one after another are in error: **"The grave housekeeper brought bread and set it before them, and many dainties besides, giving freely of her store. And the carver lifted up platters of meat and set them before them."** For if the housekeeper had already set out the "dainties," it is clear that the carver did not need to bring in leftovers of meat. Therefore, the first two lines are sufficient on their own. When the diners were finished, the tables were carried away, as was the case with the suitors and the Phaeacians, of whom he says: **"The handmaids cleared away the abundant food."** <note>original: "σῖτον ἄπλαστον" — usually referring to a great quantity of food.</note> It is clear he means the vessels. Indeed, they call the protective parts of armor—the breastplates, greaves, and similar items—"vessels" <note>original: "σκεύη" (skeue), often meaning equipment or containers</note>, just as they are the "equipment" for the parts of the body. 

Homer calls the larger rooms of heroic houses "halls" <term>megara</term>, "dwellings" <term>domata</term>, and "lodgings" <term>klisiai</term>. People today call them "guest-rooms" or "private suites." What then, my friends, should we call the banquet which was given by **Antiochus**, the king who was titled "Epiphanes" <note>The Illustrious</note> but was nicknamed "Epimanes" <note>The Madman</note> because of his actions? He was one of the Seleucid kings of Syria, and Polybius says of him: 

<margin>Antiochus the Madman.</margin>
"Sometimes he would escape from the court, slipping away from his attendants, and would be seen wandering with one or two others in the city. He was most often found at the silversmiths' and goldsmiths' workshops, talking technicalities with the engravers and other craftsmen. Then he would go down and socialize with any common people he happened to meet, drinking with the cheapest of the foreign visitors. Whenever he heard of young men gathered for a party, he would arrive without any warning, crashing the feast with a jar of wine and a band of musicians, so that most of the guests would flee in terror at the absurdity of it. Often, he would lay aside his royal robes, put on a Roman <term>tebenna</term> <note>a toga</note>, and go around the marketplace as if he were a candidate for office. He would shake hands with some and embrace others, begging them to give him their vote—sometimes for the office of market-overseer, sometimes for tribune. Having obtained the office and sitting upon the ivory chair after the Roman fashion, he would listen to the lawsuits concerning marketplace transactions and judge them with great seriousness and zeal. This behavior left sensible people at a total loss; some thought he was a simple, plain man, while others thought he was a complete lunatic."

His gift-giving was of a similar nature. To some, he would give knuckle-bones made of gazelle bone; to others, dates; to others, gold. If he happened upon people he had never seen before, he would bestow unexpected gifts upon them. Yet, in the sacrifices he sent to cities and the honors he paid to the gods, he surpassed all previous kings. One can see evidence of this in the temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens and the statues surrounding the altar at Delos. 

It is also told that in the public baths, when the baths were full of common citizens, jars of the most expensive perfumes would be carried in for him. On one occasion, someone said, "You kings are fortunate to use such things and smell so sweet!" Without saying a word to the man, the king waited until the next day when the man was bathing, then stood over him and ordered a massive jar of the most expensive perfume—called "sakte"—to be poured over the man's head. The result was that everyone jumped up to roll themselves in the spilled perfume, and because of the slipperiness, they kept falling down, providing a great laugh for the king himself.

When this same king heard about the games organized in Macedonia by the Roman general Aemilius Paullus, he wished to surpass Paullus in the magnificence of his display. He sent ambassadors and sacred observers to the various cities to announce the games he was going to hold at Daphne, so that there was a great rush among the Greeks to visit him. 

<margin>The Procession of Antiochus.</margin>
The beginning of the festival was the procession, which was conducted as follows: Leading the way were five thousand men in the prime of life, equipped in the Roman fashion with coats of chainmail. After them came five thousand Mysians, then three thousand Cilicians armed in the manner of light infantry, wearing gold crowns. Following these were three thousand Thracians and five thousand Galatians. Then came the "Silver Shields" <note>original: "ἀργυράσπιδες" — an elite infantry unit</note>, followed by two hundred and forty pairs of gladiators. Behind these were the cavalry: a thousand Nisaean horses and three thousand citizen cavalry. Most of these had gold trappings and gold crowns, while the others had silver trappings. After these came the so-called "Companion Cavalry" <note>original: "ἑταῖροι" — an elite social and military rank</note>, numbering one thousand, all with gold trappings. Next to them was the "Corps of Friends," equal in number and equipment. Then came a thousand elite troops. Last of the cavalry were the "Cataphracts" <note>original: "κατάφρακτος" — heavily armored cavalry where both horse and rider are plated in mail</note>, appropriately named because both horses and men were covered in armor; they numbered one thousand five hundred. All those mentioned so far wore purple cloaks, many of them embroidered with gold or animal figures. There were one hundred six-horse chariots, forty four-horse chariots, then a chariot drawn by elephants and one by a pair of mules. These were followed by thirty-six individual elephants in full regalia. It is difficult to describe the rest of the procession, but to speak in summary, there were eight hundred youths in the parade...

# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS

...eight hundred, wearing gold crowns, and a thousand well-fed oxen. The sacrifices fell only slightly short of three hundred. There were eight hundred elephant tusks. As for the multitude of statues, it is impossible to describe them fully. For images of all those who are called or considered gods or spirits among men, and furthermore of heroes, were led along in the procession—some gilded, others dressed in robes interwoven with gold. And to all of these were attached the appropriate myths and traditional stories, represented through costly displays. Among them were also figures of Night and Day, of Earth and Heaven, and of Dawn and Noon. 

The quantity of gold and silver plate might be guessed from this: one of the king’s friends, Dionysius the secretary, had a thousand boys following in his train in the procession, carrying silver plate of which no single piece weighed less than a thousand drachmas <note>A drachma was a standard Greek silver coin; a thousand drachmas' weight (roughly 4.3 kg) represents an immense amount of silver for a single vessel.</note>. Six hundred royal servants passed by carrying gold plate. Then followed about two hundred women sprinkling perfumes from gold pitchers. Next in the procession were eighty women carried in litters with gold feet, and five hundred in litters with silver feet, all sitting sumptuously arrayed. These were the most conspicuous parts of the procession. 

When the games, gladiatorial combats, and hunts were finished—lasting thirty days during which he performed the sacrifices—for the first few days he anointed everyone in the gymnasium with saffron oil from gold jars; there were fifteen of these jars, and an equal number of jars containing cinnamon and nard oil. Following this, other oils were brought in: <margin>† lily-scented.</margin> wallflower, marjoram, and † iris-scented oil <note>original: "εἰρινόν" (irinom), though the margin suggests "κρίνινον" (krinon), meaning lily-scented.</note>, all of them remarkable for their fragrance. For the banquets, sometimes a thousand couches were laid, and sometimes fifteen hundred, with the most luxurious equipment. 

The management of these affairs was handled by the king himself. Riding a cheap, common horse, he would run alongside the procession, ordering some groups forward and holding others back. At the drinking parties, he would stand at the entrances, bringing some guests in and seating others. He even brought in the servants and the courses of food himself. Walking around the room, he never sat down or reclined. Sometimes he would put down a morsel of food or his cup and jump up, moving elsewhere. He would go around the party taking toasts, standing up now with one group, now with another, while also joking with the performers. As the party went on and many had already left, the king would be carried in by mimes, entirely covered up. He would be placed on the ground as if he were one of the performers, and when the music signaled, he would jump up and dance and act with the jesters, so that everyone felt ashamed and fled the party. 

All these things were funded partly by the revenues he brought from Egypt when he went to court against the young king Philometor <note>Ptolemy VI Philometor, the nephew of Antiochus IV.</note>, and partly by contributions from his friends. He also plundered most of the temples. 

<margin>The procession of Philadelphus.</margin>
While the guests marveled at the king’s character—how he was not "Epiphanes" <term>Epiphanes</term> <note>meaning "Illustrious" or "God Manifest," the title Antiochus IV took for himself.</note> but truly "Epimanes" <term>Epimanes</term> <note>meaning "The Madman," a pun on his official title.</note>—Masurius added an account of the procession held in Alexandria by that most excellent king, Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, who ruled Egypt in the 3rd century BCE and was famous for his patronage of the Arts and the Library of Alexandria.</note>. He cited Callixeinus of Rhodes, who describes it in the fourth book of his *History of Alexandria*: 

"Before I begin, I will describe the tent that was prepared within the citadel's enclosure, separate from the space for receiving the soldiers, craftsmen, and visitors. For it was exceedingly beautiful and well worth hearing about. In size, it was large enough to hold one hundred and thirty couches arranged in a circle. Its design was as follows: wooden columns were set up, five on each side along the length, being fifty cubits high, and one fewer on each side along the width. Upon these a square architrave was fitted, which supported the entire roof of the banquet hall. The roof itself was covered in the center by a scarlet canopy with a white border. On either side it had beams with white centers, covered by turreted hangings. Within these, painted panels were arranged in the center. Of the columns, four were made to look like palm trees, while those in the middle had the appearance of thyrsoi <term>thyrsos</term> <note>A ritual staff associated with the god Dionysus, usually topped with a pine cone.</note>. 

Outside these columns, a peristyle corridor was built on three sides with a vaulted roof, where the attendants of the guests were meant to stand. The interior of this was surrounded by scarlet curtains. In the spaces between the columns, extraordinary animal skins, remarkable for both their variety and size, were hung. The surrounding open-air area was shaded by myrtle, laurel, and other suitable branches. The entire floor was strewn with all kinds of flowers. For Egypt, both because of the mildness of the surrounding air and because of the skill of its gardeners, produces in abundance and at all times flowers that grow only rarely or in specific seasons elsewhere. Neither roses, nor white violets, nor any other flower is ever easily lacking there. Therefore, even though the reception took place in mid-winter, there was a wonderful sight for the foreign guests. For flowers that could not easily be found for a single garland in another city were supplied in abundance for the garlands of this great multitude of guests. Indeed, they were strewn thickly over the floor of the tent, truly creating the appearance of a divine meadow. Around the tent stood one hundred marble animals made by the finest craftsmen. In the spaces between them were paintings by the Sicyonian artists..."

# BOOK V.

...writing. There were choice carpets <note>original: "ψιλαὶ" (psilai); specifically smooth, non-shaggy woven rugs</note> of every variety of pattern, and tunics shining with gold, and most beautiful cloaks, some having images of the kings woven into them, and others depicting mythological scenes. Above these were placed gold and silver shields. In the spaces above these, which were eight cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> high, grottoes had been constructed. Along the length of the tent on each side, and four across the width. These contained banquet scenes representing figures from tragedy, comedy, and satyr plays <note>Satyrs were the wild, half-man half-goat followers of the god Dionysus.</note>, wearing real clothing. Beside them were placed gold drinking cups. In the middle of the grottoes, nymphs were fashioned, among whom stood gold Delphic tripods <note>A tripod is a three-legged stand, often used as an altar or to hold a basin.</note> with bases. At the highest point of the roof, facing one another, were gold eagles <note>original: "αἰετοὶ" (aetoi); the OCR reads "αὐτοὶ," but the context of Ptolemaic architecture confirms these were gold eagles, symbols of royal power.</note>, fifteen cubits in size. There were also a hundred gold couches with sphinx-shaped feet <note>original: "σφιγγόποδες" (sphingopodes)</note> along the two sides, for the side facing the front was left open. Over these were spread purple rugs made of the finest wool. On top were various coverlets distinguished by their craftsmanship. Persian carpets covered the area between the feet of the couches, featuring precise and beautiful depictions of woven animals. Near those reclining were placed gold tripods, two hundred in number, so that there were two for each couch, resting on silver bases. Behind the couches for the guests stood a hundred silver basins and an equal number of pitchers. Opposite the banquet, another couch was set up for the display of the cups, goblets, and everything else intended for use in the arrangement. These were all made of gold and studded with precious gems, marvelous in their artistry. To describe the brilliance and individual craftsmanship of these items would be a long task. However, the total weight of the silver alone used for the entire arrangement amounted to ten thousand talents <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight; ten thousand talents is approximately 260 metric tons.</note>. Having finished the description of the tent's construction, we shall also provide an account of the procession. It was led through the city’s stadium. First walked the Dawn Star <note>original: "ἑωσφόρου" (Heosphoros); the morning star, Phosphorus.</note>, for the procession began at the time when that star appears. Then followed the group named for the parents of the kings, and after these, the sections belonging to all the gods, each containing a historical display appropriate to them. The final section happened to coincide with the time of the Evening Star. Those who wish to know the details of these groups may look at the records of the four-year festivals <note>original: "πεντετηρίδων" (penteteridon); grand festivals held every four years.</note>. In the Dionysian procession, those who held back the crowd went first: Silenoi <note>Older, drunken forest spirits in the train of Dionysus.</note> dressed in purple cloaks, and others in scarlet. These were followed by Satyrs, twenty in each part of the stadium, carrying gilded ivy-shaped torches. After them came Victories <note>original: "νῖκαι" (nikai)</note> with gold wings. They carried incense burners seven cubits high, decorated with ivy and gold branches, and they were dressed in tunics with girdles. These wore a great deal of gold jewelry. Behind them followed an altar six cubits high, covered with double-layered gold ivy leaves, having a gold vine-leaf crown wrapped with white ribbons. Following this were boys in purple tunics carrying frankincense, myrrh, and saffron, along with one hundred and twenty gold platters. After them were forty Satyrs crowned with gold ivy wreaths. Their bodies were painted, some with purple dye <note>original: "ὀστρέῳ" (ostreo); dye derived from shellfish</note>, others with red earth <note>original: "μίλτῳ" (milto); red ochre</note>, and other colors. They also carried a gold vine-crown crafted of gold. After them came two Silenoi in purple cloaks and white boots. One of them held a broad-brimmed hat <note>original: "πέτασον" (petason)</note> and a gold herald's staff, and the other a trumpet. Between them walked a man over four cubits tall in the costume of a tragic actor, carrying a gold horn of plenty <note>original: "ἀμαλθείας κέρας" (Amaltheia's horn)</note>. He was addressed as "The Year" <note>original: "ἐνιαυτός" (Eniautos); the personification of the passing year.</note>. He was followed by a most beautiful woman of impressive height, decorated with much gold and magnificent ornaments. She carried a crown of persea-leaves in one hand and a palm branch in the other. She was called "Penteteris" <note>The personification of the four-year festival cycle.</note>. She was followed by the four Seasons <note>original: "ὧραι" (Horai)</note>, dressed accordingly, and two gold ivy-clad pillars six cubits high, with a square gold altar between them. Again, Satyrs with gold ivy crowns followed, wrapped in scarlet cloaks. Some carried a gold wine-jug, others a goblet. After them walked the poet Philiskos, being the priest of Dionysus, and all the craftsmen associated with Dionysus. Following these were carried Delphic tripods, prizes for the sponsors of the athletic contests. One, <margin>for a boy.</margin> intended for the boys' contest, was nine cubits in height; the other, twelve cubits high, was for the men's. After these, a four-wheeled wagon <note>original: "τετράκυκλος" (tetrakuklos)</note> with fourteen wheels and a width of eight cubits was led by one hundred and eighty men. On it was a statue of Dionysus, ten cubits tall, pouring a libation from a gold goblet, wearing a purple tunic that reached his feet. Over it was a transparent saffron-colored garment. He was wrapped in a purple cloak embroidered with gold. Before him was placed a Spartan mixing bowl of gold holding fifteen measures <note>original: "μετρητῶν" (metretōn); one metretes was roughly 39 liters.</note>, and a gold tripod on which stood a gold incense burner, and two gold bowls full of cassia and saffron. Around him was a canopy decorated with ivy, vine, and other seasonal fruits. Attached to it were crowns, ribbons, thyrsoi <note>A thyrsos is a staff associated with Dionysus.</note>, drums, headbands, and masks for satyrs, comedians, and tragedians. On the wagon were priests and priestesses, Bacchic initiators, all kinds of religious troupes, and women carrying the sacred winnowing fans. After the—

### FROM ATHENAEUS'S *THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED*

Following him were the so-called Mimallones, and Bassarids, and Lydian women <note>These are various groups of female followers of Dionysus, often depicted as being in a state of religious ecstasy.</note> with their hair flowing loose and wearing crowns, some of bindweed, and others of bindweed combined with grapevines and ivy. In their hands, some held daggers and others held snakes. After these women, a four-wheeled wagon was led, eight cubits wide, pulled by sixty men. Upon it was an eight-cubit-high statue of Dionysus <note>Dionysus was the god of wine, theater, and ritual madness.</note> sitting down, dressed in a yellow tunic embroidered with gold, and he was wrapped in a Laconian cloak. The statue rose up by a mechanical device without anyone touching it; it would pour a libation of milk from a golden bowl and then sit back down again. In his left hand, he held a thyrsus <note>term: "thyrsus" (original: θύρσον) — A ritual staff made of a giant fennel stalk topped with a pine cone and wrapped in ivy.</note> polished with <unclear>ribbons</unclear>. The statue was crowned with ivy made of gold and with clusters of grapes made of precious gems. It was shaded by parasols, and at the corners of the four-wheeled wagon, four gilded torches were fixed. Next came another four-wheeled wagon, twenty-four cubits long and fifteen wide, full of grapes. 
<margin>10</margin> Sixty Satyrs <note>original: "Σάτυροι"; mythological creatures, half-man and half-goat, known for their rowdy behavior.</note> were treading them while singing a grape-treading song to the sound of a flute. Silenus <note>The eldest and wisest of the satyrs, often depicted as the tutor of Dionysus.</note> presided over them, and throughout the entire route, the fresh wine flowed out. Next was carried a four-wheeled wagon, twenty-four cubits long and fourteen wide, pulled by six hundred men. Upon it was a wineskin holding three thousand metretes <note>term: "metretes" (original: μετρητὰς) — An ancient liquid measure roughly equal to 9 gallons or 39 liters.</note> made of stitched leopard skins. This too flowed out little by little, being opened along the entire route. Following it were twenty Satyrs and twenty Sileni, all wearing crowns and carrying, some of them wine-pitchers, others bowls, and others large Thericleian cups <note>A specific style of luxury drinking vessel, named after the Corinthian potter Thericles.</note>, all of which were made of gold. Next was led a silver mixing bowl <note>original: "κρατὴρ" (krater); a large vessel used for mixing wine and water.</note> that held six hundred metretes, pulled on a four-wheeled wagon by six hundred men. It had animal figures embossed under the rim, the handles, and under the base; and in the middle, it was encircled by a gold crown set with gems. Next were brought two silver wine-cups, twelve cubits across and six cubits high. These had decorative projections at the top and around their middle sections. And on the feet were many animal figures, some half a cubit and others a cubit in size. There were also ten large wash-basins and sixteen mixing bowls,
<margin>20</margin> of which the largest held thirty metretes and the smallest five. There were seven cauldrons and twenty-four incense burners on five stands. There were two silver coolers upon which sat twenty-four jars. There was also a table made entirely of silver, twelve cubits long, and thirty other tables six cubits long. In addition to these, there were four tripods, one of which had a circumference of sixteen cubits and was entirely gilded, while the other three were smaller and set with gems in the center. After these were carried eighty silver Delphic tripods, smaller than those mentioned before. At the corners of these were four-meter <note>original: "τετράμετροι" (tetrametroi); the scribe shifts from cubits to meters here.</note> vessels, twenty-six water jars, sixteen Panathenaic amphorae <note>Large ceramic jars traditionally awarded as prizes at the games in Athens, though these were likely of precious metal.</note>, and one hundred and sixty coolers, the largest of which held six metretes and the smallest two. All these items were made of silver. Following these in the procession came those carrying the gold plate: four Laconian mixing bowls with crowns made of vine leaves.
<margin>30</margin> There were another two four-meter Corinthian-style bowls; these had embossed animal figures sitting on top, and on the neck and the rounded bodies were carefully crafted faces. Each held eight metretes and sat on stands. There was also a wine-vat twenty cubits by ten, and two buckets, each holding five metretes. There were two jars holding two metretes each, and twenty-two coolers, of which the largest held thirty metretes and the smallest one. There were four large gold tripods used as footstools and a gold chest set with gems, ten cubits long and six steps high. Inside it were many carefully made animal figures four palms high, as well as two wine-cups and two gold-glass cups. There were two gold stands four cubits high, and three other smaller ones, ten water jars, a three-cubit altar, and twenty-five bread-trays. After these marched one thousand six hundred boys dressed in white tunics, crowned some with ivy and others with pine branches. Two hundred and fifty of them held gold pitchers, and four hundred held silver ones. Another three hundred and twenty carried gold coolers, and others silver. After them, other boys
<margin>40</margin> carried jars for the service of the sweet drink, of which twenty were gold and fifty were silver. Three hundred were painted with white designs in all colors; when the contents were mixed in the water jars and vats, everyone in the stadium was treated to the sweet drink in an orderly fashion. Next to these, he lists tables four cubits long, upon which many spectacles worth seeing and luxuriously constructed were carried around. Among these was the bridal chamber of Semele <note>Semele was the mother of Dionysus.</note>, in which some wore tunics stitched with gold and set with very precious stones. It would not be right to omit this four-wheeled wagon, being twenty-two cubits long and fourteen wide, pulled by five hundred men. Upon it was a cave, exceedingly deep, covered in ivy and red lead <note>original: "μίλτῳ" (milto); a red pigment used for decoration.</note>. From this cave, pigeons, doves, and turtle-doves flew out throughout the entire route, having ribbons tied to their feet so they could be easily caught by the spectators. Two fountains also gushed from it, one of milk and the other of wine. All the nymphs standing around it had golden crowns.
<margin>50</margin> Hermes <note>The messenger god, often associated with Dionysus.</note> carried a golden herald’s staff and wore luxurious clothing. On another four-wheeled wagon was the representation of Dionysus's return from India; the statue of Dionysus was twelve cubits high, reclining upon an elephant, dressed in a purple robe and wearing a gold crown of ivy and vine leaves. ### THE GRAND PROCESSION (CONTINUED)

Following these was a five-cubit-high <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters. A five-cubit figure would be about 7.5 feet tall.</note> figure of a little satyr crowned with a golden pine wreath. In his right hand, he held a golden goat-horn to signal the start of the movements. An elephant followed, draped in golden trappings, with a golden crown fastened around its leg <note>original: "μισθὸν"; likely referring to a prize or honorary decoration.</note>. Following this were five hundred young girls dressed in purple tunics and cinched with golden belts. One hundred and twenty of them led the way, clad in suits of armor—some made of silver and others of bronze.

After them came five troops of donkeys, ridden by crowned Sileni and Satyrs. The donkeys wore frontlets <note>term: "frontlets" (original: προμετωπίδας) — Decorative plates or bands worn on the foreheads of animals.</note> and harnesses made of gold or silver. Behind them followed twenty-four elephant-drawn chariots, sixty pairs of goats, twelve pairs of colts, seven oryxes <note>A type of large antelope with long, straight horns.</note>, and fifteen buffaloes. There were also eight pairs of ostriches and seven pairs of deer. These were followed by four pairs of wild donkeys pulling four chariots. 

All these animals were mounted by young boys wearing charioteers' tunics and broad-brimmed hats <note>term: "petasoi" (original: πετάσους) — Traditional Greek sun hats with flat brims.</note>. Little girls also rode along, equipped with small shields <note>The Greek text reads "νιλταρίοις," which is likely a scribal error for "πελταρίοις" (small shields).</note> and spear-thyrsi; they were adorned with fine robes and gold jewelry. The boy-drivers wore pine wreaths, while the girls wore ivy wreaths.

There were also six pairs of camels, three on each side, followed by wagons drawn by mules. These wagons carried "barbarian" tents, inside which sat Indian women and others dressed as captives. Some camels carried three hundred pounds <note>term: "minas" (original: μνᾶς) — A unit of weight roughly equal to one pound.</note> of frankincense, while others bore two hundred pounds of myrrh, cassia, cinnamon, iris-root, and various other spices. 

Next came Ethiopians bearing gifts: some carried six hundred elephant tusks, others two thousand logs of ebony, and others sixty gold and silver mixing bowls <note>term: "krater" (original: κράτηρα) — A large vessel used for mixing wine and water.</note> along with gold dust. Behind them marched hunters holding gilded hunting spears, leading two thousand four hundred dogs of various breeds—Indian, Hyrcanian, Molossian, and others.

Then followed one hundred and fifty men carrying cages filled with all kinds of wild animals and birds. Numerous parrots were carried in special containers. After describing many other things and listing herds of animals, the author mentions one hundred and thirty Ethiopian sheep, two hundred Arabian sheep, and twenty from Euboea. There were twenty-six white Indian oxen, eight Ethiopian oxen, one large white bear, fourteen leopards, sixteen panthers, four lynxes, a giraffe <note>original: "καμηλοπαρδάλεις" — Literally "camel-leopard," the ancient name for a giraffe.</note>, and a single Ethiopian rhinoceros.

Next, on a four-wheeled wagon, was a scene of Dionysus seeking refuge at the altar of Rhea <note>Rhea was an ancient Mother Goddess; the scene likely refers to a myth where she purified Dionysus of his madness.</note> while being pursued by Hera. Dionysus wore a golden crown, and a figure of Priapus <note>A god of fertility and gardens.</note> stood beside him, crowned with golden ivy. The statue of Hera also wore a golden crown, as did the statues of Alexander the Great and King Ptolemy, who were crowned with ivy made of gold. A statue of Virtue <note>term: "Arete" (original: Ἀρετῆς) — The personification of excellence or virtue.</note> stood next to Ptolemy, wearing a golden olive crown. Beside them was another Priapus with a golden ivy wreath. A figure representing the city of Corinth stood near Ptolemy, wearing a golden diadem. 

Near these was a sideboard full of gold plate and a golden mixing bowl holding over forty-five gallons <note>term: "metretas" (original: μετρητῶν) — A Greek liquid measure equal to about 9 gallons.</note>. This wagon was followed by women in expensive clothing representing the cities of Ionia and other Greek settlements in Asia and the islands that had been under Persian rule; all wore golden crowns. 

On another wagon was carried a golden thyrsus ninety cubits long, a silver spear sixty cubits long, and a golden phallus one hundred and twenty cubits long, decorated with golden ribbons and topped with a golden star six cubits in circumference.

Though many diverse things were described in these processions, we have selected only those involving gold and silver. There were many other sights worth hearing about: vast numbers of wild animals and horses, and twenty-four enormous lions. There were other wagons carrying not just images of kings, but of many gods. After these came a choir of six hundred men, among whom were three hundred gilded harpers <note>term: "citharistae" (original: κιθαρισταὶ) — Players of the cithara, a professional version of the lyre.</note> with golden crowns. Next came two thousand bulls, all of the same color, with gilded horns, golden frontlets, and golden aegis-plates <note>term: "aegis" (original: αἰγίδας) — A protective breastplate or shield, often associated with Zeus or Athena.</note> on their chests. Everything about them was gold. 

Then came the procession of Zeus and many other gods, and finally an image of Alexander, who was carried on a chariot drawn by real elephants; he was made of gold, with figures of Victory and Athena on either side. Many thrones made of ivory and gold followed; on one lay a golden crown, on another a golden horn, and on another a solid gold horn. On the throne of Ptolemy Soter <note>Ptolemy I Soter, the founder of the dynasty and father of the current king, Ptolemy II.</note> rested a crown made of ten thousand gold coins. There were also three hundred and fifty golden censers and gilded altars crowned with gold. Around one of these were fixed four golden torches, fifteen feet high. Twelve golden hearths also passed by, one of which was fifteen feet wide and sixty feet high, while another was fifteen stories tall. Finally, there were nine golden Delphic tripods <note>A three-legged stand or altar, originally associated with the oracle at Delphi.</note> six feet tall, eight others nine feet tall, and one massive tripod forty-five feet high, decorated with golden figures and a golden vine-wreath. Seven gilded palm trees twelve feet tall also passed, and a gilded herald’s staff...

There was also a gilded temple, the circumference of which was forty cubits. Every double-fold wall was eight cubits high. A great multitude of gilded animals also joined the procession, most of them twelve cubits in size, along with wild beasts of extraordinary proportions and eagles twenty cubits tall. There were 3,200 golden crowns carried in the parade, as well as another "musical" crown <note>Likely a crown awarded for a musical or poetic competition.</note> made of gold and adorned with precious stones, eighty cubits in size. This was placed at the entrance of the Bereniceion <note>The shrine or portal dedicated to Queen Berenice I.</note>, alongside a golden dawn-flower <note>original: "αὐγῆς"; likely a decorative floral ornament or a representation of light.</note> of similar design. Many other golden crowns were carried by young boys dressed in costly garments. One of these crowns was two cubits in height and sixteen cubits in circumference.

A golden breastplate twelve cubits long was also displayed, along with another of silver eighteen cubits long, which featured two golden thunderbolts twelve cubits long and a crown of oak leaves set with gems. There were twenty golden shields, sixty-four golden suits of armor, and two golden greaves <note>Leg armor.</note> three cubits high. Also seen were twelve golden basins, a vast number of bowls, thirty-six wine pitchers, ten large oil vessels, twelve water jars, fifty bread-chargers <note>term: "mazonomia" (original: μαζονόμια) — Large, flat plates used for serving barley cakes or bread.</note>, various tables, and lampstands made of golden materials many cubits high, as well as a lyre of solid gold thirty cubits long. 

All these golden items were in addition to those carried in the procession of Dionysus. Furthermore, there were four hundred wagons of silver vessels, twenty wagons of golden vessels, and eight hundred wagons of spices. Following all these came the military forces, both cavalry and infantry, all marvelously armed. The infantry numbered 57,600, and the cavalry numbered 23,200. All these marched in the procession dressed in the uniforms appropriate to their rank and carrying their proper suits of armor. Besides the armor these men wore, there were many other sets kept in storage, the number of which is not easy to record; however, Kallixinos <note>Kallixinos of Rhodes, a 3rd-century BCE historian whose lost work on Alexandria is preserved here by Athenaeus.</note> has listed them. 

In the athletic games, twenty people were crowned with golden crowns. Ptolemy I and Berenice were honored with twenty [crowns] on golden chariots... <note>The text here is somewhat corrupt or compressed in the original.</note> The total expenditure in coinage amounted to 2,235 talents and 50 minae <note>An astronomical sum, equivalent to millions of silver coins.</note>. All this was accounted for by the treasurers because of the enthusiasm of those presenting the crowns before the spectacle began. Their son, Ptolemy Philadelphus, was honored with twenty golden crowns... 

<margin>The wealth of Philadelphus.</margin> What other kingdom has ever been so rich in gold? This was not because he had processed minerals or money taken from the Persians or Babylon, nor because he possessed the Pactolus River which carries down gold dust. For only the Nile, truly called "the gold-flowing," carries down unadulterated gold along with its abundant food, harvested without risk, so that it suffices for all men—like the gifts of Triptolemus <note>A mythological figure who spread the knowledge of agriculture to the world.</note> sent to every land. For this reason, the poet of Byzantium, nicknamed Germanus, says, "O Nile, Egyptian Zeus." 

Philadelphus surpassed many kings in wealth through his history and exceeded all in his grand constructions and his competitive spirit. He also surpassed everyone in the number of his ships. He possessed the largest vessels: two "thirty-rowers," one "twenty-rower," four "thirteen-rowers," two "twelve-rowers," fourteen "eleven-rowers," thirty "nine-rowers," thirty-five "seven-rowers," five "six-rowers," and seventeen "five-rowers." The number of ships from "four-rowers" down to "one-and-a-half-rowers" <note>term: "trihemiolia" (original: τριημιολίας) — A fast, light galley with a specific oar arrangement often used by pirates and navies for pursuit.</note> was double this. The ships sent to the islands and other cities he ruled, including Libya, numbered more than four thousand. Regarding the number of books, the collection of the libraries, and the equipment for the Museum <note>The Mouseion of Alexandria, the famous research institute and home of the Great Library.</note>, why need I speak, as these are in everyone's memory? 

But since we have mentioned the construction of ships, let us speak of them. Worthy of hearing are the vessels built by King Philopator <note>Ptolemy IV Philopator, who reigned 221–204 BCE.</note>. 

<margin>The ship of Philopator.</margin> Regarding these, the same Kallixinos records in the first book of his *Account of Alexandria*, saying: Philopator built the "forty-rower" ship <note>term: "tessarakonteres" (original: τεσσαρακοντήρη) — A massive catamaran-style galley, the largest ship of antiquity.</note> with a length of 280 cubits and a width of 38 cubits from deck-edge to deck-edge. Its height to the figurehead was 48 cubits. From the stern ornaments to the part submerged in the sea was 53 cubits. It had four steering oars, each 30 cubits long. The oars for the highest row <note>term: "thranite" (original: θρανιτικὰς) — The highest of the three levels of rowers in a standard galley, here used for the largest oars.</note> were 38 cubits long—the largest of all—which, because they had lead in the handles and were very heavy, were well-balanced for use during rowing. It was double-prowed and double-sterned and had seven rams—one leading the way, others trailing, and some by the "ear-timbers" <note>Supports for the anchors and oars near the bow.</note>. It used twelve under-girding cables, each 600 cubits long. The ship was exceptionally well-proportioned. 

The other decorations of the ship were also wonderful. It had figures twelve cubits long at the bow and stern, and every part of the vessel was decorated with encaustic painting <note>gloss: Painting using pigments mixed with hot wax.</note>. All the oar-space down to the keel was surrounded by ivy leaves and Dionysian wands <note>term: "thyrsoi" — Staffs topped with pine cones, associated with Dionysus.</note>. There was a great array of weaponry which filled the necessary parts of the ship. Upon its trial, it held more than 4,000 rowers, 400 attendants, and 2,850 marines on the deck. Besides these, there was another multitude of men beneath the decks and a significant supply of provisions. They were launched from a single [apparatus]...

...with a slipway constructed from the timber of fifty festive ships, which they say was used to support the weight. It was launched by a great crowd accompanied by shouting and trumpets. Later, however, a certain Phoenician devised a new method for the general launching, having constructed a trench equal in length to the ship, which he dug near the harbor. In this trench, he built a foundation of solid stone five cubits deep, and across it, he laid transverse rollers spanning the width of the trench, leaving a space four cubits deep. 

<margin>10</margin>

By creating an inlet from the sea, he filled the entire excavated space with water, into which he easily floated the ship with the help of just a few men. After closing the original entrance, he pumped the seawater out again using mechanical engines. Once this was done, the ship rested securely on the aforementioned rollers.

King Philopator <note>Ptolemy IV Philopator, reigned 221–204 BCE.</note> also constructed a river-ship, the so-called <term>Thalamēgos<note>original: θαλαμηγός; literally "room-carrier." This was a floating palace or pleasure barge designed for leisure and travel on the Nile.</note></term>. It had a length of half a stadium <note>Approximately 300 feet or 90 meters.</note> and a width 

<margin>20</margin>

of thirty cubits at its broadest point. Its height, including the structure of the pavilion, reached nearly forty cubits. Its shape was neither like a "long ship" <note>A narrow war galley.</note> nor a "round ship" <note>A wide merchant vessel</note>, but was modified in depth to suit the requirements of the river. Below the waterline, it was flat and broad, but its bulk rose high into the air. The sections at its extremities, especially toward the bow, extended considerably, with the curve of its lines appearing very graceful. It was double-bowed and double-sterned, and it rose high above the water because the waves in the river often become quite large. 

In the middle of its hull, banquet halls and sleeping quarters were constructed, along with all the other amenities required for a luxurious lifestyle. Around the ship, double walkways ran on three sides, the circumference of which was 

<margin>30</margin>

no less than five <term>plethra<note>A plethron is approximately 100 feet; five plethra would be about 500 feet.</note></term>. The arrangement of the lower level was similar to a peristyle <note>A courtyard surrounded by columns.</note>, while the upper level was enclosed with screens and windows on all sides. As one first entered toward the stern, there was a vestibule that stood open. Around it was a walkway, and at the section facing the bow, a gateway <note>propylaion</note> had been constructed, made of ivory and the most precious materials. Passing through this, one found a sort of stage-front <note>proskenion</note> that had been built as a covered area. 

Again, in the middle, there was another similar arrangement; toward the sides, there were portals that led into it. To the left and right of these, windows were placed to provide excellent ventilation. Connected to these was the largest hall. It was surrounded by columns and could accommodate twenty couches. Most of it was constructed of split cedar and Milesian cypress. The twenty doors of the surrounding colonnade were fitted with panels of 

<margin>40</margin>

cypress wood, featuring ivory decorations. The plating on their front surfaces and the door-knockers were made of red bronze, which had been fire-gilded. The shafts of the columns were made of cypress, while the capitals were of the Corinthian style, decorated with ivory and gold. The entire architrave was made of gold, upon which was fitted a frieze featuring ivory figures over a cubit in height. These were of modest workmanship but were wonderful for their lavish materials. Over the banquet hall lay a beautiful square ceiling of cypress wood; its ornaments were carved, with a gilded surface. 

Adjacent to this banquet hall was a bedroom with seven couches, joined to which was a narrow corridor that ran the width of the hull, separating the women's quarters. In these quarters was a banquet hall with nine couches, similar in luxury to the large one, and a bedroom with five couches. Such were the arrangements up to the first deck. 

Upon ascending the stairs located near the aforementioned bedroom, there was another room with five couches, having a coffered ceiling with a diamond pattern. Near it was a circular temple of Aphrodite, containing a marble statue of the goddess. Opposite this was another lavish banquet hall surrounded by columns; for its columns 

<margin>50</margin>

were made of Indian stone. Next to this banquet hall was a bedroom with furnishings corresponding to those already described. 

As one proceeded toward the bow, there was a chamber dedicated to Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note> that held thirteen couches, surrounded by columns and featuring a gilded cornice as far as the surrounding architrave. The ceiling was decorated according to the character of the god. In this room, on the right side, a grotto had been constructed, the color of which appeared like real stone, though it was crafted from genuine minerals and gold. Within it were set portrait statues of the King’s family made of "Lychnite" stone <note>A high-quality, translucent Parian marble.</note>. 

There was also another very pleasant banquet hall situated on the roof of the largest hall, arranged like a tent, so that its center was open to the air. Purple canopies were spread over it during the voyage. After this open-air space was a gallery that occupied the level above the underlying vestibule, where a winding staircase led to the covered walkway, and a nine-couch banquet hall designed in the Egyptian style. For the columns built there were round, with alternating drums of black and white marble placed one upon the other. Their capitals were also circular in shape; their entire outline was similar to roses that are slightly opened. Around what is called the "basket" of the capital, there were no scrolls <note>volutes</note> as on Greek columns, but rather the calyxes of river lotuses and the fruit of newly-sprouting palms. Regarding the city and the ship constructed by Hiero of Syracuse, for which Archimedes the geometer was the overseer, it is not right to remain silent, since a certain Moschion has published a treatise on it, which I happened to read with some care. Moschion writes as follows: Diocleides of Abdera is admired <margin>† Iliad</margin> for the <term>Helepolis<note>original: ἑλεαπόλει; literally "city-taker." A massive siege tower used by Demetrius Poliorcetes.</note></term> brought against the walls of Rhodes by Demetrius. Timaeus is admired for the funeral pyre built for Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily; Hieronymus for the construction of the carriage in which the body of Alexander was transported; and Polyclitus for the lamp-stand made for the Persian King. 

Hiero, the King of the Syracusans, who was in all things a friend to the Romans, was earnest about the construction of temples and gymnasiums. He was also ambitious regarding shipbuilding, constructing grain-transport ships, of which I shall mention the construction of one. From the forests of Etna, a quantity of timber was prepared sufficient to complete sixty triremes. When he had prepared the bolts, the ribs, the planks, and the other materials needed—the wood coming from Italy, and for the ropes, white fiber from Iberia <note>Likely esparto grass from Spain.</note>, and hemp and linen from the river Rhone—he gathered all other necessities from many places. He assembled shipbuilders and other craftsmen, appointing Archias of Corinth as the lead architect over them all. He urged them to take up the construction with enthusiasm, remaining present himself throughout the days. 

One half of the entire ship was finished in six months, and as each part was built, it was covered with tiles made of lead. This was done by three hundred craftsmen working on the materials, not counting the assistants. It was then ordered to launch this part into the sea so that the rest of the construction could be completed there. However, since there was much debate about how to launch it into the sea, Archimedes the mechanic alone brought it down with the help of only a few people. For by constructing a <term>helix<note>original: ἕλικα; a screw-based winch or windlass mechanism.</note></term>, he brought that enormous hull down into the sea. Archimedes was the first to discover the construction of the helix. When the remaining parts of the ship were completed in another six months, the whole was secured with bronze nails. Most of these weighed ten minas <note>About 10-12 pounds.</note>, and the others were half as large again, fitted through holes to hold the planks together. These were protected from the wood by leaden tiles, with cloths soaked in pitch placed underneath. 

As for the interior arrangement, the ship was built with twenty banks of oars and three decks. The lowest deck held the cargo, accessed by many sets of ladders. The second deck was designed for those who wished to enter the living quarters. The last deck was for those stationed under arms. Along each side of the middle deck were thirty cabins, each with four couches for the men. The captain’s quarters had space for fifteen couches and included three chambers with two couches each; the kitchen was located toward the stern. 

All of these rooms had floors composed of <term>tesserae<note>original: ἀϐακίσκοις; small tiles used in mosaics.</note></term> of all kinds of stones, in which the entire story of the *Iliad* was wonderfully depicted. In the fittings, the ceilings, and the doorways, all these things were exquisitely crafted. On the uppermost deck was a gymnasium and walking-paths, their scale proportionate to the size of the ship. In these were all kinds of gardens, producing wonderful plants through leaden planters. There were also shaded areas of white ivy and grapevines, the roots of which were in large jars filled with earth, receiving the same irrigation as the gardens. These shaded areas covered the walking-paths. 

Next to these was a shrine of Aphrodite with three couches, having a floor made of agate and other beautiful stones found on the island. The walls and ceiling were made of cypress wood, and the doors were of ivory and citrus wood, excessively decorated with paintings and statues, as well as drinking vessels. Next to this was a library with five couches, its walls and doorways made of boxwood, containing a collection of books. On the ceiling was a celestial sphere, modeled after the sundial at Achradina. There was also a bath with three bronze tubs and a wash-basin holding fifty units of water, decorated with colorful Taormina stone. Many more rooms were built for the passengers and those who guarded the pumps. Apart from these, there were stables for ten horses on each side of the walls. Near these was the fodder for the horses and the equipment for the riders and the servants. There was also a water tank...

### BOOK 5

A water-tank was built at the prow, sealed and holding two thousand <term>metretas<note>An ancient Greek liquid measure, roughly 9 gallons or 37 liters.</note></term>, constructed from wooden planks, pitch, and linen cloth. Beside this was a closed-off fish-pond made of lead and wood. It was kept full of seawater, and many fish were raised within it. Along both sides of the walls, there were projecting supports placed at regular intervals, upon which were built wood-stores, ovens, kitchens, mills, and many other service rooms. Around the outside of the ship stood <term>Atlantes<note>original: ἀτλαντές; statues of powerful men used as architectural pillars to support weight.</note></term> six cubits high <note>About 9 feet.</note>, which supported the upper weights and the decorated <term>triglyph<note>A tablet with three vertical grooves, a standard feature of the Doric style of architecture.</note></term>, all standing at even intervals. The entire ship was painstakingly decorated with appropriate paintings. There were also eight towers on board, sized in proportion to the ship’s massive bulk. Two were at the stern, two at the prow, and the rest in the middle of the vessel. To each of these towers were attached two yards <note>Large wooden beams.</note>, upon which crates were built; from these, stones were dropped upon any enemy ships sailing underneath. Upon each tower stood four fully armed youths and two archers. The entire interior of the towers was kept full of stones and missiles.

A wall with battlements and decks had been built across the ship, supported by trestles. On this stood a stone-throwing engine <note>A catapult or ballista.</note> which could hurl a three-talent stone <note>Roughly 170–180 pounds (78 kg).</note> and a twelve-cubit bolt <note>An 18-foot long arrow.</note>. This machine was designed by **Archimedes**. Each of these projectiles could be thrown a distance of one <term>stadium<note>About 600 feet or 185 meters.</note></term>. Behind this, screens made of thick mats were hung by bronze chains. Under each mast, there were two yards equipped for dropping stones, from which iron "harps" and lead weights were released against attackers. There was also an iron palisade surrounding the ship to prevent boarding, and iron "crows" <note>Grappling hooks.</note> all around the ship, which could be dropped by mechanical devices to seize enemy vessels and pull them into a position where they could be struck. On each side of the walls, sixty fully armed young men stood on guard. An equal number were stationed around the masts and the stone-dropping yards. High up on the masts were copper "crows-nests." In the first nest, three men were stationed; in the following ones, two; and then one. Stones and missiles were supplied to these men in woven baskets, hoisted up by pulleys to the defensive breastworks by children.

The ship carried four wooden anchors and eight iron ones. As for the masts, the second and third were easily found, but the first <note>The main mast.</note> was found with great difficulty in the mountains of **Britain** <note>original: Βρεττανίας; most scholars believe this is a scribe's error for "Bruttia" in Southern Italy, as it is unlikely a mast would be sourced from Britain at this time.</note> by a swineherd. It was brought down to the sea by Phileas of Tauromenium, the engineer. The bilge-pump, despite its incredible depth, could be emptied by a single man using a "screw," an invention of **Archimedes**.

The ship was named the *Syracusia*, but when King Hiero sent it away, he renamed it the *Alexandria*. It had several tenders: the first was a *kerkouros* <note>A fast, light ship of Phoenician origin.</note> capable of carrying three thousand talents. This was entirely powered by oars. After that came royal fishing boats of fifteen hundred talents, and many other smaller vessels. The crew was no less than six hundred men in addition to those already mentioned, with another six hundred stationed at the prow to watch for orders. A court of justice was established for any crimes committed on board, consisting of the captain, the pilot, and the prow-officer, who judged according to the laws of the Syracusans.

<margin>† of rams <note>original: κρίων; possibly a note regarding the beams or the grain measurements.</note></margin> They loaded the ship with sixty thousand measures of grain, and ten thousand jars of Sicilian salt-fish. There were twenty thousand talents of wool, and twenty thousand talents of other cargo. This was in addition to the provisions for the crew and passengers. When Hiero heard that some harbors could not receive the ship and others were dangerous for it, he decided to send it as a gift to **King Ptolemy** in **Alexandria**. For there was a shortage of grain in Egypt at that time, and so he did. The ship was brought to Alexandria and hauled up onto the docks. Hiero also honored **Archimelus**, the epigrammatist, who wrote a poem about the ship, by sending him one thousand <term>medimni<note>A dry measure of about 1.5 bushels.</note></term> of wheat to Piraeus at his own expense. The epigram goes as follows:

I have intentionally passed over the "sacred trireme" of Antigonus, which the general of Antigonus once surrendered... to the people of Kos, since he dedicated it to Apollo. That ship was not even a third, perhaps not even a quarter, the size of this *Syracusia* or *Alexandria*.

We have now listed these things regarding ships—not starting with the Boeotian catalogue of ships <note>A reference to the list of ships in Homer's Iliad.</note>, but from festival processions. ### FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS

<margin>vessel-stands</margin> Concerning the **vessel-stand** <note>original: ἐγγυοθήκη (*eggyotheke*); a stand or support for jars and cups.</note>, there was a speech attributed to the orator Lysias titled *Concerning the Vessel-stand*, which begins: "If the judges promote a just or moderate examination..." In this speech, he goes on to say that it is not right to argue about the vessel-stand itself, or that it is not worth thirty drachmas. That this stand was made of bronze is stated next: "Last year, wishing to have it repaired, I sent it to a bronze-foundry. For it is of complex design, featuring the faces of Satyrs and small ox-heads." He adds that there was another of the same size: "For the same craftsman makes many such vessels identical to one another." In these passages, Lysias clearly established that the stand was bronze. However, according to Callixenus, they should be called **supports** <note>original: ὑποθήματα (*hypothemata*).</note>. Polemon the traveler says the same in the third book of his *Address to Adaeus and Antigonus*, explaining the arrangement in the Phliasian <note>A city in the Peloponnese.</note> hall and the painted porch of the polemarch <note>A high-ranking military official.</note> by Sillax of Rhegium, which are mentioned by Epicharmus and Simonides, saying: "a vessel-stand, and upon it a cup." Hegesandros of Delphi, in his treatise *On Statues and Images*, says regarding Glaucus of Chios that the <margin>book 1</margin> **support** <note>original: ὑπόστημα (*hypostema*).</note> at Delphi is like a sort of iron vessel-stand, a dedication by Alyattes. Herodotus mentions this, calling it a **bowl-stand** <note>original: ὑποκρητηρίδιον (*hypokreteridion*); a stand used to hold a large wine-mixing bowl (krater).</note>. These are the words of Hegesandros. We ourselves also saw it dedicated at Delphi, and it is truly worth seeing for the small figures, animals, and plants carved upon it. The stand called an *anggotheke* by the Alexandrians is triangular and hollow in the middle, through which jars are lowered. The poor have wooden ones, but the wealthy have them in bronze or silver.

<margin>Antiochus’ banquet</margin> Having spoken concerning the vessel-stand, we shall next recall the banquet-loving kings. For the king of the same name as the one mentioned before, Antiochus <note>Antiochus VII Sidetes.</note>, the son of Demetrius—as Posidonius relates—used to host massive daily gatherings. Apart from the food consumed, he would allow each guest to carry away whole portions of meat from land, air, and sea animals, prepared as if they were undivided, enough to fill a wagon. After this came heaps of honey-cakes and crowns made of myrrh and frankincense, along with golden ornaments as long as a man. Another king, Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes.</note>, celebrating games at Daphne, also hosted magnificent receptions, as Posidonius tells us. First, he distributed portions of meat to every man. Later, he gave away live animals: geese, hares, and gazelles. Golden crowns were given to the diners, along with a multitude of silver vessels, slaves, horses, and camels. Each guest was told to mount a camel, drink, and then keep the camel and the servant standing by it. He says all the inhabitants of Syria, because of the fertility of the land, would hold constant gatherings to feast together, free from the labor of necessities. They used the gymnasia as if they were baths, anointing themselves with costly oils and perfumes, and treated the *grammateia* <note>original: γραμματείοις; likely referring to public halls or offices used as dining clubs.</note> as if they were their own homes. Most of the day was spent stuffing themselves with wine and food, even carrying away leftovers, all while listening to the loud sound of the "swallow-song" flute. The whole city echoed with such noise.

<margin>Alexander’s banquet</margin> I also praise, dear friends, the banquet held by Alexander, the king of Syria <note>Alexander Balas.</note>. This Alexander was the supposed son of Antiochus Epiphanes, put forward because of the hatred everyone felt for Demetrius; our companion Athenaeus discusses this in his history of the Syrian kings. Here is how that banquet went: Diogenes the Epicurean—a man of considerable skill in his chosen school of thought, originally from Seleucia near Babylon—was well-received by the king, even though the king usually delighted in Stoic teachings. Alexander treated him with great honor despite Diogenes being a man of poor character, foul-mouthed and spiteful, not even sparing kings from his ridicule. When Diogenes made a strange request to the king—asking for a purple tunic and a golden crown featuring the **Face of Virtue** <note>An allegorical representation of Virtue (*Arete*).</note> in the center so he could be called her priest—the king granted it and gave him the crown as a gift. Diogenes, having fallen in love with a female performer <note>original: Λυσιωδοῦ (*lysiode*); a performer of satirical or erotic songs.</note>, gave these items to her. When Alexander heard of this, he gathered a banquet of philosophers and notable men and invited Diogenes. When he arrived, the king asked him to recline for the meal wearing his crown and robes. After he made some ill-timed excuse, the king signaled for the entertainment to be brought in, including the woman, who entered wearing the Crown of Virtue and the purple robe. While everyone burst into great laughter, the philosopher remained unbothered and never stopped praising the woman. Later, Antiochus <note>Antiochus VI Dionysus.</note>, who succeeded to the throne, could not endure Diogenes’ insults and ordered him to be executed. Yet Alexander himself was gentle to all and a lover of learning in his conversations—not like Athenion the Peripatetic philosopher, who also taught school in Athens and Messene, and even in Larissa.

<margin>Philosophers who became tyrants</margin> We shall later speak of this Athenion who became a tyrant of the city, whose history Posidonius of Apamea records in detail. Even if the account is long, it is worth setting it out so that we may carefully examine all those who claim to be philosophers, and not trust their coarse cloaks and unkempt beards. ### BOOK 5

If I speak the truth, I will not bring joy. If I bring joy to some, I will not be speaking the truth. But since they say truth is dear <note>A reference to the proverb "Plato is dear, but truth is dearer."</note>, we shall set forth the facts concerning this man as they happened, and the school named after the **Peripatetics** <note>original: περιπατητικῶν (*peripatetikon*); the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, known for walking while lecturing.</note>. For I shall dwell upon the accounts concerning the man at Athens, who, having purchased an Egyptian slave-woman, associated with her. While she was in his house and giving birth, the child—born of someone else but given the same name as his master, **Athenion**—was raised by him. Having learned his letters, he acted as a guide for his master in his old age, along with his mother. And upon his master’s death, having inherited the estate, he was enrolled as an Athenian citizen by fraudulent means, and he married a beautiful young girl. After these events, he set his heart on practicing philosophy, hunting for "scholarly" youths and teaching philosophy in Messene and in Larissa in Thessaly; having amassed a great deal of money, he returned to Athens. He was elected as an ambassador by the Athenians when affairs were shifting toward **Mithridates** <note>Mithridates VI Eupator, the King of Pontus and a major rival to the Roman Republic.</note>; having ingratiated himself with the King, <margin>10</margin> he became one of his inner circle, attaining the highest advancement. Consequently, he stirred up the Athenians through letters, claiming he had the greatest influence with the "Cappadocian" <note>Referring to Mithridates, whose kingdom was in the region of Cappadocia and Pontus.</note>, suggesting that not only would they be released from the burden of their debts and live in harmony, but they would also recover their democracy and receive great gifts both privately and publicly. The Athenians boasted of these things, being convinced that the Roman empire had been destroyed. But since affairs in Asia had already changed, Athenion returned to Athens. Being troubled by a storm, he was carried down to Carystus. When the "Descendants of Cecrops" <note>original: Κεκροπίδαι (*Kekropidai*); a poetic name for the Athenians, after their mythical king Cecrops.</note> learned of this, they immediately sent warships to bring him back, and a silver-footed litter. Almost the entire city, and many others besides, ran out to welcome him, marvelling at the paradox of fortune: that the "re-enrolled" Athenion was being brought back to Athens upon a silver-footed litter and purple coverings—he who had never before seen purple even on his philosopher's cloak, <margin>20</margin> at a time when not even any of the Romans had ever behaved with such ostentatious luxury in Attica. Men, women, and children all ran together for this sight, expecting the greatest things from Mithridates. When Athenion, the performer who had once held "contribution-lectures" <note>original: ἐρανικὰς ἀκροάσεις (*eranikas akroaseis*); lectures where the audience paid a contribution to attend.</note>, paraded through the countryside and the city because of the King, the **Guild of Dionysus** <note>original: οἱ περὶ τὸν Διόνυσον τεχνῖται (*hoi peri ton Dionyson technitai*); the professional guild of actors and musicians.</note> met him, calling him the "messenger of the New Dionysus" <note>Mithridates styled himself as a "New Dionysus."</note>, inviting him to the common hearth and the prayers and libations associated with it. He, who previously had gone out from a rented house, was brought into the house of Aristion, which was decorated with rugs, paintings, statues, and a display of silver vessels. From this house he emerged wearing a brilliant cloak and a gold ring engraved with the image of Mithridates. A great many servants preceded and followed him. In the sacred precinct of the artists, sacrifices were performed to mark Athenion’s presence, and libations were made with the announcement of a herald. On the following <margin>30</margin> day, many people came to the house and waited for his appearance. The **Kerameikos** <note>The "Potters' Quarter," a prominent area of Athens used for public gatherings and burials.</note> was full of citizens and foreigners, and there was a spontaneous rush of the crowds to the assembly. He finally came forward, guarded by those who wished to be in high favor with the people, each of them eager even just to touch his garment. Having ascended the **bema** <note>The speaker's platform.</note> built in front of the Stoa of Attalos for the Roman generals, he stood there and, looking around at the circular crowd, raised his eyes and said: "Men of Athens, circumstances and the interest of the fatherland compel me to report what I know. But the magnitude of what is about to be said, due to the unexpected nature of the news, hinders me." When the crowds shouted all at once for him to take heart and speak, he said: "I tell you, then, of things never hoped for, nor even imagined in a dream. King Mithridates is master of Bithynia and Upper Cappadocia. He is the natural master of all Asia as far as Pamphylia and Cilicia. Kings of the Armenians and Persians serve as his bodyguards. <margin>40</margin> He rules the nations around Lake Maeotis <note>The Sea of Azov.</note> and the whole Black Sea, a circuit of thirty thousand stadia. The Roman general of Pamphylia, **Quintus Oppius**, has been handed over and follows him in chains. **Manius Aquillius**, the man of consular rank who celebrated a triumph over Sicily, is dragged on foot by a horseman, bound by a long chain five cubits long. Of the other Romans, some have prostrated themselves before the statues of the gods, while the rest have changed their clothes into square cloaks <note>Adopting Greek dress to hide their Roman identity.</note> and call themselves by their original homelands once more. Every city meets the King with honors beyond those of men, calling him the 'God King.' Oracles from everywhere prophesy his rule over the inhabited world. Therefore, great armies have been sent toward Thrace and Macedonia, and all parts of Europe have collectively shifted toward him. For ambassadors are present with him, not only from the Italian nations but also from the Carthaginians, asking for an alliance for the destruction of Rome." After pausing a <margin>50</margin> day on these matters, and having allowed many to talk amongst themselves about the paradoxes announced, he wiped his forehead and said: "What then do I advise? Do not tolerate the anarchy which the Roman Senate has caused to be poured over you, while it decides for itself how you must be governed. Let us not allow the temples to be closed, the gymnasia to be parched, the theater to be without assemblies, and the law courts to be silent."

### FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS

The **Pnyx** <note>The traditional meeting place of the Athenian democratic assembly.</note>, which had been consecrated by the oracles of the gods, was snatched away from the people and handed over to him. The Athenians saw the sacred voice of **Iacchus** <note>A ritual cry or deity associated with the Eleusinian Mysteries.</note> silenced, the venerable sanctuary of the two goddesses <note>Demeter and Persephone at Eleusis.</note> closed, and the lecture halls of the philosophers left voiceless. After many such things were said by the attendants, the crowds spoke with them and, sharing their enthusiasm, rushed into the theater and elected **Athenion** as General over the Infantry. The Peripatetic philosopher then stepped forward into the orchestra, walking with a stride equal to that of Pythocles. He thanked the Athenians and said: "Now you are your own generals; I said before that if you would nod your approval, this would happen, as much as it concerns the common good of you all." Having said this, he appointed the other magistrates he wanted, suggesting their names.

A few days later, having declared himself tyrant, he showed his true intentions regarding his plot—by the god of friendship, what a "philosophy" it was! It was just as the handsome **Pythagoras** introduced, as **Theopompus** recorded in the eighth book of his *History of Philip*. But **Hermippus**, the follower of Callimachus, immediately noticed that this man acted contrary to the teachings of **Aristotle** and **Theophrastus** regarding sensible citizens, proving the truth of the proverb: <note>original: μὴ παιδὶ μάχαιραν (*me paidi machairan*)</note> "Do not give a sword to a child." He immediately removed those citizens who were of sound mind. He stationed guards at the gates so that many Athenians, fearing what was to come, were prevented from letting themselves down over the walls by ropes to flee at night. Athenion sent out cavalry to pursue them; some he slaughtered, and others he brought back in chains, accompanied by many bodyguards from among those called the "rag-bearers."

He frequently gathered assemblies and pretended to favor the Roman cause. However, bringing charges against many—accusing them of sending messages to the exiles or of plotting revolution—he put them to death. He placed thirty guards at each gate, allowing no one who wished to enter or leave. He also seized the property of many and gathered so much money that he filled several wells with it. He sent agents into the countryside like highwaymen to catch those who were retreating; they brought them back to him, and he destroyed them without trial after torturing and racking them. He also brought treason charges against many, alleging they were assisting the exiles in their return. Some fled out of fear before their trial, while others were condemned in the courts, with Athenion himself casting the deciding vote. A shortage of the necessities of life soon occurred in the city; during the famine, he rationed a small amount of barley to the people. He also sent out heavy-armed soldiers into the territory to hunt down anyone who had retreated within the borders, or any Athenian traveling abroad; anyone caught was beaten to death. He publicized these murders, which he preceded with tortures, and he proclaimed that everyone must stay indoors after sunset, and that no one should walk about with a lamp-bearer.

He did not only plunder the property of citizens, but eventually laid his hands even on the property of the gods. He stretched out his hands toward the treasures of the god at **Delos** <note>Apollo.</note>. <margin>Apellicon.</margin> He sent **Apellicon of Teos** to the island. Apellicon had become an Athenian citizen and lived a very colorful and fickle life. He claimed to be a philosopher and a follower of the Peripatetic school; he had purchased the library of Aristotle and many others, for he was very wealthy. He also used to steal the original <note>original: αὐτόγραφα (*autographa*)</note> decrees of the ancients from the temple of the Mother of the Gods, as well as anything ancient or hidden from other cities. When he was caught in Athens for these thefts, he would have been in danger if he had not fled. He returned not long after, having flattered many. The Athenians enrolled him in their ranks, as if he were truly of their same philosophical sect.

Athenion, holding to the doctrines of the Peripatetics, measured out a small ration <note>original: χοίνικα (*choinika*); roughly a quart, a meager daily portion.</note> of barley to last four days for the foolish Athenians—food fit for poultry, giving it to them as if they were not men. Meanwhile, Apellicon set out for Delos with a military force. He conducted himself more like he was at a festival than on a campaign, keeping a very careless guard over the Delian side. Especially on the side of the island facing **Thespiae**, he left the area unguarded and did not even dig a trench. Instead, he went to sleep. When **Orobius**, the Roman general guarding Delos, realized this, he waited for a moonless night. Landing his soldiers, he fell upon the Athenians while they were sleeping and drunk. He slaughtered the Athenians and those campaigning with them like cattle—six hundred in number. He took about three hundred prisoner. The "noble" general Apellicon secretly fled from Delos. When Orobius saw many others had fled into farmsteads, he burned them down along with the houses. He also destroyed all their siege engines, including the **Helepolis** <note>original: ἑλεπόλει (*helepolei*); a massive "city-taker" mobile siege tower.</note> which Apellicon had constructed upon arriving at Delos. Having set up a trophy and an altar on the site, Orobius inscribed the following:

> The strangers who died here have this tomb, they who fought for Delos,
> And lost their lives in the sea.
> When the Athenians were ravaging the sacred island,
> Having joined in a common war for the King of the Cappadocians <note>Mithridates VI.</note>.

And there was also this Epicurean philosopher who became a tyrant, named **Lysias**. Having been elected as a "Crown-bearer" by his country—which is to say, a priest of Heracles—he did not lay down his office, but remained a tyrant while wearing the robe. He wore a white-centered purple tunic, and over it he threw a costly cloak decorated with animal patterns; he wore white Laconian shoes and was crowned with a wreath of golden laurel. He distributed the property of the rich to the poor, after committing many murders of those who would not give.
