...a soldier of irreproachable strength. For Plato says that Socrates served in three campaigns, <margin>The campaigns of Socrates.</margin> one to Potidaea, another to Amphipolis, and a third against the Boeotians, which was when the Battle of Delium took place. Yet none of the historians mention this; Plato himself says that Socrates even received the prize for valor <note>term: *aristeia*—the award given to the bravest soldier after a battle</note> when all the other Athenians were in flight and many were being killed. All of these claims are false. For the campaign against Amphipolis <margin>5</margin> occurred during the archonship of Alcaeus <note>term: archon—the chief magistrate of Athens; their names were used to date years</note>, under the leadership of Cleon, and consisted of "picked men," as Thucydides says. Socrates would necessarily have had to be one of these picked men, yet he possessed nothing but a worn cloak and a staff. What historian or poet mentions this? Where has Thucydides ever recognized the Socrates of Plato’s imagination as a soldier? For what does he know of his private habits or his staff? And when did he ever serve at Potidaea, as Plato has said in the *Charmides*, claiming that he even yielded the prize for valor to Alcibiades at that time? <margin>10</margin> Neither Thucydides nor Isocrates mentions this in his speech *On the Team of Horses*. In what battle did Socrates receive the prize, and what notable deed did he perform? It is entirely unrecorded; no such battle coincided with the events as Thucydides has narrated them. Not content with this fabrication, Plato also introduces the heroic deeds at Delium—or rather, the invented heroism. For if Socrates had behaved at Delium as Herodicus of Cratete records in his *Against the Friend of Socrates*, he would have fled ingloriously along with the <margin>15</margin> masses when Pagondas sent two companies of cavalry around the hill from a hidden position. For the account says some of the Athenians fled toward Delium, others toward the sea, others toward Oropus, and others toward Mount Parnes. The Boeotians followed and killed them, especially the cavalry, both their own and those of the Locrians. In the midst of such chaos and fear overtaking the Athenians, did Socrates alone stand there "looking sideways and stalking like a pelican" <note>original: βρενθυόμενος, καὶ τὰ ὀφθαλμὼ παραβάλλων — a famous description of Socrates’s walk from Aristophanes and Plato</note>, holding back the Boeotian and Locrian cavalry? <margin>20</margin> Neither Thucydides nor any other poet mentions this "courage" of his. And how could anyone yield a prize for valor to Alcibiades, who did not participate in that campaign at all? In the *Crito*, that "friend of memory" Plato even says that Socrates never once went abroad, except for a single trip to the Isthmus. Antisthenes the Socratic records the same things about the prize for valor as Plato. But this story is not true. For this "Dog" <note>original: Κύων — a reference to Antisthenes being the founder of the Cynic (dog-like) school of philosophy</note> grants many favors to Socrates. Therefore, <margin>25</margin> neither of them is to be trusted, if we look to Thucydides as our guide. Antisthenes even toys with the false writing, saying: "We hear that you also received the prize for valor in the battle against the Boeotians." He knew the bad reputation of the story, saying to Alcibiades: "The honor is not mine, but yours, for you gave it to me, as we hear." But Plato’s Socrates says he was present at Potidaea and yielded the prize to Alcibiades—yet according to all historians, the campaign at Potidaea, which Phormio commanded, preceded the one at Delium. In every respect, <margin>30</margin> <margin>Xenophon erring in his chronology.</margin> these philosophers lie and write many things regarding dates without realizing their errors. Just like the "fair" Xenophon, who in his *Symposium* posits that Callias, the son of Hipponicus, held a banquet because he was in love with Autolycus, the son of Lycon, who had won the pancratium <note>term: pancratium—a brutal ancient Greek combat sport combining wrestling and boxing</note>. He places those present at the feast with the other guests, though they were perhaps not even born yet, or were still in their childhood. This was the time when Aristion was archon; it was under him that Eupolis produced the play *Autolycus* through Demostratus <margin>35</margin> and mocked the victory of Autolycus. Again, Xenophon makes Socrates say these things in the *Symposium*: "And Pausanias, the lover of Agathon the poet, speaking in defense of those who wallow in lack of self-control, said that the strongest army would be one made of boyfriends and lovers. For he said he thought they would be most ashamed to abandon one another." These are marvelous things to say, as if those who disregard blame would be ashamed before each other! They are usually the ones most ashamed to do anything disgraceful. <margin>40</margin> That Pausanias never said any of these things can be learned from Plato’s *Symposium*. I know of no writing by Pausanias, nor is he introduced by anyone else speaking about the use of lovers and boyfriends except by Plato. Whether Xenophon lied or simply came across a version of Plato's *Symposium* that was written differently, let it pass. But we must address the chronological failure: Aristion, under whom the symposium is set as a fiction, was archon four years after Euphemus, under whom Plato writes that Agathon's victory feast took place—the setting where Pausanias discusses erotic matters. It is, therefore, wondrous and monstrous if things not yet spoken were being critiqued four years before they were said. In general, Plato’s *Symposium* is nonsense. For when Agathon won, Plato was fourteen years old. Agathon was crowned at the Lenaia <note>term: Lenaia—an annual Athenian festival with dramatic competitions</note> under the archon Euphemus. Plato was born under Apollodorus, who was archon after Euthydemus. Having lived eighty-two years, he passed away under Theophilus, who came after Callimachus—who is the eighty-second archon. From Apollodorus and the birth of Plato, <margin>50</margin> Euphemus is the fourteenth archon, the one under whom Agathon’s victory feast was held. And Plato himself indicates that this gathering happened a long time ago, so that even I might report it.

> "For I," he said, "how should I know? Perhaps I am Glaucon. Do you not know that for many years Agathon has not lived here?"

And proceeding, he says,

<meta>This page continues the critique of Plato’s historical accuracy, specifically addressing his dialogues the *Symposium*, *Gorgias*, and *Protagoras*. The author is demonstrating that the timelines Plato provides for famous events and people do not align with the records of historians.</meta>

"But tell me, when did this gathering take place?" And I said, "While we were still children, when Agathon won the prize for his first tragedy." <margin>Plato's chronological errors.</margin> It is clear from many instances that Plato often errs regarding chronology. For, to quote a poet who is not present, he does not let his tongue wander "out of season," nor does he write without making distinctions. He did not speak without preparation, but with great deliberation. As he writes in the *Gorgias*: 

> "Then this Archelaus <note>Archelaus I, King of Macedon from 413 to 399 BCE.</note> is miserable according to your logic, if indeed, my friend, he is unjust."

Then, after explicitly stating that Archelaus held the sovereignty over the Macedonians, he proceeds to write the following: 

> "And we found that Pericles had recently died." 

Now, if Pericles had "recently died," Archelaus was not yet master of the kingdom; but if Archelaus was king, Pericles had died a very long time before. Perdiccas <note>The king of Macedon before Archelaus.</note> reigned before Archelaus, for forty-seven years according to Nicomedes of Acanthus; Theopompus says thirty-five; Anaximenes says forty; Hieronymus says twenty-eight; Marsyas says seventeen; and Philochorus says twenty-three. Even if we take the shortest of these recorded periods, twenty-three years, it still fails to align. Pericles died in the third year of the Peloponnesian War <note>429 BCE</note>, during the archonship <note>term: archon—the chief magistrate of Athens; years were named after them</note> of Epameinon, which is when Perdiccas died and Archelaus succeeded to the throne. How then could Pericles have "recently" died according to Plato? And in the same *Gorgias*, he makes Socrates say: 

> "Last year, when I was chosen by lot to serve on the Council <margin>Memoirs <note>Likely referring to Xenophon's *Memorabilia*.</note></margin>, and my tribe held the presidency, and it was my duty to put the matter to a vote, I provided a laugh because I did not know how to put it to the vote."

Socrates was not so much ignorant as he was stubborn <note>original: *authadian*—willfulness or self-will</note>, as they say. For he was unwilling to break the laws of the democracy. Xenophon makes this clear in the first book of his *Hellenica*, setting it out thus: 

"When some of the presidents refused to put the motion to a vote because it was contrary to the law, Callixenus again stood up and accused them. The people shouted for those who refused to be summoned. All the presidents, seized with fear, agreed to put the motion to the vote except Socrates, the son of Sophroniscus. He said he would not, but would act in every way according to the laws." 

This was the vote taken against the generals who served under Erasinides, because they did not pick up those who perished in the sea battle at Arginusae <note>406 BCE; the generals were executed for failing to rescue shipwrecked sailors</note>. This battle took place during the archonship of Callias, twenty-four years after the death of Pericles. 

Furthermore, in the dialogue *Protagoras*, which is set after the death of Hipponicus <note>A wealthy Athenian general</note> when Callias had already inherited the estate, Plato has Protagoras arriving for the second time only a few days prior. But Hipponicus, while serving as general during the archonship of Euthydemus, was stationed with Nicias against the Tanagrans and defeated the Boeotians who came to their aid in the battle. He likely died not long before the production of Eupolis’s play *The Flatterers* <note>original: *Kolakes*—a comedy from 421 BCE</note> in the year of Alcaeus. For the play portrays Callias’s lifestyle as if he had only recently come into his inheritance. In this same play, Eupolis introduces Protagoras as being in town. But Ameipsias, in his play *The Commoners* <note>original: *Konnos*</note>, produced two years earlier, does not include him in the chorus of "thinkers." It is clear, then, that he arrived between these dates. 

Yet Plato makes Hippias <note>Hippias of Elis, a famous Sophist</note> also present in the *Protagoras* with some of his own fellow citizens, though it was not likely he could stay safely in Athens before the truce was concluded in the month of Elaphebolion during the archonship of Isarchus. But Plato sets the dialogue much later than these times when these events had recently occurred. He says, at least: "For if there were such wild men as those the poet Pherecrates exhibited last year at the Lenaea <note>A winter festival for drama in Athens.</note>." The play *The Savages* <note>original: *Agrioi*</note> was performed during the archonship of Aristion, after whom came Astyphilus, who was the fifth archon from Isarchus, under whom the truce was made. For first was Isarchus, then Ameinias, after whom was Alcaeus, then Aristion, <margin>Socrates.</margin> and then Astyphilus. Contrary to history, then, Plato brings Hippias into Athens in his dialogue while the citizens were still enemies and before the truce was in effect. 

In other places, Plato says that Chaerephon asked the Pythian priestess if anyone was wiser than Socrates, and she replied, "No one." Even in this, he does not agree with Xenophon, who says: "For when Chaerephon once asked at Delphi concerning me, Apollo replied in the presence of many that no man was more just or more temperate than I." How is it reasonable or plausible that Socrates, who admitted he knew nothing, should be declared the wisest of all by a god who knows everything? For if this is wisdom—to know nothing—then to know everything would be a flaw. 

And what need was there for Chaerephon to bother the god by inquiring about Socrates? Socrates himself was a credible witness regarding himself, saying he was not wise. It was a foolish thing to ask the god such things, as if one were to ask: "Are there any Athenian wools softer than these?" or "Are there any people among the Bactrians or Medes more oily than others?" or "Is there anyone more snub-nosed than Socrates?" For the god sharpens his wit against those who ask such things. Like the person—whether it was Aesop the fable-writer or someone else—who mockingly asked, "How might I become rich, O son of Zeus and Leto?" and the god answered, "If you acquire the land between Corinth and Sicyon." 

Furthermore, none of the comic poets ever mentioned the things Plato said about Socrates: neither that he was the son of a "Sturdy Midwife" <note>original: *Maia Blosura*—a joke or alternative name for his mother Phaenarete</note>, nor that Xanthippe was a difficult wife who poured washtubs <note>term: *nitēras*—basins of dirty water or lye</note> over his head. Nor did they mention that Alcibiades slept under Socrates' own cloak—though it would have been necessary for Aristophanes to trumpet this abroad, especially since Plato has him present at the symposium. For he would not have been silent

### BOOK 5

They seem to resemble Aristophanes in his portrayal of Socrates as a corrupter of youth. Aspasia, the wise teacher of rhetoric to Socrates, in the verses attributed to her which Herodicus the Cratetean set forth, says the following: "Socrates, you did not escape my notice when your heart was bitten by desire for the son of Dinomache and Cleinias <note>original: "παιδὸς Δεινομάχης καὶ Κλεινία"—referring to Alcibiades</note>. But listen if you wish to fare well with your beloved; do not disobey my messenger, but be persuaded, and it will be much better for you. And when I heard this, I let my body be anointed with joy. With tears in my eyes, I unwillingly send forth a groan, having covered my heart with the restraints of a captive. Or you will capture him with the terror of songs and desires. For the beginning of friendship lies in both. Having restrained him in this way, you will win him over by appealing to his senses." So the handsome Socrates goes hunting, with the woman from Miletus <note>Aspasia was from Miletus</note> as his teacher of love; but he is not the one being hunted, as Plato said, trapped in the nets of Alcibiades. Indeed, he speaks through tears, as I think, being in a state of distress. For seeing him in such a condition, Aspasia says: "Why have you been weeping, dear Socrates? Has desire, struck by the eyes of the unconquerable youth, been rekindled in your chest? I promised to make that gathering of followers for you." That he was truly in love with Alcibiades is made clear by Plato in the *Protagoras*, even though the boy was nearly thirty years old. He writes thus: "Where have you come from, Socrates? Surely from the hunt after the youthful beauty of Alcibiades? And indeed, when I saw him just the other day, the man still seemed handsome to me. A man, indeed, Socrates—to speak among ourselves—already filling out with a beard." Then he asks: "What of it? Are you not an admirer of Homer, who said that the most graceful bloom of youth is that of the first beard, which Alcibiades now has?" <margin>Philosophers and accusers.</margin> Most philosophers are naturally more prone to accusation than even the comic poets. Take Aeschines the Socratic: in his *Telauges*, he mocks Critobulus, the son of Crito, for his ignorance and the filthiness of his life; and he reports that Telauges himself died wearing a garment that cost only half an obol <note>term: obol—a small silver coin of ancient Greece; half an obol represents extreme poverty or stinginess</note> every day. He ridicules him in a comedy-like fashion for being girt and wearing rotting sandals tied with scraps, and he mocks the orator quite immeasurably. In his *Aspasia*, he calls Hipponicus, the son of Callias, a "foolish person" <note>original: "μοάλεμον"—likely meaning a simpleton or dullard</note>. He summarizes the women from Ionia as "adulteresses and courtesans." His *Callias* contains the dispute between Callias and his father, and the mockery of the sophists <note>term: sophist—a paid teacher of philosophy and rhetoric in ancient Greece</note> Prodicus and Anaxagoras. For he says that Prodicus turned Theramenes into a student. The other philosopher, Philoxenus, mentions Eryxidias and Ariphrades (the brother of Arignotus the cithara-player), wanting to reveal their wickedness and the source of their base gluttony from the teaching of those who educated them. In the *Axiochus*, he bitterly attacks Alcibiades as a drunkard and as one who behaves licentiously with other men's wives. Antisthenes, in one of his *Cyrus* dialogues, slanders Alcibiades, saying he is lawless in his conduct toward women and in his general way of life. For he says he slept with his mother, his daughter, and his sister, just like the Persians. His *Statesman* dialogue contains an attack on all the demagogues in Athens. His *Archelaus* attacks the orator Gorgias. His *Aspasia* is a slander of Pericles' sons, Xanthippus and Paralus. For he says that one of them, Archestratus, was a roommate who lived like those working in small brothels. He says the other was a companion and acquaintance of Euphemus, mocking him for vulgar and cold jokes when they met. Plato, renaming a work *Sathon* <note>original: "Σάθωνα"—a crude term referring to the male member; used here as a mocking nickname for Antisthenes</note>, published that dialogue against him in an improper and vulgar manner. For to these men, not one person seems to be a good counselor, or a general, or a noteworthy mime, or a sophist, or a useful poet, or a sensible populace. But Socrates, after his time with Aspasia, spent his time with the flute-girls of the workshop, and talked with Gison the breastplate-maker. And he taught Theodote the courtesan how she should enjoy her lovers, as Xenophon introduces him in the second book of his *Memorabilia*. For he makes him give such advice to Theodote as neither Nico the Samian, nor Callistrate the Lesbian, nor Philaenis the Leucadian, nor even the Athenian Pythonicus ever devised as charms for desire. Indeed, these things follow in a circular fashion. Time would fail me if I wished to set out all the "solemn" censures of the philosophers. For according to Plato himself, a "multitude of such Gorgons and Pegasuses" flows in upon me, and other impossible things in number and strange monstrosities of nature. Therefore, I shall remain silent. <margin>Gorgon.</margin> After Masurius had said these things and was admired by everyone for his wisdom, Ulpian, when silence fell, said: "It seems to me, fellow diners, that you have been drenched in fierce words, quite beyond expectation, like one who has had too much unmixed wine. For a man drawing wine like a horse draws water speaks in the Scythian fashion <note>The Scythians were famous for drinking wine undiluted, which the Greeks considered barbaric</note>. Or perhaps, knowing the letter 'Koppa' <note>original: "κόππα"—an archaic Greek letter; here referring to a brand for horses or a specific type of cup</note>, he dives down speechless into the jar. He is fast asleep as if drinking poppy-juice drugs, as Parmenon of Byzantium says. Or perhaps you have been turned to stone by the aforementioned Gorgons. As to whether there really are certain animals that cause petrification in humans, Alexander of Myndus records in the second book of his *History of Beasts* as follows: the nomads in Libya call the animal the Gorgon, which is also where it is found. It looks downward. Most say it is similar to a wild sheep, marked by its skin. Some say it is like a calf. They say it has such a..."

<meta>This page concludes the final discussions of Book 5, including accounts of exotic African beasts and a polemic against pedantic grammarians, before transitioning into the opening of Book 6, which focuses on the merits of Greek drama.</meta>

<margin>Backward-grazing oxen, according to the records...</margin>
...it breathes out a foul air, so that it destroys anyone who encounters the animal. It carries a mane from its forehead hanging down over its eyes; whenever it barely manages to part it because of its weight and looks out, it kills whoever is seen by it. It does not do this with its breath, but by the natural force emanating from its eyes, which turns the viewer into a corpse. It became known in this way: Some of the soldiers with Marius <note>Gaius Marius (157–86 BCE), the Roman general</note> campaigning against Jugurtha <note>The King of Numidia</note>, seeing the Gorgon <note>original: "Γοργόνα"—here refers to the Catoblepas, a mythical creature often described as a downward-looking beast</note> and thinking—because it was bowed down and moved slowly—that it was a wild sheep, rushed at it to dispatch it with the swords they held. But the creature, being startled, parted the mane lying over its eyes and immediately turned those who had rushed toward it into corpses. Again and again, when others did the same and those who approached were always killed, some of the men inquired among the locals about the nature of the animal. At Marius’s command, some Numidian horsemen shot it from a distance with arrows. They killed it and brought the beast back to the general. It was either this creature, or its skin, that was a testament to Marius's campaign. What is told by the historians regarding this is not entirely credible, such as the claim that there are certain cattle in Libya called "backward-grazers" <note>original: "ὀπισθονόμοι" (opisthonomoi)</note>, because they do not graze while moving forward. Instead, they do so while retreating backward. They say their horns are an obstacle to natural grazing because they do not curve upward, like those of other animals,
<margin>10</margin>
but rather they curve downward and overshadow the eyes. This is equally hard to believe, as no other historian bears witness to it. When Ulpian had said these things, Larensis <note>The host of the banquet</note> bore witness and, agreeing with the account, said that Marius had indeed sent these skins to Rome, and no one was able to guess what animal they belonged to because of their extraordinary appearance. These skins were dedicated in the Temple of Hercules, through which generals leading triumphs enter the city, just as many of our own poets and writers have stated. Therefore, you grammarians, do not record anything of this sort, according to Herodicus of Babylon. "Fly, you followers of Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace, the famous librarian and critic</note>, over the broad back of the sea, away from Greece, more cowardly than a young deer! You corner-buzzers <note>original: "Γωνιοβόμβυκες"—a derogatory term for scholars who mutter in corners</note> who care only for monosyllables, you whose concern is with 'sphin' and 'sphoin' and 'min' and 'nin' <note>These are obscure Greek pronoun forms that grammarians obsessed over</note>. Let this be your wretched lot, but let Greece and god-born Babylon always remember Herodicus." For according to the comic poet Anaxandrides, it is a private pleasure: "Whenever someone finds a new thought, they must show it to everyone. But those who are truly wise first have a judge of their craft, then they are envied. One must bring it to the crowd, everything that seems to have some novelty." After these words, most of the guests quietly withdrew and the gathering broke up.

# ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE
<margin>30</margin>
## BOOK SIX

<margin>Tragedy.</margin>
Since you constantly ask when we meet, my friend Timocrates, for the things said among the Deipnosophists <note>The "Banquet of the Learned"</note>, thinking we are finding something new, we will remind you of what is said by Antiphanes regarding poetry, in this manner: "Tragedy is a happy creation in every way, especially because the stories are first recognized by the spectators before anyone even speaks. The poet only needs to remind them. If I say 'Oedipus,' they know all the rest: his father was Laius, his mother Jocasta, his daughters and sons. They know what he will suffer and what he has done. Again, if someone says 'Alcmaeon,' even the children immediately say he went mad and killed his mother, and Adrastus will arrive soon in a rage. When they have nothing more to say, they completely give up on the plays and lift the stage-crane like a finger <note>A gesture of surrender or an appeal to the 'deus ex machina'</note>, and it is enough for the audience. But for us (comic poets), this is not possible; we must find all new names, then the previous circumstances, the current situation, the resolution, and the opening. If one of these is left out, some Chremes or Pheidon <note>Typical names in Comedy</note> is hissed off the stage. But Peleus and Teucer are allowed to do these things." And Diphilus says in *The Orchard-Keepers*: "O you who made this place most dear to the gods, the sanctuary of Brauron... daughter of Leto and Zeus..." as the tragic poets say, who alone have the power to say and do everything. Timocles the comic poet also says that tragedy is useful to life in many ways, stating in *The Women at the Dionysia*: "Oh my friend, listen to what I am about to tell you. Man is an animal burdened by nature, and life carries many painful things in itself. He therefore discovered these consolations for his cares. For the mind, forgetting its own troubles and being led by the suffering of another, departs with pleasure, having been educated at the same time. Consider first the tragic poets, if you will, how they benefit everyone. For the man who is poor, learning that Telephus was even more of a beggar than himself, now bears his poverty more easily. He who is madly ill looks upon Alcmaeon. If someone has a disease of the eyes, there are the blind sons of Phineus. If someone's child has died, Niobe provides comfort. If someone is lame, there is Philoctetes..."

# BOOK 6

"Look at Philoctetes! An old man in misfortune, yet his mother did not allow him to learn his fate. For by contemplating the greater misfortunes that have befallen others, a man bears his own calamities more easily." <note>This is a quotation from the comic poet Timocles, suggesting that watching tragedies—like that of the suffering hero Philoctetes—is a form of therapy for the audience.</note> And so, we too, Timocrates, are delivering to you the "leftovers" of the *Deipnosophists* <note>original: "Δειπνοσοφιστῶν λείψανα" — literally the "scraps" or "remains" of the learned banquet-goers' conversations.</note>. We are "restoring" them to you, rather than just "giving" them, as the orator from Kothokidai <note>Hegesippus, an Athenian orator and ally of Demosthenes</note> said when mocking Demosthenes. He advised the Athenians not to accept the island of Halonnesus from King Philip if he "gave" it, but only if he "restored" it <note>This refers to a famous diplomatic quibble: "giving" implies a gift of something Philip owned; "restoring" implies returning something that always belonged to Athens.</note>. The comic poet Antiphanes teased this distinction in his play *The Nestling* in this manner: "The master has received back <note>original: "ἀπέλαβεν" (apelaben)</note> all his father's property. Just as he 'received' it, he would have loved the word 'received back'—the very word Demosthenes took up." Alexis also says in *The Soldier*: "You received this back; this is what I took from you as a boy and now return." How can you not like the word "restore," since it belongs to us? It was yours, you gave it to me, we did not simply give it back. <margin>10</margin> Why have we "restored" what was not mine to take? And in *The Brothers*: "I have given something to these men, not as a gift, but as a restoration, for they do not have it though they took it." Anaxilas in *Euandria* says: "And I am not conceding the wrestling grounds to you because of the land, but give them back! I am leaving because of the taxes."

Timocles says in *The Heroes*: "Now command him to speak of everyone else's troubles rather than his own—I shall tell you everything! First, will you not stop? Demosthenes is angry! He is like Briareus <note>A mythological giant with a hundred hands</note>, a man who eats catapults and spears, a hater of words, who never says a pleasant thing but looks like a curse." Following these poets, and "restoring" the sequence of what was previously announced, we shall speak of what followed in our banquet. 

A multitude of children <note>Slaves or attendants</note> entered, carrying such a quantity of fish—from the sea and the lakes—on silver platters that I marveled at the size and the luxury. It was as if Nereids <note>Sea nymphs</note> themselves had gone shopping for us. <margin>20</margin> One of the flatterers present wittily remarked that Poseidon was sending these fish to our friend Neptunius <note>The host or a guest whose name evokes the sea god Neptune</note>. These were not sold by the fish-sellers in Rome who charge an equal weight of money for an equal weight of fish, but were brought from Antium, others from Terracina and the Pontine Islands, and others from Pyrgi—this being a city in Tyrrhenia <note>Etruria</note>. 

The fishmongers <term>ichthyopōlai (ἰχθυοπῶλαι) <gloss>fish-sellers notorious in Greek comedy for their greed and arrogance</gloss></term> in Rome are not much different from those once mocked in Attic comedy. Antiphanes says in *Young Men*: "I used to think the Gorgons were a mere myth, but whenever I go to the fish market, I believe in them instantly. For looking at the fishmongers, I am immediately turned to stone! <note>A pun on the Gorgon's gaze; the high prices "freeze" the customer.</note> So I am forced to talk to them while looking away. If I see how big a fish is and hear the price they ask, I am chilled to the bone." Amphis says in *The Wanderer*: "It is easier to get an audience with a general and receive an answer to a question than it is to deal with the cursed fishmongers in the market! If you ask one of them a question, or pick up something lying there, he stoops down like Telephus <note>A tragic hero often depicted as a silent, brooding beggar</note> <margin>30</margin> and remains silent at first. And they do this with good reason, for they are all man-slayers! He pretends to be busy, doesn't listen, and just beats a polypus <note>octopus</note>. Another might snap off a syllable of the price: 'Eight obols' becomes 'Eight 'bols.' This is the kind of thing one must hear when buying fish."

Alexis says in *The Man with the Glaucous Eyes*: "When I see generals with their eyebrows raised, I think it's a bit much, but I don't really wonder at it, for they are honored by the city. But when I see those damned fishmongers looking down but keeping their eyebrows on top of their heads <note>A sign of extreme arrogance</note>, I choke! If you ask, 'For how much are you selling those two mullets?' he says, 'Ten obols.' 'That’s steep; will you take eight?' 'Only if you buy the other one as well!' Is this not more bitter than gall itself?" Diphilus says in *The Busybody*: "I used to think fishmongers <margin>40</margin> were wicked only in Athens. But it seems the species is a beastly race by nature, and everywhere the same! Here there is a certain 'trans-Pontic' fellow <note>Perhaps from the Black Sea region</note> who grows his hair long, claiming it is sacred to the god. But that’s not why; he has a brand on his forehead and uses his hair as a curtain to hide it! If you ask him, 'How much for the sea-bass?' he answers, 'Ten obols.' He doesn't tell you the currency! Then, when you lay down the money, he demands Aeginetan coins <note>Aeginetan drachmas were heavier and worth more than Attic ones</note>. But if he has to give change, he pays you back in Attic coins! He takes his profit from both sides of the exchange."

Xenarchus says in *The Purple-Fish*: "The poets are full of nonsense; they find nothing new, they just toss the same things up and down. But there is no race more 'philosophical' than the fishmongers—nor more unholy! Since the law forbids them from sprinkling their fish with water, if one of these god-hated men sees his fish drying out, he purposely starts a fight <margin>50</margin> in the middle of the market. Blows are struck, and pretending to have been hit, he falls down and acts as if he has fainted, lying there like a corpse among the fish! Someone shouts for water! A fellow tradesman immediately grabs a pitcher and pours a tiny bit on the 'fainted' man, but pours the rest all over the fish! You would swear the fish had just been caught. You are selling dead fish as fresh, you scoundrel!"

...mystery. In his play *The Merchant*, Diphilus says that there is a certain law among the Corinthians:
> "This is a most excellent custom here among the 
> Corinthians, my good man: if we see someone 
> shopping for gourmet food <note>original: "ὀψωνοῦντ'" (opsonounta). In Athens, buying 'opson'—the 'relish' eaten with bread—usually meant buying expensive fish.</note> 
> with such splendor all the time, we 
> cross-examine him to see where he gets his 
> living and what he does. If he has an estate 
> whose income covers his expenses, we let him 
> enjoy his life. But if he happens to be 
> spending beyond his means, they forbid him 
> from doing it any longer. If he does not obey, 
> they impose a fine. And if he lives 
> luxuriously despite having nothing at all, 
> they hand him over to the public

> impossible for such a man to live without 
> doing some evil. He must necessarily either 
> rob people of their clothes at night, or 
> break into houses, or share the loot with

> "Rightly so, by Zeus! But what does this have 
> to do with me?"
> "We see you shopping for gourmet food every 
> single day, my friend, not in moderation but 
> with arrogance. It is not possible for anyone 
> else to get a share of fish while you are around. 
> You have driven our city to eat only greens; 
> we have to fight over sprigs of celery as if

> <margin>Law</margin> cannot even see one flying anymore because of 
> you! You have driven up the price of foreign 
> wine considerably."

Sophilus, in *The Flower-Gatherer*, suggests that this custom should also exist in Athens, claiming that two or three supervisors should be chosen by the Council for this purpose. Lynceus of Samos even wrote a *Manual on Marketing* <note>original: "τέχνην ὀψωνητικὴν" (techne opsonetike)—a guide for buying gourmet food.</note> addressed to someone who was a "bad buyer" <note>original: "δυσώνην" (dysonen)—someone who pays too much or gets bad quality.</note>, teaching him what to say to those "murderous fishmongers" to buy profitably and get what he wants without being pained.

Picking up the "thorns" <note>A metaphor for difficult or sharp questions.</note> from these previous discussions, Ulpian asked if we could show that the ancients used silver cups or plates during their dinners, and whether "platter" <note>original: "πίναξ" (pinax).</note> is a truly Greek name. For although Homer said in the *Odyssey*:
<margin>Od. 17</margin>
> "Beside them the swineherd placed platters of 
> meat,"

Aristophanes of Byzantium <note>A famous grammarian from the 3rd century BCE.</note> says that serving gourmet dishes on platters is a more modern practice. He was apparently unaware that the poet also said elsewhere:
<margin>Od. 1</margin>
> "The carver lifted platters of meat and placed 
> them beside them."

Ulpian also asks whether some people owned a great multitude of slaves, just as people do now; whether the word for frying pan <note>original: "τήγανον" (teganon)</note> is correctly used (rather than only *tagenon*); and whether we should not "drink or eat everything" like those who are called "parasites" <note>originally meaning those who ate at the public expense, later becoming 'moochers'</note> or "flatterers" because of their bellies.

To him, Aemilianus replied: "You have the word 'platter' used for a vessel by the comic poet Metagenes in *The Thurio-Persians*. As for 'frying pan,' the excellent Pherecrates uses it in *The Man-Haters* as follows:
> 'And they said they were letting the small 
> fry go from the frying pan.'"

And in his *Persians*, the same author says: "Setting it upon frying pans, set the rushes on fire." Philonides in *The Buskins* speaks of "putting on shoes made of rays <note>A type of flatfish.</note> in frying pans," and again mentions someone "smelling something from a frying pan." Eubulus in *Orthanes* says: "A fan wakes up the guard-dogs of Hephaestus <note>A poetic way of referring to fire/sparks.</note>, provoking them with the heat and the breath of the frying pan." And again: "Every beautiful woman who is in love frequents the frying pan and delights in sautéing." And in *The Titans*: "The cooking pot smiles at us and bubbles with a barbarian babbling." Gnathaena likewise mentions "fish in hated frying pans." The verb "to fry up" is used by Phrynichus in *The Tragedians*: "It is sweet to fry oneself up for a contribution." And Pherecrates says in *The Ant-Men*: "But you, having fried it up..." Hegesander of Delphi says that the Syracusans call small dishes "frying pans," and they call the actual frying pan a "dry-frying-pan." This is why Theodoridas says in a certain poem: "A frying pan's double-handled vessel in an eight-measure pool," referring to the dish as a "frying pan." Without the letter 't', the Ionians say *ēganon*, as Anacreon does: "To throw the hand into the frying pan."

Your question, noble Ulpian, brings me back to consider the use of silver plate, specifically what was said by Alexis in *The Fugitive*: "For the hired pottery that the cooks use would bring a horse." For until the times of the Macedonians, those who dined were served with earthenware vessels, as my friend Juba says. But when the Romans were already changing their lifestyle to something more 
<margin>By Alexis</margin> luxurious, Cleopatra—the one who brought an end to the kingdom of Egypt—imitated them. Since she could not change the traditional name, she called her silver and gold vessels "pottery." 
<margin>the</margin> These "pottery" items <note>original: "κέραμα" (kerama)—literally 'ceramics'.</note> were given as take-home gifts to the guests. This was the peak of luxury: Cleopatra spent daily minas <note>A unit of currency; a silver mina was a significant sum.</note> on this "pottery," specifically the high-quality Rhosian kind, which was extremely fragrant.

King Ptolemy, in the eighth book of his *Memoirs*, discussing Masinissa the king of the Libyans <note>Masinissa was the first King of Numidia.</note>, says the following: 
"The dinners were prepared in the Roman fashion with 'pottery,' but everything was provided in silver. He decorated the second tables <note>The dessert or fruit course.</note> according to Italian customs. The baskets were all made of gold, but fashioned to look like they were woven from reeds. He also employed Greek musicians."

Aristophanes the comic poet—as Heliodorus of Athens says in his work *On the Acropolis* regarding the earth of Naucratis—says in his play *Wealth*, during the appearance of the god of the same name, that the fish-platters were seen to become silver. Having learned this, he says the following:
"Every vinegar-cruet, small dish, and cooking pot has become bronze. But the rotten little platters—the ones for fish—you can now see them as silver!"

->ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS<-

The oven suddenly became made of ivory. And Plato <note>Plato Comicus, a writer of Old Comedy, not the philosopher.</note> in *The Ambassadors* says: "I caught Epicrates and Phormisius <note>Athenian politicians often accused of taking bribes from Persia.</note> receiving many bribes from the King—gold bowls and small silver plates." Sophron, in his *Mimes of Women*, says: "My house gleamed with bronze and silver plate." Philippides, in *The Disappearance of Silver*, mentions such things as a sign of vulgarity. When some newly-rich resident aliens were bothering him, he says: "But a certain pity for the whole situation has fallen upon me when you, a common slave, drive away free men, while a silver plate worth a mina <term>mina: a unit of currency equal to 100 drachmas, a very high price for a single dish</term> carries a piece of dried fish worth two or three obols, or three-farthings worth of capers on a tray that costs fifty silver drachmas."

In earlier times, it was a difficult task to even see a sacrificial bowl <note>original: "φιάλη" (phiale), a shallow bowl used for pouring libations to the gods.</note> dedicated in a temple. Indeed, this was still the case then: if someone dedicated one, someone else immediately snatched it. Alexis, in *The Little Horse*, introduces a young man in love showing off his wealth to his mistress, and makes him say: "I told them all—for I brought two sets of plate from home for everyone to see. There was a silver ladle, and two sets of plate weighing two drachmas each; perhaps another set of cups weighing four, and a small wine-cooler worth ten obols—thinner than a play by Philippides <note>A joke comparing the literal thinness of the silver to the 'thin' or weak quality of the poet's writing.</note>. But all this was not badly conceived for the purpose of boasting. I myself know a certain fellow citizen of ours, a 'Poor-Braggart' <term>Ptochalazon: a comic character type who acts wealthy despite being destitute</term>, who, though he possessed silver plate worth only a drachma in total, would shout for his servant—he had only one—calling him by many names: 'Psammakisios! Bring us the conch-shell cup from the winter silver—no, not those, the summer ones!'"

Such a man is also found in the play titled *The Kings* by Nicostratus. He is a braggart soldier of whom the poet says: "There is a vinegar-cruet left, and a cooler thinner than a membrane." For even then, some people used to beat out silver until it was as thin as a skin. Antiphanes also says in *The Women of Lemnos*: "A tripod was set out, by the honored gods, holding a silver bowl of honey." And Sopater the parodist says in *Orestes*: "A silver plate holding rotten catfish." In the play titled *Lentil Soup*, he says: "But bring silver vinegar-cruets on double-handled stands, shaped like dragons." Such a vessel was once possessed by Theron, son of Tantalus—a man softened by the weight of many talents <term>talent: the largest unit of currency, representing a massive fortune</term>.

Theopompus of Chios, in his *Advice to Alexander*, speaking of his fellow citizen Theocritus, says: "He drinks from silver and gold vessels, and uses other such things for his table service, though previously he not only lacked silver to drink from, but even bronze; he drank from earthenware, and those were chipped." Diphilus says in *The Painter*: "It would please the locals if some new or desirable sweet fish were served, a whole phalanx of varied small platters. A heap of roasted meat from the frying pan was brought to them with sauces in silver mortars." He also mentions a doctor named Philimus and a certain chest of silver plate. Menander says in *The Self-Tormentor*: "Maidservants, a bath, silver plate." And in *Hymnis*: "But I have come wishing to take the silver plate." Lysias, in his speech *On the Golden Tripod*, if the speech is genuine, uses the terms "silverware" or "goldware." Those who speak correct Greek would say "silver ornament" or "gold ornament."

After Aemilianus said all this, Pontianus remarked: Gold was truly rare among the Greeks in the old days, and silver was scarce in the mines. Therefore, Duris of Samos says that Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon.</note>, the father of Alexander the Great, possessed only one small gold saucer, and always kept it under his pillow. It is said there was once a golden lamb belonging to the house of Atreus, which caused the eclipse of the sun and the change of kings <note>A reference to the myth of Atreus and Thyestes, where the possession of a golden lamb determined the right to rule Mycenae.</note>, a common theme in tragedy. Herodorus of Heraclea says there was a silver saucer with a golden lamb in the middle. Anaximenes of Lampsacus says in the first of his *Histories* that Eriphyle's necklace became famous because gold was so rare among the Greeks at that time. Even a silver cup was a marvelous sight to see then.

But after the seizure of Delphi by the Phocians <note>The Third Sacred War (356–346 BC), when the Phocians seized the temple treasures to pay for mercenaries.</note>, everything of that sort spread through their hands. Even very wealthy men used to drink from bronze cups, or they called the chests that held them "bronze-chests." Herodotus <margin>Book 2.</margin> says that Egyptian priests drink from bronze cups. He also says that when their kings once sacrificed together, it was found that no silver saucers had been given out; Psammetichus, being younger than the other kings, used a bronze saucer while the others were given silver ones. Once the Pythian temple <note>The Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note> was plundered by the Phocian tyrants, gold and silver shone upon the Greeks and came in like a flood. Later, when the great Alexander took the treasures of Asia, the "Wealth of the Eurymedon" <note>Quoting a fragment of Pindar; the Eurymedon was a river in Asia Minor where the Greeks won a major victory over Persia.</note> truly rose like the sun. The silver and gold offerings at Delphi were first dedicated by Gyges, King of the Lydians. Before his reign, the Pythian temple was without silver or gold, as Phanias of Eresus and Theopompus say in the fortieth book of his *Philippics*. They record that the Pythian temple was adorned first by Gyges, and after him by Croesus. After them, it was adorned by Gelo and Hiero of Sicily, the former dedicating a tripod and a golden Victory...

# BOOK VI

->ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS<-

...offerings made of gold at the time when Xerxes <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BCE.</note> marched against Greece. However, the temple once held similar items made of other materials. Theopompus <note>A 4th-century BCE historian.</note> says the following: "In ancient times, the temple was adorned with bronze offerings—not of unworked gold, but with cauldrons and tripods made of bronze." When the Spartans wished to gild the face of the statue of Apollo at Amyclae <note>An ancient sanctuary near Sparta.</note> and could find no gold in Greece, they sent messengers to the oracle to ask the god where they might buy some. The god replied that they should go and buy it from Croesus the Lydian <note>A king famous for his legendary wealth.</note>. So they went and purchased it from Croesus. Similarly, Hieron of Syracuse, wishing to dedicate a tripod and a statue of Victory to the god, found himself for a long time in want of gold. Later, he sent men to search throughout Greece. After much difficulty, they arrived in Corinth and found some in the possession of Architeles the Corinthian, who had been buying it up little by little over a long period and had amassed a considerable treasure. He sold the messengers as much as Hieron needed. In addition, Architeles filled his hand with as much more as it could hold and gave it to them as a gift. In return, Hieron sent him a ship full of grain and many other gifts from Sicily. Phanias <note>A student of Aristotle.</note> records the same facts in his work *On the Tyrants of Sicily*, stating that ancient offerings were of bronze: tripods, cauldrons, and hand-daggers <note>original: "ἐγχειριδίων" (enkheiridion), a small sword or dagger.</note>. He even mentions an inscription on one of them:

> Behold me truly; for I was once in the towers of Troy
> When we fought for the sake of fair-haired Helen.

And Antilochus <note>A Greek hero in the Trojan War, son of Nestor.</note> carried me... Now I occupy the divine floor of Leto’s son <note>Leto's son is the god Apollo.</note>. On a tripod, which was one of the prizes set out for Patroclus' funeral games:

> I am a bronze tripod, dedicated as an ornament at Pytho <note>Pytho is another name for Delphi.</note>.
> And swift-footed Achilles set me as a prize for Patroclus.
> Diomedes, the son of Tydeus, dedicated me as a prize,
> Having won the horse-race by the wide Hellespont.

Ephorus (or perhaps his son Demophilus) in the thirtieth book of his *Histories*, speaking of the temple at Delphi, says: "Onomarchus, Phayllus, and Phalaecus <note>Phocian leaders who seized the temple of Delphi during the Third Sacred War (356–346 BCE).</note> not only carried away all the god's treasures, but eventually their wives even took the ornaments of Eriphyle, which Alcmaeon had dedicated at Delphi by the god's command, as well as the necklace of Eriphyle which was an offering from Menelaus." For the god had given an oracle to both: to Alcmaeon, when he asked how he might be cured of his madness:

> You ask me for a precious gift to end your madness.
> So bring me a gift of honor, such as your mother
> Once hid beneath the earth along with Amphiaraus and his horses.

And to Menelaus, when he asked how he might take vengeance on Alexander <note>Another name for Paris of Troy.</note>:

> Bring the all-golden ornament, taking it from your wife’s
> Neck, which Cypris <note>The goddess Aphrodite.</note> once gave to Helen
> As a great joy; thus she will grant you vengeance on your most hated enemy, Alexander.

It happened that a rivalry broke out between the wives as to which of them would receive which ornament. They drew lots, and the one who was somber and dignified in her life received the necklace of Eriphyle. The other, who was wanton and inclined toward adultery, received the necklace of Helen; she eventually fell in love with a young man from Epirus and ran away with him. The first wife, however, plotted death for her husband in that very place.

The divine Plato and Lycurgus of Sparta <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note>, who did not allow such things in their own states, believed that the rest of the citizens should conduct their affairs accordingly. They did not allow silver or gold, believing that iron and bronze were sufficient for those who mine the earth. They cast those precious metals out as things that ruin the health of cities. Zeno of the Stoa <note>Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoic philosophy.</note>, however, considered all such things "indifferent" <term>indifferent: "adiaphora," things that are neither morally good nor bad in themselves, but depend on how they are used</term> except for using them in a lawful and beautiful way. While he did not forbid their possession or command men to flee from them, he ordered that one should primarily use what is simple and easy to obtain, so that the soul’s disposition remains unbridled and unawed by things that are neither noble nor shameful. Nature, it seems, has not entirely cast these metals out of the world, but has created underground veins for them, involving much toil and difficult labor. This was done so that those who pursue such things might do so with great effort, for not only the miners but also those who collect the mined metal hunt for this much-envied wealth with countless hardships. Some gold is found with difficulty because it occurs only on the surface, such as in the furthest reaches of the inhabited world where even ordinary rivers wash down gold dust. These grains are separated by women and physically weak men who wash the sand and then take it to the furnace, as my friend Posidonius <note>A Stoic philosopher and polymath.</note> says regarding the coastal tribes. This also occurs among certain Celts, and in the mountains once called the Rhipaean, then the Olbian, and now the Alps. It is said that in Gaul, when a forest caught fire spontaneously, the silver actually flowed together and ran out of the earth.

<margin>The same from Posidonius in Strabo, Book 3.</margin>

However, the majority of this metal is found through deep and painful mining. According to Demetrius of Phalerum <note>An Athenian orator and statesman.</note>, greed hopes to drag Pluto <note>The god of the underworld, whose name also means "wealth."</note> himself up from the depths of the earth. He says, by way of a joke, that people often spend what is visible for the sake of what is hidden, and they do not receive what they hoped for, while losing what they already had—a misfortune that resembles a riddle. The Spartans, being forbidden by their customs from bringing gold and silver into Sparta (as the same Posidonius records), nonetheless acquired it, but they deposited it for safekeeping with their neighbors, the Arcadians. Eventually, they became enemies...

...that he might have money instead of friends, so that his faithlessness might go unpunished because of the enmity it caused. It is said that the gold and silver previously sent by the Spartans was dedicated to Apollo at Delphi in equal weight. However, when Lysander <note>A Spartan admiral and politician who brought vast wealth into Sparta after defeating Athens in 404 BCE.</note> brought it publicly into the city, he became the cause of many evils. 
<margin>Plutarch, in *Life of Lysander*.</margin>
Indeed, there is a story that Gylippus <note>The Spartan general who led the defense of Syracuse against Athens.</note>, the man who liberated the Syracusans, died of starvation after being condemned by the ephors <note>The five senior overseers of the Spartan state.</note> for embezzling part of the Lysandrian money. It was not easy for a mortal to treat with neglect that which was dedicated to a god and granted to the people as a sacred ornament and possession.

Among the Gauls <note>Specifically the Scordisci, a Celtic tribe in the Balkans.</note>, those called the Scordistae do not bring gold into their own country. Yet, they do not cease from plundering the lands of others and committing injustices. Their nation is a remnant of the Gauls who marched with Brennus <note>The Gallic leader who famously attacked the Oracle of Delphi in 279 BCE.</note> against the Delphic oracle. A certain leader named Bathanatius led them to the regions around the Ister <note>The ancient name for the Danube River.</note>, after whom they still call the road by which they returned the "Bathanatian Way." They have renounced gold and do not bring it into their homelands because they suffered many terrible things for its sake. They use silver instead, and for its sake, they do many terrible things. And yet, it was necessary to banish not the type of metal stolen, but the sacrilegious impiety itself. If they did not even bring silver into their land, they would surely sin over bronze and iron. And if even these were not among them, they would continue to behave like violent mobs over food and drink and other necessities. 

After Pontianus had said these things—for many guests were competing to resolve the questions proposed by Ulpian—Plutarch, having taken up the remaining points, spoke as follows:

The name of <term>parasite</term> <note>original: "παράσιτος" (parasitos). In modern English, this implies a social leech, but in ancient Greece, it originally meant "one who eats alongside" or "at the table of."</note> was anciently venerable and sacred. Polemon of Samos (or Sicyon, or Athens, for he enjoys all these names, as Heraclides the Molossian says when listing his various citizenships) was also nicknamed "The Pillar-Cutter" <note>original: "στηλοκόπας" (stelokopas). Likely a reference to his habit of collecting and copying inscriptions from stone pillars.</note>, as Herodicus the follower of Crates says in his work *On Parasites*. He writes as follows: "The name of the parasite is now held in low esteem, but among the ancients, we find the parasite to be a sacred office, similar to a fellow-banqueter." 

In the Heracleion <note>A sanctuary of Heracles.</note> at Cynosarges <note>A gymnasium in Athens specifically for "nothoi," or those of mixed/illegitimate parentage.</note>, there is a certain pillar on which is inscribed a decree of Alcibiades, with Stephanus, son of Thucydides, as the secretary. In it, concerning the <term>proskoreia</term> <note>A preliminary sacrifice or ritual cleaning.</note>, it says: "The priest shall perform the monthly sacrifices with the parasites. The parasites shall be selected from among the illegitimate sons and their children according to the law." It is also written on the *kyrbeis* <note>Rotating wooden blocks used for displaying laws in ancient Athens.</note> that the herald, chosen from the family of heralds involved in the Mysteries, should also act as a parasite for the Delian Apollo for one year. 

In the sanctuary at Pallene, the following is inscribed on the offerings: "The Archons and Parasites dedicated this, having been crowned with a golden crown in the year of Pythodorus's archonship." And from the priestly tribe, the parasites dedicated: "Pericles of Gargettus, son of Lycostratus; Pericleitus of Pithus; Charinus of Gargettus, son of Demochares." Also, in the laws of the King <note>Referring to the King Archon (*Archon Basileus*), the magistrate in charge of religious matters in Athens.</note>, it is written: "Concerning Apollo, the parasites shall be chosen from the Acharnians." 

Clearchus of Soli, one of Aristotle’s pupils, writes the following in the first book of his *Lives*: "The term 'parasite' is now used for one who is ready to be fed, but then it referred to one chosen to live and eat together with others. In ancient laws, most cities—and even today the most honorable magistracies—include parasites among their ranks." Cleidemus says in his *Atthis*: "Parasites were also chosen for Heracles." And Themison in his *Pallene* says: "The King who is currently reigning shall take care of the parasites whom they select from the districts, as well as the elders and the <term>protopokai</term> women." <note>original: "πρωτοπόκας" (protopokas). This refers to "first-shorn" ewes or, by extension, women who have just borne their first child; Ulpian later asks for a clarification of this term.</note> You may now ask me here, Ulpian, who these "first-bearing" women are! 

But truly, since the conversation is about parasites, it is also written on a pillar in the Anakeion <note>The temple of the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux).</note>: "Of the two oxen selected for the god, one third part shall be for the contest, and of the remaining two parts, one shall go to the priest and the other to the parasites." Crates, in the second book of *The Attic Dialect*, says: "The parasite is now considered a thing of no reputation, but formerly parasites were those chosen to select the sacred grain." In an ancient law regarding parasites, the following is written in the King's code: "The King shall oversee the archons to ensure they are appointed and that they choose the parasites from the districts according to the written laws. Each parasite shall choose from his own portion a sixth of a bushel of barley to be used for the feast of the Athenians in the temple according to ancestral custom. The parasites from the Acharnians shall provide the grain for the sanctuary of Apollo from their selection of barley." 

That their office was ancient is shown in the same law: "For the repair of the ancient temple, the <term>parasition</term> <note>A building or room where the sacred grain was stored and where the parasites ate.</note>, and the sacred house, the money shall be given as much as the inspectors of the sacred buildings shall contract for." From this, it is clear that the place where the parasites deposited the first-fruits of the sacred grain was called the *parasition*. Philochorus also records these facts in his work titled *The Tetrapolis*, mentioning the parasites enrolled for Heracles. And Diodorus of Sinope, the comic poet, in his play *The Heiress*, provides testimony which I will cite a little later. Aristotle, in his *Constitution of the Methoneans*, says that parasites...

# BOOK VI

->ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS<-

...for the rulers there were two [parasites] for each, but for the war-leaders <note>Greek: *polemarchois*, high-ranking military officials</note> there was one. These men received a fixed portion of food from various sources, including fish from the fishermen. However, the modern sense of the word "parasite" was first found in the works of Alexis, according to Carystius of Pergamum in his treatise *On Dramatic Records*. He seems to have forgotten that Epicharmus <note>A celebrated comic poet from the 5th century BCE, known for his Doric dialect plays</note> introduced the character in his play *Hope* (or *Wealth*), speaking in this manner: "But here stands another who follows at my heels, hoping to easily snatch something to drink and eat for his pleasure; yet he drinks down the cup in one gulp <note>original: *amystin*, a way of drinking without closing the eyes or breathing</note>." Epicharmus depicts the parasite himself saying the following to someone questioning him:

> I dine with anyone who wishes to invite me—and only me. And at the Festival of the Gamelion <note>An Athenian month associated with marriage and family feasts</note> I am quite a soul-stirring fellow. At such times I am full of charms, I create much laughter, and I praise the host. And then, after having eaten much and drunk much, I depart. No slave carries a lamp for me; I crawl home slipping and in the dark. If I happen to run into the night-patrol, I thank the gods that they don't want to strike me, but only whip me. I accept my punishment as my due, so long as the unmixed wine still rules my senses.

The parasite of Epicharmus says other such things as well. And the character in Diphilus says this:

> When a rich man invites me to a banquet, I do not notice the triglyphs <note>Architectural ornaments in the frieze of a building</note> nor the ceilings. I do not judge the quality of the Corinthian columns. Instead, I fix my gaze on the smoke from the cook; if it rises thick and straight, I rejoice and flutter with excitement. But if it is slanted and thin, I immediately realize that this dinner of mine will have no blood in it <note>meaning it will be meatless or meager</note>.

Some say that Homer was the first to introduce a parasite,
<margin>Iliad 17</margin> when he spoke of Podes, calling him the "dear banquet-companion" of Hector. For there was among the Trojans one Podes, son of Eetion, wealthy and brave, whom Hector honored most of all among the people, because he was his dear companion at the feast.
<margin>Iliad 17</margin> For he was a friend at the banquet... <note>The text here is somewhat corrupted in the original Greek</note>. This is why Homer depicts him being wounded in the belly by Menelaus. Demetrius of Scepsis says that Pandarus was also wounded in the tongue because he had broken his oath; thus each man is struck where he sinned. But the ancient poets called parasites "flatterers" <note>Greek: *kolakes*</note>, from which Eupolis took the title for his play, making the chorus of flatterers say the following:

> We will tell you of the lifestyle flatterers lead. Listen, for we are all very refined men. First, each of us has a servant, usually someone else's, though we may have a small claim on him. I have two fine cloaks; I take turns wearing them when I head out to the marketplace. There, when I spot a man who is foolish but wealthy, I am immediately at his side. Whatever that rich man says, I praise it excessively, pretending to be struck with wonder and delighting in his words. Then we go off to dinner, one here, one there, to a stranger's table, where a flatterer must immediately say many witty things or be thrown out the door. I know Acestor himself, the branded one <note>Likely a reference to a slave or foreigner with a mark of infamy</note>, suffered this. For if he told a joke that failed, the slave led him out by the neck and handed him over to the stocks.

Aristophon mentions the name of "parasite" in his play *The Physician* in these lines:

> There is no way you are not a parasite, my dear friend; for Ischomachus <note>A well-known Athenian wealthy figure</note> provides for you.

The name is very common among the more recent writers. The verb "to parasite" <note>Greek: *parasitein*</note> appears in Plato the philosopher’s *Laches*, where he says:

> ...who parasites us youngsters.

Alexis describes the different types of parasites in *The Pilot*:

> There are two types of parasites, Nausinicus. One is the common, comic type—those of us who are "the black ones" <note>A possible reference to theater masks or lower-class status</note>. But I seek the other kind: the "stately-parasites" <note>Greek: *semnoparasiton*</note>, who are satraps and famous generals. They maintain a dignified look, with furrowed brows, pretending to manage affairs of a thousand talents. You know the type. In both kinds, the method is the same: the contest of flattery. Just as in life, fortune assigns some of us to the great and others to the small. If some of us prosper and others just leap about, am I teaching you anything, Nausinicus, or is this foolish? But I praise you anyway, and you will ask for more.

Timocles also characterizes the parasite in his play *The Dragon* like this:

> Shall I allow anyone to speak ill of a parasite? No, for there is no class of men more useful. If a man is a lover of his friends, the parasite does this to the end. Are you in love? He becomes your unhesitating co-lover. Are you doing something? He is there to do whatever is needed. This is only fair to the one who feeds him. He is a wonderful praiser of his friends, and they enjoy their pleasures without having to pay a contribution <note>Greek: *asymbolois*, dining without paying one's share</note>. What mortal, hero, or god would reject such a pastime? Not to be long-winded, I think it is a huge proof of how honored the life of a parasite is. For the same rewards given to Olympic victors are given to them: free meals <note>original: *sitesis*</note> for the sake of their "gold" <note>A pun on the golden rewards of winners versus the "gold" of the rich host</note>. For where no contributions are required, every place is a Town Hall <note>Greek: *Prytaneum*, where honored citizens ate for free at public expense</note>.

And Antiphanes says in *The Twins*:

> If you look at it correctly, how many things a parasite is...

# BOOK VI

->ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS<-

...sharing in both their fortune and their life. No parasite ever prayed for his friends to be unlucky; on the contrary, he wishes for everyone to be forever prosperous. If a man lives a life of luxury, the parasite does not envy him, but rather prays to be by his side and share in those riches. He is a noble and steady friend, not prone to fighting, nor irritable, nor spiteful. He is excellent at enduring anger, and if someone mocks him, he simply laughs. He is amorous, witty, and cheerful in his manner. Furthermore, he is a soldier of extreme excellence—if the "rations" <note>Greek: *sitarchêma*, a soldier's pay or provisions</note> are decent enough to keep him breathing.

And indeed, Aristophon says to a doctor: 

> "I want to tell him beforehand what my character is like. If anyone hosts a feast, I am there first—so much so that for a long time now I’ve been nicknamed 'The Soup.' If there’s a need to haul away a drunkard by the waist, consider me a self-taught wrestler for the job. If a house needs to be stormed, I am a battering ram. If a little ladder needs to be scaled, I am Capaneus <note>A hero from the myth of the Seven Against Thebes, famous for scaling the city walls with a ladder</note>. I can endure blows like an anvil, and punches too. 

Plato calls him "the support" <note>original: *telamôn*, likely a pun on the hero Ajax Telamon and the word for a supporting strap or pillar</note> where the smoke is finest. And if he 'plays the Pythagorean' <note>A reference to the followers of Pythagoras, who were known for their strict vegetarianism and asceticism</note>, he says:

> "I’ll go to the feast, provided I don't see so much as a single spurge-plant or a bit of chicory. As for drinking water, I am a frog. As for enjoying thyme and greens, I am a caterpillar. As for not washing, I am filth itself. To spend the winter in the open air, I am a blackbird. To endure the sweltering heat and chatter at midday, I am a cicada. To neither use nor look at oil, I am a cloud of dust. To walk about barefoot at dawn, I am a crane. To sleep not even a wink, I am a bat."

Antiphanes says in *The Ancestors*: 

> "You know my way: there is no vanity in me. I am such a man toward my friends that if someone wants to hit me, I am hit. If someone wants to strike me hard, I am blinded by the lightning. If a wind needs to carry someone away, I am that wind. If someone needs to be choked, I am the noose. To break down doors, I am an earthquake. To hop in uninvited, I am a locust. To dine uninvited, I am a fly. To never leave, I am a deep well. To throttle, to play the executioner, to bear witness—I am all of these, and not just by chance. Because I do all these things without a second thought, the younger men call me 'The Thunderbolt.' But come with me and your jokes; for I am a friend to my friends, a man of deeds and not just words."

Diphilus, in his play 
<margin>The Parasite.</margin> 
*The Parasite*, when a wedding is about to take place, makes the parasite say: 

> "Are you unaware of the ancient curses? That if someone does not point out the way, or if someone does not provide a light for a fire, or if someone spoils the water for those about to use it... or if someone prevents a man from spending his money on a feast!" 

And Eubulus says in his *Oedipus*: 

> "The man who first discovered how to dine at the expense of others was, it seems, a man of the people <note>original: *dêmotikos*, meaning democratic or common</note> in his ways. But whoever invites a friend or a stranger to dinner and then demands a contribution <term>symbolas</term> <note>A *symbolê* was a "potluck" contribution or a fee paid by guests to cover the cost of a shared meal</note>—may he be an exile and never bring anything home from his own house!"

Diodorus of Sinope, in *The Heiress*, also speaks elegantly regarding the life of a parasite: 

> "I want to show clearly how grand this practice is, how it is an art of our own, and a discovery of the gods. No god showed us the other crafts; they were found by wise men. But 'parasitism' was discovered by Zeus Philios <note>Zeus in his role as the god of Friendship and Hospitality</note>, who is admittedly the greatest of the gods. For he enters houses without distinguishing between the poor and the rich. Wherever he sees a well-spread couch 
<margin>10</margin> 
and a table set with everything necessary, he lies down in a dignified manner, feasts himself, drinks his fill, and then departs for home without paying a contribution. I do the same now. Seeing the couches spread, the tables ready, and the door open, I enter quietly to drink, making myself agreeable so as not to annoy the other guests. Having enjoyed everything served and having drunk, I go home just like Zeus Philios."

That this practice was always glorious and honorable can be seen even more clearly from the following: the city, honoring Heracles magnificently, performs sacrifices in all the districts. For these sacrifices, it never failed to appoint "parasites" to the god. It did not choose just anyone for this, but selected 
<margin>40</margin> 
twelve men from the citizens with great care, choosing from those who had served as judges and lived honorable lives. Later, imitating Heracles, some of the wealthy chose a great many parasites, not selecting the most charming men, but those capable of flattery and praising everything. To these men, if the host ate rotten radishes and silphium, they would say he had been served violets and roses. And if the host sneezed while lying next to them, the parasite would say: "Bless you!" and "Tell me, where did you get that incense for your nose?" Because of such people who use the art so lewdly, what was once honorable and noble is now considered shameful.

And Leonicus says in *The Chalcidian*: 

> "When I first fell in love with being a parasite, along with Philoxenus 'The Heel-Cutter' <note>original: *pternokopidês*, a nickname for a parasite who follows closely at one's heels</note>, I was still a youth. I endured sweet punches and wounds from the spits, sometimes having at least eight wounds. For it was profitable; I am a slave to pleasure. And besides, I have come to believe the practice is profitable in a way: if someone is quarrelsome and fights with me, I simply change my mind and say, 'how right you are!' No matter how much he 
<margin>50</margin> 
insults me, I immediately agree and suffer no harm. If someone says a wicked man is actually good, I praise him and receive a favor in return. If I eat a piece of boiled grayling today, and tomorrow it’s leftovers, I don't mind. Such is my way and my nature."

Antidotus, in the play entitled *The First Chorus*, introduces a character similar to those who today are sophists <note>The "sophists" here refers to the pretentious intellectuals or teachers of rhetoric in the time of Athenaeus</note> under the emperor Claudius...
<meta>The catchword "ζόνουσιν" (sophists) bridges to the next page's discussion of modern parasites who mimic intellectualism.</meta>
