# BOOK VI.

...they show things not even honorable to mention, saying such things about the parasitic art. "According to the gift, everyone listens to me about being enrolled and receiving the short cloak <note>Greek: *chlamydion*, the characteristic dress of a certain class of citizens or travelers, here perhaps implying a uniform of sorts</note>, concerning the act of being a parasite in whatever conversations might fall out. Let this little art of mine swallow it down." And let us see how he views the mind itself. There were parasites known by name: Tithymallus <note>Literally "Spurge," a plant with a milky sap; here the name of a famous parasite</note> for one, whom Alexis mentions in *The Milesian* and in *Odysseus Weaving*. And in his *Fables* he says: "Let your health be sweet. Just as death is a 're-born' old age <note>original: Δίδλαχ' ὁ θάνατος τὸ γῆράς</note>, so they say. At any rate, Tithymallus-Death goes about." In *The Female Psaltery Player*, he says: "A dance-song, a holy thing—Mellon, the one who never pays his share <note>original: ἀσύμβολος (*asumbolos*), meaning someone who attends a feast without contributing to the cost</note>, has returned again. Everything is shameful. I saw Tithymallus, more careless and redder than a cuckoo-fruit <note>original: κόκκυ</note>, walking about; he turns so red because he never pays his contribution." Timocles, in *The Centaur* or *Dexamenos*, calls him both Tithymallus and a parasite. In 
<margin>10</margin> *The Men of Iconium*: "What is this 'victory-glory' waiting for? You will strip him. Oh, everything! For this Tithymallus, by the hearth of the tavern, softened eight lupine-seeds <note>term: *thermes*, a cheap, bitter legume often eaten by the poor</note> for an obol. He did not endure it, but he suffered it, my friend." Gynon, in his *Letters*: "Alas, miserable me, how I love, by the gods! Tithymallus never loved eating so much, nor was he so eager to receive a cloak as a garment. Not even Nalos, the barley-man, nor Corydus <note>term: *Corydus*, meaning "The Lark," a famous parasite</note> who never pays—grinding his teeth." Antiphanes in *The Tyrrhenian*: "For you say that he himself serves his friends for free, and that Tithymallus will be rich. For by Eupraxiton's wage in your speech, among those with whom he dined for free, you will collect a great deal."

And Corydus was one of those named as parasites. Timocles mentions him in *The Rejoicer in Evil* thus: "To see a market well-stocked with fish is sweet for a wealthy man; but if a man is poor, it is most wretched. Corydus, at least, having become uninvited as it seems to me, buys fish for his own home. 
<margin>20</margin> Oh, what a ridiculous suffering! A man with only a copper coin <note>original: χαλκός</note> looks at eels, tuna, electric rays, and crabs, and his teeth are set on edge <note>original: ἡμωδία</note>. And after going around all these and asking how much they cost, he runs off to the cheap sprats <note>term: *membradas*, small, inexpensive fish</note>." Alexis in *Demetrius* or *Philetaerus*: "But let us be ashamed before Corydus, if I seem to have snatched something away from someone. So readily, because we answered back nonetheless. For not even if someone calls him..." In *The Nurse*: "This Corydus, the one accustomed to saying funny things, wants to be a 'Blepaeus' <note>A reference to a famously wealthy man of the time</note>, since he has sense. For Blepaeus is rich." Cratinus the Younger in some play: "Beware of Corydus the 'copper-beater' <note>note: perhaps a joke on his tough skin from being hit, or his constant handling of small coins</note>. Lest you think he says nothing against you, never dine with him at all. I tell you beforehand about Corydus: he has a strong hand like a tireless smith, much stronger than fire itself." 

Because Corydus spoke jokes and wished to be laughed at by these men, the same Alexis says in *The Poets*: "I certainly wish to be laughed at in this way and to always say funny things, especially after Corydus and many of the Ethiopians." 
<margin>30</margin> Lynceus of Samos records him in his *Memoirs*, saying his proper name was Eukrates, the son of Eukrates. He writes as follows: "Eukrates, also known as Corydus, was drinking at someone's house that was in decay; he said he was dining there while propping up the roof with his left hand, just like the Caryatids." Philoxenus, nicknamed "The Ham-Cutter" <note>original: *pternokopis*</note>, when the conversation turned to the fact that thrushes are expensive, and Corydus being present—who was eating some small scraps—said: "But I remember when Corydus was only worth an obol." And Philoxenus was also one of the parasites, just like Axionikos in *The Chalcidian*. The evidence is already laid out. Menander also mentions him in *The Hair-Net*, calling him only "Ham-Cutter." 

Machon the comic poet also mentions him—Machon was a Corinthian or Sicyonian by birth, but lived out his life in my own Alexandria. 
<margin>40</margin> He became a teacher there of the parts of comedy to Aristophanes the Grammarian, and he died in Alexandria. This inscription is on his tomb: 

> "To the comic writer, bring ivy over the tomb of the living Machon, you who love song, onto his light dust. For you do not hold a 'scoured sponge' <note>original: κηφῶνα (*kephôn*), a drone or a person who lives off others without wit</note>, but you cover a worthy remnant of the art, worthy of the ancients. This old man the city of Cecrops <note>note: Athens</note> loved much by the Nile; sometimes among the initiates the spirit was born..." 

In these lines, he clearly shows he was Alexandrian by residence. Machon mentions Corydus in these lines: 

> "Eukrates once asked Corydus how Ptolemy <note>note: Likely Ptolemy I Soter or Ptolemy II Philadelphus</note> had used him; I don't know, he then said clearly. For he made me drink just like a doctor—he never gave me anything to eat or bread." 

Lynceus, in the second book of *The Sayings of Menander*, says of those who gained a reputation for jokes: "Eucleides, also called Smikrines, and Philoxenus the Ham-Cutter." Of these, Eucleides' utterances were worthy of a book and of memory, but in other things he was unpleasant and cold. Philoxenus did not do anything by halves in his speech; if he were to speak or be bitter toward any of those coming in, he would describe everything regarding sex, and he was full of grace. And it so happened that while Eucleides was [unclear] in his life, Philoxenus was loved and honored by all. Alexis mentions a certain parasite named Moschion in *Trophonius*, 
<margin>50</margin> calling him "The All-Chewer" <note>original: *pasamasêtês*</note> in these lines: "Moschion the All-Chewer, auspicious among mortals." In *The Pancratiast*, Alexis, listing those who are ready at hand, says: 

> "First there was Callimedon 'The Crab,' then Corydus, Kobios, Kyrybion, the Mackerel, the Fine Flour—dear Heracles! You have named the purchases for a banquet." 

Epikrates was nicknamed "Kyrybion" <note>note: likely referring to 'bran' or 'husks,' a joke on his low quality or poverty</note>; he was the brother-in-law of Aeschines the orator, as he says...

...as Demosthenes says in his speech *On the False Embassy*. Regarding such epithets which the Athenians, in their mockery, used to say to everyone
during their lives, Anaxandrides mentions them in *Odysseus* as follows: "For you are always mocking one another,
I know it well. For if someone is handsome, you call him 'Holy Marriage' <note>original: *Hieros Gamos*; a ritual wedding of gods, here used as a sarcastic nickname for a 'perfect' looking man</note>. If he is a tiny little 
human, you call him 'The Droplet.' If a resplendent man goes out, he is 'The Hullabaloo.' The oily Demo-
<margin>5</margin> kles walks about, and he is named 'The Soup.' Someone enjoys being parched or filthy? 'The Dust-cloud' has appeared! Behind him 
follows a flatterer? He is nicknamed 'The Telemeter' <note>Literally "Far-measurer," perhaps implying someone who keeps a certain distance while following</note>, walking like a little brother for the most part. He is a 'Caper-fish' of the island, how well
and beautifully he looks, 'Empty' <note>original: *Kenos*</note>. If a stage-manager jumps up playing a lamb, he is called 'Atreus' <note>A mythological king associated with a golden lamb</note>. If he plays a ram,
'Phelios.' If he carries a little fleece, 'Jason.' Chairephon the parasite is mentioned by those who came before 
these. Indeed, Mnesandros also mentions him in *The Hair-Net*, and says regarding his temper, 'A man differs from Chai-
<margin>10</margin> rephon not even a bit—one who will come when invited at any time to a banquet, standing upright like a twelve-foot shadow.'
He would turn toward the moon, and seeing his shadow, he would think he was late and should have been there at daybreak. He says after other things: 'For 
that most elegant Flower-Chairephon wore me out, claiming he would perform a "Holy Marriage" on the twenty-second, 
at his own expense, so that on the fourth day he might feast at the expense of others. For matters pertaining to a god would be good in every way.'
He mentions him also in *The Hermaphrodite* or *The Cretan*. Timokles, in his *Letters*, also mentions how he 
<margin>15</margin> stood beside Demotion the profligate. Demotion, thinking he was being squeezed by him, said: 'The money
is not for me, but it turned aside for anyone who wanted it.' Chairephon thought he was walking home entirely
unburdened. 'And yet, it is only worth it then for the "squeezer" to receive the two-pronged wood' <note>original: *dikroon xylon*, a type of pillory or punishment device</note>.
'For he is neither graceful in appearance, nor without money.' Antiphanes says in *The Scythian*: 'To a revel, as it seems, 
just as we are. Should we not then take a torch and garlands and thus go after them and sing the praises of
<margin>20</margin> the "Ever-hungry"?' <note>original: *aeilipnos*</note>. Timotheus in *The Companion* says: 'Let us leave after paying for the dinner. I will go to a seven-couch room
as he told me, unless that sweetest Chairephon has squeezed himself in.' Apollodorus of Carystus in *The Priestess*: 
'They say it is a new thing for Chairephon to have slipped into weddings uninvited like a debtor; 
taking a basket and a garland, as if in the dark, claiming he has come from the bride, the one bringing the birds—
he seems to have arrived late for the feasting.' In *The Slain Woman*: 'I call upon those who conquer in my vinegar-sauces. I call 
<margin>25</margin> Chairephon. For even if I do not call him, he will come uninvited.' Machon the comic poet says: 'When Chairephon once went 
a long way to a wedding dinner, they say the poet Diphilus said: "In your own jaws, Chairephon,

<margin>30</margin> they say he spoke to the butcher quite piously; when a piece of meat by chance hit him,

<margin>40</margin> and even more the sea-weed fish—a man quite stuffed by the sprats and the Phaleric anchovies. 
But he restrained himself most firmly from the gobies. The matter having become quite ridiculous, 
and the king having asked Alciphron if Archephon had overlooked the gobies. The hunchback said, "Quite the

For it is not his ancestral custom to eat fish that are 'un-contributing' <note>original: *asumbolon*; a pun on fish that are 'worthless' and a guest who pays no share</note> and have no 'vote' <note>original: *apsēphon*; a pun on fish with no scales and a man who has no political vote</note> in any injustice."' me more than your father? For he does not feed me, but you feed me splendidly. And it is always my prayer to all the gods that you live. 
For if anything happens to you, how shall I live?' Axionikos the comic poet in *The Tyrrhenian* 
<margin>50</margin> mentions Gryllion the parasite in these words: 'There is no wine in them now; they use their companions as a pretext 
for certain revels, which Gryllion is always accustomed to do.' Aristodemos, in the second book of his *Humorous Memorabilia*, 
records the parasites: Sopatros of King Antiochus, Evagoras the Humpback of Demetrius the Besieger, 
and Phormion of Seleucus. Lynceus of Samos in his *Sayings*...

# BOOK 6

Silanus the Athenian says that when he was asked who the parasite of Gryllion was, he replied: "A great-man of the seashore" <note>original: *Meganthropos aeigianathos*; a mocking play on high-sounding names, perhaps implying he is a "big man" only in the wasteland of the coast</note>. Regarding Chairephon, it is said by everyone that he once entered a wedding uninvited and sat down in the very last place. When the women-inspectors <term>gynaikonomoi; magistrates responsible for maintaining decorum and enforcing sumptuary laws at private gatherings</term> were counting the guests and ordered him to leave because he was the thirty-first person—exceeding the legal limit of thirty—he replied: "Count again, but this time start with me!"

That it was the custom for the women-inspectors to oversee banquets and examine the number of guests to see if it followed the law is confirmed by Timocles in *The Litigious Man*:

> Open the doors at once, so that we may be 
> clearly seen in the light, in case the woman-inspector 
> wishes to come on her rounds and take a count. According to the law,
> the new one which she is accustomed to observe regarding those who enter.

However, the practice was actually the opposite: they would examine the houses of those who were *not* dining. Menander says in *The Hair-Net*:

> We have learned that all the cooks serving at weddings 
> must be registered with the women-inspectors, according to some new law, 
> so they may find out who the guests are, in case someone happens 
> to enter in greater numbers than is permitted.

And Philochorus says in the seventh book of his *Atthis* <note>A history of Attica/Athens</note>: "The women-inspectors, along with the members of the Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens</note>, used to inspect gatherings in private houses, both at weddings and other sacrifices." 

Lynceus records the following witty sayings of Corydus <note>nickname meaning "The Lark"</note>. Once, while Corydus was drinking with a courtesan named Gnome <note>meaning "Opinion" or "Judgment"</note>, and some cheap wine was still left, he urged everyone to contribute two obols. He told Gnome she should contribute "whatever seems good to the people" <note>A pun on the standard formula for Athenian decrees: *edoxe to demo*, "it was decided by the people/it seemed good to the people"</note>. 

When Polyctor the cithara-player was slurping lentil soup and bit down on a stone, Corydus said: "You poor man, even the lentil soup hits you!" <note>original: *he phake se ballei*; a pun on *phake* (lentil) and *Phake*, a place name, or perhaps a play on "the lens/lentil strikes you"</note>. Machon also mentions this, saying:

> A certain man, seemingly a very poor stone-mason,
> intending to build his house, asked a friend
> for stones. I will bring him
> many more, he says, from the boiling pot.

When someone told Corydus that he kisses his own wife’s neck, breasts, and navel, Corydus replied: "That is already a bad sign. For even Heracles moved from the 'Navel' to the 'Pleasant'." <note>A pun on Omphale, the queen whom Heracles served, whose name sounds like *omphalos* (navel)</note>. When Physomachus dipped into some lentil soup and overturned the bowl, Corydus said he was "justly fined," because he registered for a meal without knowing how to spend. At the table of King Ptolemy, when a delicacy <term>mattye; a spiced meat dish</term> was being passed around but always ran out before it reached him, he said: "Ptolemy, am I drunk, or does it only *seem* to me that these dishes are revolving?" 

When Chairephon told a parasite that he could not "carry his wine," the man replied: "Neither can you carry what goes *into* the wine" <note>Implying Chairephon was too poor to contribute his share</note>. When someone at a dinner mocked Chairephon while he was stripped, Chairephon said: "I see you are like the oil-flasks; I see how much hatred you hold" <note>A pun on the narrow neck of an oil flask and "narrow-minded" spite</note>. 

During the time when Demosthenes accepted the cup from Harpalus, this man, calling the others "unmixed-cup-heads" <note>original: *akratokothonas*; those who drink wine unmixed with water, a sign of excess</note>, drained the large cup himself. It was his habit to bring rolls of bread to dinners, and when someone called him out for bringing even blacker bread than usual, he said he wasn't supplying "wood-bread," but rather "the shadows of bread."

Philoxenus the parasite, nicknamed "The Ham-Cutter," was dining at Python's house. Olives were served first, and shortly after, a platter of fish was brought in. He struck the bowl and said: "He whipped the olive!" <note>original: *mastichen d' elaon*; a parody of Homer's phrase "he whipped the horses to drive them" (*mastichen d' elaunon*)</note>. When a host who invited him to dinner served black bread, he said: "Don't serve any more, or you'll cause a total eclipse."

Gausimachus said that a parasite supported by an old woman suffers the opposite of his patroness; for he says that she "takes him into her womb" <note>Meaning she supports his stomach/appetite, playing on the phrase for becoming pregnant</note>. Machon writes of this as well:

> Seeing the water-drinker called Morion,
> they say he was being fed by a wealthy old woman, 
> acting as a parasite in the Lyceum. He does a very sharp thing, 
> for that old woman always takes you into her womb.

The same parasite, hearing that he was supported by an old woman and slept with her every day, said: "Now everything happens, or else she simply does not conceive. But he 'takes into his womb' every day."

Ptolemy the son of Lysarchus, a citizen of Megalopolis, says in the second book of his *Histories of Philopator* that the King gathered drinking companions from the whole city who were addressed as "The Jesters" <note>original: *geloiastai*</note>. 

Posidonius of Apamea says in the twenty-third book of his *Histories* that the Celts, even when going to war, take companions with them whom they call "parasites." These men sing their praises both before large crowds and to individuals who listen to them in turn. Their performers are the ones called "Bards." These are poets who deliver praises through song. 

In the thirty-fourth book, the same author records a certain Apollonius who became a parasite to Antiochus, nicknamed "Grypus" <note>The Hook-Nosed</note>, the King of Syria. Aristodemus relates that Bithon, the parasite of King Lysimachus, jumped up in terror when Lysimachus threw a wooden scorpion onto his cloak. When he realized what had happened, he said: "I shall terrify you too, O King—give me a talent!" <note>A talent was a massive sum of money</note>. Lysimachus was known for his generosity. 

Agatharchides of Cnidus says in the twenty-second book of his *European Histories* that Anthemocritus the wrestler became the parasite of Aristomachus, the tyrant of Argos. Regarding parasites in general, Timocles mentions them in *The Boxer*, calling them "provision-seekers":

> You will find some of these provision-seekers 
> who spend the property of others unsparingly, 
> offering themselves as punching bags for athletes.

Pherecrates says in *The Old Women*: "But you won't get your provisions any faster than Smikythion." Who is this...

### FROM ATHENAEUS' DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...still. Let us look everywhere at the work of a single member of the "Holy-Gulleters" <note>original: *Hagialaryngitai*; a mock-religious title for a club of gluttons</note>. For those who served for the sake of their food were called **hirelings** <term>episitioi; literally "those on provisions," workers who receive food as their primary wage</term>. For Plato says in the fourth book of the *Republic*: "And these people are hirelings, and receive no wages beyond their food, unlike the others." Aristophanes says in *The Storks*: "For if someone again bears false witness in an unjust lawsuit, there will be twelve hirelings for the others." And Eubulus in *Daedalus* says: "He wishes to remain as a hireling without pay." Diphilus, in *The Pair of Horses*—which is the name of a courtesan—mentions Euripides. There is also a certain throw of the dice called by this name. Playing with the word's varied meanings and the city of parasites, he says: "Have you then, having escaped from that 'Die' <note>original: *Kybos*; a pun on a dice-throw and perhaps a person or place</note>, become a citizen? Lay down two drachmas, it is set. How could I not throw a 'Euripides'?" Euripides, "A woman will save you," <note>This likely refers to a famous line from a tragedy, here used in a comedic context</note> do you not see in the tragedies how he mocks them? But he loved to speak of parasites. For he says: "A man who possesses a good life, if he does not support at least three 'non-contributors' <term>asymbolous; guests who bring nothing to the feast</term>, may he perish! May such a plague never come to my fatherland." By the gods, where are these lines from? What of it? Is it the black broth? For we do not look at the food, but at the mind. In his *Disakes*, speaking of a parasite who is very angry at the food itself, he says: "He is angry, being a parasite, he is angry! No, but he is bespattering the table with his bile, just as children are weaned from the breast." And following this: "You see how the parasite's craft is ridiculed. I do not know why the parasite is judged second only to the lyre-player." In the play entitled *The Parasite*, he says: "It is not possible to be a parasite while being extremely hard to please." Menander, in *Anger*, speaking of a friend who does not answer a dinner invitation, says: "This is truly a companion; he does not ask what time dinner is, like the others. And what prevents him from feasting when he is present? Then he looks toward another dinner with his nose, and then another dinner again." Alexis in *Orestes*, Nicostratus in *Wealth*, Menander in *Drunkenness*, and Philonides in *The Buskins* say: "I, being a 'non-feeder' <note>original: *apositos*; one who goes without food</note>, am not ashamed of having drunk."

There are names similar to the **parasite**. There is the **hireling** <term>episitios</term>, who was mentioned before, and the **boarder** <term>oikositos</term>, and the **small-eater** <term>oligositos</term>. Anaxandrides mentions the "boarder" in *The Hunters*: "For a 'boarder' becomes sweet." A **boarder** <term>oikositos</term> is called one who serves the city not for pay, but for free <note>literally "eating at one's own house," meaning they do not drain the public or host's resources</note>. Antiphanes in *The Scythian*: "For he quickly becomes a 'boarder' of the Assembly." Menander in *The Finger*: "We have found a 'boarder' bridegroom who needs no dowry." And in *The Lyre-Player*: "You do not take 'boarders' as listeners." Regarding the **hireling**, Crates says in *The Deeds of Daring*: "He shepherds the hireling. In the cold, he will receive food for pay." Peculiarly, in *Women Dining Together*, he says it was "citizen-like" not to bring women together, nor to feast a crowd, but to have made the wedding for "boarders" <note>meaning guests who provide for themselves</note>. Alexis mentions the **bread-clipper** <term>sitokouros</term> in *The Night-Festival* or *The Laborers*: "You will be a walking bread-clipper." Menander called the useless man who is fed in vain a **bread-clipper** in *Thrasyleon*: "Hesitant in everything, a miserable, useless bread-clipper, admitting he is fed merely for a laugh." And in *The Slave-Market*: "You are still standing at the doors having put down your burden; we have taken a miserable bread-clipper into the house." Crobylus mentioned the **self-feeding parasite** <term>autositos</term> in *The Man Hanging Himself*: "Supporting himself as a self-feeding parasite, he contributes the most to his master." Eubulus mentions the **bad-eater** <term>kakositos</term> in *Ganymede*: "Sleep supports him, since he is a bad-eater." Phrynichus mentions the **small-eater** in *The Solitary Man*: "What is the small-eating Heracles doing there?" And Pherecrates (or Stratis) in *The Good Men*: "How small-eating he is, even if he runs long distances or days for his food." 

<margin>Flatterers.</margin> After Plutarch had said these things about parasites, Democritus took up the discourse and said: "Indeed, I myself, speaking of nature, just as 'wood by wood' (as the Theban poet said), will speak about **flatterers** <term>kolakes</term>. For what does the flatterer do better than all, if not the beautiful things Menander describes?" The flatterer is not far removed from the name of the parasite. Cleisophus, for instance—who was recorded by everyone as a flatterer of Philip, the **King** of the Macedonians—is called a parasite by Lynceus of Samos in his *Memoirs*, as Athenaeus says in *The Barley-Meal* (according to Satyrus the Peripatetic in the *Life of Philip*). He says: "Cleisophus, the parasite of Philip, when Philip rebuked him because he was always asking for things, said: 'I keep forgetting.' When Philip gave him a wounded horse, he sold it. When asked by the King after some time where it was, he said it had 'died of its wound.' When Philip mocked him and he was faring well, Philip said, 'Shall I not support you?'" And Hegesander the brother, in his *Commentaries*, records these things about Cleisophus: When King Philip said that letters had been brought to him from King Cotys, Cleisophus, being present, said, "By the gods, you are right!" When Philip asked, "What do you know of what is written?" he replied, "By Zeus the greatest, you have rebuked me perfectly!" Satyrus says in the *Life of Philip* that when Philip's eye was knocked out, Cleisophus went around with a bandage over the same eye; and again, when the King's leg was injured, he went out limping along with the King. And if Philip ever ate something sharp or bitter, Cleisophus would twist his own face as if sharing the meal. But in the land of the Arabs, they did not do this out of flattery, but according to a certain law...

# BOOK 6

-> λ 3 <-

When a King suffers some injury in his limbs, it is said his followers imitate that same suffering; for they consider it ridiculous to be buried with him when he dies, yet not to grant him the same appearance of suffering while he lives. Nicolaus of Damascus <note>A historian and philosopher (c. 64 BC – 4 AD) who served as a tutor to the children of Antony and Cleopatra and was a friend to Herod the Great.</note>, being one of the Peripatetic school, says in the nineteenth book of his *Universal History* (which consists of one hundred and forty-four books): Adiatomus, the king of the Sotiates (which is a Celtic nation), had six hundred chosen men around him, whom the Gauls call "Silodouri" <term>Silodouri; likely a Latinized Celtic term *soldurii*, meaning "devoted ones" or "vassals"</term> in their native tongue. In Greek, this term means "those bound by a vow." These men live and die alongside their kings, performing this service for them. Those who share his power also wear the same clothing and follow the same lifestyle, and they must necessarily die when he dies, whether the king meets his end by disease, in war, or in any other way. And no one can say that any of these men ever showed cowardice regarding death when the time came for the king to pass away.

Theopompus says in the forty-fourth book of his *Histories* that Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great.</note> established Thrasydaeus the Thessalian as a tyrant over his fellow countrymen, though he was small in intellect but a very great flatterer. However, Arcadion the Achaean was not a flatterer, though the same Theopompus and Duris (in the fifth book of his *History of Macedon*) write about him. This Arcadion hated Philip and went into voluntary exile from his fatherland. Because he was very witty, many of his sayings are remembered. It happened once, while Philip was staying at Delphi, that Arcadion was also present. The Macedonian king, seeing him and calling him over, said: "How much longer will you flee, Arcadion?" And he replied: "Until I reach those who do not know Philip." Phylarchus says in the twenty-first book of his *Histories* that Philip laughed at this and even invited Arcadion to dinner, and in this way their enmity was dissolved.

Regarding Hegesias' son, Nicisias, the flatterer of Alexander: Agandrus relates that when Alexander was being bitten by flies and was zealously brushing them away, Nicisias, who was present, said: "Truly these flies are far superior to all others, for they have tasted your blood." The same author says that Chirisophus, the flatterer of Dionysius <note>Dionysius I, the tyrant of Syracuse.</note>, seeing Dionysius laughing with some acquaintances, stood some distance away from them so he could not hear. When Dionysius asked him why he was laughing when he had not heard what was said, he replied: "I trust you, because what was said must have been ridiculous." 

His son, Dionysius <note>Dionysius II of Syracuse.</note>, also had many who flattered him, whom the common people called "Dionysian Flatterers" <term>Dionysiokolakas; a pun combining the king's name with the word for flatterer</term>. These men used to pretend they could not see clearly at dinner because Dionysius himself had poor eyesight; they would touch the dishes as if they could not see them until Dionysius guided their hands to the bowls. When Dionysius spat frequently, they would offer their own faces to be spat upon, and licking up his saliva—and even his vomit—they would claim it was sweeter than honey.

Timaeus says in the twenty-second book of his *Histories* that Democles, the flatterer of the younger Dionysius, noticed a custom in Sicily of making sacrifices in houses to the Nymphs and spending the night drinking near their statues. Democles, leaving the Nymphs to dance around the goddesses, said there was no need to pay attention to soulless gods, and went and danced before Dionysius instead. Later, when he was on an embassy with others to Dionysius, and all were being carried on a trireme, he was accused by the others of behaving badly during the journey and harming the common interests of Dionysius. When Dionysius became very angry, Democles claimed the dispute between him and his fellow ambassadors arose because, after dinner, they would sing the paeans <note>Hymns of praise or triumph.</note> of Phrynichus, Stesichorus, and Pindar, while he, with those who wished, sang the poems composed by Dionysius himself. He offered clear proof of this: his accusers did not even know the number of the songs, while he was ready to sing them all in order. When Dionysius' anger subsided, Democles said: "You would do me a favor, Dionysius, if you ordered someone who knows it to teach me the paean composed for Asclepius; for I hear you have been working on it."

Once, when friends were invited by Dionysius to dinner, Dionysius entered the room and said: "Friends, letters have been sent to us again from the generals stationed at the New City <note>Probably Neapolis (Naples).</note>." And Democles, interrupting, said: "By the gods, they have done well, Dionysius!" The king looked at him and asked: "How do you know whether what they have written is to our liking or the opposite?" "By the gods, you have rebuked me well, Dionysius!" he replied. Timaeus also records a certain Satyrus as a flatterer of both the Dionysii.

Hegesander relates that Hiero the tyrant also had dimming eyesight, and his friends who dined with him would purposely miss the dishes so they could be guided by him, making it appear that he had sharper vision than the others. Hegesander also says that Euclides, nicknamed "The Bundle" <note>original: *Styplax*</note> (who was also a parasite), when many figs were served to him at dinner, said: "Capaneus <note>One of the Seven against Thebes, famously struck down by Zeus's lightning.</note>, who was..."

### FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS

Euripides, introduced in his play *The Suppliants*, defends the modest life, saying: "I hate the tables of those who puff themselves up too much." <note>original: "μισῶ τραπέζας ὅς τις ἐξογκοῖτ’ ἄγαν" — Euripides, Suppliants 865.</note> It is said that the Athenian demagogues during the Chremonidean War <note>A conflict (c. 267–261 BC) between a coalition of Greek city-states and Macedonia.</note>, seeking to flatter the Athenians, claimed that while everything else was common to all Greeks, only the Athenians knew the road that leads through the gates of heaven to mankind. Satyrus, in his *Lives*, says that Anaxarchus the "Eudaemonic" <note>Meaning "The Joyful" or "The Happy."</note> philosopher was one of the flatterers of Alexander the Great. While traveling with the King, when it started to thunder so violently that everyone cowered in fear, he asked, "Did you do something like that, Alexander, son of Zeus?" Alexander laughed and replied, "I do not wish to be terrifying, as you suggest I should be, you who command me to have the heads of kings and princes served to me at dinner." Aristobulus of Cassandrea says that Dioxippus the Athenian, a <term>pancratiast</term> <note>An athlete in the "pancration," an ancient Greek martial art combining wrestling and boxing.</note>, once saw Alexander wounded and bleeding, and remarked: "Ichor, such as flows in the veins of the blessed gods." <margin>li. 1.</margin> <note>A quote from Homer’s *Iliad* (5.340), referring to the divine fluid that serves as the blood of the gods.</note> <margin>10</margin> Epicrates the Athenian, who served as an ambassador to the royal court <note>The Persian court.</note>—as Hegesander relates—having received many gifts from the King, was not ashamed to flatter him so openly and boldly that he even said that instead of electing nine archons <note>The highest magistrates in Athens.</note> each year, they should elect nine ambassadors to send to the King. I, for my part, wonder at the Athenians: how they could let such a man go without trial, yet they fined Demades ten talents because he proposed that Alexander be recognized as a god. They also put Evagoras to death because, while serving as an ambassador, he performed <term>proskynesis</term> <note>The act of prostrating oneself before a ruler, which Greeks considered an act of worship fit only for gods.</note> before the King. Timon of Phlius, in the third book of his *Silli* <note>Satirical poems.</note>, says that Aristo of Chios, an acquaintance of Zeno, became a flatterer of the philosopher Persaeus because Persaeus was a companion of King Antigonus. Phylarchus, in the sixth book of his *Histories*, says that Nicias, a flatterer of Alexander, seeing the King exhausted by a medicine he had taken, said: "O King, what must we do when even you gods suffer such things?" <margin>20</margin> Alexander, barely looking up, replied: "What kind of gods? I fear we are enemies of the gods."

In the twenty-eighth book, the same Phylarchus says that when Antigonus (called the "Caretaker") captured the city of the Lacedaemonians <note>Sparta.</note>, Apollophanes became his flatterer, telling Antigonus that he possessed the "Fortune of Alexander." Euphantus, in the fourth book of his *Histories*, says that Callicrates was a flatterer of Ptolemy III, the King of Egypt. This man was so extreme that he not only carried an image of Odysseus on his signet ring, but even gave his children the names Telegonus and Anticleia <note>The names of Odysseus's son and mother.</note>. Polybius, in the thirteenth book of his *Histories*, says that Procleides of Tarentum was a flatterer of Philip—the one who was defeated by the Romans—and that he handed over the entire kingdom to him. In the fourteenth book, he mentions Agathocles the son of Oenanthe, and Philo, a friend of another king, Ptolemy Philopator; and for Hieronymus, the tyrant of the Syracusans, he names Thraso, nicknamed "the Shark." Castor of Sinope records in his work on the tyranny of Hieronymus that the tyrant used to consume a great deal of unmixed wine. <margin>30</margin> Another flatterer, whose name was Achen, caused a man to be executed by Hieronymus; this same Achen persuaded Hieronymus himself to wear the diadem, the purple robe, and all the other regalia that the tyrant Dionysius used to wear. Agatharchides, in the thirtieth book of his *Histories*, says that Haeresippus the Spartan was an exceptionally base man, unfit for administration, but possessing a persuasive tongue for flattery, and he cultivated the wealthy as far as their fortunes would allow. Such a man was also Heraclides of Maroneia, the flatterer of Seuthes, the King of the Thracians, whom Xenophon mentions in the seventh book of the *Anabasis*. Theopompus, in the eighteenth book of his *Histories*, speaking of Nicostratus of Argos and how he flattered the King of the Persians, writes the following:

"As for Nicostratus of Argos, how can one not consider him base? Though he was a leader of the city of Argos, and inherited high birth, wealth, and a great estate from his ancestors, he surpassed everyone in flattery and servility, <margin>40</margin> not only those who served in the army at that time, but also those who came before. First, he so craved honor from the Barbarian <note>The Persian King.</note> that, wishing to please him and be trusted more, he handed over his own son to the King—something no one else had ever done so openly. Then, every day when he was about to dine, he would set a table, calling it the 'Table of the King's Spirit,' and fill it with bread and other provisions. He had heard that those of the Persians who lived at the King's gates did this, and he thought that through this service he would gain more money from the King. For he was greedily fond of profit, and a slave to money as much as any man I know." After the King, there came a flatterer and teacher named Simachus, whom Callimachus records as being the son of Theodorus, though Hermippus lists him among the pupils of Theophrastus. This man wrote many books on the education of Attalus <note>Likely Attalus I of Pergamum.</note>, which were full of every kind of flattery. Polybius, in the eighth book of his *Histories*, says that Cauarus the Gaul, though otherwise a good man, was corrupted by his flatterer Sostratus, <margin>50</margin> who was a Chalcedonian by birth. Nicolaus, in the hundred and fourteenth book, says that Andromachus of Carrhae was a flatterer of Licinius Crassus, the one who campaigned against the Parthians. Crassus confided everything to him, only to be betrayed to the Parthians by him and perish. And he...

### BOOK 6.

Andromachus was set over these matters by the divine power <note>original: "ὑπὸ τοῦ δαιμονίου" — implying a stroke of fate or divine providence</note>, for having received the tyranny of his homeland as a reward for his deeds, he and his entire household were burned alive by the people of Tauromenium <note>The OCR reads "Karpiaion," but historical context identifies them as the inhabitants of Tauromenium in Sicily</note> because of his cruelty and violence. Posidonius of Apamea, who later styled himself a Rhodian, says in the fourth book of his *Histories* that Hierax of Antioch—who previously accompanied <term>lysiode</term> singers <note>A "lysiode" was a performer of male roles in female dress, often in a style associated with Simos or Lycus</note> on the flute—later became a flatterer of Ptolemy VII, the king called Euergetes <note>Ptolemy VIII Physcon (often confused in numbering as VII), titled "The Benefactor."</note>. He possessed the greatest power under him, just as he did later under Philometor, before being destroyed by him. Mithridates records a flatterer named Sosipater, a man who was a sorcerer, as does Nicolaus the Peripatetic. Theopompus, in the ninth book of his *Hellenic History*, says that Sisyphus of Pharsalus was the flatterer and servant of Athoneus the Eretrian.

Even the Athenian people came close to this sort of flattery. <margin>5</margin> Demochares, the nephew of the orator Demosthenes, in the twentieth book of his *Histories*, describes the kind of flattery the Athenians practiced toward Demetrius the Besieger. He writes that although it was not Demetrius's own wish at the time, the situation was shameful and debased. <margin>10</margin> Temples were dedicated to Leaina and Lamia <note>Lamia and Leaina were famous courtesans and mistresses of Demetrius Poliorcetes</note> under the name of "Aphrodite," as well as to Adeimantus and Oxythemis, his flatterers. Altars, hero-shrines, and libations were established for each of them, and <term>paeans</term> <note>Hymns originally dedicated to Apollo</note> were sung, so that even Demetrius himself was amazed at what was happening, saying that no Athenian of his time had ever been great and noble of soul. The Thebans also, flattering Demetrius when he was at war, founded a temple to "Aphrodite Lamia" in Sicyon. She was the mistress of Demetrius, just like Leaina. What then could be more paradoxical than the Athenians, acting as flatterers of flatterers, singing paeans and processional hymns to Demetrius himself?

Demochares, writing in his twenty-first book, says that when Demetrius returned from Leucas and Corcyra to Athens, the Athenians received him not only with incense, crowns, and libations, but even processional songs, choruses, and <term>ithyphalloi</term> <note>Suggestive, upright-phallus songs often associated with Dionysian revelry</note> with dancing and song met him. <margin>20</margin> Standing among the crowds, they danced and sang that he was the "only true god," while the others were either sleeping, or away, or did not exist; and that he was the offspring of Poseidon and Aphrodite. They said he was distinct in beauty and common to all in his philanthropy. They approached him with prayers and supplications. Demochares says this much about Athenian flattery.

Duris of Samos, in the twenty-second book of his *Histories*, preserves the very ithyphallic hymn they sang, claiming that the greatest and dearest of the gods were present in the city. 

> For the time has brought us Demetrius.
> The other gods are either far away,
> or have no ears,
> or do not exist, or heed us not at all.
> But you we see present, 
> not of wood or stone, but a true god. 
> To you we pray: first, make peace,
> O dearest one, for you have the power. 
> And this Sphinx that prowls not just around Thebes
> but all of Greece—this Aetolian <note>Referring to the Aetolian League, which was then a threat to Athens</note> 
> who sits upon a rock, just like the one of old, 
> snatching away all our bodies—
> we cannot fight him, for it is the Aetolian way
> to snatch the property of neighbors, 
> and now even those far off. 
> Most of all, punish him yourself; 
> if not, find some Oedipus who will 
> either hurl this Sphinx down the cliffs
> or make him cease his deeds.

<margin>30</margin> These things were sung by the "Men of Marathon"—not only in public but in their private homes!—those very people who had once put to death the man who merely prostrated himself before the Persian King, and who had slaughtered countless myriads of barbarians. Alexis, in his play *The Pharmacist* (or *The Girl in Power*), introduces someone offering a toast to one of his fellow drinkers, saying:

> Pour four cups of friendship for the great Zeus,
> from those present. Having first pledged your loves to you,
> then to the victory of King Antigonus,
> and a cup for the young prince.
> Bring a third for dear Aphrodite,
> and hail to the fellow-drinker of men;
> I shall drink this full cup of good things.

Such were the Athenians, when the wild beast of flattery cast a terrible madness <note>original: "λύσσαμ" — lyssa, often used to describe the rabies of dogs or divine madness</note> upon the city—the city which the Pythian oracle once proclaimed the "hearth of Greece." <margin>40</margin> Even the most hostile Theopompus, who said elsewhere that Athens was full of "Dionysian-flatterers," sailors, and cutpurses, as well as false witnesses, sycophants, and false summons-servers—even I am persuaded that like a rainstorm or some terrible omen from the gods, flattery entered into everything.

Regarding this, Diogenes used to say very well that it was much better to go to the crows <note>original: "κόρακας" — korakas</note> than to the flatterers <note>original: "κόλακας" — kolakas</note>; for crows devour the dead, but flatterers devour the living while they are still "good." <margin>50</margin> Some say that the flatterers of the wealthy are like "the worms in a lekythos" <note>A small oil flask; the proverb suggests they crawl into every crevice of a person's life</note>. Each one crawls into the habits of men in their own way, sitting there until they have sucked them dry like an empty husk of grain. As Plato says in the *Phaedrus*: "To the flatterer, that dangerous beast and great harm, nature has mixed in a certain pleasure that is not without its reward." Theophrastus, in his work *On Flattery*, says that Myllus <note>Possibly a corruption of a name like Myiscus</note> the ancient used to call Cleonymus the dancer—who was also a flatterer—one who often sat beside him and...

->FROM THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED BY ATHENAEUS<-

...to him and his fellow jurors. Wanting to be seen enjoying himself with those in the city, he took him by the hand and dragged him to the council chamber, saying in the presence of many: "The lyre shall not dance, nor shall he hear our voices." Diphilus <note>A poet of New Comedy, contemporary with Menander</note> says in *The Marriage*: "For the flatterer subverts generals and rulers, both friends and cities, with wicked words, providing pleasure for only a short time." He adds that a kind of "bad habit" <note>original: "κἀχεξία" — a state of ill health or a morbid condition of the soul</note> has crept into the masses. Our judgments are diseased, and there is too much focus on pleasing others. Therefore, the Thessalians did well to raze the city called Flattery <note>original: "Κολακεία" — Kolakeia</note>, which the Malians once inhabited, as Theopompus says in his thirtieth book. Phylarchus says in the thirteenth book of his *Histories* that the Athenians living in Lemnos were also flatterers. Out of gratitude to the descendants of Seleucus and Antiochus <note>Successor kings of Alexander the Great</note>—since Seleucus himself had not only rescued them when they were harshly ruled by Lysimachus but also restored both their cities to them—the Athenians from Lemnos built temples not only to Seleucus but also to his son Antiochus. Furthermore, when pouring a cup of wine at their social gatherings, they invoke "Seleucus the Savior" <note>original: "Σελεύκου Σωτῆρος" — Seleukos Soter</note>.

Some people, trying to avoid the stigma of this word "flattery," call it "complaisance" <note>original: "ἀρέσκειαν" — areskeia; the quality of being overly eager to please</note>, as Anaxandrides says in *The Woman from Samos*: "For flattery now goes by the name of complaisance." But those who practice flattery do not realize that this "art" is short-lived. Alexis, at any rate, says in *The Liar*: "The life of a flatterer blooms for a short time; for no one enjoys a grey-haired parasite." <margin>15</margin> Clearchus of Soli, in the first book of his *On Love*, says: "No flatterer remains constant in friendship, for time consumes the falsehood of their pretense. The lover, however, is a 'flatterer of friendship' due to youth or beauty." Among the flatterers of King Demetrius, those around Adeimantus of Lampsacus built a temple and set up statues at Thria, naming them "Phila-Aphrodite" <note>Combining the name of Demetrius's wife/mother, Phila, with the goddess of love</note>. <margin>20</margin> They called the place the "Philaeum" after Demetrius's mother, Phila, as Dionysius the son of Tryphon says in the tenth book of *On Names*.

Clearchus of Soli, in the work titled *Gergithios*, explains where the name of "flatterers" originated. He introduces Gergithios himself—after whom the book is named—as one of the flatterers of Alexander the Great. He explains it this way: flattery makes the character of the flatterers base, as they feel contempt for those around them (a sign of which is that they endure things while knowing what they are daring to do). Meanwhile, the characters of those being flattered are puffed up by the flattery, becoming empty and vain, leading them to believe that their superiority is acknowledged by everyone. Following this, he tells a story about a certain youth, Paphian by birth but a king by fortune. This youth (whose name he does not mention) would lie down, due to excessive luxury, upon a silver-footed couch covered with a very expensive Sardian carpet. <margin>30</margin> Over him was spread a purple rug with an Amorgian <note>A fine, silk-like linen from the island of Amorgos</note> coverlet. He had three pillows of fine linen with purple borders under his head, which were held in place by the coverlet. Two more pillows, dyed with sea-purple and of the so-called "Doric" style, were under his feet, upon which he lay dressed in a white cloak.

All the monarchs in Cyprus have adopted the race of "noble flatterers" as something useful. Indeed, this "possession" is entirely suited to tyrants. It is a group like the Areopagites <note>The high court of Athens</note>, whom no one among the common people knows by sight, except for the most prominent members. The flatterers in Salamis are divided into two groups by kinship, from whom the flatterers in the rest of Cyprus are derived: they call one group the "Gergini" and the other the "Promalangae." The Gergini mingle with the people in the city, in the workshops and the marketplaces, acting as spies <note>original: "ὠτακουσοῦσι" — literally "ear-listeners" or eavesdroppers</note>. Whatever they hear, they report each day to the so-called "lords" <note>original: "ἀνάκτας" — anaktas</note>. The Promalangae then investigate the reports brought by the Gergini. Their skill and persuasiveness in social interaction are so great that it seems to me, as they themselves say, that the "selection" <note>original: "αἴρεμα" — referring to the choicest or most skilled</note> of distinguished flatterers spread from them to other places. They are not merely moderately proud of their profession because of the honor they receive from kings; they even claim that one of the Gergini was a descendant of those people whom Teucer <note>The legendary founder of Salamis in Cyprus after the Trojan War</note> took as captives and settled in Cyprus. This descendant supposedly sailed along the coast and, following a divine light, founded a city near Trojan Mount Ida in the land of his ancestors, taking some Mysians with him. That city was formerly called Gergitha after the race, but is now called Gergitha. It seems that some people, having been separated from this stock, settled in the region of Cyme <note>In Aeolis, Asia Minor</note>, being of Cypriot descent—though some say they came from Tricca in Thessaly, an ignorance which I believe not even the sons of Asclepius <note>The god of healing</note> could cure. <margin>50</margin> There existed in our region, during the time of Glutus, women who served the "lords" <note>the kings</note> who were called "female flatterers" <note>original: "κολακίδες" — kolakides</note>. Some of their remnants went across the sea, having been sent for by the wives of Artabazus and Mentor, and were renamed "ladder-women" <note>original: "κλιμακίδες" — klimakides</note> because of their practice: to please the women who sent for them, they made a "ladder" of themselves so that the women could climb...

<meta>catchword: ...up onto their backs.</meta>

# BOOK VI

...it is their custom to make both the ascent and descent in wagons, reaching such an insolence of luxury that they might not be worn out by any hardship. Dionysius <note>Likely referring to Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse known for his excesses</note>, having been moved by his craft away from his excessively soft lifestyle, lived harshly in his old age. But those among us who inherited these habits, having fallen from power, went down to Macedonia; it is not even honorable to describe the manner in which they accustomed the mistresses and queens there to their company, except to say that they became like "Bull-riding" processions <note>original: "ταυροπολικὰ" — likely referring to the wild, frenzied festivals of Artemis Tauropolos</note>, truly full of all kinds of impurities. It seems that flattery of this sort becomes the cause of so many evils for those who accept it through being flattered. Moving forward again, Clearchus says the following: "But someone might find fault with the youth's need for attendants, as I said." For some, being a little away from their children, used the tunics of Philoxenes. Since there were three of them through whom the whole story is now told, and who are truly famous among us, one sat on the couch at the feet of the youth, having wrapped the youth's legs over his own knees with a thin cloth. What he was doing is not unclear, even if I do not say it. This man is called **Side-door** <note>original: "Παράθυρος" — Parathyros</note> by the locals, because of his skill in slipping into conversations even when people do not welcome him. Another was **Epitinos**, who stayed by a chair placed near the couch itself. Hanging from the youth's outstretched hand, he cooled it and, taking each of the fingers in turn, he pulled and stretched them, so that the person who first nicknamed him **The Gourd** <note>original: "σικύαν" — sikya; a cupping-glass used in medicine to draw blood, here implying he 'sticks' to his patron</note> seemed to have spoken quite accurately. The third was that "sweetest beast," who was Philocrates, the protagonist; he leaned quite affectionately against the youth's head, which was resting on fine linen pillows. With his left hand he groomed the youth's hair, and with the other he moved a sort of "whispering brush," making a pleasant sound as if invisible, yet not actually shooing anything away. It seems to me that some noble spirit, feeling indignation, sent a fly to the youth—one of no ordinary kind—just as Homer says Athena put courage into Menelaus <note>A reference to the *Iliad*, where Athena gives Menelaus the persistence of a fly</note>, so strong and fearless was its soul. When the fly bit him, the man cried out so loudly on the youth's behalf and was so angry that, because of this single offense, he rushed out and drove the fly from the house. From this, it became clear he had stationed himself for this purpose; but Leucon, the tyrant of Pontus, was not such a man. When he perceived that many of his friends were being plundered by the flatterers around him, and seeing a man slandering one of his remaining friends, he put him to death, saying: "By the gods, if the tyranny did not require it, we would not ask for villains." Antiphanes, the comic poet, in *The Soldier*, says similar things regarding the luxury of the kings in Cyprus; he depicts someone asking a soldier these things:

> Tell me, you say you spent a long time in Cyprus
> While the war lasted. In what place
> Did you stay most? Tell me. For you say
> There was a remarkably delicate thing to see,
> Otherwise unbelievable. What kind? He was fanned
> By pigeons, and by nothing else,
> The King, while dining. How? Tell me,
> For I am asking. We know how he was anointed
> With a special perfume brought from Syria, made from a fruit
> Which they say the pigeons like to eat.
> Because of its scent, they came flying there,
> And were able to settle upon his head.
> But boys sitting nearby would shoo them away,
> Raising them just a little, but not so far
> That they left entirely, thus they fanned him
> So that the breeze they made for him was perfectly
> Measured and not too harsh.

Thus, the flatterer of the aforementioned youth would be a "malleable flatterer," as Clearchus says. For how could one not be flattered by such a person, when the very shape of the one being flattered is molded by him, as he positions and wraps himself around the person in front of him? This is why some call him a "side-dish-licker" <note>original: "παραψωνικυλιστήν"</note>, and others a "body-rubber." In truth, the flatterer seems to be the same as **Proteus** <note>A sea god capable of changing into any shape</note>. At least, he becomes all sorts of things, not only in his form but also in his speech; he is so multifaceted in his mind. Androcydes the physician used to say that flattery <note>original: "κολακεία" — kolakeia</note> got its name from "sticking to" <note>original: "προσκολλᾶσθαι" — proskollasthai</note> conversations. But it seems to me it is because of his ease, because he slips into everything like a submissive beast of burden through the character of his soul, and is not burdened by any shameful act. One would not be wrong to call the life of that Cypriot youth **Fluid** <note>original: "ὑγρόν" — hygros; meaning soft, moist, or dissolute</note>. Alexis says there is a great teacher and prize-master of this in *The Brazier*, speaking thus:

> I desired to make trial of the other life,
> Which everyone is accustomed to call "fluid."
> So, having walked for three days in the Ceramicus,
> I found teachers—I do not say of life—
> But perhaps thirty from a single workshop.

And Crobylus says in *The Deserted Woman*: "The fluidity of your life has stunned me, or rather your wastefulness." For some now address luxury as "fluidity." Antiphanes, in *The Lemnian Women*, suggests that flattery is a kind of craft when he says:

> If there is any good fortune for a city,
> Or any other source of income than fawning
> Cleverly, which a painter toils and suffers for,
> Or a farmer, in all the dangers he faces...
> Again, care and toil are present in all.
> But for us, life is spent with laughter and luxury.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of flatterers, specifically transitioning from general descriptions of their behavior to historical examples of how flatterers have overthrown kings and corrupted the courts of rulers like Philip of Macedon and Dionysius of Syracuse.</meta>

# FROM THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

For it is no small task, no mere game, to laugh all at once, to mock someone, or to drink a great deal. Such things are not pleasant to me—at least, not compared to being wealthy. Menander <note>A famous Athenian playwright of the New Comedy, known for his character studies</note> has characterized the flatterer as carefully as possible in the play of the same name, as has Diphilus with the parasite in his *Telesias*. Alexis, in his play *The False Accuser*, introduces a certain flatterer who speaks of his nature in this way: "By Zeus the Olympian and by Athonas <note>original: "Ἀθωνᾶ" — likely a local epithet or reference to Mount Athos</note>, I am happy! Not because I will feast at a wedding on the very same day, but because I shall burst, if God wills it. May it be my lot to meet death in this way!" It seems to me that this man is Philo the "Beautiful Belly" <note>original: "γάστρις" (gastris) — a glutton</note>; I would not hesitate to apply to him the words from the *Omphale* of Ion the tragic poet: "I must call the festival an 'acquaintance,' as it is a daily occurrence."

Hippias of Erythrae, in the second book of his *Histories of his Native Land*, recounts how King Knopos was overthrown by his own flatterers, saying the following: When Knopos consulted the oracle about his safety, the god commanded him to sacrifice to Hermes the Guileful <note>original: "Ἑρμῇ δολίῳ" — Hermes Dolios, the patron of thieves and tricksters</note>. After this, when he set out for Delphi, those who wished to overthrow his kingship in order to establish an oligarchy—namely Ortyges, Iros, and Echaros—accompanied him. These men were called his "flatterers" because of their extreme attendance upon his eminent person. While they were sailing with Knopos and were already far from land, they bound Knopos and threw him into the deep sea. They then landed at Chios and, receiving forces from the tyrants there, Amphiclus and Polytecnus, they sailed by night to Erythrae. At the same time, Knopos’s body was washed up on the shore of Erythrae at the place now called Liopodion. While Knopos’s wife, Cleonice, was occupied with the burial of the body, a festival and assembly for Artemis Sophia <note>Artemis the Wise</note> was being held. Suddenly, the blast of a trumpet was heard; the city was captured by Ortyges and his followers, and many of Knopos’s friends were put to death. Cleonice, having learned of this, fled to Colophon.

Ortyges and his fellow tyrants, bolstered by the force from Chios, destroyed those who opposed their affairs. Having abolished the laws, they managed the city’s business within the walls, admitting none of the common citizens. Outside the gates, they set up a tribunal and conducted trials, dressing themselves in sea-purple robes <note>original: "ἁλουργὰ" — robes dyed with expensive murex purple</note> and tunics with purple borders. During the summer, they wore intricate sandals, but in winter, they walked about in women's shoes made of mesh. They grew their hair long and practiced wearing tresses, binding their heads with yellow and purple headbands. They also wore solid gold ornaments, just like women. They forced some of the citizens to be their litter-bearers, others to be their staff-bearers, and others to sweep the roads. They would summon the wives and daughters of the noblemen to their public gatherings, and those who disobeyed were subjected to the most extreme punishments. If anyone from their circle of associates died, they would gather the citizens with their wives and children and force them to mourn the deceased, beating their breasts by force and crying out loudly and shrilly, while lash-bearers stood over them to compel this behavior. This continued until Hippotes, the brother of Knopos, attacked Erythrae with a force during a festival. With the help of the Erythraeans, he fell upon the tyrants, tortured many of their followers, stabbed Ortyges as he fled, and killed those with him. Having severely punished their wives and children, he liberated his fatherland. From all these events, one can see <margin>Love of flatterers.</margin> what great evils flattery causes in life.

For Theopompus also says in the nineteenth book of his *History of Philip* that Agathocles, who had been a slave and one of the Thessalian serfs <note>original: "πενεστῶν" (penestai) — a class of unfree laborers in Thessaly</note>, became very powerful with Philip because of his flattery. Because he would mock Philip at banquets, dance, and provide laughter, Philip sent him to destroy the Perrhaebians and manage affairs there. The Macedonian always kept such men around him, with whom he spent most of his time and held counsel on the most important matters due to their love of drinking and buffoonery <note>original: "βωμολοχίαν" (bomolochian) — low-brow or scurrilous jesting</note>. Hegesander of Delphi records these things about them: <margin>Diomeia, see Suidas.</margin> that when a group of jokers used to gather at the temple of Heracles in Diomeia <note>A district in Athens known for its temple of Heracles and its "club" of sixty wits</note>, Philip sent them a significant sum of money and ordered certain people to write down their jokes and send them to him.

Theopompus, in the twenty-sixth book of his *Histories*, says that Philip, knowing certain Thessalians were unrestrained and lewd in their lifestyle, organized gatherings for them and tried to please them in every way, even by dancing, reveling, and enduring every kind of debauchery. He was a buffoon by nature and got drunk every day, delighting in practices that tended toward such things. Among men, he preferred those called "gifted" <note>original: "εὐφυέσι" — witty or clever</note>, who said and did funny things; he chose more of the Thessalians who approached him for his social circles than for his gifts. Dionysius of Sicily acted in a similar way, as Eubulus the comic poet presented in his play of the same name, *The Tyrant*: "But he is more stubborn toward the solemn, and more pleasing to all flatterers and those who mock him. He loved these alone as free men, and they were his friends."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of flatterers (kolakes) by moving from general types to specific historical examples, focusing on the courts of Philip II of Macedon and Dionysius of Syracuse. It explores how these rulers preferred the company of the debauched over the virtuous.</meta>

# BOOK VI

Indeed, not only Dionysius <note>Dionysius I, the tyrant of Syracuse (c. 432–367 BC)</note> but also Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon (382–336 BC), father of Alexander the Great</note> welcomed those who squandered their estates on drinking and dice, and on such forms of licentiousness. Theopompus <note>A 4th-century BC Greek historian known for his biting critiques of contemporary figures</note> records this regarding each of them; in the forty-ninth book of his *Histories*, he writes as follows: "Philip rejected those who were orderly in their habits and took care of their private affairs; but those who were extravagant and lived their lives in gambling and drinking, he honored and promoted. Therefore, he not only encouraged them to possess such vices but also made them champions of every other kind of injustice and foulness. For what shameful or base thing did they lack, or what noble and serious thing did they not disregard? Did they not persist in being shaved and smoothed <note>original: "λειαινόμενοι" — referring to the practice of removing body hair to appear more effeminate</note> even though they were men? And they dared to make sexual advances toward one another despite having beards. They would travel about with two or three male prostitutes, yet they provided the same services to others. Thus, one might justly have considered them not companions <note>original: "hetairoi" — the title of Philip’s elite cavalry and inner circle</note> but courtesans <note>original: "hetairai" — the female equivalent, a sharp pun on their status</note>.
<margin>10</margin> Nor would one call them soldiers, but rather street-walkers. For though they were man-killers by nature, they were man-prostitutes by habit. In addition to this, instead of being sober, they loved being drunk; instead of living orderly lives, they sought to plunder and murder. They did not consider it their duty to tell the truth or abide by agreements; rather, they believed that perjury and cheating were the most solemn of things. They neglected what they possessed and yearned for what they did not have. And this, despite them holding a portion of Europe. For I believe that the 'Companions'—who were no more than eight hundred in number at that time—harvested no less land than ten thousand Greeks, even those who possessed the best and most extensive territory." Regarding Dionysius, he records similar things in the twenty-first book: "Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, favored those who squandered their
<margin>Laughter-lovers</margin> estates on drinking and dice and such licentiousness. For he wanted everyone to be corrupt and base, and these were the ones he treated well." Demetrius Poliorcetes <note>Demetrius "the Besieger," a Successor to Alexander the Great</note> was also a lover of laughter, as Phylarchus records in the
<margin>20</margin> tenth book of his *Histories*. And in the fourteenth book, he writes as follows: "Just as Demetrius saw those who flattered him at banquets and tried to claim that Demetrius alone was King, but Ptolemy was only an Admiral, Lysimachus a Treasurer, and Seleucus an Elephant-master <note>These titles were intended as insults to Demetrius's rivals, suggesting they were mere subordinates rather than sovereign kings</note>. From these things, he gathered much hatred at random."
<margin>Book 2</margin> Herodotus says that Amasis, the king of the Egyptians, was a playful man who mocked his fellow drinkers; even when he was a private citizen, he was a lover of drinking and a lover of jokes, and not a man of serious character. Nicolaus <note>Nicolaus of Damascus, a historian and tutor to the children of Antony and Cleopatra</note> says in the twenty-seventh book of his *Histories* that Sulla, the Roman general, so delighted in mimes and jesters because he was a lover of laughter, that he even granted them many acres of public land. His cheerful disposition in these matters is revealed by the satyric comedies he wrote in his native tongue <note>original: "τῇ πατρώῳ φωνῇ" — Latin</note>. Theophrastus, in his work *On Comedy*, says that the people of Tiryns <note>An ancient city in the Peloponnese</note> were so fond of laughter that when they found themselves unable to handle serious matters, they fled to the oracle at Delphi
<margin>30</margin> seeking to be rid of the affliction. The god replied that if they could sacrifice a bull to Poseidon and throw it into the sea without laughing, they would be cured. Fearing they might fail the oracle's condition, they even forbade children from being present at the sacrifice. However, one boy found out and mingled with them; when he saw them trying to drive him away, he said, "What are you afraid of? That I'll overturn your victim?" When they laughed at this, they learned by experience that the god was teaching them that a long-standing habit is impossible to cure. Sosicrates, in the first book of his *Cretica*, says there is something peculiar about the people of Phaestus. For they seem to practice from childhood the art of saying funny things, which is why they often happen to speak wittily in season because of this early habit. Consequently, everyone in Crete attributes jokes to them. 
<margin>Boasters</margin> Alexandrides the comic poet gives place to boastfulness alongside flattery in *The Drug-Diviner*, saying: "I am a boaster among the esteemed. But for what reason? For this art, along with
<margin>40</margin> flattery, is far superior." Antiphanes mentions "crumb-flatterers" <note>original: "ψωμοκόλακας" (psomokolakas) — those who flatter just for a morsel of food</note> in *Gerytades* as follows: "You are called a whisperer, a flatterer, and a lewd fellow; where are you off to, you cursed crumb-flatterers?" Philemon notes: "This man is a crumb-flatterer." Philippides says in *Aulonia*: "Always crumb-flattering and wagging his tail." The term *kolax* (flatterer) is properly derived from this; for *kolon* is food <note>An ancient etymological theory linking the flatterer to the stomach or the limbs/food</note>, hence also *boukolos* (herdsman). Also *dyskolos* (difficult/fretful), which means someone hard to please and fastidious. And *koilia* (belly), which receives the food. Diphilus in *Theseus* uses the term "crumb-slap" <note>original: "ψωμοκόλαφον" (psomokolaphon)</note> saying: "He will call you a runaway crumb-slap." After Democritus said these things and asked for a drink from a "Sambeia" narrow-necked jar, Ulpian asked, "And what is the 'Sambeia'?" As he was about to go through many points from his miscellaneous learning, a multitude of servants appeared bringing in the things for the feast.
<margin>Slaves</margin> <margin>50</margin> Starting again, Democritus said: "I have always wondered at the race of slaves, how they are so self-controlled while wallowing in such dainties. These they do not gulp down, not only because of fear, but also by training—not the kind from Pherecrates's *Slave-Teacher*, but by habit." He noted that this was the case in the island of Cos when they sacrifice to Hera. For Macarius says in the third book of his *Coica* that whenever the Coans sacrifice to Hera, no slave enters the temple, nor does any slave taste any of the prepared dishes. And Antiphanes says in *Dynastratos* that one can see half-eaten cakes lying about...

...half-eaten, and scraps of bird, which the women say it is not lawful to eat even if caught. Epikrates <note>A 4th-century BC Athenian comic poet</note>, in his play *The Hard-to-Sell Man*, shows a servant complaining and saying: "For what is more hateful than being called 'boy' during a drinking party? And even worse, for a beardless youth to have to carry the chamber-pot <note>original: "amida"</note> for someone, and to see and smell the foul, half-eaten scraps and bird-meat? It is not even lawful to eat these if caught, as the women say." He calls the stomach a "gluttonous reaper" for those who won't eat any of these things of ours. From this un-iambic iambic verse, it is clear that Epikrates has borrowed these lines from Antiphanes <note>Another prolific comic poet of the Middle Comedy period</note>. Archiadas, in his *History of Megara*,

<margin>Beginnings [according to] Stephanus <note>Referring to the 16th-century editor Henri Estienne (Stephanus)</note></margin>
says that the islands called the † Araiai <note>meaning "The Cursed" or "The Thin/Scattered"</note> are located between the Cnidians and Rhodes. He explains that a dispute arose among those who had set out with Phorbas <note>A legendary figure often associated with Rhodes</note> after his death. While some retreated to their quarters, those who remained with Phorbas came to Ialysos. However, those following the "meddler" <note>original: "priergos"</note> occupied the chambers. At that time, it is said that the "meddler" cursed Phorbas. And because of this, the islands were called *Araiai* <note>original: "araias" — the Cursed Islands</note>. Phorbas was shipwrecked, and Phorbas’s daughter, Parthenia, and the meddler's sister were carried on a raft to the place called Ialysos. There, they were met by Thamnus, who happened to be an avid hunter. He led them to his home to host them and sent his servant to tell his wife to prepare the necessary eggs <note>original: "pita ōa"</note>, as he was bringing guests. But when Thamnus arrived home and found nothing prepared, he himself threw grain onto the griddle and did the other necessary things, then entertained them with ground meal. Phorbas was so pleased with this hospitality that, when his life was ending, he commanded his friends that only free men should perform the funeral rites for him. This custom remains in the sacrifice to Phorbas, for those who serve are all free men. It is clear that this must be done in a holy manner. Since Ulpian has put forward questions regarding "city-slaves," let us open up a discussion about them, based on what we have long ago read. Pherecrates <note>A 5th-century BC Athenian comic poet</note> says in his play *The Savages*: "For back then, no one had a slave like a Maues or a Sacas <note>Foreign names typical of the slave trade</note>, but the women had to perform all these labors in the house themselves."

"Then everyone who came by at dawn found them grinding grain, so that the village echoed with the sound of the mills."
And Anaxandrides <note>A Middle Comedy poet</note> says in *Anchises*: "There is no city at all, my good men, where slavery does not exist. Fortune shifts the bodies of all people. Many who are not free today will be citizens of Sunium tomorrow, and on the third day, they will frequent the marketplace. For a divinity turns the tiller for each person." Poseidonios of the Stoa <note>A famous 1st-century BC Stoic philosopher and historian</note> says in the eleventh book of his *Histories* that many people, being unable to govern themselves due to a weakness of the mind, give themselves over to the service of those more intelligent. In return, they receive the care they need for their basic necessities, and they, in turn, provide whatever services they are capable of. In this way, the Mariandynoi <note>A people of northern Anatolia</note> became subject to the people of Heraclea, promising to serve them as long as they provided their needs; they stipulated that none of them should be sold outside the territory of Heraclea, but only within their own land. Perhaps for this reason, Euphorion the epic poet <note>A 3rd-century BC poet and librarian</note> called the Mariandynoi "gift-bearers" <note>original: "dorophoroi"</note>. "They are called gift-bearers, who serve their masters." Callistratus, the follower of Aristophanes, also says that they named the Mariandynoi "gift-bearers" to take away the bitterness of the name "slaves," just as the Spartans did with the Helots, the Thessalians with the Penestai, and the Cretans with the Klarotai. The Cretans call those in the city slaves "gold-bought" <note>original: "chrysonētas"</note>, but those in the country they call *amphamiōtai*—these are locals who were enslaved in war and were called *Klarotai* <note>original: "klarōtas"</note> because they were distributed by lot <note>original: "klēros"</note>. Ephorus, in the third book of his *Histories*, says the Cretans call their slaves *Klarotai* from the lot that was cast for them. Certain festivals are customary for these people in Cydonia <note>A city in Crete</note>, during which no free men enter the city, but the slaves rule over everything and are masters who may even whip the free men. Sosicrates, in his second book of *Cretan Affairs*, says the Cretans call general slavery *mnoia* <note>the public slave class</note>, but private slavery they call *aphamiota*, and the subjects are called *perioikoi* <note>those living in outlying districts</note>. Dosiadas records similar things in his fourth book of *Cretan Affairs*. Regarding the Thessalians, who call those who are not slaves by birth but were captured in war *Penestai* <note>laborers or "the poor"</note>, the comic poet Theopompus, using the word, says: "Master, become a counselor of the Penestai." Philocrates, in his second book of *Thessalian Affairs*—if the writings are genuine—says the Penestai are also called "Thessalian-servants." Archemachus, in his third book of *Euboean Affairs*, says that when the Boeotians settled Arna, those who did not depart for Boeotia but remained out of love for the land gave themselves over to the Thessalians to be slaves by agreement. The condition was that the masters would neither take them out of the country nor kill them. They, in turn, would work the land for them and pay a contribution. These people who remained according to the agreements and surrendered themselves were then called *Menestai* <note>Those who stayed</note>, but are now called *Penestai*. For this reason, many of them are wealthier than their masters. Euripides, in his play *Phrixus*, calls them "Latreis" <note>hired servants</note> in these words: "A Penestian servant <note>original: "latris"</note> of my ancient house." Timaeus of Tauromenium, in the ninth book of his *Histories*, says that it was not an ancestral custom for Greeks to be served by silver-bought <note>chattel</note> slaves in ancient times, writing as follows: "Generally, they accused Aristotle of having erred regarding the customs of the Locrians. For they did not even possess..."
