### BOOK 6.

It was the law for the Locrians, and likewise for the Phocians <note>Central Greek regions</note>, to have neither handmaids nor domestic slaves, at least until very recently. However, Philomela, the first woman to seize Delphi <note>A reference to the Third Sacred War, c. 356 BC, when the Phocians occupied the sanctuary</note>, was followed by two handmaids. Similarly, Mnason, the companion of the philosopher Aristotle, was slandered among the Phocians for acquiring a thousand slaves, as he was seen as depriving so many citizens of their necessary food. For it was the custom in households for the younger members to serve the elders.

Plato says in the sixth book of his *Laws* that the management of slaves is difficult in every way. This is because, of all the Greeks, the Lacedaemonian system of "Helots" <note>A class of unfree laborers in Sparta who were tied to the land</note> provides the greatest difficulty and dispute—some saying it was established well, others that it was not. The enslavement of the Mariandyni <note>A tribe in Bithynia enslaved by the Greek city of Heraclea Pontica</note> causes less dispute. Then there is the "Penestic" <note>A class of serfs in Thessaly similar to the Helots</note> nation of the Thessalians. Looking at all these examples, we must ask: what should we do regarding the ownership of slaves? 

<margin>10</margin> For there is nothing healthy in the soul of a slave. That one should trust them or that they possess a sound mind is not to be believed. 

<margin>Iliad</margin> As the wisest of poets <note>Homer</note> says: "For wide-seeing Zeus takes away half of a man’s mind <note>original: "noou" — often translated as "virtue" or "worth"</note> on the day that the day of slavery seizes him." <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 17.322–323</note> Thus, owning them is often shown to be a difficult matter in practice, as seen in the frequent revolts of the Messenians and the evils that occur in cities that acquire many slaves who speak the same language. 

<margin>The Dinner-Sophists</margin> Furthermore, there are the deeds and sufferings involving the various thefts by the so-called slaves in the cities of Italy. Anyone looking at all these things would be at a loss as to what should be done about such matters. Two methods alone remain: first, that those who are to serve more easily should not be from the same country, and as much as possible, they should speak different languages <note>original: "asymphonous" — meaning not in agreement or discordance in speech</note>. Second, one should nourish them correctly, not only for their sake, but more out of respect for oneself. One should treat them with the least possible insolence; slaves must be punished with justice, and not pampered by being admonished like free men, which makes them conceited. Almost every address to a slave should be a command, and one should never play with slaves, whether female or male. 

<margin>20</margin> Many Athenians treat their slaves with great foolishness and pampering, making life harder for the slaves to be ruled and for themselves to rule. I know that the Chians were the first of the Greeks to use "silver-bought" <note>chattel slaves purchased with money, as opposed to populations conquered in war</note> slaves, as Theopompus reports in the seventeenth book of his *Histories*. The Chians were the first Greeks after the Thessalians and Lacedaemonians to use slaves, though they did not acquire them in the same way. For it will be seen that the Lacedaemonians and Thessalians established their slavery from the Greeks who previously inhabited the land they now hold—the Achaeans in the case of the Lacedaemonians, and the Perrhaebians and Magnetes for the Thessalians. They called these enslaved people "Helots" and "Penestae" respectively. But the Chians possess "barbarians" <note>Non-Greeks, typically from Thrace or Asia Minor</note> as their domestic servants, paying a price for them. 

Theopompus recorded these things. I believe the divine power <note>original: "daimonion"</note> was angry with the Chians for this reason. For in later times, they were brought to war because of a slave girl. 

<margin>30</margin> Nymphodorus of Syracuse, in his *Voyage of Asia*, records these things about them: In Chios, the slaves run away from their masters, and gathering in large numbers in the mountains, they harass the farmsteads, for the island is mountainous and heavily wooded. A little before our time, there was a certain slave—of whom the Chians themselves tell legends—who ran away and lived in the mountains. He was a brave man who led the runaway servants in war, like a king of armies. Although the Chians often campaigned against him, they achieved nothing. When Drímakos (for that was the runaway's name) saw that they were being destroyed in vain, he said to them: "O Chians and masters, this business of the slaves will never cease. For how could it, since it is an oracle given by a god? But if you listen to me and let us live in peace, I will be the source of many benefits to you." 

They stayed in Chios and made a truce for a time. 

<margin>40</margin> He prepared his own measures, weights, and a personal seal, and showing them to the Chians, he said: "When I take something from any of you, I will take it according to these measures and weights. And having taken enough, I will leave the valuables sealed with this seal. As for the slaves who run away from you, I will examine their reason. If they seem to me to have run away because they suffered something incurable, I will keep them with me. But if they have no just cause to speak of, I will send them back to their masters." 

Seeing that the Chians gladly accepted this arrangement, the remaining slaves ran away much less often, fearing his judgment. The runaways who were with him feared him much more than their own masters, and they did everything necessary for him, obeying him as if he were a general. For he punished those who were disorderly, and allowed no one to plunder a field or do any other injustice without his permission. On feast days, he would go out and take wine and fine sacrificial animals from the farms. 

<margin>50</margin> Whatever the masters gave him [he accepted], but if any of them tried to act unjustly or set traps for him, he punished them. Then, because the city had proclaimed that they would give a great deal of money to whoever captured him or brought his head, this Drímakos, having grown old, called his beloved to a certain place and said to him: "I have loved you most of all men, and you are to me both child and son, and all other...

# FROM THE ATHENAEANS’ DEIPNOSOPHISTS
<meta>catchword: men,</meta>

...all other things. As for me, I have lived a sufficient amount of time. But you are young, and you are in the prime of your life; what you must do now is become a truly noble and good man. Since the city of the Chians is offering great rewards to whoever kills me, and promises them their freedom, you must cut off my head and carry it to Chios. Once you have received the money from the city, you may live in happiness." Although the young man argued against it, Drimakos eventually persuaded him to do this. And so, the youth cut off his head and received the bounty that had been proclaimed by the Chians. After burying the body of the runaway leader, he departed to his own land. 

Later, when the Chians were once again being mistreated and plundered by their domestic slaves, they remembered the fairness of the deceased Drimakos and established a hero’s shrine <note>Greek: *heroon*, a shrine dedicated to a person who has attained semi-divine status after death</note> in that region. They named him the "Benevolent Hero." Even to this day, runaway slaves bring him the first-fruits of everything they have taken. It is also said that he appears to many Chians in their sleep to warn them of plots by their servants. Those to whom he appears go to the place where the shrine is located and offer sacrifices to him.

This is the account recorded by Nymphodorus. However, in many copies of the text, I have not found him mentioned by name. I believe you are also aware of what the fine historian Herodotus recorded concerning Panionios of Chios and the punishment he suffered for his practice of castrating free-born boys and selling them. 

<margin>book 6.</margin> Nicolaus the Peripatetic and Posidonius the Stoic both state in their histories that the Chians were eventually enslaved by Mithridates of Cappadocia and handed over in chains to their own slaves to be resettled in the land of the Colchians. In this way, the divine truly showed its anger toward them for being the first to use "bought" slaves <note>The text distinguishes between "chattel" slavery (buying people like property) and older forms of serfdom where people were tied to the land but not traded as commodities</note>, whereas most others performed their own service. Perhaps it is because of this that the proverb arose: "A Chian bought a master," which Eupolis also uses in his play *The Friends*. 

The Athenians are the most exempt from blame in this regard, as they look out for the fortunes of slaves, even enacting laws that allow for "indictments for outrage" <note>Greek: *graphe hybreos*. In Athens, a citizen could be prosecuted for assaulting or insulting a slave, a rare legal protection in the ancient world</note> on behalf of slaves. Indeed, the orator Hypereides says in his speech *Against Mantitheus* that the lawgivers established penalties for battery not only regarding free men, but also ordered that an indictment be filed against anyone who commits an outrage against the body of a slave. Lycurgus says similar things in his first speech *Against Lycophron*, as does Demosthenes in his speech *Against Meidias*. 

Malacus, in his *History of the Siphnian Territories*, records that the slaves of the Ephesians, numbering one thousand, were originally from Samos. They first revolted and fled to the mountain on the island, where they caused many troubles for the Samians. Six years later, following an oracle, the Samians came to an agreement with the servants. These slaves left the island unharmed, sailed away, and occupied Ephesus, becoming the ancestors of the current Ephesians. 

Chrysippus says that a "slave" differs from a "domestic servant" <note>Chrysippus distinguishes between the legal status (*doulos*) and the social/functional role (*oiketes*)</note>. In the second book of his work *On Concord*, he writes that while freedmen are still "slaves" in a legal sense, domestic servants are those who have not been released from ownership. For a domestic servant, he says, is a slave assigned to a specific household. 

Slaves are called by many names: Cleitarchus, in his *Glossary*, says they are called *azoi*, "attendants," "followers," "ministers," and "servants," as well as "laborers" and "hired hands." Amerias says that domestic servants in the fields are called *erkitas*. Hermon, in his *Cretan Glossary*, mentions *mnotas*, whom he calls "noble servants." Seleucus mentions *azas* for female servants and "attendants." He also notes the term *epophthasai* for a slave girl at the mill, and *syndroma* for a group of slaves. A "handmaid" is a servant at the feet of her mistress, and a "leader" is one who walks in front. Proxenus, in the second book of the *Laconian Constitution*, says that the Lacedaemonians call female servants *epikulathas*. Ion of Chios, in his play *Laertes*, refers to his servant as a "trickster" <note>Greek: *dolos*</note> when he says: "Woe is me, Damon my servant, weep with wings lest any mortal come." Achaeus, in *Omphale*, speaking of the Satyrs, says how "servant-like" <note>Using the word *eudolos*</note> and "well-housed" they are, meaning they are useful in their service. 

It is common for "domestic servant" to mean one who stays in the house, even a free person. But the poets of Old Comedy, when speaking of the ancient life, explain that there was no need for slaves then. They describe it as follows:

Cratinus says in *The Gods of Wealth*: "Those for whom King Cronus was the ruler in the old days, when men played dice with loaves of bread." And "barley cakes were tossed about in the gymnasiums, ripe and thick with lumps." 

Crates says in *The Wild Beasts*: "Then no one shall possess a male slave or a female one, but an old man shall serve himself." 
"Not at all!" says another, "for I shall make all these things happen myself." 
"What more will they gain from this?" 
"Nothing. Listen—when someone calls for his belongings to be set out: 'Table, prepare yourself!' 'Knead, little bag!' 'Pour, cup!' 'Where is the goblet? Go wash yourself!' 'Rise up, barley cake!' 'The pot must empty out its beets!' 'Fish, come here!' 'But I’m not roasted on the other side yet!' 'Well then, turn yourself over and baste yourself with oil!'"

<margin>good things automatically.</margin> Next after this, the character taking the opposing view says: "But consider this instead: I will bring hot baths on the sea for my people on pillars. The water will flow into each man's tub, and the holy water will splash out, and a jar of perfume will come automatically, along with a sponge and sandals." 

Teleclides is even better than these in his *Amphictyons*: "I will tell you of the life from the beginning which I provided for mortals. Peace was the first of all things, like water poured over one's hands. The earth bore neither fear nor disease, but all necessities grew of their own accord. For every gully flowed with wine; barley cakes fought with wheat loaves at the mouths of men..."

# BOOK 6. 151

...of men, begging to be swallowed: "If you love us at all, the whitest ones!" And the fish, coming home and roasting themselves, would lay themselves out upon the tables. A river of broth <note>original: *zomos*, a thick meat soup or stock</note> would flow past the couches, rolling along warm pieces of meat. Channels of seasoned sauces were available for those who wished, so there was an abundance to swallow down or soak into a soft piece of bread. There were platters, and even pounded pomegranate seeds sprinkled with seasonings. Roasted thrushes, served with little honey-cakes <note>original: *amētiskōn*</note>, flew right into the gullet. There was an unspeakable crowding of flat-cakes around the jaws. The children played at knucklebones with slices of sow’s womb and tidbits of tripe. Men were fat back then, and truly a great race of giants.

By Demeter, my friends, if things were like this, what need would we have of servants? But the ancients, through their poems, were educating us to be self-reliant <note>original: *autourgos*, one who works their own land without slaves</note> even as they feasted us with their words. Since I have, like a small torch, just lit up the most wonderful Cratinus and shared the passage before us—and showed how those who came after him imitated and refined his work—I will follow the order of the plays as they were produced. And if I am not annoying you (for the concern for Comedies is not the smallest matter), I will recount in order what was said by the other poets. One of these is the most refined Pherecrates, who in his play *The Miners* <note>original: *Metalleis*</note> says: 

"Everything there was mixed with Wealth, and worked in every way with all good things. Rivers of porridge and black broth flowed through the alleyways, gurgling with small pieces of bread and chunks of barley-cake. Thus, the oily food was ready to flow spontaneously into the throats of the dead. Sausages and slices of boiling blood-pudding lay sizzling by the rivers like shells on a beach. And truly, there were dressed cuts of meat, beautiful with all sorts of sauces. Entire roasted ribs, most tender, were near at hand on small platters. There were savory trotters <note>original: *akrokōlia*</note> steaming most sweetly, and cow's intestines, and ribs of pork seasoned with flowers. Sizzling small fish sat upon fine flour-cakes. There was grain-pudding washed with milk, lying in bowls that poured forth... Oh, how you will destroy me if you continue here, when I could be diving into Tartarus <note>The speaker is likely a character describing the Underworld as a paradise of food</note>! What else can one say? For roasted thrushes, seasoned and ready, flew around the mouth, begging to be swallowed, nestled under branches of myrtle. And the most beautiful apples hung overhead—no one had ever seen such beauty. Girls in freshly-made, thin robes, blooming and smelling of roses, drew full cups of dark, fragrant wine through funnels for anyone who wished to drink. And each of these things, whatever one ate or drank, immediately became double again from the start."

And in his play *The Persians*, he says: "Who would still have need of a plow, or a yoke-maker, or a sickle-smith, or bronze-work, or seed, or vine-props? For rivers of broth and black soup flow spontaneously through the crossroads, surging with oily Achillean barley-cakes <note>A high-quality type of barley bread named after the hero Achilles</note>. The cups of the wealthy flow from the springs for those who sacrifice. Zeus, raining down wine, gives us a bath with his jars. From the roofs, gutters of grapes together with little honey-cakes and cheese-filled pastries will flow warm with pea-soup. And the trees on the hills will shed their leaves of goat-gut sausages and tender squids and roasted thrushes."

What more is there to say about these things, given what Aristophanes <note>original: *Areisophanēs*</note> has set forth regarding the frying pan? For everyone in his *Acharnians* is full of such things. But I will conclude my speech by mentioning Metagenes from his *Thurian Persians*, giving a small greeting to the words of Nicophon, in which it is written: "Let it snow with fine flour, let it drizzle with loaves of bread, let it rain with pea-soup. Let broth roll through the streets, and let the meat-cakes command themselves to be eaten!" But Metagenes says this: "The river Crathis <note>A river in Magna Graecia, near Sybaris</note> brings down to us enormous barley-cakes, kneaded spontaneously. The other river, called the Sybaris, pushes a wave of pastries and meat, and even small fish being hauled up right there. These little streams here flow on one side with roasted squid and lobsters, and on the other with sausages and mincemeat. <unclear>† Here with small fry, there with sweet things</unclear> and dried slices of meat flow spontaneously, smothered in sauce, into the mouth. Some fall right at one's feet, while fine flour-cakes swim around us in a circle."

I know that both *The Thurian Persians* and the play by Nicophon have not been performed publicly. For that reason, I mentioned them last. When Democritus had clearly and sharply gone through these things, the guests praised him. But Cymaulcus said: "Fellow diners, while I am extremely hungry, Democritus has not unpleasantly entertained me by leading me through rivers of ambrosia and nectar. My soul has been watered by these words, yet I have become quite parched by merely swallowing his tales. So, let us finally cease this endless talk and, according to the orator from Paeania <margin>He means Demosthenes.</margin>, take part in some of those things which we neither <unclear>know as soup</unclear> nor die leaving behind. For there is no love for beautiful things in an empty stomach. As Achaeus says in his satyr play *Aethon*: 'Cypris <note>Aphrodite, the goddess of love</note> is bitter to those who are hungry.' And the wise Euripides, following him, said: <margin>Erasmus reads 'something in fullness.'</margin> <unclear>† Love is found in fullness, but not in the hungry.</unclear>" Toward...

...[Ctesicles says in his *Chronicles*] that in the one hundred and tenth Olympiad <note>The 110th Olympiad was approximately 340–337 BCE</note>, a census was held in Athens by Demetrius of Phalerum <note>A statesman and philosopher who governed Athens</note> of those inhabiting Attica. It was found that there were twenty-one thousand Athenians, ten thousand resident aliens <term>metoikoi: foreign residents who lived in Athens but did not have citizenship rights</term>, and four hundred thousand slaves. Nicias, the son of Niceratus—as the noble Xenophon says in his treatise *On Revenues*—owned a thousand slaves whom he leased to Sosias the Thracian to work in the silver mines, on the condition that Sosias pay him one obol <note>A small silver coin, one-sixth of a drachma</note> per day for each slave. Aristotle, in his *Constitution of the Aeginetans*, says that among them as well there were four hundred and seventy thousand slaves. Agatharchides of Cnidus, in the thirty-eighth book of his *History of Europe*, says that the Dardanians <note>An ancient tribe in the Balkans</note> owned slaves—some a thousand, some even more. Each of these slaves would farm in times of peace, but in times of war they would serve as soldiers, with their own master as their leader. 

Responding to these points, Larisios said: "But every Roman—and you know this accurately, noble Massurius—owns a vast number of servants. Indeed, very many own ten thousand, twenty thousand, or even more; and not for the sake of income, like the wealthy Greek Nicias. Rather, most Romans have the majority of their slaves as an entourage for when they go out. And those many tens of thousands of Athenian slaves worked in the mines in chains. Poseidonius the philosopher, whom you mention constantly, says that they even revolted and slaughtered the guards of the mines; they seized the citadel at Sunium and for a long time plundered Attica. This was the same time when the second slave uprising occurred in Sicily. These revolts were many, and more than a million slaves perished. Caecilius the orator, from Cale Acte, published a treatise *On the Slave War*. And Spartacus the gladiator, having revolted from Capua, a city in Italy, around the

And if he had not died in the battle against Licinius Crassus, he would have caused no small 'sweat' <note>A Greek metaphor for labor or trouble</note> for our 
<margin>Praise of the Romans.</margin>
people, just like the 'Kindly One' <note>A sarcastic reference to Eunus, the leader of the first Sicilian slave revolt</note> did in Sicily. 

But the ancient Romans were temperate and excellent in all things. Scipio, surnamed Africanus, for instance, when he was sent out by the Senate to settle the kingdoms across the inhabited world so they might be entrusted to their proper rulers, took only five slaves with him, as Polybius and Poseidonius record. And when one of them died during the journey, he wrote to his family to buy another and send him to replace the one who was lost. Julius Caesar, the first of all men to cross over to the British Isles with a thousand ships, took with him only three servants in total, as Cotta records—who was then his lieutenant—in his treatise *On the Roman Constitution*, which is written in our native tongue <note>Meaning Latin; the speaker is Roman</note>. 

But Smindyrides of Sybaris <note>Sybaris was a Greek city in Italy famous for its extreme luxury</note> was not such a man, nor were the Greeks; when he set out to marry Agariste, the daughter of Cleisthenes, he took with him a thousand slaves because of his luxury and refinement: fishermen, bird-catchers, and cooks. This man, wanting to be loved for the prosperity of his life, as Chamaeleon of Pontus records in his *On Pleasure* (though the same book is also attributed to Theophrastus), claimed that he had not seen the sun rising or setting for twenty years. And this he considered a great and wonderful thing for his happiness. He, it seems, slept early and woke up late—unfortunate in both respects! But Hestiaeus of Pontus used to boast, with good reason, that he had never seen the sun rising or setting because he was devoted to his education at all hours, as Nicias of Nicaea records in his *Successions*. 

Why then did both Scipio and Caesar have slaves? They did. But they guarded the ancestral laws and lived with restraint, maintaining the customs of the state. For it is the mark of wise men to abide by ancient pursuits. Through these pursuits, they conquered others in military campaigns, and while taking the captives of war, they also took whatever was useful and beautiful among them to imitate—which is what the Romans did in ancient times. For while preserving their ancestral ways, they adopted much from those they subdued if they found any remnant of good practice, leaving the useless things to those people, so that they might never be able to recover what had been taken from them. For example, having learned about siege engines and machines from the Greeks, they defeated them in naval battles with these very things. They also took the practice of charging in phalanx formation from the Etruscans when they met in battle, and from the Samnites they learned the use of the shield <term>thyreos: a large, door-shaped shield</term>. From the Iberians, they took the javelin <term>gaison: a heavy iron spear</term>. And learning other things from other peoples, they worked to make them better. Having imitated the Spartan constitution in all things, they preserved it better than the Spartans themselves. But now, in making a selection of useful things, they are brought together by their opposites and by wicked rivalries. For their ancestral way, as Poseidonius says, was endurance and a simple diet, and a plain, unadorned use of other possessions. Furthermore, they had a wonderful piety toward the divine, justice, and great caution against doing wrong toward all men, along with the practice of agriculture. There is still [a remnant] in the ancestral sacrifices...

# EXTRACTS FROM ATHENAEUS'S BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

...sacrifices, which we perform privately; for we conduct ourselves in an orderly and defined manner. We move with discipline, and we speak in our prayers, and we act in our sacred rites with things that are simple and plain <note>Greek: *aphele te tauta kai lita*</note>. We wear nothing beyond what is natural, nor do we possess anything more than our bodies before we begin the offerings. We have humble clothing and footwear, and we wear thick hats of sheepskin on our heads; we carry our serving vessels made of ceramic or bronze. We consider it strange to consume the most meager foods and drinks—those which are most basic—while sending to the gods what is traditional, but providing for ourselves according to a life of excess. Furthermore, what is spent on ourselves is measured by our needs, while what is given to the gods consists of first-fruits.

In Rome, Mucius Scaevola was the third to observe the Fannian Law <margin>See Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 3, Chapter 17.</margin>, along with Nautius Caecilius Tubero and Rutilius Rufus, the man who wrote the history of his ancestors. The law commanded that one should not host more than three guests from outside the household. In the market, it allowed for only three fish per month. It did not permit spending more than two and a half drachmae on delicacies <term>opsonion: specifically the "relish" or expensive additions to a meal, usually fish or meat</term>. It allowed for the expenditure of fifteen talents' weight of smoked meat per year, and as many vegetables and legumes as the earth brings forth in the season. 

Even though the allowed expenditure was very small, because the market prices had been driven up by those who break the law and spend without restraint, how could those of more noble character proceed legally? For Tubero used to buy birds for a drachma each for those on his own estates. Rutilius once found that one of his slaves who went fishing for him had purchased a two-pound portion of delicacies—specifically what is called "Thyrian" <note>Probably a specific, expensive variety of fish</note>—which was part of a sea-dog <note>A type of shark or dogfish</note>, as it was called. Mucius Scaevola, regarding the things used by him, would spend based on the price-list. Out of so many tens of thousands of people, these alone kept the law under oath, and they would not accept even the smallest gift. Yet they gave great gifts to others and to friends who were driven by a love of learning, for they followed the doctrines of the Stoa <note>The Stoic school of philosophy, which emphasized virtue and simple living</note>.

However, when luxury was at its peak, the first leader into it was Lucullus, the man who defeated Mithridates in a naval battle, as Nicolaus the Peripatetic records. For arriving in Rome after the defeat of Mithridates, and also that of Tigranes the Armenian, and having celebrated a triumph and given an account of his actions in the war, he moved into a luxurious way of life, departing from the old moderation. He became the first to introduce luxury to the Romans, having harvested the wealth of the two aforementioned kings. 

The famous Cato, as Polybius records in the thirty-first book of his *Histories*, was distressed and used to cry out that some people had introduced foreign luxuries into Rome, buying a jar of salt-fish from the Black Sea for three hundred drachmae, and also beautiful young boys at prices exceeding those of the markets. Previously, those inhabiting Italy were so content with little that even in our own time, says Poseidonius, those who were quite well-off led simple lives, drinking water for the most part and eating whatever was at hand. He says a father or mother would often ask a son whether he wanted pears or nuts for dinner, and having eaten some of these, he was satisfied and went to sleep. 

But now, as Theopompus records in the first book of his *History of Philip*, there is no one—even among those of moderate means—who does not set out a luxurious table; they possess cooks and many other servants, and they spend more daily than they used to spend on festivals and sacrifices. Since the discussion of these recorded memories has reached a sufficient length, let us end the discourse here.

-># BOOK VII.<-

After everyone had praised the refined learning of Cynulcus, Plutarch spoke in a similar vein, saying: "In my own city of Alexandria, there is a certain festival celebrated called the *Lagynophoria* <note>original: Λαγυνοφορία; literally 'The Carrying of the Bottle' (lagynos)</note>, about which Eratosthenes provides an account in his treatise titled *Arsinoe*. <margin>Bottle-bearing.</margin> He says that when Ptolemy Philadelphus was instituting various kinds of festivals and sacrifices—especially those concerning Dionysus—he asked Arsinoe <note>Arsinoe II, the sister-wife of Ptolemy II Philadelphus</note> what day the people were currently observing, as she was carrying certain olive branches. When he was told that it was called the 'Bottle-bearing,' where people recline on beds of straw and drink from their own bottles which they have brought themselves, she looked at us and remarked that it seemed like a 'squalid gathering.' For, she said, the assembly of a mixed crowd must result in a stale feast that is in no way respectable. However, if the nature of the festival had pleased her, the Queen would surely not have found it tiresome to prepare the same things herself, just as is done during the festival of the *Choes* <note>The 'Pitchers' festival, part of the Anthesteria in honor of Dionysus</note>. At that festival, guests feast privately, but the one who issued the invitation provides the meal."

One of the grammarians present, looking at the preparations for the dinner, said: "And how shall we digest <term>diapnesomen: literally 'breathe through' or 'evaporate,' referring to the ancient belief that digestion was a form of internal cooking or ventilation</term> so many dishes, perhaps throughout the entire night? As the witty Aristophanes says in his *Aeolosicon*: 'drinking all night long.' This is much like the Homeric line: <margin>Iliad 10</margin> 'stretching it out through the sheep,' <note>original: διὰ μήλων; a pun or misquotation of Iliad 10.334, here used to emphasize the great size or duration of the meal</note> indicating its magnitude."

To this, the physician Daphnus replied: "My dear friend, late-night dinners are actually most beneficial for the whole body. For the star of the moon is suited to the nourishment of everything, as it possesses a certain power of putrefaction. And digestion is essentially a form of putrefaction <note>The ancients believed that food was 'cooked' or 'broken down' (sepsis/pepsis) in the stomach through heat and moisture, processes they associated with the moon's influence</note>. Certainly, victims sacrificed at night are more easily decomposed, as is wood cut during the moon's cycle; even fruits ripen more quickly under the moon. 

Since there are many and various fish prepared here, both in size and variety, Myrtilus spoke up: "Rightly so, my friends! <margin>20</margin> Among all the 'relishes' <term>opson: originally any food eaten with bread, but eventually synonymous with fish due to its popularity</term> called side-dishes, fish has emerged as the winner because of its exceptional flavor. It alone is called 'the relish' because people are so passionately obsessed with this food. Indeed, we call people 'relish-eaters' <note>original: opsophagoi</note>, but we do not mean those who eat beef (such as Heracles, who ate green figs with his beef) nor do we mean a 'fig-lover' like the philosopher Plato, as Phanocritus records in his work *On Euboea*. He also records that Arcesilaus was a 'grape-lover.' Rather, we use the term for those who frequent the fish-market. Philip of Macedon and his son Alexander were also lovers of long-dishes <note>referring to long platters for fish</note>, as Dorotheus says in the sixth book of his *Histories of Alexander*. Chares of Mitylene records that when Alexander found the most beautiful apples in the region of Babylon, he filled his boats with them and started an 'apple-fight' from the ships, which was a most pleasant sight to behold. 

I am well aware that 'relish' <note>opson</note> strictly refers to anything prepared by fire for eating—it is named either from 'boiling' <note>hepsesis</note> or from 'roasting' <note>optesis</note>. Since there are many fish, then, which we enjoy in their various seasons, most wonderful Timocrates—for as Sophocles says: 'A choir of voiceless fish splashed about, wagging their tails not at their mistress, but at the cooking pots'—and according to Achaeus: 'A great crowd of the sea’s circle, a marine spectacle, rejoicing in the calm of the sea.' I will recount to you what the *Deipnosophists* said about each one. For all of them contributed their 'book-portions' to the conversation, though I will omit their names because of their great number. As Amphis says in *The Woman from Leucas*: 'Anyone who, when buying relish and having the chance to enjoy real fish, desires to buy radishes instead, is mad!' 

So that what was said may be easy for you to remember, I will arrange the names in alphabetical order. For when Sophocles in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer* called fish 'voiceless' <note>original: ellous; a rare poetic term for fish</note>, saying 'destruction to the voiceless fish,' someone asked if any of his predecessors had used that name. <margin>Note.</margin> Zoilus replied: 'Though I am not a great "relish-eater"'—as Xenophon used the term in his *Memorabilia*, writing 'he is both a relish-eater and a slacker'—'I know that the author of the *Titanomachy* (whether it be Eumelus of Corinth or Arctinus, or whoever he chooses to be called) said in his second book: "In it there are swimming, gold-faced, voiceless <note>ellous</note> fish; they play as they swim through the ambrosial water."' Sophocles was fond of the Epic Cycle, even following its mythology to create whole plays. 

When some **amia** <note>a type of tuna or bonito</note> were served, <margin>Amia.</margin> someone said: 'Aristotle records that these have covered gills, jagged teeth, and are schooling, carnivorous fish. They have a gall bladder as long as their intestine. It is said that when they are caught, they leap up and escape by biting through the fishing line.' Archippus mentions them in his play *The Fish*, saying: 'When you ate fat amia.' And Epicharmus in *The Sirens* says: 'In the morning we breathe out the scent of small fry—round ones and little pigs—roasted meats and octopus, and we drank sweet wine with them; alas, where is the sign calling me? It says "Phoo!" at the bad things; and besides the red mullets and frost-fish, two large **amia** were laid out in the middle, and many wood-pigeons and sea-scorpions.' Aristotle, providing an etymology for the name, says it is called so because they 'go together' <note>original: hama ienai; a pun on amia and hama (together)</note> with others of their kind, for it is a schooling fish."

# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS

...Dionysius says in his work *On Matter* that they are succulent and tender, but asks how their excretions can be black or so very fragrant. <margin>Archestratus.</margin> The master of culinary arts, Archestratus, in his *Gastrology* <note>original: Γαστρολογία; also known as "The Life of Luxury," this was a mock-epic poem on fine dining</note>—for so Lycophron says it is titled in his works *On Comedy*—just as Cleostratus of Tenedos wrote a *Gastrology* regarding the stars, speaks thus about the <term>amia</term> <note>original: ἀμία; likely the Atlantic bonito, a relative of the mackerel and tuna</note>: 

"When the Pleiades set in the autumn, prepare the bonito in every way you like. Why do I tell you this? For it cannot be spoiled, even if you try. But if you wish, my dear Moschus, to know the best way to serve it: wrap it in fig leaves with a little oregano—not too much—no cheese, no nonsense. Simply prepare it thus: wrap it in fig leaves and tie it with a reed from above. Then place it deep under hot ashes, knowing by your own wit the right moment when it is roasted, and do not let it burn. Let this fish be from lovely Byzantium. If you get a good one, even if you are near the threshing floors of that place, you will take it; but if it comes from far across the sea, from the Hellespont, you will rejoice at a new treat. But if it crosses the salt path of the Aegean Sea, it is no longer the same, but puts its former praise to shame."

This Archestratus, driven by a love of pleasure, traveled over every land and sea—it seems to me—because he wished to examine with great care everything pertaining to the belly. And just as those who have made accurate descriptions of the world or coastal voyages, he wishes to set forth where every food and drink is best. Indeed, he himself promises this in the introduction to those fine instructions he gives to his companions, Moschus and Cleanthrus, as if he were an oracle telling them to seek: "A Thessalian horse, a Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> woman, and men who drink the water of beautiful Arethusa." <margin>Hedonists.</margin> 

Chrysippus <note>a famous Stoic philosopher</note> says that Archestratus was truly a "philosopher of the senses" and a pioneer for Epicurus and his followers, who at that time understood how to ruin everything with pleasure. For even if Epicurus speaks while veiling his meaning, he says in a loud voice: "For my part, I cannot conceive of the Good if I take away the pleasures of the palate, and take away the pleasures of sex." For the wise man believes that the life of a profligate is blameless if fear and pain are removed. Therefore, the comic poets, when attacking pleasure and lack of self-control, cry out against the "Epicuruses" and "Buthuses." 

For Plato <note>the comic poet, not the philosopher</note> portrays a man who is indignant at someone leading others astray, speaking to a tutor: "You have destroyed my boy by taking him, you filthy man! You have persuaded him to enter a life foreign to him." Then, when asked if the boy has learned how to live, he says: "If he has learned to live, master, you complain? To 'live' is what the wise call this!" For Epicurus says that the Good is found in pleasures; you cannot look at life beautifully unless you give in to them. "Have you not seen," he says, "some philosopher drunk on these things you speak of?" All those who have their eyebrows raised high, seeking 'the wise man' in the walkways and schools as if he were a runaway slave—as soon as a <term>glaukiskos</term> <note>original: γλαυκίσκος; a type of grey-colored fish, perhaps a sea bream or snapper</note> is served to them, they know exactly which part to touch first! They seek the head as if it were a matter of great importance, so that everyone is stunned. 

And in the play titled *The Manslayer*, the same Plato, mocking one of the Epicurean philosophers, adds: "Having a wife, lying down comfortably, and taking two cups of Lesbian wine—this is the 'wise' thing; this 'good' is what Epicurus said, the same things I say now. If everyone lived the life I lead, there would be no strange behavior and no trouble." 

Hegesippus, in his *Friends of Philetaerus*, says: "When someone asked the wise Epicurus what the 'Good' was that all people seek through to the end, he said 'Pleasure.' Well said, O greatest and wisest of men! For there is nothing better than chewing; for pleasure is the Good." 

And it is not only the Epicureans who embrace pleasure, but also the Cyrenaics and those called the Mnesistratians. For these also delight in living pleasantly, as Posidonius says. Not far from these was Speusippus, the pupil and relative of Plato. Dionysius the Tyrant, in his letters to him, went through his love of pleasure and his greed, proving that he collected contributions from many, and reproached him for his love of the Sardian courtesan, Ladineia. To him and to all, he says: "You reproach some for greed, while you yourself have not failed in any shameful profit. For what have you not done for the sake of 'gifts of Hermes' <note>lucky gains</note>, delighting in collecting contributions?"

Regarding Epicurus, Timon says in his *Satires*: "Indulging a belly than which nothing is more gluttonous." For the sake of this and other pleasures of the flesh, the man flattered both Idomeneus and Metrodorus. And Metrodorus himself, not hiding these "noble" doctrines, says: "For concerning the belly, O natural philosopher Timocrates, the discourse that proceeds according to nature has its whole focus." For Epicurus was the teacher of all, and he cried out: "The beginning and the root of every good is the pleasure of the belly; even wisdom and culture must be referred back to this." And in his work *On the End*, he says,

# BOOK VII

...he [Epicurus] <note>original: Ἐπίκουρος; the philosopher Epicurus (341–270 BCE) was often associated by later writers with a purely physical pursuit of pleasure</note> says something like this: "For my part, I cannot conceive of the Good if I take away the pleasures of taste, if I take away the pleasures of sex, and if I take away the pleasures of hearing and the delightful motions of beautiful forms seen by the eyes." And going further, he says that even if one speaks of "the beautiful" and "virtue" and such things as being more honorable, if they provide no pleasure, they should be dismissed. But long before Epicurus, the tragic poet Sophocles <note>original: Σοφοκλῆς</note> said these things about pleasure in his *Antigone*: "For when men lose their pleasures, I do not consider such a man to be truly alive, but I look upon him as a living corpse. You may be as wealthy as you like at home, and live with the outward style of a king; but if joy is absent from these things, I would not buy the rest from a man for the shadow of smoke, compared to his pleasure." Philetairus, the comic poet, says: "Why, being mortal, should I pray for anything else but to live my daily life pleasantly, if one has the means? But one must also look upon human affairs with a watchful eye." To worry about what tomorrow will bring is a waste of time, something some call "stale" <note>original: ἔωλον; literally "yesterday's food," used here metaphorically for outdated concerns</note>, but he calls money. And the same author says in *Oinopion*: "Of all mortals who live wretchedly despite having an abundant life, I say they are miserable. For when you are dead, you won't get to eat eel, nor is a wedding feast sent among the dead." Apollodorus of Carystus, the playwright <note>original: γραμματιοποιός; here likely referring to a writer of comedies</note>, says: "O all you people, why is it that we neglect to live pleasantly when we are here, and instead occupy ourselves with doing harm and making war on one another? Is it perhaps because Fortune, who presides over our life, is without a dowry? She knows nothing of education, neither what is evil nor what is good, being completely ignorant; and then, I suppose, she rolls us along in whatever way she happens to. For who would truly choose, being Greek, to see people grieving at their own hands and falling dead, when it is possible to be cheerful, playing, drinking, and listening to the flute? O sweetest lady, let us prove that our Fortune is unrefined." And going further, he says: "For living is not truly about the so-called life of the gods, but about how much more pleasant things are in the cities. Look now, if we spent our life changing our ways—drinking without fear, and if battles were forgotten for twenty years, and no cavalry—we could go on a ten-day revel to Corinth wearing crowns... [for] five days, and some of the Megarians who sell radishes would go to the bath with their allies to mix the wine immediately with luxury, and that would truly be life! But instead, we are slaves to an uneducated fortune."

<margin>The myth of Tantalus</margin>

The poets say that Tantalus of old was also a lover of pleasure. For the author of *The Return of the Atreidae* <note>original: Νόστοι; a lost epic poem of the Trojan Cycle</note> says that when he reached the gods and lived among them, he obtained the authority from Zeus to ask for whatever he desired. Because he was predisposed to uncomplicated enjoyments, he made a request for these very things: to live in the same manner as the gods. <margin>30</margin> Zeus was annoyed by this, but fulfilled the prayer because of his promise. However, so that Tantalus might not actually enjoy the things set before him, but instead remain in a state of agitation, Zeus hung a stone over his head, because of which he is unable to reach the pleasure laid out before him.

In the Stoic school, too, some advocated for this kind of pleasure. Eratosthenes of Cyrene, for instance, who was a pupil of Aristo of Chios (one of the philosophers from the Stoa), in his work titled *Aristo*, blamed his teacher for later turning toward luxury, saying: "And yet, I have already caught him digging through the wall between pleasure and virtue, and appearing on the side of pleasure." This was well known to all of Aristo's acquaintances. In the work titled *Aristo*, the author himself reveals his teacher's love of pleasure. Much was said about Dionysius of Heraclea <note>original: Διονύσιος ὁ Μεταθέμενος; known as "Dionysius the Renegade" because he abandoned the Stoic belief that pain is indifferent after suffering from an eye infection</note>, who immediately stripped off the cloak of virtue and, changing his clothes and his mind, delighted in being called "the Renegade." He abandoned the words of the wise and went over to the school of Epicurus. Timon <note>original: Τίμων; likely Timon of Phlius, the skeptical poet</note>, who is often very ungrateful, says: "When it was time to be silent, he now begins to enjoy himself; a time to love, a time to marry, and a time to cease." Apollodorus of Athens, in the third book of *On Sophron*, presenting the most lewd of human mimes, mentions the "alpheketai" <note>original: ἀληκεταί or ἀλφησταί</note>.

Some fish are called <term>alphestai</term> <note>original: ἀλφησταί; possibly a species of wrasse or grouper</note>; they are generally dark blue, but purple in certain parts. They say these fish are caught in pairs, and one is seen following the other at its tail. Because one follows the other with a soul-like attachment, some of the ancients called people who are lacking in self-control and prone to lust by this name. Aristotle, in his work *On Animals*, says that the *alphestikos* is single-spined and yellowish. Nymphis of Heraclea also mentions it in his work *On Fishing*, saying: "the wrasses and the *alphestai*, red in their skin color." Like the Scorpion-fish. And Epicharmus <note>original: Ἐπίχαρμος; a 5th-century BCE comic poet famous for his lists of food</note> in the *Marriage of Hebe* says: "there are *alphestai* mice and coracines <note>original: κορακῖνοι; a dark fish, possibly the 'crow-fish' or a type of perch</note>." Mythaecus also mentions it in his *Culinary Art*.

<margin>Anthiai.</margin>

The <term>anthias</term> <note>original: ἀνθίας; often identified as the Mediterranean sea-bass or a red sea bream</note> and the "beautiful-fish" (*kallichthys*). Epicharmus mentions them in the *Marriage of Hebe*, as does Skipias. "The chromis <note>original: χρόμιος; the 'drummer' fish</note> in the spring... and <margin>50</margin> we increase the whole [stock]; of all fish, the *anthias* is best in winter." Ananius says it thus: "In the spring, the *chromis* is best, but the *anthias* in winter. Of fine dishes, the best is a cake baked in a fig leaf, and to eat a lot of autumn-flood meat." And he says to eat young pigs when they are dipped and trodden, and dogs in the second season, and hares and foxes. But when the summer comes and the cicadas chirrup, then there is nothing from the sea [better than] the <term>thynnos</term> <note>original: θύννος; the tuna</note>,

# FROM THE ATHENAEAN DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...is not a bad food, but conspicuous among all fish, though not [suitable] for a suitor. A fattened ox, I think, is sweet in the middle of the night as well as by day. I have mentioned the many [arguments] of Aianias, thinking that these instructions would be set out for the lustful. Aristotle says in his *On the Habits of Animals* that the anthias <note>original: "ἀνθίας"; likely the Mediterranean red snapper or a similar sea bream</note> is not a wild beast. Sponge-divers use this as a sign when they dive, calling it a **sacred fish**. Dorion also mentions it in his work *On Fish*. Some people call the anthias the *kallichthys* <note>meaning "beautiful fish"</note>, and also the *kallionymos* <note>meaning "beautifully named"</note> and the *ellops*. Hicesius, in his writings *On Matter*, says that the "wolf-fish" <note>original: "λύκον"; likely the sea bass</note> is a different species, though others call it the *kallionymos*. He says it has excellent flesh, is juicy and easy to digest, though not very good for the stomach. Aristotle says the *kallichthys* has serrated teeth, is a meat-eater, and travels in schools. Epicharmus, in his *Muses*, lists the *ellops* but is silent regarding the *kallichthys* or *kallionymos*, as if they were the same. He speaks of the *ellops* as follows: "And the highly honored *ellops*." And the same author says, "Zeus was amazed <unclear>by the bronze price of a single one</unclear> <note>original: "χαλκὸς ὤνιος... ὁ Ζεὺς ἔλαθεν"; the Greek here is corrupt and difficult to reconstruct</note>... he built it for his wife." 

Dorion, in his *On Fish*, says that the anthias, the *kallichthys*, the *kallionymos*, and the *ellops* are all different. As for what the so-called **sacred fish** is, the author of the *History of the Tilchinians*—whether it be Epimenides the Cretan, or Teleclides, or someone else—says that dolphins and the *pompilos* <note>original: "πομπίλους"; the pilot-fish</note> are sacred. The pilot-fish is an erotic animal, having been born from the blood of Uranus <note>the sky god</note> at the same time as Aphrodite. Nicander says in the second book of his *Oitaika*: "The pilot-fish, which is pleasant to sailors on their paths, mimicking those in love in their voiceless <unclear>environment</unclear>." Alexander the Aetolian, in his *Kriskas*, if the poem is genuine: 

<margin>The Pilot-fish <note>original: Πομπίλος</note></margin> "On the tip of the steering-oar, the pilot-fish hovers. And below, behind the gods, the pilot-fish is a fish." Pancrates the Arcadian, in his work titled *Sea Labors*, says that the pilot-fish, which seafarers call the **sacred fish**, is held in honor not only by Poseidon but also by the gods of Samothrace <note>the Cabeiri, protectors of sailors</note>. He tells a story of a certain old woman of the sea named Epopis who lived during the Golden Age of humanity. She was from Icarus and went to the island. While she was fishing with her son, they had great success catching many fish, including pilot-fish. However, they did not abstain from eating them, and she and her son devoured them all. Not long after, she paid the penalty for her impiety. A sea monster <note>original: "κῆτος"; a generic term for a whale, shark, or sea beast</note> came upon the ship and swallowed Epopis in front of her child's eyes. Pancrates also records that the pilot-fish is an enemy of the dolphin, and the dolphin does not escape unpunished if it eats a pilot-fish. It becomes old <note>or perhaps "slow"</note> and thrashes about when it eats one, and being washed up on the shores by the waves, it becomes food for gulls and shearwaters. Sometimes it is also killed by men who specialize in hunting sea monsters. Timachidas the Rhodian mentions pilot-fish in the ninth book of his *Dinners*: "Sea gobies and pilot-fish are sacred fish." And Cosmas, who wrote a short poem attributed to him: "O pilot-fish, sending a fair voyage to sailors, pilot-fish from the stern, my companion of the sea." 

Apollonius of Rhodes (or perhaps of Naucratis), in his *Founding of Naucratis*, says the pilot-fish was formerly a man who was transformed into a fish because of the love of Apollo. Near the city of Samos flows the river Imbrasus. "To the daughter of this swift-flowing [river], the beautiful nymph Ocypete, Chesias bore a child of noble father after lying in love, Ocypete, to whom the Seasons gave boundless beauty." Apollo fell in love with her and tried to seize her. She crossed over to Miletus during a festival of Artemis, and when she was about to be snatched away, she was cautious and implored a certain fisherman named Pompilus, who was a friend of her father, to save her and bring her to her homeland, saying: "Keep my heart's virtue safe within my womb, Pompilus, from the deep-sounding sea; save me!" He took her across to the shore. But Apollo appeared, snatched the girl, turned the ship into stone, and transformed Pompilus into the fish named after him, making him a companion of the swift ships in the sea. 

Theocritus of Syracuse, in his poem *Berenice*, calls the fish named the "wolf-fish" <note>sea bass</note> sacred. In these lines: "And a man prays for a good catch and wealth from the sea, by which these nets live as his plows, sacrificing the <unclear>choice parts</unclear> to this goddess as a **sacred fish**; that which they call the wolf-fish. For it is the most sacred of others; and may he dry his nets and draw them from the sea full." 

<margin>The Sacred Fish <note>original: Ἱερὸς ἰχθῦς</note></margin> Dionysius, nicknamed Iambus, writes in his *On Dialects*: "We have heard from a rowing fisherman about the sacred fish, and many other fishermen call the pilot-fish by this name." It is a deep-sea fish and frequently appears near ships, looking like a variegated bonito. A certain character in "The Poet" <note>referring to Homer</note> "pulls a sacred fish while sitting on a jutting rock," unless there is some other fish called sacred. Callimachus in his *Galatea* mentions the "gilt-head bream" <note>original: "χρύσοφρυν"; Sparus aurata</note>, or rather "the golden-browed sacred fish," or "fat ones and whatever else the unharvested brine of the deep brings." In his *Epigrams*, the same poet says, "A certain sacred fish is sacred." Others understand the "sacred fish" to be the anthias, as...

# BOOK 7

They cry out that the same fish is "sacred." Others call the "great fish" sacred, just as Homer says: "the sacred strength of Alcinous." <note>original: "ἱερὸν μῦνον Ἀλκινόοιο"; a Homeric formula where "sacred strength" simply means the person himself</note> Some apply the name to the fish that swims against the current. Clearchus, in his *On Dialects*, says: "Sailors address the pilot-fish <note>original: "πομπίλον" (pompilos)</note> as a 'sacred fish' because it escorts ships from the deep sea until they reach the harbor." For this reason, it is called the "pilot," though it is actually a gilt-head bream <note>original: "χρυσόφρυν" (chrysophrys)</note>. Eratosthenes also says in his *Hermes*: "Ares left a portion of still-living fish, either the sea-thrush <note>original: "κίχλην" (kichlē)</note> near the newly built wall, or the swift-running gilt-head, the sacred fish of the hearth." Should our culinary discussion <note>original: "ὀψολογία" (opsologia)</note> proceed from this? Let the noble Ulpian <note>A character in the dialogue known for his pedantic questioning</note> investigate whether Archestratus, in his excellent *Instructions*, said anything about the salted fish of the Bosporus <note>The region around the Black Sea, famous for preserved fish</note>, saying: "When sailing out of the Bosporus, seek the very white ones... nor let the flesh of the sturgeon <note>original: "κέσσερας" (kesseras)</note> from the Maeotian Lake <note>The Sea of Azov</note> escape you, a fish grown so large it is not lawful to speak of it in meter." Who is this fish that he says is unlawful to mention in verse?

### Anchovies
<margin>Anchovy.</margin>
In the singular, they call it the *aphye* <note>original: "ἀφύη" (aphye); a general term for "small fry," including anchovies, sardines, and larval fish</note>. Aristonymus, in *The Sun Feeling Cold*, says: "So that he never simply saw even a single anchovy." There are several kinds of anchovies. The one called the "foam-anchovy" <note>original: "ἀφρῖτις" (aphritis)</note> is not born from spawn, as Aristotle says, but from the foam that floats on the sea when a great collection forms after heavy rains. 
<margin>Book 6.</margin>
Another is the "goby-anchovy" <note>original: "κωβῖτις" (kōbitis)</note>, which is born from the small, common gobies found in the sand. From this anchovy, certain "pitted" ones are produced, which are called *enkrasicholoi* <note>original: "ἐγκρασίχολοι"; literally "mixed-with-bile," likely referring to the bitter taste of the gut, our modern European anchovy</note>. There is also another anchovy which is the offspring of the *mainis* <note>a small Mediterranean fish</note>, and another from the *membras* <note>a type of small herring or sprat</note>, and yet another from the small grey mullets found in the sand or born in the mud. Of all these, the foam-anchovy is the best. Dorion, in his *On Fish*, mentions a "cooked" goby-anchovy and one made from the *atherina* <note>original: "ἀθερίνη"; a smelt-like fish</note>. *Atherina* is the name for these small fish. He also says there is a "red-mullet-anchovy" <note>original: "τριγλῖτιν" (triglitis)</note>. Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, lists anchovies alongside *membrades* and *kamaro* <note>shrimps or small crustaceans</note>, mocking what is called the "offspring." Hicesius says: "The anchovy that is white, very thin, and foamy, which some also call the 
<margin>† goby-anchovy.</margin>
'goby-anchovy,' is superior. There is another that is dirtier and thicker. The clean, thin one is different."

Archestratus, the artist of gourmet food, says: "Despise all anchovies except the Athenian ones; I mean the 'offspring' which the Ionians call 'foam.' Take it fresh when caught in the beautiful curves of the sacred Phaleron <note>The port of Athens, famous for its small fry</note>, or in the wave-washed hills of Rhodes, when it is in season. If you desire to taste it, you must buy it along with the bushy sea-anemones <note>original: "ἀκαλήφας" (akalēphas)</note> of Knidos. Mix them together in a frying pan, then roast them after rubbing in fragrant herbs and oil." Clearchus the Peripatetic, in his *On Proverbs*, says that because the anchovy needs very little fire in the frying pan, most people follow Archestratus's advice: as soon as the pan is hot and it begins to sizzle, take it off; as soon as it cooks and sizzles, it is done immediately. Therefore, there is a proverb: "anchovy to the fire." 

Chrysippus the Philosopher, in his *On Things Desirable for Their Own Sake*, says that people in Athens look down on the anchovy because of its abundance, calling it "beggar’s food." But in other cities, they marvel at it, even when it is of much worse quality. He says: "While people here strive to raise Adriatic birds <note>likely pigeons or ducks</note> which are quite useless because they are much smaller than our own, people there conversely send for the ones we have here." Hermippus uses the singular form in *The Townsmen*. Callias, in *The Cyclopes*, says: "How could you wrong an anchovy?" Aristonymus in *The Sun Feeling Cold*: "As if this were simply an anchovy." Aristophanes uses the diminutive "little anchovies" in *The Fryers*: "And don't forget those little Phaleric anchovies." 

Lynceus of Samos, in his letter to Diagoras, praises the Rhodian anchovies and contrasts many Athenian products with those of Rhodes, saying that against the Phaleric anchovies they set those called "Aeniatid" anchovies. Against the *glaukiskos* <note>a gray fish</note> he sets the *ellops* <note>sturgeon or similar</note>, and the *orphos* <note>sea perch</note> against the other. "How can I compare the Eleusinian flatfish and mackerel, and if there is any other fish in the land of Cecrops <note>Athens</note> that has gained fame? I set the fox-shark <note>original: "ἀλώπεκα" (alōpeka)</note> against them." The author of *The Sub-Passions* <note>original: "ὑποπάθειαν"</note> advises those who cannot satisfy their desire through price to obtain their gourmet food through "injustice" <note>i.e., by stealing it</note>. Archestratus tells the Cynthian in his much-celebrated poem, regarding the houndfish <note>original: "γαλεοῦ" (galeou); a small shark</note>: "In Rhodes, if you want a 'fox-shark' and you are about to die if you don't get it—if they won't sell it to you, snatch it! The Syracusans call it the 'fat dog,' then later suffer whatever fate is destined for you."

### The Gaper
<margin>The Gaper.</margin>
The *achanis* <note>original: "Ἄχανος"; literally "the gaper," likely a type of wide-mouthed fish or sea perch</note>. Callias in *The Cyclopes*: "Roasted *libaris* and ray <note>original: "Βατὶς" (batis)</note> are the main part of the feast, along with eels, crabs, and the *achanis*." Thus also the ray, the *barachos*, and the *batos* <note>all species of skates or rays</note>. Aristotle mentions the "little ray" <note>original: "βατίδιος"</note> and the *barachos* in his *On Animals*, listing them among the cartilaginous fish <note>original: "σελάχεσιν" (selachesin)</note>. Eupolis, in *The Flatterers*, says: "At Callias's house there is much joy, for there are crabs, rays, hares, and 'rolling-footed' women." Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "I see electric rays <note>original: "νάρκαι"</note> and the ray. I see hammerhead sharks <note>original: "ζύγαιναι"</note>, *preties*, *kamatai*, the skate, and the rough-skinned shark-rays <note>original: "ῥίναι"</note>... in Megara, their sides are like the ray..." Sannyrion in *Laughter*: "O rays, O heads of gray-fishes!" Aristotle, in the fifth book of *History of Animals*, says the cartilaginous fish are the shark-ray, the ox-ray, the 
<margin>† kamaro.</margin>

In these matters, there are some fine fish mentioned in the verses. There are *mesrai* <note>original: "μέσραι"; an unidentified species</note> and *anthiai* <note>original: "ἀνθίαι"; likely the Mediterranean sea-perch or barberfish</note>, though perhaps he is referring to some kind of plant. The most wise Archestratus <note>A 4th-century BCE poet known as the "Daedalus of tasty dishes"</note> gives much advice concerning the **Anglerfish** <note>original: "βάτραχος" (batrachos), literally "frog-fish"</note> in these maxims:

> Boil the anglerfish if you
> see it among the market delicacies, preparing it in its own belly.

And somewhere he says regarding the **Ray**: <note>original: "βατίς" (batis); specifically the skate or ray</note>

> And I had to eat the ray in the winter
> season; and with this, touch the flesh with cheese and silphium <note>original: "σίλφιον"; a prized, now-extinct medicinal and culinary plant from Cyrene</note>
> Lest the children of the sea have fatty flesh. One must prepare it
> with the juice of the laserwort; this is what I say, and I speak of it further.

Ephippus, the comic poet, says in his play *The Linden Tree* (the name refers to a courtesan):

> Cutting the conger eel and the ray into slices,
> I will boil them in a bowl, or roast them in the Sicilian fashion.

<margin>
The Bogue.
See Hermolaus on Pliny.
</margin>
**The Bogue.** <note>original: "Βῶκις" (bōkis); a common Mediterranean fish, *Boops boops*</note> Aristotle, in the work titled *On Animals* (or *On Fish*), says that the *bōx* has markings along its back, while the *kolias* <note>Spanish mackerel</note> has crooked markings. Epicharmus mentions them in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "Then again, there were bogues, small fry, anchovies, and prawns." Nymphiodorus, in his *Art of Fishing*, calls them *boēkes* in these lines: "The white sea-bream, the bogues, and the sardines." Speusippus and other Attic writers call them *boakas*. Aristophanes says in *Women at the Skira*: "But having a belly full of bogues, they walked away home." The fish was named after its "shout" <note>original: "βοή" (boē); the ancients believed this fish could make sounds</note>. For this reason, legend says the fish is sacred to Hermes, just as the lyre-fish is sacred to Apollo. Pherecrates, in *The Ants*, claims that while other fish have no voice at all, "By the two gods, there is no other fish that speaks but the Bogue!" <note>original: "Βόαξ" (boax)</note> However, Aristophanes of Byzantium says we are wrong to call the fish a *Bōx*; it should be *Bōps* <note>original: "Βῶπα"; literally "ox-eyed"</note>, since despite being small, it has large eyes. If it has the eye of an ox, how should it be named? For if we name things poorly, as when we say *iserakinos* instead of *korakinos* <note>A crow-black fish; the text discusses linguistic shifts</note>. For it was named from its "moving its pupils" (*koras kinein*). And why do we not say *seisouros* instead of *silouros*? <note>The catfish</note> For it would be named from "continually shaking its tail" (*seisein tēn ouran*).

<margin>Sprats.</margin>
**Sprats.** <note>original: "Βεβράδες" (bebrades); also known as *membrades*, likely small fry or Mediterranean sprats</note> Phrynichus the tragedian says: "O golden-headed sprats of the sea!" Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, calls them *bebradonai*: "The sprats, the wrasses, and the brave dragon-fish." And Sophron in his *Mimes*: "A needle for a sprat." Nymphiodorus in his *Art of Fishing*: "The ray and the sardine... prepare these in two layers." Dorion, in his book *On Fish*, says: "If you decapitate the sprat and wash it in fine salt and water, boil it in the same manner as the red mullet." He says a specific preparation is made only from the sprat, called "Bebraic," which Ariston mentions in *Shivering in the Sun*. Certainly, the Sicilian sprat resembles the small anchovy. However, the Attic writers say *membrades* <note>With an 'm'</note>. Aristomenes says in *The Sorcerers*: "Bringing sprats for an obol." Aristonymus in *Shivering in the Sun*: "Neither are there anchovies now, clearly, nor yet the wretched sprat." Aristophanes in *Old Age*: "Nourished on grey-skinned sprats." Plato in *The Ambassadors*: "By Heracles, what sprats!" In the plays of Eupolis, one can find the spelling with the 'm'. Antiphanes in a comedy says: "They herald a place for the fish—a proclamation!—not for someone's greasy sprat, but claiming to have sprats sweeter than great honey." If that is so, nothing prevents the honey-sellers from crying out that they sell honey more rotten than sprats! Alexis in *The Chorus Leader* uses the 'm' spelling: "He who served at the funeral feasts a jar of gudgeon and sprats in olive-pressings." And in the *Lead Singer*: "By Dionysus, I have not had a harder time since I became a parasite; it would be better for me to have sprats..."

<margin>The Belunnos.</margin>
**The Belunnos.** <note>An unidentified small fish</note> Sophron mentions this in the work titled *The Fisherman*: "the most wild *belunnos*." It is similar in appearance to a goby. Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, calls some fish *baiones* in these lines: "Bring the red mullets and the curved prawns and the *baiones*." Among the Athenians, there is a proverb: "No bad fish is small <note>original: "βαιὸν" (baion)</note> for me."

<margin>The Sole.</margin>
**The Sole.** <note>original: "Βούγλωσσος" (bouglossos), literally "ox-tongue"</note> Archestratus, that practitioner of Pythagorean self-restraint <note>An ironic joke; Archestratus was actually a glutton</note>, says: "Then take a large flatfish and catch that 'ox-tongue' where it lies near Chalcis." Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, says: "ox-tongues and lyre-fish were within." Different from the soles are the "dog-tongues" <note>original: "κυνόγλωσσοι" (kunoglossoi)</note>. Concerning these, Epicharmus says in the same work: "The swimmers and the dog-tongues and the *skiathides*." The Athenians call the sole a *psetta*.

<margin>Conger Eels.</margin>
**Conger Eels.** <note>original: "Γόγγροι" (gongroi)</note> Hicesius says these are tough-skinned and live in shoals, thin-fleshed and lacking in good juice, though they are good for the stomach. Nicander the epic poet, in the third book of his *Glossary*, says they are also called *gryllai*. Eudoxus, in the sixth book of his *Tour of the Earth*, says that many conger eels the weight of a man are caught in Sicyon <note>A city in the Peloponnese</note>, some of which are large enough to fill a wagon. Philemon the comic poet also mentions the excellent congers of Sicyon, portraying a cook boasting of his craft in the play *The Soldier*:

> How a desire came over me to tell to earth and sky
> How I prepared the dish! By Athena, it is sweet to succeed,
> How tender the fish became for me—not at all
> Seasoned with cheese or overwhelmed from above,
> But as it was in life, so it was when roasted.
> I gave it such a gentle fire, I will not even be believed;
> Like when a bird snatches a fish,
> It seeks to swallow it down whole, watching the cooking
> To gulp it down.

Regarding his own boasting, another play follows this one. The pleasure was the same for the first man who learned of it...

These are the stories now being told at the Athenaeans' table: Menecrates of Syracuse spoke in this way, he who was called "Zeus." He was a man of great pride because he believed himself to be the sole cause of life for mankind through his medical skill. Thus, when he cured those suffering from the so-called "sacred disease," <note>original: "ἱερὰς νόσους" (hieras nosous); a common ancient term for epilepsy</note> he compelled them to sign a written agreement that they would follow and obey him as his attendants. One of these was a man dressed as **Heracles**, <note>the famous Greek hero known for his strength and lion-skin cloak</note> and he was indeed called Heracles. This was Nicostratus of Argos, who had been cured of the sacred disease. Ephippus mentions them in his play *The Dearest One*, saying that Menecrates claimed to be a God, while Nicostratus of Argos was a second Heracles. Another followed as **Hermes**, <note>the messenger god</note> wearing a traveler's cloak and carrying a herald's staff. How bitter this was for others, as seen with the zealot Nicephorus, who also held a tyranny over his homeland, as Baeton records in his work *On the Tyrants at Ephesus*. Hegesander also says that Menecrates cured a man named Astycreon and thereafter called him **Apollo**. <note>the god of light, music, and prophecy</note> Yet another of those he saved took up the robe of **Asclepius** <note>the god of healing</note> and †was led around with him. "Zeus" himself was dressed in purple, wore a golden crown upon his head, held a scepter, and wore high-soled buskins as he went about with his "choir" of gods. In a letter to King Philip, he wrote the following: "Menecrates Zeus to Philip, greeting. You rule over Macedonia, but I rule over Medicine. You are able to destroy those who are healthy if you wish, but I can save those who are sick. And those who are robust obey me, for I keep them alive until old age. Therefore, the Macedonians serve as your bodyguards, but all those who are to be born serve as mine. For I, Zeus, grant them life." To this, Philip wrote back to Menecrates, as if to a madman, wishing him "sanity." <note>original: "ὑγιαίνειν" (hygiainein); Philip's response is a clever pun—it is the standard greeting "to be well," but in this context, it pointedly wishes the delusional doctor "good mental health."</note> He also sent similar letters to Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, and to others to whom he wrote, never refraining from the title of "Zeus." Once, Philip invited him to a banquet along with his personal gods. He had them all sit together on the middle couch, which was the highest, most magnificent, and decorated in a manner fit for a temple. He placed a table before them on which an altar stood, featuring the first-fruits of all the earth's produce. And whenever food was carried around to the other guests, the servants would only offer incense and libations to Menecrates and his followers. In the end, this "New Zeus," hungry along with his subject gods, fled from the banquet, as Hegesander records. Menecrates is also mentioned by Alexis in *Minos*. Furthermore, Themison of Cyprus, the favorite of King Antiochus, is mentioned by Pythermus of Ephesus in the eighth book of his *Histories*. Not only was he proclaimed at the public festivals as "Themison of Macedonia, the Heracles of King Antiochus," but all the locals sacrificed to him, addressing him as "Heracles Themison." He would appear whenever any of his "fellow gods" was invoked, reclining by himself and dressed in a lion's skin. He also carried Scythian bows and held a club. Yet even this Menecrates, being the sort of man described, never performed a feat like the aforementioned cook who, leaning on his elbows, boasted: "I have found immortality! Even those already dead, whenever they smell my cooking, I make them live again." Indeed, the whole race of cooks is boastful, as Hegesander also pointed out in his *Delphic Memoirs*. He introduces a cook who says:

The boastfulness of cooks.

> **B**est of men, many have said much to me about the art of cooking. Tell me, do you appear to be saying something new, or something I have heard before? If not, do not bother me.
> No, but I alone know the secrets of the culinary art, a discovery of things usually recognized only by me. For I did not learn this casually in two years while wearing an apron, but through my whole life, seeking the sharpest points of the craft part by part.
> I know the types of vegetables, how small fry should be handled, and every kind of lentil soup—I tell you the limit of it. For when I happen to be serving at a funeral feast, as soon as the guests arrive from the burial wearing their mourning clothes, I take the lid off the pot and make those who were weeping laugh! Such a thrill runs through their bodies, a tickling sensation as if they were at a wedding.
> Tell me, do you say this while serving lentils and small fry?
> These are just my side projects. But if I get the proper ingredients and set my kitchen in order just once, you will see the same thing happen as when I pulled the celery before. For a man will hardly be able to pass by this mustard-pot because of the smell.
> Everyone walking past the door will immediately stand there open-mouthed, rooted to the spot, speechless, until some other friend runs up and pulls him away by the nose, so great is the craftsman.
> You do not know the man you are talking to! I know many of those sitting here who have devoured their entire estates because of me. By the gods, how do we differ from the Sirens? This man seems to me like one of those rolling things in Pindar, who in the same way made their listeners forget their food because of the pleasure—they simply vanish.
