# FROM THE ATHENAEAN "BANQUET OF THE LEARNED"

"You display a character that is quite refined and gentle, but you have acted with great negligence. What do I mean? Have you not investigated who we are in our craft, or did you first inquire of those who know accurately before you hired me?"
"By Zeus, I did not think it necessary. Perhaps there is no difference between a servant and a cook? I do not know, but you will find out from what you say."
"Taking fish already bought from the market and simply delivering them after preparation in a musical manner—that is the job of any ordinary servant. By Heracles, the perfect **cook** <note>original: "μάγειρος" (mageiros); in Greek comedy, the cook is often a boastful, highly-trained professional for hire, not a household slave</note> is a completely different disposition! You might find many arts that are very famous, but it is not possible for one who wishes to learn them correctly to approach them immediately. But first, one must understand that painting and cookery are the same; one must first learn other arts, which it is better for you to know before you take up the craft: **Astrology**, **Medicine**, and **Geometry**."
"For from these, you will know the powers and the qualities of the fish by following the seasons, seeing when <margin>10</margin> each is out of season or when it is ripe. For there are great intervals in the quality of pleasures. Sometimes a tuna is better than a cow."
"So be it, but what does **Geometry** have to do with you?"
"Because we consider the whole to be a sphere; having divided this and taken its place, the art consists of skillfully partitioning it by type, with each part being transferred from its place. I shall believe that, but do not speak of the rest!"
"But regarding **Medicine**: since some foods are gas-inducing and hard to digest, and carry a penalty of stomach-turning—not of simple cramps, but of those where everyone becomes acidic and lacks self-control. For the most pleasant foods, remedies have been found for each transition of the art. Everything pleasant is mine, provided it is mindful and symmetrical. Where each dish will be placed in the battle-array—to perceive the quantity of the cookery by number—no one else can do this as I can. Let me be called a minor part of the universe. Do not mock yourself or me. Let us pass the day without trouble."

And the cook in the play by the "reaper of returns" Philemon <note>a celebrated poet of New Comedy</note> wishes to be something of a teacher, <margin>20</margin> speaking such things as: "Keep the fire only this way; make the roasts for me without blood. For if you make them too roasted, you actually boil them. Do not let the fire be sharp, for it burns whatever it catches on the outside, but then it does not penetrate into the flesh. A man is not a cook if he simply comes with a ladle and a knife, nor if someone just throws fish into the pans—rather, there is a kind of wisdom in the matter."

And the cook in the play by Diphilus <note>another major Athenian comic poet</note> speaks to the painter, saying how he selects his clients through a teacher, speaking thus: "I will not take you on—I do not shout this often—you shall not continue in this work for the day, preparing tables for many good things to be poured out. For I do not walk in before I have tested who the one sacrificing is, or from where the dinner is organized, or what kind of people he has invited. I have a description of all the types, to know for which ones I should be hired and whom I must avoid. For instance, consider the Market-place <note>original: "Ἐμπορίον" (Emporion); the commercial district of a city</note> now, if you wish to use it. A sea-captain is sacrificing because he just lost <margin>30</margin> a mast or broke a yard-arm, or threw his cargo overboard with a very bad judgment—I let such a man go. He makes a pleasant mackerel dish, but not for the sake of the Law. While he eats, he calculates the shares of the voyage with his crew, and each man eats as if he were devouring his own innards. But there is another, a guest-lover from Byzantium, a merchant on his third day, calm, well-off, and full of joy. Having received ten or twelve silver coins for his freight, he comes up from the harbor smelling of the Aphrodisian rites <note>implying he has just visited the temple of Aphrodite or the brothels</note> under the influence of beautiful pimps, immediately showing off his right hand, swollen with money; by Zeus the Savior, I stick to that servant! Such is the way. Again, a youth in love devours and squanders his father's inheritance. I go there! But those who collect from a common contribution—by Zeus, elsewhere! He puts his findings into a ceramic pot, putting away the scraps and shouting, 'Who can make a cheap little fish better?' I let him shout. For one must expect blows upon arriving there, and serving the whole night. For if you ask for your small wage, he says, 'Bring me a chamber-pot <margin>40</margin> first!' or 'The lentil soup has no vinegar.' If you ask again, he says, 'You'll wail for a long time!' That is the first of the cooks. I could list ten thousand other such things. But where I am leading you now is a expensive brothel where things are wasted, a courtesan leading a pour-out with her fellow prostitutes. Drip yourself in and run away with whatever is in your pocket."

And in Archedicus’s *The Treasure*, another culinary sophist says these things: "When the first guest has not yet tasted the raw fish, the invited ones will bring it. Having taken the dish in hand, I let it go; putting the pans on the fire of the coals, I splash everything with oil and create a flame, in which the vegetables and the side-dishes delight my man with their scent. For in delivering a boiled fish that has its juice within it, and the peak of the brine, every free man would dip into it. With a pint of oil consumed, I have perhaps saved fifty dining rooms."

Philostephanus, in his *Man of Delos*, also lists the names of famous cooks in these lines: "Knowing that you excel all in the art and in sharpness after Theron, O Daedalus, <margin>50</margin> the one from Athyla called 'the Savior,' I have come here to bring you, giving the wage you asked." And Sopater—not the Maronite poet of Ionian songs, but the poet of Middle Comedy—also makes a certain cook speak in his play *The Women Shut In* (for so he titles the drama): "I took some shrimp first, and I fried these..."

I wrapped it in a leaf and hid it like a treasure in many hot ashes, and I received from it a **Phaleric whitebait** <note>whitebait from the port of Phalerum were considered the finest in Athens</note>. Into a cup, much plant-water was poured. Cutting a scale of greens and more, the oil-flask was overturned. What remains? Nothing else of the craft, nor of the inventory, nor of the records. And enough of the cooks. Now concerning the <margin>Conger Eel.</margin> **conger eel** <note>original: "γόγγρος" (gongros)</note> we must speak. For Archestratus <note>a 4th-century BCE poet known as the "Hesiod of Diners"</note> in his *Gastronomy* explains where each part of it should be bought, saying: "Friend, in **Sicyon** <note>a city in the Peloponnese famous for its fish market</note> get the head of a large, strong conger, and all its hollow parts. Then boil it for a long time in brine with greens." Next, going through the places in Italy, this fine prince of poets says: "A noble conger is caught, so much so that it surpasses all other fish, just as the most excellent feast-fire <margin>20</margin> surpasses the poorest of crows." And at Helice and near Thebes, there is a conger with fatty members under the flesh. Archedicus, in *The Treasure*, introduces a certain cook saying from where he bought his wares: "A small *glaukos* for three drachmae. A conger head and the first slices for five drachmae—O, what a wretched life! Drachmae for the necks! But by the sun, it is possible for me to get another neck from elsewhere and buy it, so that I have water flowing in..." He related these things. "No one is more hardworking than a Sicyonian. At the same time, we buy many things, and many very expensive things. At the same time, if we buy anything good, we lose it..." <margin>Dogfish.</margin> **Dogfish.** Hicesius, in his writings *On Material*, says that of the dogfish, the best and most tender are those called **starred dogfish** <note>original: "ἀστερίας" (asterias)</note>. Aristotle says there are several other kinds: the spiny, the smooth, the variegated, the young, and the fox-dogfish; <margin>30</margin> he says it has one fin near the tail, but none along the spine. Aristotle, in the fifth book of *History of Animals*, says there is a certain dogfish that is also called 'notidanos.' Epaenetus says in his *Art of Cookery* that the back-parts are good. He says the kind with a sting is worse and foul-smelling. It is recognized by having a sting at the first fin, which others of the same kind do not have; it has neither suet nor fat, nor is this fish oily because it is cartilaginous. Specifically, the spiny dogfish has a five-sided heart. The dogfish gives birth to three young, and takes the newborns back into its mouth and releases them again. This is especially true of the variegated and the fox-dogfish. The others do not do so because of their roughness. Archestratus, who lived the same life as Sardanapalus, speaking of the dogfish in Rhodes, considers it to be the same as the one which among the Romans is carried around to banquets with flutes and crowns, the carriers themselves being crowned, called the **acipenser** <note>original: "ἀκκιπινσήρᾳ"; likely referring to the sturgeon, a status symbol at Roman feasts</note>. But this <margin>40</margin> one is small and has a longer snout, and is more triangular in shape than the other. Of these, the cheapest and smallest is sold for no less than a thousand Attic drachmae. Appion the grammarian, in his book *On Attic Luxury*, says that the fish called 'elops' is the *acipenser*. But Archestratus, speaking of the Rhodian dogfish and advising his companions in a fatherly way, says: "In Rhodes, get the 'fox-dogfish,' and even if you are about to die, if they will not sell it to you, snatch it! The Syracusans call it a fat 'dog.' Later, suffer whatever fate is destined for you." Mentioning these verses, Lynceus of Samos, in his letter to Diagoras, says that the poet rightly encourages one who cannot pay the price to satisfy his desire through wrongdoing. For he says that Theseus, being handsome, took the fish from Tlepolemus... Timocles says in *The Finger*: "Dogfish and rays and all those flat fish <margin>50</margin> which are gathered in an acidic-fatty sauce." **Glaukos.** Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe* says: "Variegated scorpions, <margin>Glaukos.</margin> lizard-fish, and *glaukos* fish come." Numenius in *The Art of Fishing* says: "At Sicyon, or for the beautiful-fish... at other times the sea-perch, or the *glaukos* provide shining meat." Archestratus says: "But for me, boil a *glaukos* head in brine. And at Megara, for they are caught there in noble sizes." And Antiphanes in...

Thatta says: "Boeotian **eel**, **Pontic mice** <note>original: 'μῦς ποντικοί'; likely referring to a type of shellfish or small fish, though literally 'mice'</note>, Megarian **tunny**, Carystian **sprats**, Erythraean **snapper**, and Skyrian **lobsters**." The same author, in his play *Philantides*, also says the following: "So, the little **glaukos-fish** <note>original: 'γλαυκίδιον'; a small grey-fish or sea-perch</note> should be boiled in brine as usual, but this **sea-bass** should be roasted whole; the **dogfish** in a spicy sauce <note>original: 'ἀποτρίμματι'; a rubbed or pounded sauce, similar to pesto</note> of Zeuthus; the **eel** with salt, oregano, and water. The **conger eel** and the **ray** are prepared the same way, with greens. You shall roast a slice of **tunny** meat, but for the **kid-goat**, the roasting is the opposite... the island of Sisachthon." Eubulus, in *Kampylion*: "Bring out the dishes of those fair-faced ones, of this sea-born **Glaukos**; bring also a noble **sea-bass**, boiled in a simple brine." Anaxandrides, in *Nereus*: "The first to discover a costly large slice. This face of a **Glaukos** and the blood-red tunny... and all the other foods of the sharp salt sea; Nereus dwells in this whole place." Amphis, in *Seven Against Thebes*: "Whole **Glaukoi**, the fleshy parts of the spines." And in *Philetaerus*: "Cleanly I cooked a little **eel** and **glaukos** heads and slices of **sea-bass**." Antiphanes, in *The Cyclops*, surpassing the poet Archestratus, says: "Within we have Hymettian **gray mullet**, choked **torpedo** <note>the electric ray</note>, striped **perch**, stuffed **squid**, roasted **synodon**, a head of **glaukos**, a head of **conger**, the belly of a **fishing-frog** <note>monkfish</note>, the flank of a **tunny**, the back of a **ray**, the loin of a **cuttlefish**, a **thrush-fish**, a burnt **sprat**, a **red mullet**, and a **wrasse**. Let nothing of life's bounty be absent." Nausicrates, in *The Ship-Owners*, says: "Two soft and beautiful ones appearing to sailors in sea-embraces, whom they say announce the sufferings of mortals. You speak of Glaucus; you have recognized him."

<margin>Glaucus of the sea: myths.</margin> Concerning the sea-daemon **Glaucus**, Theolytus of Methymna says in his *Bacchic Verses* that he fell in love with Ariadne after she was stolen by Dionysus on the island; and when he tried to force her, Dionysus bound him with vine-tendrils, but then released him after he spoke: "Anthedon is the city on the shores of the sea, opposite Euboea, near the streams of the Euripus. Thence is my race. My father was Nopes." Promathidas of Heraclea says in his *Iambics* that Glaucus was the son of Polybus (son of Hermes) and Euboea (daughter of Larymnus). Mnaseas, in the third book of his *On Europe*, genealogizes him as the son of Anthedon and Alcyone. He says Glaucus was a sailor and an excellent diver, and thus called "The Marine." He further relates that Glaucus abducted Syme, the daughter of Iclemon and Dotis, and sailed away to Asia, where he settled a deserted island near Caria and named it Syme after his wife. Evanithes the epic poet, in his *Hymn to Glaucus*, calls him the son of Poseidon and a Naiad nymph, and says he lay with Ariadne on the island of Dia when she was abandoned by Theseus. Aristotle, in his *Constitution of Delos*, says he settled in Delos with the Nereids and gave prophecies to the gods. Possis of Magnesia, in the third book of the *Amazoniad*, says Glaucus was the builder of the *Argo* and its helmsman, and when Jason fought the Tyrrhenians, Glaucus was the only one unhurt in the sea-battle; by the will of Zeus he appeared in the depths of the sea, and thus became a sea-daemon, seen only by Jason. Nicanor of Cyrene, in his *Changes of Names*, says Melicertes was renamed Glaucus. Alexander the Aetolian also mentions much about him in his poem entitled *The Fisherman*, saying that after tasting a certain herb, he threw himself into the sea: "In the Islands of the Blessed, a thin plant grows in the morning soil for the sun-god Phaethon. The Sun gives it to his horses as a delightful meal... so they may complete their course without weariness." Aeschrion of Samos says in one of his iambic poems that the sea-god Glaucus fell in love with Scylla, the daughter of the diver Hydne. He speaks particularly about the herb: "By eating which he became immortal, and found the secret food of the gods, which Cronus had sown." Nicander, in the third book of his *On Europe*, records that Glaucus was the beloved of Nereus. The same Nicander, in the first book of his *Aetolian History*, says that Apollo was taught the art of prophecy by Glaucus. He recounts that while Glaucus was hunting on a high mountain in Aetolia, he caught a hare that was fainting from the chase; he brought it to a spring and wiped it with the surrounding grass. When the hare was revived by the herb, Glaucus recognized its power and tasted it himself; becoming divinely inspired, he threw himself into the sea during a storm by the will of Zeus. Hedylogos of Samos (or Athens) says Glaucus threw himself into the sea out of love for Melicertes. Hedyle, the poetess, and mother of the iambic poet Moschine of Attica, in her poem entitled *Scylla*, relates that Glaucus fell in love with Scylla and came to her cave: "Bringing her a gift of a hollow shell from the Red Sea rock, or the still-wingless chicks of the halcyons, as toys for the nymph. But his tears and his sighs the maiden pitied not." For he was driven away by her, and by the fires of Etna.

<margin>Gnapheus.</margin> **Fuller-fish** <note>original: 'Γναφεύς'; literally 'Fuller' (one who cleans cloth). Likely a species like the pufferfish or something with detergent-like properties</note>. Dorion, in his work *On Fish*, says that the liquid from cooking the fuller-fish cleans every stain. Epainetus also mentions it in his *Art of Cookery*.

<margin>Eel.</margin> **Eel**. Epicharmus mentions sea-eels in his *Muses*. Dorion, in his *On Fish*, mentions those from Lake Copais and praises them. These grow to an immense size.

For instance, Agatharchides says in the sixth book of his *History of Europe* that the Boeotians <note>People from the region of Boeotia in central Greece, famous for their love of eels.</note> take the unusually large eels from Lake Copais, and after crowning them with garlands like <term>hieria</term> <note>sacrificial victims</note> and offering prayers, they throw barley-groats upon them and sacrifice them to the gods. When a stranger, perplexed by this strange custom, asked for the reason, the Boeotian would only say that one must maintain ancestral customs and that it is not right to offer explanations to others for them. We should not be surprised that eels are sacrificed like ritual victims, since Antigonus of Carystus, in his work *On Language*, says that those who perform a sacrifice to Poseidon <note>God of the sea</note> during the tunny-fishing season—whenever they have a good catch—sacrifice the caught tunny to the god; and this sacrifice is called the *Thynnaion* <note>original: "θυνναῖον"; the "Tunny-offering"</note>. Salt fish, too, are offered as sacrifices among the people of Phaselis. Heropythus, at any rate, in his *Annals of the Colophonians*, while relating the founding of the city through Phaselis, says that Lacius, who led the colony, gave the shepherd Cylabras (who was grazing sheep in that spot) some <term>tarichoi</term> <note>dried or salted fish</note> as payment for the land, because the shepherd requested it. For when Lacius gave him the choice of receiving either barley-meal, wheat, or salt fish for the site, Cylabras chose the salt fish. Because of this, the people of Phaselis even now sacrifice salt fish to Cylabras every year. Philostephanus, in the first book of his *On the Cities of Asia*, writes as follows: "Lacius the Argive, one of those who arrived with Mopsus—whom some say was a Lindian and the brother of Antiphemus, the founder of Gela—was sent to Phaselis by Mopsus with a group of men according to a prophecy of Manto, the mother of Mopsus. This was when their ships reached the island and they gathered at the Chelidonian islands; those with Lacius arrived late because they had landed during the night. It is said he bought the land where the city now stands, just as Manto had foretold, from a certain Cylabras, paying with salt fish. For Cylabras was told to take whatever they were carrying; hence, every year the people of Phaselis sacrifice salt fish to Cylabras, honoring him as a hero."

<margin>Eels.</margin>
Regarding eels, Hicesius says in his *On Materials* that eels are the most succulent of all fish and that they surpass most others in being easy on the stomach; for they are "slippery" and very nourishing. He says he classifies the Macedonian eels among the salt-fish type. Aristotle, however, says that eels delight

<margin>Book 8.</margin>
in the clearest water, which is why eel-breeders pour clean water over them; for they choke in muddy water. This is also why those who hunt them stir up the mud so that they will be suffocated. They have thin gills, and their pores are immediately blocked by the mud. For the same reason, they are suffocated in winter when the water is disturbed by the winds. They mate by intertwining, and they release a certain slimy substance from themselves which, when it settles in the mud, comes to life. Those who keep eels say they feed at night, but during the day they remain motionless in the mud. <unclear>as if a rotting occurs</unclear>, just as is said of the so-called "earth-worms." This is why Homer, in distinguishing them from the general nature of fish, said: "The eels and the fish were distressed in the eddies" <note>Iliad 21.203. Ancient scholars noted that Homer treats eels as distinct from other fish.</note>. Epicharmus, a certain banqueter among those dining with us, when an eel was served, called it the "Helen of Dinners" <note>Comparing the eel to Helen of Troy—a prize so beautiful and desirable that men would go to war for it.</note>. "I then shall be Paris," he said, and before anyone else could stretch out a hand for it, he fell upon it and stripped its side right down to the backbone. This same man, when a hot flat-cake was once served and everyone was holding back, exclaimed: "I shall eat it myself," and even though it was likely to burn his hands, he rashly threw himself upon it and, swallowing it while it was burning hot, he was quite overcome. He also said of the Cyclops: "The seagull is carried off from the throat-battle." And regarding the eel, Archestratus writes the following:

> I praise every kind of eel, but by far the best
> Is that caught in the sea-strait opposite Rhegium.
> There you, above all other mortal men,
> Gain the advantage by placing such a food within your mouth.
> Nevertheless, a very great reputation for excellence is carried
> By the eels of Copais and the Strymon; for they are large
> and wonderful in their thickness. Yet I believe the queen
> Of all our diet, and the leader in pleasure,
> Is the eel, which is by nature the only fish without scales.

When Homer said, "the eels and the fish were distressed," Archilochus followed suit: "He pursued many blind eels." The Attic writers, as Tryphon says, were familiar with the singular uses of the word, but they did not consistently follow suit in the plural forms. Aristophanes, for instance, in the *Acharnians*, says: "Children, look at the finest **eel**." And in the *Women of Lemnos*: "The Boeotian **eel**." And for the nominative case in the *Daedalus*: "And a stone like an **eel**." And Cratinus in the *Ploutoi*: "Tunny, sea-perch, gray-fish, **eel**, dogfish." However, they do not use the plural forms in the same way as the poet [Homer]. Aristophanes in the *Knights*: "For you have suffered just like those who hunt for **eels**." And in the second version of the *Clouds*: "imitating my images of the **eels**." In the *Wasps*, he uses the dative: "I do not delight in rays, nor in **eels**." Strattis in *The Rivers*: "He was born a cousin of the **eels**." Simonides in his *Iambics*: "Like an **eel** through the slime," and he also uses the accusative: "For a heron, finding an **eel** eating in the Maander-like coil, took it away." Aristotle, in his books *On Animals*, explains why he used the form *egcheleis*. When Aristophanes says in the *Knights*: "For you have suffered just like those who hunt for **eels**. When the lake is calm, they catch nothing. But if they stir the mud up and down, they take them. So too you take things if you stir up the city." This clearly shows that the eel is caught from the mud, hence also...

->### FROM THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED<-

<margin>Sacrificial victims</margin> ...the matter was brought to a conclusion. The poet <note>Homer, in the *Iliad* 21.353, describing the god Hephaestus burning the river Scamander</note>, wishing to show that the heat reached the very depths of the river, said: "The eels and the fish were tormented." He specifically mentions the eels apart from the other fish to demonstrate that even the deep-dwelling creatures felt the boiling water. Antiphanes, in his play *Lycon*, mocks the Egyptians, saying: "They say the Egyptians are clever in other ways, but especially in considering the eel equal to a god. In fact, it is far more precious than the gods! For we can reach the gods just by praying, but to even get a smell of an eel, we have to spend at least twelve drachmas or more. The creature is not holy in any sense at all."

Anaxandrides, in his play *The Cities*, addresses the Egyptians directly, saying: "I could never be an ally to you, for neither our manners nor our laws agree. They stand very far apart from each other. You worship a cow, but I sacrifice it to the gods. You consider the eel a very great divinity, but we consider it by far the greatest of delicacies. You do not eat pork, but I find it most delightful. You worship the dog, but I beat it whenever I catch it eating my food. Among us, it is the law that priests should be whole and unblemished, but among you, it seems they are mutilated <note>A reference to circumcision, which Greeks found strange.</note>. If you see a cat in distress, you weep; but I would most gladly kill and skin it. Among you, the shrew-mouse has power, but with me, it has none."

Timocles, in *The Egyptians*, says: "How could an ibis or a dog save anyone? For where people commit sacrilege against the acknowledged gods and are not punished immediately, what sort of punishment could a cat's altar inflict?"

That eels are even more delicious when wrapped in beet leaves is a point frequently made by the ancient comic poets. Eubulus says in *Echo*: "O nymph, a bride of the beet, covering your body in a white-skinned veil, you appear—the eel! O, what a great, great light you are to me!" And in *Ion*: "And after these, the wealthy tunnies were present, all under-cooked on the coals; and there were the divine Boeotian eels from the lake, wrapped in their beet-leaf robes." And in *Medea*, he calls it the "maiden of Boeotian Copais" <note>Referring to Lake Copais, famous for its eels.</note>, for they call her a goddess. Antiphanes also mentions that the eels of the river Strymon were famous, saying in *Thamyras*: "And you, whose name is famous among the tales of mortals, a river flowing down through Thrace—the Strymon—having produced the largest eels." Regarding the river Eucleia, mentioned by Antimachus in his tablets titled *The Tablets*: "Coming to the springs of the swirling Eucleia." Demetrius of Skepsis, <margin>Ellops</margin> in the sixteenth book of *The Trojan Array*, says that many different types of eels exist. 

**The Ellops** <note>A type of sturgeon or similar prized fish.</note>. Some things have been said about it before, but Archestratus says this: "Eat the *ellops* especially in famous Syracuse, the very best kind. For that fish is native to that place. Even if it is caught near islands, or if it reaches some other land, or Crete, it becomes thin, tough, and battered by the waves."

<margin>Erythrinoi</margin> **The Erythrinoi** <note>Red mullets or sea breams.</note>. Aristotle, in his work *On Animals*, and Speusippus say that the *phagros*, the *erythrinos*, and the *hepatos* are similar. Dorion says the same in his book *On Fish*. The people of Cyrene call the *erythrinos* a *lynkin*, as Cleitarchus says in his *Glossary*. 

<margin>Anchovies</margin> **The Anchovies**. Aristotle mentions these as very small fish in his work *On Animal Parts*. Dorion, in his book *On Fish*, mentions anchovies among the boiled fish, saying: "Either boiled anchovies, or *iopas*, or *atherines*, or gobies, or small red mullets, and small squids and crabs." 

<margin>Epsitos</margin> **The Epsitos** <note>Literally "the boiled one," referring to a small fry or smelt.</note>. This is one of the thin, small fish. Aristophanes says in *Anagyrus*: "This is not a dish of *epsitoi*." Archippus says in *The Fish*: "The anchovy fell down with the soul of an *epsitos*." Eupolis in *The Goats*: "O Graces, for whom the *epsitoi* are destined." Eubulus in *Pronousia* or *The Swan*: "I love even a day-old *epsitos* on the boats, even if it has been boiling for twelve days." Alexis in *The Blinded Man*: "For some of us were present with skillfully prepared *epsitoi*—for they call all beautiful works 'Daedalean' <note>After the mythical inventor Daedalus.</note>." And again: "So you don't take any of the *korakinos* fish, nor the *trichidion*, nor even any *epsitoi*?" They mostly use the word *epsitos* in the plural. Aristophanes in his plays or in *Niobe*: "By Zeus, I will not even mention a dish of *epsitoi*." Myanthos in *The Little Boy*: "The child came in carrying an *epsitos*." Nicostratus uses the singular in *Hesiod*: "The *bembras*, the anchovy, the *epsitos*." Poseidippus in *The Woman Chosen by Lot*: "Someone to buy an *epsitos*." In Naucratis <note>A Greek trading city in Egypt.</note>, they call the small fish caught in the canals "epsitoi" when the Nile finishes its flooding.

<margin>Hepatos</margin> **The Hepatos** <note>Literally "the liver-colored fish," likely a species of sea bream or grouper.</note> or **Lebias**. Diocles said it is one of the rock-dwelling fish. <margin>Lebias</margin> Speusippus says the *hepatos* is similar to the *phagros*. It is a solitary fish, as Aristotle says, a meat-eater with jagged teeth, dark in color, with eyes larger than its body size would suggest, and a white, triangular heart. Archestratus, the leader of banquets, says one should catch the *lebias* or *hepatos* in the waters around Delos. 

<margin>Spindle-fish</margin> **The Spindle-fish** <note>original: "hlakatines"; possibly a type of large tuna or kingfish.</note>. Mnesimachus in *The Horse-breeder*: "Mackerel, tunny, goby, spindle-fish." These are whale-like in size and suitable for salting. Menander says in *The Limping Men*: "Goby, spindle-fish, and dog-fish tail." Mnaseas of Patrae says that from the fish called *hesychia* come sisters called *galiai*, and the moray eel, and the spindle-fish. 

<margin>Tunny</margin> **The Tunny**. Aristotle says this fish swims into the Black Sea keeping the land on its right, but swims out keeping it on its left. This is because it sees more sharply with its right eye and is dim-sighted with its left.

->### BOOK VII ###<-

<sig>y 4</sig>

It has under its fins the so-called gadfly <note>original: οἶστρος (*oistros*); likely referring to a parasitic crustacean that plagues tuna</note>. It delights in saltiness, which is why it approaches the sandy shores. It becomes edible once it is free of this gadfly. It mates after its period of hibernation, as Theophrastus says. As long as it carries small embryos, it is difficult to catch; but when they grow larger, it is easily taken because of the gadfly's irritation. The tuna also hibernates during the season of many waves. Archestratus says: "Around holy and wide Samos you will see the tuna caught with speed—the great one, which they call the *orkynos* <note>original: ὄρκυνος; the giant tuna or albacore</note>. 
<margin>5</margin> Others call it a sea-monster. One must buy this from the gods, as it were, quickly and regardless of price. Furthermore, the noble tuna of Byzantium is caught in its prime; and also in the famous island of the Sicilians. The shores of Tyndaris also nourish tuna that are much better than these. And if ever you go to Hipponion in sacred Italy, a place surrounded by water, there they are by far the best of all, and they hold the prizes of victory. 
<margin>10</margin> Those that are found in other places are from far away, having crossed many seas through the deep water. When we ourselves hunt them, we are like heroes." The tuna (*thunnos*) was named from its "rushing" (*thyein*) and "dashing" <note>An ancient etymological pun: *thunnos* from *thyein* (to dart/rush)</note>. For the fish is impulsive because, during certain seasons, it has a gadfly on its head, by which Aristotle says it is driven mad. He writes as follows: 
<margin>lib. 8.</margin> "The tuna and the swordfish go into a frenzy <note>original: οἰστρῶσι (*oistrōsi*) - to be driven by the gadfly</note> around the rising of the Dog Star <note>The star Sirius, associated with the hottest part of summer</note>; for at that time they both have near their fins a sort of small worm called the gadfly, which resembles a 
<margin>15</margin> scorpion and is about the size of a spider. This causes them to leap out of the water, no less than dolphins do, and they often fall into ships." And Theodoridas says: "The tuna shall dash in a frenzied race." Polybius of Megalopolis, in the thirty-fourth book of his *Histories*, discussing the region of Lusitania in Iberia <note>Modern-day Portugal/Spain</note>, says that there are "acorns" <note>original: βάλανοι (*balanoi*); likely the fruit of the sea-oak or Posidonia seagrass</note> produced in the depths of the sea there, 
<margin>20</margin> which the tuna eat and thereby grow fat. Therefore, one would not be wrong to call the tuna "sea-pigs," for like pigs they are fattened by acorns. The most praised part of this fish is the belly (*hypogastrion*), as Eubulus says in *The Ion*: "After these things, bring the roasted belly of a great-fleshed tuna." Aristophanes in *The Lemnian Women*: "No Boeotian eel, no sea-grayling, no belly of a tuna." Stratis in *Atalanta*: "He said the belly of a tuna and a ham cost a drachma." In 
<margin>25</margin> *The Macedonians*: "Sweet are the bellies of tuna." Eriphus in *Meliboea*: "For these things are not cheap; one cannot buy a tuna's belly in the market, nor a sea-bass head, nor conger eel, nor cuttlefish. I think the gods do not look upon such things from afar." And when Theopompus says in *Callaeschrus*: "Bring the belly of the fish, O master." It is worth noting that they use the term "belly" (*hypogastrion*) primarily for fish, and rarely for pigs 
<margin>30</margin> and other animals. It is unclear which animal's belly Antiphanes refers to in *The Man from Pontus*, when he says: "Whoever has bought fish... perhaps you receive the worst ones, but going for the belly, then how many will you slip away with? Everything is prepared sweetly, the side along with them." Alexis in *The Slave-Girls Weaving*, praising the head of the tuna, says: "And I will throw the fisherman onto the bench; they catch small fish for me like those for freedmen—little sprats and squids and some fried bits. No one previously 
<margin>35</margin> took a tuna head, but used to think of eels and having tuna." They also praised what are called the "collarbones" <note>original: κλεῖδες (*kleides*); the pectoral region of the fish</note> of the tuna, as Aristophon says in *The Parallels*: "And indeed the side-dishes are completely unspoiled. Two roasted collarbones are prepared, with which he will close the doors. The eating of a female tuna is a solemn thing, and a third Spartan dish." Antigonus of Carystus, in his work *On Diction* addressed to Poseidonius, says that a tuna is sacrificed, as we mentioned before. Heracleon of Ephesus says that the term *orkynos* is not used in the Attic dialect. Sostratus, 
<margin>40</margin> in the second book *On Animals*, says that the young tuna (*pelamys*) is called a *thunnid*. I believe that as it grows it becomes a tuna (*thunnos*), and when even larger, an *orkynos*. When it grows excessively large, it becomes a "whale" (*ketos*) <note>Used here to mean any huge sea monster</note>. Aeschylus also mentions the tuna, saying: "I tell you to receive the hammers and forge them; he who bears the sparks without a groan, silent as a tuna." And elsewhere the same poet: "Glancing sideways like a tuna." This refers to the tuna looking with its left eye, 
<margin>45</margin> as Aristotle has said... <note>Ancient Greeks believed tuna could only see well with one eye or migrated keeping the shore on a specific side</note> and in Sophron there is "The Tuna-Hunter." Some call them *thunnoi*, but the Athenians call them *thunnides*.

<margin>The female tuna. lib. r.</margin> **The Female Tuna.** Aristotle says the male differs from this one by having a fin under the belly which is called the *apharea*. In his work *On Animals*, he says the female tuna gives birth in the month of Hekatombaion <note>Roughly July</note> to a sack-like mass in which there are many small eggs. Speusippus, in the second book of *Similitudes*, says they are similar to the male tuna, as does Epicharmus in *The Muses*. Cratinus says in *The Wealthy Men*: "For I am a female tuna, either black, or even a tuna, a sea-perch, a sea-grayling, an eel, a dogfish." Aristotle, in his book *On Fish*, says the female tuna is a shoaling and migratory fish. Archestratus, the glutton, says: "And 
<margin>50</margin> have the tail of the female tuna—I speak of the large female tuna whose mother-city is Byzantium. Then, having cut it correctly, roast it all, sprinkling it only with fine salt and brushing it with oil. Eat the noble slices while hot, dipping them into a sharp brine. Even if you wish to eat them dry, they are excellent, like the immortal gods in form and nature. But if you sprinkle vinegar over it, you have ruined it."

<summary>This page explores the biology, etymology, and culinary preparation of the tuna, featuring Aristotle's observations on its parasites and Archestratus's specific instructions for roasting the fatty belly and tail.</summary>

# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS #

And Antiphanes, in *The Pederast*, says regarding a piece of "Biltiske" <note>This name may refer to a specific person or a well-known courtesan of the time</note> or a middle cut of a Byzantine tuna: "In this, it is hidden within torn coverings." Regarding the tail of the tuna, Antiphanes also praises it in *Korydidos*, speaking of one who was raised in the country: "He eats nothing from the sea; he might try a sweet conger-eel or a torpedo-fish—I mean those lower parts of the tuna that are on the ships—those you might eat. For I have never considered fish to be man-eaters in any other sense." <note>A comedic joke implying that expensive fish "eat" the men who buy them by consuming their wealth</note>. And in *The Absence of Fear*: "This evil is such that you call the eels of Lake Copais 'ships' <note>original: κωπαΐδας (Kopaïdas); a pun on the famous eels from Lake Copais and the word for 'oar'</note>, quite wildly. For I happen to be a farmer by the lake, and I am charged with the 'desertion' of these little eels. For I have not gone to my estate at all." One can find one of these iambic verses also in *The Ill-Treatment*, and in *The Rustic*, or *Boutalion*. And Hipponax, as Lycanias cites in his works *On the Iambic Poets*, says: "For another of them was taking his ease and drinking, eating tuna and garlic-sauce <note>original: μυττωτὸν (myttoton); a pungent spread made of garlic, leeks, cheese, and honey</note> every single day, feasting like a Lampsacene eunuch." And again: "He devoured the hard parts, as it is necessary to dig, eating modest figs from the mountain rocks and a small barley cake for fodder." Strattis also mentions tuna-fish in *Kallippides*.

<margin>Hippouroi</margin> **The Hippouroi.** <note>original: ἵππουροι; likely the Coryphene or Mahi-mahi, literally "horse-tails"</note> Aristotle, in the fifth book of *History of Animals*, says that the *hippouroi* lay eggs, and that these grow from the smallest size to the largest, just like those of the moray eel. They lay eggs in the spring. Dorion, in his work *On Fish*, says that the *hippouros* is also called the *koryphaina* <note>original: κορυφαίναν; the dolphin-fish or mahi-mahi</note>. Hicesius himself addresses them as *ippereas*. Epicharmus mentions them in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "and sharp-snouted needle-fish, *hippouroi*, and gilt-heads." Nymphodius, in *The Art of Fishing*, describing the nature of the fish, says that it leaps continuously, which is why it is also named the "leaper" <note>original: ἀρνευτὴν (arneuten); a tumbler or diver</note>. He speaks of it thus: "Whether the great leaping 'leaper,' the *hippouros*." Archestratus says of its nature: "The *hippouros* from Carystus is the best; it is an excellent dish from many places, but especially Carystus."

<margin>Hippos</margin> Epaenetus, in his *Art of Cookery*, says it is also called the *koryphaina*. **The Hippos.** <note>original: ἵππος; literally "horse," likely a horse-mackerel</note> Perhaps Epicharmus calls them *ippidia* <note>little horses</note> when he says: "Both the crows and the crow-like fish... fat little horses... sea-slugs." Noumenius, in *The Art of Fishing*: "Either the parrot-fish or the nourishing sea-bream or the shameless stone-fish. The gaping *tithanas*, eels, and the pitch-black wrasse-eel, or mussels, or *hippoi*, or the grey-blue *koryphalen*." Antiphanes of Colophon mentions it in the *Thebaid*, saying: "either the *hykken*, or the *hippos*, or what they call the wrasse."

<margin>Ioulides</margin> **The Ioulides.** <note>original: ἰουλίδες; the Rainbow Wrasse</note> Regarding these, Dorion says in *On Fish* that one should eat *ioulides* in brine, either roasted or from the frying pan. Nymphodius says: "And you might see the *tyke* and the greedy *ioulida* turning away from many things, and the venomous centipede." He himself names the insects of the earth *ioulou* <note>woodlice or millipedes</note> in these lines:

"And you might remember the trickery because near the edge of the divine shore, the 'earth-eaters' <note>original: γαιηφάγοι; earth-eaters, referring to worms or wrasses that root in the sand</note> of the land, the black wrasse... or the little-footed creepers when the sandy rocks are washed by the pure edge of the wave; from there you may gather them all together into a vessel."

<margin>Kichlai. Kossyphoi.</margin> **The Kichlai and Kossyphoi.** <note>original: κίχλαι (thrush-fish/wrasse) and κόσσυφοι (black wrasse)</note> The Attics say *kichle* with the letter *eta*. The rule is this: feminine nouns ending in -le that have another *lambda* before the *lambda* include *skylla* (scylla), *skilla* (squill), *kolla* (glue), *bdella* (leech), *amilla* (contest), *amalla* (sheaf). But those with only one *lambda* do not: *omichle* (mist), *phytle* (race), *geuthle* (lineage), *aigle* (gleam), *trogle* (hole). Similarly, then, *kichle*. Cratinus: "if a *prigle* should increase..." Diocles, in the first book of *Health Matters*, says: "Those called the rock-fish—the *kossyphoi*, *kichlai*, perches, *mobidai*, *phykides*, and *alpheisikoi*—are soft-fleshed." Nymphodius in *The Art of Fishing*: "The *glaukoi*, or the sea-perch, or the sea-bream, or the dark-skinned *kossyphos*, or the sea-colored *kichlas*." Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "The *bambalones* and *kichlai* and *logoi*, and the mighty dragon-fish." Aristotle in his *History of Animals* says some are black-spotted, like the *kichle*. Pancrates the Arcadian, in *Sea Works*, says the *kichle* is called by many names: "The fishermen will call the wine-colored *kichle* a 'lizard' <note>original: σαυρὸν (sauron)</note>, and also the 'glittering one' with the most observant head." And Nicander, in the fourth book of *Transformations*, says: "either the parrot-fish or the many-named *kichlen*."

<margin>Kapros. Krimis.</margin> **The Kapros and Krimis.** <note>original: κάπρος (boar-fish) and κρίμις</note> Aristotle in *The Nature of Animals* says the following: "Some have teeth in their palate and are smooth like the needle-fish; some are stone-headed like the *huremys*; some are very hard and rough-skinned like the *kapros* (boar-fish). Some are fatty, like the *sesrinos*. Some are many-striped and red-lined, like the *salpe*." Both Dorion and Epaenetus mention the *kapros*. Archestratus says: "But when you come to the prosperous land of Ambracia, if you see the *kapros*, buy it and do not leave it, even if it costs its weight in gold, lest the terrible nemesis from the immortals breathe upon you; for it is the flower of nectar. It is not lawful for all mortals to eat this, nor even to look upon it, except for those who are used to vibrating the counting-pebbles with a glowing mind, holding the woven rope of the hollow oil-press in their hands, throwing gifts upon the limbs of the apple-trees." <note>This dense metaphorical passage suggests that this fish is the "nectar" of laboring men or those who work the presses</note>

<margin>Kitharos</margin> **The Kitharos.** <note>original: κίθαρος; a species of flatfish or turbot</note> Aristotle in *On Animals* or *On Fish* says the *leibaros* <note>another name for the kitharos</note> has jagged teeth, is solitary, eats seaweed, has a loose tongue, and a white, broad heart. Pherecrates in *The Slave-Teacher*: "the *leibaros* is sweet... and buying a *kitharos*." How good the *kitharos* is! And how they say it is entirely Apollo's—what a good nature there is in the *leibaros*, it has nothing bad. Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "there were *hyainides*, soles <note>original: βουγλώσσοι; literally 'ox-tongues'</note>, and the *kitharos*." Apollodorus says it was considered sacred to Apollo because of its name <note>A pun on *kithara*, the lyre of Apollo</note>.

<meta>This page continues the encyclopedic catalog of fish, focusing on the Kitharos (a flatfish), the Coryphene (Dolphinfish), various crustaceans, the Karcharias (shark), and an extensive discussion of the Kestreus (Grey Mullet). # BOOK 7 #

Callias or Diocles says that the **kitharos** <note>original: κίθαρον (kitharon); likely a species of flatfish like a turbot, or possibly a gurnard</note> is good roasted, as is the **batis** <note>a species of ray or skate</note>; this sums up the matter. Archestratus, in his *Life of Luxury*, says: "As for the **kitharos**, if it is white and firm by nature, boil it in clear brine with green leaves. But if it is reddish to the eye and not too large, roast it after piercing the body with a freshly sharpened knife, and smear it with plenty of cheese and oil. For it delights in seeing those who spend freely, being itself extravagant."

<margin>Coryphaenus</margin>
**Coryphaenus** <note>The Dolphinfish or Mahi-mahi</note>. Aristotle says it is amphibious and dies from the sun when it surfaces. Nymphiodorus, in his *Art of Fishing*, calls it a **kerylos** <note>usually the name for a kingfisher bird</note>. "For them all things are prepared, and you should set aside the perfumes, whether it be a **coryphaenus**, a **parion**, or a sea-dwelling **eripillam**." He also mentions a **koryphainis** <note>a feminine or smaller form of the same fish</note> in these verses: "Either minas, or horses, or a gray-fish for a **koryphainis**."

<margin>Cammari</margin>
**Cammari** <note>original: κάμμαροι (kammaroi); a term for lobsters or crayfish</note>. Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe* says: "furthermore, there were sea-breams, smelts, anchovies, and **cammari**." Sophron also mentions them in his *Mimes for Women*. They are a genus of shrimp, and are called thus by the Romans.

<margin>Karcharias</margin>
**Karcharias** <note>original: καρχαρίας (karcharias); literally "jagged-toothed," referring to the Great White or similar predatory sharks</note>. Numenius of Heraclea says in his *Art of Fishing*: "At another time the **karcharias**, when the sandy shore is in a foam." Sophron, in *The Tuna Hunt*, says: "Your belly is a **karcharias** <note>a metaphor for an insatiable appetite</note>." Nicander of Colophon, in his *Glossary*, says the **karcharias** is also called a **lamia** or a **skylla** <note>referring to man-eating sea monsters of myth</note>.

<margin>Kestreus</margin>
**Kestreus** <note>The Grey Mullet</note>. Hicesius says: Of the so-called "white-fish" there are several kinds. Some are called **kephaloi** <note>large-headed mullets</note>, some **kestreis**, others **chelones** <note>thick-lipped mullets, literally "tortoises"</note>, and others **myxinoi** <note>slime-mullets</note>. The **kephaloi** are the best both for flavor and for being succulent. Second to these are the so-called **kestreis**, and last are the **myxinoi**. The **chelones**, also called **bakchoi**, are of lower quality than all the others. They are very juicy but not very nourishing and are easily digested. Dorion, in his *On Fish*, praises the sea-dwelling **kestreus** but does not approve of the river variety. He names the sea-mullet's head as the **kephalon** and the **nestis** <note>"the faster"</note>, and he calls the bump on the head of the **kestreus** the "vertebra." He says the **kephalinos** is a smaller **kephalos**, which is also called a **blennos** <note>the blenny</note>.

<margin>† Chelones</margin>
Aristotle, in the fifth book of his *History of Animals*, says that among the **kestreis**, the **chelones** begin to breed in the month of Poseideon <note>roughly December</note>, as do the **sarchos**, the so-called **myxos**, and the **kephalos**. They are pregnant for thirty days. Some of the **kestreis** do not arise from mating, but grow out of the mud and the sand. In another place, Aristotle says that the **kestreus**, though it has jagged teeth, does not eat other fish, as it does not eat flesh at all.

<margin>lib. 8</margin>
Furthermore, one type is the **kephalos**, another the **chelon**, and another the **pheraios**. The **chelon** stays near the ground, while the **pheraios** does not use food <note>ancient observers often believed mullets lived on nothing because their stomachs were usually found empty</note>. The 

<margin>† Pheraias</margin>
**pheraios** lives on the slime produced by itself, and the **chelon** on sand and mud. It is also said that no wild beast devours the spawn of the **kestreis**, since the **kestreis** themselves devour no other fish. Euthydemus the Athenian, in his *On Salt-Fish*, says there are varieties of **kestreis** called **sphyraia** <note>hammer-like</note> and **daktylia** <note>finger-like</note>. The **kephaloi** are so named because they have a heavier head. The **sphyraia** are square-shaped. The **daktylia** have a width less than two fingers. The **kestreis** caught in Abdera are wonderful, as Archestratus has also said. Second are those from Sinope. These fish are called "floaters" (*plotoi*) by some, as Polemon says in his *On the Rivers in Sicily*. Epicharmus also names them thus in *The Muses*: "Aioliai, and the dog-tongues of the floaters, and the skiathides."

<margin>lib. 9</margin>
Aristotle, in his *On the Habits and Lives of Animals*, says that **kestreis** live even when their tails are removed. The **kestreus** is pursued by the **labrax** <note>the voracious sea bass</note>, and the conger-eel by the moray. The proverb "the mullet fasts" <note>original: κεστρεύς νηστεύει (kestreus nesteuei)</note> is applied to those who act justly, since the mullet does not eat flesh. Anaxilas in *The Solitary*, mocking the sophist Maton for his gluttony, says: "Maton snatched up and devoured the skull of the **kestreus**, and I am undone!" The noble Archestratus says: "Purchase a **kestreus** from sea-girt Aegina... you will deal with well-to-do men." Diocles says: "The **kestreus** leaps for joy in the sea." That the **nestis** <note>"the faster"</note> is a type of **kestreus** is stated by Archippus in *The Marriage of Heracles*: "The **nestis** mullet, the **kephalos**." Antiphanes says to Lampon: "You happen to be a **nestis** <note>a pun on 'fasting' and the fish name</note> while having other **kestreis** as soldiers." Alexis in *The Phrygian*: "I, a fasting (**nestis**) **kestreus**, run back home." Ameipsias in *The Cottabus-Players*: "I, an ordinary man, will try to escape notice at the marketplace; surely a **nestis** would follow me like a **kestreus**." Euphron says: "Aeschramidas has come, walking about like a **nestis**." Philemon in *The People Dying Together*: "I was buying a **nestis kestreus**, a great delicacy." Aristophanes in *Gerytades*: "From which we see the colony of **kestreis**-men." It is known that they are called **nestides** <note>fasters</note>. Anaxandrides in *Odysseus*: "He walks about without dinner most of the time; he is a fasting (**nestis**) **kestrine**." Eubulus in *Nausicaa*: "Who is baptized for a whole day... I lead the wretched life of a fasting **kestreus**." When these things were once said regarding this fine delicacy, one of the companions of the comic poets came and said: "Friends, are we not also keeping the Fast of the Thesmophoria <note>a festival for Demeter where women fasted</note> because we are fasting like two **kestreis**?" For as Diphilus says in *The Women of Lemnos*: "These men have dined, but I, wretched as I am, will be a **kestreus** again, fasting to the extreme." Myrtilus, taking up the conversation, 

<margin>†</margin>
said: "And we shall make the chorus of the **kestreis** in Theopompus's *Hedychares* grow hair, like men who have been guests of the snow. For you shall not partake of anything until either we or your fellow-student Ulpian says why the **kestreus** alone of fish is called **nestis** <note>the faster</note>." And Ulpian said, "Because no bait..."

<meta>This page continues the catalog of fish in Book 7 of Athenaeus's Deipnosophistae. The previous page discussed the Kestreus (Grey Mullet) and its reputation for fasting; this page concludes that discussion before moving on to the Korakinos (Crow-fish), Kyprianos (Carp), Kobios (Goby), and Kokkyx (Gurnard), citing various culinary and biological authorities.</meta>

### FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE OF ATHENAEUS ###

...eats living things, and it is never caught with meat or any other living bait, as Aristotle records, claiming that even when it fasts it is a poor creature <note>original: φαῦλος (phaulos); meaning simple or even foolish in this context</note>, and that if it is frightened, it hides its head as if the whole body were then hidden. And Plato <note>Plato the comic poet, not the philosopher</note> says in *The Festivals*: "As I was watching, a fisherman approached me bringing me **kistrias** <note>original: κιστρίας; another name for the mullet</note> fish; he brought them to me fasting and not at all bad." But you, tell me, O Myrtilus, you "wrestler of the Thessalians" <note>a playful nickname for a clever debater</note>, why are fish called **ellopes** <note>original: ἔλλοπες; an ancient poetic epithet for fish</note> by the poets? He replied: it is because they are voiceless. For they wish, by analogy, to be called *illopes*, because they are "shut off" from voice. For the word *illein* means to be shut off. If you don't know this, it's because you yourself are an *ellops* <note>a pun: both "voiceless" and "fish-like" or "ignorant"</note>. But I, following the wise Epicharmus, when the fellow gave no answer, spoke again, providing the answer myself, and I say they are called *ellopes* because they are scaly <note>original: λεπιδωτούς (lepidotous)</note>. I say this even if no one asks. And why do the Pythagoreans touch other living things in moderation, and even sacrifice some, but never touch fish at all? Is it because of their "rule of silence" <note>original: ἐχεμυθίαν (echemythian)</note>? For they <margin>10</margin> consider silence to be a divine thing. Since, then, you Molossian dogs are all silent, you are playing the Pythagorean with us, while we others will talk of fish.

<margin>Crow-fish</margin>
**Crow-fish** <note>original: Κορακῖνοι (Korakinoi); likely a species of sea-bass or umbrine</note>. The sea-dwelling ones, says Hicesius, are not very nutritious and are easily digested, though they are lacking in good juice. Aristotle, in the fifth book of his *History of Animals*, says it happens that nearly all fish grow quickly, <margin>† Not least.</margin> but least of all the **crow-fish**. It spawns near the shore, and in <margin>† [Text unclear]</margin> mossy and shady places. Speusippus, in the second book of his *Resemblances*, says the **black-tail** and the **crow-fish** are similar. Numenius, in his *Art of Fishing*, mentions "the slender *ilkoi* and the dappled **crow-fish**." Perhaps, then, the fish called *aioliai* <note>dappled ones</note> in the works of Epicharmus are actually **crow-fish**. For he says: "*Aioliai* and swimming **dog-tongues** <note>a species of sole</note>." In his *Marriage of Hebe*, he mentions the *aioliai* as distinct: "mice, and *alphetai*, and honey-colored **crow-fish**; *aioliai* and swimming **dog-tongues**." Euthydemus, in his book *On Salt-Fish*, says that the **crow-fish** is called a **saperdes** by many, and Heracleon <margin>20</margin> of Ephesus says the same; Philotimus says so too in his *Cookery*. Parmenon of Rhodes, in the first book of his *Instructions in Cookery*, says that the **saperdes** is called "the flat-one," just like the **crow-fish**. Aristophanes, in *The Telmessians*, spoke of "black-finned **crow-fish**." Pherecrates used a diminutive name for them in *The Forgetful Man*: "How shall I be silent about your little **crow-fish** and little **anchovies**?" Amphis says in *The Dirge*: "He who eats the sea-dwelling **crow-fish** when Glaucus is present has no wits." The **crow-fish** of the Nile are sweet, fleshy, and pleasant, as those who live by the Nile know. They were named because they "continually move their pupils" <note>original: τὰς κόρας κινεῖν (tas koras kinein); a pun on 'korakinos'</note>, or because they never stop doing so; the Alexandrians call them *platakas* <note>flat ones</note>, from their being burnt-colored <note>original: πυρίχοντες (pyrichontes)</note>.

<margin>Carp</margin>
**Carp** <note>original: Κυπριανός (Kyprianos)</note>. It is one of the carnivorous fish, as Aristotle records, and it is gregarious. Its tongue is not attached to the body, but is very thin and separate from it. Dorion, listing them among the lake and <margin>30</margin> river fish, writes: "the scaly one, which some call the **carp**."

<margin>Gobies</margin>
**Gobies** <note>original: Κωβιοί (Kobioi)</note>. They have much juice, as Hicesius says, and are distinguished by their good flavor; they are easily digested, provide little nourishment, and have poor juice. The white-fleshed ones are superior in flavor to the black ones. The flesh of the green **gobies** is softer and less fatty, and yields less and thinner juice, but they are more nutritious because of their size. Diocles says that those from rocky islands have soft flesh. Numenius, in his *Art of Fishing*, calls them *kobos*, "or a **parrot-fish** or a **kothon** with nutritious and shameless slavery."

And Sophron in his *Rustic Mimes* mentions "sea-washers," and he perhaps called the son of a tuna-fisher *Kothonias* after this fish. It is the Sicilians who call the **goby** a **kothon**, as Nicander of Colophon says in his *Glossary*, and Apollodorus in his work *On Sophron*. Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe* names the **gobies**: "sting-rays with <margin>† Chalaroi.</margin> stings behind, and **chalaroi gobies**." Antiphanes, in *Timon*, praises the **gobies** and shows where the best ones come from:

> I have come, having spent a great deal for the wedding <margin>40</margin>
> on incense for the gods and goddesses
> all of them, and for the heroes I give the grain-cakes.
> But for us mortals I bought **gobies**.
> Having thrown them down, I ordered that burglar,
> the fishmonger—I tell you, I added

their whole tribe, for they are from Phaleron <note>a port of Athens famous for its small fish</note>. Others, it seems, sold them as *troiskous* <note>small rounds or cakes</note>. Menander says in *The Ephesians*: "One of the fishmongers was just now pricing **gobies** at four drachmas—a very high price." <margin>Gurnards</margin> Dorion mentions river **gobies** in his book *On Fish*. **Gurnards** <note>original: Κόκκυγες (Kokkyges); literally 'cuckoos' because of the sound they make</note>. Epicharmus: "and the splendid **gurnards**, which everyone cooks, and how they would be sweetened by their gaping." Dorion says one should roast them after slitting them along the back, and season them with greens, cheese, pomegranate, silphium <note>a now-extinct medicinal herb and spice</note>, salt, and oil. While turning them, one should grease them and sprinkle a little salt, and after removing them, sprinkle with vinegar. Numenius calls it "the red one" from its appearance, saying: "Another is the red **Gurnard**, or a few *pemphides*, or another **sauron** <note>horse-mackerel</note>." <margin>Dogfish</margin> **Dogfish**. **Shark** <note>original: Καρχαρίας (Karcharias)</note>. Archestratus, the "Hesiod or Theognis <margin>50</margin> <margin>Shark</margin> of the gourmands," says it is a great fighter. And Theognis, seeing it, wrote about good living, as he himself says in these lines:

> When the sun, having his single-hooved horses in the sky,
> signals that it is midday.
> Let the feast begin, as sweet as one's heart commands,
> gracing the belly with all kinds of good things.

### BOOK VII ###

->Let a girl quickly carry the lustral water out of doors, and let a beautiful Spartan girl, with slender hands, bring the garlands within.<-

Nor did this wise man <note>Likely referring to Sophocles or a philosopher mentioned in the preceding lost context</note> reject the love of boys. At any rate, he says: "Then I shall embrace him while singing a fleeting song, and setting a prize in the middle—himself being beautiful—let them contend with me and you concerning wisdom, and you would know how much better mules are than horses." Thus, Archestratus in these beautiful instructions advises:

> In the city of the Toronaeans <note>Torone was a city in Chalcidice known for its fish</note>, one should buy the hollow under-belly of the sharp-toothed shark <note>original: κεκαρχαρία (kekarcharia); a species of shark or dogfish</note> from the lower parts. Then, sprinkle it with a little salt and cumin and roast it. 
> Do not add anything else to this dear head, except for green oil. When it is roasted 
> already, bring some seasoning sauce to serve with it. Whatever you boil in the hollow depths of a pan, 
> mix in neither a spring of water nor wine 
> vinegar, but pour over it only oil, 
> and dry cumin with fragrant leaves. 
> Cook it over the heat of the coals without letting the flame touch it, 
> and move it frequently so that it does not burn 
> secretly. But not many mortals know this divine food, 
> nor are they willing to eat it—those who have the soul of a 
> weak-hearted bird. Such mortals are struck senseless, 
> claiming the beast is a man-eater. Yet every 
> fish loves human flesh, if it can only happen upon it.

Then there is the part of the fish called the *thyrsion* <note>a choice cut, perhaps the porpoise-flesh or a similar firm cut</note> by the Romans, which is the sweetest and most delicate.

<margin>Sea Bass.</margin>
The Sea Bass <note>original: Λάβραξ (Labrax)</note>. As Aristotle records, this fish is solitary and carnivorous. They have a bony tongue that is fused to the mouth, and a triangular heart. In the fifth book of his *History of Animals*, he says they spawn just as the *kestreus* <note>grey mullet</note> and the *chrysophrys* <note>gilt-head bream</note> do, especially where rivers flow into the sea. They spawn in winter, and they spawn twice. Hicesius says that sea bass are juicy, but not very nourishing. As for how they eliminate waste, they are judged to be among the first in terms of good flavor. The fish was named for its greediness <note>original: λαβρότητα (labrotis); a play on the name *labrax*</note>. It is said that its intelligence differs from other fish, being clever at finding ways to save itself. Therefore, the comic poet Aristophanes says, "The Sea Bass, the wisest of all fish." Alcaeus the lyric poet says that it swims high in the water. But the wise Archestratus says:

> Take the "son of the gods," the sea bass, and the head of the *kephalos* <note>mullet</note> from Gaison when you come to Miletus. 
> For there they are the best. For the place is of such a nature. 
> Many others are born in famous Calydon, 
> and in Ambracia, and in the Bolbe lagoon. 
> But those do not have a belly crowded with foreign filth <note>likely referring to the mud-eating habits of fish in lesser waters</note>, 
> nor are they so pungent. Those Milesian ones are 
> wonderful in their excellence. In general, roast it without scales, 
> roasting it gently and serve it simply with brine. 
> Let no one ever approach you while you are preparing this dish— 
> neither a Syracusan nor any Italian. 
> For they do not know how to prepare good fish, 
> but they ruin them miserably by cheesing everything, 
> and sprinkling them with liquid vinegar and silphium brine <note>silphium was a prized, now-extinct medicinal and culinary herb from Cyrene</note>. 
> Regarding the thrice-cursed little fish of the shoals, 
> they are the best at knowing how to fry them, 
> and they can elegantly present many forms at a feast, 
> reaching for sticky, expensive appetizers.

Aristophanes in *The Knights* also mentions that the sea bass around Miletus are superior when he says: "But you, having devoured the sea bass, might throw the Milesians into confusion." And in *The Lemnian Women*: "not to eat the brain of a sea bass nor a lobster," implying that the brain of the sea bass is exceptional, just as it is with the *glaukos* <note>the "gray" fish, possibly a bluefish or species of sea bream</note>. Eubulus also says in *The Nurses*, not extravagantly but cleanly: "...on account of the shopping, little cuttlefish or squids, or the small tentacles of an octopus, or the womb of a sow, or a large-sized head of a sea bass." As for Gaison, which Archestratus mentions, the Gaisonian Lake is between Priene and Miletus, connected to the sea, as Neanthes of Cyzicus records in the sixth book of his *Hellenic History*. Ephorus, in his fifth book, says that the river Gaison flows around Priene and into a lake. Archippus, mentioning sea bass in his *Fishes*, says: "The most foul fishmonger of all, the Egyptian Hermaeus, who by force skins sharks and dogfish to sell, and is the murderer of the sea bass."

<margin>Latos.</margin>
The Latos <note>A large perch-like fish, likely the Nile Perch</note>. Archestratus says this is best in Italy, speaking thus:

> And the famous Latos in wooded Italy 
> The Strait of Scylla holds, a marvelous food.

But the *latos* fish found in the Nile River are found to be of great size, even weighing over two hundred pounds. This fish is very white and most sweet however it is prepared, being very similar to the *glanis* <note>a type of catfish</note> found in the Danube. The Nile also bears many other kinds of fish, and all are very sweet. This is especially true of the various kinds of *korakinos* <note>crow-fish</note>, for there are many types of these. It also produces the "diving" Maeotian fish, which Archippus mentions in *The Fishes*: "those which are Maeotian, and Sapresian, and catfish." There are many fish along the Black Sea that take their name from Lake Maeotis <note>The Sea of Azov</note>. Then there are the "Nile fish," if indeed the name I recall indicates a costly migration. There is the Narce <note>Electric Ray</note>, the pig-fish, the flat-nose, the sea-bream, the sharp-snout <note>sturgeon</note>, the allabes, the silurus, the synodontis, the marsh-eel, the eel, the thrissa, the abramis, the blind-fish, the lepidotus, the bellows-fish, and the mullet. There are also many others.

<margin>Lobatos.</margin>
The Lobatos. This is also called the *rhine* <note>file-fish or rasp-fish</note>. It is white-fleshed, such that it is praised by the gourmets. Plato says in *The Sophists*: "even if there be a dogfish and a lobatos and an eel."

<margin>Moray Eels.</margin>
The Moray Eels <note>original: Μύραιναι (Myrainai)</note>. Theophrastus, in his fifth book *On those that live in dry places*, says that the eel and the moray can live for a long time out of the water, because...

### FROM THE ATHENAEAN DEIPNOSOPHISTS ###

...having small gills, and holding very little fluid. Hicesius says that they are no less nutritious than <term>eels</term> <note>original: ἐγχέλεων (encheleon)</note>, and even the <term>conger eels</term> <note>original: γόγγρων (gongron)</note>. Aristotle, in the fifth book of *The History of Animals*, says they grow rapidly from a small size and are <term>saw-toothed</term> <note>original: καρχαρόδοντα (karcharodonta)</note>. They lay small eggs at all seasons. Epicharmus, in his *Muses*, distinguishes them and calls them *myrainas*, saying: "Neither any of the thicker congers, nor the <term>moray eel</term> <note>original: μύραινα (myraina)</note> is like mustard; she is similar and modest." Plato (or perhaps Cantharus) in *The Alliance* mentions the moray along with the *sibatis*. Dorion says that among the river varieties, the moray has only a single bone, similar to the so-called "milk-white" <term>hake</term> <note>original: ὀνίσκωι (oniskou)</note>. Andreas, in his work *On Fishing*, says that the moray kills <term>sea-vipers</term> <note>original: ἔχεις (echeis)</note>. He notes they are smaller, rounded, and variegated in color. Nicander, in his *Theriaca*, says:

> The moray's fury is terrible; often leaping from the
<margin>10</margin> briny deep, she would saw through the fishing-poles, plunging back into the sea after escaping the grips. If the story be true, she leaves the ways of the sea to mate with venomous vipers on the dry land. <note>This reflects a common ancient myth that moray eels came onto land to mate with land snakes.</note>

However, Andreas, in his work *On False Beliefs*, says it is a lie that the moray mates with vipers by coming to marshy places. For vipers do not feed in marshes, preferring hungry, sun-scorched deserts. Sostratus, in his
<margin>The Myros.</margin> *On Animals* (consisting of two books), agrees that this mating occurs. **The Myros.** The *myros*, as Aristotle says in the fifth book of *The History of Animals*, differs from the moray. The moray is variegated and weaker, while the *myros* is of a solid color <note>original: λεόχρως (leochros)</note> and strong; its color is like that of the <term>wryneck bird</term> <note>original: ἰύγγι (iyngi)</note>, both inside and out. Dorion says the *myros* has no bones throughout its flesh, but is entirely useful and exceedingly tender. There are two kinds: some are black, and others are <term>white-bellied</term> <note>original: ἀσπρινειλοῦντον (asprinilounton)</note>. The darker ones are superior. Archestratus, the philosopher of pleasure, says:

> Between Italy and the straits where the purple waves swell,
<margin>20</margin> if the floating moray, as it is called, should ever be caught, buy it! For there it is a marvelous delicacy.

<margin>Sprats.</margin> **Sprats.** <note>original: Μαινίδες (Mainides), often identified as picarel or sprats.</note> Hicesius says these are more succulent than gobies. They are prized for their fine flavor and for being an aid to the bowels. Speusippus, in the second book of *Resemblances*, says the <term>bogue</term> <note>original: βόακα (boaka)</note> and the <term>picarel</term> <note>original: σμαρίδας (smaridas)</note> are similar to the sprat. Epicharmus also mentions them in *Earth and Sea*, saying: "Many bogues and picarels." Epinicus, in his *Art of Cookery*, says that the inhabitants of Lousioi call the picarel "the dog’s bed." Antiphanes, in *The Countryman* (or *The Byzantine*), calls sprats "the food of Hecate" <note>Hecate was a goddess of the underworld; small fish were often left as offerings for her at crossroads.</note> because of their smallness, saying: "For everyone knows these large fish are man-eaters. What are you saying, my dear man? A man-eater? How could a man eat them? Clearly these are the foods of Hecate,
<margin>In Book 8, these verses are read slightly differently.</margin> which he says are sprats and red mullets." Some are also called "white-sprats," and some people call them bogues. Polyochus, in his *Corinthian Woman*, says:

> So that no one of the gods may take the fire from you, 
<margin>30</margin> he calls the bogues "white-sprats."

<margin>The Saddled Seabream.</margin> **The Saddled Seabream.** <note>original: Μελάνουρος (Melanouros), literally "black-tail."</note> Concerning this fish, Numenius says in his *Art of Fishing*:
> ...or the black-tail, the leader of the perches.

Hicesius says its flesh is similar to the <term>white seabream</term> <note>original: σάργῳ (sargo)</note>, but it is inferior in succulence and flavor; it is slightly fatty and nutritious. Epicharmus mentions it in *The Marriage of Hebe*:
> ...and the small sargos and the black-tails.

Aristotle, in his writings *On Animals*, writes that the black-tail and the sargos are "straight-tailed" fish, and they are marked with many black stripes.
<margin>The Melandrinos.</margin> **The Melandrinos.** This is said to be similar to the black-tail. Speusippus, in the second book of *Resemblances*, mentions the so-called *psychros* (cold-fish), which Numenius calls *psoros*, saying:
> Either the psoros, or the goldline, or the coastal bogue.

<margin>The Striped Seabream.</margin> **The Striped Seabream.** <note>original: Μορμύρος (Mormyros).</note> This is very nutritious, as Hicesius says. Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, calls them *myrmas*, unless they are different in nature. He writes:
> ...and the sea-swallows and the *myrmiai*, which are larger in the belly.

Lynceus of Samos, in his *Art of Food-Shopping*, says to a friend named Dysōnis or Zenon: "Do not stare at them like chaff without lowering the price, just like those who greedily hang around the fish-stalls." He brings up Archestratus, the poet of *Hedypatheia* (Pleasant Living), who writes in meter:
> The coastal striped seabream is a bad fish, never good. 
> And: buy the <term>bonito</term> <note>original: ἀμίαν (amian)</note> in autumn; but now it is spring. 
> The <term>mullet</term> <note>original: Κεστρία (Kestria)</note> is marvelous when winter arrives. 
> Now it is summer, when many such things are available. 
> For by brushing away many of the windy talkers and hangers-on, 
> you will compel the seller to let you take what you think is best.

<margin>The Electric Ray.</margin> **The Electric Ray.** <note>original: Νάρκη (Narke), from which we get 'narcotic'.</note> Plato (or Cantharus) says in *The Alliance*:
> For the electric ray became a meal for the sake of grace.

The philosopher Plato, in the *Meno*, mentions the sea-ray. For it makes anyone who approaches it grow numb. The name is also found in Homer:
> His hand grew numb
> at the wrist.

Menaechmus says in his *Lantern*:
> A certain numbness (*narka*) came over my whole skin, 
> such as none of the ancients ever described.

Hicesius says it is less nutritious and less succulent, but it has a certain cartilaginous substance that is very good for the stomach. Theophrastus, in his work *On Animals that Burrow*, says the ray can hide under the earth because of the cold. In his work *On Biting and Stinging Animals*, he says the ray sends its numbing power even through wooden poles and fishing spears, causing those holding them in their hands to grow numb. Clearchus of Soli stated the cause of this in his work *On the Electric Ray*. From a long distance...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Mediterranean sea creatures from Book 7 of Athenaeus’s *Deipnosophists*.
