### BOOK 7 ###

...having been forgotten, I refer you back to the treatise itself. The <term>electric ray</term> <note>original: νάρκη (narke)</note>, as Aristotle says, is one of the <term>cartilaginous fish</term> <note>original: σελαχωδῶν (selachodon)</note> and those that <term>produce live young</term> <note>original: σκυμνοτοκούντων (skymnotokounton)</note>. It hunts small fish for its food by touching them, causing them to grow numb and motionless. Diphilus of Laodicea, in his work *On Nicander’s Antidotes*, says that it does not produce numbness in the whole animal, but only in certain parts of itself, claiming to have reached this conclusion through much experimentation. Archestratus says: "A boiled electric ray in oil and wine is sweet, with fragrant herbs and a little grated cheese." Alexis, in *Galatea*, says: "They say the electric ray should be roasted whole and stuffed." And in *Demetrius*: "Then I took an electric ray, keeping in mind that when a woman brings her tender fingers near its spine, she suffers none of these effects."

<margin>Swordfish.</margin>
**Swordfish.** Aristotle says this fish has an internal part—the lower portion is small, but the upper part is sword-like and large, equal to its total size. This is called the <term>sword</term> <note>original: ξίφος (xiphos)</note>. The fish has no teeth. Archestratus says: "But take a steak of <term>swordfish</term> <note>original: ξίφια (xiphia)</note> when you come to Byzantium, specifically the vertebra of the tail—it is excellent—even at the narrows where the great currents of the gates flow." Who is such an accurate tactician, or such a judge of delicacies, as this poet—or rather, this "mock-poet"—who, out of pure gluttony, sailed across the straits to examine the qualities of every part of every fish and their juices, as if he were laying down a treatise for the benefit of human life?

<margin>Grouper.</margin>
**Grouper.** It is also called the *orphos*. Pamphilus says this. Aristotle, in the fifth book of *The History of Animals*, says that growth in fish is rapid, and the <term>grouper</term> <note>original: ὀρφὼς (orphos)</note> becomes very large from a small size in a short time. It is a meat-eater and <term>saw-toothed</term> <note>original: καρχαρόδους (karcharodous)</note>, and is also a solitary creature. A unique feature in it is that the passage for milt cannot be found, and it can live for a long time after being cut open. It is one of the fish that hide in holes during the coldest days of winter, and it prefers being near the land rather than in the open sea. It lives no longer than seven years. Numenius mentions it, saying: "Those you might easily lift from their rocky dens, the scorpion-fish or the circling grouper." And again: "The grey-fish or the grouper... or the black-skinned wrasse." Dorion says that the young grouper is called an *orphakinis* by some. Archippus, in *The Fish*, says: "For a grouper came to them as a priest of the god." Cratinus in *The Odysseys*: "A hot steak of grouper." Plato in *Cleophon*: "For your flesh was settled as food for rotten groupers, sharks, and sea-breams." Aristophanes in *Wasps*: "If someone buys a grouper but does not want small fry." The Attics pronounced the singular nominative with an acute accent. Archippus uses it in *The Fish*, as shown above. The genitive is used by Cratinus in *The Odysseys*: "With a hot steak of grouper."

<margin>Large Tuna.</margin>
**Large Tuna.** <note>original: Όρκυνος (Orkynos), often identified as the Orcyn or a large variety of tuna.</note> Dorion, in his work *On Fish*, says that the large tunas travel toward the Pillars of Hercules from our sea, which is why they are caught in large numbers in the Iberian and Tyrrhenian seas. From there, they scatter into the other sea. Icesius says those caught at Gades <note>Modern Cádiz, Spain</note> are fatter. After these are the ones in Sicily. Those far from the Pillars of Hercules are lean because they have swum a greater distance. At Gades, the "collar" parts are pickled by themselves, as are the jaws and palates of the *autakiai* <note>A type of tuna</note>, and the so-called <term>dark-meats</term> <note>original: μελανδρίαι (melandriai)</note> are pickled from them. Icesius says their bellies, being fatty, differ greatly in flavor from the other parts, and the collar parts are even more delicious than these.

<margin>Hake. Small Hake.</margin>
**Hake**, or **Small Hake.** <note>original: Όνος (Onos), literally 'donkey-fish'; usually identified as hake or a cod-like fish.</note> Aristotle says in his work *On Animals* that it has a wide-gaping mouth like the sharks. It is a schooling fish. It is the only fish that has its heart in its belly, and in its brain it has stones like millstones. It alone hides in holes during the hottest days under the Dog Star, whereas others hide during the coldest winter days. Epicharmus mentions them in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "Wide-gaping, solitary and hollow, variegated-bellied hakes." The hake differs from the small hake, as Dorion says in his work *On Fish*, writing: "The hake, which some call the *gados* <note>Cod or Hake</note>; the *kallarias*, which some call the small hake and also the *mazeinos*." Euthydemus, in his work *On Salt-Fish*, says some call it the *bakchos*, some the *gelathein*, and others the small hake. Archestratus said: "I will pass over the hake, which they call the *kallarias*; it grows to a great size, and both have flesh that is—to me at least—not sweet, but divine. For one delights in its offspring, the other in praises."

<margin>Octopus.</margin>
**Octopus.** <note>original: Πολύπους (Polypous), literally 'many-foot'.</note> So the Attics call it, as does Homer: "As when the octopus is dragged from its hole." It is formed by analogy... or they use the accusative *polypoda*, as they do with Alcinous and Oedipus. Aeschylus is said to have called a cauldron this, and the word is also used for "adamantine" from the simple root of "foot." The form *polypou* is Aeolic. The Attics say *polypous*. Aristophanes in *The Revellers*: "These things willingly, octopuses and cuttlefish." And again: "He set the octopus before me." Again, springs are said to be "fat with octopuses." Alcaeus in *The Adulterous Sisters* says it is foolish "to have the mind of an octopus." Ameipsias in *The Diver*: "Because of which, it seems, many octopuses..." Plato in *The Child*: "Just like the octopus, first of all you..." Alcaeus: "I swam like an octopus." Others pronounce *polypoda* according to the pattern of "foot, of a foot, to a foot." Eupolis in *The Demes*: "A citizen man of an octopus-like character." Diocles, in the first book of *On Hygiene*, says that <term>mollusks</term> <note>original: μαλάκια (malakia)</note> for...

### FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS ###

...pleasure and how they mate. The <term>octopuses</term> <note>original: πολύποδες (polypodes)</note> are especially noted for this. Aristotle records that the octopus has eight feet, of which the top two and the bottom two are the smallest, while those in the middle are the largest. It also has two rows of <term>suckers</term> <note>original: κοτυληδόνας (kotyledonas)</note>, which it uses to draw in its food. Its eyes are positioned above the two top feet. Its mouth and teeth are located in the center of its feet. When dissected, it is found to have a brain divided into two parts. It also possesses what is called <term>ink</term> <note>original: θολὸν (tholon)</note> or "the black," just like the cuttlefish, but it is reddish in the part called the <term>mecon</term> <note>original: μήκωνι (mekoni), literally "poppy-head," referring here to the digestive gland or milt</note>. This mecon lies above the stomach, like a bladder. It does not have a corresponding gut-sac. It feeds on everything, sometimes even the flesh of <term>bivalves</term> <note>original: κογχυλίων (konchylion)</note>, throwing the shells outside its den; this is how hunters identify their location. It mates by intertwining, and stays close for a long time because it is <term>cold-blooded</term> <note>original: ἄναιμος (anaimos), literally "bloodless," as ancient biology categorized invertebrates</note>. It lays eggs in what is called a "blower," which is a passage in the body. It lays its eggs in clusters like grapes. 

Some say that if it runs out of food, it eats itself. One of those who says this is the comic poet Pherecrates; in the play titled *The Savages*, he says:

> O you who live on <term>thryskes</term> <note>a type of wild green or small fish</note> and <term>brakanes</term> <note>wild vegetables</note> and pine-cones. But whenever they are very hungry, just like the octopuses, you gnaw around your own fingers at night.

And Diphilus says in *The Merchant*:

> An octopus having once for all its entire tentacles... It has not eaten itself, my dearest.

However, this is a falsehood. For it is actually when they are being chased by <term>conger eels</term> <note>original: γόγγρων (gongron)</note> that their feet are damaged. It is also said that if one sprinkles salt into their dens, they come out immediately. It is recorded that out of fear they change their colors and make themselves look like the places where they hide. As Theognis of Megara says in his elegies:

> Adopt the temperament of the complex octopus, which appears to the eye just like the rock to which it clings.

Similarly, Clearchus records in the second book of *On Proverbs*, citing these verses:

> It is not just, my son, to have the mind of an octopus, O hero Amphilochus, adapting yourself to those among whose people you arrive.

Regarding the area around Troezen in ancient times, the same Clearchus says it was not customary to hunt the "octopus-shrine" or the "rowing-neighbor." But of all these things, the rule was not to touch the sea turtle. 

The octopus is silent and very foolish. For how else does it walk right into the hands of its pursuers, and when chased, sometimes it does not even retreat? After spawning, the females become weak and silent, which is why they are easily caught. They have sometimes been seen coming out onto dry land, especially in rugged places. For they flee smooth surfaces and take pleasure in the olive tree and olive groves; they are often found with their tentacles wrapped around the trunk. They have also been seen clinging to fig trees by the sea, spending time out of the water and eating the figs, as Clearchus says in his work *On Aquatic Creatures*. A proof of the octopus's affinity for the olive is that if one lowers a branch of this plant into the sea where there are octopuses and waits a little while, he can pull up as many as he wants clinging to the branch at night. While their other parts are very strong, their neck is weak. 

It is said that the male has something like a sexual organ in one of its tentacles, where there are two large suckers. It is equally sinewy up to the middle of the tentacle, entirely attached. In the fifth book of *History of Animals*, Aristotle says the octopus mates in winter and lays eggs in spring. It stays in its hole for about two months. The animal is very prolific. The male differs from the female in having a longer head and having what the fishermen call a penis in its tentacle <note>Modern biology identifies this as the hectocotylus, a specialized arm for transferring sperm</note>. The female broods when she lays her eggs, which is why they are at their worst as food during this time. The octopus lays its eggs either in dens, or in a ceramic jar, or some other hollow vessel. After fifty days, little octopuses crawl out of the eggs, looking like spiders in great numbers. The female octopus sometimes sits on the eggs and sometimes at the entrance of the den, holding on with a tentacle. 

Theophrastus, in his work *On Creatures that Change Color*, says that the octopus most especially likens itself only to rocky places. They do this out of fear and for the sake of protection. In the work *On Animals that Live on Dry Land*, <margin>Book 9.</margin> Machion speaks of octopuses in the sea. In his work *On Regional Differences*, Theophrastus says octopuses are found near the Hellespont. For that sea is cold and less salty, both of which are hostile to the octopus. 

The creature called the <term>nautilus</term> <note>original: ναυτίλος (nautilos), referring to the Paper Nautilus or Argonaut</note>, Aristotle says, is not actually an octopus, though it is similar in its tentacles. It has a shell-covered back. It rises from the depths with its shell held over itself so it doesn't draw in seawater. Turning over, it floats on the surface, raising two of its tentacles which have a thin membrane growing between them, just as the feet of birds are seen to have a leathery web between the toes. It lowers two other tentacles into the sea to act as rudders. But when it sees something approaching, out of fear it pulls in its feet, fills the shell with seawater, and sinks to the bottom as fast as possible. In his work *On Animals and Fish*, someone says the octopus is called the *pontilos* by some and the *nautilus* by others. It is to the nautilus that the epigram of Callimachus the Cyrenean refers, which goes like this:

> I was a shell, O Zephyritis, an ancient one;
> but now you, Cypris, have me as the first offering from Selene—a Nautilus, I who used to sail upon the seas, 
> if there were winds, stretching a sail from my own forestays. But if the Goddess of the Calm were shining, I would row with all my strength...

->To the Cnosian woman, that her name might be fitting: "Let me sail along the shores of Ioulis, that I may be for you, Arsinoe, a far-seen toy." <note>This is a fragment of a famous epigram usually attributed to Callimachus, though here discussed as Poseidippus, regarding a nautilus shell dedicated to Queen Arsinoe.</note> No longer in the sea-chambers as before, for I am breathless; I was born from the egg of a sea-faring halcyon. "This sanctuary of Arsinoe, both on the river and on the land of the sibling-loving <term>Cypris</term> <note>original: Κύπριδος (Kypridos), an epithet for Aphrodite</note>, I shall appease; she whom Callicrates the admiral established as ruler over the Zephyrian shore. The tragic poet Ion also mentions the <term>octopus</term> <note>original: πολύποδος (polypodos)</note> in his work *Phoenix*, saying: "And I loathe the octopus, the bloodless skin-changer of the rocks with its many coils." He also mentions the octopus, the <term>eledone</term> <note>original: ἐλεδίωνα (elediona)</note>, the <term>polyponine</term>, the <term>bolbotine</term>, and the <term>osmylos</term> <note>A variety of small, foul-smelling octopus</note>, as Aristotle and Speusippus record. In his work *On Animals*, Aristotle says that the <term>mollusks</term> <note>original: μαλάκια (malakia), literally "soft-bodied creatures"</note> consist of octopuses, the osmylos, the eledone, the <term>cuttlefish</term> <note>original: σηπίαν (sepian)</note>, and the <term>squid</term> <note>original: τευθίδα (teuthida)</note>. Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, says: "Octopuses and squids with their fins; the <term>bolbitis</term> <note>a type of small octopus</note> which is hard to catch, and old women like red-faced ones." Archestratus says that octopuses are best in Thasos and Caria, and that Corcyra produces many and of great size. The Dorians call it a <term>polypon</term> <note>original: πώλυπον (polypon)</note> with an 'o' sound, as Epicharmus does; Simonides also said "seeking the octopus." But the Athenians call it <term>polypoun</term>. They are among the <term>cartilaginous fish</term> <note>original: σελαχωδῶν (selachodon)</note>—the gristly ones are named so: octopuses, sharks, and rays; but the <term>teuthis</term>-like ones are called mollusks.

<margin>Crabs.</margin> **Crabs** <note>original: Πάγουροι (Pagouroi)</note>. <margin>Bonito. Hair-tail.</margin> **Bonito** <note>original: Πηλαμύς (Pelamys)</note>. Phrynichus mentions this in *The Muses*. Sophocles also mentions them in *The Shepherds*: "If the neighboring bonito is storm-tossed, a rustic inhabitant, a seasonal beauty in summer for the Bosporite, for there he frequents."

<margin>Perch. Perch.</margin> **Perch** <note>original: Πέρκαι (Perkai)</note>. Diocles mentions these, as does Speusippus in his second book on *Similar Things*, saying that the perch, the <term>chaine</term> <note>a species of sea-bass or comber</note>, and the <term>phykis</term> <note>a wrasse</note> are similar. Epicharmus says in his comedies: "Perches and dappled perches." Nythodius <note>The OCR likely misspells Nymphodorus or a similar author</note> in his *Art of Fishing* says: "At another time again the perches, when they are at the rock. Aristotle, in his work *On Animals*, says they are spiny-finned and variegated in color, specifically the wrasses. Of those with striped markings or those with horizontal bands, he names the perch. There is also a proverb: "Like the perch to the black-tail" <note>An ancient expression for things that are inseparable or very similar</note>.

<margin>Needlefish.</margin> **Needlefish** <note>original: Ῥαφίδες (Rhaphides)</note>. Epicharmus also mentions these, speaking of "sharp-beaked needlefish and sea-horses." Speusippus also calls it the *belone*.

<margin>Ray.</margin> **Ray** <note>original: Ῥίνη (Rhine)</note>. Dorion, in his work *On Fish*, says that the rays in Smyrna are excellent. <margin>Parrotfish.</margin> **Parrotfish** <note>original: Σκάρος (Skaros)</note>. I have found that Aristotle says it is saw-toothed, solitary, and carnivorous. It has a small mouth and a tongue that is not very attached, a triangular heart, whitish and three-lobed. It has a gallbladder and a black gall. Of its gills, some are double and one is single. It is the only one among the fish that <term>ruminates</term> <note>original: μηρυκάζει (merykazei); ancient naturalists believed the parrotfish chewed the cud like a cow</note>, and it delights in feeding on seaweed. Therefore, it is hunted with these. It is at its best in summer. Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, says: "You take away the salty one and the parrotfish, whose very dung it is not lawful for the gods to cast out." Seleucus of Tarsus, in his *Art of Fishing*, says the parrotfish is the only fish that sleeps, which is why it is never caught at night. This perhaps happens to it out of fear. Archestratus, in his *Gastronomy*, says: "Seek the parrotfish in Ephesus. In winter, they will quickly catch the red mullet in Miletus, at the gates of the crooked-legged ones." In another part he says: "Roast the great parrotfish in coastal Carthage; it is sweet. You will also find it in Byzantium, equal in size to a shield. Prepare the whole thing in this way: when you have taken it, and when it is well covered with cheese and oil, hang it in a hot oven and then bake it. Sprinkle it with cumin-salted grains and golden oil, pouring it from your hand over the god-receiving tail." Nicander says there are two kinds of parrotfish: one called the <term>onias</term> and the other the <term>aiolos</term> <note>dappled</note>.

<margin>Annular Bream.</margin> **Annular Bream** <note>original: Σπάρος (Sparos)</note>. I found that Hicesius says it is more flavorful than the <term>mainis</term> <note>a small sprat or pickerel</note> and more nutritious than most others. <margin>Scorpion-fish</margin> **The Scorpion-fish.** <note>original: Σκορπίος (Skorpios); likely the red scorpion-fish, *Scorpaena scrofa*, prized for its firm flesh.</note> Diocles, in the first book of his *Health Studies* addressed to Pleistarchus, says that among the fresh fish, the flesh of the scorpion-fish, gurnards, turbots, "karuchoi," and horse-mackerel is drier. And Mnesimachus, in *The Horse-Breeder*, mentions the sharp-toothed "numb-fish,"
<margin>The Skipinos. The Umbrine.</margin>
the angler-fish, perch, horse-mackerel, hair-tail, fig-fish, *beigkos*, beet-fish, and gurnard. **The Skipinos.** Dorion, mentioning this fish in his treatise *On Fish*, says it is also called the "soft-fish." **The Umbrine.** <note>original: Σκίαινα (Skiaina); a member of the drum or croaker family, likely *Sciaena umbra*.</note> Epicharmus, in *The Wedding of Hebe*, says: "Dappled swimmers, dog-tongues, and little umbrines." Nymphodius, in his *Descriptions*, calls it the "shade-fish," which he says cleanses itself after being seized by a longing for other fish, "either the great shade-fish or the broken horse-fish, or the sea-bream." 
<margin>The Smagris. The Barracuda.</margin>
And when they gather, they are called "shade-gatherers." **The Smagris.** <note>The picarel or *Spicara smaris*.</note> Epicharmus mentions these in *The Wedding of Hebe* and in *Earth and Sea*. **The Barracuda.** <note>original: Σφύραινα (Sphyraina); literally "hammer-fish," often identified with the Mediterranean barracuda.</note> Hicesius says these are more nutritious than conger eels, but they are unyielding in taste and smell, and only moderately juicy. Dorion says that some call the barracuda a "pike." Epicharmus, in *The Muses*, names the "pike" but no longer mentions the "barracuda," implying they are the same. He lists "chalcid-fish and dog-fish, pikes and perches and dappled-fish." And Sophron, in *Mimes of Men*, says: "the pikes snapping at the *botis* fish." Speusippus, in the second book of *Resemblances*, sets them out in succession: "the pike, the needle-fish, the lizard-fish." The Athenians mostly call the barracuda a "pike" and rarely use the name "barracuda." Strattis, at least, in *The Macedonians*, has an Athenian ask—as if ignorant of the name—"What is the barracuda?" and the other replies: "It is what you Athenians call a pike." Antiphanes, in *Euthydicus*, says: "A very large barracuda—or a pike, as the Athenians would say." Nicophon, in *Pandora*, mentions "pikes and sea-bass." Epicharmus, in *The Wedding of Hebe*, says: "pikes, perches, and dappled-fish." 
<margin>The Cuttlefish.</margin>
**The Cuttlefish.** <note>original: Σηπία (Sepia); the common European cuttlefish.</note> Aristophanes, in *The Reclining Feast*, says: "And these having cuttlefish and octopus." As for the causes of the name, as Philemon relates, it is similar to words like "little child," "headband," or "house." Aristotle says the cuttlefish has eight feet, of which the two lowest are the largest, and two proboscises <note>tentacles</note>, and between them the eyes and mouth. It also has two teeth, one above and one below. It has what is called a "shell" <note>the cuttlebone</note> in its back. The ink is located in the "mytis" <note>ink sac</note>. This is situated near the mouth, acting like a bladder. Its belly is flat and smooth, similar to the abomasum <note>fourth stomach</note> of cattle. Small cuttlefish feed on tiny fish, extending their proboscises like fishing lines and hunting with them. It is said that when a storm of the "whispering winds" <note>seasonal winds</note> occurs, they hold onto rocks with their proboscises like anchors. When pursued, the cuttlefish releases its ink and hides within it, appearing to flee forward while actually retreating. It is said the females are hunted with a trident, and the males come to their aid.
<margin>Book 5.</margin>
But if the males are caught, the females flee. The cuttlefish does not make a sound, just like the octopus. In the fifth book of *Parts of Animals*, Aristotle says cuttlefish and squid swim while entwined in their bodies, fitting their tentacles against one another. They also fit their blowholes together. Among the mollusks, the cuttlefish are the first to spawn in the spring; they do not carry eggs at all seasons, and the young are born in fifteen days. When they spawn, the male follows and blows upon the eggs to protect them. They walk in pairs. The male is more variegated and has a darker back than the female. Epicharmus, in *The Wedding of Hebe*, says: "octopuses, cuttlefish, and winged squids." There is some mockery of Speusippus for saying that the cuttlefish and the squid are similar. Hipponax, in his *Iambics*, mentions "cuttlefish blood-sauce," and the commentators explain this as the ink of the cuttlefish. This "blood-sauce" <term>hypotri-mma: a thick, pounded sauce or relish</term>, as Erasistratus says in his *Art of Cookery*, is a condiment. He writes: "the blood-sauce for roasted meats is made of blood stirred with honey, cheese, salt, cumin, silphium, and boiled vinegar." Glaucus the Locrian, in his *Art of Cookery*, writes: "blood-sauce consists of boiled blood, silphium, boiled wine or honey, vinegar, milk, cheese, and chopped fragrant leaves." The most learned Archestratus says: "May I have cuttlefish in the middle of Maroneia." Aristophanes, in *The Women at the Thesmophoria*, says: "someone bought a fish or a little cuttlefish." And in *The Daughters of Danaus*: "little smelts and little sprats and little cuttlefish." Theopompus, in *Aphrodite*: "but eat up the cuttlefish that was divided, and the octopus." Regarding the boiling of little cuttlefish, Alexis in *The Wicked Woman* introduces a cook saying: "Cuttlefish—how much? One drachma. Take them; as for these, I will cut up the tentacles and fins and boil them. The rest of the body I will cut into many cubes, mix with fine salt, and bring them sizzling from the frying pan."
<margin>The Red Mullet.</margin>
**The Red Mullet.** <note>original: Τρίγλα (Trigla).</note> Like the thrush-fish, it is spelled with a 't'. For feminine nouns ending in '-la' usually take another letter, like "Skylla." Those that have a 'g' combined with the ending end in '-le', such as "hole" (*trogle*), "radiance" (*aigle*), or "yoke" (*zeugle*). Aristotle says in the fifth book of *History of Animals* that the red mullet spawns three times a year, and he notes that fishermen do not always see the spawn appearing three times in certain places. Perhaps the name comes from this <note>The Greek "tri" means three</note>, just as "amiae" are so named because they do not travel alone (*mia*), but in schools. **The Parrot-fish** (*Skaros*) is named from "skairon" <note>skipping or leaping</note>, or from "spaeis" <note>to draw/gasp</note>. **Small fry** (*Aphuai*) are so called because they are "unnatural" (*aphueis*), that is...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Mediterranean fish from Athenaeus’s "The Banquet of the Learned" (Deipnosophistae), Book 7. The previous page ended with a discussion of the barracuda; this page begins by concluding a point about the "double-natured" qualities of certain species before launching into an extensive discussion of the Red Mullet.</meta>

...double-natured. Two types, according to Bion the Cynic <note>original: Bion ho Drymikos; likely Bion of Borysthenes, a philosopher known for his wit</note>, and their nature is linked to the rising of the Dog Star because they are driven by the heat from its head. This fish is sharp-toothed, gregarious, and eats all kinds of things; it is a carnivore. The third type of this fish is sterile. This is because certain small worms grow in its uterus which consume the developing offspring. For this reason, Epicharmus happens to call them "bent" in his play *The Marriage of Hebe*, saying: "Come now, bring the bent red mullets and the tiny *karcharis*." Sophron, in his *Mimes of Men*, gives them various names, such as the "navel-cutting mullet" and the "well-living mullet." In the work titled *Kapoi*, he mentions "fat red mullets" and "roasted mullet," and in his *Mimes of Women* he speaks of the "sacrificial mullet."

Diocles, in his writings *To Cleitarchus*, says that the red mullet <note>original: τρίγλα (trigla); the Red Mullet, *Mullus barbatus*</note> has firm flesh. Speusippus says it is similar to the cuckoo-fish, the swallow-fish, and the red mullet itself; hence Typhon, in his works *On Animals*, says some people think the mullet is the same as the cuckoo-fish because of its dryness when roasted, as Sophron noted when he spoke of "fat mullets" and "roasted mullet." Plato <note>the comic poet, not the philosopher</note> says in his play *Phaon*: "The Red Mullet would not be a maiden who desires to return home to her master. For she is born a creature that hates the possessions of Artemis." The red mullet is dedicated to Hecate because of the similarity in their names; for Hecate is "of the three ways" <note>original: τριοδῖτις (trioditis)</note> and "three-eyed" <note>original: τριγλήνων (triglenon)</note>, and people bring these fish to her at the ritual dinners offered at the crossroads. 

Furthermore, the *plasios* is most closely associated with Apollo, as is the *kitharos*; the *boax* belongs to Hermes, the *kyttis* to Dionysus, and the *phalaris* to Aphrodite—as Aristophanes says in *The Birds*, due to its name's similarity to the phallus. Some associate the duck <note>original: νῆττα (netta)</note> with Poseidon. There is also the "sea-born" fry, which we call *aphye*, but others call *aphrye* and some call *aphros* (foam). This is said to be most dear to Aphrodite because the goddess herself was born from foam. Apollodorus, in his work *On the Gods*, says the red mullet is sacrificed to Hecate because of the kinship of the name; for the goddess is "three-formed." Melanthius, in his book *On the Eleusinian Mysteries*, says both the red mullet and the sprats are offered because Hecate is also a goddess of the sea.

Hegesander of Delphi says that all red mullets are brought to the festivals of Artemis because they appear to hunt and consume sea-hares, which are deadly. Therefore, as they act as a benefit to humans by hunting, they are dedicated to the hunting goddess. Sophron says the red mullet belongs to women because those who possess its "sweetness" are more pleasure-seeking than others. There is also a place called Trigla, where there is a dedicated offering to "Hecate of the Mullets." Thus Charicleides says in *The Chain*: "Mistress Hecate of the crossroads, three-formed, three-faced, charmed by red mullets." 

If a living red mullet is suffocated in wine and someone drinks that wine, they will be unable to engage in sexual intercourse, as Heracleides records in his work *On Aphrodisiacs*. And if a woman drinks the same wine, she will not conceive. The same applies to birds. The learned Archestratus, after praising the red mullets of Teichiussa in Miletus, says: "And if you are in Thasos, you will buy mullets no worse than these. The best for hunting is the very red one of the shore." Cratinus says in *Trophonius*: "It is a fine thing to eat a three-obol fish," referring to the red mullet; "I do not accept the black-tail instead of the mullet." Nausicrates the comic poet praises the mullets bought for a few obols in his *Sea-Captains*, saying: "Among them are those of remarkable nature, the golden-colored ones, which the waves of the market...
<margin>The Ribbon-fish.</margin> 
...breed in various places. With these, goddesses are honored at the dinners of the Light-bearing Maiden <note>Artemis or Hecate</note> whenever sailors send gifts. You speak of Red Mullets." 

**Ribbon-fish.** 
<margin>Ribbon-fish.</margin>
<margin>Ribbon-fish.</margin>
Epicharmus also mentions these: "The ribbon-fish are thin but sweet when cooked over a little fire." Mithaecus, in his *Culinary Art*, says of the ribbon-fish <note>original: ταινία (tainia); likely the Band-fish or Ribbon-fish, *Cepola macrophthalma*</note>: "Gut it, cut off the head, wash it, and after cutting it into slices, pour on cheese and oil." They are found in great numbers and at their best near Canopus in Alexandria and in Seleucia near Antioch. When Eupolis says in *Those Requesting More*: "His mother was a goddess who sold ribbons," he is referring to the woven bands and small trinkets that women use for profit.

**Horse-mackerel.** 
<margin>Horse-mackerel.</margin> 
Diocles mentions these as being of a drier nature. 
<margin>Horse-mackerel.</margin>
Numenius, in his *Art of Fishing*, mentions "the needle-fish, the wagtail, and the other horse-mackerel" <note>original: τράχουρος (trachouros); the horse-mackerel or scad</note>. 

**The Taulopias.** 
<margin>Taulopias.</margin> 
Archestratus records concerning this: "Indeed, a large *taulopias* is a great purchase in the hunt, when the sun is at its zenith; put it in a hot dish quickly with a sauce. Cook the underbelly of it on a spit." 

**The Squid.** 
<margin>Squid.</margin> 
Aristotle says this is one of the gregarious fish. 
<margin>Squid.</margin>
It has a body like the cuttlefish, the same number of feet, and tentacles. Of its feet, the lower ones are small and the upper ones are larger. Of the tentacles, the right one is thicker, and the whole body is tender and somewhat elongated. It has ink in its bladder, not black, but pale, and its internal shell is very small and cartilaginous. 

**The Large Squid.** 
<margin>Large Squid.</margin> 
The *teuthos* <note>the larger species of squid</note> differs from the *teuthis* <note>the smaller squid</note> only in size. 
<margin>Large Squid.</margin>
It can grow to three spans in length. Its color is reddish, and of its teeth, it has a smaller one below and a larger one above. Both are black and resemble the beak of a hawk. When opened, it has a stomach similar to that of a pig. In the fifth book of *Animals*, Aristotle says both the squid and the cuttlefish are short-lived. Archestratus, who traveled through every land and sea for the sake of gluttony, says: "You will see squids in Pierian Dium near the stream of Baphyrus, and in Ambracia in great numbers." Alexis, in *The Eretrian*, has a cook say: "Squids, rays, the people's fish, anchovies..." Criades in his own...

-># BOOK 7.<-

...but as for the "straight-fish," <note>original: εὐθείας (eutheias); likely a species of fish named for its straight shape</note> I roast their fins after mixing a little dough and smearing it over them, seasoning them with delicate green spices. And the fish which the physician calls "straight," Pamphilos says is also called the "bread-maker" fish.

<margin>Swine-fish.</margin> **Swine-fish.** <note>original: Ὕες (hyes); literally "pigs" or "swine," likely referring to the Triggerfish or a type of Sea Bream</note> Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, says: "There were swine-fishes, bugloss-fish, and the *kitharos* <note>a species of flatfish</note>." He speaks of certain "swine" in these lines: "Chalcid-fish, swine-fish, hawk-fish, and the 'can't-see-it' dogfish." Unless, perhaps, these are the same as the wild boar-fish. Numenius, in his *Art of Fishing*, explicitly lists a certain "hyena-fish" <note>original: ὑαίναν (hyainan)</note> among them: "The hyena-fish and the red mullets appear in the Kantharisian waters." And Dionysius mentions the hyena-fish in his *Cookery Book*. Archestratus, the tutor of gourmets, says: "In Aenus and the Pontus, buy the swine-fish, which some mortals call the 'dug-up sand-fish.' At that time, boil the head without adding any seasoning, but boil it in water alone, stirring it frequently; serve it with hyssop and other pungent things, dipping it into vinegar and hurrying so that you are almost choked by the heat <note>original: αὐσθῆς (austhēs); referring to the steaming heat or breath</note> while gulping it down. Roast the back fin and the rest of the parts." Perhaps Numenius also calls the swine-fish a "sand-dweller" in his *Art of Fishing* when he says: "At one time the shark, at another the Rhodian sand-dweller."

<margin>Hykai.</margin> **Hykai.** <note>original: Ὕκαι (hykai); a small, gregarious fish, possibly a wrasse</note> Of the *hykai*, Callimachus in his *Epigrams* calls them a "sacred fish" in these lines: "A god gave him the sacred *hykes*." Numenius, in his *Art of Fishing*, says: "Either the parrot-wrasse, or the herding *hykkas*, or the sea-dwelling sea-bream." Timaeus, in the thirteenth book of his *Histories*, discussing the small Sicilian town (I mean the one below Hykkara), says the town was named because the first people to arrive at the place found the fish called *hykkas*, and these were pregnant; taking this as an omen, they named the place Hykkara. Zuodotus says the Cydonians <note>people of Crete</note> call the *hykes* the "red-fish." Hermippus of Smyrna, in his writings *On Hipponax*, uses the term *hykkion* instead of "rainbow wrasse" <note>original: ἰουλίδα (ioulida)</note>. These fish are also hard to cure. For this reason, Philetas said: "Not even the *hykes* fish escaped the gaping mouth."

<margin>Sea Bream.</margin> **Sea Bream.** <note>original: Φάγροι (phagroi); the Common Sea Bream or Braize</note> Speusippus, in the second book of his *Resemblances*, says the sea bream, the red-fish, and the liver-fish are similar. Numenius also mentions it in the passages cited above. Aristotle says it is a carnivore and a solitary fish; it has a triangular heart and is at its peak mainly in the spring. Epicharmus says in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "Sea breams and sea bass." Metagenes also mentions them in *The Thurio-Persians*. Ameipsias says in *Konnos*: "You will be weighed down with sea-perch, rays, and sea breams." Hicesius says that sea breams, sea-drums <note>original: χρόμις (chromis)</note>, the *anthias*, the *akarnan*, sea-perch, the *skiosthontos*, and the *synagris* <note>the Dentex</note> all have similar colors (for they are sweet, somewhat fatty, and nutritious), and accordingly, they are difficult to distinguish. Those of them that are fleshier are more nutritious and sweeter, having less fat. Archestratus says: "When the Dog Star rises, one should eat sea bream in Delos and Eretria in the well-harbored houses of the sea. Buy only the head of it." Stratis mentions the sea bream in *The Queens of the Lake*: "Many large sea breams having stooped down." And in *Philoctetes*: "Then going into the market, they buy up all at once large sea breams, Copaic eels, and a tender, round-ribbed slice of fish." There is also a "stone-bream" <note>original: λίθου φάγρος (lithou phagros)</note>; for the whetstone is called *phagros* among the Cretans, as Simmias says.

<margin>Gapers.</margin> **Gapers.** <note>original: Χάνναι (channai); the Comber or Painted Sea Bass, known for its wide mouth</note> Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe* mentions "big-mouthed gapers and the large-bellied *skepēros*." Numenius in his *Art of Fishing* mentions "the mature gaper and the *gingylios*." Dorion also mentions it in his book *On Fish*. Aristotle, in his work *On Animals*, calls them "red-speckled" or "black-streaked" because they are variegated with black lines.

<margin>Sea-drums.</margin> **Sea-drums.** <note>original: Χρόμις (chromis); the Umbrine or Drum-fish, named for the sound it makes</note> Epicharmus also mentions this fish, saying: "The sea-drums and the *skioas* which, on the <unclear>shore</unclear>, is the best of all voiceless fish." Numenius in his *Art of Fishing* says: "The *hykkion* and the *pallichthon* among the sea-drums, and the sea-perch." And Archestratus calls the sea-drum "large in gray Pelon," and says it is fat in Anthedon, or even in Ambracia.

<margin>Gilt-heads.</margin> **Gilt-heads.** <note>original: Χρύσοφρυς (chrysophrys); literally "golden-brow," the Gilt-head Sea Bream</note> Archippus says in *The Fish*: "The gilt-head, sacred to Aphrodite of Cythera." Hicesius says these fish are the best of all in sweetness and general flavor. They are also highly nutritious. Aristotle says they spawn in the same way as the gray mullets, in places where rivers flow. Epicharmus mentions them in *The Muses*, and Dorion in his *On Fish*. Eupolis in *The Flatterers* says: "At the fish-market he bought for a hundred drachmas only eight sea bass and twelve gilt-heads." The wise Archestratus in his *Instructions* says: "Do not pass by a fat gilt-head from Ephesus, which they call the 'little Ionian'; take it, that creature of the sacred celery-blossom, and cook it properly even if it is ten cubits long."

<margin>Chalcids.</margin> **Chalcids.** <note>original: Χαλκίδες (chalkides); likely sprats or small sardines</note> And similar to these are the *thrissa* <note>shad</note> and the prized *ischides*. Hicesius says the so-called *chalkides*, the *rapsides*, and the *thrissai* are chaff-like, lean, and without juice. Epicharmus in *The Marriage of Hebe* mentions: "Chalcid-fishes, swine-fishes, hawk-fishes, and the 'can't-see-it' dogfish." Dorion calls them "Chalcidic fishes." Numenius says: "You in turn among those *chalkides*, eat likewise the small *maenidia* <note>picarel</note>." The *chalkeus* <note>John Dory</note> is different from the *chalkis*, which Heracleides mentions in his *Cookery Book*, and Euthydemus in his work *On Salt Fish*, saying they are found in the region of Cyzicus and are circular in shape. Aristotle mentions the *thrissai* in his works on animals and fish, in various places: "The stationary *thrissa*, the anchovy, the *membras*, the *korakinos*, the red-fish, and the *trichis* <note>a hairy or bristly fish</note>." Eupolis mentioned them in *The Flatterers*...

# FROM ATHENAEUS’S THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

That man was cheerful who had a little substance <note>original: ὑπῆν (hypēn); literally "was underneath" or "supported" his life</note> in his life; before the war, he bought sprats <note>original: τριχιδίας (trichidias); a small, bony fish like an anchovy or sardine</note> just once, because a "sama" <note>a measure of fish</note> could be bought for half an obol <note>a small Greek coin</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*: "If sprats should become a hundred for a single obol." Dorion, in his work *On Fish*, mentions the "dripping-fish" <note>original: στακτίας (staktias)</note> in sulfur-broth, and calls the sprat a "hair-fish." Nicochares, in *The Women of Lemnos*, says that they called young tunas "sprats." <gloss>†</gloss> Plato <note>Plato Comicus, a playwright, not the philosopher</note> in *Europa* says: "Fishing once, I saw him with coals and young tunas, and then he arrived at the shout." Aristotle says the same in the fifth book of his *History of Animals*. He says that the variety called the "living sprat" <note>original: ζωϊκὴν τριχιδία (zōikēn trichidia)</note> is named so because it is stirred to growth by dancing and song, and having heard <note>original: ἀκούσας (akousas)</note> music, it leaps out of the sea. Dorion mentions "highly-prized fish" <note>original: ἐριτίμων (eritimōn)</note>, saying they are the same as the *chalcis* <note>a type of sardine</note>, though some say they are the scrapings of the catch. Epainetus, in his *On Fish*, says that the "myrnid-catshark," which some call a type of dogfish, and the *chalcides* are what some call "highly-prized sardines." He also mentions the "hawk-swallow." Aristotle, in the fifth book of his *History of Animals*, calls them sardines. Callimachus writes as follows in his *National Names*: "Engrasicholos, the highly-prized fish of the Chalcedonians. The sprat, the chalcis, and the iktar-atherina." And in another part, listing the names of fish, he mentions: "Oaina, osmylion, thyrios, iopis, the highly-prized fish, and the athyoi." Nicander mentions the *iopes* in his *Boeotics*: "As when around the well-woven schools of *iopes*, either sea-breams or unlit scops-owls or even groupers." Aristophanes in *The Merchant Ships* says: "O wretched man, who was just now dipped in the brine <note>original: ἅλμη (halmē)</note> of sprats!" For a fish not <margin>Thasian brine. See Suidas.</margin> suitable for grilling was dipped into brine, so as to call it "Thasian brine," as the same poet says in *The Wasps*: "For previously, having twice drunk the brine of small coals." Since we are at this point in the discussion, and are speaking about "Thracian-women" <note>original: θραττῶν (thratton); a pun on a type of fish and Thracian slave-girls</note>, come, let us say who these "Thracian-women" are in the play *The Fish* by Archippus. For he has made these "contracts of the fish" for the Athenians, and they shall perish when they hold us against each other: "Us Thracian-girls to the flute-playing *atherina*, the cuttlefish to the *thyrsos* and the red mullets, and Euclides who was the leader, and those from Anagyros who are 'little crows' <note>original: κορακινούς (korakinous); likely a type of dark fish</note>. And just as for the woman of Salamis, her offspring, and 'Little Frog' <note>original: βάραχον (barachon)</note> the assistant of those from Oreus." In these lines, someone might ask what kind of "Thracian-women" among the fish happen to be those who agree to destroy men. Since I have written a specific treatise on this, I will now say only the most essential points. The "Thracian-fish" <note>original: θρᾶττα (thratta)</note> is a small sea-fish. Mnesimachus mentions it in *The Horse-Breeder*; he is a poet of the Middle Comedy. He says: "Gray-mullet, *lebias*, *sparos*, *aiolias*, Thracian-fish, swallow-fish, *katheis*, squid." Dorotheos of Ascalon, in the one hundred and eighth book of his *Collection of Words*, says it is a "divine spelling," perhaps having encountered the name by error, or having believed he corrected it himself because of the name's unusual nature. Generally, the name of the "Thracian-fish" is not found in any Attic writers. But that they called a small sea-fish a "Thracian-fish" is established by Anaxandrides in *Lycurgus*, saying: "And he consorted with little crow-fish along with little pigs and little Thracian-fish." And Antiphanes in *The Tyrrhenian* says: "There is a fisherman for the People. For the rest of the land is the same to me, and I shall be spoken of badly; why then, instead of Thracian-fish or some flatfish or a moray eel, will he give me some great sea-evil?"

<margin>Flatfish.</margin> **Flatfish.** <note>original: Ψῆται (Psētai); generally referring to turbot, brill, or other flatfishes</note> Diocles lists these in his *Articles of Diet*. Speusippus, in the second book of *Similar Things*, says the flatfish is similar to the sole <note>original: βούγλωσσον (bouglosson); literally "ox-tongue"</note> and the ribbon-fish. Aristotle writes in the fifth book of *History of Animals*: "Similarly, most small fish spawn only once, such as the *chytoi*, those caught in nets, the *chromis*, the flatfish, the tuna, the young tuna, the mullet, the *chalcides*, and such." In his work *On Animals*, he says the cartilaginous fish are the ox-ray, the stingray, the torpedo, the ray, the fishing-frog, the sole, the flatfish, and the sea-mouse. Dorion writes in his *On Fish*: "Of the flat fishes, there is the sole, the flatfish, and the *epsaros*, which they also call the *koris*." Epicharmus also names soles in *The Marriage of Hebe*: "Hyenas and soles and the *kitharos*." Lynceus of Samos, in his *Letters*, says the finest flatfish are found near Eleusis in Attica. Archestratus says: "Then let us take a large and roundish flatfish. Serve the sole with the noble *chalcis*." The Romans call the flatfish a *rhombus* <note>original: ῥόμβον (rhombos); the source of the modern word "rhombus," describing its shape</note>, and the name is Greek. Nausicrates in *The Shipowners*, having spoken first about the gray-fish, adds: "Those golden-haired ones whom the Byzantine wave [brings]."

Having breakfasted on the belly in these places, he is educated, by which they also honor the goddess Phosphoros <note>The Light-bringer, usually Hecate or Artemis</note>, when sailors send gifts. You speak of the *teugla*, milk-colored, which the Sicilian crowd fixes as a *rhombus*. Having filled up the chatter about the small round fish for the diners, O Timocrates, he brought the discussion to a close, unless we were to set out other foods, such as those Eubulus spoke of in *The Laconians* or *Leda*: "In addition to these, serve slices of tuna, pig meat, guts of a kid, boar's liver, ram's testicles, beef tripe, lamb's heads, kid's fat, hare's stomach, sausage, tripe, small fry, and others."

->Having been filled, leave us and these things, and take care<-
->of the little body, so that you may be able to<-

# ATHENAEUS: THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED
## BOOK EIGHT.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated woodcut initial 'T' begins the main text, featuring ornate floral and scrolling patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

Regarding the prosperity of the region of Lusitania <note>modern-day Portugal and western Spain</note>—which is a part of Iberia that the Romans now call Hispania—Polybius of Megalopolis, my excellent friend Timocrates, gives an account in the thirty-fourth book of his *Histories*. He says that because of the excellent temperature of the air, both animals and humans are very fertile, and the fruits of the land never spoil. For instance, pomegranates, white violets, asparagus, and similar plants do not cease to bloom for more than three months of the year. The sea-fish, both in terms of quantity, quality, and beauty, are vastly superior to those produced in our own sea <note>the Mediterranean</note>. He notes that a *siklos* <note>a measure</note> of barley costs one drachma, and a *medimnos* <note>about 12 gallons</note> of wheat costs nine <note>original: φινικα, likely a corruption of ἐννέα (ennea)</note> Alexandrian obols. A *metretēs* <note>about 9 gallons</note> of wine costs one drachma, and a good-sized kid or a hare costs one obol. The price of lambs is three or four obols. A fat pig weighing one hundred minas <note>about 100 lbs</note> costs five drachmas, and a sheep costs two. A talent's weight <note>about 60 lbs</note> of figs is three obols. A calf <note>original: μάγος, likely a corruption of μόσχος (moschos)</note> costs five drachmas, and a yoke-ox costs ten. As for the meat of wild animals, it is hardly considered worth a price at all, but people exchange them as a free gift or a favor.

Yet our fine friend Larisius, by providing Rome with its own "Lusitania" at every turn, fills our high-minded bellies daily with all sorts of good things through his generosity, while we bring nothing from home but our "little words" <note>original: λογάρια (logaria); academic discussions or speeches</note>. After many speeches had been made regarding fish, Cynulcus was clearly becoming annoyed. But the handsome Democritus anticipated him and said: "But truly, no fish was overlooked in the works of Archippus <note>a comic poet who wrote a play titled 'The Fish'</note>."

<margin>Stephanus mentions.</margin>
Therefore, it is right for us to briefly mention the so-called "fossil fish" <note>original: ὀρυκτοὺς ἰχθύας (oryktous ichthyas); fish literally dug out of the earth</note> which are found in Heracleia and near Tium, the Milesian colony in the Pontus. The same philosopher, Theophrastus, writes about them and about those fish that are frozen by the winter's ice like a garden <note>original: ἰσόκηπον, likely a corruption of ἰσόπηκτον meaning 'solidly frozen'</note>; these do not feel anything or move until they are thrown into the cooking pots and boiled. A unique thing happens among those in Paphlagonia called fossil fish. For they dig in deep places where there are neither overflows from rivers nor hot springs, and they find living fish in the soil. Mnaseas of Patrae, in his *Circumnavigation*, says that in the Cleitor river there are fish that make sounds, even though Aristotle says that the only fish that make sounds are the *scaphros* <note>parrot-fish</note> and the "river-hog" <note>a type of grunting fish</note>. Philostephanus—a Cyrenaean by birth and an acquaintance of Callimachus—in his work *On Remarkable Rivers*, says that in the Ladon river, which flows with a voice, the fish "sing" just like thrushes <note>original: κίχλαις (kichlais)</note>. He says they are called "variegated ones."

Nymphodorus of Syracuse, in his *Circumnavigations*, says that in the Helorus river there are sea-bass and large eels so tame that they accept food from the hands of those who offer it to them. I myself have seen in Arethusa at Chalcis—and perhaps most of you have too—tame mullets and eels wearing silver and gold bracelets <note>original: ψέλλια (psellia)</note>, taking food from people who offer it, including the entrails of sacrificial victims and fresh cheese. Semus, in the sixth book of his *History of Delos*, says that when the Athenians were sacrificing in Delos at the spring called Batas, a fish appeared in the bowl with the water. The Delian seer told them they would become masters of the sea.

Polybius, in the thirty-fourth book of his *Histories*, says that near the river Narbonne there is a plain through which the rivers Ilebernis and Roscynicus flow, past cities of the same name inhabited by Celts. In this plain, there are the so-called fossil fish. The plain has thin soil and is covered with much couch-grass. Beneath this, the ground is sandy for two or three cubits, and water from the rivers flows through it. Fish swim under the earth through these seepages in search of food (for they love the root of the couch-grass), making the whole plain full of underground fish, which people catch by digging them up. Theophrastus says that among the Indians, fish come out of the rivers onto the land and then jump back into the water, just like frogs; in appearance, they are similar to the fish called "muranas" <note>original: μαξανοῖς, likely a corruption of μυξίνοις (myxinois), a type of mullet</note>. 

Nor has Clearchus the Peripatetic escaped my notice, who spoke about the fish called the "out-of-sleeper" <note>original: ἐξωκοίτου (exōkoitou); so named because it was believed to sleep on the shore</note> in his work titled *On Aquatic Animals*. He says—and I believe his wording is as follows: "The out-of-sleeper fish, which some call the Adonis. It received its name because it often takes its rest outside of the water. It is reddish, and from the gills along the depth of the body to the tail it has one continuous white stripe. It is round, not flat, and in size it is equal to the mullets found near the shore. These are about eight fingers long. In general, it is very similar to the small fish called the 'goat-fish' <note>original: τράγῳ (tragō)</note>, except it lacks the black part under the stomach which they call the 'goat's beard.' This 'out-of-sleeper' is one of the..."

->FROM ATHENAEUS'S BANQUET OF THE LEARNED<-

They swim, then, to these places. But as for the species of dogfish <note>original: γαλιῶν (galeōn), a type of small shark or dogfish</note>, they are carried in by the waves and lie upon the rocky ground for a long time, resting themselves on the dry land. They even turn themselves toward the sun. But when they have had enough rest, they roll themselves back toward the moisture until the wave takes them up again, carrying them back into the sea with the outgoing tide. When they happen to be awake on the dry land, they keep a lookout for the water-birds, specifically those called the kingfisher <note>original: κήρυλος (kerylos)</note>, the plover <note>original: τροχίλος (trochilos)</note>, and the "prey-taker" <note>original: ἐλώριος (elōrios)</note>, which resembles a hawk. For these birds, while feeding along the dry shore during calm weather, often fall upon the fish. When the fish see them coming, they flee by leaping and gasping until they can dive back into the water.

The same Clearchus <note>Clearchus of Soli, a student of Aristotle</note> also says these things about Sapherus the Cyrenaean, the lover of wreaths—a man not previously celebrated in song. He notes that some fish, though they have no lungs, still make sounds. Among these are the fish near Cleitor in Arcadia, in the river called the Ladon. <margin>10</margin> For they do indeed speak and produce a loud sound.

And Nicolaus of Damascus, in the hundred and fourteenth book of his *Histories*, says that near Phrygian Apamea, at the time of the Mithridatic wars, earthquakes occurred, and lakes appeared in the surrounding country where none had been before; even rivers and other springs were opened up by the movement. Many others, however, vanished. So much other water—both bitter and sea-colored—burst forth from the earth, even though the sea was far distant from those places, that the whole neighboring region was filled with oysters and fish <margin>A rain of fish.</margin> of the kind that the sea nourishes.

I also know that in many places the god has rained fish. Phaenias, for instance, in the second book of his *Chronicles of Eresus*, says that in the Chersonese it rained fish for three days. And Phylarchus, in his fourth book, says that people have seen the god raining fish in many places. The same thing often happens with wheat, just as it does with frogs. Heraclides Lembos <note>A 2nd-century BC historian</note>, in the twenty-first book of his *Histories*, <margin>20</margin> says that regarding Paeonia and Dardania, the god rained frogs. The multitude of them was so great that the houses and roads were full of them. For the first few days, the people endured it by killing them and locking their houses. But when they achieved nothing—for their vessels were filled with them, and frogs were found in their food, being boiled and roasted along with it—and besides this, they could not use the water, nor could they set foot on the ground because of the heaps of frogs, and being overcome by the stench of the dead ones, they fled the country.

I also know that Posidonius the Stoic spoke of a great multitude of fish appearing at the time when Tryphon of Apamea, who had seized the Syrian kingdom, was being attacked by Sarpedon, the general of Demetrius, near the city of Ptolemais. As Sarpedon, after being defeated, retreated into the interior with his own soldiers, Tryphon’s men were marching along the shore after their victory in the battle; suddenly, a wave from the sea, rising to an extraordinary <margin>30</margin> height, came upon the land and overwhelmed them all, destroying them beneath the waters. When the wave receded, it left behind a vast heap of fish along with the corpses. When Sarpedon and his men heard of the disaster, they came and were delighted by the sight of their enemies' bodies, but they also carried away an abundance of fish and sacrificed to Poseidon of the Trophy in the suburbs of the city.

I will not remain silent, either, about the fish-diviners <note>original: ἰχθυομάντεις (ichthyomanteis)</note> in Lycia, whom Polycharmus records in the second book of his *History of Lycia*, writing as follows: "When they go down to the sea, where there is a grove of Apollo on the shore, and where there is a whirlpool on the sand, those seeking an oracle arrive holding two wooden skewers, each having ten pieces of roasted meat. The priest sits by the grove in silence. The person seeking the oracle throws the skewers into the whirlpool and watches what happens. After the skewers are thrown in, the whirlpool fills with seawater, and such a great number and variety of fish appear <margin>40</margin> that the sight is astounding. They are so large that one might even be afraid. When the seeker reports the types of fish seen, the prophet receives the oracle from the priest and gives it to the seeker regarding the matters he inquired about. There appear groupers, gray-fish, and sometimes whales and saw-fish, as well as many invisible fish and some strange to the sight."

Artemidorus, in the tenth book of his *Geographical Works*, says it is reported by the inhabitants that a spring of fresh water bubbles up there, which causes the whirlpools. He says that large fish appear in the swirling place, and those who offer sacrifice throw in the first-fruits of the victims on wooden skewers, pinning on pieces of boiled and roasted meat, as well as barley-cakes and bread. <margin>Pliny, Book 32, ch. 2; Book 31, ch. 2</margin> The harbor and this place are named Dinos <note>meaning "Whirlpool"</note>.

I also know that Phylarchus spoke about large fish and the green figs sent along with them. He says that Patroclus, the general of Ptolemy, sent them to King Antigonus as a riddle, just as the Scythians sent gifts to Darius when he was invading their country. <margin>50</margin> For they sent—or so Herodotus says—a bird, an arrow <margin>Herodotus, Book 4.</margin>, and a frog. But Patroclus, as Phylarchus says in the third book of his *Histories*, sent the aforementioned figs and fish. The king happened to be drinking at a banquet <note>original: κωδωνιζόμενος (kōdōnizomenos), literally "being tested like a bell," an idiom for drinking</note>, and while everyone was puzzled by the gifts, Antigonus laughed and told his friends that he knew what the host-gifts meant. "For Patroclus says," he remarked, "that either we must rule the sea, or we must eat figs <note>a metaphor for poverty or simple living, implying they would lose their kingdom</note>."

# BOOK VIII.

It does not escape my notice that fish were commonly called "gapers" <note>original: καμασιῶτες (kamasiōtes), likely referring to how fish open their mouths</note> by Empedocles the natural philosopher <note>Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously proposed the four elements</note>, in this way: "How also the long-spawned and the ocean-dwelling gapers." And the author of the epic poem *The Cypria* <note>The *Cypria* was a lost epic of the Trojan Cycle, detailing the events leading up to the Trojan War</note>—
<margin>Nemesis is the mother of Helen.</margin>
whether he be a certain Cyprian, or Stasinus, or whoever he prefers to be called—represents Nemesis being pursued by Zeus and transforming into a fish, in these verses: "After them, she bore Helen, a wonder to mortals, whom once the fair-haired Nemesis, having joined in love with Zeus the king of the gods, bore under harsh necessity. For she fled, and did not wish to join in love with Father Zeus, the son of Cronus; for her heart was worn with shame. And she fled Nemesis now throughout the harvestless dark water. But Zeus pursued her, wishing in his heart to catch her; at one time in the waves of the loud-roaring sea, where she, in the form of a fish, stirred up the great deep; at another time along the river Ocean and the ends of the earth; and then again along the fertile land—always she became whatever wild beasts the dry land nurtures, so that she might escape him." I also know
the stories concerning the city called Apopyris <note>Literally "Fire-baked" or "Smoked-fish" city</note> and the lake Bolyke, about which Hegesander says the following in his *Commentaries*: "In Chalcidice, near Apollonia, flow two rivers, the Ammites and the Olynthiacus. Both empty into Lake Bolyke. There stands the monument of Olynthus, the son of Heracles and Bolyke. In the months of Anthesterion <note>roughly February/March</note> and Elaphebolion <note>roughly March/April</note>, the locals say that Bolyke sends the 'fire-baked' fish <note>original: ἀπόπυριν (apopyrin)</note> to Olynthus at this season in such an infinite multitude that it is sufficient for all the neighboring people to prepare enough salt-fish <note>term: τάριχος (tarichos) - dried or salted fish, a staple protein in the ancient Greek diet</note> for their own needs. It is a wonder that they do not pass the monument of Olynthus. They say that previously the rites for the dead were performed in Apollonia during Elaphebolion, but now in Anthesterion. For this reason, in these months alone, the fish do not make their ascent, during which times they are accustomed to honor the departed." And so much for these things and the fish themselves. For you all, having gathered everything as fodder, have thrown us to the fish; and it was not enough for us that one should say so much—not even the Megarian philosopher Ichthyas <note>His name literally means "Fish"</note>, nor the name 'Fish' itself, which is a proper name mentioned by Teleclides in the *Amphictyons*. But I might also charge you, boy, to remember the things mentioned by Pherecrates: "Never serve me fish, O Deucalion, nor even here."
<margin>Brizo. <unclear>ed. m.</unclear></margin>
For in Delos, as Semus the Delian says in the second book of his *History of Delos*, whenever they sacrifice to Brizo <note>A local Delian goddess of sleep and prophecy</note>—she is the prophetess in sleep, for the ancients called sleeping 'brizing'—they place offerings there... In this way, when the Delian women sacrifice, they bring her bowls full of all good things, except for fish, because they pray to her for all things and especially for the safety of their ships. My friends, though I admire many things about Chrysippus <note>A major Stoic philosopher</note>, the leader of your sect, I praise him even more for this:
<margin>Philainis.</margin>
for ranking the much-talked-about Archestratus <note>Archestratus of Gela (4th c. BCE), author of the first 'gastronomy' or guide to fine dining</note> alongside Philainis <note>Philainis of Samos, to whom an ancient sex manual was falsely attributed</note in his discussion on gluttony. To her is attributed that licentious work on sexual matters, which Aeschrion of Samos, the iambic poet, says was actually written by Polycrates the Sophist to slander the woman, who was actually very modest. The iambic verses go like this:
> I, Philainis, famous among men,
> Lie here in the sleep of long old age.
<margin>'Lathnen' should be read; see Hesychius under 'Lichisratoi'.</margin>
> O foolish sailor, do not, as you round this cape,
> Make me a target of mockery, laughter, and abuse <note>original: λάθνην (lathnēn), a rare word for insult or mockery</note>.
> For by Zeus, and by the youths below,
> I was not a man-chaser among men, nor common.
> But Polycrates, from an wretched lineage
> Of words, a trickster and a foul tongue,
> Wrote what he wrote. I myself do not know it.

But anyway, the most wonderful Chrysippus says in the fifth book of *On the Beautiful and Pleasure* that both the books of Philainis and the *Gastronomy* of Archestratus, which deals with powers of eating, and likewise the handmaids who are experienced in movements and postures and the practice of these things... and again, he says that they should learn such things by heart and acquire the writings on these matters by Philainis and Archestratus and those who have written similar things. And in the seventh book he says: "Just as it is not necessary to learn the works of Philainis and the *Gastronomy* of Archestratus as if they contributed anything to living better." But you have often filled the banquet with licentiousness by mentioning this Archestratus. For what has this 'noble' epic poet left out of things that can ruin a man? He alone emulated Sardanapalus <note>The legendary last king of Assyria, a symbol of extreme decadence</note>, the life of 'Anakyndaraxes' <note>This may refer to a specific type of decadent dance or posture</note>, which Aristotle said was even more senseless in its name than that of his father. Upon whose tomb Chrysippus says these words were inscribed:
> Knowing well that you were born mortal, indulge your heart,
> Delighting in feasts; when you are dead, there is no benefit.
> For I am but dust, though I was king of great Nineveh;
> I have only what I ate and the wanton pleasures I enjoyed, and the joys
> I felt in love. But all those many and blessed things are lost.

This is a wise advice for life...
<margin>Od. 9.</margin>
and I shall take it from her; let anyone who wishes jump upon the boundless gold. And the Poet <note>Homer</note> said concerning the Phaeacians: "Always the feast is dear to us, the lyre and the dances, changes of clothes, warm baths, and the bed." And another person says something similar to Sardanapalus, advising those who are not prudent as follows: "I wish to advise all mortals to live their daily life pleasantly. For he who has died is nothing, and a shadow beneath the earth. While living, it is necessary to enjoy a short life."

# BOOK VIII.

And **Amphis** <note>A Middle Comedy poet of the 4th century BCE.</note> the comic poet says in his play *Ialemus*: "Whoever is a mortal and does not make use of life, but seeks something pleasant to enjoy while ignoring the rest, is a fool in my eyes and in the eyes of all wise judges, and is cursed by the gods." And indeed, in the play titled *Rule of Women*, he says much the same: "Drink, boy! Life is mortal, the time to live is short; death is immortal once a man has died." And a certain **Bacchidas**, who lived the same kind of life as **Sardanapalus** <note>The last king of Assyria, legendary in the Greek world for his extreme decadence and luxury.</note>, has this inscribed upon his tomb after his death:

> Drink, eat, and give all things to your soul.

For I have always considered these things to be Bacchidas's own. **Alexis** <note>A major poet of Middle and New Comedy.</note> says in *The Master of the Profligate*—as **Sotion of Alexandria** <note>A biographer and doxographer of the 2nd century BCE.</note> notes in his works on the satires of **Timon**—"For I have not sworn off the drama, having read more than eight hundred plays of Middle Comedy and made selections from them, yet I did not come across *The Master of the Profligate*. Nor am I aware of it being deemed worthy of a catalog entry; for neither Callimachus nor Aristophanes cataloged it, nor did those who made the records at Pergamon." But Sotion says that in the play, a certain servant named Xanthias was represented as a companion to **Pythagoras**, and he says:

<margin>See Suidas regarding "without fear."</margin>
> Why do you babble this nonsense, prating 
> up and down the Lyceum, the Academy, and the gates? <note>Referring to the famous schools of philosophy in Athens.</note>
> All that chatter of the sophists is not worth a single thing.
> Let us drink, let us drink deep! Let us rejoice while 
> it is possible to feed the soul with festivities; 
> nothing is sweeter than the belly. She is your father, 
> and she alone is your mother. Virtues, embassies, and 
> generalships are but empty boasts—noises instead of dreams. 
> Fate will rub you out at your appointed time. You will 
> possess only what you eat and drink; the rest is ashes—
> even the "Sea-Bream" Pericles, the "Gudgeon" Cobyoi, and Cimon. <note>original: περικλῆς, κόβοιοι, κίμων. This is a series of puns on the names of famous Athenian statesmen (Pericles, Cimon) and types of fish.</note>

It would have been better, says **Chrysippus** <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his vast output and logical precision.</note>, if he had changed the inscription on Sardanapalus’s tomb to this:

> Knowing well that you were born mortal, 
> indulge your spirit; taking pleasure in food is your only profit.

For I too am a wretch, though I have eaten as much and as pleasantly as possible.

> I have what I learned and thought upon, and with these, 
> I have enjoyed good things; but all the rest 
> and all the pleasures have been left behind.

**Timon** <note>Timon of Phlius, a Skeptic philosopher and satirical poet.</note> also spoke very beautifully: "Above all things, one should not have a wicked heart." And **Clearchus** <note>A student of Aristotle.</note> says in his *On Proverbs* that Terpsion was the teacher of **Archestratus** <note>Archestratus was a famous ancient gourmet who wrote a poem on gastronomy.</note>; it was Terpsion who first wrote a "Gastronomy" and instructed his students on what things to avoid. Terpsion also improvised a rule about the tortoise: "Either eat it, or do not eat it." <note>A proverb implying that some things should be done thoroughly or not at all, as tortoise meat was thought to cause cramps unless eaten in large quantities.</note> Others say it this way:

<margin>Dorion.</margin>
"Either eat the meat of a tortoise, or do not eat it." But from where, O most wise men, did the gourmand **Dorion** come to you, as if he were some sort of writer? I know him to be called a "suspender-of-meat" by Philiscus, but not a writer. **Machon** the comic poet mentions him as a meat-hanger in this way:
<margin>Mylen is a city in Egypt, according to Stephanus.</margin>
The gourmand Dorion once went to Mylen, and being unable to find any lodging for rent, he sat down at a certain temple—the one belonging to the goddess of Fortune. Seeing the temple-keeper approaching, he said, "By Athena, O best of gods, whose temple is this, tell me?" The man said to him, "Zeus the Healer <note>original: νοσοστάδιος (nosostadios)</note> occupies it." And Dorion replied, "How then could one find a place to stay here?"

And again, they say he lived with a fellow-drinker. **Lynceus of Samos**, a student of Theophrastus and brother of **Duris** (who wrote histories and was tyrant of his homeland), says in his *Apophthegms* that when someone said to Dorion the flute-player that the ray was a good fish, he replied: "It's as if someone said they were eating boiled triangles." When another praised the bellies of tunas, he said, "Yes, quite so; for I eat them as if they were my own." When asked, "How?" he replied, "With pleasure!" On another occasion, he said a crab was "expensive but elegant in its feasting and appearance." While dining in Cyprus with **Nicocreon**, he praised a certain cup. Nicocreon said, "Whatever you wish, the same craftsman will make another for you." Dorion replied, "He can make one for you, but give this one to me." The flute-player was not acting without sense in saying this. For there is an old saying that the gods did not plant sense in flute-players:

> But as soon as they blow, their sense flies out.

**Hegesander** says the following about him in his *Commentaries*: Dorion the fish-glutton, when his servant had bought some fish, whipped him and ordered him to name the best fishes. When the boy counted off "the grouper, the sea-bass, and the conger eel," and other such fish, Dorion said, "I ordered you to name the gods, you divine boy!" <note>Likely a pun or a hyperbole suggesting that high-quality fish are equivalent to deities.</note> The same Dorion, mocking the storm in Timotheus's *The Sailor*, remarked that he had seen a greater storm boiling in a cooking pot. **Aristodemus** says in the second book of his *Laughable Memoirs* that Dorion the meat-hanger was club-footed, and once at a symposium, his shoe for his lame foot went missing. He said he could wish nothing more on the thief than that the sandal would actually fit him. That this Dorion was notorious for his fish-gluttony is clear from what **Mnesimachus** the comic poet says in the play *Philip*:

> Is it not beautiful that even at night Dorion 
> is inside our house, blowing on the cooking-pots?

<margin>Lasus.</margin>
I also know that **Lasus of Hermione** <note>A lyric poet and music theorist of the 6th century BCE.</note> joked about fish, which **Chamaeleon of Heraclea** recorded in his book about Lasus, saying this: Lasus said that a raw fish was "roasted." When many wondered at this, he attempted to prove it by saying that as whatever is "heard" is "audible," and whatever is "thought" is "thinkable," so also whatever is "eatable" <note>original: ἐσθίειν (esthiein)</note> is "eatable" <note>original: ἐσθλ' (esthl') - a pun on 'roasted' or 'good'</note>. Therefore, since the fish is eatable, it is roasted <note>A sophisticated linguistic pun involving the Greek words for 'eatable' and 'roasted'.</note>. And once, while joking with some fishermen...

<summary>This page catalogs anecdotes and poetic fragments regarding gluttony and wit, focusing on the decadent inscriptions of Sardanapalus and the humorous exploits of the gourmand Dorion.</summary>
