# BOOK VIII.

...he stole from the fishermen, and having hidden it, he gave it to one of those standing by. When put under oath, he swore that he himself did not have the fish, nor was he aware of anyone else who had taken it; for while he had hidden it himself, another person now held it, whom he had pointed out. He swore again that he neither took it himself nor knew of anyone else having it. For the one who received it had "taken" it, but the thief himself "held" it <note>This is a play on the Greek verbs for "taking" and "having/holding," a common type of sophistical wordplay used to evade the literal truth of an oath.</note>. **Epicharmus** <note>A 5th-century BCE comic playwright from Sicily, known for his philosophical parodies.</note> plays with such things as if in a story, saying: "Zeus invited me to a **contributing meal** <note>term: *eranos* — a meal where each guest contributes a share of the cost or food.</note> for Pelops." Or: "O friend, the **crane** <note>term: *geranos* — crane (the bird).</note> is a most wicked dish!" "But I am not speaking of a crane (*geranos*), but a contributing meal (*eranos*)!"

<margin>Fish-lover.</margin> **Alexis** says in his play *Demetrius*, mocking a certain Phayllos as a fish-lover: "Previously, whether the North wind or the South wind blew on the sea, no one could eat a splendid fish. But now, with all these winds, a third storm has been added to our misfortunes. For whenever a **cloud-burst** <note>term: *eknephias* — a sudden storm or squall breaking from a cloud.</note> happens to rush down upon the market, it carries off everything that was caught, shield and all, so that for the rest of us, the battle takes place over the vegetables." 

<margin>Gourmands.</margin> **Antiphanes** in *The Fisherwoman*, listing certain people who are "dear to fish," says: "First, the household Heracles themselves, they have crammed everything into their bags; won't you throw them back into the sea? And those swimming things—let the Dorians not call you anything but 'shadows' <note>original: *skias* — a type of fish (the umbrina), but also meaning 'ghosts' or 'shadows'.</note> even if you have caught them. And this **crayfish** <note>term: *karabos* — a spiny lobster or large crayfish.</note> here—how? Give back the sprats! By Zeus, you are thick indeed! O Zeus, whoever should look upon you, **Callimedon** <note>An Athenian orator and politician nicknamed "The Crayfish" because of his gluttony and perhaps his appearance.</note>, and your circle of friends, there is no one who would not pay their contribution. And how did he station you here? What a beautiful dish of red mullet is this of Callimedon's! At any rate, he would waste his whole estate on a single one. And the **conger eel** from Sinope already has thicker spines. This man shall no longer take it, though he be the first to approach." 

For **Smigolas**, you do not eat of these at all, but there is no **cithara-fish** <note>term: *kitharos* — a species of flatfish (Lepidorhombus boscii), often used in puns involving cithara players.</note> that you would let out of your hands if you saw it. And truly, it escapes notice how much this man has naturally grown attached to all **cithara-players** <note>term: *kitharōdos* — a professional singer who accompanies themselves on the kithara (lyre).</note>. "I must send this little man, this little fleece of feet, to the beautiful **Pythionice** <note>A famous and wealthy Athenian courtesan (hetaira) of the 4th century BCE.</note>... for he is stuffed full, but nevertheless he will not taste it. I am going for the cured fish! For I have rushed for the anchovies or these 'peeled' fish into the red mullet; it was found to be apart from the tuna and of equal weight." 

Most persuasively, in these lines, **Antiphanes** has mocked **Smigolas** as being intensely devoted to beautiful cithara-singers and cithara-players. For the orator **Aeschines** says in his speech *Against Timarchus* concerning him: "Smigolas, the son of Naucratis, O Athenians—a man who in other respects is noble and good, and whom no one would ever find fault with—is strangely obsessed with this matter, and is accustomed to having certain cithara-singers or cithara-players around him. I say this not to be vulgar, but so that you may recognize who he is." And **Timocles** says in *Sappho*: "Smigolas, who does not admit it, but appears to be wreathed by those in their youth." 

**Alexis** says in *The Contest* (or *The Letter*): "O mother, I beseech you, do not marry me to Smigolas, for I am no cithara-singer!" He also says that Pythionice is "dear to cured fish," because she had as lovers the sons of Chaerephilus, the **sellers of cured fish** <note>original: *tarichopōla* — vendors of salted or smoked fish, a trade often looked down upon but very lucrative.</note>, as **Nicocles** says in *The Small Ones*: "How is 'Thick' Anytus when he comes to eat something of Pythionice's?" For they say she calls to him whenever she hosts the two mackerel of Chaerephilus... and again: "Pythionice will receive you gladly, and she will perhaps devour what you now have, which you will bring from us, for she is insatiable. Nevertheless, it seems to you that her path is one of baskets of cured fish. For she happens to be well-off, and you will know her... and these things are unsalted for certain 'broad-beaked' ones." Before these, she had a lover named **Cobios** <note>A name meaning "Gudgeon" (a small fish).</note>. 

And somewhere, **Callimedon**, going after the cithara-fish and being a "fish-lover," is called "the squint-eyed one." **Timocles** in *The Busybody* says: "Then Callimedon the Crayfish suddenly approached; they are looking at me. And how he laughed at the chatter of another man. I, naturally understanding nothing of what they were saying, moved about. For they look apart, however their **pupils** <note>original: *korai* — a pun meaning both 'pupils of the eyes' and 'young girls' (daughters).</note> are." **Alexis** in *Cratiya* (or *The Pharmacist*): "For I have been treating the *korai* <note>The "pupils" or "daughters."</note> of Callimedon for four days now." "Had he daughters who were girls?" "The ones in his eyes, which not even **Melampus** <note>A legendary healer and soothsayer who cured the daughters of Proetus of madness.</note>, who alone cured the daughters of Proetus from their madness, could restore." 

He mocks him similarly in the play titled *The Assemblies*. Regarding his **gluttony** <note>term: *opsophagia* — the obsessive love of delicate food, especially fish.</note>, Phaidon (or Phaidria) says: "You shall be a market-clerk if the gods will it, so that you may stop Callimedon—if you love me—from storming the fish-market all day long. It is a task for tyrants, not for market-clerks' speeches. For he is a warlike man, yet useful to the city." These same iambic verses are also found in the play titled *At the Well*. "And you, being marketed, if I love any other strangers more than you... eels, so that Callimedon the Crayfish might buy me." And in *Cratiya*: "And Callimedon the Crayfish with Orpheus." **Antiphanes** in *Gorgithos*: "I would be less shaken by those I chose than if Callimedon should buy a grayling from Cratias." **Eubulus** in *The Rescued*: "Others, entangled with the gods, in the company of the Crayfish, who alone of mortals can swallow down whole slices from boiling platters so that nothing remains." **Theophilus** in *The Doctor*, mocking him and his "cold" words: "But the son, out of ambition for his father, set before him a young eel... and a good squid... 'How are you? How is the crayfish?' 'It is cold,' he says, 'take it away; I will not taste of orators!'" **Philemon** says... when someone served a crayfish, seeing it, he said, "Hail, dearest father!"

<meta>This page continues the catalog of anecdotes concerning famous gluttons and "fish-lovers" in Athenian society, transitioning from general observations on pleasure to specific satirical attacks found in Middle and New Comedy. It focuses on historical figures like the poet Antagoras, the painter Androcydes, and the orator Hyperides.</meta>

-> FROM ATHENAEUS' DEIPNOSOPHISTS <-

...he made his father a convict. **Herodicus of Cratete** <note>A 2th-century BCE scholar and follower of Crates of Mallus.</note> says in his *Miscellaneous Notes* that he will demonstrate that the money belonged to **Callimedon** <note>A pro-Macedonian orator nicknamed "The Crab" because of his love for seafood.</note>. There have also been many notable **gourmands** <note>term: *opsophagoi* — literally "relish-eaters," referring to those obsessed with fine food, especially expensive fish.</note>. They say that **Diagoras** the poet did not just give a boy fish, but—as the story goes—he "released" them while they were half-dead. In a military camp, they say he was once boiling a dish of **conger eels** <note>original: γόγγρων (*gongrōn*)</note> and dissolved it into a broth.

**King Antigonus** <note>Likely Antigonus II Gonatas, King of Macedon.</note> once came upon **Antagoras** the poet while he was boiling eels in a pan, and asked: "Do you think, Antagoras, that **Homer**, who recorded the deeds of **Agamemnon**, would have done so if Agamemnon had been boiling eels?" To which Antagoras replied quite cleverly: "And do you think, O King, that Agamemnon accomplished those great deeds by being a busybody, wandering about the camp to see who was boiling eels?" 

Another time, while Antagoras was boiling a bird, he refused to go to the bathhouse with the King, fearing that his servants would gulp down the broth. When someone remarked that his mother would watch it for him, he replied: "Should I then trust the broth of a little bird to my mother?" 

**Androcydes of Cyzicus**, the painter, was also a fish-lover. As **Polemon** records, he reached such a state of passion for it that when he painted the **Scylla** <note>The legendary sea monster from the Odyssey.</note>, he surrounded her with the specific fish he himself found most delicious. 

Regarding **Philoxenus of Cythera**, the **dithyrambic poet** <note>term: *dithyrambopoios* — a composer of wild, emotional choral hymns.</note>, the comic writer **Machon** writes the following: "They say that Philoxenus, the poet of dithyrambs, was a superlative gourmand. Once, in Syracuse, he bought an octopus two **cubits** <note>term: *pechys* — a unit of length roughly 18 inches; thus a three-foot octopus.</note> long. After preparing it, he ate nearly the whole thing himself, except for the head. He was then seized by such a severe case of indigestion that he was in a very bad way. When a doctor came in and saw him in such a desperate state, he said: 'Philoxenus, if you have any affairs unsettled, set them in order quickly, for you will die by the seventh hour.' Philoxenus replied: 'Everything is finished, doctor, and has been settled long ago. By the grace of the gods, I leave behind my dithyrambs in their prime—all of them crowned with victory—which I dedicate to the Muses, my companions, with Aphrodite and Dionysus as my executors. These are my last wishes. But since the **Charon** <note>The ferryman of the dead.</note> from Timotheus' play does not let me linger, but shouts for me to come to the ferry—as the dark fate calls, which one must obey—so that I may depart for the world below with all my possessions, **give me the rest of my octopus!**'"

In another passage, it is said that Philoxenus of Cythera once prayed to have a neck three cubits long: "So that I might swallow for the longest possible time," he said, "and let all my food provide me with pleasure at once." **Diogenes the Cynic** <note>The famous philosopher who lived in a tub.</note> also died—so they say—after eating a raw octopus which he had craved. 

Regarding Philoxenus, the parodist **Sopater** also says: "For in the midst of two servings of fish, you sit in the center, aiming your sights on them." 

The orator **Hyperides** <note>One of the ten great Attic orators, known for his wit and lifestyle.</note> was also a gourmand, as the comic poet **Timocles** says in his play *Delos*, describing those who took bribes from **Harpalus** <note>A treasurer of Alexander the Great who fled to Athens with stolen wealth, sparking a massive corruption scandal.</note>. He writes: 

"Demosthenes has fifty talents; he is blessed, provided he shares it with no one. And Metrocles has taken much gold—look there, Anagyros! Lucky is the man who receives. Demon and Callisthenes have also taken some, and so they have our forgiveness. And the formidable Hyperides, the prince of the gourmands, has taken his share too; he is the one making our fishmongers rich. For he is a glutton, like the gulls of the sea."

The same poet says in his play *The Icarians*: "There is Hyperides, a river flowing with fish, who overcomes you with the thunderous sounds of sensible speech, bubbling over with boastful, gentle thickets of words... a hired man who has given himself over to persuasion." 

**Philetaerus**, in his play *Asclepius*, says that Hyperides, in addition to his gluttony, was also a gambler. Just as the orator Callippe... **Axionicus**, in *The Lover of Euripides*, says: "Another man, bringing a great salted fish to these places, comes like some Glaucus of the sea, a shark among gourmands, the darling of greedy men. I carry it on my shoulder, telling of its preparation: 'Having soaked the curls of the fish in a green sauce, or fattening its body with the drippings of wild brine, I will hand it over to the all-consuming fire.' Someone said that a man named **Moschion**, a lover of flutes, would eat it boiled in hot brine. And it shouts its own reproach: 'O miserable man, you rejoice in figs and salt-fish, while the gourmand passes by with a choice dish in brine!'" 

The mention of "figs" is a way of mocking him as a **sycophant** <note>term: *sykophantēs* — literally "fig-shower," a term for professional informers or slanderers.</note>, while "salt-fish" perhaps suggests those of low character. **Hermippus** says in his work *On the Pupils of Isocrates* that Hyperides used to take morning walks in the fish market. 

**Timaeus of Tauromenium** even claims that **Aristotle** the philosopher was a gourmand. And **Matron the Sophist** was also a gourmand. This is perhaps shown by **Antiphanes** in *The Cithara Player*, or in *The Beginning*: "No flea ever dug into anyone's eye," he says, "as quickly as Matron approaches a fish." 

**Anaxilas**, in *The Solitary Man*, describes someone snatching the head of a **mullet** <note>original: κεστρέως (*kestreōs*)</note>: "Matron snatched it up, while I am perishing from his excessive gluttony and his snatching of food!" And this was just the head of a mullet. Unless, of course, those who are clever at such things know that there is something useful in a mullet's head, which I will allow the fans of **Archestratus** <note>The author of a famous ancient cookbook/travelogue on fine dining.</note> to explain to you. 

**Antiphanes**, in his play *The Rich Men*, gives a list of gourmands: "Enthymus is there, wearing sandals and a seal-ring, and perfumed; he was calculating his affairs, I know not what. **Phoenicides** and the dearest **Andron**—old-fashioned gourmands, the type who would gulp down whole slices of fish in the marketplace. Those who saw them were amazed at the feat, and they bore the lack of fish very poorly... The circle of those who gather figs..."

# BOOK VIII

<margin>o 2</margin>
<meta>catchword: katamy-</meta>

...they were saying these things: that life is not worth living, nor can it be endured, if some of you lay claim to the sea and spend so much money on it, especially when you get no enjoyment from it, nor should you have to. What use, then, are the islanders? Perhaps they should be broken down by law to provide a regular escort of fish, so that you might finally silence the fishermen. Indeed, **Diogeiton** <note>A figure mentioned in comedy, possibly a well-known gourmand.</note> has ceased his efforts for these reasons, so that we might bring the fish to him. And he said it was "democratic" to hunt such things, for he loved them; those were the youthful "marriages" I once had. **Euphanes** <note>A comic poet of the Middle Comedy.</note> says in his *Muses*, and **Phoenicides** <note>Another comic poet.</note> describes how, when he saw a dish <note>original: λοπάδα (*lopada*) — a flat earthenware dish or casserole</note> boiling over with a multitude of ships full of the "children of Nereus" <note>A poetic way of saying fish.</note>, he raised his hands in a fit of passionate excitement. Who is so skilled by nature to flee from the common crowd, or who would snatch the hot portions from the middle? Where is **Corydus**, or **Phyromachus**, or the "Force of the Hollow"? Let them come to us; perhaps they would receive nothing.

-> <-

**Melanthius** <note>A tragic poet of the late 5th century BCE, often mocked for his gluttony and skin disease.</note>, the tragic poet who also wrote elegies, was of this same character. They lampoon 
<margin>10</margin> him for his **fish-gluttony** <note>term: *opsophagia* — an obsessive craving for "relish," almost exclusively referring to expensive fish.</note>: **Leucon** in *The Clansmen*, **Aristophanes** in *Peace*, and **Pherecrates** in *Petale*. In the play *The Fish*, **Archippus** depicts him as a glutton and has him bound and handed over to the fish to be eaten by them in return. Furthermore, **Aristippus** the Socratic <note>A philosopher and student of Socrates who founded the Cyrenaic school, which emphasized pleasure.</note> was a fish-glutton. When he was once rebuked by **Plato** for his love of fine food, as **Sotion** and **Hegesander** relate, the Delphian writes as follows: Aristippus, when Plato criticized him for buying a great quantity of fish, replied that he had bought them for only two **obols** <note>A small silver coin; roughly the price of a cheap loaf of bread.</note>. When Plato remarked that he would have bought them himself at such a price, Aristippus said: "You see then, O Plato, it is not that I am a glutton, but that you are a **miser** <note>original: φιλάργυρος (*philargyros*) — literally "silver-lover."</note>." 

**Antiphanes**, in *The Flute-Girl* or *The Twins*, mocks a certain Phoenicides for his gluttony, saying: "**Menelaus** fought the Trojans for ten years because of a woman with a beautiful face <note>original: *opsin* — a play on words with *opson* (fish/relish).</note>, but **Phoenicides** fought **Tauria** for the sake of an **eel**." The orator **Demosthenes** also insulted **Philocrates**, because he used the gold he received from his treachery to buy prostitutes and fish, accusing him of licentiousness and gluttony. **Diocles** 
<margin>20</margin> was also a fish-glutton; as Hegesander tells us, when someone asked him which fish was better, the **conger eel** or the **sea bass**, he replied: "The boiled one," while the other said: "The roasted one." 

**Leontius** of Argos, the tragic actor and a student of **Aethylion**, was also a glutton. He was a servant to the King of the **Mauretanians** in his ways, as **Amarantus** says in his *On the Stage*, claiming that he wrote this epigram for himself when he performed the role of **Hypsipyle** poorly: "Do not look upon me, Leontius, the eater of delicacies, who pours out tragic sounds as Hypsipyle with a wicked heart. Truly, I was once a friend to **Bacchus**, nor was I healed through the gold-flecked ears of any through old age. But now, earthenware pots and dry frying pans have taken the place of my voice, as I gratify my stomach." 

Hegesander says that **Phoroscus** the fish-eater was silent about how much of the fish he wanted to take, but when more people followed him, he said: "The things that resist are destroyed by the saw," and he consumed the whole fish. When someone had already eaten the top part of a fish, **Bius** turned it over and ate it greedily, saying: "Ino is working on the other side" <note>A literary joke referencing the mythological figure Ino.</note>. 

<margin>30</margin> **Theocritus of Chios** <note>A 4th-century BCE orator and wit.</note>, when the wife of the glutton Diocles died, saw him making the funeral offerings while weeping and eating fish at the same time. He said: "Stop weeping, you wretch! You won't make the fish-eating any better by it." When the same man had "eaten up" his farm to pay for his fish-habit, he once swallowed a piece of fish so hot he cried out that his palate was burnt. Theocritus remarked: "The only thing left for you to do is to drink up the sea, and then you will have made the three greatest things disappear: the earth, the sea, and the heavens." 

**Clearchus**, in his work *On Lives*, records a certain lover of pleasure as follows: **Technon**, an old flute-player, when **Charmos** the flute-player died (who was a great lover of fish), sent an offering to his tomb. The poet **Alexis** was also a fish-glutton, as **Lynceus of Samos** says; when he was teased by certain "starvelings" for his gluttony and one of them asked what he would eat if he could have anything, Alexis replied: "Roasted starvelings." 

**Nothippus** the tragic poet—whom **Hermippus** mentions in *The Fates*—was also mocked: "If any of the race of men today could fight, and a large roasted **ray-fish** and a side of pork were leading them, no others would need to stay at home, for we would send Nothippus alone. He by himself could swallow down the whole **Peloponnese**." That this was the poet is clearly shown by **Teleclides** in *The Hesiods*. 

**Myiscus** the tragic actor is lampooned by **Plato** <note>The comic poet Plato Comicus, not the philosopher.</note> in *The Rabble* as a glutton: "This is indeed a sea-perch from Anagyrus; let our friend Myiscus the Chalcidian eat it." "You speak well." They also lampoon **Lampon** the diviner for the same reasons: **Callias** in *The Shackled Men*, **Lysippus** in *The Bacchic Women*, and **Cratinus** in *The Runaways*, where he says that for Lampon, no vote of mortals is as powerful as a hot offering of fish. He adds: "Now someone belches. For he devours everything present, and would even fight for a **red mullet**." 

**Hedylus**, in his epigrams, listing various gluttons, mentions a certain **Phaidon** in these lines: "Phaidon always says 'yes' to seaweed and **Chordias** the harper, for he is a fish-glutton." He mentions **Agisis** in these: "The boiled **beaked-fish** has now been thrown into the 'Acorn-snatcher.' <note>A humorous name for a dish or perhaps a person.</note> Let not the holy **Proteus** <note>The shape-shifting sea god.</note> come and turn the contents of the dishes into water and fire. But he will not escape; for he will arrive transformed into something like a 'Golden-flowing Zeus' to enter the 'Acorn-snatcher’s' casserole." He also mocks a woman named **Cleo** for the same vice, calling her "Cleo the fish-glutton."

# FROM THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED (ATHENAEUS)

...and even when their eyes are closing, they still want to eat. Such is the nature of the **conger eel** <note>original: γόγγρος (*gongros*) — a large marine eel, highly prized in antiquity</note>, whether it be at its peak or just a portion. Whether one speaks of Zenion or some other such sign, we don't just speak of the sight of it. We would be most relieved if everything was long ago settled, and not just concerning these eels. For the wretched eels end up in the casserole dish. **Aristodemus**, in his *Laughable Memorabilia*, says that **Euphranor** the gourmand, upon hearing that another fish-eater had died from swallowing a burning hot piece of fish, cried out: "That death is sacrilege!" **Kindon** the gourmand, and **Detylos**—another fellow of that sort—were once served a **gray mullet** <note>original: γλαύκου (*glaukou*) — likely the Bluefish or a similar prized species</note> and nothing else. Kindon snatched the eye, but Detylos pressed his hand over Kindon’s eye and forced him, shouting: "Let go, and I’ll let go!" On another occasion, when a beautiful dish of food was served at a dinner, Detylos, having no other way to ensure he could eat it all himself, spat into the dish. 

**Zopyrus of Citium**, a follower of the Stoic school, acted similarly toward a gourmand who remained silent for a long time. As **Antigonus of Carystus** relates in his *Life of Zeno*, when a single large and expensive fish was served and nothing else was prepared, Zopyrus took the whole thing off the platter as if he intended to eat it all himself. When the other man stared at him, Zopyrus asked: "What do you think those who are silent with you must suffer, if you yourself cannot endure my 'fish-gluttony' <note>original: ὀψοφαγίαν (*opsophagian*) — specifically the craving for rich food, usually fish</note> for even one day?" **Istros** says that the poet **Choerilus**, who received four minae a day from **Archelaus**, spent it all on fish-eating, becoming quite the gourmand. 

I am also aware of the "fish-eating boys" whom **Clearchus** mentions in his work *On Lives*, claiming that **Psammetichus**, the King of Egypt, raised children as fish-eaters because he wanted to discover the sources of the Nile. He also trained others to go without thirst so they could search the sands of Libya, though few of them survived. I also know of the cattle of the **Moschi** in Thrace, who eat fish that are thrown into their mangers. **Phoenicides**, when serving fish to those who had contributed to a shared meal, used to say that while the sea is common property, the fish in it belong to those who bought them. The term "gourmand" <note>original: ὀψοφάγος (*opsophagos*)</note> is used by others, as is the verb "to be a gourmand." **Aristophanes** uses it in the second version of *The Clouds*, and **Cephisodorus** said: "You are a gourmand and a licker of sauces." **Machon** says in a letter: "I am a gourmand; this is the foundation of our art." He goes on to say that one must not be a "bad man" at the table, but must consider the cleanliness of the dining room and not miss the chance to add salt if something needs it. Again, he speaks of the "harmony of sweetness," comparing it to tuning a lyre until everything sounds in accord, and then introducing the "Myconian Nicolaides." 

I also know of a "Gourmand Apollo" <note>original: ὀψοφάγον Ἀπόλλωνα (*opsophagon Apollona*)</note> who is honored among the people of **Elis**. **Polemon** mentions him in his letter to **Attalus**. I also know of the painting of the **Satidae** dedicated in the temple of **Artemis Alpheiusa**. There is also a work by **Cleanthes of Corinth** in which **Poseidon** is depicted bringing a tuna fish to **Zeus** while the latter is in labor <note>A bizarre mythological reference, perhaps related to the birth of Dionysus or Athena</note>, as **Demetrius** records in the eighth book of his *Trojan Array*. After saying this much, **Democritus** himself addressed you, saying he would go and eat his fish, despite the "customs of the Syrians" which have deprived us of fish...

<margin>Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 1, Ch. 23</margin>

...And yet **Antipater of Tarsus**, the Stoic, says in the fourth book of his *On Superstition* that some say **Tatis**, the Queen of the Syrians, was such a gourmand that she issued a decree that no one should eat fish except **Atargatis** <note>The chief Syrian goddess, often depicted as a mermaid</note>. Out of ignorance, the common people call her "Atargatis" and abstain from fish. **Mnasias**, in the second book of his *History of Asia*, says: "It seems to me that Atargatis was a harsh queen who ruled her people sternly, even forbidding them to eat fish, ordering instead that every fish be brought to her because she found the food so delicious. Because of this, the custom still remains that when people pray to the goddess, they dedicate silver or gold fish. However, the priests serve real fish on the goddess's table every day—both boiled and roasted—which the priests of the goddess then consume themselves." 

Coming a little further, he says again: "**Atarchatis** (as **Xanthus the Lydian** says), having been captured by **Mopsus the Lydian**, was drowned with her son **Ichthys** <note>original: Ἰχθύος — literally "Fish"</note> in the lake near **Ascalon** because of her pride, and she was eaten by the fish." Perhaps you, my friends, have intentionally left out the "sacred fish" mentioned by the comic poet **Eriphus**, which he says was prepared for **Geryon** in his play of the same name. In these lines he says:

# BOOK VIII.

...lest the night-storm wash over it. I am not unaware that Ephippus says these same things in his play *Philyta*, through which the same points are arranged. "Prattling such things without drawing breath, he is admired among the youths, though he knows nothing of calculating with pebbles <note>original: ψήφῳ (*psepho*) — referring to an abacus or counting-board</note>; he is solemn, solemnly dragging his fine cloak." For whom Ephippus intended these barbs, it is time for you to seek, noble **Ulpian** <note>Ulpian is a frequent character in this dialogue, often teased for his pedantry</note>, and to teach us. If you find anything ambiguous, stammering, or difficult to utter, repeat it and learn it clearly. "I have more leisure than I wish," as **Aeschylus** says in his *Prometheus*. Even the cook himself—what great thing would he take into his mind, if not a fish? He who is always picking out the bones of the tiny fry and the smelts. And if anything is more unfortunate than a late-arriving little fish, it is the passing over of the large slices. For just as among the "fortunate women," as **Eubulus** says in his *Ixion*: "Eating fine cakes whenever they are present, but also dill and celery and such nonsense, and shredded cress." So it seems to me, even the "white-armored" <note>original: λευκοθώραξ (*leukothorax*) — likely a pun on Ulpian's clothing or perhaps his pale complexion</note> Ulpian, according to my fellow citizen **Cercidas**, knows nothing of what befits a man, but only watches those eating to see if they overlooked a bone, or a piece of gristle, or if some cartilaginous bit was served. We should always keep in mind the words of the noble and brilliant Aeschylus, who said that his tragedies were "slices from the great banquets of **Homer**." Aeschylus was a philosopher among children, who also—when unjustly accused at some point, as **Theophrastus** or **Chamaeleon** says in his work *On Pleasure*—said he dedicated his tragedies to Time, knowing that he would receive the honor due to him. 

<margin>Stratonicus' pun.</margin>
It is also possible for all to be well, as **Stratonicus** the citharist <note>term: citharist — a professional performer on the *kithara*, a sophisticated ancient Greek lyre</note> declared to **Tropis** the Rhodian singer. For **Clearchus**, in his works *On Proverbs*, says that Stratonicus, seeing Tropis—who was physically massive but a poor artist, and smaller in skill than in body—inquired what sort of man he was. He replied: "Nobody, bad, big, fish." Hinting that, first, he was a "nobody"; second, that he was "bad"; and further, that he was "big," but a "fish" because of his voicelessness <note>Greek folklore often described fish as "mute" or voiceless; here it implies Tropis is a silent, talentless singer</note>. **Theophrastus**, in his work *On the Ridiculous*, says the proverb was spoken by Stratonicus, but directed at the actor **Simylas**, dividing the proverb thus: "No big fish is rotten." **Aristotle**, in his *Constitution of the Naxians*, writes about the proverb as follows: Of the wealthy among the Naxians, many lived in the city, but others were scattered throughout the villages. In one of the villages named **Lesades** lived **Telesagoras**, who was exceedingly rich and well-regarded, honored by the people in all things, and especially by the daily gifts sent to him. Whenever people came down from the city and found the goods for sale too expensive, it was a custom for the sellers to say they would rather give them to Telesagoras for free than sell them at such a price. Some young men, while buying a large fish, heard the fisherman say the same thing; being annoyed at hearing this so often, and having been drinking, they went to his house in a rage. Though Telesagoras received them kindly, the youths insulted both him and his two daughters of marriageable age. The Naxians, outraged by this, took up arms and attacked the young men. A great civil strife <note>term: stasis — a period of internal conflict or civil war within a Greek city-state</note> then arose, and the Naxians were led by **Lygdamis**, who through this command emerged as the tyrant of his homeland. 

I do not think it is out of place to speak further, being generous myself with the stories of the citharist Stratonicus, to say something of his witty responses. When he was teaching cithara players, he had in his schoolroom nine statues of the **Muses** and one of **Apollo**, but only two students. When someone asked how many students he had, he said: "With the help of the gods, twelve." 

<margin>Mylasa, a city of Caria, according to Stephanus.</margin>
Upon visiting **Mylasa**, seeing many temples but few people, he stood in the middle of the marketplace and shouted: "Listen, O Temples!" **Machon** records these things in his *Memorabilia*. Once, when Stratonicus visited **Pella**, having heard from many people before that the city used to make "flute-like" <note>original: αὐλωνικούς (*aulonikous*) — a pun on *aulon* meaning both a flute and a narrow channel or gutter</note> sounds in the bathhouse, he observed many youths exercising near the fire, having elegantly trained their color and bodies; he said those who told him were mistaken. But when he was leaving and noticed the "flute" of the belly was twice as wide, he sat down where he could see the clothes-keepers watching the entrances and the gutters, so he wouldn't be defeated by nature or a narrow space. 

A bad harp-player once met Stratonicus and showed off his skill during a drinking party. As the reception was brilliant and ambitious, and Stratonicus, being played to, had no one else to talk to, he smashed his cup and asked for a larger one. Taking many ladles of wine, he showed the cup to the sun, drank it down quickly, and went to sleep, leaving the rest of the revelry to chance. When some other acquaintances of the harp-player arrived, as it seems, the wine-soaked Stratonicus woke up immediately. When they asked if he had been drunk from drinking too much wine, he replied shortly: "For the treacherous and ignorant harp-player," he said, "has killed me like an ox at the manger." 

When Stratonicus once traveled to **Abdera** for the games held there, seeing that each of the citizens possessed their own private herald <note>term: herald — a public messenger or crier</note> and that each would have them proclaim the New Moon whenever they wished, and that almost everyone...

# FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS

When there were far more heralds <note>original: κήρυκας (*kerykas*) — officials who made public announcements, often seen as noisy or self-important</note> in the place than there were citizens, he walked through the city almost on the tips of his toes, staring intently down at the ground. When strangers asked him what sudden ailment had affected his feet, he replied: "I am perfectly healthy, stranger, but I am running away from the dinner-invitations of these flatterers much more than the dinner itself. I am anxious lest I trip over the nets of the heralds and catch my foot in one." When a bad flute-player was about to perform to some hero-shrines, Stratonicus said: "We must speak only good omens; let us pray to the gods as he stands up." Cleon the kitharode <term>kitharode: a professional singer who accompanies themselves on the kithara (a large lyre)</term>, who was nicknamed "The Ox," was singing terribly out of tune and not even using his lyre correctly. Upon hearing him, Stratonicus remarked that while people used to say "an ass at the lyre" <note>A common Greek proverb for someone with no appreciation for art</note>, they now say "an ox at the lyre." When Stratonicus the kitharode sailed to the Black Sea to visit King Berisades, after a long time had passed, he wished to return to Greece, but it seems the king would not let him go. He is said to have replied to Berisades: "Why do you intend to keep me here? Do you want me to stay forever?" Once, while he was visiting Corinth, an old woman stared at him and would not look away, at which Stratonicus said: "By the gods, mother, tell me what it is you want and why you keep looking at me?" She replied, "I was wondering if your mother carried you for ten months and survived the labor." He retorted: "A city that has you for a single day suffers enough." Biothia, the wife of Nicotheontos, went down to the river with her dainty servant girls and was trapped. Then, stepping on some Sicyonian almond shells, she slipped and fell. Stratonicus said: "The sound of a fall at night is not the same." But for this woman, the brilliance did not last, for you destroyed your freedom of speech in the deep sea. Once in Ephesus, when a talentless kitharode was presenting his student to friends, Stratonicus said: "You haven't made a sea-change of him yet" <note>A pun on 'saltiness' or wit</note>. Clearchus says in his second book *On Friendship* that Stratonicus the kitharistes <term>kitharistes: a teacher or player of the lyre</term>, when he was about to rest, always ordered his slave to bring him a drink. "Not because I am thirsty," he said, "but so that I *won't* become thirsty." In Byzantium, when a kitharode performed the introduction well but failed in the rest, Stratonicus stood up and made a proclamation: "Whoever can fall asleep during the introduction of all kitharodes shall receive a thousand drachmas." When asked by someone who were the most wicked people in Pamphylia, he said the Phaselians were the most wicked, but the Sidetae were the most wicked in the whole inhabited world. Again, when asked (as Hegesander tells it) whether the Boeotians or the Thessalians were more barbaric, he said the Eleans were. He even once set up a trophy in his schoolroom and inscribed it "against those who play the kithara badly." When asked by someone which ships are the safest, the long ones or the round ones, he replied: "Those that have been hauled up on shore." In Rhodes, when he was giving a performance and no one applauded, he left the theater, saying: "Where you do not even give what costs you nothing, how can I expect to receive a contribution from you?" He said the Eleans should organize gymnastic games, the Corinthians musical ones, and the Athenians theatrical ones. And if anyone should commit a musical error, he should be flogged, as Charicles says in the first book *On the Contest of the Flute*. When King Ptolemy was discussing kithara-playing with him somewhat contentiously, Stratonicus said: "It is one thing, O King, to hold a scepter, and another to hold a plectrum" <term>plectrum: a small tool used to pluck the strings of a lyre</term>, as Capito the epic poet says in the fourth book of his *Commentaries to Philopappus*. Once, having been invited to hear a kitharode, after the performance he said: "One thing his father gave, but another he won for himself" <note>A parody of a line from the Odyssey</note>. When someone asked what he meant, he said: "His father gave him the gift of being a bad player, but he won his own worthiness by doing it so well." Once, when a beam fell and killed a wicked man, he said: "I believe there are gods; and if there are not, then beams exist." He also records the following after the aforementioned memories of Stratonicus: Stratonicus said to the father of Chrysogonus, who was saying that everything belonged to him—that he was a contractor, and of his sons, one would teach and the other would play the flute. Stratonicus laughed and said: "There is still one thing: you are a plague to all of Greece, not staying in just one city." He said that all Greeks had received a 'payment' from the Muses, from whom he collected a 'fee for lack of music.' He said that Phaon played the flute not with 'harmony' but with 'Cadmus' <note>original: Κάδμον (*Kadmon*) — likely a pun on 'building' or 'founding,' implying his music was as heavy as masonry</note>. When Phaon pretended to be a great flute player and claimed to have a chorus in Megara, Stratonicus said: "You are talking nonsense; for you don't 'have' one there, you 'are' one." He said he most admired the mother of the sophist Satyrus, because no city could bear him for ten days, yet she bore him for ten months. Hearing that Satyrus was visiting Ilium during the Trojan festivals, he said: "Always evils for Ilium" <note>A reference to the proverbial 'Iliad of woes'</note>. When Minnacus disputed with him about music, he said he would not listen to him, because he spoke from a place higher than his ankle. He said that a bad doctor sends those he treats straight to Hades. Meeting an acquaintance whose shoes were well-polished, he expressed sympathy as if the man were doing poorly; he believed the shoes wouldn't be so well-polished unless the man had polished them himself. When someone asked him if Miletus was a great city to live in, and he saw that all the tombs belonged to foreigners, he said: "Let us leave, boy. Here the foreigners seem to be the only ones who die, and none of the citizens." When Zethus the kitharistes was discoursing on music, Stratonicus said he had no right to talk about music, seeing as he chose the most unmusical of names, for if you...

# BOOK VIII

...ten months, and you call Zethus the son of Amphion <note>A reference to Euripides' play *Antiope*, where Zethus mocks his brother Amphion’s devotion to music</note>. While teaching a certain Macedonian to play the kithara, Stratonicus became frustrated that the man was doing nothing he was supposed to do, and told him to "go to Macedonia" <note>This likely implies going back to the uncivilized wilds or is a pun on the cold climate</note>. Once, seeing a cold bathhouse that was poorly built but lavishly decorated, he remarked as he emerged after washing: "I am not surprised that many people dedicate votive tablets here. For every person who bathes here likely dedicates a tablet as a survivor of a great peril" <note>Votive tablets were typically dedicated by those saved from shipwrecks; here, Stratonicus suggests the cold water is a life-threatening ordeal</note>. He used to say that for eight months it was cold, and for the other four it was winter. He said that those coming from the Black Sea <note>original: *Pontos*</note> came from the "Sea of Destruction" <note>original: *ek tou olethrou* — a pun on the harsh conditions of the region</note>. He called the Rhodians "white Cyrenaeans" <note>The people of Cyrene were famous for luxury; "white" implies the Rhodians were even softer or more effeminate</note> and their city the "City of Suitors" <note>A reference to the lazy, gluttonous suitors of Penelope in the *Odyssey*</note>. 

He called Heracleia "Man-Corinth," and Byzantium the "armpit of Greece." He referred to the Leucadians as "stale Corinthians," and the Ambraciots as "anchovy-ots" <note>original: *membrakiotas*, a pun on *membras*, a cheap little fish</note>. As he was leaving the gates of Heracleia and looking all around, someone asked him what he was looking for; he replied that he was ashamed and didn't want to be seen, as if he were walking out of a brothel. Seeing two men bound in the harbor, he remarked that it was "small-town politics" not to be able to fill a whole prison.

When a music theorist <term>harmonikos: a scholar of music theory rather than a performer</term> was talking nonsense to him about harmony, he said: "Wretches! If only each of you actually knew your own craft." In Maroneia, while drinking with some locals, he said he wanted to know which part of the city he was in, even if they led him there blindfolded. When they led him and asked, he said he was "at the tavern," because the entirety of Maroneia is one big tavern. To Telephanes <note>A famous flute player</note>, when he began to blow into his flute, Stratonicus, reclining nearby, said he sounded like someone 
<margin>soap, according to the Suda</margin>
belching. To a bath-attendant in Cardia who provided terrible soap <note>original: *rymma*</note> and salty water, he said he felt he was "being besieged by land and by sea." After defeating his rivals in Sicyon, he dedicated a trophy in the temple of Asclepius with the inscription: "Stratonicus, from the spoils of the bad kithara-players." 

When someone sang a song and he was asked whose melody it was, and the person said it was by Carcinus <note>original: *Karkinos*, which means "Crab"</note>, he replied: "It certainly sounds more like a crab's work than a human's." In Maroneia, he said there was no spring, only "warmth" <note>original: *alean* — a pun on the local wine or climate</note>. In Phaselis, when a bath-attendant was arguing about the fee (claiming that foreigners should pay more), he said: "You rascal, for the sake of a small bit of copper you have made me a 'Phaselite'" <note>A pun on a type of bean or boat, implying he was being squeezed or cheated</note>. When someone praised him just to get something from him, he said the man was "a beggar of the highest order." Teaching in a small city, he said: "This isn't a city (*polis*), it's a 'barely' (*molis*)." In Pella, he went to a well and asked if it was drinkable. When the locals hauling the ropes said, "We drink it," he replied, "Then it isn't drinkable," for the people there happened to look sickly and pale <note>original: *chloroi* — greenish-yellow</note>.

Upon hearing the song of Timotheus, he said if the man had given birth to a "contractor" <note>original: *ergolabon* — implies someone who works for hire/money rather than art</note> and not a god, what kind of noises would he have made? When Polyidus boasted that his student Philotas had defeated Timotheus, Stratonicus said he marveled that Polyidus didn't know that Philotas makes "decrees," but Timotheus makes "laws" <note>Implying Timotheus's work has more permanence and authority</note>. To Areius the harper who was annoying him, he said, "Go harp to the crows!" <note>A Greek idiom equivalent to "Go to hell"</note>. In Sicyon, when an unfortunate man was insulting him, he simply called him "unlucky." 

Stratonicus himself, observing the Rhodians to be luxurious and heavy drinkers, said they were "white Cyrenaeans." He also called Rhodes the "City of Suitors," thinking that while they differed from the Homeric suitors in their complexion (being prone to luxury), they were just like them in their downward slide into pleasure. Stratonicus became an emulator of these witty sayings from the poet Simonides, as Ephorus says in the second book of his *On Inventions*, claiming that Philoxenus of Cythera also studied such things. Phanias the Peripatetic says in his second book *On Poets* that Stratonicus the Athenian seems to have been the first to introduce many-stringed playing to the solo kithara, and was the first to take students in music theory and to set up a diagram for it. He was also quite talented at making jokes. He also says that he died because of his frankness in joking, having been forced to drink poison by Nicocles, the King of the Cyprians, for mocking the king’s sons.

I have often marveled at the works of Aristotle, whom the wise have made so famous—by Zeus, and at Democritus too! If one were to believe his words, as one might trust other philosophers and orators, one would think he learned with great accuracy—perhaps from some Proteus or Nereus rising from the depths—exactly what fish do and how they live. For he wrote these things down so that they are "wonders for fools," as the comic poet says. For he claims that for the trumpet-shell <note>original: *keryx*</note> and all the shell-skinned creatures, their kind is produced without mating. And he says that the purple-fish and the trumpet-shell are long-lived. How could he know that the purple-fish lives six years? And he says that the mating of the viper takes a very long time, and that the wood-pigeon is the largest, the rock-dove second, and the turtle-dove the smallest. 

How does he know that the male horse lives thirty-five years, but the female more than forty, and even claims some live to seventy-five? He records that nits are born from the mating of lice, and that a caterpillar comes from a changing worm, from which comes a moth <note>original: *bombylios*</note>, which is then called a *enekydalos*. Furthermore, he says that bees live up to six years, and some even seven. But he says no one has ever seen a bee or a drone mating, which is why it is not clear which of them are male or female. How can he know how many bees there are? For they always maintain the same number in their life and do not change, but gather together and work without spiritlessness. Yet he speaks as if he knew the number of bees, full of the same conceit as...

### FROM THE ATHENAEUS DEIPNOSOPH[ISTAE]

...that those [flies] are of honey, where does it say they suffice? He says in his work *On Longevity* that a certain fly lives for six or seven years. For what is the proof of these things? And where does he say that ivy grows on a stag’s horn? He says that owls and crows are unable to see during the day, which is why they hunt for their own food at night. And not all night, but only at twilight. He also says the characteristics of their eyes are not similar. For some are gray-blue, some black, and others fierce-looking. To perceive that every eye has a persuasive difference, he says, is a task for the eyes. For he does not say how the Egyptians, among men, are naturally well-disposed toward sharpness of vision, but in their character are the best.

<margin>On the Nature of Animals, Book 1</margin>
And of the others, some have eyes on the outside, though not by nature, and others perhaps not. And of some, they are most sharp-sighted, while others are most malicious. He says those who have eyes in the middle are reasonable, while some are also blinkers. He says that some are shameless, while those who stare fixedly are unstable. Those with eyes in the middle have the best characters. He claims that man alone among animals has his heart on the left side, while other animals have it in the middle. He says it has been observed that males have more teeth than females, and that this is even the case with sheep, pigs, and goats. He says not a single fish has a tongue, and that neither fish nor birds have breasts.

He says the dolphin alone does not have a gall bladder. But some say that they do not have a gall bladder in the liver, but near the intestines, such as the *ellops* <note>original: *ellops* — an unidentified prized fish, perhaps a sturgeon</note>, the *synagris* <note>original: *synagris* — a type of sea-bream</note>, the moray eel, the swordfish, and the swallow-fish. The *amia* <note>original: *amia* — likely the bonito</note> has its gall bladder stretched out along the entire intestine. He also discussed how the kite <note>a bird of prey</note> has it in the liver and the intestines. And how the "goat-head" <note>original: *aigokephalos* — likely a bird like the godwit or owl</note> has it in the liver or the stomach. As for the pigeon, quail, and swallow, some have it in the intestines, others in the stomach. He says that the soft-shelled <note>mollusks</note>, the shell-skinned <note>crustaceans</note>, the cartilaginous fish <note>sharks and rays</note>, and the insects mate for a long time. He says the dolphin and certain fish mate by lying alongside one another. He claims that the mating of dolphins is slow, but that of fish is quick.

Furthermore, he says the lion has bones so hard that when they are struck together, fire flashes out as if from stones. The dolphin has bones and not a spine. The cartilaginous fish have both cartilage and a spine. Of the fish, some are land-dwellers, some are water-dwellers, and some are "fire-dwellers" <note>original: *pyribia* — mythical creatures believed to live in fire, like the salamander</note>. There are also some called "ephemerals" which live for only a single day. Others are amphibious, such as the hippopotamus, the crocodile, and the seal.

He says all animals have two "leading" feet, but the crab has four. He says that whatever animals did not need to be... are either legless, two-footed, or four-footed. Whatever animals have more than four feet are bloodless. Therefore, everything that moves does so by four points: man with two feet and two hands, a bird with two feet and two wings, and an eel or conger eel with two fins and two bends of the body.

Furthermore, of animals, some have hands, like man. Others seem to, like the monkey. For none of the irrational animals teaches or receives, though he explains how hands are given as tools. Again, of animals, some have joints, like man, the donkey, and the ox. Others are without joints, such as snakes, *aria* <note>uncertain: perhaps a type of worm or sea creature</note>, and "lungs" <note>original: *pneumones* — likely referring to sea-lungs or jellyfish</note>. Many animals do not appear in every season, such as those that hibernate. Even those that do not hibernate do not always appear, such as swallows and storks.

Though I have many more things to say about the nonsense spoken by "the pharmacist" <note>A derogatory nickname for Aristotle, referring to a rumor that he sold drugs before becoming a philosopher</note>, I shall stop. And yet, I know that even Epicurus, that greatest lover of truth, said these things about him in his *Letter on Occupations*: that after squandering his inheritance, Aristotle rushed into military service, and that faring poorly in that, he turned to the drug-selling business; then, as Plato's Walk <note>the Peripatos</note> was being filled up, he presented himself and sat in on the lectures, not being without talent. And little by oily little, he emerged into the field of study. I know that only Epicurus said these things against him; neither Eubulides nor Cephisodorus dared to say any such thing against the sophist, nor did those who published treatises against the man.

<margin>Gellius, Book 5, Ch. 3</margin>
In the same letter, Epicurus also says that Protagoras the sophist was originally a porter and a wood-carrier, and first became a scribe for Democritus. Having been admired by him for a particular way he bound wood together, he was taken up by him from that beginning, and taught letters in a certain village, from which he was spurred on to become a sophist.

And I, in turn, fellow guests, am moved by these many words to finally turn the cooks toward the business of the belly, because of this feast of many words, lest they serve the food cold. For as Cynulcus said, quoting the comic poet Alexis in his *Milkon*: "No one would eat cold food."

He says: "If they do not serve it hot... you say the good Plato is good everywhere; you understand that the sweet is certainly sweet here too." Not without charm is the story of Sphaerus, who studied under Cleanthes after leaving Chrysippus. When he was sent for and came to a fishing party...

But he cleverly declared that he did not consent to the idea that they *were* birds, but only that it was *reasonable* <note>original: *eulogon*</note> that they were birds. He argued that an "apprehensive perception" <note>original: *katalēptikē phantasia* — a Stoic term for a clear, undeniable truth</note> differs from a "reasonable belief." For the one is infallible, while the "reasonable" can turn out otherwise. And so for us, according to the apprehensive perception, and the...

Among the rock-fish, the wrasse <note>original: "phykis"</note>—and there are two types of wrasse—being very tender little fish, are flavorless and easily digested. ->FROM ATHENAEUS' DEIPNOSOPHISTAE<-

...and a large octopus, and delicate fish. The **pelamys** <note>original: "pelamys" — a young tunny or Atlantic bonito</note> is very nourishing and heavy, suitable for boiling but hard to digest. When salted, it is better, similar to the belly pieces, and acts as a thinning agent. The larger version is called the **synodontis** <note>original: "synodontis" — literally "with joined teeth," likely a larger variety of sea bream or tuna</note>. It is analogous to the *pelamys*, but the *palamys* <note>original: "palamys" — likely a spelling variant or slightly different growth stage</note> is tougher. The **swallow-fish** <note>original: "chelidonion" — likely a type of flying fish</note>, which resembles the octopus, has a fluid of its own that causes difficulty in flow <note>original: "dysroian" — possibly referring to digestion or bile</note> and stirs the blood. The **orkynos** <note>original: "orkynos" — a very large tuna</note> is mud-dwelling, and the larger ones resemble the swallow-fish in their toughness. Its belly-parts <note>original: "hypogastria"</note> or the collar-bone area are flavorful and tender. Those called **korai** <note>original: "korai" — literally "damsels" or "puppets," referring to small young fish</note> are good when salted. Xanthias says it is smelly and more tender than the *orkynos*. These things Diphilus has said. But Mnesitheus the Athenian, in his book *On Foods*, says there is a genus of larger fish called "sliced fish" <note>original: "tmeton"</note> by some, and "deep-sea fish" <note>original: "pelagion"</note> by others. Examples include the **gilt-head sea bream** <note>original: "chrysophrys"</note>, the **grey-fish** <note>original: "glaukos"</note>, and the **phagros** <note>original: "phagros" — the common sea bream</note>. These are difficult to process. 
<margin>10</margin>
When processed, however, they provide many times more nourishment. The genus of scaled fish, such as **tunny**, **mackerel**, **small tunny**, **conger eels**, and the like, happens to be migratory. Those that are seen neither by themselves nor in schools are more easily digested, such as conger eels, **sharks** <note>original: "karchariai"</note>, and similar types. Among these migratory fish, the edible ones should be eaten after a period of fasting (as they are very fatty), because they are heavy and hard to process. For this reason, they are best when salted. These are the finest of the salted meats. They are also useful when roasted, as they are naturally fatty. Those called **fleshy fish** <note>original: "sarka" — likely referring to cartilaginous fish like sharks and rays</note> generally have a smell like that of a goat <note>original: "tragia"</note> on the surface of their skin; they do not have scales, but rather skin like that of **rays** <note>original: "batides"</note> and **angel-fish** <note>original: "rhinai"</note>. All these are easily crumbled but not fragrant; they create moist humors in the body and are the most laxative of all boiled fish. 
<margin>20</margin>
When roasted, they are inferior. The genus of **mollusks** <note>original: "malakia" — "soft-bodied creatures" including cephalopods</note>, such as octopuses and cuttlefish and the like, have flesh that is hard to digest, which is why they are suited for sexual arousal <note>original: "aphrodisiasmous"</note>. For they are themselves "windy" <note>original: "pneumatodeis"</note>, and the time of sexual intercourse requires a windy or spirited condition <note>original: "pneumatodous diatheseos"</note> <note>Ancient medicine taught that erections were caused by "pneuma," a mixture of air and vital spirit.</note>. These become better when boiled, for they contain poor-quality fluids—specifically the kind they release when washed. Boiling draws these out of the flesh. Because they require gentle heating with liquid, the boiling acts as a kind of washing for them, whereas roasting dries out their moisture. Furthermore, since their flesh is naturally tough, it is logical that they should be prepared this way. **Small fry** <note>original: "aphyai"</note>, **small sardines** <note>original: "membrades"</note>, **hair-fish** <note>original: "trichides"</note>, and all others where we eat the bones along with the flesh, all make digestion "windy" or bloated. They provide moist nourishment. Thus, the digestion does not happen evenly, as the flesh is digested too quickly while the bones are dissolved much later. Because the small fry are naturally bony, they hinder the processing of each other; 
<margin>30</margin>
moisture results from the nourishment, and gas from the digestion. They are better when boiled, but they affect the bowels unevenly. Those called **rock-fish** <note>original: "petraia"</note>—**gobies**, **scorpion-fish**, **turbots** <note>original: "psettai"</note>, and the like—provide our bodies with a dry nutritional state; they are bulky and satisfying, digest quickly, do not leave behind much waste, and do not produce gas. Every side-dish <note>original: "opson"</note> becomes more digestible when simply seasoned, and the rock-fish are simply prepared for pleasure. Similar to these is the genus called **soft-fleshed** <note>original: "malakosarkon"</note>, like the **wrasse** <note>original: "kichlai"</note> and **sea-blackbird** <note>original: "kossyphoi"</note>. These are moister than the former. For recovery, they provide more enjoyment; they are more laxative for the bowels and more diuretic than the rock-fish because they have moister and more abundant flesh. If one wishes to move the bowels, one should give them boiled; if the bowels are moderate, they are nourishing when roasted. 
<margin>40</margin>
For urination, they are useful prepared either way. Those parts of the sea where rivers and lakes empty, and where there are great depths and gulfs, are places where the fish are entirely moist-nourished and tend to be fatter. They are sweeter to eat, but worse for digestion and nutrition. On rocky shores and very open seas, most fish are tough, thin, and battered by the waves. However, in places that are deep near the shore and not subject to great winds, and where there are coastal outflows, there one finds the most kinds of fish that are consistent in terms of pleasure, digestibility, and bodily nourishment. The heaviest of sea fish are those that migrate from the sea into rivers and lakes, such as **mullets** <note>original: "kestreis"</note>, and generally any fish that can live in both types of water. Of those that live entirely in rivers and lakes, the river fish are better. 
<margin>50</margin>
For lake water is a kind of decay <note>original: "sepsis"</note> of waters. Among river fish themselves, the best are those in the swiftest-flowing rivers, and those that are "fiery-eyed"; these do not exist unless the river is swift and cold. They differ from other river fish in their ability to swim. These things you might learn from us, as many of you as wish to buy fish according to your ability to do so healthily. For according to the parasite in Antiphanes' play...

-># BOOK 8.<-

I was not at all pushed regarding the marketing <note>original: "opsonia" — the purchasing of relish or fish, a central part of Greek daily life</note>, nor was I very honored by those who discovered things in other ways; wherever one might escape a hangover in the Greek fashion. However, I am not such a **fish-lover** <note>original: "philichthys"</note> as the character in the same poet's *Boutalion*, who seems to have devised a way for country-folk to eat. For he says: "Indeed, I will feast you today, and you will go to the market for us, taking † some money, for otherwise I do not know how to shop well; tell me which relish you love and enjoy, speak of each one specifically, what fish you would most gladly eat. He went to the field bringing some fish-monger's sprats <note>original: "mainides"</note> and red mullets <note>original: "triglides"</note>. And by Zeus, it pleased us all greatly, and so now tell me: Would you eat these yourself, even if the other is small? For we know all these large ones are man-eaters—man-eaters because they have taken [us]—but these are the foods of Elene <note>This name is likely a corruption or refers to a local deity/character</note>, sprats and 
<margin>10</margin> red mullets." In *The Countryman*, he said the sprats and red mullets were "the foods of Hecate" <note>Hecate was an underworld goddess to whom offerings were left at crossroads; these small fish were considered cheap or ritual offerings</note>. And Philippus, disparaging even small fish, says in *The Linden Tree*: "Papias, do you want to run to the market and buy for me? Tell me what? Fish with sense, father, not babies <note>meaning small fry</note>; I don't know what the money will be for silver." And very pleasant is the young man in the same poet's *The Spit-Bearers* <note>original: "Obeliaphoroi"</note> who diminishes everything regarding the marketing, speaking thus: "Buy cheaply. For everything is enough, tell me sometime. Not expensively, but cleanly whatever there is, for the sake of piety... small squids, little cuttlefish, and some spiny lobster <note>original: "karabos"</note> if he catches one, that will suffice. How sweet on the table are little eels <note>original: "egchelyia"</note>, sometimes Thebes sends them; from there take a little rooster-flesh, a little partridge-ling. If someone brings such things, 
bring them; how small-minded you are, you say I am too expensive. Will someone mix † meat for us of all things? No, but bring it immediately. Tomorrow we will dine on the **little calf of the Crow**."
<margin>20</margin> The difficult man in Mnesimachus’ play of the same name, being very stingy, says to the profligate youth: "But I entreat you, do not order too many things for me, nor things too wild, nor those plated in silver. But moderate things for your uncle—how can they be even more moderate, you divine man? How concise? And deceive me: do not call it 'fish' for me, but 'fishlet' <note>original: "ichthydion"</note>. For I will perish much more pleasantly."
Since the term occurred in the preceding lines, my dearest Ulpian, and you sons of grammarians, tell me what meaning the character in the aforementioned lines meant by "tomorrow we will dine on the little calf of the Crow." For I think there is some history to it, and I long to learn. And Plutarch said that those called **Crow-singers** <note>original: "Koronistai"</note> are part of Rhodian history; he cannot recite the history from memory at the moment, because it has been a very long time since he encountered the book containing these things. But I know that Phoenix of Colophon, the iambic poet, mentions certain men who collect [donations] for the Crow, and say these things:
> "Noble people, give a hand of barley to the Crow,
<margin>30</margin> > Or to the child of Apollo <note>referring to the crow</note> a bed of wheat,
> Or bread, or a half-obol, or whatever anyone wishes;
> Give, O good people, † each what he has in his hands to the Crow,
> And she will receive a grain of salt. For she loves to feast on these entirely.
> He who gives salt now, will later give a honeycomb.
> O boy, open the door, Wealth has heard,
> And a maiden brings figs to the Crow.
> May the gods allow the girl to be sent for [in marriage],
> And find a wealthy and famous husband.
> And may she place a boy in the hands of her old father,
> And a girl on her mother's knees...
> To nourish a wife for her brothers.
> But I, wherever my feet carry me, an eye,
> I pass through the courtyard, singing at the doors,
> To the giver and the non-giver, more than these."

And at the end of the iambic poem he says:
> "But O good people, reach out from what your inner chamber abounds;
> Give, O Lord, and you, bride, many things to me,
> It is the custom for the Crow. And a hand begging.
> Knowing such things, give something and you will make use of it."

Those who collect for the Crow were called "Crow-singers," as Pamphilus of Alexandria says in his work *On Names*, and the songs 
<margin>40</margin> sung by them are called **Crow-songs** <note>original: "koronismata"</note>, as Agnocles the Rhodian relates in *On Crow-singing*. 
<margin>Swallow-singing.</margin>
And another type of collection among the Rhodians is called **Swallow-singing** <note>original: "chelidonizein"</note>. Regarding this, Theognis says in his second book *On the Sacrifices in Rhodes*, writing thus: "The Rhodians call a certain type of collecting 'swallow-singing,' which happens in the month of Boedromion. It is called swallow-singing because of the habitual refrain:
> The swallow has come, has come, bringing beautiful seasons and a beautiful year.
> White on the belly and black on the back.
> Do you not roll out a fruit-cake from your rich house,
> And a cup of wine and a basket of cheese and wheat?
> The swallow does not even reject pulse-bread;
> Shall we go away or shall we receive? If you give something—
> But if not, we will not permit it; either we will carry away the door, or the lintel,
> Or the woman sitting inside.
> She is small, we will carry her easily.
> But if you bring something, may you bring something great.
> Open, open the door for the swallow,
> For we are not old men, but children."

This collection was first introduced by Cleobulus of Lindus in Lindus when a need arose for a 
<margin>50</margin> collection of money. Since we have mentioned Rhodian histories, 
<margin>Fish-divination.</margin>
let us "talk fish" <note>original: "ichthyologēsōmen" — a pun on "speak of fish"</note> and I myself come to you from beautiful Rhodes, where the most pleasant Lynceus says [fish] are shown to be. Ergeias the Rhodian, in his work *On Phoenician Matters*, relating something about the Phoenicians who settled the island, says that those around Phalanthus held a very strong and ancient city in Ialysus...

...holding out against Iphiclus. For there was an oracle <note>original: "thesphaton," a divine decree</note> or a prophecy given to them that he should leave the land once **white crows** appeared and fish were seen in the mixing bowls <note>original: "krateres," large vessels used for mixing wine and water</note>. Expecting that this would one day happen, they were somewhat more relaxed regarding the war. But Iphiclus, having learned of these oracles from one of the Phoenicians, laid an ambush for Phalanthus’s servant, whose name was Larcas, while he was going to fetch water. After making a pact of trust with him, Iphiclus caught some small fish or trapped them in a net, threw them into the water jar, and gave them to Larcas. He then commanded him, as he carried the water, to pour it into the mixing bowl from which the wine was poured for Phalanthus. Larcas did this; meanwhile, Iphiclus caught some crows and, having smeared them with white chalk <note>original: "gypsos"</note>, released them.

<margin>Fish-divination.</margin>
When Phalanthus saw the crows, he went to the mixing bowls. As soon as he saw the fish as well, he supposed the land no longer belonged to them. He then sent a herald to Iphiclus, wishing to depart under a truce along with those under his command. When Iphiclus agreed, Phalanthus devised a trick of his own. Having slaughtered [animals], he cleaned out their bellies and attempted to smuggle out gold or silver inside them. But Iphiclus perceived this and prevented it. When Phalanthus brought up the oath he had sworn—that he would allow him to take out what he was "carrying in his belly"—Iphiclus argued back. He offered them ships to be carried away, but he disabled the rudders, the oars, and the sails, swearing that he would provide ships "of a kind," but nothing else. Being held by this helplessness, the Phoenicians buried much of their wealth, marking the spots so that they might recover them later upon returning. However, they left much behind for Iphiclus. In this way, the Phoenicians were removed from the country, and the Greeks took control of affairs. Polyzelus tells the same story in his *Rhodian History*, mentioning the fish and the crows, though he alone says it was Phakas <note>A variant name for the leader</note> and his daughter Dirce. She, having fallen in love with Iphiclus and making a marriage agreement through her nurse, persuaded the water-carrier to bring fish and throw them into the mixing bowl. It was also she who whitened the crows and released them.

Creophylus, in his *Annals of the Ephesians*, says that those who founded Ephesus, after suffering much from a lack of space, finally sent one of their number to the god <note>The Oracle at Delphi</note> to ask where they should establish their city. The god declared: "Establish a city where a fish shall show you, and a wild boar shall lead the way." It is said that at the place where the fountain called Hypelaeus now stands and the Sacred Harbor is, some fishermen were eating their breakfast. One of the fish, leaping out with a hot coal, set fire to some brushwood, which in turn stirred up a wild boar that happened to be in the thicket. Disturbed by the fire, the boar ran far up the mountain called Tracheia, and finally fell when it was struck by a javelin at the spot where the Temple of Athena now stands. The Ephesians then crossed over from the island and, after living there for twenty-two years, founded Tracheia and the area near Corissus; they also established the Temple of Artemis in the marketplace and the temple of Pythian Apollo by the harbor. 

While many things were still being said, there suddenly arose throughout the whole city the booming of flutes and the sound of cymbals, together with the beat of drums accompanied by singing. It happened to be the festival of the *Thyea*. This was anciently called the *Paselgia*, but is now called the **Roman Festival**, established in honor of the Fortune of the City <note>The goddess Tyche or Roma</note> and the temple consecrated by that most excellent and most musical Emperor, **Hadrian**. Every year on that notable day, all those dwelling in Rome celebrate a festival, 

<margin>Odyssey, Book 1.</margin>
<margin>Ballismus (Dancing).</margin>
those who [live] in the city. But Ulpian spoke up again: "What is this? A banquet or a wedding? Since this is certainly no <term>eranos</term> <note>a "potluck" or meal where guests contribute</note>." And he asked of what kind of "booming" they spoke—"Since everyone in the city is <term>ballizousin</term> <note>dancing or prancing</note> for the goddess, my good man," Ulpian said with a laugh—"and which of the Greeks ever used the word <term>ballismos</term>? Is it the same as saying everyone in the city is revelling, or dancing, or any of those other terms? You, having purchased a word from a 'land of iron' <note>i.e., a foreign or harsh place</note>, have ruined the wine by pouring in water." 

And Myrtilus said: "Nevertheless, I shall show you that the name is quite Greek, my friend, since you value such things. For we observe that everyone is silenced by ignorance—but you show yourself to be emptier than a kettle. **Epicharmus**, most wonderful sir, mentions the *ballismos* in his *The Spectators*, and Italy is not far from Sicily. In that play, the spectators, looking at the offerings at Delphi, say the following about each one: 'speaking of bronze mixing bowls.' And the rest... <unclear>how great a thing the dancing (ballismos) was</unclear>. And **Sophron**, in his work titled *The Bridesmaid*, says: 'and then taking it, he leads the way for those who were dancing (*eballizon*),' and again, 'those who were dancing filled the chamber with <unclear>shadows</unclear>.' Furthermore, **Alexis** says in *The Girl with the Haircut*: 'For I see a crowd of revellers approaching, and I hope that these fine and good men, who are doing well for themselves with their dancing (*ballismon*), do not meet me alone at night; for they would never let me go without stripping me of my cloak.'"

<margin>Odyssey, Book 1.</margin>
"I know the name from elsewhere too, and I will bring it to mind later. But you are the one who ought to tell us—since you remember those Homeric lines: 'What feast, what throng is this? What need have you of it? Is it a banquet (*eilapine*) or a wedding? Since this is certainly no <term>eranos</term>.' How do these differ from one another? Since you are silent, I shall speak. For already, following the words of the Syracusan poet... the ancients used to call sacrifices and the more magnificent preparations **banquets** (*eilapinai*), and those who partook in them were 'banqueters.' But <term>eranoi</term> are the gatherings where contributions are made by the participants, from the act of mixing and bringing things together..."
