<meta>This page continues the discussion of social gatherings and terminology related to dining, following the previous page's focus on historical and mythological anecdotes regarding food and divine signs. Here, the author analyzes the religious and etymological origins of different types of feasts.</meta>

-># BOOK 8.<-

...each thing. The same gathering is called both a "subscription feast" <note>original: "eranos," a meal where guests contribute</note> and a "religious guild" <note>original: "thiasos," a group associated with a specific god</note>, and those who come together are called guild-members or contributors. The crowd that follows Dionysus is also called a *thiasos*, as Euripides says: "I see three guilds <note>original: "thiasous"</note> of female dancers." The term *thiasos* was given in honor of the god; for the Laconians <note>The Spartans</note> call the gods *sious* <note>original: "sious," a dialectal variation of "theous"</note>. On the other hand, the word for a lavish banquet <note>original: "eilapine"</note> comes from the preparation and expense involved. For "to empty out" <note>original: "laphuxai" and "lapaxai"</note> means to clear out and spend. 
<margin>Lavish Banquet.</margin>
Hence, poets also use the word "to sack" <note>original: "alapaxai"</note> for plundering, and things snatched away to be consumed are called "spoils" <note>original: "laphura"</note>. Aeschylus and Euripides call such festivities *eilapinas*, from the word meaning "to have been emptied." For the word "to lap up" <note>original: "lapto"</note> means to gulp down, and when something is emptied, it becomes "slack" <note>original: "lagaron"</note>, from which we get the words for "hollow" <note>original: "lagona"</note> or "thin wafer" <note>original: "laganon"</note>. From the word for "emptying" <note>original: "lapaxai"</note> comes the word for "flank" <note>original: "lapara"</note>. To "gluttonize" <note>original: "laphuxai"</note> is to devour greedily, derived from emptying and clearing out. Even "to spend" <note>original: "dapanan"</note> is said to come from "lapping up."

For if it is connected to gluttony, that is why the term "to devour" <note>original: "dapsai"</note> or "to tear apart" <note>original: "dardaptein"</note> is used for those who eat greedily and like beasts.
<margin>Odyssey, Book 3.</margin>
Homer says: "Then the dogs and birds devoured <note>original: "katedapsan"</note> him." They called feasts *euochiai* not because of the "nourishment" <note>original: "trophē"</note> involved, but because of the "well-being" found in coming together to honor the divine and to move themselves toward cheerfulness. They called the drink *methu* <note>wine</note> because it was "after the sacrifice" <note>original: "meta to thuein"</note>—whatever amount they set aside for the god—and they addressed the god as Methymnaean, or Lyaeus <note>the Deliverer</note>, or Euius and Heïus. Similarly, they called someone who was not gloomy or pensive "cheerful" <note>original: "hilaros"</note>. Therefore, they ask for the divinity to be "propitious" <note>original: "ileon"</note>, crying out "ie, ie!" Hence, they named the place where this was done "holy" <note>original: "hieron"</note>. That they used "propitious" and "cheerful" to mean the same thing is shown by Epicharmus in the play entitled *Hope*. In a passage where he speaks of needing a certain companion, he says:

"Then, if one of us happens to enter while grieving, 
she flatteringly entertains him with pleasure,
and kisses him—not with a mouth that clashes like an enemy's,
but like little sparrows with gaping beaks, so that she consoles him.
She immediately made him **cheerful** <note>original: "hilaron"</note>, 
removed all his grief, and showed him to be **propitious** <note>original: "ileon"</note>."
<margin>Gods present at feasts.</margin>
The ancients, having imagined the gods in human form, arranged their festivals accordingly. For they saw that while it is impossible to turn men away from their impulse toward enjoyment, it is useful and beneficial to ensure they conduct themselves in an orderly and decent manner by setting aside a specific time. After sacrificing to the gods first, they then allowed themselves relaxation, so that each person, believing the gods had come to receive the first-fruits and libations, would conduct their social gathering with reverence. 
<margin>Odyssey, Book 1.</margin>
Homer, at least, says: "Athena came to share in the rites." And Poseidon "went to the distant Ethiopians to receive a hecatomb of bulls and rams." 
<margin>Iliad, Book 1.</margin>
And Zeus "went yesterday to a feast, and all the gods followed with him." And if an elderly man is present anywhere, he is respected by choice; they are ashamed to say or do anything unseemly. As Epicharmus says somewhere: "But in silence, something good and better." 

Supposing, then, that the gods were near them, they spent their festivals in a decent and sober manner. 
<margin>30</margin>
Hence, it was not the custom among the ancients to recline, but they feasted while sitting. Nor did they drink to the point of intoxication; rather, when they had poured out as much as their heart desired, each went home. 

But those today who claim to sacrifice to the gods, and invite those they consider friends (and not just members of the household) to the sacrifice, end up cursing their children, insulting their wives, and beating the servants. They threaten the crowd, almost 
<margin>Iliad, Book 2.</margin>
saying the words of Homer: "Now go to dinner, so that we may join the battle." They take to heart the things said by those who have made things worse, as Pherecrates says in his *Hosia*, or in *Nicomachus the Rhythm-Master*—whoever the author may be:

"Do not, after calling a friend to a rich feast, 
be annoyed when you see him arrive; 
for it is a base man who does this. 
Rather, with a very easy mind, delight your own heart and delight him."

But nowadays, people do not remember these words at all. They learn by heart the following lines, which are certainly added from the *Great Eoiae* or the *Great Works* attributed to Hesiod:

"If one of us, while sacrificing, invites someone to dinner, 
we are annoyed if he comes, and we look askance as he enters, 
wishing he would go out the door as quickly as possible."

Then, knowing this, how could one repay it? As one of the fellow-drinkers said, "How can you get rid of this?" The host himself is annoyed at the one who lingers, and immediately recites elegiac verses: "Do not force anyone to stay among us against their will, nor wake Simonides when he is sleeping." For such are the things we say while feasting a friend over wine. We even add these words: "Do not be a host of a guest-crowded feast that is troublesome; from a communal contribution comes the greatest pleasure and the least expense." <margin>Hesiod in *Works and Days*</margin> 

And when sacrificing to the gods, we spend the very least on the sacrifices, just whatever happens to be at hand, as the excellent Menander presents it in *Drunkenness*:

"Don't we do everything and sacrifice in this way? 
For the gods, I bring a little sheep worth ten drachmas, 
but for the flute-girls, the perfume, the harpers, 
the Mendaean and Thasian wine, the eels, the cheese, and the honey, 
the bill comes to nearly a talent! 
It is worth ten good drachmas for us to receive a favorable sign from the gods. 
But when someone spends all this on the other things, 
is he not bringing a penalty upon himself rather than a blessing from the sacred rites? 
If I were a god, I wouldn't allow it; I'd leave the fat on the altar, 
unless someone also consecrated the eel at the same time, 
so that Callimedon <note>A famous Athenian glutton known for his love of eels</note>, one of the relatives, would die."

<margin>Extra dishes.</margin>
The ancients also gave the name *epidosima* <note>original: "epidosima," voluntary additions or contributions</note> to certain dinners, which the Alexandrians now refer to as "extra servings" <note>original: "epidomata"</note>.

Alexis, at any rate, says in *The Woman at the Well*: "Now my master toasted <note>original: "proupinen"</note> me with a jar of wine for those who would bring idle talk, and indeed I understand that everything else will now be a bonus <note>original: "epidosimon"</note>; I love a perceptive old woman." And Crobylus says in *The False Supposititious Child*: "Laches, how do I lead you on? To where you ask me, since I have come as a friend. Let our side-dishes be 'contributions' <note>original: "epidoxima"</note> as they were yesterday; again you forced a hundred cups, though you only gave twelve." The ancients also knew the dinners now called "communal flute-playing gatherings" <note>original: "apo synaulias"</note>. Pherecrates somewhere shows these 
<margin>Dinner from a basket.</margin>
to the forgetful or the sea in this way: "Having prepared a dinner, he has come 'from a basket' <note>original: "apo spyridos"</note>. He walked as if toward a benefit." This clearly explains the "dinner from a basket," which is when someone prepares a dinner for themselves, puts it into a small basket, and goes to someone else's house to dine. Lysias also used the term "social dining" <note>original: "syndeipnetikon"</note> in his *Symposium* and in the speech *On the Murder of Mykines*. For he says, "the whole social-dining group having been invited." And Plato also says, "to the fellow-diners <note>original: "syndeipnois"</note> who are varied." And Aristophanes in *Gerytades* uses the term for "fellow-diners" while praising Aeschylus. Therefore, 
<margin>Social gatherings.</margin>
some people even think it right to title the play of Sophocles in the neuter as *The Social Dinner* (*Syndeipnon*). They also call some "gathering dinners" <note>original: "synagogima"</note>, as Alexis says in *The Lover of Beauty*: "O nymphs, burn those beautiful things as well; let us make a 'social gathering' <note>original: "synagogimon"</note>. But I know well that your way has long been that of a cumin-splitter <note>A common Greek idiom for a miser or skinflint.</note>." And Ephippus in *Geryon*: "And assign a social-gathering banquet." They used the verb "to gather" (*synagein*) for drinking together, and called the banquet itself a "gathering" (*synagogion*). Menander says in *The Woman Who Was Sold*: "And they are 'gathering' alone on behalf of these things." Then immediately after he says: "Fill up the gathering-fund <note>original: "synagogion"</note>." Perhaps this is what is called the dinner "from contributions" <note>original: "apo symbolon"</note>. Alexis himself indicates what "contributions" (*symbolai*) are in *The Woman Drugged by Mandrake* through these lines: 
<margin>Contributions.</margin>
"I will come bringing contributions and giving them at the same time." "How can the people of Chalcis call ribbons 'contributions,' and you, old woman, call alabaster jars 'contributions'?" The people of Argos, as Hegesander says in his *Commentaries*, write that the contribution (*symbolen*) brought in by the drinkers for banquets is called a *chon* by the Argives, while they call a portion an *aisan*. It is not unfitting, my friend Timocrates, having reached the end of this volume, to stop the discourse here, lest someone think we have, according to Empedocles, once been fish. For the natural philosopher <note>Empedocles (c. 494–434 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously proposed a theory of reincarnation.</note> says: "For I have already been a boy and a girl, a bush and a bird, and a fiery fish out of the sea."

# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS
## BOOK NINE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Χ' featuring several figures in classical attire within a square frame.</image-desc><margin>water for hands.</margin>Let us again remember the fodder <note>original: "chortou," meaning greens or vegetables</note> and let them pour water over our hands. Let us see from where the stories proceed for both me and you, O Timocrates. For when some hams <note>original: "kolinon"</note> were brought in, and someone asked if they were "tender" (*takera*), Ulpian asked where the word "tender" is used, and if anyone has called mustard <note>original: "napy"</note> *sinapi*. For I see mustard being brought in on side-dishes with the hams. I know that the ham is also called *kolion* in the masculine. Epicharmus, at any rate, says in *The Woman of Megara*: "little mountain things, marrows, vertebrae, but not a single one of the edible things." And in *The Cyclops*: "sausages and, by Zeus, a pig's ham <note>original: "kolios"</note>." Learn this also from me, O most wise ones: that Epicharmus also named the ham *kolen* when he was calling it a bird. I also see seasoned salts in other side-dishes. The comic poets are full of such salts; in their works, according to Antiphanes, someone says in *The Leather Bag*: "And of the sea-dogs always, he had a side-dish; he spoke over the salt, and everything was roasted; let us drink a little wine, and by Zeus, some house-vinegar <note>original: "rosbilon"</note>, for it is good for those present. Altogether, a saucer-full of seasoning." I also see garum mixed with vinegar. 
<margin>Tender.</margin>
I know that now some people prepare "vinegar-garum" (*oxygaron*) specifically by itself. Zoilus, having met these points, said: "Aristophanes, my friend, in *The Women of Lemnos* applied the word 'tender' (*takeron*) to things that are delicate, saying: 'Lemnos, which nourishes tender and beautiful beans.' And Pherecrates in *The Deserters*: 'To make the chickpeas tender right there.'" Nicander of Colophon named mustard *sinkipi* in his *Theriaca* thus: "either a mouse or the copper-colored cucumber *sinki*." And in his *Georgics*: "the eye-biting seeds of mustard (*sinepios*)." And again: "cress and sharp black-leaved mustard (*sinepi*)." Crates, in his *Attic Dialect*, presents Aristophanes as saying: "And he looks like mustard <note>meaning he looks sharp or angry</note>, and he knit his brows." As Seleucus says in his *Hellenism*, the verse is from *The Knights* and goes like this: 
<margin>Mustard.</margin>
"And he looked mustard (*napy*)." The Attic writers say either *sinapi* or *napy*, and there is a reason for each. *Napy*, because it is "lacking in nature" (*naphy*), being weak and small, just as they call small fry *aphue*. But they call it *sinapi* because it "hurts the eyes" (*sinetai tous opas*) with its smell, just as the onion (*krommuon*) is so named because we "close the pupils" (*koras muomen*). Xenarchus the comic poet says in *The Scythians*: "This evil is no longer an evil; the little daughter has 'mustarded' <note>seasoned with mustard</note> the slice of fish through her skill." And the beautiful Aristophanes mentions salts and vinegar in his lines about Sthenelus the tragic poet, saying: "And how could I eat a word of Sthenelus..."

...dipped into vinegar or white salt. "Well then, my good man, we have kept silent while you were searching for these things. It is only right that you answer us: among which authors is the 'side-dish' <note>original: "paropsis"</note> used to refer to the vessel itself? For I know Plato <note>The comic poet, not the philosopher.</note> said in *Festivals* that 'wherever there might be barley-cake and a side-dish.' And in *Europe* he speaks of it again as a delicacy through many lines, including: 'let honor be given; for I am learning slowly, your side-dishes are gold-trimmed. She alone is a much better thing to take for pleasure.' Are these not side-dishes? Then I entreat you, they go on in the following lines, just as I say regarding the 'side-dish.' And in *Phaon*: 'Other people's things are like side-dishes, for a little bit is seen and quickly consumed.' Aristophanes in *Daedalus*: 'To all women he is of one character, just like a side-dish prepared as an adulterer.'"

While Ulpian remained silent, Leonides said: "But I am the one who ought to speak; having been silent for so long, I no longer wish to let so many things go uncontradicted. See how one argument suffices against an old one. I will serve you as I can, for my own sake. Using my own words, speaking as quickly as possible, since these are matters of teaching, regarding the vessels in which he spoke, my dear Myrtilus (for you have already started the argument): Antiphanes in *The Boeotian* says, 'Having called her, she sets out a side-dish.' And Alexis in *Hesione*, 'When he saw two men carrying in a table filled with an array of side-dishes, he no longer looked at me.' And the author of the works attributed to Magnes in the first *Dionysus*: 'And these side-dishes are my evils.' Achaeus in the satyr-play *Lithon*: 'Of small coins, other side-dishes for me...'

'...scorched and toasted scraps.' Sotades the comic poet in *The Person Being Ransomed*: 'If I appear as a side-dish to any Crobylus, he chews on that, but he bites me in small pieces.' The term is used ambiguously by Xenophon in the first book of the *Education of Cyrus*. For the philosopher says: 'there were brought to him side-dishes <note>original: "paropsides"</note> and all sorts of sauces and foods.' And in the work attributed to Pherecrates, *The Worse Man*, the word 'side-dish' refers to a condiment. However, Didymus, in his work *On Words Corrupted by Use*, applies it to the vessel. For he says: 'By Zeus, just as if side-dishes of the causes contain the seasonings, which he calls worthy of nothing.' Nicophon in *The Sirens*: 'another with his foot [attacks] the seat of the side-dish.' Aristophanes in *Daedalus*: 'To all women he is of one character, just like a side-dish prepared as an adulterer.'

Plato in *Festivals*: 'wherever there might be barley-cake and side-dishes.' He is speaking about the seasoning and preparation of bulbs <note>likely wild onions or similar tubers</note>. But the Athenians, as you know, Pliny, also use the term 'sauce' <note>original: "embamma," literally something to dip into</note>, as Theopompus says in *Peace*: 'For while bread is sweet, the sauce that comes on the plate for the bread becomes a poor thing.' 

They also use the term 'ham' <note>original: "kolea"</note> and 'thigh.' Eupolis in *The Goat-Peddlers*: 'Squills and hams straight to the...'. Euripides in *Sciron*: 'nor the hams of the dead.' From 'ham' <note>kolea</note> it is contracted, just as *sykia* becomes *syke* (fig-tree) or *leontia* becomes *leonte* (lion-skin), so *kolea* becomes *kolea*. Aristophanes in the second *Plutus*: 'Alas for the hams, oh my poor little jar!' In *The Banqueters*: 'and hams of tender piglets and scraps of meat.' In *The Storks*: 'heads of lambs, hams of kids.' Plato in *Gold*: 'fish, hams, sausages.' Ameipsias in *Konnos*: 'Priestly portions are given, a ham, a flank, and a left half-head.' Xenophon in *On Hunting*: 'fleshy hams, supple flanks.' And Xenophanes of Colophon says in his elegies: 'For having sent the ham of a kid, he obtained a fat leg of a prize bull, a thing for a man to obtain. Whose fame will reach all of Greece, and will not cease as long as the race of Greek songs exists.' 

Following these many and varied things being brought in, we note what is worthy of memory. For there was always a multitude of birds and geese. And regarding young birds, which some call *hippai*, and piglets, and 'Priapic' birds from Phasis <note>pheasants</note>. Having previously set forth matters concerning vegetables, I will now describe the rest. Turnips.

<margin>Turnips.</margin>
Apollas, in his work *On the Cities in the Peloponnese*, says these are called 'bellies' <note>original: "gasteres"</note> by the Lacedaemonians. Nicander of Colophon in his *Glossary* says that among the Boeotians, cabbages are called 'bellies,' but turnips are called *sekeltides*. Ameilas and Timachidas say that pumpkins are called *zakeltides*. Speusippus in the second book of *Similar Things* says that radish, turnip, rape, and *anarrhinon* are similar. Glaucus, in his *Art of Cookery*, calls the 'rape' <note>original: "rhapys"</note> by the name *rhapon*. Nothing else is similar to these, except what is now called the *bounias* <note>a type of French turnip or napus</note>. Theophrastus names the *bounias*, and calls a certain turnip 'male,' which is perhaps this *bounias*. <margin>The Bounias.</margin> Nicander in his *Georgics* mentions the *bounias*: 'You might sow turnips in the winnowing-place of the earth so that, lower than the plane trees, the *bounias* may bloom equally; but inside the radishes, let the turnips lie hidden. For the green sprout of the radish appears long in the garden-bed.' Crates mentions the 'Cephisian turnips' in *The Orators* as follows: 'all similar to Cephisian turnips.' Theophrastus says the turnip is a sweet thing, existing as both male and female. Both grow from the same seed. Posidonius the Stoic, in the twenty-seventh book of his *Histories*, says that in Dalmatia there are turnips and wild carrots...

### FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS

...carrot <note>original: "staphylinos"; in ancient Greek, this could refer to a parsnip or a wild carrot.</note>. Diphilus of Siphnos, the physician, says that the turnip <note>original: "gongylis"</note> is thinning, pungent, and hard to digest; it also causes flatulence. However, the variety from Boeotia is considered more appetizing, for it is sweeter and easier to digest, being both good for the stomach and nutritious. He further states that when the turnip is roasted, it is better digested and becomes more refined in its effect on the body. Eubulus mentions this in *Ankylion* as follows: "I bring here these turnips for roasting." And Alexis in *The God-Possessed* says: "Glycera is talking to me; the turnip-cutter is roasting them." 

<margin>Cabbage.</margin>
The pickled turnip is more thinning than the boiled variety, especially when prepared with mustard, as Diphilus claims. **Cabbage.** <note>original: "krambe"</note> Eudemus of Athens, in his treatise *On Vegetables*, says there are three types of cabbage: the so-called "salty" variety, the smooth-leafed, and the celery-like <note>original: "selinousia"</note>. He judges the salty kind to be the first in terms of flavor. It grows in Eretria, Kyme, Rhodes, and also in Cnidus and Ephesus. The smooth-leafed variety, they say, grows in every land. The celery-like variety gets its name from its curliness, for it resembles celery in its dense texture. Theophrastus writes as follows: "Of the radish (by which I mean the cabbage), one is curly-leafed and the other is wild." Diphilus of Siphnos says that the finest cabbage grows in the sweet soil of Kyme, while in Alexandria it is bitter. However, if seeds from Rhodes are brought to Alexandria, they produce sweet cabbage for one year, after which time it returns to its local bitter nature. Nicander says in his *Georgics*: "Smooth cabbage, or when the wild type is filled out, if sown it becomes many-leafed... or the curly kind, and the Tyrian bush-variety with its five petals, or the reddish kind similar to the 'frog-plant' and the ill-colored one from Kyme—one of which looks like the soles used by cobblers to patch old sandals, which the ancients called the 'prophet' <note>original: "mantis"</note> among vegetables." Perhaps Nicander called the cabbage a 'prophet' because it was considered sacred. Indeed, even in the iambics of Hipponax, there is a saying that goes "know it." Sophocles also invoked the cabbage: "the seven-leafed cabbage," or "die by drinking the juicy medicine at Pandora's festivals." Ananius also says: "I love you most of all men, yes, by the cabbage!" And Teleclides said to the presiding officials: "Yes, by the cabbages!" Epicharmus says: "For there is earth and sea; yes, by the cabbage!" Eupolis in *The Dippers*: "Yes, by the cabbage!" This oath is said to be of Ionian origin. It is not surprising that they swore by the cabbage, since Zeno of Citium <note>The founder of Stoicism.</note> used to swear "by the caper-bush," imitating Socrates’ oath "by the dog," as Empedus says in his *Memoirs*. Aithonios says that cabbage was even prepared for initiation rites as a kind of antidote against "the dark" <note>likely referring to a hangover or intoxication; cabbage was famously believed to prevent drunkenness.</note>. Ephippus says in *Geryon*: "Then every man—there is no one who does not stand before the doors—the smell of fat does not strike the tips of the nostrils, even though the 'Naming Day' rites <note>original: "Amphidromia"; a family festival held a few days after a child's birth.</note> are occurring, during which it is customary to roast slices of Chersonese cheese, to boil a cabbage embraced by oil, to stifle the spleens of fat lambs, to pluck pigeons and thrushes together with small squids and cuttlefish, and to twist many tentacles together, and to drink many cups of unmixed wine." Antiphanes, in *The Parasite*, mentions cabbage as a cheap food in these lines: "I know a woman very well—cheese, a kind of cake, matters for a free man, dried fish—not with seasonings from a lamb, but stuffed with crumbs and mixed up; these pots are the ruin of men. And indeed, they boil glistening cabbages—O gods! A nation that marvels at its own pea-soup." Diphilus says in *The Glutton*: "Quickly we bring it, along with every good thing: a glistening cabbage, many little furrow-born pieces of meat, and nothing, by Zeus, to compare to my own. And similar things, not even compared to the sea-olives." Alcaeus in *The Wrestling School*: "He ate a whole pot of cabbages." Polyzelus in *The Birth of the Muses* says they call them "cabbages" specifically: "and many high-leafed cabbages." 

<margin>Beets.</margin>
**Beets.** <note>original: "seutla"</note> Of these, Theophrastus says the white is juicier than the black and produces fewer seeds, and is called "Sicilian." The "beet-leaf" <note>original: "seutlis"</note> is different from the beet itself, which is why Diphilus the comic poet, in his play *The Hero*, rebukes someone for speaking poorly and calling beets "pitainas." Eudemus, in his work *On Vegetables*, says there are four kinds of beets: the common, the stalked, the white, and the "panodikos," which is grey in color. Diphilus of Siphnos says the beet is juicier than the cabbage and moderately nutritious. When boiled and taken with mustard, it is more thinning and kills intestinal worms. The white beet is more laxative for the bowels, while the black is more diuretic. Their roots are also quite firm and more nutritious. 

<margin>Carrot.</margin>
**Carrot.** <note>original: "staphylinos"</note> This is pungent, says Diphilus, quite nutritious and moderately good for the stomach; it is purgative and flatulent, hard to digest, diuretic, and quite stimulating for sexual desire. Because of this, it is even called a "love potion" by some. Neumenius says in his *Work on Fishing*: "As many leaves as are rooted at the ends of the fields, in winter and whenever the flowery spring comes, the dry thistle and the wild carrot, and the firm radish and the wild-growing stalk." Nicander says in the second book of his *Georgics*: "And also the deep stalk and root of the fennel-flower, together with the parsnip <note>original: "staphylinos"</note> on the dry ground, and the smyrnium, the sow-thistle, and the ox-tongue and chicory, and you might crumble the half-eaten leaves."

->### BOOK 9<-

And there is that which is called "bird's milk" <note>original: "ornithos gala"; likely referring to the Star-of-Bethlehem plant (*Ornithogalum*), known for its white flowers</note>. Theophrastus also mentions the wild carrot <note>original: "staphylinos"; in antiquity, this term covered both wild carrots and parsnips</note>. Phanias, in the first book of *On Plants*, writes as follows: "According to the nature of the seed itself is the so-called *sips* and the seed of the wild carrot." And in the first book, in his classification of seeds, he mentions: anise, fennel, wild carrot, bur-parsley, hemlock, coriander, *skias*, and the "mouse-killer" <note>original: "myoktonon"; a poisonous plant, possibly aconite</note>. Since Nicander mentioned the arum plant, we should first note that Phanias, in the aforementioned book, writes: "Some call the dragon-plant <note>original: "drakontion"</note> 'silent arum'." Diocles, in the first book of his *Health Manual*, calls the wild carrot *astaphylinos*. As for the variety called *karron* <note>the source of our word 'carrot'</note>, it is a large and well-grown wild carrot. Diphilus records that it is juicier than the common wild carrot, and more warming, more diuretic, good for the stomach, and easy to digest.

<margin>
Headed-leek.
Small leek.
</margin>
**Headed-leek.** The same Diphilus says that the arum and the "leek-green" are called by this name, and it is juicier than the *karta* <note>potentially a corruption in the text referring to a specific sharp vegetable</note>. It is moderately thinning, nutritious, but causes flatulence. Epainetus, in his *Art of Cookery*, says that headed-leeks are called *gethyllides* <note>small leeks or onions</note>. I found this name used by Eubulus in *The Pimp* as follows: "I couldn't eat any bread. For at Gnathaenion's I just ate bread, and he caught her and chilled a small leek." <note>The Greek text here is fragmented and the meaning is somewhat obscure</note>. Others say this is what is called the *gethyon*. Didymus, in his work *On Foodstuffs*, says that these leeks are similar to what are called "vine-leeks" <note>original: "ampeloprasa"; wild leeks often found in vineyards</note>, and that they are also called *epiduthyllides*.

Epicharmus mentions these small leeks in *Philoctetes*, saying: "where there are two cloves of garlic and two small leeks." Aristophanes, in the second edition of *Aeolosikon*, says: "the roots of the leeks having a garlic-like nature." Polemon the Guide, in his treatise *On Samothrace*, says that Leto <note>the mother of Apollo and Artemis</note> once craved small leeks, writing as follows: "For this reason, at the sacrifice of the *Theoxenia* <note>a festival where gods were invited to a banquet</note> among the Delphians, whoever brings the largest leek to Leto receives a portion from the table; and I myself have seen a leek no smaller than a round turnip or a large radish." They tell the story that Leto craved leeks while she was pregnant with Apollo, which is why this plant has been held in such honor.

<margin>
Gourd.
</margin>
**Gourd.** <note>original: "kolokyntē"</note> Once, when gourds were brought to us during the winter season, everyone was amazed, thinking they were fresh. We were reminded of what the witty Aristophanes said in *The Seasons*, praising beautiful Athens in these lines: "You can see in the middle of winter cucumbers, grapes, autumn fruit, crowns of violets, and dust that blinds you." He says again: "The same man sells thrushes, pears, swallows, olives, colostrum, tripe, celandine, cicadas, and embryos. You can see baskets full of figs and myrtles together, then gourds alongside turnips, so that no one knows what time of year it is; it is the greatest blessing if one can have whatever they desire throughout the year." It would be a great evil if these were not available, for then they would not crave them or spend money on them. I would say that for a short time I would take these things away from other cities, but they belong to the Athenians because they revere the gods. "Have you then made their city into an Egyptian one instead of Athens?" we joked. So we marveled at eating these gourds in the month of January. For they were green and yielded their own juice, having been preserved underground by cooks who know how to manage such things. The gluttonous man asks if the ancients also knew this use. And Ulpian said: Nicander of Colophon, in the second book of his *Georgics*, mentions this use, calling the gourds *sikya*. For that is what they were called, as we said before. He speaks thus: "Slice the gourds into segments and dry them in the air, then hang them in the smoke, so that when the wide-bellied pots are filled, they may be tossed in with various legumes when they are ground; put the rings of the gourd in after washing them." And in another place: "Long ago, people mixed sliced stalks with flat cakes..."

<margin>
Bird.
</margin>
**Bird.** <note>original: "ornis"; usually referring to poultry</note> Since birds are served after the gourds and other rich vegetable dishes—Aristophanes says in *Daedalus*: "Chopped vegetables smelling of fat or olive-pulp"—Myrtilus said: "Indeed, only common custom now calls the females 'birds' <note>specifically hens</note>, of which I see a great number being carried around. Chrysippus the philosopher, in the fifth book of *On the Beautiful and Pleasure*, writes: 'Just as some people say white hens are more pleasant than black ones, even though the males are called *alektryones* and the females *alektorides*.' Among the ancients, the word 'bird' (*ornis*) was used for both males and females of other winged creatures, not just this specific kind, whereas common speech today says 'to buy birds' meaning hens." Homer says: "Many birds fly under the rays of the sun." And elsewhere in the feminine: "With a baneful bird." And: "As a bird brings morsels to her unfledged chicks when she finds them, though it goes badly for herself." Menander, in the first *Inheritress*, clearly uses the word in its common sense, showing it thus: "A rooster crowed loudly; will someone not shoo the birds <note>hens</note> away from us?" And again: "This woman will hardly be able to drive the birds out." Cratinus also used the diminutive "little birds" in *Nemesis*: "and all the other little birds." Regarding the masculine use, not only the word "bird"...

->### EXCERPTS FROM ATHENAEUS'S BANQUET OF THE LEARNED<-

...but also a "bird" <note>original: *ornin*</note>. The same Cratinus <note>a famous comic poet of Athens</note>, in the same play, mentions a "crimson-winged bird" <note>original: *ornitha phoinikopteron*; this is the flamingo</note>. And again, "I drink a bird" because it becomes large. Sophocles in *The Root-Cutters* <note>original OCR: *authonotheias*; corrected to *Rhizotomois*</note> says, "a bird, and a herald, and a servant." Aeschylus in *The Women of Etna* <note>original OCR: *kathaiois*; likely *Aitnaiai*</note> says, "But I do not make you a bird of my path." Xenophon, in the second book of the *Education of Cyrus*, says: "regarding birds in the harshest winter." Menander in *The Twins* says, "I have come bringing a bird." And following this, he says "cutting off the birds." That they also use "bird" <note>original: *ornis*</note> for the plural is shown by the testimony of Menander. But also Alcman <note>a Spartan lyric poet</note> says somewhere: "The young girls fled fruitlessly like a bird when a hawk flies beneath." Eupolis in *The Demes* says: "he who scares me with a piece of meat... and birds likewise, for whom a chick is like a father."

The ancients spoke of the "rooster" <note>original: *alektruona*</note> in the feminine gender as well. Cratinus in *Nemesis* says: "Leda, your task is to ensure you do not differ at all in your ways from a rooster, so that you may sit upon the egg and hatch something beautiful and wonderful for us from this bird." Strattis in *The Souls* says: "all the hens <note>original: *alektruones*</note> whose piglets and small birds have died." Anaxandrides in *Tereus* says: "they gladly watch the sows being leaped upon and the hens."

<margin>Anaxandrides</margin>
Since I have mentioned this comic poet, and I know that his play *Tereus* is not ranked among his first-rate works, I will set out for you, my friends, the judgment which Chamaeleon of Heraclea stated about him in the sixth book of *On Comedy*, writing as follows: "Anaxandrides, when competing as a producer of dithyrambs, once entered on a horse and recited part of the song. He was handsome and tall in appearance, wore his hair long, and dressed in a purple robe with golden fringes. Being bitter in character, he acted in such a manner regarding his comedies: whenever he did not win, he would take the play and give it to be cut up for incense-wrappers <note>i.e., he destroyed the manuscript rather than keep it</note>, and he did not revise them like most poets. Thus, he destroyed many of his plays that contained clever passages, being ill-tempered toward the spectators because of his old age." He says "because of old age" lightly regarding his brilliant career. I wonder, then, how *Tereus* was preserved since it did not win a victory, along with other plays of the same sort.

<margin>10</margin>
And Theopompus in *Peace* also categorized the "rooster" as feminine, saying: "I am annoyed at having lost a hen <note>original: *alektruona*</note> that laid such beautiful eggs." Aristophanes in *Daedalus* says: "It has laid a massive egg, like a hen." And again: "Often, by force of sleepiness, hens lay many eggs." In *The Clouds*, while teaching the old man about the difference in names, he says: "Now how should I call it? A 'hen-ess' <note>original: *Alektruaina*; a humorous feminine form created by the character Socrates</note>, and the other a 'rooster' <note>original: *alektora*</note>." They also say *aliktheis* and *alektor*. Simonides called it "the lovely-voiced rooster." Cratinus in *The Seasons* says: "just like the Persian bird, the loud-voiced rooster that sounds at every hour." This has been said regarding the additions such as those in the examples before you.

The Dorians say *ornix* <note>bird</note>; in the genitive case, because of the 'eta', they say *ornichos*. Alcman expresses the 'eta' of the goddess thus: "the sea-purple bird of spring." In the genitive: "I know the songs of all birds <note>original: *ornichon*</note>."

<margin>Piglet.</margin>
**Piglet.** <note>original: *Delphax*</note> Epicharmus calls the male hog by this name in *Odysseus the Deserter*: "And the piglet of the neighbors, which you were guarding for the Eleusinians, you destroyed wondrously though not willingly; and for these things you bargain with me," he said, "swearing to me by the piglet tied to the hog-pens." Anaxilas in *Circe* also used "piglet" in the masculine, and applied the name to a full-grown animal: "to make some of you fish-eating piglets, and others wild panthers, wolves, or lions." Aristophanes categorized the name as feminine in *The Fryers*: "or a piglet <note>original: *delphakos*</note> from the autumn harvest." And in *The Acharnians*: "For she is young, but a piglet <note>original: *delphax*</note>... she has grown great and fat." "But if you wish to be reared, you are a fine pig <note>original: *choiros*</note>."

<margin>Odyssey 14</margin>
Eupolis in *The Golden Race*, and Hipponax also said "as a piglet <note>original: *delphax*</note>." The females are called *delphines* <note>not to be confused with dolphins</note> when they have given birth. For this reason, the wombs are called *metrai*, from which the word "brothers" <note>original: *adelphoi*, literally 'from the same womb'</note> is etymologically derived. Regarding the age of the animal, Cratinus says in *The Archilochoi*: "already piglets <note>original: *delphakas*</note>, and pigs <note>original: *choiroi*</note> with their salt." Aristophanes the Grammarian, in his work *On Ages*, says: "among swine, those that are already firm are called *delphakes*, and those that are tender and young are *choiroi*." From this, the Homeric passage becomes clear: "What is present for the servants are young pigs <note>original: *choiroi*</note>, but the suitors eat the fatted hogs <note>original: *sialous*</note>."

Plato the comic poet used it in the masculine in *The Poet*: "he led away the piglet <note>original: *delphaka*</note> in silence." There was also an ancient law, as Androtion (or Epigones) says, that for the sake of the hundred cattle, one should not slaughter a sheep that was "childless" or had not yet given birth. Because the full-grown ones are sweeter: "but the suitors eat the fatted hogs." Even now, the priestess of Athena in Athens does not sacrifice a lamb, nor does she taste cheese. Philochorus says that when cattle once failed for a time, a law was passed because of the scarcity to abstain from the animal, gathering those who wished to increase the population by not sacrificing them.

The Ionians call the female a *choiros*, as Hipponax says: "in the pasture and with the entrails of a wild pig." Sophocles in *Taenarii* says: "Guard like a pig <note>original: *choiros*</note> in a snare." Ptolemy II, the King of Egypt, in the ninth book of his *Memoirs*, says: "When I visited Assos, the Assians presented me with a delicious pig which was two and a half cubits in height, and its length was in proportion, white as snow in color." He said the king found such animals and bought them carefully, giving four thousand drachmas for one. Aeschylus says: "And I will place a very well-fed pig in the Dutch oven <note>original: *kribano*</note>; for what dish could be better than this?" And again: "A white one... and beautifully..."

->## BOOK IX.<-

"Come, pig, be boiled, and do not be grieved to die." And even after sacrificing this pig, which was once a sow, you have indeed done many evils in the houses of the gods, now fittingly your fortune turns up and down. These things were first noted by Chamaeleon <note>A Peripatetic philosopher and literary critic</note> in his work *On Aeschylus*. He says they sacrifice the pig because the animal is sacred among the Cretans. Agathocles of Babylon, in the first book of his *History of Kyzikos*, says that the birth of Zeus took place in Crete on Mount Dikti, where a secret sacrifice is performed. For it is said that a sow offered her teat to him, and by mingling her grunting with the whimpering of the infant, she made his crying inaudible to those passing by. Therefore, everyone considers this animal most 
<margin>Praisos: a city of Crete. Steph.</margin>
pious, and he says they do not feast upon its flesh as they do with rams. The people of Praisos also perform sacred rites with it, and this sacrifice is considered by them to be a preliminary rite of initiation. Similar things are related by Neanthes of Kyzikos in the second book of his work *On Initiation*. 
<margin>Petalid sows.</margin>
Achaius of Eretria mentions "petalid" <note>original: *petalidon*; meaning broad or spreading</note> sows in his satyr play *Aethon*, saying: "they followed the forms of these petalid sows." He calls them "petalid" by transferring the term from calves. For calves are called "petalos" <note>broad-horned</note> based on their horns when they have them widely spread out. Similarly to Achaius, Eratosthenes in his *Arterinnys* called pigs "larine," transferring the term from 
<margin>Larine cattle.</margin>
"larine" cattle. These were so called either from the word "larineuosthai" (which means to be well-fed), as Sophron says, "the cattle are fattened" <note>original: *larineuontai*</note>, or from a certain village in Epirus called Larine, or from the man who herded them. A "larinos" man was also a term used.

Once, a young pig <note>original: *delphakos*</note> was brought in to us, half of which was carefully roasted to a crisp, while the other half was tenderly boiled as if in water. While everyone was marveling at the cook’s skill, he, being very proud of his art, said: "Truly, can any of you point out where the killing blow was struck, or how the belly itself was filled with all sorts of good things? For it contains within itself thrushes and other small birds, parts of sows' bellies, slices of wombs, and the golden yolks of eggs, as well as the wombs of birds filled with delicious juices. These are meats chopped into fine pieces and molded together with pepper." I am ashamed to use the term "isicia" <note>original: *isikia*; a Latin loanword for minced meat or sausages</note> in front of Ulpian <note>A character in the dialogue known for his strict adherence to pure Attic Greek and hatred of foreign words</note>, even though I see him enjoying them, but the author Paxamus mentions "isicia," and I do not care for Atticisms. "But you all, show me how the pig was slaughtered, and how one half is roasted and the other boiled." While we were still searching, the cook said: "Do you think I have less skill than those ancient cooks of whom the comic poets speak?" For 
<margin>Cooks' boastfulness.</margin>
Poseidippus in *The Dancing Girls* has a cook speaking to his disciples thus: "Disciple of Leucus, and you fellow-servants, for every part of the house is a place to learn the truth about our art—what do you say is the strongest seasoning in the culinary art? Boastfulness! <note>original: *alazoneia*; the comic trope of the 'braggart cook'</note> Generally, the appearance of the arts depends on the leader. 

He is like a general who does not wear a scale-armored breastplate, or a dragon embroidered with silk, like Briareus. And if it happens to be a hare, the cook, if he has an assistant looking at him like a commoner, and his disciples are all 'cumin-splitters' <note>original: *kyminopristas*; a term for misers or those who split hairs over small things</note>, it is a beautiful hunger. Stop right there. If you throw yourself into the truth and put aside your pillows, give space to the common ground where you are placed, and know the mouths of those invited. For just as in the markets, this is the test of the art: how the body will serve. Now there is a wedding; the sacrifice is an ox; the person receiving it is eminent. He receives it eminently; of the women, there are priestesses to the goddess, gods, Corybantes, flutes, all-night festivals, and bustling about. This is the racetrack of the culinary art; remember this, boy." And regarding another cook (whose name is Synthos), the same poet says: "Synthos is a great commoner to them; I know that he seems to differ in no way from a good general. When the enemy is deep, the general by nature holds back and accepts the situation. The enemy is the drinking crowd. For when they come in all at once, having looked forward to the dinner for ten days, full of impulse and exhausted, watching for someone to bring something to their hands, understand that this is a crowd gathered in rags." The cook in Euphron’s *Companions* says: "Licentious things as always, when you serve guests at a club-dinner <note>original: *eranisais*; a meal where everyone contributes a share</note>, it is no time for playing. Do what you have learned; yesterday you were victorious, you ate whatever was available. For generally they were empty. The brain was altered... when you come inside to the rabble and the porters, and you ask for your whole wage together, it's only fair. We aren't going to a wedding now to see a man-slayer. You are my disciple and either a cook or a bad one; the opportunity is prayerfully helpful; the old man is a miser... I will ruin you now for not sitting still; by the coals, you are lost! Go inside. For the old man himself is approaching, and how stingily he looks! He is a great thinker, and nothing leads to boastfulness." And Sosipater the cook says, speaking falsely: "Our art is not entirely to be despised if you consider our people, but the matter has fallen, and almost everyone says they are cooks, knowing nothing. By such as these, the art is ruined. For if you take a true cook, one led correctly into the matter from childhood, knowing its powers and having learned all the lessons in order, the matter will perhaps appear to be something else, such as we who remain..."

# FROM THE ATHENAEUS'S LEARNED BANQUETERS

Of small cattle <note>original: "boidion"</note> and Chariades and I, and for the rest... but what do you say? I am. We preserve the teaching of our master Sikon <note>A famous stock character of a cook in Greek comedy, known for his arrogance and skill</note>, who was the founding leader of this art. He taught us first to study astrology, then immediately after that, architecture. He poured out all his discourses concerning nature, and upon all these things he spoke of military strategy. Before the art of cooking itself, he urged us to learn these things. Are you, then, a person capable of chopping, my dearest friend? No—but while the boy is returning from the market, I will stir you up a little concerning these matters, so that by talking we may occupy this idle time. Apollodorus, it is a laborious task. Listen, my good man; for a cook must first of all know about the heavens, the settings of the stars and their risings, and when the sun returns for the long and short days, and in which signs of the zodiac it is. 

<margin>10</margin> For they say that all relishes <note>original: "opsa"; refers to seasoned dishes or delicacies eaten with bread</note> and foods, in the revolution of the whole celestial arrangement, take on a different pleasure within themselves. Therefore, he who understands such things, seeing the season, will use each of these as is appropriate. But he who is ignorant of these things is naturally beaten. Again, you perhaps wondered about architecture: how does it contribute to the art? I indeed wondered. But nevertheless, I will explain. To lay out the kitchen <note>original: "toptanion"</note> correctly, to let in as much light as is necessary, and to see from where the breeze comes, is of great use to the matter. For the smoke, being carried here and there, is accustomed to produce a certain difference in the dishes being boiled. Furthermore, the cook must possess knowledge of military strategy. Order <note>original: "taxis"</note> is a wise thing everywhere and in every art, but in ours, it practically leads the way. For to serve and to clear away each thing in an orderly fashion, and to see the right moment for these—when to bring them in more rapidly, and when at a slow pace, and how the guests feel toward the dinner, and when it is the right time for the dishes themselves to be served hot, some cooling down, some in the middle, 

<margin>20</margin> and some completely chilled—all these things are examined through the lessons of military strategy. Who, having shown me what is necessary, will go away and keep quiet himself? And the cook in Alexis’s play *The Milesians* says things not far from this: "Do you not know, as in most arts, that the master architect is not the only lord of pleasure, but that a portion also belongs to those who use it, if they use it well?" For instance? "For I, the cook, must learn to prepare the relish well, but that is all. If, then, the person who is going to eat and judge these things arrives at the proper moment, he aids the art. But if he is later than the appointed peak of perfection, so that the meat must either be warmed again after being roasted, or finished off quickly without being fully roasted, he robs the art of its pleasure." At any rate, I enroll the cook among the experts. Be silent, I tell you; the fire is burning for me; already the frequent sparks of Hephaestus <note>The god of fire and the forge</note> fly lightly through the air, and at the end, someone mocks life with the unseen law of necessity. 

<margin>30</margin> And Euphron, whom I briefly mentioned before...

<margin>The Seven Sages of Cooking.</margin>

...having judged you, we did not hesitate to call you back, and I will remind you of our senses... for his brothers... by making a certain cook very learned and well-educated, remembering all his fellow craftsmen and what private virtue each had, and in what he excelled. Nevertheless, he mentioned nothing of the sort which I often happen to prepare for you. He speaks thus: "Many pupils having come to me, Lycus, because of my intellect... having become a cook from a house in which for ten whole months... as far as a Rhodian, he alone roasted fish to perfection. Nereus the Chian boiled the conger eel for the gods—the white part was the limit—and Chariades with yellow-haired broth. 

<margin>40</margin> Black broth was first refined by Lamprias. Aphthonetus made blood-sausages. Euthymus made lentil soup. From contributions they gathered... These, after those Seven Sages who existed long ago, are our Second Sages. But I, seeing that most things were already occupied, discovered stealing first, so that not one... because of this... Did you discover something unique? And this is yours: the Teians were sacrificing on the fifth day. Guests of an old man, of one who had sailed... a kid, and I do not let a small portion go... then a white-bearded man, you did not even manage to provide for the teacher, you forced two kids. For their liver being frequently chopped, just as you took one hand and threw it boldly into the pit, you made the kidney cause much noise. They did not notice the kidney, I say, and those present shouted out 'a loss!' and sacrificed another. And the second one—I saw you swallowing the heart, glowing hot, long ago. You are great, know this! For you alone have discovered the art of not gaping like a wolf in vain. 

<margin>50</margin> Having extinguished two raw fish in the fire... skewers of guts... and how you chirped the double-stringed tune. That food was like a song, or like a game. Did any of those who were named the Second Seven Sages devise such a thing? Where is the pig? Every part and the belly is full, and part of it must be roasted, and part boiled. But it is invisible." While we were wondering and entreating him to show his wisdom, he says, "I will not speak, by those who risked their lives at Marathon, and furthermore those who fought the sea-battle at Salamis." It seemed best to everyone, because of such a great oath, not to force the man.

<margin>A half-boiled pig.</margin> Where does the idea of a half-roasted, half-boiled pig stuffed with unslaughtered creatures come from? The pig was slaughtered with a small cut under the shoulder and laid on the ground. When much of the blood had flowed out, and all the small animals <note>original: "zoodidia"; likely referring to birds or small game used as stuffing</note> were put inside after the disemboweling—for the word 'disemboweling' <note>original: "exairesis"</note> is used for when it is easily gutted—I rinsed it thoroughly with wine several times and hung it up by its feet. Then I soaked it again in wine, and having rubbed the gaping openings with plenty of pepper, I "sacrificed" <note>A cook's jargon for "cooked"</note> it by pouring a very well-made broth through the body. After this, I filled half the pig, as you see, with a great deal of barley meal, having kneaded it with wine and oil. Then I placed it in a covered oven <note>original: "kribanos"</note>, setting it upon a bronze tray, and adjusted the fire so as neither to burn it nor leave it raw. And since it is now a succulent, crispy treat, I bring it to you and serve it, having added the other half or the "half-god" portion by throwing in the barley.
<margin>22</margin> <margin>Disemboweling.</margin> Regarding the 'disemboweling' <note>original: "exairesis"</note>, my dear Ulpian, the comic poet Dionysius says the following in the play of the same name, depicting a certain cook speaking to his students: "Come now, if I know anything elegant, or wise, or polished in these matters, make the teacher’s work manifest. Now I shall tell you the demonstration of the art. Run boldly into the enemy's fray <note>A metaphor for a busy kitchen or market</note>, divide the meats by number, and keep watch over them. Having done this, and having boiled them vigorously, confuse the number just as I tell you. A delicate fish is present; it is yours. And if you turn aside a slice of meat, that too is yours, so long as it is raw. But when I perform the **disemboweling**, the other consequences are such that they can neither be counted nor checked. 
<margin>30</margin> Bring the scraps in order or by position; tomorrow these things will delight you and me, and give a share to the scrap-seller entirely, so that you may have an entrance through the doors. Why should I say many things that you already know? You are my student, and I am your teacher. Remember these things and walk here with me."
<margin>Platonic cooks and the arrogance of cooks.</margin> When we all praised the cook for his ready speech and the elaborateness of his art, our noble host Larensis said: "How much better it is for cooks to learn such things thoroughly, rather than what happened with one of our citizens. Out of wealth and luxury, he forced his cooks to learn the dialogues of Plato! When they brought in the dishes, they had to say: 'One, two, three—but where is the fourth of us, my dear Timaeus, who was our guest yesterday but is now our host?' <note>This is a parody of the opening lines of Plato's *Timaeus*</note>. Another would answer: 'Some illness has fallen upon him, Socrates.' They would go through most of the dialogue in this way, so that the guests were annoyed and that all-wise man <note>Plato</note> was insulted, and the banquets at his house became a source of dissatisfaction because of this excessive 'refinement.' But these men of ours, by learning these things briefly, provide us with a little cheer." Then the boy, praised for his culinary wisdom, said: "What such thing have the poets found or said? I pride myself on my diligence; and indeed, the first man to win the race at the Olympics, Coroebus of Elis, was a cook! Yet he was not so puffed up by his art as the cook in Straton's *The Phoenician*, of whom the man being mocked says:
'I have taken into my house not a cook, but an unspeakable Sphinx! Simply by the gods, I understand nothing of what he says. He comes with a supply of strange words. For as soon as he entered, he looked at me grandly and asked: "How many **articulate mortals** <note>original: "meropes"; a Homeric term for humans</note> have you invited to dinner? Speak!" I said, "I have invited *mortals* to dinner? You are mad! Do you think I know these *mortals*? No one is here. For by Zeus, why would I call *mortals* to dinner for the rest of time?" "Is there not then a **banqueter** <note>original: "daitymon"; an archaic/poetic term for a guest</note> present?" "None at all; I don't think there's any *banqueter*." I started calculating: there was Philinus, Moschion, Niceratus, so-and-so and so-and-so—as I went through the names, there was not a single *banqueter* among them. "I tell you, no one is here!" "What are you saying?" he cried, "Not even one?" He was greatly indignant as if he had been wronged, because I had not invited a *banqueter*. How very clumsy!
Not even then...'

"You do not then sacrifice an 'earth-shaker' <note>original: *erysichthon*, a Homeric epithet for a bull</note>?" "I am undone!" "I shout for a 'broad-browed' one." "I am sacrificing a bull, you wretch!" "Do you sacrifice 'apples' <note>original: *mēla*, which in Homeric Greek refers to sheep, but in Attic means apples</note> then?" A certain smothered dish, a suckling pig already... then he burnt it; do not worry. For the suffering is curable in this way: taking vinegar, pour it into a basin, mixing in cold water, then place the hot pot into the vinegar. For while it is still glowing hot, it will draw moisture through itself, and being leavened, just like a pumice stone, it will take in through the porous passages, through which it will receive the moisture. The meat will not be dried out, but succulent, and I will release the flow like dew. Apollo! How medically you do this, O gray-eyed one! I will do these things, or set them all out. When you set them out, you learn good agility. For so that the steam does not escape through the nose, but eating with the mouth wide open, it seems you have become much better then." Whether it is a speech-writer or a cook speaking, he does not speak, but reproaches the art. Of the cooks, you will discuss their arrogant way of life enough, lest one of them, grumbling from Menander’s *The Grump* <note>original: *Dyskolos*</note>, should shout these things: "Not a single cook has escaped the Attic laws unharmed; how sacredly our art is held." And I will set before you the most pleasant Diphilus, a whole lamb in the middle, stuffed and seasoned, with whole suckling pigs arranged around it; <margin>Fattened fodder</margin> I bring a goat with the puffing of the wind. "Chilo" <note>referring to fodder or fattened animals</note>. When these and other well-prepared "fodders" <note>original: *chilōn*</note> were brought around, someone said, "the fattened fodder." And Ulpian asked, "With whom is the term 'fattened fodder' <note>original: *siteutos chilo*</note> found?" How then does Plutarch say: Theopompus the Chian said in the *Hellenica*, and in the thirteenth book of the *Philippica*, that when Agesilaus the Spartan arrived in Egypt, the Egyptians sent him fodder and fattened calves. And Epilycus the comic poet says in *The Bacchants*: "But if someone took and reared it for me like fodder, a fattened one." Archestratus in his famous poem says, "as the fattened fodder together with the thin..." simply in this way. And you, Ulpian, are right to tell us—you who demand an account of everything from everyone— <margin>Pliny book 10 ch 11</margin> whether these expensive livers of fattened animals were deemed worthy of memory among the ancients. For that he is a "green-watcher" <note>original: *chlōroskopos*</note> of the road, Cratinus is a witness in *Dionysalexandros*, saying "green-watching herdsmen." Homer used the masculine for the feminine, bringing "fodder" <note>original: *chilo*</note> himself. And: "who did not even seize the fodder in the well-tended house," and "twenty measures of wheat for me in the house with the fodder." Of "fodder-livers" (which Rome has now made common), Eupolis mentions them in *The Female Garland-Sellers*, saying: "Unless <margin>Half-heads</margin> you have a liver or a soul of fodder." There were also many "half-heads" <note>original: *hēmichrairai*</note> of suckling pigs. Crobylus mentions them in *The False Supposititious Son*: "A tender half-head of this pig came in; by Zeus, I didn't leave a bit of it." <margin>Ram-pot</margin> After these things, the so-called "ram-pot" <note>original: *kriokakkabos*</note>. These are internal organs chopped up with blood and fat in a sweetened broth. Aristophanes the Grammarian says this, as Myrtilus the Achaean noted. Anticleides says in the seventy-eighth book of *Returns*, that when the Chians and Erythraeans were about to be destroyed in an attack, someone who learned what was to happen said, "O Chians, for pride breaks much, flee from the pig's meat roasted over the fire, and do not... <margin>Boiled up</margin> Aristomenes mentions "boiled-up" <note>original: *anabraston*</note> meats in *The Sorcerers* thus... <margin>Testicles</margin> and "testicles" <note>original: *orchas*, also a type of olive</note> most sweet, which he also called kidneys. When he said that other sweet things had been made, and a chicken with "vinegar-fat" <note>original: *oxyliparon*</note>, the fault-finder Ulpian, lying down alone, eating little and watching those who spoke, said: "What is 'vinegar-fat' unless..."

...unless you stop biting us and leave off, you are going to name the ancestral customs of my food. But Timocles, the comic poet, in his play *The Dactyl*, mentions "sour-fat-sauce," <note>original: *oxyliperdes*</note> speaking as follows:

> A fisherman or a Batidas and all those
> juices prepared with the sour-fat-sauce seasoning.

And Alexis in *The Wicked Woman* has called certain men "surface-fat" <note>original: *akroliparous*, meaning those who are slightly oily or sleek on the outside</note> like this:

<margin>a small fish or relish.</margin>
> Surface-fat ones; some have a body like wood underneath.

Once, when a large fish’s eye was served, someone remarked that every "little fish" <note>original: *opsarion*—Ulpian will soon object to this word being used for a single part of a fish</note> served in the eye is most delicious. Ulpian, that collector of thorns <note>a nickname for Ulpian due to his prickly habit of catching people on small linguistic errors</note>, knitting his brows, said: "Where is the 'eye' laid down as a 'little fish'? For I know of that term being used by no living soul." Most of the guests, telling him to go hang, continued dining, but Cynulcus, while taking up the sixth portion, called out: "But my good man, let us dine, and afterward ask me everything you wish. For now, being hungry, I am somewhat unscientifically forgetful." And Myrtilus, joining him with a certain pleasure so that he might share in nothing but speak of everything, said: "Cratinus in *The Odysseys* has spoken of eyes in these lines:

> In return for which, having seized all of you, my noble companions,
> roasting, boiling, and charcoal-grilling, and baking,
> dipping into brine and vinegar-brine, and then into garlic-brine,
> whichever of you appears to me the most well-baked of all,
> I shall gobble you up, O soldiers!"

And Aristophanes in *The Wasps* says: "Having blown it off, drop it into hot vinegar-brine." We use the term "little fish" <note>original: *opsarion*</note> for those that are no longer living. But even Plato <note>the comic poet, not the philosopher</note> says regarding the fish in his *Peisander*:

<margin>a small fish or relish.</margin>
> Having most pleasantly eaten such a "little fish" as is made, you fell ill and the same thing did not happen to you. But I, last year, having eaten a crayfish...

Pherecrates in *The Deserters* says: "Someone placed this 'little fish' around us." Philemon in *The Treasure*:

> It is not true to reckon thus, nor to have good 'little fish.'

Menander in *The Carthaginian*:

> Having a desire for a private 'little fish' from the North Wind, I gave and I took; boil the lentils!

And in *The Ephesian*: "So that I might sing having taken the 'little fish'." And one of the fishmongers adds: "He was selling a gudgeon for five obols." Anaxilas in *Hyacinthus the Pimp*:

> I, being your 'little fish,' will buy for you.

And a little later:

> Prepare the whole 'little fish' for yourselves.

And Aristophanes in *The Anagyros*:

> If there were not a consolation with 'little fish' each time, I would be heard by the trimmings themselves.

For even Alexis in *The All-Night Festival*, putting the speech in the mouth of a cook, says:

> You always delight in 'little fish' that are hotter, either in the middle or lower down.
> Lower down? What are you saying? How? Whenever a man
> does not know how to live, shall I serve everything cold to you?
> Not at all. But boiling? By Apollo, then it will be in the middle...
> No one of the common people treats me like the other one; I don’t think so,
> nor from wherever you are now doing this. But I will tell you, for to those being cured
> I give back the right moment of the mixing... You sacrifice all the nations of the gods,
> do not chop the kid for me, but boys, bring the meat along,
> boys, to the divine kitchen.

It is clear that it should be kept in the smoke, but not for me; rather, it is bad to have smoke if the pride <note>original: *typhou*—a pun on smoke and vanity</note> cuts you off thus. These things are recorded by us "living souls" for you, O scanty-eating Ulpian. For it seems that after me and the others, you will partake of no "living thing," <note>original: *empsychon*—referring to the Pythagorean/Orphic vegetarianism</note> as someone says in this Attic piece:

<margin>Living things, specifically.</margin>
> The first person who said that a scholar gives nothing to a "living thing" was some wise man. For I have now come having bought no "living thing": I purchased fish—dead ones; and I intend to eat large portions of fat lamb—not living ones, for that is not possible; yes, I took an additional roasted liver. If any of these bites back, or has a voice or a soul, I confess I am doing wrong and breaking the law.

On these terms then, allow us to dine. For look, while I am talking to you, the pheasants <note>original: *phasianoi*</note> have sailed past, overlooking us because of your ill-timed wordiness. "But oh, you said 'to me,'" said Ulpian, "Myrtilus, my teacher, where did you get 'happy-bellied' <note>original: *olbiogastōr*</note>? And if any of the ancients mentions 'pheasant birds,' I will not sail away from you, but going to the market, I will buy a pheasant which I will look at with you." And Myrtilus said: "I speak on these conditions." He mentions "happy-bellied" again in *The Woman-Madness* speaking thus: "Eurybates Cetolaches, you were not then a 'happy-bellied' man."

<margin>a roasted dish.</margin>
<margin>Pheasants. The subject of the Birds of Aristophanes.</margin>
Regarding the pheasant bird, the most delightful Aristophanes mentions it in his play *The Birds*. There are two old Athenians who, out of a desire for a quiet life, seek a city in which they may dwell undisturbed. And the life among the birds is chosen by them; until a certain point, fearing the sight of them and consoling themselves, they say among other things: "Is there any bird you won't name? I am an angry pheasant." And in *The Clouds* I hear something of these birds, as many do from the horses. "The pheasant which Leogoras rears." To you a horse rears, to you a pheasant bird. For Leogoras is satirized as a glutton by Plato in *Priyalges*. Mnesimachus in *Philip* (he too is one of the poets of the Middle Comedy) says that even the so-called "bird's milk" will be provided, and "a well-plucked pheasant."

Theophrastus of Eresus, the student of Aristotle, in the third book of *On Animals*, mentioning them, says something like this: "There is also such a difference among birds. For those that are short-winged and not flight-oriented, such as the woodcock, the partridge, the domestic fowl, and the pheasant, are immediately walkers and ground-dwellers." And Aristotle in the seventh book of the *History of Animals* writes this: "Of birds, some are dusters, some are bathers, and some are neither dusters nor bathers. As many as are not flight-oriented, but ground-dwelling, are dusters, such as the hen, the partridge, the woodcock,

->FROM THE ATHENAEUS DEIPNOSOPHISTS<-

...pheasant, and crested lark. Speusippus also mentions them in the second book of *Similar Things*. Some have called the pheasant "phasianos" and not "phasianikos." Agatharchides of Cnidus, in the thirty-fourth book of his *History of Europe*, while discussing the Phasis River <note>The Phasis River is in modern-day Georgia; the bird’s name "pheasant" is derived from this river</note>, writes the following: "A great number of the birds called pheasants frequent the mouths of the river for the sake of food." Callixenus of Rhodes, in the fourth book of his *Account of Alexandria*, describing the famous procession of King Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, a 3rd-century BCE ruler of Egypt known for his lavish spectacles</note>, writes about these birds as a great marvel: "Then parrots were carried in cages, along with peacocks, guinea-fowl, pheasants, and a great number of Ethiopian birds." 

Artemidorus, the follower of Aristophanes, in his work titled *Culinary Terms*, and Pamphilus of Alexandria in his *On Names and Terms*, claim that Epænetus—in his book on *The Art of Cookery*—says the pheasant bird is also called a "tatyras." Ptolemy Euergetes <note>Ptolemy VIII, another king of Egypt who wrote memoirs</note>, in the second book of his *Commentaries*, says the pheasant bird is named a "tetartos." This is as much as I have to tell you about pheasants, which I have seen carried around not only for the benefit of those suffering from fevers. But if you do not fulfill your agreements and pay what was promised tomorrow, I shall sue you publicly for deception. Or rather, I will send you to live by the Phasis—just as Polemon the Geographer says that the writer Callimachus "consecrated" a namesake of his by throwing him into the river of the same name.

<margin>Francolin.</margin>The Francolin <note>original: *attagas*; likely the Black Francolin</note>. Aristophanes says in his *Storks*: "The francolin's meat is the sweetest to serve at a victory feast." Alexander the Myndian says it is slightly larger than a partridge, with its back entirely mottled and tile-colored, though tending toward reddish. It is easily caught by hunters because of its heavy weight and short wings. It is a bird that bathes in the dust, is very prolific, and is a "deserter" <note>likely meaning it escapes easily or changes its habits</note>. Socrates, in his work *On Mountains*, says that when they were brought from Lydia to the city gates, they initially made a sound like a quail. But when they hatched near the "Hollow River" and a famine occurred, and many in that region were dying, they never ceased imitating the stammering of the children, saying even now: "Evils to those who do evil." Once caught, they not only cannot be tamed but they lose their voice entirely. However, if they are released, they become vocal again. Hipponax mentions them: "Neither francolin nor silagas..." and Aristophanes mentions them in *The Birds* and *The Acharnians*, noting they are abundant in Megara. The Attic writers formed the name contrary to strict grammatical rule. For words ending in *-as* with two syllables and a long *a* in the penult are usually recessive in accent, like *akamas* or *adamas*. One should say "attagas" and not "attaglon."

<margin>Purple Swamphen.</margin>The Purple Swamphen <note>original: *porphyrio*</note>. It is clear that Aristophanes mentions this bird too. Polemon, in the fifth book of his *Remarks against Antigonus and Adaeus*, says that the swamphen, when kept in a house, keeps a watch on the women for adultery. It has such a sense for when a woman is unfaithful that when it suspects such a thing, it signals the master by "prescribing a noose for itself" <note>an ancient belief that the bird would commit suicide if it witnessed infidelity in the home</note>. He says it will not take food until it has walked to a place suitable for it, nor until it has bathed in the dust, and then it feeds. Aristotle says it has "snow-feet" <note>possibly meaning white or pale legs</note>, is blue in color, has long legs, and a red beak starting from the head, being the size of a rooster. A peculiarity of this bird is that it uses its foot like a hand to bring small morsels to its mouth, and it gulps as it drinks. It has five toes, with the middle one being the largest. Alexander the Myndian, in the second book of his *History of Birds*, says the bird is Libyan and is sacred to the gods of Libya.

<margin>Purple-bird.</margin>The Purple-bird <note>original: *porphyris*</note>. Callimachus, in his work *On Birds*, says that the *porphyrio* is different from the *porphyris*, listing them separately. He says the *porphyrio* hides while eating so that no one sees it, for it hates anyone approaching its food. Aristophanes also mentions the *porphyris* in *The Birds*. What birds does Ibycus call "dark-purples"? Because of their backs, they appear one way, but on their tips they are yellow and mottled: "The colorful, tawny-necked ducks, and the purple-birds and the long-winged halcyons." In other verses he says: "Always, my friend, the long-winged one, like the purple-bird."

<margin>Partridge.</margin>The Partridge. Many authors mention these, including Aristophanes. Some shorten the middle syllable of the name, like Archilochus: "Crouching like a partridge." They do the same with "quail" and "choenix." The word is often used as a pun by the Attic writers. Sophocles says in a comedy: "A multitude of birds named after the partridge on the famous hills of Athens." Pherecrates, the author of *The Worse Man*, said: "He came here against his will, in the manner of a partridge." Phrynichus the tragic poet says: "Cleombrotus, the son of the partridge." This animal is used symbolically to represent lust. Nicophon in *The Hand-bellies* says: "Not even a boiled partridge like that one." Epicharmus in *The Revelers* says: "You seem like a small fig-pecker and a <margin>Book 9.</margin>chattering partridge." Aristotle says the following about the animal in his *History of Animals*: "The partridge is a land bird with split toes. It lives for about fifteen years, and the female even longer, for female birds are longer-lived than the males. It broods and rears young just like a hen. When it realizes it is being hunted, it moves away from the nest and rolls about at the feet of the hunter <margin>Pliny book 10 ch. 33.</margin>, creating the hope that it will be caught, and thus deceives him until the chicks fly away, and then it flies off itself." The animal is...
