### BOOK IX.

...malicious and cunning; furthermore, it is highly lustful. For this reason, the male even crushes the eggs of the female, so that he may enjoy her sexual favors <note>Ancient naturalists believed male partridges destroyed eggs to force the female back into heat</note>. Knowing this, the female flees and lays her eggs in secret. Callimachus relates the same things in his work *On Birds*. The bachelors among them fight with one another, and the loser is mounted by the winner. Aristotle, however, says that they take turns mounting the one who has been tended to. Tame ones also mount the wild ones. Whenever one is mastered by a second, he is mounted in secret by the victor. This happens at a certain season of the year, as Alexander the naturalist <note>original: "mythios"; likely Alexander of Myndus, a writer on zoology</note> says. They nest on the ground. The males do not share a single home, <margin>Perhaps "governed/distributed" (original: διοικουμένοι).</margin> but wherever they happen to be while hunting, the leader of the wild ones thrusts himself forward in battle. When he is caught, another comes forward to fight. They do this when the one hunting is a male. But when the one hunting and singing is a female, the leader <margin>admits/approaches.</margin> approaches her, and the others gather and drive him away from the female. For they attend to her, and not to themselves. Thus, for this reason, he often approaches in silence, so that no other bird, hearing his voice, might come and fight him. Sometimes the female silences the male as he approaches. <margin>stands up/rises.</margin> Often she sits still <note>The text here is slightly corrupt; it suggests a submissive or waiting posture</note> when she perceives the male approaching the female decoy, and she endures being mounted so that she may draw him away from the decoy. Indeed, both partridges and quails are so crazed with the desire to mate that they fall right into the hands of the hunters, <note>textual variant suggests: "settling upon their heads"</note>. Those who lead female partridges out for the hunt say that when the females see or smell the male downwind, or see them flying nearby, they become so excited that some even lay eggs on the spot. Both females and males gape their mouths and stick out their tongues during the mating season. Clearchus, in his work *On Panic*, says that <margin>or: "the one sitting upon the hives"</margin> sparrows, partridges, and even cocks and quails, discharge their seed not only upon seeing the females, but even upon hearing their voice. The cause of this is the mental impression <term>phantasia</term><note>A technical term for a mental image or sensory impression that triggers a physical response</note> regarding mating that occurs in the soul. This becomes most apparent during mating when they are hunted using mirrors. For they approach because of the reflection and are caught, discharging their seed—except for the cocks. In their case, the perception of the reflection leads only to a fight. These are the words of Clearchus.

Partridges are called "kakkabai" by some, as in the works of Alcman, who speaks thus: "Alcman composed a melody, having discovered the tongue-sounded name of the 'kakkabides'." He clearly shows that he learned to sing from the partridges. For this reason, Chamaeleon of Pontus said that the invention of music was devised by the ancients from birds singing in the deserts, from whose imitation he says music was derived. Not all partridges, however, make the "kakkabe" sound. Theophrastus, at any rate, in his work *On the Different Voices of Similar Animals*, says that the partridges at Athens which sit on this side of Corydallus toward the city chirp <note>Greek: "tithubizousin"; an onomatopoeic word for a sharp, twittering sound</note>, while those on the other side make a different sound. Bassilis, in the second book of his *Indian History*, says that the small men <note>The legendary Pygmies of Greek myth, often said to be at war with cranes</note> who wage war against cranes use partridges as mounts. Menecrates, in the first book of his *Collection*, says that the Pygmies war against both partridges and cranes. There is another genus of partridges in Italy, dark in plumage and smaller in build, and not having a vermilion beak. The partridges around Cirrha have meat that is uneatable because of their pasture. Those around Boeotia either do not cross over into Attica, or if they do, they are distinguished by their voice, as we said before. Theophrastus says that the partridges found around Paphlagonia have two hearts. Those on the island of Sciathos eat snails. They sometimes lay fifteen or sixteen eggs. They fly only for short distances, as Xenophon writes in the first book of the *Anabasis*: "As for the bustards, <margin>bustards (otides).</margin> if one starts them up quickly, they can be caught. For they fly only a short distance, like partridges, and soon tire out. Their meat is delicious." Plutarch, however, says that Xenophon is talking about the bustard. He says these animals are brought in great numbers to Alexandria from the nearby regions of Libya, where they are hunted in the following way. The animal is mimetic, much like the *otos* <note>The "otos" is a species of eared owl; its name shares a root with "otis" (bustard)</note>, especially of whatever it sees a man doing. It does the same things it sees the hunters doing. The hunters, standing opposite them, smear their eyes with a certain drug, having prepared other drugs that are sticky to the eyes and eyelids, which they place in small bowls nearby. The bustards, watching the men smearing themselves, do the same thing, taking from the bowls, and are quickly caught. Aristotle writes about them thus: "It is a migratory and winter-visiting bird, three-toed, the size of a large cock, with the plumage of a quail, a long head, sharp claws, a thin neck, large eyes, a bony tongue, and it has no crop." Alexander the naturalist says it is also called the "lagoidia" <note>"Hare-bird," likely due to its speed or the color of its feathers</note>. They say it is also forced into friendship and takes pleasure in a horse. If someone puts on a horse-hide, he can hunt as many as he wants, for they approach him. In other passages, Aristotle says again: "The *otos* is similar to the owl, but it is not nocturnal. It has two tufts of feathers by its ears. It is called *otos* (eared), is the size of a pigeon, and is a mimic of humans."

### BOOK IX.

...the author himself has called them quails <note>original: "ortyges"</note>, saying: "Have you ever raised any quails?" "I have indeed, small ones." "And then what?" Antiphanes, in *The Countryman*, mentions a "male quail," implying that it has a spirit capable of doing the work of a quail. Pratinas, in *The Women of Dyme* or *The Tailoresses*, uniquely calls the quail "sweet-voiced," unless perhaps he means it has a voice among the Phliasians or the Spartans, just as partridges do. Didymus says the *siklis* <note>A small bird, perhaps a type of wagtail or lark</note> may have been named from this sound, for almost most birds get their names from the sounds they make. Then there is the so-called "quail-mother" <note>original: "ortygometra"; likely the Corncrake</note>, which Crates mentions in *The Worse Men*, saying: "the quail-mother is a distinct species." Alexander of Myndus <note>The OCR reads "Mydios" here, a common transcription error for Myndios</note> says of her that she is the size of a turtle-dove, has long legs, and is difficult to handle and cowardly. Concerning the hunting of quails, Clearchus of Soli tells a unique story in the work entitled *On the Mathematical Passages in Plato’s Republic*, writing as follows: "Around the time of mating, if someone places a mirror opposite the quails and a snare in front of it, they run toward their own reflection in the mirror and fall into the snare." He tells similar stories about the birds called jackdaws <note>original: "koloioi"</note>. Because of their natural affection—and they differ so much in their overall craftiness—nevertheless, when a bowl full of olive oil is set out, they perch on the rim and, looking down at their reflection, they try to seize it. Because of this, the olive oil causes a fire <note>perhaps referring to the oil's reflective sheen or its role in trapping them</note>, or the sticking together of their feathers becomes the cause of their capture. The Athenians lengthen the middle syllable of the name <note>referring to "ortyx"</note>, as Demetrius of Ixion says in his work *On the Alexandrian Dialect*. But Aristophanes in *Peace* shortened it for the sake of the meter, saying "home-bred quails." Regarding the birds called *chennia*, they are a small kind of quail; Cleomenes mentions them in his letter to Alexander <margin>Chennia.</margin>, writing: "ten thousand salted birds, five thousand cushions, and ten thousand salted *chennia*." And Hipparchus in his *Egyptian Iliad* says: "The life of the Egyptians did not please me, the way they pluck *chennia* and smoke the dizzying little things."

<margin>Swans. Book 9.</margin>
Swans were also frequently present at our banquet. Concerning them, Aristotle says: "The swan is gregarious and combative; at least, the warlike ones kill each other. They even fight the eagle, though they do not start the fight themselves. They are musical, especially near the end of their lives <note>This is the origin of the 'Swan Song' myth</note>. They cross the sea singing, but they are not dung-eaters in their slow-footed nature." But Alexander of Myndus says that although he followed many dying swans, he never heard them sing. Hegesianax of Alexandria, who composed the *Trojan Histories* under the name of Cephalion, says that Cycnus <note>The name means 'Swan'</note>, who fought a duel with Achilles, was raised in Leucophrys by a bird of the same name. Boios in his *Ornithogonia* (or Boio, as Philochorus calls her), says that Cycnus was turned into a bird by Ares. And in a humorous passage, by the river Sybaris, he approached a crane. He also says that he [Cycnus] planted the plant called *lygaia*. Boios also says concerning the crane that there was a famous woman named Gerana among the Pygmies. She was honored as a goddess by her citizens, and she herself came to think she truly was a goddess, despising especially Hera and Artemis. Hera, becoming angry, transformed her into an ugly bird <note>the crane</note> and made her an enemy and a loathed creature to the Pygmies who had honored her. He says that from her and Nicodamas was born the land-tortoise. In general, the poet of these verses records that all birds were formerly humans.

<margin>Pigeons. Book 9.</margin>
Pigeons <note>original: "phassai"</note>. Aristotle says they are a genus of the dove family, but of five distinct types, writing as follows: "the domestic pigeon <note>peristera</note>, the rock-dove <note>oinas</note>, the wood-pigeon <note>phaps</note>, the ring-dove <note>phassa</note>, and the turtle-dove <note>trygon</note>." In the fifth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, he does not name the *phaps*. Aeschylus in his *Proteus* mentions the bird thus: "the wretched, fattened *phaps*, its blackened ribs crushed and cooked." And in *Philoctetes*, he mentions the "sweet rest of the *phaps*." Now, the rock-dove, says Aristotle, is larger than the domestic pigeon, but smaller than the *phaps*. The ring-dove is the size of a cock, and its color is like ash. The turtle-dove is the smallest of all and its color is greyish. It appears in summer and hides in the winter. But the *phaps* and the domestic pigeon are seen all year round. The rock-dove appears only in autumn. The ring-dove is said to be the longest-lived of these, for it lives thirty and even forty years. Neither the males nor the females leave their mates until death, but if one dies, the survivor remains widowed. Ravens, crows, and jackdaws do the same. The entire pigeon-like race takes turns incubating the eggs. When the chicks are born, the male spits on them so that they are not bewitched <note>original: "baskanthosi"; to protect against the 'evil eye'</note>. It lays two eggs, the first of which produces a male and the second a female.

<margin>* they lay. † Still later, the "peleias" is the domestic pigeon. The "peleias" is smaller to me. They lay eggs, and more are born in their rough parts. The "peleias" is both black and small, and more reddish and rough, because of where it is raised.</margin>
They lay eggs in every season of the year, and they produce ten or eleven clutches a year * [as they lay]. In Egypt, they lay twelve times, for after giving birth, she conceives again on the following day. Furthermore, Aristotle says in the same work † that there is another pigeon, the *peleias*, which is smaller. The *peleias* becomes tame, but the common pigeon <note>peristera</note> is black, small, reddish, and rough, and therefore spares nothing. He says a peculiarity of the pigeon is that they kiss when they are about to mate, or even when the female is about to lay. The older bird leads and initiates the mating without kissing, but the younger ones always do this when they mate. Even females mount one another when no male is present, after having kissed; but they produce nothing from each other, laying only "wind-eggs" <note>infertile eggs</note> from which no chick is born. ->## ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS<-

...you will make the wild pigeon <note>original: "peleias"</note> itself tamer than a house pigeon <note>original: "peristera"</note>, as Sophron says in his *Mimes of Women*. Callimachus, in his work *On Birds*, lists them as distinct species: the wood-pigeon <note>original: "phassa"</note>, the fire-red bird <note>original: "pyrallis"</note>, the house pigeon, and the turtle-dove. Alexander of Myndus <note>A Greek writer on natural history</note> says that the wood-pigeon is not a "self-cuckoo" <note>An imitation of its call</note>, unlike the turtle-dove, and that it remains silent in winter unless there is fair weather. It is also said that if the rock-dove <note>original: "oinas"</note> eats a moderate amount of laurel, it becomes capable of mating for some time, and produces mistletoe. Daimachus, in his *History of India*, records that pigeons the color of quinces <note>original: "melinas"; yellowish-gold</note> are found in India. Charon of Lampsacus, in his *History of Persia*, while discussing the city of Mardonia and the destruction of the fleet at Mount Athos <note>The Persian fleet was wrecked here in 492 BCE</note>, writes the following: "And then white pigeons were seen for the first time among the Greeks, <margin>Book 9. Pigeons.</margin> having never existed there before." Aristotle says that when the young pigeons are born, the parents masticate salty earth and spit it into the chicks' open mouths, preparing them in this way for their food. In Sicily, at Eryx <note>Home to a famous temple of Aphrodite</note>, there is a festival of the gods called the *Anagogia* <note>The "Leading Away" or "Departure"</note>, during which they say the goddess departs for Libya. At that time, the pigeons in the area disappear, as if they have gone abroad with the goddess. Nine days later, at the festival called the *Katagogia* <note>The "Return"</note>, a single golden-colored pigeon is seen flying in from the sea toward the island, and then the rest arrive. All the inhabitants who are wealthy enough to have heard the news of the festival of Cronus celebrate with feasts; the rest celebrate with joy. At that time, the whole place smells of butter, which they use as evidence of the goddess’s divine return. Autocrates, in his *History of Achaia*, records that Zeus changed his form when he fell in love with a girl named Pythoe in Aegium. The Athenians use the masculine form, "pigeon-cock" <note>original: "peristeron"</note>. Alexis says in *The Syrians*: "I am the white pigeon of Aphrodite. Dionysus knows only how to get drunk; whether the wine is new or old, he does not care." In his play *The Rhodian*, he uses the feminine form for a bird that chirps, and notes that the Sicilian ones are distinct: "the nature of the Sicilian pigeon is exceptionally elegant." Pherecrates says in *The Old Women*: "Send away the male pigeon as a messenger." And in *Petale*: "O little pigeon, fly like Calliphon <note>A famous runner or messenger</note>, and carry me to Cythera and Cyprus." Nicander, in the second book of his *Georgics*, mentions Sicilian pigeons, saying: "You might raise dragon-like hawks, or Sicilian pigeons in your halls; neither are they obvious, nor are they mentioned as those that dwell in the thickets." <margin>Ducks.</margin> **Ducks.** Of these, as Alexander of Myndus says, the male is larger and more colorful. The bird called the golden-eye <note>original: "glaukion"</note> gets its name from the color of its eyes; it is slightly smaller than a duck. Of those called teals <note>original: "boskades"</note>, the male is more patterned than the duck. The males have smaller, flatter beaks in proportion to their size. <margin>Grebe.</margin> The little grebe <note>original: "kolymbis"</note> is the smallest of all the waterfowl; it is blackish in color, has a sharp beak, and its eyes are constantly watching as it dives frequently. There is another kind of teal, larger than a duck but smaller than a shelduck <note>original: "chenalopex"</note>. Those called garganeys <note>original: "phaskades"</note> are slightly larger than the little grebes, but otherwise similar to ducks. The bird called the gadwall <note>original: "oueia"</note> is not much smaller than a duck; it is a dirty-grey color and has a long, narrow beak. The coot <note>original: "phalaris"</note> also has a narrow beak, is more rounded in appearance, and is ash-colored on its belly and back. Ducks and grebes—from which the words "to swim" <note>original: "nechein"</note> and "to dive" <note>original: "kolymban"</note> are derived—are mentioned along with many other marsh-birds by Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*: "ducks, divers, teals, coots, grebes." Callimachus also mentions them in his work *On Birds*. Often there were served to us the birds called "leek-colored" <note>original: "prasatoi"</note>, which Epainetus mentions in his *Art of Cookery* and Simarus in the sixth book of his *Synonyms*. In the fourth book, he says these are actually testicles so named. While some meats "smothered" in broth <note>original: "pnikta"; a method of cooking in a sealed pot</note> were being served, one of the guests asked what kind of meats these were. Ulpian <note>A character in the dialogue known for being a pedantic grammarian</note>, the "Daedalus of names," said: "I will choke myself <note>A pun on "smothered" (pniktos)</note> if you don't tell me where you found the word for such meats! I won't eat them until I learn." He then cited Stratis in *The Macedonians*: "Or some Cinnysian, I drink down much 'smothered' meat before bed." And Eubulus in *The Glue-Maker*: "and Sicilian smothered porridges." Aristophanes says in *The Wasps*: "smothered in a dish." Cratinus in *The Flask*: "what part of the clean little 'smothered' meat should I take?" Antiphanes in *The Countryman*: "First, I lift up the longed-for barley cake, the gift of Demeter that brings joy to mortals. Then, the tender, smothered limbs of bleating kids, <margin>Sucklings.</margin> fresh-slaughtered meat covered in greens." "What do you say, should we eat?" I advise you with the words of Sophocles. **Suckling pigs.** When some suckling pigs were brought in, it was asked if the name "suckling" <note>original: "galathinos"; literally "milk-fed"</note> had been used before. Someone said: Pherecrates in *The Teachers* says "sucklings, missing but not yet complete." In *The Deserters*: "You who are about to sacrifice a suckling." Alcaeus in *The Wrestling School*: "For he is the same... if I should rub on more than a suckling pig." Herodotus says in his first book that in Babylon, it is not permitted to sacrifice anything except sucklings on the golden altar. Antiphanes in *The Friend of his Comrades*: "A clever little piece of meat, this suckling." Heniochus in *Polydyctus*: "The bronze ox goes... and of old, he perhaps took the pig as a suckling." And Anacreon says: "Like a tender, suckling fawn, which, left behind in the woods by its antlered mother, is terrified." Crates in *The Neighbors*: "Now, let it not be for you like the suckling..."

# BOOK 9.

...still of suckling animals <note>original: "galathenoi"; refers to young animals still feeding on milk</note> and young pigs. Simonides, describing Danae with the infant Perseus, makes her say: "O child, what a burden I bear, yet you sleep with a suckling's <note>original: "galathenon"</note> heart." And elsewhere, speaking of Alcmene, he says that she "gave birth to a suckling babe <note>original: "galathenon tokos"</note> who breathed out a sweet soul." Clearchus, in his *Lives*, says that the tyrant Phalaris <note>A notoriously cruel ruler of Akragas in Sicily</note> reached such a height of cruelty that he would feast on suckling infants. The term is feminine for those who suck milk. For Hector, being mortal, "sucked a woman’s breast," and there is a poetic line: "A hind having put to sleep her suckling <note>original: "galathenas"</note> fawns." We must now move on to gazelles <note>original: "dorkades"</note>, because Palamedes, the namer of things, said they provide quite a pleasant meat. Myrtilus asked, "How is it that they are only called *dorkades* and never *dorkones*?" <margin>Gazelles.</margin> Xenophon, in the first book of the *Anabasis*, writes: "There were also bustards and gazelles."

<margin>The Peacock.</margin> **The Peacock.** This bird was once rare. Antiphanes, in *The Soldier* or *Tykon*, says: "He brought only a single pair of peacocks, the thing being so rare." But now they are more numerous than quails. And Eubulus in *The Phoenix* says: "For the peacock is admired because of its rarity." Aristotle says the peacock <note>original: "taos"</note> is blue-colored and variegated. It breeds when it is three years old, at which time it also acquires the variety of its plumage. It sits on its eggs for thirty days. It lays twelve eggs once a year—not all at once, but every other day. Those laying for the first time lay eight. It also lays "wind-eggs" <note>original: "hypunemia"; unfertilized eggs</note>, like a hen. It hatches its eggs by sitting on them just like a hen. Eupolis, in *The Draft-Dodgers*, says: "I will never keep pigeons, but rather the life of peacocks, who do not even wake those who are sleeping." Antiphon the orator <note>An influential Athenian politician and speechwriter</note> wrote a speech entitled *On Peacocks*. In the speech itself, the name "peacock" is never used, but he frequently calls it a "variegated bird," claiming that people were granted a view of them by a decree of the people. He describes how many people came out of a longing to see the birds, arriving from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> and Thessaly, and that they even tried to obtain some of the eggs. Speaking of their appearance, he writes: "If someone wanted to introduce such birds into the city, it is not from where they are sent back. For if you cut their wings, you take away their beauty; for their feathers are their beauty, not their body." He also mentions in the same speech that the sight of them was a public spectacle: "On the new moons, those who wish may enter, but on other days, if anyone comes wishing to see them, there is no time they cannot. This has not been the case just since yesterday or the day before, but for more than thirty years."

The Athenians say *taōs* <note>peacock</note>, as Tryphon says, using a circumflex accent on the last syllable and a rough breathing <note>an "h" sound at the start of the syllable</note>. They read it this way in Eupolis’s *Draft-Dodgers*, as cited before. And in *The Birds*, Aristophanes writes: "For Tereus has turned into a winged bird or a peacock?" And again: "What on earth is this bird? Surely a peacock." They also use the Ionized form *taōni*, as Aristophanes does in that same play. It is impossible among the Athenians and Ionians for names of more than one syllable that begin with a vowel at the last syllable to be pronounced with a rough breathing. For they will certainly follow a smooth breathing. For example: *neōs* <note>temple</note>, *Menelēōs*, *Lakonikos*, *eunēōs*, *prāos* <note>gentle</note>, *huios* <note>son</note>, *Chios*, *dios* <note>divine</note>, *chaos*, *pleios* <note>full</note>, *laios* <note>left</note>, *baios* <note>small</note>, *phaios* <note>grey</note>, *choos* <note>soil</note>, *thoos* <note>swift</note>, *roos* <note>stream</note>, *zōos* <note>alive</note>. Philarchus says that the rough breathing is naturally dominant and is silently enclosed in the final parts of names. The peacock is named *taōs* from the stretching <note>original: "tasis"</note> of its feathers. Seleucus, in the fifth book of *On Hellenism*, says the Athenians use the rough breathing and circumflex on *taōs* without a logical reason. But for the first vowels of names, they wish to bring out the simple pronunciation, and to set it forth more quickly. The Athenians judge the nature of the accent from the vowels, just like other things. I believe the ancients shaped the rough breathing for their own reasons. This is why the Romans <margin>lib. 6.</margin> prefix a *k* <note>likely referring to the Latin 'h' or 'c' sounds</note> before all words that have a rough breathing, signifying its dominance. If such is the nature of the rough breathing, perhaps it is not without reason that the final syllable of *taōs* is aspirated by the Athenians.

Many things having been said at the banquet about each item brought in, Larentius said: "But I, too, now propose to the excellent Ulpian: what are we eating? What do you think the *tetrax* <note>a grouse or guinea-fowl</note> is? After whom is it named? Is it a type of bird?" <margin>The Grouse.</margin> It is the custom of grammarians to propose questions about everything—a type of plant, a bird, or a stone. Larentius said to the man: "Aristophanes mentions it charmingly in *The Birds*, in a place I know: 'to the purple gallinule, the pelican, the spoonbill, the phlexis, the *tetrax*, and the peacock.' I seek to learn from you if there is any mention of it in any other author." Alexander of Myndus, in the second book of *On Winged Creatures*, mentions it not as a large bird, but as one of the smallest. He says: "The *tetrax* is equal in size to a 'seed-collector' <note>original: "spermalogos"; possibly a sparrow</note>, with a brick-colored plumage. It is variegated with small spots and large lines, and it eats fruit. When it lays eggs, its call is *tebaxa*." Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, mentions them being served: "taking quails and sparrows and crested larks, red-necked grouse <note>original: "tetragas"</note>, seed-collectors, and splendid fig-peckers." And in other works he says: "there were many herons with long curved necks, and grouse <note>original: "tebages"</note>, and seed-collectors." Since you have nothing to say and remain silent, I will show you the bird itself. For they are making a noise in the...

# ATHENAEUS: THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED
### BOOK 9 (Continued)

<margin>Budé, *On the Ancient Coinage*, Book 2 <note>original: "Bud. 2. de Asse"; a reference to the 16th-century scholar Guillaume Budé</note></margin>
...as if it were the emperor's, for whom I have presided over the affairs of that province. I have seen in that region the quail <note>original: "ortyx"</note>, which, having learned it is called so among the Mysians <note>People of northwest Asia Minor</note>, I present here, being reminded of it by the words of Aristophanes <note>Likely Aristophanes of Byzantium, the grammarian</note> regarding the bird. I believe also that the animal was deemed worthy of mention by the most learned Aristotle in his very costly treatise (for the story goes that he received eight hundred talents <note>A massive sum; one talent was roughly 60 lbs of silver</note> from Alexander the Great to support his *History of Animals*). Although I found nothing specifically said by him there, I was happy to have the most graceful Aristophanes as a very close witness. While he was saying this, someone came in carrying a grouse <note>original: "tetrax"</note> in a basket. In size, it was larger than the largest rooster, and in appearance it resembled a purple coot; from its ears on both sides it had hanging bits, just as roosters have wattles <note>original: "kallaia"</note>, and its voice was deep. While we were marveling at the bird's bright colors, it was brought in shortly after having been prepared, and its meat was very similar to that of the large sparrow <note>The ostrich</note>, which we have often eaten.

<margin>The Loins.</margin>
**The Loins.** The author of *The Return of the Descendants of Aeneas*, in his third book, says: "having loins <note>original: "psyas"</note> equal to his swift and back-turning feet." Simaristus, in the third book of his *Synonyms*, writes: "the fleshy parts gathered at the sides of the spine are called the loins <note>original: "psyai"</note>." The hollows on either side are called *kybai* or *galliai*. Clearchus, in his second book *On Skeletons*, says: "the fleshy muscles on each part, which some call loins, others 'foxes' <note>original: "alopekas"</note>, and others 'womb-sinews' <note>original: "neurometras"</note>." Hippocrates the most holy <note>The famous physician of Kos</note> also mentions these loins. They were named so because they are easily rubbed off <note>original: "apopsasthai"</note>, like the flesh upon the ridges of the back, even if they are on superficial bones. Euphron the comic poet also mentions them in *The Women at the Festival*: "a certain lobe and what are called loins—having learned to prize these before even seeing them." 

<margin>The Udder.</margin>
**The Udder.** Telecleides says in *Hard Men*: "As a female udder <note>original: "outhar"</note>, I naturally carry water." Herodotus, in the fourth book of his *Histories*, says: "Coming back whenever he finds the udder <note>original: "outhar"</note>," a term used for other animals as well. 

<margin>The Under-belly.</margin>
**The Under-belly.** The term *hypogastrion* is used specifically for fish. Stratis in *Atalanta* mentions "the under-belly <note>original: "hypogastrion"</note> of a tuna and a pig's trotter." Theopompus in *Kallaischros* mentions "the under-bellies of fish." 

<margin>Drinking-vessels.</margin>
In *The Sirens*, he calls the under-bellies "drinking-vessels" <note>original: "hypoteria"</note>, saying: "the drinking-vessels of white Sicilian tunas." 

<margin>The Hare.</margin>
**The Hare.** Regarding this most sweet creature, Archestratus <note>A 4th-century BCE poet known as the 'Hesiod of Gout'</note> says: "There are many ways and many styles of preparing the hare. But this one is best: bring the roasted meat to each guest while it is still hot, simply sprinkled with salt and snatched from the spit while it is still a bit rare <note>original: "psomostomon"</note>. Do not let it grieve you to see the juices <note>original: "ichora"</note> dripping from the meat, but eat it greedily! All other preparations are, to my mind, unnecessary: sticky sauces, or covering it in cheese and too much oil, as if they were cooking for a cat!" Naucrates the comic poet says in *The Persian Woman* that it is rare to find a "shaggy-foot" <note>a nickname for the hare</note> in Attica: "In Attica, has anyone ever seen lions or any other shaggy beast? One cannot even easily find a hare <note>original: "dasypoda"</note>." Alcaeus in *Callisto* suggests they were once common, saying that if you catch them, you should have salt ready to sprinkle on them. Tryphon says that Aristophanes used the form *lagon* <note>The author is here debating the specific Attic Greek spelling of 'hare'</note> in *The Danaids*, saying: "A wolf might perhaps snatch our hare <note>original: "lagon"</note>." In *The Banqueters*, he says: "I am ruined; I shall be seen plucking the hare." Xenophon, in his *Treatise on Hunting*, uses the form *lago* without the 'n'. Just as we say *naos* (temple) and they say *neos*, or *laos* (people) and they say *leos*, so where we say *lagon*, they say *lagon*. Sophocles also uses the plural *lagoi* in his satyr play *Amlycus*: "cranes, crows, owls, kites, hares." Eupolis also uses the form *lago*. Some writers accent the word on the final syllable without reason. Since nouns ending in -os are usually accented the same way even when changed to the Attic -os (like *naos/neos*), the name is used this way by Epicharmus, Herodotus, and the author of *The Helots*. In the Ionian dialect, it is *lagos*, as in "having disturbed the sea-hare." In the Attic dialect, it is *lagos*. Hegesander of Delphi in his *Commentaries* says that in the time of Antigonus Gonatas <note>Macedonian King, 3rd century BCE</note>, such a multitude of hares was produced in Astypalaea <note>An island in the Dodecanese</note> that the inhabitants consulted the oracle. The Pythia <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi</note> told them to breed dogs and hunt, and in one year more than six thousand were caught. This population explosion happened because a man from Anaphe had released two hares on the island; previously, a man from Astypalaea had released two partridges on Anaphe, which resulted in such a 

<margin>
Anaphe is one of the Sporades, according to Stephanus, book 4.
</margin>
multitude of partridges on Anaphe that the inhabitants were in danger of being driven out. Originally, Astypalaea had no hares, only partridges. The hare is a most prolific animal, as Xenophon said in his *Treatise on Hunting*. Herodotus says: "The hare is hunted by everything—beasts, birds, and men—and yet it is so prolific. It is the only animal that can conceive while already pregnant <note>original: "epikyisketai"; the biological phenomenon of superfetation</note>."

## BOOK 9

...in the female. Some of the young are formed in the belly with hair, some are bald, some are just being shaped in the uterus, and others are still in the early stages of conception. 

<margin>The Rabbit <note>original: "Koniklos"</note></margin>
Polybius, in the twelfth book of his *Histories*, says that there is an animal very similar to the hare called the **rabbit** <note>original: "koniklos"</note>, writing as follows: "The so-called rabbit, when seen from a distance, appears to be a small hare. However, when one takes it in their hands, there is a great difference, both in its outward appearance and in its taste. It lives for the most part underground." Posidonius the philosopher also mentions them in his *History*, and we ourselves saw many of them during the voyage from Dicaearchia <note>modern Pozzuoli, near Naples</note> to Naples. For there is a long island off the coast where the final parts of Dicaearchia lie, which is sparsely inhabited but has a great many of these rabbits. 

<margin>Swallow-hares <note>original: "Chelidonioι lagōoι"</note>. Gellius, Book 16, Chapter 15. Carthaginian swine.</margin>
Some are also called "swallow-hares." Diphilus of Laodicea mentions them in his play *Ignorance*, saying: "For what country is this swallow-hare <note>original: "chelidonios dasupous"</note> from? And the *memarkus* is a gray-fish." Theopompus, in the twentieth book of his *Histories*, says that in Bisaltia <note>a region in Macedonia</note> hares are born having two livers. 

Regarding the wild sow <note>original: "suos agrios"</note> which surpassed all in size, which was no smaller than me—I mean the one famously called the **Calydonian boar**—I propose a question to you, our meticulous researcher Ulpian: Who recorded that the Calydonian boar was actually female and white in color? 

He, having thought deeply and then remaining silent on the problem, said: "But to you, you gluttons <note>original: "gastrones"</note> who never seem to have your fill of delicacies, you seem to me to exceed all those who have become notorious for overeating. And you ask who these people are, though it is only right that you should now bring forward the facts about the pig <note>original: "sus"</note> more accurately." For the animal is called *sys* from *sthueisthai* <note>original: "σθύεισθαι"</note>, meaning to be impetuous or rushing. Others say it comes from *syorethein* <note>to be stirred up</note>, as if it were *thuein* <note>to sacrifice</note>, as it is the most suitable animal for sacrifice. 

<margin>The Wild Boar <note>original: "Suagros"</note></margin>
"If you please, answer me this: who mentions the hunting of the pig under the name **syagros** <note>a compound of 'pig' and 'wild/field'</note>, referring to the wild boar?" 

For Sophocles, in his *Lovers of Achilles*, applied the name to a dog, saying it 'violently haunts the fields' <note>original: "agrous bia"</note>: "And you, O *Syagros*, an ancestral sword." 

<margin>Syagros</margin>
In Herodotus, the name **Syagros** is a proper noun belonging to a Spartan who went as an ambassador to Gelon of Syracuse regarding an alliance against the Medes <note>the Persians</note>, in his seventh book. In Aetolia, I also know of a general named Syagros, whom Phylarchus mentions in the fourth book of his *Histories*. 

And Democritus said: "If ever you, O Ulpian, are accustomed to partake of the strength of the dishes prepared before you, you must first learn if the use of these names is ancient. You risk one day having these worries dissolve you, just as the Coan poet Philitas did." 

<margin>Suidas <note>a reference to the Byzantine encyclopedia, likely a later annotator's note</note></margin>
Philitas of Cos, while investigating the so-called 'Liar' paradox of logic <note>the 'pseudologos'—a famous logical puzzle where a statement contradicts itself</note>, became quite thin in body because of his researches and died, as the epigraph on his monument shows: 

*Stranger, I am Philitas; the 'Liar' argument destroyed me,* 
*And the evening cares of nighttime study.* 

Lest you too disappear while searching for the *Syagros*, learn that Antiphanes, in *The Girl Who was Carried Off*, named it so: "I will bring the wild boar (*syagros*) back to the house tonight to face the lion and the wolf." Dionysius the tyrant, in his *Adonis*, says: "I hear the Nymphs... the wild boar (*syagros*)... to whom I offer many first-fruits." Lynceus of Samos, in his letter to Apollodorus, writes: "So that you may have the wild things for the children, and the wild boar meat (*syagria*) for yourself with your friends." Hippolochus the Macedonian, whom we mentioned in the letter to Lynceus, speaks of being "affected by many wild boars." 

Since you have avoided answering the question of where the Calydonian boar comes from and who recorded it as white, I will tell you. The evidence is from Cleomenes of Rhegium in his dithyrambs. In the one entitled *Meleager*, he records this history. 

<margin>Achedoros</margin>
I am not unaware that those living in Sicily call the wild boar an **achedoros**. Aeschylus, in his *Phorcides*, comparing Perseus to this wild beast, says: "He entered the cave like a wild boar (*achedoros*)." And Sciras (he is a poet of the so-called Italian Comedy, a Tarentine by birth) says in his *Meleager*: "A shepherd thinks it right to pasture his flocks where no wild boar (*achedoros*) comes to mate." It is not surprising that Aeschylus, having spent time in Sicily, used many Sicilian words. 

<margin>Kids <note>original: "Eriphoi"</note></margin>
**Kids** are also frequently served, prepared in various ways, some with much seasoning, which provide no small pleasure to us. Indeed, goat meat is very nourishing. Cleitomachus of Carthage, who was second to none in the theory of the New Academy <note>a school of skeptical philosophy</note>, says that a certain Theban athlete surpassed everyone in strength by feeding himself solely on goat meat. For its juices are tough and sticky, and able to remain in the muscles for a long time. This athlete was joked about, however, because of the bad smell of his sweat. Pork and lamb, which remain unexhausted by boiling, spoil most easily because of their fat. 

The dinners described by the comic poets provide more pleasure to the ears than to the throat, such as those in Antiphanes' *The Female Seamstress*: "He would gladly eat the meat of some animal," he says, "For the sake of economy, sheep that have neither wool nor lamb's cheese, my dear friend. And of goats, in the same way, those that produce no cheese. For I endure eating the poorest of things for the sake of the profit from the fertile ones." And in *The Cyclops* he says: "Of land animals, there shall come to you before me..."

<meta>This page continues the catalog of animals and foodstuffs discussed during the banquet, moving from the natural history of hares and pigs into a sprawling poetic list of ingredients and a philosophical defense of the art of cookery.</meta>

->ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED<-
# BOOK 9

...here are oxen from the herd, mountain-roaming goats, "celestial" goats <note>A poetic or perhaps breeds-specific term for high-climbing goats</note>, castrated rams, castrated boars, castrated swine, suckling pigs, hares, kids, fresh cheese, dry cheese, pounded cheese, grated cheese, sliced cheese, and curdled cheese.

Mnesimachus, in his play *The Horse-Breeder* <note>original: "Hippotrophos"</note>, prepares the following scene: "Come out from the cypress-roofed chambers, Manes; go out to the market... see how well Hermes <note>The god of commerce</note> protects it, for the tribal leaders do not frequent it. Tell the students who are learning to mount horses that I am sparing in my descent, just as I tell their ears. Tell them this: the cold things are four, the drink is hot, the mixture is dry, the loaves are dry, and the offal is being roasted anew. You have snatched meat from the brine; a slice of sausage has been taken out, and a slice of stomach-tripe. One of small-intestine, another of large-intestine. It is all being counted out by the voting-pebbles <note>A metaphor for accounting or perhaps the noise of the kitchen</note>, and let the mixing-bowl flow out whenever the wine-offering proceeds. Only the *skordax* <note>A lewd dance associated with comedy</note> remains; it acts lewdly among the youths. Everything dear to them is turned upside down. Remember what I say, pay attention to my words! You stand there gaping; look here and see if you can repeat these things, for I will tell you to come back from the beginning if you fail. And tell the cook not to ruin anything, as the delicacies are being boiled, roasted, or served cold."

The speaker then lists them one by one:
**Bulb, olive, garlic, cabbage, gourd, pea-soup, sulphur-wort, leafy-greens, pieces of cedar-smoked meat, gray-fishes, sharks, squat-rays, conger eels, a whole phyxikinos, a whole black-tail, sprats, mackerel, tunny-fish, gudgeon, spindle-fish, the tail of a gudgeon, stingrays, frog-fish, perch, lizard-fish, zygiai, wrasses, belechos, red mullets, gurnards, sea-pigeons, moray eels, sea-breams, myllos, libias, aparos, parrot-fish, speckled-fish, Thracian-fish, swallow-fish, shrimp, squid, flounder, brakainis, cuttlefish, groupers, lobsters, grilled-fish, whitebait, needle-fish, mestreus, scorpion-fishes, eels, and aphthoi.**

As for other meats, the quantity is unspeakable:
**Pig, ox, lamb, sheep, boar, goat, rooster, duck, jay, partridge, and fox-meat.** And after dinner, what a wonder of good things! Throughout the house there are small barley-cakes, flat-cakes, plucked fowl, minced meats, drums of bread, eggs, and joy; one plays, there are garden-herbs, dinners, and fine things; one leaps and dances. The voices of the flutes are venerable and I admire them, with song and clangor...

<margin>Rhodunthia: a servant-boy.</margin>
...cassia-horn from the holy land, and from the sea and the swine. A venerable scent of long-burning frankincense shakes the nostrils, along with myrrh, reed-spice, Syrian balsam, and deep-dyed linen, and mint. The house is filled with a mist of all good things.

Upon these words being spoken, there was brought in the dish called a **rhodunthia** <note>likely a dish flavored with roses or pink in color</note>. Concerning this, that Phrygian cook spoke like a tragic actor before showing what he was carrying. He mocked the celebrated master cooks of old, and in mentioning them, he said: "What is more acute than this? The cook in Antiphanes' comedy *The Man Who Veiled Himself* <note>original: "Enkalyptomenos"</note> boasted in this way."

<margin>Culinary instructions.</margin>
It is not easy to reach the pinnacle of Sophon or Damoxenus, who were fellow students in the art. They were taught by Labdacus of Sicily. These men wiped the old and legendary seasonings out of the books and vanished that way of life from our midst. I mean things like **cumin, vinegar, silphium, cheese, and coriander**—the seasonings that Cronus <note>i.e., people from the ancient, "Golden Age" or simply "old-fashioned"</note> used to use. They considered anyone who dealt with common grocers to be a friend of the old ways.

They themselves used oil and new pots, and they created a sharp fire, blown frequently, by which they raised the whole dinner to a higher level. They were the first to remove the "tears" and "mucus" from the table—that is, the heavy, unrefined parts of the food—and they purified the palates of the eaters. Indeed, a certain Rhodian died from drinking a kind of brine; the drink was contrary to nature, and rightly so. Sophon, however, holds all of Ionia in his thrall.

"My teacher, father, was a man of spirited temper, and having left behind philosophical writings himself, I strive to make my own discoveries in the art. I do not just chop up whatever we are about to sacrifice at dawn; I hold the cookbooks in my hands and seek out the science... You will know if I am called upon: I do not always serve the same foods to everyone. I distinguish how each person lives. Different things are needed for those in love, for philosophers, and for tax-collectors. For a youth who has a lover, I serve cuttlefish and squid and various fish from Piraeus, served in elegant sauces. For such a person is not a 'heavy' diner, but one whose mind is turned toward love. To the philosopher, I serve knuckle-bones and feet, for that animal <note>the philosopher</note> is excessively gluttonous. For a tax-collector, I serve gray-fish, eel, and aparos-fish when they are available. For the elderly, I prepare a dish of lentils and make the 'after-funeral' feast <note>original: "peridipnon"</note> look brilliant for their life. The bodies of the elderly are sluggish, quite different from those of the young. I serve them **mustard** and make sharp juices to stir up their internal 'air.' By looking at a man's face, I will know what he seeks to eat."

In Dionysus's play *The Law-Giver* <note>original: "Thesmophoros"</note>, a cook says to the banqueters (for it is good to remember these things): "I always feel a great sense of gratitude, by the gods, when you tell the cook these things before he enters. For those who are about to prepare a dinner must always be prepared well in advance. For if someone only looks at how to make a dish 'properly'—in what manner to serve it or how to season it—without foresight or thought, he is not a 'Cook,' he is perhaps just a 'Dresser of Meat' <note>original: "opsopoios"</note>. There is a great difference. It is like a General: anyone can take command of a force, but not everyone can manage the situation and..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the high art of professional cookery, moving from a philosophical defense of the chef’s status to a specific recipe for a rose-infused dish, followed by a historical and literary account of legumes and the famous parodist Hegemon of Thasos.</meta>

->ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED<-
# BOOK 9

...and not to overlook anything, one is a General, but the other is a Leader. Thus it is in our power to prepare or to honor; any random person can fill the seasonings and blow the fire. Such a person is merely a sauce-maker <note>original: "opsopoios"</note>, but a true cook <note>original: "mageiros"</note> is something else entirely. He must consider the place, the season, the host, and the guest, as well as when and what fish to buy. You can get almost everything, for it is always available, but not always at the right time. Archestratus <note>A 4th-century BCE poet known as the "Hesiod of Gorging" for his culinary travels</note> has written on these things and is held in high regard by some, as if his words were useful. But he has ignored the most important things and tells us nothing. Do not listen to everything, nor learn everything from those who write by force without purpose. Nor is there a man who can truly master the culinary art, for as they say: "The moment has no fixed limit, but is its own mistress." If you do not use the art properly, and you lose the right moment, the art itself is lost. Man, this is a great thing! Now, regarding what you just said about a pouch <note>An idiom likely referring to carrying ingredients or a "bag of tricks"</note> making us forget many expensive dinners, I will provide signs of all things divine. I will speak only of these: set the limit of the feast, even if unwillingly draining the urban bilge-water. Let me not be burdened with vulgar foods or agonies, unless I make you doze over a side-dish.

To this, Aemilianus said: "My best friend, many have spoken about cookery, and not just Hegesippus’s brother. Do you appear as a 'Thunderer' <note>A play on words suggesting a loud or boastful person</note> who brings something new compared to those who came before? Or will we never see what you are carrying? Speak, in the name of the gods!" The other replied: "Do you look down on me because I am a cook? Perhaps as much as I have earned from this art, so did the comic poet Demetrius, who in his play titled *The Man of the Areopagus* said these things: 'No actor has ever earned so much. This art is a smoky tyranny! I was a flour-maker for Seleucus <note>One of Alexander the Great's generals and founder of the Seleucid Empire</note>. And under Agathocles <note>The tyrant of Syracuse</note>, I was the first to introduce the 'Sicilian-style' lentil soup. I haven't even mentioned the greatest thing: when Lachares <note>A tyrant of Athens during the 3rd century BCE</note> was facing famine, I provided relief for his friends, and I did not bother him even though I am bothering you now.'" Aemilianus said: "If you don't show us what you're carrying..." and he finally spoke.

<margin>Rose-colored casserole dish.</margin>
"I call this dish 'Rose-style' <note>original: "rhodonia"</note>. It is prepared so that you don't just wear a fragrant garland on your head, but you also feast on its appearance, so that the meal may feast your whole body. Rub the most fragrant roses in a mortar, then add the brains of birds and pigs, which have been boiled and thoroughly cleaned of their membranes, along with the yolks of eggs. After these, add oil, fish sauce <note>original: "garos" or garum, the ubiquitous fermented fish condiment of the ancient world</note>, pepper, and wine. Having mixed these carefully, put them into a new casserole dish over a gentle and steady fire." And as he spoke, he uncovered the dish, which released such a fragrance through the banquet that one of those present truly quoted:

<margin>Iliad, Book 2.</margin>
> "From the moving Zeus unto the bronze-floored house..." <note>A parody of Homer's description of divine fragrance</note>

The scent reached neither earth nor heaven, yet such a fragrance of roses was diffused. After this, roasted birds were brought around, along with lentil soup and peas in their own pots. Regarding these, Phanias of Eresus <note>A philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> writes the following in his work *On Plants*: "Every nature of legumes, whether cultivated or wild, is 'seed-bearing' <note>original: "anermatine"</note>. Some are harvested for standing use, such as the bean and the pea—for a filling meal is made from these. Others are whitened, like the vetch. Some are for the lentil-dish, like the lentil. Others are for the fodder of four-footed animals, like the bitter vetch for plowing oxen, and the wild lentil for sheep." Eupolis also mentions the 'Dardanian pea' in his play *The Golden Race*. Heliodorus the Periegete <note>A travel writer</note>, in his first book *On the Acropolis*, says that when the placement of wheat was devised, the ancients called it 'bean,' but people now call it 'whole-wheat.'

While many more things were being said, Democritus said: "Let us also partake of the lentil soup, or the pot itself, lest one of you be hit with stones, according to Hegemon of Thasos <note>The inventor of the literary parody</note>."

<margin>Hegemon the Parodist.</margin>
Ulpian asked: "What is this 'stone-throwing' <note>original: "balletys"</note>?" At my Eleusis <note>The site of the Eleusinian Mysteries</note>, there is a festival called *Balletys*, about which I would speak if I hadn't already taken enough from everyone else. But Democritus said: "I am not a greedy time-keeper <note>A metaphor for someone who hoards the conversation</note> like Timon’s prologue-speaker; I will tell you about Hegemon. Chamaeleon of Pontus, in his sixth book *On Ancient Comedy*, says that Hegemon of Thasos, who wrote parodies, was nicknamed 'The Lentil.' He wrote in one of his parodies: 'These things Athena many-counselled stood beside me, holding a golden rod... she told a tale: having suffered from a disgusting lentil-dish, he went into the contest.' He once entered the theater to perform a comedy with his cloak full of stones; he began throwing them into the orchestra, confusing the spectators. After a short pause, he said: 'Here are the stones; throw them if anyone wishes!' Lentils are good in both summer and winter. The man was highly esteemed for his parodies and was famous for his delivery. He acted with such total theatricality that on that day he made everyone laugh. And yet, even when the news of the great disasters in Sicily <note>The catastrophic defeat of the Athenian expedition in 413 BCE</note> was announced to them in the theater, no one left, even though nearly all of them had lost relatives. They wept while covering their faces, but stayed in their seats so as not to be seen grieving the disaster by visitors from other cities. They remained to listen. And because of this, Hegemon himself, realizing they had decided to remain silent, continued his performance at a time when the Athenians, while masters of the sea, were bringing the lawsuits of the islanders into the city..."

->FROM THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS<-
# BOOK 9

...someone brought a lawsuit against the leader <note>Referring to Hegemon of Thasos, a famous parodist</note> and brought him to Athens. He, being brought there, gathered the performers of Dionysus <note>original: "Dionysou technitas" — the professional guild of actors and musicians</note> from somewhere and approached with them, asking Alcibiades for help. Alcibiades encouraged him and told everyone to follow. He went to the Metroon <note>The sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods in Athens, which housed the city's official archives</note>, where the records of lawsuits were kept. Weting his finger from his mouth, he wiped out <note>original: "dieleipse" — literally smeared or erased the ink</note> the leader's lawsuit. While the clerk and the magistrate were indignant, they kept quiet because of Alcibiades's influence, and the one who filed the suit fled to safety. This, Ulpian, is our "Vellectys" <note>A rare term, possibly referring to a clever trick or a "knock-out" blow</note>. And whenever you wish, you will say...

<margin>Telemachus’s pot.</margin>
...at Eleusis. And Ulpian said: "But do not give them these beautiful things, Democritus, nor the pots, so they might learn often what 'Telemachus’s pot' was, and who this Telemachus happened to be." And just as everyone was greeting him, he said to me, "My good man, you who joined the beans to the pots." After these things were said, seeing Philip the son of Chaerephilus from afar—one of the 'fat ones' <note>original: "pacheon" — a slang term for the wealthy or the politically influential</note>—he watched him and then ordered him to send flat-cakes <note>original: "laganas"</note>. Since Telemachus of Acharnae was also of the people, the same inhabitant says in *Dionysus*: "But Telemachus of Acharnae is still making speeches." He seems like the young Syrians:

> "How or what to do. For I want to know, he carries a beautiful death-bringing pot." He says not justly to the Satyrs, as if they had nothing. "For our sake, having spent the night in misery, first let me not sleep harshly, then the 'lion-horse' played with us completely, then hunger led us to Dion or Diapyron. But he did not have it immediately. How, having swallowed the gold, Telemachus of Acharnae, a heap of beans... snatching these with a twist, but he does not see us. Cephisodorus once wore down the speaker's platform."

From these things it is clear that Telemachus, always eating from a pot of beans, led a festival procession of "all-boiled" <note>original: "panepsian" — likely a reference to the Pyanopsia, a festival where pulse and beans were boiled in a common pot</note> foods. Some mention the "bean-man" <note>original: "kyaminos"</note>, such as the comic poet Heniochus in *Trachylios*, saying: "For being angry with myself, by the gods, how much figs differ from cress, and you... Nor do you say to Pauson <note>A painter often mocked in comedy for his poverty</note> to have kicked the thing, and a very difficult matter first for me. Having many troublesome cares, say it, for we are not perhaps announcing the 'bean-nation.' Because it blows up the stomach, and the fire in which those known things rejoice, the affair of Pauson. As always... regarding the beans... this squeeze at the end."

While such things were being said often, water was brought for the hands and for greetings. And again Ulpian asked if the term "hand-basin" <note>original: "chernibion"</note> is used as we say it, or if it is uncommon. And someone answered him, quoting the *Iliad*: "The old man should have ordered the maid-servant to pour pure water on the hands, and she stood by holding a hand-basin <note>original: "chernibion"</note> along with a pitcher." But the Attic writers say "hand-basin," as Lysias does in the speech *Against Alcibiades*, saying:

<margin>Hand-washing vessel.</margin>
> "Burn incense in the hand-basins... of the hand-washer. And when some good or useful citizen wins, being golden..."

Epicharmus in *The Spectators* used the word "hand-washings" <note>original: "cheironiba"</note> through these lines: "Libations, tripods, chariots, bronze cloaks, hand-washings, and these little bronze basins." The more common usage is to say "water over the hand" <note>original: "kata cheiros hydor"</note>, as Eupolis says in *The Golden Race*, and Amphias in *The Sling*, and Alcaeus in *The Sacred Marriage*. "Mold it because it is water." Philyllius in *The Goat* used "over the hands" thus: "And indeed the women have brought them, but come, bring the tables to us in due time, then sweep up. Then water over the hands for each, and give some perfume." Menander in *The Water-Pot*: "Those having received water over the hands are waiting, my dearest ones." Aristophanes the Grammarian <note>The librarian of Alexandria, famous for his work on Greek literature</note>, in his *Tablets against Callimachus*, mocks those who do not know the difference between "over the hand" and "washing off." For among the ancients, the first was said before dinner, and the latter after it. It seems the grammarian had his own observations on Attic usage. Since Homer sometimes says "to wash," and sometimes "entering to the table." And elsewhere: "The heralds poured water over their hands, and the maids piled grain in baskets." And Sophron in *Women's Mimes*: "Wretched in her vices, water over the hand when the table is set aside for us." Sometimes in the tragedians and comedians, you read "lustral water" <note>original: "cherniba"</note>, as in Euripides' *Heracles*: "As the son of Alcmene throws it into the lustral water." And in Eupolis' *Goats*: "Stop the lustral water yourself." Furthermore, the lustral water was that in which they dipped a torch taken from the altar on which they performed the sacrifice; and sprinkling the bystanders with this, they purified them. It must still be pronounced properly. For compound verbal nouns ending in 'ps' derived from the perfect tense... [a grammatical note on the accentuation of words like *aigilips* (goat-deserted), *oikotrips* (house-slave), and *boikleps* (cattle-thief)]. Sometimes in Sophocles, "Hermes of the downcast gaze" <note>original: "katobleps"</note>. Sometimes in Archelaus of the Chersonese in his *Oddities*. "Drink!" or in such oblique cases, the accent is preserved on the same syllable. Aristophanes in his first [play] used "hand-basin." They used these to wash their hands, and also soap <note>original: "smegmati"</note> for the sake of scrubbing, as Antiphanes says in *The Knapsack*:

> "While I listen to you, order someone to bring water to wash and soap."

They also anointed their hands with fragrant oils, despising the "hand-wipes" <note>original: "apomagdalias" — pieces of bread used as napkins</note> which the Spartans called "dog-bits" <note>original: "kynadas"</note>, as Polemon says in his *Letter on Kindred Names*. Sometimes using fragrant...

# BOOK 10

...they use their hands; regarding sweets, Antiphanes says in *The Disappearance of the Silver*: "And then you will walk about the garden, brushing the fragrant earth with your hands <note>original: "tas cheiras... ten gen" — implying using the soil or scented earth as a cleanser</note>." Philoxenus also says in the work titled *The Banquet*: "Then boys brought washing-water for the hands, with cleansers rubbed with wild figs <note>original: "smegmasin erinoshmektois" — a type of natural soap made using the sap or fruit of the wild fig tree</note>, and they poured over them chilled water. Then they wiped them with bright, fine-woven linens <note>original: "sindonyphe"</note>, and he gave them ambrosial-scented ointments and violet-blooming garlands." And Dromon says regarding a harper-girl: "We sat down quickly; the boys held the wash-water for the tables, for those who were washing themselves, but not the garlands." Again, Autophanes says: "Having received them, we were crowned with garlands." They called the water used for washing the hands and feet "wash-water" <note>original: "aponiptron"</note>. Aristophanes says:
<margin>Wash-water.</margin>
"Just like one pouring out wash-water in the evening." Perhaps they also called the basin by this name, in the same way they use the term "hand-basin" <note>original: "cheironiptron"</note>. Among the Athenians, the term "wash-water" <note>original: "aponimma"</note> is specifically used for the water used in honors for the dead, and for those purifying the polluted, as Cleademus says in the work titled *The Exegesis*. For he says, regarding the source of sanctifications, he writes the following: "It requires birds and a pit for each body; then, looking into each pit, pour down water, saying these words: 'Wash-water for you, for whom it is right and for whom it is lawful.' Then, afterwards, pour down myrrh." Dorotheus also cited these things, stating that in the ancestral rites of the descendants, the following was written regarding the purification of suppliants: "Then, having washed himself, he and the others who are handling the entrails, taking water, he purifies and washes away the blood of the one being purified. And after moving the wash-water into the same place, pour it out." A "hand-towel" <note>original: "cheiromaktron"</note> is what they called that with which they wiped their hands, made of raw linen <note>original: "omolino"</note>.
<margin>Hand-towel. Raw linen.</margin>
In the same way, Philoxenus of Cythera, in the passages mentioned before, called it a "wipe-cloth" <note>original: "ektrimma"</note>. Aristophanes in *The Fryers* says: "Boy, bring water for the hands quickly; pass the hand-towel." It should be noted that they used the phrase "water for the hand" even after dining, though Aristophanes the Grammarian says that before eating the Athenians said "water for the hand," but after dining they said "to wash oneself" <note>original: "nipsasthai"</note>. Sophocles in *Oenomaus* says: "With a Scythian hand-towel <note>original: "skythisti cheiromaktron" — a grim reference to the Scythian practice of using an enemy's scalp as a towel</note> hanging from him." And Herodotus says in his second book—Xenophon also writes in the first book of the *Education of Cyrus*: "Whenever you touch any of these things, you immediately wipe your hand on the hand-towels," as if he were very annoyed that he had been defiled by them. Polemon, in the sixth book of his *Response to Antigonus or Adaeus*, speaks about the difference between "water for the hand" and "washing." Demonicus, in *The Achelous*, refers to the washing before dinner in these words: "Each of you, go in as if to eat, he has dined both as a man and as a Boeotian." At any rate, he describes the "water on the hand" in a way that suggests it happens for him after dinner. Cratinus mentions raw linen in *The Archilochuses*: "Hair teeming with raw linens, full of dishonor." And when Sappho says in the fifth book of her lyric poems to Aphrodite: "And laughing, she sent purple hand-towels, these things she sent as precious gifts, after scorning them." By "hand-towels," she means ornaments for the head <note>original: "kephales... cheiromaktra"</note>, as Euctaeus also shows, or whoever wrote the *Periegesis* titled *In Asia*. He says that women wear hand-towels under their heads. Herodotus says in his second book: "After these things, they said that the King descended alive to the place which the Greeks consider to be Hades. And there he played dice with Demeter; sometimes he won, and sometimes he was defeated by her, and he returned again having a gold hand-towel as a gift from her." Regarding the boy who sprinkled the basin and gave water for the hands to Hercules, whom Hercules killed with a punch <note>original: "kondylo" — literally with a knuckle or fist</note>:
<margin>To speak of little children.</margin>
Hellanicus says in his *Histories* that he was called Archias, and because of this, Hercules went into exile from Calydon. But in the second book of the *Phoronis*, he calls him Chereias. Herodorus, in the seventeenth book of his *Account of Hercules*, calls him a young lad. Some say it was Cyathus, the brother of Antimachus, and Hercules killed him while he was serving as his wine-pourer, as Nicander relates in the second book of his *Oetaica*; he says a sacred precinct was dedicated to him by Hercules in Prochoros, which to this day is called "The Wine-Pourer" <note>original: "Oinochoos"</note>. We, having brought this discussion to a close here, will make the beginning of the next part from the gluttony of Hercules.

**B**ut just as a poet must provide a refined and varied feast for the spectators, O Timocrates, so that someone might take something from it, whether drinking or eating, lest the preparation be lacking in artistry <note>original: "mousike" — literally "the things of the Muses," implying poetic skill</note>. Astydamas the tragic poet says in his satyr play *Hercules*: "Come, friend Timocrates, let us say here the things that follow from what was said before: that Hercules was indeed a glutton <note>original: "adephagos" — a voracious eater</note>." Nearly all poets and historians demonstrate this. Epicharmus says in *Busiris*: "First, if you saw him eating, you would die! His throat roars inside, his jaw rattles, his molar thuds, his canine-tooth squeaks, he snorts through his nostrils, and he even moves his ears." And Ion in *Omphale*, showing him in his gluttony, adds: "Out of hunger he swallowed even the limbs and the coals..."

# FROM THE ATHENAEUS DEIPNOSOPHISTAE

...not merely embers. And where did Pindar get the idea when he said they boiled hot meat through the carcasses of oxen upon the coals, and the bodies of fire-breathing <note>original: "pyripnoon"</note> creatures? At that time, I saw the smell of flesh and the heavy groan of bones—it took much time to distinguish them. Because he indulged himself in such voracious gluttony, they even gave him the nickname "The Gull" <note>original: "laros" — a bird known for its scavenging and greed</note>, or called him the "Ox-eater" <note>original: "buphagos"</note>. Heracles is also introduced competing with Lepreus in a contest of excessive eating; having challenged him, Heracles emerged victorious. Zenodotus, in the second book of his *Epitomes*, says that Lepreus was the son of Poseidon and Astydameia (or Phorbas), and that Lepreus ordered Heracles to compete in games when Heracles demanded his wages from Augeas. After Heracles finished his labors, he came to the Caucones, and at the request of Astydameia, he reconciled with Lepreus. But after this, Lepreus challenged Heracles to a contest with the discus, to a water-drawing contest, and to see who could consume a bull faster—which he swallowed whole. Then, having fortified himself with drink <note>original: "thorechtheis" — literally "armored," but colloquially used for being drunk or "steeled" by wine</note>, he challenged Heracles to a fight and died in the battle. Matris, in his *Encomium of Heracles*, says that Heracles was also challenged by Lepreus to a drinking contest, and again Lepreus was defeated. The Chian orator Caucalus, brother of the historian Theopompus, relates the same things
<margin>See also...</margin>in his *Encomium of Heracles*. Homer also portrays Odysseus as a glutton and a greedy man, when he says: "But let me eat, though I am followed by grief. For there is nothing more shameless than the hateful belly, which commands a man to remember it by necessity." And even when one is greatly worn down, the belly commands him to be filled. For in these lines his greediness appears excessive, especially since he speaks so openly about his stomach to those he has not even seen yet. For he ought to have endured in his lack, or not dwelt so long on the subject of food. Finally, at the very end, he displayed greed and gluttony, saying: "For though I have grief in my heart, yet the belly always commands me to eat and drink. It makes me forget all I have suffered and bids me to be filled." For even that famous Sardanapalus would never have dared to say such things. Even as an old man, Odysseus ate meat greedily and drank sweet wine. Theagenes of Thasos, the athlete, ate a whole bull by himself, as Poseidippus says in his *Epigrams*. "And once I ate a whole bull at a meal..." <note>The following lines in the source text appear corrupted or fragmentary</note>
<margin>Budé, *On the As* <note>original: "Bud. r. de Asse" — a reference to the 16th-century scholar Guillaume Budé's work on ancient weights and measures</note></margin>...and Milo of Croton <note>Milo was a 6th-century BC wrestler famous for his incredible strength</note>, as Theodorus of Hierapolis says in his work *On Contests*, used to eat twenty minas of meat and as many of bread, and he drank three *choes* of wine <note>A "mina" is about 1 pound (.45kg); a "chous" is roughly 3 liters. Milo was consuming roughly 40 lbs of food and 9 liters of wine.</note>. At Olympia, he put a four-year-old heifer on his shoulders and, after carrying it around the stadium, he carved it up and ate it all by himself in a single day. Titormus the Aetolian used to compete with him over an ox, as Alexander the Aetolian records. Phylarchus says in the third book of his *Histories* that Milo ate the bull while reclining before the altar of Zeus, which is why the poet Dorieus wrote these lines about him:
<margin>Gluttonous athletes.</margin>
"Such was Milo when he lifted the heavy weight from the earth, a four-year-old heifer at the feasts of Zeus; and placing the monster on his shoulders as if it were a young lamb, he carried it lightly through the entire assembly. It was a marvel, but he performed an even greater wonder: before the sacrifices of the priest, the very ox he had led in procession as a victim, he butchered and feasted upon every bit of it alone."
Astydamas of Miletus, a three-time Olympic victor, and a champion in the *pancratium* <note>A brutal ancient Greek combat sport combining wrestling and boxing</note>, was once invited to dinner by Ariobarzanes the Persian. Upon arrival, he promised to eat everything that had been prepared for all the guests, and he did so. The Persian, not knowing him well (as Theodorus records), asked him to do something worthy of his strength; Astydamas then broke a bronze leg off the couch, bent it, and straightened it out again. When he died and was cremated, his bones could not fit into a single urn, and barely into two; yet he alone had eaten the dinner prepared for nine men at Ariobarzanes' house. It was not surprising then that the "embers" <note>Possibly a pun or reference to "charred-ones" or those with burning appetites</note> became gluttonous. For all those who compete in gymnastics are taught to eat a great deal.
<margin>Slander of the athletes.</margin>
Therefore, Euripides says in the first *Autolycus*: "Of the countless evils throughout Greece, none is worse than the race of athletes. First, they neither learn how to live well, nor could they. For how could a man who is a slave to his jaw and a servant to his belly acquire wealth greater than his father's? Nor can they endure poverty or serve their fortunes, for having not been habituated to good character, they change harshly when they meet difficulties. They shine in their youth and walk about as ornaments of the city, but when bitter old age falls upon them, they go away like worn-out cloaks that have lost their thread. I blame the custom of the Greeks, who hold assemblies for the sake of these men and honor useless pleasures for the sake of a feast. For what man, by wrestling well, or being swift of foot, or throwing a discus, or striking a jaw skillfully, has ever defended his city by winning a crown? Will they fight the enemy with discuses in their hands, or will they drive the enemy from their fatherland by kicking through shields? No one is so foolish as to do these things when standing near the iron sword. We ought to crown the wise and the good with leaves, and whoever leads the city most nobly, being a prudent and just man. Whoever by his words removes evil deeds, taking away battles and seditions. For such things are good for the whole city and all the Greeks." Euripides took these views...
