# BOOK 10

From the elegies of Xenophanes of Colophon <note>Xenophanes was a 6th-century BCE philosopher known for his social critiques</note>, who spoke as follows: "But if someone should win a victory through swiftness of foot, or competing in the pentathlon where the precinct of Zeus is, by the streams of Pisa <note>Pisa was an ancient district or town near the site of Olympia</note> in Olympia; or in wrestling, or holding the painful art of boxing, or that terrible contest they call the pancration <note>original: "pankration" — a no-holds-barred combat sport combining boxing and wrestling</note>; he would appear more glorious to his fellow citizens, and he would win a conspicuous front-row seat at the games. He would even be fed from the public stores and receive a gift from the city that would be a treasure for him. Even if he won with horses, all these things would fall to him. Yet he is not as worthy as I am. For our wisdom <note>original: "sophie"</note> is better than the strength of men and horses. But this custom is practiced quite at random, and it is not just to prefer strength over good wisdom. For even if there were a good boxer among the people, or one skilled in the pentathlon or wrestling, or even in swiftness of foot—which is the most honored display of strength in the games of men—the city would not, because of him, be in a state of better law and order. A city would find very little joy in a man winning a victory by the banks of the Pisa, for such things do not fatten the city's storehouses." Xenophanes, in accordance with his own wisdom, struggles against many other things as well, disparaging the pursuit of athletics as useless and unprofitable. And Achilleios, who investigates the sacrifices of athletes, relates:
<margin>Athletes</margin>
"Naked, they push their shining arms, swelling with youth they go about, young men. Shining again with strong shoulders, satiated with oil <note>original: "aden t’ elaiou" — soaked or glutted with oil, used by athletes for massage and protection</note> on their chests and the hollow of their feet, as if they possessed their nature from home." Heraclitus, in the work titled *The Refutation*, says that a certain woman ate the greatest amount. And Poseidippus, in his epigrams, mentions Phylomachus; as if one were to write this upon him: "Phylomachus ate everything like a gluttonous crow at an all-night festival; but he has a grave like a trench, or a double-layered cloak of grey. But you, send this man and his meat to the Goddess of Death <note>original: "Ker"</note> and his crown..." <unclear>his eyes were dim looking out from a ship...</unclear> He who destroyed his hair with a single oil-flask... Amarantus of Alexandria, in his books *On the Stage*, says that Herodorus of Megara was a trumpeter, three and a half cubits tall <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches, making him about 5'3" — perhaps short but exceptionally broad</note>. He says the man’s ribs were incredibly strong. He ate six *choenixes* of bread <note>A choenix was a daily ration of grain, roughly 1 quart</note> and twenty pounds <note>original: "litras"</note> of whatever meat he could find. He drank two *choes* of wine <note>A chous is about 3 quarts</note>, and could blow two trumpets at once. He had the habit of sleeping only on a lion’s skin. This trumpeter gave the signal when Demetrius, son of Antigonus, was besieging Argos; when the soldiers were unable to bring the siege-engine <note>original: "helepolis" — the famous "city-taker" tower</note> to the walls because of its weight, he sounded his two trumpets, and by the sheer volume of the sound, he forced the soldiers to take heart and move the machine. He won ten Olympic victories in this manner, and he always ate while sitting down, as Nesos records in his *Theatrical Commentaries*. And a woman also played the trumpet: Aglais, daughter of Megalocles, in the first great procession held in Alexandria. She wore a wig and a crest on her head, as Poseidippus shows in his epigrams. She herself ate twelve pounds of meat and four *choenixes* of bread, and drank a *chous* of wine. Lityerses was the bastard son of Midas. He was a king of Celaenae in Phrygia, a man wild and savage to look upon, and a powerful glutton. Sositheus the tragic poet speaks of him in the play *Daphnis* or *Lityerses* as follows: "He himself eats three whole packs <note>original: "kanthelios" — a large basket or pack-load</note> three times in a short day. At the same time, he drinks a fine *metreter* <note>A liquid measure of nearly 10 gallons</note>, this fruit-bearing jar." Such a man is also found in Pherecrates’ *The Woman Soldier* or *Good Men*, where someone says: "I barely eat half a *medimnos* <note>A medimnos is about 12 gallons of dry grain</note> a day, if I force myself. What a small eater he is, who eats the provisions of a whole trireme <note>A warship with 170 rowers</note> during a long day." Xanthus, in his *Lydian History*, says that Cambles, who reigned over the Lydians, was a great eater and drinker, and moreover, a glutton. One night, having chopped up his own wife, he ate her. Then, in the morning, finding his wife’s hand still in his mouth, he killed himself when the deed became notorious. Horus, king of the Paphlagonians, is also mentioned as being a great eater, and they compare him to the account by Theopompus in his twenty-fifth book. Archilochus, in his tetrameters, attacked Cheilas for similar things, just as the comic poets attacked Cleonymus and Peisander. And Chaerippus, as they say, is mentioned in Phylarchus: "Thirdly, besides these, look at how the most wise Chaerippus eats as you know, until I see who he is, or if he bursts unawares; he has a storehouse like a house." Nicolaus the Peripatetic, in the hundred and first book of his *Histories*, says that Mithridates, the king of Pontus, held a contest of eating and drinking (the prize was a talent of silver) and won both. He gave the prize to the runner-up, the athlete Kalanobrounios of Cyzicus. And Timocreon of Rhodes, the poet and pentathlete, was a great eater, as the epigram on his tomb shows: "Having drunk much, and eaten much, and spoken much evil of men, here I lie, Timocreon of Rhodes." Thrasymachus of Macedon, in one of his prefaces, says that when Timocreon came to the Great King and was entertained by him, he stuffed himself with much food; when the king asked him what he would do after this...

# ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

...he would work, even if countless Persians bowed down together; and on the following day, having defeated many one by one, he afterward made gestures with his hands <note>original: "echeironomēse" — a form of rhythmic pantomime or shadow-boxing</note>. When asked the reason for his absence, he said that if anyone should receive so many blows, [they would likewise be absent]. Clearchus, in the fifth book of his *Lives*, says that Kanthisbaros the Persian, whenever his jaws grew tired from eating, would have his servants pour food into his open mouth as if into a lifeless vessel. Hellanicus, in the first book of the *Deucalioneia*, says that Erysichthon the son of Myrmidon was called "Aithon" <note>original: "Aithona" — meaning "Blazing" or "Burning," referring to the burning sensation of insatiable hunger</note> because he was insatiable for food. 

Polemon, in his work *Against Timaeus*, says that there is a temple to Gluttony <note>original: "adēphagia"</note> in a city of the Sicilian Greeks, and a statue of Demeter of the Grain <note>original: "Sitos"</note> is established nearby, as well as one of Imalis, just as there is one of Hermochthe at Delphi. And in Scape in Boeotia, there are statues of "Great-Loaf" <note>original: "Megalartō"</note> and "Great-Cake" <note>original: "Megalomazō"</note>. The poet Alcman also records that he himself was a glutton in his third book, through these lines: "And one day I will give you a tripod bowl in which there is a cauldron, but for now it is empty; yet soon it will be full of the pea-soup <note>original: "etnos"</note> that the all-devouring Alcman loved, hot after the winter solstice." For he still eats what is beaten together, but he seeks out new things just like the common people. Everywhere he displays his gluttony, saying: "He created three seasons—summer, winter, and autumn—and a fourth, spring, when things bloom but one cannot eat enough." 

Anaxilas the comic poet, speaking about a certain Ktesias in the play *The Goldsmith*, says: "Almost everything is sweet to you, Ktesias. For this man dines, as the wise say, alone knowing neither beginning nor end." And even if he were rich, he would burst without restraint.

If someone dines well, do not keep it to yourself. For what prevents you? For this man dines, as the wise say, never having learned of a beginning or an end. And if he should be listed among the graces of some Kranaus. It is not for nothing that some who approach ask: "Does Kranaus really sleep with Ktesias's stag <note>Possibly a metaphor for a large portion of meat or a specific person</note>, or do they both drink heavily?" Philetaerus says in *Atalanta*: "Even if I run more stadium-lengths than Sotades, surpassing the bull-like men in my labors, I would still outrun Ktesias in eating."

Anaxippus says in *The Thunderbolt*: "For I see Damippus approaching me from the wrestling school. You call him 'the pitch-man,' but know that Diphilus will call for you. Now they rightly call his courage 'the thunderbolt,' for I believe he strikes the tables with his very jaw." In these lines, the comic poet made it clear why the play itself was titled *The Thunderbolt*. Theophilus in *Epidaurus* says that a certain captain who gathered some Mantineans was able to eat more than all other men. In *The Pancratiast*, introducing an athlete as a great eater, he says: "I eat nearly three minas <note>A mina was about 1 pound or 0.5 kg</note> of meat, a pig's snout, and four trotters, by Heracles! And three oxen, by Apollo!" Another says: "You swallowed two minas of figs, and in sickness, twelve jugs of unmixed wine." Apollodorus says this in *Sabazius*.

Whole nations were also mocked for their gluttony, such as the Boeotians. Eubulus, for instance, says in *Antiope*: "They toil...

<margin>The Boeotians are gluttons.</margin>

...truly they are human in eating and endurance, but I say to the Athenians: eat little; but to the Thebans: eat much." And in *Europa*: "Found a city of Boeotians, for a man who is best at eating all day long." and in *Ion*: "He is so Boeotian in his ways that he is never, as they say, filled with dinners." And in *Cercopes*: "After this I went to Thebes, where they dine all night and all day, and every man has a dung-heap at his door. For there is no greater good for mortals than to relieve oneself after walking a long way and eating much; the man who bites his lips [to hold it in] is a ridiculous sight." In *The Mysians*, he makes someone say: "You, leaving the plain of Thebes as you say, where a man is best at eating for whole days, and where there are no privies nearby." Diphilus in *The Boeotian* says: "The sort who begins eating at daybreak, or rather, spends the whole day." Mnesimachus in *Busiris*: "For I am a Boeotian: a man of few words but much eating." Alexis in *Trophonius*: "Now, lest I seem entirely Boeotian to those accustomed to mocking you—as if I were someone who only knows how to work like an ox and understands that a dinner is the only goal, or dines the whole night—strip yourselves, everyone!" Achaeus in *The Contests*: "Do you see them as spectators or athletes? They eat with strength, as is the custom of those in training. For what land are the strangers from? They are Boeotians." From this, it is likely that Eratosthenes, in his letters to Prithellus, when asked what he thought of the Boeotians, replied: "What else? They talk such things as even vessels would say if they had a voice, regarding how much each one holds." 

Polybius of Megalopolis says in the twentieth book of his *Histories* that the Boeotians, after gaining great glory following the Battle of Leuctra <note>A battle in 371 BCE where Thebes defeated Sparta</note>, soon lost their spirit and, turning to feasting and drunkenness, formed social clubs. Many of those who had families bequeathed the greater part of their property to these dining clubs <note>original: "syssitia"</note>, so that many Boeotians had more formal dinners scheduled in a month than there were days in that month. Therefore, the Megarians, hating this state of affairs, went over to the Achaeans. The Pharsalians are also mocked as gluttons.

<margin>The Thessalians are gluttons.</margin>

Mnesimachus says in *Philip*: "Has someone from the Pharsalians come to eat up the tables? No one is present, though one is shouting 'bravo'—is he perhaps already eating the hoof of an Achaean city?" And that all Thessalians were slandered as gluttons, Crates says in *Lamia*: "But when a Thessalian approached..."

...cut into large pieces. This is why people speak of "Thessalian-cut" meat, referring to how the Thessalians cut great portions. Philetaerus says in *The Torch-Bearers*: "And hand-heavy pieces of swine's flesh, a Thessalian-cut of meat." They also used the term "Thessalian puffing" to describe anything massive. Hermippus says in *The Fates*: "But Zeus, taking no thought of these perfumes, fashioned the Thessalian puffing." Aristophanes mentions these "wagon-sized" portions in *The Fry-Cooks*: "How can these meager things be compared to the Thessalian style, and are the Thessalian ways not much more 'wagon-like'?" By this, he means as large as a wagon <note>original: "hamaxiai" — a metaphor for something massive enough to fill a cart</note>. For the Thessalians called their carriages *mapanas* or *kapanas*. In the play *The Scythians*, someone asks: "What do you mean by 'wagons' <note>original: "kapanas"</note>? On which wagon did you bring the kid to Olympia?" The reply is: "Everyone calls carriages *apēnas*, I understand."

The extreme simplicity of Pythagoras.
</margin>
Neochabis used very moderate food. Pythagoras of Samos also used moderate food, as the physician Lycon records in his work *On Pythagoras*. He abstained from living creatures <note>original: "empsychōn" — referring to meat or anything with a soul</note>, as Aristoxenus has said. However, Apollodorus the mathematician says that Pythagoras actually sacrificed a hecatomb <note>original: "hekatombē" — a massive sacrifice of 100 oxen</note> upon discovering that in a right-angled triangle, the square of the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares of the sides containing it <note>The Pythagorean Theorem</note>. "When Pythagoras found that famous geometric figure, for which he offered a celebrated sacrifice of oxen."

The frugality of various men.
</margin>
Pythagoras was also a small drinker and lived most frugally, often being satisfied with honey alone. Similar things are recorded about Aristides, Epaminondas, Phocion, and Phormion, even though they were generals. Manius Curius, the Roman general, lived on turnips <note>original: "gongylidi"</note> all his life; when the Sabines sent him a great amount of gold, he said he had no need of gold as long as he could dine on such things. Megacles records this in his work *On Illustrious Men*. Many people are content with moderate meals, as Alexis relates in *The Woman in Love*: "But I, having what is necessary, hate excess. 

<margin>
20
</margin>
For in extravagance there is no real pleasure, only high cost." In *The Fake Drunkard*, he says: "I hate excess. For in extravagance there is expense, but no pleasure whatsoever. Live temperately, for everything moderate is sweet; therefore, let us not overfill. I depart now, still empty, but happy with myself." For Mnesitheus says that the gods tell us to avoid all excess. Ariston the philosopher, in the second book of his *Love Stories*, says that Polemon of the Academy advised those going to a banquet to ensure they make their drinking pleasant not only for the present moment, but also for the next morning. 

When Timotheus, the son of Conon, was taken from his usual lavish general's dinners by Plato to a symposium at the Academy, he was entertained so simply and intellectually <note>original: "mousikōs" — literally "in the manner of the Muses"</note> that he remarked: "Those who dine with Plato feel well the next day too." Hegesander, in his *Commentaries*, says that the next day Timotheus met Plato and said: "You, Plato, dine better for the sake of the next day than for the day that is passing." 

<margin>
30
</margin>
Pyrrho of Elis, when one of his acquaintances received him quite lavishly, as he himself relates, declared for the future: "I will not come to you again if you receive me like this; I do not want to see you spending money unnecessarily, nor do I want to be distressed by your hardship. For it is better for us to benefit from one another's company than from the multitude of dishes which mostly benefit the servants." 

<margin>
Menedemus's symposium.
</margin>
Antigonus of Carystus, in his *Life of Menedemus*, describing the regular symposia held by the philosopher, says that they did not have a formal lunch <note>original: "ariston"</note> individually. The gathering for the rest of the meal was at nightfall. Menedemus would invite guests to the meal; it seems that when some arrived before the hour, they would walk back and forth near the doors and ask the servants coming out what was being served and at what stage the meal was. If they heard "vegetables" or "salt-fish," they would go away. But if they heard "a bit of meat," they would enter the room already prepared for this. In the summer, 

<margin>
40
</margin>
mats were laid on each couch; in winter, a fleece. Each guest brought his own pillow. The drinking cup was small, about a half-pint <note>original: "kotyliaion" — roughly 0.25 liters</note>. The snacks were lupine-seeds or beans. Sometimes seasonal fruits were brought in: in summer, pomegranate; in spring, peas; and in the winter season, dried figs. 

Lycophron of Chalcis bears witness to these things in his satyr play *Menedemus*, where Silenus says to the Satyrs: "Children of a most noble father, you most worthless lot, I am showing off for you, as you see. For by the gods, never in Caria, nor in Rhodes, nor in Lydia, have I had such a dinner. It was a heaven-sent feast, Apollo, how beautiful!" And going further: "But the boy carried around a diluted cup in a five-obol vessel, slowly passing it around... and Demonicus, a generous local man, was a warm companion to those drinking in the dining room." He says further that there were philosophical inquiries during the drinking. For a temperate discourse was in the midst of them all. It is recorded that often when they gathered, the bird <note>the rooster</note> would catch them at dawn with its calling, and they were not yet satiated with the conversation. 

<margin>
50
Arcesilaus's lack of dinner.
</margin>
Once when Arcesilaus was entertaining some guests and the bread ran out, and the servants realized there was no more, he burst out laughing and clapped his hands saying: "What a banquet ours is, friends of gods and men! We have forgotten to buy enough bread; run, boy!" And he said this laughing, and a roar of laughter broke out from all present, and the party became even more enjoyable.

<page-num>101</page-num>
<header>ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS</header>

...and it was a pastime such that the banquet would end up unwashed due to the breadcrumbs. On another occasion, Arcesilaus <note>A Greek philosopher and founder of the Second Academy</note> ordered his acquaintance Apelles to strain the wine. But Apelles, in his confusion, disturbed some parts and soaked others, making the wine appear much muddier. Smiling slightly, Arcesilaus said, "I ordered a man to strain the wine who is no better at it than I am. So, you stand up, Aridicus, and you, Apelles, go and sweep up the crumbs." These things brought such joy and cheer to those present that they were filled with good spirits.

<margin>
Foreign
Nurses.
</margin>
But those who gather for dinners nowadays—especially those from the "beautiful" Alexandria—shout, scream, and heap abuse upon the wine-pourer, the servant, and the cook. The slave boys weep, being struck with knuckles from every side. The guests dine with total unpleasantness; even if it happened to be a sacrifice, the god would cover his head and depart, leaving not only the house but the entire city. For it is ridiculous for a man to proclaim a holy silence <note>original: "euphēmian" — the ritual call for silence/good speech before a sacrifice</note> and then immediately curse his wife and children. To such diners, one might say: "Yes, come here to dinner so that we may join in a curse, for the house is filled with the smell of incense and, at the same time, with songs and groans."

When these things were said, one of those present remarked that we must avoid these behaviors by looking at the nature of gluttony. For a cheap dinner does not produce drunken violence, as Amphis says in *The Cloth*, nor does it lead to outrages and insults. Alexis, in *The Weaver*, testifies through these words: "For long companionship and frequent banquets, and daily mockery, tend to bring pain more than pleasure. Mockery is the beginning of speaking ill; once you have spoken once, you immediately hear a response. Then comes the cursing, then the blows from drunken behavior. For these things are born of such a nature and happen to some who eat."

Mnesimachus, in his play *Philip*, because of the excessive satiety at dinners, introduces the banquet as a preparation for war, as Xenophon most elegantly called war a "workshop" <note>original: "ergastērion"</note>. He speaks thus: "Do you know that you must fight against men who sharpen their swords and swallow half-burned torches for snacks?" Immediately following this, he brings in the dessert: "To us, a boy brings Cretan arrows after dinner like chickpeas, and fragments of spears, and we have shields for pillows and breastplates for mats, and we have bows at our feet instead of slings. We are even crowned with catapults." And Phoenix of Colophon says: "Wine jars are the knives, and the cup is the spear-point; the hair is the bow, and the mixing bowls are auspicious. Horses are the unmixed wine and the battle-cry of perfume."

In *The Parasite*, Alexis, speaking of some gluttonous person, says: "All the younger men call him 'The Parasite' <note>A term for one who eats at another's table</note> as a nickname, but he is as sweet as honey. He is like Telephus <note>A mythological king who was struck dumb</note> at dinner, only nodding to those who ask him anything, so that often the man who invited him thinks he has a Samothracian <note>Likely referring to the silent initiations of the Samothracian mysteries</note> guest who has finally ceased his breathing and become calm. But the lad is a winter storm to his friends." Diphilus, in *Heracles*, speaking similarly of someone at dinner: "You don't see me drinking, already being 'breastplate-deep' in wine <note>original: "akrothōraka" — a slang term for being tipsy/armed for drink</note>, and becoming angry. My brother is a master of discord, already nearly twelve cups deep."

Therefore, Bion of Borysthenes used to say well that pleasures should not be sought from the table, but from the mind. They say Euripides, when encountering a poor diet, would say, "I eat to satisfy my body," as if the pleasure from food belonged much more to the body than the soul. Aeschylus says in a certain passage: "And many false-dinners of a gluttonous jaw, like a discharge of the body in its first joy." In *Dictys*, Euripides, speaking of communal contributions, says: "Life is like the purple sea; it does not strike you, but provides a manger on the shore. The moist mother and the pious nurse is the sea, and the life we draw from her comes home in nets and woven traps."

<margin>
Slander
against the
belly.
</margin>
For the stomach is a great evil for men. As Alexis says in *Dying Together*: "You might learn what an evil the stomach is for men; it teaches and compels so much. If someone were to remove this part from our bodies, no one would do wrong, nor would anyone commit outrages willingly. But now, all troublesome things happen because of this." Diphilus says in *The Parasite*: "Well said, O golden Euripides: 'Necessity and my wretched stomach conquer me.' For there is nothing more wretched than the stomach, into which you first throw everything, unlike any other vessel. If you carry bread, you bring it there; if you have soup, you ruin it there; you put cakes in a basket, but you don't put lentils there; you put wine in a flask, but not crayfish. But into this enemy stomach, one carries everything, though they are not at all alike. And I add the rest: because everywhere, all these things happen because of that wretched thing."

<margin>
Diogenes Laertius
reports the
same.
</margin>
And Crates the Comic <note>Correction: Likely Crates the Cynic philosopher</note>, as Sosicrates says in his *Successions*, slapped Demetrius of Phalerum with his wallet of bread. And when Demetrius sent him a flask of wine, Crates said, "I wish the springs also produced bread." Stilpo <note>A philosopher of the Megarian school</note> was amazed at his own self-control after eating garlic and then falling asleep in the Temple of the Mother of the Gods. It was forbidden for anyone who had eaten such things to enter. The goddess appeared to him in his sleep and said, "O Stilpo, being a philosopher, do you transgress the laws?" He seemed to reply in his sleep, "Provide me with food, and I will not use garlic." But concerning these things—

# BOOK 10

Ulpian said: "Since Alexis has mentioned dinners in *The Woman of Cos*, and since we have long since 'finished dining' <note>original: "dedeipnēkamen"—the perfect tense indicating a completed action</note>... Eubulus also uses this term in *Procris*: 'we have finished dining.' And again: 'You knew long ago that we must have finished dining.' Antiphanes in *Leonidas* says: 'But you come along before we have finished dining.' Aristophanes, in *The Preliminary Contest*, says: 'It is time for me to go to my Master now, for I think they have already finished dining.' And in *The Daughters of Danaus*: 'To everyone, before I have finished dining.' And the comic poet Plato—Epicrates of Ambracia (who is a poet of Middle Comedy) says in *The Amazons*: 'For they seem to me to have finished dining quite opportunely.' Aristophanes also used the term 'we have had breakfast' <note>original: "ēristamen"—referring to the morning or midday meal</note> in *The Frying-Pan Men*: 'Gentlemen, we have fallen under the table, or rather, we have breakfasted well.' And Hermippus in *The Soldiers*: 'To have breakfasted and to drink these things.' Theopompus in *Callaeschrus* says: 'We have breakfasted; for if he is silent in some way by word of mouth.' Antiphon in *The Politician* used 'has consumed' <note>original: "katēristēken"—literally "has breakfasted away"</note> in this way: 'When she herself has consumed her own affairs or those of her friends,' or 'for the children finished dining long ago.'"

Plato, speaking to the gods, as he says in *Philebus*: "Let us move on and mix the drink, whether it be Dionysus or Hephaestus or whichever god has been allotted this honor of the mixing. For just as we are certain wine-pourers who have chosen to judge, one might compare the quality of pleasure to honey, but the quality of wisdom to the sober and wineless austerity of some healthy water, which we must strive to mix as beautifully as possible." It is therefore time for us to drink, and let one of the servants take the cups away from the drinking-vessels. For I see a multitude of beautiful and varied cups. 

Lothytus <note>Likely a corruption in the transcription for a speaker's name or a reference to a cup type</note> then said of a large cup: "But pour it out more 'undiluted' <note>original: "akratesteron"—stronger wine with less water</note> for me, boy, filling the ladle <note>term: "kyathos" — a small ladle used for measuring and transferring wine from the mixing bowl to the cup</note> into the cup. Let it not be as the comic poet Antiphanes says in *The Twins*: 'Bring me the large cup, taking and pouring in unmixed wine, not a child's ladle's worth of a myriad of gods and goddesses.' Then, upon all these, for the sake of the venerable goddess and the sweetest king."

<margin>Stronger wine.</margin>
"A double portion. Therefore, boy, mix it 'stronger' <note>original: "zōroteron"</note> for me." For we were just speaking about the number of ladles, but I shall explain both that the term 'ladle' was used and where the term 'undiluted' comes from, and who the wine-pourer was. But first, you shall tell me where the term 'stronger' comes from. Antiphanes in *Melanion* says: "In this I judge, after the wineless offerings for the sake of health, to drink, using a 'stronger' wine-pourer." And in *Lampon*: "But he, like a horse-man, mixed it stronger." Ephippus in *The Youth*: "Having mixed it stronger, let each of the two be." 

<margin>Iliad 9.</margin>
Some say that the passage in Homer—"mix it stronger" <note>original: "zōroteron de keraire"—Achilles' command to Patroclus in Iliad 9.203</note>—means 'pure wine,' while others say it means 'warm,' from the word 'vital' <note>original: "zōtikou"</note> and 'boiling,' which would be strange for a mixing bowl being prepared for companions to drink from at the start. Others say it means 'more unmixed,' just as 'right-handed' is used for 'the right.' Some, since years are called *hōroi* and animals likewise, say it signifies size or abundance, and that 'strong' means 'much.' Diphilus says in *The Pederasts*: "Pour out for me to drink, even 'stronger,' if there are two boys. For water is entirely a bad thing for the soul." Theopompus, in his work *On Drunkenness*, says that 'stronger' refers to the mixture, citing these lines of Empedocles: "And immediately those things grew mortal which before had learned to be immortal, and 'strong' things <note>original: "zōra"—pure or unmixed</note> which before were unmixed, changing their paths."

<margin>The Ladle.</margin>
Plato mentioned the 'ladle' <note>original: "kyathos"</note> as a vessel for drawing liquid in *Phaenon*: "Having taken the ladle thus for the body." And in *The Ambassadors*: "As many ladles as you leave behind each time." Archippus in *The Fishes*: "I bought a ladle from the fair side." Such is also the reference in Aristophanes’ *Peace*: "having black eyes." For black eyes <note>original: "hypōpia"</note> are diminished when bruised with ladles <note>note: Cold metal ladles were used as a folk remedy to reduce swelling and bruising around the eye</note>. Xenophon also mentions the ladle in the first book of the *Cyropaedia*, as does Cratinus. Furthermore, Aristophanes mentions it in many places, and Eubulus in *Orthannes*. Pherecrates, in *Trifles*, named it a 'silver ladle.' Timon, in the second book of his *Silli*, called it an 'extractor' <note>original: "arysana"</note> or 'dipper.' And others call them 'pourers' or 'scrapers.' Simonides says: "He gave it thus, and the dipper was curved." Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: "For I had these dippers." Phrynichus in *The Female Revelers*: "a dipper-cup." From which also comes the word 'ladle-bucket.' They also used to call a vessel for water 'eiphthobon,' as Xenophanes says in his *Related Matters*. Polydeuces <note>Pollux</note>, in the ninth book of his *Histories*, even records a certain river called 'Kyathos' <note>Ladle</note> near the city of Arsinoe in Aetolia. Hypereides also used the term 'more unmixed' in his speech *Against Demosthenes*, writing: "If someone drank it more unmixed, it caused pain." Similar to this is 'more annoying' and the phrase in Aeschylus’ *The People of the Sun*: "more abundant libation." Epicharmus in *Pyrrha* said 'more vital.' 

<margin>He drank.</margin>
And in the speech *Against Demades*, Hypereides called the city 'more easy-going.' Plato also uses 'to mix' in the *Philebus*: "Let us mix while praying to the gods, O First Principle." And Alcaeus in *The Holy Marriage*: "They both mix and make things disappear." Hypereides in the *Heliastic* speech: "The Greeks in common mix the bowl of the Ionians." 

<margin>Noble Wine-pourers. Odyssey 4.</margin>
In ancient times, the wine-pourers were the most noble boys, such as the son of Menelaus: "the son of glorious Menelaus poured the wine." And Euripides the poet served as a wine-pourer when he was a boy. Theophrastus, at any rate, in his work *On Drunkenness*, says: "I myself have learned that the poet Euripides used to pour wine at Athens for those called the 'Dancers.' They used to dance around the city and the temple of Delian Apollo, being among the foremost of the Athenians, and they wore garments of the *terēsikoi* type. This Apollo is the one in whose honor they lead the *Thargelia* festival. A record of these things is preserved among the guardians in the *Daphnephoreion* <note>The place of the laurel-bearers</note>." Hieronymus of Rhodes, a disciple of Aristotle, records the same things in his own work *On Drunkenness*. And the beautiful Sappho everywhere praises her brother Larichus...

# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

I praise the way he serves as a wine-pourer <note>original: "oinochoounta"</note> in the Town Hall <note>The "Prytaneion," the seat of government where official guests were entertained.</note> for the people of Mitylene. Among the Romans, too, the sons of the highest nobility perform this service, imitating the gods in all things during public sacrifices, even down to the tones of their voices. Similarly, the luxury of the ancients reached such extravagance that they did not only have wine-pourers, but also "wine-inspectors" <note>original: "oinoptas"</note>. In fact, the "wine-inspector" was an official office among the Athenians, as Eupolis mentions in *The Cities*: "those wine-inspectors whom you would never see elsewhere, we now see washing as generals. O city, city, how much luckier you are than you are wise!"

The wine-inspectors either oversaw what happened at the drinking parties to see if the guests were drinking in equal amounts, or perhaps the office was of secondary importance, as the orator Philip says in *The Legal Proceeding over the Lamp-stand*. There were three wine-inspectors who gave orders to the drinkers regarding lamps and wicks; some people also called these officials "eyes." Among the Ephesians, the young men who poured wine at the festival of Poseidon were called "bulls," as Amerias says. The people of Hellene <note>referring to a specific local dialect or tribe</note> call the wine-pourer an "infuser" <note>original: "epichytēn"</note> and meat-carving "distribution" <note>original: "krionomian"</note>, as Demetrius of Scepsis says in the twenty-sixth book of *The Trojan Array*. Some record that Harmonia acted as a wine-pourer for the gods, as Capito the epic poet (an Alexandrian by birth) records in the second book of his *Love Stories*. Alcaeus also introduces Hermes as their wine-pourer, as does Sappho when she says: "And there a mixing bowl of ambrosia had been mixed, and Hermes took the ladle <note>original: "olpin"</note> to pour for the gods." The ancients called those who performed these services 
<margin>Iliad 3</margin> heralds. Homer says: "Heralds through the city brought the gods' faithful pledges: two lambs and cheering wine, the fruit of the earth, in a goatskin bottle; and the herald Idaios carried a shining mixing bowl and golden cups." And again: "But the noble heralds gathered the gods' faithful pledges, and mixed wine in a bowl; then they poured water over the hands of the kings." Cleidemus says that cooks were also called heralds. Some also imagined Hebe pouring wine for the gods, perhaps because symposia used to be called the <unclear>cup-storage</unclear> <note>original: "kylikeia"</note>. King Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus, mentions a statue of a "Wine-Pouring Woman," 
<margin>In Suidas</margin> as does Ptolemy son of Agasarchus in the third book of his *Histories of Philopator*. He says that statues of her stood in many parts of Alexandria, dressed in a single tunic and holding a drinking horn <note>original: "rhyton"</note> in her hands. After these words, Ulpian, draining his cup, said: "Naming the whole sacred group for a reward, I drink to you, my kinsmen, a pledge of friendship." When he was still drinking, one of those present added the remaining iambic lines: "Gulp down your love now—for I am choking—but drink it up!" And Ulpian, having finished the cup, said: "These lines are from Clearchus in *The Cithara-Singer*, but I shall return to the *Hired Laborers* of Amphis: 'Let the boy keep the cup moving quickly, and you fill mine, and I will give it back to you in turn.'"

<margin>Mixing of wine.</margin> "Let almond play with almond." These words were spoken by Penocharton in *The Twins*. When some were asking for more wine, and others were saying it should be mixed "equal to equal" <note>A 1:1 ratio of wine to water, considered quite strong by Greek standards.</note>, and someone mentioned that Archippus said in the second book of *Amphitryon*: "Who mixed it for you, you unlucky man, equal to equal?" and Cratinus in *The Flask*: "Or bringing the equal to equal, but I am filled up," it seemed good to everyone to discuss the mixing ratios used by the ancients. And someone said that Menander said in *Early Morning*: "And yet it is much more pleasant; for otherwise they would never drink three parts water and only one of wine." But Alexis, in *The Woman of Thue*, advises a more sober mixing: "Look, the wine is here; therefore, Crito, pour it much better than four parts water <note>To one part wine</note>, so that you might say it is light; nevertheless, after drinking this, tell us what we should believe regarding what we have made about this." And Diocles in *The Bees* says how to drink a mixture: "Wine again after four and two." This mixture, being contrary to custom, perhaps gave rise to the famous proverb: "Either drink five or three, but not four." For he says one should drink either two parts wine to five parts water, or three parts wine to three parts water <note>which is the 1:1 ratio</note>. The iambic poet Pythes, in his work *On Chios*, says that the seer Euryon (or Palamedes) prophesied that "It would be sweet for the Greeks drinking three parts water to one of wine." Those who used the drink more intensely drank two parts wine to five of water. Nicochares, at any rate, playing with the name in *Amymone*, said: "Oenomaus, greetings to you, five and two, and may both I and my fellow drinkers become so." Ameipsias says something similar in *Those Playing Cottabus*: "I am Dionysus to all of us, five and two." Eupolis in *The Goats*: "Greetings, Dionysus; is it not five and two?" Hermippus in *The Gods*: "When we drink or are thirsty, we pray—how this wine is ill-timed in its kind! For I bring not only wine but mud as well, just as it has become five and two." In Anacreon, regarding the drinking of wine with water: "Come now, boy, bring us a bowl, so that I may drink it at a gulp; pour in ten measures of water and five of wine, so that I may again decently <note>without becoming rowdy</note> celebrate the god." And further on, 
<margin>Scythian drinking.</margin> he calls drinking unmixed wine "Scythian drinking": "Come now, let us no longer practice Scythian drinking with such clatter and shouting over our wine, but drink moderately amidst beautiful hymns." And the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, as he says...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on drinking customs, transitioning from the roles of wine-servers to the cultural perceptions of intoxication, the history of the "Cottabus" game, and legal restrictions on wine consumption across different civilizations.</meta>

# BOOK X

...for Herodotus says in his sixth book that Cleomenes the King, after associating with the Scythians and becoming a drinker of unmixed wine <note>original: "akratopotin"; the Greeks usually diluted their wine with water, and drinking it "neat" was considered a barbaric Scythian habit</note>, went mad from his drunkenness. The Spartans themselves, whenever they wish to drink their wine stronger than usual, use the term "to Scythianize" <note>original: "episkuthisai"</note>. Chamaeleon of Heraclea writes about this in his treatise *On Drunkenness*: "The Spartans say that even Cleomenes the Spartan went mad because he learned to drink unmixed wine from his time with the Scythians; hence, when they want to drink more heavily, they say 'to Scythianize.'" Achaius, in his Satyr play *Aethon*, depicts the Satyrs <note>Nature spirits in the train of Dionysus, often depicted as rowdy and obsessed with wine</note> being annoyed at drinking watery wine and saying: "Was there much Achelous <note>original: "Achelōos"; the name of a river god, often used by poets as a metaphor for water</note> mixed in? Yet it is not lawful for anyone to cease from this... It is well, then, to compete in drinking in the Scythian fashion."

Theophrastus says in his work *On Drunkenness* that the whole practice of pouring out the dregs of the wine was an ancient custom. Originally, one part was offered to the gods, while the <margin>Playing the Cottabus.</margin> "Cottabus" <note>A popular Greek drinking game where players threw the last drops of wine from their cups at a target</note> was dedicated to one's beloved. They practiced the Cottabus game with great care, as they were Sicilian by heritage <note>The game was believed to have originated in Sicily</note>, just as Anacreon of Teos has written: "playing the Sicilian Cottabus with a flick of the wrist." For this reason, the so-called "skolia" <note>social songs sung at banquets</note> of the ancient poets are full of such references. They say that Pindar also wrote: "I brought the favors of Aphrodite’s loves, while drunk with the game, as a Cottabus-offering to the handsome Agathon." To their deceased friends, they would also set aside the remnants of food from the tables. This is why Euripides says in his *Stheneboea*—since I think Bellerophon is dead—"No drink should be spoken of from my hand, but straightaway let these things go to the Corinthian... <note>original: "*" indicates a break or corruption in the source manuscript</note> so as not to get drunk, nor to revel... saying what kind of person you happen to be, not what you pretend to be. For brass is a mirror for the face, but wine is a mirror for the mind." This is why those who speak in prologues aptly say that wine has no rudder <note>meaning wine removes self-control</note>.

Xenophon, the son of Gryllus, once when he was with Dionysius the Sicilian tyrant and the wine-pourer was forcing him to drink, addressed the tyrant by name and said: "Why is it, O Dionysius, that the cook, who is skilled and prepares varied dishes, does not force us to eat when we are feasting and do not wish to? Instead, he sets the food before us on the table in silence. Yet the wine-pourer forces us to drink." And Sophocles says in a Satyr play: "So it seems that to drink by force is as great an evil as to thirst by force." Hence it is also said: "Wine leads even an old man to dance against his will." The poet Sthenelas said elegantly: "Wine casts even the wise into foolishness." And Phocylides said: "In a banquet, while the cups go round, one should sit and chat pleasantly while drinking."

Even now, we see this among some of the Greeks. Since they began to live luxuriously and in splendor, they collapsed from their stools onto couches, and taking rest and ease as their allies, they practiced drunkenness in a relaxed and disorderly way, the preparation of the feast catering, I suppose, to their pleasures. As Hesiod said in his *Catalogue of Women*: "What a joy and a burden Dionysus gave to men! Whoever drinks his fill, for him the wine becomes a raging thing. It binds feet and hands together, and tongue and mind, with invisible bonds; and soft sleep loves such a man." And Theognis says: "I have come after drinking as much wine as is most pleasant for a man to have drunk; I am neither sober nor too drunk. But whoever exceeds the measure of drinking is no longer master of his own judgment or mind. He speaks reckless things that are shameful to the sober, and performs disgraceful deeds when he is drunk, though he was previously sensible and kind. But you, knowing these things, do not drink wine to excess. Rise and leave before the drunkenness begins. Let not your belly compel you, like a wretched daily laborer."

Anacharsis the Wise, when he was learning about the power of the vine from the King of the Scythians, said that its branches grew so thick that if the Greeks did not prune the vine every year, it would have reached Scythia by now. Those who sculpt or paint Dionysus as drunk are not acting rightly, nor are those who lead him through the middle of the marketplace on a wagon in a drunken state. They are showing the spectators that wine is stronger than the god himself. For I think not even an ordinary man could endure this. If they depict him in this state because he "shines" the wine for us, it is clear they will also depict Demeter harvesting or eating. In this regard, I would say even Aeschylus was in error. For he was a gentle man, and not, as some say, like Euripides, who introduced the sight of drunkards into tragedy. In his *Cabiri*, Aeschylus introduces Jason and his companions as drunkards; but what the playwright did himself, he attributed to his heroes. For he used to write his tragedies while drunk. Therefore, Sophocles, reproaching him, said: "O Aeschylus, even if you do what is required, you do it without knowing it," as Chamaeleon records in his work *On Aeschylus*. Those who say that Epicharmus was the first to bring a drunkard onto the stage are ignorant, followed by Crates in *The Neighbors*.

<margin>Alcaeus.</margin> Alcaeus the lyric poet and Aristophanes the comic poet also wrote their poems while drunk. And many others, when intoxicated, fought more brilliantly in war. Among the Locrians in Italy, if anyone drank unmixed wine without a doctor's prescription for the sake of medical treatment, the penalty was death, according to the law established by Zaleucus. Among the Massalians, another law forbade women from drinking anything but water. Theophrastus says this is still the custom in Miletus even now. Among the Romans, neither a slave, nor a free woman, nor the sons of free men drank wine until they were thirty years old. Anacreon is tireless in this, having hung his entire poetry upon drunkenness. Having given himself over to softness and luxury, he is criticized in his poems, not...

# ATHENAEUS: THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...while many are aware that a writer <note>Likely referring to a specific poet or playwright like Aeschylus, who was said to write while drunk</note> may be sober and skilled in his craft but only pretends to be drunk because it is expected. However, those who are ignorant of the true power of wine claim that Dionysus is the cause of madness among men, slandering the god beyond measure. For this reason, Melanippides <note>A famous Greek dithyrambic poet of the 5th century BCE</note> said: "All once detested water, being before then unaware of the delights of wine. Soon, indeed, some found great joy in it, while others poured out a distracted voice <note>original: "paraplēkton cheon omphan"; implying the incoherent speech of the intoxicated</note>."

<margin>Macrobius, Saturnalia, Book 7, Chapter 15.</margin>
Aristotle, in his treatise *On Drunkenness* <note>A lost work by the philosopher Aristotle</note>, says that if wine is moderately boiled, it is less intoxicating when drunk. This is because its "strength" is taken away and becomes weaker. He also notes that elderly people are naturally more prone to drunkenness because of the scarcity and weakness of the natural heat within them. Because of this, they are easily overcome by the heat added from the wine. Among the irrational animals, even pigs get drunk if they are fed on the skins of pressed grapes, as do crows and dogs if they eat the herb called "oinanthe" <note>original: "oinanthē"; likely water-dropwort or a similar plant whose name means "wine-flower"</note>. Even monkeys and elephants can be intoxicated by drinking wine. For this reason, people hunt monkeys and <margin>10</margin> crows by getting them drunk—the former with wine, the latter with the "oinanthe" herb. Crobylus, in his play *The Woman Who Left*, asks what pleasure there is in loving to get drunk: "Depriving oneself while alive of the ability to be prudent, which is the greatest good nature has given us." Alexis, in *The Phrygian Adaptation*, says: "If the hangover <note>original: "kraipalan"</note> came before the drinking, not a single one of us would ever take more than a moderate amount of wine. But as it stands, not expecting the punishment of drunkenness, we drink too readily and without dilution."

Aristotle says that the wine called "Hamagethian" <note>An exceptionally strong wine, possibly from a specific region</note> is so potent that three *kotylai* <note>about a pint and a half</note> of it, when mixed, can make more than forty men drunk. Having said these things, Democritus took a drink and said: "Let anyone who disagrees speak first." For you shall hear, according to Eunomus: "To you these things seem right, but to me, those." But since I have digressed into a discussion about ancient mixing ratios, I shall resume the argument, <margin>20</margin> keeping in mind the words spoken by Alcaeus the lyric poet.

<margin>The mixing of wine.</margin>
For Alcaeus says somewhere: "Pour in and mix one to two." Some do not believe he is speaking here of the mixing ratio <note>The proportion of water to wine</note>, but rather that he was a sober man who drank one cup of unmixed wine and then two more. This was the view of Chamaeleon of Heraclea <note>A student of Aristotle</note>, who was perhaps unfamiliar with Alcaeus's love for wine. For this poet is found drinking in every season and every circumstance. In winter, for instance: "Zeus sends rain, and a great storm comes down from the sky; the streams are frozen... drive away the winter by piling up the fire. Mix the honey-sweet wine unsparingly, and wrap a soft cushion around your head." In summer: "Soak your lungs with wine, for the star <note>Sirius, the Dog Star, associated with the heat of midsummer</note> is coming round again; the season is harsh, and everything is thirsty from the heat." In spring: "I heard the flowery spring <margin>30</margin> coming." And further on he says: "Mix the honey-sweet bowl as quickly as possible." In times of misfortune, he says: "One must not give one's heart over to evils. We shall gain nothing by grieving, O Bacchus; the best medicine is to bring wine and get drunk." And in times of joy: "Now one must get drunk and drink with force, since Myrsilus is dead!" <note>Myrsilus was a tyrant of Mytilene and an enemy of Alcaeus</note> And generally giving advice, he says: "Plant no other tree before the vine." How then could such a wine-lover be considered "sober" or one who drinks only one or two ladles? Indeed, as Seleucus says, the poem itself bears witness against those who interpret it that way. For it says: "Let us drink! Why wait for the lamp? Daylight is but a finger's breadth. Take down the large cups... for the son of Semele and Zeus <note>Dionysus</note> gave wine to men to forget their sorrows. Pour it out, mixing one part to two <margin>40</margin> full cups, and let one cup push the other out of the head." This "one to two" means one part wine to two parts water, or perhaps three parts total. Pherecrates, in *The Girlfriends*, speaks of two parts water to four of wine: "Give it here, you sweet-pourer... certainly not water! How could you, you cursed woman, pour two of water? And why four of wine? To the crows with you! Leave it for the frogs." Ephippus, in *The Lyrists*, says: "You might drink more safely at three parts water to four of wine, very watery. No, by the Earth! Let me have three and four of the unmixed kind." Timocles, in *The Satyr Covered in Dust*, says: <margin>50</margin> "I shall strike with 'equal to equal' <note>original: "ison isō"; a mixture of half water and half wine, considered very strong</note> in large cups to tell the whole truth." And Alexis in *Dorkis, or the Flute-Player*: "I drink healths of the 'equal to equal' mixture." And Xenarchus (or Timocles) in *The Purple Fish*: "By Dionysus, this is not just 'equal to equal'!" Sophilus, in *The Dagger*, says: "Unmixed wine was given continuously, 'equal to equal' again, in the larger cup." Alexis in *The Money-Lender*: "Do not give it to him completely watery; you understand, 'equal to equal' is almost right. The drink is sweet, a river of Bromios <note>A title for Dionysus</note>, like Thasian luxury, and it is not right that we, having no foreign wine, should drink the local stuff." In *The Supposititious Son*: "Drinking without taking a breath, like a whole city, 'equal to equal' mixed." Metaneira in *The Brothers*: "Pour in eight parts and then twelve <margin>60</margin> cups until you settle down, striving to win the drinking match." They used the term "Katasame" for those who did not succumb to their drinks, a metaphor taken from grain that does not fall from the stalk. Alexis says in *The Man Being Cut Off*: "He was not the master of the feast <note>term: "symposiarch"; the person who decided the mixing ratio at a party</note>, but an executioner! Chaereas, drinking twenty cups of 'equal to equal,' until the larger cup arrived."

# BOOK 10

Diodorus of Sinope, in his play *The Female Flute-Player*, says: "Whenever someone drinks ten cups <note>original: "kyathoi"; a small ladle used for measuring wine, about 1.5 ounces</note>—as Crito does—if one examines each cup individually, it will be found that his reasoning is no longer sound. Consider how he behaves." And Lysander the Spartan was not without wit, as Hegesander says in his *Commentaries*; when the wine sold by the retailers <note>original: "kapēloi"; small-scale merchants or tavern keepers</note> during military campaigns was already watered down, he ordered them to sell it as it was, so that the soldiers would buy it in its weaker state <note>This was a tactical move to ensure the army remained sober and disciplined</note>. Alexis says something similar in his play *Aesop*: "This is a clever custom of ours, O Solon, and one skillfully invented in Athens. For drinking at symposia is managed so that you do not drink your wine entirely unmixed <note>original: "akraton"; wine served without water, which was considered barbaric by the Greeks</note>. For it is not easy to find it so; they sell it from wagons already mixed, not to make a profit, but taking care that the heads of those who buy it remain healthy. Thus, you will see a Greek drinking session avoiding a hangover by using moderate cups, where they chat and joke pleasantly with one another. For that other way of drinking—from buckets and jars throughout the night—is not a drinking party, but a bath, or rather, it is death itself."

<margin>What Plato says about wine.</margin>
Plato says in the sixth book of his *Laws* that "drinking to the point of drunkenness is nowhere appropriate, except in the festivals of the god who gave the wine <note>Dionysus</note>. Nor is it safe, especially for someone serious about marriage; for at that time, more than any other, the bride and groom ought to be in their right minds, as they are undergoing a great change in their lives. At the same time, children should be conceived by parents who are as sensible as possible. For it is uncertain what kind of night or light will produce the child." In the eleventh book of the *Laws*, he says: "The Lydians use drunkenness, as do the Persians, Carthaginians, Celts, Iberians, and Thracians, and such nations; but you, O Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, abstain from it entirely. The Scythians and Thracians, however, drink their wine completely unmixed—both the women and all the men—and they consider it a beautiful and happy practice to pour it over their clothes."

<margin>Mix barley-meal with wine.</margin>
The Persians also indulge greatly in other luxuries which you reject. But most people do not drink wine this way simply for pleasure, but rather they add barley-meal <note>original: "alphita"</note> to the wine, as Hegesander of Delphi says. Epinicus, for instance, in his play *Mnesiptolemus*—or perhaps he was mocking him—wrote about Mnesiptolemus reading his histories, in which it was written how King Seleucus "barley-mealed" his wine. Mimicking his voice, he wrote: "I saw Seleucus the King drinking with barley-meal during the summer, and I wrote it down, looking closely at many details; for even a common or very cheap thing can be made grand by its own power. He took Thasian wine and the sweet swarm of the Athenian bee <note>honey</note> and mixed it with the fruit of Demeter <note>grain/barley</note> to soothe the summer heat." This same author records that the Thracians, when imposing taxes on the islands, demanded a flask <note>original: "lekythos"</note> of barley-meal wine, and this drink was called "the better drink made from barley."

<margin>The Spartan toast.</margin>
It was not the custom for the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> to offer toasts at symposia, nor to pledge friendship to one another through them. Critias explains this in his elegies: "For this is a custom and a settled practice in Sparta: to drink from the same wine-vessel, and not to give gifts of toasts by naming someone, nor to pass the cup around the circle to the right. The Lydian hand may prepare the vessels, but here we do not have toasts given to the right, nor do we call out the name of the one to whom we wish to drink. For from such drinking, tongues are loosened into shameful stories, the body is made weak, and a dim mist settles upon the eyes. Memory fades and slips from the mind, the intellect is tripped up, and characters become undisciplined. Then comes the household-wasting expense. But the Lacedaemonians drink only enough to lead their minds toward cheerful hope, and their tongues toward friendly conversation and moderate laughter. Such drinking is beneficial for the body, the mind, and the estate; it is good for the works of Aphrodite and for sleep—that harbor from labors—and for health, the most pleasant of gods to mortals, and for self-control, the neighbor of piety." He says further: "For toasts made with cups beyond measure, though they delight for the moment, bring pain for all time. But the Spartan way of life is balanced: eating and drinking together just enough to nourish. The drinking is purposeful, not to excess, and not to intoxicate the body with unmeasured draughts during the day."

<margin>Nestor's love of drinking.</margin>
A "wine-lover" <note>original: "philoinos"</note> is one ready for wine; a "party-lover" <note>original: "philopotēs"</note> is one ready for drinking-bouts; but a "cup-lover" <note>original: "philokōthōnistēs"</note> is one who drinks to the point of drunkenness. Among the heroes, the three-generations-old Nestor was clearly more devoted to wine than the others, even more than Agamemnon himself, whom Achilles rebukes as a "heavy drinker." Even when the greatest battle was raging, Nestor did not abstain from drinking; as Homer says: "The cry of battle did not escape Nestor, though he was drinking." Homer mentions the cup of this hero alone, just as he mentions the shield of Achilles. Nestor went to war with his cup, just as Achilles went with his shield, of which Hector said its fame reached to heaven. One would not be wrong to call Nestor's cup the "Shield of Ares," following the example of Antiphanes in his *Caeneus*, where it is said: "Is it not clear that the shield is the 'cup of Ares' according to Timotheus?" Indeed, because of his love of drinking, Nestor receives a gift even from Achilles: a deep bowl <note>original: "phialē"; a shallow drinking bowl</note> during the funeral games held for Patroclus.

<summary>This page explores the social and moral dimensions of drinking in the Greek world, contrasting the disciplined sobriety of the Spartans with the perceived excess of "barbarian" nations and the habits of Homeric heroes like Nestor.</summary>

It was not because Achilles did not also give a cup to the one who was defeated. For victory does not welcome those who love drink, due to their laziness. Or perhaps it is because winners suffer most from thirst, because they have to hold their hands up <note>original: "bas-tazein tas cheiras anateinontes"; likely referring to the posture of athletes or victors in competition</note>. Eumelus, however, receives a breastplate—a small prize for a precarious effort, yet a weapon of safety won without much toil.

<margin>Thirst.</margin>
Indeed, nothing is more desired than thirst. Because of this, Archilochus called the poet "much-thirsting" <note>original: "polydipsion"</note>, meaning "much-desired" on account of wine. For thirst creates a powerful desire in everyone for the enjoyment of drinking. Therefore, Sophocles also says: "For to a thirsty man, though you offer all wise things, you would not please him more than by giving him a drink." And Archilochus says: "I shall speak of your battle even as I long to drink to satisfy a thirst." One of the tragic poets also said: "holding joy that empties thirsty blood." Anacreon says: "For you are dear to strangers; let me drink, for I am thirsty." Xenophon, in the third book of his *Education of Cyrus* <note>The *Cyropaedia*</note>, makes Cyrus say these words: "I
<margin>10</margin>
thirst to do you a favor." And Plato says in the *Republic*: "Whenever, I think, a democratic city, having become thirsty for liberty, happens upon bad wine-pourers as its leaders, and is intoxicated with unmixed wine <note>original: "akratou"; wine served without water, a metaphor for extreme or dangerous freedom</note> beyond what is proper." Indeed, Proteas the Macedonian also drank much, as Ephippus says in his work *On the Burial of Alexander and Hephaestion*, 

<margin>Alexander's heavy drinking.</margin>

Proteas took it, and after praising the king at length, he drank so much that he was cheered by everyone. A little later, Proteas asked for the same cup, and having drunk again, he toasted the king. Alexander took it and pulled at it nobly, bringing it back to his lips, but then he leaned back against his pillow, letting the cup fall from his hands. From that point on he fell ill and died, because Dionysus <note>The god of wine</note> was angry with him, because he had besieged the god's own homeland,
<margin>20</margin>
Thebes. Alexander used to drink a great deal, so that from his intoxication he would frequently sleep for two days and two nights. This is made clear in his *Royal Diaries* <note>original: "ephemerisin"; the daily records of the king's court</note>, which were written by Eumenes of Cardia and Diodotus of Erythrae. Menander, in *The Flatterer*, says: "In Cappadocia, I drank a golden *kondylos* <note>a type of drinking vessel</note> holding ten *kotylai* <note>about 2.5 liters</note> of unmixed wine three times. Alexander, you have drunk more than the king!" "Not less, by Athena, but a great deal!" And Nicobulus, or perhaps Anticlides, says in his writings that while Alexander was dining with Medius the Thessalian, he drank twenty toasts at the banquet, toasting everyone and receiving the same in return while playing, and rising from the banquet, he went to rest shortly after. Callisthenes of Ophis, as Lynceus of Samos says in his *Memoirs*, and Aristobulus, and Chares in their *Histories*, say that at the banquet, when the cup of unmixed wine came to Alexander, he pushed it away as someone was absent, asking "Why are you not drinking?" Darius <note>Darius III, the Persian King</note>, who followed the ways of the Magi, had inscribed upon his
<margin>30</margin>
tomb: "I was able both to drink much wine and to bear it well." Ctesias says that among the Indians, it is not possible for the king to become intoxicated. But among the Persians, it is permitted for the king to get drunk on one single day: the day on which they sacrifice to Mithra <note>The Persian sun-god</note>. Duris writes about this in the seventh book of his *Histories*: "Only during the festival celebrated by the Persians for Mithra does the king get drunk and dance the *Persica* <note>a traditional Persian dance</note>. And they believe that the movement from this activity provides a rhythmic exercise for the strength of the body." Alexander was so prone to

For Aristotle says in his *Physical Problems* that the heat of wine destroys the seed. Hieronymus, in his *Letters*, says that Theophrastus claims Alexander was not well-disposed toward

Olympias <note>Alexander's mother</note>, at any rate, and Philip, sensing this, provided him with Callixeina, the Thessalian courtesan, who was very beautiful (for they were cautious lest he be womanish <note>original: "gynnis"; meaning effeminate or lacking virility</note>), and she often had to urge Alexander to be with her. And Philip, Alexander’s father, was a lover of drink, as Theopompus records

->### BOOK 10<-

Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great</note> used to say, whenever he was inclined to get drunk: "One must drink, for Antipater is sober enough for us all." It is told that once, when a certain sculptor was coming up to him while Antipater was present, Philip hesitated as if caught in the act.
<margin>Lover of drinking <note>original: "Philopotes"</note></margin>
Theopompus lists Dionysius the Younger, the tyrant of Sicily, as both a lover of drinking and a drunkard; he says Dionysius’s eyesight was actually ruined by wine. Aristotle, in his *Constitution of the Syracusans*, says that Dionysius would sometimes remain intoxicated for ninety consecutive days, which is why his vision became quite dim. Theophrastus further relates that his companions, seeking to flatter the tyrant, would pretend they could not see well either; they would allow themselves to be led by the hand by Dionysius himself and would feign an inability to see the dishes set before them or the drinking cups. For this reason, they were nicknamed "Dionysian-Flatterers" <note>original: "Dionysokolakes"</note>.

Nysaeus, who later became tyrant of Syracuse, and Apollocrates were also heavy drinkers. These were the sons of the elder Dionysius, as Theopompus records in the fortieth and subsequent books of his *Histories*. Regarding Nysaeus, he writes: "Nysaeus, who later ruled Syracuse, lived like a man under a death sentence; knowing he likely had little time to live, he spent his days gluttonizing and drunk." In the thirty-ninth book, he says: "Apollocrates, the son of the tyrant Dionysius, was debauched and a lover of drinking." Some of his flatterers even tried to turn him against his father. He also says that Hipparinus, another son of Dionysius, was murdered while reigning in a state of intoxication.

Regarding Nysaeus, he further writes: "Nysaeus, the son of the elder Dionysius, while in Syracuse, stayed in charge of affairs, but he would fit out a trireme <note>a Greek warship</note> just to put on his embroidered robes. He indulged in gourmet gluttony, wine-bibbing, and the abuse of boys, women, and others, as much as he was capable of doing, leading a life of total excess."

In the forty-fifth book, the same author says of Timolaus the Theban: "Though many have lived lives of daily excess in their cups, I believe no man in public life was ever more intemperate, gluttonous, or more obviously so than Timolaus." In the twenty-third book, discussing Charidemus of Oreus (whom the Athenians made a citizen), he says: "You would have seen his daily life as one of debauchery and fattening himself up. He was always drinking to the point of intoxication and dared to corrupt free women. He reached such a peak of intemperance that he even attempted to seduce a certain handsome and graceful boy in the council of the Olynthians. This boy had been taken captive along with Derdas the Macedonian."

Arcadion was also a heavy drinker, though it is unclear if this is the same man who was an enemy of Philip, as indicated by the epigram recorded by Polemon in his work *On the Inscriptions found in Cities*. This was the hero Arcadion, the "man of many bells."

> Eagle-like, he spoke these words by the path, sweet Dorcon
> and noble Charmylus; but the man was a fellow
> who drank deep from the flaring cup.

Of a certain Eriphigenus, who had drunk a great deal, an epigram says:

> No shallow wine-drinker was Eriphigenus; for twice in a row,
> the cup of unmixed wine <note>original: "Akrite"</note> clearly carried him off.

Alcetas the Macedonian was also a heavy drinker, according to Aristus of Salamis, as was Diotimus the Athenian. The latter was nicknamed "The Funnel" <note>original: "Chone"</note> because he would attach the vessel to his body and drink unceasingly as the wine was poured in. Polemon confirms he was called "The Funnel" for this reason. We have already mentioned that Cleomenes the Spartan was a drinker of unmixed wine.
<margin>Book 6.</margin>
Herodotus records that Cleomenes, in a fit of drunkenness, cut himself to pieces with a knife. The poet Alcaeus was also a lover of drinking, as I mentioned before. Baton of Sinope, in his writings *On the Poet Ion*, says that Ion was both a lover of drinking and extremely amorous. In his own elegies, Ion admits to loving Chrysilla of Corinth, the daughter of Teleus, whom Teleclides says in his *Hesiods* was also loved by Pericles "The Olympian."

Xenarchus of Rhodes was nicknamed "The Gallon-Measure" <note>original: "Metretas"; a metretes was about 9 gallons</note> because of his vast capacity. Euphorion mentions him in his *Thousands*. Chares of Mytilene, in his *Histories of Alexander*, tells of the Indian philosopher Kalanos, who died by throwing himself onto a funeral pyre; he says that Alexander held gymnastic, musical, and oratorical contests at his tomb. Because of the Indians' love of wine, he also held a contest for drinking unmixed wine. The prize for first place was a talent, for second thirty minae, and for third ten minae. Of those who drank the wine, thirty-five died immediately from the chill <note>likely the shock to the system or "cold" quality ancient medicine attributed to unmixed wine</note>, and six more died shortly after in their tents. The man who drank the most and won was named Promachus; he drank four pitchers <note>original: "choas"; roughly 12 liters</note> of unmixed wine.

Timaeus says that the tyrant Dionysius, at the Festival of the Pitchers <note>original: "Choes"</note>, offered a gold crown as a prize to the first person to drain a pitcher. The philosopher Xenocrates was the first to finish. He took the gold crown and, as he was leaving for his home in the evening, placed it upon the statue of Hermes that stood in his courtyard, just as he was accustomed to doing with his floral crowns every day. He was greatly admired for this. Phanodemus says the Festival of the Pitchers was established in Athens by King Demophon, who wished to welcome Orestes when he arrived in Athens. Wanting Orestes to participate in the sacred rites but not wanting him to share the communal cup before he was purified... <note>The text cuts off here, explaining the origins of the custom where each guest at the Anthesteria festival drank from their own separate vessel to avoid ritual pollution from the matricide Orestes.</note>

### ATHENAEUS: THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...not yet judged <note>This refers to the myth of Orestes arriving in Athens while still polluted by the murder of his mother, before his trial at the Areopagus</note>, he ordered the temples to be closed and a measure of wine <term>choa (about 3 liters)</term> to be set before each guest, announcing that a cake would be given as a prize to the first person to finish drinking. He also ordered that when they finished, they should not lay down the wreaths they were wearing—as was the custom at sacred rites—because they had shared a roof with Orestes. Instead, each man was to tie his wreath around his own pitcher and deliver it to the priestess at the sanctuary "in the Marshes." Afterward, they were to perform the remaining sacrifices in the temple. From that time on, the festival has been called the *Choes* <note>The "Festival of Pitchers," part of the Anthesteria</note>. At this festival, it is customary to send gifts and pay fees to the teachers <note>original: "sophistais"</note>, who themselves invite their acquaintances to a feast of hospitality, as Eubulides the dialectician says in a comic play:

<margin>Dionysius of Heraclea</margin>
"You most wretched of teachers, by the justice of the dance, you who receive fees and feast on more than just snacks." Antigonus of Carystus, in his *Life of Dionysius of Heraclea* (surnamed "the Renegade" <note>original: "metathemenou," referring to his switch from Stoicism to the pursuit of pleasure</note>), says that Dionysius used to celebrate with his servants during the Festival of Pitchers. Being unable in his old age to enjoy the company of his former mistress, he turned to his fellow diners and said, "I can no longer stretch the bow; let another take it" <note>A parody of the contest of the bow from the *Odyssey*</note>. From his youth, as Nicias of Nicaea says in his *Successions*, Dionysius was mad for sexual pleasures and would visit public prostitutes without distinction. Once, while walking with some acquaintances, he came to the brothel where he had been the previous day and still owed some copper coins; having money on him by chance, he reached out his hand and paid the debt in full view of everyone. Anacharsis the Scythian, while at the court of Periander, was offered prizes for drinking; he demanded the victory prize because he was the first to get drunk.

<margin>A lover of drinking</margin>
He claimed this was the goal of a drinking bout, just as the goal of a race is to reach the finish line. The philosophers Lacydes and Timon, having been invited by one of their acquaintances for two days and wishing to adapt to those present, drank quite eagerly. On the first day, Lacydes left early as the drink was getting the better of him. Timon, seeing him depart, said:

<margin>Iliad 22</margin>
"We have won great glory; we have slain the noble Hector" <note>original: "eramentha mega kydos ephenomen Hektora dion"</note>. On the following day, when Timon was toasted but was unable to finish the cup set before him, Lacydes, seeing him recoil, said:

<margin>Iliad 9</margin>
"But later the children will meet my strength" <note>original: "hystero de te paides emo menei antiosi"</note>. Herodotus records that Mycerinus the Egyptian, upon hearing from an oracle that he would live only a short time, had many lamps made. Whenever night fell, he would drink and enjoy himself, ceasing neither day nor night. He wandered into the marshes and groves, or wherever he heard there were gatherings of young people, to get drunk. Herodotus also says that Amasis, another king of the Egyptians, drank heavily. Hermeias of Methymna, in the first book of his *History of Sicily*, says that Nicoteles the Erelinthian was a lover of drinking. Phanias of Ephesus, in his work *The Killing of Tyrants Out of Revenge*, says that Scopas, the son of Creon and descendant of the elder Scopas, was a lifelong heavy drinker; he would return from symposia sitting on a throne, carried home by four men.

<margin>Antiochus the drinker</margin>
Phylarchus, in the sixth book of his *Histories*, says that King Antiochus was a lover of wine and would get so drunk that he slept for long periods; then, waking up in the evening, he would drink again. He says the king transacted very little business while sober, doing most of it while drunk. Consequently, two men managed the kingdom for him: Aristeus and Themison, Cypriots by birth and brothers, both of whom were favorites of Antiochus. King Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes <note>"The Illustrious"</note>, who had been a hostage in Rome, was also a heavy drinker. Ptolemy Euergetes <note>Ptolemy VIII, "The Benefactor"</note> records in the first and fifth books of his *Memoirs* that this king turned to Indian-style revelry and drunkenness and spent vast sums. He spent most of his money reveling by day; sometimes he would stand in the public streets and shout, "To whom does Fortune give it to take?" and then toss the money and leave. Often, wearing a woven crown of roses on his head and a golden Roman toga <note>original: "tebennan"</note>, he would walk alone with stones tucked under his arm, which he would throw at his own followers. He also used to bathe in the public baths, anointed with precious ointments.

<margin>See Book 5</margin>
Once, a commoner seeing him said, "You are blessed, O King, for you smell so expensive."

<margin>Kings who were heavy drinkers</margin>
Pleased by this, the king said, "I will give you your fill of this," and ordered a large jar <note>original: "hydrisken"</note> containing more than two pitchers of thick ointment to be poured over the man’s head, so that the crowd of common people rolled around in the spill. As the floor became slippery, Antiochus himself burst out laughing, and most of the bathers suffered the same fate <note>meaning they also slipped and fell</note>. Polybius, in the twenty-sixth book of his *Histories*, calls him "the Madman" <note>original: "epimane," a pun on his title Epiphanes</note> because of his actions. For he not only mingled with common people but also drank with the cheapest foreigners and the lowest sorts. If he heard that any young men were feasting anywhere, he would show up with a portable jar and a band of musicians, so that most people, startled by the absurdity, would get up and flee. Often, he would cast off his royal robes, put on a Roman toga, and wander around the marketplace. In the thirty-first book, the same Polybius says that while celebrating games in Antioch, he invited all the Greeks and anyone else who wished to come to the spectacle.
