### BOOK X

He poured out iris-scented perfume from golden vessels, as well as cinnamon, nard, marjoram, and lily-scented oils. Calling people together for a feast, he would sometimes fill a thousand dining couches, and at other times fifteen hundred, with the most lavish preparations. The distribution of duties was managed by the king himself. Standing at the entrances, he would lead some guests in and seat others, and he even personally led in the servants who carried the courses. During the banquets, he did not remain seated but would jump up before the others. Sometimes he would set down a morsel of food, other times his cup, and leap up and move about the drinking party, accepting toasts while standing, moving from one person to another. At the same time, he would joke with the musical performers, and he would even be carried in by the mimes, completely covered up, and placed on the ground as if he were one of the performers himself. When the music struck up, the king would leap up and dance and joke with the mimes, so that everyone felt ashamed for him. Such is the effect that a lack of education regarding drunkenness has upon the wretched. 

Antiochus, the one nicknamed "the Median" <note>original: "Madeia," likely referring to Antiochus VII Sidetes who fought the Parthians/Medes</note> who campaigned against Arsaces, was also a lover of drink, as Poseidonius of Apamea records in the sixteenth book of his *Histories*. Indeed, after he was killed, it is said that Arsaces, while burying him, remarked: "Your boldness and drunkenness tripped you up, Antiochus. For you hoped to drink up your kingdom in large cups." 

Antiochus, the one called "the Great," whom the Romans defeated, as Polybius records in his twentieth book, arrived at Chalcis in Euboea and celebrated a wedding when he was fifty years old—a man who had taken up two of the greatest tasks: the liberation of the Greeks (as he himself promised) and the war against the Romans. <margin>Plutarch, in the *Life of Flamininus*.</margin> Having fallen in love with a girl of Chalcis, he neglected the timing of the war to marry her out of this ambition, being a wine-drinker and delighting in drunkenness. She was the daughter of Cleoptolemus, one of the prominent citizens, and surpassed all others in beauty. While celebrating the wedding in Chalcis, he spent the entire winter there, taking no thought whatsoever for the pressing matters of state. He even gave the girl the name "Euboea." When he was defeated in the war, he fled to Ephesus with his new bride. 

In his second book, Polybius records that Agron, the king of the Illyrians, after defeating the Aetolians, was so overcome by the pleasure of victory that—being a heavy drinker—he turned to drunkenness and feasting, contracted pleurisy, and died. In his twenty-ninth book, the same author says that Genthius <note>original: "Tenthiona"</note>, the king of the Illyrians, committed many outrages in his life because of his heavy drinking, being drunk both night and day. He even killed his brother Plator <note>original: "Glydyraton"</note> when he was about to marry the daughter of Monunius, so that he could marry the girl himself, and he treated his subjects cruelly. 

He also says that Demetrius (Soter), who escaped from Rome where he was a hostage, as recorded in the thirty-third book, became king of the Syrians and was a heavy drinker, remaining intoxicated for the greater part of the day. Orophernes also, who ruled Cappadocia for a short time and abandoned his ancestral ways, as Polybius says in the thirty-second book, introduced Ionian and "artistic" <note>Referring to the extravagant lifestyle of professional performers or "artists of Dionysus"</note> wastefulness. 

Therefore, the most divine Plato rightly legislates in his second book <note>Plato's *Laws*</note> that children should not taste wine at all until they are eighteen years old. For one must not "channel fire upon fire." One should taste wine in moderation until thirty years of age. But the young man must abstain from drunkenness and heavy drinking altogether. However, when a man reaches forty years, he may feast in the common messes and call upon the other gods, and especially invite Dionysus to the "rite of the elders" <note>original: "teleten," a sacred mystery or initiation</note> and to their play. For God gave wine to humans as a helper against the austerity of old age—a medicine, so that we might regain our youth and that gloominess might be forgotten. And he says further, following the flow of the argument, that this god's soul and mind were corrupted by his mother Hera. For this reason, she inflicts him with Bacchic frenzies and all kinds of mad choral dancing as a punishment, which is also why wine was given by them. 

Phalaecus, in his epigrams, writes of a certain woman who was a heavy drinker named Kleo, who "belted her saffron-robed tunic three times for Chrysopus": 

"To this Dionysus, Kleo gave a gift, 
Because she excelled in drinking parties; 
no one of men contended with her to drink joyfully, 
nor from a cup." 

That the female race is fond of wine is common knowledge. But Xenarchus in his *Pentathlon* specifically introduces a woman swearing this most terrifying oath: 

"May it be my lot, while I live, my free child, to squeeze out wine <note>i.e., to drink deeply</note> until I die." 

<margin>Gellius, Book 10, Chapter 23.</margin> Among the Romans, as Polybius says in his sixth book, women are forbidden from drinking wine. But they do drink what is called raisin wine <note>original: "passon" (passum)</note>. <margin>The "good voice" of Roman women.</margin> This is made from raisins, and when drunk, it tastes similar to sweet unfermented must or cooked wine. Therefore, they use it to satisfy urgent thirst. But it is impossible for a woman to drink wine in secret. For, first of all, the woman does not have control over the wine. In addition to this, she must kiss her own relatives and those of her husband, down to cousins, and do this every day whenever she first sees them. Since it is unclear whom she will meet, she must be on her guard. For if she has merely done the deed, it provides all the grounds needed for an accusation. 

Alcimus the Sicilian, in his book entitled *On Italy*, says that all women in Italy do not drink wine for the following reason: Hercules, once being in the territory of Croton, went to a house because he was hungry from his journey and asked for something to drink. It happened that the woman of the house had secretly opened a jar of wine, and to him...

# BOOK 10.

<sig>T 2</sig>

...these symposia lead men astray, and they are all of a dissolute character, girding their bellies with wide belts whenever they drink. At first, when they drink in moderation, they laugh quite loudly; but as they drink more, they continue to tighten their belts further. The Ariaei <note>A Thracian or Illyrian people known for their heavy drinking.</note> are said to have been subdued in a similar way, numbering some three hundred thousand. Every day they get drunk and hold assemblies, eating and drinking without restraint. Because of this, the Celts, while at war with them and knowing their lack of self-control, ordered all their soldiers to prepare a most magnificent feast in their tents, but to mix into the food a certain medicinal herb capable of cramping the bowels and purging the system. When this happened, some of them were captured and killed, while others threw themselves into the rivers, having lost all control of their guts. After Democritus had listed many such examples in succession, Pontianus spoke: "I say that wine is the mother-city of all these horrors, for because of it come drunkenness, madness, and drunken violence, which men fall into when they partake so passionately." Nor was Dionysius—nicknamed "The Brazen"—wrong when he called those who serve wine "rowers of cups" in his elegies. And someone else, addressing Dionysius of Philistia, said, "Sailors of the banquet and rowers of cups." Concerning this, the love of it has not perished.

<margin>Drunkenness is the mother-city of evils.</margin>

Alexis, in his play *The Hairdresser*, speaking of someone who drank too much, says: "My son, such as he just left you, has become a sort of wine-drinker, or a Marops, or a shopkeeper." Or as Timocles says: "He is drunk on nothing else." Another might be called a "clod of earth," a "plow," or an "earth-born man." It is a difficult thing, then, for a man who is a friend to be drunk, and Alexis says it well in his play *The Season* (the title is the name of a courtesan) that drinking wine not well-mixed with water makes one vomit, and then people blame the wine. If drunkenness is an evil above all others, it is the greatest and most harmful thing to mankind. And as the proverb says: "Much wine makes one commit many errors."

Crobylus says in *The Woman Leaving*: "For what pleasure is there in being constantly drunk, depriving oneself of reason while still alive? Reason is the greatest good that nature has given us." One should not, therefore, get drunk. For a democratic city, as Plato says in the eighth book of the *Republic*, when it thirsts for freedom and happens upon "bad cupbearers" <note>original: "κακῶν οἰνοχόων"—Plato uses the metaphor of wine-service to describe political leaders who offer too much liberty too quickly.</note> and becomes drunk on "unmixed" <note>original: "ἀκράτου"—wine served without water, here a metaphor for pure, dangerous freedom.</note> freedom further than is necessary, it punishes its rulers unless they are very mild and provide a great deal of liberty, accusing them of being filthy oligarchs. In turn, it insults those who are obedient to the rulers. In the sixth book of the *Laws*, he says the city should be mixed like a wine-bowl (*krater*); when the wine is poured in, it boils and rages, but when corrected by another, sober god <note>The "sober god" is water, which tempers the wine/city.</note> and receiving a beautiful partnership, it produces a good and moderate drink. For to behave like a drunkard is to become intoxicated. Therefore, Antiphanes says in *Arcadia*: "A sober man should never behave like a drunkard anywhere, nor even when he decides to drink, if he has any sense." He who thinks more highly of himself than a mortal should, trusting in a bit of wretched money, will see himself as equal to everyone else when he goes to the brothels. If he examines the evidence of the physicians regarding life—where the veins lead, both those above and those below—he will see how the whole of mortal life is steered. And in *Aeolus*, criticizing the terrible things done by those who drink too much, he says: "Blessed was his love for a woman of similar character; sweet it was, and for a time he mastered his misfortune and restrained himself. But then, taking Wine as his general—who alone brings daring to mortals to lead them beyond good counsel—he rose up at night and obtained what he desired." 

<margin>Wine is the milk of Aphrodite.</margin>

Aristophanes was right, then, to call wine "the milk of Aphrodite," saying: "Sweet it is to drink wine, the milk of Aphrodite." For some people, after drinking much of it, develop a craving for unlawful sexual pleasures. Hegesandros of Delphi also called certain people "wine-gods" (*theoinous*), saying: "Among the clever people of Rhodes who were involved in politics, or even foreigners, one of them, mocking Rhodophon for his gambling, said: 'O old man, truly the young gamblers wear you out.'" He reproached Rhodophon for being very lawless with women and for his lack of self-control, sparing no insult. Theopompus, in the sixteenth book of his *Histories*, speaking of another Rhodian, says: "Hegesilochus, who by ancient lineage was of high birth, was ruined by wine-drinking and dice; he had no special reputation among the Rhodians, but was slandered by all his companions and fellow citizens for the wastefulness of his life." Then, speaking of the oligarchy he established with his friends, he adds: "They brought in many noble women, the wives of the leading men. And they corrupted not a few girls and youths. They reached such a point of licentiousness that they even saw fit to gamble with one another for free-born women." 

<margin>The Rhodians' gambling regarding women.</margin>

They agreed that those who threw the lower number with the knucklebones (*astragaloi*) must bring one of the female citizens to the winner for sexual intercourse, making no excuses, but persuading or forcing each one as they were able; thus they joined in this contest. Some other Rhodians also played at this gambling. 

<margin>Antheas, a composer of songs or of a dissolute life...</margin>

Most notoriously, Hegesilochus himself, the leader of the city, took part in this. Antheas of Lindos, who claimed to be a relative of Cleobulus the Wise, as Philodemus says in his work on the...

# ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...an elderly and prosperous man, naturally gifted in poetry; he lived his whole life in a Dionysian manner <note>Living "Dionysianly" implies a life dedicated to wine, theater, and ritual revelry.</note>, wearing Dionysian dress and maintaining many companions. He led a revel-procession (*komos*) constantly, both by day and by night. He was the first to invent the style of poetry composed of compound words, which Asopidorus of Phlius later employed in his prose iambics. This man also composed comedies and many other works in this poetic style, which he would lead as the conductor for his fellow phallus-bearers <note>Participants in Dionysian processions who carried symbolic phalli.</note>. 

<margin>Drunkard.</margin>
Upon hearing this, Ulpian said: "But as for the term 'drunkard' (*paroinos*), my dear Pontianus, where is it found? For as Agathon the Fair once said, you are 'destroying me with questions,' and you and your new-fashioned ways use language in an unseemly manner." Since it has been decided that we must all give ourselves over to good cheer, I note that Antiphanes says in *The Lydian*: "A Colchian man, a drunkard." But you, in your drunken behavior, are never satisfied, nor do you take it to heart that Eumolpus of Pergamum died from intoxication. 

<margin>The nephew of the King of Pergamum, as Ctesicles records in the first book of his *Chronicles*.</margin>
This Eumolpus was the nephew of the King of Pergamum, as recorded in the first book of *Chronicles*, and he was quite unlike Perseus, who was overthrown by the Romans. For Perseus did not imitate his father Philip in anything; he was neither eager for women nor a lover of wine. Indeed, at dinner, he not only drank moderately himself, but so did the friends who were with him, as Polybius records in his twenty-sixth book.

<margin>Unrhythmic drinker.</margin>
But you, Ulpian, are an "unrhythmic drinker" (*arrhythmopotas*), according to Timon of Phlius. For it was he who gave this name to those who gulp down a great deal of unmixed wine in one breath without stopping, writing in the second book of his *Silli* <note>Satirical poems.</note>: "Either a heavy, striking leather-thonged man, or a wolf-worker, who rebuked Dionysus as an unrhythmic drinker. And from the flow, he kept throwing the ladles of those insatiable for wine." 

<margin>Given to drinking.</margin>
Alcaeus used the term "given to drinking" (*potikos*) for Ganymede. 

<margin>Drunkenness confuses the vision.</margin>
That drunkenness causes our vision to wander was clearly shown by Anacharsis through his words regarding "God-lookers" <note>Anacharsis likely meant that drunkards see "divine" or false images.</note>, noting that false opinions arise in those who are drunk. For when a certain fellow-drinker saw Anacharsis's wife at a banquet and said, "O Anacharsis, you have married an ugly woman," he replied, "Indeed, so it seems to me as well. So, boy, pour me a stronger cup of unmixed wine, so that I may make her beautiful." 

After this, Ulpian, drinking a toast to one of his companions, said: "Consider also our friend Antiphanes, who says in *The Rustics*: 'Closing his eyes, he gulps down the whole great load, not like one who needs to be an expert.' Drink, my friend, and let us not always draw hatred. The same Antiphanes says in *The Wounded Man*: 'Let someone strike a calculation into the center, and let someone go through a Milesian turn.' By this, he means that there is a change in every deed except one. Let everyone follow me in drinking 'unmixed-born wine,' as Euripides called it." 

<margin>Drink!</margin>
For Euripides did use that phrase. But as for Philoxenus, it makes no difference, my good man; if you challenge me, he will say it is a matter of a single syllable. But who has used the form "Drink!" (*pithi*)? Ulpian replied, "You have been darkened by shadows, my dearest friend, having rushed off to such wine. Cratinus said 'Drink!' in *The Odysseys*: 'There now, take this and drink (*pithi*) at once, and then ask me my name immediately.' And you, drink, lest we be deprived; for the shape of the cup is somehow seductive and worthy of its fame—remember the festival! For just now we were drinking from small earthenware bowls. May the gods give many good things to the craftsman who made you for the sake of the mixture and for safety." 

Diphilus, in *The Bath-house*, says: "Pouring it out, he filled the mortal cup and covered the goddess, saying 'Drink!' (*pithi*)." These things are for us, O Father Zeus of the Companions! Ameipsias says in *The Miser*: "Stirring the jar, drink (*pithi*) the sea-water." Menander in *The Flute-Girls*: "Throw in to your heart's content, or have you ever drunk so much? Sosila, everyone drink (*pithi*) now, for I am drinking poorly." 

<margin>I shall drink.</margin>
One must say "I shall drink" (*piomai*) or "you will drink," lengthening the 'i'. For so it is in the Homeric phrase "I shall drink (*piomai*) from the pasture," and Aristophanes in *The Knights*: "Where will you ever drink (*piesai*) from this?" and in other places: "I shall drink (*piomai*) the most bitter wine." This is perhaps derived from the word for "a poem" (*poiema*), though sometimes they shorten the 'i', as Plato [the comic poet] does in *Those from the Temples*: "Nor he who drinks up (*ekpietai*) the money." And in *The Rabble*: "O, drink (*pithe*) much water." Diphilus says in *The Dagger*: "I will force the temple-robber first, and there, drink (*pie*), drink (*pine*), drink (*pine*)." And you, my friend, consider also Alexis, who says in *The Twins*: "Drink a toast (*propithi*) to this man, so that he may drink to another," and there arises what is called an "over-toast" (*episios*) in Anacreon. For the lyric poet says: "Do not babble like a sea-wave, drinking the over-toast (*episios*) greedily with a loud, gift-bearing belly." 

<margin>Over-toast.</margin>
We usually say "ever-living" (*aieisona*). But you, having drunk, do not fear that you will fall down. For are they not loosened <note>Originally "unbound" or "relaxed" in a physical sense.</note> who drink the wine that, according to Simonides, is "mind-destroying and burden-some"? 

<margin>Drinking.</margin>
But as Aristotle says in his work *On Drunkenness*, those who have drunk the barley-beverage—which they call *pinon*—fall on their backs. He writes as follows: "However, something peculiar happens regarding the barley-drink called *pinon*. For from all other intoxicating drinks, those who are drunk fall in every direction—to the left, to the right, on their faces, or on their backs. But only those who are drunk on *pinon* lean backward and fall flat on their backs." 

<margin>Beer (*Bryton*).</margin>
Some also call barley-wine *bryton*, as Sophocles does in *Triptolemus*: "...and not to any [man] the land-born beer (*bryton*)." And Archilochus: "Like a Thracian or a Phrygian man, he gulped his beer (*bryze*) through a pipe..." Aeschylus mentions the drink in *Lycurgus*: "And from these he drank beer (*bryton*), thinning it over time, and he boasted of it in his manly house." Hellanicus, in his *Foundations*, says that *bryton* is prepared from roots, writing: "They drink beer (*bryton*) made from roots..."

<summary>This page explores various Greek terms for drinking and intoxication, citing numerous poets and Aristotle’s scientific observation that barley-beer (pinon) uniquely causes drinkers to fall backward.</summary>

# BOOK 10.

...from roots, just as the Thracians make drink from barley. Hecataeus, in the second book of his *Description of the Earth* <note>Hecataeus of Miletus was an early Greek historian and geographer (c. 550–476 BC).</note>, after stating that the Egyptians are bread-eaters, adds that they "grind up barley for a drink." In his description of Europe, he says that the Paeonians drink *brytos* <note>original: βρύτον — a type of fermented barley ale.</note> made from barley, and *parabie* made from millet and fleabane. He also says they anoint themselves with "oil made from milk" <note>This likely refers to butter, which was a curiosity to the Greeks who preferred olive oil.</note>. So much for these matters. "But in our own time, wine is a friend, thyrsus-bearing <note>The thyrsus was the staff of Dionysus, topped with a pine cone and wrapped in ivy.</note>, and Dionysus is held in great honor," as Ion of Chios says in his elegies. For this is the occasion for all-divine oracles, and the gatherings of all the Greeks, and the feasts of kings: 

> From the time the grape-bearing vine, 
> sending up her underground shoot, 
> embraced the sky with her flourishing arm, 
> and from the eyes of the air sprouted 
> thick clusters of children who keep silence 
> until they arrive, one after another. 
> But when they cease their shouting, 

<margin>Dionysus.</margin>

> milking the nectar that is the only blessing for men, 
> a common, self-grown medicine for joy, 
> whose children are the feasts, 
> and kindliness, and the dances, 
> wine, the king of all good things, has shown its nature. 
> You, father Dionysus, who delights in festivals, 
> the presiding officer of cheerful symposia, 
> hail! Grant a long life for beautiful deeds, 
> and for drinking and playing, and for thinking just thoughts. 

Amphis also praises wine in *The Philadelphians*, saying: "To have the mind only in the forehead, like those who are much sought after among you who are accustomed to think clearly." For indeed, some forms of wisdom are cautious because they examine everything slowly and frequently, thus defining matters by impulse and readiness; but another kind, because it does not calculate clearly what will happen from each action, shouts out something youthful and hot-headed.

When someone was about to drink, Aemilianus said to Ulpian: "It is time for us, dear friends, to seek out something concerning riddles <note>original: γρίφων (griphoi) — intellectual puzzles or word-games played at dinner parties.</note>, so that we might 'rinse out the cup' for a moment, or perhaps consider the *Grammatical Tragedy* of the Athenian Callias. But let us first seek the definition of the 'griphos.' Some were even proposed by Cleobulina of Lindos <note>A famous female poet of the 6th century BC known for her riddles.</note> among her enigmas. Our companion Diotimus the Olympian has spoken sufficiently about them, but let us see how the comic poets mention them, and what penalty they say is required of those who do not solve them."

<margin>Riddles.</margin>

And Laertius said that Clearchus of Soli defines it thus: "A riddle is a playful problem proposed for the purpose of finding the intended meaning by intellectual search, often said for the sake of an honor or a penalty." In his work *On Riddles*, the same Clearchus says there are seven kinds of riddles. First, based on a letter: for example, we might be told to say a name of a fish or a plant starting with alpha. Similarly, he might order a name that includes a certain letter or lacks one, such as the so-called "sigma-less" riddles <note>Riddles where the letter 'S' (sigma) must be avoided, a common literary challenge.</note>; hence Pindar composed an ode against the letter 'S,' as if a riddle had been proposed in the composition of the music. 

Riddles are also told by syllable: for example, we might speak a verse and ask for a word that begins with 'ba' like 'basileus' (king), or ends in 'nax' like 'Callianax,' or begins with 'leon' like 'Leonides,' or conversely ends in 'an' like 'Thrasylean.' In terms of names, we might ask for simple or compound two-syllable names, perhaps those with a tragic appearance, or lowly names, or names of the gods like 'Cleonymus' or 'Dionysius.' And among these, whether they are from one god or several, like 'Hermaphroditus,' or beginning with Zeus like 'Diocles,' or with Hermes like 'Hermodorus,' or perhaps ending in '-nikos.' Those who did not answer as commanded had to drink a certain cup of wine as a penalty. Clearchus defines it this way, but he also asks Ulpian what this cup is. Antiphanes also mentions riddles in *The Knossians*, or perhaps *Gastron*:

> I used to think that when people ordered 
> riddles to be told over drinks, they were 
> clearly talking nonsense, saying nothing 
> that anyone could grasp. When they said 
> 'What a man carries but does not carry,' 
> I laughed, thinking it was just talk, 
> and never did I think there was a real point to it. 
> It seemed like a trap. But now I know it is true! 
> For we are bringing a contribution (*eranos*), 
> and the men are here, but not one of them 
> 'carries' his share. So clearly, 'what a man carries 
> but does not carry' is this—and thus the riddle 
> is solved and makes sense to everyone. 
> But what nonsense they make of the matter, 
> those who do not put down their money! 

Philip says in his play *Good Fortune*: "By Zeus! As for the matters of Aphrodite, when I am about to speak, do I say 'the pot' (*chytra*), or do I say: 

> A hollow-bodied vessel fashioned from earth, 
> baked in another mother’s womb, 
> which protects the stewed, milk-fed 
> newborn of the flock within it, 
> melting their flesh with its nets? 

By Heracles, you will kill me if you don't speak plainly! You speak well of a pot of meat. And if I mean a 'honey-cake' (*plakous*), should I say: 

> A clot of the tawny bee's streams 
> mixed with the discharge of bleating goats, 
> sitting in a broad vessel of a pure 
> maiden daughter of Demeter, 
> feasting on thin-composed, myriad coverings? 

Or shall I say 'honey-cake' plainly? I want 'honey-cake.' And instead of 'wine,' say 'the sweat of the Bromian spring' in short. And skip the 'gray dew of the spring' for a song—just say 'water.' Tell me 'myrrh' instead of 'the breeze of the Casiopian air.' Speak at length, and don't tell me anything else, or I might say the opposite—that it seems this task is like kneading dough, as some say: you say nothing yourself, but you wrap many other things around it." And Alexis in *Sleep* proposes such riddles: 

> Not mortal, nor immortal, but having a certain 
> mixture, so that it lives neither in the 
> portion of man nor in the portion of god, 
> but always grows... 
> You delight in playing, O woman...

# BOOK 10

### T 4

For instance, the one concerning the shadow. For he <note>Likely referring to a poet like Sophocles or Simonides, though the attribution is debated.</note> said there was a certain nature which, at its birth and its passing, is largest, but at its peak is smallest. He speaks as follows:

> Of all the natures that the nourishing earth brings forth, or the sea,
> none has a growth similar to mortals;
> But where it is first sown, it is largest;
> in its middle prime it is small; but in its old age
> it is once again greater than all others in form and size.

<margin>5</margin> And in the tragedy *Oedipus*, he says that he spoke riddlingly of the Night and the Day: "There are two sisters, sun-born; one gives birth to the other, and she who gave birth is in turn born from the one she birthed." <note>A classic Greek riddle: Day gives way to Night, and Night to Day.</note> Something similar is also told by Callisthenes in his *Hellenica*, that when the Arcadians were besieging Cromnus (which is a small town situated near a large city), Hippodamus the Spartan, who was one of those being besieged, gave instructions to the herald sent to them from the Lacedaemonians. He intended to reveal their situation to them in a riddle, telling him to report to his mother "to release the little woman within seven days, the one depicted in the Apollonium," as it would no longer be possible to release her if they delayed. This message was quite clear in its meaning. For in the Apollonium <note>A temple of Apollo.</note>, next to the throne of Apollo, there is a painting representing "Famine" <note>original: λιμός — Limos</note>, having the form of a woman. Thus it became clear to everyone that the besieged could only hold out for ten more days because of the famine. <margin>15</margin> Understanding the message, the Spartans came with all their might to the aid of those in Cromnus. 

There are many such riddles, such as: "I saw a man glue bronze to a man with fire, so closely that he made them of one blood." This signifies the application of a <term>cupping-glass</term> <note>original: σικύα — a medical instrument used to draw blood to the surface of the skin using heat and a vacuum.</note>. Among the riddles of this type, as Clearchus says in his work *On Riddles*, is this: "A man and not a man hit a bird and not a bird sitting on a tree and not a tree with a stone and not a stone." These refer respectively to a eunuch, a bat, a fennel-stalk, and a pumice-stone. <note>The eunuch (man/not-man) hit the bat (bird/not-bird) on the fennel-stalk (wood/not-wood) with a pumice (stone/not-stone).</note> <margin>20</margin> Even Plato in the fifth book of the *Laws* <note>Actually Republic 479c.</note> mentions the riddles of children, saying they are like those who invite guests to a feast and offer ambiguous things, such as the children's riddle about the eunuch's throw and the bat, from which they even riddle about the thing thrown. 

The riddles of Pythagoras are also of this kind, as Demetrius of Byzantium says in the fourth book of *On Poets*: "Do not eat the heart," meaning to practice freedom from sorrow. "Do not poke the fire with a sword," meaning do not provoke an angry man; for the anger is the fire and the strife is the sword. <margin>25</margin> "Do not step over the balance," meaning to flee from all greed and to seek the equal, for the balance represents fairness. "Do not walk the highways," meaning do not follow the opinion of the many; for each person responds randomly with whatever seems right to them, but one should use the mind as a guide to love the straight path. "Do not sit on a bushel," meaning not to look only to the needs of the day, but always to look forward to the coming one; for death is the boundary and end of life. Therefore, one should not approach it with grief and worry. 

<margin>30</margin> "The Dog" <note>Referring to Diogenes the Cynic, or perhaps a student of the Cynic school.</note> used to play with riddles and jokes in a manner similar to Theodectes, as Clearchus says, as did Aristonymus the Cithara-player, and also Cleon, who was called the "Flute-Mime." This Cleon became the best "face-actor" of the Italian mimes; for he even surpassed Nymphodorus among the famous mimes. Ichomachus the herald also became a follower of his, performing his imitations in public circles. Because he was so well-regarded, he moved on to perform mimes among the "wonder-workers" <note>Traveling entertainers and magicians.</note>. <margin>35</margin> The riddles they made were of this sort: for instance, a certain countryman was overstuffed and feeling unwell, and when the doctor asked him if he had "passed anything on top" <note>Referring to vomiting.</note>, he replied, "I haven't passed anything on top, but only into my belly." Or a certain poor woman whose stomach was aching, when the doctor asked if she had "anything in her womb," <note>A common euphemism for pregnancy.</note> she said, "How could I, when I haven't eaten for three days?" Of the sayings of Aristonymus, many were witty. Sosiphanes the poet said to Cephisocles the actor, seeing him looking proud: "I would have hit you in the ribs with a stone, if I weren't afraid of splashing those standing around you." <note>An insult implying the actor is full of nothing but liquid or filth.</note> 

<margin>40</margin> The oldest and most logical riddle, and most characteristic of the nature of "griphoi," is: "What do we all teach without knowing it?" and "What is the same nowhere and everywhere?" and in addition, "What is the same in heaven, on earth, and in the sea?" This is based on <term>homonymy</term>. For the names "Bear," "Snake," "Eagle," and "Dog" exist in heaven (as constellations), on earth, and in the sea (as animals). The second riddle signifies Time; for it is the same for everyone at once, yet it is nowhere because its nature is not in one place. <margin>45</margin> The first refers to the soul; for no one among us knows it, yet we teach it to our neighbor. 

Callias of Athens (as research was done into this even earlier) who lived a little before the time of Strattis, composed what is called the *Grammar Tragedy*, arranging it thus: its prologue is made of the letters of the alphabet, which must be recited by dividing the letters according to their various forms, ending with Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, E, Zeta, Eta, Theta, <margin>50</margin> Iota, Kappa, Lambda, Mu, Nu, Xi, O, Ou, Pi, Rho, Sigma, Tau, U, Phi, Chi, Psi, and ending at Omega. The chorus consists of women, and is composed by him in meter and set to music in this manner: "Beta-Alpha: Ba; Beta-E: Be; Beta-Eta: Bee; Beta-Iota: Bi; Beta-Omicron: Bo; Beta-Upsilon: Bu; Beta-Omega: Boo." And then again in the antistrophe of the melody in the same meter: "Gamma-Alpha: Ga; Gamma-E: Ge; Gamma-Eta: Gee; Gamma-Iota: Gi; Gamma-Omicron: Go; Gamma-Upsilon: Gu; Gamma-Omega: Goo." And so on for the rest of the

<meta>This page continues the scholarly discussion from the *Deipnosophistae* (The Learned Banqueters) by Athenaeus, focusing on "letter riddles"—literary devices where characters describe the shapes of letters to spell out a name, usually because the character is illiterate.</meta>

# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

Each syllable then likewise had its measure and the melody to which all parts have this same correspondence. Thus, it is suspected that Euripides did not only compose his *Medea* in this specific way entirely, but that he also clearly adapted the melody itself. They say that in Sophocles’s *Justice*, he ventured to compose the poem using the meter of a woman he had heard, but he did not do so in his *Oedipus*. "Thus I, when I shall pain you, having been told these things myself." Therefore, all the others, it seems, in their tragedies, maintained the responding stanzas from those models, and after the chorus, they would introduce a speech starting again with vowels, in this manner. If, through the paragraph markers, one were to divide the speech similarly to those mentioned before, so that the performance intended by the poet might be preserved—the power of "alpha" alone, O women, whether one must say the second alone, or you will speak the third alone, then I shall let go of the fourth, of the "iota" alone, and for the fifth, it says "theta" alone, and for the sixth, "upsilon" alone. <note>This passage is somewhat corrupt in the original Greek, referring to complex experiments in poetic meter and the specific phonetic qualities of vowels and consonants.</note> I speak a song of the seven vowels, yet only seven in the meters. If she ceases, she speaks herself seven times. Since he also gave the line through the iambics, he was the first to speak. The thought is somewhat more unrestrained, but the style is phrased in this way: "For I am a bitch <note>original: Κυνω — Kyno</note>, O women, but perceive it, friends. A child found the name of the wise in letters: a straight long line, and from its middle, a small one lying sideways on each side." <note>This describes the letter **H** (Eta) in its archaic or specific form.</note>

Hence later, as one might suspect, Maandrius the historian—having slightly slanted the imitation through his elegance—wrote the speech more vulgarly in his instructions. But Euripides, in his *Theseus*, seems to have composed a speech for an illiterate man. There is an illiterate man who reveals to himself the name of Theseus, which was inscribed, in this way:

> I am not skilled in letters,
> but I will describe the shapes and clear signs.
<margin>20</margin> <margin>Θ</margin> > A certain circle, as if measured out by a compass;
> this has a clear mark in its middle. <note>The letter **Θ** (Theta).</note>
<margin>Η</margin> > The second consists of two lines first.
> Another single line in the middle keeps these apart. <note>The letter **Η** (Eta).</note>
<margin>Σ</margin> > The third is like a certain lock of hair, all curled. <note>The letter **C** (Lunate Sigma).</note>
<margin>Ε</margin> > The fourth, again, is one line standing upright,
> and three slanting lines are fixed upon it. <note>The letter **Ε** (Epsilon).</note>
<margin>Υ</margin> > The fifth is not easy to describe in words:
> for there are two lines from separate points,
> but these run together into one base. <note>The letter **Υ** (Upsilon).</note>
<margin>30</margin> <margin>Σ</margin> > The last is similar to the third. <note>The letter **Σ** (Sigma).</note>

The tragedy-writer Agathon did the same thing in his *Telephus*. For there, an illiterate man likewise reveals the inscription of Theseus as follows: "The first of the writing was a circle with a navel in the middle; then two lines joined by straight rulers; the third was similar to a Scythian bow. Then a trident <note>original: τριόδους — triodous</note> was lying sideways, and two lines joined on a single ruler. And that which was third was the last again." And Theodectes of Phaselis also brings on a certain countryman who is illiterate, and who signifies the name of Theseus to him: "The first of the writing was a soft-eyed circle. Then two rulers of exactly equal measure, and a horizontal ruler binds these through the middle. The third is like a curled lock of hair. Then a trident lying sideways, as it appeared. Fifth, two rods of equal measure from above, <margin>40</margin> and these stretch together to a single base. The sixth is that which was before: the lock of hair." And Sophocles did something similar to this in his satyr play *Amphiaraus*, introducing the letters through a dance. Neoptolemus of Parium, in his work *On Epigrams*, says that in Chalcedon, this epigram is inscribed on the tomb of Thrasymachus the Sophist: "The name: Theta, Rho, Alpha, Sigma, Upsilon, Mu, Alpha, Chi, Omicron, Sigma. <note>Spells **Θρασύμαχος** (Thrasymachus).</note> The fatherland is Chalcedon, and the craft is wisdom." And the poem of Castorion of Soli to Pan, as Clearchus says, is of such a kind: each of the feet is comprised of whole words, and it has all the feet together as both leading and following, such as: "Thee, who over the snow-beaten, storm-lashed heights... [moving as a noble beast-tender, for the land of the Arcadians I shall celebrate in writing, and for the wise king having composed a prayer for all, let him hear my song, he who wears the wax-coated tunic of the Muse, pouring forth honey.]" <note>A highly complex poem where words and meters are interchangeable.</note> and the rest in the same manner. Each of these feet, however you place them in order, will yield the same meter, thus: <margin>50</margin> "Thee, who over the snow-beaten heights, Thee, who over the storm-lashed heights." And also that each of the feet has the same number of letters <note>original: ἑκασταγράμματος — hekastagrammatos</note>. For the method is not unique, but can be done otherwise, so that by placing more, it may have something useful from the one, speaking thus: "Tell me the measure of the feet, taking the measure for me of the feet, the measure tell me." For we wish to take the measure of the feet. And Pindar, regarding the song composed without the letter sigma, as he himself...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of literary curiosities and intellectual games from Book 10 of the *Deipnosophistae*. While the previous page focused on "letter-riddles" where shapes of letters were described, this page moves into "sigmaless" poems (poems omitting the letter 'S') and complex allegorical riddles by famous poets like Simonides and Theognis.</meta>

# BOOK 10

<margin>1</margin>Clearchus says that just as if a riddle <term>grīphos; a verbal puzzle or enigma</term> had been proposed in a musical composition, many people were offended by the letter **sigma** <note>The letter 'S', which some ancient critics found hissing and unmusical.</note> because it was possible to exclude it. Because he did not approve of the letter, Lasus of Hermione composed "sigmaless" odes, such as the one titled *The Centaurs*. Also, the hymn composed by Lasus to Demeter of Hermione is sigmaless, as Heraclides of Pontus states in the first book of his treatise *On Music*. The opening line is: *I sing of Demeter and the Maiden, the wife of Clymenus.* <note>original: Δάματρα μέλπω κόραν τε Κλυμένοιο ἄλοχον. Note the absence of the letter sigma (ς) in the Greek.</note> You might also encounter other riddles appearing openly, such as: *My father is the salt water that surrounds me, and my mother is the child of the number eight.* <note>original: οκτώ — okto</note> He is clearly speaking of the island of **Delos**, which is surrounded by the sea; its mother is Leto, who is the daughter of Coeus. <note>The riddle relies on a Macedonian dialectal pun where "Coeus" sounds like a word for the number eight.</note> The Macedonians call the number eight *kotos*. And regarding **barley-groats**, one must "knead the juice of peeled barley and drink it." For he created the name for barley-water from the words "to crush" and "to strip."

<margin>10</margin>In the odes, there is a description of a **snail**. It is recorded this way in the *Definitions* of Teucer: *A homeless animal, spineless, boneless, shell-backed, with unblinking eyes, moving forward by stooping.* Antiphanes, in his play *The Lover*, says: *You mean "parsley-fleshed curd-chunks" when you say "cheese".* And Anaxandrides uses shameful language, recently describing a pot as: *When the continuous parts of the body are kneaded in the fire-struck earth,* as Timotheus said, when he was once again trying to describe a cooking pot. Timocles, in his *Heroes*, says: *The seated nurse of life, the enemy of hunger, the guardian of friendship, the physician of exhausted appetite.* He means a **Table**. By heaven, that is an elaborate way to speak when one could simply say "table" briefly! 

Plato <note>The comic poet, not the philosopher.</note>, in his *Adonis*, says an oracle was given to Cinyras regarding Adonis: *O Cinyras, king of the hairy-rumped Cyprian men, a son is born to you, most beautiful and marvelous of all men, but two divinities possess him:* 

<margin>20</margin>*One is driven by secret desires, the other is the driver.* He means **Aphrodite** and **Dionysus**, for both were in love with Adonis. 

And as for the **Riddle of the Sphinx**, Asclepiades in his *Tragedians* records it thus: *There is a thing on earth that is two-footed and four-footed, which has one voice, and is also three-footed; it changes its form alone of all creatures that move on the ground, through the air, or in the sea. But when it walks leaning on the most feet, then the speed of its limbs is at its weakest.* <note>The answer is "Man": a baby (crawling on four), an adult (standing on two), and an old man (using a cane as a third foot).</note>

There is also this riddle-like epigram by **Simonides**, as Chamaeleon of Heraclea says in his book *On Simonides*: *The father of the kid and the fish of the handle leaned their heads against the child of the gray one. Receiving the child of night upon their eyelids, they do not wish to nurse the ox-slaying servant of Lord Dionysus.* 

Some say this was inscribed on one of the ancient offerings at Chalcis, and that it depicted a goat and a dolphin. Others say it refers to a dolphin and a goat crafted onto the peg of a **psaltery** <term>a stringed instrument</term>. They say the "ox-slayer" and the "servant of Dionysus" is the **dithyramb** <term>a choral hymn to Dionysus</term>. 

<margin>30</margin>However, others say that in Ioulis, when an ox was being sacrificed to Dionysus, it was struck by some young men with an axe. As the festival was approaching, the axe was given to a blacksmith. Simonides, who was still young, went to the smith to fetch it. Seeing the craftsman asleep, with a bellows <note>The "father of the kid," being made of goatskin.</note> and a pair of tongs <note>The "fish of the handle," resembling a crab.</note> lying there, and their front parts resting on one another, he went back to his companions and spoke the aforementioned puzzle. For the "father of the kid" is the bellows, the "fish of the handle" is the crab-like tongs, and the "child of night" is sleep. The "ox-slaying servant of Dionysus" is the axe. 

Simonides also wrote another epigram which causes difficulty for those unfamiliar with the history: *I say that he who is unwilling to carry the prize of the cicada shall give a great dinner to the Panopid Epeius.* It is said that while he was staying in Carthaea, he was teaching the choruses. 

<margin>40</margin>The rehearsal hall was high up near the temple of Apollo, far from the sea. Everyone, including Simonides' group, had to fetch water from below where the spring was. A donkey carried the water for them, which they called **Epeius**, because of the myth that Epeius performed this task; there was an image in the temple of Apollo depicting the Trojan myth in which Epeius carries water for the sons of Atreus, as Stesichorus also says: *The daughter of Zeus took pity on him as he carried water for the kings.* 

Because of these circumstances, they say a rule was set: any member of the chorus who did not arrive at the appointed hour had to provide a <term>choenix; about a quart</term> of barley for the donkey. This is what the poet meant by: "He who does not carry the prize of the cicada" (referring to the singing), or "is unwilling to compete," shall give the "great dinner" (the measure of barley) to the "Panopid" <note>An epithet likely referring to the donkey's wide eyes or perhaps a mock-heroic title.</note> donkey. 

Similar is this by the poet Theognis: *For already a dead sea-corpse has called me home, speaking with a living mouth.* He means a **conch shell** <note>used as a trumpet or signal horn</note>. 

<margin>50</margin>Similar also is the use of words that sound like the names of men, such as: "Having taken Aristonicus <note>Meaning "Best-Victory".</note> in battle, he conquered," and the popular verse: *Before they ran down again with ten ships to a single place, where they fought with stones, but no stone could be picked up; they were dying of thirst, yet water was above their chins.* <note>This describes a battle on a stone jetty or ship, where the "water above the chin" refers to the sea surrounding them, which they cannot drink.</note>

What punishment did those in Athens undergo who could not solve a proposed riddle? Either they had to drink a cup of unmixed wine, as Clearchus stated in his second book...

# BOOK 10

### THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

**Riddles.** In the first book of his treatise *On Proverbs*, Clearchus writes as follows: "The investigation of riddles <term>grīphoi; verbal puzzles or enigmas</term> is not foreign to philosophy. The ancients used to make these a demonstration of their education, proposing them during drinking parties. They were not like the people of today, who ask each other what the best sexual position is, or which fish is the tastiest, or which is in its prime. Furthermore, they do not ask what should be eaten after the rising of the star Arcturus, the Pleiades, or the Dog Star. For such questions, the prizes for the winners are kisses—which are worthy of hatred to those with a free and refined sense—while they set a penalty for those who are defeated: to drink unmixed wine <note>Drinking wine 'unmixed' with water was considered boorish and dangerous to health by the Greeks, who usually diluted their wine.</note>, which they drink to the detriment of their health. For these things are truly close to riddles. 

<margin>
The penalty for those ignorant of riddles.
</margin>

Instead, they should propose things like this: when one person says an iambic verse, another must recite a verse from another poet expressing the same thought, or each person must recite an iambic line. In addition to this, each person must recite a metrical line of a specific length, or ones that involve observations about letters or syllables. Similarly, they might require guests to name the leaders of the Greeks who went to Troy, or the Trojan leaders. Or to name a city in Asia starting with a given letter, while the next person must name one in Europe, and the rest must alternate between Greek and foreign cities in a certain order. This was done so that their play was treated as a branch of education, and the prizes offered were a crown and words of praise, through which mutual affection is most sweetened."

These are the words of Clearchus, and the types of challenges he says should be proposed. I believe such things include reciting a verse of **Homer** starting with the letter **Alpha** and ending with the same letter. <note>Greek: α</note> For example: *Archē d' isauthen epea pteronenta prosēuda* <note>original: Ἀρχὴ δ' ἰσαυθὲν ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα — "He spoke winged words to him."</note> Or: *All' age nyn mastiga kai hēnia sigaloenta* <note>original: Ἀλλ' ἄγε νῦν μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία σιγαλόεντα — "But come now, take the whip and the shining reins."</note> Or: *Aspidas eukuklous laisēia te pteronenta* <note>original: Ἀσπίδας εὐκύκλους λαισήϊα τε πτερόεντα — "Well-rounded shields and fluttering targets."</note> And again, similarly with iambic verses: *Agathos authis legoit' an, ho pherōn tagatha* <note>original: Ἀγαθὸς αὖθις λέγοιτ' ἂν, ὁ φέρων τἀγαθά — "A good man may again be called so, if he brings good things."</note>

<columns>2</columns>
"Again, a man is good who bears his evils well."
"To our city, since I was not then about to..."
"In health that is deeply thoughtful and worthy of the enclosure."
Starting with **Eta**: "So she spoke and departed, bright-eyed Athena." <note>original: ἡ — Eta</note>
**Aphrodite.** In iambics: "Let the loyalty of your friends be well-tempered."
"May they perish from Ilium, unheeded and unseen."

blameless and strong."

"...how I have everything upright in my soul." One can also propose "sigmaless" verses <note>Verses that omit the letter 'S'.</note>, such as: "I am willing to give all, whether from home or to add more." And again, Homeric verses where the first syllable and the last syllable together reveal a name. For example: ***Ai**as d' ek Salaminos agen duo kai deka ne**as***. <note>original: Αἴας... νῆας. The first syllable 'Ai' and the last syllable 'as' spell out 'Aias', the Greek name for Ajax.</note>

"The soul in the heart of the Olympian Danaans grieves."
"He speaks according to fate, just as another would think."
"Being wretched, lest he should suffer some even greater evil."

**Apples** <note>Spells *mē-la*</note>
<columns>1</columns>

Since we have made a sufficient digression regarding riddles, we must now state what punishment those who failed to solve the proposed riddle had to endure. They had to drink **brine** <note>Salt water.</note> mixed into their own drink, and they had to finish the cup in a single breath <note>original: ἀπνευστί — apneusti</note>, as **Antiphanes** shows in *Ganymede* through these lines: "Woe is me, these complications! You ask too much. But I will tell you clearly if I know anything of the boy’s kidnapping. You must speak quickly before you are hung up! Have you proposed a **riddle** to me, master? Then, if I know anything about the boy’s kidnapping—whatever that phrase means—let someone bring a strap quickly, as if I didn't know. Then do not punish me at all. But he must carry around a cup of brine."

"I know how you must drink it: quite cold as he brings it to you." "No, but you must put your hands behind your back and drain it in one breath." After the **Deipnosophists** <term>The 'learned banqueters' of the book's title</term> had said this much about riddles, and since evening is catching up with us, let us recount what has been said. Let us postpone the discussion about **drinking cups** until tomorrow. For, according to the *Philothutēs* of **Metagenes**, I will change the subject to a new 'episode,' so that I may entertain the theater with many new side-dishes, making the discourse on drinking cups the next thing in order.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book 11 of the *Deipnosophistae*. While Book 10 concluded the discussion on riddles and excess, Book 11 shifts the focus specifically to the material culture of the banquet: the history, variety, and naming of drinking vessels. The transition is managed through a literary debate on whether the ancients used large or small cups.</meta>

# BOOK 11. ATHENAEUS THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS BOOK ELEVEN.

<margin>
On drinking vessels <term>ekpōmata; a general term for cups</term>.
</margin>

**C**ome then, "what shall be the beginning of our words," as the comic poet Cephisodorus asks, since we have gathered, Timocrates, at the appointed hour with great enthusiasm? Because of the interest in drinking vessels, Ulpian, before anyone else could speak, addressed the company as they were taking their seats. In the works of Adrastus, he notes, "the chieftains sat down again as friends." <note>original: "παρὰ μὲ τῷ Ἀδράστῳ αὖθις φίλοι καθίσαντες οἱ ἀριστεῖς"</note> Similarly, Polydotus, while performing a sacrifice, says that as he was departing he held back the victim, and having broken off a branch of foliage, he immediately set out tables of the sacrificial meats. And when Autolycus came to the "rich land of Ithaca," <note>A reference to Homer’s *Odyssey*.</note> the nurse sat him down; for while the men of that time were dining, as the poet of the *Odyssey* says, "Eurycleia placed the young child on the knees of his mother's father <note>referring to Autolycus, Odysseus's grandfather</note> as he was finishing his supper." He sat him *upon* the knees, rather than standing him by the knees. Therefore, let us not waste time, but let us now recline, so that Plutarch may pay the debt of the discourse he promised us about drinking cups, and make all our goblets full. I know that my ancestor, the poet Simonides, was the first to use the name "drinking cups" <term>potēria</term> in his iambic poems, saying: "he took the drinking cups from the table." <note>original: "ἀποτράπεζαν εἷλέ νιν ποτήρια"</note> And in the *Alcmaeonid*, the author says:

<margin>
Drinking cups <term>potēria</term>.
</margin>

"The corpse lay either on the ground or on some shield, and to these he set out branches and drinking cups and siphons <term>siphūnas; tubes for drawing wine</term>, and there he placed a mixing-bowl." These vessels were named from the act of drinking <term>posis</term>. Just as the Athenians use the term "drinking vessel" <term>ekpōma</term>, they also use the verbs "to drink a little" or "to drink wine." Aristophanes says in *The Knights*: "Gulping it down with your jaws, you blood-drinking demon." And in the same play: "Bakis has spoken much in the drinking cup." Pherecrates says in *The Tyranny*: "The mixing-bowl holds a thousand drinking cups." Anacreon said: "I have become a wine-drinker." The verb is also found in the Poet <note>Homer is traditionally referred to simply as 'the Poet'.</note>, for he spoke of "drinking wine." Sappho also said in her second book: "and many countless drinking cups with beautiful...". Alcaeus says: "drinking from cups that are being passed around." Demeter is also honored among the Achaeans as "The Cup-Bearer" in the region of Anthia, as Autocrates records in the second book of his *Achaean History*. I think it is worthwhile for you to acquire a catalog of the drinking cups with which this sideboard <term>kylikeion</term> is filled. For it is called thus: the storehouse for drinking vessels. In Aristophanes' *Farmers*, he says: "as if a cloth from the sideboard flew toward him." It is also mentioned by Alexandrides in *The Gentle Man*. Eubulus says in *Lydia*: "just as if you were giving a washing, he has smashed the cups in the sideboard." And in *The Female Psaltery-Player* he said: "he dug out the sideboards for us." In *Semele or Dionysus*: "Hermes, son of Maia, being made of stone, with the washings of those rubbed bright in the sideboard." Cratinus says in *The Younger Men*: "I have come home from the enemy with many kinsmen, clansmen, and fellow-demesmen..."

<margin>
Ancient small drinks.
</margin>

"...having barely been enrolled into the sideboard <note>This is a play on words between 'kylikeion' (sideboard) and the civic registers</note>, Zeus is still my protector of the courtyard and of the clan." But we must investigate whether the ancients drank from large drinking cups. For Dicaearchus of Messene, the pupil of Aristotle, says in his work *On Alcaeus* that they used small vessels and drank their wine quite diluted. However, Chamaeleon of Heraclea, in his book *On Drunkenness*, reminds us of the following: those who use their power and prefer this drunkenness because of their wealth—which is no surprise. For having no other pleasure more beautiful or powerful than this, they naturally flee to wine. Thus, large drinking vessels became customary among them. This is not an ancient practice, nor is it a Greek custom, but was recently invented, having been transferred from the barbarians. For those people, being deprived of education, rush toward much wine. They provide all sorts of elaborate excuses. Neither in the ancient places of Greece, nor in paintings, nor among the people of former times, will we find a large-sized cup manufactured, except for those belonging to the heroes. For the so-called *rhyton* <term>a horn-shaped vessel</term> was granted to heroes alone. There is even a certain opinion that this was established because of the sharp appearance of the divine spirits. For they believe the heroes to be harsh and striking, especially by night rather than by day. So, in order that they might appear this way not because of their character, but because of drunkenness, they depict them drinking from large vessels. And they seem to me to speak correctly who say that a large cup is a "silver well." In these matters, Chamaeleon seems to be ignorant that the ivy-wood bowl <term>kissybion</term> given to the Cyclops by Odysseus in Homer is not small. For he would not have been so overcome by drunkenness after drinking only three times, being so massive. Therefore, large cups existed even then. Unless someone blames the strength of the wine—which Homer himself described—or the Cyclops' lack of habit in drinking, since he mostly drank milk. Or perhaps the cup was of barbarian origin and was large, having been taken from the Cicones as booty. What then can we say about Nestor's cup, which a young man could scarcely lift, but "Nestor the old man raised it without effort"? Plutarch will discuss this with us, not "plowing the soil of men" <note>A poetic metaphor for tedious or earthly work</note> as the Phliasian poet Pratinas said, but...

<meta>This page continues the opening of Book 11, which investigates the history and naming of drinking vessels. Having introduced the general term for cups, the text now explores specific tribes and locations named after the 'kylix' (a shallow wine cup) and shifts into a beautiful anthology of 'sympotic' poetry—verses written to be sung at drinking parties.</meta>

# ATHENAEUS THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

<margin>The Kylikranes.</margin> "I come to speak of the cup, but I am not one of the Kylikranes." <note>This is likely a pun on the word *kylix* (cup). The speaker is playing with the name of a real tribe to make a joke about his interest in drinking vessels.</note> The comic poet Hermippus mocks them in his iambic verses, saying that the kingdom of the Kylikranes was destroyed. I have seen Heraclea, a very beautiful city. These people are Heracleots who live at the foot of Mount Oeta, as Nicander of Thyatira says; he claims they were named after a certain Kylix, a descendant of Lysis, who was one of those who campaigned with Heracles. Scythinus of Teos also mentions them in the work titled *History*, writing: "Heracles, having captured Eurytus and his sons, killed them for demanding tribute from the Euboeans; he then plundered the Kylikranes, who were living as pirates, and built the city called Trachinian Heraclea." Polemon, in the first book of his *Address to Adaeus and Antigonus*, says: "Of Heraclea under Oeta and Trachis, some of the inhabitants who arrived from Lydia with Heracles were called Kylikranes, and others Adamantes; the places where they lived are named after them. The Heracleots did not grant them citizenship, regarding them as foreign neighbors." They are called Kylikranes because they had <term>kylikes</term> <note>shallow, stemmed wine cups</note> tattooed on their shoulders. I also know that Hellanicus, in his *Names of Nations*, says that among the nomadic Libyans, there are some who possess nothing but a cup, a knife, and a water jar. He adds that they live in houses made of asphodel stalks, which are little more than small patches of shade, and they carry these houses with them wherever they go. To many...
<margin>The Kylikes. The Tomb of Cadmus.</margin> ...for the place in Illyria is famous from which the so-called Kylikes come. Near them is the monument of Cadmus and Harmonia, as Phylarchus records in the twenty-second book of his *Histories*. Polemon, in his work *On the Morychus at Syracuse*, says that at the tip of the island, near the temple of Olympia and outside the walls, there is a certain altar. From this altar, he says, sailors departing by sea take a cup <note>original: *kylika*</note> and sail out until the shield of the statue of Athena on the Acropolis becomes invisible. Then they let a ceramic cup drop into the sea, filling it with flowers, honeycombs, un-cut frankincense, and various other spices. And so I see your...
<margin>Sympotic poems.</margin> ...and the banquet itself, according to Xenophanes of Colophon, is full of every kind of joy:

> For now the floor is clean, and the hands of all, and the cups;
> one puts woven wreaths around our heads, 
> another proffers fragrant ointment in a bowl.
> The mixing-bowl <term>krater</term> stands there full of good cheer,
> and more wine is ready in the jars, which says it will never fail, 
> smelling of flowers, sweet and mild.
> In the midst, the frankincense sends up its holy scent,
> and there is water, cold and sweet and pure.
> Yellow loaves of bread are set out, and a venerable table 
> is weighed down with cheese and thick honey.
> The altar in the middle is covered all over with flowers,
> and song and celebration fill the house.
> First, cheerful men must hymn the god 
> with auspicious stories and pure words.
> After pouring a libation and praying for the power 
> to do what is right—for that is the most obvious duty—
> it is no outrage to drink as much as will allow you 
> to reach home without a guide, unless you are very old.
> Praise the man who, after drinking, reveals noble thoughts, 
> as his memory and his striving for virtue guide him.
> He does not recount the battles of Titans or Giants, 
> nor the Centaurs, those fictions of the men of old,
> in which there is nothing useful; 
> but it is always good to have a holy regard for the gods.

And the charming Anacreon says: "I do not love the man who, while drinking wine by a full mixing-bowl, speaks of strife and tearful war. Rather, I love him who, mixing the bright gifts of the Muses and Aphrodite, remembers lovely festive joy." And Ion of Chios says: "Hail to our king, our savior and father! Let the wine-pouring servants prepare our bowl with silver pitchers. Let the gold vessel containing the wine wash the floor. <note>referring to a ritual libation</note> Pouring holy libations to Heracles, the son of Alcmene, and to Procles, and starting from Zeus, let us drink. Let us play; let song go through the night; let someone dance. Lead the way in friendship with a willing heart, for a blooming maiden awaits... even if one drinks from other toasts." The so-called Seven Sages also held sympotic conversations. For "wine consoles even the despondency of old age," as Theophrastus says in his work *On Drunkenness*. Therefore, let no one of sound mind begrudge us these Dionysian chats... or the words of Alexis in *The Tarentines*, which harm no one: "I know that what is called 'living' is just a name, a pet-name for human fate, used for the sake of passing the time. For whether someone says I judge well or ill, I would not know how to say. 
<margin>For what...</margin> I have realized, upon considering it, that all human affairs are entirely mad. We who are living are always in a state of travel, as if we had arrived at a sort of festival <term>panēgyris</term> <note>a grand public festival or assembly</note> out of the darkness of death and the underworld, into this light which we see. He who laughs and drinks the most, and enjoys the favors of Aphrodite during this time granted to him, and who happens to love someone—he has celebrated the festival and goes home most happily." And as the beautiful Sappho says: "Come, Cypris <note>Aphrodite</note>, and in golden cups pour nectar delicately mixed with our festivities for these companions," 
<margin>Different drinking bouts.</margin> both mine and yours. # BOOK 11

The Athenian style of drinking is to pass the cup skillfully to the right <note>original: "epideia"—referring to the custom of passing the wine bowl in a clockwise circle</note>. The Thessalians, however, use large cups to toast whoever they wish. The Spartans each drink from their own cup, and the slave refills it as soon as they have finished drinking. Anaxandrides mentions this "drinking to the right" in his play *The Rustics* as follows: "In what manner should we drink now? Speak! In whatever way you please. Would you have us, father, drink to the right, as if one were speaking to a dying man? <note>This is a joke suggesting that 'drinking to the right' or 'passing the word' was a solemn or old-fashioned ritual</note> Oh, Apollo!" We should also mention ceramic <term>pottery</term> drinking vessels. Ctesias, in his writings on the Persians, says that whomever

<margin>Ceramics</margin>
the King wishes to dishonor, he makes them use ceramic vessels <note>In the Persian court, gold and silver were the standard; using clay was a mark of social demotion</note>. The epic poet Choerilus says:

> In my hands I hold the wealth of a cup, a broken shard,
> A shipwreck of banqueting men, such as the many 
> Winds of Lord Dionysus toss out in insolence.

But I know well that ceramic drinking vessels are often the most pleasant, such as those among us made from dust and earth. For the clay is baked after being mixed with aromatic spices.

<margin>And Rhodian pots.</margin>
Aristotle, in his work *On Drunkenness*, says that the so-called "Rhodian pots" are brought into drinking parties both for the pleasure they give and because, when they are heated, they make the wine less intoxicating. For they contain myrrh and similar substances which, when thrown into the wine and boiled, or poured into the wine, make it less heady. In another part of the work he says: "Rhodian pots are made from myrrh, rushes, saffron, balsam, spice-plant, and cinnamon all rubbed together; when the wine is poured from them, it becomes so dark that it even dampens sexual desire by constricting the breath." Because of this, we should not drink madly, looking only at the quantity of beautiful cups or the various crafts used to make them. Chrysippus, in his *Introduction to the Treatise on Goods and Evils*, says that a kind of madness affects most people, just like "wine-madness" or "quail-madness" <note>An obsession with quail-fighting, a popular pastime</note>. Some

<margin>And various types of madness.</margin>
who are "wisdom-mad" <note>original: "sophomaneis"</note> call those who love glory by that name, just as those who love women are called "woman-mad" and those who love birds are "bird-mad." These names signify the same thing, so that other obsessions are not wrongly named in this manner. For the self-lover and the glutton are also "food-mad," and the wine-lover is "wine-mad." Likewise, in similar cases, the term "madness" is not misplaced, since they err madly and wander far from the truth. But we, as was the custom among the Athenians, drink while listening to these jesters and mimes, as well as other performers. Philochorus speaks of this as follows: "At the Dionysian contests, the Athenians first go to the spectacle having breakfasted and drunk, and they watch while wearing crowns. Throughout the entire contest, wine is poured for them and treats are brought round; when the choruses enter, they are given wine to drink, and when they finish their performance and leave, they are given more." The comic poet Pherecrates also testifies that until his own time, the spectators were never left without food. Phanodemus says that at the temple of Dionysus "in the Marshes," the Athenians bring the new wine from the vats to mix it for the god and then partake of it themselves; hence Dionysus is called "of the Marshes," because the wine was mixed with water there.

<margin>Something Dionysian.</margin>
It was then that mixed wine was first drunk, which is why springs were called "Nymphs" and the "nurses of Dionysus," because water increases the volume of the wine when mixed. Delighted by this mixture, they sang to Dionysus in songs, dancing and calling him "Beautiful-Flowered," "Dithyrambus," "Bacchic," and "The Roarer."

<margin>And why Nymphs are the nurses of Dionysus.</margin>
Theophrastus, in his work *On Drunkenness*, says that the Nymphs are truly the nurses of Dionysus. For vines pour out a great deal of liquid when they are cut, and they naturally "weep." Therefore Euripides says the horse of the sun is the "fiery Bacchic friend of flowers," ripening the autumnal rows of vines, from which mortals call wine "sparkling." And Odysseus gave "honey-sweet red wine,"

<margin>"Filling one cup," etc.</margin>
and "poured twenty measures of water for it, and a sweet smell wafted from the mixing bowl" <note>A reference to the incredibly strong Maronian wine mentioned in Homer's Odyssey</note>. Timotheus, in his *Cyclops*, says: "He poured one ivy-wood cup of the dark, immortal drop, frothing with foam; and twenty measures 

<margin>The possession of many cups.</margin>
he poured in. He mixed the nymph-tears <note>water</note> with the freshly-flowing Bacchic tears <note>wine</note>." I know some men who were members of sacred clubs and were very proud of their wealth, specifically in their possession of many silver and gold cups. One of these was Pytheas the Arcadian, from Phigalia, who even as he was dying did not hesitate to instruct his kin to inscribe the following on his tomb:

> This is the monument of Pytheas, a good and temperate man,
> Who possessed a countless multitude of cups.
> Of silver, gold, and shining amber-gold,
> He acquired more than all those who came before him.

Harmodius of Lepreum records this in his work *On the Customs of Phigalia*. Xenophon, in the eighth book of the *Education of Cyrus*, writing about the Persians, says: "Indeed, they pride themselves on having as many cups as possible. Even if they are clearly obtained through injustice, they are not ashamed; for injustice and greed for gain have greatly increased among them." Oedipus also cursed his sons regarding their drinking vessels, as the author of the epic *Thebaid* says, because they set before him vessels he had forbidden. He writes:

> But the divinely-born hero, fair-haired Polynices,
> First set a beautiful table before Oedipus,
> The silver table of the god-like Cadmus; then he filled

# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

...he filled a beautiful cup with sweet wine. But when he <note>Referring to one of the sons of Oedipus, likely Polyneices or Eteocles</note> noticed his father’s precious honors <note>original: "gera"—prized possessions or heirlooms</note> set before him, a great evil fell upon his heart. At once, he called down grievous curses upon both his sons, and the Fury of the gods did not fail to notice. He prayed that they might never divide their father's wealth in friendship, but that both should always have war and strife. 

Caecilius the rhetorician, in his work *On History* regarding the "Beautiful Coast," says that Agathocles the tyrant <note>Agathocles of Syracuse (r. 317–289 BCE), who rose from being a potter to a king</note>, when showing off gold drinking cups to his companions, used to say that he had fashioned these from the profits of his pottery-making. 

And the character of Acrisius in Sophocles' play *The Larissaeans*, where he himself held games, as the tragic poet says: "A great contest for all guests is proclaimed, setting out bronze-forged cauldrons to be carried away, and hollow gold-inlaid vessels, and silver 

<margin>Grammatical cup.</margin>
drinking cups, sixty-two in number." Posidonius, in the twenty-eighth book of his *Histories*, says that Lysimachus the Babylonian invited Himerus to dinner—Himerus who had acted as tyrant not only over the Babylonians but also the Seleucians by force—and after the tables were cleared, he gave each of the three hundred guests a silver cup weighing four minas. After making a libation, he toasted them all together and allowed them to take the cups home. 

Anticleides the Athenian, in the sixteenth book of his *Returns* <note>original: "Nostoi"—a genre of literature about the return voyages of Greek heroes</note>, relates the story of the colony sent to Lesbos by the kings under Aeolus. There was an oracle that they should cast a maiden into the open sea for Poseidon while sailing across. Some say this happened near Methymna. They say one of the leaders named Enallus fell in love with her and dived into the sea, wishing to save the girl. At that time, they were both hidden by a wave and disappeared. But later, once Methymna was inhabited, Enallus reappeared and told his story: the maiden was living among the Nereids <note>sea nymphs</note>, while he himself was herding the horses of Poseidon. He said that once, when a great wave rushed in, he swam with it and came ashore holding a small, very old, round cup with badly damaged handles, which had gold letters inscribed around it—truly a divine thing—saying "To Zeus the Savior." This gold cup was so marvelous that when compared to their own gold, theirs seemed no better than bronze. 

Furthermore, there is another remarkable "lettered" cup <note>original: "grammatikon"—a cup with an inscription</note> dedicated to Artemis in Capua, Campania. It is made of silver and embossed with verses from the Homeric epics, having its letters in gold just as Nestor’s cup did. Achaeus of Eretria, in his play *Omphale*, also describes "lettered cups," making the Satyrs say: 

> "The god’s cup has been calling me for a long time, 
> Showing the letters Delta, Iota, and a third... 
> Which you have present, even if unworthy, 
> To announce your drinking face to face." 

In these lines, the letter Upsilon (U) is missing. This is because 

<margin>And to all.</margin>
all the old Greeks used the letter Omicron (O) not only for the sound it currently has, but also when it signified the diphthong (OU). Similarly, they would write the Upsilon sound simply as O when it was pronounced by itself or joined with Iota. Thus, in the passage above, the Satyrs indicated the name "Dionysou" <note>of Dionysus</note> with the last syllable carved as a single O, implying the U sound was included. 

They also used the letter "San" for Sigma in the Doric fashion. For musicians, as Aristoxenus often says, used to avoid saying the "Sigma" because of its harsh sound, which was unsuitable for the flute. They frequently preferred the "Rho" instead due to the difficulty. They also call horses branded with the letter "S" <term>samphoras</term>. Aristophanes says in *The Clouds*: "Neither myself, nor this yoke-horse, the samphoras." And Pindar says: "Before, you used to sing the long-drawn song and the counterfeit 'San' from your mouths." 

Eubulus mentions the "lettered cup," using it as a name for a poem, in his play *The Nereid*: "I hate that most wicked 'lettered cup' ... which my son went off with, having a small bowl, and many things are made 

<margin>Gyala.</margin>
similar to it." 

**Gyala.** Philitas, in his *Miscellaneous Notes*, says the Megarians call cups <term>gyalae</term>. Parthenius, the student of Dionysus, says in the first book of his *Inquiry into Historical Terms* that it is a type of cup, as Marsyas, the priest of Heracles, writes: "When the king enters the city, the attendants 

<margin>Danos.</margin>
bring a <term>gyala</term> full of wine. He takes it and performs a libation." 

**Danos.** This is also a name for a cup. Dionysius of Sinope, in his play *The Woman Who Saves*, listing the names of cups, mentions this one, saying: 

> "Of all the types of fine Thericlian cups— 
> *Gyiai*, *diktyloi*, *bikotyloi*, and the great *danos* 
> Holding a gallon, the *kymbion*, the *skyphoi*, the *rhyta*— 
> The old woman sees these drinking vessels and nothing else." 

Cleanthes the philosopher, in his work *On Figures of Speech*, says that the Thericlian cup and the "Atheniad" are named after their creators. Seleucus, saying that the *danos* is a type of drinking vessel, cites Stratis from his play *Medea*: "You know, Creon, your skull seems to be a *danos*..." Archedicus, in *The One Who Errs*, describing someone speaking about a child of the courtesans, says: "I will snatch away that fine 'Nicostratian' ball, nicknamed 'Skotodane' <note>lit. 'dark-cup' or 'cup-of-darkness'</note>, because it once brought a silver 'Deinos' <note>a large bowl</note> in the dark." "Deinos" and "Danos" were the same to them. There is also a type of dance called *danos*, as Apollophanes says in *The Torch*: "Some *danos* and this little basket here." Telisilla of Argos calls the threshing floor "beautiful"...
