# BOOK 11

...beautiful cups <note>original: "kala depa"</note>. Most properly, they call a foot-basin a *depas*, as Philetas says in his *Attic Words*.

**Depastra**. Silenus and Cleitarchus say in their *Glossaries* that these cups are named similarly to "invitation vessels" <note>original: "kletoria"</note>. Antimachus of Colophon, in the fifth book of his *Thebaid*, says: "Adrastus ordered these things to be prepared as she approached, and he poured out water and unmixed honey into a silver mixing-bowl, blending them. They quickly distributed the *depastra* <note>a type of drinking vessel or ladle</note> to the kings of the Achaeans as they entered, and they immediately poured a libation from a golden pitcher." And again: "Another shall bring a solid silver mixing-bowl, or golden *depastra* which lie in my halls." And in the following verses he says: "Both golden *depastra* and a sturdy *kelebeion* <note>another form of cup</note> full of honey, which would be more to his liking." 

**Finger-cup** <note>original: "daktyloton ekpoma"</note>. This is mentioned <margin>Finger-cup.</margin> by Ion of Chios in his play *Agamemnon*: "I brought a gift worthy of the first-fruits, a finger-cup <margin>10</margin> untouched by fire." Gelias calls it a great prize, while Casi says it is a "work of the feet." Epimeleides understands it to be a cup with handles on both sides into which one can insert the fingers. Others say it has finger-like moldings or patterns in a circle, or that it has protrusions like the glass cups from Sidon <note>A famous center for glassmaking in Phoenicia</note>, or that it is simply smooth. The phrase "untouched by fire" <note>original: "achranton pyri"</note> is a reference to the Homeric "fireless cauldron" <note>original: "apyron lebēta"</note>, meaning it was either suitable for receiving cold water or perhaps for a difficult-to-arrange cold-drinking session. Some say it refers to a horn, around the base of which the horns of oxen naturally grow. Theopompus records its construction, from which it is likely you fashioned it; and near the "place of the molopidia" is Iolcus, where games were held by Pelias. 

Didymus says it is better to read "the fragment" <note>This part of the OCR is slightly garbled; it refers to a textual variant in Homer</note> and notes that Homer says, "and for the fifth he set out a double-handled bowl, unfired by fire" <margin>Iliad 23</margin>. For it seemed to be a drinking vessel because it was a wide-mouthed, cauldron-like piece of bronze, well-suited for holding cold water. It is called "finger-cup" because the bowl has hollows around it on the inside, as if <margin>20</margin> made by fingers, or because it is gripped by the fingers of those drinking. Some call a horn an "unfired bowl" because it is not made by fire. Perhaps one could also call it a "pouring vessel" metaphorically. Philemon, in his *Attic Names* or *Glossaries*, lists it and says a finger-cup is a double-handled vessel into which one can place the fingers on each side. Others say it has finger-shaped patterns around it. 

**Elephant** <margin>Elephant.</margin>. This was the name of a certain cup, as Damoxenus says in his *The Self-Persuader*: "And if it is not enough for you that the boy has come bringing the 'elephant'—and what is more unique, by the gods?—a double-pronged *rhyton* <note>a drinking horn with two outlets</note> so large it holds three *choes* <note>approximately 9 liters or 2.4 gallons</note>." It is a work of Alcaeus, and it sits as pleasantly as if it were in a chest. <margin>Elephant.</margin> Epinicus also mentions this in *The Supposititious Women*, where I will provide evidence regarding the *rhyton*. <margin>Embasis.</margin>

**Embasis** <note>literally "an entry" or "a base"</note>. Epigenes mentions them in *The Heroine*: "Coolers, a ladle, small bowls, four *rhytons*, three *hedypotides*, all silver." Cratinus the Younger says: "Twelve *hedypotides* from Archephon."

When he was in the open sea, Oceanus, testing him, caused the goblet to be tossed by waves, appearing in various forms. Heracles was about to shoot him with an arrow, and Oceanus, being afraid, commanded him to stop.

<margin>Ethaneion.</margin>
**Ethaneion** <note>A strainer</note>. Hellanicus, in his *Egyptian History*, writes as follows: "In the houses of the Egyptians, there lies a bronze bowl <note>original: "phiale"</note> and a bronze ladle <note>original: "kyathos"</note>, and a bronze strainer." 

<margin>Hemitoos.</margin>
**Hemitoos** <note>A half-cut or half-measure cup</note>. A type of drinking vessel among the Athenians, named for its shape, as Pamphilus says in his *Glossary*. 

<margin>Thericleios.</margin>
**Thericleios** <note>The Thericlean cup</note>. This cup is deep-set around the sides, quite hollowed out, and has short handles as a drinking cup should. Perhaps Alexis, in his play *Hesione*, depicts Heracles drinking from a Thericlean cup when he says: "Becoming intoxicated with wine, he could barely move in a circle; then, taking the vessels one after another, he drained them rapidly, according to the proverb: 'Once a hide is well-filled, it is a skin-bag.'" 

<margin>Book 5.</margin>
"A well-filled man is a sack." That the Thericlean vessel is indeed a drinking cup is clearly shown by Theophrastus in his *History of Plants*. In his discussion of the terebinth tree, he says that "Thericlean cups are turned from it so perfectly that no one can distinguish them from earthenware ones." It is said that this type of vessel was first fashioned by **Thericles**, a Corinthian potter <note>Thericles was a famous craftsman from the 5th century BCE</note>, from whom it takes its name; he lived around the same time as the comic poet Aristophanes. Theopompus also mentions the cup in his *Nymphs*:

> Come here, equal child of Thericles,
> Let us give you a noble name...
> A mirror of nature or a full gift...
> I hate that old woman... why do you call me, my dearest?
> To whom shall I give this greeting? ... Among the young men, it is called a "Spark" and other such playful names. I will drink a "Friendship Cup" to your health. Drink as much as your heart desires, or mine.

This is the first entrance <note>original: "parodos"</note>. Cleanthes, in his treatise *On Metalepsis*, says: "Therefore, the inventions and all such things and the rest of the people's names, such as the Thericlean, the Deinian, the Iphicratean—these were originally named after those who discovered them." This is still evident today. If the name does not change, it would be a small matter. But as has been said, it comes from the person who happened to make them. Others, however, record that the cup was named "Thericlean" because the skins of wild beasts <note>original: "theria"</note> were embossed upon it. Pamphilus of Alexandria says it was named because Dionysus used these cups to scatter the wild beasts by pouring libations against them. Antiphanes also mentions the vessel in his *Similar People* as follows: "When they had finished dinner in silence..."

> For I want the middle...
> and of Zeus the Savior. Let the Thericlean instrument come, 
> the delicate vessel from Lesbos, full and foaming, 
> each person took it in their right hand.

And Eubulus in his *Dolon*: "No cup was ever more thirsty... for I was working it cleaner than pottery, when Thericles was young and making cups." And in *The Gluttons*: "Just now, the Thericlean cups are foaming over... polished, reflecting light, washed clean... calling upon the house of Zeus the Savior." Araros (or Eubulus) in *Lampylion* says:

> O ceramic earth, did Thericles once 
> fashion you, widening the depth of your hollow side? 
> Or did he adapt the design to the nature of women, 
> who do not enjoy drinking from small cups?

Alexis in *The Knight*: "And a certain Thericlean cup having a rim of gold around it, or some such acquired ornament." And in *The Little Knight*: "In the middle, he drained a Thericlean cup of unmixed wine, a sacrifice to the liver." Timaeus, in the twenty-eighth book of his *Histories*, calls the cup "Thericleia" writing: "A certain Polyxenus, one of those from Tauromenium who had been appointed to an embassy, returned having received other gifts from Nicodemus and a Thericlean cup." Adatus, in his work *On Arrangement*, says the Thericlean and the *karchesion* <note>a large, waisted cup with handles</note> are the same. But that they differ is clearly shown by Callixenus in his account *Of Alexandria*, stating that some people in the procession carried Thericlean cups, while others carried *karchesia*. What a *karchesion* is will be explained in what follows. There is also a "Thericlean Mixing-Bowl" <note>original: "krater"</note> mentioned by Alexis in *The Swan*: "A bright Thericlean mixing-bowl in the center..."

> It was full of white, ancient nectar, 
> foaming, which I took when it was empty, 
> rubbed it to make it shine and gave it a stable base, 
> then crowned it with fruitful branches of ivy.

Menander used the feminine form of the name in *The Possessed Girl*: "Half-drunk, holding a three-pint Thericlean cup." And Dioxippus in *The Miser*: "I have need of the great Thericlean cup, I know well, and the Rhodian ones too. For I am accustomed to drinking most pleasantly from those pointed cups." # BOOK 11

<margin>Iomos <note>likely a reference to a specific shape or name, possibly corrupted in the transcription</note>.</margin>

...on the Acropolis at Athens, he did not name it otherwise, saying that Neoptolemus dedicated "the gold Thericlean cups <note>original: "Therikleia," a famous style of pottery named after the Corinthian potter Thericles</note> carved from wood." Apollodorus of Gela, in his play *The Philadelphians* or *The Man Starving Himself to Death*, says in succession: "silverware, carpets, and those delightful, expensive Thericlean cups." Aristophanes, in his *Aiolosikon*, writes: "Therefore, because of the excellence of the Thericlean cups, my master Marteios gave me a well-rounded shield <note>original: "aspida," used here metaphorically for a large cup</note>, overflowing and luxurious, mixed in equal parts, and offered it to me, I believe, for the sake of his goodness. Then he set me free, having dipped me in the depths of love." Theophilus, in his play *Boeotia*, says: "He mixes a ceramic cup holding four kotylai <note>a kotyle was about half a pint</note>, one of the Thericlean type—how do you think it looks? Foaming beautifully!" And Autocles says: "Thus, having raised it rhythmically with the right hand to the shoulders, he drinks a toast and brings in a Thericlean cup, holding more than a kotyle, for good luck." **Idion** <note>Meaning "Unique" or "Special"</note>. In his *Bridal Songs*, it is peculiar to call the cup by this name among the prizes.

**Kados** <note>A large jar or jug, typically for wine</note>. Simmias, quoting Anacreon, says: "I had a breakfast of a small piece of thin honey-cake, but I drank off a *kadion* <note>diminutive of kados</note> of wine." In his *Grave Epigrams*, he says: "Leave for him the sacred jar of the mixing bowl... it is for the skull-cups, but let each speak of them specifically."

For you yourself say that you have arrived late from the King's banquet... <unclear>gift of drink</unclear>. Hedylus in his *Epigrams* says: "Let us drink, for we may find something new and delightful in the wine, some subtle and honeyed word. But soak me, soaking me in *kadoi* <note>jars</note>, and say, 'Play, Hedylus! I am drinking myself into the void.'" And in another: "For six nights now, Pasisocles has been at the wine, four hundred *kadoi*. Then suddenly he is gone; but over the wine I play the Sicilian way, something sweeter than honey. It is much more robust, as the grace of the wine shines so that I may write of it as a friend." Clearchus says in his *Glossaries* that the Ionians call a ceramic vessel a *kados*. Herodotus, in his third book, speaks of "a Phoenician *kados* of wine."

<margin>Kadiskos.</margin>
**Kadiskos** <note>A small jar or bucket</note>. Philemon, in the aforementioned work, says it is a type of cup. It is also the vessel in which they establish the "Ktesian Zeus" <note>Zeus of the Storeroom or Household</note>, as Anticlides writes in his *Exegesis*: "The signs of Zeus Ktesios should be established thus: one should take a new *kadiskos* with two handles, crown the handles with white wool, and hang it from the right shoulder and the forehead... and put in whatever food you find, including dried figs and 'ambrosia.' Ambrosia is pure water, oil, and a mixture of all kinds of fruits; throw these in." The comic poet Strattis also mentions the *kadiskos* in his *Limnomedusa*, saying: "Some draw from a pitcher, and others from *kadiskoi* mixed in equal parts."

<margin>Kantharos.</margin>
**Kantharos** <note>A deep drinking cup with two high vertical handles</note>. It is both a common name for a ship and for a drinking vessel. Ameipsias says in *The Cottabus Players*: "Mother, bring the vinegar-saucers and the *kantharoi*." Alexis in *The Priestess*—the speech is about someone drinking in a tavern: "Then I see Hermaiskos, and someone else shouting, draining a *kantharos*, and nearby a camel with its blankets and knapsack." Eubulus, mentioning the name frequently in his *Pamphilus*, says: "I happened to be opposite a great new tavern, and there I watched the nurse of the girl, having ordered the tavern-keeper to mix me a *chous* <note>about 3 liters</note> for an obol—as large a *kantharos* as possible."

And again: "The *kantharos* has long been empty and is drying out." And further: "At the same time, taking it, she made it vanish; imagine what a size it was!" Aristias says: "He made a very large and deep, dry *kantharos*." Xenarchus says in his *Priapus*: "Do not pour it, boy, into silver, into the deep vessel; rather, let us bring it back to the *kantharos*—pour it, by Zeus, into the *kantharos*!" <unclear>The honeyed heroine</unclear>. "But he does not even conquer the potters who make those *kantharoi*, those massive ones, but everything low and smooth, just like the cups themselves, as they are not drinking the wine." Sosicrates in *The Philadelphians*: "The breeze of the girl Keironos, with a quiet foot, gently and beautifully brought the *kantharos* to laugh with its curved waves." Phrynichus in *The Revelers*: "Then working as a potter, if he lived temperately at home, Chaerestratus would break a hundred *kantharoi* of wine a day." Nicostratus in *The Slanderer*: "Is the ship a twenty-oared one, or a 'Swan,' or a 'Kantharos'? For if I learn this, I will know why he brings these things—surely a 'Swan-Kantharos,' a mixture of both." Menander in *The Shipmaster*: "Having left the salty depths of the Aegean..." Theophilus: "To us, O Straton, how beautiful it is to see a son successful and safe. I first give you the golden *kantharos*—the ship itself." And a few lines later: "You tell me the ship is safe; I call my new ship the 'Euphranor,' built by Callicles and steered by a Thurian." Polemon, in his work *On Painters* addressed to Antigonus, says: "At Athens, in the painting of the *Wedding of Peirithous*, Hippeus depicted the wine-pourer and the cup as made of stone, with gold leaf around the rims, and the couches made of fir wood decorated on the ground with various colors, and the drinking vessels as ceramic *kantharoi*, and the lamp likewise hanging from the ceiling, with its flames turning upward." That the cup was named after a potter named Kantharos is stated by Philetaerus in his *Peleus*: "Peleus

# BOOK 11

**Karchesion** <note>a tall, slender drinking cup with a "waist" in the middle</note>. Callixenus of Rhodes, in his writings *On Alexandria*, says that it is a tall cup, moderately constricted in the middle, with handles that extend all the way down to the base. The *karchesion* is quite elongated, and perhaps it was named this because it is "stretched upwards" <note>original: "anatetastai," a play on words regarding the cup’s height</note>. The *karchesion* is a very ancient type of vessel; it is said that Zeus, after his union with Alcmene, gave it to her as a gift for their night together, as recorded by Pherecydes in his second book and by Herodorus of Heraclea. 

Asclepiades of Myrlea, however, claims it is named after certain parts of a ship’s rigging. For on a mast, the lowest part is called the "heel," which is fixed into the mast-step; the middle part is called the "neck"; and the part toward the top is the *karchesion*. This part has "ears" <note>braces or yard-arm supports</note> extending upwards on either side, and upon it sits what is called the "breastwork," which is square on all sides except for the base and the top. The top part projects slightly outward in a straight line, rising above the breastwork and tapering to a point; this is called the "distaff."

Sappho also mentions *karchesia* <note>plural of karchesion</note>: "And then for all of them they held *karchesia* and poured libations. They prayed for every blessing for the bridegroom." Sophocles, in his play *Tyro*, says: "A table was set in the middle with food and *karchesia*," claiming that serpents approached the table to partake of the food and the vessels. It was a custom among the ancients to place ceramic cups on the tables, just as Homer describes. The *karchesion* was named so because it has "roughness" or "hairy" textures, or perhaps from "thirst"; for this reason, Homer called those who are parched by thirst "karchaleoi" <note>rough or dry</note>. Charon of Lampsacus says in his *Boundaries* that among the Spartans, the very cup given to Alcmene by Zeus—when he took the form of Amphitryon—is still on display.

<margin>Kalpion.</margin>
**Kalpion** <note>a small pitcher or jug</note>. A certain Erythraean cup, as Gamelus says, and I think it is similar to the *skaphion* <note>a bowl-shaped cup</note>. 

<margin>Kylike.</margin>
**Kelebe**. Anacreon mentions this drinking vessel: "Come now, boy, bring us a *kelebe*, so I may drink a long draught <note>original: "amystin," a way of drinking without closing the eyes or taking a breath</note>. Pour in ten measures of water and five of wine." It is unclear what specific shape of cup he refers to as a *kelebe*, but it is named either from "pouring" <note>original: "cheein"</note> libations into it or from "taking" <note>original: "labein"</note> it. If it was used commonly for liquids, it may be related to the word *lebes* <note>a kettle or cauldron</note>. Silenus and Clitarchus say the Aeolians use this name for a cup. Pamphilus says the *kelebe* is the same as the cup called a "hot-drinker." 

Nicander of Colophon, in his *Glossary*, says the *kelebe* is a poetic vessel used for honey. Indeed, Antimachus of Colophon says in the fifth book of his *Thebaid*: "The heralds brought dark wine for the immortals; they used to carry it in a full skin, and a *kelebeion* <note>a variant of kelebe</note> full of honey was placed in their halls." And again: "But taking up the double-handled *kelebeion*, full of the finest honey..." And elsewhere he says: "And golden cups, and a sturdy *kelebeion* full of the finest honey." Here he clearly lists the *kelebeion* as a specific storage vessel alongside the drinking cups. Theocritus of Syracuse says in *The Sorceresses*: "Crown the *keleba* with fine crimson wool." And Euphorion: "Lest you draw water from the river with a *kelebe*." Anacreon says: "She poured honeyed wine from a ladle into a *kelebe* for her attendant." Dionysius the Lean, in his song for the *Encomium of Theodorides*, says the *kelebe* is an upright cup, somewhat like a *Thericlean* bowl.

<margin>Keras.</margin>
**Keras** <note>Horn</note>. It is said that the first people drank from the horns of oxen. This is evident from the fact that even now, when people mix water with wine, they call it "mixing" <note>original: "kerasai," which sounds like "keras" (horn)</note>. The vessel in which wine is mixed is called a *krater* because the mixing <note>original: "kyrnasthai"</note> happens in it, deriving from the word for "horn" (*keras*), as if it were a "kirater" <note>a vessel for pouring into a horn</note>. The manufacture of horn vessels continues to this day. Some call these *rhyta* <note>drinking horns often shaped like animal heads</note>. Many poets mention the ancients drinking from horns. Pindar, speaking of the Centaurs, says: "When they smelled the scent of honey-sweet wine, they pushed the white milk away from the tables with their hands, and drinking from silver horns, they became intoxicated." 

Xenophon, in the seventh book of his *Anabasis*, describing the banquet with the Thracian Seuthes, writes: "When Xenophon had finished drinking with him, everyone from Seuthes' party entered; they first greeted one another and, according to the Thracian custom, offered horns of wine." In the sixth book, speaking of the Paphlagonians, he says: "Lying on straw mats, they dined and drank from horn cups." Aeschylus, in his *Perrhaebians*, represents them using horns instead of cups in these lines: "With silver-wrought horns fitted with golden mouthpieces." Sophocles also says in *Pandora*: "And for one who drinks a full golden horn..." Hermippus says in his *Moirae*: "I know what you should do; do not give me that one now, let me drink once from the horn." 

Lycurgus the orator, in his speech against Demades, says that King Philip used to toast with a horn to those he wished to honor. Theopompus, in the second book of his *Philippics*, says that the kings of the Paionians make drinking vessels from the horns of their local oxen—which grow so large they can hold three or four *choes* <note>a chous was about 3 liters, so these horns held 9 to 12 liters!</note>—by plating the rims with silver and gold. Philoxenus of Cythera, in his...

# BOOK 11

In the work entitled *The Banquet*, it says he drank the nectar-like drink from golden <term>protomes</term> <note>original: "protomais"; ornamental busts or the foreparts of animals used as vessels</note> instead of other horns; it was exceptional and small. The Athenians also make silver horns, and I drank from them. In the Pythion <note>the Temple of Apollo</note>, among the lists of items for public sale, it is recorded as follows from a pillar dedicated on the Acropolis which lists the offerings: "horns, a silver drinking cup, and a leg-support." There is also the <term>kernos</term> <note>a complex ritual vessel</note>, a ceramic vessel having many small cups <note>original: "kotyliskoi"</note> attached to it, in which they say are placed white poppies, wheat, barley, peas, chickpeas, and lentils. Basalas says that whoever carries this in a procession <note>original: "liknophoresas"; literally "carrying the winnowing-fan"</note> tastes these items, as reported by Ammonius in his book *On Altars and Sacrifices*.

<margin>Kissybion</margin> **Kissybion**. This is a one-handled cup. Philemon and Neoptolemus of Parium, in the third book of *Glossary*, say it refers to an ivy-wood cup in the works of Euripides, specifically in *Andromeda*: "All the shepherd folk were flowing in, one carrying a cup of milk made of ivy-wood <note>original: "kissinon"</note>; a refreshment after labors, while drinking the joy." For the *kissybion*, he says, is described as a rustic bowl <note>original: "skyphos"</note>, where a wooden cup is most appropriate. Clitarchus says the Aeolians call the bowl a *kissybion*. Marsyas calls it a bowl or a wooden cup. Eumolpus says it is a "sweet cup," perhaps because it was originally constructed from ivy wood <note>original: "kissinou xylou"</note>. Nicander of Colophon, in the first book of *Aetolian History*, writes that in the sacred rites for Zeus Didymaios, libations are made using ivy leaves, which is why ancient drinking cups are called *kissybia*. Homer says: "Holding a *kissybion* of dark wine in his hands" <margin>Odyssey 9</margin>. Asclepiades of Myrlea says regarding the "Cup of Nestor" that no one in the city or of moderate means used the *kissybion*, but only swineherds, shepherds, and those in the country. Polyphemus used the *kissybion*, and in another passage, Eumaeus did as well. Callimachus seems to have erred in his use of names <margin>Odyssey 14 and 17</margin> when speaking of his own guest who was feasting with him in the city of Athens: "For he drained a Thracian draught at a single gulp, drinking unmixed wine, and was delighted with a small *kissybion*." He who uses the terms "bowl" and "kissybion" interchangeably does not preserve the accurate placement of the names. One might guess that the *kissybion* was first made by shepherds out of ivy wood. Others derive its name from "to pour" <note>original: "cheisthai"</note> or "to contain" <note>original: "chorein"</note>. [There follows an unclear etymological comparison to the hiding place of a snake and a vessel for dice]. Dionysius of Samos, in his work *On the Cyclops*, calls the Homeric *kissybion* a <term>kymbion</term> <margin>Kymbion</margin>, writing: "And Odysseus, seeing him doing these things, filled a *kymbion* with wine and gave it to him to drink."

<margin>Kiborion</margin> **Kiborion**. Hegesander of Delphi says that the poet Euphronion made a costly cup for Grytanis the Spartan, which was shaped much like a bell; having taken the *kiboria* as established shapes, he used them while drinking. Didymus says it is a type of drinking cup; they are also called *skyphia* because they narrow at the bottom like Egyptian *kiboria* <note>the seed-pods of the Egyptian water-lily</note>.

<margin>Kondy</margin> **Kondy**. An Asiatic drinking cup. Meganthes says it holds ten <term>kotylae</term> <note>about 2.7 liters</note>, and in the land of Cappadocia, the *kondy* is a golden libation bowl. Hipparchus mentions them. "Why do you pay attention to this soldier? He has no silver, nor both, I say—but either a little flask or a beloved variegated Persian cup, some double-handled things of the Persian sort—to the crows with them, you scoundrel!—and a *kondy*, and a cooler, and a *kymbion*." Nicomachus, in the first book *On Egyptian Festivals*, says: "The *kondy* is Persian; in the silver-work there is an astrological design like the cosmos, from which the gods produce wonders and the fruits of the earth." Pancrates, in the first book of the *Konchereis*: "But he, having poured a libation from a silver *kondy*, stepped out toward the foreign people."

<margin>Kononeion</margin> **Kononeion**. Histros, the follower of Callimachus, in the first book of his *History of Ptolemais* in Egypt, writes: "A pair of *Kononeian* cups, a pair of gold-inlaid Thericlean cups."

<margin>Kotylos</margin> **Kotylos**. One-handled cups are called *kotyloi*, which Alcaeus also mentions. Diodorus says in his work *On Lycophron* that this cup is common among the Sicyonians and that it resembles a deep wash-basin. It also has handles like a <term>phiale</term>. Ion of Chios mentions it, speaking of "more than a *kotylos* of wine." Hermippus, in *The Gods*, mentions the *kotylos* as the first thing brought by neighbors. Plato mentions the *kotylos* in *Zeus Ill-Treated*, and Aristophanes in *Babylonians*. Eubulus says: "And the priest, standing in their midst, wearing his fine equipment, poured out a *kotylos* of wine." Pamphilus says it is a drinking cup with a sticky coating <note>original: "glyios"</note> and that it is sacred to Dionysus. Polemon, in his work *On the Fleece of Zeus*, says: "After these things he performs the rite, and takes it from the chamber, and distributes it to those who have carried the *kernos* around; this is a ceramic vessel having many small cups <note>original: "kotyliskous"</note> attached to it. Inside them are: sage, white poppies, wheat, barley, peas, vetch, chickpeas, lentils, beans, spelt, oats, a fruit-cake <note>original: "palathion"</note>, honey, oil, wine, milk, and unwashed wool. He who carries this tastes of these things."

<margin>Kotyle</margin> **Kotyle**. Aristophanes in *Cocalus*: "Other older women use the dark wine... they would pour it into large *kotylae*... they are forced by desire for unmixed dark wine." Silenus, Clitarchus, and Zenodotus also mention it.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ancient Greek drinking vessels, transitioning from the "Keras" (horn) and "Kissybion" (ivy-cup) mentioned on the previous page to the "Kotyle" (a deep cup or measure) and its variants, followed by the "Kottabis" (vessel for the game of kottabos), the "Kratanion," and beginning the discussion of the "Kylix" (the standard shallow cup).</meta>

# ATHENAEUS: THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

"Everywhere around the corpse the blood flowed by the cupful" <note>original: "kotylēryton aima"; a phrase describing blood flowing as if poured from a cup</note>. And there is the proverb: "Many things happen between the cup and the edge of the lip." Simaristus says that the white cup is called by this name. Diodorus says that among some people, the *kotylos* <note>a variant of kotyle</note> was the name given to a variegated, wheaten vessel; he notes that it was not exactly a <term>kylix</term> <note>the standard shallow drinking cup</note> because it lacked handles, but rather resembled a deep basin or a simple drinking vessel. Diamadas says that among the Aetolians, the so-called *kotylai* of the Ionians are similar to those previously mentioned which lack handles. Crates mentions them in his *Educations*, as does Hermippus in *The Gods*. The Athenians also call a certain measure a <term>kotyle</term> <note>approximately 0.27 liters</note>. Thucydides writes: "They gave to each of them for eight months a *kotyle* of water and two *kotylas* of grain." Aristophanes in the *Proagon* says: "He who bought three <term>choenixes</term> <note>a dry measure</note> of barley-meal reckons them as three *kotylai* short when he gets home." Apollodorus describes it as a type of cup that is high and hollow. He says the ancients called everything hollow a *kotyle*, such as the hollow of the hands; hence "blood flowing by the cupful" refers to blood scooped up with both hands. A certain game is called *Enkotyla*, in which those who have been defeated hollow their hands and hold the knees of the winners, carrying them along. Diodorus, in his *Italian Dialects*, and Heracleitus (as Pamphilus says) state that the *kotyle* is called a 

<margin>Hemina.</margin>
**hemina** <note>the Roman equivalent of the kotyle measure</note>. Epicharmus mentions the *hemina* when he says: "to drink twice as much lukewarm water, two *heminas*." And Sophron says: "Turn the *hemina* over, my child." Pherecrates mentions a "little cup" <note>original: "kotyliskion"</note> in *Korianno*, but says a *kotyliskis* should never be used. Aristophanes in *The Acharnians* refers to a "little cup" with a broken rim. The term *kotyle* is also applied to the cavity of the hip-socket and the suckers on the tentacles of polyps, which leads to the derivative verb "to have suckers" <note>original: "kotylēdonisai"</note>. Aeschylus in *The Edonians* even called cymbals *kotylai*: "The bronze-bound cup <note>original: "kotylē"</note> rings out." Marsyas says that the bone in the hip is called both an *aleiphos* and a *kylix*. The "sacred little cup" <note>original: "kotyliskos"</note> of Dionysus is also called by this name, and it is used by initiates, as Nicander of Thyatira says when he cites a line from Aristophanes' *Clouds*: "nor the siphon of the little cup." Simmias, however, defines 

<margin>Kottabis.</margin>
the *kotyle* as an *aleiphos*. **Kottabis**. Armodius of Lepreum, in his work *On the Customs of Phigalia*, writes the following regarding local banquets: "After performing the sacrifices, each person drinks a small amount from a ceramic *kottabis*, and the one who serves it must maintain a ritual silence." Agesarchus, his brother, in his *Commentaries* (which begin with "In the best constitution..."), says that the game called *kottabos* was introduced to banquets by the people of Sicily, as Dicaearchus reports. There was such great enthusiasm for this practice that they brought prizes, called *kottabia*, into the banquets. These were cups specifically constructed to be most useful for the game, and they were called *kottabides*. Every arrangement in the houses was made in a circular fashion so that everyone, aiming at the center of the *kottabos* mark, might compete for victory from similar positions. For they took pride not only in hitting the target, but also in doing everything gracefully. It was necessary to lean on the left elbow and, with the right hand, flick the <term>latagus</term> <note>the drop of wine dregs</note> in a smooth, circular motion. This was the name they gave to the liquid falling out of the cup, and some people were more proud of being a "good kottabos-player" than others were of being great javelin-throwers. 

<margin>Kratanion.</margin>
**Kratanion**. Perhaps the ancients gave this name to the drinking vessel now called a *kranion*. Polemon (or whoever wrote the work entitled *Helladikos*), when speaking of the Metapontine treasury at Olympia, writes: "The temple of the Metapontines, in which there are one hundred and thirty-two silver bowls <note>original: "phialai"</note>, two silver wine-pitchers <note>original: "oinochoai"</note>, a silver sacrificial vessel, and three gilded bowls. Also the temple of the Byzantines, in which there is a Triton in white marble <note>original: "leukaneilsin"; likely referring to Parian marble</note> holding a silver *kratanion*, a silver chain, two silver *marchesia*, a silver *mylix*, a golden wine-pitcher, and two horns. In the ancient temple of Hera, there are thirty silver bowls, two silver *kratania*, a silver *kypros*, a golden sacrificial vessel, a golden krater dedicated by the Cyrenaeans, and 

<margin>Krounia.</margin>
a silver *batianeion*." **Krounia**. Epigenes in *The Tomb* mentions: "Kraters as large as tubs, which are indeed *krounia* <note>vessels associated with springs or fountains</note>." 

<margin>Kyathis.</margin>
**Kyathis**. A cup-like vessel. Sophron, in the mime entitled *The Women who say they are goddesses*, writes: "A small *kyathis* is buried beneath, containing a stretch of antidotes." 

<margin>Kylix.</margin>
**Kylix**. Pherecrates in *The Slave-Teacher* says: "And now, washing the *kylix*, I will give you a drink, placing a knee-pad over the pour-spout." These are ceramic drinking cups, and the name is derived from "to roll" <note>original: "kyliesthai"</note> on the potter’s wheel; from this comes the term *kylikographein*, meaning to speak over a cup. The Athenians also call a doctor's medicine box a *kylikis* because it is turned <note>rolled</note> on a lathe. Both Argive and Attic cups were famous. Pindar mentions the Attic ones in an ode: "O Thrasybulus, I send this lovely chariot of songs to you as an after-supper treat. May it be sweet to fellow-drinkers and a fruit of Dionysus, a sting <note>original: "kentron"</note> in Attic cups." The Argive cups seem to have a different shape than the Attic ones. They had "shaggy" rims <note>original: "phobai"</note>, as Simonides of Amorgos says. The term "shaggy-rimmed" refers to a rim that tapers to a point, like the vessels called *ambikoi*. They apply the word *phoxon* <note>peaked or warped</note> to this, just as Homer says of Thersites: "he was peaked <note>original: "phoxos"</note> of head," which means something like "tapered toward the light" when viewed. There are various types of cups...

# BOOK XI

...and in the works of our fellow-diner, Athenaeus of Naucratis <note>The author, Athenaeus, playfully refers to himself as a character in his own dialogue</note>. For there are bowl-shaped vessels made on the lathe, but finished as if by hand, having four handles and a broad, extended base. There are many potters in Naucratis, after whom the nearby gate of the Ceramicus <note>the potters' quarter in Athens</note> is called the Ceramic Gate, and they are distinguished for their work in silver-style pottery. Chian cups are also highly praised, as Hermippus mentions in *Soldiers*: "A Chian <term>kylix</term> <note>the standard shallow, two-handled drinking cup</note> hangs high on a peg." Glaucon, in his work on *Glossaries*, says that the *kotylia* are what some call "squalid" cups. Hipponax, in his *Synonyms*, writes the following list: "bowl, cup, goblet, two-eared jar, skyphos, kylix, kothon, beaker, phiale." Archaeus of Eretria, in his *Alcmaeon*, uses a derivative form of the word, calling them "small cups" (*kylychnidia*), in these lines: "But bring them here to me as quickly as you can; we must have a common mixing bowl and small cups." And Alcaeus says: "Let us drink! Why wait for the lamp? The day is but a finger's breadth. Take down the great <term>kylychnai</term> <note>a variant of the kylix</note> from the shelf. For the son of Semele and Zeus gave wine to men to make them forget their cares. Pour it out, mixing it, let the cups be full to the brim!" And in his tenth book, he mentions the "drop" <note>original: "latagon"; the last drop of wine thrown in the game of kottabos</note> falling from the cup. Pherecrates says in *Corianno*:

-> "I come from the bath-house ruined, with a parched throat; I shall relieve it by drinking. My spit is dry, by the two goddesses! If I take the cup, let it not be a small one at all, for it stirs my bile if I do not have a medicinal drink." <-

<margin>Small cups.</margin>That women used large drinking vessels is stated by Pherecrates himself in *The Tyranny*: "Then someone, having made pottery of wide-walled cups, held them; but it was just the vessel itself, not a small gift or a shell-measure, resembling beakers. They say they carried these deep cups around like merchant ships, wine-bringers, circular and thin in the middle, not simply made, but finished with splendor so that the wine might be drunk in its full breadth. Then, whenever we accuse them of drinking too much, they curse and swear they haven't drunk anything but one cup. Yet that one cup is greater than a thousand."

<margin>Kymbion.</margin>**Kymbion.** These are hollow and small drinking vessels, according to Simaristus. Dorotheus says the <term>kymbion</term> <note>literally "little boat"</note> is a type of deep cup that has neither a straight base nor handles. Ptolemy, the follower of Aristonicus, calls them "curved." Nicander of Thyatira says that Theopompus in *The Mede* used the name for a cup without handles. Philemon says in *The Ghost*: "Since the girl has prepared a *kymbion* of unmixed wine for you." Dionysius of Samos, in the sixth book of his work *On the Circle*, thinks that the *kissybion* <note>the rustic ivy-cup</note> and the *kymbion* are the same thing. He says that when Odysseus filled a *kymbion* with unmixed wine, he offered it to the Cyclops. However, the *kissybion* given to him in Homer is not small; for even a giant like the Cyclops was quickly brought down by drunkenness after drinking it. Demosthenes also mentions the *kymbion* in his speech *Against Meidias*, mentioning "silverware and boat-cups," and again in the speech *Against Euergus and Mnesibulus*. Didymus the Grammarian says it is a vessel that is oblong and narrow in shape, resembling a boat. Anaxandrides says in *The Peasants*: "Perhaps large cups were pledged to you, and with unmixed wine, these boat-cups have made your heads heavy." Alexis says in *The Knight*: "And those boat-cups with gold on their prows." Eratosthenes, in his letter to Agenor the Spartan, describes the *kymbion* as a useful ladle-like vessel, writing: "They wondered how a ladle was not used, but only a boat-cup was attached to the bowl. It seems to me that one was used for human needs and the other for the honor of the gods. They did not use ladles or small measures (*kotylai*) then; they offered silver mixing-bowls to the gods, not set with stones, but made of fine clay. Whenever they filled them with water to pour a libation, they would scoop from the mixing-bowl with the *kymbion*, just as we still do today in the <term>phiditia</term> <note>the communal mess halls of Sparta</note>." 

When Ephippus says in *The Youths*: "Chaereamon does not bring the meal in a *kylix*... Euripides has not fought with boat-cups," he is not referring to the famous tragic poet, but to someone of the same name—either a certain Philinus or someone who had an unsavory reputation, as Antiochus of Alexandria says in his work on the poets of Middle Comedy. For it was common to bring *kymbia* to feasts and to seem to fight with them. Anaxandrides also mentions him in *The Nereids*: "Give him the pitcher, fellow-reveler, and bring the boat-cup; a certain Euripides will drink today." And Ephippus says in *Those Alike*: "One would have to learn the songs of Dionysius, and what Demophon did to the small measure... and Euripides would enter bringing boat-cups." That the *kymbe* is also a boat is confirmed by Sophocles in *Andromeda*: "Whether you travel the land by horse or by boat-ships." 

<margin>Kypellon.</margin>**Kypellon.** Regarding this drinking vessel, Apollodorus of Paphos says it is the same as others, differing only in name. "Then the sons of the Achaeans pledged one another from different sides with golden cups (*kypellois*)" <note>A quotation from Homer's Iliad</note>. The shape was either identical to the *depas* <note>a large, two-handled goblet</note> or...

# ATHENAEUS: THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

...the double-goblet cup, and thus it is. It is simply curved. For the term *kypellon* <note>original: "κύπελλον"</note> comes from its curvature (*kyphotes*), or because it is similar to the *pellis* <note>a milk pail or bowl</note>, though more drawn together into a curve. The double-goblets are like those curved on both sides from the handles, because of their construction. For the Poet <note>Homer</note> says, "a golden two-handled cup." Antimachus, in the fifth book of his *Thebaid*, says: "And the heralds, attending to all the leaders, distributed beautiful golden cups well-wrought." Silenus says that *kypella* are drinking vessels similar to *skyphoi* <note>deep wine cups</note>, as does Nicander of Colophon: "The cup-bearer distributed the goblets." Eumolpus says it is a type of cup named from being curved. Simaricos, in his twentieth book, says it is a two-handled cup; for the Cyprians call the two-handled one a *kypellon*, while the Cretans use the term for a four-handled one. Philetas says that the Syracusans call the crusts of barley-cakes and bread *kypella* because of their hollowed shape.

**Kymbe.** Philemon, in his *Attic Words*, says it is a type of *kylix* <note>the standard shallow Greek wine cup</note>. Apollodorus, in his work *On Etymologies*, says the people of Gaza call a cup a *kymba*. **Kothon.** A Laconian <note>Spartan</note> drinking vessel, mentioned by Xenophon in the first book of the *Education of Cyrus*. Critias, in his *Constitution of the Lacedaemonians*, writes as follows: "Apart from these things, they wear the smallest <term>Laconian shoes</term> <note>noted for their simple, functional design</note> and Laconian cloaks, which are the most pleasant and useful to wear. The *kothon* is a Lacedaemonian drinking vessel, most useful for military service and very easy to carry

<margin>
Plutarch in the Life of Lycurgus.
</margin>
in a soldier's knapsack. The reason is that a soldier is often forced to drink water that is not clean. First, the vessel prevents the drink from being too visible <note>the dark clay hid the murkiness of the water</note>; second, because the *kothon* has an inward-curving rim (*ambon*), it catches the impurities within itself." Polemon, in his work *Against Adaeus and Antigonus*, writes that the Lacedaemonians used earthenware vessels: "But truly, this kind of simple living is archaic, and it is still practiced among some Greeks where it began, at public banquets. In Lacedaemon, during festivals—such as victory celebrations or the weddings of maidens—they drink from earthenware cups; but at other drinking parties, the ambitious drink from large jars." Archilochus also mentions it in his elegies as a common drinking vessel: "But come, go with the *kothon* through the benches of the swift ship, draw the drinks from the hollow jars. Pour the red wine from the dregs, for we shall not be able to stay sober on this watch." It is spoken of as a type of *kylix*. Aristophanes in *The Knights*: "They jumped into the horse-transports, having bought *kothons* like men; and some bought garlic and onions." Heniochus in *Gorgons*: "Someone, having grabbed a fire-colored, round, narrow-mouthed, thick-bodied *kothon*, the child of the throat." Theopompus in *Female Soldiers*: "For I would drink from a *kothon*... with its neck bent back." Alexis in *Vetches*: "Since it's a four-turn episode, give me a *kothon*. It's a greater possession than a house." This vessel is also why they call those who drink too much unmixed wine "kothonizers," as Hyperides says in his speech *Against Demosthenes*. Callixenus, in his fourth book *On Alexandria*, describing the processions of Philadelphus and listing many vessels, writes: "Two *kothons*, two cubits in diameter." Regarding the act of "kothonizing" <note>heavy drinking/carousing</note>, and why it is considered useful: Mnesitheus, the Athenian physician, says in his *Letter on Heavy Drinking*: "It happens that those who drink much unmixed wine at social gatherings are greatly harmed in both body and soul. However, to 'kothonize' <note>original: κωθωνίζεσθαι; to indulge in a heavy drinking bout</note> every few days seems to me to provide a certain cleansing for the body and a relaxation for the soul. For from our daily gatherings, some superficial residues remain. For these, the most natural channels for the body are through urination. Among cleansings, that which comes through periodic heavy drinking is most appropriate. For the body is bathed by the wines—wine being moist and hot. The urine filtered through us is consumable <note>Mnesitheus is likely referring to its use as a detergent</note>; indeed, fullers use it as a wash for cleaning clothes. Three things must be secured when one drinks heavily: do not drink bad wine, nor unmixed wine <note>wine was usually diluted with water</note>, nor engage in business during the bout. When you have had enough, do not sleep before you have vomited using more oil <note>to induce vomiting</note>. Then, after you have vomited enough, rest after walking a little. If you cannot move yourself enough, make more use of the bath; lie down in the tub in very hot water." Polemon, in his fifth book *Against Adaeus and Antigonus*, says that Dionysus Tilphos <note>a title for the god of wine</note> is depicted sitting on a rock, and to his left is a

<margin>
Labronia.
</margin>
bald satyr holding in his right hand a ribbed *kothon*. **Labronia.** A type of Persian drinking vessel, named from the "greed" or "violence" (*labrotes*) involved in drinking; it is wide in construction and large. It also has large handles. Menander in *The Fisherman*: "To be wealthy is to drink from golden cups; those Persian robes are purple, and inside there are vessels, spoils of war, and labronia cups embossed with the faces of 'goat-stags' <note>a mythical creature like a griffin</note>." In *The Lovers of Siblings*: "This pourer, these jewel-encrusted labronia—the Persians stood there holding them." Hipparchus in *Thais*: "By Heracles, this bird-shaped labronius is a cup made of two hundred pieces of gold, which he offers as a gift to his dearest." Diphilus in *Tithraustes*, listing other kinds of cups, says: "Goat-stag, saw-cup, batiake, labronios; you see no slaves here, but names of vessels for every hearth." The gold labronios

### BOOK XI

The **lepaste** <note>original: "λεπαστή", a large, often limpet-shaped drinking vessel</note> is said to be named either from the clay, like Attic vessels, or from the shape that became popular there, just as *thyrikleia* <note>a type of cup named after a potter</note> are named. Aristophanes says in *The Banqueters*: "And costly feasts and Chian wine from Laconian 
<margin>The Lepaste.</margin> cups <note>original: "κυλίκων"</note>, drinking sweetly and fondly." **The Lepaste.** Some say the name comes from the way they "lap up" <note>original: "λάψαι", meaning to gulp or lap like a dog</note> the final dregs, like wine-vats. Others say it is because they "grow large" <note>original: "παραφύουσιν"</note>. The cup was named from those who spend much on their bellies and on wastefulness, whom we call "gluttons" <note>original: "λαφύκτας"</note>; these were large cups. Aristophanes says in *Peace*: "Why then do you give the children a *lepaste* cup of wine, from which one can lap up, to drink down at once?" This is the opposite of the vessel called a *bomylios* <note>a narrow-necked bottle that gurgles when poured</note>. For he says somewhere himself: "The blood cut like a whirlwind, O Lord and Master, as if you drank me dry." And in *Gerytades*, and in *The Farmers*, he says: "The boy went around in a circle, quickly bringing us the *lepaste*." The comic poet presented the depth of the cup as being very cold and "dark-clashing" <note>original: "κυανοκτυπᾶτο", a poetic epithet usually reserved for the sea</note>.

Antiphanes in *Asclepius* says: "Turning a little from the things impossible for everyone of old with the root of the beer-drinkers <note>original: "βρυτικῶν", perhaps referring to a Thracian drink</note>, and being afraid of the sweetness of its size, he made him drink from a hollow *lepaste*." Phillyllius in *Auge*: "For all the young men were drinking together, and likewise the old women, rejoicing in large *lepaste* cups of wine." Theopompus in *Pamphile*: "A shallow basin... a very thick *lepaste* to drink down the unmixed wine of the Good Spirit <note>original: "ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος", the traditional toast at the end of a meal</note>." In *The Mede*: "As once Callistratus covered the sons of the Achaeans, why do you deceive your friends, Cyrnus, when he loved the alliance?" As if the thin lip of a vessel... gave him a *lepaste* before the cup of Lysander. Amerias says that the wine-jug is called a *lepaste*. Aristophanes and Apollodorus say it is a type of *kylix* <note>a shallow wine cup</note>. Pherecrates in *The Petal-less*: "Whichever of the spectators is thirsty, let him take a full *lepaste* and swallow it down." Nicander of Colophon says the Dolopes call the *kylix* by this name. Lycophron, in his work *On Comedy*, citing much from Pherecrates, also said the *lepaste* was a type of *kylix*. Moschus, in his *Explanation of Rhodian Words*, says they are "wide-faced," similar to the vessels called *psematides*, but flatter.

Artemidorus, the follower of Aristophanes, says it is a certain kind of cup. Apollophanes in *The Cretans*: "And a *lepaste* ever-flowing with wine gladdens through the day." Theopompus in *Pamphile*: "A very frequent *lepaste*, drink down the unmixed wine of the Good Spirit; it makes the village a spinning top." Nicander in *The Geatrians* says a cup is placed beside a barley-cake. Teleclides in *The Prytanes*: "And to draw sweet wine, sharp-breathed, from a *lepaste*." Hermippus in *The Fates*: "If I suffer anything from drinking these *lepaste* cups, I give all my money to Dionysus."

<margin>The Loibasion.</margin> **The Loibasion.** <note>A libation vessel; from "loibe," a drink offering</note> In his *Glossary*, Clearchus and Nicander the Geatrian say it is the vessel with which they pour oil upon the sacred offerings. Antimachus of Colophon mentions it along with
<margin>The Spondeion.</margin> **The Spondeion** <note>A vessel for libations, from "sponde"</note> and small libation-cups. 

<margin>The Lisbion.</margin> **The Lisbion.** Hedylus shows that this is a cup in his *Epigrams*, speaking thus: "The woman who drinks with men, a wonder to behold, Neisis, drank three *choes* <note>about 9 liters</note> at once. Beside her was the fragrant, unmixed wine, and she drained the purple *lisbion* of glass, so that she might bring you the spoils of sweet desires."

<margin>The Louterion.</margin> **The Louterion.** <note>Literally a wash-basin</note> Epigenes in *The Monument*, in his catalog of cups, says: "mixing bowls, jars, buckets, sacred ewers, wash-basins (*louteria*)." But why speak of each individually? For he sees them himself.

<margin>The Lykiourges.</margin> **The Lykiourges.** <note>Lycian-wrought</note> Some are called so from Lykon, the one who manufactured them, just as *kononioi* are named after Konon. Demosthenes mentions Lykon in his speech *On the Crown*, and in the speech *Against Timotheus* regarding an assault, saying: "two Lycian-wrought bowls" <note>original: "φιάλας λυκιεργεῖς"</note>. In the speech *Against Timotheus*, he writes: "He gave them to Phormion to store with the money, and two other Lycian-wrought bowls." Hesiod in the *Seventh Book* calls them "two Lycian-wrought javelins, double-edged," either because they are javelins suitable for hunting wolves <note>a pun on "lykos", wolf</note> or because they were worked in Lycia. Didymus the grammarian, explaining this, says they were manufactured by Lykios. This Lykios was a Boeotian by birth, from Eleutherae, the son of Myron the sculptor, as Polemon says in the first book of *The Acropolis*. But the grammarian is ignorant that one would not find such a name derived from proper names, but rather from cities or nations. For Aristophanes says in *Peace*: "The boat shall be a Naxian-wrought beetle." Critias in his *Constitution of the Lacedaemonians* mentions a "Milesian-wrought bed" and a "Chian-wrought table." Herodotus in the *Seventh Book* mentions "two Lycian-wrought javelins." Perhaps, then, in Demosthenes too one should write *lykierges*, meaning those worked in Lycia.

**The Mele.** Certain cups are called this, mentioned by Anaxippus in *The Well*: "You, Syriskos, take this *mele* and bring it to that monument, you understand, and the small bucket <note>original: "καπέκιον"</note>."

<margin>The Metaniptron.</margin> **The Metaniptron.** <note>Literally "after the washing"</note> The cup shared after dinner, once hands have been washed. Antiphanes in *The Torch*: "To gulp down the *metaniptron* of the Good Spirit." They have washed their hands. Diphilus in *Sappho*: "Archilochus, receive this *metaniptris* cup full of Zeus the Savior and the Good Spirit." Some say it is the drink taken after washing, as Seleucus says in his *Glossary*. Callias in *The Iron-Beaters*: "And receive this *metaniptris* of Health." Philetaerus in *Asclepius*: "Having poured it full of half-and-half wine, the *metaniptris*...

<margin>Manes.</margin> 
Pamphilus says it is perhaps a type of drinking vessel or a measure like a *kyathos* <note>a small ladle or measure</note>, but Diodorus renders it as a *kylix* <note>a shallow, wide-mouthed wine cup</note>. **Manes.** A type of drinking vessel. Nikon says to the cithara-player, and a certain man very opportunely drinking a toast says in a proverb: "Bring the earthenware *Manes* in abundance, holding five *kotylai* <note>roughly 1.3 liters</note>; perhaps I shall shine." Didymus and Pamphilus set out these iambic verses. It is also called a 
**manes** when it refers to the figurine placed upon the *kottabos* <note>A popular Greek game where players flicked the dregs of their wine at a target</note> stand, from which the wine-drops fell during the game. Sophocles in *Salmoneus* called this a "brazen head," saying: "And there is the tickling and the sound of kisses; for the one who plays the *kottabos* well, I set prizes of victory, even for the one who hits the brazen head." Antiphanes in *The Birth of Aphrodite* says: "I will show you the way down if you flick the *kottabos* toward the scale-pan; what then would be the underlying object, if you mean the little small plate? That is, the scale-pan, if it is at the very top. How then does it stand unsteady if it just happens to fall upon the *manes* itself? And there will be a very loud noise for the *kottabos* player." There is also a certain *manes* that is like a household servant. Hermippus in *The Fates* says: "You will see the *kottabos* rod rolling in the chaff. The *manes* hears nothing of the wine-drops anymore, and you might see the wretched 
<margin>Nesoris.</margin> 
scale-pan lying by the hinge of the garden-gate among the sweepings." **Nesoris.** Concerning the 
<margin>About the Cup of Nestor.</margin> 
<margin>Iliad, Book 11.</margin> 
form of the **Cup of Nestor**, the Poet <note>Homer</note> says:

->Next to them he placed a cup, most beautiful, which the old man brought from home,<-
->studded with golden nails; and its handles<-
->were four; and two pigeons about each<-
->were feeding, made of gold, and there were two bases below.<-
->Another man could only move it from the table with effort<-
->when it was full, but the old man Nestor lifted it with ease.<-

In these verses, it is first asked what exactly is meant by "studded with golden nails," and then why there were "four handles." For other cups, says Asclepiades of Myrlea in his treatise *On the Nesoris*, usually have two handles. And how can there be pigeons "feeding about each of the handles"? And how does he say there are "two bases" for the cup? It is specifically remarked as a point of equality that while others struggled to lift the cup, the old man Nestor lifted it without effort. Having proposed these questions, Asclepiades seeks to know where or how it was "studded with nails" through the body of the vessel. Some say that the gold was hammered onto the silver cup from the outside through the skill of the embosser's art. As it says regarding Achilles: "So he spoke in anger, and cast the scepter to the ground, 
<margin>Iliad, Book 1.</margin> 
studded with golden nails." For it appears that the nails were driven in, just as on clubs. And regarding the sword of Agamemnon:

->And about his shoulders he threw the sword, and on it the nails<-
->shone in gold; and the sheath around it was of silver.<-

Apelles the engraver, he says, shows us the placement of nails in certain Corinthian works. For they have, in a small space on the sides, elongated pieces that look like the heads of nails. To say it was "studded" might not mean by the Poet that they were added from the outside, or that they were literally driven through, but that they *resembled* driven nails, projecting slightly outward and being raised above the rest of the surface. And concerning the handles, they define it thus: that it had two handles, just like other cups; but each handle had two parts at the curve from both sides, similar to Corinthian water-jars. But Apelles says that he showed that the use of four handles was like this: they grow as if from one root where they join the base, and on each side there are two branched rods, not standing at a great distance from one another. These extend to the lip of the cup, and rising a little higher, they maintain the gap for the hand. And where they end at the lip, they are joined again. In this way, there are four handles. This style of construction is not seen on all cups, but on some, especially those called *Seleukides*. As for the question of the two bases, "there were two bases below," some resolve it this way: some cups have one base that is natural and forged with the whole cup, like the vessels called *kymbia* and *phialai* <note>shallow bowls</note>, or anything bowl-like in appearance. Others have two, like the *ooskyphia*, the *kantharia*, the *seleukides*, the *karchesia*, and those similar to *kykyioi*. One base is the one forged with the whole vessel at the curve. The second is the one added as a stand, starting from a sharp point and ending in a wider base upon which the cup stands. They say the Cup of Nestor was of this sort. It is also possible to suppose two bases in another way: one that supports the whole bulk of the cup, having a circular outline proportionate to its height; and another with a smaller circle...

### BOOK XI

...moving in a larger circle, it generally happens that the base tapers to a point at the natural bottom of the cup, so that the vessel is supported by two bottoms. It is said that Dionysius Thrax, while in Rhodes, constructed a version of the "Cup of Nestor" <note>A legendary golden cup described in the Iliad, famous for its four handles and two bottoms</note> using money contributed by his students. Promathidas of Heraclea, explaining Dionysius's design, says it is a deep cup (*skyphos*) with handles that curve outward like the prows of bireme ships. Around the handles are the doves, and two "rods" <note>original: ῥοπάλια (rhopalia)</note> lie beneath the cup, extending sideways along its length. These, he says, are what the poet calls "two bottoms." Today, one can see a cup dedicated to Artemis in the city of Capua in Campania, which they claim is the actual cup of Nestor. It is made of silver and has the Homeric verses inscribed upon it in gold letters.

But I say that there are countless things to be said about this cup. For the ancients, who first organized human diet and realized that the world is spherical—taking evidence from the visible shape of the sun and the moon—believed it right to make their food and the vessels that contain it resemble the shape of the universe. For this reason, they fashioned tables to be circular. From these, they made three-legged stands consecrated to the gods, which they called *syllaiai* <note>original: σιλλαίας</note>, appearing like stars. They even called bread *artos* <note>original: ἄρτος</note> because the circle is the most complete and perfect of shapes. Consequently, they made the cup, which receives liquid nourishment, circular in imitation of the cosmos. The cup of Nestor reveals something even more specific: it contains stars, which the poet called "studs" <note>original: ἥλους (hēloi), literally nails or rivets</note>, because stars are round like the heads of nails and appear fixed in the heavens, just as Aratos says:

> They are like silver images of the night, fixed in the heavens themselves.

The poet expressed this poetically by placing gold studs on the vessel; for by the nature of the stars and the sky, he represented their essence through color. The sky resembles silver, while the stars resemble gold because of their fiery nature. Having assumed that Nestor’s cup was decorated this way, he then moves on to the most important of the "fixed stars" by which men judge the affairs of life. I speak of the **Pleiades**. For when the poet says "two golden *peleiades* <note>doves/stars</note> were feeding around each handle," he does not mean birds, as some mistakenly suppose them to be doves. Aristotle says that a "Pleiad" is one thing and a "dove" (*peristera*) is another. The poet here calls the **Pleiades** by the name *peleiades*, which refers to both a star and a fruit. For they represent the beginning of growth and harvest for all things, as Hesiod says:

> At the rising of the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas,
> Begin the harvest, and the plowing when they set.

And Aratos says:

> Though they are small and dim, they are famous as they revolve,
> Both in the morning and evening; Zeus is the cause.
> He ordained them to signal the coming of summer,
> The beginning of winter, and the time for plowing.

Therefore, the poet appropriately carved upon the cup of the most wise Nestor the Pleiades, which signal the birth and ripening of crops. For the cup is a vessel that receives water and other nourishment. This is also why he says the "doves" (*peleiades*) bring ambrosia to Zeus:

> By that way not even winged things pass, not even the timid doves
> That bring ambrosia to Father Zeus.

We must not believe that actual doves bring ambrosia to Zeus, as many think—for that would be undignified—but rather the **Pleiades**. It is appropriate that these stars, which signal the seasons for human life, should "bring" ambrosia to Zeus; thus he uses the name *peleiades* instead of Pleiades. "By that way not even winged things pass, not even the *peleiades*." That he understood the Pleiades to be among the fixed stars is clear from how he lists them alongside others:

<margin>Iliad 18</margin>
> Therein he wrought all the constellations with which heaven is crowned,
> The Pleiades, the Hyades, and the might of Orion,
> And the Bear, which men also call the Wagon.

Many were led astray thinking the Pleiades were birds, first because of the poetic phrasing and the arrangement of letters. Secondly, they accepted "timid" <note>original: τρήρων (trērōn)</note> as an epithet only for doves, since that bird is fearful by nature. However, it is plausible to apply the epithet of "being fearful" to the Pleiades as well. For the myth says they "flee" from Orion, as their mother Pleione was pursued by him. The variation of the name, where the Pleiades are called *peleiai* or *peleiades*, is common among many poets. Moero of Byzantium <note>A female poet and scholar of the 3rd century BCE</note> was the first to correctly grasp the sense of Homer’s poems, stating in her work titled *Memory* <note>original: Μνημοσύνῃ (Mnēmosynē)</note> that it is the Pleiades who bring ambrosia to Zeus. Crates the Critic <note>Crates of Mallus, a famous grammarian</note> then usurped her opinion and put forth the argument as his own. Simonides also called the Pleiades "peleiades" in these verses:

> The son of Hermes, god of the games, gives it—the son of lovely-haired Maia.
> Atlas fathered seven daughters of violet hair, surpassing in beauty, 
> Who are called the heavenly *peleiades*.

He clearly calls the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, *peleiades*, just as Pindar does: "It is likely that Orion follows not far from the mountain Pleiades." For Orion is very close to the edge of the Pleiades, which is why the myth says they flee from Orion with their mother Pleione. They are called "mountainous"...

<meta>catchword: ...is said (γεται)</meta>

# ATHENAEUS: THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...calls the Pleiades by a name similar to "tail" <note>original: οὐρίᾳ (ouria)</note> by omitting the letter 'u,' since in that context they are part of the "tail of the Bull" <note>the constellation Taurus</note>. 

Aeschylus also more clearly greets the name through homonymy: "And those who are named the daughters of Atlas, they used to bewail the great labor of their father [carrying] the heavens and the earth, where they hold the forms of wingless doves <note>original: πελειάδες (peleiai)</note> as nightly apparitions." He called them "wingless" because of their shared name with the birds. 

The poetess Moero <note>A 3rd-century BCE poet from Byzantium</note> also spoke of this in a similar way, saying: "Great Zeus was raised in Crete, and none of the blessed gods knew of him; he grew in all his limbs. Timid doves <note>original: τρήρωνες (trerones)</note> fed him in a sacred cave, bringing him ambrosia from the streams of the Ocean. And the great god himself, always drawing nectar from a rock with his beak, would carry it to wise Zeus. And when Zeus had conquered his father, the wide-seeing Cronus, he made them immortal and settled them in the heaven. 
<margin>10</margin>
In the same way, he granted honor to the timid doves, who truly are the messengers of summer and winter." 

And Simmias, in his *Gorgo*, says: "Those doves became the swift attendants of the ether." Lamprocles the dithyrambic poet also explicitly says they are named after pigeons because of the shared name: "Those who bear the same name as the winged doves are situated in the ether." And the author of the *Astronomy* attributed to Hesiod always calls them "Pleiades," saying: "Those whom mortals call Pleiades." And again: "The wintry Pleiades are setting." And again: "Then the Pleiades are hidden." 

There is therefore nothing unbelievable in Homer having named the Pleiades "doves" according to poetic law. It has been accepted among scholars that the "doves" on the cup <note>The cup of Nestor mentioned in the Iliad</note> were Pleiades, with two placed under each of the handles—whether one wishes to imagine them as small birds or as human-like figures, but dappled with stars. As for the phrase "each of them were feeding on gold," this does not mean that each one was separate, for that would make eight in total. Rather, since each of the two handles has two
<margin>20</margin>
branches, and these are joined at the base of the last part, "each" could be said of each of the total branches of the handles. Each pair, insofar as they grow together at the end, becomes their point of origin. 

When he says, "Two doves were feeding around each [handle] made of gold, and two were under the bottoms," we should understand that there was one dove for each branch of the handles, appearing as "two" because they are naturally joined and paired. For the word "double" <note>original: δοιοὶ (doioi)</note> and "twain" signify both the number two—as in "two tripods, ten talents of gold, and two attendants"—and also that which is naturally joined or paired by number. As he says in these lines: "A double bush grew from the same spot, one of buckthorn and one of olive." 

Thus, there are four doves upon the handles; and when he adds "two doves were feeding around each made of gold, and two were under the
<margin>30</margin>
bottoms," we should not understand "two bottoms," nor should we read it with a division as Dionysius the Thrax does, but as a compound word "under-bottoms," so that we hear the total of the Pleiades. Thus, there were four on the handles and two "under-bottoms"—that is, beneath the bases—as if the cup were being held up by two doves placed under the bottom. This brings the total to six Pleiades, since that is how many are actually seen. 

Though people say there are seven, as Aratus says: "They are called seven-pathed among men, though only six are visible to the eyes. Not that a star has been lost from the heavens without a trace since we first heard of their birth, but it is commonly said so; those seven are called by that name in speech, even though only six are visible to the eyes." Therefore, the poet appropriately fashioned what is seen in the stars into the visible construction of the cup. 

However, many are convinced that the poet means something regarding Zeus <margin>Odyssey, Book 12</margin> when he says: "No birds pass by there, not even the timid doves that carry ambrosia to Father Zeus. But the smooth rock always takes one away. 
<margin>40</margin>
But the Father always sends another to make up the number." Because of the sharpness and smoothness of the "Clashing Rocks" <note>The Planctae/Symplegades from the Odyssey</note>, I say that one of the Pleiades is "taken away," but in another sense, for Zeus's sake, he preserves their number, hinting poetically that although only six Pleiades are seen, their number is not actually lost. They are called seven in both number and name. 

How, then, can they say it is inappropriate for the Pleiades to be embossed on the cup, being significant markers of the harvest? It must be said that the cup is capable of receiving both types of nourishment <note>liquid and solid</note>. For a *kykeon* <note>A restorative mixed drink of wine, meal, and cheese</note> is made in it; it is a drink that contains cheese and barley-meal in the mixture. The poet says both these things are stirred together and drunk this way: <margin>Iliad, Book 11</margin> "For them, Hecamede of the beautiful hair prepared a *kykeon*; she first set before them a table, 
beautiful with its dark-cyan base and well-polished, and upon it 
<margin>50</margin>
a bronze basket. And with the drink, an onion as a relish, and pale honey, and the grain of sacred barley-meal. Beside it, a very beautiful cup, which the old man had brought from home. In it, the woman, like the goddesses, mixed for them a drink of Pramnian wine, and over it she grated goat's cheese with a bronze grater. She sprinkled white barley-meal over it, and she told them to drink once she had prepared the *kykeon*." 

While another man would struggle to move the table when it was full, the old man Nestor could lift it without effort. We should not hear this as applying only to Machaon and Nestor, as some think when they say "the one who struggled to move it from the table," but...
<meta>catchword: ...from the table, [he]</meta>

<meta>This page continues the philological examination of Nestor’s cup from the Iliad. Having previously discussed the symbolic meaning of the doves on the handles, the text now addresses a famous "problem" in Homeric scholarship: how the elderly Nestor could easily lift a cup that other, younger heroes found heavy. It includes a famous anecdote about the critic Sosibius and King Ptolemy Philadelphus.</meta>

# BOOK XI

...from the table, believing that for Machaon, the act of "prying" <note>original: μοχλεῖν (mochlein)</note> it is indicated because he had been wounded. However, it has been determined elsewhere that according to Homer, Machaon was not wounded <note>This refers to a scholarly debate about whether Machaon was too injured to lift the cup himself</note>. He also ignores that Homer did not apply the word "another" <note>original: ἄλλος (allos)</note> solely to Machaon and Nestor. For while two people are drinking, another person may stir the mixture; for just as there were two cups, so too there were two people. It is similar to the phrase, "One was white, but the other blinded the dark one." Furthermore, the word "who" <note>original: ὃς (hos)</note> is used as a prefix, as in: "There lived Sisyphus, who was the craftiest of men." The word "someone" <note>original: τὶς (tis)</note> was elided. For the full sense is: "Anyone else would have struggled to move that table, old as he was, but the elder Nestor lifted it without toil." This suggests that while any other man could scarcely move the cup from the table, Nestor lifted it easily, without labor or hardship. 

The cup is understood to be large and its vessel heavy in weight, but Nestor, being a lover of drink, was accustomed to lifting it easily through constant habit. 

<margin>Sosibius the Solver.</margin>

Sosibius "the Solver" <note>A 3rd-century BCE scholar known for "solving" contradictions in Homer</note>, having set forth the lines: "Another old man would have moved it from the table, but the elder Nestor lifted it without toil," writes exactly the following: "The poet is being criticized because he depicts the rest of the men needing to 'pry' the cup to lift it, while Nestor alone lifts it without toil. It seemed irrational that Nestor, being advanced in age, should be introduced as stronger than Diomedes, Ajax, or even Achilles." 

Having faced these accusations, they "solve" the poet's problem by using a transposition <note>original: ἀναστροφῇ (anastrophe) — a re-ordering of words</note>. For if we take the hexameter, "Old as he was, the elder Nestor lifted it without toil," and remove the word "elder" from the middle and place it in the first line, we complete the beginning following the word "another." It would read: "Another old man would struggle to move it from the table, but Nestor lifted it without effort." Now, with the words arranged this way, Nestor appears to be the only one of the *other old men* who could lift the cup without toil. 

These things the wonderful "Solver" Sosibius proposed, not without charm. However, Ptolemy Philadelphus mocked these much-discussed and forced solutions. When Sosibius was due to receive his royal stipend, the King summoned the treasurer and ordered that if Sosibius came to demand his payment, he should be told he had already received it. 

When Sosibius arrived a little later and asked if he might have his payment in peace, the King approached and blamed the treasurer. Ptolemy himself then summoned the treasurer to his chamber along with the books containing the registers of those receiving stipends. Taking these in his hands, the King looked at them and declared that Sosibius had indeed been paid. There were names written there: **So**ter, **Sosi**genes, **Bi**on, and Apollon**ios**. Looking at these, the King said: "O wonderful Solver, if you take the '**So**' from Soter, the '**si**' from Sosigenes, the '**bi**' from Bion, and the final syllable '**os**' from Apollonios, you will find you have received your payment in full, according to your own clever methods!" Thus, Sosibius was caught by his own bitter devices, just as the wonderful Aeschylus was, by laboring over "Dionysian-less" solutions <note>A proverbial expression meaning "irrelevant" or "beside the point"</note>.

<margin>Olmos.</margin>

**Olmos.** A cup fashioned in the manner of a horn. Minucis, in the fourth book of his *Treatise on the State*, writes: "a twisted *albatan* made of a golden *olmos*." The *olmos* is a cup fashioned like a horn, about a cubit in height.

<margin>Oxybaphon.</margin>

**Oxybaphon.** Common usage gives this name to a vessel that holds vinegar <note>original: ὄξος (oxos)</note>. However, it is also the name of a drinking cup mentioned by Cratinus in *The Flask*: "How can one stop him from drinking too much? I know—I will scatter his jugs, and smash his pitchers like thunderbolts, and all the other vessels for the drinking bout; he shall not even possess a wine-filled *oxybaphon* anymore." That the *oxybaphon* is a type of small ceramic cup is clearly shown by Antiphanes in *The Mysian Girl*: "Philynus praises a large cup and disparages the small cup as cheap." When someone asks "How?", he replies: "For the thing itself is somehow attractive; this cup is worthy of the fame of Thericles. If it were a cheap piece, we would be drinking out of ceramic *oxybaphia*. May the gods give many blessings to the craftsman who made this for its symmetry and stability." 

And in the *Babylonians* of Aristophanes, we hear of the *oxybaphon* as a cup when Dionysus says he makes the Athenian demagogues pay two *oxybaphia* as a fine. We should consider it nothing other than a drinking vessel; it is also the *oxybaphon* used by those playing *kottabos* <note>A Greek drinking game where dregs of wine were thrown at a target</note> to catch the wine-drops. It would be nothing other than a shallow, wide-mouthed cup. Eubulus also mentions the *oxybaphon* as a cup in *The Mill-Woman*, describing drinking without measure: "an *oxybaphon* into the void... if the wine is pure, it makes him feel the vinegar; if it is vinegar, it makes the wine feel even stronger."

<margin>Oineskeia.</margin>

**Oineskeia.** Pamphilus says that those about to cut their hair <note>a rite of passage for young men</note> bring a large cup filled with wine to Heracles, which they call an *oineskeia*; after pouring a libation, they give it to those assembled to drink.

<margin>Onyx.</margin>

**Onyx.** Pamphilus, in his *Glossary of Attic Terms*, identifies this as a wooden Panathenaic cup. Posidonius the philosopher, in the thirty-sixth book of his *Histories*, mentions certain cups called by this name, writing: "There were also *onyx* bowls, and sets of these up to the size of two pints, and very large Panathenaic ones, some holding two gallons..."

<meta>This page continues the catalog of drinking vessels in Athenaeus’s "The Banquet of the Learned."
