# ATHENAEUS: THE DEIPNOSOPHISTAE

<margin>Prokromos.</margin>
...and very much so. **Prokromos**: a wooden mixing bowl <term>crater: a large vessel used for mixing wine and water</term> in which the Ethiki <note>A tribe in Epirus</note> mix their wine, as Pamphilus says in the third book of *Glossaries*. 

<margin>Pelike.</margin>
**Pelikai**: Callistratus, in the third book of his *Commentaries on the Thracian Women* by Cratinus, identifies this as a *kylix* <term>kylix: a broad-beamed, shallow wine cup with two handles</term>. However, Crates, in the second book of his *On the Attic Dialect*, writes as follows: "The *choes* <note>pitchers</note> were called *pelikai*." Formerly, the shape of the vessel resembled the Panathenaic jars when it was called a *pelike*, but later it took the form of an *oinochoe* <term>oinochoe: a wine jug or pitcher</term>, such as those used in the festival <note>The Anthesteria festival</note>. These were also called *olpai* and were used for pouring wine. As Ion of Chios says in *The Sons of Eurytus*: "Drawing from the casks with pitchers <note>original: ὄλπαις (olpais)</note>, you make the strong wine splash." Nowadays, such a vessel is set out in a specific ceremonial way only during the festival. For practical use, it has been reshaped to resemble a ladle <note>original: ἀρυταίνῃ (arytainē)</note>, which is what we call a *choa*. Regarding the *olpe*, Seleucus says that the Corinthians and Byzantines identify it with the *lekythos* <term>lekythos: a flask for storing oil or perfume</term>, but the Thessalians identify it with the *prochoos* <note>a small jug</note>. 

<margin>Pisa.</margin>
<margin>Pella.</margin>
Seleucus also says the Boeotians call the *kylix* a **pilichna**. Euphronius, in his *Commentaries*, identifies the **pella** as a *choa*. The **Pella** is a boat-shaped vessel with a wide base, used for milking. Homer says: "as when flies swarm in the sheepfold around the milk-pails <note>original: πέλλας (pellas)</note>." Hipponax refers to these as *pellisia*, saying: "drinking from a *pella*, for they had no *kylix*; the servant fell and broke it." I believe he is making it clear that it is primarily a vessel for milk, but they used it for drinking due to a lack of proper cups. And again: "he drank from the *pella*, and he toasted her, and she toasted him." Phoenix of Colophon, in his *Iambics*, uses the word for a bowl <note>original: φιάλης (phialēs)</note>, saying: "Thales, who was the most helpful of the astronomers... received a golden *pella* as a prize." In another passage, he mentions a silver *pella*. Cleitarchus, in his *Glossary*, says the Thessalians and Aeolians call the milking-pail a *pellikter*, but call the drinking cup a *pella*. Philitas, in his *Miscellaneous Notes*, says it is a Boeotian cup.

<margin>Pentaploa.</margin>
**Pentaploa**: Philochorus mentions this in the second book of the *Atthis*. Aristodemus, in the third book of his *Life of Pindar*, says that at the festival of the Scira, a race for young men <note>ephebes</note> is held. They run while carrying a vine branch heavy with fruit, called an *oschos*. They run from the sanctuary of Dionysus to the sanctuary of Athena Skiras, and the winner receives a cup called the **Pentaploa** <note>literally "five-fold"</note> and joins a celebratory procession with a chorus. The cup is called "five-fold" because it contains wine, honey, cheese, meal, and a little bit of oil. 

<margin>Pitachnon.</margin>
<margin>Plemochoe.</margin>
**Pitachnon**: a cup made of metal leaf <note>original: πετάλου (petalou)</note>. Aristophanes mentions it in *The Dramas*, saying "everyone's favorite *pitachnon*." **Plemochoe**: a ceramic vessel shaped like a spinning top with a steady base, which some call a *kotyliskos*, as Pamphilus says. It is used at Eleusis on the final day of the Mysteries, which is itself named "Plemochoai" after the vessel. On this day, they fill two *plemochoai* and, turning one toward the East and the other toward the West, they tip them over while reciting a mystical formula. The author of *The Peirithous*—whether it be the tyrant Critias or Euripides—mentions them: "so that we may reverently pour the *plemochoai* into the chasm of the earth."

<margin>Peisis.</margin>
<margin>Prochytes.</margin>
**Peisis**: This was a type of cup, as previously mentioned in the discussion of the *batiakes*. **Prochytes**: a type of drinking vessel, as Simaristus says in the fourth book of *Synonyms*. Ion of Chios in his *Elegies* writes: "The servants mix for us a bowl <note>crater</note> with silver *prochytai*." Philitas says it is a wooden vessel from which country folk drink. Alexander the Aetolian also mentions it. Xenophon, in the eighth book of the *Cyropaedia*, mentions certain cups called *prochoidas*, writing that it was a Persian custom not to bring *prochoidas* into symposia, evidently believing that not over-drinking would result in fewer stumbles of body and mind. But nowadays, they still practice the custom of not bringing them in, yet they drink so much that instead of the cups being carried in, the men themselves are carried out when they can no longer walk upright.

<margin>Preusias.</margin>
**Preusias**: This cup was mentioned before in the discussion of the *diorthou*. Nicander of Chalcedon, in the fourth book of his *Persian Affairs*, records that it takes its name from King **Prusias** of Bithynia, who was notorious for his luxury and effeminacy. 

<margin>Rheonta.</margin>
**Rheonta** <note>literally "flowing things"</note>: This was the name of certain cups. Deudiamas mentions them in his *Hermes*, saying: "ten silver bowls <note>craters</note>, and two of gold, and another golden *rheontas*." 

<margin>Rhysis.</margin>
<margin>Rhodias.</margin>
**Rhysis**: a golden vial <note>phiale</note>, according to Theodorus. Cratinus, in *The Laws*, mentions a silver *rhysis*. **Rhodias**: Diphilus mentions it in *The Wall-Breaker*. Callimachus also mentions it in his *Epigrams*, saying: "He drank from either a Rhodian cup or a *rhyton*." 

<margin>Rhyton.</margin>
Dioxippus mentions it in *The Miser*, and Aristotle in his work *On Drunkenness*. Lynceus of Samos, in his *Letters*, says the **rhyton** <term>rhyton: a horn-shaped vessel, often ending in an animal head</term> is short and pointed. Demosthenes mentions *kymbia* and *phialai* in his speech *Against Meidias*. Diphilus says in *The Soldier*: "He drinks from either a Rhodian cup or a *rhyton*." Epinicus says in *The Supposititious Women*: "The greatest *rhyta* in existence... have come to us today."

# BOOK 11

...of those living on couches <note>original: ἐκλινοβίων (eklinobiōn)</note>, and "streaming-juice" <note>original: Κρουνοζόμηνον (Krounozomēnon)</note>; I consider both names to be omens. It is possible for an elephant—I mean to buy ivory <note>The author puns on "elephas," which can mean both the animal and the ivory material</note>—in the Chorokota to buy two *choas* <term>choas: a liquid measure, roughly 3 liters</term>, from which an elephant drank. I myself, drinking often, have never drunk from an ivory vessel, for you are no different. Another vessel is the **Trireme**, named after the ship in that region. He says that the Bellerophon in the poem is named from the rudder, having killed the fire-breathing Chimera. Take it and drink!

### THE RHYTON
The **Rhyton** <term>rhyton: a drinking horn, often ending in an animal's head, with a hole at the bottom for a steady stream</term> was formerly called a "horn" <note>original: κέρας (keras)</note>. It seems to have been first crafted under King Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II, who ruled Egypt in the 3rd century BCE</note> to be carried by the statues of Arsinoe <note>Arsinoe II, his deified wife-sister</note>. In her left hand, she carries this creation, which is full of all the seasonal fruits; the craftsmen intended to show that this horn is even more fertile than the horn of Amaltheia <note>The mythological "cornucopia" or horn of plenty</note>. Theocles mentions it in his *Ithyphalloi* as follows: "For today we craftsmen have all sacrificed offerings of salvation, with whom he drank, toasting the horn to our dearest King." 

Dionysius of Sinope, in his *The Woman Being Saved*, provides a certain catalog of cups and mentions the rhyton, as I said before. Hedylus <note>OCR reads "Eidolos"</note>, in his *Epigrams*, mentions the rhyton constructed by Ctesibius the engineer <note>A famous Alexandrian inventor known for hydraulics and pneumatics</note>, saying: "Come, drinkers of unmixed wine, to this temple of the friendly Zephyritis <note>An epithet for Arsinoe</note>; here is the rhyton that sounds a shrill trumpet blast when the fountain's flow is tilted. Like the roar of a Nile-born lord, it finds a melody for the initiated from its divine waters. But come, drink from this wise invention of Ctesibius, and give honor to the victory in the shrine of Arsinoe."

Theophrastus, in the first book of his *Laws*, mentions its sale. Dorotheus of Sidon says that rhytons are similar to horns, but are pierced through so that men drink from the bottom as the liquid flows out in thin streams <note>original: κρουνιζόντων (krounizontōn)</note>; they are named from this "flowing" <note>original: ῥύσεως (rhyseōs)</note>.

<margin>Sannakra.</margin>
**Sannakra**. Crates, in the fifth book of *The Attic Dialect*, says this is the name for a drinking cup, and that it is Persian. Philemon, in *The Widow*, mentions "Batiaka" cups and plays with the silliness of the names, saying: "Sannakra, horse-goat-stags <note>original: ἱπποτραγέλαφοι (hippotragelaphoi), a mythical hybrid animal often depicted on Persian vessels</note>, Batyakia, Sannakia."

<margin>Seleukis.</margin>
**Seleukis**. This cup receives its name from King Seleucus, as previously mentioned based on the history by Apollodorus of Athens. Polemon, in the first book of *To Adaeus*, says there are cups called "Apollosian," "Seleukis," "Rhodian," and "Antigonis." There is also the **Kallion**, a small cup <note>original: λυλίκιον (lylikion) - possibly a corruption of kylikion</note> used by the Aeolians when they are being wanton, as Philetas says in his *Miscellany*.

<margin>Skyphos.</margin>
**Skyphos**. Some people pronounce this with a "u" sound <note>Athenaeus is discussing the spelling "skyphos" vs. "skypphos"</note>, but we will treat the masculine form **Skyphos** as being like *lychnos* (lamp). When it is used in the neuter form, **to skyphos**, we decline it like *teichos* (wall) or *tachos* (speed). Attic writers use the nominative in both the masculine and neuter. 

Hesiod, in the second book of the *Melampodia*, calls it a *skypphos* with a double "p": "And to him the messenger god Mars came through the house, and shaking it, he brought the silver *skypphos* and gave it to the king." And again: "And then the prophet took it in his hands... Iphiclus climbed upon the backs of the cattle, holding a *skypphos* in one hand, and in the other raising a staff." Similarly, Anaximander in his *Heroic Genealogies* says: "Amphitryon, having distributed the spoils to the allies, kept the *skypphos* which he had chosen for himself." And again: "Poseidon gives the *skypphos* to his own son Teleboas, and Teleboas gives it to Pterelaus; having taken it, he sailed away." 

Anacreon also says: "And I, holding the *skypphos*, drank it all down to the white-crested middle," using the word for "drinking a toast" <note>original: προέπινον (proepinon)</note>. For the essence of "toasting" <note>original: προπίνειν (propinein)</note> is to give the drink to another after oneself. Dionysius says that in Homer, Arete <margin>Odyssey 15</margin> "placed a two-handled cup <note>original: δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον (depas amphikypellon)</note> in his hands." And in the Iliad <margin>Iliad 9</margin>: "Filling a cup of wine, he pledged it to Achilles." <margin>Toasting.</margin> For they used to toast one another while filling the cups and addressing them. 

Panyasis, in the first book of the *Heracleia*, says: "Having mixed a great, shining golden crater, we took up frequent *skyphoi*, drinking the sweet drink." Euripides used the masculine form in his *Eurystheus*: "There was no wine in the *skyphos*." Forming the word uniquely from *skyphos*, he also used it in the neuter, as did Epicharmus in *The Cyclops*: "Bring it and pour into the *skyphos*." And Alexis in *The Woman from Leucadia*: "Wine to the aged lips of the great *skyphos*." Epigenes in *Bacchia*: "You were happy receiving the *skyphos*." Phadimus in the first book of the *Heracleia*: "A wooden *skyphos* broad with honey-sweet drink." 

In Homer, Aristophanes of Byzantium <note>The famous librarian and grammarian</note> writes: "Having filled it, he then gave him the *skyphos* from which he himself drank." But Aristarchus <note>Aristophanes' successor</note> writes it as *skyphon* (masculine). Asclepiades of Myrlea, in his work *On the Cup of Nestor*, says that no one in the city or of the middle class used the *skyphos* or the *kissybion* (ivy-wood cup); rather, they were used by swineherds and shepherds and those in the fields, such as Eumaeus, who "filling it, gave the *skyphos* from which he drank, full of wine." 

Alcman also says: "Often on the mountain peaks, when the gods are pleased by the torch-lit festival, you held a golden vessel, a great *skyphos*, such as shepherd men have, and with your hands you milked a lioness and made a great, unbroken cheese." Aeschylus, in the *Perrhaebians*, says: "Where are my many gifts and first-fruits? Where are the gold-wrought and silver *skyphomata* <note>cups in the style of a skyphos</note>?" Stesichorus calls the drinking cup given to Pholus the Centaur a *skyphion depas*, perhaps meaning it was "skyphos-shaped." Regarding Heracles, he says: "Taking the *skyphion*, a measured cup about the size of three flagons <margin>Lagynos.</margin>, he drank it off after Pholus had mixed it and set it before him." Archippus, in *Amphitryon*, uses the neuter form. They say the **Lagynos** <term>lagynos: a flagon or decanter with a long neck and bulging body</term> is a standard name among the Greeks, like the *choas* or *kotyle*, and it holds twelve Attic *kotylai* <term>kotyle: roughly a half-pint</term>...

# BOOK 11

...He said that these three measures are the standard for the **flask** <term>lagynos: a long-necked wine flask with a swollen body</term>. Nikostratos, in his play *Hecate*, uses the word *lagynos* in the masculine: "or a flask marked for us, of what size." It is also used in the masculine in the play titled *The Couch*: "and this difficult flask smells nearby." Diphilus likewise, in *The Rejuvenated*, says: "having an empty flask in his hands, like a bag or a middle lamp." Samius, in his letter *How to Describe*, writes: "During the time you were staying in Samos, I knew you often attended our drinking parties, in which a flask is placed for each man to serve everyone with pleasure, giving each a cup." 

Aristotle, in his *Constitution of the Thessalians*, says that the *lagynos* is called in the feminine by the Thessalians. And Rhianus the epic poet says in his epigrams: "Half of every *kopis* <note>original: κωπιτίδος; a measure or a type of cleaver/cup</note>, and half of the wine of Archinus; but the flask holds it." And Lipoteres says: "I know the meat of a kid, he who sent Aeneas in the clay, Hippocrates, who is worth everything."

Diphilus uses the word in the neuter in *The Brothers*, as in "that lucky-souled <margin>τ</margin> little flask" <note>original: λαγύνιον (lagynion), the diminutive form</note>, "which I carry under my arm to the tastings, and sell wine until the collection is over." One remaining woman, a tavern-keeper, was pleased by the wine-sellers. Regarding the term *gauonidi* used by Stratis, there is an ambiguity in the other tongue as to whether it refers to a *lagynos*. 

Eratosthenes says that a certain flat Samian vessel is mentioned, and that the **skyphos** <term>skyphos: a deep, two-handled wine cup with a flat base</term> was named after the *skaphis* <note>original: σκαφίδος (skaphidos), a small boat or tub</note>, being similarly a round wooden vessel for receiving milk and <margin>receiving whey</margin> whey, as is also said in Homer: "and all the vessels swam with whey, the milk-pails and the bowls, well-wrought, into which he milked." <note>original: Γαυλοί τε σκαφίδες τε (Gauloi te skaphides te). Homer, Odyssey 9.222</note> Unless the *skyphos* is named after the Scythians <note>original: Σκύθας (Skythas)</note> because of the custom of drinking in the Scythian manner <note>The Greeks believed Scythians drank their wine "neat" or undiluted, which they considered barbaric</note>. Hieronymus of Rhodes, in his work *On Drunkenness*, says that "to Scythianize" <note>original: σκυθίσαι (skythisai)</note> means to drink deep, for it is related to the love of wine. 

Later, they crafted ceramic and silver *skyphoi*, for which the Boeotians were the first to become <margin>Boeotian Skyphoi</margin> famous, those called "Heracleotic" because Heracles used them first on his campaigns; for this reason, they are called Heracleotic by some. They have a certain difference in their handles, for they have what is called the "Heraclean knot" upon them. Bacchylides mentions these Boeotian cups in these lines where he addresses the Dioscuri <note>Castor and Pollux</note>, inviting them to a feast: "No golden vessels are here, nor purple rugs, but a kindly spirit, a sweet muse, and pleasant wine in Boeotian **skyphoi**." After the Boeotian ones, those called Rhodian and the Syracusan ones are distinct. 

The *skyphos* is called a *lyrtos* by the people of Epirus, as Seleucus says. <margin>Scythian/Engraved</margin> By the Methymnaeans, it is called a *skythos*, according to Parmenon in his work *On Dialects*. Derkylidas the Spartan was also called "Skyphos," as Ephorus says in his eighteenth book: "The Lacedaemonians sent Derkylidas to Asia instead of Thimbron, hearing that the barbarians in Asia were accustomed to doing everything with deceit and guile; therefore they sent Derkylidas, thinking he was least likely to be deceived. For he had nothing of the typical Spartan character, nor was he simple, but had much of the cunning and the beastly; for which reason the Lacedaemonians addressed him as 'Skyphos' <note>This implies he was 'deep' or 'crafty' like the cup</note>." 

**Tabaitai.** <margin>Tabaitai</margin> Amipsas, in the first book of his *Stations of Asia*, discussing the place where "air-honey" <note>original: ἀερομέλιτος (aeromelitos), likely manna or honeydew</note> is found, writes: "Nursing it with leaves, they put it together, molding it into the shape of a Syrian fruit-cake. Others make spheres, which, when they are about to consume them, they break into wooden cups they call *tabaitai*, pre-soak them, and after straining, they drink it; and it is like drinking honey and wine, or even more so."

**Tragelaphos.** <margin>Tragelaphos</margin> Certain cups are called this <note>literally "goat-deer," a mythical creature</note>, which Alexis mentions in *The Whitewasher*: "shallow bowls, phialae, *tragelaphoi*, cups." Eubulus in *The Glued-Together* says: "but there are five phialae, two *tragelaphoi*." Menander in *The Fisherman* says: "Labronian *tragelaphoi*." Antiphanes in *The Gold Coin*: "They say to the bridegroom: talents of property, slaves, stewards, teams, camels, bedding, silver plate, phialae, *kynides*, *tragelaphoi*, *karchesia*, *gauloi*, all-gold, ships." These vessels which some call *gauloi*, everyone addresses as such.

**Trireme.** <margin>Trireme</margin> That the *trireme* <note>original: Τριήρης (Triērēs)</note> is also a type of drinking cup; for Epinicus in *The Supposititious Women* has shown this, where the evidence was previously cited.

**Hysiakon.** <margin>Hysiakon</margin> A kind of cup; Rhinthon in *Herakles* says: "and with a *hysiakon* you gulped down pure flour-cakes and pure unbaked groats."

**Phiale.** <margin>Phiale</margin> When Homer speaks of a "double-handled" <note>original: ἀμφίθετον (amphitheton)</note> **phiale** <term>phiale: a broad, shallow bowl for drinking or libations, often without handles</term> <margin>Double-handled</margin> that is "unfired," he placed both a golden *phiale* or a double-layered one, he means the cup, but something made of bronze and thin-plated, perhaps having two ears on both sides. But Parthenius, the student of Dionysius, understands "double-handled" to mean a *phiale* without a base. Apollodorus of Athens, in his work *On the Bowl*, says it is one that cannot be set down on its base or rested, but only on its mouth. Some say that in the same way a jar is called *amphiphoreus* because it can be carried by handles on both sides, so too is the "double-handled" *phiale*. But Aristarchus says it is one that can be set down on both sides, both on its base and on its mouth. Dionysius Thrax says it is round and double-handled, being circular in shape. Asclepiades of Myrlea says that the *phiale* is named by letter-permutation as *piale*, or as having enough (*halis*) to drink (*piein*), for it is larger than a regular cup. The "double-handled" and "unfired" one is "cold-edged," or not placed over a fire, just as the poet calls one cauldron "fire-trodden" and another "unfired": "And he set out an unfired cauldron, worth an ox, patterned with flowers."

...perhaps containing cold water, so that even the **bowl** <term>phiale: a shallow, broad drinking vessel, often with a central boss</term> is made of bronze, resembling a leaf split in two to hold cold water. Some call it "placed on both sides" <note>original: ἀμφίθετον (amphithetos)</note>, whether because it has two bases, or because it is thought to be used from either side. Some say the word "ambiguous" <note>original: ἀμφισήμαινε (amphisēmaine)</note> refers to what is desired, and he called it circular, so that it is said to be "circularly decorated" <note>original: περιφερῶς πεποικιλμένην</note>. It is called "placed on both sides" because "to decorate" <note>original: ποικίλαι</note> was a term used by all the ancients. It can also be placed on its rim, its bottom, or its mouth; such a placement of bowls is Ionian. Indeed, even now, the people of Marseille <note>original: μασσαλιῶται (Massaliotes)</note> place their bowls face down in this ancient manner. Cratinus, having spoken of this, says they will dip "bath-bossed" bowls <note>original: βαλανειομφάλους (balaneiomphalos)</note>. Eratosthenes, in the eleventh book of *On Comedy*, says that Lycophron was ignorant of this term. For the bosses <note>original: ὀμφαλοί (omphaloi); the central raised knob of a phiale</note> of the bowls and the domes <note>original: θόλοι (tholoi)</note> of the bathhouses are very similar, and they play on the appearance not without rhythm. Apion and Herodorus say they are a specific type of bowl whose boss is similar...

<margin>10</margin> Asclepiades of Myrlea says regarding the "bath-bossed" bowls in Cratinus that their bosses and the domes of the baths are alike. Didymus, saying the same things, cites Lycophron, [explaining] how they relate to the bosses in the women's tubs <note>original: πυελοῖς (pyelois)</note>, from which they are scooped up with small ladles. Timarchus, in the fourth book of his work on Eratosthenes, asks if the term was used playfully there, because the ceilings of the baths in Aegina, being circular in construction, have their outlets in the center, upon <margin>15</margin> which a bronze boss is placed. Ion, in his play *Omphale*, says: "Then bring out the Pythian cups and the middle-bossed ones." Thus, for the "bath-bossed" ones mentioned by Cratinus, call them "bath-bossed bowls." Theopompus said in other works: "taking a full golden middle-bossed bowl." Teleses used to call unmixed wine "unmixed," as if Teleses had spoken of the unmixed wine of the bowls. Pherecrates, or whoever wrote the *Persians* attributed to him, says: "And a crown for all, gold cups with bosses." The Athenians call the silver <margin>20</margin> bowls *argyrides* and the golden ones *chrysides*. Regarding the silver bowl, Pherecrates in *The Little Dogs* mentions it thus: "Hey you, where are those silver bowls <note>original: ἀργυρίδια (argyridia)</note> you are carrying?" Concerning the gold bowl, Cratinus in *The Laws* wrote: "giving them to drink from a pure gold bowl <note>original: χρυσίδι (chrysidi)</note> like snakes." Hermippus in *The Porters* says: "Having drunk all the wine from the gold bowl, he stole it." And even I, the substitute Ptolemy, the king's son, having taken a fourth gold bowl of unmixed wine from my sister's portion, [said]: "Having drunk this from the king's [cup], so that again I might [drink] it most pleasantly mixed half-and-half; and for the sake of Harmony, why should I not revel now without a lamp, for it desires such <margin>25</margin> light." Herodotus, in the fifth book of his *Histories*, says that the people of Argos and Aegina made a law not to bring anything Attic to the sacrifices, not even pottery, but that for the future it should be the custom there to drink from local gold bowls. And Meleager the Cynic, in his *Symposium*, writes: "And he gave him a heavy toast from deep Lydian gold bowls."

<margin>Psykter.</margin> **The Psykter (Wine-Cooler).** Plato, in the *Symposium*, says: "But, boy, bring that **wine-cooler** <term>psykter: a vessel used for cooling wine, often placed inside a larger krater filled with snow or cold water</term>," seeing that it held more than eight *kotylai* <note>about 2 liters</note>; "so having filled it, <margin>30</margin> he first drank it himself, then ordered [the boy] to pour for Socrates." Archibulus, while pouring most opportunely, [says]: "the boy, pouring the wine, overturns the wine-cooler." Alexis, in *The Settler*, says: "coolers before the cup." Dionysius, in *The Miser*, says: "from Olympichus he received two very sharp wine-coolers in the Thericlean style." Menander, in the play entitled *The Bronze Vessels*, says: "for the current custom is to give the large wine-cooler of unmixed wine; whoever toasted them, they perished miserably." Epigenes, <margin>35</margin> in *The Heroine*, listing many cups, also mentions the "cooler" <note>original: ψυγεῖος (psygeios)</note> thus: "Give me the Thericlean cup, or bring the Rhodian ones; taking the girls, you alone shall bring in the wine-cooler, the ladle, and the small bowls." Stratis, in *The Psychastae*, says: "one stole a wine-cooler, another a bronze ladle, and being at a loss, he searches for a small cup among the palms." Alexis, in *The Little Horse*, calls it a "little wine-cooler" <note>original: ψυκτηρίδιον (psykteridion)</note> in these lines: "going away to the guest at the lodging, <margin>40</margin> the parched man said to the boys: 'For I brought two drinking vessels from home, worth two obols.'" Philippides says it is "thinner." Heracleon of Ephesus says: "what we call 'coolers' <note>original: ψυγεῖα (psygeia)</note>, some name 'cooling-vessels' <note>original: ψυκτηρεῖα (psyktereia)</note>." The Attic writers of comedy call them "coolers," regarding the other as a foreign name. Euphorion, in *The Toadeaters*, whenever he calls the wine-cooler a *psygeion*, [asks]: "the little pillar or the ladle, the lentil-soup or the lentil-pot, what are we to do?" For we said well, as if paying back a voice of gold to Pyrgothemis the money-changer. Antiphanes, in *The Knights*, [says]: <margin>45</margin> "How then do we live? The little chest is our bedding, the beautiful hat is a beautiful wine-cooler; why do you want everything to be a 'Horn of Amaltheia'?" In his *Carna*, it is clearly shown that they used this vessel for pouring wine. For having mentioned a tripod and having set a jar beside it, he makes him say in the following lines: "When will the wine-cooler be stronger?" Therefore, if anyone should speak, he will not press, to ladle wine from the jar, and taking the cup, carry away everything else. Dionysius, the son of Tryphon, in his <margin>50</margin> *On Names*, says the ancients called wine "coolers." Nicander of Thyatira says that wine-coolers are also called the shady vessels dedicated to the gods, in which one can cool oneself. Aeschylus, in *The Youths*, says: "lizards lurking in the wine-coolers." Euripides, in *Phaethon*: "Inlaid wine-coolers." It is mentioned in Philemon's *The Women of Olpai*. And the author of the *Aigimios*, whether it is Hesiod or Cercops the Milesian, [says]...

# ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED
### BOOK 11

<margin>Cooler</margin>
...where my cooler <note>original: ψυκτῆριον (psykterion); a vessel for cooling wine</note> will one day be, O leader of the people. **Oiblos**. This was the name of a cup, as Tryphon says in his *Treatise on Names*; it was the name given to the cup used when singing a drinking song <note>original: σκόλιον (skolion); a song sung by guests at a banquet</note>, as Antiphanes shows in *The Doubles*:
> "What then should happen to the gods," he said, "if one does not mix the drinks? Take the **song-cup** <note>original: ὠδὴν (oden); a pun on 'oiblos' and 'ode' (song)</note>, and then do not offer him any of those old-fashioned tunes, neither the *Telamon* nor the *Paean* nor the *Harmodius*." <note>These were famous traditional Greek drinking songs.</note>

<margin>Hyoskyphion</margin>
**Hyoskyphia**. Regarding the shape of these cups, Asclepiades of Myrlea, in his work *On the Cup of Nestor*, says that it has two bases: one which is forged together with the body of the cup itself, and another added base which begins as a sharp point and ends in a wider flat part, upon which the cup stands.

<margin>Egg</margin>
**Oon** <note>literally "The Egg"</note>. Dinon, in the third book of his *Persian History*, says the following: "There is the *potibazis* <note>a Persian bread</note>, made of barley and wheat, and a cypress wreath; and wine mixed in a **golden egg**, from which the King himself drinks." After saying these things, Plutarch <note>a character in the dialogue, not the famous biographer</note>, having been applauded by everyone, asked for a bowl <note>phiale</note>. Having made a libation from it to the Muses and their mother Mnemosyne <note>Memory</note>, he drank a toast of friendship to everyone, quoting the passage: "As when one takes from a wealthy hand a cup foaming within with the dew of the vine, and toasts a young son-in-law..." <note>A quotation from Pindar’s seventh Olympian Ode.</note>

<margin>Drinking in a circle</margin>
...but he also gave it to all his dearest friends, and ordered the servant to pass the drink around in a circle <note>original: περισοβήσην κύκλῳ (perisobesen kyklo)</note>, saying: "That which we set aside." From Menander’s *The Woman from Perinthos*: "The old woman did not leave a single cup alone, but drinks the one going around the circle." And again: "Let the unmixed wine be passed around to them quickly." And Euripides says in *The Cretan Women*: "Farewell to the rest, as the cup creeps in a circle."

<margin>Cup</margin>
<margin>To 'Crater-ize'</margin>
When Leonidas the Grammarian asked for a larger cup and said, "Let us 'crater-ize' <note>original: κρατηρίζωμεν (kraterizomen); to drink from the large mixing bowl (crater) rather than small cups</note>, my friends." Dysanias of Cyrene says that Herodorus told these things to those people, since after they had finished dinner, they turned to the mixing bowls, to festivities, and to songs of praise. And the author of the mimes, whom they say the wise Plato always had at hand <note>original: διὰ χειρὸς ἔχειν (dia cheiros echein); a reference to the tradition that Plato slept with the mimes of Sophron under his pillow</note>, says: "If we should happen to have drunk from a full mixing bowl..." But Pontianus asked, "How did Dionysius say he drank from a large cup, or a 'drinking-bowl' <note>original: ποθίσου (pothisou)</note>, or a 'most graceful one,' when we have Xenophon before our eyes?" For Xenophon says in his *Symposium*: "Then Socrates said, 'Indeed, gentlemen, it seems quite right to me that we should drink.'"
> "For in truth, wine, by moistening the soul, lulls sorrows to sleep just as mandrake <note>used as an anesthetic in antiquity</note> puts men to sleep, but it awakens friendly feelings just as oil awakens a flame. However, it seems to me that the bodies of men suffer the same thing as plants growing in the earth. For when the god waters them too abundantly all at once, they cannot stand upright, nor can the breezes blow through them. But when they drink only as much as gives them pleasure, they grow quite upright and reach full fruitfulness. So it is with us: if we pour the drink in all at once, both our bodies and our minds will soon stumble, and we will not be able to breathe, let alone speak. But if the servants sprinkle us frequently with small cups—to use a phrase of Gorgias <note>Gorgias of Leontini, a famous rhetorician known for his flowery style</note>—then, not being forced into drunkenness by the wine, but being persuaded by it, we shall arrive at a more playful state."

Looking at these words of the noble Xenophon, one can recognize the jealousy that the most illustrious Plato felt toward him, or perhaps these men had a spirit of rivalry toward each other from the beginning,

<margin>Aulus Gellius, Book 14, chapter 3</margin>
each being aware of his own excellence, and perhaps they disagreed over who was the greatest. We can judge this not only from what they said regarding Cyrus, but also from their choice of the same subjects. 

<margin>Xenophon or Plato, having once been envious of one another.</margin>
For both wrote *Symposia*, in which one (Xenophon) dismisses the flute-girls while the other (Plato) introduces them; one (Xenophon), as previously stated, declines to drink from large cups, while the other (Plato) brings Socrates forward drinking from a cooler <note>psykter</note> until dawn. And in his *On the Soul* <note>The Phaedo</note>, though Plato lists everyone who was present, he does not mention Xenophon even slightly. Also, regarding Cyrus, one (Xenophon) says he was educated in all ancestral customs from his earliest youth, but Plato, as if in opposition, says in the third book of the *Laws*:
> "I divine concerning Cyrus that, while he was in other respects a good and patriotic general, he had not touched upon right education at all, and seems to have paid no attention to household management; rather, he seems to have spent his life on campaigns from his youth, handing his children over to the women to be raised."

Again, Xenophon, having marched up with Cyrus to Persia with the Ten Thousand Greeks, and knowing accurately the betrayal of Menon the Thessalian—that he himself was the cause of the destruction of Clearchus and his men by Tissaphernes—and describing what sort of man he was in character, how harsh and how licentious; yet the noble Plato, as if saying "this story is not true," goes through a long eulogy of him. Plato, who once and for all spoke ill of all others, casting Homer and imitative poetry out of his *Republic*, yet he himself wrote his dialogues in an imitative style—a form of which he was not even the inventor. 

<margin>Alexamenos in the dialogues.</margin>
For before him, Alexamenos of Teos invented this type of discourse, as Nicias of Nicaea and Soterion record. Aristotle, in his work *On Poets*, writes as follows: "Should we then not say that the so-called 'Mimes' of Sophron, though not in meter, are discourses and imitations? Or the works of Alexamenos of Teos,

<margin>Slander of Plato</margin>
the first Socratic dialogues to be written?" Thus the most learned Aristotle says outright that Alexamenos wrote dialogues before Plato. Furthermore, Plato slanders Thrasymachus...

# ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED
### BOOK 11
Page 549

...regarding Thrasymachus the Chalcedonian, saying he is like a sophist in name only. He also mentions Hippias and Gorgias in the *Parmenides* and includes much in the dialogue *Protagoras*. Plato said such things in the *Republic*, such as: "When, I suppose, a city under a democracy, thirsting for liberty, happens upon bad cup-bearers and gets drunk on unmixed <note>original: ἀκράτῳ (akrato); wine not diluted with water, which Greeks associated with loss of self-control</note> wine." It is also said that when Gorgias himself read the dialogue named after him, he remarked to his companions: "How well Plato knows how to write lampoons!" <note>original: ἰαμβίζειν (iambizein); referring to iambic poetry, which was the traditional meter for satire and personal attacks</note>. 

Empedus says in his work *On Gorgias* that when Gorgias visited Athens—after he had dedicated a golden statue of himself at Delphi—Plato saw him and remarked: "The beautiful and golden Gorgias has come to us." Gorgias replied: "Athens has truly found a new and beautiful Archilochus <note>Archilochus was a famous 7th-century BC poet known for his biting, aggressive satire</note> in this man." Others say that after Gorgias read Plato’s dialogue, he told those present that he "neither said nor heard such things" from Plato. Phaedo said the same thing after reading the dialogue *On the Soul* <note>The *Phaedo*</note>. Therefore, Timon did well to say of him that Plato "fashioned wonders, knowing how to mold fictions." 

For as to Parmenides, the age of Plato’s Socrates hardly allows for them to have even met in conversation, let alone for such long discourses to have been spoken or heard. But the most outrageous thing of all—said for no pressing reason—is the claim that Zeno, his fellow citizen, had been Parmenides' "favorite" <note>original: παιδικά (paidika); a term for the younger partner in a pederastic relationship</note>. He said in the *Phaedrus* that Zeno was not only Socrates' friend but had also been his beloved. Furthermore, in the *Protagoras*, Paralus and Xanthippus, the sons of Pericles, are shown conversing with Protagoras during his second visit to Athens, even though they had died during the plague some time before. One could say much more to demonstrate how he fabricated his dialogues.

<margin>That Plato spoke ill of everyone.</margin>
That he was ill-disposed toward everyone is clear, even from the dialogue titled *Ion*, in which he first speaks ill of all the poets, and then of those men honored by the people as courageous, such as Apollodorus of Cyzicus, and Heraclides of Clazomenae. In the *Meno*, he attacks the greatest Athenians, Aristides and Themistocles. He praises Meno for being willing to betray the Greeks, while he insults Euthydemus and his brother Dionysiodorus, mockingly calling them "late-learners" <note>original: ὀψιμαθεῖς (opsimatheis); those who start studying late in life, often implying they lack deep culture</note> to reproach them. They were exiles from their homeland of Chios who settled in Thurii. Nor does he spare Melesias, the son of Thucydides <note>The politician, not the historian</note> who was a rival to Pericles, nor Lysimachus the son of Aristides, claiming they were unworthy of their fathers' virtue. 

What he said about Alcibiades in the *Symposium* is not even fit to be spoken in the light of day. Nor is it fit in the earlier of the dialogues named after him—though some say this one is by Xenophon, just as the *Alcyone* is said to be by Leon the Academic, as Nicias of Nicaea says. I will remain silent regarding what was said about Alcibiades. 

He also called the Athenian people a "judge with his sleeves rolled up" <note>original: πρόκωπον (prokopon); literally "with sword in hand" or "ready for action," implying a hostile or aggressive stance</note>. While praising the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, he also praises the Persians, the enemies of all Greeks. He portrays the brother of Alcibiades and Nicias as madmen, and their sons as idiots, and Midias as a "quail-striker" <note>original: ὀρτυγοκόπον (ortygokopon); a gambler who plays a game of flicking quails</note>. He says the Athenian people are "ugly-faced," and that one must strip them to see them clearly; for then, he says, their supposed dignity will be seen as a mere cloak covering a beauty that is not real. 

In the *Cimon*, he does not spare Themistocles from accusation, nor Alcibiades and Myronides, nor even Cimon himself. The *Crito* also contains an attack on Sophocles. The *Gorgias* attacks not only the man for whom it is named, but also Archelaus, the king of Macedonia, whom he reproaches not only for his favors but for killing his master. 

This is the same Plato of whom Speusippus says that, being a dear friend to Archelaus, he was the cause of Philip obtaining the kingship. Carystius of Pergamum writes in his *Historical Notes*: "Speusippus, hearing that Philip was speaking ill of Plato, wrote in a letter something to the effect that people seem to be unaware that Philip gained the beginning of his reign through Plato. For Plato sent Euphraeus of Oreus to Perdiccas, who persuaded him to allot a certain territory to Philip. Supporting his forces there, when Perdiccas died, Philip fell upon the state of affairs with a ready army." As to how much truth there is in this, God only knows. 

His "beautiful" *Protagoras* contains an attack on many poets and wise men, and he puts the life of Callias on public display more than Eupolis did in his play *The Flatterers*. In the *Menexenus*, not only is Hippias the famed mockingly treated, but also Antiphon of Rhamnus and the musician Lamprus. The day would fail me if I wished to go through everyone who was spoken ill of by "the wise one." 

Indeed, he did not even praise Antisthenes. For though Antisthenes spoke ill of many, he did not even spare Plato, but gave him the vulgar name "Saton" <note>A crude pun on 'Platon,' derived from 'sathe' (the male member); Antisthenes wrote a dialogue with this title to mock Plato</note> and published a dialogue under that title. 

Hegesander of Delphi, in his *Notes*, speaking of Plato's malice toward everyone, writes this: "After the death of Socrates, when his companions were despondent, Plato, who was present, took up a cup and exhorted them not to be discouraged, for he himself was capable of leading the school. He then toasted Apollodorus; but Apollodorus said he would have more gladly received the cup of poison <note>original: φαρμάκου (pharmakou)</note> from Socrates than..."

# ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED
### BOOK 11
Page 250

-> Α Θ Η Ν. Δ Ε Ι Π Ν Ο Σ Ο Φ. <-
<note>ATHEN. DEIPNOSOPH. (Athenaeus, The Banquet of the Learned)</note>

...had taken a cup of poison, or received from you a toast of wine. For it seemed that Plato was envious, and his character was by no means beyond reproach. Although he criticized Aristippus for traveling abroad to the court of Dionysius <note>Dionysius I and II were the powerful tyrants of Syracuse in Sicily</note>, Plato himself sailed to Sicily three times: once to see the lava flows <note>original: ῥυακῶν (rhuakon); referring to the volcanic eruptions of Mount Etna</note>, during which time he met the elder Dionysius and put his life in danger; and twice to visit the younger Dionysius. Furthermore, though Aeschines was poor and had only one student, Xenocrates, Plato lured this student away from him. He was also caught bringing a lawsuit of slavery against Phaedo. In general, he had a "stepmotherly" disposition <note>i.e., hostile or unkind</note> toward all the disciples of Socrates. For this reason, Socrates—aiming at him with no small effort—said in the presence of many people that he had seen a dream. He said it seemed that Plato had become a crow and hopped onto his head, pecking at his bald spot <note>original: φαλακρόν (phalakron)</note> and looking around triumphantly. "I think, Plato," Socrates said, "you will tell many lies against my head." Plato was not only malicious but also hungry for glory <note>original: φιλόδοξος (philodoxos)</note>; it was he who said that we only strip off the "tunic of glory" at the very moment of death—even in our wills, funerals, and tombs, as Dioscorides says in his *Memoirs*. And his desire to found a city and to give laws—what is that if not a natural passion for glory? It is clear that what he said in the *Timaeus* was true: that he felt a certain passion for his state <note>original: πολιτείαν (politeian)</note>, just as a painter might wish to see his own works moving and active; so too did he wish to see the political systems he had sketched. And as for what he said in his dialogues, what more can one say? For the idea that the soul is fashioned as immortal <margin>In. P. <note>original: In Platonem; Against Plato</note></margin> and is separated from the body at death was first stated by Homer. For Homer said that the soul of Patroclus "went down to Hades, lamenting its fate, leaving behind its manliness and youth."

<margin>Against Plato.</margin> If, then, Plato claims this discourse as his own, I do not see what benefit we have gained from it. For even if one concedes that the souls of the dead migrate into other natures and rise to a higher place because they possess lightness, what is that to us? If there is neither a memory of what we once were, nor any perception of our former existence, what grace is there in such immortality? And the laws composed by him, and even before those, his *Republic*—what have they achieved? Certainly, if they were useful, then just as Lycurgus served the Spartans, Solon the Athenians, and Zaleucus the Thurians, some of the Greeks should have made use of his laws. For a law, as Aristotle says, is a reason defined according to the common agreement of a city, indicating how each thing must be done. Is it not strange that of the three famous Athenian lawgivers—Draco, Solon, and Plato himself—the citizens abide by the laws of the first two, while they actually laugh at those of Plato? As he himself says regarding his *Republic*: if it is not the best in the eyes of all, but only to us in our feelings, what is the gain? It seems, then, that Plato did not write his laws for real men, but for those "molded" by him, so that people would have to be searched for to use them. He should have either spoken things that everyone could follow or written laws that were not merely like prayers, but suited for those who pursue the study of nature. Furthermore, if one were to go through his *Timaeus*, his *Gorgias*, and his other such dialogues in which he discusses mathematics, natural philosophy, and many other topics, even then he is not to be wondered at for these. For one could find these things elsewhere, either better stated or at least no worse. Theopompus of Chios, in his work *Against the School of Plato*, says that one would find most of his dialogues to be useless and false. He claims most of them were borrowed from the lectures of Aristippus, some from Antisthenes, and many from Bryson of Heraclea. But why do we look for what he promises in his writings regarding the nature of man? We do not find it; instead, we find banquets and discourses spoken about love <note>referring to the *Symposium* and *Phaedrus*</note>, which are quite unbecoming, and which he composed while looking down upon his readers. Indeed, many of his students became tyrannical and slandering men.

<margin>Plato's students were tyrannical.</margin> For Euphraetus, while staying with King Perdiccas in Macedonia, ruled no less than the king himself; he was a base man and a slanderer, who so coldly organized the king's inner circle that no one was permitted to share the common meal unless they knew geometry or philosophy. Because of this, when Philip took over the rule, Parmenion killed him in Oreus, as Carystius says in his *Historical Notes*. Callippus the Athenian, who was himself a student of Plato and a companion and fellow-student of Dion, traveled with him to Syracuse; but when he saw Dion attempting to make the monarchy his own, he killed him and attempted to become a tyrant himself through slaughter. Then there was Euagon of Lampsacus, as Eurypylus and Dicaeocles of Cnidus say in the twenty-first book of their *Lectures*. Furthermore, Demochares the orator, in his speech *On Behalf of Sophocles against Philon*, says that Euagon lent money to his city on the security of the acropolis and plotted to become tyrant until the people of Lampsacus ran together against him, paid back the money, and cast him out. Timaeus of Cyzicus, as the same Demochares says...

...he says, by distributing money and grain to the citizens. Because of these acts, as is your custom, he was held in high esteem among the people of Cyzicus. But after waiting a short time, he attacked the constitution; having been judged by Aristoteles <note>original: Ἀριστοτέλους; this refers to Aristoteles of Cyzicus, a student of Plato, not the famous philosopher</note> or having been deemed worthy of a salt-tax <note>This passage is difficult; it implies a fall from grace or a legal penalty</note>. If he had not used great care, he would have lived out his old age in dishonor and obscurity. There are some of the Academic school even now who live in an unholy and inglorious manner. For having gained control of wealth through impiety and unnatural means—by way of sorcery—they are now much-admired.

Such a man was Chaeron of Pellene, who not only attended the lectures of Plato, but also those of Xenocrates. He, having become a bitter tyrant in his homeland, not only drove out the best of the citizens, but also gave the property of the masters to their slaves as a gift, and settled the wives of those masters into a "marriage community" <note>original: γάμου κοινωνίαν (gamou koinonian); a mocking reference to Plato’s theory of communal wives in the *Republic*</note> with the slaves. These were the benefits he derived from that "Beautiful Republic" and those "Lawless Laws." 

For this reason, the comic poet Ephippus, in his play *The Shipwrecked Man*, mocks Plato himself and some of his associates. He bitingly portrays them as sycophants who hunt for money, showing that they dressed with great extravagance—perhaps because of their beauty, or perhaps because they took more care for their own wantonness than for us. He speaks as follows:

> Then one of those youths from the Academy
> Who studied under Plato, and was struck
> By the bold-reasoning schemes of Bryson <note>Bryson of Heraclea was a mathematician and sophist</note>,
> Was forced by the "peg-seizing" art <note>A pun on logical "pegs" or perhaps a dental instrument</note>
> To keep silent, though he could not stop speaking. 
> He says, "Good day, sir," with a polished lifestyle,
> Having carefully arranged the depths of his beard,
> And placing his feet well into his sandals,
> Under the strap of the shin-wrap with equal folds,
> Well-protected by the bulk of his fine cloak,
> Leaning his weight upon a worthy staff—
> A borrowed look, not his own, it seems to me—
> He spoke to the breezes of the Athenian land.

Let us bring our collection of stories to an end here, my dear and sweet Timocrates; next, we shall speak of those who became notorious for their luxury.

# ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED
## BOOK TWELVE

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A featuring a classical figure holding a staff or instrument.</image-desc>

<margin>pleasure.</margin>
"You seem to me to be a man of Cyrene," <note>A reference to the Cyrenaic school of philosophy, which held that pleasure was the supreme good</note> according to the joke Timocrates made in the *Tantalids* of Alexis. For the dinner was once again fine in this way: eighteen were present, and others in ten-horse chariots, and a heap of fifteen more. Regarding these things, I must throw the necessities to you, so that it is best not to invite anyone else. And for me, it is best to keep silent, and not to add further things to the many already said. 

But since you so very persistently demand from us the account of those who became notorious for luxury <note>original: τρυφῆς (truphes); luxury, soft living, or voluptuousness</note>, and of their enjoyment of pleasure—for enjoyment follows first upon desire, and then comes with pleasure. And where the poet Sophocles, speaking of enjoyment as one of those things, so that he might not blame old age, as if he had found temperance to have rebelled against him—I mean the pleasure regarding sexual enjoyments—said that he was gladly rid of them as if from a "mad master." 

But I say that the Judgment of Paris was also created by the ancients as a comparison of pleasure against virtue. When Aphrodite was preferred—and she represents Pleasure—everything was thrown into turmoil. And it seems to me 
<margin>from the Memoirs.</margin>
that our noble Xenophon also fashioned the myth about Hercules and Virtue from the very beginning. For even Empedocles says:

> Nor was there among them any god of war, nor any battle-din,
> Nor was Zeus their King, nor Cronus, nor Poseidon,
> But Cypris <note>Aphrodite</note> was Queen.

They appease her with the most pious images: with painted animals and expertly fashioned perfumes, and sacrifices of pure myrrh and fragrant frankincense, throwing libations of yellow honey upon the ground. And Menander, in *The Lyre Player*, says of certain people who were "music-mad," that one was very much a lover of the Muses, "And always a sound trained for luxury." 

And yet some say that pleasure is according to nature, because all living creatures have been enslaved by it, just as they are by cowardice and fear, and the other passions that belong to all in common. But among those who use reason, pleasure is rejected. Therefore, if one pursues pleasures headlong, one must eventually hunt for pains.
<margin>according to pleasure.</margin>
For this reason, Homer, wishing to make pleasure a thing of reproach, says that even the greatest of the gods are not helped by their own power, but are harmed in the greatest ways when led forward by it. For all the things that Zeus, while lying awake, planned for the sake of the Trojans, he lost in a day when he was overcome by pleasure <note>Referring to the "Deception of Zeus" in the Iliad, where Hera seduces him to distract him from the war</note>. And Ares, being the most valiant, was bound by the weakest Hephaestus—an instance of both shame and loss, because they gave themselves over to irrational loves. He says to the gods, when they came to see him bound:
<margin>in the Odyssey.</margin>
> "Ill deeds do not prosper.
> The slow catches the swift, just as now Hephaestus,
> Though he is slow, has caught Ares, though he is the swiftest 
> Of the gods who hold Olympus, being lame, he caught him by his art."

No one speaks of the life of Sadus as "sweet," but rather that of Smindyrides the Sybarite, and that of Sardanapalus. And yet, according to reputation, they say in the book *On Pleasure* that Theophrastus is not similarly brilliant, but he did not puff himself up like those men, nor like Agesilaus the King of the Lacedaemonians, but was rather more fortunate or lived without such 
<margin>invisible</margin>
distress.

-> ATHEN. DEIPNOSOPH. <-
<note>original: ΑΘΗΝ. ΔΕΙΠΝΟΣΟΦ. — Athenaeus, The Deipnosophistae</note>

...is being invisible to reputation. For it was not so among the demigods at Troy, but much more among those of today; and naturally so, for the former lived without elaborate preparation, like a spring of water flowing of its own accord, with neither civic refinement nor the perfected arts. But the modern man is equipped in every way for ease and every kind of enjoyment, and for other modes of passing the time. Plato says in the *Philebus* that pleasure is the greatest of all boasters. As the argument goes, even in the pleasures of sex—which seem to be the greatest—perjury has received forgiveness from the gods, as if pleasures were like children, not even possessing the faculty of reason. 

In the eighth book of the *Republic*, the same Plato previously pointed out what is commonly discussed by those in power: that among desires, some are natural and necessary, while others are neither natural nor necessary. He writes as follows: "Would not the desire to eat until one reaches health and well-being, and the desire for bread and relish <note>original: ὄψου (opsou); refers to any seasoning or side-dish eaten with bread, often fish or meat</note>, be necessary?" "I think so." "The desire for bread is necessary for both reasons: because it is beneficial and because it is capable of sustaining life." "Yes." "And the desire for relish is necessary insofar as it provides some benefit toward well-being?" "Certainly." "What then of the desires that go beyond these, for other kinds of foods or drinks—desires which can be eliminated if they are checked from youth and disciplined by many means, and which are harmful to the body, and harmful to the soul in respect to wisdom and temperance—would these not rightly be called unnecessary?"

<margin>On pleasure.</margin>
"Most rightly indeed." Heraclides of Pontus, in his work *On Pleasure*, says the following: "Tyrants and kings, being masters of all good things and having experienced everything, put pleasure first; for pleasure makes the natures of men more large-minded." <note>original: μεγαλοψυχότερας (megalopsychoteras); literally "great-souled" or magnanimous</note> At any rate, all those who honor pleasure and choose to live in luxury are large-minded and magnificent, like the Persians and the Medes. For these people, more than any other men, honor pleasure and luxury, being the most courageous and large-minded of the barbarians. Indeed, to enjoy oneself and to live in luxury belongs to free men, for it relaxes and enlarges their souls; but to toil belongs to slaves and the lowly, which is why their natures are contracted. 

The city of Athens, as long as it lived in luxury, was at its greatest and nurtured the most large-minded men. For they wore purple garments, and put on tunics of varied colors, and binding their hair in knots, they wore golden grasshoppers <note>original: τέττιγας (tettigas); these were ornamental golden pins used by ancient Athenians to signify their "autochthony" or being born from the land</note> around their foreheads and hair. Their servants carried folding stools for them, so that they might not sit down just anywhere. And yet these were the very men who won the battle at Marathon, and who alone subdued the power of all Asia. And the most prudent men, he says, those held in the highest reputation for wisdom, believe that pleasure is the greatest good. Simonides says it this way: "For what life of mortals is desirable without pleasure? Or what tyranny? Without her, even the life of the gods is not to be envied." Pindar, in his praise for Hiero, the ruler of the Syracusans, says: "Do not diminish the delight in your life; a pleasant life is by far the best thing for a man." And Homer says that "good cheer" and "making merry" is a more graceful end, "whenever the banqueters listen to the singers, and the tables are full." He says that the gods "live easily," and "easily" means "without toil," as if indicating that the greatest of evils

<margin>Hercules, lover of pleasure. <insert><unclear>and [holy?]</unclear></insert></margin>
is the misery and toil involved in living. Therefore, Megacleides finds fault with the poets after Homer and Hesiod—those who have spoken about Hercules as if he led armies and captured cities. For Hercules actually spent his life among men with the greatest pleasure, marrying the most women and fathering children from the most maidens in secret. Indeed, he asks those who do not accept this: "Where else, O men, do you get the idea of his devotion to food? Or why is there a custom among men that nothing should be left in the libation cup, if they did not recognize his devotion to pleasures? Or why are the hot baths that appear from the earth everywhere said to be sacred to Hercules? Or why do they habitually call soft bedding 'the beds of Hercules,' if he despised those who live pleasantly?" 

Later, he says, the younger poets depicted him in the guise of a robber, walking alone, holding a club and wearing a lion skin and a bow; and they say Stesichorus of Himera was the first to invent this fiction. But Xanthus the lyric poet, who was older than Stesichorus—as Stesichorus himself bears witness, according to Megacleides—did not give him this outfit, but rather the Homeric one. Stesichorus has adapted many things from Xanthus, just as he did with the poem called the *Oresteia*. Antisthenes, while claiming that pleasure is a good, added "the kind that brings no regret." And Odysseus in Homer seems to have become a leader of the much-celebrated "Epicurean" pleasure, for he says: "For I say there is no end more graceful than when good cheer possesses the whole people... and the banqueters in the halls listen to the singer, sitting in order, and beside them the tables are full of bread and meat, and the cupbearer, drawing wine from the mixing bowl, carries it round and pours it into the cups; this seems to my mind to be the most beautiful thing." Megacleides says that Odysseus, adapting to the circumstances so as to seem of like mind with the Phaeacians, embraced their luxurious lifestyle after learning of it from Alcinous: "Always to us the feast is dear, and the lyre and dances, and changes of clothing, and hot baths and bed." For only in this way did he think he would not fail to get what he hoped for.

They spent the autumn in Persepolis and the rest of the year in Babylon. The kings of the Parthians spend the spring in Rhagae and the winter in Babylon, and the rest of the year elsewhere. The kings of the Persians also placed a <term>petasmon</term> <note>A broad-brimmed hat or head-covering</note> upon their heads, appearing in it as a display of their enjoyment of much suffering <note>The Greek "poly-patheia" here implies a refined sensitivity or susceptibility to sensation</note>. For it was prepared, as Dino says, from myrrh and the so-called <term>labyzus</term>. This <term>labyzus</term> was a fragrant plant, more highly valued than myrrh. And whenever the king descended from his chariot, Dino says, even if the height to the ground was small, he never jumped down nor leaned on anyone's hands; instead, a golden stool was always placed for him, and he stepped onto this to descend. The king’s stool-bearer followed him for this purpose. He is guarded by three hundred women, as Heracleides of Cyme records in the first book of his *Persian History*. These women sleep during the day so that they may be awake at night; they spend the night singing and playing the harp by the light of burning lamps. The king often makes use of them in the court of the <term>melophoroi</term> <note>original: μηλοφόροι; "Apple-bearers," the elite royal guard whose spears were tipped with golden apples</note>. These men were part of the bodyguard, all Persians by birth, having golden apples on the butts of their spears, numbering one thousand. They were chosen from ten thousand Persians called the "Immortals." The king would pass through their court on foot, walking upon thin Sardian carpets on which no one else set foot except the king. When he reached the last court, he would mount his chariot, or sometimes a horse; but he was never seen on foot outside the palace unless he was exiting the gate, and his concubines went out with him. The throne on which he sat to conduct business was golden, and around it stood four small golden columns encrusted with precious stones, over which was stretched a patterned purple cloth. Clearchus of Soli, in the fourth book of his *Lives*, having spoken previously about the luxury of the Medes and how they castrated many of their neighbors because of it, notes that the Persians inherited this "softness" from the Medes—not only as a punishment for what they had suffered, but also through the luxury of their bodyguards, a memorial to the extent of their shamelessness. For it seems their untimely and vain luxury in life weakened even those armed with spears, making them "silver-shields" <note>likely meaning they became more decorative than functional</note>. Going further, he writes that when the king provided a sweet food for himself, he would give prizes to those who provided it, but he would not grant these honors to others; rather, being sensible, he preferred to enjoy them himself. This is, I believe, what is called the "Brain of Zeus and the King" <note>A proverbial expression for an exquisite delicacy</note.
<margin>
Budé, Book 4, *On the As*.
</margin>
Chares of Mytilene, in the fifth book of his *History of Alexander*, says that the Persian kings reached such a level of luxury that a five-couch chamber was kept above the head of the royal bed, in which five thousand talents of gold were always kept; this was called the "Royal Pillow." At his feet was another three-couch chamber, where three thousand talents of silver were kept, called the "Royal Footstool." In the bedchamber, there was also a golden vine encrusted with precious stones over the bed. Amyntas says in his *Stathmoi* <note>A work on Persian geography/stages of travel</note> that this vine even had clusters of grapes made from the most expensive jewels. Not far from this was dedicated a golden mixing-bowl, the work of Theodorus of Samos. Agathocles, in the first book of his *History of Cyzicus*, says that among the Persians there is a water called "Golden Water." It consists of seventy springs, and no one may drink from it except the king and his eldest son; if anyone else drinks it, the penalty is death. Xenophon, in the eighth book of his *Education of Cyrus* <note>The Cyropaedia</note>, says that they still practiced the Persian education then, but they adopted the Median dress and refinement. "But now," he says, "they allow the Persian endurance to be extinguished, while they preserve the Median softness." I wish to clarify their daintiness; for first, it is not enough for them to have their beds softly spread, but they now even place the feet of their couches upon carpets, so that the floor does not resist them, but the carpets give way. Moreover, regarding what is served at the table, nothing that was previously discovered has been abandoned, but they are always devising new things, and the same with side-dishes; for they possess inventors for both of these, but...

<margin>Omphale.</margin> one of the outraged women named Omphale. Having gathered the mistresses there by force, she shut them in with the slaves. ...as told in the preparatory verses of the household books <note>original: φαμήλοις παρασκευασικοῖς ἐπῶν — likely referring to household records or instructional verses</note>, it is written that in the Frankincense-bearing land <note>the region of Lebanon or Southern Arabia</note> there is a king who is autonomous and a subject to no one. He exceeds all others in luxury and indolence; for he spends all his time in the baths, passing his life in luxury and expense. He performs not a single duty of state, nor does he grant audiences to many, but instead appoints judges himself. If anyone believes they have been judged unjustly, there is a small window in the highest part of the palace, and it is tied with a chain. The person who believes they have been treated unfairly takes hold of the chain and pulls the window; when the king notices this, he summons the person and judges the case himself. If the judges are found to have ruled unjustly, they are put to death. But if they ruled justly, the one who moved the window is executed. He says the daily expenses for the King, and the women and friends around him, amount to fifteen Babylonian talents.

They dine <gloss>to dine</gloss> not with their own husbands, but with whichever of the men present they happen to be with, and they toast whomever they wish. They are also formidable drinkers and are very beautiful in appearance. The Etruscans raise all children that are born, not knowing who the father of each one is. These children live in the same manner as those who raised them, holding many drinking parties and having relations with all the women. It is not considered shameful among the Etruscans to be seen either performing <note>original: ποιοῦντας (active sexual role)</note> or receiving <note>original: πάσχοντας (passive sexual role)</note> a sexual act in public; for this is a local custom among them. When they have sexual gatherings in groups, they do as follows: first, when they have finished drinking and are about to sleep, the servants bring in to them—while the lamps are still burning—sometimes courtesans, sometimes very handsome boys, and sometimes wives. When they have enjoyed these, they then bring in vigorous young men, who have relations with those people themselves. They carry out their unions sometimes in view of one another, but for the most part they place screens <note>original: λαβίδας (labidas) — literally 'grips' or 'tongs', here referring to folding screens or lattices</note> around the couches, which are woven from rods, and clothes are draped over them. ### ATHENAEUS: THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

<margin>Masinissa’s love of animals.</margin>
...Maltese puppies, which they even take to see the gymnasiums. How then did Masinissa, the king of the Maurusians <note>modern-day Numidians of North Africa</note>, answer those like them? As Ptolemy says in the eighth book of his *Commentaries*, when people were seeking to buy monkeys, he asked: "Do the women among you people not bear children?" For Masinissa delighted in small children, and he kept his own sons' children with him to be raised. He had many children, and daughters likewise; he raised all of them himself until they were three years old, after which he sent them back to their parents when others arrived to take their place. Eubulus the comic poet said the same things in his play *The Graces*:

> For how much better it is to raise
> -> a human being into a man, if one has the means, <-
> -> than a flapping and <-
> -> gaping goose, <- or a sparrow, or a wicked, plotting monkey.

And Athenodorus, in his work *On Serious Study and Play*, says that Archytas the Tarentine <note>a famous Pythagorean philosopher and statesman</note>, who was both a politician and a philosopher, had many domestic servants and delighted in having them join the symposium when they were released from their work. But the Sybarites <note>citizens of Sybaris, a Greek colony in Italy known for extreme wealth</note> delighted in Maltese puppies and in "humans who were not humans" <note>likely referring to jesters, dwarfs, or people kept for amusement rather than labor</note>. The Sybarites also wore garments made of Milesian wool <note>renowned in antiquity for its supreme softness</note>, which was the basis for the friendship between the two cities, as Timaeus records. For among those from Italy they loved the Etruscans, and among those from abroad they loved the Ionians, because they were all devoted to luxury <note>original: τρυφῇ (tryphe)</note>. The cavalry of the Sybarites, being more than five thousand in number, used to parade wearing saffron-colored robes over their breastplates. During the summer, their younger men would travel away to the caves of the Nymphs at Lousiades and spend their time in total luxury. When their merchants traveled into the countryside, even when traveling by carriage on the road, they would take three days to complete a single day's journey. Some of the roads leading into their fields were even covered with awnings. Most of them possessed wine-cellars near the sea, into which they would let the wine flow from the estates through pipes; some of it was sold abroad, while some was brought into the city by boats. They also held many frequent public banquets, and they honored those who were magnificently ambitious with gold crowns. They would announce these honors at public sacrifices and games, proclaiming not their goodwill, but their lavish provision of dinners. They also honored the cooks who prepared the presented dishes with the greatest skill. Among the Sybarites, steam-baths <note>original: πύελοι (pyeloi)</note> were also invented, in which they would lie down and be steamed. They were also the first to invent chamber pots, which they brought into their symposia. While mocking those who traveled away from their homelands, they themselves took pride in having grown old upon the bridges of their rivers. It seems that a great part of their prosperity was due to the fact that their land, though lacking harbors, lay along the sea, and almost all the produce was consumed by the citizens themselves. Both the location of the city and an oracle from the god signaled that everyone should indulge in luxury and live beyond measure in a relaxed state. Their city lay in a hollow, and in the summer, it was excessively cold in the mornings and evenings, but the heat of midday was unbearable, so that many of them believed the rivers were vital for their health. Thus it was said that anyone in Sybaris who did not want to die before his time should see the sun neither setting nor rising.

<margin>The luxury of the Sybarites.</margin>
Once, they even sent messengers to the god’s oracle at Delphi—among whom was Isamyris—asking how long their prosperity would last. The Pythia <note>the priestess of Apollo</note> said:

> Happy are you, equal in honor to the ever-living gods,
> So long as you honor a mortal man after a god.
> But when that changes, war and
> civil strife shall come upon you.

Upon hearing this, they thought the god meant they would never cease their luxury, for they believed they would never honor a man more than a god. But the change in their fortune happened when one of the masters was whipping a servant, and the servant fled to the temples but was whipped anyway. But when he finally fled to the tombs of his master's ancestors, the master let him go out of shame. They eventually destroyed themselves through competing with each other in luxuries. Their city vied with all others in luxury, and then not long after—following many omens and signs of ruin which I will not list now—they were destroyed. They had driven their luxury to such an extent that even at their feasts, they trained their horses to dance to the flute. The Crotonians <note>rivals of the Sybarites in Southern Italy</note>, knowing this when they went to war with them (as Aristotle records in his *Constitution of the Sybarites*), played the dance-tune for the horses. For they had flute-players with them in military gear, and as soon as the horses heard the flutes,
<margin>Horses dancing to the flute in battle formation.</margin>
they not only danced away but, carrying their riders with them, they defected to the Crotonians. Charon of Lampsacus tells a similar story about the people of Cardia in the second book of his *Boundaries*, writing as follows: The Bisaltae marched against Cardia and conquered it. The leader of the Bisaltae was Onaris. This man had been sold as a child in Cardia, and having served a certain Cardian as a slave, he became a barber. Now, the Cardians had a prophecy that the Bisaltae would come against them, and they spoke of this often while sitting in the barber shop. Onaris escaped from Cardia to his own country and led the Bisaltae against the Cardians, having been appointed leader by the Bisaltae. But the Cardians all...
