# BOOK 12

They taught their horses to dance at banquets to the sound of flutes; standing on their hind legs, they would dance with their forelegs <note>literally "faces," but referring to the front limbs in a dancing posture</note> in time with the elaborate flute melodies. Knowing this, Onaris <note>a leader of the Bisaltae, a Thracian people</note> acquired a flute-player from Cardia <note>a Greek city in the Thracian Chersonese</note>. When she arrived among the Bisaltae, she taught many flute-players, with whom Onaris then marched against the Cardians. When the battle was joined, he ordered them to play the melodies that the Cardian horses were trained to recognize. As soon as the horses heard the flute, they stood up on their hind legs and turned to dancing. Since the strength of the Cardians lay in their cavalry, they were easily defeated. 

Once, a certain Sybarite <note>a citizen of Sybaris, famous for its extreme wealth and love of ease</note> wishing to sail from Sybaris to Croton hired a private vessel on the condition that he should not be splashed, that no one else should board, and that he could take his horse with him. When the pilot agreed, he brought the horse on board and, having coaxed the animal, ordered it to be still. Then, when one of those seeing him off asked to sail with him, saying he would tow the ferry so it could sail along the shore, the Sybarite replied: "I would hardly have listened to you if I were going to sail by the sea, and not by the land." <note>A joke illustrating the Sybarite's comical avoidance of even the slightest discomfort of the open sea</note>.

<margin>Law of the Syracusans</margin>
Phylarchus says in the twenty-fifth book of his *Histories* that there was a law among the Syracusans that women should not adorn themselves with gold, nor wear flowered patterns, nor have garments with purple borders, unless one of them admitted to being a common prostitute. There was another law that a man should not beautify himself, nor use elaborate or distinctive clothing, unless he confessed to being an adulterer or a catamite <note>term: catamite — a passive male partner in a sexual relationship, often used here as a term of legal or social shaming</note>. Furthermore, a free woman was not to go out after sunset, unless she was going to commit adultery, and even during the day she was prevented from going out without the <term>gynaikonomoi</term> <note>magistrates who supervised the conduct and dress of women</note>, with a single maidservant following her.

<margin>And the luxury of the Sybarites.</margin>
It is said the Sybarites were puffed up with luxury; they passed a law that those inviting women to festivals and sacrifices must give notice a year in advance, so that they might prepare clothes and other finery worthy of the occasion before attending. If any caterer or cook discovered a private and excellent dish, no one else was allowed to use it for a year; instead, the discoverer himself held the exclusive right so that the first inventor might profit from the work, and so others might be encouraged to excel in such industrious labors. Likewise, they exempted from taxes those who sold eels, as well as the dyers, those who dyed with sea-purple, and those who imported it. 

Having thus drifted entirely into insolence <note>original: "hubris"</note>, they finally killed all thirty ambassadors who came from the people of Croton and threw their bodies before the walls to be devoured by wild beasts. 

<margin>The destruction of the Sybarites.</margin>
This was the beginning of their calamities. It is said that after a few days, all their magistrates saw the same vision on the same night: they saw Hera come into the middle of the marketplace and vomit bile. A spring of blood also bubbled up in her temple, but even so they did not cease from their arrogance until they were all destroyed by the Crotoniates. Heraclides Ponticus, in his work *On Justice*, says that when the Sybarites overthrew the tyranny of Telys, they slaughtered those who had taken part in the government, murdering them at the very altar. Because of these murders, the statue of Hera turned away, and the floor sprouted a spring of blood, so that they had to cover the entire area with bronze grates, wishing to stop the upwelling of blood. For this reason they were uprooted and all destroyed—they who even wished to eclipse the ancient fame of the Olympic games. For observing the time when they were held, they attempted to lure the athletes to themselves by offering an excess of prizes.

<margin>Of the Crotoniates.</margin>
The Crotoniates, as Timaeus says, after destroying the Sybarites, also drifted into luxury, so that even their chief magistrate went about the city dressed in a sea-purple robe, crowned with a golden crown, and wearing white sandals. But some say this did not happen because of luxury, but because of Democedes the physician, who was a Crotoniate by birth. He lived with Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos, and after the tyrant's death, he was taken prisoner by the Persians and brought to the King, after Oroetes had killed Polycrates. Democedes cured Atossa—the wife of Darius and daughter of Cyrus—who was suffering from a breast ailment, and asked as his reward to be sent back to Greece, promising to return. Having obtained this, he came to Croton and wished to remain there. 

<margin>Herodotus book 3.</margin>
When one of the Persians seized him, saying he was the King’s slave, the Crotoniates rescued him; stripping the Persian of his robe, they dressed the attendant of the chief magistrate in it. Since then, dressed in Persian robes, he walks around the altars on the seventh days with the magistrate—not for the sake of luxury or insolence, but to insult the Persians. Later, Timaeus says, the Crotoniates also attempted to destroy the Olympic festival at the same time by offering a very wealthy silver-prize contest. But some say it was the Sybarites who did this. Those who say the Tarentines...

# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

Phylarchus, in his fourth book, says that they not only acquired power but progressed to such a degree of luxury <note>original: "tryphe"</note> that they began to smooth their entire bodies by removing hair, and were the first to lead others in this practice of depilation. By nature and through their way of life, they wore very transparent garments, of the kind that women nowadays use to make themselves look elegant. Secondly, having been led by luxury into insolence <note>original: "hybris," meaning a prideful violation of others' rights</note>, they laid waste to Carbina, a city of the Iapygians. From there, they gathered boys, virgins, and women in their prime into the temples of the Carbinates, where they set up tents and displayed their naked bodies for all to see. Anyone who wished would then feast upon the beauty of those gathered there, as if upon a herd fallen into misfortune, satisfying their desires in the sight of all—and especially in the sight of the gods, whom those men least expected to care. For this reason, the divine power was so outraged that it struck all the Tarentines who had committed these lawless acts at Carbina with lightning. Even to this day in Tarentum, every house has a number of pillars standing before the doors—equal to the number of those sent out into Iapygia—at which, on the anniversary of their destruction, the people neither lament the departed nor pour the customary libations, but instead offer sacrifices to **Zeus the Descender** <note>Zeus Kataibates, the aspect of the god who strikes with lightning</note>.

<margin>
The luxury and destruction of the Iapygians.
</margin>
As for the Iapygian race itself, they are originally from Crete, having arrived and settled there while searching for Glaucus. These people, after some time, forgot the Cretan way of life and reached such a point of luxury and later insolence that they were the first to paint their faces and wear hairpieces and false hair, and to clothe themselves in flowery robes. They considered it a disgrace to work or perform manual labor, and many of them made their private houses more beautiful than the temples. The leaders of the Iapygians, in their mockery of the divine, even plundered the statues of the gods from the temples, ordering them to be removed from the sacred grounds. Because of this, they were struck from heaven with fire and bronze, which served as their punishment. For a long time, the evidence was visible in the form of bronze pieces forged by the heavenly strikes; and even to this day, all their descendants live with their heads shaven and wearing mourning clothes, deprived of all the goods they formerly possessed.

The Iberians, on the other hand, though they go about in painted robes and varied patterns, and use tunics that reach to their feet, are in no way hindered in their strength for war.

<margin>
Of the Massalians.
</margin>
The people of Massalia <note>modern Marseille</note> became effeminate, wearing garments that were an insult to their dignity. Indeed, they behaved indecorously because of the softness in their souls, acting like women out of a love for luxury. Hence, a proverb arose: "May you sail to Massalia," <note>an insult implying the person will become soft or "ladylike"</note> referring to those who are wealthy and decadent.

<margin>
The luxury of the Sirites and Milesians.
</margin>
Those who inhabited Siris—which was first occupied by those coming from Troy and later by the Colophonians—drifted into luxury no less than the Sybarites, as Timaeus and Aristotle tell us. It was their local custom to wear flowery tunics, which they cinched with expensive girdles; because of this, they were called "girdle-tunic wearers" <note>original: "mitrochitones"</note> by their neighbors, whereas Homer calls those who are ungirded "without girdle-tunics." The poet Archilochus greatly admired the land of the Sirites for its prosperity; speaking somewhere of Thasos, he says it is less desirable:

> For it is not a beautiful place, nor charming, nor lovely,
> such as the land around the streams of the Siris.

Siris was named, as Timaeus and Euripides say in the *Captive Melanippe*, after a woman named Siris; but according to Archilochus, it was named after the river. Not a little of their luxury and the general prosperity of the entire Italian region, as well as the great number of people, led to the whole settlement in Italy being called **Great Greece** <note>original: "Megale Hellas" or Magna Graecia</note>. The Milesians, as long as they did not indulge in luxury, defeated the Scythians (as Ephorus says) and founded the cities of the Hellespont. They settled the Black Sea with magnificent cities, and all the local nations were under the sway of Miletus. But when they were led astray by pleasure and luxury, the manliness of the city dissolved, as Aristotle says, and a proverb was born regarding them:

> Once upon a time, the Milesians were brave.

Heracleides of Pontus, in his second book *On Justice*, says: "The city of the Milesians fell into misfortunes because of luxury." Driven by hatred and refusing to love fair dealing, they uprooted their enemies. When a civil war broke out between the wealthy and the common people—whom they called Gergithes—the commoners first gained the upper hand. They drove out the rich, gathered the children of the fugitives onto threshing floors, brought in oxen, and trampled them to death in a most lawless manner. Consequently, when the rich gained power again, they burned everyone they could catch, including their children. It is said that while they were burning, many omens appeared, and a sacred olive tree caught fire spontaneously. For this reason, the god <note>the Oracle at Delphi</note> shut them out from his prophecy for a long time, and when they asked why they were being excluded, he said:

> I care not for the slaughter of the Gergithes, nor the fate of the Gisiri, nor the unflowering men.

Clearchus, in his fourth book, says that the Milesians, having envied the luxury of the Colophonians, spread it to their neighbors and then fell into a state of self-forgetfulness.

<margin>
Scythian insolence and goodness.
</margin>
The Milesian customs were local, but Clearchus records the following about the Scythians: "The Scythian nation was the first to use common laws, but then they became the most wretched of all mortals through their insolence. For they indulged in luxury like no others, being insolent in their wealth and the rest of their abundant resources."

# BOOK 12

...at hand. It is clear from this that their leaders, even now, have fallen back into seeking an arbitrator. Having indulged in luxury <note>original: "tryphe"</note> and, most notably, being the first of all mankind to rush toward such decadence, they advanced to such a point of insolence <note>original: "hybris"</note> that they would even insult the faces of those they encountered in the most degrading ways; from this, their descendants, even now, still carry a name derived from that shameful behavior. As for their wives, they treated the wives of the Thracians living toward the west and north in a similar manner, pricking their bodies with pins to create patterns—the art of tattooing <note>The Greeks viewed tattooing as a mark of slavery or punishment, unlike the Thracians who saw it as a sign of nobility.</note>. Many years later, the Thracian women who had been so mistreated sought to erase their misfortune by tattooing the rest of their skin, so that the original mark of shame and insolence might be integrated into a larger pattern, thus using the name "decoration" to mask the original disgrace. They stood so arrogantly above all others that the story of their eventual slavery was told with many tears, reporting that they could not even endure the "Scythian speech," whatever that may have been. Because of the magnitude of the disasters that overwhelmed them—since the destruction of their lives and the cutting of their hair was common to the whole nation—outsiders began to call the act of shaving one’s head as an insult "to Scythianize" <note>original: "aposkythisai"</note>. 

<margin>To Scythianize.</margin> 

Callias, or perhaps Diocles in *The Cyclopes*, examines all the Ionians together, asking: "For what is the tender and <margin>The flight from Abydos, or Ephesus.</margin> beautiful Ionia up to now?" The people of Abydos, who are colonists of the Milesians, were also abandoned to their lifestyles and were condemned for it, as Hermippus says in *The Soldiers*. "I rejoice at a certain army that was eager to advance, soft in appearance of body, with youthful hair fleeing from their arms; for the man of Abydos has been pledged as something sweet." And Aristophanes in *Triphales* mentions many Ionian women: "When they were present, they were notable for their fine clothes... one to Clazomenae, another to Ephesus, others to Abydos—I hail all those holy things." Regarding the people of Abydos, Antiphon <note>An influential Athenian orator and statesman.</note> speaks thus in his mockery of Alcibiades <note>The famous and controversial Athenian general known for his beauty and excess.</note>: "When you were approved by your guardians and received your inheritance from them, you sailed away to Abydos, not to collect any personal debt nor to serve as a consul for any city, but to learn ways of lawlessness and licentiousness of mind from the women in Abydos, so that you might employ them for the rest of your life." The Magnesians near the Maeander River were also destroyed because they flourished too greatly, as Callinus says in his elegies, as does Archilochus; for they were captured by the Ephesians.

Concerning the Ephesians themselves, Democritus of Ephesus, in the first book of his work *On the Temple at Ephesus*, recounts their luxury and the dyed garments they wear, writing the following: "The Ionian garments are dyed violet, purple, and saffron, woven with diamond patterns; the borders are decorated with figures of animals at equal intervals. There are also tunics <term>sarapes: a Persian-style loose-fitting tunic</term> in apple-yellow, purple, and white, while others are sea-purple. There are also Corinthian-made <term>kalasiris: a fringed linen tunic or garment</term>. Some are purple, others violet, and some hyacinth-colored. One might also see those the color of flame or the sea. There are also Persian fringed tunics, which are the most beautiful of all. One might also see," he says, "the so-called <term>aktaia: a costly Persian outer garment</term>, which is the most expensive of the Persian robes. It is as light as a shadow for the sake of comfort, yet it is encrusted with golden beads. These beads are all fastened to the inside with purple thread at intervals in the middle." He says that the Ephesians used all these things when they gave themselves over to luxury.

Regarding the luxury of the Samians, Duris in his history quotes the poems of Asius of Samos, noting that they wore bracelets on their arms, and when they celebrated the festival of Hera, they would walk with their hair carefully combed back over their necks and shoulders. This custom is also attested by the following proverb: "To walk like a Samian at the festival of Hera, with braided hair." The verses of Asius are as follows:

> They would go in this manner, whenever they had combed their locks,
> To the sacred precinct of Hera, wrapped in beautiful garments;
> With snow-white tunics they covered the floor of the wide earth,
> And golden ornaments like cicadas <note>The Greeks often wore golden cicada-shaped pins to fasten their hair, symbolizing they were "children of the soil."</note> were upon them,
> Their hair tossed by the wind in golden bonds,
> And skillfully wrought bracelets were around their arms...

Heraclides of Pontus, in his work *On Pleasure*, says that the Samians indulged in luxury to such an excess that they destroyed their city through their petty squabbles with one another, just as the Sybarites did. The Colophonians, as Phylarchus says, were originally harsh in their discipline; but when <margin>The flight of the Colophonians.</margin> they drifted into luxury after making a friendship and alliance with the Lydians, they would go out with their hair elaborately adorned with gold ornaments, as Xenophanes says: 

> Having learned useless luxuries from the Lydians,
> While they were still free from hateful tyranny,
> They went to the marketplace wearing robes of all-purple,
> No fewer than a thousand in all,
> Boasting in their beautiful, well-groomed hair,
> Drenched in the scent of prepared ointments.

They became so dissolved by untimely drunkenness that some of them never saw the sun either rising or setting <note>Meaning they slept all day and stayed awake all night partying.</note>. They even established a law, which was still in effect in our time, that female flute-players, harp-players, and all such performers should receive their wages from early morning until midday, and from the lighting of the lamps until the rest of the night...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ancient peoples who were corrupted by excessive luxury (tryphē). It follows a discussion on the Ionians and transitions into the decadent habits of the Byzantines, Thessalians, and various Italian groups like the Syracusans and Capuans, often citing the historian Theopompus and the philosopher Plato to show how such lifestyles lead to political ruin.</meta>

-> ATHENAEUS: THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS <-

...they were inclined toward drunkenness. Theopompus, in the fifteenth book of his *Histories*, says that one thousand of them wore purple robes, a garment that was once rare <note>original: "stolas," a long, flowing robe</note>, which is why it was even sought after by kings. Purple dye was considered equal in weight to silver when its value was tested. Because of this kind of upbringing, they succumbed to tyranny and various misfortunes, and their homeland was eventually destroyed. Diogenes the Babylonian also says much the same about them in the first book of his *Laws*. Regarding the luxury <note>original: "tryphē"</note> of the Ionians in general, Antiphanes says the following in *Phaon*: “From where has this delicate, pleasure-loving crowd of Ionians, with their soft cloaks, set out?” 

<margin>Budé, Book on the Asse <note>A reference to Guillaume Budé’s 16th-century scholarly work on ancient Roman coinage and weights.</note></margin>

Theophrastus, in his treatise *On Pleasure*, says that because of the Ionians' extreme luxury, even now there is a famous "golden proverb" told about them. 

<margin>The decline of the Ionians and Byzantium.</margin>

Theopompus, in the eighth book of his *History of Philip*, also says that some of the king's companions lived in great luxury. Regarding the Byzantines and Chalcedonians, the same Theopompus says: “The Byzantines, because they had long lived under a democracy and their city was situated at a commercial center, spent all their time in the marketplace and the harbor; they were undisciplined and accustomed to gathering and drinking in the taverns.” As for the Chalcedonians, before they shared in the government with the Byzantines, they devoted themselves to better pursuits and a more orderly life. But once they had a taste of the Byzantines' democracy, they were corrupted by luxury; from being the most sober and moderate of people in their daily lives, they became hard drinkers and extravagant spenders.

In the first book of the *History of Philip*, he also says that the nation of the Umbrians, as well as those living near the Adriatic Sea, were quite decadent; he notes they were similar to the Lydian Boeotians and possessed a fertile land, which led them to great prosperity. 

<margin>Luxury of the Thessalians.</margin>

Speaking of the Thessalians in his fourth book, he says that some spend their lives with dancing girls, while others pass the day in dicing, drinking, and similar debaucheries. They are more concerned with how to set their tables with all kinds of side dishes <note>original: "opson," meaning delicacies or seasonings eaten with bread</note> than with how to order their own lives. He says the Pharsalians are the laziest and most extravagant of all men. It is generally agreed, as Critias says, that the Thessalians became the most extravagant of all Greeks in both their lifestyle and their clothing; this was the reason they brought the Persians into Greece, for the invaders envied their luxury and opulence.

<margin>Of the Aetolians.</margin>

Regarding the Aetolians, Polybius says in the thirteenth book of his *Histories* that due to continuous wars and their extravagant lifestyle, they became burdened with debt. Agatharchides, in the twelfth book of his *Histories*, says that the Aetolians are more ready to face death than other men precisely because they live so luxuriously and seek out pleasure more intensely than others. 

<margin>Of the Syracusans.</margin>

The Sicilians and Syracusans are also notorious for their luxury, as Aristophanes says in *The Banqueters*: “But you did not learn these things when I sent you there; instead, you learned to drink, and then to sing badly at a Syracusan table, with Sybaritic feasts <note>Sybaris was a Greek city in Italy famous for such extreme wealth and pleasure-seeking that it gave us the word "sybarite."</note> and Chian wine from Spartan cups.” Plato says in his *Letters*, having this same thought: “With this mindset, I went to Italy and Sicily when I first arrived. Once I got there, the life I found did not please me at all—stuffing oneself twice a day and never sleeping alone at night, and all the other habits that follow such a lifestyle. For from these habits, no man under heaven could ever become wise if he were raised in them from youth, nor would he ever strive to become temperate.” In the third book of the *Republic*, he writes: “A Syracusan or Sicilian table, and the variety of Sicilian side dishes—you do not seem to approve of these, but you find fault with the Corinthian girl who is a favorite of men who intend to be in good physical condition, and you dislike Attic pastries, which are thought to be treats.” 

Posidonius, in the sixteenth book of his *Histories*, speaking of the cities in Syria and how they lived luxuriously, writes this: “Because of the abundance of their land, the people in the cities held frequent gatherings where they feasted constantly, using the gymnasia as if they were baths—anointing themselves with expensive oil and perfumes. They treated the communal clubhouses <note>original: "grammateia," likely referring to guild halls or dining clubs</note> as if they were their own homes, spending most of the day filling their bellies with wine and food, even taking much of it home with them. They were entertained by the sound of the lyre <note>original: "chelônidos," literally "of the tortoise," referring to the lyre's shell</note>, so that the entire cities echoed with such noises.” 

<margin>Luxury of the Lucanians.</margin>

Agatharchides, in the thirty-fifth book of his *Histories*, says that the Lucanians, who are neighbors of the Lycians, became heavily in debt due to their wastefulness and luxury. Because of their laziness and love of pleasure, they were unable to repay their loans and pinned their hopes on Mithridates, considering the cancellation of debts to be their prize. In the thirty-first book, he says the Zacynthians are inexperienced in war because they are accustomed to luxury and wealth. 

<margin>Of the Capuans.</margin>

Polybius, in his seventh book, says the people of Capua in Campania, having acquired great wealth due to the fertility of their land, drifted into luxury and extravagance, even surpassing the fame of Croton and Sybaris. 

<margin>Livy, book 3 of the Punic War.</margin>

Being unable to bear their current prosperity, he says, they called in Hannibal. Because of this, they suffered incurable calamities at the hands of the Romans. The Petelini <note>original: "Pitilinioi"</note>, however, maintained their loyalty to the Romans with such great fortitude...

It cites philosophers like Plato and historians like Polybius to argue that indulgence breeds laziness, debt, and eventual conquest by enemies.</summary>

-> BOOK XII <-

...they showed a great amount of endurance when besieged by Hannibal <note>The Carthaginian general during the Second Punic War (218–201 BCE).</note>, so that after eating all the hides <note>animal skins</note> in the city, and consuming not just the bark but the tender shoots of all the trees around the city, and having endured the siege for eleven months with no one coming to their aid—neither the Romans nor the
<margin>The Curetes.</margin> Curetes—they finally surrendered. Regarding the Curetes, Phylarchus says in the eleventh book of his *Histories* that Aeschylus claims they were so called because of their "high fortune," and they did not use common greetings, but rather wore their hair in luxurious locks like delicate young girls, which is why the term "to shear the people" <note>original: "keirai laon," a pun on Curetes and the Greek word for shearing/cutting hair</note> was used. Agathon, in his play *Thyestes*, says that those who came to woo the daughter of Pronax were dressed exquisitely in all other respects and wore their hair long; but when they failed to win the marriage, he says, "we sheared our hair as witnesses of our luxury," for it is surely a desirable thing to toy with one's mind. At any rate, we immediately have a
<margin>The luxury of the Cumaeans.</margin> namesake for this fame, that the Curetes are so named for the "shorn" grace of their hair. And the Cumaeans in Italy, as Hyperochus says (or whoever wrote the *Cumaean History* attributed to him), lived their lives wearing gold jewelry and flower-patterned clothing, and would go out to the fields with their wives riding in horse-drawn chariots.
Now, regarding the luxury of nations and cities, I have mentioned these many things. But concerning the luxury of individual men, I have heard the following. Ctesias <note>A Greek physician and historian who lived at the Persian court.</note>, in the third book of his *Persian History*, says that all those who ruled Asia were very devoted to luxury, but especially Ninyas, the son of Ninus and
<margin>Regarding Ninyas.</margin> Semiramis. This man remained indoors and was seen by no one except his eunuchs and his own women. Such a man was also
<margin>Regarding Sardanapalus. 35.</margin> Sardanapalus <note>The legendary last king of Assyria, often portrayed in Greek literature as the ultimate symbol of decadence.</note>, whom some say was the son of Anacyndaraxes and others the son of Anabaxarus. When Arbaces, one of the generals under him and a Mede by birth, managed through one of the eunuchs to be admitted to see Sardanapalus, it was with great difficulty that he was permitted. When the Mede entered and saw him, he found him painted with white-lead <term>psimythion: a white lead-based cosmetic used to whiten the skin</term> and adorned in a womanly fashion, carding purple wool among his concubines, sitting with them with his eyebrows painted, wearing a woman’s robe, his beard closely shaved and his skin smoothed with pumice—being whiter than milk—and his eyes lined with makeup. Most historians, including Duris, report that Arbaces was so outraged that such a man should rule them that he stabbed him to death. But Ctesias says that Sardanapalus actually went to war, and having gathered a great army, he was eventually defeated by Arbaces and died by setting himself on fire in his palace. He built a pyre <note>a funeral wood-pile</note> four plethra <note>roughly 400 feet</note> high, upon which he placed one hundred and fifty golden couches and an equal number of golden tables. He also built a chamber one hundred feet long out of wood within the pyre, and there he spread couches and lay down himself with his wife, while his concubines lay on the other couches. For he had three sons and two daughters, and seeing that his affairs were failing, he sent them away to Nineveh to the king there, giving them three thousand talents of gold. He roofed the chamber with large, thick beams and then placed many thick logs all around it so that there was no way out. Inside, he placed ten million units of gold and one hundred million talents of silver, along with garments, purple robes, and all sorts of apparel. Then he ordered the pyre to be lit, and it burned for fifteen days. Those who saw the smoke from a distance marveled and thought he was performing a sacrifice, for only the eunuchs knew the truth. Thus Sardanapalus, having lived in extreme pleasure, died in a noble manner. But Clearchus, in the fourth book of his *Lives*, tells us that the king offered prizes to those who could invent a new delicious food, having no law for his own conduct. There is a delicacy called, I believe, the "Brain of Zeus and the King" <note>a metaphor for the most exquisite luxury</note>. Hence Sardanapalus, who honored pleasures throughout his entire life, shows in the sculpture on his tomb his fingers in a snapping gesture, as if laughing at the fact that human affairs are
<margin>Sardanapalus</margin> worth no more than the snap of a pair of fingers—a gesture he is depicted making twice, as if to say the rest of the world will hear of it. It seems then that Sardanapalus was not entirely idle, for the inscription on his tomb reads: "Sardanapalus, son of Anacyndaraxes, built Anchiale and Tarsus in a single day, but now he is dead." Amyntas, in the first book of his *Stations*, says there is a high mound in Nineveh which Cyrus tore down during the siege to use for his own earthworks against the city. This mound was said to be that of Sardanapalus, the king of Nineveh, and upon it was a stone pillar with Chaldean <note>Assyrian/Babylonian</note> writing, which Choerilus translated into verse as follows: "I was king, and as long as I saw the light of the sun, I drank, I ate, I loved, knowing that the time humans live is short and subject to many changes and hardships; whatever goods I leave behind, others will enjoy. Therefore, I did not miss a single day of doing this." But Cleitarchus, in the fourth book of his *History of Alexander*, says that Sardanapalus died of old age after the fall of the Syrian Empire. Aristobulus says that at Anchiale (which he says Sardanapalus founded), Alexander the Great camped while marching against the Persians, and not far away was the tomb of Sardanapalus, upon which stood a stone figure with the fingers of the right hand joined as if snapping them. On it was inscribed:

<vocab>karteria (endurance), Annibas (Hannibal), Kouretes (Curetes), Phylarchos (Phylarchus), Aischylos (Aeschylus), Agathon, Kymaioi (Cumaeans), Ktesias (Ctesias), Ninyas, Sardanapalos (Sardanapalus), Arbikes (Arbaces), Louris (Duris), Klearchos (Clearchus), Amyntas, Choirilos (Choerilus), Alexandros (Alexander), Aristoboulos (Aristobulus), Anchiale</vocab>

# ATHENAEUS: THE LEARNED BANQUETERS
### Book XII (Continued)

...it was written for him in unintelligible characters: "Sardanapalus, son of Anacyndaraxes, built Anchiale and Tarsus in a single day. Eat, drink, and play, as all other human things are not worth a snap of the fingers" <note>original: "apokrotēmatos"—literally the sound of a finger-snap; a gesture of dismissive contempt</note>; this is what it seems to say. But Sardanapalus was not the only one honored this way; there was also Anthrocolus the Phrygian. For he too was ashamed of himself <note>meaning he hid his true nature or was excessively modest in a strange way</note> and wore a woman’s garment, adorning himself more beautifully than a woman, as Mnaseas says in the third book of his *History of Europe*.

<margin>Whose last relief?</margin>
Clearchus, in the fifth book of his *Lives*, says that Sagaris the Mariandynian was so decadent that he was fed from a wet nurse’s breast until old age, so that he would not have to labor by chewing his food. He never brought his hand lower than his navel, which is why Aristotle, mocking Xenocrates of Chalcedon <note>a philosopher and head of Plato's Academy</note> because he would not use his hand to hold his genitals while urinating, said: "He has pure hands, but a defiled mind." Ctesias records that Annaros, a governor under the King and ruler of Babylon, wore women's clothing and ornaments. He also relates that while the King was at dinner, one hundred women would enter his banquet, playing harps and singing. They would play while he was dining.

<margin>Ninus.</margin>
Phoenix of Colophon, a poet, speaking of Ninus <note>the legendary founder of Nineveh</note> in the first book of his *Iambics*, says: "There was a man named Ninus, as I hear, an Assyrian, who possessed a sea of gold and other things more numerous than the sands of the Caspian. He never saw a star, nor perhaps even desired to; he did not maintain the sacred fire among the Magi, as is the law, touching the gods with a straight wand; he was no sacrificer, nor a judge of the people, nor did he learn to speak to the masses or to count. Instead, he only knew how to drink and mix wine, and all other such things; he lived like a commoner. When the man died, he left a saying for everyone where Ninus is now: 'Look at my tomb, hear it, whether you be Assyrian or a teller of tales, or a long-haired Indian from the distant lakes. For I proclaim something else: I, Ninus, was once a breath of life, but now I am nothing, made only of earth. I have only what I ate, and what I sang, and what I loved <note>This is a famous epitaph format emphasizing that only sensual pleasures remain with the dead in memory</note>. Our riches are carried off by strangers coming together, just as the Bacchants tear a raw kid-goat. When I went to Hades, I took neither gold, nor horse, nor silver chariot; I am now much ash, and he who wore the miter lies here.'"

<margin>Straton's luxurious living.</margin>
Theopompus, in the fifteenth book of his *Philippic Histories*, says that Straton, the King of the Sidonians, surpassed all men in luxury and decadence. He lived much like the Phaeacians described by Homer—continually feasting, drinking, and listening to harp-players and rhapsodes. Straton continued this lifestyle for a long time, but he was even more deranged in his pursuit of pleasure than the Phaeacians; for while they, as Homer says, held their drinking parties with their own wives and daughters, Straton prepared his gatherings with flute-girls, harp-players, and lyre-players. He summoned many courtesans from the Peloponnesus, many musicians from Ionia, and young girl-courtesans from all of Greece, some for singing and others for dancing, for whom he organized competitions among his friends. He spent his time in these gatherings, rejoicing in such a life, being by nature a slave to his pleasures.

<margin>Straton and Nicocles against each other.</margin>
He was even more motivated by his rivalry with Nicocles. For they happened to be exceedingly ambitious toward one another, each striving to make his own life more pleasant and extravagant. They reached such a point of competition, as we hear, that they would inquire from travelers about the furnishings of each other’s houses and the costliness of the sacrifices performed by the other, and they vied to surpass one another in such things. They were eager to appear happy and blessed, but they did not meet with a fortunate end to their lives; both were destroyed by a violent death. Anaximenes, in the work titled *The Successions of Kings*, reporting the same things about Straton, says that Nicocles, who reigned in Salamis in Cyprus, rivaled him in luxury and licentiousness, and that both died violently. In the first book of the *Philippics*, Theopompus, speaking of Philip, says that on the third day he arrived at Onocarsis, a place in Thrace, which had a large, beautifully arranged grove, very pleasant for living in, especially during the summer season. For it was one of the spots favored by Cotys, who, of all the kings who have lived in Thrace, was the most driven toward luxury and decadence. As he traveled through the country, wherever he saw places shaded by trees and flowing with water, he built banquet halls. Visiting them whenever it happened, he would offer sacrifices to the gods and spend time with his subordinates, being happy and blessed until he began to blaspheme against Athena and commit outrages. The author explains next that Cotys prepared a banquet as if Athena were being married to him, and having prepared a bridal chamber, he waited for the goddess in a drunken state. Having already lost his mind, he sent one of his bodyguards to see if the goddess had arrived at the chamber. When the man returned and said there was no one in the room, Cotys shot him with an arrow and killed him. He killed a second man for the same reason, until a third, understanding what was happening, said that the goddess had been waiting for him for a long time. This king, once becoming jealous of his own wife, with his own hands...

<summary>This page recounts the extreme and often delusional decadence of ancient rulers like Sardanapalus, Ninus, and Straton of Sidon. It highlights how their pursuit of luxury (tryphē) led to moral decay, competitive extravagance with rivals, and ultimately, madness or violent deaths.</summary>

### BOOK XII

<margin>The luxury of Chabrias.</margin>
...he would lift a man up with his hands, starting from the genitals. In the thirteenth book of his *Philippic History*, Theopompus <note>a 4th-century BCE historian known for his biting critiques of moral character</note>, while recording the story of Chabrias the Athenian, says that he was unable to live in the city, partly because of his licentiousness and his own expensive lifestyle, and partly because of the Athenians themselves. For the Athenians are harsh toward everyone. Because of this, their most famous men chose to live outside the city: Iphicrates in Thrace, Conon in Cyprus, Timotheus in Lesbos, Chares in Sigeum, and Chabrias himself in Egypt.

<margin>And of Chares.</margin>
Regarding Chares, Theopompus says in his forty-fifth book that although Chares was sluggish and slow, he lived a life of great luxury. When he went on military campaigns, he was accompanied by flute-girls, harpists, and common prostitutes. Part of the money contributed for the war he spent on this arrogance <note>original: "hybris"—here referring to insolent luxury or excess</note>, and the rest he left behind in Athens for the orators who proposed the decrees and for those private citizens who served as jurors in the courts. For these actions, the Athenian people never grew indignant; on the contrary, they loved him more than any other citizen, and with good reason. For they themselves lived in such a manner that the young men spent their time among flute-girls and at the houses of courtesans, while those a little older spent theirs in gambling and similar profligacies. Indeed, the entire populace spent more on public banquets and meat distributions than on the administration of the city. In the work by Theopompus titled *On the Treasures Plundered from Delphi*, he says that sixty talents were given to Chares the Athenian through Lysander, with which he feasted the Athenians in the marketplace, offering sacrifices to celebrate a victory in a battle against Philip’s mercenaries. These mercenaries were led by Adaeus, who was nicknamed "The Cock" <note>original: "alektryōn"</note>. Heracleides, the comic poet, mentions him in this way: "Taking Adaeus, Philip’s Cock, while he was crowing and wandering about, he cut him down. For he did not yet have a single crest <note>original: "lophon"—a play on a helmet crest and a rooster's comb</note>; but after cutting him down, he spent quite a lot, and Chares was then treated like a noble by the Athenians."

<margin>The Peisistratids and Pasiphane.</margin>
Duris <note>an historian and ruler of Samos</note> records the same things. But Idomeneus says that the Peisistratids, Hippias and Hipparchus, invented festivals and revelries. Because of this, a great number of horses became common among them, which is why their rule became burdensome. Their father, Peisistratus, also indulged in countless pleasures, to the extent that he did not even place guards in his fields or gardens, as Theopompus records in his twenty-first book; instead, he allowed anyone who wished to enter and enjoy themselves, taking whatever they needed. Later, Cimon did the same, imitating him. Concerning Cimon, Theopompus says in the tenth book of the *Philippic History*: "Cimon the Athenian did not station any guard over the fruit in his fields and gardens, so that any citizen who wished could enter to pick the fruit and take whatever they needed from the estates. Furthermore, he kept his house open to everyone, and a simple meal <note>original: "deipnon eutele"—an inexpensive but sufficient meal</note> was always prepared for many people, so that any of the poor Athenians who approached could enter and dine." He also looked after those who were in need every day. They say he was accompanied by two or three young men carrying small coins, and he would order them to give money whenever someone approached him in need. They say he even contributed toward burials; and doing this often, whenever he saw a citizen poorly dressed, he would command one of the young men following him to exchange clothes with that person. Because of all these things, he was held in high regard and was the first among the citizens. However, Peisistratus also became burdensome in many respects; indeed, some say that the mask of Dionysus at Athens is an image of him.

<margin>And the profligacy of Pericles.</margin>
Heracleides of Pontus, in his work *On Pleasure*, says that Pericles "the Olympian" <note>a nickname for Pericles suggesting his god-like authority and oratorical thunder</note> drove his wife out of his house and chose a life of pleasure. He lived with Aspasia, the courtesan from Megara, and spent the greater part of his property on her. As for Themistocles, at a time when the Athenians were not yet given to drunkenness or the use of courtesans, he openly harnessed four courtesans to a chariot and drove through the crowded Cerameicus <note>a prominent neighborhood and cemetery in Athens</note> at dawn. Idomeneus mentions this ambiguously, whether he harnessed the four courtesans like horses or whether he simply had them ride upon the four-horse chariot. Phasis, in the third book of his *History of Magnesia*, says that when Themistocles held the office of "Wreath-Bearer" <note>original: "stephanēphoros"—a high magistracy in certain Greek cities</note> in Magnesia, he sacrificed to Athena and named the festival the Panathenaea, and while sacrificing to Dionysus with a mask, he also established the Festival of the Pitchers <note>original: "Choes"</note> there.

<margin>The lack of control of Themistocles.</margin>
Clearchus, in the first book of his *On Friendship*, says that Themistocles, having built a most beautiful dining room <note>original: "triklinon"—a room for three couches</note> in Magnesia, said he would be content if he could fill it with friends.

<margin>The luxury of Artemon.</margin>
Chamaeleon of Pontus, in his work *On Anacreon*, cites the verse: "Blonde-haired Artemon, who now frequents Eurypyle," and says that Artemon received the nickname "Artemon of the Litter" <note>original: "periphoretos"—meaning 'carried around'</note> because he lived so luxuriously that he was carried about on a couch. Indeed, Anacreon says that he turned toward a luxurious life after a period of hardship, in these lines: "Formerly he wore a Berberean <note>foreign/shabby</note> covering, and wooden earrings in his ears, and around his ribs a hairless, newly-washed ox-hide from a wretched shield; he associated with bread-sellers and voluntary outcasts, the wicked Artemon, finding a fraudulent life. Often he put his neck in the stocks, often on the wheel, often his back was whipped with a leather lash and his beard was plucked out. But now he rides in a carriage, wearing golden earrings and delicate things..."
<meta>catchword: boy</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the decadent lifestyles and excessive generosity of famous Athenian leaders like Chabrias, Chares, and Cimon, arguing that their luxury either forced them into exile or was used to manipulate public favor. It also details the transition of figures like Artemon from poverty to extreme, effeminate luxury.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of famous figures known for their excessive luxury (tryphē). It transitions from general Athenian commanders to a detailed and scandalous portrait of Alcibiades, the famous and controversial Athenian statesman, before touching on the Persian-influenced habits of later leaders like Pausanias, Alexander the Great, and Demetrius Poliorcetes.</meta>

# ATHENIAN DEIPNOSOPHISTS

<margin>Alcibiades</margin>
...a young servant followed him, and he even carried an ivory sunshade for his wives. Regarding the handsome Alcibiades, Satyrus <note>Satyrus of Kallatis, a 3rd-century BCE biographer known for collecting scandalous anecdotes</note> says in his *Histories* that when he was in Ionia, he appeared even more luxurious than the Ionians themselves; but in Thebes, by training his body and exercising, he was more "Boeotian" than the Boeotians themselves. In Thessaly, he raised horses and drove chariots more competitively than those most devoted to the sport. In Sparta, he practiced such endurance and austerity that he outdid the Spartans. He even surpassed the Thracians in their habit of drinking unmixed wine <note>The Greeks usually diluted their wine with water; drinking it "neat" was considered a sign of barbarian excess or alcoholism</note>. Regarding his wife Hipparete, whom he neglected, some say he paid a fine of a thousand drachmas. Being most beautiful in form, he grew his hair long quite late into his youth and wore a particular style of shoes which were called "Alcibiades" after him. Whenever he served as a chorus leader and marched in procession wearing a purple robe, he was admired as he entered the theater not only by the men, but also by the women. This is why Antisthenes the Socratic, who had seen Alcibiades with his own eyes, says that he was strong, manly, bold, and beautiful even as he aged. Whenever he set out on travels abroad, he treated four of the allied cities as if they were his personal handmaidens.

<margin>The Chians (Plutarch)</margin>
For him, the Ephesians constructed a Persian-style tent; the Chians provided fodder for his horses; the Cyzicenes provided the sacrificial animals and the victims for his priestly duties; and the Lesbians provided the wine and everything else needed for his daily living. When he arrived at the Olympic Games to compete, he dedicated two paintings by the artist Aglaophon <note>a famous painter and the father of Polygnotus</note>. One showed the personified cities of Olympia and Pythia crowning him. In the other, Nemea <note>the personification of the Nemean Games</note> was seated, with Alcibiades on her knees, appearing more beautiful than any of the female faces. Even when serving as a general, he wished to remain beautiful; he had a shield made of gold and ivory, upon which was an emblem of Eros holding a thunderbolt <note>original: "keravnon ankylemenos"—a provocative symbol suggesting his charisma was as powerful as Zeus's weapon</note>. Once, when he went on a drunken revel to the house of Anytus <note>a wealthy Athenian, later one of Socrates' accusers</note>, who was his lover, he was accompanied by his friends, including Thrasyllus (who was a poor man). After drinking to Thrasyllus’s health with half of the cups and bowls laid out, he ordered his attendants to carry the rest off to Thrasyllus’s house. Having shown this "affection," he left Anytus. When some guests remarked that Alcibiades had acted ungratefully, Anytus, in a very gentlemanly and loving manner, replied, "By Zeus, no! He has acted most kindly; for when he had the power to take everything, he left us half." The orator Lysias, speaking of his luxury, says that when Axiochus and Alcibiades sailed together to the Hellespont, they both married Medontiada of Abydos out of sheer recklessness and lived with her together. Later, a daughter was born to them, and they claimed they could not tell which of them was the father. 

<margin>Alcibiades and his eunuchs</margin>
When the girl reached a marriageable age, they both slept with her; and if Alcibiades was the one with her, they said she was Axiochus's daughter, but if it was Axiochus, she was Alcibiades's. He was also mocked by the comic poet Eupolis for his licentiousness regarding women and his sycophants: "Let Alcibiades come out from the women! Why do you talk nonsense? Go home and exercise your own wife, Lamarta." And Pherecrates says: "For Alcibiades was not a man, as it seems, but is now the man of all women." While in Sparta, he even seduced Timaea, the wife of King Agis. When some rebuked him for this, he claimed he did it not out of lust, but so that a son of his might rule over Sparta, and so that the kings would no longer be called descendants of Heracles, but of Alcibiades. Even while acting as general, he brought along with him Timandra, the mother of the famous Corinthian courtesan Lais, and Theodote, the Athenian courtesan. After his exile, when he had gained control of the Hellespont for the Athenians and taken five thousand Peloponnesians as prisoners, he sent them to Athens. Returning to his homeland after these events, he crowned the Athenian triremes <note>warships</note> with olive branches, headbands, and ribbons, and towed the captured ships with their figureheads removed. He sailed in with two hundred captured ships full of spoils, Laconian armor, and Peloponnesian gear. The trireme on which he himself sailed approached the docks of Piraeus with purple sails. As they drew near and the rowers took up their oars, Chrysogonus played the flute for the rowing rhythm, dressed in the sacred robe of a Pythian victor. Callippides the tragic actor gave the signals, dressed in his theatrical costume. Because of this, someone remarked wittily: "Sparta could not endure two Lysanders, nor Athens two Alcibiades." Alcibiades even imitated the "Medism" <note>the adoption of Persian customs</note> of Pausanias, and while socializing with Pharnabazus, he learned the Persian language, just as Themistocles had. Duris, in the twenty-second book of his *Histories*, says that Pausanias, the King of the Spartans, set aside his ancestral cloak and put on Persian dress. Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, wore a fine robe and a golden crown over his sacred tragic vestments. Alexander, after he became master of Asia, also used Persian robes. But Demetrius <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes, the "Besieger"</note> surpassed everyone: he had footwear made at great expense. 

<margin>Extravagant Persian-style robes, and Pausanias's decadent lifestyle.</margin>

-># ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS<-

...and Dionysius, who became the scourge of all Sicily, arrived at the city of the Locrians. Because his mother, Doris, was a Locrian by birth, he prepared a house there in the city, the largest one available, carpeting the floors with wild thyme and roses. He would summon the daughters of the Locrians in turn, and stripped naked among naked girls, he felt no shame as he rolled about on that flowered carpet. Not long afterward, however, those who had been so insulted rose up. Having seized his wife and children, they brought them under their power. To avenge the outrages committed against them, they first tortured the women by thrusting needles under their fingernails and then killed them. After they had died, they ground up their bones in <term>mortars</term> <note>Large stone bowls used for crushing grain or spices</note> and distributed the remaining flesh, swearing an oath that anyone who did not taste of it would be cursed. This is why they ate their flesh to fulfill that unholy curse, so that the food they prepared would be consumed; then they cast the remains into the sea. As for Dionysius himself, he ended his life as a <term>metragyrtes</term> <note>A wandering beggar-priest of the Great Mother goddess, Cybele</note>, carrying a tambourine and ending his life miserably. He had always been careful to avoid losing his life in the so-called "House of Phlous," yet he ultimately considered <term>hybris</term> <note>Arrogant insolence or outrage against others</note> to be the destruction of all things. 

<margin>Gelon's pool and the Horn of Amalthea.</margin>
Diodorus Siculus, in his work *On the Library*, says that the people of Akragas constructed a magnificent pool for Gelon <note>Gelon was the tyrant of Syracuse and Gela in the 5th century BCE</note>, which had a perimeter of seven <term>stades</term> <note>Roughly 0.8 miles</note> and a depth of twenty cubits. Into this, river and spring water was diverted to create a fish-pond, providing a great many fish for Gelon's luxury and enjoyment. He also kept a multitude of swans there, making it a most delightful sight. Later, however, it was neglected and became filled with earth. Duris, in the tenth book of his *History of Agathocles*, says that near the city of Hipponium there is another grove of surpassing beauty, well-watered, in which there is a place called the <term>Horn of Amalthea</term> <note>A mythical horn that could provide unlimited food and drink; here, a metaphor for a lush, fertile spot</note>, which Gelon is said to have constructed. Silenus of Calatia, in the third book of his *History of Sicily*, says that near Syracuse there is a garden sumptuously prepared which is called "The Myth," where King Hiero <note>Hiero II of Syracuse</note> used to conduct his business. Indeed, the entire Panormus region of Sicily is called "The Garden" because it is entirely full of wild and cultivated trees, as Callias says in the eighth book of his *Histories*. Speaking of Damophilus the Sicilian—the one whose luxury ignited the <term>Servile War</term> <note>The first major slave revolt against Rome, roughly 135–132 BCE</note>—he writes the following: "Being a slave to luxury and wickedness, he used to travel through the country in a four-wheeled carriage, leading along horses, handsome servants, and outrunners, as well as a swarm of flatterers and boys." Later, he and his whole household met a shameful end, having been prostituted by his own servants.

<margin>The luxury of Demetrius of Phalerum.</margin>
Demetrius of Phalerum, as Duris says in the sixteenth book of his *Histories*, came into possession of twelve hundred talents every year. Spending only a small portion of this on his soldiers and the administration of the city, he squandered all the rest through his innate lack of self-control. He held magnificent banquets every day, hosting a great number of guests. In the expense of his dinners, he surpassed even the Macedonians, and in their refined cleanliness, he surpassed the Cyprians and Phoenicians. Perfumes were sprinkled upon the ground. Many of the floors in the men’s quarters were decorated with floral patterns worked by skilled craftsmen. There were also secret encounters with women and nocturnal love affairs with young men. Although Demetrius laid down laws for others, he arranged his own life to be entirely lawless. He even took great care of his appearance, dyeing the hair on his head blonde, rubbing his face with <term>youth-restoring unguents</term> <note>original: paiderote; likely a cosmetic lead-based white or a specific skin-clearer</note>, and anointing himself with other cosmetics; for he wished to appear cheerful and pleasant to those who met him. In the procession of the Dionysia, which he led when he was Archon, a chorus sang a poem for him composed by Seiramenes, in which he was called "sun-like"—"The Archon, exceptionally sweet and gentle-natured, honors you with god-like honors." Carystius of Pergamum, in the third book of his *Notes*, says that after his brother Himeraeus was executed by Antipater, Demetrius of Phalerum himself lived with Nicanor, being accused of the same things as his two brothers. Having become a friend of Cassander, he gained great power. At first, his lunch was simple, consisting of a dish of various olives and island cheese. But when he became wealthy, he bought Mochion, the best chef and banquet-manager of that time. So much was prepared every day that he would give the leftovers to Mochion. Within two years, Mochion bought two tenement houses and began to insult free-born boys and the wives of the most prominent citizens. The boys’ lovers, like Theognis, were all investigated, and Demetrius became so indulgent that after he had taken a walk after lunch, a great many of the most beautiful boys would gather in the same place on the following days just to be seen by him. 

Nicolaus the Peripatetic, in the hundred and tenth book of his *Histories*, says that Lucullus,

Silius was also notorious among the Romans for luxury and soft living, as Rutilius says (we have already spoken of Apicius). Almost all historians record that Pausanias and Lysander also became notorious for their luxury. This is why Agis said to Lysander that "Sparta has given birth to a second Pausanias." <meta>This page continues the discussion of "tryphē" (luxury and soft living) among the famous figures of antiquity. Having previously discussed tyrants and kings, the text now turns to the paradoxical cases of the Spartan general Lysander, the extravagant painter Parrhasius, and the pleasure-oriented philosophy of Aristippus.</meta>

-># BOOK XII<-

In the tenth book of his *History of Greece*, [Theopompus] says the opposite about Lysander: that he was hardworking, able to court both private citizens and kings, temperate, and superior to all pleasures. At least, though he was master of nearly all Greece, he will not be seen in any of the cities to have rushed toward sexual pleasures or to have indulged in untimely drunkenness and drinking bouts. Among the ancients, the habits of luxury and expenditure were practiced to such an extent that even Parrhasius the painter wrapped himself in purple and wore a golden crown on his head, as Clearchus records in his *Lives*. For this man, having indulged in luxury through his painting beyond all measure, laid claim to virtue in word and inscribed the following on the works he completed: 

->Parrhasius, a man of delicate life <note>original: "habrodiaitos," referring to a lifestyle of refined luxury</note> who honors virtue, painted this,<-
->From his famous fatherland, Ephesus.<-
->Nor did I forget my father Euonymus, who sired<-
->A genuine son of the Greeks, foremost in art.<-

He boasted without fear of divine retribution about these things, saying things that were incredible to hear. For he said: 

->I say that the clear boundaries of this art have now been found<-
->By my own hand, and a limit is fixed that cannot be surpassed.<-
->But nothing born of mortals is blameless.<-

Once, when he was competing in Samos against an inferior artist on the subject of Ajax <note>The Greek hero who committed suicide after losing a contest for Achilles' armor</note> and was defeated, he said to his friends who were grieving with him <margin>See Hermolaus in his corrections of Pliny</margin> that he himself cared little, but he felt for Ajax, who had now been defeated a second time. Due to his luxury, he wore a purple robe and a white headband on his head; he also carried a staff entwined with gold spirals and fastened the straps of his slippers with golden laces. Yet he did not find the labor of his art burdensome, but painted easily while singing, as Theophrastus records in his work *On Happiness*. He used to tell wondrous tales—for instance, when he was painting the Heracles at Lindos, he claimed the god appeared to him in a dream and posed himself in the proper stance for the painting. Thus he inscribed upon the panel:

->Just as he appeared many times visiting in the night,<-
->To Parrhasius in sleep, such is he here to behold.<-

<margin>Aristippus the happy.</margin>
Even entire schools of philosophers made claims regarding luxury. The so-called Cyrenaic school, which took its start from Aristippus the Socratic, accepted "soft living" and claimed that this was the "end" <term>telos</term> <note>The ultimate goal or purpose of life</note>, and that happiness was established in it. He said that happiness exists only in the moment of enjoyment <note>original: "monochronos," meaning "single-moment" or "fleeting"</note>, not considering it to consist in the memory of past enjoyments or the hope of future ones, but judging the "good" by the single present moment. He thought that having enjoyed or being about to enjoy meant nothing to him, for the one is no longer and the other is not yet and is uncertain—a feeling common to those who live in luxury, who think only of making the present well. He agreed with this doctrine in his own life, for he thought happiness for all lay in luxury and the lavish use of perfumes, fine clothing, and women. For instance, he openly kept Lais the <term>hetaira</term> <note>A high-status companion or courtesan in ancient Greece</note>, and he delighted in the extravagances of Dionysius, even if he was often insulted by him. Hegesander, at any rate, says that when he happened to be at a banquet with Dionysius, and Dionysius asked how the seating arrangement seemed compared to yesterday, he replied that it was an "enjoyment." For the former had said... <note>The text here is somewhat corrupted in the original Greek</note>... "Today it has become most excellent because of your presence, whereas yesterday it was pleasant when you were not there," and Hegesander relates other such things. Aristippus, though appearing to be a servant to Dionysius, was mocked by Antiphon; but he replied, "If I happened to be a fisherman, would I have left my work?" Aristippus spent most of his time living luxuriously in Aegina. Therefore, Xenophon says in his *Memorabilia* that Socrates often admonished him, and having fashioned a fable, he introduced the figures of Virtue and Pleasure. Regarding Lais, Aristippus used to say, "I possess her, I am not possessed by her." Through Dionysius he came into conflict with some regarding the honor of three women, and he bathed in perfumes and claimed that even in Bacchic revels, a chaste woman will not be corrupted. It is also recorded that a fisherman named Galatea makes a certain servant narrate these things about one of the disciples: "My master... once spent time, when he was a youth, with the philosopher Epicurus, who was a Cyrenaic, as Aristippus says, a gifted <term>sophist</term> <note>A teacher of rhetoric and philosophy</note>, or rather the leader of all then, differing from others in his lack of restraint. Having given him a talent <note>A very large sum of money</note>, he became a disciple. My master, even if he did not fully learn the art, certainly snatched up the 'windpipe' <note>A metaphor for greed or gluttony</note>."

<margin>The luxury of philosophers.</margin>
Antiphanes, in his play *Antaeus*, speaking about the luxury of philosophers, says: "My friend, do you perceive who this old man is? From his appearance he looks Greek: a white cloak, a fine gray tunic, a soft little hat, a rhythmic cane. A sturdy table—why need I speak at length? I think I see the Academy itself!" <margin>Polyarchus, nicknamed 'the Pleasure-seeker'.</margin> Aristoxenus the musician, in his *Life of Archytas*, says that the younger Dionysius sent ambassadors to the city of the Tarentines, among whom was Polyarchus, nicknamed "the Pleasure-seeker," a man devoted to bodily pleasures not only in deed but in word. He was an acquaintance of Archytas, and though entirely a stranger to philosophy, he would attend their gatherings and walk with the circle of Archytas, listening to their discourses. Once, when a discussion and inquiry arose concerning desires, and generally concerning bodily pleasures, Polyarchus said: "To me, men, having often remained silent while considering..."

<header>->ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED<-</header>

<margin>
It has often seemed [to be] secure.
</margin>

...the structure of these virtues [is artificial], and far removed from nature. For when nature speaks with her own voice, she commands us to follow pleasures; she says that it is not the mark of a rational person to resist or be enslaved by desires, nor is it the mark of a wise, happy, or practical person to perceive the constitution of human nature as such. A strong proof of this is that all men, when they seize power of significant magnitude, descend into bodily pleasures, as if they believe that such enjoyment is the very purpose of power; they treat almost everything else as secondary or, quite simply, as a matter of trifling concern. 

One can cite as examples the kings of the Persians, or anyone who happens to be the master of a significant tyranny—and before them, the kings of the Lydians and the Medes, and even further back, those of the Syrians. For these men, no pleasure under the sun was too great for their enjoyment. It is even said that among the Persians, rewards were offered to those who could invent a new pleasure—and quite rightly so. For human nature quickly becomes sated with long-standing pleasures, even if they are deeply ingrained. Since novelty has great power in making pleasure appear greater, one must not neglect it, but rather take great care in its pursuit. 

For this reason, many types of foods were invented, many drinks, many incenses and perfumes, many styles of clothing and bedding, as well as drinking cups and other vessels. All these things contribute to various pleasures when the underlying material is something admired by human nature. This seems to be the case with gold and silver, and most things that are pleasing to the eye and rare, which appear meticulously crafted by the resulting arts. 

If one were to list in order the many luxuries of the Persian king’s court—the types and number of attendants he has, his sexual indulgences, the scents applied to his skin, the beauty and conversation he enjoys, and the various spectacles and musical performances he witnesses—one would say that the Persian king is the happiest of men. For he is able to mold for himself the most perfect, prepared pleasure. Second to him, one might place our own tyrant <note>referring to Dionysius of Sicily</note>, though he falls far behind; for while all of Asia was the Persian king's provider, the resources of Dionysius would appear utterly cheap by comparison. 

That such a life is worth fighting for is clear from historical events. The Medes took the kingdom from the Syrians through the greatest of dangers for no other reason than to become masters of the Syrian power. The Persians did the same to the Medes for the same reason—the enjoyment of bodily pleasures. 

However, the lawgivers, wishing to level the human race and ensure that no citizen lived in luxury, created the "form of the virtues." They wrote laws concerning contracts and other matters that seemed necessary for political society, including regulations on clothing and the rest of one’s lifestyle to ensure it remained uniform. Since the lawgivers were at war with the "grasping" <term>pleonexia: the desire to have more than one's fair share</term> nature of man, praise for Justice was first magnified, and some poet or other proclaimed:

> Justice has a golden face, and again, the golden eye of Justice watches.

The very name of Justice was deified, so that by custom there are altars and sacrifices to Justice. After this, they introduced Temperance and Self-control, and they labeled the excess of enjoyment as "greed," so that those who obey the laws and public opinion would moderate their bodily pleasures. 

Duris says in the twenty-fourth book of his *Histories* that the ancients also lost their dynasties through a desire for drunkenness. He claims Homer shows this when Achilles insults Agamemnon, saying:

> You wine-heavy man, with the eyes of a dog. <note>Iliad 1.225</note>

And when signaling the king's death, he says:

> We lay around the mixing bowl, a struck-down multitude,

indicating that he met his death in the very midst of his drunken desires.

<margin>
Speusippus, Philoxenus, and the Epicureans.
</margin>

Philoxenus of Leucas [was one such man]. So too was Speusippus <note>Plato’s nephew and his successor as head of the Academy</note>. Indeed, Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily, in a letter to him, spoke against his love of pleasure, reproaching him for his love of money and his passion for Lastheneia of Arcadia, who had been a student of Plato. Not only Speusippus and his followers embraced the pleasure of movement, but also Epicurus and his school. 

And so that I do not have to speak of the "titillations" and "refined luxuries" which Epicurus often brings forward—the ticklings and the riddles he spoke of in his work *On the Goal*—I will mention them all. For he says:

> For I, at least, am unable to conceive of the Good if I take away the pleasures of taste, take away the pleasures of sex, take away the pleasures of listening to music, and take away the pleasant movements of the sight of beautiful forms.

And Metrodorus <note>a close disciple of Epicurus</note> says in his letters:

> O Timocrates, student of nature, the argument that proceeds according to nature centered on the belly contains the whole of existence.

And Epicurus himself says:

> The beginning and root of every good is the pleasure of the belly; even wisdom and cultural refinements have their reference point in this.

And in his book *On the Goal*, he says again:

> We must honor the Beautiful and the virtues and such things if they produce pleasure; but if they do not produce it, we must bid them farewell.

Clearly...

...making pleasure a servant to virtue, and holding the rank of a handmaid, even if others say it is appropriate for noble things, and those who admire him in vain when they produce no pleasure. Therefore, the Romans acted well—judging all things with scrutiny—when they expelled the Epicureans Alcius and Philiscus from the city 
<margin>Persecutions of philosophers.</margin> during the consulship of Lucius Postumius <note>original: "Ποσομίου" (Posomios), likely a transcription error for Postumius, consul in 173 or 155 BCE</note>, because of the pleasures they introduced. King Antiochus <note>Likely Antiochus VII Sidetes or Antiochus Grypus</note> also expelled all philosophers from his kingdom, writing as follows: "King Antiochus to Phanias. We wrote to you previously that there should be no philosopher in the city or in the country. We hear, however, that there are not a few, and that they are corrupting the youth. Since you have done nothing of what we wrote regarding these matters, as soon as you receive this letter, order a proclamation to be made that all philosophers must depart from these places immediately; and if any of the young men are caught associating with them, they shall be hanged, and their fathers will face the gravest charges, if it should happen otherwise." For every man is an eager promoter of pleasure. This is why Sophocles the poet, 
<margin>Sophocles says this in Antigone.</margin> speaking these words in *Antigone* <note>original: "Ἀντιγόνῃ"</note>: "For when men betray their pleasures, I do not consider such a man to be alive, but I look upon him as a living corpse. You may be as wealthy at home as you wish, and live with the outward status of a tyrant, but if the power to rejoice is absent from these things, I would not purchase the rest for the shadow of smoke compared to the man's pleasure." <note>This quote emphasizes that without joy, life and wealth are worthless.</note>

And Lycon the Peripatetic <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's school</note>, as Antigonus of Carystus says, when he first arrived in Athens for his education, was accurately aware of the fees for the "dinner-bell" <note>original: "κώδωνος" (bell); likely referring to the cost of admission to lectures or school meals</note> and how much each person was charged for the "bull-tax." Later, when he presided over the Peripatetics, he used to entertain his friends with great vanity and much extravagance. For aside from the musical performances, silver plate, and bedding brought in for these occasions, the rest of the preparation—the elaborateness of the meals and the crowd of table-setters and cooks—was so great that many were terrified and those wishing to approach the school were deterred; it was as if they were entering a corrupt state filled with expensive public duties <term>liturgies; compulsory public services performed by the wealthy</term>. For it was necessary to take a turn in the office recognized by the Peripatos. This office involved managing the contributions of those paying a few obols, to host not only those who had contributed, but also whomever Lycon might invite. Furthermore, they had to provide for the elders who met diligently at the school, so that the collected money was not even sufficient for the perfumes and crowns; they also had to perform sacrifices and act as overseers of the Muses. All these things appeared to be foreign to reason and philosophy, and more suited to luxury and excess. Even if someone who could not afford these expenses was provided for, starting from an ancient and meager supply, it was nonetheless quite out of place. For it was not so that they might enjoy a table lasting from evening until dawn, or for the sake of sexual indulgence, that the followers of Plato and Speusippus held these gatherings, but so that they might appear both to honor the divine and to associate naturally with one another, and mostly for the sake of relaxation and literary study. All these things later became secondary among them, replaced by fine cloaks and the luxury that followed. For I do not even exclude the rest. 

But Lycon, out of vanity and in the most conspicuous part of the city, in the house of Conon, had a room with twenty couches, as it was suitable for his receptions. Lycon was also a good and skillful ball-player. And concerning Anaxarchus, Clearchus of Soli writes thus in the fifth book of his *Lives*: when a great abundance fell to Anaxarchus—who was called "the Happy"—through the ignorance of his providers, a young maiden of marriageable age, chosen for her superior beauty, would pour his wine while naked, exposing her charms—how can this be true?—to the lack of self-control of those who used her so. The baker wore gloves <note>original: "χειρίδας"</note> and a wax mask over his face so that no sweat might drip into the dough, nor might he breathe upon the loaves as he kneaded them. Therefore, one might appropriately say to this "wise" philosopher the words of Anaxilas about the bread-maker: "Anointing his skin with yellow perfumes, dragging fine cloaks, trailing slippers, eating bulbs, devouring cheese." He also drank from trumpets <note>original: "κήρυκας"; likely shell-shaped or trumpet-shaped vessels</note> and wore all these things in stitched leather garments with beautiful letters on his hearth. 

How much better than these was Gorgias of Leontini, of whom the same Clearchus says in the eighth book of his *Lives* that, because he lived temperately, he lived for nearly eighty years with his faculties intact. When someone asked him by what diet he lived so harmoniously and with such perception for so long a time, he said he never did anything for the sake of pleasure. And Demetrius of Byzantium, in his work *On Poems*, says that Gorgias of Leontini, when asked what was the cause of his living more than a hundred years, said it was never having done anything for the sake of another. As he had acquired a sufficient supply for life for a long time in the kingdom and the rest of the city, when he was dying, his eldest son asked him what he had done to preserve his kingdom for so many years so that he might imitate his example. He replied: "By doing what is just toward all men and gods." Carystius of Pergamum says in his *Historical Notes* that Cephisodorus the Theban says Polydorus the Teian physician used to dine with Antipater, and possessed a love of expensive carpets...

Then there is Python of Byzantium, the orator, who—as his fellow citizen Leon records—was exceptionally fat in body. Once, when the Byzantines were engaged in civil strife <note>original: "στασιάζουσι" (stasiazousi), referring to internal political conflict.</note> against one another, he tried to encourage the citizens toward friendship by saying: "O fellow citizens, you see what my body is like, but I also have a wife who is much fatter than I am. <margin>10</margin> How much better is it then, good Timocrates, to be thin from drinking, as Hermippus <margin>Leotrophides.</margin> lists in his play *The Monkeys*, than to be excessively wealthy and resemble the Tanagraean judge <note>A reference to a proverb or specific anecdote about a judge from Tanagra, likely known for his bulk.</note>, like the men mentioned before?
