Aristophanes, in his play *Gerytades*, also lists those who are thin, whom he says are sent as ambassadors to the underworld by the poets, describing the poets there in this way: "And who would dare to go down to the bottom of the dead and the dark gates?" He says that they chose one from each art in a common assembly: "Those who signify the 'genital-walkers' <note>original: "αἰδοφοίτας" (aidophoitas), a punning term likely referring to their frailty or a specific comedic costume.</note> and frequent that place often—for there are certain men among you, by Zeus, who are 'genital-walkers', especially like the Thracians, who have everything." And who were they? First, Sannyrion from the comic poets, Meletus from the tragic choruses, and Cinesias from the circular (dithyrambic) choruses. 

<margin>20</margin> Then he says in order: "How strongly you were carried along then on thin hopes! For it was possible to select many of these, taking them together as a river of diarrhea that will flow out." Sannyrion, mocking his own frailty, says this in his play *Laughter* regarding Meletus: "Meletus, the corpse from Aeneas." 

In reality, Cinesias was extremely tall and thin, and Stratis wrote an entire play about him, calling him "Phthiotic Achilles" <note>A pun on "Phthia" (Achilles' home) and "phthisis" (wasting disease/consumption).</note> because in his own poetry he constantly used the word "phthiota" (wasted). Playing on his appearance, he said, "O wasted Achilles!" Others, like Aristophanes, have often called him "Linden-wood Cinesias" because he wore a corset made of linden-wood planks strapped around him so that he would not bend over due to his height and thinness. 

That Cinesias was sickly and terrible in other ways too is mentioned by the orator Lysias in the speech titled *Against Phanias for Illegal Proposals*. Lysias claims that Cinesias gave up his craft to become a professional informer <term>sykophantēs: a professional accuser in Athenian law who sought profit from lawsuits</term> and grew rich from it. That this poet is the same person is clearly indicated by the 
<margin>30</margin> fact that he is shown being mocked in comedy for his atheism. The orator describes him as such: "I wonder if he is not burdened by the fact that it is Cinesias who does such things, a man who, while sinning against the gods, has a reputation in other matters so shameful it is disgraceful even to speak of it. But you hear the comic poets every year! Was it not with him that Apollophanes, Mysalides, and Lysitheus once met, choosing a single day of the 'unlucky days' <note>original: "ἀποφράδων" (apophradōn), days when temples were closed and no business was conducted.</note>, and instead of 'New-Moon-Observers' <note>original: "νουμηνιαστῶν" (noumeniastōn), a religious club.</note>, they gave themselves the name 'Devil-Worshipers' <note>original: "κακοδαιμονιστάς" (kakodaimonistas), literally those who worship an evil spirit.</note>?"

This name suited their fortunes, not because they intended to act that way in their hearts, but as a way of mocking the gods and our laws. Consequently, each of those men perished, as is natural for such people. But the gods have dealt with this man, who is known to many, in such a way that his enemies would rather see him live than die—as an example to others. This is so they may know that for those who are excessively insolent toward divine matters, the gods do not store up punishments for their children, but destroy the men themselves miserably, 
<margin>40</margin> inflicting greater and more difficult disasters and diseases upon them than upon other humans. For to die or to fall ill in a normal way is common to us all; but to remain in such a state for so long a time, dying every day and yet unable to end one's life, belongs only to those who have committed such sins as this man." So the orator spoke regarding Cinesias.

Philitas of Cos, the poet, was even thinner; it is said that because of his physical frailty he wore lead spheres on his feet so that he would not be overturned by the wind. Polemon the Geographer, in his work *On Marvels*, says that Archestratus the seer, when he was captured by enemies and placed on a scale, was found to weigh only an obol <note>A small silver coin.</note>, so thin was he. The same author records that Panaretus never associated with doctors but listened to the philosopher Arcesilaus; he stayed with Ptolemy Euergetes <note>Ptolemy III of Egypt.</note>, receiving twelve talents a year, 
<margin>50</margin> though he remained extremely thin. Metrodorus of Scepsis, in the second book of his *On Athletics*, says that the poet Hipponax was not only small in stature but also thin, yet so high-strung <note>original: "ἀκρότονον" (akrotonon)</note> that he could throw an empty oil-flask <term>lēkythos: a narrow-necked bottle used for oil</term> a vast distance—unlike most people with light bodies who cannot cut through the air because their throw lacks forceful momentum. Philippides was also thin...

But when his brother Crito returned from Sicily, he seized him and handed him over to a doctor, and he was cured of his madness. He used to recount that never in his life had he felt more pleasure, for no pains ever came to him, while the abundance of his pleasures was beyond measure."

## BOOK THIRTEEN.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' depicting two seated figures in classical robes within an architectural setting.</image-desc>Antiphanes the comic poet, my friend Timocrates, was once reading one of his own comedies to King Alexander, but it was clear that the king did not quite approve of it. For the king said that the man who approves of such things must have often dined at potluck meals <note>original: "συμβόλων" (symbolōn), referring to meals where each guest contributed a portion of the cost or food.</note>, and must have frequently given and received blows over a courtesan, as Lycophron of Chalcis says in his work *On Comedy*. Since we are now about to arrange our discourse concerning erotic matters—for many discussions often arose regarding wives and courtesans, setting out history for those who know it—let us call upon the Muse Erato to bring to our memory those noteworthy erotic tales, and from that point we shall make our beginning. "Then, since Erato stood beside me, speak to me..." <note>A poetic invocation to the Muse of erotic poetry.</note> What discourses were spoken concerning love itself and erotic affairs? For our noble host, praising wives, said it was a delightful thing to recount the history of legislators: that in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta.</note> all the <margin>Number of wives.</margin> maidens were shut up in a dark room, and the unmarried young men were shut in with them, <margin>Mother.</margin> and whichever girl each man grabbed, he led her away without a dowry. For this reason, they even fined Lysander because, having left his first wife, he wished to marry another who was much more beautiful. And Clearchus of Soli says in his work *On Proverbs* that in Lacedaemon, the women at a certain festival drag the bachelors around the altar and whip them, so that to escape the insult of the practice, they might be affectionate and come to marriage in due time. 

In Athens, Cecrops <note>The legendary first king of Athens, often depicted as half-man, half-serpent.</note> was the first to yoke one man to one woman, whereas previously there had been promiscuous unions and communal marriages; for this reason, some thought he was called "double-natured," because the men of earlier times did not know their own fathers due to the number of partners. Proceeding from these facts, one might find fault with those who attribute two wives to Socrates—Xanthippe and Myrto, the granddaughter of Aristides (for the dates do not allow her to be called his daughter, but rather his great-granddaughter). Among these authors are Callidichus, Demetrius of Phalerum, Satyrus the Peripatetic, and Aristoxenus, to whom Aristotle gave his own reputation, recounting the same in his work *On Nobility of Birth*—unless perhaps a decree was passed at that time because of the shortage of men, so that anyone who wished was permitted to have two wives, which is why the comic poets are silent on the matter, though they often mention Socrates. Hieronymus of Rhodes cited a decree concerning women, which I will send to you in this book. Panaetius of Rhodes is also among those who speak about Socrates' wives. Among the Persians, the kingship tolerates a multitude of concubines, because the king rules over his wife as a master. Furthermore, as Dinon says in his *Persian History*, the queen is even worshipped by the concubines; they certainly bow down to her. Priam also made use of many women, which Hecuba found distressing. Priam says: "Nineteen were born to me from one womb, but the others the women in my halls bore for me." <margin>Wives suspecting concubines.</margin> But among the Greeks, the mother of Phoenix cannot tolerate the concubine of Amyntor. And Clytemnestra, becoming overcome with passion, kills Cassandra along with Agamemnon himself—Cassandra whom the ruler had brought into Greece, having followed a custom that was...

One must call all these prostitutes "Theban Sphinxes," for they speak simply of nothing, but rather in certain riddles about how they desire, love, and sleep together so pleasantly. Then he says: "Let a two-footed girl or a four-footed couch or a throne be mine," then some "three-footed" thing <note>This is a parody of the Sphinx’s riddle: "What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening?" Here, it refers to the expensive furniture and servants a courtesan demands.</note>, then a two-footed girl again. The man who does not understand these things leaves at once, just like the one who, thinking he is saving her by his own reputation, is instead the only one held against his will. Those who expect to be loved are immediately carried off. And how they are lifted up like Aethra! To be brief: nothing is gained. <margin>On courtesans versus wives.</margin> Then, consider the courtesans—what kind of beasts are more destructive?

While Lariosthenes was saying many such things, Leonides, disparaging the very name of "wife," quoted from the seers and from Alexis, saying: "O wretched are we who have sold the freedom of our lives and our luxury! We live as slaves to women instead of free men. Then, to have a dowry—is this not a bitter price we pay, full of feminine gall? For their 'ambrosia' is nothing compared to that bitterness. For while men who are wronged are usually forgiven, she herself commits the wrong and yet still accuses him besides. They do not rule over what they should, and they neglect what they ought to rule; they commit perjury, and if they are not suffering some evil, they claim to be sick at every opportunity."

And Xenarchus says in *Sleep*: "Then, are not the Cicadas <note>original: "Τεττίγες" (Tettiges). This is a famous ancient joke: only the male cicadas sing, while the females are silent.</note> happy, in whom the wives have not even a bit of voice?"

Philetaerus says in *The Corinthianizer*: "By Zeus, how melting and soft a look she has! It is not for nothing that there is a temple to the Courtesan everywhere, but nowhere in Greece is there one for a Wife."

And Amphis says in *Athamas*: "Is not a courtesan more well-disposed than a wife? Much more so, and with good reason. For the wife stays at home, despising you by law; but the courtesan knows that she must either win a man over by her manners, or she must go off to find another."

Eubulus says in *Chrysilla*: "Cursed be he who marries a second time! For I will not speak ill of the first wife. The first man was, I suppose, inexperienced in evils, but the second man knew exactly what kind of evil a woman was." And proceeding further he says, "O highly honored Zeus, if I ever speak ill of women, by Zeus, let me perish then, for they are the best of possessions. If Medea was a bad woman, Penelope was a great thing. If someone says Clytemnestra was bad, I set the good Alcestis against her. Perhaps someone will speak ill of Phaedra; but by Zeus, there was someone else who was good—alas, who was she? Woe is me, I am miserable! Quickly indeed the good women have run out, but of the wicked ones I still have many to name."

Aristophon says in *Callonides*: "May he who marries a second time perish miserably; for the first man did no wrong, as he did not yet know what kind of evil he was taking in a wife. But he who took one later, took her knowing full well the evil he was walking into."

And Antiphanes in *The Father-Lover*: "Has he really married? What are you saying? Is it true? He has married now, who was just recently alive and walking about!"

Menander in *The Girl Carrying the Sacred Vessels* or *The Flute-Player*: "You will not marry if you have any sense, leaving behind this life. For I myself have married; and as for what those who do not marry might suffer, let the die be cast—the matter is decided! You might be saved, or you might find yourself thrown into a literal sea of troubles—not the Libyan or the Aegean, where thirty ships out of thirty are destroyed. But of those who marry, not a single one has ever truly been saved."

And in *Those Set on Fire*: "May he perish utterly who was the first to marry, then the second, then the third, then the fourth, and then whoever came after."

Carcinus the tragic poet says in *Semele*: "O nights, O Zeus, why is it necessary to speak of women as an evil? It would be enough just to say 'woman'."

Nor are those who marry young women in their old age unaware that they are throwing themselves into obvious evil. The poet of Megara <note>Referring to Theognis of Megara.</note> would have advised them: "A young wife is not suitable for an old man; for she does not obey the rudder like a boat. She does not hold to the anchor, but having broken her cables, she often finds another harbor at night."

And Theophilus in *Neoptolemus* said: "A young woman is not profitable for an old man. For like a boat, she does not obey a single rudder in the least; but having broken all her ropes, she is found in another harbor during the night."

<margin>Wars because of women.</margin> I think none of you are ignorant, dear friends, that the greatest wars have happened because of women. The Trojan War because of Helen; the plague because of Chryseis; the wrath of Achilles because of Briseis. And the 'Sacred War' (as it is called) happened because of another wife, as Duris says in the second book of his *Histories*: a Theban woman named Theano was carried off by a certain Phocian. This war lasted ten years, and in the tenth year, when Philip became an ally, it came to an end; for then the Thebans took Phocis. And the war called the Crisaean War, as Callisthenes says in his work *On the Sacred War*, when the inhabitants of Cirrha went to war against the Phocians, lasted ten years after the Cirrhaeans snatched away Megisto, the daughter of Pelagon the Phocian, and the daughters of the Argives as they were returning from the Pythian temple; in the tenth year, Cirrha was captured.

Entire houses have also been overturned because of women. That of Philip, the father of Alexander, because of his marriage to Cleopatra. That of Hercules because of his marriage to Iole, the daughter of Eurytus. That of Theseus because of Phaedra, the daughter of Minos. That of Athamas because of Themisto, daughter of Hypseus. That of Jason because of Glauce, the daughter of Creon. That of Agamemnon because of Cassandra. And the expedition of Cambyses against Egypt, as Ctesias says, was because of a...

...he lied about his wife. For Cambyses <note>King of Persia, 530–522 BCE.</note>, having heard that Egyptian women were superior in their physical intimacies to all others, sent a request to Amasis, the King of the Egyptians, asking for one of his daughters in marriage. Amasis, however, did not give his own daughter, suspecting she would not hold the rank of a wife but rather that of a concubine; instead, he sent Nitetis, the daughter of Apries <note>The former king of Egypt whom Amasis had overthrown.</note>. Apries had fallen from the Egyptian kingship. Because of her lineage, she was the only one chosen by Amasis to go to the Persians. Cambyses was pleased with Nitetis, but becoming intensely provoked after learning the whole truth from her, and seeking to avenge the murder of Apries by a calculated plan, he went to war against the Egyptians. But Dino, in his *History of Persia*, and Lynceus of Naucratis in the third book of his *History of Egypt*, say that Nitetis was actually sent by Amasis to Cyrus <note>Cambyses’ father.</note>, and that Cambyses was her son; they claim he undertook the expedition to Egypt to avenge his mother. Furthermore, Duris of Samos says in his first book that a war <margin>10</margin> once broke out between two women, Olympias and Eurydice <note>Olympias was the mother of Alexander the Great; Eurydice was the wife of Philip III Arrhidaeus.</note>. One of them, Olympias, advanced in a more Bacchic fashion <note>Like a follower of Dionysus.</note> with drums, while Eurydice came forward armed in the Macedonian style, having been trained in warfare by Cyane the Illyrian.

After these accounts, it seemed right to the philosophers present to speak <margin>On Love.</margin> again about Love and Beauty. Many philosophical discourses were delivered, in which some even recalled songs from the "philosopher of the stage," Euripides, including these lines: "Love is the greatest education in wisdom and virtue, and in social grace; this divinity is by nature the sweetest of all to mortals, for he brings a joy free from pain and leads us toward hope. May I never associate with those uninitiated in his labors, but may I live apart from those of uncultured ways. I advise the young never to flee from Love, but to use him rightly when he comes." Another guest quoted Pindar, saying that it is right to love and to yield to Love when the timing is right, and another added these lines of Euripides:

> But you, O Love, tyrant over gods and men,
<margin>20</margin> > either do not teach us what is beautiful, or for those who love—
> since you are their creator—help them labor through their struggles to a happy end.
> If you do this, you will be honored by the gods; but if you do not,
> the very grace by which you are honored will be taken from you
> by the one who loves to learn from you.

Pontianus then noted that Zeno of Citium <note>The founder of Stoic philosophy.</note> believed Love to be the god of friendship and freedom, and moreover, the provider of harmony—and nothing else. Therefore, in his *Republic*, Zeno said that Love is a god who acts as a fellow-worker for the safety of the city. Furthermore, the elders of that time who revered philosophy said that Love is separated from everything shameful. This is evident from the fact that in the gymnasia <note>Ancient Greek centers for both physical training and education.</note> he is established alongside Hermes and Heracles—the former presiding over Reason <note>original: *logos*</note>, the latter over Strength <note>original: *alkē*</note>. From the union of these two come friendship and harmony, through which the most beautiful freedom increases for those who pursue these things.
<margin>30</margin> The Athenians were so far from thinking Love presided over base physical intimacy that, although the Academy <note>The school founded by Plato.</note> was clearly consecrated to Athena, they established an altar to Love there and sacrifice to him. The Thespians also honor the *Erotideia* <note>A festival for Eros.</note>, just as the Athenians honor the *Panathenaea*, the people of Elis the *Olympics*, and the Rhodians the *Halia*. In public gatherings and social unions, Love is generally honored. The Spartans even offer sacrifices to Love before their battle lines are drawn, believing that safety and victory lie in the friendship of those standing together in the ranks. And the Cretans, in their battle lines, adorn the most beautiful of their citizens and through them sacrifice to Love, as Sosicrates records. What is called the "Sacred Band" among the Thebans <note>An elite military unit consisting of 150 pairs of male lovers.</note> was composed of lovers and their beloveds, manifesting the dignity of the gods by embracing a glorious death rather than a life of shame and reproach. The Samians, as Erxias says in his *History of Colophon*, dedicated their gymnasia to Love, and called the festival celebrated through them the "Festival of Liberty" <note>original: *Eleutheria*</note>, because of the god through whom the Athenians attained freedom. Indeed, when the Peisistratids <note>Tyrants who ruled Athens in the 6th century BCE.</note> were expelled, they first tried to slander the deeds associated with the god. After these things were said, Plutarch recalled the lines from the *Phaedrus* by Alexis. A character, frustrated by his education or by evils, says:

> A philosophical perplexity has come upon me, and it seems to me
> that painters do not know Love—to speak most soberly—
<margin>40</margin> > as many as make images of this divinity.
> For he is neither female nor male, and again,
> neither god nor man, neither a fool
> nor, on the other hand, wise, but a mixture
> from everywhere, bearing many forms in a single type.
> For he has the daring of a man, the cowardice of a woman,
> the folly of madness, the reason of the wise,
> the violence of a wild beast, the endurance of adamant,
> and the ambition of a divinity. By Athena and the gods,
> I do not know what he is, but he is certainly something
> like this... if not in name. Eubulus says in *Campylion*:
> "Who was the first man to paint or mold in wax
> a winged Love? He knew how to paint nothing but swallows,
> and was ignorant of the god's ways.
> For he is neither light nor easy to be rid of
> for the one bearing the disease, but quite heavy. How then could he have wings?
> Such a thing is nonsense, even if someone claims it."

### ATHENAEUS: THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

...vigorously, the practice of shaving the beard came into fashion under Alexander <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE), who famously ordered his soldiers to shave so enemies could not grab their beards in battle.</note>, as your own Chrysippus says in the fourth book of *On the Beautiful and Pleasure*. I will recall his words, not without good reason, I believe; for I take great pleasure in the man because of his vast learning and the mildness of his character. The philosopher speaks thus: "The practice of shaving the beard was introduced under Alexander, the first people to adopt it being those who were in his favor." Indeed, Timotheus the flute-player used to play the flute with a long beard, and among those living in Athens, it is not a very ancient custom for the first man who shaved to have the nickname "Cutter" <note>original: "κόρσην" (korsē), referring to the hair on the temples or a nickname for a barber.</note>. Therefore, Alexis <note>A poet of Middle Comedy.</note> said somewhere:

> If you see a man acting solemn 
> or being shaved, he has one of two reasons: either he seems to me to be planning to be a soldier, and to shout everything in opposition to his beard, or we have some artificial evil falling upon us.
> By the gods, why do hairs 
> distress you, through which each of us appears a man? Unless you suspect that these hairs are doing something against you. 

And Diogenes <note>Diogenes of Sinope, the famous Cynic philosopher who lived in a tub.</note>, seeing someone with a beard like that, said: "Have you some complaint against nature, because she made you a man and not a woman?" And seeing another man, a horseman, who was smooth-shaven and wearing perfume, and dressed accordingly, he said that previously he used to ask what a "horse-prostitute" was, but now he had found out. In Rhodes, although there is a law against shaving, no one is prosecuted because everyone shaves; and in Byzantium, though a fine is imposed on any barber who possesses a razor, everyone uses them nonetheless. These things were said by that wonderful Chrysippus. 

But that wise Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, founder of the Stoic school.</note>, as Antigonus of Carystus says, prophesying about our way of life and the pursuit of imported habits, said that those who merely listened to his discourse without understanding it would be like "hallway flute-players" <note>original: "αὐληθύθυροι" (aulēthuthuroi), meaning those who hang around the doors of flute-parties but never get inside; superficial followers.</note>, just like those who were led astray by the sect of Aristippus—extravagant and bold. And indeed, many of you are of this sort, sent out together, and "adorned" <note>ironic usage</note> not only in your character but in your appearance. For while you wish to be loved for your self-sufficiency and your frugality, you are found at the doors of greed, living filthily and wrapping yourselves in small, worn-out cloaks. Your ears are filled with the cheap talk of taverns, and you call those who use perfume or wear slightly softer clothing "effeminate." 

Yet a man dressed like that <margin>An image of hypocrisy.</margin> somewhere makes money from his poetry, and vigorously goes about with his chin and his rump shaved—those who will perish in the Lyceum <note>The gymnasium where Aristotle taught.</note> with the sophists—by Zeus, lean, starving men, as thin as leather! 

In the works of Antiphanes, beauty itself is also discussed; for in the *Thyadresiae*, they select the most beautiful men <margin>On Beauty.</margin> and entrust them with the first-fruits, if a judgment of beauty takes place based on age; and the first prize is given to carry the fortunes, the second to lead the ox, and the third to lay on the sacrificial cakes. 

Heraclides Lembus records that in Sparta, the most beautiful man and the most beautiful woman are most admired, as Sparta produces the most beautiful women. Therefore, they say that once when Archidamus the king <note>Archidamus II, King of Sparta.</note> was presented with a beautiful woman and another who was ugly but rich, and he inclined toward the rich one, the Ephors <note>The high overseers of Sparta.</note> fined him, telling him that he chose to beget "kinglets" instead of "kings" for the Spartans. 

Euripides also said: "First, a beautiful appearance is worthy of sovereignty." And the elders of the people in Homer <margin>Iliad, Book 3.</margin>, marvelling at the beauty of Helen, say:

> "No shame that Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans 
> should suffer agonies for a long time for such a woman; 
> she is dreadfully like the immortal goddesses in her face."

Indeed, Priam himself is struck by the beauty of the woman, even though he is in the midst of terrible dangers. At any rate, he admires Agamemnon for his beauty, exclaiming:

> "So beautiful a man 
> I have never yet seen with my eyes, 
> nor so majestic; for he is like a kingly man."

Many nations also appoint the most beautiful as kings, such as the Ethiopians (who are called "the immortals" even to this day), as Bion says in his *Ethiopica*. For it seems that beauty is native to kingship. The goddesses contended for beauty, as everyone has heard; and because of beauty, the gods snatched away Ganymede to be a cupbearer, "for the sake of his beauty, that he might be among the immortals." And whom do the goddesses snatch away if not the most beautiful? Think of—and then silence—how they took Cephalus, Cleitus, and Tithonus; how Demeter took Iasion, and Aphrodite took Anchises and Adonis. Because of beauty, even the greatest of the gods <note>Zeus.</note> comes as gold through the roof-tiles, becomes a bull, or is often "drunk" as in Aegina. 

Socrates the philosopher, who looked down on everything, was no less sharp regarding the beauty of Alcibiades, just as the most solemn Aristotle was toward his Phaselitan disciple. Do we not also prefer the most beautiful among inanimate things? I praise the Spartan custom of showing the young maidens naked to strangers. In the island of Chios, too, it is a noble sight to go to the gymnasiums of the youths and see the young men wrestling with the girls. 

And you, Cynisulcus <note>A character in the dialogue, a Cynic philosopher whose name literally means "Dog-dragger."</note>, you "golden-fingered" one, dare you say such things against Karkinos? You who have one leg made of dung, like that poet of the same name as you whose memory you carry, who always lives in taverns and inns! And yet Isocrates the orator says in the *Areopagiticus*: "To eat or drink in a tavern was something no decent servant would ever dare to do." For they practiced being dignified, not acting like buffoons. And Hyperides <margin>Areopagites.</margin> in his speech *Against Patrocles* (if the speech is genuine) says that the Areopagites <note>The members of the supreme court of Athens.</note> forbade a man who had lunched in a tavern from ascending to the Areopagus.

### BOOK 13

<margin>Books on courtesans.</margin>
But you, O sophist, are mixed up in the taverns, not with male companions but with many long-wandering <term>hetairai</term> <note>original: "ἑταιρῶν" (hetairōn). These were high-class female companions in ancient Greece, often highly educated, who provided conversation and companionship as well as sexual services.</note> around you, carrying about such books as those by Aristophanes, Apollodorus, Ammonius, and Antiphanes, and even Gorgias of Athens—all of whom have written treatises about the courtesans of Athens. In this, your "fine learning" has in no way imitated Thomhasidion the "Most Authoritative," who, as Theophrastus says in his work *On Happiness*, used to go about promising to teach people how to be lucky. O teacher of sacred things, you are no different from Amasias of Elis, whom Theophrastus says in his *Erotikos* was remarkably skilled in matters of love. Indeed, one might not be wrong to call you a "painter of prostitutes" <note>original: "πορνογράφον" (pornographon), from which we derive the word "pornography." In this context, it refers to artists who specialized in erotic subjects.</note>, like the painters Aristeides, Pausanias, and Nicophanes. Polemon mentions them as being excellent at painting such subjects in his treatise *On the Tablets in Sicyon*. O most shameful friends of "fine learning": you even mention this "branded" <note>The Greek text here is somewhat corrupted, but suggests something shameful or marked.</note> behavior, where they do not even cover themselves but openly quote Eubulus from his play *The Cercopes*:

> I went to Corinth with pleasure; there,
> somehow, I ate some "basil" <note>original: "ὤκιμον" (okimon). This is a double entendre; while it is the name of the herb basil, it was also a slang term or a proper name for a courtesan.</note> that was quite lively...
<margin>Names of courtesans.</margin>
> And there they were caught in the Diomeia <note>A district or festival in Athens.</note>.

And that sophist of the Corinthians was quite foolish to explain to his students that "Basil" was the name of a courtesan. There are many other plays which take their titles from the shameless names of courtesans: Diocles’ *Thalatta*, Pherecrates’ *Corianno*, Eunicus’ (or Philyllius’) *Anteia*, Menander’s *Thais* and *Phannion*, Alexis’ *Opora*, and Eubulus’ *Clepsydra*. This last courtesan was given that name because she used to have sex by the <term>clepsydra</term> <note>original: "κλεψύδραν" (klepsydran), a water-clock used in Athenian courts to time speeches. Here, she used it to time her sessions until the water ran out.</note> until it was empty, as Asclepiades, the son of Areius, says in his treatise *On Demetrius of Phalerum*, claiming her real name was Metiche. Furthermore, a courtesan—as Antiphanes says in *The Rustic*—is a disaster for the man who supports her:

> For she rejoices while having a great 
> evil at home; therefore, someone 
> lead her out while lamenting:

As Timocles says in *Neaira*: "But I, wretched man,"

> falling in love with Phryne <note>Phryne was one of the most famous and wealthy courtesans of the 4th century BCE, famous for her beauty and for being the model for the painter Apelles and the sculptor Praxiteles.</note>, when she was still 
> gathering capers, I once 
> had as much as any prostitute has, 
> spending a vast amount, yet at every 
> single door I was shut out.

And in the play titled *The Bath*, the same Timocles mentions the most wretched women:

> Nannion, Glachon, Lyca, 
> Gnathaena, Phryne, Pythionice, Myrrhine, 
> Chrysis, Conallis, 
> Hierocleia, and the little dish <note>original: "λοπάδιον" (lopadion), likely a nickname for a courtesan.</note> are all asleep.

Amphis also mentions these courtesans in *The Girl*, saying:

> Wealth seems to me to be blind, 
> since he did not come to me for this girl,

And with Sinope, Lyca, and Nannion, and other such "traps of life,"

> he sits inside as if paralyzed and does not come out.

<margin>Tricks of the courtesans.</margin>
<margin>Pollux Book 7, Chapter 11.</margin>
Alexis, in the play titled *Equal to a Weight*, sets out the "preparations" of courtesans and their hairstyles achieved through artificial means as follows:

> They sew on attachments for everyone; whenever 
> they are at a loss, they take on new courtesans 
> who are beginners in the craft. 
> Immediately they reshape them, 
> so that neither their habits 
> nor their appearances remain the same. 
> If one happens to be short, cork is 
> enclosed in the soles of her shoes. 
> If one is too tall, she wears a thin sandal 
> and goes out with her head 
> slumped toward her shoulder; 
> this takes away from her height. If one has no hips, 
> she puts on stitched-under padding, 
> so that those who see her shout about 
> her "fine buttocks." If she has a belly, 
> they have upright paddings, such as 
> comic actors have, to place there; 
> for such things pull the belly 
> forward as if with poles. 
> If one has red eyebrows, they paint them with soot. 
> If she happens to be dark-skinned, 
> she plasters herself with white lead. 
> If she is too pale, she rubs on rouge. 
> If she has some beautiful part 
> of her body, she shows that part naked. 
> If she has fine teeth, she must laugh by necessity, 
> so that those present may see 
> her mouth and how charmingly she wears it. 
> But if she does not enjoy laughing, she spends 
> the day inside, just as 
> what is laid out at the butcher's 
> when they sell the heads of goats: 
> they have a thin, upright stick of 
> myrtle between their lips, 
> so that in time they appear to be grinning; 
> they want this instead of not 
> looking the part, because of the craft they practice.

<margin>Regarding cheap little prostitutes.</margin>
Therefore, I advise you to frequent the common brothels and the women in the "rooms," and not to waste the small change of young men on nothing necessary. For truly, choosing a "lame" <note>Likely a reference to a specific type of cheap or accessible prostitute.</note> woman makes you sensible, teaching you to look at the leather <note>Perhaps a reference to the cheapness of the trade compared to the high-cost hetairai.</note>. Or do you not know the "all-night festival" of Eubulus and the cheerful "fanning of coins"?

> Girls of Cyprus, well-practiced, 
> standing naked in a row, conveniently arranged, 
> standing in thin-spun veils, such as 
> the girls the Eridanus <note>A mythical river.</note> nurtures with pure 
> waters; for a small bit of 
> coin, one can surely say to you 
> that pleasure is bought safely.

And in Eubulus' play *Nannion*, and also in Philippides:

> For whoever marries in secret and darkness, 
> how is he not the most wretched of all? 
> When it is possible to behold them in the sun, 
> standing naked in a row, conveniently 
> arranged, standing in thin-spun veils, 
> such as the girls the Eridanus nurtures 
> with pure waters, and to buy 
> pleasure for a small bit of coin. 
> And not a secret "Cypris" <note>Cypris is a title for Aphrodite, goddess of love; here used to mean sex.</note> which is most shameful, 
> and which comes through 
> insult rather than through the grace of desire. 
> I groan for the city of wretched 
> Hellas, which sent out such 
> a "cup-like" admiral.

Xenarchus also censures lives similar to yours in *The Pentathlete*, speaking thus of the high-priced courtesans in the city and the free women:

> Dreadful and intolerable 
> things the young men do in the city; 
> for where it is possible for the serving lads 
> to be seen at the brothels, 
> or those dressed in thin robes, 
> naked in a row...

# ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

...arranged in order, so that one might pick out what one likes and leave the rest—whether she be thick, round, long, wrinkled, young, old, middle-aged, or riper. One does not need to ask for a ladder to enter in secret, nor to sneak out through a hole in the roof, nor to be smuggled in through tricks in the chaff. For these women force themselves on you and are lewd, calling those who are old "little fathers" and the younger ones "daddies." And each of these may be enjoyed without fear and cheaply, by day or evening, in every way. One need not see them—nor even see them clearly while looking—perpetually worn out and afraid, holding one's soul in one's hand most fearfully. How on earth, O Lady of the Sea, Kypris <note>original: "Κύπρις" (Kypris). An epithet for Aphrodite, the goddess of love, referring to her birth in Cyprus.</note>, can they manage to make love under the "draconian laws" <note>A reference to the famously harsh laws of Draco, or perhaps a pun on "serpentine" laws.</note> when they remember them while being worshipped?

And Philemon in *The Brothers* points out that Solon was the first, because of the vigor of young men, to establish women in houses after buying them. Nicander of Colophon also records this in the third book of his *History of Colophon*, saying that he also first founded the temple of Aphrodite Pandemos <note>original: "πάνδημον ἀφροδίτης" (pandēmon aphroditēs). This title means "of all the people," suggesting a civic or public cult associated with the common people.</note> from the money earned by those who offered themselves in the houses. But Philemon says it this way:

"But you, O Solon, having found this for all mankind—for they say you were the first to see this—a democratic, O Zeus, and saving thing. And it is fitting for me to say this to you, Solon, seeing the city full of young men, and these having necessary natural urges, and erring where they should not; you stood having purchased women in places common to all and prepared. They stand naked; do not be deceived, look at everything. If you are not feeling well, you have... How the door will be open; a single obol <note>An ancient Greek coin of small value, making the services accessible to everyone.</note>, jump in! There isn't even one piece of coquetry or nonsense, nor does she snatch herself away, but immediately as you wish and in the many ways you wish. She goes out; tell someone else to go howl <note>An idiom roughly equivalent to "go to hell" or "go lament your own luck."</note>."

The Socratic Aspasia is also said to have had a multitude of beautiful women, and she filled Greece from her own ranks, as the witty Aristophanes hints, speaking of the Peloponnesian War, that Pericles, because of his love for Aspasia and because her maids were snatched away by the Megarians, broke the terrible decree against the Megarians:

"But some young men, drunk and playing at *kottabos* <note>original: "μεθυσοκότταβοι" (methysokottaboi). Kottabos was a popular Greek drinking game involving flinging wine dregs at a target; being "drunk at kottabos" implies rowdy, youthful partying.</note>, went to Megara and stole a prostitute. Then the Megarians, stung with garlic-sharp pains, stole in return two of Aspasia's prostitutes; and from there the beginning of the war broke out for all Greeks, from three whores."

But regarding the high-priced courtesans, he speaks most precisely, for he says of the others that one can see them playing the flute, all flute-girls according to the law of Apollo. Epicrates says of Lais:

<margin>
Description of Lais.
</margin>

"This Lais is lazy and a drunkard, seeing only how to drink and eat every day. It seems to me she has suffered what happens to eagles: when they are young, they eat sheep and hares from the mountains, snatching them up from on high by their strength. But when they get older, they sit on the temples hungry and miserable, and then it is considered a portent. And Lais might rightly be considered a portent. For when she was a fledgling and young, made wild by the satyrs, you would have seen her faster than Pharnabazus <note>A Persian satrap known for his wealth and speed; here it implies she was very much in demand and active.</note>. But since she has now advanced far in years, and the harmonies of her body are loosened, it is easier for me to see her and spit; she goes out everywhere now drinking. She accepts a three-obol piece, and admits both old and young. She has become so tame, O my dearest, that she now takes money right from the hand."

Anaxandrides also mentions Lais in *Old Age Madness* and lists other courtesans with her in these lines: "I know Lais from Corinth—for how could I not? Every day, oh, that dear one Anteia, and that was our plaything. By Zeus the Purifier, and Lagiska! And the one who was then Theolyte, with a very fair face and beautiful, and Niphus, who was to be, and Ocymon, quite brilliant."

I have these things to advise you, my companion Myrtilus, even according to the *Huntress* by Philetaerus: "Stop being a man of old-fashioned ways; do you not know that there is nothing sweeter than to die while living, just as they say Phormisios died?" Or is it sweeter for you, as Timocles says in *The Marathonians*: "It is a divine thing to sleep the night between a young girl or a common whore—bravo!—sweet skin, breath like the gods, not having everything be too ready. If one still has to struggle and even be slapped and take blows from soft hands, that is sweet indeed!"

By greatest Zeus, while Cynulcus <note>The "Cynic-dog," a nickname for the character in the dialogue.</note> wanted to say much more, and Magnus wanted to slap him to honor Myrtilus, Myrtilus anticipated him. For he was hostile to the Syrian, and said: "My hopes did not labor so as to call an enemy to alliance," as Callimachus says. "For we ourselves shall defend our self-sufficiency, O Cynulcus! How clumsy and rustic you are! You carry your tongue on the left side of your body <note>A Greek idiom suggesting someone is uncouth or "backwards."</note> according to Ephippus’s *Philyra*. You seem to me to be one of those whom the Muses taught left-handed letters <note>Meaning an improper or distorted education.</note>." As he said in his parodies: "I, O flute-player, am not your messmate according to the breezes of Metaglys, nor the one who complained to Aristagoras about you dancing girls, whom I once called 'ripe courtesans' but now I say this to you no longer. He asks for flute-girls just now sprouting their first down, who for a fee pull themselves under the knees of vulgar men."

But I have made my speech about many of those who were truly courtesans, capable of maintaining a friendship without guile, which Cynulcus failed to notice...

### BOOK 13

...it is sweet to mock. Of all other women, only these are addressed by the name of "friendship," derived from the title "Aphrodite the Companion" <note>original: "ἑταίρας τῆς Ἀφροδίτης" (hetairas tēs Aphroditēs). A title for the goddess suggesting her role in social bonding.</note> among the Athenians. Regarding this, Apollodorus of Athens says the following in his work *On the Gods*: "Aphrodite is called the Companion because she brings together male companions (*hetairoi*) and female companions (*hetairai*)."

Indeed, they even call free women "friends," and even now they call young girls who are close associates and friends *hetairai* <note>The word "hetaira" (ἑταίρα) literally means "female companion," though it later became a technical term for high-status courtesans.</note>. As Sappho says: "Now these things for my companions (*hetairai*) I shall sing beautifully and delightfully," and she also notes that "Leto and Niobe were very dear companions (*hetairai*)." But they also call those who work for hire *hetairai*, and the act of working for hire from sexual union is called "to act as a companion" (*hetairein*), no longer referring back to the original meaning of the word but rather to a more decorous term. Thus Menander, in *The Deposit*, distinguishes between male companions and female courtesans, saying:

> These are the works of a neighbor,
> Not a companion's; for these words,
> Being what they are, do not make the address very decorous.

Regarding courtesans, Euphemus says these things in *The Merchant*:

> Then, if one of us enters feeling grieved,
> She happened to flatter him, or
> Kissed him—not pressing her mouth tight like an enemy,
> But like a gaping sparrow—the same way as one she desired;
> She made him cheerful and immediately took away all his pain,
> Leaving him gentle and favorable thereafter.

And Eubulus, in *The Hunchback*, introducing a well-behaved courtesan, says that she dined modestly, not like the others who make a scene:

> Smaller mouthfuls than
> Cheeks, and tearing at the meat
> Like a sow; instead, she tasted a little of everything
> Like a Milesian maiden.

Antiphanes in *The Hydra*—I will not speak of this one, but of a certain neighbor of his, an individual's courtesan whom Hades reached for in love; she was destitute of a guardian or relatives, but possessed a character worth gold in terms of virtue:

> Truly a companion (*hetaira*); the others
> Harm the name by their ways, but hers is truly a beautiful name.

Anaxilas in *The Young Bird* says that if someone speaks moderately, so as to please her when she is in need:

> From the word for companionship (*hetaireia*), the name 
> "Companion" (*hetaira*) was addressed; and you now, not as you say
> To a prostitute (*porne*), but you have come to the love
> Of a companion (*hetaira*); so in truth she is
> Simple indeed—and charming, by Zeus!

Our fellow young-lover here is just like that, such as Alexis or Antiphanes introduces in *Sleep*. For this reason, this "male prostitute" <note>A term used here as an insult or a specific social category.</note> does not even seek out everything with us, so as to avoid grieving his lover when kissing. Erippus speaks well of such people in *Sappho*:

> For whenever a bastard child
> Entering, sees another's face,
> And lays an un-contributing hand upon the food,
> Consider that you must give an account of him by night.

The orator Aeschines said the same things in his speech *Against Timarchus*. Regarding courtesans, in *The Friend of Courtesans* and *The White-Robed*, it says: "There is no sanctuary for a courtesan; it is everywhere."

But we do not know of a sanctuary for a married wife in Greece. I also know of a festival called the *Hetairideia* <note>The "Festival of Companionship."</note> celebrated in Magnesia, not because of the courtesans but for another reason, as Hegesander mentions in his *Commentaries*, writing: "The Magnesians celebrate the festival of the *Hetairideia*." They record that Jason, the son of Aeson, first brought the Argonauts together to Zeus the Companion (*Hetairios*), offered sacrifice, and called the festival the *Hetairideia*. The kings of the Macedonians also sacrifice at the *Hetairideia*.

<margin>Aphrodite the Prostitute.</margin> There is a temple of Aphrodite the Prostitute (*Porne*) among the people of Abydos, as Pamphilus says. For when the city was held in slavery by a garrison, the men once sacrificed to the Earth, as Cleanthes records in his *Mythical Matters*; they brought in several courtesans, one of whom, seeing the guards fallen asleep, took the keys, climbed over the wall, and reported it to the people of Abydos. They immediately arrived with arms, killed the guards, and having gained control of the walls and regained their freedom, they paid a debt of gratitude to the prostitute by founding a temple to "Aphrodite the Prostitute."

Alexis of Samos, in the second book of his *Samos Annals*, says that the Aphrodite in Samos—whom some call "in the reeds" and others "in the marshes"—was founded by the courtesans who followed Pericles when he was besieging Samos, after they had earned sufficient money from their beauty. Eualkes, in his *Ephesian History*, also says that temples were founded to "Aphrodite the Companion" in Ephesus.

Clearchus, in the first book of his *Erotics*, says that Gyges the King of the Lydians, who became famous not only for his longing for his mistress while she was alive—risking himself and his entire empire for her—but also when she died, he gathered all the Lydians from the countryside and built what is still called "The Courtesan’s Monument" to a great height, so that as he traveled through the territory of Tmolus, wherever he might turn, he could see the monument, and it would be visible to all who inhabit Lydia.

The orator Demosthenes, in the speech *Against Neaera*—if it is genuine, which Apollodorus spoke—says: "We have courtesans (*hetairai*) for the sake of pleasure, concubines (*pallakai*) for the sake of daily service to the body, and wives (*gynaikes*) for the sake of bearing legitimate children and having a faithful guardian of the household."

I shall further list... <margin>Corinthian courtesans.</margin> ...beginning with beautiful Corinth, since I have found a certain speech concerning courtesans even before Aeschylus, showing the religious practice there. For it was an ancient custom in Corinth, as Chamaeleon of Heraclea records in his book *On Pindar*, that whenever the city prays to Aphrodite concerning great matters, they enlist as many courtesans as possible to join the supplication, and these pray to the goddess and later are present at the sacrifices. And when the Persian led his expedition against Greece, as both Theopompus and Timaeus record in his seventh book, the Corinthian courtesans prayed for the salvation of the Greeks, having gone into the temple of Aphrodite...

### BOOK 13

...for this reason, Simonides also composed an epigram when the Corinthians dedicated a tablet to the goddess—which remains there even now—depicting the individual courtesans who made a public supplication for the safety of Greece and were present at the event. He wrote the following:

> These women, on behalf of the Greeks and their brave citizens,
> Stood to pray to divine Cypris <note>Cypris is a common epithet for Aphrodite, referring to her mythical birth on the island of Cyprus.</note>.
> For divine Aphrodite did not intend to allow the archer
> Persians to betray the acropolis of the Greeks.

Even private citizens make vows to the goddess that if they obtain what they pray for, they will bring her a specified number of courtesans. Such a custom being established at the temple, Xenophon of Corinth, when setting out for the Olympic games, vowed that he himself would bring courtesans to the goddess if he were victorious. Pindar first wrote an encomium <note>A formal hymn of praise.</note> for him, which begins: "Praising a house thrice-victorious at Olympia." Later, he also composed a *skolion* <note>A "drinking song" performed at banquets.</note> to be sung during the sacrifice, in which the opening address is directed immediately to the courtesans who followed Xenophon during the sacrifice to Aphrodite. Therefore he said:

"O Mistress of Cyprus, here to your grove Xenophon has led a herd of a hundred grazing girls to fulfill his vows." He began the end of the poem like this: "O hospitable young women, handmaidens of Persuasion in wealthy Corinth, you who often burn the amber tears of frankincense for us, flying in thought to the heavenly mother of loves, Aphrodite... who granted you, O girls, to harvest the fruit of soft youth in lovely beds of necessity." Having started in this way, he says later: "But I wonder what the masters of the city will say of me, finding this honey-minded beginning of a drinking song joined with common women." For it is clear that in addressing the courtesans, he was anxious about how the matter would appear to the Corinthians. But, trusting in himself, it seems, he immediately wrote: "Gold tested by a touchstone has shone forth."

<margin>
Aphrodisia:
This [festival] of the Corinthians.
</margin>

That the courtesans celebrate the festival of Aphrodisia privately there, Alexis says in *Natures*: "The city celebrated the Aphrodisia for the courtesans; there is another festival separately for the free women. On these days it is the custom to revel, and it is the law for the courtesans to sing with us."

In Lacedaemon <note>Another name for Sparta.</note>, as Polemon the Guide says in his work *On the Dedications in Lacedaemon*, there is a famous statue of a courtesan named Kotinna, who they say also dedicated a bronze cow. He writes: "And the small statue of the courtesan Kotinna, who because of her fame has a building named after her very near the hill where the temple of Dionysus stands, a place well-known to many in the city. Her dedication stands above the 'Bronze House' <note>The temple of Athena Chalkioikos (Athena of the Bronze House).</note>, the aforementioned small bronze cow."

And the beautiful Alcibiades—about whom one of the comic poets said, "O earth and gods, the beautiful Alcibiades, whom Lacedaemon desires to catch as an adulterer"—while being loved by the wife of Agisilaus, used to revel at the doors of common courtesans, leaving behind both the Spartan and Athenian women. At any rate, he fell in love with a certain Medontis of Abydos by reputation alone, and having sailed to the Hellespont with Axiochus (who was his lover at the time, as the orator Lysias says in the speech against him), he shared her with him. Alcibiades always took two other courtesans with him: a certain Damasantra and the younger Laïs, and also Theodote, by whom he was buried after his death in the village of Melissa in Phrygia, having been plotted against by Pharnabazus.

<margin>
Synnada, see Stephanus.
</margin>

We ourselves have seen the tomb of Alcibiades in Melissa when traveling from Synnada to the Metropolis <note>Synnada and Metropolis were important cities in the Roman province of Phrygia, in modern-day Turkey.</note>. At this tomb, a bull is sacrificed every year by the command of the most excellent Emperor Hadrian, who also set up a statue of Alcibiades in Parian marble upon the tomb.

One should not wonder if some have fallen in love with people by report alone, since Chares of Mitylene, in the tenth book of his *History of Alexander*, says that some have fallen in love after seeing people in dreams whom they had never seen before. He writes as follows: "Hystaspes had a younger brother named Zariadres; both were very beautiful, and the locals say they were the children of Aphrodite and Adonis. Hystaspes ruled over Media and the lower country, while Zariadres ruled the region above the Caspian Gates as far as the Tanais river. Beyond the Tanais ruled Omartes, king of the Marathi, who had a daughter named Odatis. It is written in the histories about her that she saw Zariadres in a dream and fell in love with him, and the same passion befell him for her. They continued to desire one another through the visions seen in sleep. Odatis was the most beautiful woman in Asia, and Zariadres was also handsome. So, when Zariadres sent to Omartes desiring to marry the woman, Omartes would not agree because he was destitute of male children and wanted to give her to one of his own household. Not long after, Omartes gathered the lords, friends, and relatives of his kingdom to celebrate the wedding, without having said beforehand to whom he intended to give his daughter. When the drinking was at its height, the father called Odatis into the banquet and said in the hearing of the guests: 'O daughter, we are now making your marriage.' Looking around and seeing them all, she took a golden cup and filled it; he said, 'Give it to whom you wish to be married,' for that was the sign of being chosen for marriage. She, looking around at everyone, did so while weeping, longing to see Zariadres—for she had sent word to him that the wedding was about to take place. He, who was encamped by the Tanais, slipped away from his camp and crossed over with only his charioteer, and having run by night on his chariot, he passed through the city..."

### BOOK 13

...having chased on foot for nearly eight hundred stadia <note>A stadium is roughly 600 feet; 800 stadia is nearly 92 miles.</note>, and arriving near the village where they were to celebrate the wedding, he left his chariot and charioteer in a certain place and went forward, having found a Scythian robe during the night. Passing into the courtyard and seeing Odatis standing before the sideboard, weeping as she slowly mixed the wine in the bowl <note>original: "φιάλην" (phiale), a shallow ceramic or metal bowl used for drinking and libations</note>, he stood near her and said: "O Odatis, I am here as you desired—I, Zariadres." She, recognizing a strange and handsome man, similar to the one she had seen in her sleep, became overjoyed and gave him the bowl. He seized her, led her away to the chariot, and fled with Odatis. The servants and handmaidens, knowing of their love, kept silent, and when her father ordered them to call her, they claimed they did not know where she had gone. This love story is remembered among the barbarians who inhabit Asia, and is exceedingly popular; they paint the myth in their temples, palaces, and even in private houses, and many name their own daughters Odatis.

Aristotle records a similar custom in his *Constitution of the Massaliotes* <note>Massalia is modern-day Marseille, France.</note>, writing as follows:
<margin>Marriage customs of the Massaliotes.</margin>
"The Phocaeans <note>Greeks from Ionia, in modern Turkey.</note> who were engaged in trade founded Massalia. Euxenus the Phocaean was a guest of King Nanos—for that was his name. This Nanos, while celebrating his daughter's wedding, invited Euxenus, who happened to be present, to the feast. The marriage was conducted in this manner: after the meal, the girl had to enter and give a bowl of mixed wine to whichever of the present suitors she wished; and to whomsoever she gave it, he was to be the bridegroom. The girl entered and gave it, whether by chance or for some other reason, to Euxenus. The girl's name was Petta. When this happened, her father, believing the gift had been made by divine will, allowed him to have her. Euxenus took her as his wife and lived with her, changing her name to Aristoxene. There is still a family in Massalia descended from them called the Protiadae, for Protis was the first son of Euxenus and Aristoxene."

Themistocles also, as Idomeneus says, did not hitch a chariot of horses, but drove into the city when the marketplace was full with a chariot drawn by four courtesans—these were Lamia, Scione, Satyra, and Nannion. Themistocles himself was born of a courtesan <note>original: "ἑταίρας" (hetaira)</note> named Abrotonon, as Amphicrates records in his treatise *On Famous Men*. 
<margin>On various courtesans who became queens.</margin>
"Abrotonon was a woman of a certain race, but they say she gave birth to the great Greek, Themistocles." However, Neanthes of Cyzicus, in the third and fourth books of his *Grecian Histories*, says he was the son of Euterpe.

And did not Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Younger, who attempted to seize the Persian throne from his brother Artaxerxes II.</note>, who marched against his brother, have with him the Phocaean courtesan who was the wisest and most beautiful of her time? He had her on his campaign, and Zosophanes says she was previously called Milto but was renamed Aspasia. A Milesian concubine also followed him. 

The Great Alexander also had with him Thais, the Athenian courtesan. Cleitarchus says she was the cause of the burning of the palace at Persepolis. This same Thais, after Alexander's death, was married to Ptolemy, the first king of Egypt, and bore him children: Leontiscus and Lagus, and a daughter, Irene, who married Dionysius, the king in Cyprus. 

The second king of Egypt, Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus.</note>, as the benefactor Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, who wrote memoirs.</note> records in the third book of his *Commentaries*, had many mistresses: Didyme, one of the local women who was very beautiful in appearance, and Bilistiche. Furthermore, he had Agathoclea and Stratonice, whose great monument exists by the sea near Eleusis, and Myrtion, and many others, being rather inclined toward sexual pleasures. Polybius, in the fourteenth book of his *Histories*, says that many statues of Cleino, his cupbearer, are dedicated throughout Alexandria, depicting her wearing only a tunic and holding a drinking horn <note>original: "ῥυτὸν" (rhyton)</note> in her hands. He says the finest of the houses are named after Myrtion, Mnensis, and Pothane. Indeed, Mnensis and Pothane were flute-players, and Myrtion was one of the well-known and common dancers. 

King Ptolemy Philopator <note>Ptolemy IV.</note> was ruled by the courtesan Agathoclea, who threw the whole kingdom into turmoil. Eumachus of Naples, in the second book of his *Histories of Hannibal*, says that Hieronymus, the tyrant of the Syracusans, took a woman named Peitho who had lived in a brothel and declared her queen. Timotheus, the Athenian general, was born of a famous courtesan whom he knew was Thracian by birth, but otherwise noble in her manners. For some women change their ways toward modesty and are better than those who pride themselves on it. When Timotheus was once mocked for having such a mother, he said, "I am grateful to her, for because of her I am the son of Conon." 

Carystius, in his *Historical Notes*, says that Philetaerus of Pergamon, who ruled this territory now called the "New Land," was the son of a flute-playing courtesan named Boa, a Paphlagonian by birth. Aristophon the orator, who introduced the law under the archonship of Euclides <note>403/402 BCE.</note> that anyone not born of a citizen-mother should be a bastard, was himself shown by the comic poet Calliades to have had children by the courtesan Choregis, as Carystius himself records in the third book of his *Notes*. 

Demetrius the Besieger <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes.</note> was divinely in love with the flute-player Lamia, by whom he also had a dear daughter. Polemon says, in his work *On the Painted Stoa in Sicyon*, that Lamia was the daughter of Cleanor of Athens, and that she constructed the aforementioned stoa for the Sicyonians.

# ATHENAEUS — THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

Demetrius <note>Demetrius I Poliorcetes (337–283 BCE), a successor to Alexander the Great known for his flamboyant lifestyle and many mistresses.</note> was also desperately in love with **Leaena** <note>The name means "Lioness."</note>, a courtesan who was then at her peak, as well as many others. **Machon**, the comic poet, says in his work titled *Anecdotes*: "Demetrius was exceedingly pleased with Leaena. Persinomides, who was a favorite in Demetrius's court, says that the King jokingly ordered **Lamia** <note>One of the most famous courtesans of antiquity, a flute-player and long-term mistress of Demetrius.</note> to be praised as well. She replied to this: 'Very well, if you wish, then let the Lioness [Leaena] prevail.'" Lamia was indeed very sharp and urban in her responses, much like **Gnathaena**, whom we shall speak of shortly. Again, Machon writes the following regarding Lamia: "Once our King Demetrius was showing off all kinds of perfumes to Lamia during a drinking party. Lamia was a flute-player, and she said she was quite pleased with them, but Demetrius, showing off his own skin and dismissing everything else, began to rub a certain natural nard <note>A pun on the scent of his own body or genitals; 'nard' was an expensive aromatic oil.</note> with his hand and, holding it toward Lamia’s nose, said, 'See, this has a truly divine scent.' She laughed and replied, 'But it seems to me to be the rot-smelling thing of all.'" Demetrius answered: "But by the gods, Lamia, this is a 'royal acorn' [balanos] <note>A crude double-entendre: *balanos* means both 'acorn/ben-nut' used in perfume and the 'glans' of the penis.</note>."

**Ptolemy son of Lagus** <note>Ptolemy I, King of Egypt, though some attribute this to a later historian named Ptolemy.</note>, in his histories concerning Philopator, lists the mistresses of kings and says that **Philip of Macedon** <note>Philip II, father of Alexander the Great.</note>, who expanded the power of the Macedonians, loved **Philinna** the dancer, by whom he fathered Aridaeus, who reigned after Alexander. He says Demetrius the Besieger loved **Mania** <note>A name often given to Phrygian slaves; its use for a high-class Athenian courtesan was unusual.</note> after those previously mentioned; and **Antigonus** loved **Demo**, by whom Alcyoneus was born. **Seleucus Nicator** loved **Myce**, daughter of Nysa. **Heracleides Lembos**, in the thirty-third book of his *Histories*, says that Demo became a mistress to Demetrius, and that his father Antigonus also fell madly in love with her and executed **Oxythemis** for having been a companion to Demetrius, and also tortured and killed Demo’s maidservants.

<margin>Machon on the courtesan Mania.</margin>
Regarding the aforementioned name **Mania**, Machon says the following: "Perhaps someone among the current audience might reasonably wonder whether any Athenian woman was ever called or named 'Mania.' For it is a shameful thing for a woman to have a Phrygian name, especially a courtesan in the heart of Greece, or for the city of Athens—by which all people have been civilized—to allow such a thing. In truth, her name from childhood was **Melitta** <note>Meaning 'Bee.'</note>. She was slightly smaller in stature than the other women of that time, but her voice and conversation were richly endowed. Because she was very beautiful and striking, and had many lovers among both citizens and foreigners, whenever people spoke of her, they would say that Melitta was 'Mania' [the Madwoman] because she was so lovely. She herself encouraged this even more, for whenever she made a joke, she would immediately be praised as 'Mania.' Whether she was praising or blaming someone, the word 'Mania' was attached to her speech. Therefore, by extending the nickname 'Mania,' one of her lovers seems to have called her 'Madness' [mania], and the nickname eventually took over her real name. It seems Mania was from Libya, and she and **Gnathaena** used to share the same bed. This was a rule established by **Diphilus** <note>A famous poet of the New Comedy.</note>." 

After this, Gnathaena began to mock Mania, saying: "What is this, child? If you have a stone..." Mania interrupted and gave it back to her, saying, "You take it and wipe yourself, you wretch." To show how witty she was in her replies, Machon records these things about her: "**Leontiscus** the wrestler once loved Mania and lived with her as if she were his legal wife. Later, sensing she was being unfaithful with **Antenor**, he became very angry. She, however, claimed she wasn't doing anything wrong, for she 'wanted to learn and feel at the same time what kind of blow two Olympic-winning athletes could strike in the night.'"

When King Demetrius once asked Mania to show him her backside, she requested a gift in return. When he gave it, she turned around and said, after a moment: "Now you may behold the son of Agamemnon <note>original: "Ἀγαμέμνονος παῖ" (Child of Agamemnon). This is a parody of a tragic line (likely from Sophocles' *Electra*), where the character refers to Orestes, but here she uses it to refer to her own 'rear.'</note>, since you have always been eager to see him."

There was a man who was thought to be a deserter, a foreigner, who was drinking lavishly with some athletes. He sent for Mania to join him. He had gathered some of the city's jokers who were accustomed to laughing at everything in order to get a meal. Wanting to appear refined and witty, while Mania was playing and frequently getting up, he tried to trip her up in front of the others, saying: "Young men, what do you think is the fastest beast that runs in the mountains?" Mania replied, "The deserter, my good man."

Later, when Mania came back in, she mocked the deserter, calling him a "shield-dropper" <note>original: "ῥίψασπιν" (rhipsaspin), a term of great cowardice in Greece, referring to someone who throws away their heavy shield to run faster from battle.</note> because he had once fled an attack. The soldier looked somewhat gloomy and dismissed her. The courtesan, not at all bothered, said: "Don't be upset, my dearest, for by Aphrodite, you didn't lose *your* shield, but the one who lent it to you lost it." 

At a symposium at Mania's house, a certain man was behaving very poorly and asked her rudely: "Should I go up or down?" <note>A sexual proposition regarding positions.</note> She laughed and said: "Go up, for I am somewhat afraid that you will catch me in the 'noose' [plokion] <note>A technical joke involving a hairstyle or a trap; likely implying he is clumsy or dangerous.</note>."

Machon also collected anecdotes about other courtesans, which it is not out of place to mention next. Regarding **Gnathaena**: once while Diphilus was drinking at Gnathaena’s house at a dinner, being highly honored as one of her lovers—for he was indeed very dearly loved by her—

He arrived carrying two jars of Chian wine and four of Thasian; he also brought myrrh, garlands, sweetmeats, a kid goat, and ribbons. For the main course, he brought a flute-girl and a certain Syrian stranger from Gerastos. He had filled it with snow <note>original: "χιόνα" — Snow was used by the wealthy to chill wine, a high luxury in Athens.</note>. He came in the evening, feeling ashamed of his gifts lest someone should find out, and he was especially on guard against **Diphilus** <note>Diphilus of Sinope was a famous poet of the New Comedy and a frequent target of Gnathaena’s wit.</note>, fearing he might be mocked in a play later on. He told his servant to carry them away as quickly as possible to those with whom he had agreed to share his salt. But having secretly blown the snow into the top of the vessel and ordered the boy to pour out a full measure, he offered a cup to Diphilus. Diphilus, that "prosecutor of prostitutes," drank it down suddenly, and being stunned by the unexpected chill, he cried out, "By Athena, what a god-given coldness!" Gnathaena replied, "Well, it is because we are always throwing the prologues of your plays into the well." <note>This is a famous "cold" joke; in ancient literary criticism, a boring or unsuccessful play was called "cold." Gnathaena implies Diphilus’s writing is so frigid it can chill wine.</note>

A certain scoundrel, tall and covered in scars from whippings <note>term: "mastigias" — a slave or low-life who has been frequently whipped.</note>, happened to be resting with Gnathaena. Seeing his back was completely uneven and scarred, she embraced him and said, "Poor man, poor man! My dear, where did you get these wounds?" He tried to save face and replied, "When I was a boy, I used to crawl into the fire; once, while playing with some children my own age, I fell in." She replied, "By dear Demeter, you were justly flayed, you undisciplined man!" <note>She sees through his lie; the scars are from judicial or punitive whipping, not an accidental fire.</note>

Once, when Gnathaena was with the courtesan **Dexidea**, and Dexidea was cleaning herself almost entirely of filth, Dexidea felt honored and said, "By Artemis, Gnathaena, if I had known then, I would have dined with my mother and not with you, woman!" As Gnathaena advanced in years and was by all accounts a complete old woman, they say she went out into the market, not to buy food or to meddle, but she stood at a corner where a very handsome meat-seller was standing. He was quite young. She said to him, "O beautiful youth, how do you sell the 'divine' portions? Tell me the price." He smiled and said, "Thirty, like a throw of the dice." She replied, "What? You wretch, do you use 'Carian' weights for such a price?" <note>Carian weights were notoriously unreliable or light, implying he was overcharging or cheating her.</note>

**Stratocles** used to give free gifts to his acquaintances, managing a small dish of bodies and those who associated with them, and they would wait until tomorrow to mark their morning contributions, while paying long-term dues for the rest. Gnathaena, seeing a certain lover who was a soldier paying his contributions again, said: "Stratocles makes winters for the horsemen." Seeing a very thin, dark youth, who seemed excessively lean and sleek, and even shorter than an ephebe <note>term: "ephebe" — a young man aged 18-20 in military training.</note>, she joked that he was an **Adonis**. When the young man met her in a rather rude and arrogant manner, she looked at her daughter who was walking with her and said, "By the two goddesses, my child, you are more just!" <note>The "two goddesses" are Demeter and Persephone, a common oath for Athenian women.</note>

They say a young man from the Pontus region, while resting with Gnathaena, asked for a "debt-relief" <note>term: "chreolysion" — a pun on debt cancellation, here meaning a free sexual favor.</note> early in the morning so she would provide herself to him once for free. She replied, "You wretch! <margin>Gnathaenion.</margin> An eagle hung over my nest this morning, just as the time to drive out the sows is passing." And regarding the granddaughter of Gnathaena, this too was recorded: A stranger named **Sabapes** visited Athens, a very old man of ninety years. During the festival of Cronus, he gave himself to Gnathaenion. When he was with her in an amorous way, Gnathaena, noticing his rhythm, asked with a smile how much he paid for the night. She looked at his purple clothes and his food and set the price at a thousand drachmas. He suddenly cried out, as if struck by lightning, "Good heavens, woman! You are taking a soldier’s pay! You act as if you’ve never had to work for it!" He tried to pull away, but she skillfully accepted Sabapes, saying, "If you desire the father of Zeus <note>A reference to Cronus, whose festival was being celebrated.</note>, you know accurately that you will pay double to my little daughter for the night."

In Athens, there was a very gifted bronze-worker, and when Gnathaena was nearly finished with her career and could no longer endure the work, she took up with **Andronicus** the actor. They were traveling abroad together when a son was born to him. Gnathaenion did not hesitate to receive him with a smile, and though she was very devoted to him, she also wanted to have his gold. He was a completely unrefined and vulgar man, and once, sitting in a shoemaker's shop with some others, he began to slander Gnathaena, saying that she had slept with no one but had been "ridden" five times in a row by him.

Later, when Andronicus heard what had happened after recently arriving from Corinth, he spoke of these things to Gnathaenion during a drinking session. He demanded to know if anything had happened with her or if she had ever used that "position." While others were lashing out at her as scoundrels, they say Gnathaenion replied: "Why do you embrace me? I didn't chase a barley-cake, you wretch! I endured a man who was falling apart just to get a lot of gold. I 'philosophized' so that I would take as little of his body as possible." Then they say that once, when Andronicus wanted to kiss Gnathaenion during the drinking, just as he always did in previous days, she got angry or perhaps didn't want to receive anything by force. He said, "Don't you see, Gnathaena, how haughtily your daughter is treating me?" The old woman, becoming annoyed, said, "Poor child, embrace him and kiss him if he wants."
