# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

<note>original: "ΑΘΗΝ. ΔΕΙΠΝΟΣΟΦ." — Athenaeus, *Deipnosophistae*.</note>

...of her friends, "A story was a debt owed under the cover of silence, wishing to keep the common pain as a gift." Once, during a public festival, **Gnathaenion** went down to the market to meet a certain merchant, a lover of modest means, traveling on a carriage. She had with her three little donkeys and three maids surrounding one old woman <note>term: "tethē" — an grandmother or elderly nurse/chaperone.</note>. When a crush of people occurred among them, a certain "bad wrestler" encountered them—one of those who was always diligently defeated in the games. Being unable to pass by easily but being cramped for space, he said: "O thrice-wretched donkey-driver, I'll go faster if you just fall out of the way! I shall knock down these little women from the crowd along with their little donkeys," speaking of the carriages. But Gnathaenion replied: "O miserable man, surely not, for you have never before <margin>Lais.</margin> fared so well in a struggle as you have here." <note>This is a double-entendre; she mocks him because as a failing wrestler, he finally found someone (a group of women and donkeys) he could actually "overpower."</note> Next, he records these things: They say that **Lais** the Corinthian once saw **Euripides** in a certain garden, holding a tablet with a stylus hanging from it. "Answer me, O Poet," she said, "what were you thinking when you wrote in your tragedy: 'Away, you doer of shameful things!'" <note>original: "Ἔῤῥ' αἰσχροποιέ" — a line from Euripides' lost play, *Aeolus*.</note> Euripides, struck by her boldness, said: "And who are you to speak of shameful deeds?" But she, laughing, replied: "What is 'shameful,' if it does not seem so to those who do it?" <note>This is a clever subversion of another line from the same play: "What is shameful if it does not seem so to the one who does it?"</note>

<margin>Glycerium.</margin> **Glycerium**, having received from a certain lover a new Corinthian cloak <note>term: "ledion" — a light summer garment or wrap.</note> four cubits long, gave it to a laundryman. Later, having sent her maid to fetch it with the small fee, the man refused to give back the cloak. The laundryman sent word back saying: "Bring me three more quarter-obols to collect it. The hindrance is what was owed." The maid reported this to her mistress, and Glycerium said, "The wretch! He intends to fry my cloak <margin>Nico.</margin> just like a little fish!" <note>original: "mainidos" — a sprat or small fish. She is punning on the cleaning process or perhaps the "shrinking" of the garment.</note> The poet **Sophocles**, when he was still a young man, was in love with **Demophon**. He once possessed **Nico**, who was older and nicknamed "The Goat." People always teased him that she had "devoured the great Thallos" <note>term: "thallos" — a young green shoot or branch (which goats eat), but here also the name of a wealthy lover she had exhausted.</note>. For when he was going to buy Attic honey and dried figs from Chelidonia, and loading up with Hymettian honey, it is said he knew that woman—a woman I call Isane, whom Demophon once asked to have. She, laughing well, said: "Certainly, my dearest, so that you may take Sophocles' place with me."

**Kallisso**, who was nicknamed "The Sow," was once being insulted by her own mother, whose nickname was "The Crow." Gnathaena was asked: "What is the difference between them?" She replied: "What else, except that one is a crow and the other <margin>Hippike.</margin> is a different kind of bird?" They say that **Hippike**, another mistress of Theodorus, once had a lover who dealt in hay. She herself once came late at night to a drinking party with **King Ptolemy**, as she was accustomed to drink with him. He said she was very much behind schedule. "Ptolemy," she said, "this 'Papa' is very thirsty! Let someone pour me three large cups." When she had drunk a great amount, the King said: "Into the basin with you! For it seems to me, Hippike, that you have devoured much hay today." <note>A pun on her name (meaning "Horse-like") and her lover's profession.</note>

<margin>Phryne.</margin> **Phryne** was approached by Moerichus the Theatinican, and she demanded a *mna* <note>term: "mna" — a unit of currency equal to 100 drachmas, a very high price.</note> from him. Moerichus said: "Is that not much? Did you not just recently take two gold pieces from a stranger?" "Wait then," she said, "until I am in the mood for you, and I shall take just as much from you." And **Nico**, who was called "The Goat," is said to have been left by a certain Python. Later, when he was trying to win her back, she supposedly said to the servant who came for her: "Now Python seeks me, since he is nearly finished with his weaving and is able to turn the 'Goat' back again."

<margin>Names of Hetaerae.</margin> Thus far I remember the things said by Machon. For our beautiful Athens brought forth such a multitude of courtesans—where shall I begin to enumerate them? As I think of it, no other flowering city ever had such a crowd. **Aristophanes of Byzantium** <note>A famous Alexandrian scholar and grammarian.</note> recorded one hundred and thirty-five of them. Apollodorus listed even more than these. Gorgias says many were omitted by Aristophanes, including the following: The one nicknamed "The Wine-Drinker," and *Lampyris* (Firefly), and *Euphrosyne* (Joy). The latter was a laundryman’s daughter. Others recorded by him are: *Megiste*, *Agallis*, *Thaumarion*, and *Theocleia*. The latter was nicknamed "The Crow." Also *Lysiastykisos*, *Asra*, **Gnathaena**, and her granddaughter **Gnathaenion**, and *Sige* (Silence), also called *Synaulis* (Flute-player) or *Lychnos* (The Lamp); also *Eucleia*, *Grammaia*, *Thryallis*, *Chimaira*, and *Lampas*. 

<margin>Ready answers of Gnathaena.</margin> Regarding Gnathaena's wit, as has been said before: **Diphilus** the comic poet, as Lynceus of Samos also records in his *Memoirs*, was once performing in a competition and was greatly hissed; he was driven from the theater in silence. Nonetheless, he went to Gnathaena's house. When Diphilus asked Gnathaena to wash his feet, she asked: "Why? Did you just arrive from a cliff?" <note>A "cliff" or "precipice" was a metaphor for a theatrical failure or "crash."</note> Gnathaena was extremely sharp in her replies. Other courtesans also took great pride in themselves, applying themselves to education and devoting time to studies, which is why they were so ready with their answers. For example, people once accused **Glycera** to the philosopher **Stilpo** during a drinking party, saying she was corrupting the youth. As Satyrus says in his *Lives*, Glycera interrupted and said: "We both have the same accusation against us, Stilpo. For they say that you corrupt those who encounter you by teaching them useless and erotic sophistries, and they say the same of me. Therefore, it makes no difference to those who are worn down and suffering whether they live with a philosopher or a courtesan." For according to Agathon: "A woman with an idle body does not carry an idle mind."

# BOOK 13

...And Lynceus recorded many such responses. For instance, when a certain parasite <note>In Greek culture, a "parasite" was a professional dinner guest who provided wit and flattery in exchange for a meal.</note> was being kept by an old woman and was in excellent physical condition, he wittily remarked: "Young man, you are in fine shape. What do you think would happen if you didn't even sleep 'at the door'?" <note>This implies the man was sleeping on the street or in the porch as a lover; the parasite replied that without the old woman's food, he would have died of hunger.</note> And Pausanias says that once, when a man fell into a cistern <note>original: "lakkon"</note>, he joked that the cistern had fallen into the jar. 

Once, when someone offered wine in a tiny cooler and said it was sixteen years old, Gnathaena remarked: "It's certainly small for being so many years old!" 

When some young men were drinking at her house and began mock-fighting and hitting one another, she said: "Have courage, child! The contest isn't for a crown <note>meaning a prestigious athletic prize</note>, but for silver!" 

When a man gave a *mina* <note>a unit of currency equal to 100 drachmas</note> to her daughter but brought nothing else and just kept visiting, she said: "Child, he is just like a physical trainer giving a *mina* to a wrestler—he thinks he can just keep attending classes without further payment." 

When **Phryne** said something rather bitter to her, Gnathaena replied: "If you have a stone <note>original: "lithon"</note>, you think you will be acquitted." <note>This is a layered joke: Phryne was famously acquitted in court when her lawyer exposed her beauty to the judges, but Gnathaena is also mocking Phryne for allegedly having kidney stones, while Gnathaena herself was mocked for having a protruding belly.</note>

Once, while guests were eating a dish of lentils and bulbs at her house, a slave girl accidentally spilled some of the lentils into her own lap <note>original: "kolpos"</note> while cleaning. Gnathaena remarked: "I see you are planning to make 'lap-lentils' <note>original: "kolpophagion," a pun on "bolbophagion," the dish they were eating.</note>." 

When the tragic actor **Andronicus**, returning from a contest in which he had been successful in the play *The Epigoni*, was about to drink at her house and ordered his boy to pay Gnathaena in advance, she quoted a line from the play: "O wretched fate of children, what a tale you have told!" She then joked about how he had come from the Greeks to the "first city" (likely a pun on his fame). When he asked which city, she said: "To Sigeum" <note>A pun on the Greek word "sige," meaning silence—implying his acting or the room should be quiet.</note>. 

When someone entered and saw eggs in a vessel and asked, "Are these raw <note>original: "ōma"</note>, Gnathaena?" she replied, "No, they are bronze <note>original: "enchalka"</note>, child." 

<margin>Sayings of various courtesans.</margin>

When **Cherephon** came to dinner uninvited, Gnathaena handed him a cup and said, "Take this, you arrogant man!" When he asked, "Me, arrogant? Who is more so than Gnathaena?" she replied, "You, who comes even when you aren't called!" 

**Nico**, who was nicknamed "The Goat," as Lynceus says, once saw a man who had spent an entire talent <note>a massive sum of money</note> but had grown thin through illness. She remarked, "How thin he is! It's as if he has eaten my oil-flask and my shoes in just three days."

**Metaira** the courtesan, when the parasite Democles fell into some plaster, remarked: "You didn't give yourself to the vote; these aren't pebbles." <note>A reference to the small stones or "psephoi" used for voting in Athenian courts.</note> When he later leaned over to the next couch, she said: "Watch out you don't tip over." This is recorded by Hegesander.

Aristodemus, in the second book of his *Humorous Memoirs*, says that two men—a soldier and a common rogue—hired Gnathaena. When the soldier, being rather unrefined, called her a "cistern" <note>implying she was a bottomless pit for money</note>, she replied: "Why? Is it because two 'beasts' have been thrown into me, and yet the wolf is still free?" 

When some poor lovers came to serenade Gnathaena’s daughter and threatened to tear the house down to its foundations, Gnathaena said: "If you had that much strength, you would have sent the rent you owe instead of threats." 

Gnathaena was extremely witty and even wrote a "Law for Banquets" <note>original: "nomon syssitikon"</note> which she recited from a tablet. In this, she set out rules for how lovers should behave when visiting her, imitating the way philosophers compose their treatises. **Callimachus** records this in the third volume of his *Tables of Laws*, noting it was 323 lines long.

**Callistion**, nicknamed "The Pauper-Lioness," once hired a rogue. It was summer, and as he lay naked, she saw the scars of whips on his back. "Where did those come from?" she asked. He replied, "When I was a boy, some hot soup was spilled on me." She retorted, "Then it was milk-fed trouble!" 

When the poet **Menander** <note>The most famous playwright of New Comedy.</note> visited **Glycera** and she offered him some milk to drink, he said, "I don't want any," because there was a "scum" <note>original: "graus"</note> on top. Glycera replied, "Blow the 'old woman' <note>also "graus"</note> away and take what's underneath!" 

**Thaïs**, having many cups from a certain boastful lover, heard him say he wanted to break them all and have new ones made. She replied, "Then you will just be returning to everyone what belongs to them." <note>Implying he had stolen or borrowed the cups from others.</note>

When **Leontion** was reclining with a lover and Glycera entered the party, the lover paid more attention to Glycera. Leontion, feeling slighted, turned away. When her acquaintance asked why she was upset, she said, "My 'behind' <note>original: "hystera," which means "womb" but also "the one who came later," referring to Glycera</note> hurts me." 

When a lover sent a "scrap" of meat to **Lais** of Corinth and asked her to visit him, she replied, "I cannot, for it is mud <note>original: "pelos"</note>." <note>A likely reference to the cheapness of the gift or her own "unclean" period.</note>

**Thaïs**, speaking to Grason, a man obsessed with courtesans, was asked where she was going. She replied, "I am going to live with 'The Goat' <note>Aega</note> at the house of 'The All-Giver' <note>Pandion</note>." 

When **Phryne** was dining with Grason once, she took a purple cloth and said, "Take this and eat." When one of her acquaintances sent her wine that was good but very little in quantity, saying it was ten years old, she remarked: "It is small for its age!"

When someone at a banquet asked why crowns are hung up <note>for the guests</note>, she said it was to "lead the souls." 

<margin>Various courtesans.</margin>

When a certain rogue was acting young toward her and claimed to be involved with many women, she put on a fake frown. When he asked why, she said, "I am angry at you because you have so many!" 

A certain miserly lover once called her "My Little Aphrodite of Praxiteles." She replied, "And you are my Eros of Phidias." <note>Praxiteles and Phidias were the most famous sculptors of Greece; she is matching his artistic flattery with her own.</note>

Since I also know of certain politicians who mention her, either in accusation or defense, I shall mention them. **Demosthenes**, in his speech *Against Androtion*, mentions **Sinope** and **Phanostrate**. Regarding Sinope, Herodicus says she was nicknamed "Abydos" <note>meaning "bottomless"</note> because she was an old woman. She is mentioned by **Antiphanes** in *The Arcadian*, and in *The Gardener*, *The Seamstress*, *The Fisherwoman*, and *The Little Chick*, as well as by **Alexis** in *Cleobulina*. And Callicrates mentions her in *Mochion*. As for Phanostrate...

# THE LEARNED BANQUETERS
## BOOK 13

...the orator says she was a "holy city" of competing courtesans, and that she was nicknamed "Gate of Lice" <note>original: "Phtheiropyle"</note> because she used to stand at the doors and pick lice from herself. **Hyperides**, in his speech *Against Arisagora*, says that there were others similarly called "Anchovies" <note>original: "aphyae"</note>. "Anchovies" was a common nickname for courtesans, about whom the chronographer **Apollodorus** says: "The sisters Stagonion and Anthis were called 'Anchovies' because they were pale and thin, yet had very large eyes." **Antiphanes**, in his work *On Courtesans*, says that Nicostratis was also called "Anchovy" for the same reason.

The same **Hyperides**, in his speech *On the Case of Mantitheus*, says the following about **Glycera**: "You are leading away Glycera, the woman of the sea, unfairly holding her in a yoke." This is the same woman who lived with **Harpalus** <note>Harpalus was the treasurer of Alexander the Great who fled to Athens with a massive fortune.</note>. **Theopompus**, in his *Letters to Chios*, states that after the death of Pythionice, Harpalus sent for Glycera from Athens. When she arrived, she lived in the royal palace at Tarsus and was prostrated to by the common people as if she were a queen; he even forbade anyone from crowning Harpalus with a wreath unless they also crowned Glycera. At Rhossus, he even dared to set up a bronze statue of her next to his own. **Cleitarchus** tells a similar story in his *Histories of Alexander*.

The author of the satyr play *The Agen*—whether it was **Python of Catana** or **King Alexander** himself—says: "And yet I hear that for Harpalus, tens of thousands of... <note>The text here is slightly fragmented but refers to grain shipments</note> did not escape notice." Then he suggests she was treated as a citizen: "Glycera’s grain was for ten years, but it will perhaps be the omen of destruction again, and not the engagement-earnest of a courtesan."

**Lysias**, in his speech *Against Lais* (if the speech is genuine), mentions several others: **Philyra**, who was a prostitute while still young, as well as **Scione**, **Hippaphisis**, **Theocleia**, **Psamathe**, **Dagnisca**, and **Anthia**. It is possible that "Anthia" is a misspelling of "Antia," for we find no courtesan named Anthia recorded anywhere else. However, there is a whole play titled *Antia*, which I mentioned before, by **Eunicus** or **Philyllius**; the author of the speech *Against Neaera* also mentions her.

In the speech *Against Philonides for Assault*, **Lysias** (again, if genuine) mentions a courtesan named **Naidis**. In the speech *Against Medion for False Witness*, he mentions a nickname for a courtesan: her real name was **Oia**, but **Antiphanes** says in his *On Courtesans* that she was called **Anticyra** <note>Anticyra was a region famous for producing hellebore, a plant used to treat madness.</note>, either because she mocked those who were crazy or because the doctor Nicostratus took her in and, upon his death, left her a large supply of hellebore and nothing else. <insert>¶</insert> **Lycurgus**, in his speech *Against Leocrates*, mentions a courtesan named **Irenis** who was associated with Leocrates.

**Hyperides** mentions **Nice** in his speech *Against Pasocles*; I mentioned before that she was nicknamed "Goat" <note>original: "Aks"</note> because she consumed "shoots" <note>original: "thallon," a pun on spending money or being a tavern-keeper</note>. It is well known that goats love shoots, which is why the animal is not allowed up onto the Acropolis and is never sacrificed to Athena—there is another story for why that is. But **Sophocles**, in his poetry, says the animal is a "shoot-eater": "For in the morning, before any flute-players are seen, the young goat brings its foot to the shoot, holding it by Euthystratus' salty headland."

**Alexis** mentions **Nannion** in *The Tarentines*, mocking her as "raving for Dionysus" <note>implying she was a drunkard</note>. **Menander**, in *The False Heracles*, says: "Nannion didn't take it." **Antiphanes**, in his *On Courtesans*, says Nannion was nicknamed "Proscenium" <note>original: "Proskenion," meaning a stage-front or facade</note> because she had a pretty face and wore gold and expensive clothes, but she was actually quite ugly underneath. **Corone** was Nannion's daughter; her name comes from being "the third generation of prostitutes."

**Hyperides** also mentions the flute-player **Nemeas** in his speech *Against Pasocles*. One might wonder how the Athenians allowed a prostitute to be called by the name of a sacred festival <note>The Nemean Games were one of the four great Panhellenic festivals.</note>. **Polemon**, in his works *On the Acropolis*, says that such names were given not only to courtesans but also to other slave-women. He also mentions **Ocimum** <note>meaning "Basil"</note>, whom **Hyperides** mentions in his second speech *Against Arisagora*, saying: "As for what Lais or Locara ever did... and Ocimum and **Metaneira**." **Nicostratus**, a poet of Middle Comedy, says in *Pandrosus*: "And then tell her to send the bedding... and the bronze vessels at Ocimum's house."

**Menander**, in *The Flatterer*, lists these courtesans: "**Chrysilla**, **Corone**, **Anticyra**, **Ischas** <note>meaning "Dried Fig"</note>, and you have **Nannion**, who is very ripe." **Philetaerus**, in *The Huntress*, says: "Not **Cercopa** <note>meaning "Monkey-face"</note>, who is already three thousand years old; another is **Diopithes**, and then there is **Theolytis**, whom no one knew when she was first 'carved.' Didn't the wealthy **Lais** die from too much sex? I won't mention **Galene** and **Corone**, and I'll keep silent about **Naidis**, for she has no molars left."

**Theophilus**, in *The Flute-Lover*, asks: "Why would anyone fall for **Lais**, or **Mekonid**, or **Sisymbrium**, or **Barathron** <note>meaning "The Pit," the place where criminals were thrown in Athens</note>, or **Thallusa**, or some other woman whom pimps entwine with jewels? Or Nannion, or **Malthace**?"

Having said all this, Myrtilus said with a certain rapid delivery: "Don't let these philosophers deceive you. Even those called 'Hedonists' <note>referring to the Epicureans</note> undermine the very garden of pleasure, as **Heracleides** says. My collection of the fine sayings of courtesans concludes with these. I shall now move on to another type of discourse, and first, I will mention that most truth-loving man, **Epicurus**, who in his 'General..."

# BOOK 13

...being uninitiated in higher education, he blessed you in the same way when you pursued philosophy, uttering such words as: "I bless you, sir, because you have rushed into philosophy pure of all blame." From this, **Timon** calls him a "pedagogue" <note>original: "Grammadidaskalides"</note> of the most unrefined creatures. 

<margin>Leontion of Epicurus</margin>
Did this **Epicurus** not have **Leontion** as his mistress, who became notorious for her life as a courtesan? Even when she began to study philosophy, she did not cease her profession but consorted with all the Epicureans in the gardens. She was openly with Epicurus, so much so that he took great care of her, as he reveals in his letters to **Hermarchus**.

<margin>Lais</margin>
**Lais** came from Hyccara—this is a city in Sicily—from which she became a captive and came to **Corinth**, as **Polemon** records in the sixth book of his *Reply to Timaeus*. **Aristippus** was in love with her, as was the orator **Demosthenes**. 

**Diogenes the Cynic** <note>original: "the dog"</note> also associated with her; she was also called "Aphrodite" or "Melanis" <note>Black Aphrodite</note>, appearing to her lovers at night, of whose expensive visits **Hyperides** mentions in his second speech *Against Aristagoras*. **Apelles** the painter, having seen Lais while she was still a young girl carrying water from a spring, and marveling at her beauty, once led her to a symposium of his friends. When his companions mocked him for bringing a virgin to the party instead of a courtesan, he said: "Do not wonder, for I will show her beauty to be a future delight after only three years." **Socrates** prophesied the same

<margin>Theodote. Book 3.</margin>
regarding **Theodote** the Athenian, as **Xenophon** says in his *Memorabilia* <note>Book 3, Chapter 11</note>. Because she was so beautiful that her beauty was beyond all description, Socrates said: "We must go to see the woman. For one cannot judge beauty by hearsay." Lais was so beautiful that painters used to come to her to copy the woman's breasts and chest. Lais, who was always busy with a great crowd of workers in the morning, was available to both the rich and the poor, and she did not treat them with insolence. **Aristippus** used to spend every year with her for several days in Aegina during the festival of Poseidon. When rebuked by his servant, who said, "You give her so much money, yet she sleeps with Diogenes the Dog for free," he replied: "I provide much to Lais so that I myself may enjoy her, not so that no one else may." When Diogenes said to him, "O Aristippus, you live with a common prostitute; either you should be a Cynic like me or stop," Aristippus replied: "Does it seem strange to you, Diogenes, to live in a house where others have lived before?" "No," he said. "And what about a ship in which many have sailed?" "Not that either," he said. "In the same way, then, it is not strange to be with a woman whom many have used."

<margin>Homeland and tomb of Lais</margin>
**Nymphodorus of Syracuse**, in his work *On the Marvels in Sicily*, says that Lais was from Hyccara, a Sicilian fortress. **Stratis**, in his *Macedonians* or *Pausanias*, calls her a Corinthian, and others say of her: "The girls have come from Megara, but they are Corinthians; Lais of the great fame." **Timaeus**, in the thirteenth book of his *Histories*, says she was from Hyccara, as Polemon also stated. They say she was killed by certain women in Thessaly because she had fallen in love with a man named **Pausanias of Thessaly**. Out of jealousy and spite, she was beaten to death with wooden footstools <note>original: "chelônais," literally "tortoises," referring to footstools shaped like shells</note> in the Temple of Aphrodite; for this reason, the sanctuary was called the Temple of "Impious Aphrodite" <note>original: "Anosia Aphrodite"</note>. Her tomb is shown by the Peneus river, having a stone water jar and this inscription:

> The greatness of Greece, once unvanquished in strength,
> Was enslaved by the god-like beauty of Lais,
> Whom Love fathered and Corinth nurtured,
> Now she lies in the famous plains of Thessaly.

Those who say she was buried in Corinth near the Cranion are merely improvising.

<margin>Mistresses of various famous men</margin>
Did **Aristotle the Stagirite** not father **Nicomachus** by the courtesan **Herpyllis**, with whom he lived until his death? So says **Hermippus** in the first book *On Aristotle*, stating that she received proper care in the philosopher's will. Our own noble **Plato** loved **Archeanassa**, the courtesan from Colophon, so much that he sang this to her:

> I hold Archeanassa, the courtesan from Colophon,
> On whose very wrinkles bitter Love sits.
> Ah, you wretches who met her on her first voyage,
> Through what a great fire you must have passed!

**Pericles the Olympian**, as **Clearchus** says in his first book of *Erotics*, was not less famous because of **Aspasia**. Through her, he associated with Socrates, and from her he gained a reputation for wisdom and political power, which shook all of Greece. But this man was very prone to sexual desires; even before he was with this woman, as **Stesimbrotus of Thasos** records, he had been with others before his own time, and he <note>Stesimbrotus</note> saw him in the work entitled *On Themistocles, Thucydides, and Pericles*. **Antidoxus** the Socratic says that he fell in love with Aspasia, and twice a day, when entering and leaving his house, he would embrace the woman. When she was once facing a trial for impiety, he spoke on her behalf and wept more than when he was in danger for his own life and property. And **Cimon** lived unlawfully with his sister **Elpinice**, but when she was later given in marriage to **Callias** and Cimon was exiled, Pericles took the return of Cimon as his "payment" for having relations with Elpinice. **Pythaenetus**, in the third book *On Aegina*, says that **Periander** desired **Melissa**, the daughter of Procles, after seeing her dressed in the Peloponnesian fashion—for she was without a mantle and wearing only a tunic while pouring wine for the laborers—and falling in love, he married her. And to **Pyrrhus**, the King of the Epeirots, who...

# ATHENAEUS: THE DINNER-SOPHISTS

...in the same manner, during the time when people were campaigning from the region of **Pyrrhus** <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus, the famous general who fought Rome</note> against Italy, a youth had a mistress named **Tigris of Leucadia**, whom **Olympias** (the youth's mother) killed with poison. And **Ulpian**, as if finding a stroke of luck while **Myrtilus** was still speaking, said: 

<margin>Tigris used as a masculine noun.</margin>
"Do we have any evidence for the word 'Tigris' <note>Tiger</note> being used in the masculine? For you know that **Philemon** uses it this way in his play *Neaira*. Also, **Seleucus** praises the tiger in this way—the one we saw that came from Seleucus long ago—saying: 'You honor us by sending this beast, a three-horned tiger' <note>original: "Trigerannon"</note>, for such things are born there." To which Myrtilus replied: "Since we are being hindered from making a complete list of women by an enemy catalog, isn't it true that **Sosicrates** the Phanagorean knows them? Or perhaps the *Catalog of Women* by **Nicainetus of Samos**? Or are you being unfair? Go away, you have enough; I shall be persuaded by you, 'aged Phoenix' <note>A literary reference to the tutor of Achilles</note>. Learn then, that **Alexis** has used 'tiger' in the masculine in his play *The Brazier* like this: 'Open, open the door! I was wandering about for a long time—truly—a river-donkey <note>original: "onos potamios," a humorous term for a hippopotamus</note>, a horse, a griffin, and the tiger of Seleucus.' Having other witnesses, I will set them aside for now until I have finished recounting the catalog of beautiful women."

**Clearchus** says the following regarding **Epaminondas**: "Epaminondas the Theban, though more dignified than others, was not entirely refined in his social circles and was tripped up in his judgment, if one considers his actions regarding the Laconian woman." 

The orator **Hyperides**, after casting his son **Glaucippus** out of his ancestral home, took in **Myrine**, the most expensive of courtesans, and kept her in the city. But in the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens</note> he kept **Aristagora**, and in Eleusis he kept **Phila**, whom he had purchased for a large sum of money and set free; later, he even made her his housekeeper, as **Idomeneus** records. In his speech *In Defense of Phryne*, Hyperides admitted he was in love with the woman, and not yet being cured of his passion, he brought the aforementioned Myrine into his house.

<margin>Phryne.</margin>
**Phryne** was from Thespiae. When she was put on trial by **Euthias** on a capital charge, she was acquitted. Therefore, Euthias was so angry that he never pleaded another case, as **Hermippus** says. But Hyperides, while acting as Phryne's advocate, was achieving nothing by his speech, and it seemed likely that the judges would condemn her. He then led her forward into open view and, tearing open her tunics and laying bare her breasts, he composed the closing laments of his speech based on the sight of her. He caused the judges—who were the interpreters of the divine and the ministers of Aphrodite <note>original: "zakorous aphroditēs"</note>—to feel a religious awe, so that they did not kill the handmaiden of Aphrodite. After this, a decree was passed that no one should use pity in their defense speeches, nor should the accused man or woman be seen while the case was being decided. 

Phryne was actually more beautiful in the parts of her that were not seen, which is why it was not easy to see her naked; for she wore a body-hugging tunic and did not use the public baths. But at the festival of the **Eleusinian Mysteries** and at the festival of **Poseidon**, in the sight of all the Greeks gathered there, she would take off her cloak, let down her hair, and step into the sea. It was from her that **Apelles** painted his *Aphrodite Rising from the Sea* <note>original: "Anadyomenēn"</note>. 

The sculptor **Praxiteles**, being in love with her, also modeled his *Cnidian Aphrodite* after her. On the base of his statue of **Eros**, which stands under the stage of the theater, he inscribed: 

*Praxiteles accurately depicted the Love he felt,* 
*Drawing the archetype from his own heart,* 
*Giving me to Phryne as payment for myself.* 
*I cast charms, no longer by shooting arrows, but by being gazed upon.* 

He gave her a choice of his statues—whether she wanted to take the *Eros* or the *Satyr* on the tripod. She chose the *Eros* and dedicated it at Thespiae. The inhabitants of the surrounding regions <note>original: "Periktiones"</note> had a statue of Phryne made and dedicated it at **Delphi**; it was a golden statue on a column of Pentelic marble. It was crafted by Praxiteles himself. When **Crates the Cynic** saw it, he called it "a monument to the profligacy of the Greeks." This statue stands right in the middle, between the statue of **Archidamus**, King of the Lacedaemonians, and that of **Philip, son of Amyntas** <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great</note>. It bears the inscription: "Phryne of Thespiae, daughter of Epicles," as **Alcetas** says in the second book of his work *On the Offerings at Delphi*. 

**Apollodorus**, in his work *On Courtesans*, records that there were two women named Phryne; one was nicknamed "Weeping-Laughter" <note>original: "klausigelōta"</note> and the other "Little Dried Fish" <note>original: "saperdion"</note>. **Herodicus**, in the sixth book of his *People Mentioned in Comedy*, says that the one mentioned by the orators was nicknamed "The Sieve" <note>original: "seson"</note> because she "shook out" and stripped those who associated with her. 

The Phryne from Thespiae was exceedingly wealthy and promised to rebuild the walls of **Thebes** if the Thebans would put up an inscription: "Alexander destroyed them, but Phryne the courtesan restored them," as **Callistratus** records. The comic poet **Timocles** mentions her wealth in his play *Neaira*, as cited before, as does **Amphis** in *The Girl with the Bobbed Hair*. **Gyllion**, one of the members of the Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens</note>, was a parasite <note>a social hanger-on</note> of Phryne, just as **Satyros** the flute-player was to **Pamphile**. 

**Aristogeiton**, in his speech *Against Phryne*, says her real name was **Mnesarete**. I am not unaware that the speech attributed to him is actually by **Anaximenes**, according to **Diodorus the Topographer**. The comic poet **Posidippus** says the following about her in *The Woman of Ephesus*: 

*Phryne was once by far the most famous of us courtesans.* 
*Even if you are younger than those times,* 
*You have surely heard of her trial. Though she was thought to harm society,* 
*She captured the court of the Heliaea by her body,* 
*Winning her life by pleading with her soul.* 

You also know that the orator **Demades** had a son, **Demeas**, by a flute-playing courtesan. When Demeas was once acting arrogantly on the speaker's platform, Hyperides silenced him, saying: "Be quiet, young man; you have a blast of air <note>interpreted as "hot air" or "arrogance"</note> even greater than your mother's." And in life...

# BOOK XIII

The philosopher from Borysthenes <note>Bion of Borysthenes, a 3rd-century BC philosopher known for his wit and "Cynic" lifestyle</note> was the son of a courtesan named Olympia of Laconia, as Nicias of Nicaea states in his 
<margin>Theories.</margin> *Successions of Philosophers*. Sophocles the tragic poet, even when he was already an old man, fell in love with the courtesan Theoris; he prayed for her at the shrine of Aphrodite, saying:

> Hear me as I pray, O nurse of youth, and grant that this woman 
> may reject the love and bed of young men, but let her instead 
> delight in grey-templed old men, whose strength 
> is blunted, but whose divine mind remains eager.

<margin>Human customs.</margin> These lines are actually from the works attributed to Homer <note>specifically the *Homeric Epigrams*</note>. Regarding Theoris, he mentions her by saying, "to whom my heart is steady, for Theoris is dear." But perhaps being "slow to learn" in his way of life, as Hippostratus says to Archippus, he loved the courtesan and left her as the heir to his estate. While Archippe was living with Sophocles in his old age, her former lover, Smicrines, was asked by someone what Archippe was doing; he wittily replied, "She sits there like an owl on a tomb" <note>A dark joke suggesting she is waiting for the old man to die</note>. Furthermore, even Isocrates <note>original: "Socrates," but the epithet "more modest of orators" usually refers to Isocrates</note>, the most modest of the orators, had a mistress named Metanira, according to Callias and as Lysias records in his letters. Demosthenes, in his speech *Against Neaira*, says that Metanira was the mistress of Lysias. Lysias also loved the courtesan Lagis, for whom the orator Cephalus wrote a praise-speech, just as Alcidamas the Laconian, a pupil of Gorgias, wrote a praise-speech for the courtesan Naïs. Concerning this Naïs, Lysias wrote in his speech *Against Philonides*: "There was no other woman named Naïs of whom Archias was the master." The bridegroom-to-be, the wicked Philonides who was in love with her, says this. Aristophanes also mentions her in his play *Gerytades*, and in his play *Plutus* he says, "Lais loves you, but not Philonides," though it should probably be written as "Naïs" rather than "Lais." Hermippus, in his work *On Socrates*, says that as Socrates grew older, he took a courtesan named Lagisca into his house, by whom he even had a small daughter. Stratis mentions her in these lines:

> And Lagisca, the one belonging to the bald Socrates... 
> ...who still keeps me in her bed...

And Lysias, in his speech *Regarding Lais*—if the speech is genuine—mentions her while listing other courtesans in this way: "Philyra certainly grew wealthy as a prostitute in Sicyon, as did Epaphasis the daughter of Theocles, and Psamathe, and Lagisca, and Antheia the daughter of Aristocles." There is also a story that the orator Demosthenes had children by a courtesan. 
<margin>Demosthenes' debauchery.</margin> Indeed, in his speech *On the Gold*, he brought his children before the court so that they might be pitied, though they were without their mother; it was the custom for those on trial to bring their wives, but he did this out of shame, trying to avoid public slander. The orator was unrestrained in sexual matters, as Idomeneus says. For instance, he was the lover of a certain youth named Aristarchus, and because of him, he murdered Nicodemus and even plucked out his eyes. There was once a proverb: "a youth's desire for delicacies and for women" <note>original: "voluptuosi" (Latin gloss for "pleasure-seekers")</note>. Consequently, a certain secretary once said: "What more could anyone say about Demosthenes? For in a single night, one woman undid all the speeches he had practiced." It is even said that he brought a young man named Knosion into his house while he had a wife, and that his wife was indignant at being forced to sleep in the same bed as Knosion. 
<margin>Honor remaining.</margin> King Demetrius <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes</note>, the last of the Successors <note>The Diadochi, generals who succeeded Alexander the Great</note>, had the Samian courtesan Myrine as his mistress, and she shared in his royal power outside of his diadem, as Nicolaus of Damascus says. Ptolemy, the governor of the garrison at Ephesus (who was the son of King Philadelphus), had a mistress named Irene. When a plot was formed against Ptolemy by the Thracians in Ephesus, and he fled to the Temple of Artemis for safety, she fled with him. After they killed him, Irene, clutching the ring-handles of the temple doors, splashed the altars with her blood until they slaughtered her as well. Danae, the daughter of Leontion (the student of Epicurus), was also a courtesan; she was kept by Sophron, the governor of Ephesus, and she saved him when he was the target of a plot by Laodice <note>The wife of Antiochus II</note>. However, Danae herself was thrown off a cliff, as Phylarchus records in his twelfth book. Danae, being the companion of Laodice, discovered the whole plot against Sophron; she was the daughter of Leontion, who had studied natural philosophy with Epicurus. Having previously been Sophron's mistress, she followed him; because Laodice wanted to kill Sophron, she planned to imitate the plot against him. But Sophron, catching wind of it, pretended to agree, asking for a day to consider everything, and having gained that delay, he fled to Ephesus by night. When Laodice learned what Danae had done, she had the woman thrown off a cliff, showing no regard for their previous friendship. They say that Danae, seeing the danger hanging over her when she was interrogated by Laodice, and knowing she was to be killed, said as she was being led to the cliff: "Many people rightly despise the gods, seeing that I, who saved the man who was my husband, receive such 'thanks' from the Divine, while Laodice, who killed her own, is granted such great honor." The same Phylarchus also tells the story of Mysa in his fourteenth book as follows: Mysa was the mistress of King Seleucus. When Seleucus was defeated by the Galatians and barely escaped with his life, she disguised herself in royal clothing and took on the role of a servant woman who had been captured. She was led away with the other prisoners and sold just like the other servants; she ended up in Rhodes, where she revealed who she was. She was then purchased by the Rhodians and sent back to Seleucus. Demetrius of Phalerum fell in love with Lampito, the Samian courtesan, and he lived with her happily...

-># ATHENAEUS: THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED<-

She was addressed as Lampyris <note>original: "Λαμπυριδῶ," meaning "Firefly"</note>, as Diphilus says, and was also called "Graceful-eyed." Nicarete the courtesan was the mistress of the orator Stephanus. Lysias <note>A famous Athenian speechwriter and orator</note> was in love with the sophisticated Metaneira. These women were all slaves of Casian of Elis, along with other courtesans: Anticeia, Stratola, Aristocleia, Phila, Isthmias, and Neaera. Neaera was the mistress of Stephanocleides and lived in the Xynoicladia district. Hipparchus the actor—whom the same author mentions as a lover—was the son of Demon and the nephew of Demochares. Regarding Neaera, Phrynion and the orator Stephanus had an arrangement where they each had her on alternate days, following an arbitration by their friends. Stephanus also betrothed Neaera’s daughter (then called Strobyle, though later renamed Phano) to a man named Phrastor, swearing she was his own legitimate daughter to make the match credible. Demosthenes mentions this in his speech *Against Neaera* <note>A famous legal speech from ancient Athens detailing the life of Neaera and the laws regarding citizenship and marriage</note>. He also says the following about the courtesan Sinope: "You punished Archias the high priest <note>term: "hierophant," the chief priest at the Eleusinian Mysteries</note> when he was convicted in court of impiety and for offering sacrifices contrary to ancestral tradition. Among other charges, it was alleged that he offered a sacrifice on the hearth in the courtyard at Eleusis for the courtesan Sinope, even though it was a day on which the law forbade the slaughter of victims—and he was not even the authorized priest to perform that sacrifice, but did so for the sake of the woman."

The Milesian woman Plangon also became a notorious courtesan. She was exceptionally beautiful and a young man from Colophon fell in love with her, even though he already had a mistress, Bacchis of Samos. When the young man made a proposal to her, Plangon, having heard of Bacchis's beauty and wishing to shake the young man’s affection for her (as it seemed impossible to satisfy him), demanded as her "saving-price" <note>original: "σωσίπιον μισθὸν," a play on words suggesting a fee for his soul or safety</note> the famous necklace of Bacchis. The young man, being passionately in love, begged Bacchis not to let him perish. Bacchis consented and gave him the necklace. When Plangon saw the lack of jealousy in Bacchis, she sent the necklace back to her and slept with the young man anyway. From then on, they became friends and shared the lover's attentions. Because of this, as Menetor says in his work *On Votive Offerings*, people called Plangon "Pamphila" <note>meaning "Friend-to-all" or "Beloved-by-all"</note>. Archilochus <note>A Greek lyric poet known for his sharp wit and satire</note> also testifies about them in these lines:

> A fig tree on the rocks feeding many crows,
> Easy-going receiver of strangers, friend to all.

It is common knowledge that the poet Menander loved Glycera, though he eventually fell out with her. When Philemon <note>A rival playwright of Menander</note> fell in love with a courtesan whom he named "Chryssion" <note>meaning "Golden girl"</note> in his writing, Menander wrote back that no such woman was actually "good" <note>original: "χρηστή," a pun on the name Chryssion and the word for "virtuous"</note>. 

Harpalus the Macedonian, who stole vast amounts of money from Alexander the Great and fled to Athens, fell in love with Pythionice. He spent a fortune on her, though she was a courtesan. When she died, he built her a monument costing many talents <note>A talent was a massive unit of currency; one talent was roughly 6,000 drachmas</note>. When he carried her out for burial, as Posidonius says in the twenty-second book of his *Histories*, he escorted the body with a great choir of the most famous artists, accompanied by all kinds of instruments and voices. Dicaearchus, in his work *On the Descent into the Cave of Trophonius*, says: "A traveler arriving at the city of Athens by the so-called Sacred Way from Eleusis would feel the same shock. For standing there, at the point where one first glimpses Athens, they would see a monument built by the road that surpasses all others in size. One might assume it was the tomb of Miltiades, or Pericles, or some other great man, built at public expense by the city—if they didn't think it was a temple to a god. But when they ask and hear it is for the courtesan Pythionice, they are stunned by the expectation."

Theopompus, in his letter to Alexander criticizing Harpalus’s decadence, says: "Look into and listen clearly to the reports from Babylon: how Harpalus treated Pythionice after her death. She was a slave of Bacchis the flute-player, who was herself a slave of Sinope the Thracian, who brought her trade from Aegina to Athens. Thus, Pythionice was not just a triple-slave, but a triple-harlot. Yet he built two monuments for her at a cost of more than two hundred talents. Everyone was amazed that while none of those who died in Cilicia for your kingdom and the freedom of the Greeks has had their tomb adorned by those in charge, this courtesan Pythionice has one monument in Athens and another in Babylon, both long since completed. For a woman whom everyone knew was common to all who wanted her at a common price, your 'dearest friend' dared to establish a sacred precinct and a grove, and to call the temple and altar by the name of 'Pythionice Aphrodite' <note>By identifying his dead mistress with the goddess of love, Harpalus was committing an act of extreme hubris</note>, simultaneously despising the punishment of the gods and attempting to bring shame upon your own honors."

Philemon mentions these things in *The Babylonian*: "The Queen of Babylon—or Pythionice, if it happens to be her—I know both her and Harpalus." Alexis also mentions her in *Lyciscus*. After the death of Pythionice, Harpalus sent for Glycera, who was also a courtesan, as Theopompus records. He says Harpalus even forbade anyone from crowning him with a wreath unless they also crowned the prostitute. He set up a bronze statue of Glycera in Tarsus (Syria), where he intended to place statues of you <note>Alexander</note> and himself. He allowed her to live in the royal palace in Tarsus, and she was seen being prostrated before by the people and addressed as "Queen," and honored with other gifts that would have been more fitting for your mother or your wife.

<margin>*The Agen*, a drama.</margin>

To this, the author of the *Agen* (a short satyr play) bears witness. He produced this play during the festival of Dionysus by the Hydaspes river <note>A river in modern-day Pakistan; this shows how far Greek culture traveled with Alexander's army</note>, whether it was Python...

-># BOOK 13<-

Python was either from Catana or Byzantium, or perhaps the king himself. This drama was produced when Harpalus fled to the sea <note>Harpalus was the treasurer of Alexander the Great who absconded with a vast fortune</note> and revolted. In the play, he mentions Pythionice as being dead, but Glycera as being present with him. He also accuses the Athenians of receiving gifts from Harpalus, saying: "There is a place where the reed grows... the famous people of Gorgos, whom the play *Agen* condemned because of their deeds after he fled." There, certain barbarian Magi, seeing him in a fine state, claimed he was worthy of the soul of Pythionice. The text says: "He called for Harpalus... desiring to learn from you the heights of your home and the Attic land. What fortunes or deeds call you? Why, when they said I had enough to live on, did my hands now touch the filth and the fennel? Indeed, I hear of thousands of Harpalus’s gifts, and that he sent no small amount of grain to them, making her a citizen." This grain belonged to Glycera; thus, perhaps it was their ruin and not the courtesan’s reward. 

<margin>List of courtesans.</margin>
Naukratis also produced famous courtesans of exceptional beauty, such as Doricha, who became the beloved of Charaxus, the brother of the beautiful Sappho. He had sailed to Naukratis <note>A Greek trading post in Egypt</note> for trade, and Sappho attacked Doricha in her poetry, accusing her of stripping Charaxus of much of his wealth. Herodotus calls her Rhodopis, unaware that she is a different person from Doricha—the same one who dedicated the famous iron spits at Delphi <note>term: "obelisks," though here referring to large iron roasting spits dedicated as a votive offering</note>, which Cratinus mentions. Regarding Doricha, Posidippus wrote this epigram, even though he mentions her frequently in his *Aethiopia*: 

"Doricha, your soft bones are now adorned with a binding, 
and your hair, once fragrant with perfume, is wrapped away. 
You once wrapped the charming Charaxus skin-to-skin 
and touched the morning cups of wine. 
But the white, speaking pages of Sappho’s dear song still remain. 
Naukratis shall thus guard your blessed name, 
as long as a sea-going ship shall come from the Nile." 

Archedice was also from Naukratis, and she too was a beautiful courtesan. For Naukratis somehow loves to have charming courtesans, as Herodotus says. There was also the beautiful Sappho from Ephesus, who fell in love with Phaon and became famous, as Nymphis says in his *Voyage Around Asia*. 

Nicarete of Megara was no low-born courtesan, but was desirable for both her lineage and her education. She used to listen to the lectures of Stilpo the philosopher <note>A leader of the Megarian school of logic and ethics</note>. Bilistiche of Argos was also a famous courtesan, said to preserve the lineage of the Atreidae <note>The royal house of Agamemnon</note>, as those who wrote the *Argolika* record. Leaena the courtesan was also famous for her glory, being the beloved of Harmodius who slew the tyrant <note>referring to the "Tyrannicides" who killed Hipparchus</note>; even when she was tortured by the tyrant Hippias, she died under the torments without saying a word. Stratocles the orator had as his mistress the courtesan nicknamed Lamia <note>original: "The Monster"</note> and another called Paroramos <note>original: "Overlooked"</note>, because she would go to anyone who wanted her for just two drachmas, as Gorgias says in his book *On Courtesans*. 

But as Myrtilus was about to fall silent, he said, "Friends of men, let us not forget the Lyde of Antimachus, and also another Lyde of the same name, whom Lampydius of Miletus loved. For each of these poets, as 

<margin>Courtesans of the poets.</margin>
Clearchus says in his *Erotics*, was driven to desire by a barbarian Lydian woman. One wrote the *Lyde* for her, and the other wrote the poem called *Lyde*. I also passed over Mimnermus’s flute-player Nanno and Hermesianax of Colophon’s Leontium. Indeed, because she became his beloved, he wrote three books of elegiacs, and in the third book he makes a catalog of lovers, saying something like this:

"Such was the woman the dear son of Oeagrus [Orpheus], armed with his lyre, brought back from the dead, rescuing the Thracian Agriope <note>original: "Agriope," though more commonly known as Eurydice</note>. He sailed to the evil place of Hades, where Charon drags the souls of the departed into his boat, and the lake echoes far, flowing through great reeds. Yet Orpheus braved the waves, and with his lyre he soothed all kinds of gods, even the lawless Cocytus who smiles with his brows. He endured the gaze of the most terrible dog [Cerberus], his voice sharpened in the fire, bringing fear with his three-headed gaze. From there, by his singing, he persuaded the great lords that Agriope should receive the soft breath of life. 

Nor did the son of Mene, Musaeus, the priest of the Graces, leave his Antiope without honor; she who, by the holy shore of Eleusis, 
---
breathed out the fragrance of the mystic oracles. You will know this story even in the *Aeolus*. And I say that Hesiod, the lord of all history, leaving his Boeotian home, came to the village of Ascra out of love for a girl. There, wooing the Ascraean maid, the poet suffered much, and he wrote all his books of songs beginning with that girl. 

And even that divine singer, whom the land of Ionia guards as its own, the most pleasant spirit of all the servants of the Muses—divine Homer—toiled to reach thin Ithaca for the sake of the prudent Penelope. For her sake, after suffering much, he settled in that small island, leaving far behind his wide fatherland. He wept for the kin of Icarius, the people of Amyclae, and the trials of Troy, as he touched upon his own sorrows."

### ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

> Mimnermus was a sweet poet who, after enduring much, found the sound and soft breath of the pentameter <note>The pentameter is the second line in an elegiac couplet, a meter often used for love poetry</note>. He burned with love for Nanno; and often, on the gray hill, <unclear>wearing the mouthpiece</unclear> of his flute, he led the revels in succession. He hated the meddling Hermobius and heavy-handed Pherecles, hating them as enemies because of what they said of his verses. 
> 
> Antimachus, too, was struck by love for the Lydian Lyde <note>Lyde was the title of Antimachus's most famous poem, written to console himself after her death</note>, and he went to the stream of the river Pactolus. When she died, he placed her beneath the dry earth of Colophon, weeping. He left the heights of the city and filled books with his lamentations, finding rest from all his toil. 
<margin>5</margin>
> And Alcaeus of Lesbos often took up the revels, expressing his lovely desire for Sappho. You know well how the singer of hymns <note>likely referring to Anacreon</note> loved that "nightingale of songs," vexing the Teian star <note>Anacreon was from Teos</note> with his cleverness. For indeed, the honey-sweet Anacreon frequented the company of many Lesbian women, leaving Samos behind at times, and at other times his own wine-rich homeland, to visit wine-blessed Lesbos. Often he looked across the waves toward the Aeolian shore. 
<margin>10</margin>
> And Sophocles, whom Zeus gave as a prize to Bacchus <note>Sophocles was a celebrated tragic playwright, and drama was performed in honor of Bacchus (Dionysus)</note>, I say even that guarded man was overcome. He who won honors from everyone was struck by the crooked bow of love for all women, finding no rest from the pains of the night. Eventually, he traveled through all the streets of Macedonia, following the treasurer of Archelaus <note>King Archelaus of Macedon</note>, until fate found a destruction for Euripides, when he encountered the snarling dogs of a jealous life. 
<margin>15</margin>
> I could also speak of the flute-playing man who turned the lotus-wood <note>Greek flutes, or *auloi*, were often made of lotus-wood</note> into a most faithful steward, the son of the Muses <note>likely referring to a poet like Philoxenus</note>, who was a friend to guests. He came through this city and felt a great longing for Galatea, whom he placed under the care of his ancestors among the sheep. 
> 
> I know too of the poet whom the citizens of Eurypylus placed in bronze under the plane tree on Cos—Philetas, singing of the nimble Bittis all his days, using every form of speech to praise her. 
<margin>20</margin>
> Nor did those who established a hard life sleep, those men seeking the crooked wisdom of humanity, whom bitter logic and the dread virtue of words held fast. Even they turned aside from the terrible pride of Love when it appeared, and they came under the power of the driver. Such was the madness that bound Pythagoras of Samos, who discovered the elegant secrets of geometry and how the great circle of the ether surrounds us, mapping everything in a small sphere. 
<margin>25</margin>
> And Socrates, whom the Earth declared the wisest of men in his soul—Cypris <note>Aphrodite, the goddess of love</note> was angry with him, and from the depths of his soul she brewed a fire. He lived in constant pursuit, finding no certain proof though he found many paths in logic. 
> 
> Desire also drew the Cyrenaic man <note>Aristippus of Cyrene, a philosopher who championed pleasure</note> inward with dread knowledge, when he fell in love with Lais. 
<margin>30</margin>
> The sharp Aristippus rejected all his school's discussions and, fleeing, carried his life toward her.

In these verses, Hermesianax is mistaken in thinking that Sappho and Anacreon lived at the same time; for Anacreon lived in the time of Cyrus and Polycrates, whereas Sappho lived in the time of Alyattes, the father of Croesus. Chamaeleon, in his book *On Sappho*, says that some people claim these verses were written to her by Anacreon:

> "Once more, golden-haired Love hits me with a purple ball and challenges me to play with a girl in multi-colored sandals." <note>original: "σφαίρῃ δεῦτέ με πορφυρῇ..."</note>

But she—for she comes from well-built Lesbos—finds fault with my hair because it is white, and she gapes after someone else. They also say that Sappho said this to him:

> "O Muse on your golden throne, sing that hymn from the land of beautiful women, the one that the noble elder from the Teian land sang so delightfully." <note>original: "κείνον ὦ χρυσόθρονε μοῦσα..."</note>

That this song is not actually by Sappho is obvious to everyone. I believe Hermesianax was just playing around concerning this love affair. Indeed, Diphilus the comic poet, in his play *Sappho*, made Archilochus and Hipponax her lovers. 

I think, my friends, I have made a carefree catalog of <margin>40</margin> romantic matters. I am not so "love-mad" as the Cyclops said when he slandered me, but I admit to being "amorous," though not "love-mad." 

*Is it necessary to invent misfortunes,*
*When one can stay silent and hide these things in the dark?*

As Aeschylus says in his *Alexander* and *Amphitryon*. This is the Aeschylus who, out of modesty, stayed inside the theater because of the sacred mysteries <note>Aeschylus was famously accused of revealing the secrets of the Eleusinian Mysteries on stage</note>. Since I believe Love to be a great and most powerful deity, and taking to heart the words of Euripides regarding "Golden Aphrodite," I say:

<margin>Love is everywhere</margin>

> "Do you not see how great a goddess she is? You could not describe her, nor could you measure how vast she is or how far she reaches. She nourishes you, and me, and all mortals. I will give you proof, not in words alone, but I will show you the goddess’s power through deeds. The Earth loves the rain when the dry ground is fruitless from drought and needs the moisture of friendship. The majestic Heaven, when filled with rain, loves to fall to the Earth by the power of Aphrodite. When these two are joined together, they produce and nourish all things for us, by which the human race lives and flourishes."

And the most venerable Aeschylus, in his *Danaids*, introduces Aphrodite herself saying:

> "The pure Heaven loves to wound the Earth, and Love seizes the Earth to obtain marriage. The rain, falling from the flowing Heaven, impregnates the Earth, and she gives birth for mortals..."

### BOOK 13

...the livelihood and the destroyer of life, let us ascend to the prime of those born of the damp marriage of Tellus <note>A reference to the earth-born or mortal nature of humans</note>, for which I am partly responsible. In the *Hippolytus* of Euripides, Aphrodite says once again: "As many as dwell within the boundaries of the sea and the Atlantic, seeing the light of the sun, I treat with honor those who revere my power; but I trip up those who think too highly of themselves toward me." For a young man who possessed every virtue, and whose only fault was that he dishonored Aphrodite, this became the cause of his destruction. And even when Artemis, who loved him exceedingly, was present, neither she nor any other god or spirit came to his aid. Indeed, one might ask whether such a person is a poet at all—for anyone who does not judge Love to be a god is either foolish or ignorant of beautiful things. He does not know the greatest god for men, of whom your wise Anacreon is always on everyone's lips. <margin>Anacreon</margin> Again, the great Critias says these things about him: 

"He who once wove songs of feminine limbs, the sweet Anacreon, whom Greece once brought forth, the stimulant of symposia, the deceiver of women, the rival of the flutes, lover of the lyre, sweet and painless. Your love shall never grow old or die, so long as a boy carries round the cups for toasts over his right shoulder, mixing water with wine, and as long as female choirs attend the holy all-night festivals, and the bronze daughter of the scale <note>The *plastinx*, the small bronze disc used as a target in the game of kottabos</note> sits upon the high peaks of the kottabos <note>A popular Greek drinking game where players threw wine dregs at a target</note> with the sound of splashing drops."

Archytas the musician says, as Chamaeleon reports, that <margin>5</margin> Alcman was the leader of erotic songs, and was the first to publish a song of a licentious nature, being very fond of women and bringing such a Muse into his daily activities. Because of this, he says in one of his songs: "Again, by the will of Aphrodite, sweet Love flows down and warms my heart." <margin>Alcman</margin> He also says that Alcman was moderately in love with the poetess Megalostrata, who was able to attract lovers through her conversation. He speaks of her thus: "The golden-haired Megalostrata, a blessed maiden, showed this gift of the sweet Muse." 

And Stesichorus, who was no moderate in his eroticism, composed songs in this manner which in ancient times were called *paidika* <note>Songs concerning the love of boys</note>. His treatment of erotic matters was not without struggle, yet he did not consider himself a vulgar lover. Even Aeschylus, great poet that he was, and Sophocles, <margin>Erotic poets</margin> brought love into the theaters through their tragedies: the former showed the love of Achilles for Patroclus, and the latter, in his *Niobe*, the love of the children. Because of this, some call tragedy "the teacher of pederasty," as the audience did not reject such songs. 

Ibycus of Rhegium also cries out: "In spring, the Cydonian quinces are watered by the flowing rivers, where the untouched garden of the maidens is, and the vine-blossoms grow under the shading shoots of the vines. But for me, Love rests at no season; like the Thracian North wind flaming with lightning, rushing from Aphrodite with parching madness, dark and shameless, it powerfully guards my mind from childhood."

Pindar, too, being no stranger to love, says: "May it be mine to love and to grant favors to Love, and in due season; do not pursue an older pursuit, O my soul, beyond your number." Therefore, Timon also said in his *Silloi* <note>Lampoons or satirical poems</note>: "To love in season, to marry in season, and in season to cease." Let him not sing back those things which one might utter when, as the same philosopher said, "strong and peaceful night sets." 

Pindar, remembering Theoxenus of Tenedos, who was his beloved, says: "One should gather the fruits of love in due season, O soul, along with one's youth. But whoever, seeing the rays shimmering from the face of Theoxenus, does not swell with desire—his black heart was forged from adamant or iron in a cold flame. Dishonored by the quick-glancing Aphrodite, he either toils violently for money, or with a womanly boldness is carried along, serving every cold deception. But I, for the sake of that one, melt like the wax of holy bees bitten by the heat, whenever I look upon the fresh-limbed youth of boys." And indeed, the persuasion and grace of the Tenedians reside in the son of Agesilaus. 

In general, many prefer the love of boys to that of females. For among the other powerful <margin>Love of boys</margin> cities of Greece, this custom has been accepted. The Cretans, for instance, as I have said, and the Chalcidians in Euboea, are divinely devoted to the love of boys. At any rate, in the *Cretica*, it is said that it was not Zeus who snatched Ganymede, but Minos. The aforementioned Chalcidians say that Ganymede was snatched by Zeus among them, and they show a place they call the *Harpagion* <note>The Place of Snatching</note>, in which various myrtles grow. Minos even dissolved his enmity with the Athenians, although it had arisen from the death of his son, because he fell in love with Theseus and gave him his daughter Phaedra as a wife, as Zenis (or Zonis) the Chian says in his work *On His Homeland*.

Hieronymus the Peripatetic says that the love of boys became highly valued because often the peak of youth and the shared friendship of companions working together has overthrown many tyrannies. For in the presence of their beloveds, a lover would choose to suffer anything rather than bear the reputation of a coward in the eyes of his boy. This was shown in practice by the Sacred Band <note>The *Hieros Lochos*, an elite unit of the Theban army composed of pairs of male lovers</note> organized at Thebes by Epaminondas, and the death of the Peisistratids brought about by Harmodius and Aristogeiton. In Sicily and Akragas, the love of Chariton and Melanippus—Melanippus being the beloved—as Heraclides of Pontus says in his work *On Erotic Matters*, showed this; for when they were discovered plotting against Phalaris <note>The infamous tyrant of Akragas, known for his brazen bull</note> and were being tortured and forced to speak, they did not give in...

...Phalaris <note>The notorious tyrant of Acragas, famous for his "brazen bull" torture device</note> himself was moved to pity by their endurance under torture, so much so that he released them with much praise. Because of this, Apollo was pleased with them and granted Phalaris a delay of his death. This was revealed by the Pythia <note>The priestess of the Oracle at Delphi</note> to those who asked how they might attack him; she also delivered an oracle concerning those around Chariton, ordering the use of pentameter alongside hexameter, just as Dionysius of Athens (nicknamed "The Bronze") later did in his elegies. The oracle is as follows: "Happy were Chariton and Melanippus; they were the leaders in a god-like life, a friendship most dear to mortals."

The story concerning Cratinus of Athens is also famous. When Epimenides <note>A legendary seer from Crete</note> was purifying Attica with human blood because of certain ancient grievances, Cratinus, a beautiful youth, voluntarily offered himself for the sake of his homeland <note>literally "the land that nourished him"</note>, as Neanthes of Cyzicus records in the second book of *On Initiations*. His lover, Aristodemus, died along with him, and the terrible calamity was resolved. Because of such loves, tyrants—who generally found these friendships to be their enemies—tried to banish the love of boys entirely, uprooting it from every quarter. Some even demolished the gymnasiums <term>palaestras</term> <note>Wrestling schools and social hubs for men</note>, considering them to be like defensive walls built against their own citadels, as Polycrates the tyrant of Samos did.

Among the Spartans, as Agnon the Academic says, it is the custom for girls to associate with their lovers like boys do before marriage. Indeed, the lawgiver Solon spoke of "the desire of thighs and the sweet mouth," and Aeschylus and Sophocles spoke of it openly; the former in his *Myrmidons* speaks of "reverence for the thighs" <note>original: "Σέβας δὲ μηρῶν"</note> and says, "Oh, ungrateful one after so many frequent kisses!" Sophocles, in his *Colchians*, speaking of Ganymede <note>The beautiful youth abducted by Zeus to be his cup-bearer</note>, says he "kindled the tyranny of Zeus with his thighs."

However, I am not unaware that Polemon the Traveler, in his replies to Neanthes, says the story of Cratinus and Aristodemus is a fiction. And you, Cynulcus <note>A character in the dialogue, a Cynic philosopher</note>, believe these stories to be true even if they are false, and you happily study such poems that concern the love of boys. Timaeus records that the practice of pederasty <term>paiderastein</term> passed to the Greeks first from the Cretans. Others say these loves began with Laius <note>The father of Oedipus</note> when he was a guest of Pelops and fell in love with his son, Chrysippus, whom he kidnapped, placed in a chariot, and fled to Thebes. But Praxilla of Sicyon says Chrysippus was kidnapped by Zeus. Among the barbarians, the Celts, though they have very beautiful women, delight more in youths, so that some often rest on their animal skins with two lovers. Herodotus says the Persians learned the use of boys from the Greeks.

King Alexander the Great was also madly fond of boys. Dicaearchus, in his work *On the Sacrifice at Ilium*, says he was so overcome by the eunuch Bagoas that, in full view of the entire theater, he leaned back and kissed him; and when the spectators cheered and clapped, he leaned back and kissed him again, quite undeterred. Carystius in his *Historical Notes* says that Charon of Chalcis was a beautiful boy and was loved by Alexander. Once, when Alexander praised him at a drinking party at Craterus's house, Craterus ordered the boy to kiss Alexander. When the boy was hesitant, Alexander said, "If he will please me as much as he will distress you <insert>by refusing</insert>..." For just as this king was amorous, he was also restrained regarding what was proper and most fitting. For instance, when he took the daughters of Darius captive, and his wife who was exceptionally beautiful, he not only refrained from touching them but did not even let them know they were captives; he ordered that they be provided for in every way as if Darius were still in his kingdom. Thus, when Darius learned of this, he stretched his hands to the sun and prayed that either he should remain king or Alexander should.

They say Talos became the lover of Rhadamanthus the Just. Diotimus, in his *Heracleia*, says that Eurydymas was the favorite of Heracles, which is why Heracles endured his labors. It is also said that Agamemnon fell in love with Argynnus when he saw him swimming in the Cephisus river; when Argynnus died in that river (for he drowned there), Agamemnon buried him and founded a temple to "Aphrodite Argynnis" there. Alcman of Chios says in his dithyrambs that Argynnus was the beloved of Agamemnon. The king Antigonus had the cithara-player Aristocles as a favorite, about whom Antigonus of Carystus writes in his *Life of Zeno*: "King Antigonus used to revel with Zeno, and once, coming from a party late at night, he leaped up to Zeno's house and persuaded him <margin>Sophocles was a lover of youths.</margin> to join him in a revel at the house of Aristocles the cithara-player, whom the king loved dearly."

Sophocles was a lover of youths, just as Euripides was a lover of women. Ion the poet, in his work titled *Travels* <term>Epidemiae</term>, writes as follows: "I met the poet Sophocles in Chios when he was sailing as a general to Lesbos. At a dinner, he was being served wine by a handsome boy standing by the fire. Since the boy was clearly blushing, Sophocles said, 'I see you are serving the wine with pleasure.' And again, 'Take your time bringing me the wine and taking away the cup.' When the boy blushed even more deeply, Sophocles said to the person reclining next to him: 'How well Phrynichus <note>A tragic poet</note> wrote when he said, "The light of love shines on purple cheeks."' To this, a schoolmaster from Eretria (or Erythrae) replied: 'You are indeed wise in poetry, Sophocles, yet Phrynichus did not speak well when he called the cheeks "purple"...'"

...the cheeks of the beautiful boy; for if a painter were to smear this boy’s cheeks with purple pigment, he would no longer appear beautiful. Therefore, he did not punish him because of what was beautiful, but because of what appeared unbeautiful. Laughing in this way at the man from Eretria, he said: "It seems then that you also do not care for that line of Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos, a famous lyric poet</note>, which the Greeks think was spoken quite brilliantly: 'The maiden uttering a purple voice from her lips.' Yet if a poet spoke of 'golden-haired Apollo,' and a painter made the god’s hair out of actual gold and not black, the painting would be worse for it. Or consider the one who said 'rosy-fingered' <note>A common Homeric epithet for the Dawn</note>; for if someone were to dip fingers into rose-colored dye, he would produce purple-stained hands and not those of a beautiful woman."

When the guests laughed, the Eretrian was annoyed by the rebuke. But Sophocles again occupied himself with the boy. It happened that the boy was using his little finger to remove a speck of chaff from the rim of the wine-cup; Sophocles asked if he could see the speck clearly, though it was barely visible, and then said, "Blow it away, then, so your finger doesn't get wet." When the boy brought his face close to the cup, Sophocles moved the cup closer to his own body, so that their heads came closer together. When they were very near, he caught the youth with his hand and kissed him. Everyone clapped with laughter and shouted at how cleverly he had "captured" the boy. Sophocles then said, "I am practicing my generalship, gentlemen, since Pericles <note>The famous Athenian statesman</note> told me that I knew how to write poetry, but did not know how to be a general <term>strategos</term>. Does this 'stratagem' of mine seem to have turned out correctly?" He often said and did such clever things when he was drinking or acting socially. However, in political matters, he was neither wise nor energetic, but lived as one of the ordinary, good Athenians.

Hieronymus of Rhodes also says in his *Historical Notes* that Sophocles once led a handsome boy outside the city walls for his company. The boy spread his own small cloak on the grass and wrapped himself in Sophocles’ fine mantle <term>chlanis</term> <note>An expensive, fine woolen cloak</note>. After their dalliance, the boy snatched Sophocles’ fine mantle and ran off, leaving his own childish garment behind for Sophocles. Naturally, the incident was talked about, and Euripides, hearing of it, mocked what had happened, saying that he himself had once been with that same boy but had lost nothing, whereas Sophocles had been treated with contempt because of his lack of self-control. When Sophocles heard this, he wrote an epigram against him, using the fable of the Sun and the North Wind, and hinting at Euripides’ own reputation for adultery:

"The Sun was that boy, Euripides, whose warmth made me strip; but when you were with him, it was the North Wind <note>original: "Borras"</note> that pleasured you, for you are cold. You are 'wise' indeed, you who sow love in another's field and then accuse a 'cloak-thief' of your own loss."
