Theopompus, in his work *On the Treasures Plundered from Delphi*, says that the lover of Epaminondas <note>The great Theban general</note> was so extravagant that he had a Spartan trophy engraved upon his shield; he fought with such marvelous bravery that this shield was later dedicated in the portico at Delphi. In the same book, Theopompus says that Phayllus, the tyrant of the Phocians, was a lover of women, while Onomarchus <note>Both were leaders of Phocis during the Third Sacred War, 356–346 BC, who seized the Delphic treasury to pay their mercenaries</note> was a lover of boys. From the gifts dedicated to the god, they bestowed treasures upon those who came to Delphi; to a beautiful youth who associated with them, they gave four gold scrapers <term>strigils</term> from the Sybarite dedication. To Deinia, a flute-player, Phayllus gave a silver drinking cup belonging to the Phocians and <insert>a gold one and things for the child, as she herself says</insert> she was intended to play the flute at the Pythian Games, had she not been prevented by the crowd. To Lycolas, the son of Tricholeas, because he was naturally beautiful, Onomarchus gave a laurel crown of gold, a dedication from the Ephesians. There was also a boy brought to Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon</note> by his father, and while being groomed there, he was secretly sent away. To Epilycus the Amphipolitan, because he was beautiful, Onomarchus gave a gold bowl, a dedication from Damippus. To Pharsalia, a dancer from Thessaly, Philomelus gave a gold laurel crown, a dedication from the Lampsacenes. This same Pharsalia, while in Metapontum, was the subject of a prophecy from the bronze laurel tree that the Metapontines had set up during the visit of Aristeas of Proconnesus <note>A legendary poet and miracle-worker</note>, when he claimed to have come from the Hyperboreans. As soon as she was seen entering the marketplace, the diviners went mad, and she was torn apart by them. When people later sought the cause, it was found to be because she was wearing the god’s own crown.

See to it then, you philosophers who use love in a way that is against nature, that you do not perish in a similar fashion for your impiety toward the god. For boys are only beautiful, as the courtesan Glycera used to say, for as long as they resemble women, as Clearchus records. To me, even Cleonymus the Spartan seems to have acted against nature; he was the first man to take women from the Metapontines as hostages. He released the two hundred who were the most famous and beautiful, as Duris of Samos records in his *Life of Agathocles*. And I, too, have learned these erotic songs of Anticlaides, the son of Epicrates, which are quite like the poems of Sappho, or those of Cleomela the Lamynthian. And you, O philosophers, if you ever fall in love with women, do not be seized by a murderous rage, but learn how impossible it is to succeed. Loves come to an end, as Clearchus says. For even a bull mounted the bronze cow of Pausias, and a dog tried to mate with a painted dog <gloss>which you use</gloss>, and others approached and leaped upon a painted pigeon and a tortoise. When these things proved to be inanimate to all who watched, they withdrew—just like Clasophus of Selymbria. ...the hardness of the stone <note>original: "τὸ ἀντίτυπον τοῦ λίθου"</note>, at which point his desire ceased; then, having laid out a piece of meat, he satisfied himself. The poet Alexis mentions this event in the play entitled *The Spectacle*, writing as follows: "And there have been, as some say, those in Samos who desired a girl made of stone, and one man even shut himself up in the temple." Philemon also mentions it, saying: "But once in Samos, a certain man fell in love with a stone image <note>original: "ζῶον", literally 'living thing,' but here referring to a lifelike statue</note>, and then shut himself up in the temple." The statue is the work of Ktesikles, as Adraeus of Mytilene says in his treatise *On Sculptors*. Polemon—either the one who wrote the *Description of Greece* or the one who wrote *On the Treasury of Pictures* at Delphi—says that there are two stone boys there, and the Delphians say that someone fell in love with one of them and was shut in with it, and as a result of his 'intimacy' left behind a crown; when he was caught acting like a beast, the Delphians ordered the man to be released, <margin>Animals in love with humans.</margin> for he had given them a fee. 

Indeed, even irrational animals have fallen in love with humans. In Sicyon, there was a rooster <note>original: "Ἀλεκτρυών"</note> belonging to a royal cupbearer; the rooster was called "Centaur," and the Sicyonian was a servant of the King of the Bithynians, as Nikander relates in the sixth book of his *Adventures*. In Achaia, <margin>Pliny, Book 10, Chapter 22.</margin> a goose fell in love with a boy, as Clearchus relates in the first book of his *Erotics*. Or do you think it was just a boy? Theophrastus, in his *Erotic Treatise*, says the boy was called Amphilochus, and that his race was Olenian. Hermeias, the son of Hermosothos and a Samian philosopher, says that a dog fell in love with a Laconian girl. In Leukas, Clearchus says a certain maiden fell so much in love that she even lost her life, dying along with her beloved. 

There is a story of a dolphin in Iasos falling in love with a boy, as Doris relates in her <margin>Hermolaus, Book 9, Chapter 5; citing Pliny.</margin> *History*. This is the story concerning Alexander <note>Likely Alexander the Great, who was fascinated by the story</note>, which goes as follows: the land summoned the boy of Iasos; for around this city there was a certain boy named Dionysius, who, coming from the wrestling school with the others, went to swim in the sea. A dolphin somehow met him from the deep, and taking him up on its back, carried him for a long distance while swimming, and then set him back down on the land. 

The dolphin is the most human-loving <margin>A dolphin as a lover of a boy.</margin> and most intelligent of animals, and knows how to return a favor. Phylarchus, at any rate, says in his twelfth book that a Milesian named Coeranus, seeing fishermen who had caught a dolphin in a net and were about to cut it up, gave them money and, having secured it, released it into the deep. After this, Coeranus suffered a shipwreck near Mykonos, and while everyone else perished, he alone was saved by a dolphin. When he died as an old man in his homeland, and the funeral procession happened to be passing by the sea at Miletus, a multitude of dolphins appeared in the harbor on that day, just a little distance from those escorting Coeranus, as if they were joining the procession and mourning the man. 

The same Phylarchus relates in his twentieth book the kind of affection an elephant has for <margin>And an elephant as a lover of a boy.</margin> a child; he writes the following: at that time, a female elephant was raised with a male elephant, whom they called Nicanon; the wife of an Indian, as she was dying, entrusted her thirty-day-old child to this animal. When the woman died, a terrible affection arose in the beast toward the child. For it would not endure the infant being separated from it, and it was distressed if it did not see the child. Therefore, whenever the nurse filled the child with milk, she would place it in its cradle <note>original: "σκάφῃ", literally a tub or bowl used as a cradle</note> between the feet of the beast. If she did not do this, the elephant would react appropriately. Afterward, throughout the whole day, taking up stalks of hay and the fodder placed before it, the elephant would brush away the flies while the infant slept; and whenever it cried, the elephant would move the cradle with its trunk and put it to sleep. The male elephant often did the same thing. 

But you, O philosophers, are wilder in your judgment than both dolphins and elephants, and even more inhuman! Even while Persaeus of Citium <margin>Persaeus' Memoirs.</margin> shouts in his *Sympotic Memoirs* and says that it is sometimes appropriate to make mention of sexual matters over wine. For how can we not be inclined toward these things when we have been drinking? And should we not praise those who use these things during the day and in moderation, while blaming those who do so like beasts and greedily? If dialecticians meeting for a drink should discuss syllogisms, one would suppose they were acting inappropriately for the present occasion. A gentleman might get drunk, but those who wish to be temperate maintain such a front in their drinking up to a certain point; then, when they surrender to the wine, they display every kind of indecency. This happened recently with the envoys from Arcadia who came to Antigonus. For they sat there very sullenly and indecently, as they thought—not only refusing to look at any of us, but not even at each other. But as the drinking progressed, and other entertainments entered, along with those female dancers—who, as is their custom, were dancing naked in their loincloths—those "modest" men could no longer contain themselves; they leaped from their couches and shouted as if viewing a wonderful spectacle, calling the king "blessed" because it was permitted for him to enjoy these things, and they did many other such vulgar things. 

And which of the philosophers drinking with us, when a flute-girl entered and—as there was plenty of room—the girl wished to sit beside him, did not turn away and act harshly? Yet later, when the flute-girl was being sold (as is the custom...

# BOOK XIII

### ->ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS<-

It is common for such things to happen at drinking parties; for even when he was quite a young man, he <note>Referring to the philosopher Zeno of Citium</note> was buying a girl, and when another man came forward more quickly to buy her, he disputed it—so much so that he did not even say he had sold her to him—and finally that harsh philosopher came to blows. For at first, he would not even allow the flute-girl <note>original: "αὐλητρίδι"; these were female entertainers common at Greek symposia</note> to sit down, lest Persaeus <note>A student of Zeno</note> should see her, since Persaeus himself was the type to start a boxing match over a flute-girl. For Antigonus of Carystus, writing in his work *On Zeno*, says: "When Persaeus had already bought a flute-girl at a drinking party, Zeno of Citium, having brought her to him through a servant, and being aware of his own household's violence, dragged the girl away and locked her up with Persaeus." I also know that Polystratus the Athenian, a student of Theophrastus who was nicknamed "the Blind One," used to strip the clothes off the flute-girls.

Even kings have been earnest about <margin>Female musicians [and] melodies.</margin> female musicians, as Parmenion makes clear in his letter to Alexander, which he sent to him after taking Damascus and gaining control of the baggage of Darius <note>Darius III, the Persian King defeated by Alexander the Great</note>. After listing the captives, he writes: "I found 325 concubines of the king who were musicians, 46 men who were garland-weavers, 277 cooks, 29 pot-boilers, 13 milk-producers, 17 drink-makers, 70 wine-pourers, and 40 perfumers."

And I say to you, my friends, that nothing is so delightful to the eyes as the beauty of a woman. For instance, in the play *Oeneus*, the tragic poet Chaeremon, describing certain maidens <margin>Chaeremon’s *Oeneus*: attendants and the flowers.</margin> whom he had seen, says in the drama of that name:

> One lay in the white moonlight, revealing a breast where her shoulder-strap had slipped. Another, in the dance, had loosened her left hip; to the naked air, she presented a living picture, showing her white skin to the eyes, a work of self-shining light against the dark shadows. Another exposed her beautiful arms; another was clasping her neck so that it seemed to bloom. Another, under the folds of torn cloaks, revealed a thigh, and the hope of love—though without expectation—was sealed there by her laughing youth. They fell asleep upon the helenium <note>A type of flowering plant</note>, and upon the dark-leaved wings of violets, crushing them; and the crocus, which left its sun-like image on the woven patterns of their robes. The marjoram, grown lush in the soft meadows, stretched out its neck.

This poet is quite inclined toward flowers, and speaking of those who wallow among them, he says:

> And she wrought the sights of her body, shining and distinguished by its white color, while Modesty regulated the gentlest blush, adding it to the bright complexion. Her hair, waxen-colored as if from a statue, was molded with curls, and yellow flowers grew upon her head as if on a roof.

And where the children of spring announce the flowers—the children of the air, the breezes—flowing around them... <note>The Greek text here is somewhat fragmented and difficult to translate precisely</note> some were thrown into an infinite host, and again they drew in the pleasures of the meadows’ children... those which belong to Dionysus, the ivy, lover of the dance, child of the year.

And concerning roses in his *Odysseus*, he speaks thus:

> They had roses, the flower-blooming bodies of the Seasons, in their hair—the most excellent nursing-child of spring.

And in *Thyestes*:

> The bright-shining rose together with the silver lilies... he sees much of the harvest of Cypris <note>Aphrodite, goddess of love</note> present, ripening over the unmixed vines of time.

Regarding beauty—for as Euripides says, "the aged singer still celebrates Memory"—many women have become famous. Thargelia of Miletus, who married fourteen men, was both very beautiful in form and wise, as the sophist Hippias says in the work entitled *The Collection*. Dinon, in the fifth book of his *Persian History*, says that the sister of Bagas <note>likely a courtier or official</note>, who was a paternal sister to Xerxes named Anytis, was the most beautiful of the women in Asia, and the most licentious. Phylarchus, in his nineteenth book, says that Timosa, the concubine of Oxyartes, surpassed all women in beauty; she was sent as a gift by the King of the Egyptians to Statira, the King’s wife.

Theopompus, in the fifty-sixth book of his *Histories*, says that Xenopeitha, the mother of Lysandridas, was the most beautiful of all women in the Peloponnese. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> killed her and her sister Chryse, when King Agesilaus, after a political struggle, caused her enemy Lysandridas to be exiled by the Spartans. Pantica of Cyprus was also most beautiful; Phylarchus says of her in his tenth book that she was with Olympias, the mother of Alexander, when Monimus son of Pythion sought her in marriage. Since the woman was licentious, Olympias said, "You wretch, you marry with your eyes, not with your mind."

They also say that the woman who brought Pisistratus back to his tyranny, having a beauty beyond nature as if she were Athena, was exceptionally fair, and her form was compared to the goddess. Her name was Phye; Pisistratus gave her in marriage to his son Hipparchus, as Cleidemus records in the eighth book of his *Returns*. And it is said that Hippias took another woman who was introduced to him, the daughter of Socrates (and daughter of Charmus who served as polemarch), who was very beautiful; she lived with him after he became tyrant. He says that Charmus became the lover of Hippias, and was the first to dedicate an image of Eros at the Academy, upon which it is inscribed:

> Love of many devices, for you this was dedicated...

...altar, Charmus at the shaded boundaries of the gymnasium. Hesiod, in the third book of the *Melampodia*, called Chalcis in Euboea the land of "beautiful women" <note>original: καλλιγύναικα (kalligynaika)</note>; for attractive women are born there, as Theophrastus has stated. And Nymphodorus, in his *Circumnavigation of Asia*, says that women more beautiful than any others in the world are born in Tenedos, the Trojan island. I also know that a contest for beauty <margin>contest of beauty</margin> among women was once established, as Nicias records in his *Arcadian History*. He says that Cypselus, having founded a city in the plain by the Alpheios river, settled some Parrhasians there and established a sanctuary and an altar to Eleusinian Demeter. In her festival, he also performed the beauty contest, and the first to win it was his wife, Herodice. This contest is carried out even to this day. The women who compete are called *Chrysophoroi* <term>Chrysophoroi: "Gold-bearers," likely referring to the elaborate gold jewelry worn by the contestants</term>. Theophrastus says a beauty contest takes place among the people of Elis, and the judgment is performed with great seriousness; the winners receive weapons as prizes, which Dionysius the Leuctrian says are then dedicated to Athena. The winner, crowned with ribbons by his friends, proceeds in a procession until he arrives at the temple. Myrsilus, in his *Historical Paradoxes*, records that a crown of myrtle is given to them. The same Theophrastus says that in some places, judgments are also held for women regarding temperance <note>original: σωφροσύνης (sophrosyne), a Greek virtue involving self-control and moderation</note> and household management, as is the case among the Barbarians <note>The Greeks used "Barbarian" to describe anyone who did not speak Greek, often referring to Persians or Thracians</note>. Beauty was also honored in this way as much as possible among the people of Tenedos and Lesbos. This beauty is an honor bestowed by luck or nature, whereas temperance ought to be the primary goal; for beauty of this kind is good, but if it lacks temperance, it carries the danger of licentiousness.

After Myrtilus had listed these things in order and everyone marveled at his memory, Cynulcus said: "Of polymathy <margin>Polymathy (Much learning)</margin> <note>original: Πολυμαθία (polymathia), referring to wide-ranging but superficial knowledge</note> there is nothing more empty." So said Hippon the Atheist, and even the divine Heraclitus says, "Much learning does not teach one to have sense." And Timon said, "Broad polymathy, is there any other thing more hollow?" For what is the benefit of so many names, which grammar will use to confuse everyone rather than being able to bring temperance to those who listen? Then, if someone asks you who were the ones shut inside the wooden horse, you might name one or two. And not even from the works of Stesichorus (for you lack the leisure) but from the *Sack of Troy* by Acatus of Argos, for he listed a great many in his verse. But you certainly could not list the names of Odysseus’ companions in such a rhythmic way—who among them were devoured by the Cyclops, or by the Laestrygonians, and if they were truly devoured. Since you do not even know these things, yet you constantly mention Phylarchus, claiming that in the villages of the flute-players' companions, no flute-girls are to be seen... 

And Myrtilus replied: "Perhaps Phylarchus said this somewhere, for I have read his entire history." Then, in the twenty-first book, Myrtilus said: "Do I not rightly hate all philosophers, who are really haters of learning <note>original: μισοφιλολόγους (misophilologous)</note>? King Lysimachus didn't just banish them from his own kingdom, driving them out as Carystius says in his *Historical Notes*, but the Athenians did too. Alexis, at least, says in *The Horse*: <margin>philosophers being driven out</margin> 'This is the Academy; this is Xenocrates. May the gods grant good things to Demetrius and the lawmakers, because they are sending those who supposedly teach the power of words to the youth to the crows!' They say they were driven out of Attica. A certain Sophocles also banished all philosophers from Attica by a decree. Philon, a student of Aristotle, wrote a speech against him, while Demochares, the nephew of Demosthenes, wrote a defense of Sophocles. And the Romans, who are best in everything, cast out the sophists from Rome as corrupters of the youth, though later I do not know how they let them back in. Anaxippus the comic poet also shows your folly, saying in *The Man Struck by Lightning*: 'Alas, you practice philosophy! But I find that philosophers are wise only in their words; in their deeds, I see they are fools.' It is with good reason, then, that many cities, especially the Spartans <note>original: Λακεδαιμονίων (Lacedaemonians)</note>, as Chamaeleon says in his work *On Simonides*, do not admit either rhetoric or philosophy, because of your ambition in words, your quarrels, and your untimely refutations—which caused the death of Socrates, who used to converse with those chosen by lot for the courts, who were sometimes the most thieving of men. For these reasons, Theodoros the Atheist died, and Diagoras was exiled because he suffered a shipwreck. Theotimus, who wrote against Epicurus, was prosecuted by Zeno the Epicurean and put to death, as Demetrius of Magnesia says in his *Work on Men of the Same Name*."

When he fell silent, I said: "Since, according to Clearchus of Soli, you do not practice a life of endurance, but you live a truly 'Cynic' life <margin>Cynics</margin> <note>The word "Cynic" comes from the Greek word for "dog" (kyon)</note>—even though that animal possesses a nature with four distinct qualities, of which you have taken the worse parts for yourselves. For a dog is wonderful in its sense of smell and its ability to distinguish friend from foe. It is social with humans, a housekeeper, and a guardian of the lives of those who treat it well—all of which are most desirable traits. Yet neither of these belongs to you who imitate the 'dog-like' life. You are not social, nor do you distinguish who is eating or conversing with you; lacking any sense of shame, you live idly and without watchfulness. But since the dog is by nature abusive and gluttonous, and also lives a life of hardship and nakedness, you practice both of these, and...

...discourses and altars, and besides these, people who live without homes or hearths, excluded from everything, alien to virtue, and useless for the practical needs of life. For there is nothing more unphilosophical than these so-called philosophers. Who could have expected Aeschines the Socratic to have been such a man in his character, as the orator Lysias describes <margin>Aeschines the Socratic.</margin> him in his speeches regarding business contracts? We admire him from the dialogues circulating under his name as a decent and moderate man—unless, in truth, those writings actually belong to the wise Socrates. Indeed, it is said by those around Idomeneus that they were given to him <margin>Lysias against Aeschines the Socratic.</margin> by Xanthippe, the wife of Socrates, after his death. But Lysias, in the speech entitled *Against Aeschines the Socratic regarding Debt*, mentions him in this way—and I will quote it, even if the passage is long, because of your curiosity, O philosophers. 

The orator begins as follows: "I would never have thought, O men of the jury, that Aeschines would dare to bring so shameful a case, believing that he could not easily find another more malicious than this. For this man, O men of the jury, owing money at three drachmas interest to Sosimus the banker, now denies it. Coming to us, he claimed he was being hounded by his creditors and was falling into ruin because of the interest. He said, 'I will set up a perfume-making craft <term>myrepsic art: the ancient and expensive trade of distilling and blending aromatic oils and perfumes</term>, but I need capital, and I will pay you back at an interest of nine obols per mina.' Truly, a long way from the goal of happiness is the perfume-making craft for a philosopher! And it is quite a sequel to the philosophy of Socrates—a man who even disapproved of the use of such perfumes.

Even though the lawgiver Solon prohibited men from presiding over such a craft, Pherecrates says in either *The Sleep* or *The All-Night Festival*: 'What did you learn by sitting in a perfume shop? High up, sheltered under a parasol, we sat together, not chatting with the youths all day.' Then he adds: 'Immediately after eating, he never saw a female cook, nor a fish-seller.' For each thing has its own pleasure. The tools of the trade are also fitting. Next, the orator says: 'Cease from someone speaking thus, who at the same time thought that Aeschines, having been a disciple of Socrates and speaking many solemn words about justice and virtue, would never attempt nor dare to do what the most wicked and unjust men attempt to do.' After this, he again describes his impulses: how he borrowed money, and how he pays back neither the interest nor the principal. And that he became overdue for payment by the court's judgment, being condemned in a default case, and how a branded slave <note>original: στιγματίας (stigmatias), a slave marked with a tattoo or brand as a punishment for running away or theft</note> was seized from him as collateral, and many other accusations. He adds these words: 'But indeed, O men of the jury, he is not like this only toward me, but toward all others who have dealt with him. Do not the shopkeepers who live nearby, from whom he takes appetizers and does not pay, sue him and shut up their shops? His neighbors suffer such terrible things at his hands that they abandon their own houses and rent others further away. And as for all the benefit-club loans <note>original: ἐράνους (eranous), a form of interest-free loan among friends or associates for mutual aid</note> he has collected, he does not pay back the remaining installments, but he ruins them just as he does the shopkeeper. So many people come to his house at daybreak to demand what is owed that passers-by think they have come for a funeral procession because he is dead. Those in the Piraeus are so disposed toward him that it seems far safer to sail to the Adriatic than to deal with him. For he considers whatever he borrows to be his own, much more than what his father left him. But did he not acquire the property of Hermaeus the perfume-seller by seducing his wife? She was seventy years old, yet by pretending to be in love with her, he treated her in such a way that he made her husband and sons beggars. He turned her into a retail perfume-seller. So amorously did he handle the mistress of her age, enjoying her youth—though it was easier to count her teeth, as they were so few, than the fingers on her hand! Read me the witnesses for these things.'" Such was the life of this sophist. 

Lysias, O Casuscus, speaks thus. And I, following the tragic poet Aristarchus—not starting this, but defending myself—will cease this discourse here which has bothered you and the others.

### ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

<margin>
In Xenophon: thus it is read. "One should abstain from gluttony and over-eating just as one abstains from sin." <note>original: οὕτω χρῆναι καὶ λαυμαργίας, σίτων ἀπείχεσθαι ὥς καὶ ἁμαρτίας</note>
</margin>
...if everyone drank unmixed wine <note>Ancient Greeks typically diluted their wine with water; drinking it "unmixed" was considered a sign of barbarism or lack of self-control.</note> poorly, not a single one of us would drink at all. But as it is, by taking our pleasure before we have done the work, we fall short of what is truly good. Xenophon records that Agesilaus <note>A famous King of Sparta known for his austere lifestyle.</note> believed one should abstain from drunkenness just as from madness, and from excessive food just as from idleness. But we are not like him—we who drink more than those who are present when the wine is sacrificed, and when the marketplace is full, we go off to these musical banquets. 

Indeed, the "Philip-imitating" Ulpian <note>A character in the dialogue, likely a reference to his pedantic habit of questioning every word's origin.</note> spoke up again when someone said, "I am not *exoinos*," <note>original: Ἔξοινος; meaning "out of wine" or "drunk."</note> noting that the word *exoinos* was used by Alexis in his play *The Man Moving In*. But since every day, after our usual new topics of conversation, our magnificent host Larysius introduces various entertainments, and even jesters, let us say something about them as well. 

I know that Anacharsis the Scythian, <note>A semi-legendary "noble savage" philosopher from the 6th century BCE.</note> when jesters were introduced at a banquet, remained unsmiling; but when a monkey was brought in, he laughed and said, "This creature is funny by nature, but the human is funny only by artifice." Euripides also said in his play *Melanippe the Captive*: 
"Many men practice biting wit for the sake of a laugh. But I hate all those professional jokers who, though they are wise, have unbridled mouths. They are not counted among real men, but are mere decorations for laughter. They inhabit houses and keep the ships' stores safe within the halls." <note>This quote suggests a traditional aristocratic disdain for those who trade dignity for a laugh.</note>

Parmeniscus of Metapontum—as Semus says in the fifth book of his *History of Delos*—was a man of the highest rank in birth and wealth. Having descended into the Cave of Trophonius, <note>A famous subterranean oracle in Boeotia; visitors were said to emerge so terrified they lost the ability to laugh.</note> he found upon coming back up that he could no longer laugh. When he consulted the oracle about this, the Pythian priestess replied: 
"You ask about the labor of honey-sweet laughter; Mother at home shall give you the highest honor." 
Expecting that he would laugh again upon returning to his fatherland, and thinking he had been deceived when nothing happened, he eventually chanced to go to Delos. While admiring everything on the island, he went into the Temple of Leto, expecting to see a remarkable statue of the mother of Apollo. But when he saw a shapeless wooden idol, he burst into laughter in spite of himself. Realizing the meaning of the god’s oracle—that "Mother" referred to Leto <note>Leto was the mother of Apollo and Artemis, and her temple on Delos was world-famous.</note>—and being cured of his ailment, he honored the goddess greatly.

<margin>
The Wealth-Makers. <note>original: Πλουτοποιοί; likely the title of a play by Anaxandrides.</note>
</margin>
Anaxandrides, in his play *The Old Man’s Madness*, says that Rhadamanthys and Palamedes were the inventors of jokes, writing: "And Rhadamanthys and Palamedes invented the art of saying funny things for the one who pays no contribution to the feast." <note>original: ἀσύμβολον; a guest who brings no "symbol" or contribution, essentially a "free-loader."</note> Xenophon also mentions a jester named Philippus in his *Symposium*, writing something like this: "Philippus the jester knocked at the door and told the servant to announce who he was and that he wished to be put up, saying he had come prepared with everything necessary to 'breathe through' <note>A pun on living off others.</note> someone else's property. He added that his boy was very burdened because he was carrying nothing and had not had breakfast." 

Hippolochus the Macedonian, in his letter to Lynceus, mentions the jesters Mandrogenes and Strato of Athens. There was a great abundance of this "wisdom" <note>Used ironically here.</note> in Athens. For instance, a group of sixty gathered at the temple of Heracles in Diomeia; they were so famous in the city that people would say, "The Sixty said this," or "I am coming from the Sixty." Among them were Callimedon the "Crayfish," Daneas, Masigeiton, and Menaechmus, as Telephanes says in his book *On the City*. Their reputation for idle wit became so great that Philip of Macedon, hearing of them, sent them a talent of silver <note>A massive sum of money, equivalent to about 6,000 drachmas.</note> so they would write down their jokes and send them to him. That kings have taken jokes seriously is also testified by the orator Demosthenes in his *Philippics*. 

Demetrius Poliorcetes <note>"The Besieger," a successor to Alexander the Great.</note> was also a lover of laughter, as Phylarchus says in the sixth book of his *Histories*; he used to say that the court of Lysimachus <note>A rival king.</note> was no different from a comic stage. He mocked everyone there, calling Bithys and Paris—the most powerful of Lysimachus's friends—mere actors, along with others like Rucitas, Menelaus, and Oxythemis. When Lysimachus heard this, he retorted, "I, at least, have never seen a prostitute come off a tragic stage," referring to Demetrius's mistress, the flute-girl Lamia. When this was reported back, Demetrius replied, "But the prostitute at my house lives more virtuously than the Penelope at his." 

It has been mentioned before that Sulla, the Roman general, was a lover of laughter. Lucius Aemilius Paullus, too—who also served as a Roman general, conquered the Illyrians, and led King Gentius of the Illyrians captive with his children—celebrated triumphal games in Rome and did things worthy of total laughter, as Polybius records in his thirtieth book. Pratinas <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek dramatist credited with inventing the satyr play.</note> displays his anger against those who do these things through the following choral-dance song: "What is this tumult? What are these dances? What insolence has come upon the altar of Dionysus, the loud-clattering altar? Bromios <note>An epithet for Dionysus, meaning 'The Roarer.'</note> is mine, mine! I am the one who should sing, I am the one who should make a noise, rushing through the mountains with the Naiads, like a swan leading a song of many-colored wings. The song has been established as the Queen. Let the flute dance afterwards; for it is only an assistant to the revels. It wants to lead in boxing matches, to be a general among drunken brawlers. Burn that spit-wasting reed, that babbling-heavy-voiced one, walking out of tune and rhythm, a body molded like a servant... <note>original: † υπνιολόνα δι’οσι δεξιὰ, † - this part of the Greek text is corrupted and the meaning is uncertain.</note> hear my Dorian dance, O ivy-tressed King of the triumphant dithyramb!"

Concerning the partnership of flutes with the lyre, since this joint playing <note>original: συναυλία (synaulia), music played by flutes in concert or with other instruments.</note> has often delighted us, Ephippus says in *The Merchandise*: "For, young man, the music shared by the flutes is also found in the lyre."

In harmony like this. For when they harmonize the mode for those who are listening, then the greatest pleasure is found. What exactly "joint playing" <note>original: συναυλία</note> is, Semus of Delos shows in the fifth book of his *History of Delos*, writing as follows: "Since many are ignorant of joint playing, it must be said that it is a certain contest of harmony alternating between the flute and the rhythm, without any words from a singer accompanying the melody." Likewise, Antiphanes makes it clear in *The Flute-Player*, saying: "Tell me now, what kind of joint playing is this? For he knows it, but is still playing the flute." The poets call the flute "Libyan," as Duris says in the second book of his *History of Agathocles*, because Sarkites—who is thought to have first discovered the art of flute-playing—was a Libyan among the nomads, to whom he first taught the Mother’s rites <note>Referring to the cult of Cybele, the Great Mother, whose rites often featured loud flute music.</note>. There are names for flute-tunes, as Tryphon says in the second book of *Names*: the revel-tune, the pastoral-tune, the *gingras* <note>A mournful Phoenician flute-tune.</note>, the four-revel-tune, the phallic-tune, the dance-tune, the victory-tune, the war-tune, the sweet-revel-tune, the *sikinnos-turbe* <note>A wild dance from satyr plays.</note>, the door-knocking-tune, the parched-tune and the gate-striking-tune, the tickling-tune, and the *mothon* <note>A vulgar, energetic dance.</note>. All these were played on the flute accompanied by dance.

<margin>Various songs.</margin>
The *imalios*, also called the *epimylios*, which they sang at the grain-mills, perhaps named after the *imalis*. Among the Dorians, *imalis* refers to a surplus of flour. Semus of Delos, in his work *On Paeans*, says: "The handfuls of barley themselves were called *amalas*. When many were gathered together into one bundle, they were called *oulos* and *ioulos*. ...style and arrangement. It received the name **Magody** <note>Magōidia</note> because it presents things that are almost like magic, and displays various powers as if by a drug. Among the Spartans, there was an ancient form of comic jesting, as Sosibius says; it was not very serious, since Sparta pursued simplicity even in these matters. Someone would imitate, in plain language, people stealing fruit, or a foreign doctor speaking in a particular way, just as Alexis portrayed in *The Woman Drugged with Mandrake* with these words: "If a local doctor says 'bowl,' or 'he gave him barley-water,' we look down on him immediately. But if he says 'barley-water' <note>original: πτισάνην (ptisanēn)</note> and 'gruel' <note>original: ζυβέλιον (zybelion)</note>, we admire him; and again, if he says 'beet' <note>original: σευτλίον (seutlion)</note> we ignore it, but if he says 'chard' <note>original: τευτλίον (teutlion)</note> we receive it gladly." Those who pursued such jesting among the Spartans were called <margin>Maskers.</margin> **Maskers** <note>original: δικηλισταί (dikēlistai), meaning "those who represent" or "maskers"</note>, because they were the ones who prepared the costumes as well as the imitations.

There are many local names for this type of "Masker." For the people of Sicyon call them **Phallophoroi** <note>Phallus-bearers</note>, others call them **Autokabdali** <note>Improvisers</note>, and others **Phlyakes**, as the Italians do. Most call them "Sophists," but the Thebans <margin>Evil-doers hunt for thieves.</margin> (who are accustomed to naming many things in their own unique way) call them "Volunteers." Strattis demonstrates in *The Phoenician Women* that the Thebans have a very distinct way of speaking: "The whole city of Thebes understands nothing; you call the cuttlefish a 'rear-squirter' <note>original: ὀπισθοτίλαν (opisthotilan)</note>... and the cock an 'early-riser' <note>original: ὀρτάλιχον (ortalichon)</note>, the doctor a 'bag-packer' <note>original: σακτὰν (saktan)</note>, the bridge a 'girdle' <note>original: φλέφυραν (phlephyran)</note>, figs 'tukas' <note>original: τῦκα (tyka)</note>, and swallows 'chatterers' <note>original: κωτιλάδας (kōtiladas)</note>." To laugh they call "grinding the teeth" <note>original: ἐκπρισιδίψαι (ekprisidipsai)</note>, and "scraped-out" for something dug...

Semus the Delian, in his work *On Paeans*, says that the **Autokabdali** <margin>Improvisers.</margin> (Improvisers) used to appear wearing ivy wreaths and reciting speeches. Later, both they and their poems were named **Iambs**. The **Ithyphalloi**, he says, wear masks of drunken men and are crowned with floral wreaths, wearing colorful sleeves. They use tunics with white stripes and are girded with Tarentine robes that cover them down to the ankles. Entering silently through the gateway, when they reach the middle of the orchestra, they turn toward the audience and say: "Make way, make room for the god! For the god wishes to walk upright <margin>Phallus-bearers.</margin> and firm-footed through the midst." The **Phallophoroi**, he says, do not wear masks, but put on a visor made of wild thyme, and over this they place acanthus and a thick wreath of violets and ivy; they come forward wrapped in thick cloaks, some entering from the side and others through the center, walking in rhythm and saying: "To you, Bacchus, we brighten this Muse, pouring out a simple rhythm in a varied melody, a song not used before by maidens, but pure." They begin the hymn, and then running forward, they would mock whoever they chose, standing still as they did so. But the Phallus-bearer walks straight ahead, covered in soot.

Since the flow of the conversation has reached this point, <margin>Amoebeus the Lyre-singer.</margin> I think it is not right to pass over what concerns **Amoebeus**, the lyre-singer <note>kitharōdos</note> of our own time, a gifted artist and master of musical laws. Once, arriving late to our banquet, when he learned from one of the servants that we had finished dinner, he felt he should do something liberal; so Sophon the cook came to him and, as everyone could hear, spoke these verses of Eubulus:

> Why, you wretch, do you still stand in the entryway,
> And not walk in? For these earth-born guests long ago
> Finished the warm dishes, the tender limbs of greens;
> The sacred meats of young pigs have been torn apart.
> The circle of the belly has been ground down in the middle,
> And all the extremities have been consumed.
> The noble slice of sausage has been devoured,
> And the most worthy squid has been served beside it.
> The snouts and ribs have been polished off like justice,
> As if eaten by a man caught by the Council.
> Hurry, hurry, lest you stand gaping like a wolf,
> And later howl after missing these many delicacies.

Everything is ready for us now, as the sweetest Antiphanes says in *The Theban-Lover* (or some similar title):

> While the broth is there, a Boeotian eel,
> Sliced in the hollow depths of a cooking pot,
> Is warmed, lifted, set down, bubbles, and sizzles,
> So that not even a man with bronze nostrils,
> Once he entered, could go back out again
> To throw away such a breath, the cook being so lively.
> Near her, I would stay without food for a whole day and night.
> Scaly fish and ribs, and skins all together—
> A part will come crying out with the wing of a bird,
> And a boy stands by sprinkling vinegar, 
> While a stalk of silphium <note>An extinct medicinal and culinary herb highly prized in antiquity</note> stands ready.
> Then can anyone say that incantations have no power?
> For I already see three men chewing,
> While you whistle this tune, as a companion.
> The cuttlefish, having a body with a light back,
> Armed with sword-bearing hands;
> The squid, having changed its white nature,
> Its flesh scorched by the lashes of the coals,
> Delights its whole body in the golden breezes?
> The feast prophesies an uncovered hunger,
> So do not delay, take your place!

Because we had already dined heartily, unless we were meant to suffer, he responded most tunefully to him, shouting out these lines from Clearchus’s *The Lyre-Singer*:

> For a white conger eel, a gullet for all the gluttons!

For by these things the spirit is nourished, and our little lantern becomes bright. At this, there was applause, and everyone called for him with one voice. He entered, drank, took up his lyre, and delighted us so much that everyone marveled at his speed of hand combined with his art, and the melody of his voice. To me, he seemed no less...

...it is customary according to the ancient style of Amoebeus, whom Arisias says lived in Athens as a singer to the cithara <note>original: κιθάρωι ᾠδὴν (kitharōi ōidēn)</note>. He lived near the theater, and they say that whenever he went out to sing, he received an Attic talent for the day.

Regarding music, while some say one thing and others say another every day, and all praise
<margin>Praise of Music.</margin>
this education, Masturius—a man excellent and wise in all things—spoke. For as a discoverer of laws second to none, he once compared music to a clinic <note>original: ἰατρείωι (iatreioi), a place of healing</note>. He demanded its use, and regarding the instruments, the comic poet Eupolis says to his friends that music is "a deep and winding thing," and it always finds something new for those capable of invention. For this reason, Anaxilas says in *The Hyacinth*: "By the gods, music is like Libya; every year it breeds some new beast." For, O blessed ones, according to
<margin>10</margin>
Theophilus the citharode, music is a great and stable treasure for all who have learned and been educated in it. For it educates the character, and it calms the spirited and those of diverse opinions. Clinias
the Pythagorean, for instance, as Chamaeleon of Pontus records, who was distinguished in his life and character, whenever it happened that he grew harsh through anger, would take up his lyre and play the cithara. To those who sought the reason, he would say: "I am being calmed." Even the Homeric Achilles was calmed by the cithara, which was the only thing Homer allowed him to keep from the spoils of Eetion, skillfully settling his fiery nature. At least, he is the only one in the *Iliad* who makes use of music. That music also heals diseases has been recorded by Theophrastus in his work *On Inspiration*, where he says that those suffering from sciatica <note>original: ἰσχιακούς (ischiakous)</note> remain free of the ailment if someone plays the flute over the affected part in the Phrygian mode <note>original: φρυγιστὶ ἁρμονίᾳ (phrygisti harmoniai)</note>. The Phrygians were the first to discover and employ this mode. For this reason, among the
<margin>Mode <note>term: harmonia (the arrangement of notes in a scale or "mode")</note>.</margin>
Greeks, flute-players have Phrygian names, which is quite fitting, such as Sambas, Adon, and Telos in the works of Alcman. In Hipponax, we find Comalus, Codalus, and Bathys, from whom comes the proverb
<margin>20</margin>
<margin>A bad thing; Erasmus reads the proverb "Worse than Babys."</margin>
concerning those who always play the flute for the worse: "Babys plays even worse." Aristoxenus attributes the invention of this mode to Hyagnis the Phrygian. But Heraclides of Pontus, in the third book of his *On Music*, says that the Phrygian should not even be called a "mode," just as the Lydian should not. For he says there are three true modes, since there are three races of Greeks: Dorians, Aeolians, and Ionians. There is a slight difference in their characters. The
Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, more than the other Dorians, preserve their ancestral traditions. The Thessalians—who were the ones who originally shared their race with the Aeolians—maintain a similar way of life and upbringing. But the majority of the Ionians have been altered because they conform to whoever the barbarian rulers of the time are. The style of melody that the Dorians created they called the Dorian mode.
<margin>30</margin>
<margin>Difference in music according to the shifts and colors.</margin>
The song the Aeolians sang they called the Aeolian mode. The third, they called Ionian, which they heard from the singing of the Ionians. The Dorian mode expresses manliness and majesty; it is neither diluted nor cheerful, but rather somber and intense, neither varied nor complex. The
<margin>Different modes in relation to character and colors.</margin>
character of the Aeolians possesses arrogance and bulk, and even a certain hollowness, which agrees with their horse-breeding and their hospitality to strangers. It is not cunning, but used to boldness; for this reason, drinking-bouts and romance are natural to them, along with every relaxation of diet. Thus, they embrace the character of the so-called Hypodorian mode. For this, says Heraclides, is what they used to call Aeolian, just as Lasus of Hermione says in his *Hymn to Demeter of Hermione*: "I sing of Demeter and the Maiden <note>Persephone</note>, the wife of Clymenus, a honey-voiced hymn, leading the way with a deep-booming Aeolian mode." Now, everyone sings
<margin>40</margin>
these melodies in the Hypodorian scale; since the melody is Hypodorian, Lasus reasonably says that the mode is Aeolian. Pratinas says somewhere: "Do not pursue the intense mode, nor the relaxed Ionian, but plough the middle field and 'Aeolize' in your melody." He says more clearly in the following lines that the Aeolian mode is "fitting for all song-loving singers." Previously, as I said, they called it Aeolian, but later Hypodorian. They say it was ranked this way in the flute-repertoire because they thought it was "under" <note>original: ὑπὸ (hypo)</note> the Dorian mode. But it seems to me that seeing its bulk and its claim to nobility in the characters of the mode, they called it Hypodorian, just as we call something nearly white "off-white" <note>original: ὑπόλευκον (hypoleukon)</note>. And what is not quite sweet, but close to it, we call "sweetish" <note>original: ὑπόγλυκυ (hypoglyky)</note>; thus, Hypodorian is that which is not entirely Dorian. Next
<margin>50</margin>
let us examine the character of the Milesians, which the Ionians always display—arrogant in the fitness of their bodies and full of anger. They are difficult to reconcile and contentious, displaying nothing humane or cheerful, but showing a lack of affection and a hardness in their characters. Therefore, the character of the Ionian mode is neither austere nor cheerful, but harsh and hard, though possessing a weight that is not ignoble. For this reason, the mode was beloved by Tragedy. But the characters of the modern Ionians are very luxurious, and the character of their mode has changed much. They say that Pythermus of Chios, in this very type of mode, composed "clumsy" <note>original: σκαιὰ (skaia)</note> melodies, and because the poet was Ionian, the mode was called Ionian. This is the Pythermus mentioned by Ananius or Hipponax in his iambics thus: "Pythermus says gold is everything, the rest is nothing." For Pythermus says: "It turns out there was nothing else but gold." Therefore, also according to the Ionian...

->### ATHENAEUS: THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS ###<-

...the argument is persuasive that Pythermus was sitting there, having composed the structure of his melodies to be suitable to the character <note>original: ἤθεσι (ēthesi), the moral or emotional character</note> of the Ionians. Therefore, I suspect that the "Ionian" is not a distinct musical mode, but a certain wonderful type of melodic shape. We should, then, disregard those who are unable to observe the differences in kind but instead follow only the highness or lowness of the notes, and who propose a "Trihemitolydian" mode, and others even higher than that. For I do not see that the "Hyperphrygian" has its own unique character, even though some claim to have discovered a new "Hypophrygian" mode. A mode must possess a distinct form, or a specific passion, or a moral character, just like the Locrian mode. For some of those in the circles of Simonides and Pindar once used this mode, and then it was again disregarded. It remains that there are three original modes, just as there are three Greek tribes; the Phrygian and Lydian modes, being from the barbarians, became known to the Greeks from those Phrygians and Lydians who came down into the Peloponnese with Pelops <note>A legendary king who migrated from Asia Minor to Greece, giving his name to the Peloponnese</note>. For the Lydians followed him because Mount Sipylus was part of Lydia, and the Phrygians did so not just because they are neighbors with the Lydians, but because Tantalus ruled over them as well. You can see throughout the Peloponnese, and especially in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, large mounds which they call the "Tombs of the Phrygians" who came with Pelops. The Greeks learned these modes from them; which is why Telesias of Selinus says:

"First among the mixing bowls of the Greeks,
accompanied by flutes, those who suffered much,
sang the Phrygian law of Pelops' mountain-mother."

And: "What is this two-toned Lycian hymn, pleasing to the pluckings of the *pektis* <note>original: πηκτίδων (pēktidōn), a harp-like instrument</note>?" One must not accept what
<margin>10</margin>
<margin>20</margin>
<margin>The usefulness of music.</margin>
Polybius of Megalopolis <note>A famous Greek historian of the 2nd century BCE</note> says—as Ephorus records—that music was introduced to mankind for the sake of deception and sorcery. Nor should we think that the ancient Cretans or Spartans introduced the flute and rhythm into war instead of the trumpet without a purpose. Nor did the early Arcadians adopt music into their entire civil life without reason; so much so that not only among children, but even among young men up to thirty years of age, they made it a compulsory part of their upbringing, despite being otherwise very austere in their way of life. Indeed, among the Arcadians, children are accustomed from infancy to sing according to the law the hymns and paeans with which each group, following ancestral custom, honors their local heroes and gods. After these, learning the "laws" <note>technical compositions</note> of Timotheus and Philoxenus, they dance every year to the Dionysian flutes in the theaters—the children in children's contests, and the young men in those for adults. Throughout their whole lives in their social gatherings, they do not entertain themselves with imported performers, but by commanding one another to sing in turn. While it is not considered shameful for them to deny knowledge of other subjects, it is deemed a disgrace among them to refuse to sing. Furthermore, they practice military marches with the flute and in formation, and they perform dances with great public care and expense, exhibiting them every year in the theaters.

The ancients established these customs for them not for the sake of luxury or profit, but because they observed the hardness of each person’s life and the austerity of their characters, which comes to them because of the cold and gloom of the environment that exists in most of their lands—a climate to which we humans naturally tend to assimilate. For this reason, we differ greatly from one another in character, form, and color based on national divisions. In addition to this, they established common assemblies and sacrifices for both men and women, as well as choruses of girls and boys together, looking to tame and soften the stubbornness of their nature through the establishment of these habits. When these customs were eventually neglected and held in contempt—especially in Cynaetha, which has by far the harshest land and air in Arcadia—the people were driven to such mutual slanders and rivalries that they eventually became so savage that the greatest impieties occurred among them alone. At the time they committed their great massacre, whichever Arcadian cities they entered during their passage, all the other citizens immediately ordered them to leave by herald. The Mantineans, after the Cynaethans departed, even performed a purification of their city, leading sacrificial victims in a circle around the entire territory. Agias the musician said that the *syrinx* <note>a pan-pipe or part of a flute</note> used in theaters during the festivals of Dionysus produces a Phrygian scent to those who perceive it.

In ancient times, music was an exhortation to bravery. Alcaeus the poet <note>A lyric poet from Lesbos known for his political and warrior themes</note>, for instance—if anyone else was truly musical—places matters of bravery before those of poetry, being more warlike than necessary. Therefore, boasting of such things, he says:

"The great hall gleams with bronze;
the whole roof is adorned for Ares with shining helmets,
from which white horse-hair crests
nod down, decorations for the heads of men.
Shining bronze greaves hang from hidden pegs,
a defense against strong missiles;
there are breastplates of new linen, and hollow shields
thrown down. Beside them are Chalcidian swords,
and many belts and tunics;
these things must not be forgotten,
since we have first set ourselves to this task."

And yet, perhaps it would be more fitting for the house to be full of musical instruments. But the ancients considered bravery to be the greatest of the political virtues, and to this they assigned most things, rather than to the others. Archilochus, then, being a good poet, first boasted—

->### BOOK XIV ###<-

<margin>Poets are greatly inclined toward courage, or poetry is a companion to the laws.</margin>
...the ability to participate in political struggles. Aeschylus mentioned his own poetic background when he said, "If I were not a servant of the Lord of the Sea <note>original: ἐναλίοιο ἄνακτος (enalioio anaktos), referring to Poseidon</note>, and if I did not understand the lovely gift of the Muses." Similarly, Aeschylus, despite having such great fame for his poetry, nevertheless saw fit to have his bravery inscribed upon his tomb rather than his poetic skill. As another might say: "The thick-haired Mede <note>A term for the Persians</note> knows his famous Marathonian strength." For this reason, even the most courageous Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> <margin>The utility of music.</margin> go to war accompanied by flutes <note>term: αὐλῶν (aulōn) — double-piped woodwind instruments often called "flutes" but more like oboes</note>; the Cretans do so with the lyre; and the Lydians with pipes or flutes, as Herodotus records. Many of the barbarians also carry out diplomatic missions with flutes and the <term>kithara</term> <note>A professional version of the lyre</note>, so as to soothe the souls of their opponents. Theopompus, in the forty-sixth book of his *Histories*, says that the Getae carry kitharas and play them while making diplomatic proposals. From this, it seems that Homer also preserves the ancient custom of the Greeks when he says: "The phorminx <note>An ancient stringed instrument</note>, which the gods made as a companion to the feast," implying that the art is useful during banquets. This was an established custom; first, so that each person who was driven toward drunkenness and gluttony might receive music as a "doctor" for their insolence <note>original: ὕβρεως (hybreōs)</note> and disorder; and second, because music softens one's stubbornness. By limiting gloominess, it produces gentleness and a noble joy. This is why Homer introduced the gods in the first book of the *Iliad* making use of music after their dispute over Achilles. For they continued listening "to the beautiful phorminx held by Apollo, and the Muses who sang in response with beautiful voices." For it was necessary to put an end to their strife and discord, as we have said. Most people, therefore, seem to attribute to this science the power to reform social gatherings for the sake of grace and benefit. Indeed, the ancients adopted the custom—and even laws—that everyone should sing hymns to the gods at banquets, so that through these songs our sense of beauty and temperance <note>original: σωφρονικὸν (sōphronikon), meaning self-control or moderation</note> might be maintained. For since the songs were well-harmonized, and as they were led toward the songs of the gods, the character of each guest became more dignified. Philochorus says that the ancients did not always sing, but would perform the <term>dithyramb</term> <note>A wild, passionate choral hymn usually dedicated to Dionysus</note> when they poured libations—singing of Dionysus amidst wine and drunkenness, but singing of Apollo with quietness and order. Archilochus, at least, says: "I know how to lead the beautiful song of Lord Dionysus, the dithyramb, when my mind has been struck by the lightning of wine." And Epicharmus said in his *Philoctetes*: "There is no dithyramb when you drink water." It is clear from what has been said that music did not originally enter into banquets for the sake of shallow and common pleasure, as some believe. As for the Lacedaemonians, they do not say whether they actually *learned* music, but it is agreed by them that they are able to judge the art well. They say they have already saved music three times when it was being corrupted. Furthermore, music contributes to the sharpening of the mind for physical exercise. For this reason, all Greeks and those barbarians who are well-known make use of it. Those in the circle of Damon of Athens say, not incorrectly, that songs and dances must necessarily arise whenever the soul is moved in some way. Noble and beautiful movements of the soul produce similar songs and dances, while the opposite movements produce the opposite. This is the origin of the story about Cleisthenes, the tyrant of Sicyon, regarding a sign of a disciplined mind. For when he saw one of his daughter's suitors dancing in a vulgar way—it was Hippocleides the Athenian—he told him that he had "danced away" his marriage, believing, it seems, that the man’s soul was just as vulgar as his dance. For in dancing and walking, <margin>On dancing.</margin> beauty consists of fine movement and order, while disorder and vulgarity are shameful. It was for this reason that, from the beginning, the poets arranged dances for free-born men <margin>Herodotus book 6.</margin> and used gestures only as signs of what was being sung. They maintained a sense of nobility and manliness in them, which is why they called such dances <term>hyporchemata</term> <note>A type of lively choral song and dance</note>. But if anyone should perform the gestures immoderately or, while succeeding in the songs, say nothing with his dancing, he was disapproved of. This is why Aristophanes—or perhaps Plato—in his *The Scenes*, as Chamaeleon says, spoke thus: "So that if someone danced well, it was a sight to see. But now they act strangely; they stand still like stroke victims and howl." For the style of dancing in the choruses was graceful and magnificent, as if mimicking movements made under arms. This is why Socrates, in his poems, says that those who dance best are also the best in war, saying: "Those who honor the gods most beautifully in dances are the best in war." For the dance was almost like a military drill, a demonstration not only of general discipline but also of the care of the body. Amphion of Thespiae, in the second book of his work *On the Shrine of the Muses on Helicon*, writes that there were serious dances of boys on Helicon, and he provides this ancient epigram: "I both danced and taught men the Muses' art; the flute-player was a Phialian lord, but if you mean the Bacchic dancers of Sicyon, then they were for the gods. To Sicyon a beautiful prize was laid up." The flute-player Caphyseas did not speak poorly when, seeing one of his students attempting to play the flute very loudly and practicing it, he struck him and said that excellence does not lie in greatness, but greatness lies in excellence. The statues of ancient craftsmen are also remnants of this old style of dancing; for this reason, the art of hand-gestures <note>term: χειρονομίαν (cheironomian) — the "law of hands," a system of expressive gestures used in dance and oratory</note> was more carefully studied. In this art, too, they sought beautiful and noble movements, through which they achieved greatness by embracing excellence. They then transferred these forms from the hand-gestures into the choruses, and from the choruses into the...

# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

...into the wrestling schools. For even through music, and through the care of their bodies, they cultivated **good spirits**; and they practiced how to perform movements in armor alongside song, from which the so-called **Pyrrhic dances** <note>original: πυῤῥίχαι (pyrrhichai) — a famous ancient war-dance performed in armor</note> were derived. Every such style of dancing has many names, such as the Cretan "Quails" <note>original: ὄρτυπες (ortypes)</note> and the *epikredioi*. Regarding the dance called the *apokinos* <note>A provocative dance involving hip movements</note>—which is mentioned by Cratinus in *Nemesis*, Cephisodorus in *Amazons*, Aristophanes in *Centaurs*, and many later writers—they later named it the *makrismos*. Many women used to dance it, whom I know were also called *martypiai*. Those dances that are more 
<margin>The Naming of Names.</margin> slanted and more varied, yet have a simpler style of movement, are called: *daktyloi* ("fingers"), *iambikoi*, the *molossikē emmeleia*, the *kordax* <note>A lewd dance associated with Old Comedy</note>, the *sikinnis*, the *Persian*, the *Phrygian*, the Thracian *nikatismos*, the *malabrismos*, and the *telesias*. 

This last one is a Macedonian dance, which the associates of Ptolemy used when they assassinated Philip, the brother of Alexander the son of Philip, as Marsyas records in the third book of his *Macedonian History*. There are also frenzied dances: the "Deer-bearer" <note>original: ἐλαφοφόρος (elaphophoros)</note>, the *mongchas*, and the *thermaustris*. Among private citizens, there was also the so-called *anthema* ("flower-dance"). They would dance this while reciting these words, mimicking the speakers: "Where are my roses? Where are my violets? Where is my beautiful parsley?" Among the Syracusans, there is a specific dance and flute-tune dedicated to Artemis Chitoneia. There was also an Ionian drinking-dance. Some called the *angelikē* dance a drinking-dance. There is another dance called the "Conflagration of the World," which Menippus the Cynic mentions in his *Symposium*. There are also humorous dances: the "Mortar" <note>original: ἴγδις (igdis)</note>, the *makrismos*, the *apokinos*, and the *sobas*. Furthermore, there are the *morphasmos*, the "Owl" <note>original: γλαύξ (glaux)</note>, the "Lion," the "Pouring of Meal," the "Cancellation of Debts," the *stoicheia*, and the Pyrrhic. They also danced to flutes the *keleustē* and the so-called *pinakida* ("little tablet"). The figures of dance include the "Swordplay" <note>original: ξιφισμός (xiphismos)</note>, the *malabismos*, the *kallabides*, the *skōps*, and the *skōpeuma*. The *skōps* was a figure used by those looking out at something, with the tip of the hand curved over 
<margin>20</margin> the forehead. Aeschylus mentions this in *The Spectators*: "And indeed, here are those old squinting-figures for you." Eupolis mentions the *kallabidia* in *The Flatterers*: "and he walks in the style of the *kallabidia*." There are also stylized hand gestures: the *thaumastris*, the *katiedes*, the "Watcher," the "Downturned Hand," the *mudiposismos*, the "Grabbing of the Wood," the "Elbow-gesture," the *kalabismos*, and the "Whirlwind" <note>original: στρόβιλος (strobilos)</note>. 

There is also a dance called the *telesias*; this is a military dance named after a man named Telesis, who was the first to dance it skillfully with weapons, as Hippagoras says in the first book of his *On the Constitution of the Carthaginians*. The satyric dance, as Aristocles says in the eighth book of his *On Choruses*, is called the *sikinnis*, and the Satyrs are called *sikinnistai*. Some say that a certain barbarian named Sikinnos was its inventor, while others say Sikinnos was Cretan by birth. The Cretans are indeed dancers, as Aristoxenus says. Scamon, in the first book of *On Inventions*, says it was called *sikinnis* because of the "shaking" <note>original: σείσθαι (seiesthai) — Scamon suggests a pun on the Greek word for shaking or shivering</note>, and that Thersippus was the first to dance the *sikinnis*. The movement of the feet was invented 
<margin>30</margin> before that of the hands. For the ancients exercised more with their feet in both athletic contests and in hunting. The Cretans are hunters, and therefore "swift-footed." There are some who say that the *sikinnis* was poetically named after the movement which the Satyrs dance, which is very rapid. For this dance has no "pathos" <note>Meaning it lacks heavy emotional or tragic suffering</note>, which is why it is never slowed down. In ancient times, the entirety of satyric poetry consisted of choruses, just as the tragedy of that time did; for this reason, they did not even have actors. 

There are three dances of theatrical poetry: Tragic, Comic, and Satyric. Similarly, there are three types of lyric poetry: the Pyrrhic, the *Gymnopaidikē*, and the *Hyporchēmatikē*. 
<margin>Pyrrhic.</margin> The Pyrrhic is similar to the Satyric, for both are characterized by speed. The Pyrrhic is considered a war-dance, for boys dance it in armor, and speed is necessary in war for pursuit and for fleeing when defeated—so as not to remain or be perceived as a coward. The *Gymnopaidikē* <note>A Spartan dance performed by naked youths</note> is similar to the Tragic dance, which is called the *emmeleia* <note>meaning "harmonious"</note>; in both, one sees a certain 
<margin>40</margin> weight and solemnity. The *Hyporchēmatikē* is related to the Comic dance, which is called the *kordax*; both are playful. Aristoxenus says that the Pyrrhic took its name from Pyrrhichos, who was Laconian <note>Spartan</note> by birth, and that "Pyrrhichos" remains a Laconian name to this day. The dance displays a military character, as it was an invention of the Lacedaemonians. The Spartans are a warlike people, whose sons even learn the "marching songs" <note>original: ἐμβατήρια μέλη (embatēria melē)</note> which are used before fighting in armor. The Spartans themselves, during wars, maintain a rhythmic movement by reciting the poems of Tyrtaeus. Philochorus says that after the Lacedaemonians 
<margin>On the Epic of Tyrtaeus. 50</margin> defeated the Messenians through the generalship of Tyrtaeus, they made it a custom on their campaigns that, after finishing dinner, they would sing Tyrtaeus's songs one by one. The commanding officer <note>term: πολέμαρχον (polemarchon)</note> would judge them and give a prize of meat to the winner. 

The Pyrrhic dance is no longer maintained among the other Greeks, but has died out as wars have ceased. Only among the Lacedaemonians does it remain as a preliminary exercise for war. Everyone in Sparta learns to dance the Pyrrhic from the age of five. Our modern Pyrrhic, however, seems to be a kind of Dionysian dance, being gentler than the ancient version. For the dancers hold *thyrsoi* <note>Wands wrapped in ivy</note> instead of spears, and they hurl reeds at one another and carry torches; they dance the stories of Dionysus and the Indians, as well as the stories of Pentheus. One must rank among the most beautiful things in the Pyrrhic...

# BOOK XIV

...lyric melodies and the upright rhythms. The **Gymnopaedic dance** <note>original: γυμνοπαιδικὴ (gymnopaidikē) — a Spartan festival dance performed by naked youths</note> seems similar to what the ancients called the *anapalē* <note>a dance mimicking wrestling movements</note>. For the boys dance naked, performing rhythmic movements and extending their arms in certain graceful patterns, so as to display a sort of spectacle of the wrestling school and the *pankration* <note>a brutal ancient combat sport</note>, moving their feet in time to the music. There are also the *phorikoi* and the *Bacchic* styles, such that this dance is also associated with **Dionysus**. Aristoxenus <note>A famous music theorist and pupil of Aristotle</note> says that the ancients, after practicing first in the Gymnopaedic dance, would proceed to the **Pyrrhic war-dance** before entering the theater. The Pyrrhic dance is also called *cheironomia* <note>original: χειρονομία — literally "hand-laws," referring to a system of expressive gestures</note>. Then there is the **Hyporchematic** style, in which the chorus dances while singing. Bacchylides, for instance, says: "This is no work for sitting, nor for delay." Pindar also says: "A Laconian herd of maidens." Among the works of Pindar, it is the Laconians <note>Spartans</note> who perform this dance. The Hyporchematic dance is performed by both men and women. The best styles are those used in these dances. They include the *Prosodiac* <note>processional</note> and the *Apostolic*. These are also called "Maiden-songs" (*Parthenia*), and similar to these are songs to Aphrodite or the Paean <note>A song of praise, usually to Apollo</note>, sometimes included and sometimes not.

There are also among the barbarians, just as among the Greeks, both noble and vulgar dances. For instance, the *kossabax* among the Greeks is vulgar, while the *emmeleia* <note>the dance of tragedy</note> is noble. Similarly, among the Arcadians there is the *kidaris*, and among the Sicyonians the *aletēr*. This *aletēr* is also found in Ithaca, as Aristoxenus records in the first book of his *Sympotic Miscellanies*. 

<margin>Praise of Ancient Music</margin>

So much, then, for my current discussion of dancing. In ancient times, **beauty** was strictly maintained in music, and everything followed the proper artistic decorum of its kind. Because of this, there were specific flutes for each "harmony" <note>original: ἁρμονία (harmonia) — meaning a musical mode or scale</note>, and every flute-player possessed flutes suited to each specific harmony for use in competitions. **Pronomos of Thebes** was the first to adapt all the harmonies to a single set of flutes. But nowadays, people take up music randomly and without reason. In the past, being popular with the crowds was considered a sign of poor artistry; hence Asopodorus of Phlius, when a certain flute-player was being loudly applauded, said while he himself was still waiting behind the scenes: "What's this? Clearly some great evil has happened," implying the player could not have won such popular favor otherwise. I know that some historians record a similar saying by Antigenidas. But the artists of our own day make the "theatricality" of their art their only goal. Because of this, Aristoxenus says in his *Mixed Sympotics*: "We behave like the **Posidonians** who live on the Tyrrhenian Gulf. It happened to them that, although they were originally Greeks, they became 'barbarized' by becoming Etruscans or Romans, changing their language and the rest of their customs. Yet they still observe one single Greek festival even now, where they gather to remember those ancient names and laws; having lamented and wept together, they depart. So it is with us," he says; "since the theaters have become completely 'barbarized' and this popular music has fallen into great corruption, a few of us meet in private and remember what music used to be like." These are the words of Aristoxenus.

And it seems to me that we should philosophize about music through these examples. For **Pythagoras of Samos**, who holds such a great reputation for philosophy, is clearly shown through many accounts to have taken up music with great seriousness; indeed, he even declared that the very essence of the universe is composed through music. In general, it seems that the ancient wisdom of the Greeks was especially devoted to music. For this reason, they judged **Apollo** the most musical and wise of the gods, and **Orpheus** the most musical among the demigods. They used to call all those who practiced this art "Sophists" <note>original: σοφιστής — here meaning 'master of wisdom' rather than the later negative connotation</note>, just as Aeschylus did when he wrote: "The Sophist <note>referring to Orpheus</note> plucking the strings of his lyre." 

It is clear from **Homer** that the ancients were most intimately disposed toward music. 

<margin>Homer the Poet</margin>

Because he composed all his poetry for song, he did not worry about making many "headless" lines, or "loose" lines, or even "mouse-tailed" lines. But Xenophanes, Solon, Theognis, and Phocylides—and also Periander of Corinth, the writer of elegies, and others who do not set their poems to melody—work out their lines meticulously according to the numbers and the arrangement of the meters. They take care so that none of their verses are "headless," "loose," or "mouse-tailed." **Headless** lines <note>original: ἀκέφαλοι (akephaloi)</note> are those that are crippled at the beginning, such as: *"When they reached the ships and the Hellespont"* <note>original: ἐπειδὴ νῆας τε καὶ ἑλλήσποντον ἵκοντο — a hexameter missing its first syllable</note> and *"He stretched out the cord of a slaughtered ox."* **Loose** lines <note>original: λαγαροὶ (lagaroi)</note> are those weak in the middle, such as: *"And immediately then Aeneas, the son of dear Anchises"* and *"Of them again let Asclepius' two sons lead."* **Mouse-tailed** lines <note>original: μείουροι (meiouroi)</note> are those that fall short at the end, such as: *"The Trojans shuddered when they saw the dappled snake"* and *"Beautiful Cassiepeia, in form like unto the goddesses."* Or: *"Having filled a great skin of it, and also provisions."* 

<margin>Ancient Music</margin>

The **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans</note> preserved music most of all the Greeks, using it extensively, and many composers of lyric songs arose among them. Even now they carefully preserve their ancient songs, being very learned and precise in them. Hence **Pratinas** says: "The Laconian cicada is well-suited for the dance." For this reason, the poets also continued to address songs in this way, calling the Muse the "ruler of sweetest things" and the "honey-voiced song." For in their lives, they always transitioned gladly from temperance and austerity to music, which has an inviting and educational quality. Naturally, then, it brought joy to those who heard it. They used to call the *choregos* <note>leader/sponsor of the dance</note>—as Demetrius of Byzantium says in the fourth book of his work *On Poetry*—not as we do now for those who hire the choruses, but for those who actually led the chorus, just as...

# BOOK XIV

...the name itself signifies "excellence in music" <note>original: χρηστομουσεῖν (chrēstomousein)</note> and a refusal to transgress the ancient laws of the musical art. In ancient times, it was the habit of the Greeks to be lovers of music. However, in later times, a state of disorder <note>original: ἀταξία (ataxia)</note> arose, and as nearly all the ancient customs grew old and decayed, this noble purpose was destroyed. Low-quality styles of music were introduced, through which those who practiced them—instead of gentleness—acquired a sense of effeminacy, and instead of self-restraint, they embraced licentiousness and slackness. Perhaps this decline will be seen even more clearly and progress further unless someone brings our ancestral music back into the light once more. For in the old days, men would compose songs about the deeds of heroes and hymns to the gods. Homer, for instance, says of Achilles: "And he sang of the glorious deeds of heroic men." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 9.189</note> He also says of Phemius that he knew "many things to enchant mortals, the deeds of men and gods, which singers celebrate." <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 1.337-338</note> This custom was also preserved among the barbarians, as 

<margin>10.</margin> Dinon says in his *Persian History*. At least, the singers foresaw the rise of Cyrus and the coming war against Astyages. For he says that when Cyrus began his journey to the Persians—having previously served among the staff-bearers and later among the shield-bearers—he departed after having been annoyed while with his friends at Astyages' court. There was a man named Angares <note>The OCR reads 'Agmares', but this refers to the singer Angares mentioned in other fragments of Dinon</note>. It was the custom that the most skilled of the singers would sing of various traditional matters, and at the end, he said that "a great beast has been released into the marsh, bolder than a wild boar; if it becomes master of its own territory, it will soon easily fight against many." When Astyages asked what sort of beast this was, he replied, "Cyrus the Persian." Thinking then that he had correctly suspected him, Astyages sent for him, but it did no good.
