Euphorion, in his work *On Artistic Uses*, discusses it, saying that the Parthians and the Troglodytes <note>an ancient name for various "cave-dwelling" tribes, here likely near the Red Sea</note> use it with four strings. Its form and construction are described by Biton in his letter to Attalus *On Engines*. Andreas of Panormus, in the thirty-third book of his *History of Sicily*, says it is brought against the enemy's walls from two ships lashed together; it is called a "sambyke" because when it is raised up, the shape of the ship and the ladder 

<margin>30.</margin> combined together resembles the musical instrument. Moschus, in the first book of his *Mechanics*, says the machine is Roman and that Heraclides of Tarentum invented its design. Polybius, in the eighth book of his *Histories*, says that Marcellus, when frustrated during the siege of Syracuse by the inventions of **Archimedes**, used to say that Archimedes was using his ships to "ladle" water out of the sea, while his *sambykes* had been "beaten" out of the contest in disgrace. # BOOK XIV

...the *sambyke* <note>original: Σαμβύκη; a triangular stringed instrument</note> was so named. This instrument is said to be common in Mitylene, where one of the Muses is depicted holding it in a statue made by Lesbothemis, an ancient sculptor. Menaechmus, in his treatise *On Artists*, says that the *pektis* <note>original: πηκτίς; a type of lute or harp</note> and the *magadis* are the same instrument, and that Sappho was the one who discovered it. However, Aristoxenus states that the *magadis* and the *pektis* are played by plucking the strings with the fingers <term>psalmos</term> <note>playing with the fingers rather than using a plectrum</note> without a plectrum. For this reason, Pindar also mentioned it in his drinking song <note>original: σκόλιον (skolion)</note> addressed to Hieron, calling the *magadis* a "responsive plucking" <note>original: ψαλμὸν ἀντίφθογγον (psalmon antiphthongon)</note>, because it allows for a harmony <term>synodia</term> of two strings played at the interval of an octave <term>dia pason</term>, mimicking the combined voices of men and boys. And Phrynichus, in his play *The Phoenician Women*, says:

->Singing songs pulled responsively with pluckings.<-

And Sophocles in his *Mysians* says: "And many a Phrygian triangle and responsive strains sang in harmony with the *pektis*." Some scholars are puzzled as to how the term "to magadize" <note>to play in octaves</note> could be used by Anacreon, since he mentions that many-stringed instruments appeared quite late. Anacreon says: "I pluck the *magadis* of twenty strings, O Leucaspis." Poseidonius explains this by saying that Anacreon refers to three different modes <note>original: γελωδιῶν (gelōdiōn), likely meaning melodic styles or modes</note>: the Phrygian, the Dorian, and the Lydian. Since Anacreon used only these, and each was performed on seven strings, it makes sense that he would say he plucks twenty strings, using a round number after subtracting one. But Poseidonius is unaware that the *magadis* is an ancient instrument, as Pindar clearly states that Terpander discovered the *barbitos* <note>a deep-toned lyre</note> as a responsive instrument to the *pektis* used by the Lydians. For it was Terpander of Lesbos who first discovered at banquets the Lydian plucking style:

In his work on Sappho, Menaechmus says that she, being older than Anacreon, was the first to use the *pektis*. That Terpander is also older than Anacreon

He says that there is a prose list of the metrical winners of the Carneia; the establishment of the Carneia took place during the twenty-sixth Olympiad <note>c. 676–673 BCE</note>, as Sosimus says in his work *On Chronology*. Hieronymus, in his work *On Cithara Players* (which is the fifth book of his series *On Poets*), says that Terpander was a contemporary of Lycurgus the Lawgiver.

> And so we hear the mountain-mothering Cybele’s Asiatic 
> women, daughters of the wealthy Phrygians, with drums and rumblings and the clanging of bronze, making a din with cymbals in their hands, the wise gods' hymn-singer and healer too; and I release the Lydian and Bactrian maidens, who dwell by the salt-river Halys, to worship the goddess Artemis in the laurel-shaded grove, with pluckings of triangular harps and Persian *pektides*, striking the *magadis* with responsive pulls of the strings, while the flute sounds in harmony with the golden-haired choruses in the Phrygian mode.

Phyllis of Delos, in his second book *On Music*, also says that the *pektis* differs from the *magadis*, listing them as: "Phoenician pipes, *pektides*, *magadides*, *sambykai*, *iamboi*, triangular harps, *klepsiamboi*, *skindapsoi*, and nine-stringed instruments." He notes that the instruments they used to sing iambic verses were called *eklepsybes*, and those used for spoken parts in meter were called *klepsiamboi*. He defines *magadides* as instruments played in octaves, through which the parts of the singers were harmonized. There are others besides these: the *barbitos*, the *barmos*, and many more. Some were stringed, while others were "soulless" <note>inanimate/percussive</note> constructions. Apart from wind instruments and stringed ones, there were others made only for noise, like the *krembala* <note>castanets or clappers</note>. Regarding these, Dicaearchus says in his *On the Life of Greece* that they were common in the countryside, claiming that women once used certain instruments to excess for dancing and singing, which, when struck with the fingers, made a shrill sound. This is shown in the song to Artemis, which begins: "Artemis, what has made my mind desire sleep," and continues "but someone [strikes] the gold-shining, bronze-cheeked *krembala* in their hands."

<margin>To play the clappers.</margin>
Hermippus in his *The Gods* uses the word "to play the clappers" <note>original: κρεμβαλίζειν (krembalizein)</note> when he says: "They play the clappers by striking limpets or pig-shells together." Didymus says that some people, instead of a lyre, strike together shells and pottery shards to produce a rhythmic sound for dancers, just as Aristophanes says in his *Babylonians*. Artemon, in the first book of his *On the Dionysiac Ensign*, says that Timotheus of Miletus was thought by many to have used the *magadis* with a system of too many strings. For this, he was censured by the Spartans for corrupting ancient music; and when someone was about to cut away his surplus strings, he showed them a small statue of Apollo that they possessed, which held a lyre with the same number of strings, and thus he was acquitted. Doris, in his *On Tragedy*, says the *magadis* was named after Magydis, a Thracian. Apollodorus, in his reply to the letter of Aristocles, says that what we now call a *psalterion* <note>a harp-like stringed instrument</note> is what was once called the *magadis* or *klepsiambos*. He notes that the triangular harp, the *elymos* flute, and the nine-stringed instrument have fallen into obscurity. Alcman also says: "to lay aside the *magadis*." # ATHENAEUS: THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

<margin>The Phoenix.</margin>
<margin>The Sambyx.</margin>
[Anaxandrides] says that it is a five-stringed instrument in these lines: "another, bringing in another strain, sends forth the horn-voiced *magadis* <note>original: μάγαδις; usually a twenty-stringed instrument, though here described as having five</note>, and in the five-rod number of strings he turns his hand with the speed of a double-course racer." I also know of another instrument which the kings of the Thracians use at their banquets, as Nicomedes says in his work *On Orpheus*. Ephorus and Scamon, in their books *On Inventions*, say that the instrument called the *phoenix* <note>original: φοῖνιξ; literally "palm tree" or "Phoenician"</note> was discovered by the Phoenicians and thus received its name. But Semus the Delian, in the first book of the *Deliad*, says it was named because its "elbows" <note>the curved arms of the lyre</note> were made from the palm tree found in Delos. Scamon, whom I mentioned before, says that the *sambyke* <note>original: σαμβύκη; a triangular harp</note> was first used by the Sibyl, and was named after a certain man called Sambyx who invented it. Regarding the construction of the "Tripod"—which is also a musical instrument—the aforementioned Artemon writes as follows: "There are many instruments whose origins are known, such as the Tripod of Pythagoras of Zakynthos. Because it enjoyed its peak of popularity for only a short time, and because it seemed difficult to master the hand-positioning, or for whatever reason it was quickly abandoned, it has escaped the notice of most people. It was very similar to a Delphic tripod, and it took its name from there, but it functioned as a triple cithara. Its feet stood upon a rotating base, constructed like those swivel-stools we use. He divided the empty spaces between the legs, stretching strings across them and placing a 'bridge' <term>pechus</term> <note>literally "forearm," the crossbar of a lyre</note> over each section. Below he fitted tuning pegs, and above he added a common decoration resembling a cauldron, with resonating chambers hanging from it. This gave it an elegant appearance and produced a fuller sound. He assigned to each of the three spaces one of the three harmonies <note>original: ἁρμονίαις (harmoniais); melodic modes</note>: the Dorian, the Lydian, and the Phrygian. He would sit on a stool that had a base matching the instrument's base; extending his left hand to touch the strings and using a plectrum with the other, he would use his foot to rotate the base to whichever of the modes he chose first, as it turned easily to the next. Thus, the different scales came under his hand so rapidly, thanks to the ease with which the base moved when touched by his foot, and the skill of his hand-positioning was so persuasive, that if someone heard it without seeing what was happening, they would think they were hearing three different cithara players tuned to different modes. But this instrument, though greatly admired, disappeared immediately after his death."

<margin>Inventors of various musical forms.</margin>
<margin>Poets of wicked songs.</margin>
Menaechmus says that Aristonicus of Argos, who lived at the same time as Antiochus, was the first to introduce solo cithara playing <term>psile kitharisis</term> <note>playing the cithara as a solo instrument without singing</note>, and that he came to Corcyra. But Philochorus, in the third book of the *Atthis*, says that Lysander of Sicyon, the cithara player, was the first to transform solo cithara playing; he introduced long sustained tones and rich robes, and gave a grander weight to the sound. Among those who played the cithara with their fingers <note>without a plectrum</note> was the school of Epigonus, who first diversified the intense style used by solo players; he was the first to play chromatic "colors" <note>original: χρώματα (chromata); a specific melodic genus involving smaller intervals</note>, as well as iambics and the *magadis* known as the "hissing" <note>original: συριγμόν (syringmon); likely a high-pitched or whistling tone</note>. He was the only one of his predecessors to change the instrument's nature, and by expanding its scope, he was the first to organize a chorus around it. Menaechmus also says that Dion of Chios was the first to play the libation-song of Dionysus on the cithara. Timomachus, in his *Cyprian History*, says that Stesander of Samos further expanded the art; he was the first at Delphi to sing the battles of Homer to the cithara, beginning with the *Odyssey*. Others say that Amator of Eleutherna was the first among the people of Eleutherna to play erotic songs on the cithara, and that his descendants were called "motherless" <note>a pun on Amator's name and *amētores* (motherless)</note>. Aristoxenus says that just as some people invented parodies of hexameter verse to create a laugh, Oenopas was the first to do this with cithara-singing, and he was imitated by Polyductus the Achaean and Diocles of Cyme. There have also been poets of wicked songs, about whom Phanias of Eresus speaks, saying that no one who writes such things is of sound mind. These include Telenicus of Byzantium and Argas; they were poets of wicked musical modes, and although they had a natural knack for their own style of poetry, they could not even slightly touch the dignity of the modes of Terpander or Phrynidus. Alexis mentions Argas in his play *The Dismounter* thus: "The poet Choronikos—or rather the poet of very solemn songs—is a better runner than Argas in a day's race." And Anaxandrides in his *Heracles* says: "For one man seems to be naturally gifted, having taken up the rehearsal-room with rhythm; then he teaches in the same way, 'Wow!' <note>original: πυπαῖ (pupai); an exclamation of surprise or derision</note>. Having become a man of the middle sort, how I wish to send you, Argas, to fight at the Kalanian games, so that you might defeat the sober ones, my friend!" And the author of the *Various Beggar-Women*, which is attributed to Chionides, mentions a certain Gnesippus, a writer of merry trifles, saying: "By Zeus, these are not Gnesippus' songs, nor the ones Cleomenes used to sweeten in a corner." The poet of the *Iliads* says that one should sing Stesichorus, Alcman, and ancient Simonides. But as for Gnesippus, one hears that he invented nocturnal songs for adulterers to call out women, accompanied by the *iambyke* <note>original: ἰαμβύκη; a small triangular lyre</note> and the *trigonon* <note>a triangular harp</note>. Cratinus, in *The Softlings*, says: "Who then asks me? He knows, O Gnesippus! I think many things out of bitterness, but nothing is as foul and empty as he." He also mocks him for his poems in *The Cowherds*: "He who did not give a chorus to Sophocles when he asked, but gave one to Cleomachus, whom I would not have thought worthy, though I would have been his teacher at the festival of Adonis." May the tragedy of the seasons go away, with Cleomachus as the Teacher, followed by his little twittering birds, having a chorus plucking out Lydian melodies... wicked things. Teleclides, in *The Hard Men*, says that he [Gnesippus] was involved in an act of adultery. And Clearchus, in his second book...

# BOOK XIV

In the second book of his *Erotic Matters*, he says that erotic songs and those called "Locrian" <note>original: Λοκρικά; a style of popular song from Locri in Italy, often of a romantic or suggestive nature</note> are in no way different from the works of Sappho and Anacreon. He also states that the works of Archilochus and many of the "thrush-songs" <note>original: ἐπικιχλίδια; light, popular verses, literally "songs over the thrushes" served at a meal</note> of Homer possess a certain emotional quality through their poetic symmetry. Furthermore, he mentions the erotic works of Asopodorus, and says that the sweetness of his erotic letters is like the poetry of an erotic dialogue.

<margin>Festivals in which the masters serve their slaves.</margin>
After Masurius had gone through all these matters, the "second tables" <note>original: δεύτεραι τράπεζαι; the ancient equivalent of the dessert course, brought in after the main meal</note>—which are frequently served to us—were brought in. This occurs not only on the days of the *Saturnalia* <note>original: Κρονίων; the festival of Cronus, known in Rome as Saturnalia</note>, when it is the Roman custom to feast their domestic servants while the masters themselves take on the duties of the slaves, but also among the Greeks. In Crete, for instance, a similar thing happens at the festival of Hermes <note>original: Ἑρμαίων</note>, as Carystius says in his *Historical Notes*. For while the servants feast, the masters perform the household chores. In Troezen, too, in the month of Geraestion, a festival is held lasting many days, on one of which the slaves play at dice together with the citizens, and the masters provide the feast for the slaves, as Carystius himself reports. Berosus, in the first book of his *Babylonian History*, says that on the sixteenth day of the month of Lous, a festival called the "Sakeas" is held in Babylon for five days. During this time, it is the custom for the masters to be commanded by their servants, and one of the servants, dressed in a robe like the king's, leads the household; he is called the *Zoganes*. Ctesias also mentions this festival in the second book of his *Persian History*. The opposite situation regarding food is recorded by Macarius in the third book of his *Cous*. For when they sacrifice to Hera, slaves do not attend the feast; for which reason Phylarchus says: "The Syrians alone are free priests; for all those men, let it be a day of freedom, but no slave at all may enter the temple."

<margin>Saturnalia. Peloria.</margin>
Baton of Sinope, the orator, in his work *On Thessaly and Haemonia*, clearly shows that the festival of the *Saturnalia* is thoroughly Greek, stating that among the Thessalians it is called the *Peloria*. He writes as follows: "When a public sacrifice was being held by the Pelasgians, a man named Pelorus reported to Pelasgus that in the land of Haemonia, great earthquakes had occurred, and the mountains called Tempe had split apart. Through this opening, the water of the lake rushed out into the stream of the Peneus River, and all the land that was formerly underwater was now exposed; as the waters dried up, plains appeared that were marvelous in size and beauty. Hearing this, Pelasgus had a table set for Pelorus, decorated with an abundance of food. The others, showing their friendliness, each brought the best of what they had and placed it on the table for the messenger. Pelasgus himself served him eagerly, and the other men of rank waited on him as the occasion required. Therefore, they say that after they occupied the land, they maintained an imitation of that feast. Sacrificing to Zeus Pelorus, they set out tables brilliantly decorated, conducting the festival so charitably that they even welcome all strangers to the feast, release prisoners, and have the servants recline and feast with total freedom of speech while their masters serve them. Generally, even now, the Thessalians hold this as their greatest festival, calling it the *Peloria*."

<margin>Second tables.</margin>
Since such delicacies were often served to us, as I said, one of those present remarked, "Second thoughts are somehow wiser." <note>A play on the Greek proverb that "second thoughts are better," applied here to the "second tables."</note> For Euripides says in his *Cretan Women*: "What does the table lack? With what is it not weighed down? It is full of the treasures of the sea; there are tender pieces of veal and green delicacies, and after the pounded grain, the golden-winged products of the honey-bee <note>honey or honey-cakes</note> are poured out in abundance." And as Eubulus said in *Olbia*: "In the same place everything will be sold together in Athens: heralds, grapes, turnips, pears, apples, witnesses, roses, medlars, haggis, honeycombs, chickpeas, lawsuits, and even beestings <note>the first milk after a cow gives birth</note>, ballot boxes, water-clocks, laws, and indictments." When Pontianus was about to speak about each of the dishes set before us, Ulpian said, "We will not hear about these until he has spoken about the dessert <note>original: ἐπιδορπισμάτων; after-dinner treats</note>."

<margin>Sweetmeats.</margin>
And Pontianus replied: "Crates says that Philippides, in the *Miser*, calls sweetmeats <note>original: τραγήματα; dried fruits, nuts, and sweets</note> 'desserts' in these words: 'Cakes, desserts, eggs, sesame seeds—if I listed them all, the day would fail me.' And Diphilus says in *Telesias*: 'Sweetmeats, myrtle-berries, honey-cake, almonds; these are the desserts I find most pleasant.' Sophilus in *The Deposit* says: 'It is sweet for people to gather together for pleasure; someone did not offer two cups of wine just to go carousing, but rather to recline and eat the dessert of Tanagran cakes.' Plato, in the *Critias* <note>referred to here as 'The Atlantic'</note>, calls them 'after-dinner treats' in this passage: 'The earth produced all kinds of fragrant things for the inhabitants... and it bore the fruit of the cultivated tree, and a multitude of nuts, and all those after-dinner treats that serve as a consolation for pleasure.' Tryphon says that in ancient times, before the guests entered, each person's portion was placed on the tables. Later, many various things were brought in afterwards, which is why they were called 'added-courses' <note>original: ἐπιφορήματα</note>. Philyllius in the *Miser*, speaking of the second tables, mentions 'almonds and nuts as added-courses.' Archippus also uses the term in *Heracles*, as does Herodotus in his first book."

<margin>To take dessert.</margin>
They also used the verb "to take dessert" <note>original: ἐπιδορπίσασθαι</note> for the act of eating after the main meal, as Archippus does in *Heracles*.

# BOOK XIV

...fine dessert courses <note>original: ἐπιφορήματα (epiphorēmata); literally "things brought on" after the main meal</note> for the wedding of Heracles, including cakes and other treats. And Herodotus, in his first book, says that the Persians "use little solid food, but many dessert courses." However, regarding the proverb "an Abydene dessert," it refers to a conclusion that is troublesome or burdensome, as Aristides says in the third book of his *On Proverbs*. Dionysius, the son of Tryphon, says that in ancient times, before the guests entered, each person's portion was placed on the tables, but later many varied things were "brought on" (*epipheresthai*), which is why they were called *epiphorēmata*. Philyllius, in *The Well-Digger*, describes the things brought on after dining in this way:

> Almonds and walnuts are the desserts.

Plato <note>Plato the Comic poet, not the philosopher</note>, in *Menelaus*, calls them "on-the-table-items" <note>original: ἐπιτραπεζώματα (epitrapeizōmata)</note>, meaning the foods placed upon the tables, saying:

> Tell me how few of the "on-the-table-items" are left. For that enemy of the gods has devoured them all.

Aristotle, in his work *On Drunkenness*, says that "sweetmeats" <note>original: τραγήματα (tragēmata); usually dried fruits, nuts, or confectionery</note> were what the ancients spoke of; for "nibbles" <note>original: τραγάλια (tragalia)</note> were part of the after-supper course. Pindar is the one who said, "They speak of a sweet nibble after dinner, and an abundant meal for a child." Indeed, looking at what is set before us, one might say with Euripides, "You see how sweet a life is one of good cheer at the table."

<margin>On the first dinner</margin>
That even among the ancients the "second tables" were luxuriously decorated is shown by Pindar in the *Olympian Odes*, where he recounts the story of Pelops' "joint-fitting" <note>A reference to the myth where Tantalus served his son Pelops to the gods; the "second course" here is a grim pun on the meat of the boy's body</note>: "at the second course of meats, they carved you up and ate. But for me, it is impossible to call any of the blessed gods a glutton." The older writers simply called them "tables," as Achaeus does in the satyr play *Hephaestus*:

> Feast first... but for the second course, by whatever means you devise, I will anoint your body entirely with fragrant myrrh; but you show no eagerness to wash your hands with water—yes, everything is being cleared away.

Aristophanes, in *The Wasps*, mentions bringing in the tables after water is poured over the hands. Aristotle, in *On Drunkenness*, addresses our "second tables" in these words: "One must consider the whole matter as a different thing from food, which is why the meal is called 'nibbles.' For this name is traditional to the Greeks. Since these foods are served as sweetmeats, it seems the person who first called it a 'second table' did not speak correctly." For the definition is indeed a kind of "sweetmeat-eating," served as a second course without the heavy food. Dicaearchus, in the first book of *The Descent into the Cave of Trophonius*, says: "With great expense, the 'second table' was introduced into dinners, with its intricate carvings, and crowns, and perfumes, and incense, and all that follows these things." Eggs were also given at the second table, just as hares and thrushes were brought in together with honey-cakes, as Antiphanes says in *Leptiniscus*:

> You might drink Thasian wine if someone pours it; and everyone has spoken in favor of almonds, and very soft ones which are soaked by force in honey, and the honey-cakes which he brings—I would eat those. And I would even swallow an egg.

And others are mentioned through similar means. "And if he introduced a dance or a second table, and set it down full of all kinds of treats." Amphis, in *Woman-Madness*:

> Already I ask for a life of drinking together. Clearly, unmixed sweet wine, eggs, sesame, perfume, a crown, a flute-girl—by the Dioscuri, I have run through the names of the twelve gods!

Anaxandrides in *The Peasants*:

> When the table was crowned, it was brought in, having so many foods that, by the goddesses—and I revere the goddesses—I do not eat them myself, but I will provide them so handsomely they might as well not have lived.

Clearchus in *Pandrosus*:

> "Take water for your hands." "By no means, I am fine." "Take it, good man; it's no trouble, boy. Put the walnuts and sweetmeats on the table."

Eubulus in *The Hunchback*:

> Let your table be full of sweetmeats. "I am not always a lover of nibbling."

Alexis in *Polycleia* (named after the courtesan Polycleia):

> The one who first invented sweetmeats was clever; for he found a way to pass the time at a symposium, so that the jaws are never idle.

And similar things. The same food is also mentioned by Antidotus:

> I am not a lover of dinner, by Asclepius, but I rejoice more in sweetmeats; I am quite fond of nibbling. For I know it is the custom for those seeking a bride to bring gifts to the bride, such as hares and thrushes. I rejoice in these, and in things prepared with rich sauces. O gods, I even delight in the broths!

Apion and Diodorus, as Pamphilus says, say that the sweetmeats after dinner are called "epikleia" <note>original: ἐπίκλεια; literally "famed additions"</note>. Ephippus in *The Ephebes*:

> Then came groats and Egyptian perfume, and a jar of dates was opened. Then he set out various sweetmeats: pyramid-cakes, milk-cakes, eggs, a whole "hecatomb" of treats—we devised all these and chewed them so manfully. For whatever we had, we grazed on like side-fodder.

And also quinces, and during the dinner: berries, chickpeas, beans, groats, cheese, honey, sesame-cakes, snacks, crunching-bits, downy-treats, pyramids, apples, nuts, milk, hemp-seeds, sweets, juices, and "Zeus's brains" <note>A gourmet delicacy, likely a very rich sweet or a specific part of a bird/animal</note>. Alexis in *Philiscus*:

> It is holy to wash the table; then come the crowns of the departure, perfume, wine-lees, frankincense, cooked fish, sweetmeats.

<margin>Philoxenus on the second table</margin>
Still the bath, it smells of honey-cake. Since Philoxenus of Cythera, in his *Dinner*, mentions second tables and names many of the things set before us, come, let us remember these as well. The...

# BOOK XIV

...And beforehand, they brought in again many good things, gleaming and well-anchored, which mortals now call "tables," but the immortals call "the horn of Amalthea" <note>A mythological horn of plenty that provided inexhaustible food and drink</note>. In the midst of these sat a great joy for mortals: a white marrow, sweet, covered in thin, spider-like woven veils <note>original: λεπτοῖς ἀράχνας... πέπλοις (leptois arachnas... peplois); likely referring to a very thin pastry or a spun sugar decoration</note>, as if out of shame, lest one should see it leaving the moisture of its birth, driven by necessity into the dry, well-pleasing, back-flowing springs. This he named a "mill-cake" <note>original: μυλός (mylos)</note>. They laid their soft hands upon the morsel and consumed it, for someone gives even dry crumbs to those who call for them. And whenever they were filled with the parched... wheat-and-chickpea thorns <note>The text here contains some corrupt or highly metaphorical culinary terms involving toasted grains</note>. Of every kind of food, all mixed together... small crumbs. Along with these came the "Colchian-mad" papyrus <note>A poetic or perhaps humorous reference to a specific dish or ingredient</note> for the pious ones, and all around were countless "blister-cakes" <note>original: ὁμοφλυκτὰ (homophlykta)</note>, and honey-cakes fashioned in abundance. There were also "cheese-cakes" <note>original: τυρακίνας (tyrakinas)</note> mixed with milk and honey, starch-cakes, and broad-cakes. Broad and un-pitted pastries, and cakes mixed with safflower, flourishing in the many seasons; also eggs and soft-shelled "sweet-mouthfuls," of which they gave to the children like walnuts from a son. Indeed, everything else that is fitting for a banquet of the wealthy. The drinking was accompanied by cups and thick conversation. There, a clever toy was spoken of for the child, and everyone wondered at it. These things... 

<margin>Antiphanes on Philoxenus.</margin>
...the Cytherian Philoxenus <note>A famous dithyrambic poet known for his elaborate language</note>, whom Antiphanes praises in his play *The Tritagonist*, saying: "Philoxenus is far superior to all other poets. First, he uses his own special words as well as common ones everywhere; then, he blends his melodies with shifts and 'colors' <note>term: χρώμασιν (chromasin); in ancient music, this refers to the chromatic genus or specific melodic embellishments</note>. He was a god among men, truly knowing the art of music. But the poets of today produce melodies that are ivy-struck and fountain-like, flitting about with flowery words and miserable tunes, weaving in melodies that don't belong." <margin>Cakes.</margin>
"flat-cakes" <note>original: πλακοῦντες (plakountes); the generic term for various types of ancient cakes or pastries</note>, as far as I remember, I will share these with you too. I know that Callimachus, in his *Table of Miscellaneous Writings*, recorded the treatises on cake-making by Aegimius, Hegesippus, Metrobius, and also Phaetus. As for the names of cakes that we have transcribed and will share with you—it will not be like the one sent to Socrates by Alcibiades. Xanthippe <note>Socrates' wife, famously depicted as ill-tempered in later tradition</note> trampled upon it, and Socrates said, "Well, now you won't have a share of it either!" Antiphanes mentions an "equal-voted" cake in the first book of *On Dancing*. For my part, I am not so fond of cakes that I would fight over one being insulted like that. The comic poet Plato mentions them in *The Poet*, saying: "I am left alone to enjoy the entrails, but the cake would be like incense." Indeed, I am not unmindful of the village called "Kome," which Demetrius of Skepsis says, in the twelfth book of the *Trojan Array*, is named after the "under-cake" Thebes <note>A complex geographical/linguistic pun</note>, claiming it is six stades away. They use the term *plakous* <note>flat-cake</note> as a formal noun. It is formed from "flat" (*plakos*), just as "cheese-cake" (*tyrous*) comes from "cheese" (*tyros*) and "sesame-cake" (*sesamous*) from "sesame." It is spoken as an ellipsis of "cake-bread." Those who have visited Parium will testify that they used to eat beautiful cakes there. Alexis mentions the cakes from Paros in the play entitled *Archilochus*, saying: "O aged man, inhabiting the happy and blessed Paros, a land that produces two of the most beautiful things: marble for the immortals, and flat-cakes for mortals."

<margin>Cake-makers</margin>
That the Samian cakes are also exceptional is stated by Sopater, the writer of parodies, in *The Suitors of Bacchis*. Menander mentions "poured cakes" <note>original: ἐγχύτων (enchytōn); cakes made by pouring batter into hot oil or a mold</note> in *The False Heracles*: "It is not possible to make *kandylas* <note>term: κανδύλας (kandylas); a rich Lydian dish of meat, fats, and sweets</note>, nor the things you usually season with honey and fine flour. For everything is the opposite; now the cook is making poured cakes, and toasted groats are brought in after the salt-fish, then a small door and a cluster of grapes." And the half-girl herself, standing in line, carves the meat and serves the thrushes. Evangelus, in *The Unveiled Woman*, says: "Four tables for the women in all, and six for the men. The dinner should be perfect and lacking in nothing; let the wedding be conducted splendidly. It is not a casual matter to inquire, and as an eye-witness I tell you: take from the bees everything you wish, you have took the meat, a piglet, a sow, a hare—how that cursed braggart boasts!—leaves <note>original: θρία (thria); stuffed fig leaves, similar to dolmades</note>, cheese, a poured cake, every divine thing, a *kandylos*, eggs, and finally a milk-cake. The height of the table is a cubit of life, so that one must lift the lid to take from it." The "milk-cake" <note>original: ἄμης (amēs)</note> is a type of flat-cake. Antiphanes says "a certain milk-cake made of starch." Menander in *The Substitue*: "They enjoy the milk-cake... if you persuade someone." The Ionians, as Selenus says in his *Glossary*, call it *amē*. They also use the diminutive "little milk-cakes." Teleclides says: "Thrushes with little milk-cakes flew into the gullet automatically." Then there is the "service-cake" (*diakonion*). Pherecrates says: "Because of his greed, he ate a service-cake while holding an *amphiphōn*." The *amphiphōn* is a cake dedicated to Artemis; it has small torches burning in a circle around it. Philemon says in *The Beggar*: "Dear Mistress Artemis, I bring you this fire and the *amphiphōn* cakes." Philochorus also mentions them in the *Hecate*. Philochorus says it is called *amphiphōn* <note>literally "shining on both sides"</note> because it is brought into the temples of Artemis, and also to the crossroads, because on that day the moon is overtaken as it sets by the rising of the sun, and the sky becomes "lit on both sides." # ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

Semus, in the second book of his *History of Delos*, says that on the island of Hecate <note>A small island near Delos sacred to the goddess of the underworld and crossroads</note>, the Delians sacrifice the so-called **basynias**. This is a wheat-cake boiled with suet and honey, along with what are called *kokkora* (which are a dried fig and three walnuts), twisted pastries, and freshly ground cakes. Demosthenes the orator mentions these in his speech *On the Crown* (for Ctesiphon), calling them a **"poured-over" cake** <note>original: ἐπιχύτου (epichytou); a type of pastry made by pouring batter into hot oil</note>. Nicochares mentions them in *Hand-Bellies*: "I have breads, barley-cakes, porridge,
<margin>5</margin> meal. Rolls, spit-cakes, and honey-cakes, 'poured-over' cakes, barley-water, flat-cakes, *dyndalides*, and pancakes." Pamphilus says that the so-called "bread-pancake" is also called a "poured-over" cake. Hipponax mentions the bread-pancake in these lines: "neither devouring francolins and hares, nor seasoning pancakes with sesame-seeds, nor dipping bread-pancakes into honeycombs." **Kreeion.** A flat-cake bread which the relatives of a bride bring from her to the groom.
<margin>10</margin> It is baked over coals, and friends are invited to partake of it; it is served with honey, as Philitas says in *Miscellanies*. **Glykinas.** A flat-cake made with sweet wine and oil among the Cretans, as Seleucus says in *Dialects*. **Empetas.** The same author says this is a wheat bread, hollow and mixed, similar to the so-called "slipper-cakes" <note>original: κρηπῖσιν (krepisin); pastries shaped like a soldier's boot or base</note>, into which are placed small flat-cakes made of wheat. **Enkrides.** A small pastry boiled in oil and then soaked in honey.
<margin>15</margin> Stesichorus mentions them in these lines: "groats and *enkrides* and other pastries and fresh honey." Epicharmus also mentions them, as does Nicophon in *Hand-Bellies*. Aristophanes, in *The Daughters of Danaus*, says in a varied passage that there was even a "seller of *enkrides*." Pherecrates in *The Worthless Coins* says: "Having these, he was snatching the *enkrides* in the streets." **Epikyklion.** A kind of "circular" flat-cake so called among the Syracusans, and Epicharmus mentions it in *Land and Sea*. **Gyros.**
<margin>20</margin> This is a type of flat-cake; Solon says in his *Iambics*: "Some drink and snack on thin wafers, others on their bread, others on lentils mixed with **gyros**-cakes; there is no kind of pastry missing of all those that the black earth bears for men—all are present in abundance." **Kyribanas.** Certain flat-cakes named by Apollodorus (quoting Alcman); likewise Sosibius, in his third book *On Alcman*, says they are shaped like breasts.
<margin>25</margin> The Spartans use them at women's banquets; the attendants in the chorus carry them around when they are about to sing the prepared hymn of praise for the maiden. **Krimnites.** A type of flat-cake made from coarse meal, as Iatrocles records in his treatise *On Flat-Cakes*. **Staititas.** A type of flat-cake made from flour-dough and honey; Epicharmus mentions it in *The Marriage of Hebe*. It is a liquid dough poured onto a frying pan, with honey, sesame, and cheese sprinkled on top,
<margin>30</margin> as Hierocles says. **Charisios.** Aristophanes mentions this "thanksgiving-cake" in *The Banqueters*: "I will send another *charisios* flat-cake to the two of you." Eubulus in *The Anchylion* speaks of it as if it were a type of bread: "as if he had just filled up and bought the *charisios*." **Epidaitron.** A small portion of flat-cakes given after dinner, as Philemon says in his work *On Attic Words*. **Nanos.** A cake-like bread prepared with cheese and oil. **Psathia.** These are "crumbly" cakes. Pherecrates in *The Worthless Coins* says: "You will receive in Hades a worthless coin worth three obols and some crumbly cakes." Apollodorus of Athens and Theodorus, in *Attic Dialects*, say the bread that is wiped away <note>Used as a napkin or for cleaning the hands at the table</note> is called *psathia*, which some also call *aparagos*. **Itrion.** A thin pastry made with sesame and honey. Anacreon mentions it thus: "I ate for breakfast a small piece of a thin **itrion**, and drank a jar of wine." Sophocles in *The Strife* says: "I drink to you and look again toward the **itria**." **Amorai.** These are honey-pastries. Philitas in *Miscellanies* says that honey-pastries made with oil are called *amorai*. **Tagenites.** A flat-cake fried in oil <note>The ancestor of the modern pancake</note>.
<margin>40</margin> Magnes (or the author of the comedies attributed to him) mentions them in the second *Dionysus*: "Have you already seen the warm, hissing pancakes when you pour honey over them?" And Cratinus in *The Laws*: "shaking off the morning dew, a warm pancake." **Elaphos.** A flat-cake shaped like a "stag" <note>original: Ἔλαφος (Elaphos)</note> molded for the festival of Artemis the Stag-Bolter, made of dough and sesame. **Nasos.** A type of flat-cake containing a savory stuffing. **Choria.**
<margin>45</margin> Foods made with honey and milk. **Amorbites.** A type of flat-cake among the Sicilians. But the Cretans call small flat-cakes **paisa**, as Iatrocles says. **Sesamis.** Spherical pastries made of honey, roasted sesame, and oil. Eupolis in *The Flatterers*: "who... dances the *kallabides* or the *baine*, or brings sesame-cakes, or apples, or money." Antiphanes in *Deucalion*: "sesame-cakes or honey-
<margin>50</margin> cakes, or something of that sort." Ephippus also mentions them in *Cydon*. **Mylloi.** Heracleides of Syracuse, in his work *On Customs*, says that in Syracuse, on the main day of the Thesmophoria festival <note>A festival in honor of Demeter and Persephone</note>, cakes are made of sesame and honey in the shape of female pudenda; these are called **mylloi** throughout Sicily and are carried around in honor of the goddesses. **Echinos.** Lynceus of Samos, in his letter to Diagoras, comparing the local specialties of Athens to those in Rhodes, writes: "To the city [Athens], the honey-cake will seem a new rival; for the second course, she introduces the 'dipped **echinos**' <note>literally "sea urchin," referring here to a prickly-looking pastry</note>, about which I will now speak in summary. But when you arrive, and we put things together according to the Rhodian customs..."

### BOOK 14

...chewing it over again, I will try to learn more of the account. **Small-Cups.** <note>original: Kotyliskoi; small cakes shaped like cups or made according to a specific measure</note> Heracleon of Ephesus says that certain cakes are called by this name, being those made according to a portion of a *choenix* <note>a Greek dry measure, roughly one liter</note>. **Little-Pigs.** <note>original: choirinai; likely shell-shaped or pig-shaped pastries</note> Iatrocles mentions these in his work *On Cakes*, saying that some of them differ from the so-called "pyramid cake." He says the pyramid is made of toasted wheat soaked in honey. These are offered as prizes during the all-night festivals to whoever manages to stay awake. **Chrysippus of Tyana**, in the work titled *On Bread-Making*, lists these types of cakes: the *anagrapha*, the Tarantine, the Krasian, the Sicilian, the *klestron*, *hedybia*, *marypedion*, *plikion*, *gethekou*, and the Montian; of which he says some are barley-cakes made with wine and half a portion of cheese.
There is also the *hedonikation*, the *kloustron* <note>likely related to the Latin *crustum*</note>, the Koirian, the *kresson* of Tyazos, and the Tabonian *krouston*. **Mousakia** are made with honey-wine, and there are sesame *mousakia*, the *orion krouston*, the *gastrilakion*, and the Paulian cake. Regarding cheese-cakes, he says the following are made from cheese: the *enchytos*, the *skibaitikos*, and the *bityllos*. This *bityllos* is made from groats. The *astera* and the *atos* are made from cheese, as are the *lakolloi*, the "silver-shredded" cake, the *libos*, the *kirkos*, and the *aleaphas kresos* flat-cake. He also says there is a cake called the **rice-cake**. The **phthois** <note>a thin, pressed cheese cake</note> is made this way: he grates the cheese after pressing it, puts it through a bronze sieve, then adds honey and half a *hemina* <note>a Greek and Roman unit of volume, about half a pint</note> of fine flour, and kneads it into a single mass.
The **kattillos** or "ornatus," as it is called among the Romans, is made this way: wash and cut lettuce, and putting wine into a mortar, rub the lettuce; then, after pressing out the juice, mix it with fine flour. After letting it sit for a little while, rub it again after adding a little pork fat and pepper. Having rubbed it again, stretch it into a thin sheet, smooth it out, and cut it into pieces; then boil it in very hot oil, placing the cut pieces into a cooking-pot. Other kinds of cakes include the *ostrakitis*, the *apaikis*, the *amylon* <note>literally "unmilled," referring to starch or fine flour cakes</note>. For the **cheese-sieve** cake: press the cheese well, place it in a vessel, then putting a bronze sieve over it, force the cheese through. When you are about to serve it, pour a sufficient amount of honey over it. **Hypotyris** <note>literally "under-cheese"</note> is made this way: put honey into milk, press it, and put it into a basket and let it thicken. If you have small sieves, put the vessel into them and let the whey flow out. When it seems to have thickened, take the basket and turn it onto a silver plate, and the appearance will be on the top. If there are no sieves, use new fans <note>original: phlabeliois; fans used for fanning fires</note>, for these also serve the purpose. As for the **koptoplakous** <note>pounded cake</note>, he says they make a large cake in Crete which they call **gastrin**. It is made this way: Thasian nuts, Pontic nuts, and almonds, and also poppy seeds—which you should toast and treat carefully—and rub them diligently in a clean mortar. Mix in the fruit and knead with boiled honey, adding plenty of pepper, and soften it. It becomes black because of the poppy seeds. Flatten it into a square shape. Then, having rubbed white sesame seeds, soften them with boiled honey and stretch out two thin sheets; place one underneath and the other on top, so that the black part is in the middle, and shape it neatly. These are the words of the wise pastry-expert **Chrysippus**. **Artocratius** <note>literally "Bread-Power"</note> of Mendes, in his work *On Cakes*, calls the cake known among the Alexandrians as "pankarpia" <note>"all-fruit" or "all-seed" cake</note> by that name. Regarding **itria**: these are shredded pieces boiled with honey, and after boiling, they are formed into a spherical shape and wrapped in thin papyrus so they hold together. **Alcman** mentions porridge thus: "now he will provide a porridge of beans, and white groats, and *korina* fruit." That the **puanion**, as **Sotius** says, is a mixture of all sorts of boiled sweets. "Groats" are boiled wheat. By "korina fruit" he means honey. And **Epicharmus** speaks this way: "for the earth and the sea, and in the sea at dawn." **Pherecrates** mentions the so-called honeycombs in *The Deserters* like this: "just as goats have the smell of honeycombs from their mouths."
After these things were said, the learned **Ulpian** <note>the fictional host's legalistic and pedantic friend</note> said: "Where, O most learned grammarians, and from what library did these most venerable authors **Chrysippus** and **Artocratius** appear, slandering the fine name of the philosopher by sharing his name? And who among the Greeks ever named a *hemina*, or who mentions **amylon**?" The man from Larnesius answered him, saying that the *hemina* is known to those who composed the poems attributed to **Epicharmus**, for in the work titled *Cheiron* it is said: "and to drink twice as much water as two *heminas* of lukewarm water." These are pseudepigrapha <note>falsely attributed works</note> which famous men have composed, such as **Chrysogonus** the flute-player, as **Aristoxenus** says in the eighth book of his *Political Laws* or *Constitution*. And **Philochorus** in his *On Divination* says that the race of the Locrians or the Sicyonians made these opinions their standard. **Apollodorus** records the same. **Teleclides** mentions *amylon* in *The Rigid Men*, saying: "I love a hot cake, and I struggle with excess. I rejoice in hares sitting upon *amylon*." Hearing this, **Ulpian** said: "Since you are calling out a certain exhaustion, I will speak for each boiled water... tell us, O lamps, which of the
<margin>Democritus</margin>
philologists mentions this name?" And **Democritus** said that **Dionysius of Utica**, in his *Geography*, says that the sea-leek is called a "bed." As for our honey-cakes, **Clearchus of Soli** mentions them in his *On Riddles*, saying: "ordering one to say similar things... a mat, a pot, a lamp-stand, a shore."

When everyone laughed, Democritus said: "But I did not order you, my dear 'name-hunter' <note>a nickname for Ulpian because of his obsession with the origins of words</note>, to eat it, but rather *not* to eat it. For the word 'to devour' was used in this way by the comic poet Theopompus, who says: 'Stop gambling, young man; you have a hard stomach from eating greens, so devour <note>original: apesthie</note> the small fish of the sellers.' Good counsel is the best thing, for you will find this holy thing easiest to sing in songs." They also use the word "to devour" to mean eating something away from a larger portion, as Hermippus does in *The Soldiers*: "Woe is me, this pain bites me, whether I eat away <note>original: apesthia</note> or not."

When Democritus remained silent, he continued: "Since you are at a loss, I shall teach you. Nicander of Colophon, in his *Medical Treatise on Venomous Bites* <note>original: Theriaca</note>, mentions them, saying: '...psittakia, which look like almond branches.' He also writes that *astakia* are actually almonds. And Posidonius the Stoic, in the third book of his *Histories*, writes as follows: 'Arabia and Syria also produce the *porsia* and the so-called *bisakion*, which bears its fruit in clusters; it has a white skin and is long, resembling tears. These fruits are heaped upon one another. Inside, they are green, like the seeds of hemlock or a pine cone, but they are much more fragrant.'

The brothers who wrote on agriculture write in their first book as follows: 'Both the ash-tree and the terebinth, which the Syrians now call pistachios <note>original: pistakia</note>.' These writers named them *pistakia* for that reason. But Nicander of Thasos calls them *psittakia*, and Posidonius calls them *bisakia*." Having looked around at those present, and having received praise, he continued: "Furthermore, I shall speak about all the other things set before us, so that you may admire my great learning. <margin>Konnaros.</margin>
*konnaros* <note>likely the Jujube or a related species of Ziziphus</note> and *paliouros* <note>Christ's Thorn or Mediterranean Buckthorn</note>. This tree is the size of an elm or a pine, but not as tall. It has thick, bushy branches and is somewhat thorny. The leaf is grey-green and round in shape. It bears fruit twice a year, in spring and autumn. The fruit is entirely sweet, the size of a low-quality olive, and its flesh and stone resemble the olive. It differs, however, in its pleasant flavor. The fruit is eaten while still green, and when it is dried, they make a meal from it, not by kneading it or soaking it in water, but simply

I mentioned these things first, my friends, not because they are before us now, but because I often received them as part of the second course <note>original: deutera trapeza; the dessert or snack course</note> in beautiful Alexandria. When the name was questioned there, I happened upon a book and read it.

### BOOK 14

...to the suitors, for you gave a pomegranate <note>original: rhoa</note> from your hand to him; but you should know that the Boeotians call pomegranates *sidas*. Agatharchides, in the twenty-ninth book of his *History of Europe*, writes as follows: "When the Athenians and Boeotians were disputing over the territory which they call Sidas, Epaminondas, while pleading his case, suddenly took a hidden pomegranate from his left hand and asked them what they called it. When they replied 'a pomegranate' <note>original: rhoan</note>, he said: 'But we call it a *sidan*.' Since the place at that time had that plant growing in great abundance, from which it took its original name, he won the case." Menander, in *The Self-Tormentor*, called them *rhoidia* <note>little pomegranates</note> in these lines: "For after lunch I set out some almonds, and we ate some little pomegranates." It is also said that a plant grows there in the lake near Orchomenus, right in the water, which is similar in appearance to a pomegranate; its leaves are eaten by sheep, while the shoots are eaten by pigs, as Theophrastus records in the fourth book of his *Inquiry into Plants*. He says it also grows in the Nile,
<margin>10 Dates</margin>
bearing a flower of the same name on its roots. 

**Dates.** Xenophon, in his *Anabasis*, says: "There was wine made from dates, and a cooked vinegar made from them. As for the dates <note>original: balanoi, literally 'acorns' but used here for the fruit of the palm</note> themselves, such as one can see in Greece, these were set aside for the servants. But those reserved for the masters were selected ones, wonderful in beauty and size. Their appearance differed not at all from amber, and some people dried them and stored them as sweetmeats; they were pleasant to eat while drinking, but they caused headaches." Herodotus, in his first book, speaking about Babylon, says: "There are palm trees growing there all over the plain, most of them bearing fruit, from which they make food, wine, and honey; they tend them in the same manner as fig trees. For they take the 'male' palms, as they call them, and bind their fruit to the date-bearing palms, so that the gall-wasps may enter and ripen the fruit for them, and so the fruit of the date-palm does not fall off. For the males carry gall-wasps in their fruit, just as wild figs do." Polybius of Megalopolis, an eyewitness, records similar things
<margin>20 Lotus</margin>
concerning the fruit called the **lotus** in Libya, saying in the twelfth book of his *Histories*: "The lotus tree is not large; it is rough and thorny, and has a small green leaf similar to the buckthorn, though deeper and broader. At first, the fruit is similar in color and size to ripe white sebestens <note>original: myxis; a type of plum-like fruit</note>. As it grows, it becomes Phoenician-red in color, and in size it is similar to round olives; it has a very small stone. When it is ripe, they harvest it. For the servants, they pound it with groats and pack it into jars. For free men, they remove the stones and store them in the same way, and eat them as food. The flavor is similar to a fig or a date, but better in fragrance. Wine is also made from it by soaking and crushing it in water; the taste is sweet and pleasant, similar to good honey-wine, and they drink it without adding water. However, it cannot last more than ten days, so they make it in small batches for immediate use. They also make vinegar from it." Melanippides of Melos, in his *Daughters of Danaus*, names the fruit 'Phoenicians' <note>original: phoinikas; a pun on both the fruit and the color purple/red</note>
<margin>30</margin>
when speaking of them: "For they do not bear the auspicious form of men, nor do they have a feminine voice, but they trained in chariot-driving... many sighs, delighting their sacred minds, with sacred tears of frankincense and fragrant Phoenician dates, and cassia and Syrian amomum throughout the pleasant house." Aristotle, in his work *On Plants*, speaks thus: "Of the 'testicled' dates <note>original: enorchon; meaning seeded dates</note>, which some call *psynyches*, others call them 'stoneless' <note>seedless</note>." Hellanicus also called the fruit a 'Phoenician' in his *Journey to Ammon*, if the treatise is genuine. So does Phormus the comic poet in *Atalanta*. Regarding the so-called **Nicolaus dates**, 
<margin>Nicolaus Dates</margin>
I can tell you this much: we bring them from Syria, and they were deemed worthy of this name by the Emperor Augustus because he took great pleasure in the fruit, and Nicolaus of Damascus was his companion and used to send dates to him continuously. Nicolaus was a Peripatetic philosopher who
<margin>40</margin>
wrote a great deal of history. 

**Dried Figs.** Among dried figs <note>original: ischades</note>, those from Attica <note>the region around Athens</note> were greatly admired. Dinon, in his *Persian History*, says: "There were set upon the King’s table all the foods the earth produces which the King rules over, a first-fruit of each kind. He was not permitted to use any foreign food or drink from the beginning, though this law was later relaxed. For once, when one of the eunuchs brought in some Attic dried figs among the other desserts, the King asked where they were from. When he learned they were from Athens, 
<margin>Attic Figs</margin>
he ordered his buyers to purchase them until he should have the power to take them whenever he wished, and not have to buy them. And regarding the propylaea, none of these foods can be compared at all to the francolin <note>original: atagen, a type of game bird</note>. In these matters, one must also observe the mention of the francolin. Philemon, in his work *On Attic Names*,
<margin>Aegilian dried figs.</margin>
says that the Aegilian figs are the finest dried figs <note>original: ischades</note>. Aegila is a deme <note>district</note> of Attica named after a certain hero, Aegilus.
<margin>Swallow-figs.</margin>
They also call the reddish-black dried figs "swallow-figs" <note>original: chelidonias</note>. Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, praising 
<margin>Tithrasian figs.</margin>
Tithrasian dried figs, speaks as follows:
> Barley cakes, honey-cakes, and Tithrasian dried figs.

Dried figs were so highly sought after by all men that, truly, according to Aristophanes, nothing is sweeter than dried figs. Indeed, Hegesander says that Amitrochates, the King of the Indians, wrote to Antiochus, requesting that he purchase and send him some sweet wine, dried figs, and a sophist <note>a teacher of philosophy or rhetoric</note>. And Antiochus, writing back, said: "We will send you the dried figs and the sweet wine, but it is not legal among the Greeks for a sophist to be sold." That they also ate roasted dried figs is shown by Pherecrates in *The Coriander-Seeds*, saying:
> But give me some of those roasted dried figs as a gift.

And a few lines later: "You do not know the black dried figs." Among the Mariandynians, those barbarians call the black 
<margin>Grapes.</margin>
dried figs "pots" <note>original: chytras</note>. I also know that Pamphilus mentioned *prosknides* as a kind of dried fig. As for the cluster of grapes <note>original: botrys</note>, it is clear it is not a common term. He mentions the grape-bunch and says the identity of the name is of Asiatic origin; but Crates, in the second book of *The Attic Dialect*, claiming it appears in the ancient hymns, says that *botrys* refers to the grape-cluster. [Homer says]: "There were grape-clusters <note>original: staphylai</note> heavy with black fruit." That this word is also in Homer is clear to everyone.

Plato, in the eighth book of the *Laws*, names both the grape-cluster and the grapes in these words:
> Whoever tastes the rustic fruit of grape-clusters or figs, before the season for harvesting has come—which coincides with the rising of Arcturus—whether on his own land or another's, let him owe fifty sacred drachmas to Dionysus if he plucks from his own land; if from a neighbor's, a mina; and if from others, two-thirds of a mina. But whoever 
<margin>Noble grapes.</margin>
wishes to harvest what is now called the "noble" grape, or the "noble" figs as they are named, if he takes them from his own property, let him pluck them how and when he wishes. But if he takes from others without permission, following the law of not moving what he did not set down, let him always be penalized.

These are the words of the divine Plato. But I, in turn, ask: what is the "noble" grape, and what are the "noble" figs? It is 
<margin>Hesiod, Works and Days.</margin>
time for you to investigate; while I go through the items laid before us. And Masurius said: "Do not put off until tomorrow or the day after." The philosopher calls "noble" those that are well-bred <note>original: eugeneis</note>, as Archilochus also recorded, "for you are noble," or those that are grafted. For Aristotle calls grafted pears *epibolades*. Demosthenes, in the speech *On the Crown*, mentions gathering figs, grapes, and olives.

Xenophon, in the *Oeconomicus*, says that grapes are sweetened by the sun. The poets also know of grape-clusters preserved in wine. Eubulus, following this, says: "But take it and strike it with unmixed wine, and give frequent helpings, and force him to eat many grape-clusters from the wine." And the author of *Cheiron*, which is attributed to Pherecrates, says:
> Almonds and apples and strawberry-tree fruits,
> And myrtle-berries and celery and grape-clusters from wine.

And *muchlon* <note>a type of cake or fruit</note>. That all fruits were abundant in Athens is testified by Aristophanes in *The Seasons*. What does Aethlius the Samian seem to record in the fifth book of *Samian Annals*? He says that figs, grapes, "homokles," apples, and roses appeared twice a year. Lynceus, in his letter to Diagoras, praising the "Nicostratean" grape grown in Attica and contrasting it with the Rhodian ones, says: "There is a grape-cluster there called the 'Nicostratean' or 'Hipponian' which they cultivate themselves; from the month of Hekatombaion <note>mid-summer</note>, like a good servant, it remains loyal to its owner." This is the voice of a most illustrious king, who confessed he never even tasted a pheasant, but kept them laid up like a treasure; and yet he had the birds. ...the abundance I have seen among those in Rome, where people have fled back to see the sacred senate again, as if the eagles of the kingdom had been driven out once more. For so great is the number of these birds <note>peacocks</note> in Rome that the comic poet Antiphanes seems to have spoken prophetically in his play *The Soldier* or *Tykon* when he said:

> While once a man might lead just a single pair of peacocks,

Alexis says in *The Torch*: "He himself devoured so much silver—by the gods, there wasn't even rabbit's milk or a peacock at home." Strattis also mentions that people kept them tame in their houses in his plays *The Tent-Mate* and *Pausanias* with these words:

Mnesitheus of Samos, in his work *On the Offerings at the Temple of the Samian Hera*, says: "Peacocks are sacred to Hera, and perhaps they first appeared and were bred in Samos, and from there they were distributed to outside places, just as chickens came from Persia and the birds called guinea-fowls <note>original: meleagrides</note> from Aetolia." Therefore, Antiphanes also says in *Twice a Villain*:

> They say palms grow in the city of Elis, owls in Athens, and Cyprus has 
> excellent honey-cakes. But Hera in Samos has the golden race of birds, 
> the beautiful and much-admired peacocks.

<margin>Guinea-fowls.</margin>
For this reason, a peacock was also struck upon the coinage of the Samians. Mnesitheus also mentioned the guinea-fowls, and we ourselves shall speak of them. Clytus of Miletus, a student of Aristotle, writes about them in the first book of his *History of Miletus* as follows: "Around the temple of the Virgin <note>Artemis</note> in Leros are the birds called guinea-fowls. The place is marshy. The bird is naturally unaffectionate toward its offspring and neglects its chicks, so that the priests must take care of them. It is the size of a large hen, with a small head relative to its body, which is bald; on its head is a hard, fleshy crest, round and protruding from the head like a peg, and the body is wood-colored. Near the jaws, starting from the body instead of a beard, is a long piece of flesh, redder than that of other birds. It does not have the comb that grows on other birds, which some call a 'beard' <margin>Beards.</margin> <note>original: psenoi</note>, and for this reason it is blunt in that area. It has a sharper and larger beak than a hen, and its neck is black, thicker and shorter than that of other birds. The whole body is speckled, the overall color being black but covered with white spots as thick as lentils. These spots are circles within black rhombuses <note>diamond shapes</note>, which give the rhombuses a variegated appearance, the black part having a whiter hue and the white part a darker one. The pattern on the wings is variegated with white, saw-like, fiery flows, and curved lines elsewhere. Its legs are similar to those of other birds. The females are almost identical to the males, making the species of guinea-fowl difficult to distinguish." So much the Peripatetic philosopher <note>Clytus, as a student of Aristotle</note> recorded about guinea-fowls.

Epicrates, in *The Merchant*, mentions roasted and boiled meats <note>The OCR reads "elphakon," likely a corruption of "hephthon" (boiled)</note>. "I would boast of a cook whenever Sicily boasts:

> To rear such a carver of fish,
> but I do not find boiled meats sweeter."

Alexis says in *The Voice*:

> A citizen worth three obols, very 
> high-roasted, and hot and juicy

Whenever he serves it. Philochorus says that the Athenians, when sacrificing to the Seasons <note>the Horae</note>, do not roast but boil the meat, praying to the goddesses to ward off parching heat and droughts. They ask that, with moderate warmth and seasonal rains, the crops may be brought to perfection. For they believe that roasting provides less benefit, whereas boiling not only removes the rawness but also softens hard parts through the broth and ripens the rest. Furthermore, boiling ripens the food more pleasantly and safely; hence they say "to roast what is boiled" rather than "to boil what is roasted." For the latter seems to be a degradation of the better state, as Aristotle says. Roasted meats are rawer and drier than boiled ones. Roasted meats are also called *phlogides* <note>scorched slices</note>. Strattis, for instance, in *Callippides*, says of Heracles that he:

<margin>Scorched slices.</margin>
> Snatched up hot pieces and scorched slices of wild boar, and soaked them all at once.

And Archippus in *The Wedding of Heracles*:

> The children took the trotters of pigs, 
> scorched slices of small bulls with cut-off horns, and some 
> scorched slices of wild boar.

And regarding partridges, why should I say more than what has already been said by you? However, I will not omit the story told by Hegesander in his *Commentaries*. He says that the Samians, having sailed to Sybaris and occupied the land of Siris, were so terrified when some partridges flew up making a loud noise that they fled, boarded their ships, and sailed away. Regarding the hare, Chamaeleon says in his work *On Simonides* that when Simonides was dining at the house of Hiero <note>the tyrant of Syracuse</note>, and a portion of hare was not set before him as it was for the others, but Hiero later shared some with him, he improvised:

<margin>Simonides' wit.</margin>
> For though it was large, he did not reach this far to bring it.

<margin>Success.</margin>
Truly, Simonides was a real miser and shameful in his greed...

<margin>Spartan self-restraint and simplicity in their meals.</margin>
Theopompus, in the thirteenth book of his *Philippic History*, mentions "green" <note>freshly-fed</note> fattened animals and calves. And in the tenth book of his *Hellenica*, in which he highlights the great self-restraint of the Spartans regarding their stomachs, he writes as follows: "The Thasians sent to Agesilaus as he was approaching all kinds of sheep and well-fattened oxen. In addition to these, they sent cakes and sweetmeats. He took the oxen, but at first he did not even recognize the cakes and treats, for they were covered up. When he saw them, he ordered them to be taken away, saying that it was not the custom for Spartans to use such foods. When the Thasians persisted, he said, 'Give these to those people,' pointing to the Helots <note>The state-owned serfs of Sparta</note>. He said he knew that they would be 'ruined' <note>corrupted by luxury</note> by eating them much more than himself and the Spartans present." 

That the Spartans treated the Helots in a very insulting manner is also recorded by Myron of Priene in the second book of his *Messeniaca*, writing: "They impose every insulting task upon the Helots, leading them to every kind of dishonor. For they compel each of them to wear a dog-skin cap and to be wrapped in skins, and they receive a set number of lashes every year regardless of any wrongdoing, so that they never forget they are slaves. In addition to this, if any of them grew beyond the appearance of a slave, they imposed the death penalty, and the owners were fined if they did not cut down those who were growing too sturdy." And after the land was handed over to them, they assigned a portion of the produce which they had to bring in perpetually.

And perhaps all such things were called "makidias," served after dinner. These were a kind of seasoning for the drinking cup. While Ulpian was still speaking, one of those "sophist-cooks" entered and announced a "myma" <note>A highly seasoned dish of minced meat and blood</note>. Many were surprised by the announcement. The "branded one" <note>original: "sigmatias"; likely a slave or a man with a distinctive mark</note> showed what it was and said: "I think you ignore, O banqueters, that

Cadmus, the grandfather of Dionysus, was a cook." When everyone fell silent at this, Euhemerus the Coan, in the third book of the *Sacred History*, relates this story: as the Sidonians tell it, Cadmus was the king's cook. Having taken Harmonia, a flute-girl who also belonged to the king, he fled with her. [The speaker continues]: "But I shall flee as a free man. For none of you could find a cook portrayed as a full character in a comedy, except in Posidippus alone." It is clear that cooks were first called 

<margin>Maeson.</margin>
"Maesonians" after those who first practiced the trade, or perhaps from the misfortune of captured cities. The ancients called a local cook a *maison*, and a foreign one a *tettix* <note>meaning "cicada"</note>. Chrysippus the philosopher thinks the *maison* was named from "chewing" <note>original: "masasthai"</note>, referring to someone ignorant and devoted to his belly. He was unaware that Maeson was a comic actor, a Megarian by birth, who invented the mask named after him—the "Maeson mask"—as Aristophanes of Byzantium says in *On Masks*. He claims Maeson invented the slave mask and the cook mask, and rightly so. The jokes suited to these characters are called "Maisonic." For cooks are mostly introduced as jokers, as in Menander and *The Arbitrants*. And Philemon says somewhere:

> You have taken a Sphinx, not a cook, into the house;
> For he simply says not one thing, by the gods,
> That is not a riddle—he has a supply of new words.

Polemon, in his response to Timaeus, says that Maeson was from the Megarians in Sicily, not those of Nisaea. But Posidippus, speaking of slave-cooks, says they were chosen by lot:

> These things being so, whatever happens,
> Now I am serving my master Aspius, or I shall be caught carrying out meat.

And in *The Foster-Brothers*:

> Were you walking outside the gates as an Athenian cook? Oh! What is your status then?
> I work in the market. For a fellow-craftsman I know bought me.

It was therefore not surprising if the older cooks were also experienced in the art of sacrifice. For they presided over both weddings and 

<margin>Cooks making libations.</margin>
sacrifices. Therefore, Menander in *The Flatterer*, which features a cook serving those who have sacrificed at the festival of Aphrodite Pandemos <note>Aphrodite "of all the people," a popular civic festival</note>, makes him say these things:

> Give the libation! You, follow and hold the entrails! Where are you looking?
> Bring more libation, so that you may pray well to the Olympian gods.
> We pray to all the Olympians—take the tongue—to give safety,
> Health, and many blessings; of the goods we have now, may we have the enjoyment. These things we pray for all.

<margin>Dignity of cookery.</margin>
And in Simonides, another said... knowing how to carve meat, for I know how to do even that badly. Their expertise is also shown by the letter from Olympias to Alexander. The mother, urging him to buy a cook experienced in sacrifices, says: "Take the cook Pelignas from your mother. For he knows all your father's ancestral rites, how they are sacrificed, and the secret, judicial, and Bacchic rites—whatever Olympias sacrifices beforehand, he knows. Do not neglect this, but take him and send him to me as quickly as possible." That cookery was a solemn thing can be learned from the heralds at Athens. For they held the rank of cooks and ox-slaughterers, as Cladius says... Homer uses the word "to perform" <note>original: "rexai"</note> to mean "to sacrifice." And "to sacrifice" <note>original: "thyein"</note> meant to burn incense after dinner. 

<margin>Drakton discovered.</margin>
Or the ancients called sacrificing "to flow" <note>original: "errein"</note>. For a long time, the heralds performed the duties of those of higher rank. 

<margin>Heralds.</margin>
It is recorded that the pay was not for a common cook, but for a herald. Even Agamemnon in Homer sacrifices while reigning as king; for the poet says:

> He spoke, and cut the throats of the lambs with the pitiless bronze,
> And laid them gasping on the ground, 
> Lacking life, for the bronze had taken away their strength.

<margin>Roman censors sacrificing.</margin>
And Thrasymedes, the son of Nestor, taking up the axe, strikes the ox because Nestor, due to his old age, was unable; and his other brothers assisted him. Thus, the dignity of the culinary art was glorious and great. Even among the Romans, the Censors—this is the highest office—dressed in purple-bordered robes and wearing crowns, would strike down the sacred victims with axes. It is not incidentally in Homer that heralds bring the animals for the oaths and sacrifices, as the service was ancient and appropriate to them. Hector sent two heralds "quickly to bring the lambs and call Priam." and again, "But lord Agamemnon sent Talthybius to go to the hollow ships and ordered him to bring a lamb." And Talthybius, with a voice like a god, stood by the shepherd of the people holding a boar in his hands. In the first book of the *Atthis*, the people are shown to be a tribe of cooks holding craftsman-like honors, whose work was to benefit the multitude. Appropriately, even among the Athenians... as Juba says, he introduces a cook discoursing on nature through these things: "I do not know that...
