# ATHENAEUS, THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS

The art of cookery has entirely contributed
Toward piety in every way.
This is a fact, you barbarian! <note>The cook is likely addressing a critic or a fellow banqueter as "barbarian" in a playful, theatrical manner common in Middle and New Comedy.</note>
For it released us from a wild and treacherous life.
Freeing us from the foul habit of
**Eating one another** <note>original: "allēlophagia"</note>, it brought us into a certain order,
And gave us this life that we
Now live. In what way? Pay attention and I shall tell you.
While cannibalism and many other evils existed,
A certain man, who was not a fool,
Was the first to sacrifice a victim and roast the meat.
Perhaps the meat was found to be sweeter than human
Flesh; so they did not chew upon their own kind, but
Roasting the cattle they had sacrificed, they ate them. Once
They had some experience of this pleasure,
With a beginning made, they increased the art of cookery
By adding further refinements.
Hence even now, remembering those of old,
They roast the organs for the gods, but to the flame
They do not bring **salt** <note>original: "halas"</note>, for salt had not yet been
Discovered for such use along with animal fat.
But as it pleased them later, they now
Bring salt as well, according to the sacred laws,
Preserving ancestral traditions—the very things which
For us all became the beginning of salvation:
To apply craftsmanship and, through the use of
**Seasonings** <note>original: "hedysmata"</note>,
To further increase the art of cookery.
For this art is both new and ancient.
After this, as time went on, someone introduced
A stuffed paunch <note>original: "gastria anthyleumenon"</note>,
And precisely calculated how to steam a young kid in its juices.
Someone else, striking a blow for the snacks served by hand,
Wheeled in a fish; and then there appeared
Vegetables, expensive cured fish, groats, and honey.
For the sake of these pleasures I now describe,
Everyone, having once tasted them,
Deemed it worthy to live together. A crowd
Was gathered, and cities became inhabited
Because of this art—the art of cookery, as I said.
Greetings, sir! Walk through life using us
Cooks as your masters; we sacrifice,
We make libations, so that the gods will
Especially listen to us, because we discovered these things
Which contribute most to living well.
If you stop speaking about piety, you would be
In error.

<margin>The dignity of cookery.</margin>
But come, agree with me; take these things
And make the interior look proper.
Alexis also shows in *The Little Cup*
That the art of cookery is a pursuit fit for free men. For in that play,
The cook is shown as a citizen of no mean sort. And those who
Have written on the art of seasoning—both Heracleides and Glaucus the Locrian—
Say that it is not fitting for just anyone to be a cook, but only
For those among the free men. The younger Cratinus also
Adorned the art in his play *The Giants*. And in *Thyestes*, he says:
"How sweet the earth smells! And a most savory smoke
Comes out; it seems someone lives in the chasm—
Either a frankincense seller or a Sicilian cook!"
He calls the smell from both "sweet." And Antiphanes, in *The Difficult Man*,
Praising Sicilian cooks, says: "Delicacies of the feast
Seasoned by the arts of the Sicilians."
And Menander in *The Apparition* notes: "Again, the preparation is
Cleanly and diverse." Posidippus in *The Man Who Recovered His Sight* says:
"I, having taken on a cook, have heard
All the individual complaints against cooks:
One man says the fellow doesn't have a
**Critical nose** <note>original: "rhina kritiken"</note>; another that his mouth is
Foul; another that his tongue is given to shameful
Desires; or that some of his seasonings
Are entirely too vinegary, or that he is a 'nibbler' <note>original: "chnaustikos"</note>
Who makes guests feel seasick.
Not being able to bear smoke or fire—but I, bearing it from the fire,
Came to the knives; this one eye of mine
Has come through the fire and the knives."
Antiphanes, in *Philotis*, displaying the wisdom of cooks, says:
"It was not like other times;
I say I will put the olives in brine, roast
This little sea-bass whole, boil the shark in a sauce,
And for the eel, just salt, oregano,
And water. For that, or the green ray, is enough.
There is a slice of roasted meat for the feast,
And on the other side, a roasted kid; but contrary
To that, I shall be choked with delight by this portion!"
He lists the names of famous
Seasoners of food in *The Benefactors* like this:
"Well done, O Sidonian! We do not sleep
At night, nor are we idle; the lamp burns,
And we have a book in our hands, as we
Ponder what wisdom has been left behind—who among us
Is like Actidion the Chian, or Tyndarichus the Sicyonian,
Or Zopyrinus himself? Have you discovered anything?
How many of these things are greatest for the dead!"

<margin>Myma.</margin>
And I, dear men, bring to you this food: the **myma** <note>original: "myma"</note>.
Regarding this, Artemidorus (the follower of Aristophanes) says in his
*Culinary Terms* that it is prepared from meat and blood
With many seasonings added.
Epaenetus, in his *Art of Cookery*, says the following: "One can make a
Myma from any sacrificial animal or bird. You must
Take the tender parts of the meat and cut them small, along with
The offal and the intestines; then crumble in the blood
And season it with vinegar, roasted cheese, silphium <note>A now-extinct medicinal and culinary herb highly prized in antiquity</note>, cumin,
Thyme (both green and dry), savory, coriander (both green and dry),
Small onions, and a clean leek that has been toasted—or poppy seed,
And raisins or honey, and the seeds of a sour pomegranate.
This same myma shall be your side-dish." After he had chopped up
So many things—not only the items mentioned, but us as well <note>A joke about the cook's long-windedness</note>—
Another man entered bringing the **mathene** <note>original: "mathēnē"</note>.
When a search was made for its meaning,
Ulpian spoke from the *Culinary Terms* of the aforementioned Artemidorus.
Aemilianus then told Dorotheus of Ascalon that a treatise
Had been published by him titled *Antiphanes*, and regarding the word
'mathene' used by the middle-period comic poets, which
A nursing child says is a discovery...

# BOOK XIV

...you would gratify Athens greatly during the period of Macedonian supremacy. It is generally agreed that the Thessalians became the **most extravagant** of the Greeks, both in their clothing and their lifestyle. This was the very reason they brought the Persians against Greece, as the Persians envied their luxury and extravagance. Cratinus also records their extravagance in his work *The Constitution*.

The dish called the **mattyē** <note>A "mattyē" was a famous luxury dish or dessert course, often featuring poultry or meat with rich seasonings.</note> was named, as the Athenian Apollodorus says in the first book of his *Etymologies*, from the word "to chew" <note>original: "masasthai"</note>, just like "mastic" <note>original: "masichē"</note> and similar things.
<margin>10</margin>
But we say it comes from "to knead" <note>original: "mattein"</note>, from which the word **maza** <note>A basic, common barley cake; the "daily bread" of the ancient Greeks.</note> itself was named. Also the word "magis" used by the people of Lepreum, and the expression "to live in extreme luxury beyond the *maza*." At first, they called this democratic and common food made from groats a *maza*, and "to knead" was the act of preparing it. Later, by varying this necessary food in a decadent and elaborate way, and slightly altering the name of the *maza*, they called every expensive dish a **mattyē**.

To **mattyazein** <note>The verb form: to prepare a mattyē or to live luxuriously.</note> means to prepare these dishes, whether they consist of fish, bird, vegetable, meat, or duckling. It is clear that Artemidorus cited the testimony of Alexis; for wanting to link decadence with the preparation, Alexis added the word "refined." The whole selection is from the play titled *The Demetrians*.

"Hurry to take what is on the tray, for you have bought the appetizers; drink the toasts, you refined ones, and enjoy the *mattyē*!"

The Athenians use the word "refined" <note>original: "leptas"</note> to refer to the wanton and vulgar pleasure of sexual love. Artemidorus, in his *Cookery Glossary*, declares that the *mattyē* is a general name for all expensive seasonings, writing as follows: "If anyone prepares a *mattyē* of bird, let it be slaughtered through the mouth toward the head. Let the insides remain like a partridge; or if you wish, leave it with its feathers, or pluck it."
<margin>20</margin>
Then, setting out the method of seasoning and boiling, he immediately adds: "Boil a fat nomad <note>Possibly referring to a free-range or grazing animal.</note> and chicks that are already crowing. If snails are served with the drink, take out the vegetables into a bowl, and placing the meat of the bird on top, serve it; in summer, instead of vinegar, add the juice of **sour grapes** <note>original: "omphakos"</note> to the broth, just as the clusters are. When it is boiled, take it out with the small cluster before the grapestone is removed; then crumble the vegetable in this way—thus you have *mattyē* among the sweetest things."

It is therefore clear that the name was common to the most expensive dishes. And that the style of such a feast was described in the same way. Philemon says in *The Kidnapped*: "He will order a guard for the naked man, and let him show he has enjoyed the *mattyē* through three cups." And in *The Manslayer*: "Let someone pour a drink for us, and let him make a *mattyē* quickly." Alexis, in *The Brazier*, has spoken ambiguously: "And I, whenever I find them busy, cry out: 'Will someone not give us a *mattyē*?'" as if he were speaking of the dinner itself.
<margin>30</margin>
<margin>Machon the Sicyonian.</margin>
It is also plausible that he refers specifically to the dishes. **Machon the Sicyonian**—who was himself one of the comic poets of the time of Apollodorus or Carystius—did not perform his comedies in Athens, but in Alexandria. He was an excellent poet, as good as any of those who came after the "Seven" <note>Refers to the Alexandrian Pleiad, a group of seven tragic poets.</note>; for this reason, the grammarian Aristophanes took care to study under him when he was a young man. In his play *Ignorance*, Machon wrote the following:
<margin>Mattyē.</margin>
"Nothing is sweeter to me than a *mattyē*; whether the **Macedonians** first showed this to us Athenians, or all the gods, I do not know. But it was the mark of a most cultured man, and it was brought in last of all to everyone."

Nicostratus says in *The Man Driven Away*—it is a cook who is speaking, describing how he prepared a splendid and orderly feast, having previously described what the breakfast and dinner were like—and bringing in nothing for a third course, he adds: "Well then, tomorrow in great style. But I will arrange what follows the *mattyē* in such a way as I think."
<margin>40</margin>
<margin>
Regarding "mattyē" in the neuter.
And a tender paunch, and...
Unwillingly the revolution of...
In such a way and...
</margin>
"...not yet for us as he says." And in *The Cook*: "A fig-leaf dish <note>original: "thrion"</note> and a **kandylos** <note>A rich Lydian dish made of milk, honey, and fats.</note>, or any of these things you have ever seen."

And someone else says: "I am carrying around a *mattyē*, a little pig, perhaps a womb." Dionysius in *The Man Hit by a Javelin*—the speaker is a cook: "So that while making a *mattyē* of it, I brought in the backbone at the same time, having missed one piece of meat, like a corpse." Philemon in *The Beggar*: "It was possible to be spent, spending the whole day on *mattyai* there."

Mölpis the Laconian says that the dishes called **epaikleia** <note>Literally "after-meals," the Spartan version of dessert or second course.</note> among the Spartans, which signify the after-dinner treats, are called *mattyai* by everyone else. The comic poet Menippus, in his work titled *Arcesilaus*, writes: "There was a drinking party of some revelers, and a Laconian woman ordered them to bring in a *mattyē*; and immediately a few partridges and roasted birds were carried around, and a luxury of cakes." Such a dinner the Athenians called a "dessert" <note>original: "epidorpisma"</note>; the Dorians called it "epaiklon";
<margin>50</margin>
and most of the other Greeks called it "epideipna." After so many things had been said about the *mattyē*, it was decided to depart. For it was already evening, and we dispersed in this manner.

ATHEN. DEIPNOSOPH.

# THE DEIPNOSOPHISTS OF ATHENAEUS
## BOOK FIFTEEN

If God should grant me a sweet-tongued song like that of the Sirens <note>original: "seirēneion," though the OCR reads "nesēreion"</note>, or the voice of Antenor the Phrygian, as the all-wise Euripides puts it, my friend Timocrates, I would still be unable to recount for you the things that were frequently discussed in these highly-regarded symposia. This is due both to the sheer variety and the similarity of the new topics continually being introduced. For the order of the courses was discussed many times, as were the things performed after the meal <note>original: "to d' apnon," referring to the time when eating ceases and drinking begins</note>; I can barely count them all, even after one of our companions recited the iambic verses from Plato’s *The Laconians*:

> Men have now finished almost everything.
> "Bravo! Why aren't you running to take away the tables?"
> "I’m coming in to pour out the soda." <note>original: "litron," used for washing hands</note>
> "And I shall sweep up."
> "When we have finished the libations."
> "I will bring in the kottabos-stand." <note>A kottabos-stand was the central apparatus for a popular drinking game.</note>
> "The girl's flutes should already be ready,"
> "And pour out the perfume and start blowing the fire,"
> "The Royal Egyptian kind, and then the Iris-scented."
> "I will go and give a garland to each guest's head."
> "Neocrates, who is making the mixture?"
> "It is already mixed; put on the incense."
> "Tell me, how far along are we now? I’m already drinking a toast."
> "Sing a drinking song!" <note>original: "skolion"</note>
> "The kottabos is going out the door."
> "A young girl with flutes
> Is playing a Carchic melody," <note>original: "Karchikon melos," likely a specific rhythmic tune</note>
> "I call to the fellow-drinkers
> She has a Trigonon harp," <note>A triangular stringed instrument.</note>
> "How she sings that Ionian song!"

<margin>Insult regarding the kottabos.</margin>
After this, I believe, there was an inquiry regarding the **kottabos** <note>The kottabos was a competitive game where drinkers flicked the last drops of wine from their cups at a target, usually a metal disk or small floating bowls.</note> based on those who "spit out the kottabos" <note>original: "apokottabizontōn"</note>. One of the doctors present, thinking they were referring to those who, after a bath, drink a large draught to clear the stomach and then spit it back out, said that this was not an ancient tradition. He claimed none of the ancients were known to use such a method of purging. Therefore, Erasistratus of Iulis, in his *General Treatise*, censures those who still do this, showing that the practice is harmful to the eyes and restrictive to the lower bowels. "How," he asked, "did Ulpian say: 'Look, Asclepiadae <note>Followers of Asclepius, i.e., doctors.</note>, the Charon-like cave'?" For it was not badly said by one of our companions that "If there were no doctors, nothing would be more foolish than the grammarians." For who among us does not know that this "kottabos-spitting" was not an ancient thing, if indeed you suppose that this spitting out is something related to Amphias? Since you are inexperienced in such theories, learn from me that, first, the invention of the kottabos is a **Sicilian** game. The Sicilians were the first to find it, as Critias the son of Callaeschrus says in his elegiacs:

<margin>Kottabos.</margin>
> The kottabos is a distinguished work from the Sicilian land,
> Which we set up as a target for the wine-drop bows.

Dicaearchus of Messene, a student of Aristotle, says in his work *On Alcaeus* that **latagē** <note>The wine-dregs or drops thrown during the game.</note> is also a Sicilian name. The *latagē* is the liquid remaining in the cup after it has been drained, which was held in the hand and thrown upward by those playing at the kottabos-stand. Clearchus, in his work *On Dialects*, says the Thessalians call the splashing sounds made by the kottabos-cups *rhochioi*. The prize given to the winners in the drinking bout was also called a "kottabos," as Euripides shows in *Oeneus*, saying:

> With frequent shots of Dionysus they pelted
> The old man's head; and I was appointed
> To give the kottabos-prizes to the one who hit with the siphon.

The vessel into which they threw the *latagae* was also called a kottabos, as Cratinus bites at in his *The Laws*. Plato [Comicus], in *Zeus Abused*, describes kottabos as a type of game for a drinking party, which they arranged as a piece of equipment for those being entertained. He says:

> "How might I play kottabos? While I
> prepare your dinner—I am very willing,
> but the boy is bringing a dry mortar.
> Bring the mortar! Put out water and cups.
> Let us play at the feet of the lovers' kisses anxiously."
> "I do not allow it."
> "I am setting out the kottabos-stands for you,"
> "Namely, the boots <note>original: "krēpidas"</note> she wears,"
> "And your wine-cup." "Good heavens! With these,"
> "A greater competitor approaches the Isthmian games!"

<margin>Kottabos-stand and the sunken type.</margin>
They also called certain kottabos-stands **kataktoi** <note>Meaning "sunken" or "lowered," referring to a version of the game where a vertical rod was used.</note>. These are like lampstands that are brought up and then fall together. Eubulus says in *Bellerophon*:

> Who would take hold of my legs below?
> For I am being raised up like a kottabos-stand.

And Antiphanes in *The Birth of Aphrodite*:

> "What she says, you don't understand. The kottabos
> is the lampstand. Pay attention: the winners get eggs."
> "About this joke of a kottabos—in what way?"
> "I will show you: according to how much the kottabos—"
> "Touching what sort of scale-pan?" <note>original: "plastinx," the metal plate at the top of the kottabos-stand.</note>
> "This thing lying on top."
> "You mean the small plate on top?"
> "That is the scale-pan; he who hits this is the winner."
> "How will he sing if he only happens
> To hit the **manes** <note>The *manes* was a small bronze figure placed on the stand that the scale-pan would hit when struck by the wine.</note> with it? And there will be
> A very loud noise, by the gods, from the kottabos."
> "The *manes* will be struck just like a servant."

And a few lines later:

> "And taking the cup, pass it around in order,"
> "Like a flute-player, curve your fingers,"
> "Pour in a little wine, not much,"
> "Then let it fly—look this way—in what manner."
> "Like this, O Posthion, from a great height,"
> "You shall do it. But I myself could not reach it"
> "With a sling, but..."

BOOK XV

...to learn to hook the hand very rhythmically to throw the kottabos, as Dicaearchus says. In Plato <note>The comic poet, not the philosopher</note>, in the play *The Women Who Have Been Mistreated* <note>original: "kakumenēsi"</note>, someone advises Heracles not to have a stiff hand when he is about to play kottabos. They called the discharge of the wine "from the hook" <note>original: "ap' ankylēs"</note> because of the curving of the right hand during the throws. Others, however, say that the *ankylē* is a type of cup. Bacchylides, in his love poems, says: "When she throws the wine from the hook for the young men, stretching out her white arm." And Aeschylus, in *The Bone-Gatherers*, calls the kottabos-throws "hooked" in these lines: "Eurymachus and no other, insulted me with no unseemly insults... for him the kottabos was always..." <unclear>tò mèn k' âra</unclear>. The *ankylē* of the kottabos is the target which the tongue <note>The "tongue" likely refers to the pointer or the sound made upon impact</note> of the hand aimed for. Antiphanes has already mentioned that a prize was set for the one who threw the kottabos well: "Yes, for there were both little cakes and sweetmeats." Similarly, Cephisodorus in *Trophonius*, and Callias (or Diocles) in *The Cyclopes*, go through the details, as do Eupolis and Hermippus in his iambics.

The version called the "lowered kottabos" <note>original: "katakton"</note> is as follows: it is a tall lampstand having the so-called "Manes" <note>a small bronze figure, usually of a slave</note>, upon which the falling disc <note>original: "plastinx"</note> had to fall; from there it fell into a basin <note>original: "lekanē"</note> placed below, having been struck by the wine-drop. There was a certain precise skill required for the throw. Nicochares mentions the "Manes" in *The Laconians*.

There is another type of the game played "in a basin." The basin is filled with water, and empty saucers <note>original: "oxybapha"</note> float upon it, at which they threw the drops <note>original: "latagas," the dregs of wine</note> from their deep cups <note>original: "karchēsiōn"</note> to try to sink them. The one who sank the most won the prizes. Ameipsias, in *Those Playing Kottabos* (or *The Madness*), says: "Bring the saucers and the beetle-cups <note>original: "kantharous"</note>, and pour water into the foot-basin." Cratinus in *Nemesis* says: "To those who set up the kottabos according to ancestral customs..." 

<unclear>...to throw the saucer into the sea... to the thrower I will grant every fortune.</unclear> The prize, then... <unclear>sophanēs laitaleusin</unclear>. "I have recognized you, bronze vessel, because you stand as a kottabos-stand among the myrtles." Hermippus in *The Fates*: "Fine cloaks are thrown down, everyone delights in the breastplate. Greaves are fitted to the ankles, and no one drives the wolves otherwise. You will see the kottabos-rod rolling in the chaff, but you won't see the Manes or the wine-drops, nor the wretched discs near the roof-tiles of the garden-house among the sweepings." Achaeus, in *Linus*, speaking of the Satyrs' feet, says: "Casting it out, they throw I know not what at me, saying, 'A most beautiful drop for Heracles!'" They said this because they used to remember their beloveds when they threw the so-called kottaboi at the target, which is why Sophocles says in *Inachus*: "She set the drop of Aphrodite, and the golden wine-drop of Aphrodite yields to every house." And Euripides in *Pleisthenes*: "Much clatter of kottaboi, the music of Aphrodite, echoes in the halls." And Callimachus says: "Many lovers threw the wine-missile to the ground, drinkers of the Sicilian drop <note>original: "latagas"</note> from their cups."

<margin>Kottabos was a favorite game among the Sicilians.</margin>

There was also another kind of kottabos-prize offered at the all-night festivals <note>original: "pannychisin"</note>, which Callippus mentions in *The All-Night Festival* in these lines: "He who stays awake will receive the honey-cake prize of the kottaboi, and he may kiss whichever of the women present he wishes." Certain cakes were also made at these festivals, where they spent most of their time dancing; these cakes were then called "thank-offerings" <note>original: "charisia"</note> from the joy of those who received them. Eubulus mentions this in *The Ankylion*, saying: "For I have long ago prepared the victory prizes," and he says next, "I have just now breathed out the thank-offering." Eubulus says further that a kiss was the prize: "Well then, women, see that you dance the whole night for the child's tenth-day feast; I will set three ribbons as the victory prize, and five cakes, and nine kisses."

That the kottabos was pursued with great zeal among the Sicilians is clear from the fact that they even constructed rooms <note>original: "bēmata"</note> specifically suited for the game, as Dicaearchus records in his work *On Alcman*. It is not without reason, then, that Callimachus called the wine-drop "Sicilian." Dionysius, called "The Bronze," also mentions the drops and the kottabos in his elegies: "We add the cluster of Bromios <note>Dionysus</note> to the gymnasium, for you to set up the kottabos here as a third prize for the unlucky lovers. All of you, raise your hands from the circles of the cups, and before you see the reclining air with your eye, pace out how far the pleasant drops extend."

Upon this, Ulpian was ready to drink from a large cup, quoting from the same elegies: "A hymn to pour wine to the right for you and for us. This old, far-reaching prize of yours, the oars of the tongue, we shall send forth into great praise; and as for the clever words at the symposium, let the rower send them thus to the benches for the Phaeacian's wage." For according to the younger Cratinus, who says in *Omphale*: "You become truly happy and superior, while let others care for battles and toils." Against him, the Cynic <note>Cynulcus</note>, always opposing the Syrian <note>Ulpian</note>, and never appearing fond of victory in the dispute he had with him—since a noise had taken over the banquet—said: "What is this chorus of brawlers?" And he himself, remembering some of these verses, said: "Lest Ulpian delay us with the hidden stores of the Homeridae <note>scholars of Homer</note>, having alone snatched up the kottaboi, go forth as messengers of good tidings... and you shall dissolve the strife of the cups and..."

# ATHENAEUS, THE LEARNED BANQUETERS

...entrusted his wisdom to me, and you should learn these things, as they are suitable for our present inquiry. For I see even your servants bringing us garlands and perfumes. Why is it said that if the garlands of those wearing them come loose, they are in love? For even as a boy, reading the epigrams of Callimachus <note>A famous scholar-poet of Alexandria (3rd century BCE)</note>, which we all know, I sought to learn this. The Cyrenian <note>Callimachus was from Cyrene</note> has it thus: "The roses shedding their petals / from Aeschinus's garland all fell to the ground." Therefore, you, O most musical Democritus, must now release me from this thousandth inquiry, and explain why lovers also crown the doors of their beloved. 

And Democritus replied: "But so that I too may mention the 'Bronze' poet and orator Dionysius." 
<margin>Dionysius the Bronze.</margin>
He was called "the Bronze" because he advised the Athenians to use bronze coinage; Callimachus recorded this speech in his *List of Orators*. I myself will say something from his elegies. And you, Theodore—for this is your proper name—receive this poem of mine regarding toasts. "I send this to you first from the right, mixing graces with Graces <note>A play on the 'Charites' (the Graces) and 'charis' (favor or grace)</note>, and you, receiving this gift of song, toast in return, adorning the symposium and managing your own affairs well." 

You ask then, why those wearing garlands are said to be in love if the garland is loosened. 
<margin>Garlands of lovers being loosened.</margin>
Is it because love strips away the "ordered character" <note>original: "kosmos" — meaning both 'ornament' and 'orderly behavior'</note> of the lover? Because everyone takes away from an visible ornament, Clearchus says in the first book of his *Erotics* that it is a frightening thing, and they consider it a sign of such people being stripped of their orderly character. Or is it just like in divination, where many other things are taken as a sign? For the ornament of garlands, having nothing permanent, is a sign of an unstable but beautified passion. Such is love. For no one is more inclined to beautify themselves than those in love. Since nature, acting as a divine judge over each matter, might rightly decree that lovers should not be crowned until they have conquered their love. It is a special sign for those who have subdued the beloved that they are released from desire. We therefore take the removal of the garland to be a sign that the struggle is still ongoing. Or perhaps Love itself does not allow one to be crowned in its presence, and while one is being proclaimed a winner and having the crown removed, it shows the rest a "binding" <note>original: "anedesin"</note>, signaling that they are being defeated by it; which is why everyone says such people are in love. 

Or perhaps because everything that is bound is eventually loosened. The love of those who are crowned is a "bond" <note>original: "desmos"</note>. For nothing else is bound except the garlands; then, except for the lovers, we take the loosening of the garland as a sign of the bond of love, and people seeing this say they are in love. Or is it because lovers often, due to their disposition it seems, strip off their own garlands when crowned, trying to hide the suspicion of their passion, as they would never carry a garland about unless they were in love? Or because, having spent everything specifically on the beloved, they become "sunken." Considering the loosening of the garland to be a sign of a person's sinking, people say they are in love. For lovers "sink" unless, perhaps because they have been "crowned" by Love, this garland becomes permanent for lovers. For it is difficult for a small, ordinary thing to be placed upon a great and divine crown. 

<margin>Doors of the beloved are crowned.</margin>
They crown the doors of their beloved either for the sake of honor—just as they crown the vestibules of a god—or making the offering of garlands not to the beloved, but to Love, for the beloved is the image <note>original: "agalma" — often used for a cult statue</note> of Love. Since the house is the temple, they crown the doors of the beloved. Or rather, by whom they think they have been despoiled of the truth of the "order of their soul," to these they also offer the "order of their body," being led out by their passion and despoiling themselves as an offering. Every lover, as if shouting, even when the beloved is not present (which prevents the dedication), acts accordingly; whence Lycophronides made that lover in the fable say: "I dedicate to you this beautiful thought of a rose, and sandals, and a cap, and the beast-slaying spear, since my mind is poured out elsewhere, toward the girl who is dear and beautiful to the Graces." 

<margin>Equalities of garlands.</margin>
But indeed, the most holy Plato, in the seventh book of the *Laws*, proposes a certain problem regarding garlands, which is worth solving, where he speaks as follows to the philosopher: "Distributions of certain apples and garlands fitting the same numbers for more or fewer people." Plato said this because there are few who wish to find this number, so that when the last person has entered, everyone has an equal amount of either apples or garlands. I say, therefore, that the number sixty can fulfill this equality for six fellow-drinkers. For I know that at the beginning we said no more than five should dine together, but it is clear that we are "countless as the sand" <note>original: "psammakosioi"</note>. Therefore, the number sixty: as the symposium is filled for the six drinkers, it begins thus: the first entered the symposium and took sixty garlands. When the second entered, he gave him half, so that each has thirty. When the third entered, they shared them so that all have twenty. When the fourth shared in them likewise, they have fifteen each. With the fifth, they have twelve, and with the sixth, ten. And thus, the equality of the garlands is fulfilled. 

When Democritus had said this, Ulpian, looking toward Cynulcus, said: "The divinity has truly housed me with a philosopher! According to the words of Theognetus: 'O wandering phantom, you learned your letters backwards, you wretch! Your books have overturned your life...'" 
<note>The sentence cuts off as the next page begins with "you have played the philosopher."</note>

# BOOK 15

...wasps <note>A metaphor for stinging, pedantic critics</note> talking to earth and heaven, who do not even care for your words. For from where, O Theodorus <note>Likely a nickname for a fellow banqueter</note>, did a "chorus" occur to you so opportunely? Who, being worthy of speech, remembers this musical chorus? He who said, "I will not teach you this until I receive the worthy payment from you." For I do not pick out the "thorns" of books as you do when reading, but rather those things most useful and worthy for the ears. And so Ulpian, having become annoyed, gave up something from his own store of Alexis’s writings to everyone: "I certainly do not appear to act like a Triballian <note>A Thracian tribe often characterized as uncivilized in Greek comedy</note> in these matters; they say that Daphanus saw the owner sacrificing." These same iambic verses, he said, appeared once to Antiphanes in a dream. And Cynulcus said, "Since many inquiries about garlands have already occurred, tell us, O Ulpian, what is the 'Naucratite' garland <note>A garland named after Naucratis, a Greek city in Egypt</note> mentioned by the charming Anacreon? For this honey-sweet poet says:

<margin>The Naucratite garland, and its origin.</margin>
> And each man had three garlands:
> Two of roses, and one of Naucratis.

And why are some people crowned with willow <note>original: "lyginos" — made of the *Vitex agnus-castus*, or chaste tree</note> in the work of the same poet? For he says in the second book of the *Mela*: "And the one who loves the daughter of Dike <note>Justice</note> in the middle, since he has been crowned with the willow, drinks the honey-sweet wine." For a garland of willow is strange. How can it be, since the woven willow is suitable as a bond? Since, therefore, we have matters worthy of inquiry and not just "door-named" <note>An idiom for superficial or fake</note> friendship, and while he was silent and pretending to search, Democritus said:

Aristarchus "the most grammatical," my friend, when this passage was being investigated, said that the ancients were crowned with willow. Tinarus the son of Chroscon mentions a "willow crown" in his *On the Willow*, and the other commentators have said things quite irrelevant to the subject at hand. But I, having come across the writings of Menodotus of Samos, which is titled:

<margin>The willow garland of the Samians.</margin>
*A Record of the Renowned Things of Samos*, found the answer to the inquiry. For he says that Admete, the daughter of Eurystheus, fled to Samos. Having seen the epiphany of Hera, and wishing to give a thank-offering for her safety from home, she took care of the temple that exists now. Previously, it had been established by the Leleges and Nymphs. But when the Argives heard of it and were angry, they persuaded Tyrrhenian pirates, by promising them money, to snatch the wooden statue <note>original: "bretas" — an ancient, primitive wooden cult image</note>, believing that if this happened, some evil would surely befall Admete and those inhabiting Samos. When the Tyrrhenians arrived at the Heraian harbor and disembarked, they immediately went about their deed. Since the temple was without a door, they quickly took the statue, carried it down to the sea, and threw it into their boat. But though they loosed the stern-cables and raised the anchors, and used every effort at rowing, they were unable to sail away. Thinking therefore that this was something divine, they took the statue out of the ship again, set it down by the shore, made barley-cakes as an offering to it, and departed in great fear. When Admete reported at dawn that the statue had disappeared, and a search took place, those searching found it on the beach. Thinking, as people might of "foreign girls," that it had run away of its own accord, they bound it with a fence of willow, and the longest of the branches were woven together on both sides to wrap around it completely. But Admete loosed it, purified it, and set it back on its pedestal, just as it had been established before. Because of this, every year since then, the statue is carried down to the beach and hidden. Barley-cakes are placed beside it, and the festival is called the *Tonea* <note>The "Stretching" or "Towing" festival</note>, because it happened that the statue was tightly bound by those who made the first search for it.

It is recorded by them that during that time, when they were living under the influence of religious awe regarding the harvest, they went to the oracle of the god at Hybla and asked about their offspring. Apollo prophesied that they should pay a voluntary penalty to the goddess, and without any troublesome disaster, so that in future times—just as Zeus loosed Prometheus from his most difficult bonds as a favor for the theft of fire—they should wear a symbol of this. The leader of the gods commanded that he should have this "sorrow-free" bond. Thus, Prometheus put on that aforementioned garland, and not long after, so did the men who had been benefited by him through the gift of fire. Therefore, the people were commanded by a similar custom to use willow garlands, binding their own heads with the branches with which they themselves had "captured" the goddess. He commanded them to abolish other kinds of garlands, except for the laurel, which he said he granted as a gift only to those who serve the goddess; those who used it according to the oracle would be unharmed, paying the proper penalty to the goddess not with feasts, but with this. Therefore, wishing to obey the oracle, they abolished the previously customary garlands. He himself uses the willow in abundance, but to those who serve the goddess, he permitted the wearing of the laurel crown, which still remains today. Nicainetus the epic poet also seems to mention the willow-crowning in his epigrams, being a local poet who loved the local history and did not invent it. He speaks thus:

> I do not wish, O Philotherus, to feast in the city, but in the field,
> enjoying the breezes of the West Wind;
> A bed of leaves on the ground under my ribs is enough for me. Near...

...for the bed of the porch where you drink together,

->And with the fruit of the ancient willow, a reed; but let wine be brought,<-
->and the gracious lyre of the Muses. To those drinking it is pleasant, just as the noble bride of Zeus,<-
->For in these lines Nicainetus <note>A third-century BC epic poet from Samos or Abdera</note> has spoken ambiguously whether<-

the willow refers to the nature of a mistress or to the act of crowning; but by saying it was a "reed among the ancients," he makes the object of our inquiry clear. The custom of crowning oneself with willow was well-established, even up to the time of Polycrates <note>The famous tyrant of Samos (6th century BC)</note>, as one might guess it was quite common on that island. Indeed, Anacreon says: "The friendly Megistes, for ten months now, has been crowned with the willow and drinks honey-sweet wine." These things the gods know as being first; I myself, while in beautiful Alexandria, happened upon the short treatise of Moschotus, and after showing it to many, I found the very answer to the question regarding Anacreon. But having received it

<margin>Hephaestion <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD</note> usurping the writings on the Willow.</margin>
from me, O Hephaestion—you who reproach everyone for theft—you made the solution your own and published a treatise, titling it *On the Willow Crown in Anacreon*, which we have now found in Rome in the possession of Demetrius "the Antimosyrus" <note>A nickname likely meaning "The Rival of Mosyros"</note>. Such a man is this writer Hephaestion, who also acted unfairly toward our noble Adrastus. For after Adrastus published five books on the historical and linguistic inquiries found in Theophrastus's *On Stones*, and also a work on the concepts of Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* which he generously shared with everyone—and also concerning the character Glycippe in the play by the tragedian Antiphon, and many other things, including a discussion of Antiphon himself—Hephaestion usurped these as well. He titled a book *On the Antiphon mentioned in Xenophon's Memorabilia*, having discovered nothing original of his own, just as in the case of the willow crown. For the only original thing he added then was that Phylarchus <note>A Greek historian of the 3rd century BC</note>, in the seventh book of his *Histories*, knows the story regarding the willow, but he does not know the works of Nicainetus or Anacreon. The author, having shown that he even disagrees in some points with what will be related from Moschotus. One might say more simply regarding the willow, that Megistes is crowned with the willow as a sign of supplication [TEXT MISSING]. From the sweat of every groan, having fallen from my master who is ceasing, and the great king appearing. After these things were said, Democritus spoke: "But

<margin>Aristotle's drinking song [skolion] or paean.</margin>
truly, the poem written by the most learned Aristotle for Hermias of Atarneus <note>The ruler of Atarneus and Aristotle's friend/father-in-law</note> is not a paean <note>A hymn usually reserved for a god, specifically Apollo</note>, as was claimed by Demophilus, the man who brought the indictment of impiety against the philosopher. He was incited by Eurymedon, on the grounds that Aristotle was impious for singing a paean to Hermias every day at the common meals. However, I will make it clear to you that the song provides no indication of being a paean, but is rather a specific type of drinking song [skolion], as is evident from the very beginning of the text:"

> Virtue <note>original: "Areta"</note>, won with much labor by the mortal race,
> the fairest prize in life, for your maidenly form, O Virgin,
> even to die is an envied fate in Greece, and to endure
> fierce, unwearied labors. Such is the fruit you cast upon the mind,
> immortal and better than gold or ancestors,
> or soft-eyed sleep. For your sake the divine Heracles,
> and the sons of Leda <note>Castor and Pollux</note>, endured much in their works,
> hunting after your power. And for longing of you, Achilles
> and Ajax went to the house of Hades; and for the sake of your
> dear form, the nursling of Atarneus <note>Refers to Hermias</note> widowed himself of the rays of the sun.
> Therefore he is famous for his deeds, and the Muses,
> daughters of Memory, will increase his immortality,
> honoring the majesty of Zeus the God of Hospitality and the gift of stable friendship.

<margin>Paean.</margin>
I certainly do not know if anyone can see a specific "paeonic" character in these lines, as the writer clearly acknowledges that Hermias has died by saying, "for the sake of your dear form, the nursling of Atarneus widowed himself of the rays of the sun." Nor does it have the "paeonic refrain" <note>The cry "ie paean"</note>, like the actual paean written for the Spartan Lysander, which Duris says is sung in his work titled *The Annals of Samos*. There is also the paean written for the Macedonian Craterus, which Alexander the Dialectician composed, as Hermippus the follower of Callimachus says in the first book of his *On Aristotle*. This is sung <margin>40</margin> in Delphi to the accompaniment of a lyre and the clapping of a boy. Even the one for Agemon of Corinth, the father of Alkyone, which the Corinthians sing, has the paeonic refrain. Polemon the Geographer cited it in his *Letter to Aranthius*. And the paean for Ptolemy I, the first to rule Egypt, which the Rhodians sing, also has the "ie paean" refrain, as Georgos says in his work *On the Sacrifices in Rhodes*. Philochorus says that the Athenians sang paeans for Antigonus and Demetrius, many people having composed them in the style of the aforementioned Hermocles. Furthermore, Aristotle himself says in his *Defense*—if the speech is not a forgery—"For I would never have prepared a tomb for Hermias as a mortal if I had intended to sacrifice to him as an immortal; nor would I have honored him with funeral rites if I wished to make his nature divine." While Democritus was saying such

<margin>Spicy songs.</margin>
things, Cynulcus said: "Why do you [trouble] me with the piping of 'reedy cups' <note>A metaphor for thin or hollow talk</note> according to the wise Philo? Imagine that nothing of those impious things is worth saying while the 'pot-bellied' Ulpian is present. For he welcomes 'spicy' <note>original: "kapurai" — literally dry/brittle, but here meaning wanton or scurrilous</note> erotic songs more than serious studies—the kind called 'Locrian' which are adulterous in nature, such as: 'I beseech you, do not betray us, before he comes and makes me get up, lest he do some great evil; and after him... Day is here, and already you are bringing the light through the window...'"

# BOOK 15.

...of the feast. For he says his whole Phoenicia is full of such songs; and this man, too, is "piping a whorish tune" <note>original: πορνίκα καλαμίζων; an idiom for playing suggestive or low-class music on the reed-pipe</note>.

<margin>Poets of Flatterers.</margin>
Regarding those called "collaborating flatterers"—for the name has been mentioned, my good Ulpian <note>Ulpian of Tyre, a major character in the *Deipnosophistae* who often asks for linguistic definitions</note>—Demetrius of Scepsis says the following in the tenth book of *The Trojan Array*: Ctesiphon of Athens was a poet of those called "flatterers," whom Attalus—the first of that name to rule Pergamum after Philetaerus—appointed as a royal judge over the regions around Aeolis. The same author, in the fourteenth book of the same work, says that Mnesiptolemus the historian was once highly influential with Antiochus the Great <note>ruled 222–187 BC</note>, and that Seleucus, a composer of "cheerful songs" <note>term: hilarode; a performer who sang light, often humorous songs in Greek costume</note>, composed a song of the kind they were constantly accustomed to singing:

> And I shall love boys, which is much better for me than marrying.
> For I am more fond of a boy than of a father’s battle-garden <note>original: κηπόλεμον; likely a pun on "war-garden" or "estate-battle," though the Greek text here is slightly corrupt</note>,

Then after this, looking toward him, he said, "But since I am coming to you in an angry mood, I will tell you what the Syrbitian chorus is."

<margin>The Syrbitian Chorus.</margin>
And Ulpian replied: "What a piece of refuse! Are you angry at me for what you have said? Or have you cared so little for me, you shameless dog? But since you promise to teach me, I will make a truce with you—though not a 'thirty-years' one—so you can teach me what this 'Syrbitian chorus' is." Clearchus of Soli, in the second book of his work *On Education*, says it this way: "The so-called 'Syrbitian chorus' is one in which each person sings whatever he pleases without any regard for the leader or the teacher of the chorus; but the spectator himself is far more disorderly than these." And indeed, concerning the parodist Matron <note>Matron of Pitane, a 4th-century BC poet known for parodying Homeric style to describe banquets</note>:

> For all those who were the best in former times,
> Euboeus and Hermogenes and the divine Philips,
> They are indeed dead and in the eternal halls,
> But there is a certain Cleonicus whom immortal old age has claimed.
> He is ignorant neither of poets nor of theaters,
> To whom Persephone granted the power to speak even in death.

But you, my fine fellow Ulpian, you investigate everything yet you explain nothing. And as someone once said pleasantly in verse: "My fine friend, while we are still abiding by our truce..." And Cycnicus said: "Many people have been poets of parodies, my friend."

<margin>Parodists.</margin>
The most famous was Euboeus of Paros, who lived in the times before Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon</note>. He is the one who mocked the Athenians, and four books of his parodies are preserved. Timaeus mentions them in the first book of his *Silli* <note>lampoons or satirical poems</note>. Polemon, in the twelfth book of his work *Against Timaeus*, writing the history of parody writers, says: "We should call both Boeotus and Euboeus 'learned' for writing parodies, because they contended with the ancient style and excelled the poets who came before them." Some say the inventor of the genre was Hipponax the iambic poet. For he says in his hexameters:

> Sing to me, Muse, of the daughter of Eurymedon, the sea-Charybdis,
> The gullet-sword-swallower, who eats in no orderly fashion,
> Tell me how, by a wicked vote, he may perish by a wicked fate
> By public decree beside the shore of the unharvested sea. <note>A parody of the opening lines of the *Odyssey*, substituting a glutton for Odysseus</note>

Epicharmus of Syracuse also used parody briefly in one of his plays, as did Cratinus, the poet of Old Comedy, in *The Eunids*, and his contemporary Hegemon of Thasos, whom they nicknamed "Lentil." For he says thus:

> When I came to Thasos, they pelted me while I was on high,
> With many pebbles. And someone standing nearby said,
> 'O most loathsome of all men, who persuaded you
> To step up onto such a beautiful pedestal with your feet?'

To all of them, shortly after, I spoke this verse:

> Memory persuaded an old man, even against his will, to ascend.

And he even cast many of the Thasians into a merchant ship:

> To the loathsome barbers, both the destroyers and the destroyed,
> Men who even now, there and here, rhapsodize evils upon evils,
> Upon whom I, following my faith, placed what was needed.

And again, not being master of his departure, he said to the Thasians:

> I will not hide any of the famous silver while shepherding,
> Lest some woman of the Achaeans should feel indignation at me in the house,
> When my wife hears of the 'Achaean bread' in the home.

And someone might say, seeing them a little delighted:

> As he sailed with a friendly mooring past the Athenians,
> He took fifty drachmas, but you sent only a little.

These things occurred to me as I was pondering, Pallas Athena
Holding a golden staff, and she drove me on with her voice:

> 'You go into the contest, you loathsome Lentil, having dared
> Something terrible,' and so I sang much more.

Hermippus, the poet of Old Comedy, also composed parodies. Hegemon was the first to enter the "thymelic" contests <note>contests for musicians and poets performed on the *thymele* or altar-platform of the theater</note> with these, and he won at Athens with other parodies and his *Gigantomachia* <note>Battle of the Giants; his performance of this parody famously occurred on the day news of the Athenian disaster in Sicily arrived, yet the audience stayed to laugh</note>. He also wrote a comedy in the ancient style entitled *Philinne*. Euboeus mentioned many things in his poems, mocking at one point a battle in the bathhouses:

> They threw at each other with bronze-fitted spears.

And at another point, the insults of a barber to a potter or because of a woman:

> Do not you, O good man, take away the bag of farts,

Nor you, Pelades. Because he once had a great reputation among the Sicilians, Alexander the Aetolian, the tragic teacher, wrote an elegy in the style of "silli" <note>satirical verses</note>:

> As the shaggy wits of Agathocles drove out
> The Parides of old. I am a man who knows his ancestors,
> And from my youth I have always associated with strangers,
> As many as were the lion-like guests of Mimnermus,
> With a lordly love for boys, equal to the gods,

And he wrote in the style of the splendid Homeric verses:

> He went about gurgling songs, or playing with some cloak-fringe in his wretchedness.

# ATHENAEUS, THE BANQUET OF THE LEARNED

...to the Syracusans, and being grateful; and when the Boeotian heard it, the "evoe" cry followed immediately, and in no small measure. 

As many such things were being said on each occasion, when evening finally overtook us, one person would say, "Boy, bring the lamp-stand" <note>original: λύχνειον (lykhneion)</note>, while others called it a "lamp-piece" <note>original: λυχνία (lykhnia)</note>. Some claimed that a torch made of bark was called a "bark-light" <note>original: λοφνία (lophnia)</note>. One called it a "beacon-torch" <note>original: πανός (panos)</note>, another a "lantern" <note>original: φανός (phanos)</note>. Another called it a "lamp-holder" <note>original: λυχνουχον (lykhnoukhos)</note>, and someone else called a lamp "two-wicked" <note>original: δίμυξον (dimyxos)</note>. Another used the term "driving-light" <note>original: ἐλαύνη (elaune)</note>, and someone else "sun-torches" <note>original: ἐλάνας (elanas)</note>, claiming torches were called this after the sun; this is what Neanthes says in his *History of Attalus*. And another noted that because they occasionally cause a "disturbance" <note>original: τάραχον (tarakhon)</note>, these terms are used for all such things. For a certain Silanus, the lexicographer, said that "miserable" people call torches *phanoi*. Timachidas of Rhodes said a torch is called a "peel-light" <note>original: ἔλεπτρον (eleptron)</note>, such as those used by the "night-boomers" <note>term: νυκτεροβόμενοι (nykterobomenoi); young men who carouse loudly at night</note> among the youth, which they call *elanas*. Amerias calls the torch a "grabion." Seleucus explains this word as follows: a *grabion* must be a piece of prickly oak or oak wood which, when crushed and split, is set on fire to give light to travelers. Theodoridas of Syracuse, at any rate, says in his dithyramb *The Centaurs*: "and pitch dripped from the oak-torch" <note>original: γραβίαν (grabian)</note>.

---

-> Regarding the use of the term in *The Trident-Bearer* or *The Trinket-Seller*, having first said "Take the trident and the lamp-holder," the author continues: "But I <-
-> hold on the right a certain iron-wrought bit for the limbs of wild beasts, and the <-
leg of a Cratinean light-bearing lamp." Alexis says in *Midon*: "The first man who discovered how to walk about at night with a lamp-holder, oh, what a guardian of our fingers he was!" In *The Spirit-Possessed*, the same Alexis says: "For I think some of those who meet us will rebuke me because I walk about so drunk at such an age. For what kind of torch, oh by the gods, is like the sweetest sun?" Anaxandrides in *The Ox of the Buffoon* says: "For taking a torch, you may bring me a lamp." Others claimed that a torch was called a *phanos*, and some that it was a bundle made of certain split woods. Menander says in *The People of Aenea*: "The torch must be half-full of water; it has gone out." Do not call it a "tail," but a "little foot." Nicostratus in *The Fellow-Countrymen* says: "For the shopkeeper from the neighbors, instead of wine, will give someone oil in return; instead of vinegar, the cursed man sent him away giving him water." Philippides in *The Women Sailing Together*: "The torch did not shine for us, nor did the land." Then saying "unfortunate," I was not able. 

Pherecrates, in *The False-Coins*, called what is now called a "lamp-stand" <note>original: λυχνία (lykhnia)</note> a "lamp-vessel" <note>original: λύχνειον (lykhneion)</note> in these words: "What is the workmanship of these Tyrrhenian <note>Etruscan</note> lamp-stands?" For the works among the Tyrrhenians were varied, as the Tyrrhenians were lovers of art. Aristophanes in *The Knights* says: "of the spears drawn together, we use three upright lamp-stands." Diphilus in *The Ignorance*: "We have all stretched out like a lamp on a lamp-stand." Euphorion in his *Historical Memoirs* says that Dionysius the Younger, the tyrant of Sicily, dedicated a lamp-stand in the town hall of the Tarentines capable of burning as many lamps as there are days in the year. Hermippus the comic poet, in his iambics, names the military lamp-stand thus: "But you, with light-bearing steps, and on the right as you go out, oh little lamp!" A "split-torch" <note>original: πανός (panos)</note> is the name for wood that has been split and tied together. They used a torch for fire. Menander in *The People of Aenea* says as he enters: "A torch, a lamp, a lamp-stand, because it will provide light; it only makes a lot [of smoke]." Diphilus in *The Soldier*: "But the torch is full of water." Before these, Aeschylus mentions them in *Agamemnon*. They used these torches. Alexis mentions a "wooden lamp-holder" <note>original: ξυλολυχνοῦχος (xylolykhnoukhos)</note>, and perhaps this is similar to the "spit-lamp-stand" in Theopompus. Philyllius calls torches "little pine-knots" <note>original: δᾴδια (dadia)</note>. The lamp is not an ancient invention. The ancients used the flame of the pine-torch and other torches. Clearchus says to "put the lamp to bed" <note>note: a metaphor for extinguishing a lamp</note>.

---

And Plato says in *The Long Night*: "There, on the tips of the temples, he lit a two-wicked lamp." Metagenes also mentions a two-wicked lamp in *The Lover of Sacrifices*, as does Philonides in *The Buskins*. Cleitarchus, in his *Glossary*, says the Rhodians call torches made from the bark of the vine "bark-lights" <note>original: λοφνίδας (lophnidas)</note>. Homer calls torches "tied bundles." "And the tied bundles were burning," and "rushing with fire on the three." The torch is called a "driving-light" <note>original: ἐλαύνη (elaune)</note> as Amerias says. Nicander of Colophon says an *elaune* is a bundle of reeds. Herodotus used the word for lamps in the neuter <note>original: λύχνα (lykhna)</note> in the second book of his *Histories*. Not many people say "lamp-lighting" <note>original: λυχνοκαυτία (lykhnokautia)</note>, but rather "lamp-kindling." Cephisodorus says this in *On Health*. And Cynulcus, always <margin>Candles.</margin> opposing Ulpian, said: "As for me, boy-taken-as-a-gift, buy me a penny's worth of candles <note>original: κανδήλας (kandēlas); a Greek transliteration of the Latin *candela*</note>, so that I too may cry out according to the beautiful Agathon," and the things in the sweetest Aristophanes: "Bring out the light-bearing pines according to Agathon." And having said this, he drove away to a <margin>hilarode.</margin> shady place for his walk; he left the symposium... being greatly laughed at. As the majority were shouting for a victory-song <note>original: παιᾶνα (paean)</note>, Pontianus spoke. Clearchus of Soli, being second to none of the students of the wise Aristotle, says in the first book of his *On Proverbs*...

# BOOK XV.

...he says that Leto, while bringing Apollo and Artemis up from Chalcis in Euboea to Delphi, arrived near what was called the Python’s cave. As the Python rushed toward them, Leto, holding one of the children in her arms, stepped upon the stone which still lies beneath the feet of the bronze statue of Leto <note>This refers to a specific monument at Delphi commemorating the myth</note>. This statue, made as a representation of that event, is dedicated near the plane tree in Delphi, where Apollo also happened to be holding his bow in his hands. This [cry] is, as one might say, "Shoot, boy!" and "Hit him, boy!" <note>original: ἄφιε παῖ (aphie pai) and βάλλε παῖ (balle pai)</note>. Therefore, they say that "Shoot, boy" <note>original: ἵε παῖ (hie pai)</note> and "Ie Paian" <note>original: ἰὲ παιών (ie paion)</note> were spoken then. 

But some, distorting the word and using it as a protection against dangers, say it is a kind of proverb: "Ie Paian," and not "Shoot, boy." Many others, however, use it as a refrain in their inscriptions, saying that the common cry "Ie Paian" is not simply a chorus-song but a proverb. Because it is so familiar to us, we fail to notice it is a proverb; others, speaking of the forceful nature of the cry, do not treat it as such. But the account given by Heracleides of Pontus is clearly a total invention of his leisure, for you see him first claiming the god said "Ie Paian, Ie Paian" three times. From this belief, he dedicates the so-called trimeter <note>a poetic meter</note> to the god, claiming the god invented both meters. He argues that if the first two syllables are long, it becomes a heroic verse; but if spoken short, it becomes an iambic verse. From this, it is clear that even the iambic should be dedicated to him. For if the syllables are short, and one makes the final two syllables of the whole line long, it will be the "limping" iambic of Hipponax <note>term: ἴαμβος (iambos); a specific meter often used for satire</note>. After these things were said, just as we were already intending to rise, boys entered bearing—one of them a censer, and another...

<margin>20</margin> It was the custom for one rising from dinner to offer a libation of the remaining unmixed wine to the Good Spirit <note>original: ἀγαθῷ δαίμονι (Agathoi Daimoni)</note> when the boy gives the cup to drink. Ariphron of Sicyon composed this Paean to Health:

> Hygieia <note>The personification of Health</note>, most venerable of the blessed gods! May I dwell with you for the remainder of my life, and may you be a willing resident in my home. For if there is any grace in wealth or children, or in that kingly power which makes men equal to the gods, or in the desires which we hunt with the hidden nets of Aphrodite, or if any other pleasure or respite from labors has been revealed by the gods to men, with you, blessed Hygieia, all things flourish and shine in the spring-time of the Graces. But without you, no one is happy.

-> In the play entitled as such, he speaks thus: <-

I have learned to take the Muses of Krianos and the wine of Tyrrhenian cheese <note>This appears to be a fragment of comic verse</note> along with eight [parts of water?]. These things, dearest Timocrates, are—to quote Plato—not the "playthings of a young and handsome Socrates," but the serious studies of the Banquet-Scholars <note>original: δειπνοσοφιστῶν (deipnosophistôn)</note>. For according to Dionysius the Bronze <note>A poet and orator known for his "bronze" eloquence</note>, what is more beautiful for those beginning or those ending, or what is most persuasive?

-> T H E   E N D. <-

# FINAL ILLUSTRATION AND PRINTER’S MARK

->[A large woodcut illustration is centered on the page]<-

This intricate woodcut depicts a bird—possibly a parrot or a bird of prey—perched gracefully upon the branch of a plant laden with fruit and flowers. The bird is captured in profile, grasping a small twig or vine in its beak. The artist has employed fine cross-hatching and detailed line work to define the soft texture of the feathers and the organic veins of the surrounding foliage. <note>In early modern printing, such illustrations often served as "printer’s marks," acting as a trademark for the publishing house. The bird holding a branch often symbolized peace, eloquence, or the spreading of knowledge.</note>

<insert>
->[A decorative library stamp is pressed into the lower center of the page]<-

The stamp is designed in the shape of a decorative cross surmounted by a royal crown. Within the arms of the cross, the text reads:

**VICTOR EMMANUEL**
**IN ROME**

In the center of the cross is a shield featuring a smaller cross, the coat of arms of the House of Savoy. <note>This is the official stamp of the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Roma (National Central Library of Rome). The library was established in 1876 and named after Victor Emmanuel II, the first king of a unified Italy. This indicates the manuscript or book was at one point part of the Italian national collection.</note>
